Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Minor Collection

Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Monks

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Mahākāruṇikaṃ [M 1.0001][V 1.0001][P 1.0001] nāthaṃ, ñeyyasāgarapāraguṃ;

Vande nipuṇagambhīra-vicitranayadesanaṃ.

I pay homage to the Great Compassionate Protector, who has gone beyond the ocean of knowable things, and whose teaching is subtle, profound, and of varied methods.

Vijjācaraṇasampannā, yena niyyanti lokato;

Vande tamuttamaṃ dhammaṃ, sammāsambuddhapūjitaṃ.

I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, by which those accomplished in knowledge and conduct go forth from the world, and which is revered by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Sīlādiguṇasampanno, ṭhito maggaphalesu yo;

Vande ariyasaṅghaṃ taṃ, puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ.

I pay homage to that Noble Sangha, established in the path and its fruits, endowed with virtues such as morality, the unsurpassed field of merit.

Vandanājanitaṃ puññaṃ, iti yaṃ ratanattaye;

Hatantarāyo sabbattha, hutvāhaṃ tassa tejasā.

By the merit generated through this homage to the Triple Gem, may I, by its radiant power, be free from obstacles everywhere.

Yā [V 1.0002] tā subhūtiādīhi, katakiccehi tādihi;

Therehi bhāsitā gāthā, therīhi ca nirāmisā.

The verses, free from worldly taint, spoken by the elders—such as Venerable Subhūti and others, who were accomplished and steadfast—and by the elder nuns;

Udānanādavidhinā, gambhīrā nipuṇā subhā;

Suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttā, ariyadhammappakāsikā.

Profound, subtle, and beautiful, connected with emptiness, revealing the Noble Dhamma, uttered according to the method of inspired utterance;

Theragāthāti nāmena, therīgāthāti tādino;

Yā khuddakanikāyamhi, saṅgāyiṃsu mahesayo.

Those verses which the great sages compiled within the Khuddaka Nikāya under the name ‘Theragāthā’ and likewise ‘Therīgāthā’.

Tāsaṃ [M 1.0002] gambhīrañāṇehi, ogāhetabbabhāvato;

Kiñcāpi dukkarā kātuṃ, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

Although an exposition of their meaning is difficult for me to undertake, because those verses must be penetrated by profound wisdom;

Sahasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ yasmā, dharate satthu sāsanaṃ;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, tiṭṭhateva vinicchayo.

Yet because a bold exposition upholds the Teacher's Dispensation, and the decisions of the lion-like former teachers stand firm;

Tasmā [P 1.0002] taṃ avalambitvā, ogāhetvāna pañcapi;

Nikāye upanissāya, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ.

Therefore, relying on that, having plunged into the five Nikāyas, and depending upon the tradition of the ancient commentaries;

Suvisuddhaṃ asaṃkiṇṇaṃ, nipuṇatthavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, samayaṃ avilomayaṃ.

Not transgressing the tradition of the residents of the Great Monastery, which is thoroughly pure, unadulterated, and with precise determination of meanings;

Yāsaṃ attho duviññeyyo, anupubbikathaṃ vinā;

Tāsaṃ tañca vibhāvento, dīpayanto vinicchayaṃ.

Elucidating the meaning of those verses, which is difficult to understand without a sequential explanation, and illuminating the determination;

Yathābalaṃ karissāmi, atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ subhaṃ;

Sakkaccaṃ theragāthānaṃ, therīgāthānameva ca.

I shall, according to my ability, carefully compose a beautiful explanation of the meaning of the Verses of the Elders and of the Verses of the Elder Nuns.

Iti ākaṅkhamānassa, saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiṃ;

Tadatthaṃ vibhajantassa, nisāmayatha sādhavoti.

Therefore, as one who longs for the long duration of the true Dhamma and who explains its meaning for that purpose, listen well, O worthy ones.

Kā panetā theragāthā therīgāthā ca, kathañca pavattāti, kāmañcāyamattho gāthāsu vuttoyeva pākaṭakaraṇatthaṃ pana punapi vuccate – tattha theragāthā tāva subhūtittherādīhi bhāsitā. Yā hi te attanā yathādhigataṃ maggaphalasukhaṃ paccavekkhitvā kāci udānavasena, kāci attano samāpattivihārapaccavekkhaṇavasena, kāci pucchāvasena, kāci parinibbānasamaye sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvavibhāvanavasena abhāsiṃsu, tā sabbā saṅgītikāle ekajjhaṃ katvā “theragāthā”icceva dhammasaṅgāhakehi saṅgītā. Therīgāthā pana theriyo uddissa desitā.

What, then, are these Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, and how did they arise? Although this matter has already been stated in the verses, it is said again to make it clear. Therein, the Theragāthā were first spoken by the elders beginning with Subhūti Thera. For they, having reflected on the bliss of the path and fruit that they had personally attained, spoke certain verses by way of an inspired utterance, some by way of reflecting on their own attainment and abiding, some by way of a question, and some at the time of their final extinguishment by way of clarifying the liberating nature of the Dispensation. All of these were collected together at the time of the council and compiled by the codifiers of the Dhamma simply as the “Theragāthā.” The Therīgāthā, however, were taught with reference to the elder nuns.

Tā pana vinayapiṭakaṃ, suttantapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakanti tīsu piṭakesu suttantapiṭakapariyāpannā. Dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti [V 1.0003] pañcasu nikāyesu khuddakanikāyapariyāpannā, suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthā, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ[M 1.0003], jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallanti navasu sāsanaṅgesu gāthaṅgasaṅgahaṃ gatā.

They are included in the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. They are included in the Khuddaka Nikāya among the five Nikāyas: the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the Dispensation—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—they are included in the Gāthā limb.

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dvesahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsītisahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti.

“Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks; these eighty-four thousand are the teachings that are current for me.”

Evaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena paṭiññātesu caturāsītiyā dhammakkhandhasahassesu katipayadhammakkhandhasaṅgahaṃ gatā.

Thus, among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, they are comprised of a number of sections of the Dhamma.

Tattha [P 1.0003] theragāthā tāva nipātato ekanipāto ekuttaravasena yāva cuddasanipātāti cuddasanipāto soḷasanipāto vīsatinipāto tiṃsanipāto cattālīsanipāto paññāsanipāto saṭṭhinipāto sattatinipātoti ekavīsatinipātasaṅgahā. Nipātanaṃ nikkhipananti nipāto. Eko ekeko gāthānaṃ nipāto nikkhepo etthāti ekanipāto. Iminā nayena sesesupi attho veditabbo.

Therein, the Theragāthā, in terms of sections (nipāta), are a collection of twenty-one sections: the Ekanipāta (Section of One), and so on, increasing by one up to the Cuddasanipāta (Section of Fourteen), then the Soḷasanipāta (Section of Sixteen), the Vīsatinipāta (Section of Twenty), the Tiṃsanipāta (Section of Thirty), the Cattālīsanipāta (Section of Forty), the Paññāsanipāta (Section of Fifty), the Saṭṭhinipāta (Section of Sixty), and the Mahānipāta (Great Section). A ‘nipāta’ (section) is a ‘placing down’ (nipātana), a ‘deposit’ (nikkhipana). The Ekanipāta is so called because herein is a deposit of single verses. In this way, the meaning of the remaining sections should be understood.

Tattha ekanipāte dvādasa vaggā. Ekekasmiṃ vagge dasa dasa katvā vīsuttarasataṃ therā, tattikā eva gāthā. Vuttañhi –

Therein, in the Ekanipāta, there are twelve chapters (vaggas). In each chapter there are ten elders, making one hundred and twenty elders, and just as many verses. For it is said:

“Vīsuttarasataṃ therā, katakiccā anāsavā;

Ekakamhi nipātamhi, susaṅgītā mahesibhī”ti.

“One hundred and twenty elders, their task completed, free from defilements; in the Section of One, well compiled by the great seers.”

Dukanipāte ekūnapaññāsa therā, aṭṭhanavuti gāthā; tikanipāte soḷasa therā, aṭṭhacattālīsa gāthā; catukkanipāte terasa therā, dvepaññāsa gāthā; pañcakanipāte dvādasa therā, saṭṭhi gāthā; chakkanipāte cuddasa therā, caturāsīti gāthā; sattakanipāte pañca therā, pañcatiṃsa gāthā; aṭṭhakanipāte tayo therā, catuvīsati gāthā; navakanipāte eko thero, nava gāthā; dasanipāte satta therā, sattati gāthā; ekādasanipāte eko thero, ekādasa gāthā; dvādasanipāte dve therā, catuvīsati gāthā; terasanipāte eko thero, terasa gāthā; cuddasanipāte dve therā, aṭṭhavīsati gāthā; pannarasanipāto natthi, soḷasanipāte dve therā, dvattiṃsa gāthā; vīsatinipāte dasa therā, pañcacattālīsādhikāni dve gāthāsatāni; tiṃsanipāte tayo therā, sataṃ pañca [V 1.0004] ca gāthā; cattālīsanipāte eko [M 1.0004] thero, dvecattālīsa gāthā; paññāsanipāte eko thero, pañcapaññāsa gāthā; saṭṭhinipāte eko thero, aṭṭhasaṭṭhi gāthā; sattatinipāte eko thero, ekasattati gāthā. Sampiṇḍetvā pana dvesatāni catusaṭṭhi ca therā, sahassaṃ tīṇi satāni saṭṭhi ca gāthāti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

In the Dukanipāta, there are forty-nine elders and ninety-eight verses; in the Tikanipāta, sixteen elders and forty-eight verses; in the Catukkanipāta, thirteen elders and fifty-two verses; in the Pañcakanipāta, twelve elders and sixty verses; in the Chakkanipāta, fourteen elders and eighty-four verses; in the Sattakanipāta, five elders and thirty-five verses; in the Aṭṭhakanipāta, three elders and twenty-four verses; in the Navakanipāta, one elder and nine verses; in the Dasanipāta, seven elders and seventy verses; in the Ekādasanipāta, one elder and eleven verses; in the Dvādasanipāta, two elders and twenty-four verses; in the Terasanipāta, one elder and thirteen verses; in the Cuddasanipāta, two elders and twenty-eight verses; there is no Pannarasanipāta; in the Soḷasanipāta, two elders and thirty-two verses; in the Vīsatinipāta, ten elders and two hundred and forty-five verses; in the Tiṃsanipāta, three elders and one hundred and five verses; in the Cattālīsanipāta, one elder and forty-two verses; in the Paññāsanipāta, one elder and fifty-five verses; in the Saṭṭhinipāta, one elder and sixty-eight verses; in the Mahānipāta, one elder and seventy-one verses. In total, there are two hundred and sixty-four elders and one thousand, three hundred and sixty verses. And this is also said:

“Sahassaṃ honti tā gāthā, tīṇi saṭṭhi satāni ca;

Therā ca dve satā saṭṭhi, cattāro ca pakāsitā”ti.

“Those verses number one thousand, three hundred and sixty; and the elders proclaimed are two hundred and sixty-four.”

Therīgāthā pana ekanipāto ekuttaravasena yāva navanipātāti navanipāto ekādasanipāto, dvādasanipāto, soḷasanipāto, vīsatinipāto, tiṃsanipāto, cattālīsanipāto, mahānipātoti [P 1.0004] soḷasanipātasaṅgahā. Tattha ekanipāte aṭṭhārasa theriyo, aṭṭhāraseva gāthā; dukanipāte dasa theriyo, vīsati gāthā; tikanipāte aṭṭha theriyo, catuvīsati gāthā; catukkanipāte ekā therī, catasso gāthā; pañcakanipāte dvādasa theriyo saṭṭhi gāthā; chakkanipāte aṭṭha theriyo aṭṭhacattālīsa gāthā; sattanipāte tisso theriyo, ekavīsati gāthā; aṭṭha nipātato paṭṭhāya yāva soḷasanipātā ekekā theriyo taṃtaṃnipātaparimāṇā gāthā; vīsatinipāte pañca theriyo, aṭṭhārasasatagāthā; tiṃsanipāte ekā therī, catuttiṃsa gāthā; cattālīsanipāte ekā therī, aṭṭhacattālīsa gāthā; mahānipātepi ekā therī, pañcasattati gāthā. Evamettha nipātānaṃ gāthāvaggānaṃ gāthānañca parimāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The Therīgāthā, however, are a collection of sixteen sections: the Ekanipāta, and so on, increasing by one up to the Navanipāta, then the Ekādasanipāta, Dvādasanipāta, Soḷasanipāta, Vīsatinipāta, Tiṃsanipāta, Cattālīsanipāta, and the Mahānipāta. Therein, in the Ekanipāta, there are eighteen elder nuns and eighteen verses; in the Dukanipāta, ten elder nuns and twenty verses; in the Tikanipāta, eight elder nuns and twenty-four verses; in the Catukkanipāta, one elder nun and four verses; in the Pañcakanipāta, twelve elder nuns and sixty verses; in the Chakkanipāta, eight elder nuns and forty-eight verses; in the Sattanipāta, three elder nuns and twenty-one verses; from the Aṭṭhanipāta up to the Soḷasanipāta, there is one elder nun in each, with verses corresponding to the number of each section; in the Vīsatinipāta, five elder nuns and one hundred and eighteen verses; in the Tiṃsanipāta, one elder nun and thirty-four verses; in the Cattālīsanipāta, one elder nun and forty-eight verses; and in the Mahānipāta, one elder nun and seventy-five verses. Thus the number of sections, chapters, and verses should be understood.

Nidānagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Introductory Verses

Evaṃ [M 1.0005] paricchinnaparimāṇāsu panetāsu theragāthā ādi. Tatthāpi –

Now, among these collections whose extent has been thus determined, the Theragāthā comes first. And therein—

“Sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ, dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare;

Suṇātha bhāvitattānaṃ, gāthā atthūpanāyikā”ti.

Listen to the verses, which lead to the goal, of those with developed selves, who roar like fanged lions in a mountain cave.

Ayaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle āyasmatā ānandena tesaṃ therānaṃ thomanatthaṃ bhāsitā gāthā ādi. Tattha sīhānanti sīhasaddo “sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.33) migarāje āgato. “Atha kho sīho senāpati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.34) paññattiyaṃ. “Sīhoti kho, bhikkhave, tathāgatassetaṃ [V 1.0005] adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.99; 10.21) tathāgate. Tattha yathā tathāgate sadisakappanāya āgato, evaṃ idhāpi sadisakappanāvaseneva veditabbo, tasmā sīhānaṃvāti sīhānaṃ iva. Sandhivasena saralopo “evaṃsa te”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.22) viya. Tattha ivāti nipātapadaṃ. Suṇāthāti ākhyātapadaṃ. Itarāni nāmapadāni. Sīhānaṃvāti ca sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Kāmañcettha sambandhī sarūpato na vutto, atthato [P 1.0005] pana vuttova hoti. Yathā hi “oṭṭhasseva mukhaṃ etassā”ti vutte oṭṭhassa mukhaṃ viya mukhaṃ etassāti ayamattho vutto eva hoti, evamidhāpi “sīhānaṃvā”ti vutte sīhānaṃ nādo viyāti ayamattho vutto eva hoti. Tattha mukhasaddasannidhānaṃ hotīti ce, idhāpi “nadantāna”nti padasannidhānato, tasmā sīhānaṃvāti nidassanavacanaṃ. Nadantānanti tassa nidassitabbena sambandhadassanaṃ. Dāṭhīnanti tabbisesanaṃ. Girigabbhareti tassa pavattiṭṭhānadassanaṃ. Suṇāthāti savane niyojanaṃ. Bhāvitattānanti sotabbassa pabhavadassanaṃ. Gāthāti sotabbavatthudassanaṃ. Atthupanāyikāti tabbisesanaṃ. Kāmañcettha “sīhānaṃ nadantānaṃ dāṭhīna”nti pulliṅgavasena āgataṃ, liṅgaṃ pana parivattetvā “sīhīna”ntiādinā itthiliṅgavasenāpi attho veditabbo. Ekasesavasena vā sīhā ca sīhiyo ca sīhā, tesaṃ sīhānantiādinā [M 1.0006] sādhāraṇā hetā tisso nidānagāthā theragāthānaṃ therīgāthānañcāti.

This opening verse was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council to praise those elders. Here, regarding 'sīhānaṃ,' the word 'sīha' appears in passages such as, “Monks, a lion is the king of beasts” (AN 4.33), referring to the king of beasts. It also appears as a proper name, as in passages like, “Then General Sīha approached the Blessed One” (AN 5.34). And in statements like, “Monks, ‘lion’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One” (AN 5.99; 10.21), referring to the Tathāgata. There, just as it appears for the Tathāgata by way of analogy, so too here it should be understood by way of analogy; thus, 'sīhānaṃva' means 'sīhānaṃ iva' (like lions). The vowel elision due to sandhi is like that in “evaṃsa te” (MN 1.22). Here, 'iva' (like) is a particle. 'Suṇātha' (listen) is a verb. The others are nouns. 'Sīhānaṃva' (like lions) is in the genitive case signifying relationship. Although the related entity is not explicitly stated here in form, it is stated by way of meaning. Just as when “oṭṭhasseva mukhaṃ etassā” is stated, the meaning “its face is like a camel’s face” is indeed conveyed, so too here when 'sīhānaṃva' is stated, the meaning “like the roar of lions” is indeed conveyed. If one holds that the proximity of the word 'mukha' exists there, then here too, owing to the proximity of the word 'nadantānaṃ,' 'sīhānaṃva' is a term of illustration. 'Nadantānaṃ' shows the connection with what is to be illustrated. 'Dāṭhīnaṃ' (with fangs) is its qualifier. 'Girigabbhare' (in a mountain cave) shows the location of its occurrence. 'Suṇātha' (listen) is an exhortation to listen. 'Bhāvitattānaṃ' (of those who have developed themselves) shows the source of what is to be heard. 'Gāthā' (verses) indicates the object to be heard. 'Atthupanāyikā' (leading to the goal) is a qualifier of that. Although here “sīhānaṃ nadantānaṃ dāṭhīnaṃ” appears in the masculine gender, the meaning can also be understood in the feminine gender as 'sīhīnaṃ,' etc., by changing the gender. Or, by way of ekasesa (retention of one form), 'sīhā' refers to both male lions and lionesses; therefore, these three introductory verses are common to both the Theragāthā and the Therīgāthā, as indicated by 'sīhānaṃ' and similar terms.

Tattha sahanato hananato ca sīho. Yathā hi sīhassa migarañño balavisesayogato sarabhamigamattavaravāraṇāditopi parissayo nāma natthi, vātātapādiparissayampi so sahatiyeva, gocarāya pakkamantopi tejussadatāya mattagandhahatthivanamahiṃsādike samāgantvā abhīrū achambhī abhibhavati, abhibhavanto ca te aññadatthu hantvā tattha mudumaṃsāni bhakkhayitvā sukheneva viharati, evametepi mahātherā ariyabalavisesayogena sabbesampi parissayānaṃ sahanato, rāgādisaṃkilesabalassa abhibhavitvā hananato pajahanato tejussadabhāvena kutocipi abhīrū achambhī jhānādisukhena viharantīti sahanato hananato ca sīhā viyāti sīhā. Saddatthato pana yathā kantanatthena ādiantavipallāsato takkaṃ vuccati, evaṃ hiṃsanaṭṭhena sīho veditabbo. Tathā sahanaṭṭhena. Pisodarādipakkhepena niruttinayena pana [P 1.0006] vuccamāne vattabbameva natthi.

Here, a lion is so called because it endures and because it slays. Just as the lion, the king of beasts, by virtue of its exceptional strength, faces no danger whatsoever even from sarabha deer, mighty rutting elephants, and so forth, and it endures even hardships like wind and heat; when it goes forth for prey, by its excellent majestic power, it fearlessly and unshakenly overpowers rutting scent-elephants, wild buffaloes, and so forth, when it encounters them. Having overpowered them, it indeed slays them, feasts on their tender flesh there, and dwells happily. Similarly, these great elders, by virtue of their exceptional noble strength, endure all dangers, and having overpowered and destroyed the power of defilements such as lust, abandoning them, by their excellent majestic state, they dwell fearlessly and unshaken from any quarter, enjoying the bliss of the absorptions and so forth. Thus, because they endure and because they destroy, they are like lions—hence, they are called lions. In terms of etymology, however, just as 'takkaṃ' is said by reversing the beginning and ending letters of 'kantanatthena,' so too 'sīho' should be understood from 'hiṃsanatthena' (by the act of harming). Likewise, from 'sahanaṭṭhena' (by the act of enduring). Yet, when explaining by way of the science of etymology, including the methods of Pisodara and the like, there is nothing further to be said.

Atha vā yathā migarājā kesarasīho attano tejussadatāya ekacārī viharati, na kañci sahāyaṃ paccāsīsati, evametepi tejussadatāya vivekābhiratiyā ca ekacārinoti ekacariyaṭṭhenapi sīhā viyāti sīhā, tenāha – bhagavā “sīhaṃvekacaraṃ nāga”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.30; su. ni. 168).

Alternatively, just as the maned lion, the king of beasts, dwells solitary due to its majestic power, not expecting any companion, so too these great elders are solitary wanderers due to their majestic power and their delight in seclusion. Thus, they are like lions in the sense of being solitary wanderers. Hence, the Blessed One said: “The lion, the solitary wanderer, the nāga.”

Atha [V 1.0006] vā asantāsanajavaparakkamādivisesayogato sīhā viyāti sīhā, ete mahātherā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Alternatively, these great elders are lions because they are like lions, by virtue of their special qualities such as fearlessness, speed, and prowess. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Dveme, bhikkhave, asaniyā phalantiyā na santasanti, katameva dve? Bhikkhu ca khīṇāsavo sīho ca migarājā”ti (a. ni. 2.60).

“Monks, these two do not tremble when a thunderbolt strikes. Which two? A monk whose corruptions are destroyed and a lion, the king of beasts.”

Javopi sīhassa aññehi asādhāraṇo, tathā parakkamo. Tathā hi so usabhasatampi laṅghitvā vanamahiṃsādīsu nipatati, potakopi samāno pabhinnamadānampi mattavaravāraṇānaṃ paṭimānaṃ bhinditvā [M 1.0007] dantakaḷīraṃva khādati. Etesaṃ pana ariyamaggajavo iddhijavo ca aññehi asādhāraṇo, sammappadhānaparakkamo ca niratisayo. Tasmā sīhānaṃvāti sīhasadisānaṃ viya. Sīhassa cettha hīnūpamatā daṭṭhabbā, accantavisiṭṭhassa sahanādiatthassa theresveva labbhanato.

The swiftness of a lion is unmatched by others, as is its prowess. For it can leap a distance of a hundred usabhas and pounce upon wild buffaloes and the like. Even as a cub, it breaks the charge of mighty, rutting elephants with flowing ichor and devours them as if they were a tender bamboo shoot. For these elders, however, the swiftness of the noble path and of spiritual power is unmatched by others, and their prowess in right striving is unsurpassed. Therefore, 'sīhānaṃva' means 'like those who are similar to lions.' And here, the lion should be seen as an inferior comparison, for the ultimate excellence in endurance and other such qualities is found only in the elders.

Nadantānanti gajjantānaṃ. Gocaraparakkamatuṭṭhivelādīsu hi yathā sīhā attano āsayato nikkhamitvā vijambhitvā sīhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadanti, evaṃ etepi visayajjhattapaccavekkhaṇaudānādikālesu imaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “sīhānaṃva nadantāna”nti. Dāṭhīnanti dāṭhāvantānaṃ. Pasaṭṭhadāṭhīnaṃ, atisayadāṭhānanti vā attho. Yathā hi sīhā ativiya daḷhānaṃ tikkhānañca catunnaṃ dāṭhānaṃ balena paṭipakkhaṃ abhibhavitvā attano manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pūrenti, evametepi catunnaṃ ariyamaggadāṭhānaṃ balena anādimati saṃsāre anabhibhūtapubbapaṭipakkhaṃ [P 1.0007] abhibhavitvā attano manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpesuṃ. Idhāpi dāṭhā viyāti dāṭhāti sadisakappanāvaseneva attho veditabbo.

'Nadantānaṃ' means 'of those who roar.' Just as lions, emerging from their lairs at times of hunting, exertion, or satisfaction, stretch and utter their lion’s roar, their fearless roar, so too these elders, at times of reviewing objects internal and external, or of uttering inspired verses, uttered this fearless roar. Hence it is said: 'sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ.' 'Dāṭhīnaṃ' means 'of those possessing fangs.' The meaning is 'of those with excellent fangs' or 'of those with superior fangs.' For just as lions, by the power of their four extremely strong and sharp fangs, overcome their opponents and bring their own desires to fulfillment, so too these elders, by the power of the four fangs of the noble path, overcame their opponents—never before overcome in this beginningless saṃsāra—and brought their own aspirations to their culmination. Here too, the meaning 'dāṭhā' should be understood by way of analogy: 'like fangs.'

Girigabbhareti pabbataguhāyaṃ, samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ. “Girigavhare”ti keci paṭhanti. Pabbatesu vanagahane vanasaṇḍeti attho. Idaṃ pana nesaṃ virocanaṭṭhānadassanañceva sīhanādassa yogyabhūmidassanañca. Nadantānaṃ girigabbhareti yojanā. Yathā hi sīhā yebhuyyena girigabbhare aññehi durāsadatāya janavivitte vasantā attano dassanena uppajjanakassa khuddakamigasantāsassa pariharaṇatthaṃ gocaragamane sīhanādaṃ nadanti, evametepi aññehi durāsadagirigabbharasadiseva suññāgārevasantā guṇehi khuddakānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhiparittāsaparivajjanatthaṃ vakkhamānagāthāsaṅkhātaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ, dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare”ti.

'Girigabbhare' means 'in a mountain cave'; the locative case is used here in the sense of proximity. Some read 'girigavhare.' The meaning is 'in a mountain forest-thicket' or 'in a dense wood.' This phrase indicates both their place of splendor and a location suitable for a lion’s roar. The construction is 'nadantānaṃ girigabbhare' (of those roaring in a mountain cave). For just as lions, dwelling for the most part in mountain caves—secluded from people and difficult for others to approach—utter their lion’s roar when setting out for prey in order to dispel the fear that arises in small creatures at the sight of them, so too these great elders, dwelling in secluded lodgings like mountain caves that are difficult for others to approach, uttered their fearless roar—designated as the verses about to be spoken—in order to abandon the fear caused by craving and wrong views in ordinary people who are inferior in qualities. Therefore it was said: 'sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ, dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare.'

Suṇāthāti [V 1.0007] savanāṇattikavacanaṃ, tena vakkhamānānaṃ gāthānaṃ sannipatitāya parisāya sotukāmataṃ uppādento savane ādaraṃ janeti, ussāhaṃ samuṭṭhāpento gāravaṃ bahumānañca upaṭṭhapeti. Atha vā “sīhāna”ntiādīnaṃ [M 1.0008] padānaṃ sadisakappanāya vinā mukhyavaseneva attho veditabbo. Tasmā daḷhatikkhabhāvena pasaṭṭhātisayadāṭhatāya dāṭhīnaṃ girigabbhare nadantānaṃ sīhagajjitaṃ gajjantānaṃ sīhānaṃ migarājūnaṃ viya tesaṃ abhītanādasadisā gāthā suṇāthāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yathā sīhanādaṃ nadantānaṃ sīhānaṃ migarājūnaṃ kutocipi bhayābhāvato so abhītanādo tadaññamigasantāsakaro, evaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ appamattānaṃ therānaṃ sīhanādasadisiyo sabbaso bhayahetūnaṃ suppahīnattā abhītanādabhūtā, pamattajanasantāsakarā gāthā suṇāthā”ti.

"Suṇātha" (Listen!) is an injunctive word for hearing. By arousing in the assembled audience the desire to listen to the verses about to be spoken, it generates interest in hearing, stimulating effort, and establishing reverence and esteem. Alternatively, the meaning of words such as "sīhānaṃ" should be understood primarily in their literal sense, without a figurative interpretation. Therefore, the meaning is: "Listen to these verses, which are like the fearless roar of lions—the kings of beasts—who roar a lion's roar in mountain caves, possessing exceedingly prominent, strong, and sharp fangs." This is what is meant: "Just as the fearless roar of lions, the kings of beasts, roaring a lion's roar, frightens other animals because it is utterly devoid of fear; even so, listen to the verses of the elders—who are developed in self and diligent—which are like a lion's roar, being a fearless roar because all causes of fear have been utterly abandoned, and which terrify heedless people."

Bhāvitattānanti bhāvitacittānaṃ. Cittañhi “attā hi kira duddamo (dha. pa. 159) yo ve ṭhitatto tasaraṃva ujjū”ti (su. ni. 217) ca “attasammāpaṇidhī”ti [P 1.0008] (khu. pā. 5.4; su. ni. 263) ca evamādīsu attāti vuccati, tasmā adhicittānuyogena samathavipassanābhivaḍḍhitacittānaṃ samathavipassanābhāvanāmatthakaṃ pāpetvā ṭhitānanti attho. Atha vā bhāvitattānanti bhāvitasabhāvānaṃ, sabhāvabhūtasīlādibhāvitānanti attho. Gīyatīti gāthā, anuṭṭhubhādivasena isīhi pavattitaṃ catuppadaṃ chappadaṃ vā vacanaṃ. Aññesampi taṃsadisatāya tathā vuccanti. Attatthādibhede atthe upanenti tesu vā upaniyyantīti atthūpanāyikā.

"Bhāvitattānaṃ" means 'of those with developed minds.' For the mind is called "attā" in passages such as: "Indeed, the self (attā) is hard to tame" (Dhp 159), "But one who is steadfast (ṭhitatto) is straight like a shuttle" (Snp 217), and "right establishment of the self (attasammāpaṇidhi)" (Khp 5.4; Snp 263). Therefore, it means 'of those who, through the practice of higher consciousness, have developed their minds in serenity and insight, and have reached the culmination of serenity and insight development, standing firm therein.' Alternatively, "bhāvitattānaṃ" means 'of those with developed natures,' that is, 'of those who have developed their inherent virtues such as morality.' "Gāthā" (verse) is so called because "it is sung" (gīyati); it is a composition of four or six lines, propagated by sages in meters such as Anuṭṭhubha. Others similar to it are also called thus. They are "atthūpanāyikā" (guides to the meaning) because they bring one to meanings of different kinds, such as one's own welfare, or because meanings are brought to bear in them.

Atha vā bhāvitattānanti bhāvitattābhāvānaṃ, attabhāvo hi āhito ahaṃ māno etthāti “attā”ti vuccati, so ca tehi appamādabhāvanāya anavajjabhāvanāya bhāvito sammadeva guṇagandhaṃ gāhāpito. Tena tesaṃ kāyabhāvanā sīlabhāvanā cittabhāvanā paññābhāvanāti catunnampi bhāvanānaṃ paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ dasseti. “Bhāvanā”ti ca sambodhipaṭipadā idhādhippetā. Yāyaṃ saccasambodhi atthi, sā duvidhā abhisamayato tadatthato ca. Sambodhi pana tividhā sammāsambodhi paccekasambodhi sāvakasambodhīti. Tattha sammā sāmaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ bujjhanato bodhanato ca sammāsambodhi. Sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ maggañāṇaṃ maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ “sammāsambodhī”ti vuccati. Tenāha –

Alternatively, "bhāvitattānaṃ" means 'of those whose individual existence has been developed.' For individual existence (attabhāva) is called "attā" because the 'I-conceit' (ahaṃ māno) is established (āhito) therein (ettha). And that very self has been properly developed by them through the cultivation of heedfulness and blamelessness, and made to take on the fragrance of virtue. Thus, this shows the fulfillment of all four developments for them: development of body, development of virtue, development of mind, and development of wisdom. Here, "development" (bhāvanā) is intended to mean the path to enlightenment. This enlightenment of the truth (saccasambodhi) is twofold: from the perspective of direct realization (abhisamaya) and from the perspective of its basis (tadattho). Enlightenment, however, is of three kinds: perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), solitary enlightenment (paccekasambodhi), and disciple's enlightenment (sāvakasambodhi). Among these, it is perfect enlightenment because one perfectly (sammā) awakens by oneself (sāmaṃ) to all phenomena and because one causes others to awaken. The knowledge of the path, which is the basis for omniscient knowledge, and the omniscient knowledge, which is based on the knowledge of the path, are called "perfect enlightenment." Hence it is said:

“Buddhoti [M 1.0009] yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 97; paṭi. ma. 1.161).

"'Buddha' is that Blessed One who, being self-arisen and without a teacher, by himself fully awakened to the truths in phenomena unheard of before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers."

Bodhaneyyabodhanattho [V 1.0008] hi balesu vasībhāvo. Paccekaṃ sayameva bodhīti paccekasambodhi, ananubuddho sayambhūñāṇena saccābhisamayoti attho. Sammāsambuddhānañhi sayambhūñāṇatāya sayameva pavattamānopi saccābhisamayo sānubuddho aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ saccābhisamayassa hetubhāvato. Imesaṃ pana so ekassāpi sattassa saccābhisamayahetu na hoti. Satthu dhammadesanāya savanante jātāti sāvakā. Sāvakānaṃ saccābhisamayo sāvakasambodhi. Tividhāpesā [P 1.0009] tiṇṇaṃ bodhisattānaṃ yathāsakaṃ āgamanīyapaṭipadāya matthakappattiyā satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ bhāvanāpāripūrīti veditabbā itarābhisamayānaṃ tadavinābhāvato. Na hi sacchikiriyābhisamayena vinā bhāvanābhisamayo sambhavati, sati ca bhāvanābhisamaye pahānābhisamayo pariññābhisamayo ca siddhoyeva hotīti.

For mastery over the powers serves the purpose of awakening those who can be awakened. "Enlightenment (bodhi) for oneself (paccekaṃ) alone (eva)" is solitary enlightenment (paccekasambodhi); the meaning is the realization of the truths through self-arisen knowledge, without having been taught by another. For although the realization of the truths by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones occurs by themselves through their self-arisen knowledge, it is accompanied by the teaching for others, because it is the cause for the realization of the truths by countless beings. The realization of these solitary buddhas, however, is not the cause for the realization of the truths by even a single other being. They are called disciples (sāvaka) because they are born upon hearing (savana) the Teacher's teaching of the Dhamma. The disciples' realization of the truths is the disciple's enlightenment (sāvakasambodhi). These three kinds of enlightenment should be understood as the complete fulfillment of the development of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—such as the foundations of mindfulness—through the attainment of the summit of the path leading to it, appropriate to each of the three kinds of bodhisattas, because the other kinds of direct realization are inseparable from it. For without the direct realization through personal experience, the direct realization through development cannot occur; and when the direct realization through development exists, the direct realization through abandonment and the direct realization through full understanding are certainly accomplished.

Yadā hi mahābodhisatto paripūritabodhisambhāro carimabhave katapubbakicco bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha – “na tāvimaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmi, yāva na me anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccissatī”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā aparājitapallaṅke nisinno asampattāya eva sañjhāvelāya mārabalaṃ vidhamitvā purimayāme pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena anekākāravokāre pubbe nivutthakkhandhe anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuvisodhanena cutūpapātañāṇaanāgataṃsañāṇāni adhigantvā pacchimayāme “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno jāyati ca jīyati ca mīyati ca cavati ca upapajjati ca, atha ca panimassa dukkhassa nissaraṇaṃ nappajānāti jarāmaraṇassā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57) jarāmaraṇato paṭṭhāya paṭiccasamuppādamukhena vipassanaṃ abhinivisitvā mahāgahanaṃ chindituṃ nisadasilāyaṃ pharasuṃ nisento viya kilesagahanaṃ chindituṃ lokanātho ñāṇapharasuṃ tejento buddhabhāvāya hetusampattiyā [M 1.0010] paripākaṃ gatattā sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamāya vipassanaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpento antarantarā nānāsamāpattiyo samāpajjitvā yathāvavatthāpite nāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā anupadadhammavipassanāvasena anekākāravokārasaṅkhāre sammasanto chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhena sammasanavāraṃ vitthāretvā tattha mahāvajirañāṇasaṅkhāte vipassanāñāṇe tikkhe sūre pasanne vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvena pavattamāne yadā taṃ maggena ghaṭeti, tadā maggapaṭipāṭiyā diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ khepento aggamaggakkhaṇe sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchati nāma, aggaphalakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya [P 1.0010] adhigato nāma. Sammāsambuddhabhāvato dasabalacatuvesārajjādayopi tassa tadā hatthagatāyeva hontīti ayaṃ tāva abhisamayato sammāsambodhipaṭipadā. Tadatthato pana mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva tusitabhavane nibbatti, etthantare pavattaṃ bodhisambhārasambharaṇaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbākārasampannaṃ cariyāpiṭakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vitthārato vuttamevāti tattha vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ.

When the Great Bodhisatta, having perfected the requisites for enlightenment and completed his preliminary duties in his final existence, ascended to the seat of enlightenment and made the vow, "I will not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints without clinging," he sat on the unconquered seat. Even before the evening had fully arrived, he dispersed the forces of Māra. In the first watch of the night, with the knowledge of recollection of past lives, he recollected his former existences in their many modes and details. In the middle watch, by purifying the divine eye, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings and the knowledge of the future. In the last watch, reflecting, "Alas, this world has fallen into difficulty—it is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn, yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death," and so on, he directed his mind to insight by way of dependent origination, starting from aging and death. Like one sharpening an axe on a whetstone to cut through a great thicket, the Lord of the World sharpened the axe of his wisdom to cut through the thicket of defilements. Since the causal conditions for Buddhahood had matured, he caused insight to conceive for the attainment of omniscient knowledge. Entering into various meditative attainments at intervals, he applied the three characteristics to name-and-form as they had been determined. Through insight into phenomena in succession, he contemplated the conditioned formations in their many modes and details, expanding the round of contemplation through thirty-six trillion methods. Therein, when the insight knowledge known as the Great Adamantine Knowledge was proceeding with the nature of leading to emergence—being sharp, swift, and clear—he conjoined it with the path. Then, in the sequence of the path, destroying one and a half thousand defilements, at the moment of the supreme path he attains what is called perfect enlightenment. From the moment of the supreme fruition onward, he is one who has attained it. By virtue of his state as a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, and so on, were then within his grasp. This, for a start, is the path to perfect enlightenment from the perspective of direct realization. But as for its basis, it is the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment that occurred in the interval starting from the great aspiration until his birth in the Tusita heaven. Whatever should be said on that has already been stated in full detail in the commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka, complete in all aspects; therefore, it should be understood in the manner stated there.

Paccekabodhisattāpi [V 1.0009] paccekabodhiyā katābhinīhārā anupubbena sambhatapaccekasambodhisambhārā tādise kāle carimattabhāve ṭhitā ñāṇassa paripākagatabhāvena upaṭṭhitaṃ saṃveganimittaṃ gahetvā savisesaṃ bhavādīsu ādīnavaṃ disvā sayambhūñāṇena pavatti pavattihetuṃ nivatti nivattihetuñca paricchinditvā “so ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yoniso manasi karotī”tiādinā āgatanayena catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ paribrūhentā attano abhinīhārānurūpaṃ saṅkhāre parimaddantā anukkamena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā aggamaggaṃ adhigacchantā paccekasambodhiṃ abhisambujjhanti nāma, aggaphalakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya paccekasambuddhā nāma hutvā sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyā honti.

Paccekabodhisattas, too, having made their aspiration for solitary enlightenment and having gradually accumulated the requisites for solitary full enlightenment, at such a time, established in their final existence, by the maturation of their knowledge, grasp a sign of spiritual urgency that has arisen. Having seen with distinction the danger in states of existence and so on, and having discerned with self-originated knowledge occurrence, the cause of occurrence, cessation, and the cause of cessation, they develop the meditation subject of the Four Truths according to the method that has come down, beginning with, “He wisely reflects, ‘This is suffering.’” Subduing the formations in accordance with their aspiration, having gradually and diligently developed insight, and attaining the supreme path by the sequence of the paths, they indeed fully awaken to solitary enlightenment. From the moment of the supreme fruit onwards, having become what are known as Solitary Buddhas, they are the foremost worthy of offerings in the world with its gods.

Sāvakā pana satthu sabrahmacārino vā catusaccakammaṭṭhānakathaṃ sutvā tasmiṃyeva khaṇe kālantare vā tajjaṃ paṭipattiṃ anutiṭṭhantā ghaṭentā vāyamantā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā, yadi vā paṭipadāya vaḍḍhantiyā, saccāni paṭivijjhantā [M 1.0011] attano abhinīhārānurūpasiddhiaggasāvakabhūmiyā vā kevalaṃ vā aggamaggakkhaṇe sāvakasambodhiṃ adhigacchanti nāma. Tato paraṃ sāvakabuddhā nāma honti sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyā. Evaṃ tāva abhisamayato paccekasambodhi sāvakasambodhi ca veditabbā.

Disciples, however, having heard from the Teacher or from fellow practitioners the discourse on the meditation subject of the Four Truths, either at that very moment or at a later time, undertaking the practice suitable for it, striving, and making an effort, and having diligently developed insight—or as the practice progresses—penetrate the truths. They indeed attain the enlightenment of a disciple at the moment of the supreme path, whether at the stage of a chief disciple accomplished in accordance with their aspiration, or simply as a regular disciple. Thereafter, they are called disciple-buddhas and are the foremost worthy of offerings in the world with its gods. Thus, from the perspective of direct realization, both the enlightenment of a Solitary One and the enlightenment of a disciple are to be understood.

Tadatthato pana yathā mahābodhisattānaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ satasahassañca bodhisambhārasambharaṇaṃ icchitabbaṃ majjhimaparicchedena aṭṭha [P 1.0011] asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ satasahassañca, uparimaparicchedena soḷasa asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ satasahassañca ete ca bhedā paññādhikasaddhādhikavīriyādhikavasena veditabbā. Paññādhikānañhi saddhā mandā hoti paññā tikkhā, tato ca upāyakosallassa visadanipuṇabhāvena nacirasseva pāramiyo pāripūriṃ gacchanti. Saddhādhikānaṃ paññā majjhimā hotīti tesaṃ nātisīghaṃ nātisaṇikaṃ pāramiyo pāripūriṃ gacchanti. Vīriyādhikānaṃ pana paññā mandā hotīti tesaṃ cireneva pāramiyo pāripūriṃ gacchanti. Na evaṃ paccekabodhisattānaṃ. Tesañhi satipi paññādhikabhāve dve asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ satasahassañca bodhisambhārasambharaṇaṃ icchitabbaṃ, na tato oraṃ. Saddhādhikavīriyādhikāpi vuttaparicchedato paraṃ katipaye eva kappe atikkamitvā paccekasambodhiṃ abhisambujjhanti, na tatiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyanti. Sāvakabodhisattānaṃ pana yesaṃ aggasāvakabhāvāya abhinīhāro, tesaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kappānaṃ satasahassañca sambhārasambharaṇaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Yesaṃ mahāsāvakabhāvāya, tesaṃ kappānaṃ satasahassameva, tathā buddhassa mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhākassa puttassa ca. Tattha yathā –

In terms of its meaning, however, just as for Great Bodhisattas, by the lowest reckoning, the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment is to be accepted as four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons; by the middle reckoning, eight incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons; and by the highest reckoning, sixteen incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons—and these distinctions are to be understood according to the predominance of wisdom, faith, or energy. For those in whom wisdom is predominant, faith is weak but wisdom is sharp, and consequently, due to their clear and subtle skill in means, the perfections reach fulfillment in no long time. For those in whom faith is predominant, wisdom is moderate, so their perfections reach fulfillment neither too quickly nor too slowly. But for those in whom energy is predominant, wisdom is weak, so their perfections reach fulfillment only after a long time. It is not so for Paccekabodhisattas. For them, even when wisdom is predominant, the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment is to be accepted as two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons, and not less than that. Even those predominant in faith or energy, having passed only a few aeons beyond the stated limit, fully awaken to solitary enlightenment; they do not reach a third incalculable aeon. As for Sāvakabodhisattas, for those whose aspiration is for the state of a chief disciple, the accumulation of requisites is to be accepted as one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand aeons. For those whose aspiration is for the state of a great disciple, it is one hundred thousand aeons only; and likewise for the Buddha's parents, attendant, and son. In this regard, it is as follows:

“Manussattaṃ [V 1.0010] liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamohānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

“Human existence, perfection of gender, the necessary cause, the sight of a Teacher, the going forth, the possession of virtues, a meritorious deed of service, and the will—from the conjunction of these eight factors, the aspiration succeeds.”

Evaṃ vutte aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā katapaṇidhānānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ mahābhinīhārato pabhuti savisesaṃ dānādīsu yuttappayuttānaṃ divase divase vessantaradānasadisaṃ mahādānaṃ dentānaṃ tadanurūpasīlādike sabbapāramidhamme ācinantānampi yathāvuttakālaparicchedaṃ asampatvā antarā eva [M 1.0012] buddhabhāvappatti nāma natthi. Kasmā? Ñāṇassa aparipaccanato. Paricchinnakāle nipphāditaṃ viya hi sassaṃ buddhañāṇaṃ yathāparicchinnakālavaseneva vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjantaṃ [P 1.0012] gabbhaṃ gaṇhantaṃ paripākaṃ gacchatīti evaṃ –

This having been said, for the great bodhisattas who have made their resolve by combining these eight factors, from their great aspiration onwards, even while they are diligently engaged with distinction in giving and so on, giving great gifts day by day like the gift of Vessantara, and accumulating all the qualities of the perfections such as corresponding virtue, there is no such thing as attaining the state of a Buddha in the interim, without having reached the aforementioned time limit. Why? Because their knowledge has not ripened. For just as a crop produced within a fixed time, so the Buddha-knowledge, by the power of that very fixed time, attains growth, increase, and abundance, forms its embryo, and reaches maturation. Thus—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, vigatāsavadassanaṃ;

Adhikāro chandatā ete, abhinīhārakāraṇā”ti. (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.khaggavisāṇasuttavaṇṇanā) –

“Human existence, perfection of gender, seeing one free from the taints, a meritorious deed of service, and the will—these are the causes of the aspiration.”

Ime pañca dhamme samodhānetvā katābhinīhārānaṃ paccekabodhisattānaṃ “adhikāro chandatā”ti dvaṅgasamannāgatāya patthanāya vasena katapaṇidhānānaṃ sāvakabodhisattānañca tattha tattha vuttakālaparicchedaṃ asampatvā antarā eva paccekasambodhiyā yathāvuttasāvakasambodhiyā ca adhigamo natthi. Kasmā? Ñāṇassa aparipaccanato. Imesampi hi yathā mahābodhisattānaṃ dānādipāramīhi paribrūhitā paññāpāramī anukkamena gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī buddhañāṇaṃ paripūreti, evaṃ dānādīhi paribrūhitā anupubbena yathārahaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ sāvakabodhiñāṇañca paripūreti. Dānaparicayena hete tattha tattha bhave alobhajjhāsayatāya sabbattha asaṅgamānasā anapekkhacittā hutvā, sīlaparicayena susaṃvutakāyavācatāya suparisuddhakāyavacīkammantā parisuddhājīvā indriyesu guttadvārā bhojane mattaññuno hutvā jāgariyānuyogena cittaṃ samādahanti, svāyaṃ tesaṃ jāgariyānuyogo gatapaccāgatikavattavasena veditabbo.

For Paccekabodhisattas who have made their aspiration by combining these five factors, and for Sāvakabodhisattas who have made their resolve by way of an aspiration endowed with the two factors of ‘a meritorious deed of service and the will,’ there is no attainment of the enlightenment of a Solitary One or of the aforementioned enlightenment of a disciple in the interim, without having reached the time limit stated in their respective cases. Why? Because their knowledge has not ripened. For in their case too, just as for the great bodhisattas the perfection of wisdom, cultivated by the perfections of giving and so on, gradually forms its embryo, reaches maturation, and fulfills the Buddha-knowledge, so too for them, wisdom cultivated by giving and so on, gradually and as is fit, forms its embryo, reaches maturation, and fulfills the knowledge of a Solitary Buddha and the knowledge of a disciple. For through the practice of giving, in each and every existence, due to their disposition of non-greed, they become ones with minds unattached to anything and with minds free from longing. Through the practice of virtue, being well-restrained in body and speech, with thoroughly purified bodily and verbal actions, with a pure livelihood, with guarded sense faculties, and being moderate in eating, they concentrate their minds through devotion to wakefulness. And this devotion to wakefulness of theirs should be understood by way of the practice of mindfulness in going and returning.

Evaṃ pana paṭipajjantānaṃ adhikārasampattiyā appakasireneva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañcābhiññā chaḷabhiññā adhiṭṭhānabhūtā pubbabhāgavipassanā ca hatthagatāyeva honti. Vīriyādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Yañhi paccekabodhiyā sāvakabodhiyā vā atthāya dānādipuññasambharaṇe abbhussahanaṃ, idaṃ vīriyaṃ. Yaṃ tadanuparodhassa sahanaṃ, ayaṃ khanti. Yaṃ dānasīlādisamādānāvisaṃvādanaṃ, idaṃ saccaṃ. Sabbatthameva acalasamādhānādhiṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ[V 1.0011]. Yā dānasīlādīnaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhūtesu sattesu hitesitā, ayaṃ mettā. Yaṃ sattānaṃ katavippakāresu ajjhupekkhanaṃ, ayaṃ [M 1.0013] upekkhāti. Evaṃ [P 1.0013] dānasīlabhāvanāsu sīlasamādhipaññāsu ca sijjhamānāsu vīriyādayo siddhā eva honti. Sāyeva paccekabodhiatthāya sāvakabodhiatthāya ca dānādipaṭipadā tesaṃ bodhisattānaṃ santānassa bhāvanato paribhāvanato bhāvanā nāma. Visesato dānasīlādīhi svābhisaṅkhate santāne pavattā samathavipassanāpaṭipadā, yato te bodhisattā pubbayogāvacarasamudāgamasampannā honti. Tenāha bhagavā –

Thus, for those who practice in this way, through the fulfillment of their requisites, the eight attainments, the five higher knowledges, the six higher knowledges, and the preliminary insight that serves as a foundation are obtained with little difficulty, as if in hand. Moreover, energy and the other qualities are included therein. For the exertion in accumulating the store of merit through giving and so forth for the sake of enlightenment as a Paccekabuddha or as a disciple—this is energy. The endurance of what obstructs it—this is patience. The faithfulness in undertaking giving, virtue, and so forth—this is truthfulness. The unwavering resolve in all matters—this is determination. The wish for the welfare of beings who are the basis for the practice of giving, virtue, and so forth—this is loving-kindness. The equanimity towards beings who have committed offenses—this is equanimity. Thus, as giving, virtue, and development are being accomplished, and as virtue, concentration, and wisdom are being accomplished, energy and the other qualities are accomplished as a matter of course. That very practice of giving and so forth, for the sake of enlightenment as a Paccekabuddha or as a disciple, is called ‘development’ (bhāvanā) from its developing and cultivating the mental continuum of those bodhisattas. Specifically, it is the path of serenity and insight that arises in a mental continuum well-prepared by giving, virtue, and so forth, from which those bodhisattas become endowed with the acquisition of prior meditative practice. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Pañcime, ānanda, ānisaṃsā pubbayogāvacare. Katame pañca? Idhānanda, pubbayogāvacaro diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti, no ce diṭṭheva dhamme paṭikacca aññaṃ ārādheti, atha maraṇakāle aññaṃ ārādheti, atha devaputto samāno aññaṃ ārādheti, atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño hoti, atha pacchime kāle paccekasambuddho hotī”ti (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.khaggavisāṇasuttavaṇṇanā).

“Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one with prior meditative practice. What five? Here, Ānanda, one with prior meditative practice, having made preparation, attains final knowledge in this very life. If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, then he attains final knowledge at the time of death. If not at the time of death, then, having become a deva, he attains final knowledge. If not as a deva, then in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of quick direct knowledge. Or, in a later time, he becomes a Paccekasambuddha.”

Iti pubbabhāgapaṭipadābhūtāya pāramitāparibhāvitāya samathavipassanābhāvanāya nirodhagāminipaṭipadābhūtāya abhisamayasaṅkhātāya maggabhāvanāya ca bhāvitattabhāvā buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakā bhāvitattā nāma. Tesu idha buddhasāvakā adhippetā.

Thus, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha are called ‘those with developed selves’ because their being has been developed by the cultivation of serenity and insight—which constitutes the preliminary path and is imbued with the perfections—and by the cultivation of the path—which constitutes the practice leading to cessation and is known as direct realization. Among these, it is the disciples of the Buddha who are intended here.

Ettha ca “sīhānaṃvā”ti iminā therānaṃ sīhasamānavuttitādassanena attano paṭipakkhehi anabhibhavanīyataṃ, te ca abhibhuyya pavattiṃ dasseti. “Sīhānaṃva nadantānaṃ…pe… gāthā”ti iminā theragāthānaṃ sīhanādasadisatādassanena tāsaṃ paravādehi anabhibhavanīyataṃ, te ca abhibhavitvā pavattiṃ dasseti. “Bhāvitattāna”nti iminā tadubhayassa kāraṇaṃ vibhāveti. Bhāvitattabhāvena therā idha sīhasadisā vuttā, tesañca gāthā sīhanādasadisiyo. “Atthūpanāyikā”ti iminā abhibhavane payojanaṃ dasseti. Tattha therānaṃ paṭipakkho nāma saṃkilesadhammo, tadabhibhavo tadaṅgivikkhambhanappahānehi saddhiṃ samucchedappahānaṃ. Tasmiṃ sati paṭipassaddhīppahānaṃ nissaraṇappahānañca siddhameva hoti, yato te bhāvitattāti [M 1.0014] vuccanti. Maggakkhaṇe hi ariyā appamādabhāvanaṃ bhāventi nāma, aggaphalakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya bhāvitattā nāmāti [P 1.0014] vuttovāyamattho.

Here, with the phrase ‘of lions,’ by showing the elders’ lion-like conduct, he indicates their invincibility by their opponents and their prevailing by overcoming them. With the verse ‘Of lions roaring… etc.… the verses,’ by showing the resemblance of the elders’ verses to a lion’s roar, he indicates their invincibility by the doctrines of others and their prevailing by overcoming them. With the phrase ‘of those with developed selves,’ he clarifies the reason for both of these. By virtue of their developed being, the elders are here said to be like lions, and their verses like a lion’s roar. With the phrase ‘conducive to the goal,’ he indicates the purpose in this overcoming. Herein, the opponents of the elders are the defiling states; overcoming them is abandonment by eradication, together with abandonment by substitution of opposites and abandonment by suppression. When that is present, abandonment by tranquillization and abandonment by escape are accomplished as a matter of course, which is why they are called ‘those with developed selves.’ For at the moment of the path, the noble ones are said to be cultivating the development of heedfulness, but from the point of the supreme fruit onwards, they are called ‘those with developed selves’; this is the meaning that has been stated.

Tesu tadaṅgappahānena nesaṃ sīlasampadā dassitā, vikkhambhanappahānena samādhisampadā, samucchedappahānena paññāsampadā, itarena tāsaṃ phalaṃ dassitaṃ. Sīlena ca tesaṃ paṭipattiyā ādikalyāṇatā [V 1.0012] dassitā, “ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ? Sīlañca suvisuddhaṃ” (saṃ. ni. 5.369), “sīle patiṭṭhāya” (saṃ. ni. 1.23; visuddhi. 1.1), “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti (dha. pa. 183; dī. ni. 2.90) ca vacanato sīlaṃ paṭipattiyā ādikalyāṇaṃva avippaṭisārādiguṇāvahattā. Samādhinā majjhekalyāṇatā dassitā, “cittaṃ bhāvayaṃ”, “kusalassa upasampadā”ti ca vacanato samādhipaṭipattiyā majjhekalyāṇova, iddhividhādiguṇāvahattā. Paññāya pariyosānakalyāṇatā dassitā, “sacittapariyodapanaṃ” (dha. pa. 183; dī. ni. 2.90), “paññaṃ bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23; visuddhi. 1.1) ca vacanato paññā paṭipattiyā pariyosānaṃva, paññuttarato kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ sāva kalyāṇā iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu tādibhāvāvahattā.

Among these abandonments, by abandonment by substitution of opposites, their perfection in virtue is shown; by abandonment through suppression, their perfection in concentration is shown; by abandonment through eradication, their perfection in wisdom is shown; and by the other two, the fruit of these perfections is shown. And through virtue, the initial excellence of their practice is shown, for in accordance with the sayings, “What is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified,” “established in virtue,” and “the non-doing of all evil,” virtue is the initial excellence of the practice because it brings about qualities such as freedom from remorse. Through concentration, the middle excellence is shown, for in accordance with the sayings, “the development of the mind,” and “the undertaking of the wholesome,” concentration is the middle excellence of the practice because it brings about qualities such as the psychic powers. Through wisdom, the final excellence is shown, for in accordance with the sayings, “the purification of one’s own mind,” and “developing wisdom,” wisdom is the culmination of the practice. Because wisdom is supreme among wholesome states, it is itself excellent, as it brings about a state of equanimity amidst the desirable and undesirable.

“Selo yathā ekaghano, vātena na samīrati; (Mahāva. 244);

Evaṃ nindāpasaṃsāsu, na samiñjanti paṇḍitā”ti. (dha. pa. 81) –

“Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by blame and praise.”

Hi vuttaṃ.

Indeed, it was said.

Tathā sīlasampadāya tevijjabhāvo dassito. Sīlasampattiñhi nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇanti. Samādhisampadāya chaḷabhiññābhāvo. Samādhisampattiñhi nissāya chaḷabhiññā pāpuṇanti. Paññāsampadāya pabhinnapaṭisambhidābhāvo. Paññāsampadañhi nissāya catasso paṭisambhidā pāpuṇanti. Iminā tesaṃ therānaṃ keci tevijjā, keci chaḷabhiññā, keci paṭisambhidāpattāti ayamattho dassitoti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, through the perfection of virtue, their attainment of the three true knowledges is shown. For it is by relying on the perfection of virtue that they attain the three true knowledges. Through the perfection of concentration, their attainment of the six higher knowledges is shown. For it is by relying on the perfection of concentration that they attain the six higher knowledges. Through the perfection of wisdom, their attainment of the analytical knowledges is shown. For it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that they attain the four analytical knowledges. By this it is shown, and it should be understood, that among these elders some possessed the three true knowledges, some the six higher knowledges, and some had attained the analytical knowledges.

Tathā sīlasampadāya tesaṃ kāmasukhānuyogasaṅkhātassa antassa parivajjanaṃ dasseti. Samādhisampadāya attakilamathānuyogasaṅkhātassa, paññāsampadāya majjhimāya paṭipadāya sevanaṃ dasseti. Tathā sīlasampadāya tesaṃ vītikkamappahānaṃ kilesānaṃ dasseti. Samādhisampadāya pariyuṭṭhānappahānaṃ[M 1.0015], paññāsampadāya anusayappahānaṃ dasseti. Sīlasampadāya vā duccaritasaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ, samādhisampadāya [P 1.0015] taṇhāsaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ, paññāsampadāya diṭṭhisaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ dasseti. Tadaṅgappahānena vā nesaṃ apāyasamatikkamo dassito. Vikkhambhanappahānena kāmadhātusamatikkamo, samucchedappahānena sabbabhavasamatikkamo dassitoti veditabbaṃ.

Likewise, through the perfection of virtue is shown their avoidance of the extreme known as indulgence in sensual pleasures. Through the perfection of concentration, the avoidance of the extreme known as self-mortification is shown, and through the perfection of wisdom, the cultivation of the middle way is shown. Furthermore, through the perfection of virtue is shown their abandonment of the defilements by way of transgression; through the perfection of concentration, the abandonment of the defilements by way of obsession; and through the perfection of wisdom, the abandonment of the latent defilements. Or, through the perfection of virtue is shown the purification from the defilements of misconduct; through the perfection of concentration, the purification from the defilements of craving; and through the perfection of wisdom, the purification from the defilements of wrong views. Or, by abandonment by substitution of opposites, their transcending of the planes of misery is shown; by abandonment through suppression, their transcending of the sensual realm is shown; and by abandonment through eradication, their transcending of all existence is shown. This is to be understood.

“Bhāvitattāna”nti vā ettha sīlabhāvanā, cittabhāvanā paññābhāvanāti tisso bhāvanā veditabbā kāyabhāvanāya tadantogadhattā. Sīlabhāvanā ca paṭipattiyā ādīti sabbaṃ purimasadisaṃ[V 1.0013]. Yathā pana sīhanādaṃ pare migagaṇā na sahanti, kuto abhibhave, aññadatthu sīhanādova te abhibhavati evameva aññatitthiyavādā therānaṃ vāde na sahanti, kuto abhibhave, aññadatthu theravādāva te abhibhavanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā, sabbe dhammā anattā”ti (dha. pa. 277-279) “nibbānadhātū”ti ca pavattanato. Na hi dhammato sakkā kenaci aññathā kātuṃ appaṭivattanīyato. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ parato āvibhavissati. Evamettha saṅkhepeneva paṭhamagāthāya atthavibhāvanā veditabbā.

In the phrase “of those with developed selves,” the threefold development should be understood: the development of virtue, the development of mind, and the development of wisdom, with the development of the body included therein, as it is contained within them. The development of virtue is the beginning of the practice—all else is similar to what was said before. Just as other herds of beasts cannot endure the lion's roar, much less overpower it—indeed, the lion's roar itself overpowers them—so too, the doctrines of other sectarians cannot endure the elders' teaching, much less overpower it; indeed, the elders' teaching itself overpowers them. For what reason? Because of the proclamation: “All conditioned things are impermanent, all conditioned things are suffering, all phenomena are not-self” (Dhp. 277–279) and “the element of Nibbāna.” For it is not possible for anyone to alter the nature of things, due to its irreversibility. Whatever is to be said on this point will become clear later. Thus, the exposition of the meaning of the first verse should be understood here in brief.

Dutiyagāthāyaṃ pana ayaṃ sambandhadassanamukhena atthavibhāvanā. Tattha yesaṃ therānaṃ gāthā sāvetukāmo, te sādhāraṇavasena nāmato gottato guṇato ca kittetuṃ “yathānāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Asādhāraṇato pana tattha tattha gāthāsveva āvibhavissati. Tattha yathānāmāti yaṃyaṃnāmā, subhūti mahākoṭṭhikotiādinā nayena nāmadheyyena paññātāti attho. Yathāgottāti yaṃyaṃgottā, gotamo kassapotiādinā nayena kulapadesena yāya yāya jātiyā paññātāti attho. Yathādhammavihārinoti yādisadhammavihārino, pariyattiparamatāyaṃ aṭṭhatvā yathānurūpaṃ samāpattivihārino hutvā vihariṃsūti attho. Atha vā yathādhammavihārinoti yathādhammā vihārino ca, yādisasīlādidhammā dibbavihārādīsu abhiṇhaso [M 1.0016] viharamānā yādisavihārā cāti attho. Yathādhimuttāti yādisaadhimuttikā saddhādhimuttipaññādhimuttīsu yaṃyaṃadhimuttikā suññatamukhādīsu vā yathā yathā nibbānaṃ adhimuttāti yathādhimuttā. “Nibbānaṃ [P 1.0016] adhimuttānaṃ, atthaṃ gacchanti āsavā”ti (dha. pa. 226) hi vuttaṃ. Ubhayañcetaṃ pubbabhāgavasena veditabbaṃ. Arahattappattito pubbeyeva hi yathāvuttamadhimuccanaṃ, na parato. Tenāha bhagavā –

In the second verse, this is an exposition of the meaning by way of showing the connection. Here, for those elders whose verses he wishes to recite, they are to be mentioned in a general way by name, clan, and virtue, as stated in ‘yathānāmā’ and so on. In a specific way, however, it will become manifest in each respective verse. Therein, ‘yathānāmā’ means those known by their respective names, such as Subhūti or Mahākoṭṭhika. ‘Yathāgottā’ means those known by their respective clans, such as Gotama or Kassapa, by which lineage they are known. ‘Yathādhammavihārino’ means those who dwelt in suitable meditative attainments, not being established merely in the highest degree of scriptural learning. Alternatively, ‘yathādhammavihārino’ means those who possess the Dhamma and are dwellers therein; that is, possessing such qualities as virtue, they frequently abide in the divine abidings and so forth. ‘Yathādhimuttā’ means those who are inclined in a certain way, whether inclined by faith or by wisdom, or in whatever way they are inclined toward Nibbāna through the approaches of emptiness and so on. For it is said: “For those inclined toward Nibbāna, the taints come to an end” (Dhp. 226). Both of these should be understood as pertaining to the preliminary stage. For this aforementioned inclination occurs before the attainment of Arahantship, not after. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Assaddho akataññū ca, sandhicchedo ca yo naro”tiādi. (dha. pa. 97).

“The person who is faithless, ungrateful, a house-breaker,” and so on. (Dhp. 97).

“Yathāvimuttā”ti vā pāṭho, paññāvimuttiubhatobhāgavimuttīsu yaṃyaṃvimuttikāti attho. Sappaññāti tihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya pārihārikapaññāya bhāvanāpaññāya cāti tividhāyapi paññāya paññavanto. Vihariṃsūti tāya eva sappaññatāya yathāladdhena phāsuvihāreneva vasiṃsu. Atanditāti analasā, attahitapaṭipattiyaṃ yathābalaṃ parahitapaṭipattiyañca uṭṭhānavantoti attho.

“According to their liberation” is an alternative reading, meaning liberated in whichever way, whether through liberation by wisdom or liberation in both parts. “Endowed with wisdom” means they were possessed of wisdom of three kinds: wisdom associated with three-rooted rebirth-linking, administrative wisdom, and wisdom developed through meditation. “They dwelt” means they abided with the ease they had obtained through that very wisdom. “Untiring” means not lazy; that is, they were energetic in the practice for their own welfare and, according to their strength, for the welfare of others.

Ettha ca pana nāmagottaggahaṇena tesaṃ therānaṃ pakāsapaññātabhāvaṃ dasseti. Dhammavihāraggahaṇena sīlasampadaṃ samādhisampadañca dasseti. “Yathādhimuttā sappaññā”ti iminā paññāsampadaṃ[V 1.0014]. “Atanditā”ti iminā sīlasampadādīnaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ vīriyasampadaṃ dasseti. “Yathānāmā”ti iminā tesaṃ pakāsananāmataṃ dasseti. “Yathāgottā”ti iminā saddhānusārīdhammānusārīgottasampattisamudāgamaṃ, “yathādhammavihārino”tiādinā sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ sampattisamudāgamaṃ, “atanditā”ti iminā evaṃ attahitasampattiyaṃ ṭhitānaṃ parahitapaṭipattiṃ dasseti.

Here, the mention of name and clan shows the renowned and well-known state of those elders. The mention of dwelling in the Dhamma shows their accomplishment in virtue and accomplishment in concentration. By “according to their inclination, the wise,” it shows their accomplishment in wisdom. By “untiring,” it shows their accomplishment in energy, which is the cause of the accomplishments in virtue and so forth. By “according to their names,” it shows their state of having renowned names. By “according to their clans,” it shows the arising of their attainment of the lineage of a faith-follower and a Dhamma-follower. By “according to their Dhamma-dwelling” and so on, it shows the arising of their attainment of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By “untiring,” it shows the practice for the welfare of others of those established in such accomplishment of their own welfare.

Atha vā “yathānāmā”ti idaṃ tesaṃ therānaṃ garūhi gahitanāmadheyyadassanaṃ samaññāmattakittanato. “Yathāgottā”ti idaṃ kulaputtabhāvadassanaṃ kulāpadesa kittanato. Tena nesaṃ saddhāpabbajitabhāvaṃ dasseti[M 1.0017]. “Yathādhammavihārino”ti idaṃ caraṇasampattidassanaṃ sīlasaṃvarādīhi samaṅgībhāvadīpanato[P 1.0017]. “Yathādhimuttā sappaññā”ti idaṃ nesaṃ vijjāsampattidassanaṃ āsavakkhayapariyosānāya ñāṇasampattiyā adhigamaparidīpanato. “Atanditā”ti idaṃ vijjācaraṇasampattīnaṃ adhigamūpāyadassanaṃ. “Yathānāmā”ti vā iminā tesaṃ pakāsananāmataṃyeva dasseti. “Yathāgottā”ti pana iminā pacchimacakkadvayasampattiṃ dasseti. Na hi sammāappaṇihitattano pubbe ca akatapuññassa saddhānusārīdhammānusārino gottasampattisamudāgamo sambhavati. “Yathādhammavihārino”ti iminā tesaṃ purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ dasseti. Na hi appatirūpe dese vasato sappurisūpanissayarahitassa ca tādisā guṇavisesā sambhavanti. “Yathādhimuttā”ti iminā saddhammasavanasampadāsamāyogaṃ dasseti. Na hi paratoghosena vinā sāvakānaṃ saccasampaṭivedho sambhavati. “Sappaññā atanditā”ti iminā yathāvuttassa guṇavisesassa abyabhicārihetuṃ dasseti ñāyārambhadassanato.

Alternatively, “as they are named” shows the names given to those elders by their teachers, from the mentioning of a mere convention. “As they are by clan” shows their status as sons of good family, from the mentioning of their family designation. By this, it shows their state of having gone forth out of faith. “As they dwell in the Dhamma” shows their accomplishment in conduct, by indicating their possession of moral restraint and other virtues. “As they are inclined, wise” shows their accomplishment of knowledge, by indicating their attainment of the accomplishment of knowledge that culminates in the destruction of the taints. “Untiring” shows the means of attaining the accomplishments of knowledge and conduct. Or, by “as they are named,” it simply shows their state of having renowned names. By “as they are by clan,” however, it shows their accomplishment of the latter two wheels. For the arising of the attainment of the lineage of a faith-follower or a Dhamma-follower is not possible for one whose mind is not rightly directed and who has not previously made merit. By “as they dwell in the Dhamma,” it shows their accomplishment of the former two wheels. For such distinguished qualities do not arise in one who dwells in an unsuitable place or who lacks the support of virtuous people. By “as they are inclined,” it shows their connection with the accomplishment of hearing the true Dhamma. For without the sound from another, the penetration of the truths is not possible for disciples. By “wise and untiring,” it shows the unfailing cause of the aforementioned distinguished qualities, by showing the undertaking of the right method.

Aparo nayo – “yathāgottā”ti ettha gottakittanena tesaṃ therānaṃ yonisomanasikārasampadaṃ dasseti yathāvuttagottasampannassa yonisomanasikārasambhavato. “Yathādhammavihārino”ti ettha dhammavihāraggahaṇena saddhammasavanasampadaṃ dasseti saddhammasavanena vinā tadabhāvato. “Yathādhimuttā”ti iminā matthakappattaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. “Sappaññā”ti iminā sabbattha sampajānakāritaṃ. “Atanditā”ti iminā vuttanayena attahitasampattiṃ paripūretvā ṭhitānaṃ paresaṃ hitasukhāvahāya paṭipattiyaṃ akilāsubhāvaṃ dasseti. Tathā “yathāgottā”ti iminā nesaṃ saraṇagamanasampadā dassitā saddhānusārīgottakittanato. “Yathādhammavihārino”ti iminā sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo samādhikkhandho dassito. “Yathādhimuttā sappaññā”ti iminā paññakkhandhādayo. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakaguṇānaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti ādimajjhapariyosānadassanena sabbepi [P 1.0018] sāvakaguṇā dassitā honti.

Another method: Here, in the phrase ‘according to their lineage,’ the mention of lineage indicates the accomplishment of wise attention in those elders, since wise attention is possible for one endowed with the aforementioned lineage. Here, in the phrase ‘according to their Dhamma-dwelling,’ the mention of dwelling in the Dhamma indicates the accomplishment of hearing the true Dhamma, since without hearing the true Dhamma, that dwelling is not possible. By ‘as they are inclined,’ it indicates the practice in accordance with the Dhamma that has reached its culmination. By ‘wise,’ it indicates acting with clear comprehension in all things. By ‘untiring,’ it indicates, in the manner described, the tireless nature of those who, having perfected the accomplishment of their own welfare, are established in the practice that brings welfare and happiness to others. Likewise, by ‘according to their lineage,’ their accomplishment in going for refuge is shown, through the mention of the lineage of a faith-follower. By ‘according to their Dhamma-dwelling,’ the aggregate of concentration, which is preceded by the aggregate of virtue, is shown. By ‘as they are inclined, wise,’ the aggregate of wisdom and the others are shown. Going for refuge is the beginning of a disciple’s qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end. Thus, by showing the beginning, middle, and end, all the qualities of a disciple are shown.

Īdisī [V 1.0015] pana guṇavibhūti yāya sammāpaṭipattiyā tehi adhigatā, taṃ dassetuṃ “tattha tattha vipassitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tatthāti tesu tesu [M 1.0018] araññarukkhamūlapabbatādīsu vivittasenāsanesu. Tattha tatthāti vā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ udānādikāle. Vipassitvāti sampassitvā. Nāmarūpavavatthāpanapaccayapariggahehi diṭṭhivisuddhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyo sampādetvā kalāpasammasanādikkamena pañcamaṃ visuddhiṃ adhigantvā paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā matthakaṃ pāpanavasena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā phusitvāti patvā sacchikatvā. Accutaṃ padanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi sayaṃ acavanadhammattā adhigatānaṃ accutihetubhāvato ca natthi ettha cutīti “accutaṃ”. Saṅkhatadhammehi asammissabhāvatāya tadatthikehi paṭipajjitabbatāya ca “pada”nti ca vuccati. Katantanti katassa antaṃ. Yo hi tehi adhigato ariyamaggo, so attano paccayehi uppāditattā kato nāma. Tassa pana pariyosānabhūtaṃ phalaṃ katantoti adhippetaṃ. Taṃ katantaṃ aggaphalaṃ. Atha vā paccayehi katattā nipphāditattā katā nāma saṅkhatadhammā, tannissaraṇabhāvato katanto nibbānaṃ. Taṃ katantaṃ. Paccavekkhantāti “adhigataṃ vata mayā ariyamaggādhigamena idaṃ ariyaphalaṃ, adhigatā asaṅkhatā dhātū”ti ariyaphalanibbānāni vimuttiñāṇadassanena paṭipattiṃ avekkhamānā. Atha vā saccasampaṭivedhavasena yaṃ ariyena karaṇīyaṃ pariññādisoḷasavidhaṃ kiccaṃ aggaphale ṭhitena nipphāditattā pariyosāpitattā kataṃ nāma, evaṃ kataṃ taṃ paccavekkhantā. Etena pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Purimanayena pana itarapaccavekkhaṇānīti ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇāni dassitāni honti.

Moreover, to show such an excellence of qualities which they attained by right practice, it is said, 'having insight here and there,' etc. 'Here and there' means in those various secluded dwellings such as forests, the roots of trees, mountains, etc. Or, 'here and there' means at those various times, such as during an inspired utterance. 'Having insight' means 'having thoroughly seen.' Having fulfilled the purification of view and the purification by overcoming doubt through the discernment of name-and-form and the comprehension of conditions, and having attained the fifth purification by the contemplation of aggregates, etc., in due order, they diligently developed insight and brought it to the culmination of the purification of knowledge and vision of the path, having touched, attained, and realized it. The Deathless State is Nibbāna. For it is by nature not subject to falling away, and because it is the cause of non-falling away for those who attain it, there is no falling away therein—thus it is called 'the Deathless.' And because it is unmixed with conditioned phenomena and is to be attained by those who seek it, it is called a 'state.' 'The end of what is done' means the end of what is done. For the Noble Path attained by them is called 'done' because it is produced by its own conditions. But its culmination, the fruit, is meant by 'the end of what is done.' That 'end of what is done' is the supreme fruit. Alternatively, conditioned phenomena are called 'done' because they are produced and fashioned by conditions; Nibbāna is 'the end of what is done' because it is the escape from them. That is 'the end of what is done.' 'Reflecting' means: 'Indeed, by attaining the Noble Path, I have attained this Noble Fruit; I have attained the unconditioned element.' Thus, they review the Noble Fruit and Nibbāna with the knowledge and vision of liberation, contemplating their practice. Alternatively, that which is to be done by a Noble One through the complete penetration of the truths—the sixteenfold duty of full understanding, etc.—is called 'done' because it is accomplished and concluded by one abiding in the supreme fruit. Thus, they reflect on what is done. By this, the reflection on abandoned defilements is shown. By the previous method, however, the other reflections are shown; thus, nineteen reflections are shown.

Imamatthanti ettha imanti sakalo theratherīgāthānaṃ attho attano itaresañca tattha sannipatitānaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakamahātherānaṃ buddhiyaṃ viparivattamānatāya āsanno paccakkhoti ca katvā vuttaṃ. Atthanti “channā me kuṭikā”tiādīhi [P 1.0019] gāthāhi vuccamānaṃ attūpanāyikaṃ parūpanāyikaṃ lokiyalokuttarapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ atthaṃ. Abhāsisunti gāthābandhavasena kathesuṃ, taṃdīpaniyo idāni mayā vuccamānā tesaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ gāthā attūpanāyikā suṇāthāti yojanā. Te ca mahātherā evaṃ kathentā [M 1.0019] attano sammāpaṭipattipakāsanīhi gāthāhi sāsanassa ekantaniyyānikavibhāvanena parepi tattha sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ niyojentīti etamatthaṃ dīpeti āyasmā dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko, tathā dīpento ca imāhi gāthāhi tesaṃ thomanaṃ tāsañca tesaṃ vacanassa nidānabhāvena ṭhapanaṃ ṭhānagatamevāti dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'This meaning' (imamatthanti): Herein, 'this' refers to the entire meaning of the verses of the theras and therīs. Because this meaning was revolving in the wisdom of myself and the other great elders who compiled the Dhamma and had assembled there, it was spoken of as 'near' and 'directly perceptible.' 'Meaning' (atthanti) refers to the meaning conveyed by verses such as 'My hut is roofed,' which is conducive to one's own welfare and that of others, and is connected with worldly and supramundane matters. 'They spoke' (abhāsisunti) means they related in verse form. The syntactical connection is as follows: 'Listen to these verses of those with developed minds, which are conducive to one's own welfare, which illuminate that meaning, and which are now being recited by me.' And those great elders, in speaking thus, also directed others toward right practice by making manifest the Dispensation's singular path to liberation through verses that proclaimed their own right practice. This is the meaning that the Venerable Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika (Treasurer of the Dhamma) elucidates. Moreover, it should be understood that in explaining thus, he shows that these verses serve both to praise them and to establish the basis for their statements, a position that is indeed appropriate.

Nidānagāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Introductory Verses is concluded.

1. Ekakanipāto

1. The Book of the Ones

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Subhūtittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Subhūti

Idāni [V 1.0016] channā [P 1.0020] me kuṭikātiādinayappavattānaṃ theragāthānaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Sā panāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā yasmā tāsaṃ tāsaṃ gāthānaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ pakāsetvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hoti suviññeyyā ca. Tasmā tattha tattha aṭṭhuppattiṃ pakāsetvā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmāti.

Now there is the commentary on the meaning of the elders' verses that proceed in the manner of 'My hut is roofed,' etc. Since this commentary on the meaning becomes clear and easily understood when it is explained after revealing the origin of each respective verse, I shall therefore provide the commentary on the meaning after revealing the origin in each case.

Tattha channā me kuṭikātigāthāya kā uppatti? Vuccate – ito kira kappasatasahassamatthake anuppanneyeva padumuttare bhagavati lokanāthe haṃsavatīnāmake nagare aññatarassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa eko putto uppajji. Tassa “nandamāṇavo”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto attano parivārabhūtehi catucattālīsāya māṇavakasahassehi saddhiṃ pabbatapāde isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattesi. Antevāsikānampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tepi na cireneva jhānalābhino ahesuṃ.

Therein, what is the origin of the verse 'My hut is roofed'? It is said: A hundred thousand aeons ago, before the arising of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Lord of the World, a son was born to a certain great wealthy brahmin in the city named Haṃsavatī. They gave him the name 'Nandamāṇava'. When he came of age, he mastered the three Vedas, but finding no essence therein, he went forth into the ascetic life at the foot of a mountain, together with forty-four thousand brahmin youths who were his retinue. He brought into being the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. He also taught the meditation subjects to his pupils, and they, before long, became attainers of jhāna.
