Tena [M 1.0020] ca samayena padumuttaro bhagavā loke uppajjitvā haṃsavatīnagaraṃ upanissāya viharanto ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento nandatāpasassa antevāsikajaṭilānaṃ arahattūpanissayaṃ nandatāpasassa ca dvīhaṅgehi samannāgatassa sāvakaṭṭhānantarassa patthanaṃ disvā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā pubbaṇhasamaye pattacīvaramādāya aññaṃ kañci anāmantetvā sīho viya ekacaro nandatāpasassa antevāsikesu phalāphalatthāya gatesu “buddhabhāvaṃ me jānātū”ti passantasseva nandatāpasassa ākāsato otaritvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Nandatāpaso buddhānubhāvañceva lakkhaṇapāripūriñca disvā lakkhaṇamante sammasitvā “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato nāma agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto rājā hoti cakkavattī, pabbajanto [P 1.0021] loke [V 1.0017] vivaṭacchado sabbaññū buddho hoti. Ayaṃ purisājānīyo nissaṃsayaṃ buddhoti ñatvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā, pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, āsanaṃ paññāpetvā, adāsi. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nandatāpasopi attano anucchavikaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara had arisen in the world and was residing near the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, while surveying the world at dawn, he saw the potential for arahantship among the matted-hair pupils of Nanda the ascetic, and also the aspiration of Nanda the ascetic, who was endowed with two qualities and destined for the position of a chief disciple. Having attended to his person early in the morning, the Blessed One took his bowl and robe in the forenoon and, without informing anyone, went alone like a lion. While the pupils of Nanda the ascetic had gone out to gather various fruits, the Blessed One, with the thought, 'May he know my state of Buddhahood,' descended from the sky and stood on the ground in the very sight of Nanda the ascetic. Seeing the Buddha’s majestic power and the perfection of his marks, Nanda the ascetic reflected upon the lore of marks and knew: 'One endowed with these marks, if he dwells in the household life, becomes a wheel-turning monarch; if he goes forth, he becomes a fully enlightened Buddha in the world, one with the veil uncovered. This thoroughbred of a man is undoubtedly a Buddha.' Having thus known, he went forward to meet him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Nanda the ascetic also took a seat suitable for himself and sat to one side.

Tasmiṃ samaye catucattālīsasahassajaṭilā paṇītapaṇītāni ojavantāni phalāphalāni gahetvā ācariyassa santikaṃ sampattā buddhānañceva ācariyassa ca nisinnāsanaṃ olokentā āhaṃsu – “ācariya, mayaṃ ‘imasmiṃ loke tumhehi mahantataro natthī’ti vicarāma, ayaṃ pana puriso tumhehi mahantataro maññe”ti. Nandatāpaso, “tātā, kiṃ vadetha, sāsapena saddhiṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassayojanubbedhaṃ sineruṃ upametuṃ icchatha, sabbaññubuddhena saddhiṃ mā maṃ upamitthā”ti āha. Atha te tāpasā “sace ayaṃ orako abhavissa, na amhākaṃ ācariyo evaṃ upamaṃ āhareyya, yāva mahā vatāyaṃ purisājānīyo”ti pādesu nipatitvā sirasā vandiṃsu. Atha te ācariyo āha – “tātā, amhākaṃ buddhānaṃ anucchaviko deyyadhammo natthi, bhagavā ca bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ idhāgato, tasmā mayaṃ yathābalaṃ deyyadhammaṃ dassāma, tumhe yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ phalāphalaṃ ānītaṃ, taṃ taṃ āharathā”ti vatvā āharāpetvā hatthe dhovitvā sayaṃ tathāgatassa patte patiṭṭhāpesi. Satthārā [M 1.0021] phalāphale paṭiggahitamatte devatā dibbojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Tāpaso udakampi sayameva parissāvetvā adāsi. Tato bhojanakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā nisinne satthari sabbe antevāsike pakkositvā satthu santike sāraṇīyaṃ kathaṃ kathento nisīdi. Satthā “bhikkhusaṅgho āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Bhikkhū satthu cittaṃ ñatvā satasahassamattā khīṇāsavā āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu.

At that time, forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics, carrying the finest and most nourishing fruits, approached their teacher. Observing the seat of the Buddha and their teacher, they said, 'Teacher, we have been wandering about thinking, “There is none greater than you in this world.” But this man here seems even greater than you.' The ascetic Nanda replied, 'Dear ones, what are you saying? Do you wish to compare Mount Sineru, which is sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas high, with a mustard seed? Do not compare me with the All-Knowing Buddha!' Then those ascetics thought, 'If this man were inferior, our teacher would not make such a comparison. How great indeed must this noble man be!' They fell at his feet and paid homage with their heads. Then their teacher said to them, 'Dear ones, we have no offering suitable for the Buddhas. The Blessed One has come here during his almsround; therefore, we shall give according to our ability. Whatever fine fruits you have brought, bring them forth.' Having said this, he had them brought, washed his hands, and personally placed them in the Tathāgata’s bowl. As soon as the Teacher accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence. The ascetic himself also filtered water and gave it. Then, when the meal was finished and the Teacher was seated, he summoned all his pupils and, sitting near the Teacher, engaged in courteous conversation. The Teacher thought, 'Let the community of monks come.' Knowing the Teacher's thought, a hundred thousand arahants arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.

Nandatāpaso antevāsike āmantesi – “tātā, buddhānaṃ nisinnāsanampi nīcaṃ, samaṇasatasahassassapi āsanaṃ natthi, tumhehi ajja uḷāraṃ bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca sakkāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati[P 1.0022], pabbatapādato vaṇṇagandhasampannāni pupphāni āharathā”ti. Acinteyyattā iddhivisayassa muhutteneva vaṇṇagandhasampannāni pupphāni āharitvā buddhānaṃ yojanappamāṇaṃ pupphāsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Aggasāvakānaṃ tigāvutaṃ, sesabhikkhūnaṃ aḍḍhayojanikādibhedaṃ, saṅghanavakassa usabhamattaṃ ahosi. Evaṃ paññattesu āsanesu nandatāpaso tathāgatassa purato añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhito, “bhante, mayhaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya imaṃ pupphāsanaṃ abhiruhathā”ti āha. Nisīdi bhagavā pupphāsane. Evaṃ nisinne satthari satthu ākāraṃ ñatvā bhikkhū attano attano pattāsane nisīdiṃsu. Nandatāpaso mahantaṃ pupphachattaṃ gahetvā tathāgatassa matthake dhārento aṭṭhāsi. Satthā “tāpasānaṃ ayaṃ sakkāro mahapphalo hotū”ti [V 1.0018] nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Satthu samāpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhikkhūpi samāpajjiṃsu. Tathāgate sattāhaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisinne antevāsikā bhikkhācārakāle sampatte vanamūlaphalāphalaṃ paribhuñjitvā sesakāle buddhānaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha tiṭṭhanti. Nandatāpaso pana bhikkhācārampi agantvā pupphachattaṃ dhārento sattāhaṃ pītisukheneva vītināmeti.

The ascetic Nanda addressed his disciples: 'Dear ones, the seat for the Buddha is lowly, and there are no seats for a hundred thousand monks. Today it is fitting for you to make a magnificent offering of honor to the Blessed One and the community of monks. Bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain.' Owing to the inconceivability of the range of psychic power, in a single moment they brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddha measuring a yojana. For the chief disciples, it was three gāvutas; for the other monks, it was of various sizes such as half a yojana; for the most junior monk, it was the measure of an usabha. When the seats were thus prepared, the ascetic Nanda, standing before the Tathāgata with his hands raised in reverence, said, 'Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend this flower-seat.' The Blessed One sat upon the flower-seat. When the Teacher was thus seated, the monks, knowing the Teacher's disposition, sat down on their respective, proper seats. The ascetic Nanda, taking a large flower-parasol, stood holding it over the Tathāgata's head. The Teacher, thinking, 'May this honor from the ascetics be of great fruit,' entered the attainment of cessation. Knowing that the Teacher had entered this attainment, the monks also entered it. While the Tathāgata remained seated for seven days, having entered cessation, his disciples, when the time for the almsround arrived, would consume forest roots and fruits and for the rest of the time stand with their hands raised in reverence to the Buddha. The ascetic Nanda, however, did not even go for alms but, holding the flower-parasol, passed the seven days in rapture and bliss alone.

Satthā nirodhato vuṭṭhāya araṇavihāriaṅgena dakkhiṇeyyaṅgena cāti dvīhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ ekaṃ sāvakaṃ “isigaṇassa pupphāsanānumodanaṃ karohī”ti āṇāpesi. So cakkavattirañño santikā paṭiladdhamahālābho mahāyodho viya tuṭṭhamānaso attano visaye [M 1.0022] ṭhatvā tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ sammasitvā anumodanaṃ akāsi. Tassa desanāvasāne satthā sayaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne sabbe catucattālīsasahassatāpasā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tesaṃ tāvadeva kesamassu antaradhāyi. Aṭṭha parikkhārā kāye paṭimukkāva ahesuṃ saṭṭhivassattherā viya satthāraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Nandatāpaso pana vikkhittacittatāya visesaṃ nādhigacchi. Tassa [P 1.0023] kira araṇavihārittherassa santike dhammaṃ sotuṃ āraddhakālato paṭṭhāya “aho vatāhampi anāgate uppajjanakabuddhassa sāsane iminā sāvakena laddhadhuraṃ labheyya”nti cittaṃ udapādi. So tena parivitakkena maggaphalapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Tathāgataṃ pana vanditvā sammukhe ṭhatvā āha – “bhante, yena bhikkhunā isigaṇassa pupphāsanānumodanā katā, ko nāmāyaṃ tumhākaṃ sāsane”ti. “Araṇavihāriaṅge dakkhiṇeyyaaṅge ca etadaggaṃ patto eso bhikkhū”ti. “Bhante, yvāyaṃ mayā sattāhaṃ pupphachattaṃ dhārentena sakkāro kato, tena adhikārena na aññaṃ sampattiṃ patthemi, anāgate pana ekassa buddhassa sāsane ayaṃ thero viya dvīhaṅgehi samannāgato sāvako bhaveyya”nti patthanamakāsi.

The Teacher, having emerged from cessation, commanded a disciple endowed with the two qualities of dwelling without conflict and being worthy of offerings, saying, 'Give the dedicatory sermon for the flower-seat to the assembly of seers.' That disciple, like a great warrior who has received a great reward from a universal monarch, was joyful and, standing in his own domain, he reviewed the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, and gave the dedicatory sermon. At the end of his discourse, the Teacher himself taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained Arahantship. The Teacher extended his hand, saying, 'Come, monks.' In that very moment, their hair and beards vanished. The eight requisites were placed upon their bodies, and they surrounded the Teacher like elders of sixty years' standing. The ascetic Nanda, however, due to his distracted mind, did not attain any distinction. It is said that from the time he began to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of that elder who dwelt without conflict, the thought arose in him: 'Oh, that I too, in the Dispensation of a future Buddha, might obtain the foremost position obtained by this disciple.' Because of that thought, he was unable to achieve the penetration of the path and fruit. Having paid homage to the Tathāgata, he stood before him and asked, 'Venerable Sir, the monk who gave the dedicatory sermon for the flower-seat to the assembly of seers, what is his name in your Dispensation?' 'That monk has reached the foremost position in the quality of dwelling without conflict and the quality of being worthy of offerings.' 'Venerable Sir, through the merit of this honor I have performed by holding the flower-parasol for seven days, I do not aspire to any other success. But in the future, in the Dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I become a disciple endowed with these two qualities, just like this elder.' Thus he made his aspiration.

Satthā “samijjhissati nu, kho imassa tāpasassa patthanā”ti anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pesetvā olokento kappasatasahassaṃ atikkamitvā samijjhanakabhāvaṃ disvā nandatāpasaṃ āha – “na te ayaṃ patthanā moghā bhavissati, anāgate kappasatasahassaṃ atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tassa santike samijjhissatī”ti vatvā dhammakathaṃ kathetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Nandatāpaso yāva cakkhupathasamatikkamā satthāraṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca uddissa añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. So aparabhāge kālena kālaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇi. Aparihīnajjhānova kālaṅkatvā brahmaloke nibbatto. Tato pana cuto aparānipi pañca jātisatāni pabbajitvā āraññako ahosi. Kassapasammāsambuddhakālepi pabbajitvā āraññako hutvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūresi. Etaṃ kira vattaṃ [V 1.0019] aparipūretvā mahāsāvakabhāvaṃ [M 1.0023] pāpuṇantā nāma natthi. Gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pana āgamaṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. So vīsativassasahassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā kālaṅkatvā kāmāvacaradevaloke tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti. Vuttañhetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.3.151) –

The Teacher, thinking, 'Will this ascetic’s aspiration be fulfilled or not?' sent forth his knowledge of the future and, looking forward, saw that it would be fulfilled after a hundred thousand eons had passed. He then said to the ascetic Nanda, 'This aspiration of yours will not be in vain. In the future, after a hundred thousand eons have passed, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his presence, it will be fulfilled.' Having said this and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he, surrounded by the community of monks, ascended into the sky. The ascetic Nanda stood with his hands raised in reverence towards the Teacher and the community of monks until they passed beyond the range of his sight. In the time that followed, he would from time to time approach the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma. With his meditative absorption undiminished, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma world. Passing away from there, for another five hundred births he went forth and was a forest-dweller. During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he also went forth, became a forest-dweller, and fulfilled the practice of 'going and returning.' It is said that no one who has not fulfilled this practice can attain the state of a great disciple. The practice of 'going and returning' should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the scriptures. Having fulfilled the practice of 'going and returning' for twenty thousand years, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa abode, in the desire-sphere celestial world. And this was stated in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.3.151):

“Himavantassāvidūre[P 1.0024], nisabho nāma pabbato;

Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.

“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Nisabha; my hermitage was well-made, my leaf-hut well-constructed.”

“Kosiyo nāma nāmena, jaṭilo uggatāpano;

Ekākiyo adutiyo, vasāmi nisabhe tadā.

By name I was Kosiya, a matted-haired ascetic of intense austerity. Alone, without a second, I dwelt then on Mount Nisabha.

“Phalaṃ mūlañca paṇṇañca, na bhuñjāmi ahaṃ tadā;

Pavattaṃva supātāhaṃ, upajīvāmi tāvade.

At that time, I did not eat fruit, root, or leaf. I subsisted then only on what had naturally fallen.

“Nāhaṃ kopemi ājīvaṃ, cajamānopi jīvitaṃ;

Ārādhemi sakaṃ cittaṃ, vivajjemi anesanaṃ.

I did not corrupt my livelihood, even while giving up my life. I satisfied my own mind and avoided improper seeking.

“Rāgūpasaṃhitaṃ cittaṃ, yadā uppajjate mama;

Sayaṃva paccavekkhāmi, ekaggo taṃ damemahaṃ.

When a mind associated with lust would arise in me, I myself would reflect upon it and, with one-pointedness, I would subdue it.

“Rajjase rajjanīye ca, dussanīye ca dussase;

Muyhase mohanīye ca, nikkhamassu vanā tuvaṃ.

‘You lust after what is lustful, you hate what is hateful, you are deluded by what is deluding. Depart from this forest!’

“Visuddhānaṃ ayaṃ vāso, nimmalānaṃ tapassinaṃ;

Mā kho visuddhaṃ dūsesi, nikkhamassu vanā tuvaṃ.

‘This is the dwelling of the pure, of stainless ascetics. Do not defile what is pure! Depart from this forest!’

“Agāriko bhavitvāna, yadā puttaṃ labhissasi;

Ubhopi mā virādhesi, nikkhamassu vanā tuvaṃ.

‘Having become a householder, when you obtain a son, do not fail in both ways. Depart from this forest!’

“Chavālātaṃ yathā kaṭṭhaṃ, na kvaci kiccakārakaṃ;

Neva gāme araññe vā, na hi taṃ kaṭṭhasammataṃ.

‘Like a firebrand from a pyre, a piece of wood useless for any purpose, neither in the village nor in the forest—indeed, it is not considered wood.’

“Chavālātūpamo tvaṃ si, na gihī nāpi saññato;

Ubhato muttako ajja, nikkhamassu vanā tuvaṃ.

‘You are like that firebrand from a pyre, neither a householder nor a restrained ascetic. Today you are bereft of both. Depart from this forest!’

“Siyā nu kho tava etaṃ, ko pajānāti te idaṃ;

Saddhādhuraṃ vahisi me, kosajjabahulāya ca.

‘Could this be your thought? Who would know this of you? You would bear the yoke of faith for me, and yet you are full of laziness.’

“Jigucchissanti [M 1.0024] taṃ viññū, asuciṃ nāgariko yathā;

Ākaḍḍhitvāna isayo, codayissanti taṃ sadā.

‘The wise will be disgusted by you, as a city-dweller is by filth. The seers, having dragged you forth, will constantly reprove you.’

“Taṃ [V 1.0020] viññū pavadissanti, samatikkantasāsanaṃ;

Saṃvāsaṃ alabhanto hi, kathaṃ jīvihisi tuvaṃ.

‘The wise will speak of you as one who has transgressed the teaching. Unable to find companionship, how indeed will you live?’

“Tidhāpabhinnaṃ mātaṅgaṃ, kuñjaraṃ saṭṭhihāyanaṃ;

Balī nāgo upagantvā, yūthā nīharate gajaṃ.

‘A sixty-year-old elephant, a tusker in full rut with threefold ichor flowing—a powerful bull elephant approaches and drives him from the herd.’

“Yūthā vinissaṭo santo, sukhaṃ sātaṃ na vindati;

Dukkhito vimano hoti, pajjhāyanto pavedhati.

‘Expelled from the herd, he finds no happiness, no ease; miserable and dejected, he broods and trembles.’

“Tatheva jaṭilā tampi, nīharissanti dummatiṃ;

Tehi tvaṃ nissaṭo santo, sukhaṃ sātaṃ na lacchasi.

‘In the same way, the matted-haired ascetics will expel you, you of wicked mind. Expelled by them, you will not find happiness or ease.’

“Divā vā yadi vā rattiṃ, sokasallasamappito;

Dayhati pariḷāhena, gajo yūthāva nissaṭo.

‘By day or by night, pierced by the dart of sorrow, you will burn with anguish, like an elephant expelled from the herd.’

“Jātarūpaṃ yathā kūṭaṃ, neva jhāyati katthaci;

Tathā sīlavīhino tvaṃ, na jhāyissasi katthaci.

‘Just as counterfeit gold does not shine anywhere, so you, being devoid of virtue, will not shine anywhere.’

“Agāraṃ vasamānopi, kathaṃ jīvihisi tuvaṃ;

Mattikaṃ pettikañcāpi, natthi te nihitaṃ dhanaṃ.

‘Even while dwelling in a home, how will you live? You have no stored-up wealth, neither from your mother's side nor from your father's.’

“Sayaṃ kammaṃ karitvāna, gatte sedaṃ pamocayaṃ;

Evaṃ jīvihisi gehe, sādhu te taṃ na ruccati.

‘Having done your own work, letting sweat pour from your limbs, thus you will live at home. Well now, does that not please you?’

“Evāhaṃ tattha vāremi, saṃkilesagataṃ manaṃ;

Nānādhammakathaṃ katvā, pāpā cittaṃ nivārayiṃ.

In this way I restrained my mind when it tended toward defilement. Giving various discourses on the Dhamma, I turned my mind away from evil.

“Evaṃ me viharantassa, appamādavihārino;

Tiṃsavassasahassāni, vipine me atikkamuṃ.

As I was dwelling thus, living heedfully, thirty thousand years passed by for me in the forest.

“Appamādarataṃ disvā, uttamatthaṃ gavesakaṃ;

Padumuttarasambuddho, āgacchi mama santikaṃ.

Seeing me delighting in heedfulness, seeking the ultimate goal, the Perfectly Enlightened Padumuttara came into my presence.

“Timbarūsakavaṇṇābho, appameyyo anūpamo;

Rūpenāsadiso buddho, ākāse caṅkamī tadā.

With the hue of a Timbarūsaka fruit, immeasurable, incomparable, the Buddha, unmatched in form, walked in the sky then.

“Suphullo [M 1.0025] sālarājāva, vijjūvabbhaghanantare;

Ñāṇenāsadiso buddho, ākāse caṅkamī tadā.

Like a great Sāla tree in full bloom, like lightning amidst dense clouds, the Buddha, unequaled in wisdom, walked in the sky then.

“Sīharājāvasambhīto, gajarājāva dappito;

Lāsīto byaggharājāva, ākāse caṅkamī tadā.

Fearless as a lion king, majestic as an elephant king, graceful as a tiger king, the Buddha walked in the sky then.

“Siṅghīnikkhasavaṇṇābho, khadiraṅgārasannibho;

Maṇi yathā jotiraso, ākāse caṅkamī tadā.

With the hue of Siṅgī-river gold, like embers of acacia wood, like a jotirasa gem, the Buddha walked in the sky then.

“Visuddhakelāsanibho, puṇṇamāyeva candimā;

Majjhanhikeva sūriyo, ākāse caṅkamī tadā.

Like pure Mount Kelāsa, like the moon on a full-moon night, like the sun at midday, the Buddha walked in the sky then.

“Disvā [V 1.0021] nabhe caṅkamantaṃ, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

Devo nu kho ayaṃ satto, udāhu manujo ayaṃ.

Seeing him walking in the sky, I thought thus at that time: ‘Is this being a deva, or is he a human?’

“Na me suto vā diṭṭho vā, mahiyā ediso naro;

Api mantapadaṃ atthi, ayaṃ satthā bhavissati.

I have neither heard of nor seen such a man on earth. But there are prophetic verses; this one will surely be the Teacher.

“Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādayiṃ;

Nānāpupphañca gandhañca, sannipātesahaṃ tadā.

Having thought thus, I inspired faith in my own mind. I then gathered various flowers and fragrances.

“Pupphāsanaṃ paññāpetvā, sādhucittaṃ manoramaṃ;

Narasārathinaṃ aggaṃ, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

Having prepared a delightful seat of flowers, with a virtuous mind, to the supreme Guide of men I spoke this word:

“Idaṃ me āsanaṃ vīra, paññattaṃ tavanucchavaṃ;

Hāsayanto mamaṃ cittaṃ, nisīda kusumāsane.

‘O Hero, this seat has been prepared by me, fitting for you. Gladdening my mind, please sit upon this seat of flowers.’

“Nisīdi tattha bhagavā, asambhītova kesarī;

Sattarattindivaṃ buddho, pavare kusumāsane.

The Blessed One sat there, fearless as a lion. For seven days and nights the Buddha remained on that excellent seat of flowers.

“Namassamāno aṭṭhāsiṃ, sattarattindivaṃ ahaṃ;

Vuṭṭhahitvā samādhimhā, satthā loke anuttaro;

Mama kammaṃ pakittento, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

I stood paying homage for seven days and nights. Having arisen from meditative concentration, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, proclaiming my deed, spoke this word:

“Bhāvehi buddhānussatiṃ, bhāvanānamanuttaraṃ;

Imaṃ satiṃ bhāvayitvā, pūrayissasi mānasaṃ.

‘Develop the recollection of the Buddha, supreme among meditations. Having developed this mindfulness, you will fulfill your aspiration.’

“Tiṃsakappasahassāni[M 1.0026], devaloke ramissasi;

Asītikkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjaṃ karissasi;

Sahassakkhattuṃ cakkavattī, rājā raṭṭhe bhavissasi.

‘For thirty thousand aeons, you will delight in the world of the devas. Eighty times you will be the king of devas, exercising divine sovereignty. A thousand times you will be a wheel-turning monarch, a king in the land.’

“Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Anubhossasi taṃ sabbaṃ, buddhānussatiyā phalaṃ.

‘You will enjoy vast regional kingship, innumerable by count. All this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.’

“Bhavābhave saṃsaranto, mahābhogaṃ labhissasi;

Bhoge te ūnatā natthi, buddhānussatiyā phalaṃ.

‘Wandering through existences, you will obtain great wealth. In your possessions there will be no lack; this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.’

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

‘A hundred thousand aeons from now, one born of the Okkāka clan, Gotama by name and by lineage, will be the Teacher in the world.’

“Asītikoṭiṃ chaḍḍetvā, dāse kammakare bahū;

Gotamassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajissasi.

‘Having given up eighty crores of wealth, and many male and female slaves and workers, you will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama.’

“Ārādhayitvā sambuddhaṃ, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Subhūti nāma nāmena, hessasi satthu sāvako.

Having pleased the Fully Awakened One, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans, you will be named Subhūti, a disciple of the Teacher.

“Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, dakkhiṇeyyaguṇamhi taṃ;

Tathāraṇavihāre ca, dvīsu agge ṭhapessasi.

Sitting in the Saṅgha of monks, He will establish you as foremost in two things: in being worthy of offerings and in dwelling without conflict.

“Idaṃ [V 1.0022] vatvāna sambuddho, jalajuttamanāmako;

Nabhaṃ abbhuggamī vīro, haṃsarājāva ambare.

Having said this, the Fully Awakened One named Jalajuttama, the hero, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air.

“Sāsito lokanāthena, namassitvā tathāgataṃ;

Sadā bhāvemi mudito, buddhānussatimuttamaṃ.

Instructed by the Protector of the World, having paid homage to the Tathāgata, I, being joyful, always cultivate the supreme recollection of the Buddha.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsaṃ agacchahaṃ.

By that well-done deed, and by my volition and aspiration, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

“Asītikkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Sahassakkhattuṃ rājā ca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

Eighty times I reigned as king of the devas; a thousand times I was a wheel-turning king.

“Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Anubhomi susampattiṃ, buddhānussatiyā phalaṃ.

I enjoyed vast and incalculable regional kingship and abundant prosperity—this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

“Bhavābhave [M 1.0027] saṃsaranto, mahābhogaṃ labhāmahaṃ;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, buddhānussatiyā phalaṃ.

Wandering from one existence to another, I obtained great wealth. There was no deficiency in my wealth—this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhānussatiyā phalaṃ.

One hundred thousand aeons ago, when I performed that deed, I know of no unfortunate destination—this is the fruit of the recollection of the Buddha.

“Paṭisambhidā catasso, vimokkhāpi ca aṭṭhime;

Chaḷabhiññā sacchikatā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. –

The four analytical knowledges, and these eight liberations, the six higher knowledges have been realized by me; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā subhūtitthero imā gāthāyo abhāsitthāti.

Thus indeed the Venerable Elder Subhūti spoke these verses.

Evaṃ pana so tāvatiṃsabhavane aparāparaṃ uppajjanavasena dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato cuto manussaloke anekasatakkhattuṃ cakkavattirājā ca padesarājā ca hutvā uḷāraṃ manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā atha amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthiyaṃ sumanaseṭṭhissa gehe anāthapiṇḍikassa kaniṭṭho hutvā nibbatti “subhūtī”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi.

Thus, having enjoyed divine prosperity in the Tāvatiṃsa realm by being reborn there successively, and then passing away from there, he became a wheel-turning monarch and a regional king in the human world many hundreds of times, enjoying sublime human prosperity. Then, in the time of our Blessed One, he was born in Sāvatthī in the house of the treasurer Sumana as Anāthapiṇḍika's younger brother, and his name was Subhūti.

Tena ca samayena amhākaṃ bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattavaradhammacakko anupubbena rājagahaṃ gantvā tattha veḷuvanapaṭiggahaṇādinā lokānuggahaṃ karonto rājagahaṃ upanissāya sītavane viharati. Tadā anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi sāvatthiyaṃ uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā attano sahāyassa rājagahaseṭṭhino gharaṃ gato buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ sītavane viharantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya satthāraṃ sāvatthiṃ āgamanatthāya yācitvā tato pañcacattālīsayojane magge yojane yojane satasahassapariccāgena vihāre patiṭṭhāpetvā sāvatthiyaṃ rājamānena aṭṭhakarīsappamāṇaṃ jetassa rājakumārassa uyyānabhūmiṃ koṭisanthārena kiṇitvā tattha bhagavato vihāraṃ kāretvā adāsi. Vihārapariggahaṇadivase ayaṃ subhūtikuṭumbiko anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhinā saddhiṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto saddhaṃ paṭilabhitvā pabbaji[V 1.0023]. So upasampajjitvā dve mātikā paguṇā katvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā araññe samaṇadhammaṃ karonto mettājhānapādakaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So dhammaṃ desento [M 1.0028] yasmā satthārā desitaniyāmena anodissakaṃ katvā dhammaṃ deseti. Tasmā araṇavihārīnaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Piṇḍāya caranto ghare ghare mettājhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya [P 1.0025] bhikkhaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti “evaṃ dāyakānaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Tasmā dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Tenāha bhagavā – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ araṇavihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ subhūti, dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ yadidaṃ subhūtī”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 201). Evamayaṃ mahāthero arahatte patiṭṭhāya attanā pūritapāramīnaṃ phalassa matthakaṃ patvā loke abhiññāto abhilakkhito hutvā bahujanahitāya janapadacārikaṃ caranto anupubbena rājagahaṃ agamāsi.

At that time, our Blessed One had arisen in the world and, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of the Dhamma, gradually journeyed to Rājagaha. There, by accepting the Veḷuvana Grove and performing other such acts, he brought benefit to the world, dwelling in the Sītavana, the Cool Grove, near Rājagaha. Then, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, taking goods for enterprise from Sāvatthī, went to the house of his friend, the chief merchant of Rājagaha. Hearing of the Buddha’s arising and that the Teacher was dwelling in the Cool Grove, he approached him. At the very first sight, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. He then invited the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī. Afterward, along the forty-five-yojana road, he established monasteries at every yojana, spending a hundred thousand at each. In Sāvatthī, by covering the ground with a crore of coins, he bought from Prince Jeta the park land measuring eight karīsas by the royal measure. There, he had a monastery built for the Blessed One and gave it. On the day of the monastery’s acceptance, this householder Subhūti went with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and, upon hearing the Dhamma, acquired faith and went forth. Having received the higher ordination, he mastered the two Pātimokkha codes, had a meditation subject explained to him, and practiced the duties of a recluse in the forest. Developing insight with the jhāna of loving-kindness as its basis, he attained arahantship. When teaching the Dhamma, because he taught without specifying an individual, in accordance with the method taught by the Teacher, he came to be known as the foremost among those who dwell without conflict. When going for alms, he would enter the jhāna of loving-kindness at each house and, upon emerging from it, would accept the alms-food, thinking, 'In this way, it will be of great fruit for the donors.' Therefore, he came to be known as the foremost among those worthy of offerings. For this reason the Blessed One said: 'This is the foremost, monks, among my monk disciples who are dwellers without conflict, that is, Subhūti. Among those worthy of offerings, that is, Subhūti.' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.198, 201). Thus this great elder, established in arahantship, having reached the pinnacle of the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled, became well-known and distinguished in the world. Wandering on tour through the country for the welfare of the multitude, he in due course arrived at Rājagaha.

Rājā bimbisāro therassa āgamanaṃ sutvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “idheva, bhante, vasathā”ti vatvā “nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ karissāmī”ti pakkanto vissari. Thero senāsanaṃ alabhanto abbhokāse vītināmesi. Therassa ānubhāvena devo na vassati. Manussā avuṭṭhitāya upaddutā rañño nivesanadvāre ukkuṭṭhimakaṃsu. Rājā “kena nu kho kāraṇena devo na vassatī”ti vīmaṃsanto “therassa abbhokāsavāsena maññe na vassatī”ti cintetvā tassa paṇṇakuṭiṃ kārāpetvā “imissā, bhante, paṇṇakuṭiyā vasathā”ti vatvā vanditvā pakkāmi. Thero kuṭikaṃ pavisitvā tiṇasanthārake pallaṅkena nisīdi. Tadā pana devo thokaṃ thokaṃ phusāyati, na sammā dhāraṃ anuppavecchati. Atha thero lokassa avuṭṭhikabhayaṃ visamitukāmo attano ajjhattikabāhiravatthukassa parissayassa abhāvaṃ pavedento –

King Bimbisāra, hearing of the elder’s arrival, approached him, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, please stay right here.' Saying, 'I will prepare a dwelling place,' he departed but then forgot. The elder, not receiving a lodging, spent the time in the open air. Due to the elder’s spiritual power, the rain god did not send rain. The people, afflicted by the drought, made an uproar at the king’s palace gate. The king, investigating, 'For what reason does the rain god not send rain?' reflected, 'I think it is because the elder is dwelling in the open air that he does not send rain.' Having had a leaf-hut built for him, he said, 'Venerable sir, please dwell in this leaf-hut,' paid homage, and departed. The elder entered the hut and sat cross-legged on a spread of grass. Then the rain god drizzled lightly, but did not let down a proper shower. Then the elder, wishing to quell the world’s fear of drought and to make known his own freedom from dangers related to internal and external things, declared:

1.

1.

“Channā me kuṭikā sukhā nivātā, vassa deva yathāsukhaṃ;

Cittaṃ me susamāhitaṃ vimuttaṃ, ātāpī viharāmi vassa devā”ti. –

My hut is covered, pleasant, sheltered from the wind; rain, O deva, as you please. My mind is well-concentrated, liberated; I dwell ardently. Rain, O deva!

Gāthamāha.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 1.0029] channa-saddo tāva “channā sā kumārikā imassa kumārakassa” (pārā. 296) “nacchannaṃ nappatirūpa”ntiādīsu (pārā. 383) patirūpe āgato. “Channaṃ tveva, phagguṇa, phassāyatanāna”ntiādīsu vacanavisiṭṭhe saṅkhyāvisese. “Channamativassati, vivaṭaṃ nātivassatī”tiādīsu [P 1.0026] (udā. 45; cūḷava. 385) gahaṇe. “Kyāhaṃ te nacchannopi karissāmī”tiādīsu nivāsanapārupane “āyasmā channo anācāraṃ ācaratī”tiādīsu (pārā. 424) paññattiyaṃ. “Sabbacchannaṃ sabbaparicchannaṃ (pāci. 52, 54), channā kuṭi āhito [V 1.0024] ginī”ti (su. ni. 18) ca ādīsu tiṇādīhi chādane. Idhāpi tiṇādīhi chādaneyeva daṭṭhabbo, tasmā tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā channā yathā na vassati vassodakapatanaṃ na hoti na ovassati, evaṃ sammadeva chāditāti attho.

Herein, the word 'channa' first appears in contexts such as 'that girl is suitable for this boy' (Pārā. 296) and 'unsuitable, not fitting' (Pārā. 383), where it has the meaning of 'fitting'. In phrases like 'indeed, Phagguna, the six sense bases…' it is used for the specific number six. In expressions such as 'it rains on the covered, it does not rain on the open' (Udā. 45; Cūḷava. 385), it has the meaning of 'a dwelling'. In statements like 'What can I do for you, being unclothed?' it has the meaning of 'clothing and covering'. In designations like 'the venerable Channa behaves improperly' (Pārā. 424), it is used as a proper name. In phrases like 'fully covered, fully enclosed' (Pāci. 52, 54), and 'the hut is covered, the fire is lit' (Snp 1.2), it has the meaning of 'covering with grass and so on'. Here too, it should be understood in the sense of 'covering with grass and so on'. Therefore, the meaning is: covered with grass or leaves in such a way that the rain does not get in, that the falling of rainwater does not occur, that it is not drenched; thus, 'properly covered'.

Me-saddo “kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsitu”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 8; dī. ni. 2.65; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172) karaṇe āgato, mayāti attho. “Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.182; a. ni. 4.257) sampadāne, mayhanti attho. “Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato”ādīsu (ma. ni. 1.206; saṃ. ni. 4.14) sāmiatthe āgato. Idhāpi sāmiatthe eva daṭṭhabbo, mamāti attho. Kiñcāpi khīṇāsavānaṃ mamāyitabbaṃ nāma kiñci natthi lokadhammehi anupalittabhāvato, lokasamaññāvasena pana tesampi “ahaṃ mamā”ti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā”ti (ma. ni. 1.29).

The word 'me' appears in contexts such as, 'What was attained by me with difficulty, it is not suitable to proclaim it now,' (Mahāvagga 8; Dīgha Nikāya 2.65; Majjhima Nikāya 1.281; 2.337; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.172) in the instrumental sense, meaning 'by me.' In phrases like, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to me in brief,' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.182; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.257) it appears in the dative sense, meaning 'to me.' In statements such as, 'Monks, before my enlightenment, when I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta,' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.206; Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.14) it is used in the possessive sense. Here too, it should be understood in the possessive sense, meaning 'my.' Although for those whose cankers are destroyed there is nothing that can be called 'mine' due to their being unstained by worldly conditions, by way of worldly convention, even for them there is the mere manner of speech, 'I' and 'mine.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'How might my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things?' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.29).

Kuṭikāti pana mātukucchipi karajakāyopi tiṇādicchadano patissayopi vuccati. Tathā hi –

A 'small hut' (kuṭikā), moreover, is said to be the mother's womb, the physical body, and a shelter covered with grass and the like. For thus it is said:

“Mātaraṃ kuṭikaṃ brūsi, bhariyaṃ brūsi kulāvakaṃ;

Putte santānake brūsi, taṇhā me brūsi bandhana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.19) –

"You call the mother a small hut, you call the wife a nest; you call the children a continuity, you call craving my bondage."

Ādīsu mātukucchi “kuṭikā”ti vuttā.

In such passages, the mother's womb is called a 'small hut'.

“Aṭṭhikaṅkalakuṭike[M 1.0030], maṃsanhārupasibbite;

Dhiratthu pūre duggandhe, paragatte mamāyasī”ti. (theragā. 1153) –

"In this small hut that is a skeleton of bones, stitched with flesh and sinews; shame on this body, full of foulness! You cherish another's body."

Ādīsu kesādisamūhabhūto karajakāyo. “Kassapassa bhagavato bhagini kuṭi ovassati” (ma. ni. 2.291) “kuṭi nāma ullittā vā hoti avalittā vā”tiādīsu (pārā. 349) tiṇachadanapatissayo. Idhāpi [P 1.0027] so eva veditabbo paṇṇasālāya adhippetattā. Kuṭi eva hi kuṭikā, apākaṭakuṭi “kuṭikā”ti vuttā.

In such passages, the physical body, which is a collection of hair and so forth, is meant. In passages such as, 'The hut of the Blessed One Kassapa's sister is leaking' (Majjhima Nikāya 2.291) and 'A hut is either plastered or unplastered,' and so on (Pārājika 349), a shelter with a grass roof is meant. Here too, that very same thing should be understood, because a leaf-hut is intended. For a kuṭi is simply a kuṭikā; an inconspicuous hut is called a kuṭikā.

Sukha-saddo pana “vipiṭṭhikatvāna sukhaṃ dukhañca, pubbeva ca somanassadomanassa”ntiādīsu [V 1.0025] (su. ni. 67) sukhavedanāyaṃ āgato. “Sukho buddhānamuppādo, sukhā saddhammadesanā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 194) sukhamūle. “Sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ puññānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 7.62; itivu. 22) sukhahetumhi. “Yasmā ca, kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60) sukhārammaṇe, “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ete, cunda, ariyassa vinaye”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.82) abyāpajje. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.215; dha. pa. 203-204) nibbāne. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva sukhā saggā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.225) sukhappaccayaṭṭhāne. “Sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanika”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.163; saṃ. ni. 1.130) iṭṭhe, piyamanāpeti attho. Idhāpi iṭṭhe sukhappaccaye vā daṭṭhabbo. Sā hi kuṭi anto bahi ca manāpabhāvena sampāditā nivāsanaphāsutāya “sukhā”ti vuttā. Tathā nātisītanātiuṇhatāya utusukhasampattiyogena kāyikacetasikasukhassa paccayabhāvato.

The term 'sukha,' however, appears referring to pleasant feeling in instances such as 'having turned away from pleasure and pain, as well as from joy and sorrow beforehand' (Suttanipāta 67). In instances such as 'the arising of the Buddhas is happiness, the teaching of the true Dhamma is happiness' (Dhammapada 194), it appears referring to the root of happiness. In statements such as 'this, monks, is a designation for happiness, namely, meritorious deeds' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.62; Itivuttaka 22), it appears referring to the cause of happiness. In passages such as 'because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, associated with pleasure, inclined toward pleasure' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.60), it appears referring to a pleasant object. In phrases such as 'these, Cunda, are the dwellings in the present that are happiness in the Noble One’s discipline' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.82), it appears referring to non-affliction. In declarations such as 'Nibbāna is the highest happiness' (Majjhima Nikāya 2.215; Dhammapada 203-204), it appears referring to Nibbāna. In statements such as 'so much so, monks, that it is not easy to attain by description the heavens, which are happiness' (Majjhima Nikāya 3.225), it indicates a place that is a condition for happiness. In phrases such as 'leading to heaven, resulting in happy experiences, conducive to heavenly rebirth' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.163; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.130), it means what is desirable, pleasing, and delightful. Here too, it should be regarded as referring to what is desirable or a condition for happiness. For that hut, being made complete with a pleasing appearance both inside and out and with comfortable dwelling, is called 'pleasant.' Likewise, because it is neither too cold nor too hot, it is a condition for physical and mental happiness due to its attainment of a favorable climate.

Nivātāti avātā, phusitaggaḷapihitavātapānattā vātaparissayarahitāti attho. Idaṃ tassā kuṭikā sukhabhāvavibhāvanaṃ. Savāte hi senāsane utusappāyo na labbhati, nivāte so labbhatīti. Vassāti pavassa sammā dhāraṃ anuppaveccha. Devāti ayaṃ deva-saddo “imāni te, deva, caturāsīti nagarasahassāni kusavatīrājadhānippamukhāni, ettha[M 1.0031], deva, chandaṃ janehi jīvite apekkha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.266) sammutideve khattiye āgato. “Cātumahārājikā devā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.337) upapattidevesu. “Tassa devātidevassa, sāsanaṃ sabbadassino”tiādīsu visuddhidevesu[P 1.0028]. Visuddhidevānañhi bhagavato atidevabhāve vutte itaresaṃ vutto eva hoti. “Viddhe vigatavalāhake deve”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.486; saṃ. ni. 1.110; itivu. 27) ākāse. “Devo ca kālena kālaṃ na sammā dhāraṃ anuppavecchatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) meghe pajjunne vā. Idhāpi meghe pajjunne vā daṭṭhabbo. Vassāti hi te āṇāpento thero ālapati. Yathāsukhanti yathāruciṃ. Tava vassanena mayhaṃ bāhiro parissayo natthi, tasmā yathākāmaṃ vassāti vassūpajīvisatte anuggaṇhanto vadati.

Sheltered means without wind; because its windows are bolted and closed, it is free from the danger of wind—this is the meaning. This is an explanation of the pleasant nature of that small hut. For in a windy dwelling, a suitable climate is not obtained, but in a sheltered one, it is obtained. 'Rain' means: may you rain, may you let your streams pour down properly. 'Deva'—this word 'deva' appears in the sense of a khattiya by convention in passages such as, 'These, O deva, are your eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī as the capital; here, O deva, generate a desire for life,' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 2.266). It appears in the sense of devas by rebirth in passages such as, 'The devas of the Four Great Kings are radiant and full of bliss,' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 3.337). It appears in the sense of purified devas in passages such as, 'The teaching of that deva beyond devas, the All-Seeing One,' and so on. For when the Blessed One is spoken of as a deva beyond the purified devas, it is said of the others as well. It appears in the sense of the sky in passages such as, 'When the sky is clear and free of clouds,' and so on (Majjhima Nikāya 1.486; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.110; Itivuttaka 27). It appears in the sense of a cloud or Pajjunna in passages such as, 'And the deva does not let the streams pour down properly from time to time,' and so on (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70). Here too, it should be understood as referring to a cloud or Pajjunna. For in saying 'Rain,' the elder addresses and commands them. 'As you please' means according to your wish. He speaks, showing favor to the beings who subsist on rain, saying: 'By your raining, there is no external danger for me; therefore, rain as you wish.'

Idāni abbhantare parissayābhāvaṃ dassento “citta”ntiādimāha. Tattha cittaṃ me susamāhitanti mama cittaṃ suṭṭhu ativiya sammā sammadeva ekaggabhāvena ārammaṇe ṭhapitaṃ. Tañca kho na nīvaraṇādivikkhambhanamattena; api ca kho vimuttaṃ orambhāgiyauddhaṃbhāgiyasaṅgahehi [V 1.0026] sabbasaṃyojanehi sabbakilesadhammato ca visesena vimuttaṃ, samucchedappahānavasena paṭipassaddhippahānavasena te pajahitvā ṭhitanti attho. Ātāpīti vīriyavā. Phalasamāpattiatthaṃ vipassanārambhavasena diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthañca āraddhavīriyo hutvā viharāmi, dibbavihārādīhi attabhāvaṃ pavattemi, na pana kilesappahānatthaṃ, pahātabbasseva abhāvatoti adhippāyo. “Yathā pana bāhiraparissayābhāvena, deva, mayā tvaṃ vassane niyojito, evaṃ abbhantaraparissayābhāvenapī”ti dassento punapi “vassa, devā”ti āha.

Now, to show the absence of internal dangers, he says, 'My mind,' and so on. Therein, 'my mind is well-concentrated' means my mind is excellently, exceedingly, and rightly established on its object with one-pointedness. And this is not merely through the suppression of the hindrances and so on; rather, it is liberated. It is especially liberated from all fetters included in the lower and higher fetters, and from all states of defilement; it stands having abandoned them by way of eradication and by way of subsidence. This is the meaning. 'Ardent' means energetic. 'I dwell with energy aroused for the sake of attaining fruition, by way of beginning insight, and for the sake of dwelling happily in the present life; I maintain my existence with the divine abidings and so on, but not for the sake of abandoning defilements, for there is nothing to be abandoned.' This is the intention. To show that 'Just as, O deva, on account of the absence of external dangers, you were urged by me to rain, so too is it on account of the absence of internal dangers,' he says again, 'Rain, O deva.'

Aparo nayo channāti chāditā pihitā. Kuṭikāti attabhāvo. So hi “anekāvayavassa samudāyassa avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, puggalassa taṇhāsaṃyuttassa ayañceva kāyo samudāgato, bahiddhā ca nāmarūpa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.19) kāyoti āgato. “Siñca, bhikkhu, imaṃ nāvaṃ[M 1.0032], sittā te lahumessatī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 66) nāvāti āgato. “Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhata”nti (dha. pa. 154) ca ādīsu gahanti āgato. “Satto guhāyaṃ bahunābhichanno, tiṭṭhaṃ naro mohanasmiṃ pagāḷho”tiādīsu (su. ni. 778) guhāti [P 1.0029] āgato. “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattatī ratho”tiādīsu (udā. 65) rathoti āgato. “Puna gehaṃ na kāhasī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 154) gehanti āgato. “Vivaṭā kuṭi nibbuto ginī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 19) kuṭīti āgato. Tasmā idhāpi so “kuṭikā”ti vutto. Attabhāvo hi kaṭṭhādīni paṭicca labbhamānā gehanāmikā kuṭikā viya aṭṭhiādisaññite pathavīdhātuādike phassādike ca paṭicca labbhamāno “kuṭikā”ti vutto, cittamakkaṭassa nivāsabhāvato ca. Yathāha –

Another explanation: 'Channā' means covered, concealed. 'Kuṭikā' means individual existence. For in such passages as, "Monks, for an individual who is a composite of many parts, veiled by ignorance, and yoked to craving, this very body has come to be, and externally there is name-and-form" (SN 12.19), it is referred to as 'body.' In such passages as, "Bail out this boat, monk; when bailed out, it will travel lightly for you" (Dhp 369), it is referred to as 'boat.' In such passages as, "House-builder, you are seen; the house-peak is dismantled" (Dhp 154), it is referred to as 'house.' In such passages as, "A being, much enveloped, dwells in the cave; a person stands sunk deep in delusion" (Snp 772), it is referred to as 'cave.' In such passages as, "The spotless chariot with a white canopy, the one-wheeled chariot rolls on" (Ud 6.2), it is referred to as 'chariot.' In such passages as, "You shall not build a house again" (Dhp 154), it is referred to as 'house.' In such passages as, "The hut is opened, the fire is extinguished" (Snp 19), it is referred to as 'hut.' Therefore, here too it is called 'kuṭikā.' For individual existence is called 'kuṭikā' because, like a hut called a house which is obtained in dependence on wood and so forth, it is obtained in dependence on the earth element and so forth, which are designated as bones and the like, and in dependence on contact and so forth; and because it is the dwelling place of the mind-monkey. As it is said:

“Aṭṭhikaṅkalakuṭivesā, makkaṭāvasatho iti;

Makkaṭo pañcadvārāya, kuṭikāya pasakkiya;

Dvārenānupariyāti, ghaṭṭayanto punappuna”nti ca.

"A dwelling for a monkey, in the guise of a hut of bones; the monkey, having attached itself to the five-doored hut, goes about from door to door, striking them again and again."

Sā panesā attabhāvakuṭikā therassa tiṇṇaṃ channaṃ aṭṭhannañca asaṃvaradvārānaṃ vasena samati vijjhanakassa rāgādiavassutassa paññāya saṃvutattā sammadeva pihitattā “channā”ti vuttā. Tenāha bhagavā – “sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti (su. ni. 1041). Vuttanayena channattā eva kilesadukkhābhāvato nirāmisasukhasamaṅgitāya ca sukhā sukhappattā, tato eva ca nivātā nihatamānamadathambhasārambhatāya nivātavuttikā. Ayañca nayo [V 1.0027] “mayhaṃ na saṃkilesadhammānaṃ saṃvaraṇamattena siddho, atha kho aggamaggasamādhinā suṭṭhu samāhitacittatāya ceva aggamaggapaññāya sabbasaṃyojanehi vippamuttacittatāya cā”ti dassento āha “cittaṃ me susamāhitaṃ vimutta”nti. Evaṃbhūto ca “idānāhaṃ katakaraṇīyo”ti na appossukko homi, atha kho ātāpī viharāmi, sadevakassa lokassa hitasukhūpasaṃhāre ussāhajāto bhikkhācārakālepi anugharaṃ brahmavihāreneva viharāmi. Tasmā [P 1.0030] tvampi, deva, pajjunna mayhaṃ piyaṃ kātukāmatāyapi vassūpajīvīnaṃ sattānaṃ anukampāyapi vassa sammā dhāraṃ anuppavecchāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Now, for the elder, this hut of individual existence is called 'covered' because, for him who pierces the outflows such as craving, it is, by means of the three, six, and eight doors of non-restraint, restrained and well-covered by wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "I speak of the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut" (Snp 1035). Because it is covered in the manner described, it is pleasant due to the absence of the suffering of defilements and, being endowed with non-carnal bliss, has attained happiness. For that very reason it is sheltered; its nature is sheltered because pride, intoxication, stubbornness, and contention have been struck down. And this way was accomplished for me not merely by restraining defiling states, but rather, as he shows when he says, 'My mind is well-composed, liberated,' it was accomplished by the concentration of the supreme path, through a mind thoroughly composed, and by the wisdom of the supreme path, through a mind completely liberated from all fetters. And being thus, I do not become unconcerned, thinking, 'Now I have done what was to be done.' Rather, I dwell ardently. Having become zealous in bringing about the welfare and happiness of the world with its gods, I dwell, even when on alms-round, from house to house only with the divine abidings. Therefore, you too, O god Pajjunna, out of a desire to do what is dear to me and also out of compassion for beings who live by the rains, rain down! Rightly release your streams. This is the meaning to be understood here.

Ettha [M 1.0033] ca thero “channā me kuṭikā sukhā nivātā”ti iminā lokiyalokuttarabhedaṃ attano adhisīlasikkhaṃ dasseti. “Cittaṃ me susamāhita”nti iminā adhicittasikkhaṃ. “Vimutta”nti iminā adhipaññāsikkhaṃ. “Ātāpī viharāmī”ti iminā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ. Atha vā “channā me kuṭikā sukhā nivātā”ti iminā animittavihāraṃ dasseti kilesavassapidhānamukhena niccādinimittugghāṭanadīpanato. “Cittaṃ me susamāhita”nti iminā appaṇihitavihāraṃ. “Vimutta”nti iminā suññatavihāraṃ. “Ātāpī viharāmī”ti iminā tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vihārānaṃ adhigamūpāyaṃ. Paṭhamena vā dosappahānaṃ, dutiyena rāgappahānaṃ, tatiyena mohappahānaṃ. Tathā dutiyena paṭhamadutiyehi vā dhammavihārasampattiyo dasseti. Tatiyena vimuttisampattiyo. “Ātāpī viharāmī”ti iminā parahitapaṭipattiyaṃ atanditabhāvaṃ dassetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, by the phrase, 'My hut is roofed, pleasant, sheltered,' the elder shows his own higher training in virtue, with its distinction between the mundane and the supramundane. By 'My mind is well-composed,' he shows the higher training in mind. By 'liberated,' he shows the higher training in wisdom. By 'I dwell ardently,' he shows the blissful abiding in this very life. Alternatively, by 'My hut is roofed, pleasant, sheltered,' he shows the signless abiding, as it illuminates the eradication of signs such as permanence by way of covering against the rain of defilements. By 'My mind is well-composed,' he shows the desireless abiding. By 'liberated,' he shows the emptiness abiding. By 'I dwell ardently,' he shows the means for attaining those three abidings. Or, by the first phrase, the abandoning of aversion; by the second, the abandoning of lust; by the third, the abandoning of delusion. Likewise, by the second, or by the first and second, he shows the accomplishments of abiding in the Dhamma. By the third, he shows the accomplishments of liberation. By 'I dwell ardently,' he shows his unwearied state in the practice for the welfare of others. This should be understood.

Evaṃ “yathānāmā”ti gāthāya vuttānaṃ dhammavihārādīnaṃ imāya gāthāya dassitattā tattha adassitesu nāmagottesu nāmaṃ dassetuṃ “itthaṃ suda”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ye hi therā nāmamattena pākaṭā, te nāmena, ye gottamattena pākaṭā, te gottena, ye ubhayathā pākaṭā, te ubhayenapi dassissa”nti. Ayaṃ pana thero nāmena abhilakkhito, na tathā gottenāti “itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā subhūtī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha itthanti idaṃ pakāraṃ, iminā ākārenāti attho. Sudanti su idaṃ, sandhivasena ikāralopo. Sūti ca nipātamattaṃ, idaṃ gāthanti yojanā. Āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ garugāravasappatissavacanametaṃ. Subhūtīti nāmakittanaṃ. So hi sarīrasampattiyāpi dassanīyo pāsādiko, guṇasampattiyāpi. Iti sundarāya sarīrāvayavavibhūtiyā sīlasampattiyādivibhūtiyā ca samannāgatattā subhūtīti paññāyittha sīlasārādithiraguṇayogato thero. Abhāsitthāti kathesi. Kasmā panete mahātherā attano guṇe pakāsentīti? Iminā dīghena addhunā [P 1.0031] anadhigatapubbaṃ paramagambhīraṃ ativiya santaṃ paṇītaṃ attanā adhigataṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ paccavekkhitvā [V 1.0028] pītivegasamussāhitaudānavasena sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvavibhāvanavasena ca paramappicchā ariyā [M 1.0034] attano guṇe pakāsenti, yathā taṃ lokanātho bodhaneyyaajjhāsayavasena “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato catuvesārajjavisārado”tiādinā attano guṇe pakāseti, evamayaṃ therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā hotīti.

Thus, since the abidings in the Dhamma and other qualities mentioned in the verse beginning 'yathānāmā' have been shown by this verse, the phrase 'itthaṃ sudaṃ,' etc., was said in order to show the name, among the name and clan which were not shown there. For those elders who are known by name alone are indicated by name; those known by clan alone, by clan; and those known by both, by both. This elder, however, is distinguished by name, not so much by clan; hence it is said, 'Thus the venerable Subhūti.' Therein, 'itthaṃ' means 'in this manner,' 'in this way.' 'Sudaṃ' is 'su idaṃ,' with the elision of 'i' due to euphonic combination; 'su' is a mere particle, and the connection is 'this verse.' 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment, a word of reverence and respect. 'Subhūti' is the stating of his name. For he was pleasant to see and inspiring due to his physical perfection, and also due to his perfection of virtue. Thus, because he was endowed with the splendor of beautiful bodily parts and the splendor of the perfection of virtue and so on, he became known as 'Subhūti.' He is an 'elder' (thero) due to his connection with firm qualities such as the essence of virtue. 'Abhāsitthā' means 'he spoke.' But why do these great elders proclaim their own virtues? Having reflected upon the supramundane Dhamma they had themselves attained—a Dhamma most profound, exceedingly peaceful, sublime, and never before attained over this long period—the noble ones, who have few wishes, proclaim their own virtues by way of an inspired utterance prompted by a surge of joy, and by way of clarifying the liberating nature of the Teaching. It is just as the Lord of the World, out of his intention to enlighten those who could be taught, proclaims his own virtues, saying, 'Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers, possessed of the four kinds of fearlessness,' etc. Thus, this is the elder’s verse declaring final knowledge.

Paramatthadīpaniyā theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Paramatthadīpanī, the Commentary on the Verses of the Elders

Subhūtittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Subhūti is concluded.

2. Mahākoṭṭhikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika

Upasantoti āyasmato mahākoṭṭhikattherassa gāthā. Tassa kā uppatti? Ayampi thero padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto mātāpitūnaṃ accayena kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekadivasaṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato dhammadesanākāle haṃsavatīnagaravāsike gandhamālādihatthe yena buddho yena dhammo yena saṅgho, tanninne tappoṇe tappabbhāre gacchante disvā mahājanena saddhiṃ upagato satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “ayaṃ kira imasmiṃ sāsane paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggo, aho vatāhampi ekassa buddhassa sāsane ayaṃ viya paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti cintetvā satthu desanāpariyosāne vuṭṭhitāya parisāya bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantesi. Satthā adhivāsesi. So bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sakanivesanaṃ gantvā sabbarattiṃ buddhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa ca nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ gandhadāmamālādāmādīhi alaṅkaritvā paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā tassā rattiyā accayena sake nivesane bhikkhusatasahassaparivāraṃ bhagavantaṃ vividhayāgukhajjakaparivāraṃ nānārasasūpabyañjanaṃ gandhasālibhojanaṃ bhojetvā [P 1.0032] bhattakiccapariyosāne cintesi – “mahantaṃ, kho, ahaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthemi na kho pana mayhaṃ yuttaṃ ekadivasameva dānaṃ datvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetuṃ, anupaṭipāṭiyā satta divase dānaṃ datvā patthessāmī”ti[M 1.0035]. So teneva niyāmena satta divase mahādānāni datvā bhattakiccapariyosāne dussakoṭṭhāgāraṃ vivarāpetvā uttamaṃ ticīvarappahonakaṃ sukhumavatthaṃ buddhassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā bhikkhusatasahassassa ca ticīvaraṃ datvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, yo so bhikkhu tumhehi ito sattamadivasamatthake etadagge ṭhapito, ahampi so bhikkhu viya anāgate uppajjanakabuddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti vatvā satthu pādamūle [V 1.0029] nipajjitvā patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa patthanāya samijjhanabhāvaṃ disvā “anāgate ito kappasatasahassamatthake gotamo nāma buddho loke uppajjissati, tassa sāsane tava patthanā samijjhissatī”ti byākāsi. Vuttampi cetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.54.221-250) –

The verse beginning 'Upasanto' is by the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika Thera. What was his origin? This elder, too, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, was born into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached maturity, after the passing of his parents, he established the household and lived as a householder. One day, during a discourse on the Dhamma by the Blessed One Padumuttara, he saw the citizens of Haṃsavatī with perfumes and garlands in hand, going towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—inclined, leaning, and heading towards them. Joining the great crowd, he approached the Teacher and saw him placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who had attained the analytical knowledges. He thought, 'It seems this monk is foremost among those who have attained the analytical knowledges in this Dispensation. Oh, that I too, in the Dispensation of a certain Buddha, might become foremost among those who attain the analytical knowledges, just like him!' At the end of the Teacher’s discourse, when the assembly had risen, he approached the Blessed One and invited him, saying, 'Venerable Sir, tomorrow, please accept my alms-food.' The Teacher consented. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he went to his own residence. Throughout the night, he adorned the seating place for the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks with strings of perfumes, garlands of flowers, and so forth, and had exquisite hard and soft food prepared. When that night had passed, in his own residence, he served the Blessed One, who was accompanied by a hundred thousand monks, with various kinds of gruel and snacks as his retinue, with fragrant rice-gruel having various flavors of soups and curries. At the conclusion of the meal, he thought: 'I aspire to a great position. It is not fitting for me to aspire to that position after giving alms for only a single day. I shall give alms for seven days in succession and then make my aspiration.' In that same manner, he gave great alms for seven days. At the conclusion of the meal, he had his cloth storehouse opened and, placing a supreme, fine cloth sufficient for the three robes at the feet of the Buddha, and also giving the three robes to the hundred thousand monks, he approached the Tathāgata and said, 'Venerable Sir, that monk whom you placed in the foremost position on the seventh day from today—may I, like that monk, in a future time, in the Dispensation of a Buddha who is to arise, go forth and become foremost among those who attain the analytical knowledges.' Having said this, he prostrated himself at the Teacher’s feet and made his aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, made a prediction: 'In a future time, a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. In his Dispensation, your aspiration will be fulfilled.' And this was also stated in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, sabbalokavidū muni;

Ito satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji cakkhumā.

A Victor named Padumuttara, a sage who knew all worlds, arose a hundred thousand aeons from this one, the One with Vision.

“Ovādako viññāpako, tārako sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Desanākusalo buddho, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

An exhorter, an instructor, a rescuer of all living beings; the Buddha, skilled in discourse, helped a great multitude to cross over.

“Anukampako kāruṇiko, hitesī sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Sampatte titthiye sabbe, pañcasīle patiṭṭhapi.

Sympathetic and compassionate, seeking the welfare of all living beings; he established all the sectarians who came to him in the five precepts.

“Evaṃ nirākulaṃ āsi, suññataṃ titthiyehi ca;

Vicittaṃ arahantehi, vasībhūtehi tādibhi.

Thus, the Dispensation was untroubled and devoid of sectarians; it was resplendent with Arahants, who were masters of themselves, the imperturbable ones.

“Ratanānaṭṭhapaññāsaṃ, uggato so mahāmuni;

Kañcanagghiyasaṅkāso, bāttiṃsavaralakkhaṇo.

That great sage was fifty-eight cubits in height; he was like a pillar of gold, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks.

“Vassasatasahassāni, āyu vijjati tāvade;

Tāvatā tiṭṭhamāno so, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

His lifespan at that time was a hundred thousand years; remaining for that long, he helped a great multitude to cross over.

“Tadāhaṃ haṃsavatiyaṃ, brāhmaṇo vedapāragū;

Upecca sabbalokaggaṃ, assosiṃ dhammadesanaṃ.

At that time in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin, a master of the Vedas; approaching the foremost in all the world, I listened to a discourse on the Dhamma.

“Tadā so sāvakaṃ vīro, pabhinnamatigocaraṃ;

Atthe dhamme nirutte ca, paṭibhāne ca kovidaṃ.

At that time, that hero placed a disciple—one whose intellectual range was penetrating, skilled in meaning, the teaching, etymology, and ready wit—

“Ṭhapesi [M 1.0036] etadaggamhi, taṃ sutvā mudito ahaṃ;

Sasāvakaṃ jinavaraṃ, sattāhaṃ bhojayiṃ tadā.

—in the foremost position. Hearing that, I was delighted. Then, for seven days, I fed the excellent Victor together with his disciples.

“Dussehacchādayitvāna, sasissaṃ buddhisāgaraṃ;

Nipacca pādamūlamhi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ patthayiṃ ahaṃ.

Having clothed the ocean of wisdom and his disciples with fabrics, and prostrating at his feet, I aspired to that same position.

“Tato avoca lokaggo, passathetaṃ dijuttamaṃ;

Vinataṃ pādamūle me, kamalodarasappabhaṃ.

Then the foremost in the world spoke: 'Behold this best of brahmins, bowing at my feet, radiant as the heart of a lotus.'

“Buddhaseṭṭhassa bhikkhussa, ṭhānaṃ patthayate ayaṃ;

Tāya saddhāya cāgena, saddhammassavanena ca.

'This one aspires to the position of a disciple of the supreme Buddha, through that faith and generosity, and through hearing the good Dhamma.'

“Sabbattha sukhito hutvā, saṃsaritvā bhavābhave;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, lacchasetaṃ manorathaṃ.

'Having been happy everywhere, and having wandered through existence after existence, in a future time he will attain this heart's desire.'

“Satasahassito [V 1.0030] kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

'A hundred thousand aeons from this one, one born of the Okkāka clan, Gotama by name, will be the Teacher in the world.'

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Koṭṭhiko nāma nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

'He will be that Teacher's disciple, an heir to his Dhamma, a legitimate son created by the Dhamma, known by the name of Koṭṭhika.'

“Taṃ sutvā mudito hutvā, yāvajīvaṃ tadā jinaṃ;

Mettacitto paricariṃ, sato paññā samāhito.

Hearing that, I was delighted, and for the rest of my life I attended upon that Victor with a mind of loving-kindness, mindful and established in wisdom.

“Tena kammavipākena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

By the result of that kamma, and by my volitions and aspirations, upon abandoning the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

“Satānaṃ tīṇikkhattuñca, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Satānaṃ pañcakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

Three hundred times I exercised sovereignty over the devas; and five hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch.

“Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Sabbattha sukhito āsiṃ, tassa kammassa vāhasā.

And my regional kingship was vast, innumerable by count. Everywhere I was happy, by the power of that kamma.

“Duve bhave saṃsarāmi, devatte atha mānuse;

Aññaṃ gatiṃ na gacchāmi, suciṇṇassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

I wander only in two states of existence: the divine and the human. I do not go to any other destination; this is the fruit of what was well-practiced.

“Duve kule pajāyāmi, khattiye atha brāhmaṇe;

Nīce kule na jāyāmi, suciṇṇassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

I am born only in two families: that of the warrior-noble or that of the brahmin. I am never born in a low family; this is the fruit of what was well-practiced.

“Pacchime [M 1.0037] bhave sampatte, brahmabandhu ahosahaṃ;

Sāvatthiyaṃ vippakule, paccājāto mahaddhane.

Having reached my final existence, I was a brahmin, reborn in Sāvatthī into a very wealthy brahmin family.

“Mātā candavatī nāma, pitā me assalāyano;

Yadā me pitaraṃ buddho, vinayī sabbasuddhiyā.

My mother was named Candavatī, and my father was Assalāyana. When the Buddha disciplined my father in complete purity,

“Tadā pasanno sugate, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ;

Moggallāno ācariyo, upajjhā sārisambhavo.

then, with faith in the Well-Farer, I went forth into the homeless life. Moggallāna was my teacher, and Sāriputta was my preceptor.

“Kesesu chijjamānesu, diṭṭhi chinnā samūlikā;

Nivāsento ca kāsāvaṃ, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

Even as my hair was being cut, wrong view was severed at its root. And as I was putting on the ochre robe, I attained Arahantship.

“Atthadhammaniruttīsu, paṭibhāne ca me mati;

Pabhinnā tena lokaggo, etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.

My understanding of meaning, the teaching, etymology, and ready wit became penetrating; for that reason, the foremost in the world placed me in the foremost position.

“Asandiṭṭhaṃ viyākāsiṃ, upatissena pucchito;

Paṭisambhidāsu tenāhaṃ, aggo sambuddhasāsane.

Questioned by Upatissa, I explained what was not apparent; because of my skill in the analytical knowledges, I am foremost in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

My defilements are burned up, all states of existence are uprooted. Like a great elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell free from taints.

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, mama buddhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

A good coming it was for me to the presence of the Buddha. The three true knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

“Paṭisambhidā [V 1.0031] catasso, vimokkhāpi ca aṭṭhime;

Chaḷabhiññā sacchikatā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

The four analytical knowledges, and these eight liberations, and the six super-knowledges have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Evaṃ so tattha tattha bhave puññañāṇasambhāraṃ sambharanto aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatti. Koṭṭhikotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto tayo vede uggahetvā brāhmaṇasippe nipphattiṃ gato ekadivasaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā upasampannakālato paṭṭhāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā paṭisambhidāsu ciṇṇavasī hutvā abhiññāte abhiññāte mahāthere upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchantopi dasabalaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchantopi paṭisambhidāsuyeva pañhaṃ pucchi. Evamayaṃ thero tattha [M 1.0038] katādhikāratāya ciṇṇavasībhāvena ca paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggo jāto. Atha naṃ satthā mahāvedallasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisambhidāpattānaṃ yadidaṃ [P 1.0033] mahākoṭṭhiko”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 218). So aparena samayena vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento udānavasena –

Thus, accumulating the provisions of merit and knowledge in various existences, he wandered repeatedly among gods and humans. In this dispensation of the Buddha, he was born into the family of a great brahmin householder in Sāvatthī. They named him Koṭṭhika. Having come of age, he mastered the three Vedas and became accomplished in brahminical arts. One day, he went to the Master, listened to the Dhamma, and acquired faith. After going forth and receiving higher ordination, from that time onward he worked on insight meditation. Having attained arahantship along with the analytical knowledges, he became skilled in them. Whether approaching well-known great elders or the Ten-Powered One to ask questions, he inquired only concerning the analytical knowledges. Thus, due to his aspiration made in that regard and his mastery, this elder became foremost among those who attained the analytical knowledges. Then the Master, after giving rise to the occasion for the Greater Discourse on Questions and Answers (MN I 449ff), placed him in the foremost position among those who attained the analytical knowledges, declaring: “Monks, the foremost of my monk disciples who have attained the analytical knowledges is Mahākoṭṭhika.” (AN I 209, 218) At a later time, experiencing the bliss of liberation, he uttered this inspired utterance:

2.

2.

“Upasanto uparato, mantabhāṇī anuddhato;

Dhunāti pāpake dhamme, dumapattaṃva māluto”ti. –

“Peaceful, restrained, speaking with wisdom, unagitated; he shakes off evil states, as the wind a tree’s leaf.”

Itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā mahākoṭṭhikatthero gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus indeed the Venerable Elder Mahākoṭṭhika spoke this verse.

Tattha upasantoti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ upasamanena nibbisevanabhāvakaraṇena upasanto. Uparatoti sabbasmā pāpakaraṇato orato virato. Mantabhāṇīti mantā vuccati paññā, tāya pana upaparikkhitvā bhaṇatīti mantabhāṇī, kālavādīādibhāvaṃ avissajjentoyeva bhaṇatīti attho. Mantabhaṇanavasena vā bhaṇatīti mantabhāṇī, dubbhāsitato vinā attano bhāsanavasena caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ subhāsitaṃyeva bhaṇatīti attho. Jātiādivasena attano anukkaṃsanato na uddhatoti anuddhato atha vā tiṇṇaṃ kāyaduccaritānaṃ vūpasamanena tato paṭiviratiyā upasanto, tiṇṇaṃ manoduccaritānaṃ uparamaṇena pajahanena uparato, catunnaṃ vacīduccaritānaṃ appavattiyā parimitabhāṇitāya mantabhāṇī, tividhaduccaritanimittauppajjanakassa uddhaccassa abhāvato anuddhato. Evaṃ pana tividhaduccaritappahānena suddhe sīle patiṭṭhito, uddhaccappahānena samāhito, tameva samādhiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā dhunāti pāpake dhamme lāmakaṭṭhena pāpake sabbepi saṃkilesadhamme niddhunāti, samucchedavasena pajahati[V 1.0032]. Yathā kiṃ? Dumapattaṃva māluto, yathā nāma dumassa rukkhassa pattaṃ paṇḍupalāsaṃ māluto vāto dhunāti, bandhanato viyojento nīharati, evaṃ yathāvuttapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito pāpadhamme attano santānato nīharati, evamayaṃ therassa aññāpadesena aññābyākaraṇagāthāpi hotīti veditabbā.

Therein, ‘peaceful’ (upasanto) means he is peaceful through the calming of the six sense faculties, by causing them to be non-indulgent. ‘Restrained’ (uparato) means he has refrained and ceased from all evil-doing. ‘Speaking with wisdom’ (mantabhāṇī): ‘mantā’ is a term for wisdom (paññā); he speaks after having examined with that wisdom, thus he is one who ‘speaks with wisdom’; the meaning is that he speaks while not abandoning such qualities as speaking at the proper time. Or, he is one who ‘speaks with wisdom’ because he speaks in a measured manner; the meaning is that, avoiding ill-spoken words, he speaks only what is well-spoken and endowed with four factors. He is ‘unagitated’ (anuddhato) because he is not haughty from not exalting himself on the basis of birth and so on. Or alternatively, he is ‘peaceful’ through the pacification of the three kinds of bodily misconduct and by refraining from them; he is ‘restrained’ through the cessation and abandonment of the three kinds of mental misconduct; he is one who ‘speaks with wisdom’ through the non-occurrence of the four kinds of verbal misconduct and by his measured speech; and he is ‘unagitated’ through the absence of the agitation that would arise on account of the threefold misconduct. Thus, established in pure virtue through the abandonment of the threefold misconduct, and composed through the abandonment of agitation, having made that very concentration his foundation and developed insight, by the sequence of the path he ‘shakes off evil states’—he shakes off all defiling states, which are evil in the sense of being base; he abandons them by way of eradication. Like what? ‘As the wind a tree’s leaf’: just as the wind shakes off a leaf, a withered leaf, from a tree, detaching it from its stem and carrying it away, so too, one established in the aforesaid practice removes evil states from his own continuity. Thus, this should be understood as a verse in which the Elder declares final knowledge through indirect reference.

Ettha [M 1.0039] ca kāyavacīduccaritappahānavacanena payogasuddhiṃ dasseti, manoduccaritappahānavacanena āsayasuddhiṃ. Evaṃ payogāsayasuddhassa “anuddhato”ti [P 1.0034] iminā uddhaccābhāvavacanena tadekaṭṭhatāya nīvaraṇappahānaṃ dasseti. Tesu payogasuddhiyā sīlasampatti vibhāvitā, āsayasuddhiyā samathabhāvanāya upakārakadhammapariggaho, nīvaraṇappahānena samādhibhāvanā, “dhunāti pāpake dhamme”ti iminā paññābhāvanā vibhāvitā hoti. Evaṃ adhisīlasikkhādayo tisso sikkhā, tividhakalyāṇaṃ sāsanaṃ, tadaṅgappahānādīni tīṇi pahānāni, antadvayaparivajjanena saddhiṃ majjhimāya paṭipattiyā paṭipajjanaṃ, apāyabhavādīnaṃ samatikkamanūpāyo ca yathārahaṃ niddhāretvā yojetabbā. Iminā nayena sesagāthāsupi yathārahaṃ atthayojanā veditabbā. Atthamattameva pana tattha tattha apubbaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. “Itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko”ti idaṃ pūjāvacanaṃ, yathā taṃ mahāmoggallānoti.

Here, by the statement of abandoning bodily and verbal misconduct, purity of application is shown; by the statement of abandoning mental misconduct, purity of disposition is shown. Thus, for one whose application and disposition are pure, by the statement of the absence of agitation, ‘unagitated,’ the abandonment of the hindrances is shown, due to its being of the same meaning. Among these, by purity of application, the accomplishment of virtue is revealed; by purity of disposition, the undertaking of qualities helpful for the development of serenity is revealed; by the abandonment of the hindrances, the development of concentration is revealed; and by the phrase “he shakes off evil states,” the development of wisdom is revealed. In this way, the three trainings, such as the training in higher virtue; the teaching that is excellent in three ways; the three kinds of abandonment, such as abandonment by substitution of opposites; the practice of the middle way together with the avoidance of the two extremes; and the means to transcend the planes of misery, etc., should be appropriately determined and connected. In this manner, the application of the meaning in the remaining verses should also be understood appropriately. However, we will explain only the essential meaning, which is new, here and there. The phrase “Thus indeed the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika…” is a term of veneration, just as the ‘Mahā’ in ‘Mahāmoggallāna’ is.

Mahākoṭṭhikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is concluded.

3. Kaṅkhārevatattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata

Paññaṃ imaṃ passāti āyasmato kaṅkhārevatassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi thero padumuttarabhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatto. Ekadivasaṃ buddhānaṃ dhammadesanākāle heṭṭhā vuttanayena mahājanena saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ jhānābhiratānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “mayāpi anāgate evarūpena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā desanāvasāne satthāraṃ nimantetvā heṭṭhā vuttanayena mahāsakkāraṃ katvā bhagavantaṃ āha – “bhante, ahaṃ iminā adhikārakammena aññaṃ sampattiṃ na patthemi, yathā pana so bhikkhu tumhehi ito sattamadivasamatthake jhāyīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapito, evaṃ ahampi anāgate ekassa buddhassa sāsane jhāyīnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanamakāsi. Satthā anāgataṃ oloketvā nipphajjanabhāvaṃ disvā “anāgate kappasatasahassāvasāne gotamo [M 1.0040] nāma [V 1.0033] buddho [P 1.0035] uppajjissati, tassa sāsane tvaṃ jhāyīnaṃ aggo bhavissasī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi.

The verse “Behold this wisdom…” is by the Venerable Kaṅkhārevata. What is its origin? This elder too, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, was born in the city of Haṃsavatī into a great brahmin household. One day, during a discourse by the Buddha, he went to the monastery with a large crowd, as described before. Standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who delight in jhāna. Reflecting, “It would be fitting for me also to become like this in the future,” at the end of the discourse, he invited the Teacher and, after making a great offering as described before, said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, by this foundational deed I do not aspire for any other attainment. But just as that monk was placed by you in the foremost position among meditators on the seventh day from now, so may I too, in the future, become the foremost among meditators in the dispensation of a Buddha.” He made this aspiration. The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that it would be fulfilled, declared: “In the future, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will be the foremost among meditators.” Having made this prediction, he departed.

So yāvajīvaṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ katvā kappasatasahassaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthinagare mahābhogakule nibbatto pacchābhattaṃ dhammassavanatthaṃ gacchantena mahājanena saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dasabalassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā upasampadaṃ labhitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā jhānaparikammaṃ karonto jhānalābhī hutvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So yebhuyyena dasabalena samāpajjitabbasamāpattiṃ samāpajjanto ahorattaṃ jhānesu ciṇṇavasī ahosi. Atha naṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ jhāyīnaṃ yadidaṃ kaṅkhārevato”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 204) jhāyīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Vuttampi cetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.55.34-53) –

Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons.
