In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn into a family of great wealth in the city of Sāvatthī. After the meal, while going to the monastery with a large crowd to listen to the Dhamma, he stood at the edge of the assembly, heard the discourse of the One of Ten Powers, and gained faith. He then went forth, received higher ordination, and had a meditation subject taught to him. While doing the preliminary work for jhāna, he became an attainer of jhāna and, having made jhāna his foundation, he reached arahantship. For the most part, entering into the meditative attainments that are to be attained by the One of Ten Powers, he became one with practiced mastery in the jhānas day and night. Then the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among meditators, declaring: “Monks, among my monk disciples who are meditators, the foremost is Kaṅkhārevata.” (AN 1.198, 204) And this was also stated in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, sabbadhammesu cakkhumā;

Ito satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji nāyako.

The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the one with the eye in all things, the Leader, arose a hundred thousand aeons from this one.

“Sīhahanu brahmagiro, haṃsadundubhinissano;

Nāgavikkantagamano, candasūrādhikappabho.

With the jaw of a lion, a voice like Brahmā, a sound like a swan and a great drum; moving with the gait of a majestic elephant, surpassing the sun and moon in splendor.

“Mahāmati mahāvīro, mahājhāyī mahābalo;

Mahākāruṇiko nātho, mahātamapanūdano.

Of great wisdom, a great hero, a great meditator, of great strength; the greatly compassionate Lord, the dispeller of great darkness.

“Sa kadāci tilokaggo, veneyyaṃ vinayaṃ bahuṃ;

Dhammaṃ desesi sambuddho, sattāsayavidū muni.

At one time, that supreme one of the three worlds, the Fully Enlightened One, the sage who knows the dispositions of beings, taught much Dhamma, the training for those to be disciplined.

“Jhāyiṃ jhānarataṃ vīraṃ, upasantaṃ anāvilaṃ;

Vaṇṇayanto parisatiṃ, tosesi janataṃ jino.

Praising in the assembly the heroic meditator, one who delights in jhāna, serene, and unclouded, the Conqueror gladdened the people.

“Tadāhaṃ haṃsavatiyaṃ, brāhmaṇo vedapāragū;

Dhammaṃ sutvāna mudito, taṃ ṭhānamabhipatthayiṃ.

At that time in Haṃsavatī, I was a brahmin, a master of the Vedas. Having heard the Dhamma, I rejoiced and aspired to that state.

“Tadā jino viyākāsi, saṅghamajjhe vināyako;

Mudito hohi tvaṃ brahme, lacchase taṃ manorathaṃ.

Then the Conqueror, the Guide, declared in the midst of the Saṅgha: 'Rejoice, brahmin, you shall attain that which your heart desires.'

“Satasahassito [M 1.0041] kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

A hundred thousand aeons from this one, born of the Okkāka lineage, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will be in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Revato nāma nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

His heir in the Dhamma, his true son, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher, will be named Revata.

“Tena [V 1.0034] kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

By that well-done deed and by my volitions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

“Pacchime ca bhave dāni, jātohaṃ koliye pure;

Khattiye kulasampanne, iddhe phīte mahaddhane.

And now, in my final existence, I was born in the city of the Koliyas, in a well-born khattiya family, prosperous, flourishing, and of great wealth.

“Yadā kapilavatthusmiṃ, buddho dhammamadesayi;

Tadā pasanno sugate, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ.

When the Buddha taught the Dhamma in Kapilavatthu, then, with faith in the Sugata, I went forth into homelessness.

“Kaṅkhā me bahulā āsi, kappākappe tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Sabbaṃ taṃ vinayī buddho, desetvā dhammamuttamaṃ.

I had much doubt, in aeon after aeon, here and there. The Buddha dispelled all of it, having taught the supreme Dhamma.

“Tatohaṃ tiṇṇasaṃsāro, tadā jhānasukhe rato;

Viharāmi tadā buddho, maṃ disvā etadabravi.

Then I, having crossed over saṃsāra, at that time delighted in the bliss of jhāna. As I was dwelling thus, the Buddha saw me and said this:

“Yā kāci kaṅkhā idha vā huraṃ vā, savediyā vā paravediyā vā;

Ye jhāyino tā pajahanti sabbā, ātāpino brahmacariyaṃ carantā.

Whatever doubts there may be, whether here or hereafter, whether concerning oneself or concerning others; those who are meditators abandon them all, striving ardently while practicing the holy life.

“Satasahasse kataṃ kammaṃ, phalaṃ dassesi me idha;

Sumutto saravegova, kilese jhāpayiṃ mama.

The deed done a hundred thousand aeons ago showed its fruit to me here; well-freed, like a swift arrow, I have burned away my defilements.

“Tato jhānarattaṃ disvā, buddho lokantagū muni;

Jhāyīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggo, paññāpesi mahāmati.

Then, seeing my delight in jhāna, the Buddha, the sage who has gone to the world's end, the one of great wisdom, declared me foremost among the meditating monks.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

My defilements are burned away, all states of existence are uprooted; like a great elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell without taints.

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, mama buddhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

A good coming it was indeed for me, into the presence of my Buddha; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha's instruction has been fulfilled.

“Paṭisambhidā [M 1.0042] catasso, vimokkhāpi ca aṭṭhime;

Chaḷabhiññā sacchikatā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

The four analytical knowledges, and also these eight liberations; the six super-knowledges have been realized, the Buddha's instruction has been fulfilled.

Tathā katakicco panāyaṃ mahāthero pubbe dīgharattaṃ attano kaṅkhāpakatacittataṃ idāni sabbaso vigatakaṅkhatañca paccavekkhitvā “aho nūna mayhaṃ satthuno desanānubhāvo, tenetarahi evaṃ vigatakaṅkho ajjhattaṃ vūpasantacitto jāto”ti sañjātabahumāno bhagavato paññaṃ pasaṃsanto “paññaṃ imaṃ passā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

Now this great elder, having thus accomplished his task, reflected on the state of his own mind having been afflicted by doubt for a long time previously, and now its state of being entirely free from doubt. Thinking, "Oh, surely, such is the power of my Teacher's teaching, for by it I have now become thus free from doubt, with a mind inwardly pacified," great reverence arose in him. Praising the Blessed One's wisdom, he spoke this verse: "Behold this wisdom!"

3. Tattha paññanti pakāre jānāti, pakārehi ñāpetīti ca paññā. Veneyyānaṃ āsayānusayacariyādhimuttiādippakāre dhammānaṃ kusalādike khandhādike ca desetabbappakāre jānāti, yathāsabhāvato paṭivijjhati, tehi ca pakārehi ñāpetīti attho. Satthu desanāñāṇañhi idhādhippetaṃ, tenāha “ima”nti. Tañhi attani siddhena desanābalena nayaggāhato [V 1.0035] paccakkhaṃ viya upaṭṭhitaṃ gahetvā “ima”nti vuttaṃ. Yadaggena vā satthu desanāñāṇaṃ sāvakehi nayato gayhati, tadaggena attano visaye paṭivedhañāṇampi nayato gayhateva. Tenāha [P 1.0036] āyasmā dhammasenāpati – “apica me, bhante, dhammanvayo vidito”ti (dī. ni. 2.146; 3.143). Passāti vimhayappatto aniyamato ālapati attanoyeva vā cittaṃ, yathāha bhagavā udānento – “lokamimaṃ passa; puthū avijjāya paretaṃ bhūtaṃ bhūtarataṃ bhavā aparimutta”nti (udā. 30). Tathāgatānanti tathā āgamanādiatthena tathāgatānaṃ. Tathā āgatoti hi tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathavāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgatoti evaṃ aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato. Tathāya āgatoti tathāgato, tathāya gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ gatoti tathāgato, tathāni āgatoti tathāgato, tathāvidhoti tathāgato, tathā pavattitoti tathāgato, tathehi āgatoti tathāgato[M 1.0043], tathā gatabhāvena tathāgatoti evampi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgatoti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paramatthadīpaniyā udānaṭṭhakathāya (udā. aṭṭha. 18) itivuttakaṭṭhakathāya (itivu. aṭṭha. 38) ca vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

3. Herein, 'wisdom' (paññā) is so called because it knows in various modes (pakāre jānāti) and it makes known by various modes (pakārehi ñāpeti). It knows the modes of the dispositions, underlying tendencies, conduct, inclinations, and so forth of those to be trained, and the modes in which the teachings—such as the wholesome, the aggregates, and so forth—are to be taught; it penetrates them according to their true nature, and it makes them known by those modes. This is the meaning. Here, the Teacher’s knowledge of teaching is intended; hence he says, “this.” For, having grasped it as if directly present through the power of the teaching established in himself and through his grasp of the method, it is called “this.” Or, to the extent that the Teacher’s knowledge of teaching is grasped by disciples through the method, to that same extent the knowledge of penetration in one’s own domain is also grasped through the method. Thus the Venerable General of the Dhamma said: “Moreover, venerable sir, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me” (Dī. Ni. 2.146; 3.143). “Behold” (passa) is an exclamation made spontaneously out of wonder, addressed either to no one in particular or to his own mind, just as the Blessed One, exclaiming in an inspired utterance, said: “Behold this world! A populace enveloped by ignorance, delighting in being, not freed from becoming” (Udā. 30). “Of the Tathāgatas” (Tathāgatānaṃ) means of those who are Tathāgatas on account of having 'thus come' (tathā āgamana), and so forth. For he is the Tathāgata because he has 'thus come' (tathā āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'thus gone' (tathā gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'come to the true characteristic' (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'fully awakened to the true dhammas as they really are' (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); he is the Tathāgata 'by reason of seeing thus' (tathadassitāya); he is the Tathāgata 'by reason of speaking thus' (tathavāditāya); he is the Tathāgata 'by reason of acting thus' (tathākāritāya); he is the Tathāgata 'by reason of overcoming' (abhibhavanaṭṭhena)—thus for eight reasons the Blessed One is the Tathāgata. Also: he is the Tathāgata because he has 'come to truth' (tathāya āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'gone to truth' (tathāya gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'gone to the true characteristic' (tathalakkhaṇaṃ gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'come to true things' (tathāni āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he is 'of true nature' (tathāvidho); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'thus proceeded' (tathā pavattito); he is the Tathāgata because he has 'come by true things' (tathehi āgato); he is the Tathāgata 'by the state of having thus gone' (tathā gatabhāvena)—thus also for eight reasons the Blessed One is the Tathāgata. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Paramatthadīpanī, in the Udāna Commentary (Udā. Aṭṭha. 18) and the Itivuttaka Commentary (Itivu. Aṭṭha. 38).

Idāni tassā paññāya asādhāraṇavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “aggi yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yathā aggīti upamāvacanaṃ. Yathāti tassa upamābhāvadassanaṃ. Pajjalitoti upameyyena sambandhadassanaṃ. Nisītheti kiccakaraṇakāladassanaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – yathā nāma nisīthe rattiyaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre vattamāne unnate ṭhāne pajjalito aggi tasmiṃ padese tayagataṃ vidhamantaṃ tiṭṭhati, evameva tathāgatānaṃ imaṃ desanāñāṇasaṅkhātaṃ sabbaso veneyyānaṃ saṃsayatamaṃ vidhamantaṃ paññaṃ passāti. Yato desanāvilāsena sattānaṃ ñāṇamayaṃ ālokaṃ dentīti ālokadā. Paññāmayameva cakkhuṃ dadantīti cakkhudadā. Tadubhayampi kaṅkhāvinayapadaṭṭhānameva katvā [P 1.0037] dassento “ye āgatānaṃ vinayanti kaṅkha”nti āha, ye tathāgatā attano santikaṃ āgatānaṃ upagatānaṃ veneyyānaṃ “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) soḷasavatthukaṃ, “buddhe kaṅkhati dhamme kaṅkhatī”tiādinayappavattaṃ (dha. sa. 1008) aṭṭhavatthukañca kaṅkhaṃ vicikicchaṃ vinayanti desanānubhāvena anavasesato vidhamanti viddhaṃsenti. Vinayakukkuccasaṅkhātā pana kaṅkhā tabbinayeneva vinītā hontīti.

Now, to show the unique distinction of that wisdom, the passage beginning “Like a fire” was spoken. “Like a fire” (aggi yathā) is a statement of simile. “Like” (yathā) indicates its nature as a simile. “Blazing” (pajjalito) indicates the connection with the subject of comparison. “At midnight” (nisīthe) indicates the time of performing the function. Herein, this is the meaning: just as at midnight, when a fourfold darkness prevails, a fire set blazing in an elevated place stands dispelling the mass of darkness in that region, even so, behold this wisdom of the Tathāgatas, known as the knowledge of teaching, which completely dispels the darkness of doubt for all those who are to be trained. Because they give the light of knowledge to beings through the splendor of their teaching, they are called 'givers of light' (ālokadā). Because they give the very eye of wisdom, they are called 'givers of the eye' (cakkhudadā). Showing that both of these have the dispelling of doubt as their basis, he said: “who dispel the doubts of those who have come.” Those Tathāgatas dispel, without remainder, through the power of their teaching, the doubt (kaṅkhā) and uncertainty (vicikicchā) of those to be trained who have come and approached them—such as the sixteen-based doubt that proceeds in the manner of “Did I exist in the past?” and the eight-based doubt that proceeds in the manner of “One doubts the Buddha, one doubts the Dhamma.” As for the doubt known as scrupulousness regarding the Vinaya, that is dispelled by the very dispelling of those doubts.

Aparo nayo – yathā aggi nisīthe rattibhāge pajjalito paṭutarajālo samujjalaṃ uccāsane [V 1.0036] ṭhitānaṃ obhāsadānamattena andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā samavisamaṃ vibhāvento ālokadado hoti. Accāsanne pana ṭhitānaṃ taṃ supākaṭaṃ karonto cakkhukiccakaraṇato cakkhudado nāma hoti, evameva tathāgato attano dhammakāyassa dūre ṭhitānaṃ akatādhikārānaṃ paññāpajjotena mohandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā kāyavisamādisamavisamaṃ vibhāvento ālokadā bhavanti, āsanne ṭhitānaṃ pana katādhikārānaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ uppādento cakkhudadā bhavanti. Ye evaṃbhūtā [M 1.0044] attano vacīgocaraṃ āgatānaṃ mādisānampi kaṅkhābahulānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ vinayanti ariyamaggasamuppādanena vidhamanti, tesaṃ tathāgatānaṃ paññaṃ ñāṇātisayaṃ passāti yojanā. Evamayaṃ therassa attano kaṅkhāvitaraṇappakāsanena aññābyākaraṇagāthāpi hoti. Ayañhi thero puthujjanakāle kappiyepi kukkuccako hutvā kaṅkhābahulatāya “kaṅkhārevato”ti paññāto, pacchā khīṇāsavakālepi tatheva voharayittha. Tenāha – “itthaṃ sudaṃ āyasmā kaṅkhārevato gāthaṃ abhāsitthā”ti. Taṃ vuttatthameva.

Another explanation: Just as a fire blazing in the middle of the night, with very bright flames, shining brilliantly, dispels darkness by merely providing light for those standing in an elevated place, making manifest both even and uneven ground, thus being a giver of light. For those standing very close, however, by making that ground clearly visible, it performs the function of the eye, and thus is called a giver of sight. In the very same way, the Tathāgatas, with the lamp of wisdom, dispel the darkness of delusion for those standing far from their Dhamma-body, who have not made the requisite aspiration, making manifest the even and uneven, such as bodily misconduct and so forth, thus they become givers of light. For those standing close, however, who have made the requisite aspiration, they generate the Eye of the Dhamma, thus they become givers of sight. The construction is: ‘Behold the wisdom, the supreme knowledge, of those Tathāgatas who, being such, dispel the doubt of those like me who are full of doubt and have come within the range of their speech, removing it by the arising of the noble path.’ Thus, this is also a verse of the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge through the explanation of his overcoming of doubt. For this Elder, in his time as a worldling, was scrupulous even in allowable matters and, due to his great doubtfulness, was known as ‘Kaṅkhārevata’ (Revata the Doubter). Later, even in his state as one whose cankers are destroyed, he was still referred to in the same way. Therefore, it is said: ‘Thus indeed did the venerable Kaṅkhārevata speak this verse.’ The meaning of that is as has been stated.

Kaṅkhārevatattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata is concluded.

4. Puṇṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇa.

Sabbhireva [P 1.0038] samāsethāti āyasmato puṇṇattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa dasabalassa uppattito puretarameva haṃsavatīnagare brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatto anukkamena viññutaṃ patto satthari loke uppajjante ekadivasaṃ buddhānaṃ dhammadesanākāle heṭṭhā vuttanayena mahājanena saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante nisīditvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ dhammakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “mayāpi anāgate evarūpena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā desanāvasāne vuṭṭhitāya parisāya satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nimantetvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva mahāsakkāraṃ katvā bhagavantaṃ evamāha – “bhante, ahaṃ iminā adhikārakammena nāññaṃ sampattiṃ patthemi. Yathā pana so bhikkhu ito sattamadivasamatthake dhammakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapito, evaṃ ahampi anāgate ekassa buddhassa sāsane dhammakathikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā anāgataṃ oloketvā tassa patthanāya samijjhanabhāvaṃ disvā “anāgate kappasatasahassamatthake gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tassa sāsane tvaṃ pabbajitvā dhammakathikānaṃ aggo bhavissasī”ti byākāsi.

‘One should associate only with the good’ is a verse of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. What is its origin? It is said that long before the arising of Padumuttara, the one of Ten Powers, this one was born into a great brahmin household in the city of Haṃsavatī. In due course, he reached maturity. When the Teacher arose in the world, one day, during a Dhamma discourse of the Buddha, he went to the monastery with a large crowd, in the manner previously described, and sat at the edge of the assembly, listening to the Dhamma. Seeing the Teacher establish a certain monk in the foremost position among Dhamma preachers, he thought, ‘It would be fitting for me also to become one such as this in the future.’ At the end of the discourse, when the assembly had risen, he approached the Teacher, invited him, and having made a great offering in the manner previously described, he said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, by this meritorious deed I do not aspire to any other attainment. But just as that monk was established in the foremost position among the Dhamma preachers on the seventh day from now, so may I, in the future, become the foremost among the monks who are Dhamma preachers in the dispensation of a Buddha.’ He made this aspiration. The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, made this prophecy: ‘In the future, after a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his dispensation, you will go forth and become the foremost among the Dhamma preachers.’”

So [M 1.0045] tattha yāvajīvaṃ kalyāṇadhammaṃ katvā tato cuto kappasatasahassaṃ puññañāṇasambhāraṃ sambharanto devamanussesu saṃsaritvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle kapilavatthunagarassa avidūre doṇavatthunāmake [V 1.0037] brāhmaṇagāme brāhmaṇamahāsālakule aññāsikoṇḍaññattherassa bhāgineyyo hutvā nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “puṇṇo”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So satthari abhisambodhiṃ patvā pavattavaradhammacakke anupubbena rājagahaṃ gantvā taṃ upanissāya viharante aññāsikoṇḍaññattherassa santike pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado sabbaṃ pubbakiccaṃ katvā padhānamanuyuñjanto pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvāva “dasabalassa [P 1.0039] santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti mātulattherena saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ agantvā kapilavatthusāmantāyeva ohīyitvā yonisomanasikāre kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Vuttampi cetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.1.434-440) –

There, having performed wholesome deeds for the duration of his life, he passed away from that existence. For a hundred thousand aeons, he wandered among gods and humans, accumulating the stores of merit and knowledge. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in a great brahmin household in a brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu, as the nephew of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. On his naming day, they gave him the name ‘Puṇṇa.’ When the Teacher attained supreme enlightenment and had set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, while he was dwelling near Rājagaha, Puṇṇa gradually journeyed there. He went forth in the presence of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña and received the higher ordination. Having completed all the preliminary duties and applying himself diligently to the practice, he brought the task of one who has gone forth to its culmination. Then, thinking, ‘I will go to the presence of the one of Ten Powers,’ he did not go to the Teacher’s presence with his maternal uncle, the elder, but remained behind near Kapilavatthu. There, applying himself to the practice with wise attention, he soon intensified his insight and attained arahantship. And this is stated in the Apadāna:

“Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Purakkhatomhi sissehi, upagacchiṃ naruttamaṃ.

“I was a master of recitation, a bearer of mantras, one who had gone to the far shore of the three Vedas. Surrounded by my disciples, I approached the supreme man.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama kammaṃ pakittesi, saṃkhittena mahāmuni.

“Padumuttara, the knower of the world, the recipient of offerings, the great sage, proclaimed my deed in brief.

“Tāhaṃ dhammaṃ suṇitvāna, abhivādetvāna satthuno;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, pakkamiṃ dakkhiṇāmukho.

“Having heard that Dhamma, and having paid homage to the Teacher, I raised my hands in reverential salutation and departed, facing south.

“Saṃkhittena suṇitvāna, vitthārena abhāsayiṃ;

Sabbe sissā attamanā, sutvāna mama bhāsato.

“Having heard it in brief, I spoke of it in detail; all my disciples were delighted in mind, having heard my discourse.

“Sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ vinodetvā, buddhe cittaṃ pasādayuṃ;

Saṃkhittenapi desemi, vitthārena tathevahaṃ.

“Having abandoned their own views, they made their minds serene towards the Buddha; I teach briefly, and likewise in detail.”

“Abhidhammanayaññūhaṃ, kathāvatthuvisuddhiyā;

Sabbesaṃ viññāpetvāna, viharāmi anāsavo.

“I am one who knows the method of the Abhidhamma, through purity in the points of discussion; having made it known to all, I dwell without cankers.

“Ito [M 1.0046] pañcasate kappe, caturo suppakāsakā;

Sattaratanasampannā, catudīpamhi issarā.

“Five hundred aeons from now, there were four who proclaimed well; endowed with the seven treasures, they were lords over the four continents.

“Paṭisambhidā catasso…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“The four analytical knowledges… the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.”

Tassa pana puṇṇattherassa santike pabbajitā kulaputtā pañcasatā ahesuṃ. Thero sayaṃ dasakathāvatthulābhitāya tepi dasahi kathāvatthūhi ovadi. Te tassa ovāde ṭhatvā sabbeva arahattaṃ pattā. Te attano pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakappattaṃ ñatvā upajjhāyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āhaṃsu – “bhante, amhākaṃ kiccaṃ matthakappattaṃ, dasannañcamha kathāvatthūnaṃ lābhino, samayo, dāni no dasabalaṃ passitu”nti. Thero tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “mama dasakathāvatthulābhitaṃ [V 1.0038] satthā jānāti ahaṃ dhammaṃ desento dasa kathāvatthūni amuñcitvāva desemi, mayi gacchante sabbepime bhikkhū maṃ parivāretvā gacchissanti, evaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya gantvā pana ayuttaṃ mayhaṃ dasabalaṃ passituṃ, ime tāva gantvā passantū”ti te bhikkhū āha – “āvuso, tumhe purato gantvā tathāgataṃ passatha, mama vacanena cassa pāde vandatha, ahampi tumhākaṃ gatamaggenāgamissāmī”ti. Te therā sabbepi dasabalassa jātibhūmiraṭṭhavāsino sabbe khīṇāsavā sabbe dasakathāvatthulābhino attano upajjhāyassa ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā theraṃ vanditvā anupubbena cārikaṃ carantā saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ atikkamma rājagahe veḷuvanamahāvihāraṃ gantvā dasabalassa pāde vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Now, there were five hundred sons of good family who had gone forth under the Elder Puṇṇa. The elder himself, being an obtainer of the ten topics of discussion, instructed them with those ten topics. Abiding in his instruction, they all attained arahantship. Knowing that the task of one who has gone forth had reached its culmination, they approached their preceptor and said: ‘Venerable sir, our task has reached its culmination, and we are obtainers of the ten topics of discussion. It is now time for us to see the one of Ten Powers.’ Hearing their words, the elder reflected: ‘The Teacher knows that I am an obtainer of the ten topics of discussion. When I teach the Dhamma, I teach without omitting these ten topics. If I go, all these monks will surround me and go with me. But it is not proper for me to go see the one of Ten Powers while delighting in company. Let them first go and see him.’ So he said to those monks: ‘Reverend sirs, you go ahead and see the Tathāgata. On my behalf, pay homage at his feet. I too will come by the path you have taken.’ Those elders—all of them dwellers in the region of the Buddha’s birthplace, all with their cankers destroyed, all obtainers of the ten topics of discussion—accepted their preceptor’s instruction. Having paid homage to the elder, they set out, journeying by stages. Traversing a distance of sixty yojanas, they went to the Great Monastery of the Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha, paid homage at the feet of the one of Ten Powers, and sat down to one side.

Āciṇṇaṃ kho panetaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ āgantukehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisammoditunti bhagavā tehi saddhiṃ – “kacci, bhikkhave, khamanīya”ntiādinā nayena madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kuto ca tumhe, bhikkhave, āgacchathā”ti pucchi[P 1.0040]. Atha tehi “jātibhūmito”ti vutte “ko nu kho, bhikkhave, jātibhūmiyaṃ jātibhūmakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ evaṃ sambhāvito ‘attanā ca appiccho appicchakathañca bhikkhūnaṃ kattā’”ti (ma. ni. 1.252) dasakathāvatthulābhiṃ bhikkhuṃ pucchi. Tepi “puṇṇo nāma, bhante, āyasmā mantāṇiputto”ti ārocayiṃsu. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā āyasmā sāriputto therassa dassanakāmo ahosi. Atha satthā rājagahato sāvatthiṃ agamāsi[M 1.0047]. Puṇṇattheropi dasabalassa tattha āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā – “satthāraṃ passissāmī”ti gantvā antogandhakuṭiyaṃyeva tathāgataṃ sampāpuṇi. Satthā tassa dhammaṃ desesi. Thero dhammaṃ sutvā dasabalaṃ vanditvā paṭisallānatthāya andhavanaṃ gantvā aññataramhi rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi.

It is indeed the custom of the Blessed Ones, the Buddhas, to exchange greetings with visiting monks. The Blessed One exchanged pleasant greetings with them, asking in the customary way, "I hope, monks, that you are keeping well?" and so forth, and then inquired, "From where have you come, monks?" When they replied, "From our native land," he asked further, "Monks, in your native land, which monk is so esteemed by his fellow practitioners of the holy life as one who is himself of few wishes and who speaks to the monks on the subject of having few wishes?"—thus asking about a monk who was a recipient of the ten topics of discourse. They replied, "Venerable sir, it is the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta." Hearing this, the Venerable Sāriputta became desirous of seeing the elder. Then the Teacher went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. The Elder Puṇṇa, hearing that the One of Ten Powers had arrived there, thought, "I shall see the Teacher," and went and met the Tathāgata right inside the perfumed chamber. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. The elder, having heard the Dhamma, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers and went to the Andha Grove for seclusion. Sitting at the foot of a certain tree, he passed the day in meditation.

Sāriputtattheropi tassāgamanaṃ sutvā sīsānulokiko gantvā okāsaṃ sallakkhetvā taṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ upasaṅkamitvā therena saddhiṃ sammoditvā, taṃ sattavisuddhikkamaṃ pucchi. Theropissa pucchitapucchitaṃ byākaronto rathavinītūpamāya cittaṃ ārādhesi, te aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ samanumodiṃsu. Atha satthā aparabhāge bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe nisinno theraṃ “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ puṇṇo”ti (a. ni. 1.188, 196) dhammakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So ekadivasaṃ attano vimuttisampattiṃ paccavekkhitvā “satthāraṃ nissāya ahañceva aññe ca bahū sattā saṃsāradukkhato vippamuttā, bahūpakārā vata sappurisasaṃsevā”ti pītisomanassajāto udānavasena pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ “sabbhireva samāsethā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

The Elder Sāriputta, hearing of his arrival, went looking about for him. Marking the opportunity, he approached the elder as he sat at the foot of a tree. After exchanging greetings with him, he questioned him about the sequence of the seven purifications. As the elder answered each and every question, he delighted Sāriputta's mind with the simile of the relay chariots. They mutually rejoiced in each other's well-spoken words. At a later time, the Teacher, seated amidst the assembly of monks, placed the elder in the foremost position among the preachers of the Dhamma, declaring: "Monks, foremost among my monk disciples who are preachers of the Dhamma is this one, that is, Puṇṇa." One day, reflecting on his own attainment of liberation, he became filled with joy and gladness, thinking, "Relying on the Teacher, I and many other beings have been freed from the suffering of saṃsāra. Truly, association with the virtuous is of great benefit!" And by way of an inspired utterance, impelled by a surge of joy, he spoke this verse: "Associate only with the virtuous!"

4. Tattha [V 1.0039] sabbhirevāti sappurisehi eva. Santoti panettha buddhādayo ariyā adhippetā. Te hi anavasesato asataṃ dhammaṃ pahāya saddhamme ukkaṃsagatattā sātisayaṃ pasaṃsiyattā ca visesato “santo sappurisā”ti ca vuccanti. Samāsethāti samaṃ āsetha saha vaseyya. Te payirupāsanto tesaṃ sussūsanto diṭṭhānugatiñca [P 1.0041] āpajjanto samānavāso bhaveyyāti attho. Paṇḍitehatthadassibhīti tesaṃ thomanā. Paṇḍā vuccati paññā, sā imesaṃ sañjātāti paṇḍitā. Tato eva attatthādibhedaṃ atthaṃ aviparītato passantīti atthadassino. Tehi paṇḍitehi atthadassībhi samāsetha. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā te santo paṇḍitā, te vā sammā sevantā ekantahitabhāvato maggañāṇādīheva araṇīyato atthaṃ, mahāguṇatāya santatāya ca mahantaṃ, agādhabhāvato gambhīrañāṇagocarato ca gambhīraṃ, hīnacchandādīhi daṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā itarehi ca kicchena daṭṭhabbattā duddasaṃ[M 1.0048], duddasattā saṇhanipuṇasabhāvattā nipuṇañāṇagocarato ca nipuṇaṃ, nipuṇattā evaṃ sukhumasabhāvatāya aṇuṃ nibbānaṃ, aviparītaṭṭhena vā paramatthasabhāvattā atthaṃ, ariyabhāvakarattā mahattanimittatāya mahantaṃ, anuttānasabhāvatāya gambhīraṃ, dukkhena daṭṭhabbaṃ na sukhena daṭṭhuṃ sakkāti duddasaṃ, gambhīrattā duddasaṃ, duddasattā gambhīranti catusaccaṃ, visesato nipuṇaṃ aṇuṃ, nirodhasaccanti evametaṃ catusaccaṃ dhīrā samadhigacchanti dhitisampannatāya dhīrā catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā sammadeva adhigacchanti. Appamattāti sabbattha satiavippavāsena appamādapaṭipattiṃ pūrentā. Vicakkhaṇāti vipassanābhāvanāya chekā kusalā. Tasmā sabbhireva samāsethāti yojanā. Paṇḍitehatthadassibhīti vā etaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ. Yasmā paṇḍitehi atthadassībhi samudāyabhūtehi dhīrā appamattā vicakkhaṇā mahantādivisesavantaṃ atthaṃ samadhigacchanti, tasmā tādisehi sabbhireva samāsethāti sambandho. Evamesā therassa paṭivedhadīpanena aññābyākaraṇagāthāpi ahosīti.

4. Here, 'sabbhireva' means 'with the virtuous only.' 'Santo' here refers to the Buddhas and other Noble Ones. For they, having completely abandoned the ways of the unvirtuous, having reached the pinnacle of the true Dhamma, and being exceedingly praiseworthy, are specifically called 'santo' ('the peaceful') and 'sappurisā' ('virtuous persons'). 'Samāsetha' means 'one should associate with, one should dwell together with.' The meaning is that one should live in their company, attending upon them, listening to them, and following their example. 'Paṇḍitehatthadassibhī' ('with the wise who see the goal') is a term of praise for them. 'Paṇḍā' is a name for wisdom; because this has arisen in them, they are 'paṇḍitā' ('the wise'). For that very reason, because they see without distortion the goal, which has various aspects such as one's own welfare, they are 'atthadassino' ('those who see the goal'). One should associate with those wise ones who see the goal. If it is asked, 'Why?' Because by rightly associating with them, the steadfast attain the goal, which is of unalloyed benefit, to be reached only by means of path-knowledge and so on; which is great due to its great qualities and peacefulness; profound due to its unfathomable nature and being the domain of profound knowledge; hard to see, being impossible for those of base desires to see and seen only with difficulty by others; subtle, due to its fine and subtle nature and being the domain of subtle knowledge; and minute, like an atom, due to its subtlety—this is Nibbāna. Or, the goal is the ultimate reality, being undistorted in meaning; great, because it brings about the noble state and is a sign of greatness; profound, because its nature is not superficial; hard to see, because it is to be seen with difficulty, not easily. Because it is profound, it is hard to see; because it is hard to see, it is profound—this refers to the Four Noble Truths. The steadfast, endowed with resolution, rightly realize these Four Noble Truths, especially the subtle and minute Truth of Cessation, by diligently developing meditation on them as their subject. 'Appamattā' ('heedful') means they fulfill the practice of heedfulness by not allowing mindfulness to be absent in any situation. 'Vicakkhaṇā' ('discerning') means they are skilled and expert in the development of insight. Therefore, the connection is: 'Associate only with the virtuous.' Alternatively, 'paṇḍitehatthadassibhī' is an expression in the ablative case. Because it is from the wise who see the goal, who are a collective, that the steadfast, heedful, and discerning ones attain the goal with its qualities of greatness and so on, therefore, one should associate with such virtuous persons. This is the connection. Thus, this verse also served as the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge, illuminating his penetration of the truth.

Puṇṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇa is concluded.

5. Dabbattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dabba

Yo duddamiyoti [P 1.0042] āyasmato dabbattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi padumuttarabuddhakāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā adhikārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā satthārā byākato yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaritvā kassapadasabalassa sāsanosakkanakāle pabbaji. Tadā tena saddhiṃ apare cha janāti satta bhikkhū [V 1.0040] ekacittā hutvā aññe sāsane agāravaṃ karonte disvā – “idha kiṃ karoma ekamante samaṇadhammaṃ katvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmā”ti nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā uccaṃ pabbatasikharaṃ āruhitvā, “attano cittabalaṃ jānantā nisseṇiṃ nipātentu, jīvite sālayā otarantu, mā pacchānutappino ahuvatthā”ti [M 1.0049] vatvā sabbe ekacittā hutvā nisseṇiṃ pātetvā – “appamattā hotha, āvuso”ti aññamaññaṃ ovaditvā cittarucikesu ṭhānesu nisīditvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu.

The verse beginning 'Yo duddamiyo' is that of the Venerable Dabba the Elder. What is its origin? During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, this elder was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having come of age, while listening to a Dhamma discourse in the manner previously described, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who allocate lodgings. Having performed a deed of special merit and aspired to that position, he received a prophecy from the Teacher. For the rest of his life he performed wholesome deeds, and after wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he went forth during the time of the decline of the Dispensation of Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers. At that time, he and six others—seven monks in all—became of one mind. Seeing others acting with disrespect towards the Dispensation, they thought, “What shall we do here? Let us go to a secluded place, practice the duties of a recluse, and make an end of suffering.” Having constructed a ladder, they climbed to the peak of a high mountain. Then they said, “Let those who know the strength of their own minds cast down the ladder. Let those who have a craving for life descend. May you not be remorseful later!” Having spoken thus, all being of one mind, they cast down the ladder. Exhorting one another, “Be heedful, friends!” they sat down in places that pleased their minds and began to practice the duties of a recluse.

Tatreko thero pañcame divase arahattaṃ patvā, “mama kiccaṃ nipphannaṃ, ahaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kiṃ karissāmi”ti iddhiyā uttarakuruto piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā, “āvuso, imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjatha, bhikkhācārakiccaṃ mamāyattaṃ hotu, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti āha. “Kiṃ nu kho mayaṃ, āvuso, nisseṇiṃ pātentā evaṃ avocumha – ‘yo paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ sacchikaroti, so bhikkhaṃ āharatu, tenābhataṃ sesā paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karissantī’”ti. “Natthi, āvuso”ti. Tumhe attano pubbahetunā labhittha, mayampi sakkontā vaṭṭassantaṃ karissāma, gacchatha tumheti. Thero te saññāpetuṃ asakkonto phāsukaṭṭhāne piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā gato[P 1.0043]. Aparo thero sattame divase anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā tato cuto suddhāvāsabrahmaloke nibbatto. Itare therā tato cutā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā tesu tesu kulesu nibbattā. Eko gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilānagare rājagehe nibbatto, eko majjhantikaraṭṭhe paribbājikāya kucchimhi nibbatto, eko bāhiyaraṭṭhe kuṭumbiyagehe nibbatto, eko bhikkhunupassaye jāto.

Among them, on the fifth day, one elder attained arahantship and thought, “My duty is accomplished. What shall I do in this place?” By means of his psychic power, he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said, “Friends, partake of this almsfood. Let the duty of the almsround be my responsibility. You should attend to your own tasks.” They replied, “Friend, did we declare, as we cast down the ladder, that ‘Whoever first realizes the Dhamma shall bring alms, and the others, having partaken of what he brings, shall practice the ascetic’s duty’?” He answered, “No, friends.” “You have obtained this due to your own past causes. We too, being able, shall make an end of the cycle of rebirth. You may go.” Unable to persuade them, the elder partook of the almsfood in a suitable place and departed. Another elder, on the seventh day, attained the fruit of non-returning and, passing away from there, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realm. The other elders, after passing away from there, wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one buddha-interval and were reborn in various families. One was reborn in a royal family in the city of Takkasilā in the Gandhāra country; one was reborn in the womb of a female wanderer in the Majjhantika country; one was reborn in a householder’s family in the Bāhiya country; and one was born in a bhikkhunī’s residence.

Ayaṃ pana dabbatthero mallaraṭṭhe anupiyanagare ekassa mallarañño gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa mātā upavijaññā kālamakāsi, matasarīraṃ susānaṃ netvā dārucitakaṃ āropetvā aggiṃ adaṃsu. Tassā aggivegasantattaṃ udarapaṭalaṃ dvedhā ahosi. Dārako attano puññabalena uppatitvā ekasmiṃ dabbatthambhe nipati. Taṃ dārakaṃ gahetvā ayyikāya adaṃsu. Sā tassa nāmaṃ gaṇhantī dabbatthambhe patitvā laddhajīvitattā “dabbo”tissa nāmaṃ akāsi. Tassa ca sattavassikakāle satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro mallaraṭṭhe cārikaṃ caramāno anupiyambavane viharati. Dabbakumāro satthāraṃ disvā dassaneneva [M 1.0050] pasīditvā pabbajitukāmo hutvā “ahaṃ dasabalassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti ayyikaṃ āpucchi. Sā “sādhu, tātā”ti dabbakumāraṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, imaṃ kumāraṃ pabbājethā”ti āha. Satthā aññatarassa bhikkhuno saññaṃ adāsi – “bhikkhu imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājehī”ti. So thero satthu vacanaṃ sutvā [V 1.0041] dabbakumāraṃ pabbājento tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Pubbahetusampanno katābhinīhāro satto paṭhamakesavaṭṭiyā voropanakkhaṇe sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, dutiyāya kesavaṭṭiyā oropiyamānāya sakadāgāmiphale, tatiyāya anāgāmiphale, sabbakesānaṃ pana oropanañca arahattaphalasacchikiriyā ca apacchā apure ahosi. Satthā mallaraṭṭhe yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā [P 1.0044] rājagahaṃ gantvā veḷuvane vāsaṃ kappesi.

This Elder Dabba, for his part, was conceived in the home of a Malla king in the city of Anupiya in the Malla country. His mother passed away while in labor. Her body was taken to the charnel ground, placed on a wooden pyre, and set on fire. Due to the intense heat of the fire, the skin of her abdomen split in two. The child, by the power of his own merit, flew up and landed in a clump of dabba grass. They took the child and gave him to his grandmother. When naming him, because he had survived by falling into a clump of dabba grass, she gave him the name ‘Dabba.’ When he was seven years old, the Teacher, while traveling on tour with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in the Malla country, was dwelling in the Anupiya mango grove. The boy Dabba saw the Teacher and, filled with faith at the very sight of him, desired to go forth. He asked his grandmother, “I will go forth in the presence of the Ten-Powered One.” She replied, “Very well, my dear,” and taking the boy Dabba, went to the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, please give the going forth to this boy.” The Teacher gave a sign to a certain bhikkhu, saying, “Bhikkhu, give the going forth to this boy.” That elder, having heard the Teacher’s words, while giving the going forth to the boy Dabba, taught him the meditation subject of the five skin-ending parts of the body. As a being endowed with past causes and having made a firm resolution, at the moment the first lock of his hair was being cut off, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry; as the second lock of hair was being cut off, in the fruit of once-returning; and at the third, in the fruit of non-returning. The cutting off of all his hair and the realization of the fruit of arahantship occurred simultaneously. The Teacher, having dwelt in the Malla country for as long as he wished, went to Rājagaha and took up residence in the Veḷuvana, the Bamboo Grove.

Tatrāyasmā dabbo mallaputto rahogato attano kiccanipphattiṃ oloketvā saṅghassa veyyāvaccakaraṇe kāyaṃ yojetukāmo cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ saṅghassa senāsanañca paññāpeyyaṃ bhattāni ca uddiseyya”nti. So satthu santikaṃ gantvā attano parivitakkaṃ ārocesi. Satthā tassa sādhukāraṃ datvā senāsanapaññāpakattañca bhattuddesakattañca sampaṭicchi. Atha naṃ “ayaṃ dabbo daharova samāno mahante ṭhāne ṭhito”ti sattavassikakāleyeva upasampādesi. Thero upasampannakālato paṭṭhāya rājagahaṃ upanissāya viharantānaṃ sabbabhikkhūnaṃ senāsanāni ca paññāpeti, bhikkhañca uddisati. Tassa senāsanapaññāpakabhāvo sabbadisāsu pākaṭo ahosi – “dabbo kira mallaputto sabhāgasabhāgānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ekaṭṭhāne senāsanāni paññāpeti, āsannepi dūrepi senāsanaṃ paññāpeti, gantuṃ asakkonte iddhiyā netī”ti.

There, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having gone into solitude and reflected on the accomplishment of his duty, desired to devote himself to the service of the Saṅgha and thought: “What if I were to prepare the lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign the meal tickets?” He went to the Teacher and reported his thought. The Teacher gave his approval and consented to his appointment as the preparer of lodgings and the assigner of meal tickets. Then, thinking, “This Dabba, though still young, is established in a great state,” he granted him the higher ordination even at the age of seven. From the time of his higher ordination, the elder prepared the lodgings and assigned the alms-food for all the bhikkhus dwelling in the vicinity of Rājagaha. His role as the preparer of lodgings became well-known in all directions: “It is said that Dabba Mallaputta prepares lodgings for bhikkhus of similar dispositions in one place, prepares lodgings both near and far, and even transports by his psychic power those who are unable to go.”

Atha naṃ bhikkhū kālepi vikālepi – “amhākaṃ, āvuso, jīvakambavane senāsanaṃ paññāpehi, amhākaṃ maddakucchismiṃ migadāye”ti evaṃ senāsanaṃ uddisāpetvā tassa iddhiṃ passantā gacchanti. Sopi iddhiyā manomaye kāye abhisaṅkharitvā ekekassa therassa ekekaṃ attanā sadisaṃ bhikkhuṃ datvā aṅguliyā jalamānāya purato gantvā “ayaṃ mañco idaṃ pīṭha”ntiādīni vatvā senāsanaṃ paññāpetvā puna attano vasanaṭṭhānameva āgacchati[M 1.0051]. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panidaṃ vatthu pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Satthā idameva kāraṇaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā aparabhāge ariyagaṇamajjhe nisinno theraṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ yadidaṃ dabbo mallaputto”ti (a. ni. 1.209; 214). Vuttampi cetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.54, 108-149) –

Then the bhikkhus, at proper and improper times, would ask him: “Friend, prepare a lodging for us in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove; prepare one for us in the Maddakucchi Deer Park.” Thus, having had their lodgings designated, they would depart, witnessing his psychic power. He, too, by his psychic power, would fashion mind-made bodies, providing for each elder a form resembling himself. Going before them with a blazing finger, he would say, “This is a couch, this is a chair,” and so on, preparing the lodging before returning to his own dwelling place. This is the summary here; the story is related in detail in the Pāli Canon itself. The Teacher, making this very matter the basis for his discourse, later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, established the elder in the foremost position among those who prepare lodgings, saying: “Bhikkhus, foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are preparers of lodgings is Dabba Mallaputta.” This is also stated in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, sabbalokavidū muni;

Ito satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji cakkhumā.

“A hundred thousand aeons ago from this one, there arose the Victor named Padumuttara, the sage, the knower of all worlds, the One with Vision.”

“Ovādako viññāpako, tārako sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Desanākusalo buddho, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

“An admonisher, an instructor, a deliverer of all living beings; the Buddha, skilled in teaching, brought many people across.”

“Anukampako [V 1.0042] kāruṇiko, hitesī sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Sampatte titthiye sabbe, pañcasīle patiṭṭhapi.

“Compassionate and merciful, seeking the welfare of all living beings, he established all the sectarians who came to him in the five precepts.”

“Evaṃ nirākulaṃ āsi, suññataṃ titthiyehi ca;

Vicittaṃ arahantehi, vasībhūtehi tādibhi.

“Thus, the world was untroubled, devoid of sectarians, and adorned with Arahants—such ones, who were masters of themselves.”

“Ratanānaṭṭhapaññāsaṃ, uggato so mahāmuni;

Kañcanagghiyasaṅkāso, bāttiṃsavaralakkhaṇo.

“That great sage was fifty-eight cubits tall; like a golden monument, he possessed the thirty-two excellent marks.”

“Vassasatasahassāni, āyu vijjati tāvade;

Tāvatā tiṭṭhamāno so, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

“His life-span extended for a hundred thousand years; remaining for that long, he brought many people across.”

“Tadāhaṃ haṃsavatiyaṃ, seṭṭhiputto mahāyaso;

Upetvā lokapajjotaṃ, assosiṃ dhammadesanaṃ.

“At that time, in the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a greatly renowned merchant’s son. Approaching the Light of the World, I listened to his teaching of the Dhamma.”

“Senāsanāni bhikkhūnaṃ, paññāpentaṃ sasāvakaṃ;

Kittayantassa vacanaṃ, suṇitvā mudito ahaṃ.

“Hearing the words of the Teacher as he praised a disciple of his who prepared lodgings for the bhikkhus, I was filled with joy.”

“Adhikāraṃ sasaṅghassa, katvā tassa mahesino;

Nipacca sirasā pāde, taṃ ṭhānamabhipatthayiṃ.

“Having performed a great service for that great seer and his Saṅgha, I bowed my head at his feet and aspired to that same position.”

“Tadāha sa mahāvīro, mama kammaṃ pakittayaṃ;

Yo sasaṅghamabhojesi, sattāhaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Then that Great Hero, extolling my deed, declared: ‘This one who for seven days provided meals for the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha—”

“Soyaṃ [M 1.0052] kamalapattakkho, sīhaṃso kanakattaco;

Mama pādamūle nipati, patthayaṃ ṭhānamuttamaṃ.

“‘—this one, with eyes like lotus petals, shoulders like a lion, and skin of golden hue, fell at my feet, aspiring to the supreme position.’”

“Satasahassito kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“‘A hundred thousand aeons from now, born into the Okkāka lineage, one named Gotama by clan will be the Teacher in the world.’”

“Sāvako tassa buddhassa, dabbo nāmena vissuto;

Senāsanapaññāpako, aggo hessatiyaṃ tadā.

“‘A disciple of that Buddha, renowned by the name of Dabba, will at that time be the foremost preparer of lodgings.’”

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-performed deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.”

“Satānaṃ tīṇikkhattuñca, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Satānaṃ pañcakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

“Three hundred times I ruled as king of the devas; five hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch.”

“Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Sabbattha sukhito āsiṃ, tassa kammassa vāhasā.

“Vast was my regional kingship, innumerable by calculation; everywhere I was happy, by the force of that deed.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, vipassī nāma nāyako;

Uppajji cārudassano, sabbadhammavipassako.

“Ninety-one aeons from this one, the leader named Vipassī arose, beautiful to behold, one who clearly saw all phenomena.”

“Duṭṭhacitto upavadiṃ, sāvakaṃ tassa tādino;

Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇaṃ, suddhoti ca vijāniya.

“With a corrupt mind, I slandered a disciple of that Such One, one whose influxes were utterly destroyed, though knowing him to be pure.”

“Tasseva [V 1.0043] naravīrassa, sāvakānaṃ mahesinaṃ;

Salākañca gahetvāna, khīrodanamadāsahaṃ.

“Having taken a ticket, I gave milk-rice to the disciples, the great seers, of that very hero of men.”

“Imamhi bhaddake kappe, brahmabandhu mahāyaso;

Kassapo nāma gottena, uppajji vadataṃ varo.

“In this auspicious aeon, a kinsman of Brahmā, greatly renowned, Kassapa by clan name, the best of speakers, arose.”

“Sāsanaṃ jotayitvāna, abhibhuyya kutitthiye;

Vineyye vinayitvāva, nibbuto so sasāvako.

“Having illumined the Dispensation, having overcome the false sectarians, and having disciplined those fit to be disciplined, he attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.”

“Sasisse nibbute nāthe, atthamentamhi sāsane;

Devā kandiṃsu saṃviggā, muttakesā rudammukhā.

“When the Protector together with his disciples had attained Nibbāna and the Dispensation was setting, the devas, distressed, wept with disheveled hair and tearful faces.”

“Nibbāyissati dhammakkho, na passisāma subbate;

Na suṇissāma saddhammaṃ, aho no appapuññatā.

“‘The Eye of the Dhamma will be extinguished; we shall not see the well-disciplined ones, nor shall we hear the true Dhamma—alas, our lack of merit!’”

“Tadāyaṃ [M 1.0053] pathavī sabbā, acalā sā calācalā;

Sāgaro ca sasokova, vinadī karuṇaṃ giraṃ.

“Then this entire earth, though firm, trembled and shook; and the ocean, as if grieving, roared a mournful sound.”

“Catuddisā dundubhiyo, nādayiṃsu amānusā;

Samantato asaniyo, phaliṃsu ca bhayāvahā.

“In the four directions, non-human drums resounded; on all sides, terrifying thunderbolts burst forth.”

“Ukkā patiṃsu nabhasā, dhūmaketu ca dissati;

Sadhūmā jālavaṭṭā ca, raviṃsu karuṇaṃ migā.

“Meteors fell from the sky, and a comet was seen; smoky fiery rings appeared, and the beasts cried piteously.”

“Uppāde dāruṇe disvā, sāsanatthaṅgasūcake;

Saṃviggā bhikkhavo satta, cintayimha mayaṃ tadā.

“Seeing the dreadful portents indicating the setting of the Dispensation, we, seven bhikkhus, deeply stirred, then reflected thus:”

“Sāsanena vināmhākaṃ, jīvitena alaṃ mayaṃ;

Pavisitvā mahāraññaṃ, yuñjāma jinasāsane.

“‘Without the Dispensation, enough of this life for us. Entering the great forest, let us strive in the Victor’s Dispensation.’”

“Addasamha tadāraññe, ubbiddhaṃ selamuttamaṃ;

Nisseṇiyā tamāruyha, nisseṇiṃ pātayimhase.

“Then in the forest we saw a prominent, excellent rock; having climbed it by a ladder, we cast the ladder down.”

“Tadā ovadi no thero, buddhuppādo sudullabho;

Saddhātidullabhā laddhā, thokaṃ sesañca sāsanaṃ.

“Then the Elder admonished us: ‘The arising of a Buddha is exceedingly rare; faith, exceedingly rare, has been obtained, and little remains of the Dispensation.’”

“Nipatanti khaṇātītā, anante dukkhasāgare;

Tasmā payogo kattabbo, yāva ṭhāti mune mataṃ.

“‘Those who have missed the moment fall into the endless ocean of suffering. Therefore, effort should be made as long as the Sage’s teaching endures.’”

“Arahā āsi so thero, anāgāmī tadānugo;

Susīlā itare yuttā, devalokaṃ agamhase.

“That Elder was an arahant; his follower, a non-returner. The others, being virtuous and diligent, we went to the deva-world.”

“Nibbuto tiṇṇasaṃsāro, suddhāvāse ca ekako;

Ahañca pakkusāti ca, sabhiyo bāhiyo tathā.

“One elder, having crossed saṃsāra, attained Nibbāna; another was reborn alone in the Pure Abodes. And I, and Pukkusāti, and Sabhiya, and Bāhiya likewise,”

“Kumārakassapo, ceva, tattha tatthūpagā mayaṃ;

Saṃsārabandhanā muttā, gotamenānukampitā.

“and Kumārakassapa—we thus came to be in various existences. Shown compassion by Gotama, we are freed from the bonds of saṃsāra.”

“Mallesu [V 1.0044] kusinārāyaṃ, gabbhe jātassa me sato;

Mātā matā citāruḷhā, tato nippatito ahaṃ.

“Among the Mallas, in Kusinārā, while I was in the womb, my mother died and was placed on the pyre; from there I fell forth.”

“Patito dabbapuñjamhi, tato dabboti vissuto;

Brahmacārībalenāhaṃ, vimutto sattavassiko.

“Having fallen on a heap of timber, I was thence known as Dabba. By the power of the holy life, I was liberated at the age of seven.”

“Khīrodanabalenāhaṃ[M 1.0054], pañcahaṅgehupāgato;

Khīṇāsavopavādena, pāpehi bahu codito.

“By the power of the milk-rice, I was endowed with the five factors; because of slandering one whose influxes were destroyed, I was much reproached by the wicked.”

“Ubho puññañca pāpañca, vītivattomhi dānihaṃ;

Patvāna paramaṃ santiṃ, viharāmi anāsavo.

“Now I have transcended both merit and demerit; having attained supreme peace, I dwell without influxes.”

“Senāsanaṃ paññāpayiṃ, hāsayitvāna subbate;

Jino tasmiṃ guṇe tuṭṭho, etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.

“I assigned lodgings, delighting the well-disciplined ones; the Victor, pleased with that quality, placed me foremost in this.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

“My defilements are burned away, all states of existence are uprooted; like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell without influxes.”

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, buddhaseṭṭhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

“Welcome indeed was my coming into the presence of the supreme Buddha; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

“Paṭisambhidā catasso…pe…kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“The four analytical knowledges… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Evaṃbhūtaṃ [P 1.0045] pana taṃ yena pubbe ekassa khīṇāsavattherassa anuddhaṃsanavasena katena pāpakammena bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye pacci, tāya eva kammapilotikāya codiyamānā mettiyabhūmajakā bhikkhū “iminā mayaṃ kalyāṇabhattikassa gahapatino antare paribheditā”ti duggahitagāhino amūlakena pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃsesuṃ. Tasmiñca adhikaraṇe saṅghena sativinayena vūpasamite ayaṃ thero lokānukampāya attano guṇe vibhāvento “yo duddamiyo”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Such indeed was he, who previously, by an evil deed committed through slandering a certain elder whose taints were destroyed, suffered in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. Provoked by that very karmic residue, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, holding a wrong view, slandered him with an unfounded Pārājika offense, saying, “By this one we have been alienated from the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.” And when that legal dispute was settled by the Saṅgha by means of the verdict of innocence, this elder, out of compassion for the world and revealing his own virtues, spoke this verse beginning: “He who was difficult to tame…”

5. Tattha yoti aniyamitaniddeso, tassa “so”ti iminā niyamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ubhayenapi aññaṃ viya katvā attānameva vadati. Duddamiyoti duddamo, dametuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Idañca attano puthujjanakāle diṭṭhigatānaṃ visūkāyikānaṃ kilesānaṃ madālepacittassa vipphanditaṃ indriyānaṃ avūpasamanañca cintetvā vadati. Damenāti uttamena aggamaggadamena, tena hi danto puna dametabbatābhāvato “danto”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, na aññena. Atha vā damenāti damakena purisadammasārathinā damito[M 1.0055]. Dabboti drabyo, bhabboti attho. Tenāha bhagavā imameva theraṃ sandhāya – “na kho, dabba, dabbā evaṃ nibbeṭhentī”ti (pārā. 384; cūḷava. 193)[V 1.0045]. Santusitoti yathāladdhapaccayasantosena jhānasamāpattisantosena maggaphalasantosena ca santuṭṭho. Vitiṇṇakaṅkhoti soḷasavatthukāya aṭṭhavatthukāya ca kaṅkhāya paṭhamamaggeneva samugghāṭitattā vigatakaṅkho. Vijitāvīti purisājānīyena vijetabbassa sabbassapi saṃkilesapakkhassa vijitattā vidhamitattā vijitāvī. Apetabheravoti pañcavīsatiyā bhayānaṃ sabbaso apetattā apagatabheravo abhayūparato[P 1.0046]. Puna dabboti nāmakittanaṃ. Parinibbutoti dve parinibbānāni kilesaparinibbānañca, yā saupādisesanibbānadhātu, khandhaparinibbānañca, yā anupādisesanibbānadhātu. Tesu idha kilesaparinibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā pahātabbadhammānaṃ maggena sabbaso pahīnattā kilesaparinibbānena parinibbutoti attho. Ṭhitattoti ṭhitasabhāvo acalo iṭṭhādīsu tādibhāvappattiyā lokadhammehi akampanīyo. Hīti ca hetuatthe nipāto, tena yo pubbe duddamo hutvā ṭhito yasmā dabbattā satthārā uttamena damena damito santusito vitiṇṇakaṅkho vijitāvī apetabheravo, tasmā so dabbo parinibbuto tatoyeva ca ṭhitatto, evaṃbhūte ca tasmiṃ cittapasādova kātabbo, na pasādaññathattanti paraneyyabuddhike satte anukampanto thero aññaṃ byākāsi.

5. Here, 'yo' is an indefinite pronoun; its specific referent should be understood by 'so'. By both, speaking as if of another, he speaks of himself. 'Duddamiyo' means difficult to tame, unable to be subdued. And this he says reflecting on the agitation of his mind, which was smeared with the intoxication of defilements that are wrong views and act variously, and on the lack of calm of his faculties during his time as a worldling. By 'damena' is meant by the supreme taming, the taming of the highest path. For one tamed by this is worthy of being called 'tamed' because there is no need for further taming, not by any other means. Or else, 'damena' means tamed by the Tamer, the Charioteer of Men to be Tamed. 'Dabbo' means 'of timber', the meaning is 'capable'. Therefore the Blessed One said, referring to this very elder: “Indeed, Dabba, the capable do not unravel thus.” 'Santusito' means content with contentment regarding requisites as obtained, with contentment in jhāna and attainments, and with contentment in the path and fruit. 'Vitiṇṇakaṅkho' means one whose doubt is gone because the sixteen-fold and eight-fold doubt was uprooted by the first path itself. 'Vijitāvī' means victorious because the entire side of defilements that should be conquered by a noble man has been conquered and dispelled. 'Apetabheravo' means one whose fear has departed, one who has ceased from fear, because the twenty-five fears have departed in every way. Again, 'Dabbo' is a mention of his name. 'Parinibbuto' refers to two kinds of final Nibbāna: the final Nibbāna of defilements, which is the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining, and the final Nibbāna of the aggregates, which is the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Here, the final Nibbāna of defilements is intended. Therefore, it means he is fully extinguished by the final Nibbāna of defilements, because all phenomena to be abandoned have been entirely abandoned by the path. 'Ṭhitatto' means one of steadfast nature, unmoving, unshakeable by worldly conditions due to having attained the state of being 'such' with regard to desirable things, etc. And 'hi' is a particle in the sense of cause. Therefore: he who was formerly difficult to tame, because he was capable, was tamed by the Teacher with the supreme taming, is content, has crossed over doubt, is victorious, and is without fear. Therefore that Dabba is fully extinguished and for that very reason is of steadfast nature. And towards such a one, only confidence of mind should be established, not a state other than confidence. Thus the elder, out of compassion for beings who are to be guided and can understand, declared his final knowledge.

Dabbattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Dabba is concluded.

6. Sītavaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sītavaniya

Yo sītavananti āyasmato sambhūtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ito kira aṭṭhārasādhikassa kappasatassa matthake atthadassī nāma sambuddho loke uppajjitvā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ saṃsāramahoghato tārento ekadivasaṃ mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ gaṅgātīraṃ upagacchi. Tasmiṃ kāle ayaṃ gahapatikule nibbatto tattha bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, pāraṃ gantukāmatthā”ti pucchi. Bhagavā “gamissāmā”ti avoca. So tāvadeva nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ [M 1.0056] yojetvā upanesi. Satthā taṃ anukampanto saha bhikkhusaṅghena nāvaṃ abhiruhi. So sayampi abhiruyha sukheneva paratīraṃ sampāpetvā bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca dutiyadivase mahādānaṃ pavattetvā anugantvā pasannacitto vanditvā nivatti. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaritvā ito [P 1.0047] terasādhikakappasatassa matthake khattiyakule nibbattitvā rājā ahosi cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā. So satte sugatimagge patiṭṭhāpetvā tato cuto ekanavutikappe vipassissa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā dhutadhamme samādāya susāne vasanto samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Puna kassapassa bhagavato kālepi tassa sāsane tīhi sahāyehi saddhiṃ [V 1.0046] pabbajitvā vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa “sambhūto”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gato. Bhūmijo jeyyaseno abhirādhanoti tīhi sahāyehi saddhiṃ bhagavato santikaṃ gato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ –

This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sambhūta, [beginning with] "Yo sītavanaṃ." What is its origin? Indeed, one hundred and eighteen eons ago, a Buddha named Atthadassī arose in the world. While guiding the world with its gods across the great flood of saṃsāra, one day he approached the banks of the Ganges with a great assembly of monks. At that time, this [person] was born into a householder family. Seeing the Blessed One there, his mind filled with faith, he approached, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, do you wish to go to the other shore?" The Blessed One replied, "We shall go." Immediately, he prepared a raft of boats and offered it. Out of compassion for him, the Teacher boarded the boat along with the assembly of monks. He too boarded, and having smoothly reached the far shore, he provided a great offering to the Blessed One and the assembly of monks on the second day, then followed, paid homage with a devoted heart, and turned back. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, one hundred and thirteen eons ago, he was reborn into a warrior family and became a righteous universal monarch, a just king. Establishing beings on the path to a good destination, he passed away from there and, in the ninety-first eon, went forth under the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī. Embracing ascetic practices, he lived in charnel grounds and practiced the ascetic's life. Again, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth with three companions in his dispensation and practiced the ascetic's life for twenty thousand years. After wandering among gods and humans for one intervening Buddha-period, he was reborn in this Buddha-era as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha. They named him "Sambhūta." When he came of age, he mastered the brahminical arts. Along with his three companions—Bhūmija, Jeyyasena, and Abhirādhana—he went to the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma teaching, gained faith, and went forth. This is what was referred to when it was said:

“Bhūmijo jeyyaseno ca, sambhūto abhirādhano;

Ete dhammaṃ abhiññāsuṃ, sāsane varatādino”ti.

Bhūmija and Jeyyasena, Sambhūta and Abhirādhana; these directly knew the Dhamma in the dispensation of the supreme Tādi.

Atha sambhūto bhagavato santike kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nibaddhaṃ sītavane vasati. Tenevāyasmā “sītavaniyo”ti paññāyittha. Tena ca samayena vessavaṇo mahārājā kenacideva karaṇīyena jambudīpe dakkhiṇadisābhāgaṃ uddissa ākāsena gacchanto theraṃ abbhokāse nisīditvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontaṃ disvā vimānato oruyha theraṃ vanditvā, “yadā thero samādhito vuṭṭhahissati, tadā mama āgamanaṃ ārocetha, ārakkhañcassa karothā”ti dve yakkhe āṇāpetvā pakkāmi. Te therassa samīpe ṭhatvā manasikāraṃ paṭisaṃharitvā nisinnakāle ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā thero “tumhe mama vacanena vessavaṇamahārājassa kathetha, bhagavatā attano sāsane ṭhitānaṃ satiārakkhā nāma ṭhapitā atthi, sāyeva mādise rakkhati, tvaṃ tattha appossukko hohi, bhagavato ovāde ṭhitānaṃ edisāya ārakkhāya [M 1.0057] karaṇīyaṃ natthī”ti te vissajjetvā tāvadeva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā vijjāttayaṃ sacchākāsi. Tato vessavaṇo nivattamāno therassa [P 1.0048] samīpaṃ patvā mukhākārasallakkhaṇenevassa katakiccabhāvaṃ ñatvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavato ārocetvā satthu sammukhā theraṃ abhitthavanto –

Then Sambhūta, having received the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body from the Blessed One, dwelt constantly in Sītavana. Thus, the venerable one became known as "Sītavaniya." At that time, the great king Vessavaṇa, for some purpose, was traveling through the sky towards the southern part of Jambudīpa. Seeing the elder seated in the open, attending to his meditation subject, he descended from his celestial mansion, paid homage to the elder, and commanded two yakkhas, saying, "When the elder emerges from concentration, inform him of my arrival and provide him protection," and then he departed. Standing near the elder, they informed him when he had withdrawn his mind and was seated. Hearing this, the elder said, "You, by my word, should tell the great king Vessavaṇa: 'The Blessed One has established a protection called mindfulness for those who abide in his dispensation. That alone protects those like me. You should be unconcerned about that. For those who abide in the Blessed One’s instruction, there is no need for such protection.'" Having dismissed them, he immediately developed insight and realized the three true knowledges. Later, when Vessavaṇa was returning, he approached the elder. Recognizing by the very signs of his facial expression that his task was accomplished, he went to Sāvatthī and reported it to the Blessed One. In the Teacher’s presence, he praised the elder, saying:

“Satiārakkhasampanno, dhitimā vīriyasamāhito;

Anujāto satthu sambhūto, tevijjo maccupāragū”ti. –

Endowed with the protection of mindfulness, resolute, composed in energy, a true son of the Teacher, Sambhūta, possessing the three true knowledges, has gone beyond death.

Imāya gāthāya therassa guṇe vaṇṇesi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.15-20) –

With this verse, he extolled the virtues of the elder. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Atthadassī tu bhagavā, dvipadindo narāsabho;

Purakkhato sāvakehi, gaṅgātīramupāgami.

The Blessed One Atthadassī, lord of bipeds, bull among men, preceded by his disciples, approached the bank of the Ganges.

“Samatitti kākapeyyā, gaṅgā āsi duruttarā;

Uttārayiṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ, buddhañca dvipaduttamaṃ.

The Ganges was level with the banks, drinkable by crows, and difficult to cross; I ferried the community of monks across, and the Buddha, supreme among bipeds.

“Aṭṭhārase [V 1.0047] kappasate, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, taraṇāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

One hundred and eighteen eons ago, for the deed I did then, I know of no unhappy destination; this is the fruit of that ferrying.

“Teraseto kappasate, pañca sabbobhavā ahuṃ;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

One hundred and thirteen eons from now, there were five who were universal monarchs, endowed with the seven treasures, of great power.

“Pacchime ca bhave asmiṃ, jātohaṃ brāhmaṇe kule;

Saddhiṃ tīhi sahāyehi, pabbajiṃ satthu sāsane.

And in this last existence, I was born in a brahmin family; with three companions, I went forth in the Teacher's dispensation.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burned up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.

Athāyasmā sambhūto bhagavantaṃ dassanāya gacchante bhikkhū disvā “āvuso, mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandatha, evañca vadethā”ti vatvā dhammādhikaraṇaṃ attano satthu aviheṭhitabhāvaṃ pakāsento “yo sītavana”nti gāthamāha. Te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā sambhūtattherassa sāsanaṃ sampavedentā, “āyasmā, bhante, sambhūto bhagavato pāde sirasā vandati, evañca vadatī”ti vatvā taṃ gāthaṃ ārocesuṃ, taṃ sutvā bhagavā “paṇḍito, bhikkhave, sambhūto [M 1.0058] bhikkhu paccapādi dhammassānudhammaṃ, na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ viheṭheti. Vessavaṇena tassattho mayhaṃ ārocitā”ti āha.

Then the Venerable Sambhūta, seeing some monks going to see the Blessed One, said, “Friends, on my behalf, bow your heads at the feet of the Blessed One and say this.” Having spoken thus, and while making known that he had not troubled his Teacher with a matter concerning the Dhamma, he recited the verse beginning, “Who in the cool forest.” Those monks approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and while conveying the message of the Venerable Sambhūta, said, “Venerable sir, the Venerable Sambhūta bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One and says this.” Then they recited that verse to him. Hearing it, the Blessed One said, “Monks, the monk Sambhūta is wise; he has practiced in accordance with the Dhamma, and he does not trouble me with matters concerning the Dhamma. Vessavaṇa has already informed me of this matter.”

6. Yaṃ pana te bhikkhū sambhūtattherena vuttaṃ “yo sītavana”nti gāthaṃ satthu nivedesuṃ. Tattha sītavananti evaṃnāmakaṃ rājagahasamīpe mahantaṃ bheravasusānavanaṃ. Upagāti nivāsanavasena upagacchi. Etena bhagavatā anuññātaṃ pabbajitānurūpaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Bhikkhūti saṃsārabhayassa ikkhanato bhinnakilesatāya ca bhikkhu. Ekoti adutiyo, etena kāyavivekaṃ dasseti. Santusitoti santuṭṭho. Etena catupaccayasantosalakkhaṇaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ dasseti. Samāhitattoti upacārappanābhedena samādhinā samāhitacitto, etena cittavivekabhāvanāmukhena bhāvanārāmaṃ [P 1.0049] ariyavaṃsaṃ dasseti. Vijitāvīti sāsane sammāpaṭipajjantena vijetabbaṃ kilesagaṇaṃ vijitvā ṭhito, etena upadhivivekaṃ dasseti. Bhayahetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ apagatattā apetalomahaṃso, etena sammāpaṭipattiyā phalaṃ dasseti. Rakkhanti rakkhanto. Kāyagatāsatinti kāyārammaṇaṃ satiṃ, kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ paribrūhanavasena avissajjento. Dhitimāti dhīro, samāhitattaṃ vijitāvibhāvataṃ vā upādāya paṭipattidassanametaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – so bhikkhu vivekasukhānupekkhāya eko sītavanaṃ upāgami, upāgato ca lolabhāvābhāvato santuṭṭho dhitimā kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvento tathādhigataṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā āraddhavipassanaṃ [V 1.0048] ussukkāpetvā adhigatena aggamaggena samāhito vijitāvī ca hutvā katakiccatāya bhayahetūnaṃ sabbaso apagatattā apetalomahaṃso jātoti.

6. Now, those monks reported to the Teacher the verse spoken by the Venerable Sambhūta, beginning, “He who to Sītavana…”. Therein, Sītavana refers to a large, dreadful charnel-ground forest near Rājagaha, so named. Went means he went for the purpose of residence. By this, he indicates a dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth, as permitted by the Blessed One. A monk is so called because he sees the fear in saṃsāra and because his defilements are broken. Alone means without a second person; by this, he indicates seclusion of body. Content means satisfied; by this, he indicates the noble lineage characterized by contentment with the four requisites. Of composed self means with a mind concentrated through concentration distinguished as access and absorption; by this, through the development of mental seclusion, he indicates the noble lineage of delighting in meditation. Victorious means he stands having conquered the host of defilements that are to be conquered by one practicing rightly in the Dispensation; by this, he indicates seclusion from the substrates of existence. With hair not standing on end means that because the defilements, which are the causes of fear, are gone, he is free from horripilation; by this, he indicates the fruit of right practice. Guarding means one who is guarding. Mindfulness directed to the body means mindfulness with the body as its object; not abandoning the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body by way of developing it. Resolute means wise; this indicates the practice based on being of composed self or being victorious. Herein, this is the meaning in brief: That monk, observing the bliss of seclusion, went alone to Sītavana. Having gone, being content due to the absence of fickleness, resolute, and developing the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body, making the jhāna thus attained his foundation, he roused up his practice of insight and, with his self composed by the supreme path he had attained, became victorious. Having done what was to be done, because the causes of fear were in every way gone, he became one whose hair does not stand on end.

Sītavaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder of Sītavana is concluded.

7. Bhalliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhalliya

Yopānudīti [M 1.0059] āyasmato bhalliyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira ito ekatiṃse kappe anuppanne buddhe sumanassa nāma paccekabuddhassa pasannacitto phalāphalaṃ datvā sugatīsu eva saṃsaranto sikhissa sammāsambuddhassa kāle aruṇavatīnagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatto “sikhissa bhagavato paṭhamābhisambuddhassa ujita, ojitā nāma dve satthavāhaputtā paṭhamāhāraṃ adaṃsū”ti sutvā attano sahāyakena saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā svātanāya nimantetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā patthanaṃ akaṃsu – “ubhopi mayaṃ, bhante, anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa paṭhamāhāradāyakā bhaveyyāmā”ti. Te [P 1.0050] tattha tattha bhave puññakammaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsarantā kassapassa bhagavato kāle gopālakaseṭṭhissa puttā bhātaro hutvā nibbattā. Bahūni vassāni bhikkhusaṅghaṃ khīrabhojanena upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Amhākaṃ pana bhagavato kāle pokkharavatīnagare satthavāhassa puttā bhātaro hutvā nibbattā. Tesu jeṭṭho taphusso nāma, kaniṭṭho bhalliyo nāma, te pañcamattāni sakaṭasatāni bhaṇḍassa pūretvā vāṇijjāya gacchantā bhagavati paṭhamābhisambuddhe sattasattāhaṃ vimuttisukhadhammapaccavekkhaṇāhi vītināmetvā aṭṭhame sattāhe rājāyatanamūle viharante rājāyatanassa avidūre mahāmaggena atikkamanti, tesaṃ tasmiṃ samaye samepi bhūmibhāge akaddamodake sakaṭāni nappavattiṃsu, “kiṃ nu, kho, kāraṇa”nti ca cintentānaṃ porāṇasālohitā devatā rukkhaviṭapantare attānaṃ dassentī āha – “mādisā, ayaṃ bhagavā acirābhisambuddho sattasattāhaṃ anāhāro vimuttisukhāpaṭisaṃvedī idāni rājāyatanamūle nisinno, taṃ āhārena paṭimānetha, yadassa tumhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Taṃ sutvā te uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentā, “āhārasampādanaṃ papañca”nti maññamānā manthañca madhupiṇḍikañca bhagavato datvā dvevācikasaraṇaṃ gantvā kesadhātuyo labhitvā agamaṃsu. Te hi paṭhamaṃ upāsakā ahesuṃ. Atha bhagavati bārāṇasiṃ gantvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā anupubbena rājagahe viharante taphussabhalliyā rājagahaṃ upagatā [M 1.0060] bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Tesaṃ bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. Tesu taphusso [V 1.0049] sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya upāsakova ahosi. Bhalliyo pana pabbajitvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.66-70) –

“He who drove away…”: this is the verse of the Venerable Bhalliya. What is its origin? It is said that thirty-one aeons ago from now, when no Buddha had arisen, with a confident mind he gave fruits, large and small, to a Paccekabuddha named Sumana. Transmigrating only in happy destinations, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Aruṇavatī. Having heard, “To the Blessed One Sikhī, when he first became fully enlightened, two sons of a caravan leader named Ujita and Ojitā gave the first meal,” he, together with his companion, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, invited him for the next day, held a great almsgiving, and made an aspiration: “Venerable sir, may we both, in the future, become the givers of the first meal to a Buddha like you.” Having performed meritorious deeds in various existences, transmigrating among devas and humans, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, they were reborn as brothers, the sons of the wealthy herdsman Gopālaka. For many years, they attended upon the Saṅgha of monks with milk-rice. In the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn as brothers in the city of Pokkharavatī, the sons of a caravan leader. Among them, the elder was named Taphussa, and the younger was named Bhalliya. They filled five hundred carts with merchandise and, while travelling for trade, they passed by on the great road not far from the Rājāyatana tree, where the Blessed One was dwelling at its foot in the eighth week after he had first become fully enlightened, having spent seven weeks with the bliss of liberation and contemplation of the Dhamma. At that time, their carts did not move, even on a level stretch of ground without mud or water. While they were thinking, “What, indeed, is the reason?” a deity who had been a blood relative in a past life revealed herself in the fork of a tree and said: “Sirs, this Blessed One, recently fully enlightened, has been without food for seven weeks, experiencing the bliss of liberation. He is now seated at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Honor him with food. This will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.” Hearing this, they experienced great joy and gladness, and thinking, “The preparation of a meal would be a delay,” they gave the Blessed One parched flour and honey-balls, went for refuge with the two phrases, received hair-relics, and departed. They were the first lay disciples. Then, when the Blessed One had gone to Bārāṇasī, set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, and was in due course dwelling at Rājagaha, Taphussa and Bhalliya went to Rājagaha, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One taught them the Dhamma. Of them, Taphussa was established in the fruit of stream-entry and remained a lay disciple. Bhalliya, however, went forth and became possessed of the six superknowledges. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Sumano [P 1.0051] nāma sambuddho, takkarāyaṃ vasī tadā;

Vallikāraphalaṃ gayha, sayambhussa adāsahaṃ.

“The Self-Enlightened One named Sumano dwelt in Takkara at that time; taking the fruit of a creeper, I gave it to the Self-Become One.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I gave that fruit; I have known no evil destination since then. This is the fruit of that offering of fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”
