Athekadivasaṃ māro bhalliyattherassa bhiṃsāpanatthaṃ bhayānakaṃ rūpaṃ dassesi. So attano sabbabhayātikkamaṃ pakāsento “yopānudī”ti gāthamabhāsi.

Then one day, Māra, wishing to frighten the Elder Bhalliya, manifested a terrifying form. The elder, proclaiming his complete transcendence of all fear, uttered the verse beginning, “He who drove away….”

7. Tattha yopānudīti yo apānudi khipi pajahi viddhaṃsesi. Maccurājassāti maccu nāma maraṇaṃ khandhānaṃ bhedo, so eva ca sattānaṃ attano vase anuvattāpanato issaraṭṭhena rājāti maccurājā, tassa. Senanti jarārogādiṃ, sā hissa vasavattane aṅgabhāvato senā nāma, tena hesa mahatā nānāvidhena vipulena “mahāseno”ti vuccati. Yathāha – “na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena, mahāsenena maccunā”ti (ma. ni. 1.272; jā. 2.22.121; netti. 103). Atha vā guṇamāraṇaṭṭhena “maccū”ti idha devaputtamāro adhippeto, tassa ca sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kāmādayo senā. Tathā cāha –

7. Herein, he who drove away means he who drove off, threw out, abandoned, and demolished. Of the King of Death: Death is dying, the breaking up of the aggregates. And because he makes beings follow in his own power, in the sense of being a sovereign, he is a king, thus the King of Death. His army refers to aging, disease, and so on. This is called his army because it is an instrument for bringing beings under his control. Therefore, because this army is great, of various kinds, and vast, he is called ‘one with a great army.’ As it is said: ‘For us there is no pact with that great army of Death.’ Alternatively, Death here is intended as Māra the devaputta, in the sense of the killer of virtue. And sensual pleasures and so on are his army because they become his allies. And so it is said:

“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;

Tatiyā khuppipāsā te, catutthī taṇhā pavuccati.

“Sensual pleasures are your first army, the second is called discontent; your third is hunger and thirst, the fourth is declared to be craving.”

“Pañcamī thinamiddhaṃ te, chaṭṭhā bhīrū pavuccati;

Sattamī vicikicchā te, māno makkho ca aṭṭhamī”ti. (su. ni. 438-439; mahāni. 28;cūḷani. nandamāṇavapucchāniddesa 47);

“Your fifth is sloth and torpor, the sixth is declared to be fear; your seventh is doubt, and conceit and contempt are the eighth.”

Naḷasetuṃva [M 1.0061] sudubbalaṃ mahoghoti sāravirahitato naḷasetusadisaṃ ativiya abalabhāvato suṭṭhu dubbalaṃ saṃkilesasenaṃ navalokuttaradhammānaṃ mahābalavabhāvato mahoghasadisena aggamaggena yo apānudi [V 1.0050] vijitāvī apetabheravo danto, so parinibbuto ṭhitattoti yojanā. Taṃ sutvā māro “jānāti maṃ samaṇo”ti tatthevantaradhāyīti.

The army of defilements is like a bridge of reeds because it is devoid of substance, and exceedingly weak because it is extremely powerless. He who, by means of the supreme path—which is like a great flood due to the great power of the nine supramundane states—has driven away this army, is victorious, fearless, and tamed. The connection is: he is fully extinguished, of steadfast mind. Hearing this, Māra thought, “The contemplative knows me,” and vanished on that very spot.

Bhalliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhalliya is completed.

8. Vīrattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vīra

Yo [P 1.0052] duddamiyoti āyasmato vīrattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato vasanaāvāsaṃ paṭijaggi. Ekadivasañca sindhuvārapupphasadisāni nigguṇṭhipupphāni gahetvā bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito pañcatiṃse kappe khattiyakule nibbattitvā mahāpatāpo nāma rājā ahosi cakkavattī. So dhammena samena rajjaṃ kārento satte saggamagge patiṭṭhāpesi. Puna imasmiṃ kappe kassapassa bhagavato kāle mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi hutvā kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ dānaṃ dento saṅghassa khīrabhattaṃ adāsi. Evaṃ tattha tattha dānamayaṃ puññasambhāraṃ karonto itarañca nibbānatthaṃ sambharanto devamanussesu saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagare rañño pasenadissa amaccakule nibbatti, “vīro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto nāmānugatehi pattabalajavādiguṇehi samannāgato saṅgāmasūro hutvā mātāpitūhi nibandhavasena kārite dārapariggahe ekaṃyeva puttaṃ labhitvā pubbahetunā codiyamāno kāmesu saṃsāre ca ādīnavaṃ disvā saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.21-24) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vīra, [beginning with the words] “One who is hard to tame.” What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one eons ago, he attended to the dwelling place of the Blessed One Vipassī. One day, taking nigguṇṭhi flowers resembling sindhuvāra blossoms, he offered them to the Blessed One. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, thirty-five eons ago he was reborn in a warrior clan and became a great and powerful wheel-turning monarch named Mahāpatāpa. Ruling justly and equitably, he established beings on the path to heaven. Again, in this eon, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a merchant of great wealth. Giving alms to the poor, travellers, and others, he offered milk-rice to the Saṅgha. Thus, in various lives, accumulating a store of merit consisting of generosity, and gathering other virtues for the sake of Nibbāna, he wandered among gods and humans until, during this Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn in Sāvatthī, in the family of a minister of King Pasenadi. They gave him the name “Vīra.” When he came of age, endowed with qualities befitting his name, such as strength and speed, he became a hero on the battlefield. Having taken a wife at the insistence of his parents, he fathered only one son. Urged on by a past cause, and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and in saṃsāra, he became spiritually agitated and went forth. Striving and exerting himself, before long he attained the six higher knowledges. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vipassissa bhagavato, āsimārāmiko ahaṃ;

Nigguṇṭhipupphaṃ paggayha, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“I was a park keeper for the Blessed One Vipassī. Holding up a nigguṇṭhi flower, I offered it to the Buddha.”

“Ekanavutito [M 1.0062] kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, I offered that flower in worship. I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Pañcavīse ito kappe, eko āsiṃ janādhipo;

Mahāpatāpanāmena, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Twenty-five eons ago, I was a sole lord of men, a wheel-turning monarch of great power named Mahāpatāpa.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Evaṃ pana arahattaṃ patvā phalasamāpattisukhena vītināmentaṃ theraṃ purāṇadutiyikā uppabbājetukāmā [V 1.0051] antarantarā nānānayehi palobhetuṃ parakkamantī ekadivasaṃ divāvihāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā itthikuttādīni dassetuṃ ārabhi. Athāyasmā vīro “maṃ palobhetukāmā sineruṃ makasapakkhavātena cāletukāmā viya yāva bālā vatāyaṃ [P 1.0053] itthī”ti tassā kiriyāya niratthakabhāvaṃ dīpento “yo duddamiyo”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having thus attained arahantship, while the Elder was spending his time in the bliss of fruition attainment, his former wife, desiring to make him return to lay life, repeatedly tried to entice him in various ways. One day, she went to his daytime dwelling and began to display her feminine wiles. Then the Venerable Vīra, thinking, “Desiring to entice me, this woman is as foolish as one who desires to shake Mount Sineru with the wind from a mosquito’s wing,” and showing the futility of her actions, spoke the verse beginning, “One who was hard to tame.”

8. Tattha yo duddamiyotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Idaṃ panettha yojanāmattaṃ yo pubbe adanta kilesatāya paccatthikehi vā saṅgamasīse dametuṃ jetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāyaduddamiyo, idāni pana uttamena damena danto catubbidhasammappamadhānavīriyasampattiyā vīro, vuttanayeneva santusito vitiṇṇakaṅkho vijitāvī apetalomahaṃso vīro vīranāmako anavasesato kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto, tato eva ṭhitasabhāvo, na tādisānaṃ satenapi sahassenapi cālanīyoti. Taṃ sutvā sā itthī – “mayhaṃ sāmike evaṃ paṭipanne ko mayhaṃ gharāvāsena attho”ti saṃvegajātā bhikkhunīsu pabbajitvā nacirasseva tevijjā ahosīti.

8. Therein, the meaning of the words beginning with “one who was hard to tame” has already been stated below. This is merely the application here: he who was formerly “hard to tame” due to his untamed defilements or his inability to be tamed or conquered by adversaries on the battlefield, is now tamed by the supreme taming; a “hero” (vīra) through the attainment of the fourfold right effort; content in the way described; one who has crossed over doubt; a victor; a hero whose hair no longer stands on end; the one named Vīra, who is fully extinguished through the complete extinguishing of defilements, and is therefore of a stable nature, not to be shaken by a hundred or even a thousand such women. Hearing this, that woman, filled with spiritual urgency, thought, “Since my husband has attained such a state, what use is household life to me?” She went forth among the nuns and before long became one with the three true knowledges.

Vīrattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vīra is concluded.

9. Pilindavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Pilindavaccha

Svāgatanti [M 1.0063] āyasmato pilindavacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarabuddhakāle haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule nibbatto heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ devatānaṃ piyamanāpabhāvena aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle manussaloke nibbattitvā bhagavati parinibbute satthu thūpassa pūjaṃ katvā saṅghe ca mahādānaṃ pavattetvā tato cuto devamanussesu eva saṃsaranto anuppanne buddhe cakkavattī rājā hutvā mahājanaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā saggaparāyaṇaṃ akāsi. So anuppanneyeva amhākaṃ bhagavati sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇagehe nibbatti. “Pilindo”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Vacchoti pana gottaṃ[P 1.0054]. Tena so aparabhāge “pilindavaccho”ti paññāyittha. Saṃsāre pana saṃvegabahulatāya paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā cūḷagandhāraṃ nāma vijjaṃ sādhetvā tāya vijjāya ākāsacārī paracittavidū ca hutvā rājagahe lābhaggayasaggappatto paṭivasati.

“Welcome” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Pilindavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī. As explained previously, while listening to the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position for being dear and agreeable to the deities. Aspiring to that same position, he performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life. Passing away from there, he wandered among gods and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he was born in the human world. When the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he made offerings to the Teacher's stūpa and provided great alms to the Saṅgha. Passing away from there, he wandered only among gods and humans. When a Buddha had not yet arisen, he became a wheel-turning monarch, established the great populace in the five precepts, and made heaven their destination. When our Blessed One had not yet arisen, he was born into a brahmin household in Sāvatthī. They gave him the name “Pilinda,” and Vaccha was his clan name. Therefore, in later times, he became known as “Pilindavaccha.” Due to a great sense of spiritual urgency concerning saṃsāra, he went forth as a wanderer, mastered a science called “Cūḷagandhāra,” and by means of that science, he could travel through the sky and know the minds of others. He lived in Rājagaha, having attained the pinnacle of gain and fame.

Atha [V 1.0052] yadā amhākaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho hutvā anukkamena rājagahaṃ upagato, tato paṭṭhāya buddhānubhāvena tassa sā vijjā na sampajjati, attano kiccaṃ na sādheti. So cintesi – “sutaṃ kho pana metaṃ ācariyapācariyānaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ ‘yattha mahāgandhāravijjā dharati, tattha cūḷagandhāravijjā na sampajjatī’ti, samaṇassa pana gotamassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya nāyaṃ mama vijjā sampajjati, nissaṃsayaṃ samaṇo gotamo mahāgandhāravijjaṃ jānāti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ taṃ payirupāsitvā tassa santike taṃ vijjaṃ pariyāpuṇeyya”nti. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – “ahaṃ, mahāsamaṇa, tava santike ekaṃ vijjaṃ pariyāpuṇitukāmo, okāsaṃ me karohī”ti. Bhagavā “tena hi pabbajā”ti āha. So “vijjāya parikammaṃ pabbajjā”ti maññamāno pabbaji. Tassa bhagavā dhammaṃ kathetvā caritānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So upanissayasampannatāya nacirasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Yā pana purimajātiyaṃ [M 1.0064] tassovāde ṭhatvā sagge nibbattā devatā, taṃ kataññutaṃ nissāya sañjātabahumānā sāyaṃ pātaṃ theraṃ payirupāsitvā gacchanti. Tasmā thero devatānaṃ piyamanāpatāya aggataṃ patto. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.2.55-67) –

Then, when our Blessed One had become fully enlightened and in due course arrived at Rājagaha, from that time onwards, through the Buddha’s power, that science of his no longer succeeded; it did not accomplish its purpose. He thought: “I have heard my lineage of teachers say, ‘Where the great Gandhāra science is present, the lesser Gandhāra science does not succeed.’ Since the time of the ascetic Gotama’s arrival, this science of mine has not succeeded. Without a doubt, the ascetic Gotama knows the great Gandhāra science. What if I were to attend upon him and learn that science in his presence?” He approached the Blessed One and said this: “Great Ascetic, I wish to learn a certain science in your presence. Grant me the opportunity.” The Blessed One said: “In that case, go forth.” Thinking, “Going forth must be the preliminary training for the science,” he went forth. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma and gave him a meditation subject suitable for his character. Due to his supportive conditions from the past, he developed insight before long and attained arahantship. Now, the deities who in a previous life had been reborn in heaven by following his advice, out of gratitude and with great respect, would attend upon the Elder morning and evening. Therefore, the Elder attained the foremost place for being dear and agreeable to the deities. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nibbute lokanāthamhi, sumedhe aggapuggale;

Pasannacitto sumano, thūpapūjaṃ akāsahaṃ.

“When the Protector of the World, Sumedha, the supreme person, was extinguished, with a serene and joyful mind, I made an offering to the stūpa.”

“Ye ca khīṇāsavā tattha, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā;

Tehaṃ tattha samānetvā, saṅghabhattaṃ akāsahaṃ.

“And those who were there, destroyers of the taints, possessing the six higher knowledges and great psychic power—having gathered them there, I provided a meal for the Saṅgha.”

“Sumedhassa bhagavato, upaṭṭhāko tadā ahu;

Sumedho nāma nāmena, anumodittha so tadā.

“At that time, there was an attendant of the Blessed One Sumedha, named Sumedha; he rejoiced at that time.”

“Tena cittappasādena, vimānaṃ upapajjahaṃ;

Chaḷāsītisahassāni, accharāyo ramiṃsu me.

“Through that serenity of mind, I arose in a celestial mansion; eighty-six thousand celestial nymphs delighted me.”

“Mameva anuvattanti, sabbakāmehi tā sadā;

Aññe deve abhibhomi, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Always they attend upon me with all sensual pleasures; I surpass other devas; this is the fruit of a meritorious deed.”

“Pañcavīsamhi kappamhi, varuṇo nāma khattiyo;

Visuddhabhojano āsiṃ, cakkavattī ahaṃ tadā.

“Twenty-five aeons ago, I was a khattiya named Varuṇa; I was a wheel-turning monarch then, whose food was pure.”

“Na te bījaṃ pavappanti, napi nīyanti naṅgalā;

Akaṭṭhapākimaṃ sāliṃ, paribhuñjanti mānusā.

“They do not sow seed, nor are plows used; they partake of this Sāli rice, which ripens without cultivation.”

“Tattha rajjaṃ karitvāna, devattaṃ puna gacchahaṃ;

Tadāpi edisā mayhaṃ, nibbattā bhogasampadā.

“Having reigned there, I went again to the state of a deva; even then, such abundance of possessions arose for me.”

“Na maṃ mittā amittā vā, hiṃsanti sabbapāṇino;

Sabbesampi piyo homi, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Neither friends nor foes, nor any living beings, harm me; I am dear to all; this is the fruit of a meritorious deed.”

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi[V 1.0053], yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, gandhālepassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty thousand aeons ago, I gave a gift; since then, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of anointing with perfume.”

“Imasmiṃ bhaddake kappe, eko āsiṃ janādhipo;

Mahānubhāvo rājāhaṃ, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In this auspicious aeon, I was a sole ruler of men; a king of great majesty, a wheel-turning monarch of great strength.”

“Sohaṃ [M 1.0065] pañcasu sīlesu, ṭhapetvā janataṃ bahuṃ;

Pāpetvā sugatiṃyeva, devatānaṃ piyo ahuṃ.

“Having established many people in the five precepts and led them to a happy destination, I became dear to the devas.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Tathā devatāhi ativiya piyāyitabbabhāvato imaṃ theraṃ bhagavā devatānaṃ piyamanāpabhāvena aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ devatānaṃ piyamanāpānaṃ yadidaṃ pilindavaccho”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 215) so [P 1.0055] ekadivasaṃ bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe nisinno attano guṇe paccavekkhitvā tesaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ vijjānimittaṃ bhagavato santike āgamanaṃ pasaṃsanto “svāgataṃ nāpagata”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, because of his being exceedingly beloved by the deities, the Blessed One placed this Elder in the foremost position for being dear and agreeable to the deities, saying: “Monks, foremost among my monk disciples who are dear and agreeable to the deities is Pilindavaccha.” (A.N. 1.209, 215) One day, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, reflecting on his own virtues and praising his coming into the presence of the Blessed One—which was the cause of those virtues and the sign of knowledge—he uttered the verse beginning, “Welcome, not unwelcome.”

9. Tattha svāgatanti sundaraṃ āgamanaṃ, idaṃ mamāti sambandho. Atha vā svāgatanti suṭṭhu āgataṃ, mayāti vibhatti vipariṇāmetabbā. Nāpagatanti na apagataṃ hitābhivuddhito na apetaṃ. Nayidaṃ dumantitaṃ mamāti idaṃ mama duṭṭhu kathitaṃ, duṭṭhu vā vīmaṃsitaṃ na hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ bhagavato santike mamāgamanaṃ, yaṃ vā mayā tattha āgataṃ, taṃ svāgataṃ, svāgatattāyeva na durāgataṃ. Yaṃ “bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajissāmī”ti mama mantitaṃ gaditaṃ kathitaṃ, cittena vā vīmaṃsitaṃ idampi na dummantinti. Idāni tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “saṃvibhattesū”tiādimāha. Saṃvibhattesūti pakārato vibhattesu. Dhammesūti ñeyyadhammesu samathadhammesu vā, nānātitthiyehi pakatiādivasena, sammāsambuddhehi dukkhādivasena saṃvibhajitvā vuttadhammesu. Yaṃ seṭṭhaṃ tadupāgaminti yaṃ tattha seṭṭhaṃ, taṃ catusaccadhammaṃ, tassa vā bodhakaṃ sāsanadhammaṃ upāgamiṃ, “ayaṃ dhammo ayaṃ vinayo”ti upagacchiṃ. Sammāsambuddhehi eva vā kusalādivasena khandhādivasena yathāsabhāvato saṃvibhattesu sabhāvadhammesu yaṃ tattha seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ pavaraṃ, taṃ maggaphalanibbānadhammaṃ upāgamiṃ, attapaccakkhato upagacchiṃ sacchākāsiṃ, tasmā svāgataṃ mama na apagataṃ sumantitaṃ na dummantitanti yojanā.

9. Here, svāgataṃ means a good arrival; the connection is ‘this arrival of mine.’ Or alternatively, svāgataṃ means ‘well come by me’; the case ending is to be changed to the instrumental. Nāpagataṃ means not a bad arrival, not devoid of benefit and growth. Nayidaṃ dumantitaṃ mama means ‘this was not ill-conceived by me,’ that is, not badly spoken or wrongly considered by me. This is what is meant: my coming into the presence of the Blessed One, or my having come there, was a good arrival. Precisely because it was a good arrival, it was not a bad arrival. My thought, ‘Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, I will go forth,’ whether spoken or mentally considered, this too was not ill-conceived. Now, showing the reason for this, he states the words beginning with saṃvibhattesu. Saṃvibhattesu: among the well-divided. Dhammesu: among the knowable phenomena, or the phenomena of serenity; that is, among the teachings explained and divided by various sectarians according to nature and so on, and by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones according to suffering and so on. Yaṃ seṭṭhaṃ tadupāgamiṃ: ‘I have approached that which is best.’ This means: whatever among them is best, that I have approached—the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, or the teaching of the Dispensation which leads to its realization. I approached it, thinking, ‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya.’ Or, among the natural phenomena divided by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones according to their intrinsic nature—by way of the wholesome and so on, or the aggregates and so on—whatever among them is best, supreme, and excellent, that Dhamma of the path, fruit, and Nibbāna I have approached. I have approached it through direct personal experience; I have realized it. Therefore, the connection is: ‘My coming was a good arrival, not a bad one; it was well-conceived, not ill-conceived.’”

Pilindavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Pilindavaccha is concluded.

10. Puṇṇamāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa

Vihari [M 1.0066][V 1.0054][P 1.0056] apekkhanti āyasmato puṇṇamāsattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira vipassissa bhagavato kāle cakkavākayoniyaṃ nibbatto bhagavantaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso attano mukhatuṇḍakena sālapupphaṃ gahetvā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito sattarase kappe aṭṭhakkhattuṃ cakkavattī rājā ahosi. Imasmiṃ pana kappe kassapassa bhagavato sāsane osakkamāne kuṭumbiyakule nibbattitvā pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagare samiddhissa nāma brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa jātadivase tasmiṃ gehe sabbā rittakumbhiyo suvaṇṇamāsānaṃ puṇṇā ahesuṃ. Tenassa puṇṇamāsoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ patvā vivāhakammaṃ katvā ekaṃ puttaṃ labhitvā upanissayasampannatāya gharāvāsaṃ jigucchanto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado pubbakiccasampanno catusaccakammaṭṭhāne yuttappayutto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.7.13-19) –

The verse beginning “Vihari apekkhanti” is that of the Venerable Puṇṇamāsa. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn as a ruddy goose. Seeing the Blessed One passing by, with a serene mind, he took a sāla flower in his beak and made an offering. Through that meritorious deed, while wandering among devas and humans, he became a wheel-turning monarch eight times in the seventeenth eon from the present. Then, in this eon, when the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa was in decline, he was reborn in a householder’s family. Having gone forth and practiced the ascetic’s duties, he passed away from there and, wandering among devas and humans, was reborn in this Buddha-era in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of a brahmin named Samiddhi. On the day of his birth, all the empty pots in that house became full of golden coins. For that reason, they gave him the name Puṇṇamāsa. When he came of age, having achieved mastery in the brahminical sciences, he married and had a son. Due to his possession of supportive conditions, he became disgusted with the household life. He approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. Having received the higher ordination and fulfilled the preliminary duties, he diligently applied himself to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, cultivated insight, and attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sindhuyā nadiyā tīre, cakkavāko ahaṃ tadā;

Suddhasevālabhakkhohaṃ, pāpesu ca susaññato.

“On the bank of the river Sindhu, I was then a ruddy goose; I fed on pure moss and was well-restrained from evil deeds.”

“Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, gacchantaṃ anilañjase;

Tuṇḍena sālaṃ paggayha, vipassissābhiropayiṃ.

“I saw the stainless Buddha traveling through the sky; taking a sāla flower with my beak, I offered it to Vipassī.”

“Yassa saddhā tathāgate, acalā suppatiṭṭhitā;

Tena cittappasādena, duggatiṃ so na gacchati.

“One whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established, through that confidence of mind, does not go to a bad destination.”

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, buddhaseṭṭhassa santike;

Vihaṅgamena santena, subījaṃ ropitaṃ mayā.

“Indeed, my coming to the presence of the best of Buddhas was a good one; a good seed was planted by me, who was then a bird.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I offered up that flower; since then, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Sucārudassanā [M 1.0067] nāma, aṭṭhete ekanāmakā;

Kappe sattarase āsuṃ, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“In the seventeenth eon, there were eight wheel-turning monarchs of great strength, all of the same name: Sucārudassana.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Athassa purāṇadutiyikā taṃ palobhetukāmā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā puttena saddhiṃ upagantvā piyālāpabhāvādikehi [V 1.0055] bhāvavivaraṇakammaṃ nāma kātuṃ ārabhi. Thero tassā kāraṇaṃ disvā attano katthacipi alaggabhāvaṃ pakāsento “vihari apekkha”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Then his former wife, desiring to entice him, adorned and prepared herself and approached him together with their son. Through affectionate speech, gestures, and so on, she began to perform the act of revealing her feelings. The Elder, seeing her intention and proclaiming his own state of non-attachment to anything whatsoever, uttered the verse beginning, “Vihari apekkha.”

10. Tattha viharīti visesato hari apahari apanesi. Apekkhanti taṇhaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke attabhāve vā. Huranti aparasmiṃ anāgate attabhāve vā. Idhāti vā ajjhattikesu āyatanesu. Huranti bāhiresu[P 1.0057]. Vā-saddo samuccayattho “apadā vā dvipadā vā”tiādīsu (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34; 5.32) viya. Yoti attānameva paraṃ viya dasseti. Vedagūti vedena gato maggañāṇena nibbānaṃ gato adhigato, cattāri vā saccāni pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasena abhisamecca ṭhito. Yatattoti maggasaṃvarena saṃyatasabhāvo, sammāvāyāmena vā saṃyatasabhāvo. Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalittoti sabbesu ārammaṇesu dhammesu taṇhādiṭṭhilepavasena na upalitto, tena lābhādilokadhamme samatikkamaṃ dasseti. Lokassāti upādānakkhandhapañcakassa. Tañhi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko. Jaññāti jānitvā. Udayabbayañcāti uppādañceva vayañca, etena yathāvuttaguṇānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ panettha attho – yo sakalassa khandhādilokassa samapaññāsāya ākārehi udayabbayaṃ jānitvā vedagū yatatto katthaci anupalitto, so sabbattha apekkhaṃ vineyya santusito tādisānaṃ vippakārānaṃ na kiñci maññati, tasmā tvaṃ andhabāle yathāgatamaggeneva gacchāti. Atha sā itthī “ayaṃ samaṇo mayi putte ca nirapekkho, na sakkā imaṃ palobhetu”nti pakkāmi.

10. Here, 'viharī' means one who has specifically removed, dispelled, or taken away. 'Apekkhanti' refers to craving. 'Here' (idha) means in this world or in this individual existence. 'There' (huraṃ) refers to a future individual existence. Alternatively, 'here' refers to the internal sense bases, and 'there' refers to the external ones. The word 'or' (vā) serves a conjunctive purpose, as in phrases like 'footless or two-footed.' 'Who' (yo) indicates oneself as if it were another. 'Vedagū' means one who has gone by means of knowledge (veda); that is, one who has gone to Nibbāna through the knowledge of the path, having gone to or attained it; or one who stands firm having fully understood the four truths by way of comprehension, abandonment, realization, and development. 'Yatatto' (self-controlled) means one whose nature is restrained through the discipline of the path or through right effort. 'Anūpalitto' (unattached) in all things means not stained by way of the defilement of craving and views in all dhammas as objects; through this, he shows the transcending of worldly conditions such as gain. 'Lokassa' (of the world) refers to the five aggregates subject to clinging. For it is called 'world' (loka) on account of its nature of breaking up and perishing (lujjana-palujjana). 'Jaññā' means having known. 'Udayabbayañca' means both arising and ceasing; by this is shown the preliminary practice for the aforementioned qualities. This is the meaning here: one who, knowing the arising and ceasing of the entire world of aggregates and so forth by means of fifty aspects, is a knower of the Veda (vedagū), self-controlled (yatatto), and unattached anywhere—such a one, having dispelled longing everywhere, is content and thinks nothing of such disturbances. Therefore, you blind fool, go by the very path by which you came. Then that woman, thinking, 'This ascetic is without longing for me or my son; it is not possible to entice him,' departed.

Puṇṇamāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa is concluded.

Paramatthadīpaniyā theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Theragāthā

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Cūḷavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cūḷavaccha

Pāmojjabahuloti [M 1.0068][V 1.0056] āyasmato cūḷavacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle daliddakule nibbattitvā paresaṃ bhatiyā jīvikaṃ kappento bhagavato sāvakaṃ sujātaṃ nāma theraṃ paṃsukūlaṃ pariyesantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso upasaṅkamitvā vatthaṃ datvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandi. So tena puññakammena tettiṃsakkhattuṃ devarajjaṃ kāresi. Sattasattatikkhattuṃ cakkavattī rājā [P 1.0058] ahosi. Anekavāraṃ padesarājā. Evaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane osakkamāne pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussagatīsu aparāparaṃ parivattanto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle kosambiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Cūḷavacchotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gato buddhaguṇe sutvā pasannamānaso bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami, tassa bhagavā dhammaṃ kathesi. So paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado katapubbakicco caritānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā bhāvento vihari. Tena ca samayena kosambikā bhikkhū bhaṇḍanajātā ahesuṃ. Tadā cūḷavacchatthero ubhayesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ laddhiṃ anādāya bhagavatā dinnovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ brūhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.31-40) –

‘Abounding in joy’ is the verse of the Venerable Cūḷavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a poor family and made a living by working for others. Seeing a disciple of the Blessed One, the Elder named Sujāta, searching for rag-robes, his mind became serene. Approaching him, he gave a cloth and paid homage with the five-point prostration. By that meritorious deed, he exercised the kingship of the devas thirty-three times. Seventy-seven times he was a wheel-turning monarch. Many times he was a regional king. Thus, wandering among devas and humans, during the decline of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth, practiced the ascetic’s duties, and for one Buddha-interval, he turned through the divine and human states again and again. In the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn into a brahmin family in Kosambī. His name was Cūḷavaccha. When he came of age and had achieved mastery in the brahminical arts, he heard of the Buddha’s virtues and, with a serene mind, approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. He, having gained faith, went forth. Having received the higher ordination and completed his preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject suitable to his temperament and dwelled developing it. And at that time, the monks of Kosambī had become quarrelsome. Then the Elder Cūḷavaccha, not adopting the view of either group of monks, stood firm in the instruction given by the Blessed One, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttarabhagavato, sujāto nāma sāvako;

Paṃsukūlaṃ gavesanto, saṅkāre caratī tadā.

‘A disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara, named Sujāta, while searching for a rag-robe, was at that time walking on a rubbish heap.

“Nagare haṃsavatiyā, paresaṃ bhatako ahaṃ;

Upaḍḍhudussaṃ datvāna, sirasā abhivādayiṃ.

‘In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a hired servant for others; having given half a cloth, I paid homage with my head.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

‘By that well-done deed, and by my volition and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.

“Tettiṃsakkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Sattasattatikkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

‘Thirty-three times as king of the devas, I exercised sovereignty; and seventy-seven times, I was a wheel-turning monarch.

“Padesarajjaṃ [M 1.0069][V 1.0057] vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Upaḍḍhadussadānena, modāmi akutobhayo.

‘Vast was my regional kingship, incalculable by measure; by the gift of half a cloth, I rejoice, free from fear.

“Icchamāno cahaṃ ajja, sakānanaṃ sapabbataṃ;

Khomadussehi chādeyyaṃ, aḍḍhudussassidaṃ phalaṃ.

‘If I wished, even today, I could cover this earth with its forests and mountains with linen cloths; this is the fruit of half a cloth.

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, aḍḍhudussassidaṃ phalaṃ.

‘One hundred thousand eons ago, when I gave that gift, I know of no evil destiny since; this is the fruit of half a cloth.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

‘My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.’

Atha cūḷavacchatthero arahattaṃ patvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kalahābhiratiyā sakatthavināsaṃ disvā dhammasaṃvegappatto, attano ca pattavisesaṃ paccavekkhitvā pītisomanassavasena “pāmojjabahulo”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Then the Elder Cūḷavaccha, having attained Arahantship and seeing the destruction of their own welfare by those monks through their delight in quarreling, was overcome with spiritual urgency. And reflecting on his own special attainment, out of joy and gladness he spoke the verse, ‘Abounding in joy.’

11. Tattha pāmojjabahuloti suparisuddhasīlatāya vippaṭisārābhāvato adhikusalesu dhammesu abhirativasena pamodabahulo. Tenevāha “dhamme buddhappavedite”ti. Tattha dhammeti. Sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhamme navavidhe vā lokuttaradhamme. So hi sabbaññubuddhena sāmukkaṃsikāya desanāya pakāsitattā sātisayaṃ buddhappavedito nāma. Tassa pana adhigamūpāyabhāvato desanādhammopi idha labbhateva. Padaṃ santanti nibbānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Evarūpo hi bhikkhu santaṃ padaṃ santaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ upasamabhāvato saṅkhārūpasamaṃ paramasukhatāya sukhaṃ nibbānaṃ adhigacchati vindatiyeva. Parisuddhasīlo hi bhikkhu vippaṭisārābhāvena pāmojjabahulo saddhamme yuttappayutto vimuttipariyosānā sabbasampattiyo pāpuṇāti. Yathāha – “avippaṭisāratthāni kho[P 1.0059], ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni, avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāyā”tiādi (a. ni. 10.1). Atha vā pāmojjabahuloti sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅghoti ratanattayaṃ sandhāya pamodabahulo. Tattha pana so pamodabahulo kiṃ vā karotīti āha “dhamme buddhappavedite”tiādi. Saddhāsampannassa hi sappurisasaṃsevanasaddhammassavanayonisomanasikāradhammānudhammapaṭipattīnaṃ sukheneva sambhavato sampattiyo hatthagatā [M 1.0070] eva honti, yathāha – “saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.183).

11. Therein, ‘abounding in joy’ means he is full of joy due to his perfectly pure virtue, the absence of remorse, and his delight in wholesome states of a higher order. Therefore he said, ‘in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha.’ Therein, ‘Dhamma’ refers to the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment or to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Because this was declared by the All-Knowing Buddha with his own sublime teaching, it is pre-eminently called ‘proclaimed by the Buddha.’ Moreover, since it is the means for its attainment, the teaching of the Dhamma is also included here. ‘The peaceful state’ is said with reference to Nibbāna. For such a monk attains and indeed finds Nibbāna—the peaceful state, the peaceful portion, the stilling of all formations, which is happiness because it is the ultimate bliss. Indeed, a monk of pure virtue, abounding in joy due to the absence of remorse and diligently engaged in the good Dhamma, attains all accomplishments culminating in liberation. As it is said: ‘Skillful virtues, Ānanda, are for the sake of non-remorse; non-remorse is for the sake of joy,’ and so on. Alternatively, ‘abounding in joy’ means he is full of joy with reference to the Triple Gem: ‘The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, the Saṅgha is of good conduct.’ As to what one who is full of joy does, he said, ‘in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha,’ and so on. For one endowed with faith, accomplishments are as if already in hand, because association with true persons, hearing the good Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma arise with ease. As it is said: ‘One in whom faith is born approaches; approaching, he pays close attention,’ and so on.

Cūḷavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷavaccha is concluded.

2. Mahāvacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahāvaccha

Paññābalīti [V 1.0058] āyasmato mahāvacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pānīyadānamadāsi. Puna sikhissa bhagavato kāle upāsako hutvā vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ puññakammaṃ akāsi, so tehi puññakammehi tattha tattha sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe nāḷakagāme samiddhissa nāma brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa mahāvacchoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto āyasmato sāriputtassa bhagavato sāvakabhāvaṃ sutvā “sopi nāma mahāpañño. Yassa sāvakattaṃ upāgato, so eva maññe imasmiṃ loke aggapuggalo”ti bhagavati saddhaṃ uppādetvā satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.51-56) –

This is the stanza of the Venerable Elder Mahāvaccha, beginning with 'Paññābalī.' What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he offered drinking water to the community of monks. Later, in the era of the Blessed One Sikhī, he became a lay devotee and performed many meritorious deeds conducive to liberation. Due to those meritorious deeds, he wandered through various happy realms until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a brahmin named Samiddhi in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country. His name was Mahāvaccha. When he came of age, hearing that the Venerable Sāriputta was a disciple of the Blessed One, he thought, 'If even he is a man of great wisdom, then the one whose disciple he has become, that one, I think, is indeed the foremost person in this world.' With faith arising in the Blessed One, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. Applying himself to meditation, he soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttarabuddhassa, bhikkhusaṅghe anuttare;

Pasannacitto sumano, pānīyaghaṭamapūrayiṃ.

“To the Buddha Padumuttara and his unsurpassed community of monks, with a confident and joyful mind, I filled a water pot.

“Pabbatagge dumagge vā, ākāse vātha bhūmiyaṃ;

Yadā pānīyamicchāmi, khippaṃ nibbattate mama.

“Whether on a mountain peak, in the treetops, in the sky, or on the ground—whenever I desire drinking water, it swiftly arises for me.

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dakadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“For a hundred thousand aeons, because of the gift I gave then, I have known no bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving water.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Chaḷabhiññā sacchikatā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned away… all existences are uprooted; the sixfold higher knowledge is realized, the Buddha's teaching is done.”

Evaṃ [P 1.0060] pana arahattaṃ patvā vimuttisukhaṃ anubhavanto sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvavibhāvanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ “paññābalī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having thus attained arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, to inspire his fellow spiritual practitioners by demonstrating the liberating nature of the Teaching, he spoke the stanza beginning with 'Paññābalī.'

12. Tattha [M 1.0071] paññābalīti pārihāriyapaññāya vipassanāpaññāya ca vasena abhiṇhaso sātisayena paññābalena samannāgato. Sīlavatūpapannoti ukkaṃsagatena catupārisuddhisīlena, dhutadhammasaṅkhātehi vatehi ca upapanno samannāgato. Samāhitoti upacārappanābhedena samādhinā samāhito. Jhānaratoti tato eva ārammaṇūpanijjhāne lakkhaṇūpanijjhāne ca rato satatābhiyutto. Sabbakālaṃ satiyā avippavāsavasena satimā. Yadatthiyanti atthato anapetaṃ atthiyaṃ, yena atthiyaṃ yadatthiyaṃ. Yathā paccaye paribhuñjantassa paribhuñjanaṃ atthiyaṃ hoti, tathā [V 1.0059] bhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno. Sāmiparibhogena hi taṃ atthiyaṃ hoti dāyajjaparibhogena vā, na aññathā bhojananti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhuñjiyati paribhuñjiyatīti vā bhojanaṃ, cattāro paccayā. “Yadatthika”nti vā pāṭho. Yadatthaṃ yassatthāya satthārā paccayā anuññātā, tadatthaṃ kāyassa ṭhitiādiatthaṃ, tañca anupādisesanibbānatthaṃ. Tasmā anupādāparinibbānatthaṃ bhojanapaccaye bhuñjamāno tato eva kaṅkhetha kālaṃ attano anupādāparinibbānakālaṃ āgameyya. Idha imasmiṃ sāsane vītarāgo. Bāhirakassa pana kāmesu vītarāgassa idaṃ natthīti adhippāyo.

12. Herein, 'Paññābalī' (possessed of the strength of wisdom) means being endowed repeatedly and exceedingly with the strength of wisdom through protective wisdom and insight wisdom. 'Sīlavatūpapanno' (endowed with virtue) means being accomplished with virtue that is supreme, consisting of the fourfold purification of virtue, and endowed with the vows reckoned as ascetic practices. 'Samāhito' (composed) means being composed through concentration, which is of two kinds: access and absorption. 'Jhānarato' (delighting in meditation) means delighting and constantly engaged in absorption, both in terms of the object and the characteristic. 'Satimā' (mindful) means being always mindful by way of never being separated from mindfulness. 'Yadatthiyaṃ' (for a purpose) means that which is purposeful, not deviating from purpose; that by which there is purpose is 'yadatthiyaṃ.' Just as the using of requisites serves a purpose for one who uses them appropriately, so too, when eating food. For it is purposeful either by way of the owner's use or by way of inherited use; it is not otherwise. And 'food' (bhojanaṃ) should be seen as merely an illustration. Or, 'food' means that which is eaten or consumed, referring to the four requisites. Alternatively, the reading is 'Yadatthika' (one who has a purpose). For whatever purpose, for the sake of which the requisites were permitted by the Teacher—that purpose being for the sake of the body's stability, etc., and for the sake of Nibbāna without remainder. Therefore, one who consumes the food-requisite for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging should from that very moment long for and await the time of his own final Nibbāna without clinging. Here, in this Dispensation, he is free from lust. But for an outsider who is free from lust for sensual pleasures, this does not apply—such is the meaning.

Mahāvacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mahāvaccha is concluded.

3. Vanavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vanavaccha

Nīlabbhavaṇṇāti āyasmato vanavacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira atthadassino bhagavato kāle kacchapayoniyaṃ nibbatto vinatāya nāma nadiyā vasati. Tassa khuddakanāvappamāṇo attabhāvo ahosi. So kira ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ [P 1.0061] nadiyā tīre ṭhitaṃ disvā, “pāraṃ gantukāmo maññe bhagavā”ti attano piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā netukāmo pādamūle nipajji. Bhagavā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā taṃ anukampanto āruhi. So pītisomanassajāto sotaṃ chindanto jiyāya vegena khittasaro viya tāvadeva paratīraṃ pāpesi. Bhagavā tassa puññassa phalaṃ etarahi nibbattanakasampattiñca byākaritvā pakkāmi. So [M 1.0072] tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto anekasatakkhattuṃ tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññavāsīyeva ahosi. Puna kassapabuddhakāle kapotayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā araññe viharantaṃ mettāvihāriṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā cittaṃ pasādesi.

The stanza beginning 'Nīlabbhavaṇṇā' (Blue-hued) is by the Venerable Elder Vanavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was born in the turtle species and lived in a river named Vinatā. His body was the size of a small boat. One day, seeing the Blessed One standing on the riverbank, he thought, “The Blessed One wishes to cross, I think,” and lay down at his feet, intending to carry him on his back. The Blessed One, knowing his intention, mounted him out of compassion. Filled with joy and happiness, he cut through the stream and, like an arrow shot with the speed of a bowstring, quickly reached the other shore. The Blessed One, having declared the fruit of his merit and the prosperity of his future rebirth, departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and for many hundreds of existences, he often went forth as an ascetic and always dwelt in the forest. Again, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he was born in the dove species and, seeing a monk who abided in loving-kindness dwelling in the forest, his mind became confident.

Tato pana cuto bārāṇasiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ puññakammaṃ upacini. Evaṃ tattha tattha devamanussesu saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare vacchagottassa nāma brāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa mātā paripakkagabbhā araññaṃ dassanatthāya sañjātadohaḷā araññaṃ pavisitvā vicarati, tāvadevassā kammajavātā caliṃsu, tirokaraṇiṃ parikkhipitvā adaṃsu. Sā dhaññapuññalakkhaṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. So bodhisattena saha paṃsukīḷikasahāyo ahosi. “Vaccho”tissa nāmañca ahosi. Vanābhiratiyā vasena vanavacchoti paññāyittha. Aparabhāge mahāsatte mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā [V 1.0060] mahāpadhānaṃ padahante, “ahampi siddhatthakumārena saha araññe viharissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto abhisambuddhabhāvaṃ sutvā bhagavato santikaṃ upagantvā pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe vasamāno nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49-148-163) –

Then, having passed away from there, he was reborn in a family home in Bārāṇasī. Upon reaching maturity, he was stirred by a sense of urgency, went forth into homelessness, and accumulated much meritorious action as a condition for liberation. Thus, wandering among devas and humans in various existences, he took rebirth in the household of a brahmin of the Vacchagotta clan in the city of Kapilavatthu during the appearance of this Buddha. His mother, when her pregnancy was full-term, developed a craving to see the forest, entered the woods, and wandered about. Immediately, the labor pains arose, and a screen was formed around her. She bore a son marked with signs of fortune and merit. He became a playmate of the Bodhisatta, playing in the dust with him. His name was “Vaccha,” and due to his fondness for the forest, he became known as Vanavaccha. Later, when the Great Being undertook the great renunciation and strove with great effort, he thought, “I too will dwell in the forest with Prince Siddhattha.” So he left home, adopted the ascetic life, and lived in the Himalayas. Upon hearing of the Buddha’s supreme enlightenment, he approached the Blessed One, went forth into homelessness, took up a meditation subject, and dwelling in the forest, before long diligently developed insight and realized arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Atthadassī tu bhagavā, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Vinatānadiyā tīraṃ, upagacchi tathāgato.

“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-Awakened One, the Leader of the World, the Tathāgata, approached the bank of the Vinatā River.

“Udakā abhinikkhamma, kacchapo vārigocaro;

Buddhaṃ tāretukāmohaṃ, upesiṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Having emerged from the water, I, a turtle whose resort is the water, desiring to ferry the Buddha across, approached the Leader of the World.

“Abhirūhatu maṃ buddho, atthadassī mahāmuni;

Ahaṃ taṃ tārayissāmi, dukkhassantakaro tuvaṃ.

“May the Buddha, the Great Sage Atthadassī, mount me; I will ferry you across, for you are the Ender of Suffering.

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, atthadassī mahāyaso;

Abhirūhitvā me piṭṭhiṃ, aṭṭhāsi lokanāyako.

“Knowing my intention, Atthadassī, the greatly renowned, the Leader of the World, climbed upon my back and stood there.

“Yato [M 1.0073] sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ;

Sukhaṃ me tādisaṃ natthi, phuṭṭhe pādatale yathā.

“For as long as I remember myself, for as long as I have had understanding, there has been no such happiness for me as when his feet touched me.

“Uttaritvāna sambuddho, atthadassī mahāyaso;

Naditīramhi ṭhatvāna, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Having crossed over, the Perfectly Awakened One, Atthadassī, the greatly renowned, standing on the riverbank, spoke these verses.

“Yāvatā vattate cittaṃ, gaṅgāsotaṃ tarāmahaṃ;

Ayañca kacchapo rājā, tāresi mama paññavā.

“‘As far as the mind extends, I cross the Ganges stream; and this wise turtle king carried me across.

“Iminā buddhataraṇena, mettacittavatāya ca;

Aṭṭhārase kappasate, devaloke ramissati.

“‘By this act of ferrying the Buddha, and by his mind of loving-kindness, for eighteen hundred aeons he will delight in the heavenly world.

“Devalokā idhāgantvā, sukkamūlena codito;

Ekāsane nisīditvā, kaṅkhāsotaṃ tarissati.

“‘Having come here from the heavenly world, impelled by the root of his wholesome deeds, seated in solitude, he will cross the stream of doubt.’”

“Yathāpi bhaddake khette, bījaṃ appampi ropitaṃ;

Sammādhāre pavecchante, phalaṃ toseti kassakaṃ.

Just as in a fertile field, even a little seed sown, when watered properly, yields fruit to please the farmer.

“Tathevidaṃ buddhakhettaṃ, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ;

Sammādhāre pavecchante, phalaṃ maṃ tosayissati.

Even so is this Buddha-field, taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; when offerings are properly made, the fruit will satisfy me.

“Padhānapahitattomhi, upasanto nirūpadhi;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

I am resolute in striving, calm, free from the substrates of existence; having fully understood all the taints, I dwell without taints.

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, taraṇāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

Eighteen hundred aeons ago, for the deed I did then, I know no bad destination; this is the fruit of that ferrying.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.

Evaṃ [V 1.0061] pana [P 1.0062] arahattaṃ patvā bhagavati kapilavatthusmiṃ viharante tattha gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā bhikkhūhi samāgato paṭisanthāravasena “kiṃ, āvuso, araññe phāsuvihāro laddho”ti puṭṭho “ramaṇīyā, āvuso, araññe pabbatā”ti attanā vuṭṭhapabbate vaṇṇento “nīlabbhavaṇṇā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, having attained arahantship, while the Blessed One was dwelling in Kapilavatthu, he went there, paid homage to the Teacher, and having met with the monks, was asked in a friendly manner, “Friend, was a comfortable dwelling found in the forest?” He replied, “Delightful, friend, are the mountains in the forest,” and praising the mountain where he himself had dwelt, he spoke the verse beginning, “Nīlabbhavaṇṇā.”

13. Tattha nīlabbhavaṇṇāti nīlavalāhakanibhā nīlavalāhakasaṇṭhānā ca. Rucirāti ruciyā sakiraṇā pabhassarā ca. Sītavārīti sītalasalilā. Sucindharāti sucisuddhabhūmibhāgatāya suddhacittānaṃ vā ariyānaṃ [M 1.0074] nivāsanaṭṭhānatāya sucindharā. Gāthāsukhatthañhi sānunāsikaṃ katvā niddeso. “Sītavārisucindharā”tipi pāṭho, sītasucivāridharā sītalavimalasalilāsayavantoti attho. Indagopakasañchannāti indagopakanāmakehi pavāḷavaṇṇehi rattakimīhi sañchāditā pāvussakālavasena evamāha. Keci pana “indagopakanāmāni rattatiṇānī”ti vadanti. Apare “kaṇikārarukkhā”ti. Selāti silāmayā pabbatā, na paṃsupabbatāti attho. Tenāha – “yathāpi pabbato selo”ti (udā. 24). Ramayanti manti maṃ ramāpenti, mayhaṃ vivekābhirattiṃ paribrūhenti. Evaṃ thero attano cirakālaparibhāvitaṃ araññābhiratiṃ pavedento tividhaṃ vivekābhiratimeva dīpeti. Tattha upadhivivekena aññābyākaraṇaṃ dīpitameva hotīti.

13. Herein, `nīlabbhavaṇṇā` means like a blue cloud, the color of a blue cloud. `Rucirā` means lovely, radiant, and brilliant. `Sītavārī` means having cool water. `Sucindharā` means bearing purity, due to having a pure and clean portion of earth, or due to being a dwelling place for the noble ones with pure minds. For the sake of metrical charm, the explanation is given with a nasal consonant. There is also the reading `Sītavārisucindharā`, meaning bearing cool, pure water, or possessing cool, immaculate pools of water. `Indagopakasañchannā` means covered with red insects called indagopakas, which are the color of coral; he says this with reference to the rainy season. Some, however, say, “Indagopakas are red grasses.” Others say, “They are kaṇikāra trees.” `Selā` means mountains made of rock, not mountains of earth. Therefore it is said: “Like a mountain of rock” (Ud 24). `Ramayanti maṃ` means they cause me to delight, they increase my delight in seclusion. Thus the elder, making known his long-cultivated delight in the forest, illuminates the threefold delight in seclusion. Herein, the declaration of final knowledge through seclusion from the substrates of existence is indeed shown.

Vanavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vanavaccha is concluded.

4. Sivakasāmaṇeragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Novice Sivaka

Upajjhāyoti [P 1.0063] sivakassa sāmaṇerassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ito ekatiṃse kappe vessabhussa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto ekadivasaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena araññaṃ paviṭṭho tattha pabbatantare nisinnaṃ vessabhuṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Puna tattha manoharāni kāsumārikaphalāni disvā tāni gahetvā bhagavato upanesi, paṭiggahesi bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane mātule pabbajante tena saddhiṃ pabbajitvā bahuṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vanavacchattherassa bhāgineyyo hutvā nibbatto, sivakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa mātā attano jeṭṭhabhātike vanavacche sāsane pabbajitvā pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā araññe viharante taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā puttaṃ āha – “tāta [V 1.0062] sivaka, therassa santike pabbajitvā theraṃ upaṭṭhaha, mahallako dāni thero”ti. So mātu [M 1.0075] ekavacaneneva ca pubbe katādhikāratāya ca mātulattherassa santikaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā taṃ upaṭṭhahanto araññe vasati.

‘Upajjhāyo’ begins the verse of the novice Sivaka. What is its origin? It is said that, thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, he was born into a good family. One day, having entered the forest on some business, he saw the Blessed One Vessabhu seated in a mountain cleft. With a mind full of faith, he approached, paid homage, and stood with hands reverently joined. Then, seeing delightful kāsumārika fruits there, he gathered them and offered them to the Blessed One. Out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted them. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans. In the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, when his maternal uncle went forth, he went forth with him and accumulated much wholesome merit that is a supporting condition for liberation. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn as the nephew of the Elder Vanavaccha, and his name was Sivaka. His mother, hearing that her elder brother Vanavaccha had gone forth in the Dispensation, fulfilled the duties of one who has gone forth, and was dwelling in the forest, said to her son: 'Dear Sivaka, go forth in the presence of the Elder and attend to him, for the Elder is now old.' Prompted by his mother’s single word and also due to his past resolve, he went to his uncle the Elder, went forth, and while attending to him, lived in the forest.

Tassa ekadivasaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena gāmantaṃ gatassa kharo ābādho uppajji. Manussesu bhesajjaṃ karontesupi na paṭippassambhi. Tasmiṃ cirāyante thero “sāmaṇero cirāyati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti tattha gantvā taṃ gilānaṃ disvā tassa taṃ taṃ kattabbayuttakaṃ karonto divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā rattibhāge balavapaccūsavelāyaṃ āha – “sivaka, na mayā pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya gāme vasitapubbaṃ, ito araññameva gacchāmā”ti. Taṃ sutvā sivako “yadipi me, bhante, idāni kāyo gāmante ṭhito, cittaṃ pana araññe, tasmā sayānopi araññameva gamissāmī”ti, taṃ sutvā thero taṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā araññameva netvā ovādaṃ adāsi. So therassa ovāde ṭhatvā vipassitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.38.53-58) –

One day, when he had gone to the outskirts of a village on some business, a severe illness arose in him. Although the people prepared medicine, it did not subside. When he was delayed, the elder thought, 'The novice is taking a long time, what could be the reason?' Going there and seeing him ill, he spent the day attending to his various needs. In the deep pre-dawn hours, he said, 'Sivaka, from the time I went forth, I have never before lived in a village. Let us go from here to the forest.' Hearing this, Sivaka said, 'Venerable sir, although my body is now in the vicinity of the village, my mind is in the forest. Therefore, even lying down, I will go to the forest.' Hearing this, the elder took him by the arm, led him to the forest, and gave him an exhortation. Abiding in the elder’s exhortation, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva [P 1.0064] jotantaṃ, nisinnaṃ pabbatantare;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ.

“Like a shining kaṇikāra tree, seated in a mountain cleft, I saw the stainless Buddha, foremost in the world, a bull among men.

“Pasannacitto sumano, kire katvāna añjaliṃ;

Kāsumārikamādāya, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ.

“With a serene and joyful mind, having made the gesture of reverence with folded hands, I took a kāsumārika fruit and gave it to the best of Buddhas.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from now, when I gave that fruit, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of that gift of fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

So arahattaṃ patvā upajjhāyena attanā ca vuttamatthaṃ saṃsanditvā attano vivekābhiratikataṃ katakiccatañca pavedento “upajjhāyo maṃ avacā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, comparing the meaning spoken by his preceptor and by himself, and making known his delight in seclusion and his state of having done what was to be done, he spoke the verse beginning, “Upajjhāyo maṃ avacā.”

14. Tattha upajjhāyoti vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyati hitesitaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā ñāṇacakkhunā pekkhatīti upajjhāyo. Manti attānaṃ vadati. Avacāti abhāsi. Ito gacchāma sīvakāti vuttākāradassanaṃ, sivaka, ito gāmantato araññaṭṭhānameva ehi gacchāma, tadeva amhākaṃ vasanayogganti [M 1.0076] adhippāyo. Evaṃ pana upajjhāyena vutto sivako bhadro assājānīyo viya kasābhihato sañjātasaṃvego hutvā araññameva gantukāmataṃ pavedento –

14. Herein, `upajjhāyo` (preceptor) means one who closely examines what is faulty and faultless; having established a wish for the welfare of others, he observes with the eye of wisdom—thus he is a preceptor. `Maṃ` refers to oneself. `Avacā` means he spoke. `Ito gacchāma sīvakā` shows the manner of what was said. The intention is: 'Sivaka, come, let us go from this vicinity of the village to the forest dwelling, for that alone is a suitable place for us to live.' When spoken to thus by his preceptor, Sivaka, like a fine thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, felt a sense of spiritual urgency arise and, making known his own desire to go to the forest, said:

“Gāme [V 1.0063] me vasati kāyo, araññaṃ me gataṃ mano;

Semānakopi gacchāmi, natthi saṅgo vijānata”nti. –āha;

“My body dwells in the village, my mind has gone to the forest; even while lying down, I go, for one who knows has no attachment.”

Tassattho – yasmā idāni yadipi me idaṃ sarīraṃ gāmante ṭhitaṃ, ajjhāsayo pana araññameva gato, tasmā semānakopi gacchāmi gelaññena ṭhānanisajjāgamanesu asamatthatāya sayānopi iminā sayitākārena sarīsapo viya sarīsapanto, etha, bhante, araññameva gacchāma, kasmā? Natthi saṅgo vijānatanti, yasmā dhammasabhāvā kāmesu saṃsāre ca ādīnavaṃ, nekkhamme nibbāne ca ānisaṃsaṃ yāthāvato jānantassa na katthaci saṅgo, tasmā ekapadeneva upajjhāyassa āṇā anuṭhitāti, tadapadesena aññaṃ byākāsi.

Its meaning is this: 'Although this body of mine is now in the vicinity of the village, my disposition has already gone to the forest. Therefore, even while lying down, I will go.' Because of his illness, he was unable to stand, sit, or walk, so he says 'even while lying down,' meaning 'crawling like a reptile.' 'Come, venerable sir, let us go to the forest.' Why? 'For one who knows, there is no attachment.' This is because for one who knows things as they really are—the danger in sensual pleasures and in saṃsāra, and the benefit in renunciation and in Nibbāna—there is no attachment anywhere. Thus, with a single phrase from his preceptor, his instruction was undertaken. And by means of that statement, he declared his attainment of final knowledge.

Sivakasāmaṇeragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Novice Sivaka is concluded.

5. Kuṇḍadhānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna

Pañca [P 1.0065] chinde pañca jaheti āyasmato kuṇḍadhānattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe uppanno vayappatto heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthārā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapiyamānaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā tadanurūpaṃ puññaṃ karonto vicari. So ekadivasaṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya nisinnassa manosilācuṇṇapiñjaraṃ mahantaṃ kadaliphalakaṇṇikaṃ upanesi, taṃ bhagavā paṭiggahetvā paribhuñji. So tena puññakammena ekādasakkhattuṃ devesu devarajjaṃ kāresi. Catuvīsativāre rājā ahosi cakkavattī. Evaṃ so punappunaṃ puññāni katvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapabuddhakāle bhummadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Dīghāyukabuddhānañca [M 1.0077] nāma na anvaddhamāsiko uposatho hoti. Tathā hi vipassissa bhagavato chabbassantare chabbassantare uposatho ahosi. Kassapadasabalo pana chaṭṭhe chaṭṭhe māse pātimokkhaṃ osāresi. Tassa pātimokkhassa osāraṇakāle disāvāsikā dve sahāyakā bhikkhū “uposathaṃ karissāmā”ti gacchanti.

The verse 'Pañca chinde pañca jahe...' is that of the Venerable Elder Kuṇḍadhāna. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, he approached the Blessed One as previously described, listened to the Dhamma, and saw the Teacher placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who took the first voting ticket. Seeing this, he aspired for that position and performed meritorious deeds accordingly. One day, after the Blessed One Padumuttara emerged from the cessation attainment and was seated, he offered a large bunch of bananas colored like powdered orpiment. The Blessed One accepted and partook of it. Through that meritorious deed, he became king of the gods eleven times. Twenty-four times he was a wheel-turning monarch. Thus, repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, he wandered among gods and humans until, in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he was reborn as an earth deity. For long-lived Buddhas, the Uposatha is not held every half-month. Indeed, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Uposatha was held every six years. But the Buddha Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, concluded the Pātimokkha recitation every six months. At the time of the Pātimokkha recitation, two monk companions from the surrounding regions were going, saying, “We will observe the Uposatha.”

Ayaṃ bhummadevatā cintesi – “imesaṃ dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ metti ativiya daḷhā, kiṃ nu kho, bhedake sati bhijjeyya, na bhijjeyyā”ti, sā tesaṃ okāsaṃ olokayamānā tesaṃ avidūreneva gacchati. Atheko thero ekassa hatthe pattacīvaraṃ datvā sarīravaḷañjanatthaṃ udakaphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0064] gantvā dhotahatthapādo hutvā gumbasamīpato nikkhamati bhummadevatā tassa therassa pacchato uttamarūpā itthī hutvā kese vidhunitvā saṃvidhāya sambandhantī viya [P 1.0066] piṭṭhiyaṃ paṃsuṃ puñchamānā viya sāṭakaṃ saṃvidhāya nivāsayamānā viya ca hutvā therassa padānupadikā hutvā gumbato nikkhantā. Ekamante ṭhito sahāyakatthero taṃ kāraṇaṃ disvāva domanassajāto “naṭṭho dāni me iminā bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dīgharattānugato sineho, sacāhaṃ evaṃvidhabhāvaṃ jāneyyaṃ, ettakaṃ addhānaṃ iminā saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ na kareyya”nti cintetvā āgacchantassevassa, “handāvuso, tuyhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ, tādisena pāpena saddhiṃ ekamaggaṃ nāgacchāmī”ti āha. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tassa lajjibhikkhuno hadayaṃ tikhiṇasattiṃ gahetvā viddhaṃ viya ahosi. Tato naṃ āha – “āvuso, kiṃ nāmetaṃ vadasi, ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ dukkaṭamattampi āpattiṃ na jānāmi. Tvaṃ pana maṃ ajja ‘pāpo’ti vadasi, kiṃ te diṭṭha”nti. “Kiṃ aññena diṭṭhena, kiṃ tvaṃ evaṃvidhena alaṅkatapaṭiyattena mātugāmena saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne hutvā nikkhanto”ti. “Natthetaṃ, āvuso, mayhaṃ, nāhaṃ evarūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ passāmī”ti. Tassa yāvatatiyaṃ kathentassāpi itaro thero kathaṃ asaddahitvā attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃyeva bhūtattaṃ katvā gaṇhanto tena saddhiṃ ekamaggena agantvā aññena [M 1.0078] maggena satthu santikaṃ gato. Itaropi bhikkhu aññena maggena satthu santikaṃyeva gato.

This earth-deity thought: "The friendship between these two monks is extremely strong. If a cause of division were to arise, would it break or not?" While observing for an opportunity, she went about not far from them. Then one elder, giving his bowl and robe into the other's hand, went to a place suitable for attending to his bodily needs. After washing his hands and feet, he came out from near a bush. The earth-deity, following behind that elder, took the form of an exceptionally beautiful woman. As if shaking out her hair, arranging it, and binding it, as if brushing dust from her back, and as if adjusting and putting on her lower garment, she emerged from the bush, following in the elder's footsteps. The companion elder, standing to one side, saw this and became distressed. He thought, "Now my long-standing affection for this monk is destroyed. Had I known of such behavior, I would not have placed my trust in him for so long." As the other approached, he said, "Here, friend, take your bowl and robe. I will not walk the same path with such a wicked person." Hearing these words, the heart of the scrupulous monk felt as if it had been pierced with a sharp spear. Then he said to him, "Friend, what is this you are saying? For all this time, I am not aware of having committed even an offense of wrong-doing. Yet today you call me 'wicked'—what have you seen?" "What need is there for anything else to be seen? Did you not just come out from the same place as a woman so adorned and arrayed?" "That is not so, friend. I saw no such woman." Though he spoke thus up to the third time, the other elder did not believe his words. Taking what he himself had seen as the truth, he would not go with him on the same path, but went to the Teacher’s presence by another way. The other monk also went to the Teacher’s presence by another way.

Tato bhikkhusaṅghassa uposathāgāraṃ pavisanavelāya so bhikkhu taṃ bhikkhuṃ uposathagge sañjānitvā, “imasmiṃ uposathagge evarūpo nāma pāpabhikkhu atthi, nāhaṃ tena saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā bahi aṭṭhāsi. Atha bhummadevatā “bhāriyaṃ mayā kammaṃ kata”nti mahallakaupāsakavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ gantvā “kasmā, bhante, ayyo imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito”ti āha. “Upāsaka, imaṃ uposathaggaṃ eko pāpabhikkhu paviṭṭho, ‘nāhaṃ [P 1.0067] tena saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karomī’ti bahi ṭhitomhī”ti. “Bhante, mā evaṃ gaṇhatha, parisuddhasīlo esa bhikkhu. Tumhehi diṭṭhamātugāmo nāma ahaṃ, mayā tumhākaṃ vīmaṃsanatthāya ‘daḷhā nu kho imesaṃ therānaṃ metti, no daḷhā’ti bhijjanābhijjanabhāvaṃ olokentena taṃ kammaṃ kata”nti. “Ko pana, tvaṃ sappurisā”ti? “Ahaṃ ekā bhummadevatā, bhante”ti devaputto kathento dibbānubhāvena ṭhatvā therassa pādesu nipatitvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, khamatha, etaṃ dosaṃ thero na jānāti, uposathaṃ karothā”ti theraṃ yācitvā uposathaggaṃ pavesesi. So thero uposathaṃ tāva ekaṭṭhāne akāsi, mittasanthavavasena pana puna tena saddhiṃ na ekaṭṭhāne ahosīti. Imassa therassa kammaṃ na kathīyati, cuditakatthero pana aparāparaṃ vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then, at the time for the Sangha of monks to enter the Uposatha hall, that monk, recognizing the other monk in the hall, said, 'In this Uposatha hall, there is a wicked monk of this kind. I will not perform the Uposatha with him,' and he went outside and stood there. Then the earth-deity, thinking, 'I have done a grievous deed,' approached him in the guise of an elderly lay devotee and asked, 'Venerable sir, why are you standing in this place?' 'Lay devotee, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall. I will not perform the Uposatha with him, so I am standing outside.' 'Venerable sir, do not take it so. That monk is pure in virtue. The woman you saw was I. I performed that deed to test you both, to see whether the friendship of these elders was strong or not, by observing whether it would break or not.' 'But who are you, good sir?' 'I am an earth-deity, venerable sir.' As he spoke, the divine being stood there by his divine power, fell at the elder's feet, and pleaded, 'Venerable sir, forgive me for this fault; that elder knows nothing of it. Please perform the Uposatha.' Having thus pleaded with the elder, he led him into the Uposatha hall. That elder performed the Uposatha together with him for the time being, but regarding their intimate friendship, he was not with him in the same place again. The spiritual progress of this elder is not related. However, the elder who was accused, practicing insight meditation again and again, attained Arahantship.

Bhummadevatā [V 1.0065] tassa kammassa nissandena ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ apāyabhayato na muccittha. Sace pana kismiñci kāle manussattaṃ āgacchati, aññena yena kenaci kato doso tasseva upari patati. So amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. “Dhānamāṇavo”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā mahallakakāle satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji, tassa upasampannadivasato paṭṭhāya ekā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā itthī tasmiṃ gāmaṃ [M 1.0079] pavisante saddhiṃyeva gāmaṃ pavisati, nikkhamante nikkhamati. Vihāraṃ pavisantepi saddhiṃ pavisati, tiṭṭhantepi tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ niccānubandhā paññāyati. Thero taṃ na passati. Tassa puna purimakammanissandena sā aññesaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Gāme yāguṃ bhikkhañca dadamānā itthiyo “bhante, ayaṃ eko yāguuḷuṅko tumhākaṃ, eko imissā amhākaṃ sahāyikāyā”ti parihāsaṃ karonti. Therassa mahatī vihesā hoti. Vihāragatampi naṃ sāmaṇerā ceva daharā bhikkhū ca parivāretvā “dhāno koṇḍo jāto”ti parihāsaṃ karonti. Athassa teneva [P 1.0068] kāraṇena kuṇḍadhānattheroti nāmaṃ jātaṃ. So uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya tehi kariyamānaṃ keḷiṃ sahituṃ asakkonto ummādaṃ gahetvā “tumhe koṇḍā, tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo koṇḍo, ācariyo koṇḍo”ti vadati. Atha naṃ satthu ārocesuṃ “kuṇḍadhāno, bhante, daharasāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ evaṃ pharusavācaṃ vadatī”ti. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, dhāna, sāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ pharusavācaṃ vadasī”ti vatvā tena “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti vutte “kasmā evaṃ vadesī”ti āha. “Bhante, nibaddhaṃ vihesaṃ asahanto evaṃ kathemī”ti. “Tvaṃ pubbe katakammaṃ yāvajjadivasā jīrāpetuṃ na sakkosi, puna evarūpaṃ pharusaṃ māvadī bhikkhū”ti vatvā āha –

The earth deity, due to the result of that deed, was not freed from the fear of the lower realms for an entire Buddha-interval. However, if at any time she was reborn as a human, any wrongdoing committed by others fell upon her. In the time of our Blessed One, he was born in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They named him Dhanamāṇava. When he came of age, he mastered the three Vedas. In his old age, after hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he acquired faith and went forth. From the day of his higher ordination, a woman, adorned and well-prepared, would enter the village whenever he did and leave when he left. When he entered the monastery, she entered too; when he stood, she stood—thus she was constantly seen following him. The elder did not see her. Due to the ripening of his past kamma, she appeared to others. When the women in the village offered rice gruel and alms, they joked, "Venerable sir, this portion of gruel is for you, and this one is for our companion, our friend." The elder was greatly distressed. Even when he returned to the monastery, the novices and young monks surrounded him, teasing, "Dhāna has become corrupt!" Because of this, he came to be known as Kuṇḍadhāna Thera. Unable to endure the constant mockery, he became frenzied and shouted, "You are corrupt! Your preceptor is corrupt! Your teacher is corrupt!" They reported this to the Teacher: "Venerable sir, Kuṇḍadhāna is speaking harshly with the young novices." The Teacher summoned him and asked, "Dhāna, is it true that you speak harshly with the novices?" When he admitted it was true, the Teacher asked, "Why do you speak so?" "Venerable sir, unable to bear the relentless harassment, I spoke thus." The Teacher said, "You cannot exhaust the result of your past kamma even to this day. Do not speak harshly to the monks again." Then he said:

“Māvoca pharusaṃ kañci, vuttā paṭivadeyyu taṃ;

Dukkhā hi sārambhakathā, paṭidaṇḍā phuseyyu taṃ.

Speak harshly to no one, for those you address might answer you in the same way. Painful indeed is contentious talk; retaliation might touch you.

“Sace neresi attānaṃ, kaṃso upahato yathā;

Esa pattosi nibbānaṃ, sārambho te na vijjatī”ti. (dha. pa. 133-134);

If you make yourself as still as a broken gong, you have attained Nibbāna; contentiousness is not found in you.

Imañca pana tassa therassa mātugāmena saddhiṃ vicaraṇabhāvaṃ kosalaraññopi kathayiṃsu. Rājā “gacchatha, bhaṇe, vīmaṃsathā”ti pesetvā sayampi mandeneva parivārena therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ekamante olokento aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero sūcikammaṃ karonto nisinno hoti, sāpi itthī avidūre ṭhāne ṭhitā viya paññāyati. Rājā disvā “atthidaṃ kāraṇa”nti tassā [V 1.0066] ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Sā tasmiṃ āgacchante therassa vasanapaṇṇasālaṃ paviṭṭhā viya ahosi. Rājāpi tāya saddhiṃ tameva paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā sabbattha olokento adisvā [M 1.0080] “nāyaṃ mātugāmo, therassa eko kammavipāko”ti saññaṃ katvā paṭhamaṃ therassa samīpena gacchantopi theraṃ avanditvā tassa kāraṇassa abhūtabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgamma theraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “kacci, bhante, piṇḍakena na kilamathā”ti pucchi. Thero “vaṭṭati, mahārājā”ti āha. “Jānāmahaṃ, bhante, ayyassa kathaṃ, evarūpena parikkilesena saddhiṃ carantānaṃ tumhākaṃ ke nāma pasīdissanti, ito paṭṭhāya vo katthaci gamanakiccaṃ natthi, ahaṃ [P 1.0069] catūhi paccayehi tumhe upaṭṭhahissāmi, tumhe yoniso manasikāre mā pamajjitthā”ti nibaddhabhikkhaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Thero rājānaṃ upatthambhakaṃ labhitvā bhojanasappāyena ekaggacitto hutvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tato paṭṭhāya sā itthī antaradhāyi.

They also told the king of Kosala about the elder's association with a woman. The king sent men, saying, "Go, sirs, and investigate." He himself went with a small retinue to the elder's dwelling place and stood observing from one side. At that moment, the elder was seated doing needlework, and the woman appeared to be standing not far from him. Seeing this, the king thought, "There is something to this matter," and went to the place where she stood. As he approached, she seemed to enter the elder's leaf-hut. The king also entered that same leaf-hut with her, but looking everywhere, he did not see her. Realizing, "This is no woman, but a result of the elder's kamma," he formed this perception. Though he had first approached the elder without paying respects, upon understanding the falsity of the matter, he returned, paid homage to the elder, and sat down to one side. He asked, "Venerable sir, are you not wearied by the alms-round?" The elder replied, "It is sufficient, great king." The king said, "Venerable sir, I understand your situation. Who would have faith in you, living with such a defiling association? From now on, you have no need to go anywhere. I will provide you with the four requisites. Do not be negligent in wise attention." He then established a constant alms-offering for him. The elder, having obtained the king as a supporter, with his mind unified through suitable food, developed insight and attained arahantship. From that time onward, that woman disappeared.

Tadā mahāsubhaddā ugganagare micchādiṭṭhikakule vasamānā “satthā maṃ anukampatū”ti uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nirāmagandhā hutvā uparipāsādatale ṭhitā “imāni pupphāni antare aṭṭhatvā dasabalassa matthake vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhantu, dasabalo imāya saññāya sve pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatū”ti saccakiriyaṃ katvā aṭṭha sumanapupphamuṭṭhiyo vissajjesi. Pupphāni gantvā dhammadesanāvelāya satthu matthake vitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Satthā taṃ sumanapupphavitānaṃ disvā citteneva subhaddāya bhikkhaṃ adhivāsetvā punadivase aruṇe uṭṭhite ānandattheraṃ āha – “ānanda, mayaṃ ajja dūraṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gamissāma, puthujjanānaṃ adatvā ariyānaṃyeva salākaṃ dehī”ti. Thero bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi – “āvuso, satthā ajja dūraṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gamissati, puthujjanā mā gaṇhantu, ariyāva salākaṃ gaṇhantū”ti. Kuṇḍadhānatthero “āhara, āvuso salāka”nti paṭhamaṃyeva hatthaṃ pasāresi. Ānando “satthā tādisānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ salākaṃ na dāpeti, ariyānaṃyeva dāpetī”ti vitakkaṃ uppādetvā gantvā satthu ārocesi. Satthā “āharāpentassa salākaṃ dehī”ti āha. Thero cintesi – “sace kuṇḍadhānassa salākā dātuṃ na yuttā, atha satthā paṭibāheyya, bhavissati ettha kāraṇa”nti “kuṇḍadhānassa salākaṃ dassāmī”ti [M 1.0081] gamanaṃ abhinīhari. Kuṇḍadhāno tassa pure āgamanā eva abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā ākāse ṭhatvā “āharāvuso, ānanda, satthā maṃ jānāti, mādisaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantaṃ na satthā nivāretī”ti hatthaṃ pasāretvā salākaṃ gaṇhi. Satthā taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā theraṃ imasmiṃ sāsane paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ [P 1.0070] aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Yasmā ayaṃ thero rājānaṃ upatthambhakaṃ labhitvā sappāyāhāralābhena [V 1.0067] samāhitacitto vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto upanissayasampannatāya chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.4.1-16) –

At that time, Mahāsubhaddā, living in the city of Ugga in a family of wrong view, resolved upon the Uposatha with the thought, "May the Teacher have compassion for me." Abstaining from meat, she stood on the upper terrace of the palace and made a solemn declaration: "May these flowers, without stopping in between, form a canopy over the head of the Ten-Powered One. May the Ten-Powered One, recognizing this sign, accept alms from me tomorrow along with five hundred monks." Having made this declaration of truth, she released eight handfuls of jasmine flowers. The flowers went and, at the time of the Dhamma discourse, formed a canopy over the Teacher's head and remained there.
