Seeing this jasmine flower canopy, the Teacher mentally consented to Subhaddā's alms-offering. The next day, at dawn, he said to Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, today we will go far for alms. Give the tokens only to the noble ones, not to ordinary people." The elder informed the monks, "Friends, the Teacher will go far for alms today. Ordinary people should not take tokens—only the noble ones should take them." Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna was the first to extend his hand, saying, "Friend, bring the token." Ānanda thought, "The Teacher does not have tokens given to such monks—he has them given only to the noble ones." He went and reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Give the token to the one who asks for it." The elder considered, "If it were not proper to give a token to Kuṇḍadhāna, the Teacher would prevent it. There must be a reason for this." Resolving, "I will give the token to Kuṇḍadhāna," he set out. Before Ānanda could arrive, Kuṇḍadhāna entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for the higher knowledges, and stood in the air by his psychic power. He said, "Bring it, friend Ānanda. The Teacher knows me. The Teacher does not prevent a monk like me from being the first to take the token." Extending his hand, he took the token. The Teacher, making this the occasion for a teaching, placed the elder foremost among those who are first to receive tokens in this dispensation. For this elder, having gained the support of the king and obtained suitable food, with a concentrated mind, practiced insight and, due to his supporting conditions being perfected, became endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sattāhaṃ paṭisallīnaṃ, sayambhuṃ aggapuggalaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, buddhaseṭṭhaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃ.

For seven days, the Self-Become, the foremost person, was in seclusion; with a serene and joyful mind, I attended upon the Buddha, the best of beings.

“Vuṭṭhitaṃ kālamaññāya, padumuttaraṃ mahāmuniṃ;

Mahantiṃ kadalīkaṇṇiṃ, gahetvā upagacchahaṃ.

Knowing the time he had emerged from his meditation, I approached the great sage Padumuttara, carrying a large banana blossom.

“Paṭiggahetvā bhagavā, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Mama cittaṃ pasādento, paribhuñji mahāmuni.

The Blessed One, the All-Knowing, the Leader of the World, having accepted it, the Great Sage, pleasing my mind, partook of it.

“Paribhuñjitvā sambuddho, satthavāho anuttaro;

Sakāsane nisīditvā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

Having partaken, the Fully Awakened One, the unsurpassed caravan leader, seated in his own seat, uttered these verses.

“Ye ca santi samitāro, yakkhā imamhi pabbate;

Araññe bhūtabhabyāni, suṇantu vacanaṃ mama.

'Whatever yakkhas are assembled on this mountain, and whatever beings, born and yet to be born, are in this forest, let them listen to my word.'

“Yo so buddhaṃ upaṭṭhāsi, migarājaṃva kesariṃ;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

'That person who attended upon the Buddha, who is like a lion, the king of beasts—him I shall praise. Listen to me as I speak.'

“Ekādasañcakkhattuṃ so, devarājā bhavissati;

Catuvīsatikkhattuñca, cakkavattī bhavissati.

'Eleven times he will be a king of gods, and twenty-four times he will be a wheel-turning monarch.'

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

'In a hundred thousand aeons, born of the Okkāka lineage, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will arise in the world.'

“Akkositvāna samaṇe, sīlavante anāsave;

Pāpakammavipākena, nāmadheyyaṃ labhissati.

'Having reviled ascetics, virtuous and taintless ones, through the result of his evil action, he will obtain a certain name.'

“Tassa [M 1.0082] dhamme sudāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Kuṇḍadhānoti nāmena, sāvako so bhavissati.

'A true heir in his Dhamma, his own son, fashioned by the Dhamma, that disciple will be known by the name of Kuṇḍadhāna.'

“Pavivekamanuyutto, jhāyī jhānarato ahaṃ;

Tosayitvāna satthāraṃ, viharāmi anāsavo.

'Devoted to solitude, meditative, delighting in jhāna, I, having satisfied the Teacher, dwell taintless.'

“Sāvakehi parivuto, bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhato;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, salākaṃ gāhayī jino.

'Surrounded by disciples, with the Saṅgha of monks at the forefront, the Victor, seated amidst the Saṅgha of monks, had the lots taken.'

“Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, vanditvā lokanāyakaṃ;

Vadataṃ varassa purato, paṭhamaṃ aggahesahaṃ.

'Arranging my robe over one shoulder and paying homage to the Leader of the World, I was the first to take the lot before the best of speakers.'

“Tena kammena bhagavā, dasasahassikampako;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi maṃ.

'By that deed, the Blessed One, who shakes the ten-thousand-world system, seated amidst the Saṅgha of monks, established me in the foremost position.'

“Vīriyaṃ [V 1.0068] me dhuradhorayhaṃ, yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

'My energy is like a beast of burden, leading to security from the yokes; I bear this final body in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

'My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Evaṃbhūtassapi imassa therassa guṇe ajānantā ye puthujjanā bhikkhū tadā paṭhamaṃ salākaggahaṇe “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti samacintesuṃ. Tesaṃ vimatividhamanatthaṃ thero ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā aññāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto “pañca chinde”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Although such were the virtues of this elder, those worldling monks who did not know his qualities wondered at the first taking of the lots, 'What, indeed, is this?' To dispel their doubt, the elder rose into the sky, displayed a miracle of psychic power, and, declaring his final knowledge through an indirect reference, uttered the verse beginning, 'Five one should cut off.'

15. Tattha pañca chindeti apāyūpapattinibbattanakāni pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pāde bandhanarajjukaṃ viya puriso satthena heṭṭhimamaggattayena chindeyya pajaheyya. Pañca jaheti uparidevalokūpapattihetubhūtāni pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni puriso gīvāya bandhanarajjukaṃ viya arahattamaggena jaheyya, chindeyya vāti attho. Pañca cuttari bhāvayeti tesaṃyeva uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya saddhādīni pañcindriyāni uttari anāgāmimaggādhigamato upari bhāveyya aggamaggādhigamavasena vaḍḍheyya. Pañcasaṅgātigoti evaṃbhūto pana pañcannaṃ rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhisaṅgānaṃ atikkamanena pahānena pañcasaṅgātigo hutvā. Bhikkhu [M 1.0083] oghatiṇṇoti vuccatīti sabbathā bhinnakilesatāya bhikkhūti, kāmabhavadiṭṭhiavijjoghe taritvā tesaṃ pārabhūte nibbāne ṭhitoti ca vuccatīti attho.

15. Therein, 'five one should cut off' means that one should cut off and abandon the five lower fetters, which cause rebirth in the lower realms, with the three lower paths, just as a person might cut a rope bound to their feet with a sword. 'Five one should abandon' means that one should abandon and cut off with the path of Arahantship the five higher fetters, which are the cause for rebirth in the upper celestial worlds, just as a person might abandon or cut a rope bound to their neck. This is the meaning. 'Five one should further develop' means that for the abandonment of those same higher fetters, one should further develop the five faculties, such as faith, beyond the attainment of the non-returner's path, and augment them by means of attaining the highest path. 'One who has transcended the five attachments' means that such a person, by transcending and abandoning the five attachments of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views, has become one who has transcended the five attachments. 'A monk is called one who has crossed the flood' means that he is a 'bhikkhu' because his defilements are completely broken, and he is so called because, having crossed the floods of sensuality, existence, views, and ignorance, he stands on the far shore, which is Nibbāna.

Kuṇḍadhānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna is concluded.

6. Belaṭṭhasīsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa

Yathāpi [P 1.0071] bhaddo ājaññoti āyasmato belaṭṭhasīsattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto upanissayasampattiyā abhāvena visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ pana bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito ekatiṃse kappe vessabhuṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannacitto mātuluṅgaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devesu nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatito sugatiṃ upagacchanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatto bhagavato abhisambodhiyā puretarameva uruvelakassapassa [V 1.0069] santike tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aggiṃ paricaranto uruvelakassapadamane ādittapariyāyadesanāya (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28) purāṇajaṭilasahassena saddhiṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.68-73) –

"Just as a noble thoroughbred..."—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family. After approaching the Blessed One, hearing the Dhamma, and gaining faith, he went forth and practiced the ascetic's duties. However, due to a lack of supportive conditions, he was unable to bring about any spiritual distinction. But having accumulated much merit that serves as a supportive condition for liberation, he wandered among devas and humans. Then, thirty-one aeons ago, he saw the Blessed One Vessabhū, and with a confident mind, he gave a citron fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas. Performing meritorious deeds again and again, he went from one happy state of existence to another, until, during this Buddha’s appearance, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. Even before the Blessed One’s supreme enlightenment, he undertook the ascetic life of a hermit under Uruvelakassapa. While tending the fire, at the time of the taming of Uruvelakassapa through the discourse on the Fire Sermon, he attained Arahantship along with the thousand former matted-hair ascetics. Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva jotantaṃ, puṇṇamāyeva candimaṃ;

Jalantaṃ dīparukkhaṃva, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

'I saw the Leader of the World, shining like a Kaṇikāra tree, like the moon on a full-moon day, blazing like a lamp-tree.'

“Mātuluṅgaphalaṃ gayha, adāsiṃ satthuno ahaṃ;

Dakkhiṇeyyassa vīrassa, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

'Taking a citron fruit, I gave it to the Teacher, the one worthy of offerings, the hero, pleased with my own hands.'

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

'Thirty-one aeons ago from now, when I gave that fruit, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of the gift of fruit.'

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

'My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0084] adhigatārahatto āyasmato dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa upajjhāyo ayaṃ thero ekadivasaṃ phalasamāpattito uṭṭhāya taṃ santaṃ paṇītaṃ nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ attano pubbayogañca paccavekkhitvā pītivegavasena “yathāpi bhaddo ājañño”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, this Elder, the preceptor of the Venerable Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika, having attained Arahantship, one day rose from the attainment of fruition and reflected on that peaceful, sublime, unworldly happiness and his own past practice. By the force of a surge of joy, he uttered the verse: "Just as a noble thoroughbred..."

16. Tattha yathāpīti opammapaṭipādanatthe nipāto. Bhaddoti sundaro thāmabalasamatthajavaparakkamādisampanno. Ājaññoti ājānīyo jātimā kāraṇākāraṇānaṃ ājānanako. So tividho usabhājañño assājañño hatthājaññoti. Tesu usabhājañño idhādhippeto. So ca kho chekakasanakicce niyutto, tenāha “naṅgalāvattanī”ti. Naṅgalassa phālassa āvattanako, naṅgalaṃ ito cito ca āvattetvā khette kasanakoti attho. Naṅgalaṃ vā āvattayati etthāti naṅgalāvattaṃ[P 1.0072], khette naṅgalapatho, tasmiṃ naṅgalāvattani. Gāthāsukhatthañhettha “vattanī”ti dīghaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Sikhīti matthake avaṭṭhānato sikhāsadisatāya sikhā, siṅgaṃ. Tadassa atthīti sikhī. Apare pana “kakudhaṃ idha ‘sikhā’ti adhippeta”nti vadanti, ubhayathāpi padhānaṅgakittanametaṃ “sikhī”ti. Appakasirenāti appakilamathena. Rattindivāti rattiyo divā ca, evaṃ mamaṃ appakasirena gacchantīti yojanā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā “bhaddo usabhājānīyo kasane niyutto ghanatiṇamūlādikepi naṅgalapathe taṃ agaṇento appakasirena ito cito ca parivattento gacchati, yāva kasanatiṇānaṃ parissamaṃ dasseti, evaṃ mamaṃ rattindivāpi appakasireneva gacchanti atikkamantī”ti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “sukhe laddhe nirāmise”ti. Yasmā kāmāmisalokāmisavaṭṭāmisehi [V 1.0070] asammissaṃ santaṃ paṇītaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ laddhaṃ, tasmāti attho. Paccatte cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ yathā “vanappagumbe” (khu. pā. 6.13; su. ni. 236) “tena vata re vattabbe”ti (kathā. 1) ca. Atha vā tato pabhuti rattindivā appakasirena gacchantīti vicāraṇāya āha – “sukhe laddhe nirāmise”ti, nirāmise sukhe laddhe sati tassa laddhakālato paṭṭhāyāti attho.

16. Herein, ‘just as’ is a particle used to introduce a simile. ‘Noble’ means beautiful, endowed with strength, power, capability, speed, and energy. ‘Thoroughbred’ refers to one of high breed, one who knows cause and non-cause. It is of three kinds: a bull thoroughbred, a horse thoroughbred, and an elephant thoroughbred. Here, the bull thoroughbred is intended. And it is yoked to the task of skillful plowing, hence it is said to be ‘the plow-turner.’ It is the turner of the plow, of the share; it plows in the field by turning the plow this way and that—this is the meaning. Or, it is a ‘plow-turning’ (naṅgalāvattaṃ) because the plow is turned in it; this is the plow’s path in the field, and ‘in that plow-turning’ (naṅgalāvattani) refers to that. For the sake of metrical ease in the verse, it is stated with a long vowel as ‘vattanī.’ ‘Crested’ (sikhī): because it stands on the head and is like a crest (sikhā), it is a crest, a horn. Because it has this, it is ‘crested.’ Others, however, say that ‘hump’ (kakudhaṃ) is intended here by ‘sikhā’; in either case, this word ‘crested’ is a mention of a prominent feature. ‘With little effort’ means with little fatigue. ‘Day and night’ means nights and days; thus the connection is: ‘they pass for me with little effort.’ This is what is said: just as a noble thoroughbred bull, yoked to plowing, goes on with little effort, turning this way and that, disregarding even dense grass, roots, and so on in the plow’s path, so as to overcome the toil of plowing the grass, so too for me the days and nights pass with little effort, they are transcended. Therein, he states the reason with ‘having attained the unworldly happiness.’ Because the peaceful, sublime happiness of the attainment of fruition has been attained, which is unmixed with the worldliness of sensual pleasures, the worldliness of the world, and the worldliness of the round of existence, therefore—this is the meaning. And this locative case is used in the sense of the nominative, as in ‘in the forest thicket’ and ‘by that, sir, it should be said.’ Alternatively, in response to the consideration that from that time onward his days and nights passed with little effort, he says: ‘having attained the unworldly happiness,’ meaning, when the unworldly happiness was attained, from the time of its attainment onward—this is the meaning.

Belaṭṭhasīsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa is concluded.

7. Dāsakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dāsaka

Middhī [M 1.0085] yadāti āyasmato dāsakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ito ekanavute kappe anuppanne tathāgate ajitassa nāma paccekabuddhassa gandhamādanato manussapathaṃ otaritvā aññatarasmiṃ gāme piṇḍāya carantassa manoramāni ambaphalāni adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle sāsane pabbajitvā vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ puññaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ kusalakammappasuto hutvā sugatito [P 1.0073] sugatiṃ upagacchanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatti. Dāsakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā vihārapaṭijagganakamme ṭhapito sakkaccaṃ vihāraṃ paṭijagganto abhiṇhaṃ buddhadassanena dhammassavanena ca paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji. Keci pana bhaṇanti – “ayaṃ kassapassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto aññataraṃ khīṇāsavattheraṃ upaṭṭhahanto kiñci kammaṃ kārāpetukāmo theraṃ āṇāpesi. So tena kammena amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthiyaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa dāsiyā kucchimhi nibbatto vayappatto seṭṭhinā vihārapaṭijaggane ṭhapito vuttanayeneva paṭiladdhasaddho ahosi. Mahāseṭṭhi tassa sīlācāraṃ ajjhāsayañca ñatvā bhujissaṃ katvā ‘yathāsukhaṃ pabbajā’ti āha. Taṃ bhikkhū pabbājesu”nti. So pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya kusīto hīnavīriyo hutvā na kiñci vattapaṭivattaṃ karoti, kuto samaṇadhammaṃ, kevalaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā niddābahulo viharati. Dhammassavanakālepi ekaṃ koṇaṃ pavisitvā parisapariyante nisinno ghurughurupassāsī niddāyateva. Athassa bhagavā pubbūpanissayaṃ oloketvā saṃvegajananatthaṃ “middhī yadā hoti mahagghaso cā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

‘When one is sluggish…’ is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dāsaka. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one eons ago from the present, when a Tathāgata had not arisen, he gave delightful mango fruits to a Paccekabuddha named Ajita, who had descended from Mount Gandhamādana to the human world and was walking for alms in a certain village. Through that meritorious deed, while wandering among devas and humans, he went forth in the Dispensation during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa and performed much merit that is a basis for release from the round of existence. Thus, devoted to wholesome deeds and passing from one good destination to another, during this Buddha-era he was reborn in a family home in Sāvatthī. His name was Dāsaka. He was appointed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika to the task of maintaining the monastery. While diligently looking after the monastery, he frequently saw the Buddha and heard the Dhamma, and having thereby gained faith, he went forth. Some, however, say: “This one was born in a family home during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Having reached maturity, while attending on a certain elder who was an arahant, he wished to have some work done and gave an order to the elder. Due to that deed, during the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in the womb of a female slave of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he was appointed by the great merchant to maintain the monastery and, in the way described, gained faith. The great merchant, knowing his virtuous conduct and disposition, made him a free man and said, ‘Go forth as you please.’ The monks then gave him the going forth.” From the time he went forth, he was lazy and of low energy. He did not perform any of the duties, major or minor—how then could he practice the Dhamma of a recluse? He simply ate as much as he wanted and lived full of sleepiness. Even at the time of a Dhamma discourse, he would go into a corner, sit at the edge of the assembly, and, breathing with a snore, would just sleep. Then the Blessed One, seeing his past supporting conditions, uttered the verse beginning, ‘When one is sluggish and a glutton,’ in order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency.

17. Tattha middhīti thinamiddhābhibhūto, yañhi middhaṃ abhibhavati, taṃ thinampi abhibhavateva. Yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Mahagghasoti mahābhojano, āharahatthakaalaṃsāṭakatatthavaṭṭakakākamāsakabhuttavamitakānaṃ [V 1.0071] aññataro viya. Niddāyitāti supanasīlo. Samparivattasāyīti samparivattakaṃ samparivattakaṃ nipajjitvā ubhayenapi seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ [M 1.0086] anuyuttoti dasseti. Nivāpapuṭṭhoti kuṇḍakādinā sūkarabhattena puṭṭho bharito. Gharasūkaro hi bālakālato paṭṭhāya posiyamāno thūlasarīrakāle gehā bahi nikkhamituṃ alabhanto heṭṭhāmañcādīsu [P 1.0074] samparivattetvā samparivattetvā sayateva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadā puriso middhī ca hoti mahagghaso ca nivāpapuṭṭho mahāvarāho viya aññena iriyāpathena yāpetuṃ asakkonto niddāyanasīlo samparivattasāyī, tadā so “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti tīṇi lakkhaṇāni manasikātuṃ na sakkoti. Tesaṃ amanasikārā mandapañño punappunaṃ gabbhaṃ upeti, gabbhāvāsato na parimuccatevāti. Taṃ sutvā dāsakatthero saṃvegajāto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.74, 80-84) –

17. Therein, ‘sluggish’ means overcome by sloth and torpor; for what torpor overcomes, sloth also overcomes. ‘When’ means at which time. ‘A glutton’ means one with a large meal, like one of those such as Āharahatthaka, Alaṃsāṭaka, Tatthavaṭṭaka, Kākamāsaka, or Bhuttavamitaka. ‘A sleeper’ means one who is disposed to sleeping. ‘Lying down rolling about’ shows that, having lain down rolling over and over, he is devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of his side, and the pleasure of drowsiness. ‘Nourished on fodder’ means nourished and filled with pig-feed such as bran. For a domestic pig, being raised from a young age, becomes large-bodied and, unable to exit the house, just lies sleeping, rolling over and over under beds and so on. This is what is said: when a person is sluggish and a glutton, nourished on fodder like a great boar, unable to maintain himself in any other posture, disposed to sleeping and lying down rolling about, then he is unable to pay attention to the three characteristics: ‘impermanent, suffering, non-self.’ Due to not paying attention to them, he is of dull wisdom and enters a womb again and again; he is not freed from dwelling in the womb. Hearing that, Elder Dāsaka, with a sense of spiritual urgency arisen, established insight and before long realized arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Ajito nāma sambuddho, himavante vasī tadā;

Caraṇena ca sampanno, samādhikusalo muni.

“A Sambuddha named Ajita, at that time dwelt in the Himālaya; he was a sage endowed with virtuous conduct and skilled in concentration.”

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇe sambuddhe, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahe;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjante, ambaphalamadāsahaṃ.

“When the golden-hued Sambuddha, a worthy recipient of offerings, was walking along the road, I gave a mango fruit.”

“Ekanavute ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago from this one, for the fruit I gave then, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of that gift of fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero imāya gāthāya maṃ bhagavā ovadi, “ayaṃ gāthā mayhaṃ aṅkusabhūtā”ti tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi. Tayidaṃ therassa parivattāhāranayena aññābyākaraṇaṃ jātaṃ.

Having attained arahantship, the elder recited that very same verse, thinking, “The Blessed One admonished me with this verse; this verse was my goad.” Thus, this became the elder’s declaration of final knowledge by way of the method of transference.

Dāsakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Dāsaka is concluded.

8. Siṅgālapituttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Siṅgālapitā

Ahu buddhassa dāyādoti siṅgālakapituttherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ito catunavute kappe sataraṃsiṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā attano hatthagataṃ tālaphalaṃ adāsi. Tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ [M 1.0087] puññāni katvā [V 1.0072] sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle manussayoniyaṃ nibbatto sāsane paṭiladdhasaddho hutvā pabbajitvā aṭṭhikasaññaṃ bhāvesi. Puna imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto dārapariggahaṃ katvā ekaṃ puttaṃ labhitvā tassa “siṅgālako”ti nāmaṃ akāsi. Tena [P 1.0075] naṃ siṅgālakapitāti voharanti. So aparabhāge gharabandhanaṃ pahāya sāsane pabbaji. Tassa bhagavā ajjhāsayaṃ olokento aṭṭhikasaññākammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane, athassa tasmiṃ vane adhivatthā devatā ussāhajananatthaṃ “bhāvanāphalaṃ nacirasseva hatthagataṃ karissatī”ti imamatthaṃ aññāpadesena vibhāventī “ahu buddhassa dāyādo”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

"He was an heir of the Buddha": this is the verse of the Elder Siṅgālakapitu. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-four aeons ago from the present, he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsi wandering for almsfood and, with a serene mind, paid homage and offered a palm fruit that was in his hand. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas. Subsequently performing meritorious deeds again and again and wandering only in happy destinations, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in the human realm. Having gained faith in the Dispensation, he went forth and developed the perception of a skeleton. Again, during this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a good family in Sāvatthī. Having come of age, he took a wife and had a son, whom he named "Siṅgālaka." For that reason, they called him Siṅgālakapitā. In later life, abandoning the bonds of the household, he went forth in the Dispensation. The Blessed One, discerning his inclination, gave him the meditation subject of the perception of a skeleton. Taking it, he dwelt among the Bhaggas on Mount Susumāra in the Bhesakaḷā Forest. Then, a deity dwelling in that forest, wishing to generate enthusiasm in him, revealed this meaning by way of allusion, thinking, "The fruit of his meditation will soon be within his grasp," and spoke this verse: "He was an heir of the Buddha."

18. Tattha ahūti hoti, vattamānatthe hi idaṃ atītakālavacanaṃ. Buddhassāti sabbaññubuddhassa. Dāyādoti dhammadāyādo navavidhassa lokuttaradhammadāyassa attano sammāpaṭipattiyā ādāyako gaṇhanako. Atha vā ahūti ahosi. Evaṃnāmassa buddhassa dāyādabhāve koci vibandho idāneva bhavissatīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “maññehaṃ kāmarāgaṃ so, khippameva vahissatī”ti. Bhesakaḷāvaneti bhesakena nāma yakkhena labhitattā pariggahitattā, bhesakaḷānaṃ vā kaṭṭhādīnaṃ bahulatāya “bhesakaḷāvana”nti laddhanāme araññe. Tassa bhikkhuno buddhassa dāyādabhāve kāraṇaṃ vadanto “kevalaṃ aṭṭhisaññāya, apharī pathaviṃ ima”nti āha. Tattha kevalanti sakalaṃ anavasesaṃ. Aṭṭhisaññāyāti aṭṭhikabhāvanāya. Apharīti “aṭṭhī”ti adhimuccanavasena patthari. Pathavinti attabhāvapathaviṃ. Attabhāvo hi idha “pathavī”ti vutto “ko imaṃ pathaviṃ viccessatī”tiādīsu viya. Maññehanti maññe ahaṃ. “Maññāha”ntipi pāṭho. Soti so bhikkhu. Khippameva nacirasseva kāmarāgaṃ pahissati pajahissatīti maññe. Kasmā? Aṭṭhikasaññāya kāmarāgassa ujupaṭipakkhabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo ekasmiṃ padese laddhāya atthikasaññāya sakalaṃ attano sabbesaṃ vā attabhāvaṃ [M 1.0088] “aṭṭhī”tveva pharitvā ṭhito, so bhikkhu taṃ aṭṭhikajhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanto nacireneva anāgāmimaggena kāmarāgaṃ[P 1.0076], sabbaṃ vā kāmanaṭṭhena “kāmo”, rañjanaṭṭhena “rāgo”ti ca laddhanāmaṃ taṇhaṃ aggamaggena pajahissatīti. Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā so thero “ayaṃ devatā mayhaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ evamāhā”ti appaṭivānavīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.85-90) –

18. Therein, 'ahū' means 'is' (hoti), for this past-tense word is used in the present sense. 'Buddhassa' refers to the Omniscient Buddha. 'Dāyādo' means an heir to the Dhamma, one who receives and acquires the ninefold supramundane Dhamma through his own correct practice. Alternatively, 'ahū' means 'was' (ahosi). The intention is that there will now be no obstacle to his being an heir of such a Buddha. Therefore, it is said: "I think that he will quickly sweep away sensual lust." 'Bhesakaḷāvaneti' refers to a forest named 'Bhesakaḷāvana' because it was obtained and occupied by a yakkha named Bhesaka, or because of the abundance of Bhesakaḷā wood and so on. Stating the reason for that monk being an heir to the Buddha, it is said: "Through the perception of bones alone, he suffused this earth." Therein, 'kevalaṃ' means entirely, without remainder. 'Aṭṭhisaññāya' means by the cultivation of the perception of bones. 'Apharī' means he spread it out by way of resolving, "Bones." 'Pathaviṃ' means the earth of his own person. For here, one's own person is called 'earth,' as in passages like, "Who shall conquer this earth?" 'Maññehaṃ' means 'I think.' There is also the reading 'Maññāhaṃ.' 'So' means that monk. I think that 'khippameva,' very quickly, he will abandon sensual lust. Why? Because the perception of bones is the direct opposite of sensual lust. This is what is meant: a monk who, having acquired the perception of bones in one area, abides having suffused his entire person, or the persons of all, with the thought "Bones,"—that monk, making that bone-jhāna his foundation and practicing insight, will before long abandon sensual lust with the path of non-returning, or he will abandon all craving—which is named 'kāma' in the sense of desiring and 'rāga' in the sense of lusting—with the highest path. Having heard this verse, that elder thought, "This deity spoke thus to generate enthusiasm in me," and undertaking his practice with unwavering energy, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sataraṃsī nāma bhagavā, sayambhū aparājito;

Vivekā uṭṭhahitvāna, gocarāyābhinikkhami.

"The Blessed One named Sataraṃsi, the Self-Awakened, the Unconquered; having arisen from seclusion, went forth for his alms round."

“Phalahattho [V 1.0073] ahaṃ disvā, upagacchiṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, tālaphalamadāsahaṃ.

"Seeing him, I, with fruit in hand, approached the bull of men; with a serene and joyful mind, I gave a palm fruit."

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that fruit; I know of no unhappy destination since. This is the fruit of the gift of fruit."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done."

Arahattaṃ pana patvā tāya devatāya vuttavacanaṃ patimānento tameva gāthaṃ udānavasena abhāsi. Tadevassa therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Having attained Arahantship, honoring the words spoken by that deity, he uttered that very verse as an inspired utterance. That indeed was the elder's declaration of final knowledge.

Siṅgālapituttheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Siṅgālakapitu is concluded.

9. Kulattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Kula

Udakañhi nayantīti āyasmato kulattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira thero pubbepi vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā adhikārasampanno vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ ākāse gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso nāḷikeraphalaṃ dātukāmo aṭṭhāsi. Satthā tassa cittaṃ ñatvā otaritvā paṭiggaṇhi. So ativiya pasannacitto hutvā teneva saddhāpaṭilābhena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci, satthā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ [M 1.0089] āṇāpesi – “imaṃ purisaṃ pabbājehī”ti. So pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado samaṇadhammaṃ katvā tato cuto chapi buddhantarāni devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Kulotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto sāsane laddhappasādo bhagavato santike pabbajitvā vikkhepabahulatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Athekadivasaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisanto antarāmagge bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā [P 1.0077] udakavāhakaṃ katvā icchiticchitaṭṭhāne udakaṃ nente purise disvā taṃ sallakkhetvā gāmaṃ paviṭṭho aññataraṃ usukāraṃ usudaṇḍakaṃ usuyante pakkhipitvā akkhikoṭiyā oloketvā ujuṃ karontaṃ disvā tampi sallakkhetvā gacchanto purato gantvā araneminābhiādike rathacakkāvayave tacchante tacchake disvā tampi sallakkhetvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā katabhattakicco pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā divāvihāre nisinno attanā diṭṭhanimittāni upamābhāvena gahetvā attano cittadamane upanento “acetanaṃ udakampi manussā icchikicchitaṭṭhānaṃ nayanti tathā acetanaṃ vaṅkampi saradaṇḍaṃ upāyena namento ujuṃ karonti[V 1.0074], tathā acetanaṃ kaṭṭhakaḷiṅgarādiṃ tacchakā nemiādivasena vaṅkaṃ ujuñca karonti. Atha kasmā ahaṃ sakacittaṃ ujuṃ na karissāmī”ti cintetvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.91-99) –

"Indeed, they lead water": this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kula. What is its origin? It is said that this elder, in a past life, having accumulated much merit that was a supporting condition for liberation and being endowed with the necessary qualifications, saw the Blessed One Vipassī traveling through the sky and, with a serene mind, stood wishing to offer a coconut. The Teacher, knowing his thought, descended and accepted it. He, being exceedingly serene in mind, through that very gain of faith, approached the Teacher and asked for the going forth. The Teacher commanded a certain monk, "Go forth this man." Having gone forth and received the higher ordination, he fulfilled the duties of a recluse. Passing away from there, he wandered among devas and humans for six Buddha-intervals. During this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. His name was Kula. Having come of age and gained faith in the Dispensation, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, but due to much distraction, he was unable to bring about any distinction. Then one day, while entering a village for almsfood, he saw on the way men who were digging the earth, making an irrigation channel, and leading the water to whatever place they wished. Noting this, he entered the village. He saw a fletcher who, having placed an arrow-shaft in a straightening tool, was looking with the corner of his eye and making it straight. Noting this as well and proceeding on, he saw carpenters ahead of him shaping the components of a chariot wheel, such as the felloe, spokes, and hub. Noting this as well, he entered the monastery. Having finished his meal and put away his bowl and robe, he sat down for his day's abiding. Taking the signs he had seen as similes, he applied them to the taming of his own mind: "People lead even insentient water to any place they wish. Likewise, by means of a device, they make even a crooked, insentient arrow-shaft straight. Likewise, carpenters make insentient pieces of wood crooked or straight for things like wheel-rims. Why, then, should I not make my own mind straight?" Thinking thus, he established insight, and by striving and making an effort, he attained arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nagare bandhumatiyā, ārāmiko ahaṃ tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, gacchantaṃ anilañjase.

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a park-keeper then; I saw the dust-free Buddha, traveling on the path of the wind."

“Nāḷikeraphalaṃ gayha, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Ākāse ṭhitako santo, paṭiggaṇhi mahāyaso.

"Taking a coconut fruit, I gave it to the best of Buddhas; standing in the sky, the greatly renowned one accepted it."

“Vittisañjanano mayhaṃ, diṭṭhadhammasukhāvaho;

Phalaṃ buddhassa datvāna, vippasannena cetasā.

"Generating joy for me, bringing happiness in this very life; having given the fruit to the Buddha with an utterly serene mind,"

“Adhigacchiṃ tadā pītiṃ, vipulañca sukhuttamaṃ;

Uppajjateva ratanaṃ, nibbattassa tahiṃ tahiṃ.

Then I attained joy, abundant and supreme bliss; indeed, treasure arose for me wherever I was reborn.

“Ekanavutito [M 1.0090] kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of giving a fruit.

“Dibbacakkhu visuddhaṃ me, samādhikusalo ahaṃ;

Abhiññāpāramippatto, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

My divine eye is purified; I am skilled in concentration. I have attained the perfection of direct knowledges; this is the fruit of giving a fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.

Evaṃ yāni nimittāni aṅkuse katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, tehi saddhiṃ attano cittadamanaṃ saṃsanditvā aññaṃ byākaronto “udakañhi nayanti nettikā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, having made these similes a goad, developing insight, he attained Arahantship. Comparing his own taming of the mind with those examples, he made a further declaration, reciting the verse: “Irrigators indeed guide water…”

19. Tattha udakaṃ hīti hi-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Nayantīti pathaviyā taṃ taṃ thalaṭṭhānaṃ khaṇitvā ninnaṭṭhānaṃ pūretvā mātikaṃ vā katvā rukkhadoṇiṃ vā ṭhapetvā attano icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ nenti. Tathā te nentīti nettikā. Tejananti kaṇḍaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nettikā attano ruciyā icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ nayanti, usukārāpi tāpetvā tejanaṃ namayanti ujuṃ karonti. Namanavasena tacchakā nemiādīnaṃ atthāya tacchantā dāruṃ namayanti attano ruciyā ujuṃ vā vaṅkaṃ vā karonti. Evaṃ ettakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ [P 1.0078] katvā subbatā yathāsamādinnena [V 1.0075] sīlādinā sundaravatā dhīrā sotāpattimaggādīnaṃ uppādentā attānaṃ damenti, arahattaṃ pana pattesu ekantadantā nāma hontīti.

19. Therein, in 'udakaṃ hi,' the word 'hi' is merely a particle. 'They guide' means that by digging up high ground on the earth and filling in low ground, or by making a channel, or by placing a wooden trough, they lead the water to whatever place they wish. Because they lead it thus, they are called 'leaders' (irrigators). 'Tejana' means an arrow. This is what is meant: irrigators, according to their liking, guide water to any place they wish; fletchers, by heating it, bend the arrow-shaft and make it straight. By way of bending, carpenters, while shaping wood for the purpose of wheel-rims and so on, bend the wood, making it straight or crooked according to their liking. In the same way, the wise, of good vows, with virtue and so on well-undertaken as they are, having made this much their object of meditation, tame themselves while giving rise to the path of stream-entry and so on. But when they have attained Arahantship, they are called 'completely tamed'.

Kulattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kula is concluded.

10. Ajitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajita

Maraṇe me bhayaṃ natthīti āyasmato ajitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ekanavute kappe vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannacitto kapitthaphalaṃ adāsi. Tato parampi taṃ taṃ puññaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ kappe anuppanne eva amhākaṃ satthari sāvatthiyaṃ mahākosalarañño aggāsaniyassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tassa ajitoti nāmaṃ ahosi. Tasmiñca samaye [M 1.0091] sāvatthivāsī bāvarī nāma brāhmaṇo tīhi mahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sāvatthito nikkhamitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā godhāvarītīre kapitthārāme vasati. Atha ajito tassa santike pabbajito atthakāmāya devatāya coditena bāvarinā satthu santikaṃ pesito tissametteyyādīhi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā manasāva pañhe pucchitvā tesu vissajjitesu pasannacitto satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.7-11) –

“For me there is no fear of death” is the verse of the venerable Elder Ajita. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-one aeons ago, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a confident mind he gave a wood-apple fruit. Thereafter, performing this and that merit, wandering among gods and humans, in this aeon, before our Teacher had arisen, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a brahmin who was the chief counselor to King Mahākosala. His name was Ajita. And at that time, a brahmin from Sāvatthī named Bāvarī, endowed with the three marks of a great man and a master of the three Vedas, left Sāvatthī, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt in a wood-apple hermitage on the bank of the Godhāvarī river. Then Ajita, having gone forth in his presence, was sent by Bāvarī—who had been urged by a deity desiring his welfare—to the Teacher. Approaching the Blessed One together with Tissametteyya and others, he asked questions with his mind alone. When these were answered, with a confident mind, he went forth in the Teacher's presence, took up a meditation subject, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, kapitthaṃ adadiṃ phalaṃ.

Seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One, of golden complexion, worthy of offerings, walking along the street, I gave a wood-apple fruit.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ dadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of giving a fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patto sīhanādaṃ nadanto “maraṇe me bhayaṃ natthī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained Arahantship, roaring a lion's roar, he spoke the verse: “For me there is no fear of death.”

20. Tattha maraṇeti maraṇanimittaṃ maraṇahetu. Meti mayhaṃ, bhayaṃ natthi ucchinnabhavamūlatāya parikkhīṇajātikattā[P 1.0079]. Anucchinnabhavamūlānañhi “kīdisī nu kho mayhaṃ āyatiṃ uppattī”ti maraṇato bhayaṃ bhaveyya. Nikantīti apekkhā taṇhā, sā natthi jīvite suparimadditasaṅkhāratāya [V 1.0076] upādānakkhandhānaṃ dukkhāsārakādibhāvena suṭṭhu upaṭṭhahanato. Evaṃbhūto cāhaṃ sandehaṃ sarīraṃ, sakaṃ vā dehaṃ dehasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhabhāraṃ nikkhipissāmi chaḍḍessāmi, nikkhipanto ca “‘iminā sarīrakena sādhetabbaṃ sādhitaṃ, idāni taṃ ekaṃsena chaḍḍanīyamevā’ti paññāvepullappattiyā sampajāno sativepullappattiyā paṭissato nikkhipissāmī”ti. Imaṃ pana gāthaṃ vatvā thero jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tadanantaraṃ parinibbāyīti.

20. Therein, 'of death' means on account of death, for the reason of death. 'For me' means for me. 'There is no fear' because the root of existence has been cut off, because rebirth has been exhausted. For those whose root of existence has not been cut off, there would indeed be fear of death, thinking, “Of what kind will my future birth be?” 'Longing' means craving of attachment; that does not exist in regard to life, because formations have been thoroughly crushed, and because the aggregates of clinging are well-established as being suffering, without substance, and so on. Being thus, I will lay down this aggregate of a body, or my own body, this burden of suffering designated as a body; I will cast it off. And in laying it down, thinking, 'What was to be accomplished by this body has been accomplished; now it is to be cast off completely,' I will lay it down, fully aware through having attained the fullness of wisdom, and mindful through having attained the fullness of mindfulness. Having spoken this verse, the Elder entered into jhāna and immediately after that, he attained final Nibbāna.

Ajitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajita is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Nigrodhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nigrodha

Nāhaṃ [M 1.0092][V 1.0077] bhayassa bhāyāmīti āyasmato nigrodhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira ito aṭṭhārase kappasate brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ disvā gharabandhanaṃ pahāya araññāyatanaṃ pavisitvā aññatarasmiṃ sālavane paṇṇasālaṃ katvā tāpasapabbajaṃ pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhāro vasati. Tena samayena piyadassī nāma sammāsambuddho loke uppajjitvā sadevakassa lokassa dhammāmatavassena kilesasantāpaṃ nibbāpento ekadivasaṃ tāpase anukampāya taṃ sālavanaṃ pavisitvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpanno. Tāpaso vanamūlaphalatthāya gacchanto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pupphitasāladaṇḍasākhāyo gahetvā sālamaṇḍapaṃ katvā taṃ sabbatthakameva sālapupphehi sañchādetvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pītisomanassavaseneva āhāratthāyapi agantvā namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Satthā nirodhato vuṭṭhāya tassa anukampāya “bhikkhusaṅgho āgacchatū”ti cintesi, “bhikkhusaṅghepi [P 1.0080] cittaṃ pasādessatī”ti. Tāvadeva bhikkhusaṅgho āgato. So bhikkhusaṅghampi disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Satthā sitassa pātukaraṇāpadesena tassa bhāviniṃ sampattiṃ pakāsento dhammaṃ kathetvā pakkāmi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. So tena puññakammena devamanussesuyeva saṃsaranto vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatti, nigrodhotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So jetavanapaṭiggahaṇadivase buddhānubhāvadassanena sañjātappasādo pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.190-220) –

“I do not fear what is fearful” is the verse of the venerable Elder Nigrodha. What is its origin? It is said that eighteen hundred aeons ago, he was born into a great and wealthy brahmin family. Having come of age, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, he abandoned the fetters of the home, entered the wilderness, and in a certain sāla grove, he built a leaf-hut, went forth into the ascetic life, and lived on the roots and fruits of the forest. At that time, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Piyadassī arose in the world and, with the rain of the deathless Dhamma, extinguished the fever of defilements for the world with its gods. One day, out of compassion for the ascetics, he entered that sāla grove and entered the attainment of cessation. The ascetic, while going for forest roots and fruits, saw the Blessed One and, with a confident mind, took flowering sāla branches, made a sāla pavilion, covered it completely with sāla flowers, and paid homage to the Blessed One. Out of joy and gladness, he did not even go for food but stood there paying respects. The Teacher, having emerged from cessation, out of compassion for him, thought, “Let the Saṅgha of monks come,” and, “He will also make his mind confident towards the Saṅgha of monks.” At that very moment, the Saṅgha of monks arrived. Seeing the Saṅgha of monks as well, with a confident mind, he paid homage and stood with his hands raised in reverence. The Teacher, on the pretext of revealing a smile, indicating his future success, taught the Dhamma and departed with the Saṅgha of monks. Through that meritorious deed, wandering only among gods and humans, he accumulated much wholesome karma that was a support for liberation. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a great and wealthy brahmin family; his name was Nigrodha. On the day of the dedication of the Jeta Grove, with confidence arisen from seeing the Buddha's power, he went forth, began insight meditation, and in no long time became endowed with the six direct knowledges. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Ajjhogāhetvā sālavanaṃ, sukato assamo mama;

Sālapupphehi sañchanno, vasāmi vipine tadā.

Having entered the sāla forest, my hermitage was well-made; covered with sāla flowers, I dwelt in the woods then.

“Piyadassī [M 1.0093] ca bhagavā, sayambhū aggapuggalo;

Vivekakāmo sambuddho, sālavanamupāgami.

And the Blessed One Piyadassī, the Self-become, the foremost person, the Perfectly Enlightened One desiring seclusion, approached the sāla forest.

“Assamā [V 1.0078] abhinikkhamma, pavanaṃ agamāsahaṃ;

Mūlaphalaṃ gavesanto, āhindāmi vane tadā.

Leaving the hermitage, I went to the forest; seeking roots and fruits, I wandered in the woods then.

“Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, piyadassiṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Sunisinnaṃ samāpannaṃ, virocantaṃ mahāvane.

There I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One, Piyadassī of great fame, well-seated, in attainment, shining in the great forest.

“Catudaṇḍe ṭhapetvāna, buddhassa uparī ahaṃ;

Maṇḍapaṃ sukataṃ katvā, sālapupphehi chādayiṃ.

Having placed four poles, I made a well-constructed pavilion over the Buddha and covered it with sāla flowers.

“Sattāhaṃ dhārayitvāna, maṇḍapaṃ sālachāditaṃ;

Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, buddhaseṭṭhamavandahaṃ.

Having maintained for seven days the pavilion covered with sāla, there, with a serene mind, I paid homage to the supreme Buddha.

“Bhagavā tamhi samaye, vuṭṭhahitvā samādhito;

Yugamattaṃ pekkhamāno, nisīdi purisuttamo.

The Blessed One at that time, the supreme among men, rising from his concentration and gazing a yoke's length, sat down.

“Sāvako varuṇo nāma, piyadassissa satthuno;

Vasīsatasahassehi, upagacchi vināyakaṃ.

A disciple named Varuṇa, of the Teacher Piyadassī, approached the Leader with a hundred thousand who had attained mastery.

“Piyadassī ca bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, sitaṃ pātukarī jino.

And the Blessed One Piyadassī, foremost in the world, a bull among men, seated amidst the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Conqueror, revealed a smile.

“Anuruddho upaṭṭhāko, piyadassissa satthuno;

Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, apucchittha mahāmuniṃ.

Anuruddha, the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassī, having arranged his robe over one shoulder, asked the Great Sage:

“Ko nu kho bhagavā hetu, sitakammassa satthuno;

Kāraṇe vijjamānamhi, satthā pātukare sitaṃ.

“What, indeed, O Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher’s act of smiling? When a reason is present, the Teacher reveals a smile.”

“Sattāhaṃ sālacchadanaṃ, yo me dhāresi māṇavo;

Tassa kammaṃ saritvāna, sitaṃ pātukariṃ ahaṃ.

“The youth who for seven days maintained a sāla covering for me—recalling his deed, I revealed a smile.”

“Anokāsaṃ na passāmi, yattha puññaṃ vipaccati;

Devaloke manusse vā, okāsova na sammati.

“I see no place where this merit would not ripen; whether in the world of devas or of humans, no such opportunity is found.”

“Devaloke vasantassa, puññakammasamaṅgino;

Yāvatā parisā tassa, sālacchannā bhavissati.

“For one dwelling in the world of devas, endowed with meritorious kamma, his entire assembly will be covered with sāla.”

“Tattha [M 1.0094] dibbehi naccehi, gītehi vāditehi ca;

Ramissati sadā santo, puññakammasamāhito.

“There, ever serene and composed through meritorious kamma, he will delight in divine dances, songs, and music.”

“Yāvatā parisā tassa, gandhagandhī bhavissati;

Sālassa pupphavasso ca, pavassissati tāvade.

“His entire assembly will be fragrant with scents, and at that very moment, a rain of sāla flowers will shower down.”

“Tato cutoyaṃ manujo, mānusaṃ āgamissati;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, sabbakālaṃ dharissati.

“Having passed away from there, this person will come to the human realm. Here too, he will always have a sāla covering.”

“Idha naccañca gītañca, sammatāḷasamāhitaṃ;

Parivāressanti maṃ niccaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Here, dance and song, accompanied by cymbals and rhythm, will constantly surround me. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Uggacchante [V 1.0079] ca sūriye, sālavassaṃ pavassate;

Puññakammena saṃyuttaṃ, vassate sabbakālikaṃ.

“When the sun is rising, a rain of sāla showers down; connected with meritorious kamma, it rains at all times.”

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma nāmena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“In eighteen hundred aeons from now, one born in the Okkāka lineage, Gotama by name, will be the Teacher in the world.”

“Tassa dhamme sudāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“A true heir to his Dhamma, a legitimate son created by the Dhamma, having fully comprehended all the taints, he, being taintless, will attain Nibbāna.”

“Dhammaṃ abhisamentassa, sālacchannaṃ bhavissati;

Citake jhāyamānassa, chadanaṃ tattha hessati.

“For him, while realizing the Dhamma, there will be a sāla covering; and while he is being consumed on the funeral pyre, there will be a covering there.”

“Vipākaṃ kittayitvāna, piyadassī mahāmuni;

Parisāya dhammaṃ desesi, tappento dhammavuṭṭhiyā.

Having proclaimed the fruition, Piyadassī, the Great Sage, taught the Dhamma to the assembly, satisfying them with a rain of Dhamma.

“Tiṃsakappāni devesu, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Saṭṭhi ca sattakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

“For thirty aeons I exercised sovereignty among the devas; and sixty-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.”

“Devalokā idhāgantvā, labhāmi vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, maṇḍapassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Having come here from the world of devas, I obtain abundant happiness. Here too, I have a sāla covering; this is the fruit of the pavilion.”

“Ayaṃ pacchimako mayhaṃ, carimo vattate bhavo;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, hessati sabbakālikaṃ.

“This is my last, my final existence. Here too, the sāla covering will be everlasting.”

“Mahāmuniṃ tosayitvā, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Pattomhi acalaṃ ṭhānaṃ, hitvā jayaparājayaṃ.

“Having satisfied the Great Sage, Gotama, the bull among the Sakyans, I have attained the unshakeable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.”

“Aṭṭhārase [M 1.0095] kappasate, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the eighteen hundred aeons since I worshipped that Buddha, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

“My defilements are burned up, all states of existence are uprooted; like a great elephant having broken its bonds, I dwell free of taints.”

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, buddhaseṭṭhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

“Truly, my coming to the presence of the supreme Buddha was a fortunate one. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

“Paṭisambhidā catasso, vimokkhāpi ca aṭṭhime;

Chaḷabhiññā sacchikatā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“The four analytical knowledges, and also the eight liberations, the six higher knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Evaṃ pana chaḷabhiñño hutvā phalasukhena vītināmento sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ aññābyākaraṇavasena “nāhaṃ bhayassa bhāyāmī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, having become endowed with the six higher knowledges and spending his time in the bliss of fruition, in order to demonstrate the liberating nature of the Dispensation, he spoke the verse, ‘I do not fear what is to be feared,’ by way of a declaration of final knowledge.

21. Tattha bhāyanti etasmāti bhayaṃ, jātijarādi. Bhayassāti nissakke sāmivacanaṃ, bhayato bhāyitabbanimittaṃ jātijarāmaraṇādinā hetunā nāhaṃ bhāyāmīti attho. Tattha kāraṇamāha [V 1.0080] “satthā no amatassa kovido”ti. Amhākaṃ satthā amate kusalo veneyyānaṃ amatadāne cheko. Yattha bhayaṃ nāvatiṭṭhatīti yasmiṃ nibbāne yathāvuttaṃ bhayaṃ na tiṭṭhati okāsaṃ na labhati. Tenāti tato nibbānato. Vajantīti abhayaṭṭhānameva gacchanti. Nibbānañhi abhayaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Kena pana vajantīti āha “maggena vajanti bhikkhavo”ti, aṭṭhaṅgikena ariyamaggena satthu ovādakaraṇā bhikkhū saṃsāre bhayassa ikkhanakāti attho. Yatthāti vā yaṃ nimittaṃ yassa ariyamaggassa [P 1.0081] adhigamahetu attānuvādādikaṃ pañcavīsatividhampi bhayaṃ nāvatiṭṭhati patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati, tena ariyena maggena vajanti abhayaṭṭhānaṃ satthu sāsane bhikkhū, tena maggena ahampi gato, tasmā nāhaṃ bhayassa bhāyāmīti thero aññaṃ byākāsi.

21. Herein, ‘fear’ (bhaya) is that from which they fear (bhāyanti), namely, birth, aging, and so forth. The phrase ‘of fear’ (bhayassa) is a genitive used in the sense of an ablative; the meaning is: ‘I do not fear out of fear (bhayato), that is, for the reason that should be feared (bhāyitabbanimittaṃ), namely birth, aging, death, and so on.’ Therein, he states the reason: ‘Our Teacher is skilled in the Deathless.’ Our Teacher is skilled in the Deathless, clever in bestowing the Deathless upon those who can be trained. ‘Where fear does not remain’ means that Nibbāna in which the aforesaid fear does not stand, finds no opportunity. ‘By that’ (tena) means from that Nibbāna. ‘They go’ (vajanti) means they go to the very state of fearlessness. For Nibbāna is indeed called the state of fearlessness. But by what do they go? He says, ‘The bhikkhus go by the path.’ The meaning is: by the Noble Eightfold Path, the bhikkhus, who act upon the Teacher’s instruction, are those who see fear in saṃsāra. Or, ‘where’ (yattha) means on account of which, for which reason—that is, because of the attainment of the Noble Path—the twenty-five kinds of fear, such as self-reproach, do not remain, do not find a footing. By that Noble Path the bhikkhus in the Teacher’s Dispensation go to the state of fearlessness. By that path I too have gone; therefore, ‘I do not fear what is to be feared.’ Thus the Elder declared his final knowledge.

Nigrodhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Nigrodha is complete.

2. Cittakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cittaka

Nīlāsugīvāti [M 1.0096] āyasmato cittakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarabuddhakālato paṭṭhāya vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ ācinanto ito ekanavute kappe manussayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā viññuttaṃ patto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso pupphehi pūjaṃ katvā vanditvā “santadhammena nāma ettha bhavitabba”nti satthari nibbāne ca adhimucci. So tena puññakammena tato cuto tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti cittako nāma nāmena. So bhagavati rājagahaṃ gantvā veḷuvane viharante satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññāyatanaṃ pavisitvā bhāvanānuyutto jhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānapādakaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacireneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.1-7) –

“Nīlāsugīva” is the verse of the venerable Elder Cittaka. What is its origin? It is said that from the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he accumulated wholesome karma that was a supporting condition for the rolling back of saṃsāra. Ninety-one aeons ago from now, having been reborn in a human womb and having reached discernment, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī. With a confident mind, he made an offering of flowers, paid homage, and became resolved upon the Teacher and upon Nibbāna, thinking, “There must be here what is called the peaceful Dhamma.” Through that meritorious kamma, having passed away from there, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Performing meritorious deeds again and again, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha, and was named Cittaka. When the Blessed One went to Rājagaha and was dwelling in the Veḷuvana, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. Having taken a meditation subject suitable to his disposition, he entered a forest abode and, being devoted to meditation, he produced the jhānas. Having developed insight with jhāna as its basis, in no long time he attained Arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva jotantaṃ, nisinnaṃ pabbatantare;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, vipassiṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Shining like a kaṇikāra tree, seated in a mountain cleft, I saw the dustless Buddha, Vipassī, the leader of the world.”

“Tīṇi kiṅkaṇipupphāni, paggayha abhiropayiṃ;

Sambuddhaṃ abhipūjetvā, gacchāmi dakkhiṇāmukho.

“Taking up three kiṅkaṇi flowers, I placed them as an offering. Having worshipped the Perfectly Enlightened One, I departed, facing south.”

“Tena [V 1.0081] kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsaṃ agacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.”

“Ekanavute ito kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first aeon from now, when I worshipped the Buddha, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… (and so on) … the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthāraṃ vandituṃ rājagahaṃ upagato tattha bhikkhūhi “kiṃ, āvuso, araññe appamatto vihāsī”ti puṭṭho attano appamādavihāranivedanena aññaṃ byākaronto “nīlāsugīvā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, he went to Rājagaha to pay respects to the Teacher. There, when asked by the monks, “Friend, did you dwell diligently in the forest?” he, indicating his own diligent dwelling, declared his final knowledge by speaking the verse beginning, “Nīlāsugīvā.”

22. Tattha [M 1.0097] nīlāsugīvāti nīlasugīvā, gāthāsukhatthañhettha dīgho [P 1.0082] kato, rājivantatāya sundarāya gīvāya samannāgatoti attho. Te yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇatāya nīlā. Sobhanakaṇṭhatāya sugīvā. Sikhinoti matthake jātāya sikhāya sassirikabhāvena sikhino. Morāti mayūrā. Kārambhiyanti kārambarukkhe. Kārambhiyanti vā tassa vanassa nāmaṃ. Tasmā kārambhiyanti kārambhanāmake vaneti attho. Abhinadantīti pāvussakāle meghagajjitaṃ sutvā kekāsaddaṃ karontā utusampadāsiddhena sarena haṃsādike abhibhavantā viya nadanti. Teti te morā. Sītavātakīḷitāti sītena meghavātena sañjātakīḷitā madhuravassitaṃ vassantā. Suttanti bhattasammadavinodanatthaṃ sayitaṃ, kāyakilamathapaṭipassambhanāya vā anuññātavelāyaṃ supantaṃ. Jhāyanti samathavipassanājhānehi jhāyanasīlaṃ bhāvanānuyuttaṃ. Nibodhentīti pabodhenti. “Imepi nāma niddaṃ anupagantvā jāgarantā attanā kattabbaṃ karonti, kimaṅgaṃ panāha”nti evaṃ sampajaññuppādanena sayanato vuṭṭhāpentīti adhippāyo.

22. Here, 'nīlāsugīvā' means blue-necked; the long vowel is used here for the sake of the verse's meter. The meaning is: endowed with a beautiful neck due to its stripes. For the most part, they are blue in color, thus 'nīlā.' Because of their beautiful throat, 'sugīvā.' 'Sikhino' means they are crested, being splendid by reason of the crest that has grown on their head. 'Morā' means peacocks. 'Kārambhiyanti' refers to the Kāramba tree. Or, 'Kārambhiyanti' is the name of that forest. Therefore, 'Kārambhiyanti' means in the forest named Kāramba. 'Abhinadanti' means that in the rainy season, upon hearing the thunder of the clouds, they make their 'kekā' sound, crying out as if surpassing geese and others with a voice perfected by the season's excellence. 'Te' means those peacocks. 'Sītavātakīḷitā' means, having begun to play in the cool monsoon wind, they utter sweet cries. 'Suttaṃ' refers to one who is lying down to dispel the drowsiness from a meal, or one who is sleeping at a permitted time to calm the body's fatigue. 'Jhāyanti' refers to one who is devoted to cultivation, with the nature of meditating through the absorptions of serenity and insight. 'Nibodhenti' means they awaken. The intention is: “Even these birds, not succumbing to sleep but remaining awake, do what they must do; what then of me?” Thus, by giving rise to clear comprehension, they cause one to rise from bed.

Cittakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cittaka is finished.

3. Gosālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gosāla

Ahaṃ kho veḷugumbasminti āyasmato gosālattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ ācinanto ito ekanavute kappe aññatarasmiṃ pabbate rukkhasākhāyaṃ olambamānaṃ paccekabuddhassa paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ disvā “arahaddhajo vatāya”nti pasannacitto pupphehi pūjehi. So tena puññakammena [P 1.0083] tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatto[V 1.0082]. Tato paṭṭhāya devamanussesuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe ibbhakule nibbatto gosālo nāma nāmena. Soṇena pana koṭikaṇṇena kataparicayattā tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā “sopi nāma mahāvibhavo pabbajissati[M 1.0098], kimaṅgaṃ panāha”nti sañjātasaṃvego bhagavato santike pabbajitvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sappāyaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gavesanto attano jātagāmassa avidūre ekasmiṃ sānupabbate vihāsi. Tassa mātā divase divase bhikkhaṃ deti. Athekadivasaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhassa mātā madhusakkharābhisaṅkhataṃ pāyāsaṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā tassa pabbatassa chāyāyaṃ aññatarassa veḷugumbassa mūle nisīditvā paribhuñjitvā dhovitapattapāṇī vipassanaṃ ārabhi. Bhojanasappāyalābhena kāyacittānaṃ kallatāya samāhito udayabbayañāṇādike tikkhe sūre vahante appakasireneva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā bhāvanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpento saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.8-14) –

“I am indeed in the bamboo thicket” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Gosāla. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under past Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma that served as a condition for liberation here and there, ninety-one eons ago, on a certain mountain, saw a rag-robe of a Paccekabuddha hanging from a tree branch. With a mind filled with faith, thinking, “This is indeed the banner of an Arahant!” he worshipped it with flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. From then on, wandering only through the realms of gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in the land of Magadha into a wealthy family, and was named Gosāla. Having been acquainted with Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa, upon hearing of his going forth, he thought, “Even he, so greatly wealthy, will go forth; what then of me?” Stirred by a sense of urgency, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, took up a meditation subject suitable to his temperament, and seeking a suitable dwelling place, he dwelled on a certain mountain slope not far from his native village. His mother gave him alms day by day. Then one day, when he had entered the village for alms, his mother gave him milk-rice porridge prepared with honey and sugar. Taking it, he sat at the foot of a certain bamboo grove in the shade of that mountain, ate it, and having washed his bowl and hands, he began insight meditation. Due to receiving suitable food, his body and mind became pliant. Being concentrated, with the knowledges of arising and passing away and so on being sharp, swift, and proceeding well, he diligently developed insight without much difficulty. Progressing through the stages of the path, he brought his cultivation to its culmination and realized arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassa avidūre, udaṅgaṇo nāma pabbato;

Tatthaddasaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, dumaggamhi vilambitaṃ.

“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa; there I saw a rag-robe, hanging on a treetop.

“Tīṇi kiṅkaṇipupphāni, ocinitvānahaṃ tadā;

Heṭṭhā pahaṭṭhena cittena, paṃsukūlaṃ apūjayiṃ.

“Having plucked three kiṅkaṇi flowers then, with a joyful mind I worshipped the rag-robe from below.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsaṃ agacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my intention and aspiration, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.

“Ekanavute ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pūjitvā arahaddhajaṃ.

“In the ninety-first eon from now, when I performed that deed, I do not know of an unhappy destination, having worshipped the banner of the Arahant.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana adhigantvā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ pabbatasānumeva gantukāmo attano paṭipattiṃ pavedento “ahaṃ kho veḷugumbasmi”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship and desiring to go to that same mountain slope for the sake of a pleasant abiding in this very life, he, declaring his own practice, uttered the verse beginning, “I am indeed in the bamboo thicket.”

23. Tattha veḷugumbasminti veḷugacchassa samīpe, tassa chāyāyaṃ. Bhutvāna madhupāyasanti madhupasittapāyāsaṃ bhuñjitvā. Padakkhiṇanti padakkhiṇaggāhena, satthu ovādassa sammā sampaṭicchanenāti attho. Sammasanto khandhānaṃ [P 1.0084] udayabbayanti pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayañca vipassanto, yadipi idāni [M 1.0099] katakicco, phalasamāpattiṃ pana samāpajjituṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapentoti adhippāyo. Sānuṃ paṭigamissāmīti pubbe mayā vutthapabbatasānumeva uddissa [V 1.0083] gacchissāmi. Vivekamanubrūhayanti paṭipassaddhivivekaṃ phalasamāpattikāyavivekañca paribrūhayanto, tassa vā paribrūhanahetu gamissāmīti. Evaṃ pana vatvā thero tattheva gato, ayameva ca imassa therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosi.

23. Herein, `veḷugumbasmiṃ` means near a bamboo grove, in its shade. `Bhutvāna madhupāyasaṃ` means having eaten milk-rice porridge poured with honey. `Padakkhiṇaṃ` means by taking what is excellent, that is, by properly receiving the Teacher’s instruction; this is the meaning. `Sammasanto khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ` means contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging; although he has now done what was to be done, the intention is that he establishes insight in order to enter fruition attainment. `Sānuṃ paṭigamissāmi` means “I will go, aiming for that same mountain slope where I previously dwelt.” `Vivekamanubrūhayaṃ` means developing the seclusion of calming, fruition attainment, and bodily seclusion; or, “I will go for the sake of developing that seclusion.” Having spoken thus, the Elder went right there, and this very verse was this Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Gosālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gosāla is concluded.

4. Sugandhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sugandha

Anuvassiko pabbajitoti āyasmato sugandhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ito dvānavute kappe tissassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa kāle manussayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto migabyadhanena araññe vicarati. Satthā tassa anukampāya padavaḷañjaṃ dassetvā gato. So satthu padacetiyāni disvā purimabuddhesu katādhikāratāya “sadevake loke aggapuggalassa imāni padānī”ti pītisomanassajāto koraṇḍakapupphāni gahetvā pūjaṃ katvā cittaṃ pasādesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā tato cuto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle kuṭumbiko hutvā satthu bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahādānaṃ pavattetvā gandhakuṭiṃ mahagghagositacandanaṃ pisitvā tena paribhaṇḍaṃ katvā patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi – “nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne mayhaṃ sarīraṃ evaṃsugandhaṃ hotū”ti. Evaṃ aññānipi tattha tattha bhave bahūni puññakammāni katvā sugatīsu eva parivattamāno imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa gehe nibbatti. Nibbattassa ca tassa mātukucchigatakālato paṭṭhāya mātu sarīraṃ sakalampi gehaṃ surabhigandhaṃ vāyati. Jātadivase pana visesato paramasugandhaṃ sāmantagehesupi vāyateva. Tassa mātāpitaro “amhākaṃ putto attanāva [P 1.0085] attano nāmaṃ gahetvā āgato”ti sugandhotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So anupubbena vayappatto [M 1.0100] mahāselattheraṃ disvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto sattāhabbhantare eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.15-24) –

“Anuvassiko pabbajito” is the verse of the Elder Sugandha. What is its origin? It is said that ninety-two aeons ago, during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One named Tissa, he was born in the human realm and, having attained discernment, wandered in the forest as a deer hunter. Out of compassion for him, the Teacher showed his footprint and departed. Seeing the shrines of the Teacher’s footprints, due to having made aspirations in the time of previous Buddhas, he thought, “These are the footprints of the foremost person in the world with its devas,” and, filled with joy and gladness, he took koraṇḍaka flowers, made an offering, and gladdened his mind. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. After passing away from there, he continued performing meritorious deeds, wandering between the deva and human realms. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a householder and provided great alms to the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Having ground expensive gosīta sandalwood, he plastered the fragrance chamber with it and made the aspiration: “Wherever I am reborn, may my body be so fragrant.” Thus, having performed many other meritorious deeds in various existences, he continued revolving only in good destinations. In this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was born in Sāvatthī in the house of a prosperous brahmin. From the moment he was in his mother’s womb, her entire body and the whole house exuded a sweet fragrance. On the day of his birth, an especially sublime fragrance spread even to the surrounding houses. His parents, thinking, “Our son has come having brought his own name,” named him Sugandha. In due course, having come of age, he saw the Elder Mahāsela, heard the Dhamma in his presence, and went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he attained arahantship within seven days. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 2.50.15–24):

“Vanakammiko pure āsiṃ, pitumātumatenahaṃ;

Pasumārena jīvāmi, kusalaṃ me na vijjati.

“Formerly, I was a hunter in the forest; at my parents’ behest, I made my living by slaughtering animals; no merit was found in me.

“Mama āsayasāmantā, tisso lokagganāyako;

Padāni tīṇi dassesi, anukampāya cakkhumā.

“Near my dwelling, Tissa, the world’s supreme guide, the One with Vision, showed me three footprints out of compassion.

“Akkante [V 1.0084] ca pade disvā, tissanāmassa satthuno;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, pade cittaṃ pasādayiṃ.

“Seeing the footprints where the Teacher named Tissa had trod, joyful, with a gladdened heart, I inspired faith at the sight of those footprints.

“Koraṇḍaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, pādapaṃ dharaṇīruhaṃ;

Sakosakaṃ gahetvāna, padaseṭṭhaṃ apūjayiṃ.

“Seeing a flowering koraṇḍaka, a tree growing from the earth, I took its blossoms, calyx and all, and worshipped the most excellent footprint.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my volition and aspirations, having abandoned my human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Koraṇḍakachavī homi, suppabhāso bhavāmahaṃ.

“Whatever womb I was reborn into, whether divine or human, I had skin like a koraṇḍaka flower; I was exceedingly radiant.

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, padapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-two aeons since I performed that deed then, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the footprint.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto “anuvassiko pabbajito”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

But having attained arahantship and declaring his final knowledge, he spoke this verse: “Anuvassiko pabbajito…”

24. Tattha anuvassikoti anugato upagato vassaṃ anuvasso, anuvassova anuvassiko. Pabbajitoti pabbajjaṃ upagato, pabbajito hutvā upagatavassamatto ekavassikoti attho. Atha vā anugataṃ pacchāgataṃ apagataṃ vassaṃ anuvassaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti anuvassiko. Yassa pabbajitassa vassaṃ aparipuṇṇatāya na gaṇanūpagataṃ, so evaṃ vutto, tasmā [M 1.0101] avassikoti vuttaṃ hoti. Passa dhammasudhammatanti tava satthu dhammassa sudhammabhāvaṃ svākkhātataṃ ekantaniyyānikataṃ passa, yattha anuvassiko tuvaṃ pabbajito. Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇanti tisso vijjā tayā anuppattā sacchikatā, tato eva kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ sammāsambuddhassa sāsanaṃ anusiṭṭhi ovādo anusikkhitoti katakiccataṃ nissāya pītisomanassajāto thero attānaṃ paraṃ viya katvā vadatīti.

24. Herein, `anuvassika` means `anuvassa`, one who has entered upon the rains-residence; `anuvassa` itself means `anuvassika`. `Pabbajita` means one who has undertaken the going forth; having gone forth and completed just one rains-residence, this is the meaning of `ekavassika` (of one rains-residence). Alternatively, `anuvassa` refers to a rains-residence that is past, gone, departed; one who has this is an `anuvassika`. One who has gone forth, but whose rains-residence is incomplete and thus not counted, is called this; therefore, it means `avassika` (without a rains-residence). ‘See the excellence of the Dhamma’ means: see the excellent nature of your Teacher’s Dhamma, its quality of being well-proclaimed and leading to certain liberation, wherein you, an `anuvassika`, have gone forth. The three knowledges—knowledge of the recollection of past lives, knowledge of the divine eye, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints—have been attained and realized by you. Therefore, ‘the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled,’ meaning the instruction and advice of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One’s Dispensation has been followed. Relying on this fulfillment of the task, the Elder, filled with joy and gladness, speaks as if addressing another.

Sugandhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sugandha is concluded.

5. Nandiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nandiya

Obhāsajātanti [P 1.0086] āyasmato nandiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato [V 1.0085] kāle satthari parinibbute cetiye candanasārena vedikaṃ kāretvā uḷāraṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ pavattesi. Tato paṭṭhāya ajjhāsayasampanno hutvā tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ puññakammaṃ ācinitvā devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sakyarājakule nibbatti. Tassa mātāpitaro nandiṃ janento jātoti nandiyoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto anuruddhādīsu satthu santike pabbajantesu sayampi pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto katādhikāratāya nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.15-20) –

The verse beginning “Obhāsajātaṃ” is by the Elder Nandiya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he had a railing made of sandalwood essence constructed around the cetiya and performed a grand offering and homage. From then on, being endowed with firm resolve, he accumulated much merit in various places, merit that was a supporting condition for liberation. Wandering among devas and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha’s Dispensation in the Sakyan royal family at Kapilavatthu. Because he was born bringing joy, his parents named him Nandiya. When he came of age, seeing Anuruddha and others go forth in the presence of the Teacher, he himself also went forth. Applying himself to insight meditation, he quickly attained arahantship due to his previously made aspirations. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.15.15-20):

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Jalitvā aggikhandhova, sambuddho parinibbuto.

“The Conqueror named Padumuttara, eldest in the world, a bull among men, having blazed like a mass of fire, that Perfectly Self-Enlightened One attained final Nibbāna.

“Nibbute ca mahāvīre, thūpo vitthāriko ahu;

Dūratova upaṭṭhenti, dhātugehavaruttame.

“When the Great Hero had attained final Nibbāna, a vast stupa came to be. From afar, people came to attend upon that most excellent relic-shrine.

“Pasannacitto sumano, akaṃ candanavedikaṃ;

Dissati thūpakhandho ca, thūpānucchaviko tadā.

“With a serene and gladdened mind, I made a sandalwood railing. The mass of the stupa was visible, and my work was then befitting the stupa.

“Bhave [M 1.0102] nibbattamānamhi, devatte atha mānuse.

Omattaṃ me na passāmi, pubbakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Being reborn in existence, whether as a deva or a human, I saw no inferiority in myself; this is the fruit of a past deed.

“Pañcadasakappasate, ito aṭṭha janā ahuṃ;

Sabbe samattanāmā te cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“One thousand five hundred aeons ago from now, there were eight people, all named Samatta; they were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā anuruddhattherādīhi saddhiṃ pācīnavaṃsamigadāye viharante imasmiṃ there ekadivasaṃ māro pāpimā bhiṃsāpetukāmo tassa bheravarūpaṃ dasseti. Thero taṃ “māro aya”nti ñatvā “pāpima, ye māradheyyaṃ vītivattā, tesaṃ tava kiriyā kiṃ karissati, tatonidānaṃ pana tvaṃ eva vighātaṃ anatthaṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti dassento “obhāsajātaṃ phalaga”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.
