However, having attained arahantship, while this elder was dwelling in the Eastern Bamboo Grove Deer Park with the Elder Anuruddha and others, one day Māra the Evil One, wishing to frighten him, showed him a terrifying form. The Elder, recognizing him as Māra, spoke the verse beginning “Obhāsajātaṃ phalagaṃ” to show him: ‘O Evil One, what can your actions do to those who have transcended Māra’s realm? On the contrary, from this cause you yourself will meet only with trouble and ruin.’”

25. Tattha obhāsajātanti ñāṇobhāsena jātobhāsaṃ aggamaggañāṇassa adhigatattā. Tena anavasesato kilesandhakārassa vihataviddhaṃsitabhāvato ativiya pabhassaranti attho. Phalaganti phalaṃ gataṃ upagataṃ, aggaphalañāṇasahitanti adhippāyo. Cittanti khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ sāmaññena vadati. Tenāha “abhiṇhaso”ti. Tañhi nirodhaninnatāya khīṇāsavānaṃ niccakappaṃ arahattaphalasamāpattisamāpajjanato “phalena sahita”nti vattabbataṃ arahati. Tādisanti tathārūpaṃ, arahantanti [V 1.0086] attho. Āsajjāti visodhetvā paribhuyya. Kaṇhāti māraṃ ālapati, so hi kaṇhakammattā kaṇhābhijātitāya [P 1.0087] ca “kaṇho”ti vuccati. Dukkhaṃ nigacchasīti idha kucchianuppavesādinā niratthakaṃ kāyaparissamaṃ dukkhaṃ, samparāye ca appatikāraṃ apāyadukkhaṃ upagamissasi pāpuṇissasi. Taṃ sutvā māro “jānāti maṃ samaṇo”ti tatthevantaradhāyīti.

25. Here, 'obhāsajātaṃ' (radiant with light) means the radiance born of the light of knowledge, because the supreme path-knowledge has been attained. Therefore, because the darkness of defilements has been utterly destroyed and dispelled, it is exceedingly brilliant—this is the meaning. 'Phalagaṃ' (gone to the fruit) means gone to, attained the fruit; the intention is that it is accompanied by the knowledge of the supreme fruit. 'Cittaṃ' (mind) generally refers to the mind of one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, it is said 'abhiṇhaso' (constantly). For the minds of those whose taints are destroyed, being inclined towards cessation, constantly entering the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, it is indeed worthy of being called 'accompanied by the fruit.' 'Tādisaṃ' (such a one) means one of such a nature; the meaning is an arahant. 'Āsajja' (assault) means having purified and overcome. 'Kaṇha' (Dark One) addresses Māra, for he is called 'Kaṇha' due to his dark deeds and his dark birth. 'Dukkhaṃ nigacchasi' (you will meet suffering) means here the useless bodily torment of entering a womb, etc., and in the future, you will undergo the irremediable suffering of the lower realms. Hearing that, Māra thought, 'This ascetic knows me,' and vanished on the spot.

Nandiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nandiya is concluded.

6. Abhayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya

Sutvā [M 1.0103] subhāsitaṃ vācanti āyasmato abhayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā dhammakathiko hutvā dhammakathanakāle paṭhamaṃ catūhi gāthāhi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā pacchā dhammaṃ kathesi. Tenassa puññakammabalena kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ apāyapaṭisandhi nāma nāhosi. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

“Having heard the well-spoken word”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Abhaya. What is its origin? It is said that he, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, became a Dhamma preacher, and when preaching the Dhamma, he first praised the Blessed One with four verses, and afterwards preached the Dhamma. By the power of that meritorious deed, for a hundred thousand eons there was no rebirth for him in the lower realms. For thus it was said:

“Abhitthavitvā padumuttaraṃ jinaṃ, pasannacitto abhayo sayambhuṃ;

Na gacchi kappāni apāyabhūmiṃ, satasahassāni uḷārasaddho”ti. (apa. thera 2.55.221)

“Having extolled Padumuttara, the Conqueror, the Self-existent One, Abhaya, with a serene mind, did not go to the lower realms for a hundred thousand eons, being one of great faith.”

Khettasampattiyādīhi tassa ca pubbapacchimasanniṭṭhānacetanānaṃ ativiya uḷārabhāvena so aparimeyyo puññābhisando kusalābhisando tādiso ahosi. “Acintiye pasannānaṃ, vipāko hoti acintiyo”ti (apa. thera 1.1.82) hi vuttaṃ. Tattha tattha hi bhave upacitaṃ puññaṃ tassa upatthambhakamahosi. Tathā hi so vipassissa bhagavato ketakapupphehi pūjamakāsi. Evaṃ uḷārehi puññavisesehi sugatīsu eva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rañño bimbisārassa putto [P 1.0088] hutvā nibbatti. Abhayotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa uppatti parato āvi bhavissati. So nigaṇṭhena nāṭaputtena ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ sikkhāpetvā “imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchitvā samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropehī”ti vissajjito bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā taṃ pañhaṃ pucchitvā tassa pañhassa anekaṃsabyākaraṇabhāve bhagavatā kathite nigaṇṭhānaṃ parājayaṃ, satthu ca sammāsambuddhabhāvaṃ viditvā upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi. Tato raññe bimbisāre kālaṅkate sañjātasaṃvego sāsane pabbajitvā tālacchiggaḷūpamasuttadesanāya sotāpanno hutvā puna vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.17-22) –

By the excellence of his fields and other factors, and by the exceedingly lofty nature of his initial and subsequent volitions, that immeasurable stream of merit, that stream of wholesomeness, was of such a kind. For thus it was said: “For those who are serene towards the unthinkable, the result is unthinkable.” Indeed, the merit he had accumulated in various existences became a great support for him. Thus, he made an offering of ketaka flowers to the Blessed One Vipassī. Wandering through happy destinies due to such outstanding merits, he was reborn in this Buddha-era as the son of King Bimbisāra. His name was Abhaya. His birth will be revealed later. Having been taught a two-edged question by the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta and dispatched with the instruction, “Ask this question and impute a doctrine to the ascetic Gotama,” he approached the Blessed One, posed that question, and when the Blessed One explained the indeterminacy of that question, he recognized the defeat of the Nigaṇṭhas and the perfectly self-enlightened nature of the Teacher, and declared himself a lay follower. Then, after King Bimbisāra had passed away, stirred by a sense of urgency, he went forth into the Dispensation. Upon hearing the teaching of the Sutta on the Simile of the Hole in the Yoke, he became a stream-enterer. Then, resuming his insight practice, he realized arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vinatānadiyā [V 1.0087] tīre, vihāsi purisuttamo;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.

“On the bank of the Vinatā River, the supreme person abided; I saw the stainless Buddha, concentrated and perfectly composed.”

“Madhugandhassa [M 1.0104] pupphena, ketakassa ahaṃ tadā;

Pasannacitto sumano, buddhaseṭṭhamapūjayiṃ.

“With a sweet-smelling ketaka flower, at that time, with a serene mind, joyful, I honored the supreme Buddha.”

“Ekanavute ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago from now, when I offered that flower, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattikittanena aññaṃ byākaronto “sutvā subhāsitaṃ vāca”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

However, having attained arahantship, declaring his final knowledge by praising his own practice, he spoke the verse: “Having heard the well-spoken word.”

26. Tattha sutvāti sotaṃ odahitvā, sotadvārānusārena upadhāretvā. Subhāsitanti suṭṭhu bhāsitaṃ, sammadeva bhāsitaṃ, sammāsambuddhabhāvato mahākāruṇikatāya ca kiñci avisaṃvādetvā yathādhippetassa atthassa ekantato sādhanavasena bhāsitaṃ catusaccavibhāvanīyadhammakathaṃ. Na hi saccavinimuttā bhagavato dhammadesanā atthi. Buddhassāti sabbaññubuddhassa. Ādiccabandhunoti ādiccavaṃse sambhūtattā ādicco bandhu etassāti ādiccabandhu, bhagavā. Tassa ādiccabandhuno. Ādiccassa vā bandhūti ādiccabandhu, bhagavā. Tassa bhagavato orasaputtabhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā –

26. There, “having heard” means having lent an ear, having paid attention through the ear-door. “Well-spoken” means excellently spoken, rightly spoken, spoken by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One out of great compassion without any falsehood, spoken entirely for the purpose of accomplishing the intended meaning—a Dhamma-talk that elucidates the four truths. Indeed, there is no teaching of the Blessed One that is devoid of truth. “Of the Buddha” means of the Omniscient Buddha. “Of the Kinsman of the Sun” means the Blessed One is the Kinsman of the Sun because he was born in the solar lineage, so the sun is his kinsman. Or, “kinsman of the sun” means the Blessed One, because of his being the sun's own son. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Yo andhakāre tamasī pabhaṅkaro, verocano maṇḍalī uggatejo;

Mā rāhu gilī caramantalikkhe, pajaṃ mamaṃ rāhu pamuñca sūriya”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.91);

“He who is the dispeller of darkness in the blinding gloom, the radiant one, the possessor of a disk, of mighty power; may Rāhu not swallow him traveling in the sky; release my child, O Rāhu, the sun!”

Paccabyadhinti [P 1.0089] paṭivijjhiṃ. Hī-ti nipātamattaṃ. Nipuṇanti saṇhaṃ paramasukhumaṃ, nirodhasaccaṃ, catusaccameva vā. Hī-ti vā hetuatthe nipāto. Yasmā paccabyadhiṃ nipuṇaṃ catusaccaṃ, tasmā na dāni kiñci paṭivijjhitabbaṃ atthīti attho. Yathā kiṃ paṭivijjhīti āha “vālaggaṃ usunā yathā”ti. Yathā sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiṃ susikkhito kusalo issāso usunā kaṇḍena avirajjhanto vijjheyya, evaṃ paccabyadhiṃ nipuṇaṃ ariyasaccanti yojanā.

“Paccabyadhiṃ” means “I penetrated.” “Hī” is merely a particle. “Nipuṇaṃ” means subtle, extremely refined, the truth of cessation, or indeed the four truths. Or, “hī” is a particle in the sense of cause. Because I have penetrated the subtle four truths, therefore now there is nothing more to be penetrated—this is the meaning. As to how I penetrated, he says, “like the tip of a hair with an arrow.” Just as a well-trained, skilled archer, without missing, might pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with an arrow, so I penetrated the subtle noble truths—this is the connection.

Abhayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya is concluded.

7. Lomasakaṅgiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya

Dabbaṃ [M 1.0105][V 1.0088] kusanti āyasmato lomasakaṅgiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira ito ekanavute kappe vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso nānāpupphehi pūjetvā tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto puna aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Tena ca samayena satthārā bhaddekarattapaṭipadāya kathitāya aññataro bhikkhu bhaddekarattasuttavasena tena sākacchaṃ karoti. So taṃ na sampāyāsi. Asampāyanto “ahaṃ anāgate tuyhaṃ bhaddekarattaṃ kathetuṃ samattho bhaveyya”nti paṇidhānaṃ akāsi, itaro “puccheyya”nti. Etesu paṭhamo ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle kapilavatthusmiṃ sākiyarājakule nibbatti. Tassa sukhumālabhāvena soṇassa viya pādatalesu lomāni jātāni, tenassa lomasakaṅgiyoti nāmaṃ ahosi. Itaro devaloke nibbattitvā candanoti paññāyittha. Lomasakaṅgiyo anuruddhādīsu sakyakumāresu pabbajantesu pabbajituṃ na icchi. Atha naṃ saṃvejetuṃ candano devaputto upasaṅkamitvā bhaddekarattaṃ pucchi. Itaro “na jānāmī”ti. Puna devaputto “atha kasmā tayā ‘bhaddekarattaṃ katheyya’nti [P 1.0090] saṅgaro kato, idāni pana nāmamattampi na jānāsī”ti codesi. Itaro tena saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “mayā kira, bhante, pubbe ‘imassa bhaddekarattaṃ kathessāmī’ti saṅgaro kato”ti pucchi. Bhagavā “āma, kulaputta, kassapassa bhagavato kāle tayā evaṃ kata”nti āha. Svāyamattho uparipaṇṇāsake āgatanayena vitthārato veditabbo. Atha lomasakaṅgiyo “tena hi, bhante, pabbājetha ma”nti āha. Bhagavā “na, kho, tathāgatā mātāpitūhi ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ pabbājentī”ti paṭikkhipi. So mātu santikaṃ gantvā “anujānāhi maṃ, amma, pabbajituṃ, pabbajissāmaha”nti vatvā, mātarā “tāta, sukhumālo tvaṃ kathaṃ pabbajissasī”ti vutte, “attano parissayasahanabhāvaṃ pakāsento “dabbaṃ kusaṃ poṭakila”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

The verse of the Venerable Elder Lomasakaṅgiya, beginning with 'Dabbaṃ kusaṃ'. What is the origin? It is said that ninety-one eons ago, having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, with a joyful mind he honored Him with various flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds and wandered only in happy destinations, until, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth and practiced the ascetic's way. And at that time, when the Teacher had spoken about the practice of the Excellent Night, a certain monk discussed it with him by way of the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. He could not comprehend it. Not comprehending it, he made the aspiration: 'May I be able to explain the Bhaddekaratta to you in the future.' The other made the aspiration: 'May I ask you about it.' Among these, the first one wandered among gods and humans for one Buddha-interval and was reborn in the Sakyan royal family of Kapilavatthu during the time of our Blessed One. Due to his delicate nature, hair grew on the soles of his feet like down, hence his name was Lomasakaṅgiya. The other was reborn in the heavenly world and became known as Candana. When the Sakyan princes like Anuruddha went forth, Lomasakaṅgiya did not wish to go forth. Then, to inspire him, the young god Candana approached and asked about the Bhaddekaratta. The other replied, 'I do not know.' Then the young god reproached him: 'Then why did you previously make the agreement, "I will explain the Bhaddekaratta," but now you do not even know its name?' The other then went with him to the Blessed One and asked, 'Venerable sir, is it true that in the past I made an agreement, "I will explain the Bhaddekaratta to him"?' The Blessed One replied, 'Yes, son of good family, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, you did so.' This detailed meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the Uparipaṇṇāsa. Then Lomasakaṅgiya said, 'Then, Venerable sir, ordain me.' The Blessed One refused, saying, 'Tathāgatas do not ordain a son without the permission of his parents.' He went to his mother and said, 'Mother, allow me to go forth; I will go forth.' When his mother said, 'Dear, you are so delicate, how will you go forth?' he declared his ability to endure hardships by reciting the verse: 'Dabbaṃ kusaṃ poṭakila.'

27. Tattha [M 1.0106] dabbanti dabbatiṇamāha, yaṃ “saddulo”tipi vuccati. Kusanti kusatiṇaṃ, yo “kāso”ti vuccati. Poṭakilanti sakaṇṭakaṃ akaṇṭakañca gacchaṃ. Idha pana sakaṇṭakameva adhippetaṃ. Usīrādīni suviññeyyāni. Dabbādīni tiṇāni bīraṇatiṇāni pādehi akkantassāpi dukkhajanakāni gamanantarāyakarāni ca, tāni ca panāhaṃ urasā panudissāmi urasāpi apanessāmi. Evaṃ apanento taṃ nimittaṃ dukkhaṃ sahanto araññāyatane gumbantaraṃ pavisitvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissāmi. Ko pana vādo pādehi akkamaneti dasseti. Vivekamanubrūhayanti [V 1.0089] kāyavivekaṃ cittavivekaṃ upadhivivekañca anubrūhayanto. Gaṇasaṅgaṇikañhi pahāya kāyavivekaṃ anubrūhayantasseva aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu yattha katthaci cittaṃ samādahantassa cittaviveko, na saṅgaṇikāratassa. Samāhitasseva vipassanāya kammaṃ karontassa samathavipassanañca yuganaddhaṃ karontassa kilesānaṃ khepanena upadhivivekādhigamo, na asamāhitassa. Tena vuttaṃ “vivekamanubrūhayanti kāyavivekaṃ cittavivekaṃ upadhivivekañca anubrūhayanto”ti. Evaṃ pana puttena vutte mātā “tena hi, tāta, pabbajā”ti anujāni. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Taṃ [P 1.0091] satthā pabbājesi. Taṃ pabbajitvā katapubbakiccaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisantaṃ bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “āvuso, tvaṃ sukhumālo kiṃ sakkhissasi araññe vasitu”nti. So tesampi tameva gāthaṃ vatvā araññaṃ pavisitvā bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.23-27) –

27. There, 'dabba' refers to dabba grass, which is also called 'saddula'. 'Kusa' refers to kusa grass, which is called 'kāsa'. 'Poṭakila' refers to thorny and thornless bushes, but here only the thorny ones are intended. Usīra and the like are easily understood. Grasses like dabba, kusa, and bīraṇa grass cause pain even when trodden upon by feet and create obstacles to walking. Yet, I will push them aside with my chest; I will remove them even with my chest. Thus, while removing them and enduring the pain on that account, I will enter the thickets of the wilderness and be able to practice the ascetic’s duty. This shows: what need is there to speak of treading on them with the feet? 'Developing seclusion' means developing bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from attachments. For one who abandons the company of crowds and develops bodily seclusion, mental seclusion arises when the mind settles on any of the thirty-eight meditation objects—not for one who delights in company. Only for one who is concentrated, engaged in insight, or practicing serenity and insight in tandem, is the attainment of seclusion from attachments achieved through the destruction of defilements—not for one who is unconcentrated. Therefore, it is said: 'He develops seclusion—developing bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from attachments.' When the son spoke thus, his mother consented, saying, 'Then, dear one, go forth.' He approached the Blessed One and requested ordination. The Teacher ordained him. After going forth, having completed his preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject and entered the forest. The monks said to him, 'Friend, you are delicate—how will you endure living in the wilderness?' He recited the same verse to them as well, entered the forest, devoted himself to meditation, and before long became one endowed with the sixfold higher knowledge. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.52.23-27):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, nānāpupphehi pūjayiṃ.

The gold-colored Perfectly Enlightened One, the receiver of offerings, walking along the street, I honored him with various flowers.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-one eons ago, when I worshiped with a flower, I have not known a bad destination: this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero aññaṃ byākaronto taṃyeva gāthaṃ abhāsīti.

But having attained Arahantship, the Elder, while explaining something else, spoke that very verse.

Lomasakaṅgiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya is completed.

8. Jambugāmiyaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jambugāmiyaputta

Kacci [M 1.0107] no vatthapasutoti āyasmato jambugāmiyaputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro hutvā tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ ācinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe vessabhussa bhagavato kāle ekadivasaṃ kiṃsukāni pupphāni disvā tāni pupphāni gahetvā buddhaguṇe anussaranto bhagavantaṃ uddissa ākāse khipanto pūjesi. So tena puññakammena tāvatiṃsesu nibbatto. Tato paraṃ puññāni katvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde campāyaṃ jambugāmiyassa nāma upāsakassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Tena [V 1.0090] puññakammena tāvatiṃsesu nibbatto. Tato paraṃ puññāni katvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde campāyaṃ jambugāmiyassa nāma upāsakassa putvā nibbatti. Tenassa jambugāmiyaputtotveva samaññā ahosi. So vayappatto bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaṃvego pabbajitvā katapubbakicco kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sākete añjanavane vasati. Athassa pitā “kiṃ nu kho mama putto sāsane abhirato viharati, udāhu no”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ “kacci no vatthapasuto”ti gāthaṃ likhitvā pesesi. So taṃ vācetvā, “pitā me pamādavihāraṃ āsaṅkati, ahañca ajjāpi puthujjanabhūmiṃ nātivatto”ti saṃvegajāto ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.25-30) –

'Are you not attached to robes?'—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Jambugāmiyaputta. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of previous Buddhas, he had performed meritorious deeds and, accumulating wholesome deeds that were a basis for liberation, cultivated virtues here and there. Then, in the thirty-first aeon from now, during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, one day he saw some kimsuka flowers. Taking those flowers, he recollected the virtues of the Buddha and, dedicating them to the Blessed One, he tossed them into the sky as an offering. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in Tāvatiṃsa. After that, performing more merits, he wandered through various deva and human realms until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was born as the son of a lay follower named Jambugāmika in Campā. Thus, he was known as Jambugāmiyaputta. When he came of age, he heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, and stirred by a sense of urgency, he went forth. Having fulfilled his preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject and dwelt in the Añjana Grove near Sāketa. Then his father, wondering, 'Is my son truly devoted to the Dispensation or not?' sent him a verse to test him: 'Are you not attached to robes?' Upon reading it, he thought, 'My father suspects I am living heedlessly, and indeed, I have not yet transcended the state of an ordinary person.' Filled with urgency, he strove and exerted himself, and before long, he attained the six higher knowledges. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.50.25–30):

“Kiṃsukaṃ [P 1.0092] pupphitaṃ disvā, paggahetvāna añjaliṃ;

Buddhaseṭṭhaṃ saritvāna, ākāse abhipūjayiṃ.

'Seeing the kimsuka tree in bloom, raising my joined palms; Remembering the Supreme Buddha, I worshipped him in the sky.'

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

'By that well-performed deed, and by my aspirations, Having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.'

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, for the deed I performed then, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā ñātīnaṃ vasananagaraṃ gantvā sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ pakāsento iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Taṃ disvā ñātakā pasannamānasā bahū saṅghārāme kāresuṃ. Theropi sakapitarā pesitaṃ [M 1.0108] gāthaṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā ghaṭento vāyamanto arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Aññaṃ byākarontopi pitupūjanatthaṃ “kacci no vatthapasuto”ti tameva gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, he went to the city where his relatives dwelt and displayed a miracle of psychic power, revealing the Dispensation's capacity for deliverance. Seeing this, his relatives, with faithful minds, had many monasteries built. The Elder, taking the verse sent by his father as a goad, striving and exerting himself, realized arahantship. Even when explaining something else, to honor his father, he recited that same verse: 'Surely you are not devoted to robes?'

28. Tattha kaccīti pucchāyaṃ nipāto. Noti paṭisedhe. Vatthapasutoti vatthe pasuto vatthapasuto, cīvaramaṇḍanābhirato. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ pattamaṇḍanādicāpallapaṭikkhepassāpi adhippetattā. “Kacci na vatthapasuto”tipi pāṭho, so evattho. Bhūsanāratoti attabhāvavibhūsanāya rato abhirato, yathekacce pabbajitvāpi capalā kāyadaḷhibahulā cīvarādiparikkhārassa attano sarīrassa ca maṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānāya yuttā honti. Kimeva parikkhārapasuto bhūsanārato ca nāhosīti ayamettha padadvayassāpi attho. Sīlamayaṃ gandhanti akhaṇḍādibhāvāpādanena suparisuddhassa catubbidhassapi sīlassa vasena yvāyaṃ “yo ca sīlavataṃ pajāti [V 1.0091] na itarā dussīlapajā, dussīlattāyeva dussilyamayaṃ duggandhaṃ vāyati, evaṃ tvaṃ duggandhaṃ avāyitvā kacci sīlamayaṃ gandhaṃ vāyasīti [P 1.0093] attho. Atha vā netarā pajāti na itarā dussīlapajā, taṃ kacci na hoti, yato sīlamayaṃ gandhaṃ vāyasīti byatirekena sīlagandhavāyanameva vibhāveti.

28. Herein, `kacci` is a particle in the sense of a question. `No` is in the sense of negation. `Vatthapasuto` means one devoted to robes, one who delights in adorning robes. And this is merely an example, as the rejection of frivolity such as decorating the bowl is also intended. There is also the reading `kacci na vatthapasuto`, which has the same meaning. `Bhūsanārato` means one who delights and takes pleasure in adorning his own person, just as some, even after going forth, are frivolous and much given to strengthening the body, and are devoted to the purpose of decorating and beautifying their requisites, such as robes, and their own bodies. The meaning of these two phrases here is: 'Surely you have not become one devoted to requisites and delighting in adornment?' As for `sīlamayaṃ gandhaṃ` (the fragrance of virtue): this refers to the fragrance of the fourfold virtue, perfectly pure through its attainment of the state of being unbroken, etc. The meaning is: 'The other folk' means not the other, immoral folk. Due to their very immorality, they emit a foul stench consisting of immorality. Thus, not emitting a foul stench, do you emit the fragrance of virtue? Alternatively, `netarā pajā` means not the other, immoral folk. 'Surely you are not that?' Since you emit the fragrance of virtue, it thus clarifies, by way of contrast, the very emission of the fragrance of virtue.

Jambugāmiyaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jambugāmiyaputta is concluded.

9. Hāritattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hārita

Samunnamayamattānanti āyasmato hāritattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro hutvā tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññasambhāraṃ upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe sudassanaṃ [M 1.0109] nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kuṭajapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā tena puññakammena sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagare brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatti. Hāritotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa vayappattassa mātāpitaro kularūpādīhi anucchavikaṃ kumārikaṃ brāhmaṇadhītaraṃ ānesuṃ. So tāya saddhiṃ bhogasukhaṃ anubhavanto ekadivasaṃ attano tassā ca rūpasampattiṃ oloketvā dhammatāya codiyamāno “īdisaṃ nāma rūpaṃ nacirasseva jarāya maccunā ca abhippamaddīyatī”ti saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi. Katipayadivasātikkameneva cassa bhariyaṃ kaṇhasappo ḍaṃsitvā māresi. So tena bhiyyosomattāya sañjātasaṃvego satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā gharabandhane chinditvā pabbaji. Tassa ca cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā viharantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati, cittaṃ ujugataṃ na hoti. So gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho aññataraṃ usukāraṃ usudaṇḍaṃ yante pakkhipitvā ujuṃ karontaṃ disvā “ime acetanampi nāma ujuṃ karonti, kasmā ahaṃ cittaṃ ujuṃ na karissāmī”ti cintetvā tatova paṭinivattitvā divāṭṭhāne nisinno vipassanaṃ ārabhi. Athassa bhagavā upari ākāse nisīditvā ovādaṃ dento “samunnamayamattāna”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi. Ayameva thero attānaṃ paraṃ viya ovadanto abhāsīti ca vadanti.

The verse beginning `Samunnamayamattānaṃ` is the Venerable Elder Hārita's. What is its origin? It is said that, having made his aspiration in the time of previous Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit that serves as a basis for liberation here and there, in the thirty-first aeon from now he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sudassana and, with a faithful mind, made an offering of kuṭaja flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn only in happy destinations until, during this Buddha-era, he was born into a wealthy brahmin family in Sāvatthī. His name was Hārita. When he came of age, his parents brought him a brahmin maiden, a young woman suitable in terms of family, appearance, and so on. While enjoying the pleasure of worldly possessions with her, one day he observed his own and her physical beauty and, being prompted by the nature of things, he gained a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, 'Such beauty will soon be crushed by old age and death.' A few days later, a black snake bit his wife and killed her. With his sense of spiritual urgency having arisen all the more because of this, he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, cut the bonds of the household, and went forth. While he was dwelling, having taken up a meditation subject suitable to his temperament, his meditation did not succeed; his mind did not become straight. One day, having entered a village for alms, he saw a fletcher straightening an arrow shaft by placing it in a press. He thought, 'These men straighten even an inanimate thing; why should I not straighten my mind?' Returning from there and sitting in his day-abode, he began insight meditation. Then the Blessed One, sitting in the sky above him, gave him this instruction, reciting the verse beginning `Samunnamayamattānaṃ`. Some say that the elder himself spoke this verse, admonishing himself as if he were another.

29. Tattha samunnamayanti sammā unnamento, samāpattivasena kosajjapakkhe [P 1.0094] patituṃ adatvā tato uddharanto vīriyasamataṃ yojentoti attho. Attānanti cittaṃ, atha vā samunnamayāti kosajjapakkhato samunnamehi. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Hīnavīriyatāya tava cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ nappaṭipajjati ce, taṃ vīriyārambhavasena sammā unnamehi, anonataṃ anapanataṃ karohīti [V 1.0092] adhippāyo. Evaṃ pana karonto usukārova tejanaṃ. Cittaṃ ujuṃ karitvāna, avijjaṃ bhinda hāritāti. Yathā nāma usukāro kaṇḍaṃ īsakampi onataṃ apanatañca vijjhanto lakkhaṃ bhindanatthaṃ ujuṃ karoti, evaṃ kosajjapātato arakkhaṇena onataṃ uddhaccapātato arakkhaṇena apanataṃ vijjhanto appanāpattiyā cittaṃ ujuṃ [M 1.0110] karitvāna samāhitacitto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā sīghaṃ aggamaggañāṇena avijjaṃ bhinda padālehīti. Taṃ sutvā thero vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacireneva arahā ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.35.39-43) –

29. Therein, `samunnamayaṃ` means rightly uplifting; not allowing the mind to fall into the domain of laziness, but by means of meditative attainment, lifting it from there and applying balanced energy—this is the meaning. `Attānaṃ` means the mind. Alternatively, `samunnamaya` means: uplift it from the domain of laziness. The letter `ma` is for euphonic conjunction. The intention is: if your mind, due to weak energy, does not enter upon the path of the meditation subject, then rightly uplift it by initiating energy—make it unbent and unswerving. In doing so, just as an arrow-maker straightens an arrow-shaft, so you should, 'Having straightened the mind, shatter ignorance, O Hārita!' Just as an arrow-maker, in order to pierce the target, straightens a shaft, avoiding any part that is even slightly bent down or bent away, so too should you, avoiding the mind's being bent down through not guarding against falling into laziness, and its being bent away through not guarding against falling into restlessness, having straightened the mind by means of attainment-concentration, and with a concentrated mind, having made an effort in insight meditation, swiftly break and shatter ignorance with the knowledge of the highest path. Hearing this, the elder developed insight and in no long time became an arahant. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre, vasalo nāma pabbato;

Buddho sudassano nāma, vasate pabbatantare.

Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Vasala. The Buddha named Sudassana dwells within the mountain.

“Pupphaṃ hemavantaṃ gayha, vehāsaṃ agamāsahaṃ;

Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, oghatiṇṇamanāsavaṃ.

I took a Himalayan flower and went into the air. There I saw the Fully Enlightened One, who had crossed the flood, taintless.

“Pupphaṃ kuṭajamādāya, sīse katvānahaṃ tadā;

Buddhassa abhiropesiṃ, sayambhussa mahesino.

I took a kuṭaja flower, and then placing it on my head, I offered it to the Buddha, the Self-Become, the great sage.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, for that flower with which I worshipped, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of that flower-offering.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākarontopi tameva gāthaṃ abhāsi.

However, having attained arahantship, even when explaining something else, he spoke that same verse.

Hāritattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hārita is concluded.

10. Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya

Ābādhe me samuppanneti āyasmato uttiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle candabhāgāya nadiyā mahārūpo [P 1.0095] susumāro hutvā nibbatto. So pāraṃ gantuṃ nadiyā tīraṃ upagataṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto pāraṃ netukāmo tīrasamīpe nipajji. Bhagavā tassa anukampāya piṭṭhiyaṃ pāde ṭhapesi. So haṭṭho udaggo pītivegena diguṇussāho hutvā sotaṃ chindanto sīghena javena bhagavantaṃ paratīraṃ nesi. Bhagavā tassa cittappasādaṃ [V 1.0093] oloketvā “ayaṃ ito cuto devaloke [M 1.0111] nibbattitvā tato paṭṭhāya sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto ito catunavute kappe amataṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi.

“When illness arose in me”—this verse was spoken by the Venerable Elder Uttiya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of former Buddhas, having performed meritorious deeds and accumulated merit conducive to liberation in various existences, ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn as a huge crocodile in the Candabhāgā River. Seeing the Blessed One who had approached the riverbank to cross, he was filled with faith and, desiring to carry him across, lay down near the shore. The Blessed One, out of compassion, placed his feet on his back. He, delighted and uplifted, with twice the enthusiasm due to the force of joy, cutting through the stream with swift speed, ferried the Blessed One to the far shore. The Blessed One, observing the faith in his mind, declared: “Departing from here, he will be reborn in the heavenly world, and from there onward, wandering only in happy destinations, ninety-four aeons from now, he will attain the Deathless.” Having made this prediction, the Blessed One departed.

So tathā sugatīsuyeva paribbhamanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti uttiyo nāma nāmena. So vayappatto “amataṃ pariyesissāmī”ti paribbājako hutvā vicaranto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane pabbajitvāpi sīlādīnaṃ avisodhitattā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto aññe bhikkhū visesaṃ nibbattetvā aññaṃ byākaronte disvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā saṅkhepeneva ovādaṃ yāci. Satthāpi tassa “tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.369) saṅkhepeneva ovādaṃ adāsi. So tassa ovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ ārabhi. Tassa āraddhavipassanassa ābādho uppajji. Uppanne pana ābādhe sañjātasaṃvego vīriyārambhavatthuṃ katvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.3.169-179) –

Thus, wandering only in happy realms, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin, named Uttiya. When he came of age, thinking, “I will seek the Deathless,” he became a wanderer. While wandering, one day he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and went forth in the Dispensation. Yet, because his virtue and other qualities were not purified, being unable to produce any special attainment, seeing other bhikkhus producing special attainments and declaring their final knowledge, he approached the Teacher and requested concise advice. The Teacher also gave him concise advice, saying, “Therefore, Uttiya, purify the very beginning,” and so forth (Saṃ. Ni. 5.369). Standing firm on that advice, he began insight meditation. While he was developing insight, an illness arose in him. When the illness arose, having a sense of urgency, making it the basis for arousing effort, applying himself to the work of insight, by diligently cultivating insight, he attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.3.169–179):

“Candabhāgānadītīre, susumāro ahaṃ tadā;

Sagocarapasutohaṃ, nadititthaṃ agacchahaṃ.

“On the banks of the Candabhāgā River, I was a crocodile then. Engaged in my own domain, I went to the river’s ford.

“Siddhattho tamhi samaye, sayambhū aggapuggalo;

Nadiṃ taritukāmo so, nadititthaṃ upāgami.

“At that time, Siddhattha, the Self-born, the foremost individual, wishing to cross the river, approached the river’s ford.

“Upagate ca sambuddhe, ahampi tatthupāgamiṃ;

Upagantvāna sambuddhaṃ, imaṃ vācaṃ udīrayiṃ.

“When the Fully Enlightened One had arrived, I also went there. Having approached the Fully Enlightened One, I uttered these words.

“Abhirūha mahāvīra, tāressāmi ahaṃ tuvaṃ;

Pettikaṃ visayaṃ mayhaṃ, anukampa mahāmuni.

“Ascend, Great Hero, I will carry you across. O Great Sage, have compassion on this ancestral domain of mine.

“Mama uggajjanaṃ sutvā, abhirūhi mahāmuni;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, tāresiṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Having heard my outcry, the Great Sage ascended. Delighted, with a joyful mind, I carried the Leader of the World across.

“Nadiyā pārime tīre, siddhattho lokanāyako;

Assāsesi mamaṃ tattha, amataṃ pāpuṇissati.

“On the far shore of the river, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World, encouraged me there, saying, ‘You will attain the Deathless.’

“Tamhā [M 1.0112] kāyā cavitvāna, devalokaṃ agacchahaṃ;

Dibbasukhaṃ anubhaviṃ, accharāhi purakkhato.

“Having passed away from that body, I went to the heavenly world. I experienced divine happiness, surrounded by celestial nymphs.

“Sattakkhattuñca devindo, devarajjamakāsahaṃ;

Tīṇikkhattuṃ cakkavattī, mahiyā issaro ahuṃ.

“Seven times I was king of devas, ruling the deva realm. Three times I was a wheel-turning monarch, a sovereign of the earth.

“Vivekamanuyuttohaṃ[V 1.0094], nipako ca susaṃvuto;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

“Devoted to solitude, sagacious and well-restrained, I bear this final body in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

“Catunnavutito kappe, tāresiṃ yaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, taraṇāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, I ferried that bull among men. I do not know of any bad destination—this is the fruit of ferrying across.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano sammā paṭipattiyā paripuṇṇākāravibhāvanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto “ābādhe me samuppanne”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, declaring his final knowledge by way of demonstrating the complete manner of his own correct practice, he spoke the verse, “When illness arose in me.”

30. Tattha ābādhe me samuppanneti sarīrassa ābādhanato “ābādho”ti laddhanāme visabhāgadhātukkhobhahetuke roge mayhaṃ sañjāte. Sati me udapajjathāti “uppanno kho me ābādho, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yadidaṃ ābādho vaḍḍheyya. Yāva panāyaṃ ābādho na vaḍḍhati, handāhaṃ [P 1.0096] vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi ‘appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā’”ti vīriyārambhavatthubhūtā sati tasseva ābādhassa vasena dukkhāya vedanāya pīḷiyamānassa mayhaṃ udapādi. Tenāha “ābodho me samuppanno, kālo me nappamajjitu”nti. Evaṃ uppannañhi satiṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā ayaṃ thero arahattaṃ pattoti.

30. Here, “When illness arose in me” means that illness, which is named “illness” because it afflicts the body, a disease caused by the disturbance of discordant elements, arose in me. “Mindfulness arose in me” means that mindfulness, which became the basis for arousing effort, arose in me while I was oppressed by painful feeling due to that very illness, with the thought: “An illness has arisen in me, and there is the possibility that this illness will worsen. Before this illness worsens, let me arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, the realization of the unrealized, the direct experience of the unexperienced.” Therefore, he said, “Illness arose in me; this is not the time for heedlessness.” Thus, this elder, having made this arising mindfulness a goad, attained arahantship.

Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Chapter is concluded.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter

1. Gahvaratīriyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gahvaratīriya

Phuṭṭho [M 1.0113][V 1.0095] ḍaṃsehīti āyasmato gahvaratīriyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle migaluddo hutvā araññe vicaranto addasa sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle devanāgayakkhānaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ, disvā pana pasannamānaso “dhammo esa vuccatī”ti sare nimittaṃ aggahesi. So tena cittappasādena devaloke uppanno puna aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā “aggidatto”ti laddhanāmo vayappatto bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā sañjātappasādo sāsane pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gahvaratīre nāma araññaṭṭhāne vasati. Tenassa gahvaratīrayoti samaññā ahosi. So vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.44-50) –

“Stung by insects” is the verse of the Elder Gahvaratīriya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the former Buddhas, he had made an aspiration. Then, in the thirty-first aeon from now, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was a deer hunter wandering in the forest. There, he saw the Blessed One Sikhī teaching the Dhamma to devas, nāgas, and yakkhas at the foot of a certain tree. Upon seeing him, his mind became serene, and thinking, “This is called the Dhamma,” he took the sound as a sign. Through that serenity of mind, he was reborn in the deva world. Wandering through good destinations again and again, in this Buddha-era he was reborn into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī, named Aggidatta. Having reached maturity, he saw the Blessed One's Twin Miracle, and with faith arisen, he went forth into the Dispensation. Having taken up a meditation subject, he dwelled in a forest place called Gahvaratīra. Hence, he was known as Gahvaratīriya. Developing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.52.44-50):

“Migaluddo pure āsi, araññe vipine ahaṃ;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, devasaṅghapurakkhataṃ.

“Once I was a hunter, in the wild and trackless forest; I saw the stainless Buddha, honored by a host of devas.”

“Catusaccaṃ pakāsentaṃ, desentaṃ, amataṃ padaṃ;

Assosiṃ madhuraṃ dhammaṃ, sikhino lokabandhuno.

“I heard the sweet Dhamma of Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World, proclaiming the Four Noble Truths, teaching the Deathless State.”

“Ghose cittaṃ pasādesiṃ, asamappaṭipuggale;

Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, uttariṃ duttaraṃ bhavaṃ.

“I made my mind serene at the sound, in the presence of the unequalled, peerless person. Having made my mind serene there, I crossed over hard-to-cross existence.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ghosasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from this, when I obtained that perception; I do not know of a bad destination—this is the fruit of the perception of sound.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [P 1.0097] pana patvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā sāvatthiyaṃ agamāsi. Tassa āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā ñātakā upagantvā mahādānaṃ pavattesuṃ. So katipayadivase vasitvā araññameva gantukāmo ahosi. Taṃ ñātakā, “bhante, araññaṃ nāma ḍaṃsamakasādivasena bahuparissayaṃ, idheva vasathā”ti [M 1.0114][V 1.0096] āhaṃsu. Taṃ sutvā thero “araññavāsoyeva mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti vivekābhiratikittanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto “phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, he paid homage to the Blessed One and went to Sāvatthī. Hearing of his arrival, his relatives approached and held a great almsgiving. After staying a few days, he wished to go to the forest. His relatives said, “Venerable sir, the forest is full of dangers such as gadflies, mosquitoes, and so forth; please stay here.” Hearing this, the Elder, declaring his final knowledge by way of praising his delight in solitude, spoke the verse: “Stung by gadflies...”

31. Tattha phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehi makasehīti ḍaṃsanasīlatāya “ḍaṃsā”ti laddhanāmāhi andhakamakkhikāhi, makasanaññitehi ca sūcimukhapāṇehi phussito daṭṭhoti attho. Araññasminti “pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) vuttaaraññalakkhaṇayogato araññe. Brahāvaneti mahārukkhagacchagahanatāya mahāvane araññāniyaṃ. Nāgo saṅgāmasīsevāti saṅgāmāvacaro hatthināgo viya saṅgāmamuddhani parasenāsampahāraṃ. “Araññavāso nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇito thomito”ti ussāhajāto sato satimā hutvā tatra tasmiṃ araññe, tasmiṃ vā ḍaṃsādisamphasse upaṭṭhite adhivāsaye adhivāseyya saheyya, “ḍaṃsādayo maṃ ābādhentī”ti araññavāsaṃ na jaheyyāti attho.

31. There, 'stung by gadflies and mosquitoes': This means touched and bitten by dark flies named 'ḍaṃsā' because of their biting habit, and by needle-mouthed creatures known as mosquitoes. In the wilderness: in the forest, in accordance with the characteristic of a wilderness stated as 'a minimum of five hundred bow-lengths' (Pārā. 654). In the great forest: meaning a vast forest, a wilderness, due to the density of large trees and thickets. 'Like an elephant at the head of a battle': just as a war elephant, a tusker accustomed to battle, endures the onslaught of the enemy army on the battlefield. 'Wilderness dwelling is praised and commended by the Buddhas and others'—thus, being inspired, mindful, and recollected, one should endure and bear it when such contact from gadflies and the like arises in that wilderness. One should not abandon the wilderness dwelling, thinking, 'The gadflies and such are afflicting me.' This is the meaning.

Gahvaratīriyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Gahvaratīriya is concluded.

2. Suppiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Suppiya

Ajaraṃ jīramānenāti āyasmato suppiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane vasanto tattha bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso phalāphalaṃ adāsi, tathā bhikkhusaṅghassa. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa sammāsambuddhassa kāle khattiyakule nibbattitvā anukkamena viññutaṃ patto kalyāṇamittasannissayena laddhasaṃvego sāsane pabbajitvā bahussuto ahosi. Jātimadena sutamadena ca attānaṃ ukkaṃsento pare ca vambhento vihāsi. So imasmiṃ buddhuppāde tassa [P 1.0098] kammassa nissandena sāvatthiyaṃ paribhūtarūpe susānagopakakule nibbatti. Suppiyotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Atha viññutaṃ patto attano sahāyabhūtaṃ sopākattheraṃ [M 1.0115] upasaṅkamitvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaṃvego pabbajitvā sammāpaṭipattiṃ pūretvā “ajaraṃ jīramānenā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

“The undecaying amidst the decaying” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Suppiya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family, and having gone forth as an ascetic, he lived in a forest hermitage. There, seeing the Blessed One, with a serene mind, he offered various fruits to him and likewise to the community of bhikkhus. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he was born into a warrior family. Having gradually attained maturity and, through association with a good friend, gained a sense of spiritual urgency, he went forth in the Dispensation and became very learned. Puffed up with pride of birth and pride of learning, he exalted himself and disparaged others. In this Buddha-era, as a result of that karma, he was born in Sāvatthī into the despised family of a cemetery keeper. His name was Suppiya. Later, having attained maturity, he approached his friend, the Elder Sopāka, and upon hearing the Dhamma from him, he gained a sense of spiritual urgency. He then went forth, fulfilled the right practice, and uttered the verse beginning: “The undecaying amidst the decaying.”

32. Tattha ajaranti jarārahitaṃ, nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi ajātattā natthi ettha jarā, etasmiṃ vā adhigate puggalassa sā natthīti jarābhāvahetutopi ajaraṃ nāma. Jīramānenāti jīrantena, khaṇe khaṇe jaraṃ pāpuṇantena. Tappamānenāti santappamānena, rāgādīhi [V 1.0097] ekādasahi aggīhi dayhamānena. Nibbutinti yathāvuttasantāpābhāvato nibbutasabhāvaṃ nibbānaṃ. Nimiyanti parivatteyyaṃ cetāpeyyaṃ. Paramaṃ santinti anavasesakilesābhisaṅkhārapariḷāhavūpasamadhammatāya uttamaṃ santiṃ. Catūhi yogehi ananubandhattā yogakkhemaṃ. Attano uttaritarassa kassaci abhāvato anuttaraṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – khaṇe khaṇe jarāya abhibhuyyamānattā jīramānena, tathā rāgaggiādīhi santappamānena gato evaṃ aniccena dukkhena asārena sabbathāpi anupasantasabhāvena saupaddavena, tappaṭipakkhabhāvato ajaraṃ paramupasamabhūtaṃ kenaci anupaddutaṃ anuttaraṃ nibbānaṃ nimiyaṃ parivatteyyaṃ “mahā vata me lābho mahā udayo hatthagato”ti. Yathā hi manussā yaṃ kiñci bhaṇḍaṃ parivattentā nirapekkhā gayhamānena sambahumānā honti, evamayaṃ thero pahitatto viharanto attano kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkhataṃ, nibbānaṃ paṭipesitattañca pakāsento “nimiyaṃ paramaṃ santiṃ, yogakkhemaṃ anuttara”nti vatvā tameva [P 1.0099] paṭipattiṃ paribrūhayanto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.51-77) –

32. Herein, ajaraṃ means free from aging; it is said in reference to Nibbāna. Indeed, since it is unborn, there is no aging in it; or, when it is attained by a person, aging does not exist for them. Thus, it is also called ajaraṃ (undecaying) because it is a cause for the absence of aging. Jīramānena means by that which is aging, which is reaching old age moment by moment. Tappamānenāti means by that which is being tormented, being burned by the eleven fires such as lust. Nibbutin refers to Nibbāna, which has a cooled nature due to the absence of the aforementioned torment. Nimiyan means ‘I would exchange,’ ‘I would acquire.’ Paramaṃ santin means the supreme peace, due to its nature as the complete calming of the fever of defilements and formations without remainder. Yogakkhemaṃ means security from the yokes, due to not being pursued by the four yokes. Anuttaraṃ means unsurpassed, due to the absence of anything higher than itself. Here is the brief meaning: With this aging body—overwhelmed by decay moment by moment, and likewise tormented by the fires of lust and so on, and thus impermanent, suffering, insubstantial, in every way unpeaceful and fraught with peril—I would exchange it for Nibbāna, which, being its opposite, is undecaying, the supreme state of peace, unassailed by anything, and unsurpassed, thinking: ‘What a great gain, what a great benefit has come into my hands!’ For just as people, when exchanging some goods, being unattached to what is given away, are full of high regard for what is received, so too this elder, dwelling with a resolute mind, showing his lack of attachment to his own body and life and the fact that his mind was directed towards Nibbāna, said, ‘I would exchange for the supreme peace, the unsurpassed security from the yokes.’ Then, developing that very practice, he roused his energy for insight meditation and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Varuṇo nāma nāmena, brāhmaṇo mantapāragū;

Chaḍḍetvā dasa puttāni, vanamajjhogahiṃ tadā.

“Varuṇa by name, a brahmin versed in mantras; having abandoned ten sons, he then entered the forest.”

“Assamaṃ sukataṃ katvā, suvibhattaṃ manoramaṃ;

Paṇṇasālaṃ karitvāna, vasāmi vipine ahaṃ.

“Having built a well-made hermitage, well-divided and delightful; having made a leaf hut, I dwell in the forest.”

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mamuddharitukāmo so, āgacchi mama assamaṃ.

“Padumuttara, the knower of the world, the receiver of offerings; desiring to uplift me, he came to my hermitage.”

“Yāvatā [M 1.0116] vanasaṇḍamhi, obhāso vipulo ahu;

Buddhassa ānubhāvena, pajjalī vipinaṃ tadā.

“As far as the forest grove extended, a great radiance arose; by the Buddha’s power, the forest then blazed forth.”

“Disvāna taṃ pāṭihīraṃ, buddhaseṭṭhassa tādino;

Pattapuṭaṃ gahetvāna, phalena pūjayiṃ ahaṃ.

“Having seen that miracle of the supreme Buddha, the Immovable One, taking a leaf-bowl, I made an offering of fruit.”

“Upagantvāna sambuddhaṃ, sahakhārimadāsahaṃ;

Anukampāya me buddho, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“Having approached the Fully Awakened One, I gave the shoulder-pole load; out of compassion for me, the Buddha spoke these words.”

“Khāribhāraṃ gahetvāna, pacchato ehi me tuvaṃ;

Paribhutte ca saṅghamhi, puññaṃ tava bhavissati.

“‘Take up the shoulder-pole load and come behind me; when the Saṅgha has partaken, merit will be yours.’”

“Puṭakaṃ taṃ gahetvāna, bhikkhusaṅghassadāsahaṃ;

Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, tusitaṃ upapajjahaṃ.

“Taking that container, I gave it to the community of bhikkhus; having gladdened my mind there, I was reborn in the Tusita realm.”

“Tattha [V 1.0098] dibbehi naccehi, gītehi vāditehi ca;

Puññakammena saṃyuttaṃ, anubhomi sadā sukhaṃ.

“There, with divine dances, songs, and music, connected with my meritorious deeds, I always experience happiness.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In whatever state of existence I am reborn, whether divine or human, there is no lack in my possessions; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Yāvatā caturo dīpā, sasamuddā sapabbatā;

Phalaṃ buddhassa datvāna, issaraṃ kārayāmahaṃ.

“As far as the four continents extend, with their oceans and mountains; having given fruit to the Buddha, I exercised sovereignty.”

“Yāvatā ye pakkhigaṇā, ākāse uppatanti ce;

Tepi me vasamanventi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“As many flocks of birds as fly in the sky, they too come under my control; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Yāvatā vanasaṇḍamhi, yakkhā bhūtā ca rakkhasā;

Kumbhaṇḍā garuḷā cāpi, pāricariyaṃ upenti me.

“As many yakkhas, spirits, and rākkhasas in the forest grove, and kumbhaṇḍas and garuḷas too, they come to attend upon me.”

“Kummā soṇā madhukārā, ḍaṃsā ca makasā ubho;

Tepi maṃ vasamanventi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Tortoises, dogs, bees, and both horseflies and mosquitoes, they too come under my control; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Supaṇṇā nāma sakuṇā, pakkhijātā mahabbalā;

Tepi maṃ saraṇaṃ yanti, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“The birds called Supaṇṇas, winged creatures of great power, they too come to me for refuge; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Yepi dīghāyukā nāgā, iddhimanto mahāyasā;

Tepi maṃ vasamanventi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Even those long-lived nāgas, powerful and of great glory, they too come under my control; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Sīhā [M 1.0117] byagghā ca dīpī ca, acchakokataracchakā;

Tepi maṃ vasamanventi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, wolves, and hyenas—they too come under my control; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Osadhī tiṇavāsī ca, ye ca ākāsavāsino;

Sabbe maṃ saraṇaṃ yanti, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“The spirits dwelling among medicinal herbs and grasses, and those who dwell in the sky, all come to me for refuge; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Sududdasaṃ sunipuṇaṃ, gambhīraṃ suppakāsitaṃ;

Phassayitvā viharāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“The Dhamma, extremely difficult to see, very subtle, deep, and well-proclaimed—having realized it, I dwell; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Vimokkhe aṭṭha phusitvā, viharāmi anāsavo;

Ātāpī nipako cāhaṃ, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Having attained the eight liberations, I dwell without taints; ardent and discerning am I; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Ye phalaṭṭhā buddhaputtā, khīṇadosā mahāyasā;

Ahamaññataro tesaṃ, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Those who abide in the fruit, sons of the Buddha, their corruptions destroyed, of great renown; I am one among them; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Abhiññāpāramiṃ gantvā, sukkamūlena codito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

“Having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, urged on by my wholesome roots, having fully understood all the taints, I dwell without taints.”

“Tevijjā iddhipattā ca, buddhaputtā mahāyasā;

Dibbasotaṃ samāpannā, tesaṃ aññataro ahaṃ.

“Those sons of the Buddha who possess the threefold knowledge, who have attained spiritual powers, who are of great glory, who have attained the divine ear—I am one among them.”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“One hundred thousand aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad destination since; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Kilesā [V 1.0099] jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvāpi tameva gāthaṃ aññābyākaraṇavasena abhāsi.

Even after attaining Arahantship, he spoke that same verse by way of a declaration of final knowledge.

Suppiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Suppiya is concluded.

3. Sopākattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Sopāka

Yathāpi ekaputtasminti āyasmato sopākattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro hutvā tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto kakusandhassa bhagavato kāle aññatarassa kuṭumbikassa putto hutvā nibbatto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto bījapūraphalāni satthu upanesi. Paṭiggahesi bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya[M 1.0118]. So bhikkhusaṅghe ca abhippasanno salākabhattaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅghuddesavasena tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ khīrabhattaṃ adāsi. So tehi puññakammehi aparāparaṃ devamanussesu sampattiṃ anubhavanto ekadā manussayoniyaṃ nibbatto ekassa paccekabuddhassa khīrabhattaṃ adāsi. Evaṃ tattha tattha puññāni katvā sugatīsu eva paribbhamanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde purimakammanissandena sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarāya duggatitthiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa mātā dasa māse kucchinā pariharitvā paripakke gabbhe vijāyanakāle vijāyituṃ asakkontī mucchaṃ āpajjitvā bahuvelaṃ matā viya nipajji. Taṃ ñātakā “matā”ti saññāya susānaṃ netvā citakaṃ āropetvā devatānubhāvena vātavuṭṭhiyā uṭṭhitāya aggiṃ adatvā pakkamiṃsu. Dārako [P 1.0100] pacchimabhāvikattā devatānubhāvena mātukucchito arogo nikkhami. Mātā pana kālamakāsi. Devatā taṃ gahetvā manussarūpena susānagopakassa gehe ṭhapetvā katipayakālaṃ patirūpena āhārena posesi. Tato paraṃ susānagopako ca naṃ attano puttaṃ katvā vaḍḍheti. So tathā vaḍḍhento tassa puttena supiyena nāma dārakena saddhiṃ kīḷanto vicarati. Tassa susāne jātasaṃvaḍḍhabhāvato sopākoti samaññā ahosi.

The verse of the Venerable Elder Sopāka begins with 'Yathāpi ekaputtasmiṃ.' What was its origin? It is said that in the time of previous Buddhas, having made his aspiration and accumulated wholesome karma that served as a condition for liberation in various existences, he was reborn as the son of a certain householder during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha. One day, seeing the Teacher, his mind filled with faith, he offered citron fruits to the Teacher. The Blessed One accepted them out of compassion. Having deep faith in the community of monks, he arranged a lottery meal and, by the designation of the Saṅgha, provided milk-rice to three monks for as long as they lived. Through these meritorious deeds, he enjoyed prosperity among gods and humans in successive lives. Once, reborn in the human realm, he offered milk-rice to a Paccekabuddha. Thus, having performed good deeds here and there, he wandered through happy destinies until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, due to the residual effect of past karma, he was conceived in the womb of a certain poor female adherent in Sāvatthī. His mother carried him in her womb for ten months, but when the time came for delivery, she could not give birth and fainted, lying as if dead for a long time. Her relatives, thinking she had died, took her to the charnel ground, placed her on a pyre, and left without lighting the fire because, through the power of a deity, wind and rain arose. The child, being in his last existence, emerged unharmed from his mother’s womb by the power of the deities. His mother, however, passed away. A deity took the child and, assuming human form, placed him in the house of the charnel ground keeper, nourishing him with suitable food for some time. Thereafter, the charnel ground keeper raised him as his own son. As he grew up in this way, he played with the keeper’s son, a boy named Supiya. Because he was born and raised in the charnel ground, he became known as Sopāka.

Athekadivasaṃ sattavassikaṃ taṃ bhagavā paccūsavelāya ñāṇajālaṃ pattharitvā veneyyabandhave oloketvā ñāṇajalantogadhaṃ disvā susānaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Dārako pubbahetunā codiyamāno pasannamānaso satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Satthā tassa dhammaṃ kathesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā “pitarā anuññātosī”ti vutto pitaraṃ satthu santikaṃ nesi. Tassa [V 1.0100] pitā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “bhante, imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājethā”ti anujāni. Satthā taṃ pabbājetvā mettābhāvanāya niyojesi. So mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā susāne viharanto ca cirasseva mettājhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.45.1-7) –

Then one day, when he was seven years old, the Blessed One, at dawn, cast the net of his knowledge and surveyed those who were amenable to guidance. Seeing the boy caught within the net of his knowledge, he went to the charnel ground. The boy, impelled by past causes, approached the Teacher with a serene mind, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he requested ordination. When asked, “Have you been permitted by your father?” he led his father to the Teacher. His father approached the Teacher, paid homage, and gave his permission, saying, “Venerable sir, please ordain this boy.” The Teacher ordained him and instructed him in the cultivation of loving-kindness. Taking up the meditation subject of loving-kindness and dwelling in the charnel ground, he before long developed the jhāna of loving-kindness. Having made that jhāna his foundation, he developed insight and realized arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kakusandho [M 1.0119] mahāvīro, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Gaṇamhā vūpakaṭṭho so, agamāsi vanantaraṃ.

“Kakusandha, the great hero, who had gone beyond all phenomena, withdrew from the group and went into the forest.

“Bījamiñjaṃ gahetvāna, latāya āvuṇiṃ ahaṃ;

Bhagavā tamhi samaye, jhāyate pabbatantare.

“Taking a citron fruit, I tied it with a creeper. At that time, the Blessed One was meditating in a mountain gorge.

“Disvānahaṃ devadevaṃ, vippasannena cetasā;

Dakkhiṇeyyassa vīrassa, bījamiñjamadāsahaṃ.

“Seeing the god of gods, with a mind of serene faith, I offered a citron fruit to the heroic one, worthy of offerings.

“Imasmiṃyeva kappamhi, yaṃ miñjamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bījamiñjassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In this very eon, for the fruit-kernel I gave back then, I know of no rebirth in a woeful state; this is the fruit of that citron fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahā hutvā pana aññesaṃ sosānikabhikkhūnaṃ mettābhāvanāvidhiṃ dassento “yathāpi ekaputtasmi”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having become an Arahant, while teaching the method of cultivating loving-kindness to other monks who dwell in charnel grounds, he spoke the verse beginning, “Just as with an only son…”

33. Tattha yathāti opammatthe nipāto. Ekaputtasminti punāti ca kulavaṃsaṃ tāyati cāti putto, atrajādibhedo putto. Eko putto ekaputto, tasmiṃ ekaputtasmiṃ. Visaye cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Piyasminti piyāyitabbatāya ceva ekaputtatāya ca rūpasīlācārādīhi ca pemakaraṇaṭṭhānabhūte. Kusalīti kusalaṃ vuccati khemaṃ sotthibhāvo, taṃ labhitabbaṃ etassa atthīti kusalī, sattānaṃ hitesī [P 1.0101] mettajjhāsayo. Sabbesu pāṇesūti sabbesu sattesu. Sabbatthāti sabbāsu disāsu sabbesu vā bhavādīsu, sabbāsu vā avatthāsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā ekaputtake piye manāpe mātāpitā kusalī ekantahitesī bhaveyya, evaṃ puratthimādibhedāsu sabbāsu disāsu, kāmabhavādibhedesu sabbesu bhavesu daharādibhedāsu sabbāsu avatthāsu ca ṭhitesu sabbesu sattesu ekantahitesitāya kusalī bhaveyya, “mitto udāsīno pañcatthiko”ti sīmaṃ akatvā sīmāsambhedavasena sabbattha ekarasaṃ mettaṃ bhāveyyāti. Imaṃ pana gāthaṃ vatvā “sace tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ [M 1.0120] anuyuñjeyyātha, ye te bhagavatā ‘sukhaṃ supatī’tiādinā [V 1.0101] (a. ni. 11.15) ekādasa mettānisaṃsā vuttā, ekaṃsena tesaṃ bhāgino bhavathā”ti ovādamadāsi.

33. Therein, 'yathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison. Regarding 'ekaputtasmiṃ' (in an only son): he is a 'putta' (son) because he purifies (`punāti`) and protects (`tāyati`) the family lineage; a son is distinguished as one born from oneself, and so on. 'Eko putto' is an only son; 'tasmiṃ ekaputtasmiṃ' means 'in that only son.' This locative case is used in the sense of a sphere of action. Regarding 'piyasmiṃ' (in one who is dear): in one who is a basis for love on account of being worthy of affection, being an only son, and possessing qualities such as beauty, virtue, and good conduct. Regarding 'kusalī' (wishing well): 'kusala' is said to be safety and well-being; one for whom this is to be obtained is 'kusalī,' one who wishes for the welfare of beings, whose disposition is loving-kindness. 'Sabbesu pāṇesu' (towards all living beings) means towards all beings. 'Sabbattha' (everywhere) means in all directions, or in all states of existence, or in all circumstances. This is what is meant: Just as parents would wish for the complete welfare of their beloved and dear only child, so too should one wish for the welfare of all beings situated in all directions, such as the east; in all realms of existence, such as the desire realm; and in all stages of life, such as youth. One should do so by wishing for their complete welfare, without making distinctions such as 'friend,' 'neutral person,' or 'enemy,' but by breaking down the boundaries and cultivating a loving-kindness of a single essence everywhere. Having spoken this verse, he then gave this exhortation: “Venerable sirs, if you were to apply yourselves to the cultivation of loving-kindness in this way, you would certainly become partakers in those eleven benefits of loving-kindness spoken of by the Blessed One, beginning with, ‘One sleeps in comfort’ (AN 11.15).”

Sopākattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Elder Sopāka’s verse is concluded.

4. Posiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Elder Posiya’s Verse

Anāsannavarāti āyasmato posiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā sugatīsu eva saṃsaranto ito dvenavute kappe tissassa bhagavato kāle migaluddo hutvā araññe vicarati. Atha bhagavā tassa anuggahaṃ kātuṃ araññaṃ gantvā tassa cakkhupathe attānaṃ dassesi. So bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto āvudhaṃ nikkhipitvā upasaṅkamitvā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā nisīditukāmataṃ dassesi. So tāvadeva tiṇamuṭṭhiyo gahetvā same bhūmibhāge sakkaccaṃ santharitvā adāsi. Nisīdi tattha bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya. Nisinne pana bhagavati anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedento bhagavantaṃ vanditvā sayampi ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha bhagavā “ettakaṃ vaṭṭati imassa kusalabīja”nti uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Acirapakkante bhagavati taṃ sīho migarājā ghātesi. So [P 1.0102] kālaṅkato devaloke nibbatti. “So kira bhagavati anupagacchante sīhena ghātito niraye nibbattissatī”ti taṃ disvā bhagavā sugatiyaṃ nibbattanatthaṃ kusalabījaropanatthañca upasaṅkami.

The verse of the Venerable Elder Posiya begins, 'Anāsannavarā…' What is its origin? It is said that in the time of previous Buddhas, having made his aspiration and accumulated much wholesome karma that served as a supporting condition for liberation in various existences, he wandered only through happy destinies. Ninety-two aeons from the present, during the time of the Blessed One Tissa, he was born as a deer hunter and roamed the forest. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show him favor, went to the forest and revealed himself in his line of sight. Seeing the Blessed One, his mind filled with serene faith, he laid down his weapon, approached, and stood with his hands raised in reverence. The Blessed One indicated his wish to sit down. The hunter immediately gathered handfuls of grass, spread them carefully on a level piece of ground, and offered it as a seat. The Blessed One sat there out of compassion. As the Blessed One was seated, the hunter, experiencing no small amount of joy and gladness, paid homage to the Blessed One and also sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This much is sufficient for this one’s seed of wholesomeness,' rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the Blessed One had departed, a lion, the king of beasts, killed him. Having passed away, he was reborn in the world of the gods. The Blessed One had approached him because he saw, 'If I do not approach, he will be killed by a lion and be reborn in hell,' and he did so for the sake of his rebirth in a happy destiny and to plant the seed of wholesomeness.

So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato devalokato cavitvā sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhino putto saṅgāmajitattherassa kaniṭṭhabhātā hutvā nibbatti. Posiyotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto dārapariggahaṃ katvā ekaṃ puttaṃ labhitvā antimabhavikatāya dhammatāya codiyamāno jātiādiṃ paṭicca uppannasaṃvego pabbajitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā vūpakaṭṭho hutvā [M 1.0121] catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.53.1-12) –

So, having remained there for the full lifespan, he then passed away from the heavenly world and, revolving only in fortunate realms, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain wealthy merchant, the younger brother of the Elder Saṅgāmajita. His name was Posiyotissa. When he came of age, he married and had one son. Urged on by the nature of being in his final existence, with spiritual urgency having arisen on account of birth and so forth, he went forth, entered the forest, and withdrew into solitude. Devoting himself to the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, before long, having intensified his practice of insight, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.53.1-12):

“Himavantassāvidūre, lambako nāma pabbato;

Tattheva tisso sambuddho, abbhokāsamhi caṅkami.

“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Lambaka; right there, the Perfectly Enlightened One Tissa walked in the open air.

“Migaluddo [V 1.0102] tadā āsiṃ, araññe kānane ahaṃ;

Disvāna taṃ devadevaṃ, tiṇamuṭṭhimadāsahaṃ.

“Then I was a hunter, in the forest, in the woods; seeing that God of gods, I gave a handful of grass.

“Nisīdanatthaṃ buddhassa, datvā cittaṃ pasādayiṃ;

Sambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā, pakkāmiṃ uttarāmukho.

“Having given it for the Buddha’s seat, I gladdened my mind; having paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, I departed facing north.

“Aciraṃ gatamattassa, migarājā apothayi;

Sohena pothito, santo tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Not long after I had gone, the king of beasts struck me down; struck down by a lion, I passed away there.

“Āsanne me kataṃ kammaṃ, buddhaseṭṭhe anāsave;

Sumutto saravegova, devalokamagacchahaṃ.

“A deed was performed by me near the time of death for the supreme, taintless Buddha; with the speed of a loosed arrow, I went to the heavenly world.

“Yūpo tattha subho āsi, puññakammābhinimmito;

Sahassakaṇḍo satabheṇḍu, dhajālu haritāmayo.

“There a beautiful pillar arose, created by that meritorious deed; with a thousand sections and a hundred globes, adorned with banners, made of beryl.

“Pabhā niddhāvate tassa, sataraṃsīva uggato;

Ākiṇṇo devakaññāhi, āmodiṃ kāmakāmihaṃ.

“Light radiated from it, like the rising sun with a hundred rays; surrounded by celestial maidens, I, a desirer of sensual pleasures, rejoiced.

“Devalokā cavitvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Āgantvāna manussattaṃ, pattomhi āsavakkhayaṃ.

“Having passed away from the heavenly world, impelled by the wholesome root, I came to the human state and attained the destruction of the taints.

“Catunnavutito kappe, nisīdanamadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, tiṇamuṭṭhe idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that seat; I know of no bad rebirth since then—this is the fruit of a handful of grass.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā bhagavantaṃ vandituṃ sāvatthiṃ āgato ñātiṃ anukampāya ñātigehaṃ agamāsi. Tattha naṃ purāṇadutiyikā vanditvā āsanadānādinā paṭhamaṃ upāsikā viya vattaṃ dassetvā therassa ajjhāsayaṃ ajānantī pacchā itthikuttādīhi palobhetukāmā ahosi[M 1.0122]. Thero “aho andhabālā mādisepi nāma evaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti cintetvā kiñci avatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā araññameva gato. Taṃ āraññakā bhikkhū “kiṃ, āvuso, atilahuṃ, nivattosi, ñātakehi na diṭṭhosī”ti pucchiṃsu. Thero tattha pavattiṃ ācikkhanto “anāsannavarā etā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, he came to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One and, out of compassion for his relatives, went to his family home. There, his former wife paid respects to him, offering a seat and so on, at first behaving like a laywoman. Not knowing the elder’s inclination, she later desired to entice him with feminine wiles and the like. The elder thought, “Alas, this blind fool behaves in such a way even toward one like me!” Without saying anything, he rose from his seat and went straight back to the forest. The forest-dwelling monks asked him, “Friend, why have you returned so quickly? Were you not seen by your relatives?” The elder, explaining what had happened there, spoke this verse: “These are best when not near.”

34. Tattha anāsannavarāti etā itthiyo na āsannā anupagatā, dūre eva vā ṭhitā hutvā varā purisassa seṭṭhā hitāvahā, tañca kho niccameva sabbakālameva, na rattimeva, na divāpi, na rahovelāyapi. Vijānatāti vijānantena. “Anāsannaparā”tipi pāḷi, so evattho. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – caṇḍahatthiassamahiṃsasīhabyagghayakkharakkhasapisācāpi manussānaṃ [V 1.0103][P 1.0103] anupasaṅkamanto varā seṭṭhā, na anatthāvahā, te pana upasaṅkamantā diṭṭhadhammikaṃyeva anatthaṃ kareyyuṃ. Itthiyo pana upasaṅkamitvā diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikaṃ vimokkhanissitampi atthaṃ vināsetvā mahantaṃ anatthaṃ āpādenti, tasmā anāsannavarā etā niccameva vijānatāti. Idāni tamatthaṃ attūpanāyikaṃ katvā dassento “gāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha gāmāti gāmaṃ. Upayogatthe hi etaṃ nissakkavacanaṃ. Araññamāgammāti araññato āgantvā. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro, nissakke cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Tatoti mañcakato. Anāmantetvāti anālapitvā purāṇadutiyikaṃ “appamattā hohī”ti ettakampi avatvā. Posiyoti attānameva paraṃ viya vadati. Ye pana “pakkāmi”nti paṭhanti, tesaṃ ahaṃ posiyo pakkāminti yojanā. Ye pana “sā itthī theraṃ gharaṃ upagataṃ bhojetvā palobhetukāmā jātā, taṃ disvā thero tāvadeva gehato nikkhamitvā vihāraṃ gantvā attano vasanaṭṭhāne mañcake nisīdi. Sāpi kho itthī pacchābhattaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattā vihāre therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ upasaṅkami. Taṃ disvā thero kiñci avatvā uṭṭhāya divāṭṭhānameva gato”ti vadanti, tesaṃ “gāmā araññamāgammā”ti gāthāpadassa attho yathārutavaseneva niyyati. Vihāro hi idha “arañña”nti adhippeto.

34. Here, anāsannavarā means these women are not close, not approached; they are excellent, beneficial, and best for a man when they remain at a distance—always, at all times, not just at night, not just by day, not even at a time of solitude. Vijānatā means by one who understands. The reading anāsannaparā is also found, with the same meaning. The intended meaning here is this: even fierce elephants, horses, buffaloes, lions, tigers, yakkhas, rakkhasas, and pisācas, if they do not approach humans, are excellent and best, not harmful. But if they do approach, they would cause harm only in this present life. Women, however, when they approach, destroy benefit related to this life, the next life, and even that connected with liberation, leading to great harm. Therefore, ‘these are always best when not near, for one who knows.’ Now, illustrating this point with a personal example, he says gāmā, etc. Here, gāmā means ‘to the village’; this ablative form is used in the sense of the accusative. Araññamāgammā means ‘having come from the forest.’ The ‘m’ here is a euphonic conjunction, and this is a usage in the sense of the ablative. Tato means ‘from the cot.’ Anāmantetvā means without addressing his former wife, without saying even so much as “Be heedful.” Posiyo refers to himself, speaking as if of another. For those who read pakkāmi, the construction is “I, Posiya, departed.” As for those who say, “That woman, having fed the elder who had come to her house, became desirous of enticing him. Seeing this, the elder immediately left the house and went to the monastery, sitting on the cot in his dwelling place. And that woman, after the meal, adorned and prepared, approached the elder’s dwelling in the monastery. Seeing her, the elder said nothing, rose, and went to his day-quarters”—for them, the meaning of the verse line gāmā araññamāgammā is taken according to the literal reading. For here, the monastery is intended by arañña (forest).

Posiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Posiya is concluded.

5. Sāmaññakānittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sāmaññakāni

Sukhaṃ [M 1.0123] sukhatthoti āyasmato sāmaññakānittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro hutvā tattha tattha bhave kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle manussayoniyaṃ nibbatto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ekaṃ mañcaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde aññatarassa paribbājakassa putto hutvā [P 1.0104] nibbatti. Sāmaññakānītissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto satthu yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sāsane pabbajitvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā jhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.36.30-33) –

“Happiness for the sake of happiness…”: this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sāmaññakāni. What is its origin? It is said that, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various existences, ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a human womb. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, with a confident mind, he offered a single couch. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born as the son of a certain wanderer. His name was Sāmaññakānītissa. Having attained understanding, he saw the Twin Miracle performed by the Teacher. With a confident mind, he went forth into the dispensation. Taking up a meditation subject suited to his disposition, he developed jhāna. Making jhāna his foundation, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.36.30-33):

“Vipassino bhagavato, lokajeṭṭhassa tādino;

Ekaṃ mañcaṃ mayā dinnaṃ, pasannena sapāṇinā.

“To the Blessed One Vipassī, the Eldest in the World, the Imperturbable One, one couch was given by me, with a confident mind and my own hands.
