“Hatthiyānaṃ [V 1.0104] assayānaṃ, dibbayānaṃ samajjhagaṃ;

Tena mañcaka dānena, pattomhi āsavakkhayaṃ.

“I obtained elephant vehicles, horse vehicles, and divine vehicles; through that offering of a couch, I have attained the destruction of the taints.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ mañcamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, mañcadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that couch, I have not known a bad rebirth: this is the fruit of the gift of a couch.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Therassa pana gihisahāyako kātiyāno nāma paribbājako buddhuppādato paṭṭhāya titthiyānaṃ hatalābhasakkāratāya ghāsacchādanamattampi alabhanto ājīvakāpakato theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe sākiyaputtiyā nāma mahālābhaggayasaggappattā sukhena jīvatha, mayaṃ pana dukkhitā kicchajīvikā, kathaṃ nu kho paṭipajjamānassa diṭṭhadhammikañceva samparāyikañca sukhaṃ sampajjatī”ti pucchi. Athassa thero “nippariyāyato sukhaṃ nāma lokuttarasukhameva, tañca tadanurūpaṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjantassevā”ti attanā tassa adhigatabhāvaṃ pariyāyena vibhāvento “sukhaṃ sukhattho labhate tadācara”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Now, a lay friend of the Elder, a wanderer named Kātiyāna, who, since the arising of the Buddha, had lost his gains and honor from the sectarians and was not obtaining even enough for food and clothing, his livelihood having deteriorated, approached the Elder and asked: “You followers of the Sakyan son live happily, having attained the peak of gains and fame, but we are afflicted, our livelihood difficult. How, indeed, should one practice so that happiness both in this very life and in the life to come may be accomplished?” Then the Elder, explaining indirectly the state he himself had attained, said, “Happiness, in the absolute sense, is indeed only supramundane happiness, and that is for one who undertakes the practice suitable for it,” and he spoke this verse: “One who desires happiness obtains happiness by practicing for it.”

35. Tattha [M 1.0124] sukhanti nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ idhādhippetaṃ. Tañca phalasamāpatti ceva nibbānañca. Tathā hi “ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko” (dī. ni. 3.355; a. ni. 5.27; vibha. 804) “nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (dha. pa. 203-204) ca vuttaṃ. Sukhatthoti sukhappayojano, yathāvuttena sukhena atthiko. Labhateti pāpuṇāti, atthikassevedaṃ sukhaṃ, na itarassa. Ko pana atthikoti āha “tadācara”nti tadatthaṃ ācaranto, yāya paṭipattiyā taṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjantoti attho. Na kevalaṃ tadācaraṃ sukhameva labhate, atha kho kittiñca pappoti “itipi sīlavā suparisuddhakāyavacīkammanto suparisuddhājīvo jhāyī jhānayutto”tiādinā kittiṃ parammukhā patthaṭayasataṃ pāpuṇāti. Yasassa vaḍḍhatīti [P 1.0105] sammukhe guṇābhitthavasaṅkhāto parivārasampadāsaṅkhāto ca yaso assa paribrūhati. Idāni “tadācara”nti sāmaññato vuttamatthaṃ sarūpato dassento – “yo ariyamaṭṭhaṅgikamañjasaṃ ujuṃ, bhāveti maggaṃ amatassa pattiyā”ti āha. Tassattho yo puggalo kilesehi ārakattā parisuddhaṭṭhena paṭipajjantānaṃ ariyabhāvakaraṇaṭṭhena ariyaṃ, sammādiṭṭhiādiaṭṭhaṅgasamudāyatāya aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ, antadvayarahitamajjhimapaṭipattibhāvato akuṭilaṭṭhena añjasaṃ, kāyavaṅkādippahānato ujuṃ, nibbānatthikehi magganiyaṭṭhena kilese mārento gamanaṭṭhena ca “magga”nti laddhanāmaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadaṃ amatassa asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā pattiyā adhigamāya bhāveti attano santāne uppādeti vaḍḍheti ca, so nippariyāyena “sukhattho tadācara”nti [V 1.0105] vuccati, tasmā yathāvuttaṃ sukhaṃ labhati. Taṃ sutvā paribbājako pasannamānaso pabbajitvā sammā paṭipajjanto nacirasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Idameva therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

35. Herein, by ‘happiness’ is meant unworldly happiness. And that is both the attainment of fruition and Nibbāna. For so it is said: “This concentration is pleasant in the present and also has a happy result in the future” (Dī. Ni. 3.355; A. Ni. 5.27; Vibha. 804), and “Nibbāna is the supreme happiness” (Dha. Pa. 203-204). By ‘one who desires happiness’ is meant one whose purpose is happiness, one who is desirous of the happiness spoken of. ‘Obtains’ means attains; this happiness is for one who is desirous, not for another. But who is the one who is desirous? He said, ‘by practicing for it,’ meaning one who practices for that purpose, one who undertakes that practice. Not only does one who practices for it obtain happiness, but he also attains fame. By such words as, “Thus he is virtuous, of perfectly pure bodily and verbal conduct, of perfectly pure livelihood, a meditator, devoted to jhāna,” he attains fame, a reputation spread among hundreds in his absence. ‘His fame increases’ means his renown—described as the praise of his virtues in his presence and as the accomplishment of a retinue—flourishes. Now, showing in its specific form the meaning stated generally as ‘by practicing for it,’ he said: “Whoever develops the noble eightfold path, the straight and direct way, for the attainment of the deathless.” The meaning of this is: whichever person develops the path leading to the cessation of suffering—which is called ‘noble’ because of its distance from the defilements, its sense of purity, and because it makes noble those who practice it; ‘eightfold’ because it is a collection of the eight factors beginning with right view; ‘straight’ because it is the middle practice devoid of the two extremes and thus is not crooked; ‘direct’ because it abandons bodily crookedness and so on; and has received the name ‘path’ because it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna and because one goes along it destroying the defilements—he develops it, meaning he produces and cultivates it in his own mental continuum, for the attainment of the deathless, the unconditioned element. Such a person is, in the absolute sense, called ‘one who desires happiness and practices for it.’ Therefore, he obtains the happiness spoken of. Hearing that, the wanderer, with a confident mind, went forth, and by practicing rightly, before long developed insight and attained arahantship. This itself was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Sāmaññakānittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāmaññakāni is concluded.

6. Kumāputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumāputta

Sādhu [M 1.0125] sutanti āyasmato kumāputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppati? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito ekanavute kappe ajinacammavasano tāpaso hutvā bandhumatīnagare rājuyyāne vasanto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso pādabbhañjanatelaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto. Tato paṭṭhāya sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde avantiraṭṭhe veḷukaṇṭakanagare gahapatikule nibbatto. “Nando”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Mātā panassa kumā nāma, tena kumāputtoti paññāyittha. So āyasmato sāriputtassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā laddhappasādo pabbajitvā katapubbakicco pariyantapabbatapasse samaṇadhammaṃ karonto visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto [P 1.0106] bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā sappāyaṭṭhāne vasanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.53.24-30) –

The verse beginning, 'Sādhu sutaṃ,' is that of the Venerable Elder Kumāputta. What is its origin? It is said that this elder, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, ninety-one aeons ago became an ascetic wearing a hide garment. While dwelling in the royal park in the city of Bandhumatī, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī and, with a confident mind, gave oil for anointing the feet. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in a deva world. From then on, wandering only in good destinations, during this Buddha-era he was born into a householder family in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka in the Avanti country. They gave him the name Nanda. His mother’s name, however, was Kumā, by which he became known as Kumāputta. Having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta, he gained faith and went forth. Having completed the preliminary duties, while practicing the recluse’s duties on the slope of Mount Pariyanta, he was unable to bring about a special attainment. He approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, purified his meditation subject, and, dwelling in a suitable place, developed insight and realized arahantship. Thus it was said by him in the Apadāna:

“Nagare bandhumatiyā, rājuyyāne vasāmahaṃ;

Cammavāsī tadā āsiṃ, kamaṇḍaludharo ahaṃ.

“In the city of Bandhumatī, I dwelt in the royal park; I was then clad in a hide garment, a bearer of a water pot.

“Addasaṃ vimalaṃ buddhaṃ, sayambhuṃ aparājitaṃ;

Padhānaṃ pahitattaṃ taṃ, jhāyiṃ jhānarataṃ vasiṃ.

“I saw the stainless Buddha, the Self-Became, the Unconquered, the Striving One, resolute, a meditator delighting in meditation, a master.”

“Sabbakāmasamiddhañca, oghatiṇṇamanāsavaṃ;

Disvā pasannasumano, abbhañjanamadāsahaṃ.

“And seeing him, fulfilled in all wishes, who had crossed the flood and was without taints, with a confident and joyful mind, I gave an unguent.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, abbhañjanamadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, abbhañjanassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first aeon from the present, I gave an unguent; I know of no bad destination since then; this is the fruit of that offering of an unguent.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0106] pana patvā araññe kāyadaḷhibahule bhikkhū, disvā te ovadanto sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ pakāsento “sādhu sutaṃ sādhu caritaka”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

But having attained arahantship, seeing in the forest monks who were mostly of strong constitution, he advised them, proclaiming the liberating nature of the Teaching, and spoke the verse beginning: “Good is learning, good is conduct.”

36. Tattha [M 1.0126] sādhūti sundaraṃ. Sutanti savanaṃ. Tañca kho vivaṭṭūpanissitaṃ visesato appicchatādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dasakathāvatthusavanaṃ idhādhippetaṃ. Sādhu caritakanti tadeva appicchatādicaritaṃ ciṇṇaṃ, sādhucaritameva hi “caritaka”nti vuttaṃ. Padadvayenāpi bāhusaccaṃ tadanurūpaṃ paṭipattiñca “sundara”nti dasseti. Sadāti sabbakāle navakamajjhimatherakāle, sabbesu vā iriyāpathakkhaṇesu. Aniketavihāroti kilesānaṃ nivāsanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena pañcakāmaguṇā niketā nāma, lokiyā vā chaḷārammaṇadhammā. Yathāha – “rūpanimittaniketavisāravinibandhā kho, gahapati, ‘niketasārī’ti vuccatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.3). Tesaṃ niketānaṃ pahānatthāya paṭipadā aniketavihāro. Atthapucchananti taṃ ājānitukāmassa kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthapabhedassa pucchanaṃ, kusalādibhedassa vā atthassa sabhāvadhammassa “kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusalaṃ, kiṃ sāvajjaṃ, kiṃ anavajja”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.296) pucchanaṃ atthapucchanaṃ. Padakkhiṇakammanti taṃ pana pucchitvā padakkhiṇaggāhibhāvena tassa ovāde adhiṭṭhānaṃ sammāpaṭipatti. Idhāpi “sādhū”ti padaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Etaṃ sāmaññanti “sādhu suta”ntiādinā vuttaṃ yaṃ sutaṃ, yañca caritaṃ, yo ca aniketavihāro[P 1.0107], yañca atthapucchanaṃ, yañca padakkhiṇakammaṃ, etaṃ sāmaññaṃ eso samaṇabhāvo. Yasmā imāya eva paṭipadāya samaṇabhāvo, na aññathā, tasmā “sāmañña”nti nippariyāyato maggaphalassa adhivacanaṃ. Tassa vā pana ayaṃ apaṇṇakapaṭipadā, taṃ panetaṃ sāmaññaṃ yādisassa sambhavāti, taṃ dassetuṃ “akiñcanassā”ti vuttaṃ. Apariggāhakassa, khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇadāsidāsādipariggahapaṭiggahaṇarahitassāti attho.

36. Here, ‘sādhu’ means beautiful. ‘Suta’ means hearing. Specifically, it refers to listening to the ten topics of discussion connected with contentment and so on, which are based on detachment. ‘Sādhu caritaka’ refers to that very practice of contentment and so on that has been cultivated, for ‘caritaka’ is indeed said to be good conduct. The two words also indicate extensive learning and corresponding practice as “beautiful.” ‘Sadā’ means at all times—whether in youth, middle age, or old age, or in all postures and moments. ‘Aniketavihāra’ refers to the practice aimed at abandoning dwellings, which are called ‘niketa’ because they serve as the abodes of defilements, such as the five strands of sensual pleasure or the six worldly sense objects. As it is said: “Householder, one who is bound by the diffusion of the dwelling on the sign of form is called a ‘dweller’ (niketasārī)” and so on. The practice for abandoning these dwellings is ‘aniketavihāra’. ‘Atthapucchana’ means approaching a good friend who knows and inquiring about the distinctions of meaning pertaining to the present world, the next, and the ultimate goal, or asking about the nature of wholesome and unwholesome qualities, such as: “Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless?” and so on. ‘Padakkhiṇakamma’ means, after asking, firmly resolving to follow the advice with reverence, which is right practice. Here too, the word ‘sādhu’ should be brought in and connected. ‘Etaṃ sāmañña’ refers to what is said by ‘sādhu suta’ and so on—what is heard, what is practiced, the dwelling without a fixed abode, the inquiry into meaning, and the reverential practice. This is the ascetic practice; this is the state of a contemplative. Since the state of a contemplative is achieved only by this practice and not otherwise, ‘sāmañña’ is a direct term for the path and fruit. Moreover, this is the infallible practice, and this ascetic practice is possible for one who is such. To show this, it is said ‘akiñcanassa’—for one who is without possessions, devoid of grasping and accepting fields, lands, gold, silver, male and female slaves, and so on. This is the meaning.

Kumāputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumāputta is concluded.

7. Kumāputtasahāyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumāputta's Companion

Nānājanapadaṃ [M 1.0127] yantīti āyasmato kumāputtasahāyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto araññaṃ pavisitvā bahuṃ rukkhadaṇḍaṃ chinditvā kattarayaṭṭhiṃ katvā saṅghassa adāsi. Aññañca yathāvibhavaṃ puññaṃ katvā devesu [V 1.0107] nibbattitvā tato paṭṭhāya sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde veḷukaṇṭakanagare iddhe kule nibbatti. Sudantotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. “Vāsulo”ti keci vadanti. So kumāputtassa piyasahāyo hutvā vicaranto “kumāputto pabbajito”ti sutvā “na hi nūna so orako dhammavinayo, yattha kumāputto pabbajito”ti tadanubandhena sayampi pabbajitukāmo hutvā satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkami. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So bhiyyosomattāya pabbajjāya sañjātachando pabbajitvā kumāputteneva saddhiṃ pariyantapabbate bhāvanānuyutto viharati. Tena ca samayena sambahulā bhikkhū nānājanapadesu janapadacārikaṃ carantāpi gacchantāpi āgacchantāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ [P 1.0108] upagacchanti. Tena tattha kolāhalaṃ hoti. Taṃ disvā sudantatthero “ime bhikkhū niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā janapadavitakkaṃ anuvattentā cittasamādhiṃ virādhentī”ti saṃvegajāto tameva saṃvegaṃ attano cittadamanassa aṅkusaṃ karonto “nānājanapadaṃ yantī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

“Traveling to various countries” is a verse of the Venerable Elder, the companion of Kumāputta. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of previous Buddhas, he had performed meritorious deeds, accumulating wholesome actions here and there that are a supporting condition for liberation. Ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a family of means, and having attained understanding, he entered the forest, cut many tree branches, made a traveling staff, and offered it to the Saṅgha. Having performed other meritorious deeds according to his means, he was reborn among the devas. From then on, he continued to revolve only among happy destinies until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a prosperous family in the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka. His name was Sudanta, though some call him Vāsula. He became the dear companion of Kumāputta and, while wandering, heard that Kumāputta had gone forth. Thinking, “Surely, this is no inferior Dhamma-Vinaya, where Kumāputta has gone forth,” he too, following that lead, desired to go forth and approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. With growing enthusiasm for ordination, he went forth and, together with Kumāputta, dwelt devoted to meditation on a border mountain. At that time, many bhikkhus traveling through various regions, whether going or coming, would visit that place. This caused a commotion there. Seeing this, the Elder Sudanta, stirred by spiritual urgency, thought, “These bhikkhus, having gone forth in this liberating dispensation, are following thoughts of various regions, thus disrupting their mental concentration.” Making that very spiritual urgency a goad for taming his own mind, he spoke the verse: “Traveling to various countries...”

37. Tattha nānājanapadanti visuṃ visuṃ nānāvidhaṃ janapadaṃ, kāsikosalādianekaraṭṭhanti attho. Yantīti gacchanti. Vicarantāti “asuko janapado subhikkho sulabhapiṇḍo, asuko khemo arogo”tiādivitakkavasena janapadacārikaṃ carantā. Asaññatāti tasseva janapadavitakkassa appahīnatāya cittena asaṃyatā. Samādhiñca virādhentīti sabbassapi uttarimanussadhammassa mūlabhūtaṃ upacārappanābhedaṃ samādhiñca nāma virādhenti[M 1.0128]. Ca-saddo sambhāvane. Desantaracaraṇena jhāyituṃ okāsābhāvena anadhigataṃ samādhiṃ nādhigacchantā, adhigatañca vasībhāvānāpādanena jīrantā vīrādhenti nāma. Kiṃsu raṭṭhacariyā karissatīti sūti nipātamattaṃ. “Evaṃbhūtānaṃ raṭṭhacariyā janapadacārikā kiṃ karissati, kiṃ nāma atthaṃ sādhessati, niratthakāvā”ti garahanto vadati. Tasmāti yasmā īdisī desantaracariyā bhikkhussa na atthāvahā, api ca kho anatthāvahā sampattīnaṃ virādhanato, tasmā. Vineyya sārambhanti vasanapadese arativasena uppannaṃ sārambhaṃ cittasaṃkilesaṃ tadanurūpena paṭisaṅkhānena vinetvā vūpasametvā. Jhāyeyyāti ārammaṇūpanijjhānena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena cāti duvidhenapi jhānena jhāyeyya. Apurakkhatoti micchāvitakkehi taṇhādīhi vā na purakkhatoti tesaṃ vasaṃ anupagacchanto kammaṭṭhānameva manasi kareyyāti attho. Evaṃ pana vatvā thero tameva saṃvegaṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.53.36-41) –

37. There, “various countries” means different kinds of countries separately, such as Kāsi, Kosala, and many other regions. “They go” means they travel. “Wandering” means moving through various regions, prompted by thoughts such as, “That country has abundant food and easy alms; that one is safe and free from disease.” “Unrestrained” refers to the mind being uncontrolled due to not having abandoned such thoughts about countries. “And they disrupt concentration” means they disrupt the very concentration, whether access or absorption, that is the root of all supramundane states. The word “ca” is used for emphasis. Because they have no opportunity to meditate while traveling to other lands, they fail to attain concentration not yet attained, and even the concentration they have attained deteriorates due to not bringing it to mastery—thus, they are said to disrupt it. “What will country-wandering do?”—here, ‘su’ is merely a particle. Criticizing, he says, “For those who are like this, what will country-wandering, this traveling through regions, accomplish? What purpose will it serve? It is useless.” “Therefore” means: since such travel to other lands brings no benefit to a bhikkhu, but rather brings harm by ruining his attainments, for that reason... “Having dispelled resentment” means having removed and pacified, through appropriate reflection, the mental defilement of resentment that arises due to discontent with one's dwelling place. “He should meditate” means he should meditate with both kinds of meditation: meditation by focusing on the object and meditation by focusing on the characteristics. “Not being led forward” means not being led by wrong thoughts or cravings, not submitting to their influence, but focusing only on the meditation subject. Having said this, the elder used that very spiritual urgency as a goad, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Hence, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kānanaṃ [P 1.0109] vanamoggayha, veḷuṃ chetvānahaṃ tadā;

Ālambanaṃ karitvāna, saṅghassa adadiṃ bahuṃ.

“Having entered the forest, the woodland, and having cut bamboo then, I made many supports and gave them to the Saṅgha.

“Tena [V 1.0108] cittappasādena, subbate abhivādiya;

Ālambadaṇḍaṃ datvāna, pakkāmiṃ uttarāmukho.

“Through that mental clarity, having paid homage to one of good vows, and having given a support-staff, I departed facing north.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ daṇḍamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, daṇḍadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-four aeons since I gave that staff, I do not recall any bad destination; this is the fruit of giving a staff.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Yaṃ panatthaṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā ayaṃ thero arahattaṃ patto, tamevatthaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pattopi “nānājanapadaṃ yanti”ti idameva gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tasmā tadevassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

The purpose that this elder made a goad to attain Arahantship—having placed that very purpose in his heart, even after attaining Arahantship, he spoke this very verse: “They go to various countries.” Therefore, that itself was his declaration of final knowledge.

Kumāputtasahāyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumāputta's Companion is concluded.

8. Gavampatittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gavampati

Yo [M 1.0129] iddhiyā sarabhunti āyasmato gavampatittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso pupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke uppanno aparāparaṃ puññāni karonto koṇāgamanassa bhagavato cetiye chattañca vedikañca kāresi. Kassapassa pana bhagavato kāle aññatarasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto. Tasmiñca kule bahuṃ gomaṇḍalaṃ ahosi. Taṃ gopālakā rakkhanti. Ayaṃ tattha antarantarā yuttappayuttaṃ vicārento vicarati. So ekaṃ khīṇāsavattheraṃ gāme piṇḍāya caritvā bahigāme devasikaṃ ekasmiṃ padese bhattakiccaṃ karontaṃ disvā “ayyo sūriyātapena kilamissatī”ti cintetvā cattāro sirīsadaṇḍe ussāpetvā tesaṃ upari sirīsasākhāyo ṭhapetvā sākhāmaṇḍapaṃ katvā adāsi. “Maṇḍapassa samīpe sirīsarukkhaṃ ropesī”ti ca vadanti. Tassa anukampāya devasikaṃ thero tattha nisīdi. So tena puññakammena tato cavitvā cātumahārājikesu nibbatti. Tassa purimakammasaṃsūcakaṃ vimānadvāre mahantaṃ sirīsavanaṃ nibbatti vaṇṇagandhasampannehi aññehi pupphehi sabbakāle upasobhayamānaṃ, tena taṃ vimānaṃ “serīsaka”nti paññāyittha. So devaputto ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde yasattherassa catūsu [P 1.0110] gihisahāyesu gavampati nāma hutvā āyasmato yasassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā attano sahāyehi saddhiṃ bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi[V 1.0109]. Satthā tassa dhammaṃ desesi. So desanāvasāne sahāyehi saddhiṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.53.42-47) –

The verse of the Venerable Gavampati Thera, 'He who by psychic power [restrained] the Sarabhu...' What is its origin? It is said that in the time of previous Buddhas, he had made an aspiration. In the thirty-first eon from now, having seen the Blessed One Sikhi, with a serene mind, he made an offering of flowers. By that meritorious deed, he arose in the deva world, and repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, he later had a parasol and a railing made at the shrine of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana. Then, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born in a certain family. And in that family there was a large herd of cattle. Cowherds looked after them. While wandering there from time to time, he would consider what was suitable and unsuitable. One day, seeing an elder who was an arahant, who had gone for alms in the village and was taking his meal daily in a certain place outside the village, he thought, 'The venerable one will be wearied by the sun's heat.' So he set up four sirisa poles, placed sirisa branches on top of them, and having made a branch canopy, he gave it. And they also say, 'He planted a sirisa tree near the canopy.' Out of compassion for him, the elder sat there daily. By that meritorious deed, after passing away from there, he was reborn among the Four Great Kings. Indicating his former deed, a great sirisa grove arose at the gate of his celestial mansion, adorned at all times with other flowers endowed with excellent color and fragrance; thus that mansion became known as 'Serisaka.' That deity, after wandering among devas and humans for one Buddha-interval, at the arising of this Buddha, became Gavampati, one of the four lay companions of the Elder Yasa. Hearing of the Venerable Yasa's going forth, he went with his companions to the presence of the Blessed One. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, together with his companions, he was established in arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.53.42-47):

“Migaluddo pure āsiṃ, vipine vicaraṃ ahaṃ;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ.

“Formerly, I was a deer hunter, wandering in the forest. I saw the stainless Buddha, who had gone to the far shore of all things.

“Tasmiṃ mahākāruṇike, sabbasattahite rate;

Pasannacitto sumano, nelapupphaṃ apūjayiṃ.

“To that greatly compassionate one, who delighted in the welfare of all beings, with a serene and joyful mind, I offered a stainless flower.”

“Ekatiṃse [M 1.0130] ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, since offering that flower, I know of no bad destination. This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento sākete viharati añjanavane. Tena ca samayena bhagavā mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ sāketaṃ gantvā añjanavane vihāsi. Senāsanaṃ nappahosi. Sambahulā bhikkhū vihārasāmantā sarabhuyā nadiyā vālikāpuḷine sayiṃsu. Atha aḍḍharattasamaye nadiyā udakoghe āgacchante sāmaṇerādayo uccāsaddamahāsaddā ahesuṃ. Bhagavā taṃ ñatvā āyasmantaṃ gavampatiṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha, gavampati, jaloghaṃ vikkhambhetvā bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ karohī”ti. Thero “sādhu, bhante”ti iddhibalena nadīsotaṃ vikkhambhi, taṃ dūratova pabbatakūṭaṃ viya aṭṭhāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya therassa ānubhāvo loke pākaṭo ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ satthā mahatiyā devaparisāya majjhe nisīditvā dhammaṃ desentaṃ theraṃ disvā lokānukampāya tassa guṇānaṃ vibhāvanatthaṃ taṃ pasaṃsanto “yo iddhiyā sarabhu”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, the elder, experiencing the bliss of liberation, was dwelling in Añjanavana in Sāketa. And at that time, the Blessed One, having gone to Sāketa with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, dwelt in Añjanavana. The lodgings were insufficient. Many bhikkhus slept on the sandy bank of the Sarabhu River near the monastery. Then, at midnight, as a flood of water was coming down the river, the novices and others made a loud and great noise. Knowing this, the Blessed One commanded the Venerable Gavampati: 'Go, Gavampati, restrain the flood of water and provide the bhikkhus with a comfortable abiding.' The elder replied, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and with psychic power he restrained the river's current; it stood still from afar like a mountain peak. From that time on, the elder's power became manifest in the world. Then one day, the Teacher, seated amidst a great assembly of devas, saw the elder teaching the Dhamma and, out of compassion for the world, praising him to make his virtues known, he recited the verse: 'He who by psychic power [restrained] the Sarabhu...'

38. Tattha iddhiyāti adhiṭṭhāniddhiyā. Sarabhunti evaṃnāmikaṃ nadiṃ, yaṃ loke “sarabhu”nti vadanti. Aṭṭhapesīti sandituṃ adento sotaṃ nivattetvā pabbatakūṭaṃ viya mahantaṃ jalarāsiṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Asitoti nasito, taṇhādiṭṭhinissayarahito, bandhanasaṅkhātānaṃ vā sabbasaṃyojanānaṃ samucchinnattā kenacipi bandhanena abaddho, tato eva ejānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvato anejo so, gavampati, taṃ sabbasaṅgātigataṃ tādisaṃ sabbepi rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhisaṅge atikkamitvā [P 1.0111] ṭhitattā sabbasaṅgātigataṃ, asekkhamunibhāvato mahāmuniṃ, tato eva kāmakammabhavādibhedassa sakalassapi bhavassa pāraṃ nibbānaṃ gatattā bhavassa pāraguṃ. Devā namassantīti devāpi imassanti, pageva itarā pajāti.

38. Here, 'by psychic power' (iddhiyā) means by the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi). 'Sarabhu' refers to a river of that name, which people in the world call 'Sarabhu.' 'He made it stand' (aṭṭhapesīti) means that, not allowing it to flow, he turned back the current and made a great mass of water stand like a mountain peak. 'Unattached' (asito) means not attached, devoid of reliance on craving and wrong view; or, because all fetters, which are reckoned as bonds, have been completely cut off, he is unbound by any bond. Therefore, due to the absence of defilements that cause agitation, he is unagitated (anejo). That one (taṃ), Gavampati, is ‘one who has gone beyond all attachments’ (sabbasaṅgātigataṃ) because he stands having transcended all attachments such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong views. He is a ‘Great Sage’ (mahāmuniṃ) because of his state as a sage with no more training. And he has ‘gone to the far shore of existence’ (bhavassa pāraguṃ) because he has reached Nibbāna, the far shore of all existence, which is differentiated by sensuality, kamma, becoming, and so on. 'The devas pay homage' (devā namassanti) means even the devas pay homage to this one; how much more so other beings.

Gāthāpariyosāne [M 1.0131][V 1.0110] mahato janakāyassa dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Thero aññaṃ byākaronto “satthāraṃ pūjessāmī”ti imameva gāthaṃ abhāsīti.

At the conclusion of the verse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for a great multitude of people. The elder, while giving another discourse, spoke this very verse, thinking, 'I will honor the Teacher.'

Gavampatittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Gavampati is concluded.

9. Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Tissa

Sattiyā viya omaṭṭhoti āyasmato tissattherassa gāthā. Kā uppati? Ayampi kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto tissassa bhagavato bodhiyā mūle purāṇapaṇṇāni nīharitvā sodhesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare bhagavato pitucchāputto hutvā nibbatti tisso nāma nāmena. So bhagavantaṃ anupabbajitvā upasampanno hutvā araññāyatane viharanto jātiṃ paṭicca mānaṃ karonto kodhūpāyāsabahulo ca ujjhānabahulo ca hutvā vicarati, samaṇadhamme ussukkaṃ na karoti. Atha naṃ satthā ekadivasaṃ divāṭṭhāne vivaṭamukhaṃ niddāyantaṃ dibbacakkhunā olokento sāvatthito ākāsena gantvā tassa upari ākāseyeva ṭhatvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā tenobhāsena paṭibuddhassa satiṃ uppādetvā ovādaṃ dento “sattiyā viya omaṭṭho”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

“As if struck with a spear” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Tissa. What is its origin? This one, it is said, having made an aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merit here and there in his existences as a basis for release from the round of rebirth, swept away the old leaves at the foot of the Blessed One Tissa's Bodhi tree and cleaned the place. As a result of that meritorious action, while wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in the city of Kapilavatthu as the Blessed One's paternal cousin, by the name of Tissa. Having gone forth under the Blessed One and received higher ordination, while dwelling in a forest abode, he became conceited on account of his birth, was frequently full of anger and distress, and was often given to complaining; he did not apply himself with zeal to the duties of a monk. Then one day, the Teacher, surveying him with his divine eye, saw him sleeping with his mouth open at his daytime resting place. From Sāvatthī, he went through the air and, standing above him in the sky itself, radiated light. Awakening him with that light and arousing his mindfulness, the Teacher gave him this advice, speaking the verse: “As if struck with a spear...”

39. Tattha sattiyāti desanāsīsametaṃ, ekatodhārādinā satthenāti attho. Omaṭṭhoti pahato. Cattāro hi pahārā omaṭṭho ummaṭṭho maṭṭho vimaṭṭhoti. Tattha upari ṭhatvā adhomukhaṃ dinnapahāro omaṭṭho nāma, heṭṭhā ṭhatvā uddhammukhaṃ dinnapahāro ummaṭṭho nāma, aggaḷasūci [P 1.0112] viya vinivijjhitvā gato maṭṭho nāma, seso sabbopi vimaṭṭho nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne omaṭṭho gahito. So hi sabbadāruṇo duruddharaṇasallo duttikiccho antodoso antopubbalohitova hoti, pubbalohitaṃ anikkhamitvā vaṇamukhaṃ pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati. Pubbalohitaṃ nīharitukāmehi mañcena saddhiṃ bandhitvā adhosiro kātabbo [M 1.0132] hoti, maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti. Ḍayhamāneti agginā jhāyamāne. Matthaketi sīse. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā sattiyā omaṭṭho puriso sallubbāhanavaṇatikicchanānaṃ atthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati tādisaṃ payogaṃ karoti parakkamati, yathā ca ḍayhamāne matthake ādittasīso puriso tassa nibbāpanatthaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhati tādisaṃ payogaṃ karoti, evamevaṃ, bhikkhu, kāmarāgappahānāya sato appamatto ativiya ussāhajāto hutvā vihareyyāti.

39. Therein, 'by a spear' is the heading of the discourse; the meaning is by a weapon with a single edge, and so forth, such as a sword. 'Struck down' means struck. For there are four kinds of blows: struck down, struck up, struck through, and struck around. Among these, a blow delivered downward from above is called 'struck down'; a blow delivered upward from below is called 'struck up'; a blow that goes through, piercing like a door-pin, is called 'struck through'; and all the rest are called 'struck around.' In this context, however, 'struck down' is to be understood. For this is the most terrible, a barb difficult to extract, hard to treat, with an internal affliction, and containing pus and blood within. The pus and blood do not exit but remain, covering over the mouth of the wound. By those who wish to remove the pus and blood, he must be tied to a bed and made head-down; they experience death or suffering equivalent to death. 'Burning' means being scorched by fire. 'On the head' means on the head. This is what is said: Just as a man struck down by a spear arouses energy, makes the necessary application, and exerts himself for the sake of extracting the barb and treating the wound; and just as a man with his head on fire—his head ablaze—arouses energy and makes the necessary application to extinguish it; in the very same way, O monk, for the abandoning of sensual desire, you should dwell mindful, diligent, and having become intensely energetic.

Evaṃ [V 1.0111] bhagavā tassa therassa kodhūpāyāsavūpasamāya ovādaṃ dento tadekaṭṭhatāya kāmarāgappahānasīsena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Thero imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā saṃviggahadayo vipassanāya yuttappayutto vihāsi. Tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā satthā saṃyuttake tissattherasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.84) desesi. So desanāpariyosāne arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.53.66-73) –

Thus the Blessed One, giving advice to that elder for the calming of his anger and distress, concluded the teaching with the abandoning of sensual desire as its central point for the sake of that one purpose. The elder, having heard this verse, became stirred in heart and dwelt engaged and applied to insight meditation. Knowing his inclination, the Teacher taught the Tissatthera Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 22.84). At the conclusion of the teaching, he was established in arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap Th 2.53.66–73):

“Devaloke manusse ce, anubhotvā ubho yase;

Avasāne ca nibbānaṃ, sivaṃ patto anuttaraṃ.

“Having experienced glory both in the world of devas and among humans, in the end I attained the unsurpassed, secure Nibbāna.”

“Sambuddhaṃ uddisitvāna, bodhiṃ vā tassa satthuno;

Yo puññaṃ pasavī poso, tassa kiṃ nāma dullabhaṃ.

“For the person who generates merit, having been mindful of the Sambuddha or the Bodhi of that Teacher, what indeed is difficult to obtain?”

“Magge phale āgame ca, jhānābhiññāguṇesu ca;

Aññesaṃ adhiko hutvā, nibbāyāmi anāsavo.

“In the path, the fruition, and the scriptures, and in the qualities of jhāna and the supernormal knowledges, having become superior to others, I attain Nibbāna without cankers.”

“Purehaṃ bodhiyā pattaṃ, chaḍḍetvā haṭṭhamānaso;

Imehi vīsataṅgehi, samaṅgī homi sabbathā.

“Formerly, with a joyful mind, I swept a leaf of the Bodhi tree; now, I am in every way endowed with these twenty qualities.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero aññaṃ byākaronto satthāraṃ pūjetuṃ tameva gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, however, the elder, while declaring his final knowledge, spoke that very verse to honor the Teacher.

Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tissa is concluded.

10. Vaḍḍhamānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vaḍḍhamāna

Sattiyā [M 1.0133][P 1.0113] viya omaṭṭhoti āyasmato vaḍḍhamānattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito dvenavute kappe tissassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tissaṃ bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso suparipakkāni vaṇṭato muttāni ambaphalāni adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññakammāni upacinanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ licchavirājakule nibbatti, vaḍḍhamānotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto saddho pasanno dāyako dānarato kārako saṅghupaṭṭhāko hutvā tathārūpe aparādhe satthārā pattanikkujjanakamme kārāpite aggiṃ akkanto viya saṅghaṃ khamāpetvā kammaṃ paṭippassambhetvā sañjātasaṃvego pabbaji, pabbajitvā pana [V 1.0112] thinamiddhābhibhūto vihāsi. Taṃ satthā saṃvejento “sattiyā viya omaṭṭho”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

“Like one struck down by a spear”—this is the verse of the Venerable Vaḍḍhamāna. What is its origin? This elder, it is said, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, was reborn in a good family ninety-two aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached maturity, he saw the Blessed One Tissa walking for alms and, with a confident mind, gave him fully ripe mango fruits that had fallen from their stems. Through that meritorious act, he was reborn in the world of devas. Subsequently accumulating meritorious acts, in this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in Vesālī in a Licchavi royal family, and his name was Vaḍḍhamāna. Having come of age, he became faithful, confident, a donor, delighting in giving, a benefactor, and a supporter of the Saṅgha. When, on account of some offense, the Teacher had the act of overturning the bowl performed against him, like one who has stepped on fire, he asked for forgiveness from the Saṅgha and had the act revoked. With a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, he went forth. But after going forth, he dwelt overcome by sloth and torpor. The Teacher, arousing a sense of spiritual urgency in him, spoke this verse: “Like one struck down by a spear.”

40. Tattha bhavarāgappahānāyāti bhavarāgassa rūparāgassa arūparāgassa ca pajahanatthāya. Yadipi ajjhattasaṃyojanāni appahāya bahiddhasaṃyojanānaṃ pahānaṃ nāma natthi, nānantarikabhāvato pana uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanappahānavacanena orambhāgiyasaṃyojanappahānampi vuttameva hoti. Yasmā vā samucchinnorambhāgiyasaṃyojanānampi kesañci ariyānaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni duppaheyyāni honti, tasmā suppaheyyato duppaheyyameva dassento bhagavā bhavarāgappahānasīsena sabbassāpi uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanassa pahānamāha. Therassa eva vā ajjhāsayavasenevaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

40. Therein, 'for the abandoning of craving for existence' means for the purpose of abandoning craving for existence, that is, craving for the form realm and craving for the formless realm. Although there is no abandoning of the higher fetters without having abandoned the lower fetters, yet because they are not disconnected, by the mention of abandoning the higher fetters, the abandoning of the lower fetters is also stated. Or, since for some noble ones who have already cut off the lower fetters, the higher fetters are difficult to abandon, the Blessed One, showing what is truly difficult to abandon in contrast to what is easier to abandon, spoke of the abandoning of all the higher fetters under the heading of abandoning the craving for existence. Or, it was said thus in accordance with the elder's own inclination. The rest is in the manner already explained.

Vaḍḍhamānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vaḍḍhamāna is concluded.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is concluded.

5. Pañcamavaggo

5. The Fifth Chapter

1. Sirivaḍḍhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirivaḍḍha

Vivaramanupatanti [M 1.0134][V 1.0113][P 1.0114] vijjutāti āyasmato sirivaḍḍhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā kiṅkaṇipupphehi pūjaṃ katvā tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa gehe nibbatti, sirivaḍḍhotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto bimbisārasamāgame satthari saddhamme ca uppannappasādo hetusampannatāya pabbaji. Pabbajitvā ca katapubbakicco vebhārapaṇḍavapabbatānaṃ avidūre aññatarasmiṃ araññāyatane pabbataguhāyaṃ kammaṭṭhānamanuyutto viharati. Tasmiñca samaye mahā akālamegho uṭṭhahi. Vijjullatā pabbatavivaraṃ pavisantiyo viya vicaranti. Therassa ghammapariḷāhābhibhūtassa sāragabbhehi meghavātehi ghammapariḷāho vūpasami. Utusappāyalābhena cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi. Samāhitacitto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.10-14) –

“Lightning flashes into the crevices”—this is the verse of the Venerable Sirivaḍḍha. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulated wholesome deeds that were a supporting condition for liberation here and there. Ninety-one aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a good family and reached maturity. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, he made an offering with kiṅkaṇi flowers. Through that meritorious act, he was reborn in the world of devas. Again and again performing meritorious deeds, he wandered only among happy destinations. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in Rājagaha in the home of a wealthy brahmin, and his name was Sirivaḍḍha. When he came of age, during an assembly with King Bimbisāra, confidence arose in him toward the Teacher and the good Dhamma. Being endowed with the necessary conditions, he went forth. After going forth and having completed the preliminary duties, he dwelt in a mountain cave in a certain forest retreat not far from the Vebhāra and Paṇḍava mountains, devoted to his meditation subject. At that time, a great, unseasonal cloud arose. Flashes of lightning moved about as if entering the mountain crevices. For the elder, who was overwhelmed by the torment of the heat, that torment was allayed by the winds from the moisture-laden clouds. Through obtaining suitable weather, his mind became one-pointed. With a concentrated mind, he intensified his practice of insight and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap Th 1.21.10–14):

“Kañcanagghiyasaṅkāso, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Odakaṃ dahamoggayha, sināyi aggapuggalo.

“Resembling a golden pinnacle, the All-Knowing, the Leader of the World, the Supreme Person, plunged into the water of the lake and bathed.”

“Paggayha kiṅkaṇiṃ pupphaṃ, vipassissābhiropayiṃ;

Udaggacitto sumano, dvipadindassa tādino.

“Taking up a kiṅkaṇi flower, I offered it to Vipassī. With an elated and joyful mind, I offered it to the Such-a-One, the Lord of bipeds.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Since I offered that flower ninety-one aeons ago, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping a Buddha.”

“Sattavīsatikappamhi, rājā bhīmaratho ahu;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In the twenty-seventh aeon from now, there was a king, Bhīmaratha, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0135][V 1.0114] pana patvā aññāpadesena attasannissayaṃ udānaṃ udānento “vivaramanupatanti vijjutā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, however, by way of declaring his final knowledge, he uttered a spontaneous exclamation based on his own experience and spoke this verse: “Lightning flashes into the crevices.”

41. Tattha vivaranti antarā vemajjhaṃ. Anupatantīti anulakkhaṇe patanti pavattanti, vijjotantīti attho. Vijjotanameva hi vijjullatānaṃ pavatti nāma. Anu-saddayogena cettha upayogavacanaṃ, yathā “rukkhamanuvijjotantī”ti. Vijjutāti [P 1.0115] sateratā. Vebhārassa ca paṇḍavassa cāti vebhārapabbatassa ca paṇḍavapabbatassa ca vivaramanupatantīti yojanā. Nagavivaragatoti nagavivaraṃ pabbataguhaṃ upagato. Jhāyatīti ārammaṇūpanijjhānena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena ca jhāyati, samathavipassanaṃ ussukkāpento bhāveti. Putto appaṭimassa tādinoti sīlakkhandhādidhammakāyasampattiyā rūpakāyasampattiyā ca anupamassa upamārahitassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu tādilakkhaṇasampattiyā tādino buddhassa bhagavato orasaputto. Puttavacaneneva cettha therena satthu anujātabhāvadīpanena aññā byākatāti veditabbaṃ.

41. Therein, 'vivara' means 'in between' or 'middle.' 'Anupatanti' means 'they fall' or 'they proceed in accordance with the characteristic,' meaning 'they flash.' For flashing is indeed the occurrence of lightning. Here, the word is used with 'anu,' as in 'illuminating the tree.' 'Vijjutā' means 'having brightness.' The construction is 'they flash into the crevices of Mount Vebhāra and Mount Paṇḍava.' 'Nagavivaragato' means 'he entered the mountain cave.' 'Jhāyati' means 'he meditates by focusing on the object and by focusing on the characteristic, striving to develop serenity and insight.' 'Putto appaṭimassa tādino' means 'the true son of the incomparable, the Such One, the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is matchless and without parallel in the attainment of the Dhamma-body beginning with the aggregate of virtue and the attainment of the form-body, possessing the characteristic of imperturbability regarding desirable and undesirable things.' Here, by the word 'son,' the Elder indicates his being similar to the Teacher, and it should be understood that his declaration of final knowledge is thereby made.

Sirivaḍḍhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sirivaḍḍha is concluded.

2. Khadiravaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of Khadiravaniya Thera

Cāle upacāleti āyasmato khadiravaniyarevatattherassa gāthā. Kā uppati? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare titthanāvikakule nibbattitvā mahāgaṅgāya payāgatitthe titthanāvākammaṃ karonto ekadivasaṃ sasāvakasaṅghaṃ bhagavantaṃ gaṅgātīraṃ upagataṃ disvā pasannamānaso nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ yojetvā mahantena pūjāsakkārena paratīraṃ pāpetvā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ satthārā āraññakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapiyamānaṃ disvā tadatthaṃ patthanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Bhagavā ca tassa patthanāya avajjhabhāvaṃ byākāsi. So tato paṭṭhāya tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ katvā [M 1.0136] devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe nālakagāme rūpasāriyā brāhmaṇiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Taṃ vayappattaṃ mātāpitaro gharabandhanena bandhitukāmā jātā. So [P 1.0116] sāriputtattherassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā “mayhaṃ jeṭṭhabhātā ayyo upatisso imaṃ vibhavaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajito, tena vantaṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ kathāhaṃ pacchā gilissāmī”ti jātasaṃvego pāsaṃ anupagacchanakamigo viya ñātake vañcetvā hetusampattiyā codiyamāno bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā dhammasenāpatino kaniṭṭhabhāvaṃ nivedetvā attano pabbajjāya chandaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhū taṃ pabbājetvā paripuṇṇavīsativassaṃ upasampādetvā [V 1.0115] kammaṭṭhāne niyojesuṃ. So kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā khadiravanaṃ pavisitvā, “arahattaṃ patvā bhagavantaṃ dhammasenāpatiñca passissāmī”ti ghaṭento vāyamanto ñāṇassa paripākagatattā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.1.628-643) –

The verse of the Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata begins with 'Cāle upacāle.' What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a family of ferrymen in the city of Haṃsavatī. While engaged in ferry work at the Payāga landing on the great Ganges, one day he saw the Blessed One with his assembly of disciples approaching the riverbank. With a joyful mind, he prepared a boat pontoon and, with great honor and veneration, ferried them to the other shore. Seeing a certain monk being appointed by the Teacher as foremost among forest-dwellers, he made an aspiration for that attainment and offered a great alms-giving to the Blessed One and the community of monks. The Blessed One prophesied that his aspiration would be infallible. From then on, he performed wholesome deeds that are a supporting condition for liberation, wandering among gods and humans. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country. When he came of age, his parents desired to bind him with the ties of household life. But hearing that his elder brother, the noble Upatissa, had gone forth, he thought, 'My elder brother, the noble Upatissa, has abandoned this wealth and gone forth. How could I later swallow the spittle he has vomited?' Filled with spiritual urgency, like a deer avoiding a snare, he deceived his relatives and, impelled by the maturity of his causal conditions, went to the monks. There, he announced that he was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma and expressed his desire for ordination. The monks ordained him, gave him full admission when he was twenty years old, and assigned him a meditation subject. Taking up the meditation subject, he entered the Khadiravana forest, striving with the thought, 'Having attained arahantship, I will see the Blessed One and the General of the Dhamma.' Due to the maturity of his knowledge, before long he became one endowed with the six direct knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Gaṅgā bhāgīrathī nāma, himavantā pabhāvitā;

Kutitthe nāviko āsiṃ, orime ca tariṃ ahaṃ.

The Ganges, named Bhāgīrathī, originates from the Himālaya; I was a ferryman at a difficult ford, and I ferried people across.

“Padumuttaro nāyako, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Vasīsatasahassehi, gaṅgātīramupāgato.

The leader, Padumuttara by name, the Fully Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, approached the bank of the Ganges with one hundred thousand masters.

“Bahū nāvā samānetvā, vaḍḍhakīhi susaṅkhataṃ;

Nāvāya chadanaṃ katvā, paṭimāniṃ narāsabhaṃ.

Having gathered many boats and made a covering for the boat, well-fashioned by carpenters, I paid homage to the bull among men.

“Āgantvāna ca sambuddho, ārūhi tañca nāvakaṃ;

Vārimajjhe ṭhito satthā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

Having arrived, the Fully Enlightened One boarded that boat; standing in the midst of the water, the Teacher spoke these verses.

“Yo so tāresi sambuddhaṃ, saṅghañcāpi anāsavaṃ;

Tena cittappasādena, devaloke ramissati.

He who ferried the Fully Enlightened One and the taintless Sangha, through that serene confidence of heart, will delight in the heavenly realm.

“Nibbattissati te byamhaṃ, sukataṃ nāvasaṇṭhitaṃ;

Ākāse pupphachadanaṃ, dhārayissati sabbadā.

A celestial mansion will arise for you, well-made and shaped like a boat; it will always bear a canopy of flowers in the sky.

“Aṭṭhapaññāsakappamhi, tārako nāma khattiyo;

Cāturanto vijitāvī, cakkavattī bhavissati.

In the fifty-eighth aeon from now, there will be a warrior named Tāraka; he will be a wheel-turning monarch, victorious over the four quarters.

“Sattapaññāsakappamhi[M 1.0137], cammako nāma khattiyo;

Uggacchantova sūriyo, jotissati mahabbalo.

In the fifty-seventh aeon from now, there will be a warrior named Cammaka; of great strength, he will shine like the rising sun.

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

In a hundred thousand aeons from now, born of the Okkāka lineage, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will arise in the world.

“Tidasā so cavitvāna, manussattaṃ gamissati;

Revato nāma nāmena, brahmabandhu bhavissati.

Having passed away from the Tidasā heaven, he will attain a human state; he will be named Revata and will be a brahmin by birth.

“Agārā nikkhamitvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Gotamassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajissati.

Having gone forth from the household life, urged by his wholesome roots, he will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One, Gotama.

“So pacchā pabbajitvāna, yuttayogo vipassako;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

Having gone forth, devoted to the practice and discerning, having fully understood all the taints, he will attain Nibbāna, taintless.

“Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ, yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

My energy is like a beast of burden, leading to security from bondage; I bear this final body in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

“Satasahasse kataṃ kammaṃ, phalaṃ dassesi me idha;

Sumutto saravegova, kilese jhāpayī mama.

The kamma done a hundred thousand aeons ago has shown its fruit to me here; like a swift, well-released arrow, it has burned away my defilements.

“Tato [V 1.0116] maṃ vananirataṃ, disvā lokantagū muni;

Vanavāsibhikkhūnaggaṃ, paññapesi mahāmati.

Then, seeing me delighting in the forest, the sage who has gone to the world's end, the greatly wise one, designated me as foremost of forest-dwelling monks.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burned up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā thero satthāraṃ dhammasenāpatiñca vandituṃ senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anupubbena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā satthāraṃ dhammasenāpatiñca vanditvā katipāhaṃ jetavane vihāsi[P 1.0117]. Atha naṃ satthā ariyagaṇamajjhe nisinno āraññakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āraññakānaṃ yadidaṃ revato khadiravaniyo”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 203). So aparabhāge attano jātagāmaṃ gantvā “cālā, upacālā, sīsūpacālā”ti tissannaṃ bhaginīnaṃ putte “cālā, upacālā, sīsūpacālā”ti tayo bhāgineyye ānetvā pabbājetvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojesi. Te kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuttā viharanti. Tasmiñca samaye therassa kocideva ābādho uppanno. Taṃ [M 1.0138] sutvā sāriputtatthero revataṃ “gilānapucchanaṃ adhigamapucchanañca karissāmī”ti upagacchi. Revatatthero dhammasenāpatiṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā tesaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ satuppādanavasena ovadanto “cāle upacāle”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having become one endowed with the six direct knowledges, the Elder, after putting his dwelling in order and taking his bowl and robe, gradually arrived at Sāvatthī. He entered Jetavana to pay homage to the Teacher and the General of the Dhamma, and stayed there for a few days. Then the Teacher, seated amidst the assembly of noble ones, placed him in the foremost position among forest-dwelling monks, saying: 'Monks, foremost among my disciples who are forest-dwelling monks is Khadiravaniya Revata.' Later, he went to his native village and brought his three nephews, the sons of his three sisters named Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā. He ordained them and assigned them meditation subjects. They dwelt devoted to their meditation practice. At that time, a certain illness arose in the Elder. Hearing this, the Elder Sāriputta approached Revata, thinking, 'I will inquire about his illness and his attainment.' Seeing the General of the Dhamma coming from afar, the Elder Revata, instructing those novices in order to arouse their mindfulness, spoke the verse beginning with 'Cāle upacāle.'

42. Tattha cāle upacāle sīsūpacāleti tesaṃ ālapanaṃ. “Cālā, upacālā, sīsūpacālā”ti hi itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmā te tayo dārakā pabbajitāpi tathā voharīyanti. “‘Cālī, upacālī, sīsūpacālī’ti tesaṃ nāma”nti ca vadanti. Yadatthaṃ “cālā”tiādinā āmantanaṃ kataṃ, taṃ dassento “patissatā nu kho viharathā”ti vatvā tattha kāraṇamāha “āgato vo vālaṃ viya vedhī”ti. Patissatāti patissatikā. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Āgatoti āgacchi. Voti tumhākaṃ. Vālaṃ viya vedhīti vālavedhī viya, ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – tikkhajavananibbedhikapaññatāya vālavedhirūpo satthukappo tumhākaṃ mātulatthero āgato, tasmā samaṇasaññaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā satisampajaññayuttā eva hutvā viharatha, “yathādhigate vihāre appamattā bhavathā”ti.

42. Therein, 'Cāle, Upacāle, Sīsūpacāle' is their form of address. For those three boys, having received names in the feminine gender as 'Cālā, Upacālā, Sīsūpacālā,' were addressed thus even after they had gone forth. And some say their names were 'Cālī, Upacālī, Sīsūpacālī.' Showing the purpose for which the address 'Cālā,' and so forth, was made, having said, 'Dwell mindfully, will you not?', he stated the reason therein: 'He who pierces like a hair has come to you.' Patissatā means mindful. Kho is an emphatic particle. Āgato means has come. Vo means 'your.' Vālaṃ viya vedhī means 'like one who pierces a hair.' Herein, this is the concise meaning: Due to his sharp, swift, and penetrating wisdom, your maternal uncle, the elder, who is like a hair-piercer and comparable to the Teacher, has come. Therefore, having established the perception of a recluse, dwell endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and be heedful in the dwelling you have attained.

Taṃ sutvā te sāmaṇerā dhammasenāpatissa paccuggamanādivattaṃ katvā ubhinnaṃ mātulattherānaṃ paṭisanthāravelāyaṃ nātidūre samādhiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdiṃsu. Dhammasenāpati revatattherena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā te sāmaṇere upasaṅkami, te tathākālaparicchedassa katattā there upasaṅkamante eva uṭṭhahitvā vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Thero “katarakataravihārena viharathā”ti pucchitvā [V 1.0117][P 1.0118] tehi “imāya imāyā”ti vutte “dārakepi nāma evaṃ vinento mayhaṃ bhātiko paccapādi vata dhammassa anudhamma”nti theraṃ pasaṃsanto pakkāmi.

Having heard that, the novice monks, having performed the duties of going out to meet and so forth for the General of the Dhamma, sat down not too far away, having entered into concentration at the time of the two elder uncles' friendly greetings. The General of the Dhamma exchanged friendly greetings with the Elder Revata. Rising from his seat, he approached the novice monks. Because they had determined the proper time, as the elder approached, they stood up, paid homage, and remained standing. The elder asked, "In which particular dwelling do you dwell?" When they replied, "In this one and that one," he praised the elder, saying, "Indeed, my brother, in training even these boys thus, has practiced in accordance with the Dhamma," and then departed.

Khadiravaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Khadiravaniya is concluded.

3. Sumaṅgalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sumaṅgala.

Sumuttikoti [M 1.0139] āyasmato sumaṅgalattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. So ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ nhāyitvā ekacīvaraṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā somanassappatto hutvā apphoṭesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyā avidūre aññatarasmiṃ gāmake tādisena kammanissandena daliddakule nibbatti. Tassa sumaṅgaloti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto khujjakāsitanaṅgalakuddālaparikkhāro hutvā kasiyā jīvati. So ekadivasaṃ raññā pasenadikosalena bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahādāne pavattiyamāne dānopakaraṇāni gahetvā āgacchantehi manussehi saddhiṃ dadhighaṭaṃ gahetvā āgato bhikkhūnaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ disvā “ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā sukhumavatthasunivatthā subhojanāni bhuñjitvā nivātesu senāsanesu viharanti, yaṃnūnāhampi pabbajeyya”nti cintetvā, aññataraṃ mahātheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano pabbajjādhippāyaṃ nivedesi. So taṃ karuṇāyanto pabbājetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. So araññe viharanto ekavihāre nibbinno ukkaṇṭhito hutvā, vibbhamitukāmo ñātigāmaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge kacchaṃ bandhitvā khettaṃ kasante kiliṭṭhavatthanivatthe samantato rajokiṇṇasarīre vātātapena phussante kassake disvā, “mahantaṃ vatime sattā jīvikanimittaṃ dukkhaṃ paccanubhontī”ti [P 1.0119] saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi. Ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā yathāgahitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagantvā vivekaṃ labhitvā yoniso manasikaronto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.11-19) –

The verse beginning 'Sumuttiko' is that of the venerable Elder Sumaṅgala. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences that served as a supporting condition for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was reborn as a tree deity. One day, seeing the Teacher standing in a single robe after bathing, he was filled with joy and clapped his hands. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, during this Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in a poor family in a village not far from Sāvatthī, as a result of that same kamma. His name was Sumaṅgala. When he came of age, he made his living by farming, equipped with a bent sickle, a plow, and a spade. One day, while King Pasenadi of Kosala was holding a great almsgiving for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he came along with the people who were bringing provisions for the offering, carrying a pot of curd. Seeing the honor and respect given to the bhikkhus, he thought: 'These recluses, the Sakyan sons, are well-dressed in fine robes, eat excellent food, and dwell in sheltered lodgings. Surely, I too should go forth.' Thinking thus, he approached a certain great elder and informed him of his intention to go forth. Out of compassion, the elder ordained him and taught him a meditation subject. While dwelling in the forest, he became dissatisfied and discontented in his solitary dwelling. Wishing to disrobe, he set out for his relatives' village. On the way, having tied up his loincloth, he saw farmers plowing a field. They were wearing soiled clothes, their bodies were covered all over with dust, and they were afflicted by wind and sun. Seeing them, he was stirred with spiritual urgency, reflecting: 'Truly, these beings experience great suffering for the sake of their livelihood!' As his knowledge had reached maturity, the meditation subject he had grasped presented itself to him. He went to the foot of a certain tree, found seclusion, and, applying his mind fundamentally, developed insight and, in due course, attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Atthadassī jinavaro, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Vihārā abhinikkhamma, taḷākaṃ upasaṅkami.

“The Victor Atthadassī, best of conquerors, foremost in the world, bull among men, having gone forth from the monastery, approached the lake.”

“Nhātvā pitvā ca sambuddho, uttaritvekacīvaro;

Aṭṭhāsi bhagavā tattha, vilokento disodisaṃ.

“Having bathed and drunk, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having come out with a single robe, the Blessed One stood there, looking in every direction.”

“Bhavane [M 1.0140][V 1.0118] upaviṭṭhohaṃ, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, apphoṭesiṃ ahaṃ tadā.

“Seated in my dwelling, I saw the Leader of the world; with a joyful and delighted mind, I then clapped my hands.”

“Sataraṃsiṃva jotantaṃ, pabhāsantaṃva kañcanaṃ;

Naccagīte payuttohaṃ, pañcaṅgatūriyamhi ca.

“Blazing like the sun with its rays, shining like gold; I was devoted to dance, song, and the five-part instrumental music.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Sabbe satte abhibhomi, vipulo hoti me yaso.

“In whatever birth I am reborn, whether divine or human, I surpass all beings, and my glory is vast.”

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Attānaṃ tosayitvāna, pare tosesi tvaṃ muni.

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man; having satisfied yourself, you satisfy others, O sage.”

“Pariggahe nisīditvā, hāsaṃ katvāna subbate;

Upaṭṭhahitvā sambuddhaṃ, tusitaṃ upapajjahaṃ.

“Sitting in the assembly, having laughed with joy, O you of good vows; having attended upon the Perfectly Enlightened One, I was reborn in the Tusita realm.”

“Soḷaseto kappasate, dvinavaekacintitā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“For sixteen hundred aeons, and for ninety-two aeons, endowed with the seven treasures, they were powerful wheel-turning monarchs.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā sampattiṃ attano dukkhavimuttiñca kittanavasena udānaṃ udānento “sumuttiko”tiādimāha.

But having attained arahantship, uttering an inspired utterance by way of proclaiming his own attainment and liberation from suffering, he said, “Well freed!” and so forth.

43. Tattha sumuttikoti sundarā accantikatāya apunabbhavikā mutti etassāti sumuttiko. Tassa pana vimuttiyā pāsaṃsiyatāya acchariyatāya ca apphoṭento āha “sumuttiko”ti. Puna tattha vimuttiyaṃ attano pasādassa daḷhabhāvaṃ dassento “sāhu sumuttikomhī”ti āha. “Sādhu suṭṭhu muttiko vatamhī”ti attho. “Kuto panāyaṃ sumuttikatā”ti? Kāmañcāyaṃ thero sabbasmāpi vaṭṭadukkhato suvimutto, attano pana tāva upaṭṭhitaṃ ativiya aniṭṭhabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ dassento “tīhi khujjakehī”tiādimāha. Tattha khujjakehīti khujjasabhāvehi, khujjākārehi vā. Nissakkavacanañcetaṃ muttasaddāpekkhāya. Kassako hi akhujjopi samāno tīsu ṭhānesu attānaṃ khujjaṃ katvā dasseti lāyane kasane kuddālakamme ca. Yo hi pana kassako lāyanādīni karoti[M 1.0141], tānipi asitādīni kuṭilākārato khujjakānīti vuttaṃ “tīhi khujjakehī”ti.

43. Herein, ‘sumuttiko’ means one for whom there is a beautiful liberation that is ultimate and does not lead to future becoming. As if clapping his hands with joy at the praiseworthiness and wondrousness of that liberation, he said, “Well freed!” Further, showing the firmness of his confidence in that liberation, he said, “Sādhu, I am well freed!” The meaning is, “Indeed, I am truly well freed!” Whence this state of being well freed? Although this Elder was fully liberated from all the suffering of the cycle of existence, to illustrate the extremely undesirable suffering that had first presented itself to him, he says, “by three crooked things,” and so forth. Here, ‘khujjakehī’ means ‘by crooked states’ or ‘by crooked forms.’ And this is a term of removal in relation to the word ‘freed.’ For even a farmer who is not crooked makes himself appear crooked in three situations: in reaping, in plowing, and in working with a hoe. For when a farmer performs reaping and other tasks, those tools, the sickle and so on, are also called ‘crooked things’ because of their curved shape. Thus, it is said, ‘by three crooked things.’

Idāni tāni sarūpato dassento “asitāsu mayā, naṅgalāsu mayā, khuddakuddālāsu mayā”ti āha. Tattha asitāsu mayāti lavittehi mayā muttanti attho. Nissakke cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Apare pana “asitāsu mayāti lavittehi karaṇabhūtehi mayā khujjita”nti vadanti. Tesaṃ matena karaṇatthe hetumhi vā bhummavacanaṃ. “Naṅgalāsū”ti liṅgavipallāsaṃ [V 1.0119] katvā vuttaṃ, naṅgalehi kasirehīti attho. Attanā vaḷañjitakuddālassa sabhāvato vaḷañjanena vā appakatāya vuttaṃ “khuddakuddālāsū”ti “kuṇṭhakuddālāsū”tipi [P 1.0120] pāḷi. Vaḷañjaneneva atikhiṇakhaṇittesūti attho. Idhamevāti ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Atha vāpīti vā-saddo nipātamattaṃ. Gāmake ṭhitattā tāni asitādīni kiñcāpi idheva mama samīpeyeva, tathāpi alameva hotīti attho. Turitavasena cetaṃ āmeḍitavacanaṃ. Jhāyāti phalasamāpattijjhānavasena diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ dibbavihārādivasena ca jhāya. Sumaṅgalāti attānaṃ ālapati. Jhāne pana ādaradassanatthaṃ āmeḍitaṃ kataṃ. Appamatto viharāti satipaññāvepullappattiyā sabbatthakameva appamattosi tvaṃ, tasmā idāni sukhaṃ vihara, sumaṅgala. Keci pana “arahattaṃ appatvā eva vipassanāya vīthipaṭipannāya sāsane sañjātābhiratiyā yathānubhūtaṃ gharāvāsadukkhaṃ jigucchanto thero imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā pacchā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇī”ti vadanti. Tesaṃ matena “jhāya appamatto viharā”ti padānaṃ attho vipassanāmaggavasenapi yujjati eva.

Now, showing those things in their true nature, he says, “By sickles, by me; by plows, by me; by small hoes, by me.” Herein, ‘by sickles, by me’ means ‘I was freed from sickles.’ And this locative case is used in the sense of separation. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. Others, however, say, “‘By sickles, by me’ means ‘I was afflicted by sickles as instruments.’” According to their view, the locative case is used in the sense of an instrument or a cause. ‘By plows’ is stated with a change of gender, meaning ‘by difficult plows.’ It is said ‘by small hoes’ due to the nature of a hoe used by oneself, or due to its smallness from use; there is also the reading ‘by blunt hoes.’ The meaning is ‘among digging tools excessively worn out by the very act of using them.’ In `idhameva`, the `ma` is for euphonic conjunction. Or, in `athavāpi`, the word `vā` is merely a particle. ‘Although those sickles and so forth are here in the village, right here near me, still it is enough’—this is the meaning. And this repetition is due to urgency. ‘Meditate’ means: meditate for the sake of dwelling happily in the present life by way of the jhāna of fruition attainment, and by way of the divine abodes and so forth. ‘Sumaṅgala’—he addresses himself. The repetition is made to show reverence for jhāna. ‘Dwell heedful’ means: ‘Having attained the fullness of mindfulness and wisdom, you are indeed heedful in all respects; therefore, Sumaṅgala, now dwell happily.’ Some, however, say: ‘Not yet having attained arahantship, while the path of insight was being practiced, the elder, in whom delight in the teaching had arisen, becoming disgusted with the suffering of household life as he had experienced it, spoke this verse and afterwards, having developed insight, attained arahantship.’ According to their view, the meaning of the words ‘meditate, dwell heedful’ is indeed fitting also by way of the path of insight.

Sumaṅgalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sumaṅgala is concluded.

4. Sānuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Exposition of the Verses of Elder Sānu

Mataṃ [M 1.0142] vā amma rodantīti āyasmato sānuttherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato hatthapādadhovanamukhavikkhālanānaṃ atthāya udakaṃ upanesi. Satthā hi bhojanakāle hatthapāde dhovitukāmo ahosi. So satthu ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā udakaṃ upanesi. Bhagavā hatthapāde dhovitvā bhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletukāmo ahosi. So tampi [P 1.0121] ñatvā mukhodakaṃ upanesi. Satthā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā mukhadhovanakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Evaṃ bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya tena karīyamānaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ sādiyi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa upāsakassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tasmiṃ gabbhagateyeva pitā pavāsaṃ gato, upāsikā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyitvā sānūtissa nāmaṃ akāsi. Tasmiṃ anukkamena vaḍḍhante sattavassikaṃyeva naṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike pabbājesi, “evamayaṃ anantarāyo vaḍḍhitvā accantasukhabhāgī bhavissatī”ti. “So sānusāmaṇero”ti paññāto paññavā vattasampanno bahussuto [V 1.0120] dhammakathiko sattesu mettajjhāsayo hutvā devamanussānaṃ piyo ahosi manāpoti sabbaṃ sānusutte āgatanayena veditabbaṃ.

‘Mother, they weep for the dead’ is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sānu. What is its origin? He too, having made a resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit here and there in various existences as a supportive condition for liberation, in the ninety-fourth aeon from the present, brought water for the Blessed One Siddhattha for the purpose of washing his hands and feet and rinsing his mouth. For the Teacher wished to wash his hands and feet at mealtime. Observing the Teacher’s gesture, he brought water. The Blessed One, having washed his hands and feet and eaten, wished to rinse his mouth. Knowing this too, he brought water for rinsing the mouth. The Teacher, having rinsed his mouth, completed the act of rinsing. Thus, out of compassion, the Blessed One accepted the service rendered by him. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world, and after repeatedly performing meritorious deeds while wandering among devas and humans, at the arising of this Buddha, he took rebirth in the house of a certain lay follower in Sāvatthī. While he was still in the womb, his father went away on a journey. The laywoman, after the passing of ten months, gave birth to a son and named him Sānūtissa. As he grew up, at the very age of seven, she had him ordained in the presence of the monks, thinking, “Thus, free from obstacles, he will grow up to partake of ultimate happiness.” Known as “Sānu the novice,” he was wise, accomplished in his duties, learned, a speaker of the Dhamma, and had a disposition of loving-kindness towards beings; he was beloved and dear to devas and humans—all this should be understood according to the method given in the Sānu Sutta.

Tassa atītajātiyaṃ mātā yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Taṃ yakkhā “sānuttherassa ayaṃ mātā”ti garucittikārabahulā hutvā mānenti. Evaṃ gacchante kāle puthujjanabhāvassa ādīnavaṃ vibhāventaṃ viya ekadivasaṃ sānussa yoniso manasikārābhāvā ayoniso ummujjantassa vibbhamitukāmatācittaṃ uppajji. Taṃ tassa yakkhinimātā ñatvā manussamātuyā ārocesi – “tava putto, sānu, ‘vibbhamissāmī’ti cittaṃ uppādesi, tasmā tvaṃ –

In a past life, his mother was reborn in the yakkha realm. The yakkhas, thinking, “This is the mother of Elder Sānu,” showed her great respect and paid her honor. As time passed, as if to reveal the danger of the state of a worldling, one day, due to Sānu’s lack of wise attention and the emergence of unwise thoughts, a mind desirous of going astray arose in him. His yakkha-mother, knowing this, informed his human mother: “Your son, Sānu, has given rise to the thought, ‘I will go astray.’ Therefore, you—

“Sānuṃ pabuddhaṃ vajjāsi, yakkhānaṃ vacanaṃ idaṃ;

Mākāsi pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, āvi vā yadi vā raho.

“Tell Sānu, when he is awake, this word of the yakkhas: ‘Do no evil deed, whether openly or in secret.

“Sace [M 1.0143] tvaṃ pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, karissasi karosi vā;

Na te dukkhā pamutyatthi, uppaccāpi palāyato”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.239; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.325 sānusāmaṇeravatthu) –

“‘Sace tvaṃ pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, karissasi karosi vā;Na te dukkhā pamutyatthi, uppaccāpi palāyato’’ti.

Evaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā yakkhinimātā tatthevantaradhāyi. Manussamātā pana taṃ sutvā paridevasokasamāpannā cetodukkhasamappitā ahosi. Atha sānusāmaṇero pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā [P 1.0122] pattacīvaramādāya mātu santikaṃ upagato mātaraṃ rodamānaṃ disvā “amma, kiṃ nissāya rodasī”ti vatvā “taṃ nissāyā”ti ca vutto mātu “mataṃ vā, amma, rodanti, yo vā jīvaṃ na dissatī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

‘Speak thus.’ And having spoken thus, the yakkha-mother vanished right there. The human mother, however, hearing that, was overcome with lamentation and sorrow, afflicted with mental pain. Then Sānu the novice, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and approached his mother. Seeing his mother weeping, he said, “Mother, on account of what do you weep?” And when told, “On account of you,” he recited this verse to his mother: “Mother, they weep for the dead, or for one who, though living, is not seen.”

44. Tassattho – “amma, rodantā nāma ñātakā mittā vā attano ñātakaṃ mittaṃ vā mataṃ uddissa rodanti paralokaṃ gatattā, yo vā ñātako mitto vā jīvaṃ jīvanto desantaraṃ pakkantatāya ca na dissati, taṃ vā uddissa rodanti, ubhayampetaṃ mayi na vijjati, evaṃ sante jīvantaṃ dharamānaṃ maṃ purato ṭhitaṃ passantī; kasmā, amma, rodasi?Maṃ uddissa tava rodanassa kāraṇameva natthī”ti.

44. Its meaning is: “Mother, relatives or friends weep for their own deceased relative or friend who has passed away to another world. Or they weep for a relative or friend who, though living, has gone to another country and is not seen. Neither of these applies to me. Since I am alive and present, standing right before your eyes, why, Mother, do you weep? There is no reason at all for you to weep on my account.”

Taṃ sutvā tassa mātā “maraṇañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, yo sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.63) suttapadānusārena uppabbajanaṃ ariyassa vinaye maraṇanti dassentī –

Hearing that, his mother, showing that in the Discipline of the Noble One it is a kind of death to renounce the training and return to the lower life, in accordance with the Sutta passage, “Monks, this is death: when one renounces the training and returns to the lower life,” said:

“Mataṃ [V 1.0121] vā putta rodanti, yo vā jīvaṃ na dissati;

Yo ca kāme cajitvāna, punarāgacchate idha.

“They weep, my son, for the dead, or for one living but not seen; and for one who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, returns here again.

“Taṃ vāpi putta rodanti, puna jīvaṃ mato hi so;

Kukkuḷā ubbhato tāta, kukkuḷaṃ patitumicchasī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.239; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.sānusāmaṇeravatthu) –

“They weep, my son, for that one too, for though living, he is dead. You, dear one, having been lifted from the hot embers, do you wish to fall back into the hot embers?”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

She uttered these two verses.

Tattha kāme cajitvānāti nekkhammajjhāsayena vatthukāme pahāya, tañca kilesakāmassa tadaṅgappahānavasena veditabbaṃ. Pabbajjā hettha kāmapariccāgo adhippeto. Punarāgacchate idhāti idha gehe punadeva āgacchati, hīnāyāvattanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Taṃ vāpīti yo pabbajitvā vibbhamati[M 1.0144], taṃ vāpi puggalaṃ mataṃ viyamādisiyo rodanti. Kasmāti ce? Puna jīvaṃ mato hi soti vibbhamanato pacchā yo jīvanto, so guṇamaraṇena atthato matoyeva. Idānissa savisesasaṃvegaṃ janetuṃ “kukkuḷā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – “ahorattaṃ ādittaṃ viya hutvā ḍahanaṭṭhena kukkuḷanirayasadisattā kukkuḷā [P 1.0123] gihibhāvā anukampantiyā mayā ubbhato uddhato, tāta sānu, kukkuḷaṃ patituṃ icchasi patitukāmosī”ti.

Herein, 'having abandoned sensual pleasures' means having given up the objects of sensual pleasure out of an inclination towards renunciation; and this should be understood as the abandonment of defilement-sensual-pleasures by way of temporary suppression. Herein, the going forth is intended as the relinquishing of sensual pleasures. 'He returns here' means he comes back again to this house; this is said with reference to reverting to the lower life. 'And that one too' means that for a person who, having gone forth, goes astray, women like me lament as though he were dead. If it is asked why, it is because he who lives again is indeed dead. That is, he who lives after going astray is, in essence, dead by the death of virtue. Now, to generate a special sense of urgency in him, 'hot embers,' and so forth, was said. Its meaning is this: 'The household life is called "hot embers" because it is like the Kukkuḷa hell, due to its nature of burning day and night as if ablaze. From those hot embers, I, out of compassion, have lifted you out, pulled you up. Dear Sānu, do you wish to fall into the hot embers? Are you one who desires to fall?'

Taṃ sutvā sānusāmaṇero saṃvegajāto hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.25-29) –
