Hearing this, Sānu the novice, filled with a sense of urgency, established insight meditation and, before long, attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna (Thera-apadāna 1.21.25-29):

“Bhuñjantaṃ samaṇaṃ disvā, vippasannamanāvilaṃ;

Ghaṭenodakamādāya, siddhatthassa adāsahaṃ.

“Seeing the ascetic eating, with a mind serene and unclouded, I took water in a pot and gave it to Siddhattha.

“Nimmalo homahaṃ ajja, vimalo khīṇasaṃsayo;

Bhave nibbattamānassa, phalaṃ nibbattate subhaṃ.

“Today I am stainless, pure, with doubt destroyed; for one being reborn in existence, a beautiful fruit arises.

“Catunnavutito kappe, udakaṃ yamadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dakadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave that water; I do not know any bad destination—this is the fruit of that gift of water.

“Ekasaṭṭhimhito kappe, ekova vimalo ahu;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Sixty-one aeons ago, there was one named Vimala, endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning monarch.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0122] pana patvā thero imissā gāthāya vasena “mayhaṃ vipassanārambho arahattappatti ca jātā”ti udānavasena tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

But having attained arahantship, the Elder uttered that same verse again as an inspired utterance, thinking, 'Through this verse my insight began and arahantship was attained.'

Sānuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Verses of Elder Sānu is concluded.

5. Ramaṇīyavihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin

Yathāpi [M 1.0145] bhaddo ājaññoti āyasmato ramaṇīyavihārittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha puññāni upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā koraṇḍapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devesu nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe aññatarassa seṭṭhissa putto hutvā nibbatto yobbanamadena kāmesu mucchaṃ āpanno viharati. So ekadivasaṃ aññataraṃ pāradārikaṃ rājapurisehi vividhā kammakāraṇā karīyamānaṃ disvā saṃvegajāto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā pabbaji. Pabbajito ca rāgacaritatāya niccakālaṃ susammaṭṭhaṃ pariveṇaṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīyaṃ supaññataṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ katvā viharati. Tena so ramaṇīyavihārītveva paññāyittha.

“Just as a fine thoroughbred…” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas and accumulating merit in various places, beheld the Blessed One Vipassī ninety-one aeons ago. With a confident mind, he paid homage with the five-point prostration and made an offering of koraṇḍa flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas. After repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans until, during this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a certain merchant in Rājagaha. Intoxicated with the pride of youth, he lived engrossed in sensual pleasures. One day, seeing an adulterer being subjected to various punishments by the king’s men, he was struck with a sense of urgency. After hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher, he went forth. Having gone forth, due to his passionate disposition, he dwelt keeping his monastic cell well-swept, with drinking water and water for use well-provided, and his bed and seat well-prepared. For that reason, he became known as Ramaṇīyavihārī, ‘He Who Dwells Delightfully.’

So rāgussannatāya ayoniso manasi karitvā sañcetanikaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiāpattiṃ āpajjitvā, “dhiratthu, maṃ evaṃbhūto saddhādeyyaṃ [P 1.0124] bhuñjeyya”nti vippaṭisārī hutvā “vibbhamissāmī”ti gacchanto antarāmagge rukkhamūle nisīdi, tena ca maggena sakaṭesu gacchantesu eko sakaṭayutto goṇo parissamanto visamaṭṭhāne khalitvā pati, taṃ sākaṭikā yugato muñcitvā tiṇodakaṃ datvā parissamaṃ vinodetvā punapi dhure yojetvā agamaṃsu. Thero taṃ disvā – “yathāyaṃ goṇo sakiṃ khalitvāpi uṭṭhāya sakiṃ dhuraṃ vahati, evaṃ mayāpi kilesavasena sakiṃ khalitenāpi vuṭṭhāya samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti yoniso ummujjanto nivattitvā upālittherassa attano pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā tena vuttavidhinā āpattito vuṭṭhahitvā sīlaṃ pākatikaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.35-39) –

Overcome by passion, he reflected unwisely and committed the intentional offense of emitting semen. Then, feeling remorseful, he thought, “Shame on me! How can someone like me partake of offerings given in faith?” Resolving to disrobe, he set off. Along the way, he sat down at the foot of a tree. At that time, carts were passing by on that road. One ox from a cart-team, being exhausted, stumbled in an uneven spot and fell. The carters freed it from the yoke, gave it grass and water, relieved its exhaustion, and then yoked it to the yoke again before moving on. Seeing this, the elder thought, “Just as this ox, though it stumbled once, rose again and bore the yoke, so too, though I have stumbled once due to defilements, it is proper for me to rise again and fulfill the duties of a monk.” Emerging through wise reflection, he turned back. He confessed his transgression to the Elder Upāli, and following the prescribed method, he was absolved of the offense. Restoring his virtue to its natural state, he established insight meditation and, before long, attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.21.35-39):

“Akkantañca padaṃ disvā, cakkālaṅkārabhūsitaṃ;

Padenānupadaṃ yanto, vipassissa mahesino.

“Having seen the trodden footprint of the great seer Vipassī, adorned with the ornament of the wheel, I followed along from footstep to footstep.

“Koraṇḍaṃ [M 1.0146][V 1.0123] pupphitaṃ disvā, samūlaṃ pūjitaṃ mayā;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, avandiṃ padamuttamaṃ.

“Seeing a flowering koraṇḍa plant, I offered it, roots and all. Delighted, and with a joyful heart, I paid homage to that supreme footprint.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I offered that flower; I have not known a bad destination: this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

“Sattapaññāsakappamhi, eko vītamalo ahuṃ;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Fifty-seven aeons ago, I was the one named Vītamala, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimuttisukhaṃ anubhavanto attano pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyā saddhiṃ ariyadhammādhigamanadīpaniṃ “yathāpi bhaddo ājañño, khalitvā patitiṭṭhatī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

But having attained Arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he uttered the verse, “Just as a fine thoroughbred, having stumbled, stands firm again,” which illuminates the attainment of the noble Dhamma along with his own preliminary practice.

45. Tattha khalitvāti pakkhalitvā. Patitiṭṭhatīti patiṭṭhahati, punadeva yathāṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Evanti yathā bhaddo usabhājānīyo bhāraṃ vahanto parissamappatto visamaṭṭhānaṃ āgamma ekavāraṃ pakkhalitvā patito na tattakena dhuraṃ chaḍḍeti, thāmajavaparakkamasampannatāya pana khalitvāpi patitiṭṭhati, attano sabhāveneva ṭhatvā bhāraṃ vahati, evaṃ kilesaparissamappatto kiriyāparādhena khalitvā taṃ khalitaṃ thāmavīriyasampattitāya paṭipākatikaṃ katvā maggasammādiṭṭhiyā dassanasampannaṃ, tato eva sammāsambuddhassa savanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya sāvakaṃ, tassa ure vāyāmajanitābhijātitāya orasaṃ [P 1.0125] puttaṃ bhaddājānīyasadisakiccatāya ājānīyanti ca maṃ dhāretha upadhārethāti attho.

45. Therein, 'having stumbled' means having slipped. 'Stands firm again' means stands fast, stands once more in the same place. 'Just as' means: just as a fine thoroughbred bull, while carrying a load, becomes exhausted, and coming to an uneven place, slips once and falls, but does not on that account cast off the yoke; rather, being endowed with strength, speed, and stamina, even having stumbled, it stands firm again and, standing by its own nature, carries the load. So too, you should understand me as one who, though exhausted by the defilements and having stumbled through a fault in conduct, has restored that stumble by being endowed with strength and energy; as one accomplished in vision through the right view of the path; and from that, after hearing the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, as a disciple, because of being born with the noble birth; as a true-born son, because of the noble quality born from striving in the Buddha's heart; and as a thoroughbred, because my duty is like that of a fine thoroughbred. This is the meaning.

Ramaṇīyavihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin is concluded.

6. Samiddhittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Samiddhi

Saddhāyāhaṃ [M 1.0147] pabbajitoti āyasmato samiddhittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu kattādhikāro tattha tattha puññāni upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso savaṇṭāni pupphāni kaṇṇikabaddhāni gahetvā pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe kulagehe nibbatti. Tassa jātakālato paṭṭhāya taṃ kulaṃ dhanadhaññādīhi vaḍḍhi, attabhāvo cassa abhirūpo dassanīyo guṇavā iti vibhavasamiddhiyā ca guṇasamiddhiyā [V 1.0124] ca samiddhītveva paññāyittha. So bimbisārasamāgame buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā bhāvanāya yuttappayutto viharanto bhagavati tapodārāme viharante ekadivasaṃ evaṃ cintesi – “lābhā vata me satthā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, svākkhāte cāhaṃ dhammavinaye pabbajito, sabrahmacārī ca me sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā”ti. Tassevaṃ cintentassa uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ udapādi. Taṃ asahanto māro pāpimā therassa avidūre mahantaṃ bheravasaddamakāsi, pathaviyā undriyanakālo viya ahosi. Thero bhagavato tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bhagavā “māro tuyhaṃ vicakkhukammāya ceteti, gaccha, bhikkhu tattha acintetvā viharāhī”ti āha. Thero tattha gantvā viharanto nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.30-34) –

"By faith I went forth," is a verse of the Venerable Elder Samiddhi. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made a resolution under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits here and there. Ninety-four aeons ago, he saw the Blessed One Siddhattha and, with a joyful mind, took flowers with their stalks, tied at the base, and offered them. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm. Again and again, he performed merits, revolving only among happy destinies, until in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a householder’s family in Rājagaha. From the time of his birth, that family prospered in wealth, grain, and so forth. His own person was handsome, pleasing to behold, and virtuous. Thus, he became known as "Samiddhi" due to prosperity and virtuous qualities. At Bimbisāra’s assembly, seeing the Buddha’s power, he acquired faith, went forth, and devoted himself to meditation. While the Blessed One was dwelling in Tapodārāma, one day he reflected: "Truly, I am fortunate—the Teacher is the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. I have gone forth in the well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline. My fellow monks are virtuous and of excellent character." As he reflected thus, supreme joy and gladness arose in him. Unable to bear this, Māra the Evil One, not far from the elder, made a terrifying sound, as if the earth were being swallowed. The elder reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Buddha said: "Māra intends to deceive you. Go, monk, dwell there without such thoughts." The elder went there and, dwelling without delay, cultivated insight and soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.21.30-34):

“Kaṇikāraṃva [P 1.0126] jotantaṃ, nisinnaṃ pabbatantare;

Obhāsentaṃ disā sabbā, siddhatthaṃ narasārathiṃ.

"Like a kaṇikāra tree ablaze, seated in a mountain cleft, illuminating all directions: the accomplished Siddhartha, trainer of men."

“Dhanuṃ advejjhaṃ katvāna, usuṃ sannayhahaṃ tadā;

Pupphaṃ savaṇṭaṃ chetvāna, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

"Having made the bow unerring, I then fixed the arrow; cutting the flower with its stem, I offered it to the Buddha."

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-four aeons ago, the flower which I offered; I do not recall a bad destination—this is the fruit of my homage to the Buddha."

“Ekapaññāsito kappe, eko āsiṃ jutindharo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"Fifty-one aeons ago, I was a king named Jutindhara, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0148] pana patvā tattheva viharantassa therassa khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ ajānanto purimanayeneva māro mahantaṃ bheravasaddaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sutvā thero abhīto acchambhī “tādisānaṃ mārānaṃ satampi sahassampi mayhaṃ lomampi na kampetī”ti aññaṃ byākaronto “saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

But when the elder, having attained arahantship, was dwelling there, Māra, not knowing his state of being free from defilements, made a great terrifying sound as before. Hearing that, the elder, fearless and unshaken, declared his realization, saying: "Not even a hundred or a thousand such Māras could make a single hair of mine tremble," and he spoke this verse: "By faith I went forth."

46. Tattha saddhāyāti dhammacchandasamuṭṭhānāya kammaphalasaddhāya ceva ratanattayasaddhāya ca. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati. Pabbajitoti upagato. Agārasmāti gehato gharāvāsato vā. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ, sā hi yaṃkiñci kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ ‘agārassa hita’nti agāriyaṃ nāma, tadabhāvato “anagāriyā”ti vuccati. Sati paññā ca me vuḍḍhāti saraṇalakkhaṇā sati, pajānanalakkhaṇā paññāti ime dhammā vipassanākkhaṇato paṭṭhāya maggapaṭipāṭiyā [V 1.0125] yāva arahattā me vuḍḍhā vaḍḍhitā, na dāni vaḍḍhetabbā atthi satipaññā vepullappattāti dasseti. Cittañca susamāhitanti aṭṭhasamāpattivasena ceva lokuttarasamādhivasena ca cittaṃ me suṭṭhu samāhitaṃ, na dāni tassa samādhātabbaṃ atthi, samādhi vepullappattoti dasseti. Tasmā kāmaṃ karassu rūpānīti pāpima maṃ uddissa yāni kānici vippakārāni yathāruciṃ karohi, tehi pana neva maṃ byādhayissasi mama sarīrakampanamattampi kātuṃ na sakkhissasi, kuto cittaññathattaṃ? Tasmā tava kiriyā appaṭicchitapahenakaṃ viya na kiñci atthaṃ sodheti, kevalaṃ tava cittavighātamattaphalāti thero māraṃ tajjesi. Taṃ sutvā māro “jānāti maṃ samaṇo”ti tatthevantaradhāyi.

46. Here, 'by faith' refers to faith in kamma and its results, which arises from the desire for the Dhamma, and also faith in the Triple Gem. 'I' refers to himself. 'Went forth' means he has gone forth. 'From home' means from the house or household life. 'Homelessness' refers to the going forth; for any work like farming or trade is called 'for the home' because it is for the benefit of the home. Its absence is called 'homelessness.' 'Mindfulness and wisdom have grown in me'—mindfulness characterized by recollection and wisdom characterized by understanding—these qualities have grown in me from the moment of insight onwards, by the sequence of the path, up to arahantship. Now there is no more growth to be done, for mindfulness and wisdom have reached fullness. 'And my mind is well-concentrated'—my mind is well-concentrated through the eight attainments and through supramundane concentration. Now there is no more concentration to be developed, for concentration has reached fullness. Therefore, 'O Evil One, do as you please with forms'—O Evil One, directing yourself towards me, do whatever various things you please; but you will not harass me with them, nor even be able to cause my body to tremble, much less disturb my mind. Thus, your actions are like an unaccepted gift—they serve no purpose but only distress your own mind. So the elder rebuked Māra. Hearing this, Māra thought, 'This ascetic knows me,' and vanished on the spot.

Samiddhittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Samiddhi is concluded.

7. Ujjayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ujjaya.

Namo [P 1.0127] te buddha vīratthūti āyasmato ujjayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto ito dvānavute kappe tissaṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso kaṇikārapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke [M 1.0149] nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe aññatarassa sottiyabrāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, ujjayotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto upanissayasampattiyā codiyamāno veḷuvanaṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.1-4) –

'Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero!'—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ujjaya. What is its origin? He too, having made a resolution under previous Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds in various existences, ninety-two aeons ago saw the Blessed One Tissa and, with a joyful mind, made an offering with kaṇikāra flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Again and again performing meritorious deeds, revolving among devas and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a certain brahmin of the Sotthiya clan, and his name was Ujjaya. Coming of age, he mastered the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in them, and being urged by the maturity of his supporting conditions, he went to the Veḷuvana, heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, acquired faith, and went forth. Taking up a meditation subject suitable to his disposition, he dwelt in the forest, developed insight, and before long attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.21.1-4):

“Kaṇikāraṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, ocinitvānahaṃ tadā;

Tissassa abhiropesiṃ, oghatiṇṇassa tādino.

"Seeing the Kaṇikāra tree in bloom, I then gathered them; I offered them to Tissa, the one who had crossed the flood, the Steadfast One."

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-two aeons ago, when I offered a flower, I do not recall a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Pañcatiṃse ito kappe, aruṇapāṇīti vissuto;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"Thirty-five aeons ago, I was renowned as Aruṇapāṇī, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished."

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0126] pana patvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā bhagavato thomanākārena aññaṃ byākaronto “namo te buddha vīratthū”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, he went to the Teacher, paid homage, sat down to one side, and declaring his arahantship in the manner of praising the Blessed One, he uttered this verse: 'Homage to you, O Buddha, the Hero!'

47. Tattha namoti paṇāmakittanaṃ. Teti paṇāmakiriyāya sampadānakittanaṃ, tuyhanti attho. Buddha vīrāti ca bhagavato ālapanaṃ. Bhagavā hi yathā abhiññeyyādibhedassa atthassa abhiññeyyādibhedena sayambhūñāṇena anavasesato buddhattā “buddho”ti vuccati. Evaṃ pañcannampi mārānaṃ abhippamaddanavasena padahantena mahatā vīriyena samannāgatattā “vīro”ti vuccati. Atthūti hotu, tassa “namo”ti iminā sambandho. Vippamuttosi sabbadhīti sabbehi kilesehi sabbasmiñca saṅkhāragate vippamutto visaṃyutto asi bhavasi, na tayā kiñci avippamuttaṃ nāma atthi, yatohaṃ tuyhāpadāne viharaṃ, viharāmi anāsavoti tuyhaṃ tava apadāne ovāde [P 1.0128] gatamagge paṭipatticariyāya viharaṃ yathāsatti [M 1.0150] yathābalaṃ paṭipajjanto kāmāsavādīnaṃ catunnampi āsavānaṃ suppahīnattā anāsavo viharāmi, tādisassa namo te buddha-vīratthūti.

47. Therein, 'namo' is the declaration of homage. 'Te' is the declaration of the recipient of the act of homage, meaning 'to you.' And 'Buddha, Hero' is an address to the Blessed One. For the Blessed One is called 'Buddha' because he is enlightened completely, without remainder, by self-arisen knowledge to the nature of things in its various aspects, such as the knowable. Similarly, he is called 'Hero' because he is endowed with great effort, striving in the manner of crushing all five Māras. 'Atthu' means 'may it be'; it is connected with 'namo.' 'You are liberated in every way' means: you are completely freed and detached from all defilements and from all conditioned phenomena; there is nothing in you that is unliberated. 'Because I dwell in your Apadāna, I dwell without taints' means: dwelling in your Apadāna—your instruction, the path traversed, the practice and conduct—striving to the best of my ability and strength, having thoroughly abandoned the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, I dwell without taints. Homage to you of such a kind, O Buddha, Hero—may it be so!

Ujjayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ujjaya is concluded.

8. Sañjayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sañjaya

Yato ahanti āyasmato sañjayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle mahati pūge saṃkittivasena vatthuṃ saṅgharitvā ratanattayaṃ uddissa puññaṃ karonto sayaṃ daliddo hutvā nesaṃ gaṇādīnaṃ puññakiriyāya byāvaṭo ahosi. Kālena kālaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā pasannamānaso bhikkhūnañca taṃ taṃ veyyāvaccaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti sañjayo nāma nāmena, so vayappatto brahmāyupokkharasātiādike abhiññāte brāhmaṇe sāsane abhippasanne disvā sañjātappasādo satthāraṃ upasaṅkami. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā sotāpanno ahosi. Aparabhāge pabbaji. Pabbajanto ca khuraggeyeva chaḷabhiñño ahosī. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.10.51-55) –

'Yato ahaṃ' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sañjaya. What is its origin? He too, having established a foundation under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that was a decisive support for liberation in various places, was active during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. He briefly collected materials for a great assembly, and performing merit dedicated to the Triple Gem, though he himself was poor, he was engaged in meritorious activities for those groups and others. From time to time, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and with a serene mind, performed various services for the monks. By that meritorious action, he was reborn in the deva world. Again and again performing meritorious deeds and revolving only in happy destinies, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha, named Sañjaya. When he came of age, seeing well-known brahmins like Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti, who were deeply devoted to the Dispensation, he developed faith and approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Hearing the Dhamma, he became a stream-enterer. Later, he went forth. Upon going forth, he attained the six higher knowledges at the very razor's edge. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.10.51-55):

“Vipassissa [V 1.0127] bhagavato, mahāpūgagaṇo ahu;

Veyyāvaccakaro āsiṃ, sabbakiccesu vāvaṭo.

"For the Blessed One Vipassī, there was a great assembly of followers; I was an attendant, diligent in all services."

“Deyyadhammo ca me natthi, sugatassa mahesino;

Avandiṃ satthuno pāde, vippasannena cetasā.

"And I had no offering to give to the Well-farer, the Great Sage; I bowed to the Teacher's feet with a mind of serene faith."

“Ekanavutito kappe, veyyāvaccaṃ akāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, veyyāvaccassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-one aeons ago, I performed that service; I do not recall a bad rebirth—this is the fruit of service."

“Ito [M 1.0151] ca aṭṭhame kappe, rājā āsiṃ sucintito;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"And in the eighth aeon from now, I was King Sucintita; endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Chaḷabhiñño [P 1.0129] pana hutvā aññaṃ byākaronto “yato ahaṃ pabbajito”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having become one with the six higher knowledges, declaring his final knowledge, he uttered the verse: 'Since I went forth...'

48. Tattha yato ahaṃ pabbajitoti yato pabhuti yato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ pabbajito. Pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya nābhijānāmi saṅkappaṃ, anariyaṃ dosasaṃhitanti rāgādidosasaṃhitaṃ tato eva anariyaṃ nihīnaṃ, ariyehi vā anaraṇīyatāya anariyehi araṇīyatāya ca anariyaṃ pāpakaṃ ārammaṇe abhūtaguṇādisaṅkappanato “saṅkappo”ti laddhanāmaṃ kāmavitakkādimicchāvitakkaṃ uppāditaṃ nābhijānāmīti, “khuraggeyeva mayā arahattaṃ patta”nti aññaṃ byākāsi.

48. Therein, 'Since I went forth' means: from the time, from the point when I went forth. 'I do not recall an ignoble thought connected with defilement' means: I do not recall having given rise to a thought connected with defilements such as greed, and which is therefore ignoble and base. Or, it is 'ignoble' (anariya) because it is not to be resorted to (anaraṇīya) by the noble ones, but is to be resorted to (araṇīya) by the ignoble. It is an evil 'thought' (saṅkappa), a name given to wrong thoughts such as sensual thought, because it conceives of unreal qualities in an object. By this statement, he declared his final knowledge, meaning: 'I attained arahantship at the very razor's edge.'

Sañjayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sañjaya is concluded.

9. Rāmaṇeyyakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka

Cihacihābhinaditeti āyasmato rāmaṇeyyakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsu eva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ibbhakule nibbattitvā vayappatto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe sañjātappasādo pabbajitvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharati. Tassa attano sampattiyā pabbajitasāruppāya ca paṭipattiyā pāsādikabhāvato rāmaṇeyyakotveva samaññā ahosi[V 1.0128]. Athekadivasaṃ māro theraṃ bhiṃsāpetukāmo bheravasaddaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sutvā thero thirapakatitāya [M 1.0152] tena asantasanto “māro aya”nti ñatvā tattha anādaraṃ dassento “cihacihābhinadite”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

'With the resounding 'cihacihā' cries'—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka. What was its origin? This elder, too, having established a foundation under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having attained maturity, he saw the Blessed One, and with a mind filled with faith, he made an offering of flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds, revolving only among happy destinies until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a merchant family in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he gained faith during the dedication of Jetavana and went forth. Taking up a meditation subject suited to his temperament, he dwelt in the forest. Because of his own attainments and the pleasing nature of his practice befitting a renunciant, his designation became "Rāmaṇeyyaka" (the Delightful One). Then one day, Māra, wishing to frighten the elder, made a terrifying sound. Hearing it, the elder, firm in his nature and unperturbed by it, recognized, "This is Māra," and showing his indifference, he spoke this verse: 'With the resounding 'cihacihā' cries...'

49. Tattha cihacihābhinaditeti cihacihāti abhiṇhaṃ pavattasaddatāya “cihacihā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ vaṭṭakānaṃ abhinādanimittaṃ, viravahetūti [P 1.0130] attho. Sippikābhirutehi cāti sippikā vuccanti devakā paranāmakā gelaññena chātakisadārakākārā sākhāmigā. “Mahākalandakā”ti keci, sippikānaṃ abhirutehi mahāviravehi, hetumhi cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, taṃ hetūti attho. Na me taṃ phandati cittanti mama cittaṃ na phandati na cavati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – imasmiṃ araññe viravahetu sippikābhirutahetu viya, pāpima, tava vissarakaraṇahetu mama cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānato na paripatatīti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “ekattaniratañhi me”ti. Hi-saddo hetu attho, yasmā mama cittaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya ekatte ekībhāve, bahiddhā vā vikkhepaṃ pahāya ekatte ekaggatāya, ekatte ekasabhāve vā nibbāne nirataṃ abhirataṃ, tasmā kammaṭṭhānato na phandati na cavatīti, imaṃ kira gāthaṃ vadanto eva thero vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.21.5-9) –

49. Therein, 'with the resounding 'cihacihā' cries' means: it is the cause of the resounding of the quails, which are named 'cihacihā' due to their continuous 'cihacihā' sound; the meaning is 'the cause of the loud crying'. And 'by the cries of the sippikā': the 'sippikā' are said to be tree-dwelling animals also called 'devakā', which look like sickly, starving children. Some say they are 'great squirrels'. 'By the cries of the sippikā' means by their great, loud cries; this instrumental case is used in the sense of cause, meaning 'because of that'. 'My mind does not waver at that' means my mind does not tremble or stray. This is what is said: 'O Evil One, my mind does not fall away from its meditation object on account of your making a discordant sound, which in this forest is like a cause for loud crying or the cries of the sippikā.' He states the reason for this, saying: 'For my mind delights in solitude.' The particle 'hi' is in the sense of cause. Because my mind, having abandoned socializing with groups, delights in solitude, in being alone; or, having abandoned external distraction, it delights in solitude, in one-pointedness; or, it delights in solitude, in Nibbāna which has a single nature—therefore it does not waver or stray from the meditation object. It is said that while reciting this verse, the elder developed his insight and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.21.5-9):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo bhagavā, sataraṃsī patāpavā;

Caṅkamanaṃ samārūḷho, mettacitto sikhīsabho.

"Golden-hued is the Blessed One, with a hundred rays, majestic; having ascended the walking path, Sikhī, the compassionate leader."

“Pasannacitto sumano, vanditvā ñāṇamuttamaṃ;

Minelapupphaṃ paggayha, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

"With a clear and joyful mind, having paid homage to the supreme wisdom, holding up a Minela flower, I offered it to the Buddha."

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I offered that flower in worship; I have not known a bad rebirth—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Ekūnatiṃsakappamhi, sumeghaghananāmako;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"In the twenty-ninth aeon from now, I was Sumeghaghana by name, endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning monarch."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosi.

This very verse was the elder's declaration of final knowledge.

Rāmaṇeyyakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rāmaṇeyyaka is concluded.

10. Vimalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vimala

Dharaṇī [M 1.0153][V 1.0129] ca siñcati vāti āyasmato vimalattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle saṅkhadhamanakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tasmiṃ [P 1.0131] sippe nipphattiṃ gato ekadivasaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso saṅkhadhamanena pūjaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya kālena kālaṃ satthu upaṭṭhānaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle “anāgate me vimalo visuddho kāyo hotū”ti bodhirukkhaṃ gandhodakehi nhāpesi, cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇesu āsanāni dhovāpesi, bhikkhūnampi kiliṭṭhe samaṇaparikkhāre dhovāpesi.

The verse of the Venerable Elder Vimala, beginning 'The earth sprinkles and the wind blows.' What is its origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulated wholesome actions in various existences that were a condition for the cessation of rebirth. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a family of conch-blowers, and having attained maturity, he became proficient in that craft. One day, seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, his mind became joyful, and he made an offering by blowing the conch. From then on, from time to time, he attended upon the Teacher. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Continuously performing meritorious deeds, wandering among gods and humans, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he thought, 'May my body be pure and stainless in the future,' and bathed the Bodhi tree with fragrant water. He had seats washed in the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, and also had the soiled monastic requisites of the monks washed.

So tato cavitvā devesu ca manussesu ca parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe ibbhakule nibbatti. Tassa mātukucchiyaṃ vasantassa nikkhamantassa ca kāyo pittasemhādīhi asaṃkiliṭṭho padumapalāse udakabindu viya alaggo pacchimabhavikabodhisattassa viya suvisuddho ahosi, tenassa vimalotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto rājagahappavesane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kosalaraṭṭhe pabbataguhāyaṃ viharati. Athekadivasaṃ cātuddīpikamahāmegho sakalaṃ cakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pattharitvā pāvassi. Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyimhi buddhānaṃ cakkavattīnañca dharamānakāle eva kira evaṃ vassati. Ghammapariḷāhavūpasamato utusappāyalābhena therassa cittaṃ samāhitaṃ ahosi ekaggaṃ. So samāhitacitto tāvadeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.10.56-60) –

Then, after passing away and wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha-era in a wealthy family in Rājagaha. While he was in his mother’s womb and when he was born, his body was unstained by bile, phlegm, and such, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf—just as pure as that of a Bodhisatta in his final existence. Thus, they named him Vimala. When he came of age, he saw the Buddha’s majesty upon entering Rājagaha and, having gained faith, he went forth. Taking up a meditation subject, he dwelt in a mountain cave in the Kosala country. Then one day, a great cloud that encompasses all four continents, spreading throughout the interior of the entire world-system, poured down rain. It is said that such rain falls only when Buddhas and universal monarchs are present in an evolving aeon. With the heat of feverish desire subdued and the attainment of seasonable comfort, the elder’s mind became concentrated and one-pointed. With his mind thus composed, he immediately applied himself to insight and, following the path, attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vipassissa bhagavato, ahosiṃ saṅkhadhammako;

Niccupaṭṭhānayuttomhi, sugatassa mahesino.

“I was the conch-blower for the Blessed One Vipassī; I was constantly engaged in attendance upon the Sugata, the Great Sage.”

“Upaṭṭhānaphalaṃ passa, lokanāthassa tādino;

Saṭṭhi tūriyasahassāni, parivārenti maṃ sadā.

“Behold the fruit of service to the world's protector, the steadfast one; sixty thousand musical instruments always attend upon me.”

“Ekanavutito [M 1.0154] kappe, upaṭṭhahiṃ mahāisiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, upaṭṭhānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I waited upon the great seer; I do not recall a bad rebirth—this is the fruit of service.”

“Catuvīse ito kappe, mahānigghosanāmakā;

Soḷasāsiṃsu rājāno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Twenty-four aeons ago, there were sixteen wheel-turning monarchs of great power, named Mahānigghosa.”

“Kilesā [V 1.0130] jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā katakiccatāya tuṭṭhamānaso udānaṃ udānento “dharaṇī ca siñcati vāti māluto”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, his mind content with having done what was to be done, he uttered this inspired verse while expressing his joy: “The earth sprinkles and the wind blows.”

50. Tattha dharaṇīti pathavī, sā hi sakalaṃ dharādharaṃ dhāretīti “dharaṇī”ti vuccati. Siñcatīti samantato nabhaṃ pūretvā abhippavassato mahāmeghassa vuṭṭhidhārāhi siñcati[P 1.0132]. Vāti mālutoti udakaphusitasammissatāya sītalo vāto vāyati. Vijjutā carati nabheti tattha tattha gajjatā gaḷagaḷāyatā mahāmeghato niccharantiyo sateratā ākāse ito cito ca vicaranti. Upasamanti vitakkāti utusappāyasiddhena samathavipassanādhigamena pubbabhāge tadaṅgādivasena vūpasantā hutvā kāmavitakkādayo sabbepi nava mahāvitakkā ariyamaggādhigamena upasamanti. Anavasesato samucchijjantīti. Vattamānasamīpatāya ariyamaggakkhaṇaṃ vattamānaṃ katvā vadati. Atītatthe vā etaṃ paccuppannavacanaṃ. Cittaṃ susamāhitaṃ mamāti tato eva lokuttarasamādhinā mama cittaṃ suṭṭhu samāhitaṃ, na dāni tassa samādhāne kiñci kātabbaṃ atthīti thero aññaṃ byākāsi.

50. Herein, 'the earth' (dharaṇī) is the ground, for it supports all that is borne upon it, thus it is called 'dharaṇī.' 'Sprinkles' (siñcati) means that the great cloud, filling the sky all around and pouring down rain, sprinkles the earth with showers of rain. 'The wind blows' (vāti māluto) refers to the cool wind blowing, mingled with sprinkles of water. 'Lightning flashes across the sky' (vijjutā carati nabhe)—here and there, roaring and rumbling, flashes emanate from the massive cloud, darting through the sky in all directions. 'Thoughts subside' (upasamanti vitakkā)—through the success of suitable weather conditions, and through the attainment of serenity and insight, in the preliminary stage they are temporarily suppressed by momentary suppression and so forth, and then all nine major thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, are pacified by the attainment of the noble path. They are completely eradicated without remainder. Because of the nearness to the present moment, he speaks by making the moment of the noble path as if it were the present. Alternatively, this present tense may refer to a past event. 'My mind is well-concentrated' (cittaṃ susamāhitaṃ mama)—from that very supramundane concentration, my mind is thoroughly composed; now there is nothing more to be done in regard to that concentration. Thus, the elder declared his attainment.

Vimalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verse of Elder Vimala is concluded.

Pañcamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is concluded.

6. Chaṭṭhavaggo

6. The Sixth Chapter

1. Godhikādicatuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Godhika and the Three Others

Vassati [M 1.0155][V 1.0131] devotiādikā catasso – godhiko, subāhu, valliyo, uttiyoti imesaṃ catunnaṃ therānaṃ gāthā. Kā uppatti? Imepi purimabuddhesu katādhikārā tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinantā ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patvā aññamaññaṃ sahāyā hutvā vicariṃsu. Tesu eko siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ adāsi. Dutiyo pasannacitto hutvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. Tatiyo pasannacitto ekena pupphahatthena bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Catuttho sumanapupphehi pūjamakāsi. Evaṃ te satthari cittaṃ pasādetvā pasutena tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā puna aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā sahāyakā hutvā sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle pāvāyaṃ catunnaṃ mallarājānaṃ puttā hutvā nibbattiṃsu. Tesaṃ [P 1.0133] godhiko, subāhu, valliyo, uttiyoti nāmāni akaṃsu. Aññamaññaṃ piyasahāyā ahesuṃ. Te kenacideva karaṇīyena kapilavatthuṃ agamaṃsu. Tasmiñca samaye satthā kapilavatthuṃ gantvā nigrodhārāme vasanto yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā suddhodanappamukhe sakyarājāno damesi. Tadā tepi cattāro mallarājaputtā pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā laddhappasādā pabbajitvā vipassanākammaṃ karontā nacirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.1-23) –

The four verses beginning with 'Vassati devo' are those of these four elders: Godhika, Subāhu, Valliya, and Uttiya. What is their origin? These too, having made their aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences, were reborn in good families during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, ninety-four aeons ago. Having attained maturity, they became companions and wandered together. Among them, one saw the Blessed One Siddhattha going for alms and offered him a ladleful of food. The second, with a joyful mind, paid homage with the five-point prostration and raised his joined hands. The third, with a delighted mind, honored the Blessed One with a single handful of flowers. The fourth made an offering with jasmine flowers. Thus, having inspired faith in the Teacher, they were reborn in the heavenly world due to that meritorious deed. Performing good deeds again and again, wandering between devas and humans, they were reborn in good families during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Becoming companions, they went forth into the Dispensation, practiced the ascetic life, and in the time of our Blessed One, they were reborn as the sons of the four Malla kings in Pāvā. They were named Godhika, Subāhu, Valliya, and Uttiya. They were dear friends to one another. Once, for some reason or other, they went to Kapilavatthu. At that time, the Teacher had also gone to Kapilavatthu and was staying in the Nigrodha Grove. There, he displayed the Twin Miracle and tamed the Sakyan kings, led by Suddhodana. Then, these four Malla princes, seeing the miracle, gained faith and went forth. Practicing insight meditation, they soon attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Pavarā abhinikkhantaṃ, vanā nibbanamāgataṃ.

“The golden-hued Perfectly Awakened One, recipient of offerings, the supreme one who went forth, come from the forest to the forest-free state.”

“Kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ pādāsiṃ, siddhatthassa mahesino;

Paññāya upasantassa, mahāvīrassa tādino.

“I offered a ladleful of food to the great sage Siddhattha, the great hero, the steadfast one, who is calmed by wisdom.”

“Padenānupadāyantaṃ, nibbāpente mahājanaṃ;

Uḷārā vitti me jātā, buddhe ādiccabandhune.

“Lofty joy arose in me for the Buddha, kinsman of the sun, who was following step by step, bringing peace to the great multitude.”

“Catunnavutito [M 1.0156][V 1.0132] kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bhikkhādānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that gift, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of that alms-giving.”

“Sattāsītimhito kappe, mahāreṇusanāmakā;

Sattaratanasampannā, sattete cakkavattino.

“Eighty-seven aeons ago, there were these seven wheel-turning monarchs named Mahāreṇu, endowed with the seven treasures.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Godhiko thero.

The Elder Godhika.

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, nisabhājāniyaṃ yathā;

Tidhāpabhinnaṃ mātaṅgaṃ, kuñjaraṃva mahesinaṃ.

“The golden-hued Perfectly Awakened One, like a thoroughbred bull; the great sage, like a great elephant with threefold rut.”

“Obhāsentaṃ disā sabbā, uḷurājaṃva pūritaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ apassahaṃ.

“Illuminating all directions, like the full moon, king of the stars; proceeding along the road, I saw the foremost in the world.”

“Ñāṇe cittaṃ pasādetvā, paggahetvāna añjaliṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, siddhatthamabhivādayiṃ.

Having made my mind serene through knowledge, raising my joined hands in reverence; with a serene and gladdened mind, I paid homage to Siddhattha.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ñāṇasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-four aeons ago, for the deed I then performed, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the perception of knowledge.

“Tesattatimhito kappe, soḷasāsuṃ naruttamā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

Seventy-three aeons ago, there were sixteen supreme men, mighty wheel-turning monarchs, endowed with the seven treasures.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

Subāhutthero.

The Elder Subāhu.

“Tivarāyaṃ nivāsīhaṃ, ahosiṃ māliko tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, siddhatthaṃ lokapūjitaṃ.

At that time, I was dwelling in Tivarā as a garland-maker. I saw the stainless Buddha Siddhattha, honored by the world.

“Pasannacitto sumano, pupphahatthamadāsahaṃ;

Yattha yatthupapajjāmi, tassa kammassa vāhasā.

With a serene and gladdened mind, I offered a handful of flowers. Wherever I am reborn, it is by the power of that action.

“Anubhomi phalaṃ iṭṭhaṃ, pubbe sukatamattano;

Parikkhitto sumallehi, pupphadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

I experience the pleasant fruit of my own past good deeds; surrounded by fine garlands, this is the fruit of the flower offering.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-four aeons ago, when I offered a flower, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the flower offering.

“Catunnavutupādāya[M 1.0157], ṭhapetvā vattamānakaṃ;

Pañcarājasatā tattha, najjasamasanāmakā.

Beginning from ninety-four aeons ago, excluding the present one, there were five hundred kings there, named Najjupasama.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

Valliyo thero.

The Elder Valliya.

“Siddhatthassa [V 1.0133] bhagavato, jātipupphamadāsahaṃ;

Pādesu satta pupphāni, hāsenokiritāni me.

I offered jasmine flowers to the Blessed One Siddhattha; seven flowers I joyfully scattered at his feet.

“Tena kammenahaṃ ajja, abhibhomi narāmare;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

By that action, today I surpass humans and devas; I bear this final body in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-four aeons ago, when I offered a flower, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the flower offering.

“Samantagandhanāmāsuṃ, terasa cakkavattino;

Ito pañcamake kappe, cāturantā janādhipā.

In the fifth aeon from now, there were thirteen wheel-turning monarchs named Samantagandha, lords of the four quarters, rulers of the people.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. (apa. thera 1.11.1-23);

My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

Uttiyo thero.

The Elder Uttiya.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā ime cattāropi therā loke pākaṭā paññātā rājarājamahāmattehi sakkatā garukatā hutvā araññe [P 1.0134] saheva viharanti. Athekadā rājā bimbisāro te cattāro there rājagahaṃ upagate upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā temāsaṃ vassāvāsatthāya nimantetvā tesaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ kuṭikāyo kāretvā satisammosena na chādesi. Therā acchannāsu kuṭikāsu viharanti. Vassakāle devo na vassati. Rājā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇaṃ devo na vassatī”ti cintento, taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā, tā kuṭikāyo chādāpetvā, mattikākammaṃ cittakammañca kārāpetvā, kuṭikāmahaṃ karonto mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ adāsi. Therā rañño anukampāya kuṭikāyo pavisitvā mettāsamāpattiyo samāpajjiṃsu. Athuttarapācīnadisato mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā [M 1.0158] therānaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhānakkhaṇeyeva vassituṃ ārabhi. Tesu godhikatthero samāpattito vuṭṭhāya saha meghagajjitena –

Having attained arahantship, these four elders became well-known and recognized in the world, honored and respected by kings and great ministers, and they continued to dwell together in the forest. Then one day, when these four elders arrived in Rājagaha, King Bimbisāra approached them, paid homage, and invited them to stay for the three months of the rainy season. He had individual huts built for them but, due to a lapse of mindfulness, did not have them roofed. The elders lived in those unroofed huts. During the rainy season, the sky did not rain. The king, wondering, “What indeed is the reason the sky does not rain?” and upon realizing the cause, had those huts roofed, had clay work and painting done, and while holding a festival for the huts, he offered alms to a great community of monks. Out of compassion for the king, the elders entered their huts and attained the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness. Then, from the north-eastern direction, a great cloud arose, and just at the moment the elders emerged from their meditative states, it began to rain. Among them, the Elder Godhika, rising from his absorption along with the thunder of the clouds—

51.

51.

“Vassati devo yathā sugītaṃ, channā me kuṭikā sukhā nivātā;

Cittaṃ susamāhitañca mayhaṃ, atha ce patthayasi pavassa devā”ti. –

“The god rains as if singing well; my hut is roofed, comfortable, sheltered from the wind; and my mind is well composed. So, if you wish, rain, O god!”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He recited this verse.

Tattha vassatīti siñcati vuṭṭhidhāraṃ pavecchati. Devoti megho. Yathā sugītanti sundaragītaṃ viya gajjantoti adhippāyo. Megho hi vassanakāle satapaṭalasahassapaṭalo uṭṭhahitvā thanayanto vijjutā nicchārentova sobhati, na kevalo. Tasmā siniddhamadhuragambhīranigghoso vassati [V 1.0134] devoti dasseti. Tena saddato anupapīḷitaṃ āha “channā me kuṭikā sukhā nivātā”ti. Yathā na devo vassati, evaṃ tiṇādīhi chāditā ayaṃ me kuṭikā, tena vuṭṭhivassena anupapīḷitaṃ āha. Paribhogasukhassa utusappāyautusukhassa ca sabbhāvato sukhā. Phusitaggaḷapihitavātapānatāhi vātaparissayarahitā. Ubhayenapi āvāsasappāyavasena anupapīḷitaṃ āha. Cittaṃ susamāhitañca mayhanti cittañca mama suṭṭhu samāhitaṃ anuttarasamādhinā nibbānārammaṇe [P 1.0135] suṭṭhu appitaṃ, etena abbhantaraparissayābhāvato appossukkataṃ dasseti. Atha ce patthayasīti atha idāni patthayasi ce, yadi icchasi. Pavassāti siñca udakaṃ pagghara vuṭṭhidhāraṃ paveccha. Devāti meghaṃ ālapati.

Here, ‘it rains’ means it pours, sending down showers of rain. ‘The god’ means the cloud. ‘Like a well-sung song’ means roaring like a beautiful melody. For a cloud, when it rains, rises with a hundred or a thousand layers, thundering and flashing lightning, it shines brilliantly, not just by itself. Therefore, it shows, ‘The god rains with a smooth, sweet, and deep sound.’ By this, he speaks of being undisturbed by the sound. Regarding ‘My hut is roofed, comfortable, sheltered from the wind,’ he speaks of being undisturbed by the downpour of rain because it is covered with grass and so on. It is comfortable due to the presence of comfort in use and comfort suitable to the season. It is free from the danger of wind due to its well-fitted bolts and closed windows. By both means, he speaks of being undisturbed due to the suitability of the dwelling. Regarding ‘And my mind is well-composed,’ this means: my mind is well-established, firmly fixed on the object of Nibbāna by the unsurpassed concentration; by this, he shows his freedom from anxiety due to the absence of inner dangers. Regarding ‘Now if you wish,’ this means: if you now desire, if you wish. Regarding ‘rain,’ this means: pour, let the water flow, send down a shower of rain. By ‘O god,’ he addresses the cloud.

Godhikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Godhika is concluded.

2. Subāhuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Subāhu

52. Itarehi vuttagāthāsu tatiyapade eva viseso. Tattha subāhunā vuttagāthāyaṃ cittaṃ susamāhitañca kāyeti mama cittaṃ karajakāye kāyagatāsatibhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu samāhitaṃ sammadeva appitaṃ. Ayañhi thero kāyagatāsatibhāvanāvasena paṭiladdhajhānaṃ pādakaṃ [M 1.0159] katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ sandhāyāha “cittaṃ susamāhitañca kāye”ti.

52. In the verses spoken by the others, the distinction lies only in the third line. There, in the verse spoken by Subāhu, the line is ‘cittaṃ susamāhitañca kāye,’ which means: my mind is well-composed and rightly applied to this composite body by means of developing mindfulness directed to the body. For this elder, having made the jhāna attained through mindfulness directed to the body his basis, developed insight and reached arahantship. Referring to this, he said, ‘and my mind is well-composed on the body.’

Subāhuttheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Subāhu is concluded.

3. Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Valliya

53. Valliyattheragāthāyaṃ tassaṃ viharāmi appamattoti tassaṃ kuṭikāyaṃ appamādapaṭipattiyā matthakaṃ pāpitattā appamatto ariyavihārūpasaṃhitena dibbavihārādisaṃhitena ca iriyāpathavihārena viharāmi, attabhāvaṃ pavattemīti vuttaṃ hoti.

53. In the verse of the Elder Valliya, the line is ‘tassaṃ viharāmi appamatto’ (I dwell there diligently). This means: in that hut, being diligent because I have reached the pinnacle of the practice of diligence, I dwell—that is, I maintain my existence—by means of an abiding in the four postures that is connected with the noble abidings and the divine abidings.

Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Valliya is concluded.

4. Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Uttiya

54. Uttiyattherena [V 1.0135] vuttagāthāyaṃ adutiyoti asahāyo, kilesasaṅgaṇikāya gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya ca virahitoti attho.

54. In the verse spoken by the Elder Uttiya, ‘adutiyo’ (without a second) means without a companion, devoid of the company of defilements and the company of a group—this is the meaning.

Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Uttiya is concluded.

Catunnaṃ therānaṃ gāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Four Elders is concluded.

5. Añjanavaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Añjanavaniya

Āsandiṃ [P 1.0136] kuṭikaṃ katvāti āyasmato añjanavaniyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle sudassano nāma mālākāro hutvā sumanapupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā aññampi tattha tattha bahuṃ puññaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Atha imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ vajjirājakule nibbattitvā tassa vayappattakāle vajjiraṭṭhe avuṭṭhibhayaṃ byādhibhayaṃ amanussabhayanti tīṇi bhayāni uppajjiṃsu[M 1.0160]. Taṃ sabbaṃ ratanasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (khu. pā. aṭṭha. ratanasuttavaṇṇanā; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ratanasuttavaṇṇanā) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Bhagavati pana vesāliṃ paviṭṭhe bhayesu ca vūpasantesu satthu dhammadesanāya sambahulānaṃ devamanussānaṃ dhammābhisamaye ca jāte ayaṃ rājakumāro buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji. Yathā cāyaṃ evaṃ anantaraṃ vuccamānā cattāropi janā. Tepi hi imassa sahāyabhūtā licchavirājakumārā evaṃ imināva nīhārena pabbajiṃsu. Kassapasambuddhakālepi sahāyā hutvā iminā saheva pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ akaṃsu, padumuttarassapi bhagavato pādamūle kusalabījaropanādiṃ akaṃsūti. Tatthāyaṃ katapubbakicco sākete añjanavane susānaṭṭhāne vasanto upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya manussehi chaḍḍitaṃ jiṇṇakaṃ āsandiṃ labhitvā taṃ catūsu pāsāṇesu ṭhapetvā upari tiriyañca tiṇādīhi chādetvā dvāraṃ yojetvā vassaṃ upagato. Paṭhamamāseyeva ghaṭento vāyamanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.24-28) –

“Āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā” (Having made a couch into a hut)—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Añjanavaniya. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a garland-maker named Sudassana. Having honored the Blessed One with Sumanā flowers and performed much merit here and there, he wandered among devas and humans. In the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth and practiced the ascetic life. Then, in this Buddha’s arising, he was reborn in the royal family of the Vajjis in Vesālī. When he came of age, three dangers arose in the Vajji country: the fear of drought, the fear of disease, and the fear of non-humans. All this should be understood as explained in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta (Khuddakapāṭha Aṭṭhakathā; Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā 1, Ratana Sutta Commentary). When the Blessed One entered Vesālī and the dangers subsided, and when many devas and humans attained realization of the Dhamma through the Teacher’s discourse, this prince, seeing the Buddha’s power, gained faith and went forth. And just as he did, so too did the four others mentioned immediately after. They were Licchavi princes, his companions, who also went forth in this very same way. In the time of the Buddha Kassapa as well, they had been his companions and, together with him, had gone forth and practiced the ascetic life. Even at the foot of the Blessed One Padumuttara, they had performed the planting of the seeds of merit and so on. Here, this one who had fulfilled his past duties was dwelling in a charnel ground in the Añjana forest near Sāketa. As the rains retreat approached, he obtained an old couch discarded by people. Placing it on four stones, covering it above and crosswise with grass and such, and fashioning a door, he entered the rains retreat. In the very first month, striving and exerting himself, he attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (apa. thera 1.11.24-28):

“Sudassanoti nāmena, mālākāro ahaṃ tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ.

“By the name of Sudassana, I was a garland-maker then; I saw the stainless Buddha, the world’s foremost, the bull among men.

“Jātipupphaṃ [V 1.0136] gahetvāna, pūjayiṃ padumuttaraṃ;

Visuddhacakkhu sumano, dibbacakkhuṃ samajjhagaṃ.

“Taking a jasmine flower, I worshipped Padumuttara; with pure vision and joyful mind, I attained the divine eye.

“Etissā pupphapūjāya, cittassa paṇidhīhi ca;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“By this offering of flowers and by the aspirations of my mind, for a hundred thousand aeons I was not reborn in a state of woe.

“Soḷasāsiṃsu rājāno, devuttarasanāmakā;

Chattiṃsamhi ito kappe, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“There were sixteen kings, named Devuttara; in the thirty-sixth aeon from now, they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… and so on… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento samāpattito vuṭṭhāya yathāladdhaṃ sampattiṃ paccavekkhitvā pītivegena udānento “āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi[P 1.0137].

Having attained Arahantship, experiencing the bliss of liberation, and rising from meditative attainment, he reviewed the accomplishment he had attained and, with a surge of joy, uttered this inspired verse: “Āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā”.

55. Tattha āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvāti āsandī nāma dīghapādakaṃ caturassapīṭhaṃ, āyataṃ caturassampi atthiyeva, yattha nisīditumeva sakkā, na nipajjituṃ [M 1.0161] taṃ āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā vāsatthāya heṭṭhā vuttanayena kuṭikaṃ katvā yathā tattha nisinnassa utuparissayābhāvena sukhena samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ sakkā, evaṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā. Etena paramukkaṃsagataṃ senāsane attano appicchataṃ santuṭṭhiñca dasseti. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā –

55. Therein, “having made a couch into a hut” (āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā): an āsandi is a long-legged, four-cornered stool; it can be both long and four-cornered. It is a place where one can only sit, not lie down. Having made that āsandi into a hut for dwelling, that is, by making a hut underneath in the aforementioned way, so that one sitting there can practice the ascetic life comfortably without danger from the elements—thus he made a hut. By this, he shows his own fewness of wishes and contentment regarding even the most excellent lodging. And this was said by the General of the Dhamma:

“Pallaṅkena nisinnassa, jaṇṇukenābhivassati;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 985; mi. pa. 6.1.1);

“For one sitting cross-legged, the rain does not fall upon his knees; it is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a resolute monk.”

Apare “āsandikuṭika”nti pāṭhaṃ vatvā “āsandippamāṇaṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Aññe pana “āsananisajjādigate manusse uddissa mañcakassa upari katakuṭikā āsandī nāma, taṃ āsandiṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Oggayhāti ogāhetvā anupavisitvā. Añjanaṃ vananti evaṃnāmakaṃ vanaṃ, añjanavaṇṇapupphabhāvato hi añjanā vuccanti valliyo, tabbahulatāya taṃ vanaṃ “añjanavana”nti nāmaṃ labhi. Apare pana “añjanā nāma mahāgacchā”ti vadanti, taṃ añjanavanaṃ oggayha āsandikaṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsananti viharatā mayāti vacanaseseneva yojanā. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Others, reciting the text as “āsandikuṭika,” explain its meaning as “having made a hut the size of a couch.” Still others say the meaning is: “An āsandi is a small hut made above a couch for people sitting, reclining, and so on; having made such an āsandi into a hut.” “Oggayha” means having entered, having gone into. “Añjanaṃ vanaṃ” is a forest with that name. Because of having flowers the color of kohl (añjana), the creepers are called añjanā, and due to their abundance, that forest received the name “Añjanavana.” Others, however, say, “Añjanā are great trees.” The connection should be made with the remaining words thus: “Having entered that Añjanavana and made an āsandi-hut, the three knowledges were attained and the Buddha's teaching has been done by me while dwelling there.” And this was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Añjanavaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Añjanavaniya is concluded.

6. Kuṭivihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kuṭivihārī

Ko [V 1.0137] kuṭikāyanti āyasmato kuṭivihārittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato ākāsena gacchantassa “udakadānaṃ [P 1.0138] dassāmī”ti sītalaṃ udakaṃ gahetvā pītisomanassajāto uddhammukho hutvā ukkhipi. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ ākāse ṭhitova sampaṭicchi. So tena anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. Sesaṃ añjanavaniyattherassa vatthumhi vuttasadisameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – ayaṃ kira vuttanayena pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanaṃ anuyuñjanto sāyaṃ khettasamīpena gacchanto deve phusāyante khettapālakassa puññaṃ tiṇakuṭiṃ disvā pavisitvā tattha tiṇasanthārake nisīdi[M 1.0162]. Nisinnamattova utusappāyaṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.29-35) –

“Ko kuṭikāyaṃ” and so on are the verses of the Venerable Kuṭivihārī. What is their origin? It is said that when the Blessed One Padumuttara was traveling through the sky, this one, thinking, “I will give an offering of water,” took cool water and, filled with joy and delight, faced upwards and tossed it into the air. The Teacher, knowing his intention, remained standing in the sky and accepted it in order to increase his faith. He thereby experienced no small measure of joy and delight. The rest is similar to what was said in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. But this is the difference: It is said that after going forth in the manner described and completing his past duties, he devoted himself to insight meditation. One evening, while walking near a field as it was drizzling, he saw a humble grass hut belonging to the field-guard, entered it, and sat down on a spread of grass. As soon as he sat down, having found a suitable climate, he intensified his insight meditation and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (apa. thera 1.11.29-35):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, gacchantaṃ anilañjase;

Ghatāsanaṃva jalitaṃ, ādittaṃva hutāsanaṃ.

“The Perfectly Enlightened One, golden-hued, going through the path of the wind; blazing like a ghee-fed fire, like an ignited flame.

“Pāṇinā udakaṃ gayha, ākāse ukkhipiṃ ahaṃ;

Sampaṭicchi mahāvīro, buddho kāruṇiko isi.

“Taking water in my hand, I tossed it up into the sky; the Great Hero, the compassionate Buddha, the Sage, accepted it.

“Antalikkhe ṭhito satthā, padumuttaranāmako;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“The Teacher named Padumuttara, standing in the sky, knowing my aspiration, spoke these verses:

“Iminā dakadānena, pītiuppādanena ca;

Kappasatasahassampi, duggatiṃ nupapajjati.

“By this gift of water and the arising of joy, for a hundred thousand aeons, one is not reborn in a woeful state.

“Tena kammena dvipadinda, lokajeṭṭha narāsabha;

Pattomhi acalaṃ ṭhānaṃ, hitvā jayaparājayaṃ.

“By that deed, O Chief of Bipeds, Foremost in the World, Bull Among Men, I have attained the unshakeable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.

“Sahassarājanāmena, tayo te cakkavattino;

Pañcasaṭṭhikappasate, cāturantā janādhipā.

“By the name of Sahassarāja, there were three wheel-turning monarchs; in sixty-five hundred aeons, they were lords of the four quarters, rulers of men.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… and so on… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā there tattha nisinne khettapālako āgantvā “ko kuṭikāya”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā thero “bhikkhu kuṭikāya”ntiādimāha. Tayidaṃ khettapālassa therassa ca vacanaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā –

After he had attained arahantship, while the elder was sitting there, the field-guard came and asked, “Who is in the hut?” Hearing that, the elder replied, “A monk is in the hut,” and so on. Combining the words of the field-guard and the elder:

56.

56.

“Ko [V 1.0138] kuṭikāyaṃ bhikkhu kuṭikāyaṃ, vītarāgo susamāhitacitto;

Evaṃ jānāhi āvuso, amoghā te kuṭikā katā”ti. –

“Who is in the hut? A monk is in the hut, free from passion, with a well-composed mind. Know this, friend: your hut has not been made in vain.”

Tathārūpena saṅgītiṃ āropitaṃ.

In such a form it was included in the recitation.

Tattha ko kuṭikāyanti, “imissaṃ kuṭikāyaṃ ko nisinno”ti khettapālassa pucchāvacanaṃ. Tassa bhikkhu kuṭikāyanti therassa paṭivacanadānaṃ. Atha naṃ attano anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvato taṃ kuṭiparibhogaṃ anumodāpetvā [M 1.0163] uḷāraṃ tameva puññaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ “vītarāgo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – eko bhinnakileso bhikkhu te kuṭikāyaṃ nisinno, tato eva so aggamaggena sabbaso samucchinnarāgatāya vītarāgo anuttarasamādhinā nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā suṭṭhu samāhitacittatāya susamāhitacitto, imañca atthaṃ, āvuso khettapāla, yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evaṃ jānāhi saddaha adhimuccassu. Amoghā [P 1.0139] te kuṭikā katā tayā katā kuṭikā amoghā avañjhā saphalā saudrayā, yasmā arahatā khīṇāsavena paribhuttā. Sace tvaṃ anumodasi, taṃ te bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyāti.

Here, “Who is in the hut?” is the field-guard’s question, meaning, “Who is seated in this hut?” To that, “A monk is in the hut” is the elder’s reply. Then, in order to have him rejoice in the use of that hut, due to his own supreme worthiness for offerings, and to establish that very sublime merit, the words “one free from passion,” etc., were spoken. Its meaning is this: A monk, one whose defilements are broken, is seated in your hut. Therefore, because he has utterly cut off passion by the supreme path, he is one free from passion. Having made Nibbāna his object by means of supreme concentration, his mind is well-composed due to being perfectly concentrated. And this meaning, friend field-guard, as I say, so should you know it, have faith, and be resolved. The hut you made is not in vain. The hut made by you is not in vain, not barren, but fruitful and productive, because it has been used by an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. If you rejoice in it, that will be for your long-lasting welfare and happiness.

Taṃ sutvā khettapālo “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, yassa me kuṭikāyaṃ ediso ayyo pavisitvā nisīdatī”ti pasannacitto anumodanto aṭṭhāsi. Imaṃ pana tesaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā sutvā anumodanañcassa ñatvā tambhāviniṃ sampattiṃ vibhāvento khettapālaṃ imāhi gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi –

Hearing that, the field-guard, with a confident mind, stood rejoicing, thinking, “Truly, it is my gain, my great good fortune, that such a noble one has entered and sat in my hut!” The Blessed One, however, hearing their conversation with his divine ear-element, and knowing his rejoicing, revealing his future prosperity, addressed the field-guard with these verses:

“Vihāsi kuṭiyaṃ bhikkhu, santacitto anāsavo;

Tena kammavipākena, devindo tvaṃ bhavissasi.

“A monk dwelt in the hut, with a peaceful mind, taintless. By the result of that kamma, you will become king of the devas.

“Chattiṃsakkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjaṃ karissasi;

Catuttiṃsakkhattuṃ cakkavattī, rājā raṭṭhe bhavissasi;

“Thirty-six times you will be king of the devas, ruling the divine kingdom; thirty-four times you will be a wheel-turning monarch, a king in the realm;

Ratanakuṭi nāma paccekabuddho, vītarāgo bhavissasī”ti.

You will become a Paccekabuddha named Ratanakuṭi, one free from passion.”

Kuṭikāyaṃ laddhavisesattā pana therassa tato pabhuti kuṭivihārītveva samaññā udapādi. Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthāpi ahosīti.

However, because the elder attained a special attainment by means of the hut, from then on the designation “Kuṭivihārī,” the hut-dweller, arose for him. And this itself was also the verse of the elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Kuṭivihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kuṭivihārī is concluded.

7. Dutiyakuṭivihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dutiyakuṭivihārī

Ayamāhu [M 1.0164][V 1.0139] purāṇiyāti āyasmato kuṭivihārittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato pasannamānaso pariḷāhakāle naḷavilīvehi viracitaṃ bījaniṃ adāsi. Taṃ satthā anumodanagāthāya sampahaṃsesi. Sesaṃ yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ añjanavaniyattheravatthumhi vuttasadisameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – ayaṃ kira vuttanayena pabbajitvā aññatarāya purāṇakuṭikāya viharanto samaṇadhammaṃ acintetvā, “ayaṃ kuṭikā jiṇṇā, aññaṃ kuṭikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti navakammavasena cittaṃ uppādesi. Tassa atthakāmā devatā saṃvegajananatthaṃ imaṃ uttānobhāsaṃ gambhīratthaṃ “ayamāhu”ti gāthamāha.

This verse, beginning with “Ayamāhu purāṇiyā,” is of the Venerable Elder Kuṭivihārī. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, with a devoted mind, he gave a fan made of reeds during the hot season. The Teacher praised him with a verse of appreciation. The rest that should be said here is similar to what was told in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. But this is the difference: it is said that after going forth in the manner described, while dwelling in a certain old hut, without reflecting on the ascetic’s duties, he thought, “This hut is old; it is fitting to build a new one.” Thus, he aroused the intention for new construction. A deity, wishing for his welfare and in order to stir a sense of urgency, spoke this verse of plain appearance but profound meaning, beginning with “Ayamāhu.”

57. Tattha [P 1.0140] ayanti āsannapaccakkhavacanaṃ. Āhūti ahosīti attho. Gāthāsukhatthañhi dīghaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Purāṇiyāti purātanī addhagatā. Aññaṃ patthayase navaṃ kuṭinti imissā kuṭiyā purāṇabhāvena jiṇṇatāya ito aññaṃ idāni nibbattanīyatāya navaṃ kuṭiṃ patthayase patthesi āsīsasi. Sabbena sabbaṃ pana āsaṃ kuṭiyā virājaya purāṇiyaṃ viya navāyampi kuṭiyaṃ āsaṃ taṇhaṃ apekkhaṃ virājehi, sabbaso tattha virattacitto hohi. Kasmā? Yasmā dukkhā bhikkhu puna navā nāma kuṭi bhikkhu puna idāni nibbattiyamānā dukkhāvahattā dukkhā, tasmā aññaṃ navaṃ dukkhaṃ anuppādento yathānibbattāyaṃ purāṇiyaṃyeva kuṭiyaṃ ṭhatvā attanā katabbaṃ karohīti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – tvaṃ, bhikkhu, “ayaṃ purāṇī tiṇakuṭikā jiṇṇā”ti aññaṃ navaṃ tiṇakuṭikaṃ kātuṃ icchasi, na samaṇadhammaṃ, evaṃ icchanto pana bhāvanāya ananuyuñjanena punabbhavābhinibbattiyā anativattanato āyatiṃ attabhāvakuṭimpi patthento kātuṃ icchantoyeva nāma hoti. Sā pana navā tiṇakuṭi viya karaṇadukkhena tato bhiyyopi jarāmaraṇasokaparidevādidukkhasaṃsaṭṭhatāya dukkhā, tasmā tiṇakuṭiyaṃ viya attabhāvakuṭiyaṃ āsaṃ apekkhaṃ virājaya sabbaso tattha virattacitto hohi, evaṃ te vaṭṭadukkhaṃ na bhavissatīti. Devatāya ca vacanaṃ sutvā thero saṃvegajāto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.36-46) –

57. Here, ayaṃ is a term for what is near and directly perceived. Āhu means “it was” (ahosi). It is spoken with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease. Purāṇiyā means ancient, time-worn. “You desire another new hut” means: because of the oldness and decay of this hut, you desire, you wish for, you long for another hut to be built now. But in every way, become dispassionate towards desire for a hut. Just as for the old one, for the new hut too, become dispassionate towards desire, craving, and expectation; be one whose mind is entirely detached from it. Why? Because, monk, a new hut is suffering. A hut being built now, monk, is suffering because it brings suffering. Therefore, not producing another new suffering, stay in the old hut just as it is and do what is to be done by you. This is the intention here: You, monk, thinking, “This old grass hut is decayed,” wish to build another new grass hut, not the ascetic’s duties. But one who wishes thus, by not applying himself to meditation, does not transcend the arising of renewed existence, and so is in fact one who wishes and desires to build a future hut of personal existence as well. And that new hut, like a grass hut, is suffering through the suffering of its making, and even more so because it is entangled with the suffering of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so on. Therefore, just as for the grass hut, become dispassionate towards desire and expectation for the hut of personal existence; be one whose mind is entirely detached from it. In this way, the suffering of the cycle of rebirth will not exist for you. And having heard the deity’s words, the elder, with a sense of urgency aroused, established insight, and by striving and making an effort, he was soon established in arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttarabuddhassa[M 1.0165], lokajeṭṭhassa tādino;

Tiṇatthare nisinnassa, upasantassa tādino.

“To the Buddha Padumuttara, the foremost in the world, the steadfast one, seated on a spread of grass, the peaceful, steadfast one.

“Naḷamālaṃ gahetvāna, bandhitvā bījaniṃ ahaṃ;

Buddhassa upanāmesiṃ, dvipadindassa tādino.

“Taking a garland of reeds and binding it into a fan, I offered it to the Buddha, the chief of bipeds, the steadfast one.

“Paṭiggahetvā [V 1.0140] sabbaññū, bījaniṃ lokanāyako;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsatha.

“The All-Knowing One, the Guide of the World, having accepted the fan and knowing my intention, spoke this verse:

“Yathā me kāyo nibbāti, pariḷāho na vijjati;

Tatheva tividhaggīhi, cittaṃ tava vimuccatu.

“Just as my body is cooled and the burning fever is no more, so too may your mind be freed from the threefold fires.

“Sabbe devā samāgacchuṃ, ye keci vananissitā;

Sossāma buddhavacanaṃ, hāsayantañca dāyakaṃ.

“All the devas who dwell in the forest gathered, thinking: ‘We shall listen to the Buddha’s word, which delights the donor.’

“Nisinno bhagavā tattha, devasaṅghapurakkhato;

Dāyakaṃ sampahaṃsento, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Seated there, attended by the assembly of devas, the Blessed One, delighting the donor, spoke these verses:

“Iminā bījanidānena, cittassa paṇidhīhi ca;

Subbato nāma nāmena, cakkavattī bhavissati.

“By this gift of a fan and by the aspirations of his mind, he will become a wheel-turning monarch named Subbata.

“Tena kammāvasesena, sukkamūlena codito;

Māluto nāma nāmena, cakkavattī bhavissati.

“By the remainder of that kamma, urged on by its wholesome root, he will become a wheel-turning monarch named Māluta.

“Iminā bījanidānena, sammānavipulena ca;

Kappasatasahassampi, duggatiṃ nupapajjati.

“By this gift of a fan and by abundant reverence, for a hundred thousand eons he will not be reborn in a bad destination.”

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, subbatā aṭṭhatiṃsa te;

Ekūnatiṃsasahasse, aṭṭha mālutanāmakā.

“In the thirty-thousandth eon there were thirty-eight of them named Subbata; in the twenty-nine-thousandth, eight named Māluta.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahatte pana patiṭṭhito “ayaṃ me arahattappattiyā aṅkusabhūtā”ti tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi. Sāyeva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosi. Kuṭiovādena laddhavisesattā cassa kuṭivihārītveva samaññā ahosīti.

But having become established in arahantship, thinking, “This was the goad to my attainment of arahantship,” he recited that very verse. And that very verse became the elder’s verse of the declaration of final knowledge. And because he gained a special attainment through the instruction concerning the hut, the designation ‘Kuṭivihārī’ arose for him.

Dutiyakuṭivihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dutiyakuṭivihārī is concluded.

8. Ramaṇīyakuṭikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika

Ramaṇīyā [M 1.0166][P 1.0141] me kuṭikāti āyasmato ramaṇīyakuṭikattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kusalabījaropanaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito aṭṭhārasakappasatamatthake atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto buddhārahaṃ [V 1.0141] āsanaṃ bhagavato adāsi. Pupphehi ca bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sesaṃ añjanavaniyattherassa vatthumhi vuttasadisameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso – ayaṃ kira vuttanayena pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vajjiraṭṭhe aññatarasmiṃ gāmakāvāse kuṭikāyaṃ viharati, sā hoti kuṭikā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā suparikammakatabhittibhūmikā ārāmapokkharaṇirāmaṇeyyādisampannā muttājālasadisavālikākiṇṇabhūmibhāgā therassa ca vattasampannatāya susammaṭṭhaṅgaṇatādinā bhiyyosomattāya ramaṇīyatarā hutvā tiṭṭhati. So tattha viharanto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.47-52) –

“Delightful is my hut”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika. What is their origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he planted wholesome seeds and, wandering among gods and humans, was reborn into a family home in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, at the end of eighteen hundred aeons from here. Having reached maturity, he offered the Blessed One a seat worthy of a Buddha. He honored the Blessed One with flowers, paid homage with a fivefold prostration, circumambulated him, and departed. The rest is similar to what was stated in the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. This, however, is the distinction: having gone forth in the manner described and fulfilled his prior duties, he dwelled in a hut in a certain village dwelling in the Vajjī country. That hut was beautiful, pleasing to the eye, delightful, with well-prepared walls and floors, endowed with the loveliness of a park and a pond, its ground scattered with sand like a net of pearls.
