And because of the Elder’s accomplished conduct, with its well-swept courtyard and so on, it became even more exceedingly delightful and remained so. Dwelling there, he established insight and soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera, 1.11.47–52):

“Kānanaṃ vanamoggayha, appasaddaṃ nirākulaṃ;

Sīhāsanaṃ mayā dinnaṃ, atthadassissa tādino.

“Having entered a forest grove, silent and undisturbed, I gave a lion-seat to Atthadassī, the Such One.”

“Mālāhatthaṃ gahetvāna, katvā ca naṃ padakkhiṇaṃ;

Satthāraṃ payirupāsitvā, pakkāmiṃ uttarāmukho.

“Holding a garland in my hand, and having circumambulated him, I attended upon the Teacher, and departed facing north.”

“Tena kammena dvipadinda, lokajeṭṭha narāsabha;

Sannibbāpemi attānaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā.

“By that deed, O Lord of bipeds, foremost in the world, noblest of men, I have extinguished myself; all states of being are uprooted.”

“Aṭṭhārasakappasate, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, sīhāsanassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Eighteen hundred aeons ago, I gave that gift; I do not recall an unhappy destination; this is the fruit of the lion-seat.”

“Ito sattakappasate, sannibbāpakakhattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Seven hundred aeons from here, there will be a warrior king named Sannibbāpaka, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā there tattha viharante kuṭikāya ramaṇīyabhāvato vihārapekkhakā manussā tato tato āgantvā kuṭiṃ passanti[M 1.0167]. Athekadivasaṃ katipayā dhuttajātikā itthiyo tattha gatā kuṭikāya ramaṇīyabhāvaṃ disvā, “ettha vasanto ayaṃ samaṇo siyā amhehi ākaḍḍhanīyahadayo”ti adhippāyena – “ramaṇīyaṃ vo, bhante, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Mayampi ramaṇīyarūpā paṭhamayobbane ṭhitā”ti vatvā itthikuttādīni dassetuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Thero attano vītarāgabhāvaṃ pakāsento “ramaṇīyā me kuṭikā, saddhādeyyā manoramā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

However, after the Elder had attained arahantship and was dwelling there, people who came to see the dwelling came from various places to see the hut because of its delightful nature. Then one day, some women of a wanton nature went there and, seeing the delightful nature of the hut, thought, “This ascetic dwelling here might be one whose heart we can attract.” With this intention, they said, “Venerable sir, your dwelling place is delightful. We too are of delightful form, standing in the prime of our youth,” and began to display feminine wiles and so on. The Elder, revealing his state of being free from lust, spoke this verse: “Delightful is my hut, a gift of faith, delightful to the mind.”

58. Tattha ramaṇīyā me kuṭikāti “ramaṇīyā te, bhante, kuṭikā”ti yaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ, taṃ saccaṃ. Ayaṃ mama vasanakuṭikā ramaṇīyā manuññarūpā, sā ca kho saddhādeyyā, “evarūpāya [V 1.0142] manāpaṃ [P 1.0142] katvā pabbajitānaṃ dinnāya idaṃ nāma phalaṃ hotī”ti kammaphalāni saddahitvā saddhāya dhammacchandena dātabbattā saddhādeyyā, na dhanena nibbattitā. Sayañca tathādinnāni saddhādeyyāni passantānaṃ paribhuñjantānañca mano rametīti manoramā. Saddhādeyyattā eva hi manoramā, saddhādīhi deyyadhammaṃ sakkaccaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā denti, saddhādeyyañca paribhuñjantā sappurisā dāyakassa avisaṃvādanatthampi payogāsayasampannā honti, na tumhehi cintitākārena payogāsayavipannāti adhippāyo. Na me attho kumārīhīti yasmā sabbaso kāmehi vinivattitamānaso ahaṃ, tasmā na me attho kumārīhi. Kappiyakārakakammavasenapi hi mādisānaṃ itthīhi payojanaṃ nāma natthi, pageva rāgavasena, tasmā na me attho kumārīhīti. Kumāriggahaṇañcettha upalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mādisassa nāma santike evaṃ paṭipajjāhīti ayuttakārinīhi yāva aparaddhañca tumhehi samānajjhāsayānaṃ purato ayaṃ kiriyā sobheyyāti dassento āha “yesaṃ attho tahiṃ gacchatha nāriyo”ti. Tattha yesanti kāmesu avītarāgānaṃ. Atthoti payojanaṃ. Tahinti tattha tesaṃ santikaṃ. Nāriyoti ālapanaṃ. Taṃ sutvā itthiyo maṅkubhūtā pattakkhandhā āgatamaggeneva gatā. Ettha ca “na me attho kumārīhī”ti kāmehi anatthikabhāvavacaneneva therena arahattaṃ byākatanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

58. Here, as for “Delightful is my hut”—that which you said, “Venerable sir, your hut is delightful,” is true. This dwelling hut of mine is delightful and pleasing in appearance. And it is indeed a gift of faith, given out of faith and a desire for the Dhamma, with belief in the results of kamma, thinking, “Having made such a pleasing offering to those who have gone forth, such and such a fruit will accrue.” It was not produced by wealth. And for those who see and partake of such gifts of faith, it delights the mind—thus it is “delightful to the mind” (manoramā). Indeed, it is delightful to the mind precisely because it is a gift of faith. For noble persons, when they partake of a gift of faith—which donors carefully prepare and give with faith and other qualities—they are possessed of appropriate application so as to not disappoint the donor; this is the meaning, not that their efforts and intentions are misguided as you might think. As for “I have no need for maidens”—since my mind is entirely turned away from sensual pleasures, therefore I have no need for maidens. Indeed, for one like me, there is no use for women even in terms of attending to duties, let alone out of lust; therefore, I have no need for maidens. Here, the mention of maidens should be understood as illustrative. For one like me, it is improper to behave thus. Showing that such actions would only be fitting before those of similar disposition to yourselves, even to the point of offense, he says, “Those who have need, go to them, women.” Here, “those” refers to those not rid of lust for sensual pleasures. “Need” means purpose. “There” means to their presence. “Women” is an address. Hearing this, the women, crestfallen and with slumped shoulders, returned the way they came. And here, it should be understood that by declaring, “I have no need for maidens,” the Elder revealed his arahantship through his disinterest in sensual pleasures.

Ramaṇīyakuṭikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyakuṭika is concluded.

9. Kosalavihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kosalavihārī

Saddhāyāhaṃ [M 1.0168] pabbajitoti āyasmato kosalavihārittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kusalabījaṃ ropetvā taṃ taṃ puññaṃ akāsi. Sesaṃ añjanavaniyattheravatthusadisameva. Ayaṃ [P 1.0143] pana viseso – ayaṃ kira vuttanayena pabbajitvā katapubbakicco kosalaraṭṭhe aññatarasmiṃ gāme ekaṃ upāsakakulaṃ nissāya araññe viharati, taṃ so upāsako rukkhamūle vasantaṃ disvā kuṭikaṃ kāretvā adāsi. Thero kuṭikāyaṃ viharanto āvāsasappāyena samādhānaṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.53-61) –

“Out of faith I went forth” is a verse of the Venerable Elder Kosalavihārī. What is its origin? It is said that he too, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, planted a seed of merit and performed various meritorious deeds. The rest is similar to the story of the Elder Añjanavaniya. Here, however, is the distinction: Having gone forth in the manner described above and completed his prior duties, this elder dwelt in a forest in the Kosala country, relying on a certain lay follower’s family in a village. That lay follower, seeing him dwelling at the foot of a tree, had a small hut built and gave it to him. The Elder, dwelling in the hut, obtained concentration through the suitability of his dwelling, cultivated insight, and before long attained arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.11.53–61):

“Himavantassāvidūre, vasāmi paṇṇasanthare;

Ghāsesu gedhamāpanno, seyyasīlo cahaṃ tadā.

“Not far from the Himālaya, I dwelt on a bed of leaves; addicted to food, and then I was of inferior virtue.”

“Khaṇantālukalambāni[V 1.0143], biḷālitakkalāni ca;

Kolaṃ bhallātakaṃ billaṃ, āhatvā paṭiyāditaṃ.

“Digging for tubers and stalks, and gathering biḷāli and takkala; Kola, bhallātaka, and billa—having gathered them, I prepared them.”

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, āgacchi mama santikaṃ.

“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, knowing my intention, came into my presence.”

“Upāgataṃ mahānāgaṃ, devadevaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Biḷāliṃ paggahetvāna, pattamhi okiriṃ ahaṃ.

“When the Great Nāga, the God of Gods, the Bull Among Men arrived, I took up a biḷāli and poured it into his bowl.”

“Paribhuñji mahāvīro, tosayanto mamaṃ tadā;

Paribhuñjitvāna sabbaññū, imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsatha.

“The Great Hero partook, pleasing me then; having partaken, the All-Knowing One spoke this verse:”

“Sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā, biḷāliṃ me adā tuvaṃ;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjasi.

“Having pleased your own mind, you gave me a biḷāli; for a hundred thousand eons, you will not be reborn in a bad state.”

“Carimaṃ vattate mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

“This is my last existence, all states of being are uprooted; I bear this final body in the dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

“Catupaññāsito kappe, sumekhaliya savhayo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In the fifty-fourth eon from here, he will be named Sumekhaliya; endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning monarch.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0169] pana patvā vimuttisukhappaṭisaṃvedanena uppannapītivegena udānento “saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

However, having attained arahantship, he uttered this verse as an inspired utterance, impelled by the force of joy that arose from experiencing the bliss of liberation: “Through faith, I went forth.”

59. Tattha saddhāyāti bhagavato vesāliṃ upagamane ānubhāvaṃ disvā, “ekantaniyyānikaṃ idaṃ sāsanaṃ, tasmā addhā imāya paṭipattiyā jarāmaraṇato muccissāmī”ti uppannasaddhāvasena pabbajito pabbajjaṃ upagato. Araññe me kuṭikā katāti tassā pabbajjāya anurūpavasena araññe vasato me kuṭikā katā, pabbajjānurūpaṃ āraññako hutvā vūpakaṭṭho viharāmīti dasseti. Tenāha “appamatto ca ātāpī, sampajāno patissato”ti. Araññavāsaladdhena kāyavivekena jāgariyaṃ anuyuñjanto tattha satiyā avippavāsena appamatto, āraddhavīriyatāya ātāpī, pubbabhāgiyasatisampajaññapāripūriyā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattādhigamena paññāsativepullappattiyā accantameva sampajāno patissato viharāmīti attho. Appamattabhāvādikittane cassa idameva aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi kosalaraṭṭhe ciranivāsibhāvena pana kosalavihārīti samaññā jātāti.

59. There, “out of faith” means that, upon seeing the majesty of the Blessed One as he approached Vesālī, he thought, “This teaching leads solely to liberation; surely, by following this path, I will be freed from aging and death.” Thus, moved by the faith that arose, he went forth and embraced the monastic life. “A hut was built for me in the wilderness” indicates that, in accordance with his going forth, a hut was built for him in the wilderness, showing that he lived in seclusion suited to his going forth. Hence it is said, “diligent, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.” By means of the solitude of the body obtained through wilderness dwelling, he devoted himself to wakefulness, remaining there undistracted in mindfulness—diligent through unwavering effort, ardent through sustained energy, and, through the perfection of preliminary mindfulness and clear comprehension, developing insight until, through the attainment of arahantship, he attained great fullness of wisdom and mindfulness. Thus, he dwelt as one fully comprehending and ever mindful. The declaration of his diligence and other qualities served as his own announcement of enlightenment. Due to his long residence in the Kosala country, he became known as “the Kosalan dweller.”

Kosalavihārittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kosalavihārī is concluded.

10. Sīvalittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary to the Verses of the Elder Sīvali

Te [V 1.0144][P 1.0144] me ijjhiṃsu saṅkappāti āyasmato sīvalittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle heṭṭhā vuttanayena vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ lābhīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “mayāpi anāgate evarūpena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dasabalaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ satthu bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahādānaṃ datvā “bhagavā ahaṃ iminā adhikārakammena aññaṃ sampattiṃ na patthemi, anāgate pana ekabuddhassa sāsane ahampi tumhehi so etadagge ṭhapitabhikkhu viya lābhīnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā anantarāyaṃ disvā – “ayaṃ te patthanā anāgate gotamabuddhassa santike samijjhissatī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi. Sopi [M 1.0170] kulaputto yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto vipassībuddhakāle bandhumatīnagarato avidūre ekasmiṃ gāmake paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tasmiṃ samaye bandhumatīnagaravāsino raññā saddhiṃ sākacchitvā dasabalassa dānaṃ denti. Te ekadivasaṃ sabbeva ekato hutvā dānaṃ dentā “kiṃ nu kho amhākaṃ dānamukhe natthī”ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.207) madhuñca guḷadadhiñca na addasaṃsu. Te “yato kutoci āharissāmā”ti janapadato nagarapavisanamagge purisaṃ ṭhapesuṃ. Tadā esa kulaputto attano gāmato guḷadadhivārakaṃ gahetvā, “kiñcideva āharissāmī”ti nagaraṃ gacchanto, “mukhaṃ dhovitvā dhotahatthapādo pavisissāmī”ti phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ olokento naṅgalasīsamattaṃ nimmakkhikaṃ daṇḍakamadhuṃ disvā “puññena me idaṃ uppanna”nti gahetvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Nāgarehi ṭhapitapuriso taṃ disvā, “bho purisa, kassimaṃ āharasī”ti pucchi. “Na kassaci, sāmi, vikkiṇituṃ pana me idaṃ ābhata”nti. “Tena [P 1.0145] hi, bho, idaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gahetvā etaṃ madhuñca guḷadadhiñca dehī”ti. So cintesi – “idaṃ na bahumūlaṃ, ayañca ekappahāreneva bahuṃ deti, vīmaṃsituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato naṃ “nāhaṃ ekena kahāpaṇena demī”ti āha. “Yadi evaṃ dve gahetvā dehī”ti. “Dvīhipi na demī”ti. Etenupāyena vaḍḍhetvā sahassaṃ pāpuṇi.

“These wishes of mine were fulfilled,” so said the verse of the Venerable Sīvali Thera. What is the origin? In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he too, following the previously mentioned manner, went to the monastery, stood at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, and saw the Teacher appointing one monk as the foremost among those who receive offerings. Thinking, “It is fitting for me too to become like that in the future,” he invited the Ten-Powered One and for seven days gave a great offering to the Teacher and the community of monks. Then he made this aspiration: “Venerable One, I do not seek any other attainment through this meritorious deed, but in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I too become the foremost among those who receive offerings, just like that monk you appointed to that foremost position.” The Teacher, seeing no obstacles, declared, “This aspiration of yours will succeed in the future in the presence of the Buddha Gotama,” and then departed. That clansman, having done good deeds throughout his life, wandered among gods and humans until, in the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he was reborn in a village not far from the city of Bandhumatī. At that time, the citizens of Bandhumatī, after conversing with the king, were giving offerings to the Ten-Powered One. One day, as they all gathered to give alms, they thought, “What is lacking in our offering?” and realized they lacked honey, and molasses and curd. They decided, “We must fetch some from somewhere,” and stationed a man on the road leading into the city from the countryside. At that time, this clansman, carrying a pot of molasses and curd from his village, thought, “I will bring something,” and as he approached the city, he considered, “I should wash my face and hands before entering.” While looking for a suitable spot, he saw a honeycomb on a branch as big as a plowshare, free from flies. Thinking, “This has appeared due to my merit,” he took it and entered the city. The man stationed by the city saw him and asked, “Sir, for whom are you bringing this?” “For no one, lord, but I have brought this to sell.” “Then, good sir, take this kahapana and give me this honey, and the molasses and curd.” The clansman thought, “This is not of great value, yet he offers much at once—it is worth testing.” So he said, “I will not give it for one kahapana.” “Then take two and give it.” “I will not give it even for two.” By this method, the price increased until it reached a thousand.

So cintesi – “ativaḍḍhituṃ na vaṭṭati, hotu tāva iminā kattabbakiccaṃ pucchissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ āha – “idaṃ na bahuṃ agghanakaṃ, tvañca bahuṃ desi, kena kammena idaṃ gaṇhāsī”ti. “Idha, bho, nagaravāsino raññā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhitvā vipassīdasabalassa dānaṃ dentā idaṃ dvayaṃ dānamukhe apassantā pariyesanti, sace idaṃ dvayaṃ na labhissanti, nāgarānaṃ parājayo bhavissati, tasmā sahassaṃ katvā gaṇhāmī”ti. “Kiṃ panetaṃ nāgarānameva vaṭṭati, aññesaṃ dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. “Yassa kassaci dātuṃ avāritameta”nti. “Atthi pana koci nāgarānaṃ dāne ekadivasaṃ sahassaṃ dātā”ti? “Natthi, sammā”ti. “Imesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ sahassagghanakabhāvaṃ [V 1.0145] jānāsī”ti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. “Tena hi gaccha, nāgarānaṃ ācikkha ‘eko puriso imāni dve mūlena na deti sahattheneva dātukāmo, tumhe imesaṃ dvinnaṃ kāraṇā [M 1.0171] nibbitakkā hothā’ti, tvaṃ pana me imasmiṃ dānamukhe jeṭṭhakabhāvassa kāyasakkhī hohī”ti. So paribbayatthaṃ gahitamāsakena pañcakaṭukaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0146] cuṇṇaṃ katvā dadhito kañjiyaṃ gahetvā tattha madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷetvā pañcakaṭukacuṇṇena yojetvā ekasmiṃ paduminipatte pakkhipitvā taṃ saṃvidahitvā ādāya dasabalassa avidūraṭṭhāne nisīdi mahājanena āhariyamānassa sakkārassa avidūre attano pattavāraṃ olokayamāno, so okāsaṃ ñatvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā bhagavā ayaṃ uppannaduggatapaṇṇākāro, imaṃ me anukampaṃ paṭicca paṭiggaṇhathāti. Satthā tassa anukampaṃ paṭicca catumahārājadattiyena selamayapattena taṃ paṭiggahetvā yathā aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyā bhikkhusatasahassassa diyyamānaṃ na khīyati, evaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. So kulaputto niṭṭhitabhattakiccaṃ bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito āha – “diṭṭho me, bhagavā, ajja bandhumatīnagaravāsikehi tumhākaṃ sakkāro āhariyamāno, ahampi imassa kammassa nissandena nibbattanibbattabhave lābhaggayasaggappatto bhaveyya”nti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.207). Satthā, “evaṃ hotu, kulaputtā”ti vatvā tassa ca nagaravāsīnañca bhattānumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

He thought, “It is not proper to increase it greatly. Let me first ask what needs to be done with it.” Then he said to him, “This is not of great value, yet you give so much. For what purpose are you acquiring this?” “Here, sir, the city-dwellers, competing with the king, are giving alms to Vipassī, the Ten-Powered One. Not seeing these two items among the offerings, they are searching for them. If they do not obtain these two, the city-dwellers will be defeated. Therefore, I take them for a thousand.” “But is this only suitable for the city-dwellers? Is it not proper to give to others?” “It is unrestricted to give to anyone.” “Is there anyone among the city-dwellers who gives a thousand in a single day for a gift?” “No, sir.” “Do you know the value of these two to be worth a thousand?” “Yes, I know.” “Then go, inform the city-dwellers: ‘One man does not give these two for their price but wishes to give them with his own hand. You, because of these two, should be free from worry.’ But you must be a bodily witness for me as the foremost in this act of giving.” With a māsaka coin he had obtained for his provisions, he took five pungent spices, ground them, and taking curd-gruel, he pressed a honeycomb into it, mixed it with the ground pungent spices, placed it in a single lotus leaf, prepared it, and took it. Sitting not far from the Ten-Powered One, he watched his own turn for the alms bowl from a distance as the great crowd brought offerings. Knowing the opportunity, he approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, this humble offering has arisen; out of compassion for me, please accept this.” Out of compassion for him, the Teacher accepted it with the stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings. He resolved that it would not diminish even if given to sixty-eight hundred thousand monks. That clansman, having completed the meal, paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side, saying, “Venerable sir, today I saw the city-dwellers of Bandhumatī bringing offerings to you. May I, too, through the result of this deed, attain the foremost position in gains and fame in life after life.” The Teacher said, “So be it, clansman,” and after giving a blessing of thanks for the meal to him and the city-dwellers, he departed.

Sopi kulaputto yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde suppavāsāya rājadhītāya kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Paṭisandhiggahaṇato paṭṭhāya sāyaṃ pātañca paṇṇākārasatāni sakaṭenādāya suppavāsāya upanīyanti. Atha naṃ puññavīmaṃsanatthaṃ hatthena bījapacchiṃ phusāpenti. Ekekabījato salākasatampi salākasahassampi niggacchati. Ekekakarīsakhette paṇṇāsampi saṭṭhipi sakaṭappamāṇāni uppajjanti. Koṭṭhe pūraṇakālepi koṭṭhadvāraṃ hatthena phusāpenti. Rājadhītāya puññena gaṇhantānaṃ gahitagahitaṭṭhānaṃ puna pūrati. Paripuṇṇabhattabhājanatopi “rājadhītāya puñña”nti vatvā yassa kassaci dentānaṃ yāva na ukkaḍḍhanti, na tāva bhattaṃ khīyati, dārake [P 1.0147] kucchigateyeva sattavassāni atikkamiṃsu.

That clansman, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha's dispensation, took rebirth in the womb of Suppavāsā, the king's daughter. From the moment of conception, every morning and evening, hundreds of tributes were brought to Suppavāsā by cart. Then, to examine her merit, they had her touch a seed basket with her hand. From each single seed, a hundred or even a thousand sprouts would emerge. In each karīsa of field, fifty or sixty cartloads of produce would arise. Even when filling the storehouse, they had her touch the storehouse door with her hand. By the merit of the king's daughter, the places from which they took would refill. Even from a full food bowl, saying, "This is by the merit of the king's daughter," when giving to anyone, the food would not diminish until they stopped taking from it. While the child was in the womb, seven years passed.

Gabbhe [M 1.0172] pana paripakke sattāhaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhosi. Sā sāmikaṃ āmantetvā, “pure maraṇā jīvamānāva dānaṃ dassāmī”ti satthu santikaṃ pesesi – “gaccha, imaṃ pavattiṃ satthu ārocetvā satthāraṃ nimantehi, yañca satthā vadeti, taṃ sādhukaṃ upalakkhetvā āgantvā mayhaṃ kathehī”ti. So gantvā tassā sāsanaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Satthā, “sukhinī hotu suppavāsā koliyadhītā arogā, arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti (udā. 18) āha. Rājā taṃ sutvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā attano gāmābhimukho pāyāsi. Tassa pure āgamanāyeva suppavāsāya kucchito [V 1.0146] dhamakaraṇā udakaṃ viya gabbho nikkhami, parivāretvā nisinnajano assumukhova hasituṃ āraddho tuṭṭhapahaṭṭho mahājano rañño sāsanaṃ ārocetuṃ agamāsi.

Then, when the fetus was fully developed, she endured great suffering for seven days. She called her husband and said, "Before I die, while still alive, I wish to give alms." She sent him to the Teacher with the message: "Go, inform the Teacher of this matter and invite the Teacher. Whatever the Teacher says, note it carefully, return, and tell me." He went and conveyed her message to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "May Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, be happy and free from disease; may she give birth to a healthy child." Hearing this, the king paid homage to the Blessed One and set out toward his village. Even before his arrival, the child came forth from Suppavāsā's womb like water from a water-strainer. The people gathered around her, their faces wet with tears, began to laugh joyfully. Greatly delighted, a large crowd went to inform the king of the news.

Rājā tesaṃ āgamanaṃ disvāva, “dasabalena kathitakathā nipphannā bhavissati maññe”ti cintesi. So āgantvā satthu sāsanaṃ rājadhītāya ārocesi. Rājadhītā tayā nimantitaṃ jīvitabhattameva maṅgalabhattaṃ bhavissati, gaccha sattāhaṃ dasabalaṃ nimantehīti. Rājā tathā akāsi. Sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃsu. Dārako sabbesaṃ ñātīnaṃ santattaṃ cittaṃ nibbāpento jātoti sīvalidārakotvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So sattavassāni gabbhe vasitattā jātakālato paṭṭhāya sabbakammakkhamo ahosi. Dhammasenāpati sāriputto sattame divase tena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpaṃ akāsi. Satthāpi dhammapade gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The king, seeing their arrival, thought, "I believe the words spoken by the Ten-Powered One will be fulfilled." He went and announced the Teacher's message to the princess. The princess said, "The meal for my life for which you invited him will now be an auspicious meal. Go, invite the Ten-Powered One for seven days." The king did so. For seven days, they provided a great alms-giving to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Because the child was born cooling the heated minds of all his relatives, they gave him the name Sīvalidāraka. Having stayed in the womb for seven years, from the time of his birth he was capable of all tasks. On the seventh day, the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, engaged in conversation with him. The Teacher also spoke a verse from the Dhammapada:

“Yomaṃ palipathaṃ duggaṃ, saṃsāraṃ mohamaccagā;

Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato jhāyī, anejo akathaṃkathī;

Anupādāya nibbuto, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 414);

“He who has overcome this miry path, this difficult saṃsāra and delusion; who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, is meditative, free from agitation, and without doubt; who, without clinging, is extinguished—him I call a brahmin.”

Atha naṃ thero evamāha – “kiṃ pana tayā evarūpaṃ dukkharāsiṃ anubhavitvā pabbajituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? “Labhamāno pabbajeyyaṃ, bhante”ti. Suppavāsā naṃ dārakaṃ therena [P 1.0148] saddhiṃ kathentaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho me putto dhammasenāpatinā saddhiṃ kathetī”ti theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “mayhaṃ putto tumhehi saddhiṃ kiṃ katheti, bhante”ti? “Attanā anubhūtaṃ gabbhavāsadukkhaṃ kathetvā, ‘tumhehi anuññāto pabbajissāmī’ti vadatī”ti. “Sādhu[M 1.0173], bhante, pabbājetha na”nti. Thero taṃ vihāraṃ netvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā pabbājento “sīvali, na tuyhaṃ aññena ovādena kammaṃ atthi, tayā satta vassāni anubhūtadukkhameva paccavekkhāhī”ti. “Bhante, pabbājanameva tumhākaṃ bhāro, yaṃ pana mayā kātuṃ sakkā, tamahaṃ jānissāmī”ti. So pana paṭhamakesavaṭṭiyā ohāraṇakkhaṇeyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, dutiyāya ohāraṇakkhaṇe sakadāgāmiphale, tatiyāya anāgāmiphale sabbesaṃyeva pana kesānaṃ oropanañca arahattasacchikiriyā ca apacchā apurimā ahosi. Tassa pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhusaṅghassa cattāro paccayā yāvaticchakaṃ uppajjanti. Evaṃ ettha vatthu samuṭṭhitaṃ.

Then the elder said to him, "After experiencing such a mass of suffering, is it not proper for you to go forth?" "If I may, venerable sir, I would go forth." Suppavāsā, seeing her son conversing with the elder, thought, "What is my son discussing with the General of the Dhamma?" She approached the elder and asked, "Venerable sir, what is my son discussing with you?" "He is recounting the suffering of dwelling in the womb that he himself experienced and says, ‘If permitted by you, I will go forth.’" "Good, venerable sir, please ordain him." The elder took him to the monastery, gave him the meditation subject on the five parts of the body ending with skin, and while ordaining him said, "Sīvali, you have no need for other instruction. You should reflect only on the suffering you have experienced for seven years." "Venerable sir, ordaining me is your responsibility. As for what I am able to do, that I myself will know." Then, at the very moment the first lock of hair was removed, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry; at the moment the second was removed, in the fruit of once-returning; at the third, in the fruit of non-returning. The removal of all his hair and the realization of arahantship occurred simultaneously. From the day of his ordination onward, the four requisites arose for the community of monks to the extent desired. Thus the story arose in this context.

Aparabhāge satthā sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Thero satthāraṃ abhivādetvā, “bhante, mayhaṃ puññaṃ vīmaṃsissāmi, pañca me bhikkhusatāni dethā”ti āha. “Gaṇha sīvalī”ti. So pañcasate bhikkhū [V 1.0147] gahetvā himavantābhimukhaṃ gacchanto aṭavimaggaṃ gacchati, tassa paṭhamaṃ diṭṭhanigrodhe adhivatthā devatā sattadivasāni dānaṃ adāsi. Iti so –

Later, the Teacher went to Sāvatthī. The Elder, having paid homage to the Teacher, said, "Venerable Sir, I will test my merit; please give me five hundred monks." "Take them, Sīvalī." Taking five hundred monks, he set out toward the Himalayas, traveling along a forest path. A deity dwelling in the first banyan tree he saw gave alms for seven days. Thus he—

“Nigrodhaṃ paṭhamaṃ passi, dutiyaṃ paṇḍavapabbataṃ;

Tatiyaṃ aciravatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ varasāgaraṃ.

“First, he saw the Nigrodha, second, the Paṇḍava mountain; third, the Aciravatī river, fourth, the great ocean.

“Pañcamaṃ himavantaṃ so, chaṭṭhaṃ chaddantupāgami;

Sattamaṃ gandhamādanaṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ atha revata”nti.

“Fifth, he went to the Himavanta, sixth, he approached Chaddanta; seventh, Gandhamādana, and eighth, then, Revata.”

Sabbaṭṭhānesu satta satta divasāneva dānaṃ adaṃsu. Gandhamādanapabbate pana nāgadattadevarājā nāma sattasu divasesu ekadivase khīrapiṇḍapātaṃ adāsi, ekadivase sappipiṇḍapātaṃ. Bhikkhusaṅgho āha – “imassa devarañño neva dhenuyo duyhamānā paññāyanti, na dadhinimmathanaṃ[P 1.0149], kuto te devarāja idaṃ uppajjatī”ti. “Bhante kassapadasabalassa kāle khīrasalākabhattadānassetaṃ phala”nti devarājā āha. Aparabhāge satthā khadiravaniyarevatassa paccuggamanaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā theraṃ attano sāsane lābhaggayasaggappattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

In all these places, they gave alms for seven days each. On Gandhamādana mountain, the divine king named Nāgadatta gave an alms-meal of milk-rice on one of the seven days, and an alms-meal of ghee on another. The community of monks asked, "For this divine king, neither cows being milked nor the churning of curds is apparent—so from where does this arise for you, O divine king?" The divine king replied, "Venerable sirs, this is the fruit of offering ticket-food with milk-rice during the time of Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One." Later, the Teacher, having made the occasion of Revata of the Khadira Forest coming to meet him the origin of a story, placed the Elder in the foremost position among those in his dispensation who had attained the highest gain and renown.

Evaṃ lābhaggayasaggappattassa pana imassa therassa arahattappattiṃ ekacce ācariyā evaṃ vadanti – “heṭṭhā vuttanayena dhammasenāpatinā ovāde dinne yaṃ [M 1.0174] mayā kātuṃ sakkā, tamahaṃ jānissāmīti pabbajitvā vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā taṃ divasaṃyeva aññataraṃ vivittaṃ kuṭikaṃ disvā taṃ pavisitvā mātukucchismiṃ satta vassāni attanā anubhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ anussaritvā tadanusārena atītānāgate tassa avekkhantassa ādittā viya tayo bhavā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā vipassanāvīthiṃ otari, tāvadeva maggappaṭipāṭiyā sabbepi āsave khepento arahattaṃ pāpuṇī”ti. Ubhayathāpi therassa arahattappattiyeva pakāsitā. Thero pana pabhinnapaṭisambhido chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.31-39) –

Now, regarding the attainment of arahantship by this elder who had reached the highest gain and fame, some teachers say this: "When the General of the Dhamma gave him advice in the manner previously mentioned, he thought, 'I will know what I am capable of doing.' After going forth, he took up the meditation subject of insight. On that very day, seeing a secluded hut, he entered it and recollected the suffering he himself had endured for seven years in his mother’s womb. As he contemplated the past and future in accordance with that recollection, the three realms of existence appeared to him as if ablaze. Because his knowledge had matured, he entered the path of insight and, progressing through the stages of the path, eradicated all the corruptions and attained arahantship." In both accounts, the elder’s attainment of arahantship is made known. The elder possessed the analytical knowledges and the sixfold direct knowledge. Thus it was said by him in the Apadāna:

“Varuṇo nāma nāmena, devarājā ahaṃ tadā;

Upaṭṭhahesiṃ sambuddhaṃ, sayoggabalavāhano.

By the name Varuṇa, I was then a king of the devas; I attended upon the Sambuddha, with my vehicles, forces, and mounts.

“Nibbute lokanāthamhi, atthadassīnaruttame;

Tūriyaṃ sabbamādāya, agamaṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

When the Lord of the World, the seer of the true meaning, the foremost of men, had attained Nibbāna, I took all the musical instruments and went to the supreme Bodhi tree.

“Vāditena ca naccena, sammatāḷasamāhito;

Sammukhā viya sambuddhaṃ, upaṭṭhiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

With music and dance, composed and in rhythmic time, as if in the very presence of the Sambuddha, I attended upon the supreme Bodhi tree.

“Upaṭṭhahitvā [V 1.0148] taṃ bodhiṃ, dharaṇīruhapādapaṃ;

Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāna, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

Having attended to that Bodhi tree, a tree growing from the earth, I sat cross-legged and there I passed away.

“Sakakammābhiraddhohaṃ, pasanno bodhimuttame;

Tena cittappasādena, nimmānaṃ upapajjahaṃ.

Delighting in my own kamma, with serene faith in the supreme Bodhi, through that confidence of mind, I was reborn in the Nimmāna heaven.

“Saṭṭhitūriyasahassāni, parivārenti maṃ sadā;

Manussesu ca devesu, vattamānaṃ bhavābhave.

Sixty thousand musical instruments always surrounded me, as I fared through existence after existence among humans and devas.

“Tividhaggī nibbutā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

My threefold fires are extinguished, all forms of existence are eradicated; I bear this final body in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

“Subāhū nāma nāmena, catuttiṃsāsu khattiyā;

Sattaratanasampannā, pañcakappasate ito.

Five hundred aeons ago, there were thirty-four khattiyas by the name of Subāhu, all endowed with the seven treasures.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0175] pana patvā vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedanena pītivegena udānento “te me ijjhiṃsu saṅkappā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Then, having attained Arahantship, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, with an upsurge of joy he uttered this inspired verse: 'My aspirations have succeeded.'

60. Tattha te me ijjhiṃsu saṅkappā, yadattho pāvisiṃ kuṭiṃ, vijjāvimuttiṃ paccesanti ye pubbe mayā kāmasaṅkappādīnaṃ samucchedakarā nekkhammasaṅkappādayo abhipatthitāyeva “kadā nu khvāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmi, yadariyā etarahi [P 1.0150] upasampajja viharantī”ti, vimuttādhippāyasaññitā vimuttiṃ uddissa saṅkappā manorathā abhiṇhaso appamattā yadattho yaṃpayojano yesaṃ nipphādanatthaṃ kuṭiṃ suññāgāraṃ vipassituṃ pāvisiṃ tisso vijjā phalavimuttiñca paccesanto, gavesanto te me ijjhiṃsu te sabbeva idāni mayhaṃ ijjhiṃsu samijjhiṃsu, nipphannakusalasaṅkappo paripuṇṇamanoratho jātoti attho. Tesaṃ samiddhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “mānānusayamujjaha”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā mānānusayamujjahaṃ pajahiṃ samucchindiṃ, tasmā te me saṅkappā ijjhiṃsūti yojanā. Mānānusaye hi pahīne appahīno nāma anusayo natthi, arahattañca adhigatameva hotīti mānānusayappahānaṃ yathāvuttasaṅkappasamiddhiyā kāraṇaṃ katvā vuttaṃ.

60. Therein, 'my aspirations were fulfilled'—the purpose for which I entered the hut, attaining knowledge and liberation. Those aspirations for renunciation and the like, which counteract sensual thoughts and the like, were previously wished for by me with the thought: 'When, indeed, shall I attain and dwell in that sphere which the noble ones now attain and dwell in?' These thoughts and aspirations, known as having liberation as their aim, were constantly and diligently directed towards liberation. For the sake of that purpose, for the sake of whose accomplishment I entered the hut, the empty dwelling, to practice insight, seeking and attaining the three knowledges and the fruit of liberation—all those aspirations of mine were fulfilled. They have all now succeeded for me, come to fruition. The meaning is that my wholesome aspirations have been accomplished and my heart's desire completely fulfilled. To show their successful fulfillment, it is said: 'abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit.' The connection is as follows: 'Because I abandoned, I eradicated the underlying tendency to conceit, therefore my aspirations were fulfilled.' For when the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned, there is no underlying tendency that remains unabandoned, and Arahantship itself is attained. Thus, the abandoning of the underlying tendency to conceit is stated as the cause for the fulfillment of the aspirations as described.

Sīvalittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sīvali is concluded.

Chaṭṭhavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth chapter is concluded.

7. Sattamavaggo

7. The Seventh Chapter

1. Vappattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vappa

Passati [V 1.0149] passoti āyasmato vappattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto “asuko ca asuko ca thero satthu paṭhamaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakā ahesu”nti thomanaṃ sutvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi – “ahampi bhagavā anāgate tādisassa sammāsambuddhassa paṭhamaṃ dhammapaṭiggāhakānaṃ aññataro bhaveyya”nti, satthu [M 1.0176] santike saraṇagamanañca pavedesi. So yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā tato cuto devamanussesuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ vāseṭṭhassa nāma brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, vappotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So asitena isinā “siddhatthakumāro sabbaññū bhavissatī”ti byākato koṇḍaññappamukhehi brāhmaṇaputtehi saddhiṃ gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā “tasmiṃ sabbaññutaṃ patte tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā amataṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti uruvelāyaṃ viharantaṃ mahāsattaṃ chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahantaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā oḷārikāhāraparibhogena nibbijjitvā isipatanaṃ gato. Abhisambujjhitvā satthārā sattasattāhāni vītināmetvā isipatanaṃ [P 1.0151] gantvā dhammacakke pavattite pāṭipadadivase sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito pañcamiyaṃ pakkhassa aññāsikoṇḍaññādīhi saddhiṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.20-30) –

'The seer sees'—this is the verse of the venerable Elder Vappa. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having come of age, he heard the praise that 'such and such an elder was the first to receive the Dhamma from the Teacher.' Approaching the Blessed One, he made an aspiration: 'May I too, in the future, be one of the first to receive the Dhamma from such a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha!' He also declared his going for refuge in the Teacher's presence. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he passed away from there and wandered only among devas and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in Kapilavatthu as the son of a brahmin named Vāseṭṭha, and his name was Vappa. When the sage Asita prophesied, 'Prince Siddhattha will become the All-Knowing One,' he, together with the brahmin youths led by Koṇḍañña, abandoned the household life and went forth into the ascetic life. Thinking, 'When he attains omniscience, I will hear the Dhamma in his presence and attain the deathless,' he attended upon the Great Being for six years as he strove at Uruvelā. But becoming disenchanted with the consumption of coarse food, he went to Isipatana. After the Teacher attained perfect enlightenment and spent seven weeks, he went to Isipatana. When the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. On the fifth day of the fortnight, together with Aññāsikoṇḍañña and the others, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Ubhinnaṃ devarājūnaṃ, saṅgāmo samupaṭṭhito;

Ahosi samupabyūḷho, mahāghoso avattatha.

A battle between the two kings of the devas was imminent; the forces were arrayed, and a great clamor arose.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Antalikkhe ṭhito satthā, saṃvejesi mahājanaṃ.

Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of Offerings, the Teacher, standing in the sky, stirred the great multitude.

“Sabbe devā attamanā, nikkhittakavacāvudhā;

Sambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā, ekaggāsiṃsu tāvade.

All the devas, being delighted, laid aside their armor and weapons; having paid homage to the Sambuddha, they became one-pointed at that moment.

“Mayhaṃ saṅkappamaññāya, vācāsabhimudīrayi;

Anukampako lokavidū, nibbāpesi mahājanaṃ.

Knowing my aspiration, he uttered speech; the compassionate Knower of the World pacified the great multitude.

“Paduṭṭhacitto [V 1.0150] manujo, ekapāṇaṃ viheṭhayaṃ;

Tena cittappadosena, apāyaṃ upapajjati.

A person with a malicious mind, who harms even a single living being, is reborn in a state of misery due to that corruption of mind.

“Saṅgāmasīse nāgova, bahū pāṇe viheṭhayaṃ;

Nibbāpetha sakaṃ cittaṃ, mā haññittho punappunaṃ.

You are like an elephant at the head of a battle, harming many beings. Pacify your own minds; do not be slain again and again.

“Dvinnampi yakkharājūnaṃ, senā sā vimhitā ahu;

Saraṇañca upāgacchuṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ sutādinaṃ.

The armies of both yaksha kings were astonished; they went for refuge to the foremost in the world, him of great renown.

“Saññāpetvāna janataṃ, padamuddhari cakkhumā;

Pekkhamānova devehi, pakkāmi uttarāmukho.

Having instructed the multitude, the One with Vision lifted his foot; while being watched by the devas, he departed facing north.

“Paṭhamaṃ [M 1.0177] saraṇaṃ gacchiṃ, dvipadindassa tādino;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

I first went for refuge to the leader of bipeds, the steadfast one; for a hundred thousand aeons, I was not reborn in a woeful state.

“Mahādundubhināmā ca, soḷasāsuṃ rathesabhā;

Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, rājāno cakkavattino.

And by the name Mahādundubhi, there were sixteen chariot-lords; for thirty thousand aeons, they were wheel-turning kings.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attanā paṭiladdhasampattiṃ paccavekkhaṇamukhena satthu guṇamahantataṃ paccavekkhitvā “īdisaṃ nāma satthāraṃ bāhulikādivādena samudācarimha. Aho puthujjanabhāvo nāma andhakaraṇo acakkhukaraṇo ariyabhāvoyeva cakkhukaraṇo”ti dassento “passati passo”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Then, having attained Arahantship, by way of reflecting on the accomplishment he had personally gained, he contemplated the greatness of the Teacher's qualities. To show his thought—'We treated such a Teacher with accusations of living in abundance and the like. Oh, the state of a worldling is blinding, it makes one eyeless; only the noble state creates vision!'—he uttered the verse: 'The seer sees.'

61. Tattha passati passoti passati sammādiṭṭhiyā dhamme aviparītaṃ jānāti bujjhatīti passo, dassanasampanno ariyo, so passantaṃ aviparītadassāviṃ “ayaṃ aviparītadassāvī”ti passati paññācakkhunā dhammādhammaṃ yathāsabhāvato jānāti. Na kevalaṃ passantameva, atha kho apassantañca passati, yo paññācakkhuvirahito dhamme yathāsabhāvato na passati, tampi apassantaṃ puthujjanaṃ “andho vatāyaṃ bhavaṃ acakkhuko”ti attano paññācakkhunā passati. Apassanto apassantaṃ, passantañca na passatīti apassanto paññācakkhurahito andhabālo tādisaṃ andhabālaṃ ayaṃ dhammādhammaṃ yathāsabhāvato na passatīti yathā apassantaṃ na passati na jānāti, evaṃ attano paññācakkhunā dhammādhammaṃ yathāsabhāvato passantañca paṇḍitaṃ “ayaṃ evaṃvidho”ti na passati na jānāti, tasmā ahampi pubbe dassanarahito sakalaṃ ñeyyaṃ hatthāmalakaṃ viya passantaṃ bhagavantaṃ apassantampi pūraṇādiṃ yathāsabhāvato na passiṃ, idāni pana buddhānubhāvena sampanno ubhayepi yathāsabhāvato passāmīti sevitabbāsevitabbesu attano aviparītapaṭipattiṃ dasseti.

61. Therein, 'he sees' means that with right view he sees, knows, and understands the Dhamma without distortion; thus, he is a seer. The noble one, accomplished in seeing, perceives one who sees without distortion, thinking, 'This one sees without distortion,' and with the eye of wisdom, he knows Dhamma and non-Dhamma according to their true nature. He sees not only the one who sees, but he also sees the one who does not see. The ordinary person who is devoid of the eye of wisdom and does not see the Dhamma according to its true nature—he sees even that one who does not see with his own eye of wisdom, thinking, 'Alas, this one is blind, without an eye.' One who does not see does not see another who does not see, nor does he see one who sees. This means that one who does not see, being a blind fool devoid of the eye of wisdom, just as he does not see or know another who does not see—that is, a similar blind fool who does not see Dhamma and non-Dhamma according to their true nature—so too, he does not see or know the wise one who, with his own eye of wisdom, sees Dhamma and non-Dhamma according to their true nature, thinking, 'This one is of such a kind.' Therefore, I too, formerly being without sight, did not see the Blessed One—who sees all that is to be known as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand—nor did I see Pūraṇa and others according to their true nature. But now, endowed with the Buddha's power, I see both according to their true nature. Thus, he shows his own undistorted practice in regard to what should and should not be cultivated.

Vappattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vappa is concluded.

2. Vajjiputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vajjiputta

Ekakā [M 1.0178][V 1.0151][P 1.0152] mayaṃ araññeti āyasmato vajjiputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso nāgapupphakesarehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde amaccakule nibbatti, vajjiputtotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So bhagavato vesāligamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vesāliyā avidūre aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe viharati. Tena ca samayena vesāliyaṃ ussavo ahosi. Tattha tattha naccagītavāditaṃ pavattati, mahājano haṭṭhatuṭṭho ussavasampattiṃ paccanubhoti, taṃ sutvā so bhikkhu ayoniso ummujjanto vivekaṃ vajjamāno kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā attano anabhiratiṃ pakāsento –

“Alone we dwell in the wilderness”—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Vajjiputta. What is its origin? This elder, too, had performed meritorious deeds under former Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences as a support for liberation. Ninety-one eons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a good family. Having come of age, one day he saw the Blessed One Vipassī and, with a joyful mind, made an offering with nāga flower filaments. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a minister’s family, and his name was Vajjiputta. When the Blessed One journeyed to Vesālī, he saw the Buddha’s power, acquired faith, and went forth into homelessness. Having fulfilled his preliminary duties, he took up a meditation subject and dwelled in a certain grove not far from Vesālī. At that time, a festival was taking place in Vesālī. Everywhere, dancing, singing, and music resounded, and the great multitude, delighted and elated, experienced the festivities. Hearing this, that monk, unwisely emerging from his practice, shunning seclusion, abandoning his meditation subject, and revealing his discontent, declared—

“Ekakā mayaṃ araññe viharāma, apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ;

Etādisikāya rattiyā, ko su nāma amhehi pāpiyo”ti. – gāthamāha;

“Alone we dwell in the wilderness, like a discarded log in the forest. On such a night as this, who indeed could be more wretched than we?”—he spoke this verse.

Taṃ sutvā vanasaṇḍe adhivatthā devatā taṃ bhikkhuṃ anukampamānā “yadipi, tvaṃ bhikkhu, araññavāsaṃ hīḷento vadasi, vivekakāmā pana viddasuno taṃ bahu maññantiyevā”ti imamatthaṃ dassentī –

Having heard that, the deity dwelling in the forest grove, feeling compassion for that monk, revealed this meaning: “Although you, monk, disparage dwelling in the forest, those wise ones who desire seclusion greatly esteem it.”

“Ekako tvaṃ araññe viharasi, apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ;

Tassa te bahukā pihayanti, nerayikā viya saggagāmina”nti. –

“You dwell alone in the forest, like a discarded log in the forest. Many envy you, as those in hell envy those going to heaven.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā, “kathañhi nāma tvaṃ, bhikkhu, niyyānike sammāsambuddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā aniyyānikaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkessasī”ti santajjentī saṃvejesi[M 1.0179]. Evaṃ so bhikkhu tāya devatāya saṃvejito kasābhihato viya bhadro assājānīyo vipassanāvīthiṃ [P 1.0153] otaritvā nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.11.62-66) –

Having spoken the verse, she, admonishing him, stirred him, saying, “How indeed, monk, having gone forth in the liberating dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, could you entertain thoughts that do not lead to liberation?” Thus, that monk, stirred by that deity, like a fine thoroughbred steed struck by a whip, entered the path of insight and, before long, diligently developing insight, attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, sataraṃsiṃva bhāṇumaṃ;

Obhāsentaṃ disā sabbā, uḷurājaṃva pūritaṃ.

“The Fully Awakened One, golden-hued, like the sun with its hundred rays, illuminating all directions, like the full moon.

“Purakkhataṃ [V 1.0152] sāvakehi, sāgareheva medaniṃ;

Nāgaṃ paggayha reṇūhi, vipassissābhiropayiṃ.

“Attended by disciples, as the earth is by the oceans, I took up a nāga flower with its pollen and offered it to Vipassī.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ reṇumabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, when I offered that pollen, I have not known a bad destination—this is the fruit of my worship of the Buddha.

“Paṇṇatālīsito kappe, reṇu nāmāsi khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Forty-five eons ago, there was a khattiya named Reṇu, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt away… and so on… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā “ayaṃ me arahattappattiyā aṅkuso jāto”ti attano devatāya ca vuttanayaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā –

But having attained arahantship, thinking, “This has become a goad for my attainment of arahantship,” he then recited the verse in the manner spoken by the deity to him—

62.

62.

“Ekakā mayaṃ araññe viharāma, apaviddhaṃva vanasmiṃ dārukaṃ;

Tassa me bahukā pihayanti, nerayikā viya saggagāmina”nti. –

“Alone we dwell in the wilderness, like a discarded log in the forest; many envy me, like those in hell envy those going to heaven.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this verse.

Tassattho – anapekkhabhāvena vane chaḍḍitadārukkhaṇḍaṃ viya yadipi mayaṃ ekakā ekākino asahāyā imasmiṃ araññe viharāma, evaṃ viharato pana tassa me bahukā pihayanti maṃ bahū atthakāmarūpā kulaputtā abhipatthenti, “aho vatassa mayampi vajjiputtatthero viya gharabandhanaṃ pahāya araññe vihareyyāmā”ti. Yathā kiṃ? Nerayikā viya saggagāminaṃ, yathā nāma nerayikā attano pāpakammena niraye nibbattasattā saggagāmīnaṃ saggūpagāmīnaṃ pihayanti – “aho vata mayampi nirayadukkhaṃ pahāya saggasukhaṃ paccanubhaveyyāmā”ti evaṃsampadamidanti attho. Ettha [M 1.0180] ca attani garubahuvacanappayogassa icchitabbattā “ekakā mayaṃ viharāmā”ti puna tassa atthassa ekattaṃ sandhāya “tassa me”ti ekavacanappayogo kato. “Tassa me”, “saggagāmina”nti ca ubhayampi ‘pihayantī’ti padaṃ apekkhitvā upayogatthe sampadānaniddeso daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ abhipatthentīti ca tādise araññavāsādiguṇe abhipatthentā nāma hontīti katvā vuttaṃ. Tassa meti vā tassa mama santike guṇeti adhippāyo.

Its meaning is: Like a piece of wood discarded in the forest due to being disregarded, although we dwell alone in this wilderness, solitary and without companions, yet while I am dwelling thus, many envy me. Many youths from good families, desiring their own welfare, aspire, thinking, “Oh, if only we too, like the Elder Vajjiputta, could abandon the bonds of the household and dwell in the wilderness!” To what is this comparable? Like those in hell envy those going to heaven. Just as beings born in hell due to their evil deeds envy those going to heaven or bound for heaven, thinking, “Oh, if only we too could abandon the suffering of hell and experience the bliss of heaven!”—such is the meaning here. And in this context, because the use of the honorific plural in reference to oneself is intended, it is said, “we dwell alone.” Then again, referring to the singular nature of that meaning, the singular form “of me” is used. Both “of me” (tassa me) and “those going to heaven” (saggagāminaṃ) should be understood as a dative designation in the sense of application, connected to the word “envy” (pihayanti). And “they aspire to that” is said because they are indeed aspiring to such qualities as dwelling in the forest and so on. Alternatively, “of me” (tassa me) means “the virtues in my presence”; this is the intended meaning.

Vajjiputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vajjiputta is concluded.

3. Pakkhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Pakkha

Cutā [V 1.0153][P 1.0154] patantīti āyasmato pakkhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto ito ekanavute kappe yakkhasenāpati hutvā vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso dibbavatthena pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sakkesu devadahanigame sākiyarājakule nibbatti, “sammodakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Athassa daharakāle vātarogena pādā na vahiṃsu. So katipayaṃ kālaṃ pīṭhasappī viya vicari. Tenassa pakkhoti samaññā jātā. Pacchā arogakālepi tatheva naṃ sañjānanti, so bhagavato ñātisamāgame pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharati. Athekadivasaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisituṃ gacchanto antarāmagge aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Tasmiñca samaye aññataro kulalo maṃsapesiṃ ādāya ākāsena gacchati, taṃ bahū kulalā anupatitvā pātesuṃ. Pātitaṃ maṃsapesiṃ eko kulalo aggahesi. Taṃ añño acchinditvā gaṇhi, taṃ disvā thero “yathāyaṃ maṃsapesi, evaṃ kāmā nāma bahusādhāraṇā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā”ti – kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ paccavekkhitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā “anicca”ntiādinā manasikaronto piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco [M 1.0181] divāṭṭhāne nisīditvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.1-10) –

'Cutā patantī' is a verse by the Venerable Pakkha. What is its origin? He, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, made merits in various existences. Ninety-one eons ago, he became the commander of a yakkha army and, upon seeing the Blessed One Vipassī, his mind was filled with faith. He made an offering with divine cloth. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family in the Sakyan town of Devadaha. His name was Sammodakumāra. In his youth, his legs were paralyzed due to a wind ailment. For some time, he moved about like a stool-creeper. Thus he came to be known as Pakkha. Later, even when he recovered, they still knew him by that name. At the gathering of the Blessed One’s relatives, he witnessed a miracle and gained faith. He went forth, fulfilled his preliminary duties, took up a meditation subject, and dwelt in the forest. One day, while going to the village for alms, he sat down at the foot of a tree along the way. At that time, a kite was carrying a piece of meat through the sky, and many other kites pursued it and made it fall. One kite seized the fallen piece of meat, but another snatched it away. Seeing this, the elder reflected: 'Just as this piece of meat, so too sensual pleasures are common to many, full of suffering and distress.' Contemplating the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, he established insight. Focusing on impermanence and so forth, he went for alms, completed his meal, and sat in his daytime dwelling. Developing his insight, he attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Thera 1.12.1-10):

“Vipassī nāma bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Aṭṭhasaṭṭhisahassehi, pāvisi bandhumaṃ tadā.

“The Blessed One Vipassī by name, foremost in the world, a bull among men, then entered Bandhumatī with sixty-eight thousand.”

“Nagarā abhinikkhamma, agamaṃ dīpacetiyaṃ;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ.

“Having left the city, I went to the Island Shrine; I saw the stainless Buddha, the recipient of offerings.”

“Cullāsītisahassāni, yakkhā mayhaṃ upantike;

Upaṭṭhahanti sakkaccaṃ, indaṃva tidasā gaṇā.

“Eighty-four thousand yakkhas attend upon me respectfully, as the hosts of the Tidasā gods serve Indra.”

“Bhavanā abhinikkhamma, dussaṃ paggayhahaṃ tadā;

Sirasā abhivādesiṃ, tañcādāsiṃ mahesino.

“Having gone out from my dwelling, I then raised up a cloth; I bowed with my head, and offered it to the Great Seer.”

“Aho buddho aho dhammo, aho no satthu sampadā;

Buddhassa ānubhāvena, vasudhāyaṃ pakampatha.

“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, our Teacher's accomplishment! By the Buddha's power, this earth trembled.”

“Tañca acchariyaṃ disvā, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Buddhe cittaṃ pasādemi, dvipadindamhi tādine.

“Seeing that marvel, that astonishing, hair-raising wonder, I gladdened my mind in the Buddha, the Tādī, chief of bipeds.”

“Sohaṃ [V 1.0154] cittaṃ pasādetvā, dussaṃ datvāna satthuno;

Saraṇañca upāgacchiṃ, sāmacco saparijjano.

“Having gladdened my mind and given the cloth to the Teacher, I went for refuge, along with my ministers and retinue.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first eon from now, when I performed that deed, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Ito pannarase kappe, soḷasāsuṃ suvāhanā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Fifteen eons ago from this one, there were sixteen kings named Suvāhana, mighty wheel-turning monarchs endowed with the seven treasures.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…pe… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā yadeva saṃvegavatthuṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā aññā adhigatā, tassa saṃkittanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto “cutā patantī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, having made that object of spiritual urgency a goad and developed insight, he realized final knowledge. Declaring his final knowledge by way of summarizing that event, he uttered the verse: 'Cutā patantī.'

63. Tattha cutāti bhaṭṭhā. Patantīti anupatanti. Patitāti [P 1.0155] cavanavasena bhūmiyaṃ patitā, ākāse vā sampatanavasena patitā. Giddhāti gedhaṃ āpannā[M 1.0182]. Punarāgatāti punadeva upagatā. Ca-saddo sabbattha yojetabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – patanti anupatanti ca idha kulalā, itarassa mukhato cutā ca maṃsapesi, cutā pana sā bhūmiyaṃ patitā ca, giddhā gedhaṃ āpannā sabbeva kulalā punarāgatā. Yathā cime kulalā, evaṃ saṃsāre paribbhamantā sattā ye kusaladhammato cutā, te patanti nirayādīsu, evaṃ patitā ca, sampattibhave ṭhitā tattha kāmasukhānuyogavasena kāmabhave rūpārūpabhavesu ca bhavanikantivasena giddhā ca punarāgatā bhavato aparimuttattā tena tena bhavagāminā kammena taṃ taṃ bhavasaññitaṃ dukkhaṃ āgatā eva, evaṃbhūtā ime sattā. Mayā pana kataṃ kiccaṃ pariññādibhedaṃ soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ kataṃ, na dāni taṃ kātabbaṃ atthi. Rataṃ rammaṃ ramitabbaṃ ariyehi sabbasaṅkhatavinissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ rataṃ abhirataṃ rammaṃ. Tena ca sukhenanvāgataṃ sukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhena anuāgataṃ upagataṃ accantasukhaṃ nibbānaṃ, sukhena vā sukhāpaṭipadābhūtena vipassanāsukhena maggasukhena ca anvāgataṃ phalasukhaṃ nibbānasukhañcāti attho veditabbo.

63. There, 'cutā' means dislodged. 'Patanti' means they pursue. 'Patitā' means fallen to the ground by way of being dislodged, or fallen in the sky by way of swooping down. 'Giddhā' means overcome by greed. 'Punarāgatā' means returned again. The word 'ca' should be applied everywhere. This is what is meant: 'Here, the kites pursue and fall after, and the piece of meat is dislodged from another's mouth. Having been dislodged, it has fallen to the ground, and all the kites, overcome by greed, have returned again.' Just as these kites, so too do beings wandering in saṃsāra. Those who have fallen from wholesome states fall into hells and so forth. Having fallen thus, and being established in fortunate existences, through indulgence in sensual pleasures in the sensual realm, and through craving for existence in the form and formless realms, they are overcome by greed and return again. Not being freed from existence, through whatever actions lead to those existences, they come to that suffering designated as various existences. Such are these beings. But as for me, the sixteenfold duty, distinguished as full understanding and so on, has been done. There is nothing more for me to do now. Nibbāna, which has gone beyond all conditioned things, is delighted in, lovely, and to be delighted in by the noble ones. And by this is meant the happiness that is attained, the ultimate happiness, Nibbāna, which is approached and attained through the happiness of fruition attainment. Or, the happiness of fruition and the happiness of Nibbāna are attained by means of the happiness that is the pleasant practice, that is, the happiness of insight and the happiness of the path. This is the meaning to be understood.

Pakkhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Pakkha is completed.

4. Vimalakoṇḍaññattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña

Dumavhayāya uppannoti vimalakoṇḍaññattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro [V 1.0155] tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle vibhavasampanne kule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ mahatiyā parisāya parivutaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā pasannamānaso catūhi suvaṇṇapupphehi pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāresi, yathā suvaṇṇābhā sakalaṃ taṃ padesaṃ ottharati. Taṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso hutvā [P 1.0156] bhagavantaṃ vanditvā taṃ nimittaṃ gahetvā attano gehaṃ gantvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ avijahanto kenaci rogena kālaṃ katvā tusitesu upapanno aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājānaṃ [M 1.0183] bimbisāraṃ paṭicca ambapāliyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Rājā hi bimbisāro taruṇakāle ambapāliyā rūpasampattiṃ sutvā sañjātābhilāso katipayamanussaparivāro aññātakavesena vesāliṃ gantvā ekarattiṃ tāya saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā ayaṃ tassā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Sā ca gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ tassa ārocesi. Rājāpi attānaṃ jānāpetvā dātabbayuttakaṃ datvā pakkāmi. Sā gabbhassa paripākamanvāya puttaṃ vijāyi, “vimalo”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi, pacchā vimalakoṇḍaññoti paññāyittha. So vayappatto bhagavato vesāligamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.40-48) –

"Born from the call of a tree," such is the verse of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences that was a supporting condition for liberation, ninety-one eons ago, at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, was born into a prosperous family and, having attained maturity, one day saw the Blessed One Vipassī teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a great assembly. His mind filled with faith, he offered four golden flowers in worship. To increase his devotion, the Blessed One performed such a display of psychic power that a golden radiance covered the entire place. Seeing this, his mind filled with even greater gladness, he paid homage to the Blessed One, took that as a sign, and returned home. Without abandoning his joy focused on the Buddha, he passed away due to some illness and was reborn among the Tusita devas. Continuing to perform meritorious deeds, wandering on among devas and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation he took conception in the womb of Ambapālī, on account of King Bimbisāra. For in his youth, King Bimbisāra, hearing of Ambapālī’s beauty, became desirous and went to Vesālī in disguise, accompanied by a few men. He spent one night with her. At that time, this one took conception in her womb. She informed the king that her pregnancy was established. The king, revealing his identity, gave her what was proper to give and departed. When the pregnancy reached its full term, she gave birth to a son. His name was "Vimala," and later he became known as Vimalakoṇḍañña. Coming of age, when the Blessed One visited Vesālī, he witnessed the Buddha’s power and, with a faithful mind, went forth into homelessness. Having completed his preliminary practices, he established insight and soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 1.12.40–48):

“Vipassī nāma bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Nisinno janakāyassa, desesi amataṃ padaṃ.

“Vipassī, the Blessed One, foremost in the world, the bull among men; seated amidst the assembly of people, he taught the Deathless State.”

“Tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvāna, dvipadinnassa tādino;

Soṇṇapupphāni cattāri, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“Having heard the Dhamma from him, the steadfast leader of bipeds, I offered four golden flowers to the Buddha.”

“Suvaṇṇacchadanaṃ āsi, yāvatā parisā tadā;

Buddhābhā ca suvaṇṇābhā, āloko vipulo ahu.

“As far as the assembly extended, so did a golden canopy; the Buddha’s radiance was like that of gold, and a vast light appeared.”

“Udaggacitto sumano, vedajāto katañjalī;

Vittisañjanano tesaṃ, diṭṭhadhammasukhāvaho.

“With uplifted mind, joyful, filled with rapture, with hands raised in reverence; generating delight for them, bringing happiness in this very life.”

“Āyācitvāna sambuddhaṃ, vanditvāna ca subbataṃ;

Pāmojjaṃ janayitvāna, sakaṃ bhavanupāgamiṃ.

“Having requested the Fully Awakened One, and having paid homage to the one of excellent vows, and having generated joy, I went to my own dwelling.”

“Bhavane upaviṭṭhohaṃ, buddhaseṭṭhaṃ anussariṃ;

Tena cittappasādena, tusitaṃ upapajjahaṃ.

“Seated in my dwelling, I recollected the supreme Buddha; through that clarity of mind, I was reborn in the Tusita realm.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I offered that flower; I know of no bad destination—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Soḷasāsiṃsu [V 1.0156] rājāno, nemisammatanāmakā;

Tetālīse ito kappe, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“There were sixteen kings named Nemisammata; forty-three aeons ago from now, they were powerful wheel-turning monarchs.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt away… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0184] pana patvā aññāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto “dumavhayāyā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, however, declaring his attainment indirectly by speaking as if about another, he uttered the verse beginning, “dumavhayāya.”

64. Tattha dumavhayāyāti dumena ambena avhātabbāya, ambapāliyāti attho. Ādhāre cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Uppannoti tassā kucchiyaṃ uppanno uppajjamāno ca. Jāto paṇḍaraketunāti dhavalavatthadhajattā “paṇḍaraketū”ti paññātena bimbisāraraññā hetubhūtena jāto, taṃ paṭicca nibbattoti attho. Uppannoti vā paṭhamābhinibbattidassanaṃ. Tato hi jātoti abhijātidassanaṃ. Vijāyanakālato paṭṭhāya hi loke jātavohāro. Ettha ca “dumavhayāya uppanno”ti iminā attukkaṃsanabhāvaṃ apaneti, anekapatiputtānampi visesādhigamasambhavañca dīpeti. “Jāto paṇḍaraketunā”ti iminā [P 1.0157] viññātapitikadassanena paravambhanaṃ apaneti. Ketuhāti mānappahāyī. Māno hi uṇṇatilakkhaṇattā ketu viyāti ketu. Tathā hi so “ketukamyatāpaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vuccati. Ketunāyevāti paññāya eva. Paññā hi anavajjadhammesu accuggataṭṭhena mārasenappamaddanena pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena ca ariyānaṃ dhajā nāma. Tenāha “dhammo hi isinaṃ dhajo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.241; a. ni. 4.48; jā. 2.21.494). Mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayīti mahāvisayatāya mahantā, seyyamānajātimānādibhedato bahavo ca mānappakārā, itare ca kilesadhammā samussitaṭṭhena ketu etassāti mahāketu māro pāpimā. Taṃ balavidhamanavisayātikkamanavasena abhibhavi nibbisevanaṃ akāsīti. “Mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī”ti attānaṃ paraṃ viya dassento aññāpadesena arahattaṃ byākāsi.

64. Herein, `dumavhayāya` means ‘to be called by the tree,’ that is, by the mango tree; the meaning is ‘Ambapālī.’ And this is a locative case referring to the basis. `Uppanno` means ‘born in her womb,’ and ‘coming into existence.’ `Jāto paṇḍaraketunā` means ‘born due to King Bimbisāra,’ who was known as ‘Paṇḍaraketu’ because of his white cloth banner; thus, he was born in connection with him. Alternatively, `uppanno` indicates the first arising, while `jāto` indicates the actual birth, for in the world, the term ‘born’ is used from the moment of delivery onwards. Here, the phrase `dumavhayāya uppanno` removes any self-praise and reveals that it is possible even for the sons of women with many partners to achieve distinction. The phrase `jāto paṇḍaraketunā` removes any deception of others by showing that the father is known. `Ketuhā` means ‘one who has abandoned conceit.’ For conceit, due to its characteristic of being lofty, is like a banner (ketu), and is thus called ‘ketu’. Indeed, it is said of it: ‘Its manifestation is the desire for prominence.’ `Ketunāyeva` means ‘by wisdom alone.’ For wisdom, being the highest among blameless qualities, crushing the army of Māra, and being preeminent, is called the banner of the noble ones. Hence it is said, ‘Dhamma is the banner of the sages’ (Saṃ. Ni. 2.241; A. Ni. 4.48; Jā. 2.21.494). `Mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī` means ‘he destroyed the great banner’—Māra the Evil One—who is called Mahāketu because of his vast domain, his many forms of conceit such as pride in superiority and pride in birth, and because other defilements are elevated like banners for him. He subdued him by overcoming his power, dominion, and sphere, rendering him harmless. By saying `mahāketuṃ padhaṃsayī`, he declared his arahantship indirectly, presenting himself as if he were another.

Vimalakoṇḍaññattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vimalakoṇḍañña is concluded.

5. Ukkhepakatavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha

Ukkhepakatavacchassāti āyasmato ukkhepakatavacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthāraṃ uddissa [M 1.0185] māḷaṃ karontassa pūgassa ekatthambhaṃ alabhantassa thambhaṃ datvā sahāyakiccaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena [V 1.0157] devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, vacchotissa gottato āgatanāmaṃ. So satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kosalaraṭṭhe gāmakāvāse vasanto āgatāgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti. “Ayaṃ [P 1.0158] vinayo idaṃ suttantaṃ ayaṃ abhidhammo”ti pana paricchedaṃ na jānāti. Athekadivasaṃ āyasmantaṃ dhammasenāpatiṃ pucchitvā yathāparicchedaṃ sabbaṃ sallakkhesi. Dhammasaṅgītiyā pubbepi piṭakādisamaññā pariyattisaddhamme vavatthitā eva, yato bhikkhūnaṃ vinayadharādivohāro. So tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhanto paripucchanto tattha vutte rūpārūpadhamme sallakkhetvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sammasanto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.2.13-26) –

“Ukkhepakatavacchassā” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha. What is its origin? It is said that he, too, having made a resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merit conducive to liberation in various existences, was reborn into a family ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having reached maturity, he gave a pillar to a group who were building a pavilion for the Teacher but could not find one, thus rendering assistance. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm. After repeatedly performing good deeds and wandering among devas and humans, he was born in this Buddha-era as the son of a certain brahmin in Sāvatthī, named Vaccha according to his lineage. Hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher, he gained faith and went forth. While dwelling in a village monastery in the Kosala country, he learned the Dhamma from visiting monks. However, he did not know the divisions, such as “This is the Vinaya, this is the Suttanta, this is the Abhidhamma.” Then one day, after asking the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, he discerned all the divisions accordingly. Even before the Buddhist Council, the designations of the Piṭakas and so on were established in the Dhamma of the Teachings, hence the monks’ references to Vinaya experts and others. Studying and inquiring about the Buddha’s words in the three Piṭakas, reflecting on the material and immaterial phenomena mentioned therein, he established insight and, contemplating, soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Siddhatthassa bhagavato, mahāpūgagaṇo ahu;

Saraṇaṃ gatā ca te buddhaṃ, saddahanti tathāgataṃ.

“The Blessed One Siddhattha had a great multitude of followers; and they, having gone to the Buddha for refuge, had faith in the Tathāgata.”

“Sabbe saṅgamma mantetvā, māḷaṃ kubbanti satthuno;

Ekatthambhaṃ alabhantā, vicinanti brahāvane.

“Having all gathered and consulted, they built a pavilion for the Teacher; not finding a single pillar, they searched throughout the great forest.”

“Tehaṃ araññe disvāna, upagamma gaṇaṃ tadā;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, paṭipucchiṃ gaṇaṃ ahaṃ.

“Then, seeing them in the forest, I approached the group; raising my joined hands, I questioned the group.”

“Te me puṭṭhā viyākaṃsu, sīlavanto upāsakā;

Māḷaṃ mayaṃ kattukāmā, ekatthambho na labbhati.

“Those virtuous lay followers, when asked by me, explained: ‘We wish to build a pavilion, but a single pillar is not available.’”

“Ekatthambhaṃ mamaṃ detha, ahaṃ dassāmi satthuno;

Āharissāmahaṃ thambhaṃ, appossukkā bhavantu te.

“‘Let me provide a pillar; I will give it to the Teacher. I will bring the pillar; may you be without anxiety.’”

“Te me thambhaṃ pavecchiṃsu, pasannā tuṭṭhamānasā;

Tato paṭinivattitvā, agamaṃsu sakaṃ gharaṃ.

“They entrusted the pillar to me, with pleased and joyful minds; then, turning back, they went to their own homes.”

“Aciraṃ gate pūgagaṇe, thambhaṃ ahāsahaṃ tadā;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, paṭhamaṃ ussapesahaṃ.

“Soon after the group had departed, I then brought the pillar; with a joyful and elated mind, I first raised it.”

“Tena [M 1.0186] cittappasādena, vimānaṃ upapajjahaṃ;

Ubbiddhaṃ bhavanaṃ mayhaṃ, sattabhūmaṃ samuggataṃ.

“Through that clarity of mind, I was reborn in a celestial mansion; my lofty dwelling arose, seven stories high.”

“Vajjamānāsu bherīsu, paricāremahaṃ sadā;

Pañcapaññāsakappamhi, rājā āsiṃ yasodharo.

“While the drums were being beaten, I always served. In the fifty-fifth aeon, I was a king, Yasodhara.”

“Tatthāpi bhavanaṃ mayhaṃ, sattabhūmaṃ samuggataṃ;

Kūṭāgāravarūpetaṃ, ekatthambhaṃ manoramaṃ.

“Even there, my mansion rose seven stories high, adorned with an excellent peaked chamber, delightful, supported by a single pillar.”

“Ekavīsatikappamhi[V 1.0158], udeno nāma khattiyo;

Tatrāpi bhavanaṃ mayhaṃ, sattabhūmaṃ samuggataṃ.

“In the twenty-first aeon, I was a noble named Udena; there, too, my mansion rose seven stories high.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Anubhomi sukhaṃ sabbaṃ, ekatthambhassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Whatever realm I am reborn in, be it divine or human, I experience all happiness; this is the fruit of the single pillar.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ thambhamadadaṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ekatthambhassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that pillar, I do not recall any bad destination; this is the fruit of the single pillar.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā katakiccattā akilāsubhāve ṭhito attano santikaṃ upagatānaṃ gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ anukampaṃ upādāya tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ vīmaṃsitvā dhammaṃ desesi. Desento ca ekadivasaṃ attānaṃ paraṃ viya katvā dassento –

Having attained arahantship, however, with his task accomplished and abiding in a state free from weariness, out of compassion for the householders and renunciants who came to him, he investigated the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, and taught the Dhamma. And while teaching, one day, presenting himself as if he were another, he said:

65.

65.

“Ukkhepakatavacchassa, saṅkalitaṃ bahūhi vassehi;

Taṃ bhāsati gahaṭṭhānaṃ, sunisinno uḷārapāmojjo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“That which was compiled by Ukkhepakatavaccha over many years—that he speaks to householders, well-seated and filled with sublime joy.” Thus, he spoke this verse.

Tattha ukkhepakatavacchassāti kataukkhepavacchassa, bhikkhuno santike visuṃ visuṃ uggahitaṃ vinayapadesaṃ suttapadesaṃ abhidhammapadesañca yathāparicchedaṃ vinayasuttābhidhammānaṃyeva upari khipitvā sajjhāyanavasena tattha tattheva pakkhipitvā ṭhitavacchenāti attho karaṇatthe hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Saṅkalitaṃ bahūhi vassehīti bahukehi saṃvaccharehi sampiṇḍanavasena hadaye ṭhapitaṃ. “Saṅkhalita”ntipi pāṭho, saṅkhalitaṃ viya kataṃ ekābaddhavasena [M 1.0187] vācuggataṃ [P 1.0159] kataṃ. Yaṃ buddhavacananti vacanaseso. Tanti taṃ pariyattidhammaṃ bhāsati katheti. Gahaṭṭhānanti tesaṃ yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ. Sunisinnoti tasmiṃ dhamme sammā niccalo nisinno, lābhasakkārādiṃ apaccāsīsanto kevalaṃ vimuttāyatanasīseyeva ṭhatvā kathetīti attho. Tenāha “uḷārapāmojjo”ti phalasamāpattisukhavasena dhammadesanāvaseneva ca uppannauḷārapāmojjoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, 'Ukkhepakatavacchassa' means 'of Ukkhepakatavaccha'—that is, 'by the Elder of the Vaccha clan who was established in having learned the Vinaya passages, Sutta passages, and Abhidhamma passages separately from a monk, and later, according to the divisions, placing them within the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma themselves by way of recitation.' Indeed, this is a genitive case in the sense of an agent. 'Saṅkalitaṃ bahūhi vassehi' means 'retained in the heart through compilation over many years.' Some texts also read 'saṅkhalita,' meaning 'made like a chain,' or 'uttered in a continuous flow.' The implied remainder of the phrase is 'that which is the Buddha’s word.' 'Tanti' refers to that scriptural Dhamma which he speaks or teaches. 'Householders' is said with reference to the majority of them. 'Well-seated' means properly and steadily seated in that Dhamma, not longing for gain or honor, but speaking solely while established at the very peak of the sphere of liberation. Hence it is said, 'with supreme joy'—meaning supreme joy arisen from the bliss of fruition attainment and from the very teaching of the Dhamma. For this has been said:
