“Yathā yathāvuso bhikkhu, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojja”ntiādi (dī. ni. 3.355).

“Friend, to whatever extent a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, to that extent he gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 3.355).

Ukkhepakatavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ukkhepakatavaccha is concluded.

6. Meghiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Meghiya

Anusāsi [V 1.0159] mahāvīroti āyasmato meghiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave kusalabījāni ropento ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmiñca samaye vipassī bhagavā buddhakiccassa pariyosānamāgamma āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajji. Tena pathavīkampādīsu uppannesu mahājano bhītatasito ahosi. Atha naṃ vessavaṇo mahārājā tamatthaṃ vibhāvetvā samassāsesi. Taṃ sutvā mahājano saṃvegappatto ahosi. Tatthāyaṃ kulaputto buddhānubhāvaṃ sutvā satthari sañjātagāravabahumāno uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sākiyarājakule nibbatti, tassa meghiyoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto satthu santike pabbajitvā bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhahanto bhagavati jālikāyaṃ viharante kimikālāya nadiyā tīre ramaṇīyaṃ ambavanaṃ disvā [P 1.0160] tattha viharitukāmo [M 1.0188] dve vāre bhagavatā vāretvā tatiyavāraṃ vissajjito tattha gantvā micchāvitakkamakkhikāhi khajjamāno cittasamādhiṃ alabhitvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Athassa bhagavā “aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā pañca dhammā paripākāya saṃvattantī”tiādinā (udā. 31) ovādaṃ adāsi. So tasmiṃ ovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.57-65) –

“The Great Hero Instructed”—This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Meghiya. What is its origin? This one, too, having performed deeds of merit under former Buddhas, planting seeds of wholesome kamma in various existences, was born in a family and attained maturity ninety-one aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī, having come to the end of his Buddha-work, relinquished his life-formations. When earthquakes and the like arose because of this, the great multitude became frightened and terrified. Then Vessavaṇa, the Great King, explained that matter and consoled them. Hearing that, the great multitude was stirred with a sense of urgency. There, this clansman, hearing of the Buddha's power, generated deep reverence and respect for the Teacher and experienced abundant joy and gladness. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha's arising, he was born in Kapilavatthu in the Sakyan royal family, and his name was Meghiya. Having come of age, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher, and attending upon the Blessed One while the Blessed One was dwelling at Jālikā, near the Kimikālā River, seeing a lovely mango grove on the bank, desiring to dwell there, he was twice restrained by the Blessed One, but dismissed the third time. He went there, and being plagued by wrong thoughts like flies, he did not gain concentration of mind. Returning to the Teacher, he reported that matter. Then the Blessed One gave him advice, saying, “For liberation of mind that is not yet mature, Meghiya, five things conduce to maturity,” and so forth (Ud. 4.1). Standing in that advice, developing insight, he attained arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.12.57-65):

“Yadā vipassī lokaggo, āyusaṅkhāramossaji;

Pathavī sampakampittha, medanī jalamekhalā.

“When Vipassī, foremost in the world, relinquished the life-formations, the earth shook violently, the earth with its girdle of water quaked.”

“Otataṃ vitataṃ mayhaṃ, suvicittavaṭaṃsakaṃ;

Bhavanampi pakampittha, buddhassa āyusaṅkhaye.

“My dwelling, spread out and extensive, beautifully adorned with ornaments, also shook when the Buddha's life-formations were relinquished.”

“Tāso mayhaṃ samuppanno, bhavane sampakampite;

Uppādo nu kimatthāya, āloko vipulo ahu.

“Fear arose in me when the dwelling shook; For what purpose did this great light arise?”

“Vessavaṇo idhāgamma, nibbāpesi mahājanaṃ;

Pāṇabhūte bhayaṃ natthi, ekaggā hotha saṃvutā.

“Vessavaṇa came here and calmed the great multitude; There is no fear for living beings; be unified and restrained.”

“Aho buddho aho dhammo, aho no satthu sampadā;

Yasmiṃ uppajjamānamhi, pathavī sampakampati.

“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Teacher's attainment! When he arose, the earth trembled.”

“Buddhānubhāvaṃ kittetvā, kappaṃ saggamhi modahaṃ;

Avasesesu kappesu, kusalaṃ caritaṃ mayā.

“Having extolled the Buddha's power, I rejoiced in heaven for an aeon; In the remaining aeons, wholesome kamma was performed by me.”

“Ekanavutito [V 1.0160] kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gained that perception; I do not know of a bad destination, this is the fruit of the perception of the Buddha.”

“Ito cuddasakappamhi, rājā āsiṃ patāpavā;

Samito nāma nāmena, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Fourteen aeons ago from now, I was a powerful king; named Samita, a wheel-turning monarch of great strength.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…etc…the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthu sammukhā ovādaṃ labhitvā “mayā arahattaṃ adhigata”nti aññaṃ byākaronto –

However, having attained arahantship, and having received advice in the Teacher's presence, declaring his attainment of final knowledge, he said:

66.

66.

“Anusāsi [M 1.0189] mahāvīro, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvāna, vihāsiṃ santike sato;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“The Great Hero, gone beyond all phenomena, instructed me; Having heard his Dhamma, I dwelt mindfully near him; The three knowledges are attained; the Buddha's teaching has been done.”—he recited this verse.

Tattha anusāsīti “aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā pañca dhammā paripākāya saṃvattantī”tiādinā ovadi anusiṭṭhiṃ adāsi. Mahāvīroti mahāvikkanto, vīriyapāramipāripūriyā caturaṅgasamannāgatavīriyādhiṭṭhānena anaññasādhāraṇacatubbidhasammappadhānasampattiyā ca mahāvīriyoti attho. Sabbadhammāna pāragūti sabbesañca ñeyyadhammānaṃ pāraṃ pariyantaṃ ñāṇagamanena gato adhigatoti sabbadhammāna pāragū, sabbaññūti attho. Sabbesaṃ vā saṅkhatadhammānaṃ pārabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ sayambhūñāṇena gato adhigatoti sabbadhammāna pāragū. Tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvānāti tassa buddhassa bhagavato sāmukkaṃsikaṃ taṃ catusaccadhammaṃ suṇitvā. Vihāsiṃ santiketi ambavane micchāvitakkehi upadduto cālikā vihāraṃ gantvā satthu samīpeyeva vihāsiṃ. Satoti satimā, samathavipassanābhāvanāya appamattoti attho. Ahanti idaṃ yathā “anusāsī”ti ettha “ma”nti evaṃ “vijjā [P 1.0161] anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti ettha “mayā”ti pariṇāmetabbaṃ. “Kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti ca iminā yathāvuttaṃ vijjāttayānuppattimeva satthu ovādapaṭikaraṇabhāvadassanena pariyāyantarena pakāseti. Sīlakkhandhādiparipūraṇameva hi satthu sāsanakāritā.

Here, “instructed” (anusāsī) means he gave advice and instruction, such as, “Meghiya, for an undeveloped liberation of mind, five things conduce to maturity,” and so forth. “Great Hero” (mahāvīro) means one of great vigor (mahāvikkanto), perfected in the perfection of energy, and possessing great energy through the determination of energy endowed with four factors and the attainment of the unique fourfold right exertions. “Gone beyond all phenomena” (sabbadhammāna pāragū) means he reached the far shore, the limit of all knowable things, through the journey of knowledge—thus, he is the one gone beyond all phenomena, meaning the All-Knowing. Alternatively, it means he attained Nibbāna, which is beyond all conditioned phenomena, through self-existent knowledge—thus, he is the one gone beyond all phenomena. “Having heard his Dhamma” (tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvāna) refers to listening to the teaching personally drawn forth by that Blessed Buddha, the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. “I dwelt near him” (vihāsiṃ santike) means that, troubled by wrong thoughts in the mango grove, he went to the Cālikā monastery and dwelt close to the Teacher. “Mindful” (sato) means possessing mindfulness, meaning heedful in the cultivation of serenity and insight. Here, “I” (ahaṃ) should be understood as in “instructed” (anusāsī), where it implies “me,” and similarly, in “the knowledges are attained, the Buddha's teaching has been done” (vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana), it should be understood as “by me” (mayā). And by “the Buddha's teaching has been done” (kataṃ buddhassa sāsana), he reveals the attainment of the three knowledges, as stated, by showing it as the fulfillment of the Teacher's advice, in another way. Indeed, the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth is the accomplishment of the Teacher's teaching.

Meghiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Meghiya is concluded.

7. Ekadhammasavanīyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ekadhammasavanīya

Kilesā [M 1.0190] jhāpitā mayhanti āyasmato ekadhammasavanīyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira [V 1.0161] padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatto katipaye bhikkhū maggamūḷhe mahāraññe vicarante disvā anukampamāno attano bhavanato otaritvā te samassāsetvā bhojetvā yathādhippetaṭṭhānaṃ pāpesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassape bhagavati loke uppajjitvā katabuddhakicce parinibbute tasmiṃ kāle bārāṇasirājā kikī nāma ahosi. Tasmiṃ kālaṅkate tassa puthuvindarājā nāma putto āsi. Tassa putto susāmo nāma. Tassa putto kikībrahmadatto nāma hutvā rajjaṃ kārento sāsane antarahite dhammassavanaṃ alabhanto, “yo dhammaṃ deseti, tassa sahassaṃ dammī”ti ghosāpetvā ekampi dhammakathikaṃ alabhanto, “mayhaṃ pitupitāmahādīnaṃ kāle dhammo saṃvattati, dhammakathikā sulabhā ahesuṃ. Idāni pana catuppadikagāthāmattampi kathento dullabho. Yāva dhammasaññā na vinassati, tāvadeva pabbajissāmī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ uddissa gacchantaṃ sakko devarājā āgantvā, “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti gāthāya dhammaṃ kathetvā nivattesi. So nivattitvā bahuṃ puññaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde setabyanagare seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto bhagavati setabyanagare siṃsapāvane viharante satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ [P 1.0162] nisīdi. Tassa satthā ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā, “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tassa tattha katādhikāratāya so aniccasaññāya pākaṭataraṃ hutvā upaṭṭhitāya paṭiladdhasaṃvego pabbajitvā dhammasammasanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā dukkhasaññaṃ anattasaññañca manasikaronto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.66-71) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Ekadhammasavanīya: 'My defilements have been burnt away.' What is the origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born as a tree deity. Seeing some monks wandering lost in a great wilderness, moved by compassion, he descended from his abode, comforted them, fed them, and guided them to their desired destination. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until he was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. After the Blessed One had completed his task and attained final Nibbāna, at that time, a king named Kikī ruled in Bārāṇasī. When he passed away, his son named Puthuvindarājā succeeded him. His son was named Susāma, and his son, Kikībrahmadatta, ruled the kingdom. When the Dispensation had disappeared and he could no longer hear the Dhamma, he proclaimed, “Whoever teaches me the Dhamma, I will give them a thousand.” Yet, he found not even a single Dhamma preacher. He reflected, “In the time of my father and grandfathers, the Dhamma flourished, and Dhamma teachers were abundant. But now, even one who can recite a four-line verse is hard to find. Before the perception of Dhamma is entirely lost, I shall go forth.” Abandoning the kingdom, he set out toward the Himalayas. Then, Sakka, the king of devas, approached him and taught him the Dhamma with the verse: “Impermanent, alas, are all conditioned things.” Persuaded, he turned back. After returning, he performed many meritorious deeds and wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in a wealthy merchant family in Setabyanagara. When he came of age, he approached the Blessed One, who was dwelling in the Siṃsapā forest near Setabyanagara. After paying homage, he sat to one side. The Teacher, discerning his inclination, taught him the Dhamma with the verse: “Impermanent, alas, are all conditioned things.” Due to his past accumulation of merit, the perception of impermanence arose in him more vividly. Stirred by urgency, he went forth, established reflection on the Dhamma, and by contemplating the perceptions of suffering and non-self, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.12.66-71):

“Padumuttarabuddhassa, sāvakā vanacārino;

Vippanaṭṭhā brahāraññe, andhāva anusuyyare.

“Disciples of the Buddha Padumuttara, forest-dwellers, lost in the great wilderness, wandered about as if blind.

“Anussaritvā sambuddhaṃ, padumuttaranāyakaṃ;

Tassa te munino puttā, vippanaṭṭhā mahāvane.

“Having recollected the Perfectly Enlightened One, the leader Padumuttara, those sons of that Sage were lost in the great forest.

“Bhavanā [M 1.0191] oruhitvāna, agamiṃ bhikkhusantikaṃ;

Tesaṃ maggañca ācikkhiṃ, bhojanañca adāsahaṃ.

“Having descended from my abode, I went to the presence of the monks; I pointed out the path to them, and I gave them food.

“Tena kammena dvipadinda, lokajeṭṭha narāsabha;

Jātiyā sattavassohaṃ, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

“By that deed, O lord of bipeds, foremost in the world, bull among men, at seven years of age I attained arahantship.”

“Sacakkhū nāma nāmena, dvādasa cakkavattino;

Sattaratanasampannā, pañcakappasate ito.

“Five hundred eons from now, there were twelve wheel-turning monarchs named Sacakkhū, endowed with the seven treasures.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Tassa [V 1.0162] ekeneva dhammassavanena nipphannakiccattā ekadhammasavanīyotveva samaññā ahosi. So arahā hutvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Because his task was accomplished by hearing just one Dhamma teaching, he was known by the designation ‘Ekadhammasavanīya.’ Having become an arahant, declaring his final knowledge, he spoke:

67.

67.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“My defilements are burnt up, all becomings are eradicated; the round of births is exhausted, now there is no more renewed existence.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha kilesāti yasmiṃ santāne uppannā, taṃ kilesenti vibādhenti upatāpenti vāti kilesā, rāgādayo. Jhāpitāti indagginā viya rukkhagacchādayo ariyamaggañāṇagginā samūlaṃ daḍḍhā. Mayhanti mayā, mama santāne vā. Bhavā sabbe samūhatāti kāmakammabhavādayo sabbe bhavā samugghāṭitā kilesānaṃ jhāpitattā. Sati hi kilesavaṭṭe kammavaṭṭena bhavitabbaṃ. Kammabhavānaṃ samūhatattā eva ca upapattibhavāpi samūhatā eva anuppattidhammatāya āpāditattā. Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāroti jātiādiko –

Here, ‘defilements’ (kilesā) are so called because, when arisen in a continuum, they defile, harass, or torment it; these are defilements such as lust and others. ‘Burnt up’ means that, like trees and vegetation burnt by Indra’s fire, they are utterly burnt up, roots and all, by the fire of the knowledge of the noble path. ‘My’ means by me, or in my continuum. ‘All becomings are eradicated’ means all becomings, such as sensual becoming and kamma-becoming, are uprooted because the defilements are burnt up. For when the cycle of defilements exists, the cycle of kamma must come to be. And because kamma-becoming is uprooted, rebirth-becoming is also uprooted, having been brought to a state of non-arising. ‘The round of births is exhausted’ means the cycle beginning with birth—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti. –

“The succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, uninterruptedly revolving, is called saṃsāra.” —

Vuttalakkhaṇo [P 1.0163] saṃsāro visesato khīṇo, tasmā natthi dāni punabbhavo. Yasmā āyatiṃ punabbhavo natthi, tasmā vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro. Tasmā ca punabbhavo natthi, yasmā bhavā sabbe samūhatāti āvattetvā vattabbaṃ. Atha vā vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, tato eva natthi dāni punabbhavoti yojetabbaṃ.

The saṃsāra, thus characterized, is especially exhausted; therefore, there is now no more renewed existence. Since there is no renewed existence in the future, the round of births is exhausted. And there is no renewed existence because all becomings are uprooted—it should be stated in this reverse order. Alternatively, it should be connected thus: ‘the round of births is exhausted, and for that very reason there is now no more renewed existence.’

Ekadhammasavanīyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ekadhammasavanīya is concluded.

8. Ekudāniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ekudāniya

Adhicetaso [M 1.0192] appamajjatoti āyasmato ekudāniyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle yakkhasenāpati hutvā nibbatto satthari parinibbute, “alābhā vata me, dulladdhaṃ vata me, yohaṃ satthudharamānakāle dānādipuññaṃ kātuṃ nālattha”nti paridevasokamāpanno ahosi. Atha naṃ sāgaro nāma satthu sāvako sokaṃ vinodetvā satthu thūpapūjāyaṃ niyojesi. So pañca vassāni thūpaṃ [V 1.0163] pūjetvā tato cuto tena puññena devamanussesu eva saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kālena kālaṃ satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkami. Tasmiñca samaye satthā “adhicetaso”ti gāthāya sāvake abhiṇhaṃ ovadi. So taṃ sutvā saddhājāto pabbaji. Pabbajitvā ca pana tameva gāthaṃ punappunaṃ parivatteti. So tattha vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karonto ñāṇassa aparipakkattā visesaṃ nibbattetu nāsakkhi. Tato pana cuto devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā jetavanapaṭiggahaṇasamaye buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco araññe viharanto satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiñca samaye satthā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ attano avidūre adhicittamanuyuttaṃ disvā “adhicetaso”ti imaṃ udānaṃ [P 1.0164] udānesi. Taṃ sutvā ayaṃ cirakālaṃ bhāvanāya araññe viharantopi kālena kālaṃ tameva gāthaṃ udāneti, tenassa ekudāniyoti samaññā udapādi. So athekadivasaṃ cittekaggataṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.72-81) –

“Adhicetaso appamajjato” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ekudāniya. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences as a support for emancipation, was reborn as a general of the yakkhas during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. When the Teacher attained final Nibbāna, he was overcome with lamentation and grief, thinking, “Alas for me, unfortunate am I, that I was not able to perform meritorious deeds like giving while the Teacher was still alive!” Then a disciple of the Teacher named Sāgara dispelled his grief and engaged him in the worship of the Teacher’s stupa. For five years, he worshipped the stupa, and after passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans due to that merit. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a respectable household, and upon reaching maturity, he would from time to time approach the Teacher. At that time, the Teacher frequently exhorted his disciples with the verse beginning, “Adhicetaso.” Hearing it, he was inspired by faith and went forth. After going forth, he repeatedly recited that very verse. For twenty thousand years, he practiced the ascetic life but, due to the immaturity of his knowledge, could not bring about any distinction. After passing away from there, he was reborn in a devaloka and, wandering successively through fortunate existences, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he saw the Buddha’s majesty during the dedication of Jetavana, acquired faith, and went forth. Having fulfilled his prior duties and dwelling in the forest, he approached the Teacher. At that time, the Teacher, seeing the Venerable Sāriputta nearby devoted to the higher mind, uttered this inspired saying, “Adhicetaso.” Hearing it, this elder, though dwelling in the forest for a long time engaged in meditation, would from time to time utter that same verse. Thus, he came to be known as Ekudāniya. Then one day, having attained one-pointedness of mind and developed insight, he reached arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.12.72-81):

“Atthadassimhi sugate, nibbute samanantarā;

Yakkhayoniṃ upapajjiṃ, yasaṃ patto cahaṃ tadā.

“Immediately after the Sugata Atthadassī had attained Nibbāna, I was reborn in the yakkha realm, and at that time, I attained fame.

“Dulladdhaṃ [M 1.0193] vata me āsi, duppabhātaṃ duruṭṭhitaṃ;

Yaṃ me bhoge vijjamāne, parinibbāyi cakkhumā.

An ill-gain indeed it was for me, an ill-dawn, an ill-arising; in that while my wealth was present, the Seeing One has attained Parinibbāna.

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, sāgaro nāma sāvako;

Mamuddharitukāmo so, āgacchi mama santikaṃ.

Having understood my intention, the disciple named Sāgara, wishing to uplift me, came into my presence.

“Kiṃ nu socasi mā bhāyi, cara dhammaṃ sumedhasa;

Anuppadinnā buddhena, sabbesaṃ bījasampadā.

Why indeed do you grieve? Do not fear. O wise one, practice the Dhamma. The accomplishment of the seed has been bestowed by the Buddha for all.

“Yo ce pūreyya sambuddhaṃ, tiṭṭhantaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Dhātuṃ sāsapamattampi, nibbutassāpi pūjaye.

Whether one might honor the Fully Enlightened One, the leader of the world, while he is living, or might honor even a mustard seed-sized relic of one who has attained Nibbāna,

“Same cittappasādamhi, samaṃ puññaṃ mahaggataṃ;

Tasmā thūpaṃ karitvāna, pūjehi jinadhātuyo.

When there is equal serenity of mind, the merit is equal and great; therefore, having built a stupa, worship the relics of the Conqueror.

“Sāgarassa vaco sutvā, buddhathūpaṃ akāsahaṃ;

Pañcavasse paricariṃ, munino thūpamuttamaṃ.

Having heard the words of Sāgara, I built a Buddha-stupa; for five years I attended to the Sage's excellent stupa.

“Tena kammena dvipadinda, lokajeṭṭha narāsabha;

Sampattiṃ anubhotvāna, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

By that deed, O leader of bipeds, foremost in the world, noblest of men, having experienced prosperity, I attained Arahantship.

“Bhūripaññā [V 1.0164] ca cattāro, sattakappasate ito;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

And four of extensive wisdom, seven hundred aeons from this time, endowed with the seven treasures, were wheel-turning monarchs of great might.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimuttisukhena viharanto ekadivasaṃ āyasmatā dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena paṭibhānaṃ vīmaṃsituṃ, “āvuso, mayhaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti ajjhiṭṭho cirakālaparicitattā –

Having attained Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one day, being requested by the venerable Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika, who wished to test his eloquence, 'Friend, recite the Dhamma to me,' because of their long-standing familiarity—

68.

68.

“Adhicetaso appamajjato, munino monapathesu sikkhato;

Sokā na bhavanti tādino, upasantassa sadā satīmato”ti. (udā. 37) –

Sorrows do not exist for such a one who is peaceful and ever mindful: a sage with a higher mind, who is diligent and trains in the paths to wisdom.

Imameva gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He recited this very verse.

Tattha [M 1.0194] adhicetasoti adhicittavato, sabbacittānaṃ adhikena arahattaphalacittena samannāgatassāti attho. Appamajjatoti nappamajjato, appamādena anavajjadhammesu sātaccakiriyāya samannāgatassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Muninoti “yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 269; mahāni. 149; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 21) evaṃ ubhayalokamunanena vā, monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena arahattaphalapaññāsaṅkhātena monena samannāgatatāya vā khīṇāsavo muni nāma, tassa munino. Monapathesu sikkhatoti arahattañāṇasaṅkhātassa monassa pathesu upāyamaggesu sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammesu, tīsu vā sikkhāsu sikkhato. Idañca pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Pariniṭṭhitasikkho hi arahā, tasmā evaṃ sikkhato, imāya sikkhāya munibhāvaṃ pattassa muninoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā cetadevaṃ tasmā heṭṭhimamaggaphalacittānaṃ vasena adhicetaso, catusaccasambodhipaṭipattiyaṃ appamādavasena [P 1.0165] appamajjato, aggamaggañāṇasamannāgamena muninoti evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho yujjatiyeva. Atha vā “appamajjato sikkhato” padhānahetū akkhātāti daṭṭhabbā. Tasmā appamajjanahetu sikkhanahetu ca adhicetasoti attho.

Herein, 'adhicetaso' means one possessing a higher mind; that is, one endowed with the mind of the fruition of Arahantship, which is superior to all other minds. 'Appamajjato' means not negligent; it is said to mean one endowed with the practice of diligence regarding blameless states. 'Munino' refers to a sage. As it is said: 'One who understands both worlds is thereby called a sage.' Thus, either through this understanding of both worlds, or because wisdom is called 'mona,' a taint-extinguished one is called a sage (muni) due to being endowed with that 'mona' designated as the wisdom of the fruition of Arahantship; thus, 'of that sage.' 'Monapathesu sikkhato' means training in the paths to the wisdom (mona) designated as the knowledge of Arahantship—that is, in the ways and means, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—or in the three trainings. This is stated with reference to the preliminary stage of the practice, for an Arahant is one for whom the training is completed. Therefore, 'training thus' should be understood here as 'of the sage who has attained the state of a sage through this training.' And since this is so, the meaning of these terms is indeed fitting: 'adhicetaso' by means of the minds of the lower paths and fruitions; 'appamajjato' by means of diligence in the practice of fully understanding the Four Truths; and 'munino' by means of being endowed with the knowledge of the highest path.

Sokā na bhavanti tādinoti tādisassa khīṇāsavamunino abbhantare iṭṭhaviyogādivatthukā sokā cittasantāpā na honti. Atha vā tādilakkhaṇappattassa asekkhamunino sokā na bhavantīti. Upasantassāti rāgādīnaṃ accantūpasamena upasantassa. Sadā satīmatoti sativepullappattiyā niccakālaṃ satiyā avirahitassa.

'Sorrows do not exist for such a one' means: for such a taint-extinguished sage, sorrows and mental afflictions founded on things like separation from what is dear do not exist within. Or alternatively, sorrows do not exist for the non-trainee sage who has attained the characteristic of being 'such a one.' 'Of one who is at peace' means of one who is at peace through the complete pacification of lust and so forth. 'Of one who is ever mindful' means of one who, having attained fullness of mindfulness, is at all times not bereft of mindfulness.

Ettha [V 1.0165] ca “adhicetaso”ti iminā adhicittasikkhā, “appamajjato”ti iminā adhisīlasikkhā, “munino monapathesu sikkhato”ti etehi adhipaññāsikkhā. “Munino”ti vā etena adhipaññāsikkhā, “monapathesu sikkhato”ti etena tāsaṃ lokuttarasikkhānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadā, “sokā na bhavantī”tiādīhi sikkhāpāripūriyā ānisaṃsā pakāsitāti veditabbaṃ ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosi.

Herein, by 'adhicetaso' is meant the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā); by 'appamajjato,' the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā); and by 'munino monapathesu sikkhato,' the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā). Alternatively, by 'munino' is meant the training in higher wisdom, and by 'monapathesu sikkhato,' the preliminary practice for those supramundane trainings. It should be understood that by the words 'sorrows do not exist,' and so on, the benefits of the fulfillment of the training are declared. And this very verse was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge.

Ekudāniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Ekudāniya is concluded.

9. Channattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Channa

Sutvāna [M 1.0195] dhammaṃ mahato mahārasanti āyasmato channattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagacchantaṃ disvā pasannacitto mudusamphassaṃ paṇṇasantharaṃ santharitvā adāsi. Pupphehi ca [P 1.0166] samantato okiritvā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā punapi aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle suddhodanamahārājassa gehe dāsiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, channotissa nāmaṃ ahosi, bodhisattena sahajāto. So satthu ñātisamāgame paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā bhagavati pemena, “amhākaṃ buddho, amhākaṃ dhammo”ti mamattaṃ uppādetvā sinehaṃ chindituṃ asakkonto samaṇadhammaṃ akatvā satthari parinibbute satthārā āṇattavidhinā katena brahmadaṇḍena santajjito saṃvegappatto hutvā sinehaṃ chinditvā vipassanto nacireneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.10.45-50) –

'Having heard the Dhamma, great, of great flavor'—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Channa. What is their origin? This Elder, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merit in various existences as a basis for turning away from rebirth, was born in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having come of age, one day he saw the Blessed One Siddhattha approaching the foot of a certain tree. With a confident mind, he spread out a soft couch of leaves and gave it. He also performed an act of worship by scattering flowers all around. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas. Again and again performing meritorious deeds and wandering only in happy destinations, in the time of our Blessed One, he was conceived in the womb of a female slave in the house of King Suddhodana. His name was Channa, and he was born at the same time as the Bodhisatta. He gained faith at the gathering of the Teacher's relatives and went forth. Due to his love for the Blessed One, he gave rise to a sense of possession, thinking, 'Our Buddha, our Dhamma.' Unable to cut off this affection, he did not perform the duties of a monk. After the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, having been admonished with the 'higher penalty' imposed according to the Teacher's instruction, he became filled with spiritual urgency. Cutting off his affection and developing insight, he soon attained Arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Siddhatthassa bhagavato, adāsiṃ paṇṇasantharaṃ;

Samantā upahārañca, kusumaṃ okiriṃ ahaṃ.

To the Blessed One Siddhattha, I gave a couch of leaves; and as an offering, I scattered flowers all around.

“Pāsādevaṃ guṇaṃ rammaṃ, anubhomi mahārahaṃ;

Mahagghāni ca pupphāni, sayanebhisavanti me.

In a delightful palace, I experience such a splendid quality; and costly flowers rain down upon my bed.

“Sayanehaṃ tuvaṭṭāmi, vicitte pupphasanthate;

Pupphavuṭṭhi ca sayane, abhivassati tāvade.

I turn over on a variegated bed strewn with flowers; and a rain of flowers continuously falls upon the bed.

“Catunnavutito kappe, adāsiṃ paṇṇasantharaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, santharassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave a couch of leaves; I know of no bad destination since then; this is the fruit of that couch.

“Tiṇasantharakā [V 1.0166] nāma, sattete cakkavattino;

Ito te pañcame kappe, uppajjiṃsu janādhipā.

Seven wheel-turning monarchs named Tiṇasantharaka; in the fifth aeon from this one, they arose as lords of men.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0196] pana patvā vimuttisukhasantappito pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānento –

Having attained Arahantship, satiated with the bliss of liberation, he uttered an inspired utterance impelled by a surge of joy:

69.

69.

“Sutvāna dhammaṃ mahato mahārasaṃ,

Sabbaññutaññāṇavarena desitaṃ;

Maggaṃ papajjiṃ amatassa pattiyā,

So yogakkhemassa pathassa kovido”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

'Having heard the Dhamma, great and of great flavor, taught by the Excellent One with the knowledge of omniscience, I entered upon the path for the attainment of the Deathless. He is skilled in the path to security from the bonds.' Thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha sutvānāti suṇitvā, sotena gahetvā ohitasoto sotadvārānusārena upadhāretvā. Dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ. Mahatoti bhagavato. Bhagavā hi mahantehi uḷāratamehi sīlādiguṇehi samannāgatattā, sadevakena lokena visesato mahanīyatāya ca “mahā”ti vuccati, yā tassa mahāsamaṇoti samaññā jātā. Nissakkavacanañcetaṃ “mahato dhammaṃ sutvānā”ti. Mahārasanti vimuttirasassa dāyakattā uḷārarasaṃ. Sabbaññutaññāṇavarena desitanti sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññū, tassa bhāvo sabbaññutā. Ñāṇameva varaṃ, ñāṇesu vā varanti ñāṇavaraṃ, sabbaññutā ñāṇavaraṃ etassāti sabbaññutaññāṇavaro, bhagavā. Tena sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhātaaggañāṇena vā karaṇabhūtena desitaṃ kathitaṃ dhammaṃ sutvānāti [P 1.0167] yojanā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ paramatthadīpaniyaṃ itivuttakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Magganti aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ ariyamaggaṃ. Papajjinti paṭipajjiṃ. Amatassa pattiyāti nibbānassa adhigamāya upāyabhūtaṃ paṭipajjinti yojanā. Soti so bhagavā. Yogakkhemassa pathassa kovidoti catūhi yogehi anupaddutassa nibbānassa yo patho, tassa kovido tattha sukusalo. Ayañhettha attho – bhagavato catusaccadesanaṃ sutvā amatādhigamūpāyamaggaṃ ahaṃ paṭipajjiṃ paṭipajjanamaggaṃ mayā kataṃ, so eva pana bhagavā sabbathā yogakkhemassa pathassa kovido, parasantāne vā paramanesu kusalo, yassa saṃvidhānamāgamma ahampi maggaṃ paṭipajjinti. Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosīti.

Herein, ‘having heard’ (sutvāna) means having listened, having grasped with the ear, being attentive, and having comprehended through the ear-door. ‘Dhamma’ means the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. ‘Of the Great One’ (mahato) means of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One is called ‘Great’ because He is endowed with great and most excellent qualities such as virtue, and because He is especially revered by the world with its devas; hence the designation ‘the Great Ascetic’ arose for Him. And this is an ablative expression: ‘having heard the Dhamma of the Great One.’ ‘Of great flavor’ (mahārasaṃ) means of supreme flavor, because it bestows the flavor of liberation. ‘Taught by the one with supreme knowledge of omniscience’ (Sabbaññutaññāṇavarena desitaṃ): ‘He knows all’ (sabbaṃ jānāti), thus He is ‘omniscient’ (sabbaññū); His state is ‘omniscience’ (sabbaññutā). ‘Knowledge itself is supreme’ (ñāṇameva varaṃ), or ‘supreme among knowledges’ (ñāṇesu varaṃ), thus ‘supreme knowledge’ (ñāṇavaraṃ). ‘This supreme knowledge of omniscience belongs to Him’ (sabbaññutā ñāṇavaraṃ etassa), thus He, the Blessed One, is ‘the one with supreme knowledge of omniscience’ (sabbaññutaññāṇavaro). The construction is: ‘having heard the Dhamma taught and spoken by means of that instrumental, supreme knowledge known as omniscience.’ Whatever should be said here is to be understood in the way explained in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Itivuttaka. ‘The Path’ (maggaṃ) means the Noble Eightfold Path. ‘I entered’ (papajjiṃ) means I practiced. ‘For the attainment of the Deathless’ (amatassa pattiyā): the construction is, ‘I practiced the path which is the means for the realization of Nibbāna.’ ‘He’ (so) means that Blessed One. ‘Skilled in the path to security from bondage’ (yogakkhemassa pathassa kovido): He is skilled, highly proficient, in that path to Nibbāna which is undisturbed by the four yokes. The meaning here is this: ‘Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Four Noble Truths, I practiced the path that is the means to attain the Deathless; the path of practice was undertaken by me. That Blessed One is in every way skilled in the path to security from bondage, or is adept in training others. By relying on His instruction, I too practiced the path.’ And this was the Elder’s verse of declaration of final knowledge.

Channattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Channa is concluded.

10. Puṇṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇa

Sīlamevāti [M 1.0197][V 1.0167] āyasmato puṇṇattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe buddhasuññe loke brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantappadese paṇṇakuṭiṃ katvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa vasanaṭṭhānassa avidūre ekasmiṃ pabbhāre paccekabuddho ābādhiko hutvā parinibbāyi, tassa parinibbānasamaye mahā āloko ahosi. Taṃ disvā so, “kathaṃ nu kho ayaṃ āloko uppanno”ti vīmaṃsanavasena ito cito ca āhiṇḍanto [P 1.0168] pabbhāre paccekasambuddhaṃ parinibbutaṃ disvā gandhadārūni saṃkaḍḍhitvā sarīraṃ jhāpetvā gandhodakena upasiñci. Tattheko devaputto antalikkhe ṭhatvā evamāha – “sādhu, sādhu, sappurisa, bahuṃ tayā puññaṃ pasavantena pūritaṃ sugatisaṃvattaniyaṃ kammaṃ tena tvaṃ sugatīsuyeva uppajjissasi, ‘puṇṇo’ti ca te nāmaṃ bhavissatī”ti. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sunāparantajanapade suppārakapaṭṭane gahapatikule nibbatti, puṇṇotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto vāṇijjavasena mahatā satthena saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ gato. Tena ca samayena bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Atha so sāvatthivāsīhi upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gato satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vattapaṭivattehi ācariyupajjhāye ārādhento vihāsi. So ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “sādhu maṃ, bhante bhagavā, saṃkhittena ovādena ovadatu, yamahaṃ sutvā sunāparantajanapade vihareyya”nti āha. Tassa bhagavā, “santi kho, puṇṇa, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.395; saṃ. ni. 4.88) ovādaṃ datvā sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā vissajjesi. So bhagavantaṃ vanditvā sunāparantajanapadaṃ gantvā suppārakapaṭṭane viharanto samathavipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā tisso vijjā sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.41.29-44) –

“Virtue alone”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma in various existences as a foundation for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family during a world period devoid of Buddhas, ninety-one eons ago. Having reached maturity, he mastered the brahmin arts and, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned household life and went forth as an ascetic. He built a leaf hut in the Himalayan region and dwelt there. Not far from his dwelling place, on a mountainside, a Paccekabuddha who was ill passed away into final Nibbāna. At the moment of his passing, a great light appeared. Seeing this, the ascetic wondered, “How has this light arisen?” Wandering here and there in search of its cause, he discovered the Paccekabuddha who had passed into final Nibbāna on the mountainside. Gathering fragrant wood, he cremated the body and sprinkled it with scented water. Then a deva stood in the sky and said, “Well done, well done, good man! You have generated much merit, karma that leads to a fortunate rebirth. Because of this, you will be reborn only in happy realms, and your name will be ‘Puṇṇa.’” Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, during this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a householder's family in the Sunāparanta country, in the port town of Suppāraka. His name was Puṇṇa. When he came of age, he traveled to Sāvatthī with a large caravan for trade. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī. Puṇṇa went to the monastery with the lay devotees of Sāvatthī, heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, and, having gained faith, went forth into homelessness. He lived diligently, pleasing his teachers and preceptors by fulfilling his duties. One day, he approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One give me a brief exhortation, which having heard, I may dwell in the Sunāparanta country.” The Blessed One gave him the exhortation beginning, “Puṇṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye…” (MN 145; SN 35.88), and having caused him to roar the lion’s roar, dismissed him. After paying homage to the Blessed One, Puṇṇa went to the Sunāparanta country and dwelt in Suppārakapaṭṭana. Striving in serenity and insight, he realized the three knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.41.29-44):

“Pabbhārakūṭaṃ nissāya, sayambhū aparājito;

Ābādhiko ca so buddho, vasati pabbatantare.

“Near Pabbhāra Peak, the Self-existent One, the Unconquered; though ailing, that Buddha dwells in the mountain’s interior.”

“Mama [M 1.0198] assamasāmantā, panādo āsi tāvade;

Buddhe nibbāyamānamhi, āloko udapajjatha.

“Near my hermitage, a loud noise arose at that moment; when the Buddha was passing into Nibbāna, a light appeared.”

“Yāvatā vanasaṇḍasmiṃ, acchakokataracchakā;

Vāḷā ca kesarī sabbe, abhigajjiṃsu tāvade.

“Throughout the forest grove, bears, wolves, and hyenas, wild beasts and all the lions, roared together then.”

“Uppātaṃ [V 1.0168] tamahaṃ disvā, pabbhāraṃ agamāsahaṃ;

Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, nibbutaṃ aparājitaṃ.

“Having seen that portent, I went to the mountain slope; there I saw the Sambuddha, extinguished, the Unconquered.”

“Suphullaṃ sālarājaṃva, sataraṃsiṃva uggataṃ;

Vītaccikaṃva aṅgāraṃ, nibbutaṃ aparājitaṃ.

“Like a sāl-tree king in full bloom, like the risen hundred-rayed sun; like a flameless ember, extinguished, the Unconquered.”

“Tiṇaṃ kaṭṭhañca pūretvā, citakaṃ tatthakāsahaṃ;

Citakaṃ sukataṃ katvā, sarīraṃ jhāpayiṃ ahaṃ.

“Having piled up grass and wood, I made a pyre there; having prepared the pyre well, I myself cremated the body.”

“Sarīraṃ jhāpayitvāna, gandhatoyaṃ samokiriṃ;

Antalikkhe ṭhito yakkho, nāmamaggahi tāvade.

“Having cremated the body, I sprinkled scented water; a yakkha standing in the sky proclaimed my name at that moment.”

“Yaṃ pūritaṃ tayā kiccaṃ, sayambhussa mahesino;

Puṇṇako nāma nāmena, sadā hohi tuvaṃ mune.

“For the duty you have fulfilled for the Self-existent Great Sage, may you, O sage, always be known by the name Puṇṇa.”

“Tamhā kāyā cavitvāna, devalokaṃ agacchahaṃ;

Tattha dibbamayo gandho, antalikkhā pavassati.

“Having passed away from that body, I went to the world of the devas; there, a divine fragrance rained down from the sky.”

“Tatrāpi nāmadheyyaṃ me, puṇṇakoti ahū tadā;

Devabhūto manusso vā, saṅkappaṃ pūrayāmahaṃ.

“There also my name was Puṇṇaka at that time; whether I became a deva or a human, I fulfilled my resolve.”

“Idaṃ pacchimakaṃ mayhaṃ, carimo vattate bhavo;

Idhāpi puṇṇako nāma, nāmadheyyaṃ pakāsati.

“This is my final existence, the last round of becoming is turning. Here too, the name Puṇṇaka is renowned.”

“Tosayitvāna sambuddhaṃ, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

“Having pleased the Sambuddha, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans, having fully understood all the taints, I dwell without taints.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, tanukiccassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“For the deed I did then, ninety-one eons ago, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of that small deed.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0199] pana patvā thero bahū manusse sāsane abhippasādesi. Yato pañcasatamattā purisā upāsakattaṃ pañcasatamattā ca itthiyo upāsikābhāvaṃ paṭivedesuṃ. So tattha rattacandanena candanamāḷaṃ nāma gandhakuṭiṃ kārāpetvā, “satthā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ māḷaṃ paṭicchatū”ti bhagavantaṃ pupphadūtena nimantesi[P 1.0169]. Bhagavā ca iddhānubhāvena tattakehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ tattha gantvā candanamāḷaṃ paṭiggahetvā aruṇe anuṭṭhiteyeva paccāgamāsi. Thero aparabhāge parinibbānasamaye aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, the elder inspired great confidence in the teaching in many people. Consequently, about five hundred men declared themselves lay followers, and about five hundred women declared themselves female lay followers. He then had a perfumed chamber named Candanamāḷa built there with red sandalwood, and sent a floral messenger to invite the Blessed One, saying, “May the Teacher, together with five hundred monks, accept the pavilion.” The Blessed One, by his psychic power, went there with that very number of monks, accepted the Candanamāḷa, and returned before the break of dawn. Later, at the time of his final Nibbāna, the elder, declaring his final knowledge, said:

70.

70.

“Sīlameva [V 1.0169] idha aggaṃ, paññavā pana uttamo;

Manussesu ca devesu, sīlapaññāṇato jaya”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Virtue indeed is foremost here, but the wise one is supreme; among humans and gods, victory is from virtue and wisdom.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha sīlanti sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena samādhānaṭṭhena cāti attho. Sīlañhi sabbaguṇānaṃ patiṭṭhā, tenāha – “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.23; peṭako. 22; visuddhi. 1.1). Samādahati ca taṃ kāyavācāavippakiṇṇaṃ karotīti attho. Tayidaṃ sīlameva aggaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ mūlabhāvato pamukhabhāvato ca. Yathāha – “tasmātiha, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ādimeva visodhehi kusalesu dhammesu. Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ sīlañca suvisuddha”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.369), “pātimokkhanti mukhametaṃ pamukhameta”nti (mahāva. 135) ca ādi. Idhāti nipātamattaṃ. Paññavāti ñāṇasampanno. So uttamo seṭṭho pavaroti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya gāthāya paññāyayeva seṭṭhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Paññuttarā hi kusalā dhammā. Idāni taṃ sīlapaññānaṃ aggaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ kāraṇato dasseti “manussesu ca devesu, sīlapaññāṇato jaya”nti ca. Sīlapaññāṇahetu paṭipakkhajayo kāmakilesajayo hotīti attho.

Therein, 'virtue' (sīla) is so called in the sense of composing, in the sense of being a foundation, and in the sense of harmonizing—this is the meaning. For virtue is the foundation of all good qualities, as it is said: “A wise person, established in virtue…” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.23; Peṭako. 22; Visuddhi. 1.1). And it harmonizes, meaning it makes body and speech unscattered. This very virtue is foremost among all good qualities because it is their root and because it is pre-eminent. As it is said: “Therefore, monk, here you should first purify the wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified…” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.369), and “The Pātimokkha is the beginning, it is the foremost…” (Mahāva. 135), and so on. ‘Here’ is merely a particle. ‘Wise’ (paññavā) means one endowed with knowledge. ‘He is supreme, best, excellent’—by means of this verse, which is based on the individual, it shows that supremacy belongs to wisdom alone. For wholesome states have wisdom as their chief. Now, it shows the reason for this supreme excellence of virtue and wisdom with the words: “among humans and gods, victory is from virtue and wisdom.” The meaning is: through virtue and wisdom as the cause, there is victory over the opposing side, victory over the defilements of sensual desire.

Puṇṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇa is concluded.

Sattamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Seventh Chapter is concluded.

8. Aṭṭhamavaggo

8. The Eighth Chapter

1. Vacchapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchapāla

Susukhumanipuṇatthadassināti [M 1.0200][V 1.0170] āyasmato vacchapālattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni ācinanto devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito ekanavute kappe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā aggiṃ paricaranto ekadivasaṃ mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā pāyāsaṃ ādāya [P 1.0170] dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesanto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ ākāse caṅkamantaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittajāto bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā dātukāmataṃ dassesi. Paṭiggahesi bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, vacchapālotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So bimbisārasamāgame uruvelakassapattherena iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā satthu paramanipaccakāre kate taṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā sattāhapabbajito eva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.26-34) –

“One who sees the extremely subtle and refined meaning” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vacchapāla. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences and wandering among gods and humans, was, ninety-one eons ago, born into a brahmin family. Having perfected the brahmin crafts and tending the sacred fire, one day, carrying milk-rice in a large bronze bowl while seeking a worthy recipient, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī walking in the sky, and his mind arose with wonder and amazement. He paid homage to the Blessed One and showed his desire to give. The Blessed One accepted out of compassion. Through that meritorious action, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha, and his name was Vacchapāla. At Bimbisāra’s assembly, when the Elder Uruvela Kassapa displayed miraculous power and supreme reverence was shown to the Teacher, seeing that, he gained faith, went forth, and having been ordained for only seven days, developed insight and attained the six superknowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.13.26-34):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddho, bāttiṃsavaralakkhaṇo;

Pavanā abhinikkhanto, bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhato.

“The golden-hued Sambuddha, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks, came forth from the forest, honored by the community of monks.

“Mahaccā kaṃsapātiyā, vaḍḍhetvā pāyasaṃ ahaṃ;

Āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmo so, upanesiṃ baliṃ ahaṃ.

“Having prepared milk-rice in a large bronze bowl, I, desiring to make an offering, brought the oblation near.

“Bhagavā tamhi samaye, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Caṅkamaṃ susamārūḷho, ambare anilāyane.

“The Blessed One at that time, the world’s eldest, the bull among men, had well ascended a walkway in the windless sky.

“Tañca acchariyaṃ disvā, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Ṭhapayitvā kaṃsapātiṃ, vipassiṃ abhivādayiṃ.

“Seeing that marvel, a wonder that was hair-raising, I set down the bronze bowl and paid homage to Vipassī.

“Tuvaṃ devosi sabbaññū, sadeve sahamānuse;

Anukampaṃ upādāya, paṭiggaṇha mahāmuni.

“‘You are a god, the all-knowing one in the world with its gods and humans. Out of compassion, O great sage, please accept this.’

“Paṭiggahesi [M 1.0201][V 1.0171] bhagavā, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, satthā loke mahāmuni.

“The Blessed One, the all-knowing, the world’s leader, the Teacher, the great sage in the world, accepted, having understood my intention.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pāyāsassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“For the gift I gave then, ninety-one eons ago, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of that milk-rice.

“Ekatālīsito kappe, buddho nāmāsi khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Forty-one eons ago, there was a Khattiya named Buddho, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā sukheneva attanā nibbānassa adhigatabhāvaṃ vibhāvento –

But having attained Arahantship, explaining how Nibbāna was easily attained by himself, he said:

71.

71.

“Susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā, matikusalena nivātavuttinā;

Saṃsevitavuddhasīlinā, nibbānaṃ na hi tena dullabha”nti. –

“For one who sees the extremely subtle and refined meaning, is skilled in intellect, humble in conduct, and has associated with the virtuous elders, Nibbāna is indeed not difficult to attain.”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this verse.

Tattha susukhumanipuṇatthadassināti ativiya duddasaṭṭhena sukhume, saṇhaṭṭhena nipuṇe saccapaṭiccasamuppādādiatthe aniccatādiṃ oropetvā passatīti susukhumanipuṇatthadassī, tena. Matikusalenāti matiyā paññāya kusalena chekena, “evaṃ pavattamānassa paññā vaḍḍhati, evaṃ na vaḍḍhatī”ti dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgapaññāya uppādane kusalena. Nivātavuttināti sabrahmacārīsu nivātanīcavattanasīlena, vuḍḍhesu navesu ca yathānurūpapaṭipattinā. Saṃsevitavuddhasīlināti saṃsevitaṃ āciṇṇaṃ vuddhasīlaṃ saṃsevitavuddhasīlaṃ, taṃ yassa atthi, tena saṃsevitavuddhasīlinā. Atha vā saṃsevitā upāsitā vuddhasīlino etenāti saṃsevitavuddhasīlī, tena[P 1.0171]. Hītisaddo hetuattho. Yasmā yo nivātavutti saṃsevitavuddhasīlī matikusalo susukhumanipuṇatthadassī ca, tasmā nibbānaṃ na tassa dullabhanti attho. Nivātavuttitāya hi saṃsevitavuddhasīlitāya ca paṇḍitā taṃ ovaditabbaṃ anusāsitabbaṃ maññanti, tesañca ovāde ṭhito sayaṃ [M 1.0202] matikusalatāya susukhumanipuṇatthadassitāya ca vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva nibbānaṃ adhigacchatīti, ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosīti.

Therein, 'by one who sees the extremely subtle and refined meaning' (susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā): one is a 'seer of the extremely subtle and refined meaning' because one sees the meanings of the truths, dependent origination, etc.—which are subtle in the sense of being extremely difficult to see, and refined in the sense of being delicate—by applying the perception of impermanence and so on to them. By such a one. 'By one skilled in intellect' (matikusalenāti) means skilled, clever, in the thought that is wisdom; skilled in producing the wisdom of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, knowing, “Thus his wisdom grows; thus it does not grow.” 'By one of humble conduct' (nivātavuttināti) means by one with the virtue of humble and lowly conduct towards fellow monastics, and by one who acts appropriately towards elders and new monks. 'By one who has cultivated mature virtue' (saṃsevitavuddhasīlinā): mature virtue that is cultivated and practiced is 'cultivated mature virtue'; by one who possesses this. Or alternatively, those of mature virtue have been associated with and served by him, thus he is 'one who has associated with those of mature virtue'; by such a one. The word 'hi' has the meaning of cause. The meaning is: because one who is of humble conduct, has associated with those of mature virtue, is skilled in intellect, and sees the extremely subtle and refined meaning, therefore Nibbāna is not difficult for him to attain. Indeed, due to his humble conduct and his association with those of mature virtue, the wise consider him worthy of advice and instruction. Established in their advice, and by himself engaging in the practice of insight meditation through his skill in intellect and his seeing of the extremely subtle and refined meaning, he attains Nibbāna before long. And this very verse was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Vacchapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vacchapāla is concluded.

2. Ātumattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ātuma

Yathā [V 1.0172] kaḷīro susu vaḍḍhitaggoti āyasmato ātumattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ ācinanto ito ekanavute kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ antaravīthiyaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso gandhodakena gandhacuṇṇena ca pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi, ñāṇassa pana aparipakkattā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhiputto hutvā nibbatti, ātumotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa vayappattassa mātā “puttassa me bhariyaṃ ānessāmā”ti ñātakehi sammantesi. So taṃ upadhāretvā hetusampattiyā codiyamāno “kiṃ mayhaṃ gharāvāsena, idāneva pabbajissāmī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā pabbaji. Pabbajitampi naṃ mātā uppabbājetukāmā nānānayehi palobheti. So tassā avasaraṃ adatvā attano ajjhāsayaṃ pakāsento –

“Just as a young shoot with its tip well grown” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ātuma. What was its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences that was a supporting condition for release from the round of rebirths. Ninety-one eons ago, he was born into a householder’s family and attained maturity. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī walking along the street, his mind became joyful, and he made offerings with perfumed water and scented powder. By that deed of merit, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Wandering from one good destination to another, he later went forth in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa and practiced the duties of a recluse. However, because his knowledge was not yet fully matured, he could not bring about any special attainment. Then, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī, and his name was Ātuma. When he came of age, his mother thought, “I will bring a wife for my son,” and consulted with relatives. Perceiving this, and being urged by the maturity of conditions, he thought, “What is household life to me? I shall go forth right now.” He went to the monks and ordained. Even after his ordination, his mother, wishing to make him disrobe, tempted him in various ways. He, however, gave her no opportunity, and revealing his own inclination, said:

72.

72.

“Yathā kaḷīro susu vaḍḍhitaggo, dunnikkhamo hoti pasākhajāto;

Evaṃ ahaṃ bhariyāyānītāya, anumañña maṃ pabbajitomhi dānī”ti. –

“Just as a young shoot, well-grown at the tip, having produced side branches, is difficult to extract; so too, if a wife were brought to me, I would become difficult to extract. Permit me, for I have now gone forth.”

Gāthaṃ [P 1.0172] abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 1.0203] kaḷīroti aṅkuro, idha pana vaṃsaṅkuro adhippeto. Susūti taruṇo. Vaḍḍhitaggoti pavaḍḍhitasākho. Susuvaḍḍhitaggoti vā suṭṭhu vaḍḍhitasākho sañjātapattasākho. Dunnikkhamoti veḷugumbato nikkhāmetuṃ nīharituṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Pasākhajātoti jātapasākho, sākhānampi pabbe pabbe uppannaanusākho. Evaṃ ahaṃ bhariyāyānītāyāti yathā vaṃso vaḍḍhitaggo vaṃsantaresu saṃsaṭṭha sākhāpasākho veḷugumbato dunnīharaṇīyo hoti, evaṃ ahampi bhariyāya mayhaṃ ānītāya puttadhītādivasena vaḍḍhitaggo āsattivasena gharāvāsato dunnīharaṇīyo bhaveyyaṃ. Yathā pana vaṃsakaḷīro asañjātasākhabandho veḷugumbato sunīharaṇīyova hoti, evaṃ ahampi asañjātaputtadārādibandho sunīharaṇīyo homi, tasmā anānītāya eva bhariyāya anumañña maṃ attanāva maṃ anujānāpetvā. Pabbajitomhi dānīti, “idāni pana pabbajito amhi, sādhu suṭṭhū”ti attano nekkhammābhiratiṃ pakāsesi, atha vā “anumañña maṃ pabbajitomhi dānī”ti mātu katheti. Ayañhettha attho – yadipi tāya pubbe nānumataṃ, idāni pana pabbajito amhi, tasmā anumañña anujānāhi maṃ samaṇabhāveyeva ṭhātuṃ, nāhaṃ tayā nivattanīyoti[V 1.0173]. Evaṃ pana kathento yathāṭhitova vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā kilese khepetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.35-40) –

Herein, kaḷīro means a sprout, but in this context, a bamboo shoot is intended. Susū means young. Vaḍḍhitaggo means having grown branches. Or, susuvaḍḍhitaggo means having well-grown branches, with leaves and shoots fully developed. Dunnikkhamo means difficult to extract or remove from the bamboo clump. Pasākhajāto means having produced side branches, that is, secondary shoots that have arisen at each node of the branches. “So too I, if a wife were brought to me”: just as a bamboo with a grown tip, its branches and side branches entangled among other bamboos, is difficult to remove from the bamboo clump, so too would I, if a wife were brought to me, become difficult to remove from the household life, having a “grown tip” in the sense of sons and daughters, and being attached. But just as a bamboo shoot, without the entanglement of branches, is easily removed from the bamboo clump, so too am I, without the bonds of sons, wife, and so forth, easily removed. Therefore, while a wife has not yet been brought, permit me—that is, allow me yourself. “For I have now gone forth”: with this, he declared his delight in renunciation, saying, “Now I have indeed gone forth; it is good, it is excellent!” Alternatively, he says to his mother, “Permit me, for I have now gone forth.” The meaning here is this: even if she had not approved before, now I have gone forth; therefore, permit me, allow me to remain in the state of a recluse. I am not to be turned back by you. Speaking thus, remaining as he was, he developed insight and, by the sequence of the path, eradicated the defilements and became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nisajja pāsādavare, vipassiṃ addasaṃ jinaṃ;

Kakudhaṃ vilasantaṃva, sabbaññuṃ tamanāsakaṃ.

“Seated in the excellent palace, I saw Vipassī, the Conqueror, resplendent like a Kakudha tree in full bloom, the Omniscient One, the destroyer of darkness.

“Pāsādassāvidūre ca, gacchati lokanāyako;

Pabhā niddhāvate tassa, yathā ca sataraṃsino.

“And not far from the palace, the Leader of the World proceeds; his radiance streams forth, like that of the hundred-rayed sun.

“Gandhodakañca paggayha, buddhaseṭṭhaṃ samokiriṃ;

Tena cittappasādena, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Taking up perfumed water, I sprinkled it upon the supreme Buddha; with that serenity of mind, I passed away there.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ gandhodakamākiriṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-one aeons since I sprinkled the perfumed water, I have known no bad destination—this is the fruit of homage to the Buddha.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, sugandho nāma khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Thirty-one aeons ago, I was a khattiya named Sugandha, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned away… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Chaḷabhiñño [M 1.0204] pana hutvā mātaraṃ āpucchitvā tassā pekkhantiyāyeva ākāsena pakkāmi. So arahattappattiyā uttarikālampi antarantarā tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, he took leave of his mother and departed through the air even as she watched. Even in the time after his attainment of arahantship, he would from time to time recite that same verse.

Tattha “pabbajitomhī”ti imināpadesena ayampi therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosi [P 1.0173] attano santāne rāgādimalassa pabbājitabhāvadīpanato. Tenāha bhagavā – “pabbājayamattano malaṃ, tasmā ‘pabbajito’ti vuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 388).

Here, by means of the phrase “I have gone forth,” this verse also became the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge, as it indicated the banishment of the stain of lust and other defilements from his own continuum. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Because one has banished one’s own stain, one is called ‘one who has gone forth.’”

Ātumattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ātuma is concluded.

3. Māṇavattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Māṇava

Jiṇṇañca disvā dukhitañca byādhitanti āyasmato māṇavattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā lakkhaṇadharo hutvā vipassissa bhagavato abhijātiyā lakkhaṇāni pariggahetvā pubbanimittāni sāvetvā, “ekaṃsena ayaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti [V 1.0174] byākaritvā nānānayehi thometvā abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālassa gehe nibbattitvā yāva sattavassāni, tāva antoghareyeva vaḍḍhitvā sattame saṃvacchare upanayanatthaṃ uyyānaṃ nīto antarāmagge jiṇṇāturamate disvā tesaṃ adiṭṭhapubbattā te parijane pucchitvā jarārogamaraṇasabhāvaṃ sutvā sañjātasaṃvego tato anivattanto vihāraṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.41-64) –

“Seeing the aged, the afflicted, and the sick”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Māṇava. What is its origin? This one too had made his aspiration in the time of previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome actions that support liberation in various lives. Ninety-one aeons ago, he was born into a brahmin family and became an expert in the marks of a great man. Having examined the marks on the Blessed One Vipassī at his birth and proclaimed the omens, he declared with certainty, “This one will surely become a Buddha!” He praised him in various ways, paid homage to him, circumambulated him, and departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered only in good destinations until, during this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the house of a wealthy brahmin in Sāvatthī. He grew up within the household until he was seven years old. In his seventh year, while being taken to a park for his initiation ceremony, he saw an aged person, a sick person, and a dead person along the way. As he had never seen such things before, he asked his attendants about them. Upon hearing of the nature of old age, sickness, and death, he was stirred with a sense of urgency. Without turning back from there, he went to the monastery, listened to the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence, obtained his parents’ permission, and went forth. Establishing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Jāyamāne vipassimhi, nimittaṃ byākariṃ ahaṃ;

Nibbāpayiñca janataṃ, buddho loke bhavissati.

“When Vipassī was being born, I interpreted the omens and reassured the people, saying: ‘A Buddha will arise in the world.’

“Yasmiñca [M 1.0205] jāyamānasmiṃ, dasasahassi kampati;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth the ten-thousandfold world system trembled—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, āloko vipulo ahu;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth a vast light appeared—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, saritāyo na sandayuṃ;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth the rivers did not flow—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, avīcaggi na pajjali;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth the fire of Avīci did not blaze—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, pakkhisaṅgho na sañcari;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth the flocks of birds did not fly—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, vātakkhandho na vāyati;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth the mass of wind did not blow—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, sabbaratanāni jotayuṃ;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth all the jewels shone—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānasmiṃ, sattāsuṃ padavikkamā;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“He at whose birth seven steps were taken—that Blessed One, the Teacher, the One with Vision, now teaches the Dhamma.

“Jātamatto ca sambuddho, disā sabbā vilokayi;

Vācāsabhimudīresi, esā buddhāna dhammatā.

“Just born, the Sambuddha surveyed all directions; he uttered a bull-like utterance—this is the nature of Buddhas.

“Saṃvejayitvā janataṃ, thavitvā lokanāyakaṃ;

Sambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā, pakkāmiṃ pācināmukho.

“Having stirred a sense of urgency in the people and having praised the Leader of the World, having paid homage to the Sambuddha, I departed facing east.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhithomayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, thomanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-one aeons since I praised the Buddha, I have known no bad destination—this is the fruit of that praise.

“Ito [V 1.0175] navutikappamhi, sammukhāthavikavhayo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Ninety aeons ago, I was a king named Sammukhāthavika, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Pathavīdundubhi nāma, ekūnanavutimhito;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-nine aeons ago, I was a king named Pathavīdundubhi, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Aṭṭhāsītimhito [M 1.0206] kappe, obhāso nāma khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-eight aeons ago, I was a khattiya named Obhāsa, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Sattāsītimhito kappe, saritacchedanavhayo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-seven aeons ago, I was a king named Saritacchedana, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Agginibbāpano nāma, kappānaṃ chaḷasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-six aeons ago, I was a king named Agginibbāpana, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Gatipacchedano nāma, kappānaṃ pañcasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-five aeons ago, I was a king named Gatipacchedana, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Rājā vātasamo nāma, kappānaṃ cullasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eighty-four aeons ago, I was a king named Vātasama, endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Ratanapajjalo nāma, kappānaṃ teasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

Eighty-three aeons ago, there was a king named Ratanapajjala; endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Padavikkamano nāma, kappānaṃ dveasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

Eighty-two aeons ago, there was a king named Padavikkamana; endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Rājā vilokano nāma, kappānaṃ ekasītiyā;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

Eighty-one aeons ago, there was a king named Vilokana; endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Girasāroti nāmena, kappesītimhi khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

In the eightieth aeon, there was a noble warrior named Girasāra; endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Adhigatārahatto pana bhikkhūhi, “kena, tvaṃ āvuso, saṃvegena atidaharova samāno pabbajito”ti pucchito attano pabbajjānimittakittanāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto –

However, the bhikkhu who had attained arahantship, when asked by the monks, “Friend, by what sense of urgency did you go forth while still so very young?” made his declaration of final knowledge under the pretext of stating the reason for his going forth:

73.

73.

“Jiṇṇañca [P 1.0174] disvā dukhitañca byādhitaṃ, matañca disvā gatamāyusaṅkhayaṃ;

Tato ahaṃ nikkhamitūna pabbajiṃ, pahāya kāmāni manoramānī”ti. –

“Seeing the aged, the suffering, and the sick, seeing the dead, their life’s term ended, then I went forth into homelessness, abandoning delightful sensual pleasures.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 1.0207][V 1.0176] jiṇṇanti jarāya abhibhūtaṃ, khaṇḍiccapāliccavalittacatādīhi samaṅgībhūtaṃ. Dukhitanti dukkhappattaṃ. Byādhitanti gilānaṃ. Ettha ca “byādhita”nti vuttepi dukkhappattabhāvo siddho, “dukhita”nti vacanaṃ tassa bāḷhagilānabhāvaparidīpanatthaṃ. Matanti kālaṅkataṃ, yasmā kālaṅkato āyuno khayaṃ vayaṃ bhedaṃ gato nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “gatamāyusaṅkhaya”nti. Tasmā jiṇṇabyādhimatānaṃ diṭṭhattā, “ime jarādayo nāma na imesaṃyeva, atha kho sabbasādhāraṇā, tasmā ahampi jarādike anativatto”ti saṃviggattā. Nikkhamitūnāti nikkhamitvā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Pabbajjādhippāyena gharato niggantvā. Pabbajinti satthu sāsane pabbajaṃ upagato. Pahāya kāmāni manoramānīti iṭṭhakantādibhāvato avītarāgānaṃ mano ramentīti manorame vatthukāme pajahitvā, tappaṭibaddhassa chandarāgassa ariyamaggena samucchindanena nirapekkhabhāvena chaḍḍetvāti attho. Kāmānaṃ pahānakittanamukhena cetaṃ therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi. Māṇavakāle pabbajitattā imassa therassa māṇavotveva samaññā jātāti.

Therein, “aged” means overcome by old age, afflicted with such things as broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin. “Suffering” means one who has encountered suffering. “Sick” means ill. And here, although the state of having encountered suffering is established when “sick” is said, the word “suffering” is used to emphasize the severity of the illness. “Dead” means one who has passed away; because one who has passed away is said to have reached the destruction, decay, and dissolution of life, it is therefore said, “their life’s term ended.” Thus, from having seen the aged, sick, and dead, he felt a sense of urgency, thinking, “This aging and so forth are not unique to them, but are common to all. Therefore, I too cannot overcome aging and the like.” “Then I went forth” means having gone forth; or this is the reading itself. It means having left home with the intention of ordination. “Into homelessness” means he undertook the going forth in the Teacher’s Dispensation. “Abandoning delightful sensual pleasures” means having forsaken sensual objects which are delightful because they delight the minds of those who are not free from passion, due to their being desirable and pleasing; the meaning is that he discarded them with non-attachment by eradicating the sensual desire and passion connected with them through the noble path. This statement about abandoning sensual pleasures was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge. Because this Elder went forth as a youth, he became known as “Māṇava” (Youth).

Māṇavattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Māṇava is concluded.

4. Suyāmanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Suyāmana

Kāmacchando ca byāpādoti āyasmato suyāmanattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle dhaññavatīnagare brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā [P 1.0175] vayappatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā brāhmaṇamante vāceti. Tena ca samayena vipassī bhagavā mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ dhaññavatīnagaraṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho hoti. Taṃ disvā brāhmaṇo pasannacitto attano gehaṃ netvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā tassūpari pupphasanthāraṃ santharitvā adāsi, satthari tattha nisinne paṇītena āhārena santappesi, bhuttāviñca pupphagandhena pūjesi. Satthā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā [M 1.0208] devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, suyāmanotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū paramanissamayutto hutvā gehavāsīnaṃ kāmūpabhogaṃ jigucchitvā jhānaninno bhagavato vesāligamane paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.65-74) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Suyāmana begins, “Sensual desire and ill will…”. What is its origin? This Elder too, having performed meritorious deeds under former Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in the ninety-first aeon from now, in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, in a brahmin family in the city of Dhaññavatī. Having come of age and attained proficiency in the brahminical arts, he taught the brahminical hymns. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī, together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, had entered Dhaññavatī for alms. Seeing him, the brahmin, with a serene mind, led him to his house, prepared a seat, spread a layer of flowers upon it, and offered it. When the Teacher was seated there, he satisfied him with exquisite food and, after the meal, honored him with flowers and perfumes. The Teacher gave an anumodanā and departed. By that meritorious action, he was reborn in the deva-world and, repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, wandered among the deva and human worlds. In this Buddha-era, he was born as the son of a certain brahmin in Vesālī, and his name was Suyāmana. Having come of age, mastering the three Vedas, endowed with supreme reliance, and disgusted with the sensual pleasures of household life, he was inclined to jhāna. Having gained faith when the Blessed One came to Vesālī, he went forth and attained arahantship at the very edge of the razor. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Nagare [V 1.0177] dhaññavatiyā, ahosiṃ brāhmaṇo tadā;

Lakkhaṇe itihāse ca, sanighaṇḍusakeṭubhe.

“In the city of Dhaññavatī, I was a brahmin then; skilled in the treatises on bodily marks and on legends, together with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha.”

“Padako veyyākaraṇo, nimittakovido ahaṃ;

Mante ca sisse vācesiṃ, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū.

“I was an expert in phonology and grammar, skilled in omens; I taught the hymns to my students, a master of the three Vedas.”

“Pañca uppalahatthāni, piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapitāni me;

Āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmohaṃ, pitumātusamāgame.

“Five handfuls of blue lotuses were placed by me on my back; I wished to make an offering in the presence of my parents.”

“Tadā vipassī bhagavā, bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhato;

Obhāsento disā sabbā, āgacchati narāsabho.

“Then the Blessed One Vipassī, preceded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, illuminating all directions, came, the bull among men.”

“Āsanaṃ paññapetvāna, nimantetvā mahāmuniṃ;

Santharitvāna taṃ pupphaṃ, abhinesiṃ sakaṃ gharaṃ.

“Having prepared a seat, having invited the Great Sage, and having spread those flowers, I led him into my own house.”

“Yaṃ me atthi sake gehe, āmisaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ;

Tāhaṃ buddhassa pādāsiṃ, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

“Whatever prepared food I had in my own home, that I gave to the Buddha, with a serene mind and with my own hands.”

“Bhuttāviṃ kālamaññāya pupphahatthamadāsahaṃ;

Anumoditvāna sabbaññū, pakkāmi uttarāmukho.

“When he had eaten, knowing the proper time, I gave a handful of flowers; having given his blessing, the All-Knowing One departed facing north.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“For ninety-one aeons since I gave that flower then, I know of no bad rebirth; this is the fruit of that flower offering.”

“Anantaraṃ ito kappe, rājāhuṃ varadassano;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In the aeon immediately after that, I was a king named Varadassana; endowed with the seven jewels, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā nīvaraṇappahānakittanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, he then made his declaration of final knowledge by way of proclaiming the abandonment of the hindrances:

74.

74.
