“Kāmacchando [M 1.0209] ca byāpādo, thinamiddhañca bhikkhuno;

Uddhaccaṃ vicikicchā ca, sabbasova na vijjatī”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“For a bhikkhu, sensual desire and ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and doubt—all these are entirely absent.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha kāmacchandoti kāmesu chando, kāmo ca so chando cātipi kāmacchando, kāmarāgo. Idha pana sabbopi rāgo kāmacchando aggamaggavajjhassāpi adhippetattā, tenāha “sabbasova na vijjatī”ti. Sabbepi hi tebhūmakadhammā kāmanīyaṭṭhena kāmā, tattha pavatto rāgo kāmacchando, tenāha bhagavā – “āruppe kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ uddhaccanīvaraṇaṃ avijjānīvaraṇaṃ uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 3.8.8) byāpajjati [P 1.0176] cittaṃ pūtibhāvaṃ [V 1.0178] gacchati etenāti byāpādo, “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādinayappavatto (dha. sa. 1066; vibha. 909) āghāto. Thinaṃ cittassa akalyatā anussāhasaṃhananaṃ, middhaṃ kāyassa akalyatā asattivighāto, tadubhayampi thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ, kiccāhārapaṭipakkhānaṃ ekatāya ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Uddhatabhāvo uddhaccaṃ, yena dhammena cittaṃ uddhataṃ hoti avūpasantaṃ, so cetaso vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ. Uddhaccaggahaṇeneva cettha kiccāhārapaṭipakkhānaṃ samānatāya kukkuccampi gahitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ. Yo hi katākatakusalākusalūpanissayo vippaṭisāro, taṃ kukkuccaṃ. Vicikicchāti, “evaṃ nu kho na nu kho”ti saṃsayaṃ āpajjati, dhammasabhāvaṃ vā vicinanto kicchati kilamati etāyāti vicikicchā, buddhādivatthuko saṃsayo. Sabbasoti anavasesato. Na vijjatīti natthi, maggena samucchinnattā na upalabbhati. Idañca padadvayaṃ paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ ayañhettha yojanā – yassa bhikkhuno tena tena ariyamaggena samucchinnattā kāmacchando ca byāpādo ca thinamiddhañca uddhaccakukkuccañca vicikicchā ca sabbasova na vijjati, tassa na kiñci karaṇīyaṃ, katassa vā paticayoti aññāpadesena aññaṃ byākaroti. Pañcasu hi nīvaraṇesu maggena samucchinnesu tadekaṭṭhatāya sabbepi kilesā samucchinnāyeva honti. Tenāha – “sabbete bhagavanto pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese”ti (dī. ni. 2.146).

Herein, ‘sensual desire’ (kāmacchanda) is desire for sensual pleasures; it is also sensual desire because it is both a sensual pleasure (kāma) and a desire (chanda); it is sensual lust (kāmarāga). Here, however, all lust is considered sensual desire because even that which is to be abandoned by the highest path is intended; hence it is said, “none whatsoever remains.” Indeed, all phenomena of the three realms are ‘sensual pleasures’ in the sense of being desirable; the lust arising toward them is sensual desire. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance arise in the formless realms” (Paṭṭhāna 3.8.8). ‘Ill will’ (byāpāda) is that by which the mind becomes corrupted, goes to a foul state; it is the resentment (āghāta) that arises from such thoughts as, “He has done me wrong” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1066; Vibhaṅga 909). Sloth (thina) is the unwieldiness of the mind, a lack of exertion and sluggishness. Torpor (middha) is the unwieldiness of the mental aggregates, an incapacity and fatigue. Both sloth and torpor together are called sloth-and-torpor (thinamiddha), stated as one because of the sameness of their opposition to the basis of action. Restlessness (uddhacca) is the state of agitation, that by which the mind is agitated and unquiet; this mental distraction is restlessness. By the inclusion of restlessness, worry (kukkucca) should be understood as also included here because of the similarity of their opposition to the basis of action. It has the characteristic of subsequent regret. Worry is the remorse which has as its basis wholesome and unwholesome actions that were done and not done. ‘Doubt’ (vicikicchā) is to fall into uncertainty, thinking, “Is it so or not?” Or, it is doubt because one struggles and tires while investigating the nature of phenomena; it is skepticism regarding the Buddha and other matters. ‘None whatsoever’ (sabbasova) means without remainder. ‘Does not exist’ (na vijjati) means it is not, it is not found, having been cut off by the path. These two phrases should each be applied separately. The explanation here is this: For that bhikkhu whose sensual desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt do not exist at all, having been cut off by the respective noble paths, there is nothing further to do, nor any accumulation of what has been done—thus, he declares final knowledge by way of a secondary meaning. Indeed, when the five hindrances are cut off by the path, all defilements are likewise cut off due to their being of a single nature. Hence it is said, “All those Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances, the corruptions of the mind…” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.146).

Suyāmanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Thera Suyāmana is concluded.

5. Susāradattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Susārada

Sādhu [M 1.0210] suvihitāna dassananti āyasmato susāradattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vijjāpadesu nipphattiṃ gantvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ [P 1.0177] disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantappadese araññāyatane assamaṃ kāretvā vihāsi. Atha naṃ anuggaṇhanto padumuttaro bhagavā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ upasaṅkami. So dūratova disvā pasannamānaso paccuggantvā pattaṃ gahetvā madhurāni phalāni pakkhipitvā adāsi. Bhagavā taṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde dhammasenāpatino ñātibrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā mandapaññattā susāradoti gahitanāmo aparabhāge dhammasenāpatissa santike dhammaṃ sutvā [V 1.0179] paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.75-83) –

“Good is the sight of the well-disciplined” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Susārada. What is its origin? It is said that he was born in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having attained proficiency in the sciences, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic, building a hermitage in a forest region in the Himalayas and dwelling there. Then, the Blessed One Padumuttara, showing him favor, approached him at the time of the alms-round. Seeing him from afar, with a serene mind, he went forth to meet him, took his bowl, placed sweet fruits into it, and offered them. The Blessed One accepted it, gave his blessing, and departed. By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family related to the General of the Dhamma. Being of dull wisdom, he was given the name Susārada. Later, hearing the Dhamma from the General of the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.13.75-83):

“Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Himavantassāvidūre, vasāmi assame ahaṃ.

“I am a reciter, a holder of mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas; not far from the Himalayas, I dwell in my hermitage.”

“Aggihuttañca me atthi, puṇḍarīkaphalāni ca;

Puṭake nikkhipitvāna, dumagge laggitaṃ mayā.

“I have a fire sacrifice and white mango fruits. Having placed them in a basket, I hung it on a treetop.”

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mamuddharitukāmo so, bhikkhanto mamupāgami.

“Padumuttara, the knower of the world, the receiver of offerings, desiring to uplift me, approached me while on his alms-round.”

“Pasannacitto sumano, phalaṃ buddhassadāsahaṃ;

Vittisañjanano mayhaṃ, diṭṭhadhammasukhāvaho.

“With a serene and joyful mind, I offered fruit to the Buddha; it generated satisfaction in me, bringing happiness in this very life.”

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddho, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Antalikkhe ṭhito satthā, imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsatha.

“The golden-hued Perfectly Enlightened One, receiver of offerings, the Teacher, standing in the sky, spoke this verse:”

“Iminā phaladānena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjasi.

“By this giving of fruit, and by the aspirations of your will, for a hundred thousand aeons, you will not be reborn in a state of woe.”

“Teneva sukkamūlena, anubhotvāna sampadā;

Pattomhi acalaṃ ṭhānaṃ, hitvā jayaparājayaṃ.

“By that very root of wholesome kamma, having experienced prosperity, I have attained the unshakeable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.”

“Ito [M 1.0211] sattasate kappe, rājā āsiṃ sumaṅgalo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Seven hundred aeons ago, I was King Sumaṅgala, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā sappurisūpanissayānisaṃsakittanāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto –

However, having attained arahantship, he declared final knowledge under the pretext of praising the benefits of relying on good people:

75.

75.

“Sādhu suvihitāna dassanaṃ, kaṅkhā chijjati buddhi vaḍḍhati;

Bālampi karonti paṇḍitaṃ, tasmā sādhu sataṃ samāgamo”ti. –

“Good is the sight of the well-disciplined, doubt is cut off, wisdom increases; even a fool they make wise, therefore good is association with the worthy.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this verse.

Tattha sādhūti sundaraṃ, bhaddakanti attho. Suvihitāna dassananti suvihitānaṃ dassanaṃ. Gāthāsukhatthaṃ anusvāralopo kato. Sīlādiguṇehi susaṃvihitattabhāvānaṃ parānuddayāya suṭṭhu vihitadhammadesanānaṃ ariyānaṃ dassanaṃ sādhūti yojanā. “Dassana”nti nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ savanādīnampi bahukārattā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Herein, ‘sādhu’ means beautiful; the meaning is auspicious. ‘Suvihitāna dassanaṃ’ means the sight of the well-disciplined. For the sake of the verse’s euphony, the elision of the nasal sound has been made. The explanation is that the sight of the noble ones—who are well-composed in virtues such as morality and so forth, and who teach the Dhamma well out of compassion for others—is good. ‘Sight’ should be understood as merely an indication, because listening and so on are also of much benefit. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Ye [V 1.0180] te bhikkhū sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññāsampannā vimuttisampannā vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā ovādakā viññāpakā sandassakā samādapakā samuttejakā sampahaṃsakā alaṃsamakkhātāro saddhammassa, dassanampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmi, savanaṃ…pe… upasaṅkamanaṃ…pe… payirupāsanaṃ…pe… anussaraṇaṃ…pe… anupabbajjampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahūpakāraṃ vadāmī”ti [P 1.0178] (itivu. 104).

“Those bhikkhus who are accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation—advisers, instructors, persuaders, encouragers, inspirers, gladdeners, capable explainers of the True Dhamma—I say, bhikkhus, that seeing those bhikkhus is of great benefit; hearing them… approaching them… attending on them… remembering them… and going forth after them, I say, bhikkhus, is of great benefit.” (Itivuttaka 104)

Dassanamūlakattā vā itaresaṃ dassanamevettha vuttaṃ, kaṅkhā chijjatītiādi tattha kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tādisānañhi kalyāṇamittānaṃ dassane sati viññujātiko atthakāmo kulaputto te upasaṅkamati payirupāsati “kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusala”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.296) pañhaṃ pucchati. Te cassa anekavihitesu kaṅkhāṭṭhānīyesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti, tena vuttaṃ “kaṅkhā chijjatī”ti. Yasmā ca te dhammadesanāya tesaṃ kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodetvā [M 1.0212] pubbabhāge kammapathasammādiṭṭhiṃ vipassanāsammādiṭṭhiñca uppādenti, tasmā tesaṃ buddhi vaḍḍhati. Yadā pana te vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saccāni paṭivijjhanti, tadā soḷasavatthukā aṭṭhavatthukā ca vicikicchā chijjati samucchijjati, nippariyāyena paññā buddhi vaḍḍhati. Bālyasamatikkamanato te paṇḍitā honti. So tehi buddhiṃ vaḍḍheti, bālampi karonti paṇḍitanti. Tasmātiādi nigamanaṃ, yasmā sādhūnaṃ dassanaṃ vuttanayena kaṅkhā chijjati buddhi vaḍḍhati, te bālaṃ paṇḍitaṃ karonti, tasmā tena kāraṇena sādhu sundaraṃ sataṃ sappurisānaṃ ariyānaṃ samāgamo, tehi samodhānaṃ sammā vaḍḍhananti attho.

Or, because seeing is the root of the others, seeing alone is stated here; 'doubt is cut off' and so on is the statement of the reason there. For when such good friends are seen, a discerning person, a young man of good family who desires his own welfare, approaches them, attends upon them, and asks questions such as, 'Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?' And they dispel his doubts regarding various matters that are grounds for doubt; hence it is said, 'doubt is cut off.' Moreover, because through teaching the Dhamma they dispel those doubts and in the preliminary stage generate right view regarding the path of action and right view regarding insight, their wisdom grows. And when, having developed insight, they penetrate the truths, then the sixteenfold and eightfold doubt is cut off and completely eradicated. Unconditionally, wisdom grows. Through transcending foolishness, they become wise. He increases wisdom through them, and they make even a fool wise. Therefore, and so on, is the conclusion: because seeing the virtuous, in the manner stated, cuts off doubt, increases wisdom, and turns fools into the wise, for that reason, the association with the virtuous, the noble ones, is good, beautiful. Association with them rightly fosters growth—this is the meaning.

Susāradattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Susārada is concluded.

6. Piyañjahattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Piyañjaha

Uppatantesu nipateti āyasmato piyañjahattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle himavante rukkhadevatā hutvā pabbatantare vasanto devatāsamāgamesu appānubhāvatāya parisapariyante ṭhatvā dhammaṃ sutvā satthari paṭiladdhasaddho ekadivasaṃ suvisuddhaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ gaṅgāyaṃ pulinappadesaṃ disvā satthu guṇe anussari – “itopi suvisuddhā satthu guṇā anantā aparimeyyā cā”ti, evaṃ so [P 1.0179] satthu guṇe ārabbha cittaṃ pasādetvā [V 1.0181] tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ licchavirājakule nibbattitvā vayappatto yuddhasoṇḍo aparājitasaṅgāmo amittānaṃ piyahānikaraṇena piyañjahoti paññāyittha. So satthu vesāligamane paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā araññe vasamāno vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.84-90) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Piyañjaha: 'Uppatantesu nipateti'. What was its origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences as a condition for liberation. Ninety-one eons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was a tree-deity in the Himalayas. Dwelling in a mountain ravine, he would stand at the edge of assemblies of deities to listen to the Dhamma, because his power was slight. Having gained faith in the Teacher, one day, upon seeing a very pure and delightful stretch of sand along the Ganges, he reflected on the virtues of the Teacher: 'Even purer than this are the Teacher's virtues, which are boundless and immeasurable.' Thus, having gladdened his mind with the Teacher’s virtues, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans due to that meritorious deed. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the Licchavi royal family of Vesālī. As he grew older, he became a warrior, fond of battle, invincible in combat, and known as Piyañjaha for causing the loss of what is dear to his enemies. When the Teacher visited Vesālī, he gained faith, went forth, and dwelt in the forest. Developing insight, he attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (apa. thera 1.13.84-90):

“Pabbate himavantamhi, vasāmi pabbatantare;

Pulinaṃ sobhanaṃ disvā, buddhaseṭṭhaṃ anussariṃ.

"In the Himavant mountains, I dwell in a mountain ravine; Seeing a beautiful sandbank, I recollected the best of Buddhas."

“Ñāṇe [M 1.0213] upanidhā natthi, saṅkhāraṃ natthi satthuno;

Sabbadhammaṃ abhiññāya, ñāṇena adhimuccati.

"There is no comparison to his knowledge; the Teacher's virtues cannot be enumerated. Having directly known all phenomena, he is firmly resolved through knowledge."

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Ñāṇena te samo natthi, yāvatā ñāṇamuttamaṃ.

"Homage to you, noble among men, homage to you, best of men; There is none equal to you in wisdom, as far as supreme wisdom extends."

“Ñāṇe cittaṃ pasādetvā, kappaṃ saggamhi modahaṃ;

Avasesesu kappesu, kusalaṃ caritaṃ mayā.

"Having gladdened the mind with knowledge, I rejoiced in heaven for an eon. In the remaining eons, wholesome conduct was practiced by me."

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ñāṇasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-one eons ago, when I gained that perception, I do not recall any bad rebirth—this is the fruit of the perception of knowledge."

“Ito sattatikappamhi, eko pulinapupphiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"Seventy eons ago, there was one named Pulina Pupphiyo, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Arahattaṃ pana patvā “andhaputhujjanānaṃ paṭipattito vidhurā ariyānaṃ paṭipattī”ti imassa atthassa dassanavasena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, then, explaining the meaning of 'the practice of the noble ones is distinct from the practice of blind ordinary people,' he spoke the following verse –

76.

76.

“Uppatantesu nipate, nipatantesu uppate;

Vase avasamānesu, ramamānesu no rame”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

"Among those who rise, one should fall; among those who fall, one should rise. Among those who do not dwell, one should dwell; among those who delight, one should not delight." Thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha uppatantesūti uṇṇamantesu, sattesu mānuddhaccathambhasārambhādīhi attukkaṃsanena anupasantesu. Nipateti nameyya, tesaññeva pāpadhammānaṃ parivajjanena nivātavutti bhaveyya. Nipatantesūti oṇamantesu, hīnādhimuttikatāya kosajjena ca guṇato nihīyamānesu. Uppateti uṇṇameyya, paṇītādhimuttikatāya vīriyārambhena ca guṇato ussukkeyya. Atha vā uppatantesūti uṭṭhahantesu, kilesesu pariyuṭṭhānavasena sīsaṃ ukkhipantesu. Nipateti paṭisaṅkhānabalena yathā te na uppajjanti, tathā anurūpapaccavekkhaṇāya nipateyya, vikkhambheyya ceva [V 1.0182] samucchindeyya ca. Nipatantesūti paripatantesu, ayonisomanasikāresu vīriyapayogamandatāya vā yathāraddhesu samathavipassanādhammesu hāya mānesu[M 1.0214]. Uppateti yonisomanasikārena vīriyārambhasampadāya ca te upaṭṭhāpeyya uppādeyya vaḍḍheyya ca. Vase [P 1.0180] avasamānesūti sattesu maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ ariyavāsañca avasantesu sayaṃ taṃ vāsaṃ vaseyyāti, ariyesu vā kilesavāsaṃ dutiyakavāsaṃ avasantesu yena vāsena te avasamānā nāma honti, sayaṃ tathā vase. Ramamānesu no rameti sattesu kāmaguṇaratiyā kilesaratiyā ramantesu sayaṃ tathā no rame naṃ rameyya, ariyesu vā nirāmisāya jhānādiratiyā ramamānesu sayampi tathā rame, tato aññathā pana kadācipi no rame nābhirameyya vāti attho.

There, 'among those who rise' means among those who are puffed up, among beings who are not calmed by self-exaltation through pride, restlessness, stubbornness, and hostility. 'One should fall' means one should humble oneself, one should live humbly by avoiding those very evil qualities. 'Among those who fall' means among those who are bent low, among those who are degraded in virtue due to inferior inclinations and laziness. 'One should rise' means one should strive for excellence in virtue through noble inclinations and energetic effort. Alternatively, 'among those who rise' means among those who arise, among defilements that lift their heads due to mental agitation. 'One should fall' means one should reflect appropriately so that they do not arise, suppressing and eradicating them through the power of reflection. 'Among those who fall' means among those who decline, when the qualities of serenity and insight deteriorate due to unwise attention or slack effort. 'One should rise' means one should establish, arouse, and increase them through wise attention and diligent effort. 'Among those who do not dwell' means when beings do not dwell in the life of the path, the spiritual life, and the noble life, one should oneself dwell in that life; or, when noble ones do not dwell in the dwelling of defilements, the second dwelling, one should oneself dwell in such a way that they are called 'those who do not dwell.' 'Among those who delight, one should not delight' means when beings delight in sensual pleasures or the delight of defilements, one should oneself not delight in such things. Or, when noble ones delight in the joy of jhāna and other immaterial states, one too should delight in the same way. But otherwise, one should never delight or take pleasure in anything else—this is the meaning.

Piyañjahattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Piyañjaha is concluded.

7. Hatthārohaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hatthārohaputta

Idaṃ pure cittamacāri cārikanti āyasmato hatthārohaputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ vihārato nikkhantaṃ disvā pasannacitto pupphehi pūjaṃ katvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ hatthārohakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto hatthisippe nipphattiṃ agamāsi. So ekadivasaṃ hatthiṃ sikkhāpento nadītīraṃ gantvā hetusampattiyā codiyamāno “kiṃ mayhaṃ iminā hatthidamanena, attānaṃ damanameva vara”nti cintetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvāva cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto ciraparicayena kammaṭṭhānato bahiddhā vidhāvantaṃ cittaṃ cheko hatthācariyo viya aṅkusena caṇḍamattavaravāraṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaaṅkusena niggaṇhanto “idaṃ pure cittamacāri cārika”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

"Formerly, this mind wandered on its travels." This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Hatthārohaputta. What is its origin? It is said that he, having made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that served as a basis for liberation in various existences, was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī and reached maturity. One day, seeing the Teacher emerging from the monastery surrounded by the community of monks, his mind became serene. He made an offering of flowers, paid homage with the five-point prostration, circumambulated him, and then departed. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, during this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of elephant trainers and reached maturity, attaining mastery in the art of handling elephants. One day, while training an elephant by a riverbank, prompted by the ripening of conditions, he thought: "What use is this taming of an elephant to me? Taming oneself is far better." He approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. Taking up a meditation subject suited to his disposition and working on developing insight, he restrained his mind—which through long habit strayed outside the meditation subject—with the goad of reflection, just as a skilled elephant master restrains a fierce, rutting, excellent elephant with a goad. He then uttered the verse: "Formerly, this mind wandered on its travels."

77. Tattha [P 1.0181] idanti vuccamānassa cittassa attapaccakkhatāya vuttaṃ. Pureti niggahakālato pubbe. Acārīti vicari, anavaṭṭhitatāya nānārammaṇesu paribbhami[M 1.0215]. Cārikanti yathākāmacariyaṃ. Tenāha “yenicchakaṃ yatthakāmaṃ yathāsukha”nti. Tanti taṃ cittaṃ. Ajjāti etarahi. Niggahessāmīti niggaṇhissāmi, nibbisevanaṃ karissāmi. Yonisoti upāyena. Yathā [V 1.0183] kiṃ? Hatthippabhinnaṃ viya aṅkusaggaho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – idaṃ mama cittaṃ nāma ito pubbe rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu yena yena ramituṃ icchati, tassa tassa vasena yenicchakaṃ, yattha yattha cassa kāmo, tassa tassa vasena yatthakāmaṃ, yathā yathā vicarantassa sukhaṃ hoti, tatheva caraṇato yathāsukhaṃ dīgharattaṃ cārikaṃ acari, taṃ ajjapāhaṃ bhinnamadamattahatthiṃ hatthācariyasaṅkhāto cheko aṅkusaggaho aṅkusena viya yonisomanasikārena niggahessāmi, nāssa vītikkamituṃ dassāmīti. Evaṃ vadanto eva ca thero vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.91-96) –

77. Therein, 'this' is said with reference to the mind being directly experienced. 'Formerly' means before the time of its restraint. 'Wandered' means it roamed about; due to its instability, it wandered among various objects. 'On its travels' means wandering as it pleased. Therefore, he said, "as it wished, where it wished, as it liked." 'It' refers to that mind. 'Now' means at present. 'I will restrain' means I will control it, I will make it an object not to be indulged in. 'Wisely' means by the proper method. Like what? Like a goad-wielder with a rutting elephant. This is what is meant: this mind of mine, formerly, among objects such as forms, wandered for a long time on its travels as it wished, according to whatever it desired to delight in; where it wished, according to wherever its desire was; as it liked, according to whatever way it found pleasure in wandering. Today, just as a skilled elephant master, a goad-wielder, would restrain a rutting, intoxicated elephant with a goad, so I shall restrain it with wise attention. I will not allow it to transgress. And speaking thus, the elder developed insight and realized arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddho, vipassī dakkhiṇāraho;

Purakkhato sāvakehi, ārāmā abhinikkhami.

"Golden in complexion, the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī, worthy of offerings, attended by his disciples, came forth from the monastery."

“Disvānahaṃ buddhaseṭṭhaṃ, sabbaññuṃ tamanāsakaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, gaṇṭhipupphaṃ apūjayiṃ.

"Seeing the best of Buddhas, the All-Knowing One, who dispels the darkness, with a serene and joyful mind, I offered a jasmine flower."

“Tena cittappasādena, dvipadindassa tādino;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, puna vandiṃ tathāgataṃ.

"With that serenity of mind towards the leader of bipeds, the steadfast one, joyful, with a joyful heart, I again paid homage to the Tathāgata."

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-one aeons ago, when I offered that flower, I know of no bad rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Ekatālīsito kappe, caraṇo nāma khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"Forty-one aeons ago, there was a khattiya named Caraṇa, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosīti.

And this was the elder's verse of declaration of final knowledge.

Hatthārohaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Hatthārohaputta is finished.

8. Meṇḍasirattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Meṇḍasira

Anekajātisaṃsāranti [M 1.0216] āyasmato meṇḍasirattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni karonto ito ekanavute kappe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahatā isigaṇena saddhiṃ himavante vasanto satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso isigaṇena padumāni āharāpetvā [V 1.0184] satthu pupphapūjaṃ katvā [P 1.0182] sāvake appamādapaṭipattiyaṃ ovaditvā kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sākete gahapatikule nibbatti, tassa meṇḍasarikkhasīsatāya meṇḍasirotveva samaññā ahosi. So bhagavati sākete añjanavane viharante satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samathavipassanāsu kammaṃ karonto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Teva vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.97-105) –

"Through many a birth in saṃsāra"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Meṇḍasira. What is its origin? He too, it is said, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds here and there as a basis for liberation, was born into a brahmin family ninety-one aeons ago. Having come of age, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt in the Himalayas with a great company of sages. Seeing the Teacher, his mind became serene. He had his company of sages bring lotuses and made an offering of flowers to the Teacher. After advising his disciples on the practice of diligence, he passed away and was reborn in the heavenly world. Wandering through saṃsāra again and again, during the appearance of this Buddha, he was born into a householder’s family in Sāketa. Because his head resembled that of a ram, he came to be known as Meṇḍasira. When the Blessed One was dwelling in the Añjana Grove near Sāketa, he approached the Teacher, gained faith, and went forth. Working on serenity and insight, he attained the six direct knowledges. This is as stated in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre, gotamo nāma pabbato;

Nānārukkhehi sañchanno, mahābhūtagaṇālayo.

"Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Gotama, covered with various trees, an abode for hosts of great beings."

“Vemajjhamhi ca tassāsi, assamo abhinimmito;

Purakkhato sasissehi, vasāmi assame ahaṃ.

"And in its midst, a hermitage was built; attended by my disciples, I dwelt in that hermitage."

“Āyantu me sissagaṇā, padumaṃ āharantu me;

Buddhapūjaṃ karissāmi, dvipadindassa tādino.

"'Let my company of disciples come, let them bring me lotuses; I will make an offering to the Buddha, the leader of bipeds, the steadfast one.'"

“Evanti te paṭissutvā, padumaṃ āhariṃsu me;

Tathā nimittaṃ katvāhaṃ, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

"'So be it,' they replied, and brought me lotuses; having made that a sign, I offered it to the Buddha."

“Sisse tadā samānetvā, sādhukaṃ anusāsahaṃ;

Mā kho tumhe pamajjittha, appamādo sukhāvaho.

"Having gathered the disciples then, I instructed them well: 'Do not be heedless, for heedfulness brings happiness.'"

“Evaṃ samanusāsitvā, te sisse vacanakkhame;

Appamādaguṇe yutto, tadā kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

"Having thus instructed those disciples who were amenable to my words, endowed with the quality of diligence, I then passed away."

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-one aeons ago, when I offered that flower, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Ekapaññāsakappamhi[M 1.0217], rājā āsiṃ jaluttamo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"Fifty-one aeons ago, I was a king, Jaluttama, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great might."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

So attano pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranto –

He, recollecting his own former existences, spoke this verse:

78.

78.

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Tassa me dukkhajātassa, dukkhakkhandho aparaddho”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

"Through many a birth in saṃsāra I have run on without finding the way; for me, born to suffering, this mass of suffering is now lost."

Tattha anekajātisaṃsāranti anekajātisatasahassasaṅkhyaṃ idaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ, addhuno adhippetattā [V 1.0185] accantasaṃyogekavacanaṃ. Sandhāvissanti saṃsariṃ, aparāparaṃ cavanuppajjanavasena paribbhamiṃ. Anibbisanti tassa nivattakañāṇaṃ avindanto alabhanto. Tassa meti evaṃ saṃsarantassa me. Dukkhajātassāti jātiādivasena uppannadukkhassa, tissannaṃ vā dukkhatānaṃ vasena dukkhasabhāvassa. Dukkhakkhandhoti kammakilesavipākavaṭṭappakāro dukkharāsi. Aparaddhoti arahattamaggappattito paṭṭhāya paribbhaṭṭho cuto na abhinibbattissati. “Aparaṭṭho”ti vā pāṭho, apagatasamiddhito samucchinnakāraṇattā apagatoti attho. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

Therein, 'through many a birth in saṃsāra' means this round of saṃsāra, numbering hundreds of thousands of births; since a duration of time is intended, it is in the singular case of continuous connection. 'I have run on' means I have wandered in saṃsāra, I have roamed again and again by way of dying and being reborn. 'Without finding' means not finding, not obtaining the knowledge that brings the cycle to a halt. 'For me' means for me who has been wandering thus. 'Born to suffering' means for one for whom suffering has arisen by way of birth and so on, or for one whose nature is suffering by way of the three kinds of suffering. 'Mass of suffering' means the heap of suffering which is the cycle of karma, defilements, and results. 'Is now lost' means that from the attainment of the path of arahantship onwards, it has fallen away, ceased, and will not be generated again. Or the reading is 'aparaṭṭho', meaning 'gone away' because its cause has been utterly cut off, thus it is gone. And this was the elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Meṇḍasirattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Meṇḍasira is finished.

9. Rakkhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Rakkhita

Sabbo [P 1.0183] rāgo pahīno meti āyasmato rakkhitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso desanāñāṇaṃ ārabbha thomanaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa cittappasādaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ ito satasahassakappamatthake gotamassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa rakkhito nāma sāvako bhavissatī”ti byākāsi[M 1.0218]. So taṃ sutvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devadahanigame sākiyarājakule nibbatti, rakkhitotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So ye sākiyakoliyarājūhi bhagavato parivāratthāya dinnā pañcasatarājakumārā pabbajitā, tesaṃ aññataro. Te pana rājakumārā na saṃvegena pabbajitattā ukkaṇṭhābhibhūtā yadā satthārā kuṇāladahatīraṃ netvā kuṇālajātakadesanāya (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) itthīnaṃ dosavibhāvanena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojitā, tadā ayampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.1-9) –

“All my lust is abandoned”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Rakkhita. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a good family. Having come of age, one day he listened to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and, with a serene mind, praised the knowledge displayed in the discourse. The Teacher, perceiving the serenity of his mind, made a prediction: “One hundred thousand eons from now, this one will become a disciple named Rakkhita of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One named Gotama.” Hearing this, with his mind even more serene and joyful, he repeatedly performed meritorious deeds and wandered through the round of rebirths among devas and humans. During the dispensation of the present Buddha, he was reborn into the Sākiyan royal family in the market town of Devadaha, and he was given the name Rakkhita. He was one of the five hundred princes given by the Sākiyan and Koliyan kings to be the Blessed One’s retinue, who all went forth into homelessness. However, since those princes had not gone forth out of spiritual urgency, they were overcome by discontent. When the Teacher led them to the shore of Lake Kuṇāla and, by teaching the Kuṇāla Jātaka (Jā 2.21, Kuṇālajātaka), revealed the dangers in sensual pleasures by pointing out the faults of women, he assigned them a meditation subject. Then this one too, by devoting himself to his meditation subject, developed insight and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap-Th 1.14.1–9):

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Mahato janakāyassa, deseti amataṃ padaṃ.

“The Victor named Padumuttara, eldest in the world, a bull among men, taught the deathless state to a great assembly of people.”

“Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, vācāsabhimudīritaṃ;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, ekaggo āsahaṃ tadā.

“Having heard his speech, the words he boldly uttered, I raised my hands in reverence and then sat with a concentrated mind.”

“Yathā [V 1.0186] samuddo udadhīnamaggo, nerū nagānaṃ pavaro siluccayo;

Tatheva ye cittavasena vattare, na buddhañāṇassa kalaṃ upenti te.

“Just as the ocean is the foremost of waters, and Meru, a rocky peak, is the best of mountains, so too those who live under the sway of their own minds do not attain even a fraction of the Buddha’s knowledge.”

“Dhammavidhiṃ ṭhapetvāna, buddho kāruṇiko isi;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Having established the method of the Dhamma, the Buddha, the compassionate sage, sat down in the assembly of bhikkhus and spoke these verses:”

“Yo so ñāṇaṃ pakittesi, buddhamhi lokanāyake;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ na gamissati.

“Whoever praised the knowledge of the Buddha, the leader of the world, will not go to a bad destination for a hundred thousand eons.”

“Kilese jhāpayitvāna, ekaggo susamāhito;

Sobhito nāma nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

“Having burned up the defilements, one-pointed and well-concentrated, he will be a disciple of the Teacher by the name of Sobhita.”

“Paññāse kappasahasse, sattevāsuṃ yasuggatā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“For fifty thousand eons, there were seven of lofty fame, wheel-turning monarchs of great power, endowed with the seven treasures.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up …pe… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0219] pana patvā attano pahīnakilese paccavekkhanto “sabbo rāgo”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, while reflecting on the defilements he had abandoned, he uttered the verse beginning: “All lust….”

79. Tattha “sabbo rāgo”ti kāmarāgādippabhedo sabbopi rāgo. Pahīnoti ariyamaggabhāvanāya samucchedappahānavasena pahīno. Sabbo dosoti āghātavatthukādibhāvena anekabhedabhinno sabbopi byāpādo. Samūhatoti maggena samugghāṭito. Sabbo me vigato mohoti “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 1067; vibha. 909) vatthubhedena aṭṭhabhedo, saṃkilesavatthuvibhāgena anekavibhāgo sabbopi moho maggena viddhaṃsitattā mayhaṃ vigato. Sītibhūtosmi nibbutoti evaṃ mūlakilesappahānena tadekaṭṭhatāya saṃkilesānaṃ sammadeva paṭippassaddhattā anavasesakilesadarathapariḷāhābhāvato [P 1.0184] sītibhāvaṃ patto, tato eva sabbaso kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto ahaṃ asmi bhavāmīti aññaṃ byākāsi.

79. Herein, all lust means all kinds of lust, such as lust for sensual pleasures. Abandoned means abandoned by way of eradication through the development of the noble path. All hatred means all ill will, of many different kinds based on the grounds for resentment and so on. Uprooted means extirpated by the path. All my delusion has departed: all delusion—which is of eight kinds by way of its objects, beginning with “ignorance regarding suffering” (see Dhs §1061; Vbh §909), and of numerous kinds by way of its division into defiling things—has departed from me because it has been shattered by the path. I have become cool, quenched: Thus, through the abandoning of the root defilements, and because the subsidiary defilements, sharing the same foundation, have been rightly pacified, and because there is no remaining fever and blaze of the defilements, he has attained the state of coolness. For that very reason, by the complete extinction of the defilements, he is fully quenched. Thus he declared his final knowledge.

Rakkhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rakkhita is finished.

10. Uggattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ugga

Yaṃ mayā pakataṃ kammanti āyasmato uggattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato [V 1.0187] kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso ketakapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe ugganigame seṭṭhiputto hutvā nibbatti, uggotvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto bhagavati tasmiṃ nigame bhaddārāme viharante vihāraṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.10-16) –

“Whatever deed I have done…”: this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ugga. What is its origin? This one too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and, having performed meritorious deeds in various existences, in the thirty-first eon from the present one, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, he was reborn in a good family. Having come of age, one day he saw the Blessed One Sikhi and, with a serene mind, made an offering of ketaka flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and, wandering repeatedly only in happy destinations, during the dispensation of the present Buddha, he was reborn as a banker’s son in the market town of Ugga in the country of Kosala. His name was Ugga. Having come of age, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Bhaddārāma in that town, he went to the monastery, heard the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence, and gained faith. He went forth and, by practicing insight meditation, before long he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap-Th 1.14.10–16):

“Vinatānadiyā [M 1.0220] tīre, pilakkhu phalito ahu;

Tāhaṃ rukkhaṃ gavesanto, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“On the bank of the river Vinatā there was a pilakkha tree in fruit; while searching for that tree, I saw the Leader of the World.”

“Ketakaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, vaṇṭe chetvānahaṃ tadā;

Buddhassa abhiropesiṃ, sikhino lokabandhuno.

“Seeing a ketaka flower in bloom, I then cut it at the stalk and offered it to the Buddha Sikhi, the Kinsman of the World.”

“Yena ñāṇena pattosi, accutaṃ amataṃ padaṃ;

Taṃ ñāṇaṃ abhipūjemi, buddhaseṭṭha mahāmuni.

“That knowledge by which you reached the permanent, deathless state—that knowledge I revere, O best of Buddhas, Great Sage.”

“Ñāṇamhi pūjaṃ katvāna, pilakkhumaddasaṃ ahaṃ;

Paṭiladdhomhi taṃ paññaṃ, ñāṇapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Having made an offering to knowledge, I saw the pilakkha tree. I have obtained that wisdom; this is the fruit of the offering to knowledge.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ñāṇapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, when I offered that flower, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of the offering to knowledge.”

“Ito terasakappamhi, dvādasāsuṃ phaluggatā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“In the thirteenth eon from now, there were twelve kings named Phaluggata, endowed with the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up …pe… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano vaṭṭūpacchedadīpanena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Then, having attained arahantship, declaring his final knowledge by explaining the cutting off of his own round of existence:

80.

80.

“Yaṃ mayā pakataṃ kammaṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Sabbametaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Whatever kamma I have done, whether small or great, all of it is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence.” Thus he spoke this verse.

Tattha yaṃ mayā pakataṃ kammanti yaṃ kammaṃ tīhi kammadvārehi, chahi uppattidvārehi, aṭṭhahi asaṃvaradvārehi[P 1.0185], aṭṭhahi ca saṃvaradvārehi pāpādivasena dānādivasena cāti anekehi pakārehi anādimati saṃsāre yaṃ mayā kataṃ upacitaṃ abhinibbattitaṃ vipākakammaṃ. Appaṃ vā yadi vā [V 1.0188] bahunti tañca vatthucetanāpayogakilesādīnaṃ dubbalabhāvena appaṃ vā, tesaṃ balavabhāvena abhiṇhapavattiyā ca bahuṃ vā. Sabbametaṃ parikkhīṇanti sabbameva cetaṃ kammaṃ kammakkhayakarassa aggamaggassa adhigatattā parikkhayaṃ gataṃ, kilesavaṭṭappahānena hi kammavaṭṭaṃ pahīnameva hoti vipākavaṭṭassa [M 1.0221] anuppādanato. Tenāha “natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti mayhaṃ natthīti attho. “Sabbampeta”ntipi pāṭho, sabbampi etanti padavibhāgo.

Herein, whatever kamma I have done means: whatever kamma productive of result I have done, accumulated, and generated in beginningless saṃsāra in numerous ways—through the three doors of kamma, the six doors of origination, the eight doors of non-restraint, and the eight doors of restraint, by way of evil, giving, etc. Whether small or great: it is small because of the weakness of the object, volition, effort, defilements, etc., or it is great because of their strength and its frequent performance. All of it is exhausted: all this kamma has gone to exhaustion because the supreme path that destroys kamma has been attained. For when the round of defilements is abandoned, the round of kamma is also abandoned, since the round of result is no longer produced. Therefore he said: now there is no more renewed existence. The meaning is: “There is no future generation of renewed existence for me.” There is also the reading sabbampetaṃ; the word division is sabbaṃ pi etaṃ (all this too).

Uggattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ugga is finished.

Aṭṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Eighth Chapter is finished.

9. Navamavaggo

9. Ninth Chapter

1. Samitiguttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Samitigutta

Yaṃ [V 1.0189] mayā pakataṃ pāpanti āyasmato samitiguttattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavantaṃ passitvā pasannacitto jātisumanapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena yattha yattha bhave nibbatti, tattha tattha kularūpaparivārasampadāya aññe satte abhibhavitvā aṭṭhāsi. Ekasmiṃ pana attabhāve aññataraṃ paccekabuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ muṇḍako kuṭṭhī maññe, tenāyaṃ paṭicchādetvā vicaratī”ti niṭṭhubhitvā pakkāmi. So tena kammena bahuṃ kālaṃ niraye paccitvā kassapassa bhagavato kāle manussaloke nibbatto paribbājakapabbajjaṃ upagato ekaṃ sīlācārasampannaṃ upāsakaṃ disvā dosantaro hutvā, “kuṭṭharogī bhaveyyāsī”ti akkosi, nhānatitthe ca manussehi ṭhapitāni [P 1.0186] nhānacuṇṇāni dūsesi. So tena kammena puna niraye nibbattitvā bahūni vassāni dukkhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, samitiguttotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā suvisuddhasīlo hutvā viharati. Tassa purimakammanissandena kuṭṭharogo uppajji, tena tassa sarīrāvayavā yebhuyyena chinnabhinnā hutvā paggharanti. So gilānasālāyaṃ vasati. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasenāpati gilānapucchaṃ gantvā tattha tattha gilāne bhikkhū pucchanto taṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā “āvuso, yāvatā khandhappavatti nāma, sabbaṃ dukkhameva vedanā. Khandhesu pana asantesuyeva natthi [M 1.0222] dukkha”nti vedanānupassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā agamāsi. So therassa ovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiññā sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.12.82-90) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Samitigutta: 'Whatever evil was done by me...' What is its origin? He too, having made a resolution in the presence of former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, he saw the Blessed One and, with a confident mind, made an offering of jātisumana flowers. By that meritorious deed, wherever he was reborn, he surpassed other beings in the perfection of family, beauty, and retinue. In one existence, however, seeing a Paccekabuddha walking for alms, he spat and departed, thinking, 'This shaven-headed one is a leper, I suppose; that is why he wanders about covered up.' Due to that deed, he was tormented in hell for a long time. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born in the human world and undertook the going forth of a wanderer. Seeing a lay disciple endowed with virtue and good conduct, he became filled with malice and cursed him, saying, 'May you be a leper!' He also spoiled the bathing powders placed by people at a bathing place. Due to that deed, he was reborn in hell again and experienced suffering for many years. During the time of this Buddha's appearance, he was born in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin, and his name was Samitigutta. Having come of age, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. He lived as one of exceedingly pure virtue. As a result of his former kamma, leprosy arose in him, and because of it, the parts of his body were mostly broken and oozing. He lived in the sick hall. Then one day, the General of the Dhamma, while on his inquiry after the sick, was asking after the ailing monks here and there when he saw that monk and said, 'Friend, inasmuch as there is the process of the aggregates, all of it is simply suffering. When the aggregates are absent, however, there is no suffering,' and after teaching him the meditation subject of the contemplation of feelings, he departed. Abiding in the elder's advice, he developed insight and realized the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.12.82-90):

“Jāyantassa vipassissa, āloko vipulo ahu;

Pathavī ca pakampittha, sasāgarā sapabbatā.

“When Vipassī was being born, a great light appeared; and the earth trembled, with its oceans and mountains.

“Nemittā [V 1.0190] ca viyākaṃsu, buddho loke bhavissati;

Aggo ca sabbasattānaṃ, janataṃ uddharissati.

“The diviners also declared, ‘A Buddha will arise in the world; and as the chief of all beings, he will uplift humanity.’

“Nemittānaṃ suṇitvāna, jātipūjamakāsahaṃ;

Edisā pūjanā natthi, yādisā jātipūjanā.

“Having heard the diviners, I made an offering for the birth. There is no offering such as this, like the offering for the birth.

“Saṅkharitvāna kusalaṃ, sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādayiṃ;

Jātipūjaṃ karitvāna, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Having accumulated the wholesome, I gladdened my own mind; having made the offering for the birth, there I passed away.

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Sabbe satte abhibhomi, jātipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In whatever womb I am reborn, whether divine or human, I surpass all beings; this is the fruit of the offering for the birth.

“Dhātiyo maṃ upaṭṭhenti, mama cittavasānugā;

Na tā sakkonti kopetuṃ, jātipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Nurses attend to me, compliant with my will; they are not able to anger me—this is the fruit of the offering for the birth.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pūjamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, jātipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, when I made that offering, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the offering for the birth.

“Supāricariyā nāma, catuttiṃsa janādhipā;

Ito tatiyakappamhi, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Thirty-four lords of men named Supāricariyā; in the third eon from this one, they were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…pe… the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇena etarahi anubhuyyamānarogavasena purimajātīsu attanā kataṃ pāpakammaṃ anussaritvā tassa idāni sabbaso pahīnabhāvaṃ vibhāvento –

But having attained the six higher knowledges, while reflecting on his abandoned defilements, and, prompted by the illness he was now experiencing, recalling the evil kamma done by himself in former births and elucidating its complete cessation now –

81.

81.

“Yaṃ mayā pakataṃ pāpaṃ, pubbe aññāsu jātisu;

Idheva taṃ vedanīyaṃ, vatthu aññaṃ na vijjatī”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Whatever evil was done by me in former births, it must be experienced right here; there is no other basis.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha [M 1.0223] pāpanti akusalaṃ kammaṃ. Tañhi lāmakaṭṭhena pāpanti vuccati. Pubbeti purā. Aññāsu jātisūti ito aññāsu jātīsu, aññesu attabhāvesu. Ayañhettha attho – yadipi mayā imasmiṃ attabhāve na tādisaṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ atthi, idāni pana tassa sambhavoyeva natthi. Yaṃ pana ito aññāsu jātīsu kataṃ atthi, idheva taṃ vedanīyaṃ, tañhi idheva imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vedayitabbaṃ anubhavitabbaṃ phalaṃ, kasmā? Vatthu aññaṃ na vijjatīti tassa kammassa vipaccanokāso añño khandhappabandho natthi, ime [P 1.0187] pana khandhā sabbaso upādānānaṃ [V 1.0191] pahīnattā anupādāno viya jātavedo carimakacittanirodhena appaṭisandhikā nirujjhantīti aññaṃ byākāsi.

Therein, 'pāpa' means unwholesome kamma. For it is called 'pāpa' due to its base nature. 'Pubbe' means formerly. 'In other births' means in births other than this one, in other existences. This is the meaning here: although no such evil kamma has been done by me in this existence—and now there is no possibility of it arising at all—whatever was done in other births apart from this one must be experienced right here. For its result must be felt and experienced right here in this very existence. Why? 'Because there is no other basis': for that kamma, there is no other continuum of aggregates to provide an opportunity for its ripening. But these aggregates, due to the complete abandonment of all clinging, like a fire without fuel, cease with the cessation of the final consciousness, without rebirth-linking. This is the meaning.

Samitiguttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Samitigutta is completed.

2. Kassapattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Kassapa

Yena yena subhikkhānīti āyasmato kassapattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā tīsu vedesu aññesu ca brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gato, so ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sumanapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. Karonto ca satthu samantato upari ca pupphamuṭṭhiyo khipi. Buddhānubhāvena pupphāni pupphāsanākārena sattāhaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. So taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso ahosi. Aparāparaṃ puññāni karonto kappasatasahassaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa udiccabrāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, kassapotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa daharakāleyeva pitā kālamakāsi. Mātā taṃ paṭijaggati. So ekadivasaṃ jetavanaṃ gato bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā hetusampannatāya tasmiṃyeva āsane sotāpanno hutvā mātu santikaṃ gantvā anujānāpetvā pabbajito satthari vuṭṭhavasse pavāretvā janapadacārikaṃ pakkante sayampi satthārā saddhiṃ gantukāmo āpucchituṃ mātu santikaṃ agamāsi. Mātā vissajjentī ovādavasena –

“Wherever there is abundant food,” this is the verse of the Venerable Kassapa. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a brahmin family and became proficient in the three Vedas and other brahminical arts. One day, seeing the Blessed One, his mind filled with confidence, he made an offering with sumana flowers. As he did so, he scattered handfuls of flowers all around and above the Teacher. By the Buddha's spiritual power, the flowers remained in the form of a floral canopy for seven days. Seeing this marvel, his mind became even more joyful and confident. Continuously performing meritorious deeds, he wandered for a hundred thousand eons only in happy destinations, until, at the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain northern brahmin. His name was Kassapa. In his early youth, his father passed away. His mother took care of him. One day, he went to Jetavana, heard the Blessed One's teaching on the Dhamma, and, being endowed with the necessary conditions, he became a stream-enterer on that very seat. Having gone to his mother and obtained her permission, he went forth. After he had spent the rains residence with the Teacher and completed the Pavāraṇā, when the Teacher set out on a tour of the country, he too wished to go along. He went to his mother to take leave. His mother, sending him off, said by way of advice:

82.

82.

“Yena [M 1.0224] yena subhikkhāni, sivāni abhayāni ca;

Tena puttaka gacchassu, mā sokāpahato bhavā”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“‘Wherever there is abundant almsfood, and it is safe and secure, there, my dear son, you should go; do not be overcome by sorrow.’—she spoke this verse.

Tattha yena yenāti yattha yattha. Bhummatthe hi etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, yasmiṃ yasmiṃ disābhāgeti attho. Subhikkhānīti sulabhapiṇḍāni, raṭṭhānīti adhippāyo. Sivānīti khemāni arogāni. Abhayānīti corabhayādīhi nibbhayāni, rogadubbhikkhabhayāni pana “subhikkhāni, sivānī”ti padadvayeneva gahitāni. Tenāti tattha, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ [P 1.0188] disābhāgeti attho. Puttakāti anukampantī taṃ ālapati. Māti paṭisedhatthe nipāto sokāpahatoti vuttaguṇarahitāni raṭṭhāni gantvā dubbhikkhabhayādijanitena sokena upahato mā bhava māhosīti attho. Taṃ sutvā thero, “mama mātā mayhaṃ sokarahitaṭṭhānagamanaṃ āsīsati, handa mayaṃ sabbaso accantameva sokarahitaṃ [V 1.0192] ṭhānaṃ pattuṃ yutta”nti ussāhajāto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.13.1-9) –

Herein, yena yena means 'wherever, wherever.' This instrumental expression is used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is 'in whatever region.' Subhikkhāni means 'where almsfood is easy to obtain'; the implication is 'countries.' Sivāni means 'safe and free from disease.' Abhayāni means 'free from dangers such as thieves'; the dangers of disease and famine, however, are included by the two terms subhikkhāni and sivāni. Tena means 'there'; the meaning is 'in that region.' Puttaka: she addresses him with compassion. Mā is a particle of prohibition. The meaning is: 'Do not go to countries devoid of the aforementioned qualities and be overcome by the sorrow generated by the danger of famine and so on; do not be so.' Hearing this, the elder thought: 'My mother wishes for me to go to a place free from sorrow. Well now, it is proper for me to strive to attain a state that is completely and utterly free from sorrow.' With his energy aroused, he established insight and before long attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Abbhokāse ṭhito santo, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“A reciter, a master of the sacred verses, one who had mastered the three Vedas; standing peacefully in the open, I saw the Leader of the World.

“Sīhaṃ yathā vanacaraṃ, byaggharājaṃva nittasaṃ;

Tidhāpabhinnamātaṅgaṃ, kuñjaraṃva mahesinaṃ.

“The Great Seeker, like a lion that roams the forest, like a fearless tiger king, like a great elephant in threefold rut.

“Sereyakaṃ gahetvāna, ākāse ukkhipiṃ ahaṃ;

Buddhassa ānubhāvena, parivārenti sabbaso.

“Taking a sereyaka flower, I tossed it up into the air; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they surrounded him on all sides.

“Adhiṭṭhahi mahāvīro, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Samantā pupphacchadanā, okiriṃsu narāsabhaṃ.

“The Great Hero, the All-Knower, the Leader of the World, made a determination; a floral canopy from all around showered down upon the Bull of Men.

“Tato sā pupphakañcukā, antovaṇṭā bahimukhā;

Sattāhaṃ chadanaṃ katvā, tato antaradhāyatha.

“Then that floral sheath, with stalks inside and facing outwards, having formed a canopy for seven days, then disappeared.

“Tañca acchariyaṃ disvā, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Buddhe cittaṃ pasādesiṃ, sugate lokanāyake.

“Seeing that marvel, wonderful and hair-raising, I gained confidence in the Buddha, the Fortunate One, the Leader of the World.

“Tena [M 1.0225] cittappasādena, sukkamūlena codito;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“By that confidence of mind, impelled by that wholesome root, for a hundred thousand aeons I was not reborn in a bad destination.

“Pannarasasahassamhi, kappānaṃ pañcavīsati;

Vītamalāsanāmā ca, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“In the fifteen thousandth aeon from now, there were twenty-five wheel-turning monarchs of great power by the name of Vītamalāsana.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements have been burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā “idameva mātu vacanaṃ arahattappattiyā aṅkusaṃ jāta”nti tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

But having attained arahantship, thinking, “This very word of my mother has become a goad for my attainment of arahantship,” he recited that same verse.

Kassapattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kassapa is finished.

3. Sīhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sīha

Sīhappamatto viharāti āyasmato sīhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito aṭṭhārasakappasatamatthake atthadassissa bhagavato kāle candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre kinnarayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā pupphabhakkho pupphanivasano hutvā viharanto ākāsena gacchantaṃ atthadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto pūjetukāmo añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ [V 1.0193] ñatvā ākāsato oruyha aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle pallaṅkena nisīdi. Kinnaro candanasāraṃ ghaṃsitvā candanagandhena pupphehi ca pūjaṃ katvā vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde mallarājakule nibbatti, tassa [P 1.0189] sīhoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā dhammaṃ kathesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharati. Tassa cittaṃ nānārammaṇe vidhāvati, ekaggaṃ na hoti, sakatthaṃ nipphādetuṃ na sakkoti. Satthā taṃ disvā ākāse ṭhatvā –

“O Sīha, dwell heedfully,” this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sīha. What is its origin? It is said that he, having made his aspiration in the time of former Buddhas, eighteen hundred aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, was born from a kinnara womb on the bank of the Candabhāgā River. Living as one who eats flowers and wears flowers, he saw the Blessed One Atthadassī traveling through the sky. With a confident mind, wishing to pay homage, he stood with his hands raised in añjali. The Blessed One, knowing his disposition, descended from the sky and sat down at the foot of a certain tree in the cross-legged posture. The kinnara ground sandalwood paste and made an offering with the scent of sandalwood and with flowers, paid homage, circumambulated him respectfully, and departed. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, at the arising of this Buddha, he was born in a Malla royal family. His name was Sīha. Seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind he paid homage and sat down to one side. The Teacher, seeing his inclination, taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma and gained faith, he went forth, took up a meditation subject, and dwelt in the forest. His mind ran after various objects and did not become concentrated; he was unable to accomplish his own goal. The Teacher, seeing this, stood in the sky and said:

83.

83.

“Sīhappamatto [M 1.0226] vihara, rattindivamatandito;

Bhāvehi kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, jaha sīghaṃ samussaya”nti. –

“O Sīha, dwell heedfully, untiring day and night. Develop wholesome states; quickly abandon the bodily frame.”

Gāthāya ovadi. So gāthāvasāne vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.17-25) –

He admonished him with this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:

“Candabhāgānadītīre, ahosiṃ kinnaro tadā;

Pupphabhakkho cahaṃ āsiṃ, pupphanivasano tathā.

“On the bank of the Candabhāgā River I was a kinnara then; I was one who ate flowers and also one who wore flowers.

“Atthadassī tu bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Vipinaggena niyyāsi, haṃsarājāva ambare.

“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the World’s Chief, the Bull of Men, was traveling from the forest’s edge, like a swan-king in the sky.

“Namo te purisājañña, cittaṃ te suvisodhitaṃ;

Pasannamukhavaṇṇosi, vippasannamukhindriyo.

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, your mind is so well purified; your complexion is bright, your facial faculties perfectly serene.

“Orohitvāna ākāsā, bhūripañño sumedhaso;

Saṅghāṭiṃ pattharitvāna, pallaṅkena upāvisi.

“Having descended from the sky, the one of vast wisdom, the intelligent one, spread out his outer robe and sat down in the cross-legged posture.

“Vilīnaṃ candanādāya, agamāsiṃ jinantikaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“Taking ground sandalwood paste, I went into the presence of the Jina; with a confident and glad mind, I made an offering to the Buddha.

“Abhivādetvāna sambuddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Pāmojjaṃ janayitvāna, pakkāmiṃ uttarāmukho.

“Having paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, the World’s Chief, the Bull of Men, and having generated joy, I departed facing north.

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, candanaṃ yaṃ apūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In these eighteen hundred aeons since I made that offering of sandalwood, I know of no bad destination for myself; this is the fruit of revering a Buddha.

“Catuddase kappasate, ito āsiṃsu te tayo;

Rohaṇī nāma nāmena, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Fourteen hundred aeons ago from now, there were three wheel-turning monarchs of great power, named Rohaṇī.

“Kilesā [V 1.0194] jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements have been burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Yā pana bhagavatā ovādavasena vuttā “sīhappamatto”ti gāthā, tattha sīhāti tassa therassa ālapanaṃ. Appamatto viharāti satiyā avippavāsena pamādavirahito sabbiriyāpathesu satisampajaññayutto hutvā viharāhi. Idāni taṃ appamādavihāraṃ saha phalena saṅkhepato dassetuṃ “rattindiva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho – rattibhāgaṃ [M 1.0227] divasabhāgañca “caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16; vibha. 519) vuttanayena catusammappadhānavasena atandito akusīto āraddhavīriyo kusalaṃ samathavipassanādhammañca lokuttaradhammañca bhāvehi uppādehi vaḍḍhehi ca, evaṃ bhāvetvā ca jaha sīghaṃ samussayanti tava samussayaṃ attabhāvaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena sīghaṃ nacirasseva pajaha, evaṃbhūto ca pacchā carimakacittanirodhena anavasesato ca pajahissatīti. Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero aññaṃ byākaronto tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsīti.

Now, as to the verse “O Sīha, be heedful,” spoken by the Blessed One by way of admonition: herein, Sīha is a form of address to that elder. Dwell heedfully means: dwell without departing from mindfulness, free from heedlessness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all postures. Now, to show in brief that dwelling in heedfulness along with its fruit, the words “day and night,” etc., were spoken. The meaning is this: during both the night and the day, in the way it is said, “By walking and by sitting he cleanses his mind of obstructive states,” in accordance with the four right strivings, being untiring, not lazy, with energy aroused, you should develop—that is, generate and augment—wholesome states, namely, the Dhamma of serenity and insight and the supramundane Dhamma. And having thus developed them, quickly abandon the bodily frame means: first, by abandoning the desire and lust connected with it, quickly, before long, abandon your own bodily frame, your existence. And having become thus, you will afterwards, with the cessation of the final consciousness, abandon it without remainder. But having attained arahantship, the elder, when declaring his final knowledge, recited that same verse.

Sīhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sīha is finished.

4. Nītattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nīta

Sabbarattiṃ [P 1.0190] supitvānāti āyasmato nītattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle sunando nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā anekasate brāhmaṇe mante vācento vājapeyyaṃ nāma yaññaṃ yaji, bhagavā taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ anukampanto yaññaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ākāse caṅkami. Brāhmaṇo satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso sissehi pupphāni āharāpetvā ākāse khipitvā pūjaṃ akāsi. Buddhānubhāvena taṃ ṭhānaṃ sakalañca nagaraṃ pupphapaṭavitānikaṃ viya chāditaṃ ahosi. Mahājano satthari uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. Sunandabrāhmaṇo tena kusalamūlena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, nītotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto “ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā sukhasīlā sukhasamācārā subhojanāni bhuñjitvā nivātesu senāsanesu viharanti, imesu pabbajitvā sukhena viharituṃ sakkā”ti sukhābhilāsāya pabbajitvāva satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā katipāhameva manasikaritvā taṃ chaḍḍetvā yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā divasabhāgaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo tiracchānakathāya vītināmeti, rattibhāgepi thinamiddhābhibhūto sabbarattiṃ supati. Satthā tassa hetuparipākaṃ oloketvā ovādaṃ dento –

“Having slept all night”—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Nīta. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this one was a brahmin named Sunanda who, while teaching mantras to many hundreds of brahmins, performed a sacrifice called Vājapeyya. Out of compassion for that brahmin, the Blessed One went to the sacrificial site and walked in the sky. Seeing the Teacher, the brahmin, with a confident mind, had his disciples bring flowers and scattered them in the air as an offering. By the Buddha's power, that place and the entire city were covered as if by a canopy of flowers. The great crowd experienced sublime joy and mental gladness toward the Teacher. Through that wholesome root, the brahmin Sunanda wandered among devas and humans until, during this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin in Sāvatthī. His name became Nīta. When he came of age, he thought: “These recluses, the Sakyan sons, are of comfortable habits, of comfortable conduct, eat good meals, and dwell in sheltered lodgings. If I go forth among them, I can live in comfort.” Out of a desire for comfort, he went forth and, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, he applied his mind to it for only a few days, then abandoned it. He ate to his belly’s fill, spent the daytime delighting in company and engaging in worldly talk, and at night, overcome by sloth and torpor, he slept all night. The Teacher, seeing the maturity of his causal condition, gave him this admonition:

84.

84.

“Sabbarattiṃ [M 1.0228][V 1.0195] supitvāna, divā saṅgaṇike rato;

Kudāssu nāma dummedho, dukkhassantaṃ karissatī”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Having slept the whole night through, delighting in company by day, when, pray, will that witless one make an end of suffering?”—Thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha sabbarattinti sakalaṃ rattiṃ. Supitvānāti niddāyitvā, “rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetī”tiādinā vuttaṃ jāgariyaṃ ananuyuñjitvā kevalaṃ rattiyā tīsupi yāmesu niddaṃ okkamitvāti attho. Divāti divasaṃ, sakalaṃ divasabhāganti attho. Saṅgaṇiketi tiracchānakathikehi kāyadaḷhibahulapuggalehi [P 1.0191] sannisajjā saṅgaṇiko, tasmiṃ rato abhirato tattha avigatacchando “saṅgaṇike rato”ti vutto “saṅgaṇikārato”tipi pāḷi. Kudāssu nāmāti kudā nāma. Assūti nipātamattaṃ, kasmiṃ nāma kāleti attho. Dummedhoti nippañño. Dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Antanti pariyosānaṃ. Accantameva anuppādaṃ kadā nāma karissati, edisassa dukkhassantakaraṇaṃ natthīti attho. “Dummedha dukkhassantaṃ karissasī”tipi pāḷi.

Therein, “all night” means the entire night. “Having slept” means having gone to sleep; it means not practicing the vigil spoken of thus, “During the first watch of the night he purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking back and forth and by sitting,” but simply succumbing to sleep during all three watches of the night. “By day” means during the day, the entire daytime. “In company”: company is sitting together with people who engage in worldly talk and are much concerned with physical fitness. One who delights in this, is fond of it, and whose desire for it has not faded is called one who is “delighting in company.” Saṅgaṇikārato is also a reading. “When, pray”: that is, when? Assu is a mere particle; the meaning is: at what time? “Witless one” means one without wisdom. “Of suffering” means of the suffering of the round of existence. “An end” means a termination. When will he bring about its utter non-arising? The meaning is that for such a person there is no making an end of suffering. “O witless one, will you make an end of suffering?” is also a reading.

Evaṃ pana satthārā gāthāya kathitāya thero saṃvegajāto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.26-33) –

Then, when the Teacher spoke this verse, the elder, stirred by spiritual urgency, established insight and soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sunando nāma nāmena, brāhmaṇo mantapāragū;

Ajjhāyako yācayogo, vājapeyyaṃ ayājayi.

“Sunanda was my name, a brahmin master of the hymns; a teacher devoted to sacrificial rites, I performed the Vājapeyya sacrifice.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, aggo kāruṇiko isi;

Janataṃ anukampanto, ambare caṅkamī tadā.

“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the foremost compassionate sage, feeling compassion for the people, then walked in the sky.

“Caṅkamitvāna sambuddho, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Mettāya aphari satte, appamāṇe nirūpadhi.

“Having walked, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the All-Knower, the World Leader, pervaded beings with loving-kindness, immeasurable and free from acquisitions.

“Vaṇṭe chetvāna pupphāni, brāhmaṇo mantapāragū;

Sabbe sisse samānetvā, ākāse ukkhipāpayi.

“I, the brahmin master of the hymns, having cut the flowers from their stalks, gathered all my pupils and had them toss them up into the sky.

“Yāvatā nagaraṃ āsi, pupphānaṃ chadanaṃ tadā;

Buddhassa ānubhāvena, sattāhaṃ na vigacchatha.

“A canopy of flowers then extended as far as the city; by the Buddha’s power, it did not disperse for seven days.

“Teneva [M 1.0229] sukkamūlena, anubhotvāna sampadā;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, tiṇṇo loke visattikaṃ.

“By that same wholesome root, having experienced success, and having fully understood all the taints, I have crossed beyond attachment in the world.

“Ekārase kappasate, pañcatiṃsāsu khattiyā;

Ambaraṃsasanāmā te, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Thirty-five times in eleven hundred eons I was a khattiya, a mighty wheel-turning monarch named Ambaraṃsasa.

“Kilesā [V 1.0196] jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā thero aññaṃ byākaronto tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, the elder, when declaring his final knowledge, recited that same verse.

Nītattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nīta is finished.

5. Sunāgattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sunāga

Cittanimittassa kovidoti āyasmato sunāgattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekattiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā araññāyatane assame vasanto tīṇi brāhmaṇasahassāni mante vācesi. Athekadivasaṃ tassa satthāraṃ disvā lakkhaṇāni upadhāretvā lakkhaṇamante parivattentassa, “īdisehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato anantajino anantañāṇo buddho bhavissatī”ti buddhañāṇaṃ ārabbha uḷāro pasādo uppajji. So tena cittappasādena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto [P 1.0192] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde nālakagāme aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, sunāgotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So dhammasenāpatissa gihisahāyo therassa santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā dassanabhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhito pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.34-40) –

“Skilled in the sign of the mind”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sunāga. What is its origin? This one too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome karma that serves as a basis for liberation in various existences. Thirty-one eons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was reborn in a brahmin family. Having come of age, he became a master of the three Vedas and, dwelling in a hermitage in a forest tract, he taught the hymns to three thousand brahmins. Then one day, seeing the Teacher and examining his characteristic marks, while he was reviewing the hymns on the marks, a sublime confidence concerning the Buddha’s knowledge arose in him as he thought: “One endowed with such marks will become a Buddha, an infinite victor, one of infinite knowledge.” Through that confidence of mind he was reborn in a deva world. Wandering on among devas and humans, during this Buddha’s Dispensation he was reborn in the village of Nālaka as the son of a certain brahmin and was named Sunāga. He was a lay friend of the General of the Dhamma. He went to the elder, heard the Dhamma, and became established on the plane of vision. He then went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre, vasabho nāma pabbato;

Tasmiṃ pabbatapādamhi, assamo āsi māpito.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Vasabha. At the foot of that mountain, a hermitage was built.

“Tīṇi [M 1.0230] sissasahassāni, vācesiṃ brāhmaṇo tadā;

Saṃharitvāna te sisse, ekamantaṃ upāvisiṃ.

“As a brahmin then, I taught three thousand pupils. Having gathered those pupils together, I sat down to one side.

“Ekamantaṃ nisīditvā, brāhmaṇo mantapāragū;

Buddhavedaṃ gavesanto, ñāṇe cittaṃ pasādayiṃ.

“Having sat down to one side, I, a brahmin master of the hymns, seeking the lore of the Buddha, found confidence in my mind regarding his knowledge.

“Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, nisīdiṃ paṇṇasanthare;

Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāna, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Having made my mind confident there, I sat on a spread of leaves; having folded my legs crosswise, there I passed away.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ñāṇasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-one eons since I gained that perception then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of the perception of knowledge.

“Sattavīsati [V 1.0197] kappamhi, rājā siridharo ahu;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Twenty-seven eons ago, I was a king named Siridhara, endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning monarch.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammadesanāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, when declaring his final knowledge under the guise of giving a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus,

85.

85.

“Cittanimittassa kovido, pavivekarasaṃ vijāniya;

Jhāyaṃ nipako patissato, adhigaccheyya sukhaṃ nirāmisa”nti. –

“Skilled in the sign of the mind, having known the taste of seclusion, meditating skillfully and mindfully, one may attain unworldly happiness.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

he spoke the verse.

Tattha cittanimittassa kovidoti bhāvanācittassa nimittaggahaṇe kusalo, “imasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, imasmiṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ, imasmiṃ ajjhupekkhitabba”nti evaṃ paggahaṇādiyogyassa cittanimittassa gahaṇe cheko. Pavivekarasaṃ vijāniyāti kāyavivekasaṃvaḍḍhitassa cittavivekassa rasaṃ sañjānitvā, vivekasukhaṃ anubhavitvāti attho. “Pavivekarasaṃ pitvā”ti (dha. pa. 205) hi vuttaṃ. Jhāyanti paṭhamaṃ ārammaṇūpanijjhānena pacchā lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena ca jhāyanto. Nipakoti kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇe kusalo. Patissatoti upaṭṭhitassati.
