Adhigaccheyya sukhaṃ nirāmisanti evaṃ samathanimittādikosallena labbhe cittavivekasukhe patiṭṭhāya sato sampajāno [M 1.0231] hutvā vipassanājhāneneva jhāyanto kāmāmisavaṭṭāmisehi asammissatāya nirāmisaṃ nibbānasukhaṃ phalasukhañca adhigaccheyya samupagaccheyyāti attho.

Therein, 'skilled in the sign of the mind' means skilled in grasping the sign of the mind in meditation, adept at grasping the sign of the mind that is suitable for exertion, etc., knowing: “At this time the mind should be exerted, at this time it should be gladdened, at this time it should be regarded with equanimity.” 'Having known the taste of seclusion' means having known the taste of mental seclusion developed by bodily seclusion; the meaning is having experienced the happiness of seclusion. For it is said: “Having drunk the taste of seclusion” (Dhp 205). 'Meditating' means meditating first by absorption upon the object, and afterwards by absorption upon the characteristics. 'Skillfully' means skilled in managing the meditation subject. 'Mindfully' means with mindfulness established. 'One may attain unworldly happiness' means thus, being established in the happiness of mental seclusion gained by skill in the sign of serenity and so on, being mindful and clearly comprehending, meditating with the jhāna of insight, one may attain, one may reach the unworldly happiness—the happiness of Nibbāna and the happiness of its fruit—which is unmixed with the material counterparts of sensual pleasures and the material counterparts of the round of existence. This is the meaning.

Sunāgattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sunāga is finished.

6. Nāgitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nāgita

Ito [P 1.0193] bahiddhā puthuaññavādinanti āyasmato nāgitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle nārado nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā ekadivasaṃ māḷake nisinno bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghena purakkhataṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso tīhi gāthāhi abhitthavi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare sakyarājakule nibbatti, nāgitotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So bhagavati [V 1.0198] kapilavatthusmiṃ viharante madhupiṇḍikasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.199 ādayo) sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.47-54) –

The verse of the Venerable Nāgita begins: 'Outside of this are the many with other doctrines.' What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this one was a brahmin named Nārada. One day, while sitting in a pavilion, he saw the Blessed One walking, preceded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and with a gladdened mind, he praised him with three verses. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the world of the devas. Having repeatedly performed meritorious deeds, wandering among devas and humans, during the advent of this Buddha he was reborn into the royal family of the Sakyans in the city of Kapilavatthu, and his name was Nāgita. While the Blessed One was dwelling in Kapilavatthu, having heard the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta (MN 18), he gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Visālamāḷe āsīno, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Khīṇāsavaṃ balappattaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhataṃ.

“Seated in a great pavilion, I saw the Leader of the World, the one whose taints are destroyed, who has attained the powers, preceded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

“Satasahassā tevijjā, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā;

Parivārenti sambuddhaṃ, ko disvā nappasīdati.

“A hundred thousand with the three true knowledges and the six direct knowledges, of great psychic power, surround the Perfectly Enlightened One. Who, on seeing him, would not be gladdened?

“Ñāṇe upanidhā yassa, na vijjati sadevake;

Anantañāṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, ko disvā nappasīdati.

“Whose equal in wisdom is not found in the world with its devas; the Perfectly Enlightened One of infinite wisdom—who, seeing him, would not be gladdened?

“Dhammakāyañca dīpentaṃ, kevalaṃ ratanākaraṃ;

Vikappetuṃ na sakkonti, ko disvā nappasīdati.

“Illuminating the Dhamma-body, the sole mine of gems; none can fully fathom it—who, having seen it, would not be gladdened?

“Imāhi tīhi gāthāhi, nāradovhayavacchalo;

Padumuttaraṃ thavitvāna, sambuddhaṃ aparājitaṃ.

“With these three verses, I, the affectionate one named Nārada, having praised Padumuttara, the unconquered Perfectly Enlightened One,

“Tena [M 1.0232] cittappasādena, buddhasanthavanena ca;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“Through that gladness of mind and praise of the Buddha, for a hundred thousand eons I was not reborn in a state of woe.

“Ito tiṃsakappasate, sumitto nāma khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Thirty hundred eons ago from now, I was a khattiya named Sumitta, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthu avitathadesanataṃ dhammassa ca niyyānikataṃ nissāya sañjātapītisomanasso pītivegappavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānento –

But having attained arahantship, relying on the Teacher's unerring teaching and the liberating nature of the Dhamma, with joy and gladness arisen, he uttered an inspired utterance released by the force of that joy:

86.

86.

“Ito bahiddhā puthuaññavādinaṃ, maggo na nibbānagamo yathā ayaṃ;

Itissu saṅghaṃ bhagavānusāsati, satthā sayaṃ pāṇitaleva dassaya”nti. –

“Outside of this, the paths of the many with other doctrines do not lead to Nibbāna as this one does. Thus indeed the Blessed One instructs the Saṅgha, the Teacher himself showing it as on the palm of his hand.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha ito bahiddhāti imasmā buddhasāsanā bāhirake samaye, tenāha “puthuaññavādina”nti, nānātitthiyānanti attho. Maggo na nibbānagamo yathā ayanti yathā ayaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo ekaṃsena nibbānaṃ gacchatīti nibbānagamo, nibbānagāmī, evaṃ nibbānagamo maggo titthiyasamaye natthi asammāsambuddhappaveditattā aññatitthiyavādassa. Tenāha bhagavā –

Therein, 'outside this' means in a system external to this Buddha's Dispensation. Therefore he said, 'of the many with other doctrines,' which means 'of the various sectarians.' As for 'The path does not lead to Nibbāna as this one does': just as this Noble Eightfold Path unerringly goes to Nibbāna—thus it is 'leading to Nibbāna,' 'Nibbāna-bound'—so a path leading to Nibbāna does not exist in the systems of the sectarians, because the doctrine of other sectarians has not been proclaimed by a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Idheva[V 1.0199], bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo, idha tatiyo samaṇo, idha [P 1.0194] catuttho samaṇo, suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214; ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241).

“Here, bhikkhus, is the ascetic; here the second ascetic; here the third ascetic; here the fourth ascetic. The doctrines of others are devoid of ascetics.”

Itīti evaṃ. Assūti nipātamattaṃ. Saṅghanti bhikkhusaṅghaṃ, ukkaṭṭhaniddesoyaṃ yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti. Saṅghanti vā samūhaṃ, veneyyajananti adhippāyo. Bhagavāti bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā, ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paramatthadīpaniyaṃ itivuttakavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena [M 1.0233] veditabbo. Satthāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsatīti satthā. Sayanti sayameva. Ayañhettha attho – “sīlādikkhandhattayasaṅgaho sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgiko nibbānagāmī ariyamaggo yathā mama sāsane atthi, evaṃ bāhirakasamaye maggo nāma natthī”ti sīhanādaṃ nadanto amhākaṃ satthā bhagavā sayameva sayambhūñāṇena ñātaṃ, sayameva vā mahākaruṇāsañcodito hutvā attano desanāvilāsasampattiyā hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya dassento bhikkhusaṅghaṃ veneyyajanataṃ anusāsati ovadatīti.

'Iti' means 'thus.' 'Assu' is merely a particle. 'Saṅghaṃ' means the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; this is a supreme designation, like 'the Teacher of devas and humans.' Or 'saṅghaṃ' means an assembly; the intended meaning is 'the populace to be trained.' 'Bhagavā' means the Blessed One for reasons such as being fortunate; this is a summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood in the way stated in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Itivuttaka. 'Satthā' means Teacher because he instructs appropriately in accordance with matters of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. 'Sayaṃ' means 'by himself.' This is the meaning here: Roaring the lion's roar, 'Just as the Noble Eightfold Path leading to Nibbāna—which is comprised of the three aggregates beginning with virtuous behavior and consists of the eight factors beginning with right view—exists in my Dispensation, so in external systems there is no such thing as a path,' our Teacher, the Blessed One, having known this by himself through his self-originating knowledge, or having been impelled by great compassion, instructs and advises the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the populace to be trained, showing it by the accomplishment of the grace of his own teaching like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of his hand.

Nāgitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nāgita is concluded.

7. Paviṭṭhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paviṭṭha

Khandhā diṭṭhā yathābhūtanti āyasmato paviṭṭhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ karonto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kesavo nāma tāpaso hutvā ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso abhivādetvā añjaliṃ paggayha padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule uppajjitvā anukkamena viññutaṃ patto nekkhammaninnajjhāsayatāya paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tattha sikkhitabbaṃ sikkhitvā [P 1.0195] vicaranto upatissakolitānaṃ buddhasāsane pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā “tepi nāma mahāpaññā tattha pabbajitā, tadeva maññe seyyo”ti satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji. Tassa satthā vipassanaṃ ācikkhi. So vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.55-59) –

“The aggregates are seen as they truly are,” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Paviṭṭha. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merit here and there that was a supporting condition for release from the round of existence, in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, became an ascetic named Kesava. One day, he approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and with a gladdened mind, paid homage, raised his hands in reverence, circumambulated him, and departed. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. After repeatedly performing meritorious deeds, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born in a brahmin family in the Magadha country. Gradually attaining maturity, due to his inclination and disposition towards renunciation, he went forth into the wanderer's life. Having learned what was to be learned there, he wandered about until he heard that Upatissa and Kolita had gone forth in the Buddha's dispensation. Thinking, “Even those great in wisdom have gone forth there—surely that must be better,” he went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. The Teacher instructed him in insight. He undertook insight and before long realized arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nārado [V 1.0200] iti me nāmaṃ, kesavo iti maṃ vidū;

Kusalākusalaṃ esaṃ, agamaṃ buddhasantikaṃ.

“My name is Nārada; they know me as Kesava. Seeking the skillful and the unskillful, I came to the Buddha's presence.

“Mettacitto [M 1.0234] kāruṇiko, atthadassī mahāmuni;

Assāsayanto satte so, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“With a mind of loving-kindness, compassionate, seeing the benefit, the great sage, the one with vision, comforts beings and teaches the Dhamma.”

“Sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā, sire katvāna añjaliṃ;

Satthāraṃ abhivādetvā, pakkāmiṃ pācināmukho.

Having gladdened my own mind, placing my hands in reverence upon my head, having paid homage to the Teacher, I departed facing east.

“Sattarase kappasate, rājā āsi mahīpati;

Amittatāpano nāma, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

Seventeen hundred aeons ago, there was a king, lord of the earth, named Amittatāpano, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Then, having attained Arahantship, declaring his final knowledge:

87.

87.

“Khandhā diṭṭhā yathābhūtaṃ, bhavā sabbe padālitā;

Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“The aggregates are seen as they truly are; all states of becoming are shattered. The round of births is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.” —thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha khandhāti pañcupādānakkhandhā, te hi vipassanupalakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca ñātapariññādīhi parijānanavasena vipassitabbā. Diṭṭhā yathābhūtanti vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā aviparītato diṭṭhā. Bhavā sabbe padālitāti kāmabhavādayo sabbe kammabhavā upapattibhavā ca maggañāṇasatthena bhinnā viddhaṃsitā. Kilesapadālaneneva hi kammopapattibhavā padālitā nāma honti. Tenāha “vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

Therein, “the aggregates” means the five aggregates subject to clinging. Indeed, they are to be seen with insight by way of full understanding through comprehension as known, etc., due to their being characterized for insight and by general characteristics. “Seen as they truly are” means seen without distortion by the wisdom of the path together with insight-wisdom, as “this is suffering,” and so on. “All states of becoming are shattered” means all states of becoming, such as the sense-sphere existence and others—both kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming—are split and destroyed by the sword of path-knowledge. For it is by the shattering of defilements that kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming are called “shattered.” Hence it is said: “The round of births is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.” The meaning of this has been stated previously.

Paviṭṭhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Paviṭṭha is concluded.

8. Ajjunattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ajjuna

Asakkhiṃ vata attānanti āyasmato ajjunattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto vipassissa [P 1.0196] bhagavato kāle sīhayoniyaṃ nibbatto ekadivasaṃ araññe aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ satthāraṃ [M 1.0235] disvā “ayaṃ kho imasmiṃ kāle sabbaseṭṭho purisasīho”ti pasannamānaso supupphitasālasākhaṃ [V 1.0201] bhañjitvā satthāraṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhikule nibbatti. Ajjunotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto nigaṇṭhehi kataparicayo hutvā “evāhaṃ amataṃ adhigamissāmī”ti vivaṭṭajjhāsayatāya daharakāleyeva nigaṇṭhesu pabbajitvā tattha sāraṃ alabhanto satthu yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho sāsane pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.60-65) –

“Indeed, I was able to rescue myself,” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Ajjuna. What is its origin? He, too, having made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to release from the round of existence in various lives. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a lion's womb. One day, seeing the Teacher seated at the foot of a certain tree in the forest, he, with a gladdened mind, thought, “This is indeed the supreme man, the lion among men, in this era.” Breaking off a branch of a fully blossomed sāl tree, he paid homage to the Teacher. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a merchant's family in Sāvatthī. His name was Ajjuna. Having come of age, he became acquainted with the Nigaṇṭhas and, thinking, “Thus I shall attain the Deathless,” due to his inclination towards release, he went forth among the Nigaṇṭhas in his youth. Not finding the essence there, he witnessed the Teacher’s Twin Miracle, gained faith, and went forth in the Dispensation. He began practicing insight and soon became an Arahant. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.14.60-65):

“Migarājā tadā āsiṃ, abhijāto sukesarī;

Giriduggaṃ gavesanto, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Then I was a lion, a noble one with a fine mane; seeking a mountain stronghold, I saw the leader of the world.

“Ayaṃ nu kho mahāvīro, nibbāpeti mahājanaṃ;

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ upāseyyaṃ, devadevaṃ narāsabhaṃ.

“This great hero, indeed, brings peace to the great populace. Surely, I should attend upon the god of gods, the bull among men.

“Sākhaṃ sālassa bhañjitvā, sakosaṃ pupphamāhariṃ;

Upagantvāna sambuddhaṃ, adāsiṃ pupphamuttamaṃ.

“Breaking off a branch of the sāl tree, I brought a flower with its calyx. Approaching the Perfectly Enlightened One, I offered the excellent flower.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pupphadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I offered that flower, I do not recall a bad destination; this is the fruit of that flower-offering.

“Ito ca navame kappe, virocanasanāmakā;

Tayo āsiṃsu rājāno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“And nine aeons ago from now, there were three kings named Virocana, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā anuttarasukhādhigamasambhūtena pītivegena udānaṃ udānento –

Then, having attained Arahantship, uttering a spontaneous exclamation with a surge of rapture born from the attainment of unsurpassed bliss:

88.

88.

“Asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ, uddhātuṃ udakā thalaṃ;

Vuyhamāno mahogheva, saccāni paṭivijjhaha”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Indeed, I was able to rescue myself, from the water to dry land. Though being swept away as if by a great flood, I have penetrated the truths!” —thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 1.0236] asakkhinti sakkosiṃ. Vatāti vimhaye nipāto. Ativimhayanīyañhetaṃ yadidaṃ saccapaṭivedho. Tenāha –

Therein, “asakkhiṃ” means “I was able.” “Vata” is a particle expressing astonishment. This penetration of the truths is indeed exceedingly astonishing. Therefore, he said:

“Taṃ kiṃmaññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā, yaṃ sattadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1115)?

“What do you think, monks, which is more difficult or harder to achieve: that one might pierce tip with tip of a hair split sevenfold…” and so on (SN 56.45)?

Attānanti niyakajjhattaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yo hi paro na hoti so attāti. Uddhātunti [V 1.0202] uddharituṃ, “uddhaṭa”ntipi pāṭho. Udakāti saṃsāramahoghasaṅkhātā udakā. Thalanti nibbānathalaṃ. Vuyhamāno mahoghevāti mahaṇṇave vuyhamāno viya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nāma gambhīravitthate appatiṭṭhe mahati udakoghe vegasā vuyhamāno puriso kenaci [P 1.0197] atthakāmena upanītaṃ phiyārittasampannaṃ daḷhanāvaṃ labhitvā sukheneva tato attānaṃ uddharituṃ sakkuṇeyya pāraṃ pāpuṇeyya, evamevāhaṃ saṃsāramahoghe kilesābhisaṅkhāravegena vuyhamāno satthārā upanītaṃ samathavipassanupetaṃ ariyamagganāvaṃ labhitvā tato attānaṃ uddharituṃ nibbānathalaṃ pattuṃ aho asakkhinti. Yathā pana asakkhi, taṃ dassetuṃ “saccāni paṭivijjhaha”nti āha. Yasmā ahaṃ dukkhādīni cattāri ariyasaccāni pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhiṃ ariyamaggañāṇena aññāsiṃ, tasmā asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ uddhātuṃ udakā thalanti yojanā.

“Attānaṃ” he says, referring to his own person. For whoever is not another is “attā.” “Uddhātuṃ” means to lift up; “uddhaṭa” is also a reading. “Udakā” means from the water, that is, from what is designated as the great flood of saṃsāra. “Thalaṃ” means the dry land of Nibbāna. “Vuyhamāno mahogheva” means like one being swept away in the great ocean. This is what is said: Just as a person being swept along by the current in a vast, deep, extensive, and unstable great flood of water might, upon receiving from someone desiring their welfare a sturdy boat equipped with rudder and oars, be able to easily rescue themselves from it and reach the far shore, in the same way, I—being swept along in the great flood of saṃsāra by the force of defilements and volitional formations—received from the Teacher the boat of the noble path, endowed with serenity and insight. Oh, I was indeed able to rescue myself from that flood and reach the dry land of Nibbāna! But to show how he was able, he said, “I have penetrated the truths.” The connection is thus: Because I penetrated the four noble truths—suffering, etc.—through the modes of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and cultivation by means of the knowledge of the noble path, therefore I was indeed able to rescue myself from the water to the dry land.

Ajjunattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ajjuna is concluded.

9. (Paṭhama) devasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The First Commentary on the Verses of Elder Devasabha

Uttiṇṇā paṅkapalipāti āyasmato devasabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle pārāvatayoniyaṃ nibbatto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso piyālaphalaṃ upanesi. Satthā tassa pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ taṃ paribhuñji. So tena ativiya pasannacitto hutvā kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā cittaṃ pasādeti[M 1.0237]. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde aññatarassa maṇḍalikarañño putto hutvā nibbatto taruṇakāleyeva rajje patiṭṭhito rajjasukhamanubhavanto vuddho satthāraṃ upasaṅkami, tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho saṃvegajāto rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.66-72) –

“Crossed over the mud and mire,” are the verses of the Venerable Elder Devasabha. What is their origin? He, too, having made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences conducive to release from the round of existence. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was reborn as a pigeon. One day, seeing the Teacher, his mind became serene, and he offered a piyāla fruit. The Teacher partook of it to increase his serenity. Filled with exceeding serenity of mind, he would from time to time approach, pay homage, and gladden his mind. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Performing meritorious deeds again and again, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a certain provincial king. Established in kingship at a young age, he enjoyed royal pleasures. Having grown old, he approached the Teacher, who taught him the Dhamma. Hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith, was struck with a sense of urgency, renounced the kingdom, and went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he soon attained Arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.14.66-72):

“Pārāvato tadā āsiṃ, paraṃ anuparodhako;

Pabbhāre seyyaṃ kappemi, avidūre sikhisatthuno.

“At that time I was a pigeon, not obstructing others; I made my lodging on a mountain slope, not far from the Teacher Sikhī.

“Sāyaṃ pātañca passāmi, buddhaṃ lokagganāyakaṃ;

Deyyadhammo ca me natthi, dvipadindassa tādino.

“Morning and evening I saw the Buddha, the foremost leader of the world; but I had no gift for the Lord of bipeds, the Such One.

“Piyālaphalamādāya[V 1.0203], agamaṃ buddhasantikaṃ;

Paṭiggahesi bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho.

“Taking a piyāla fruit, I went to the Buddha's presence; the Blessed One, the world's eldest, the bull among men, accepted it.

“Tato paraṃ upādāya, paricāriṃ vināyakaṃ;

Tena cittappasādena, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“From that time onwards, I attended upon the Guide; with that serenity of mind, I passed away there.

“Ekattiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from now, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad destination; this is the fruit of that fruit-offering.

“Ito pannarase kappe, tayo āsuṃ piyālino;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

Fifteen eons ago from now, there were three Piyālins, endowed with the seven treasures, mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [P 1.0198] pana patvā pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇavasena uppannasomanasso udānaṃ udānento –

Having attained arahantship and, by way of reviewing the abandoned defilements, with joy arisen, he uttered a joyful exclamation:

89.

89.

“Uttiṇṇā paṅkapalipā, pātālā parivajjitā;

Mutto oghā ca ganthā ca, sabbe mānā visaṃhatā”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Crossed over the mud and mire, the abysses avoided; freed from floods and fetters, all conceits shattered.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha [M 1.0238] uttiṇṇāti uttaritā atikkantā. Paṅkapalipāti paṅkā ca palipā ca. Paṅko vuccati pakatikaddamo. “Palipo”ti gambhīraputhulo mahākaddamo. Idha pana paṅko viyāti paṅko, kāmarāgo asucibhāvāpādanena cittassa makkhanato. Palipo viyāti palipo, puttadārādivisayo bahalo chandarāgo vuttanayena sammakkhanato duruttaraṇato ca. Te mayā anāgāmimaggena sabbaso atikkantāti āha “uttiṇṇā paṅkapalipā”ti. Pātālāti pātāyālanti pātālā, mahāsamudde ninnatarapadesā. Keci pana nāgabhavanaṃ “pātāla”nti vadanti. Idha pana agāhaduravaggāhaduruttaraṇaṭṭhena pātālā viyāti pātālā, diṭṭhiyo. Te ca mayā paṭhamamaggādhigameneva sabbathā vajjitā samucchinnāti āha “pātālā parivajjitā”ti mutto oghā ca ganthā cāti kāmoghādioghato abhijjhākāyaganthādiganthato ca tena tena maggena mutto parimutto, puna anabhikiraṇaaganthanavasena atikkantoti attho. Sabbe mānā visaṃhatāti navavidhāpi mānā aggamaggādhigamena visesato saṅghātaṃ vināsaṃ āpāditā samucchinnā “mānavidhā hatā”ti keci paṭhanti, mānakoṭṭhāsāti attho. “Mānavisā”ti apare, tesaṃ pana mānavisassa dukkhassa phalato mānavisāti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, 'uttiṇṇa' means crossed over, surpassed. 'Paṅkapalipā' means mud and mire. 'Paṅko' is called ordinary mud. 'Palipo' means deep, extensive, great mud. Here, however, 'paṅko' is like mud—it is sensual lust, due to its smearing the mind by producing impurity. 'Palipo' is like mire—it is the intense desire and lust for the objective sphere of children, wives, and so on, due to its thoroughly smearing the mind in the way stated and its being difficult to cross. These I have completely surpassed by the path of non-returning—thus he said, 'crossed over the mud and mire.' 'Pātālā' means 'they cause to fall' (pātāyālanti), hence 'abysses'; they are the lower regions in the great ocean. Some, however, say 'pātāla' is the abode of nāgas. Here, however, 'pātālā' are like abysses—they are views, in the sense of being unfathomable, difficult to plunge into, and difficult to cross. And these have been entirely avoided and eradicated by me through the very attainment of the first path—thus he said, 'the abysses avoided.' 'Freed from floods and fetters' means freed and liberated from the floods, such as the flood of sensuality, and from the fetters, such as the bodily fetter of covetousness, by means of the respective paths; the meaning is that he has gone beyond them in the sense of not being scattered upon or bound again. 'All conceits shattered' means that all nine kinds of conceit have been brought to destruction and annihilation, and have been eradicated, especially through the attainment of the highest path. Some read 'mānavidhā hatā,' meaning 'the aspects of conceit are destroyed.' Others read 'mānavisā'; for them, however, the meaning 'the poison of conceit' should be understood in terms of the suffering that is its fruit.

(Paṭhama) devasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Devasabha (the first) is concluded.

10. Sāmidattattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sāmidatta

Pañcakkhandhā [V 1.0204][P 1.0199] pariññātāti āyasmato sāmidattattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute tassa thūpe pupphehi chattātichattaṃ katvā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, sāmidattotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So anukkamena viññutaṃ patto buddhānubhāvaṃ sutvā upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gato satthāraṃ [M 1.0239] dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā tathā dhammaṃ desesi, yathā saddhaṃ paṭilabhi saṃsāre ca saṃvegaṃ. So paṭiladdhasaddho saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā ñāṇassa aparipakkattā katipayakālaṃ alasabahulī vihāsi. Puna satthārā dhammadesanāya samuttejito vipassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tattha yuttappayutto viharanto nacireneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.1-4) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Sāmidatta begins: “The five aggregates are fully understood.” What was the origin? This venerable one, too, had made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was born in a householder’s family and, having attained understanding, when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he made an offering at his stupa by making a parasol and a tiered parasol with flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Having repeatedly performed meritorious deeds, he wandered through the deva and human realms until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born as the son of a certain brahmin in Rājagaha; his name was Sāmidatta. Gradually, he attained understanding. Hearing of the Buddha’s power, he went to the monastery with lay devotees. Seeing the Teacher expounding the Dhamma, his mind became gladdened, and he sat down to one side. The Teacher, discerning his inclination, taught him the Dhamma in such a way that he gained faith and a sense of urgency towards saṃsāra. Having acquired faith and being stirred by urgency, he went forth. But because his knowledge was not yet mature, for some time he dwelt much in laziness. Again, exhorted by the Teacher with a Dhamma discourse, he took up a meditation subject for insight. Dwelling there diligently applying himself, he soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Parinibbute bhagavati, atthadassīnaruttame;

Chattātichattaṃ kāretvā, thūpamhi abhiropayiṃ.

“When the Blessed One, Atthadassī, the supreme among men, had attained final Nibbāna, having had a parasol and a tiered parasol made, I placed them on the stupa.”

“Kālena kālamāgantvā, namassiṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Pupphacchadanaṃ katvāna, chattamhi abhiropayiṃ.

“Approaching from time to time, I paid homage to the Leader of the World; having made a covering of flowers, I placed it on the parasol.”

“Sattarase kappasate, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Manussattaṃ na gacchāmi, thūpapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“For seventeen hundred eons, I exercised divine kingship; I did not go to a human state—this is the fruit of stupa worship.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

“My defilements are burnt up, all existences are uprooted; like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell taintless.”

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, buddhaseṭṭhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“Welcome indeed it was for me, in the presence of the foremost Buddha; the three knowledges are attained, the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

So aparabhāge bhikkhūhi “kiṃ tayā, āvuso, uttarimanussadhammo adhigato”ti puṭṭho sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ attano ca dhammānudhammappaṭipattiṃ tesaṃ pavedento aññābyākaraṇavasena –

Later on, when asked by the bhikkhus, “Friend, have you attained any superhuman state?” he declared to them the liberating nature of the Teaching and his own practice in accordance with the Dhamma, by way of a declaration of final knowledge:

90.

90.

“Pañcakkhandhā [V 1.0205] pariññātā, tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā;

Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“The five aggregates are fully understood, they stand with roots cut off; the cycle of birth is exhausted, now there is no further becoming.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha pañcakkhandhā pariññātāti mayā ime pañcupādānakkhandhā “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na tato bhiyyo”ti tīhi pariññāhi paricchinditvā ñātā viditā paṭividdhā. Tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakāti tathā pariññātattāyeva mūlabhūtassa [M 1.0240][P 1.0200] samudayassa sabbaso pahīnattā te idāni yāva carimakacittanirodho tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā, carimakacittanirodhena pana appaṭisandhikāva nirujjhanti. Tenāha – “vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

Herein, “the five aggregates are fully understood” means that these five aggregates of clinging have been discerned, known, and penetrated by me through the three kinds of full understanding: “This is suffering, this is the extent of suffering, there is no more than this.” “They stand with roots cut off”—because they have been fully understood in this way, and because the root cause, which is the origin, has been entirely abandoned, they now persist with roots cut off until the cessation of the final consciousness. However, with the cessation of the final consciousness, they cease without any further rebirth. Therefore, he said: “The cycle of birth is exhausted, now there is no further becoming.” The meaning of this has already been explained above.

Sāmidattattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sāmidatta is concluded.

Navamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ninth Chapter is concluded.

10. Dasamavaggo

10. Chapter Ten

1. Paripuṇṇakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paripuṇṇaka

Na [V 1.0206] tathā mataṃ satarasanti āyasmato paripuṇṇakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro dhammadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute satthu cetiye pupphādīhi uḷāraṃ pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devesu nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sakyarājakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto paripuṇṇavibhavatāya paripuṇṇakoti paññāyittha. So vibhavasampannatāya sabbakālaṃ satarasaṃ nāma āhāraṃ paribhuñjanto satthu missakāhāraparibhogaṃ sutvā “tāva sukhumālopi bhagavā nibbānasukhaṃ apekkhitvā yathā tathā yāpeti, kasmā mayaṃ āhāragiddhā hutvā āhārasuddhikā bhavissāma, nibbānasukhameva pana amhehi pariyesitabba”nti saṃsāre jātasaṃvego gharāvāsaṃ pahāya satthu santike pabbajitvā bhagavatā kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne niyojito tattha patiṭṭhāya paṭiladdhajhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.5-9) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Paripuṇṇaka begins: “Not so is a meal of a hundred flavors…” What is its origin? This venerable one, too, having made a resolve in the times of past Buddhas, was reborn in a householder’s family during the time of the Blessed One Dhammadassī and attained maturity. After the Teacher’s final Nibbāna, he made a grand offering of flowers and other items at the Teacher’s stupa. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas. Continuously performing meritorious deeds, he wandered only in happy realms until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in the Sakyan royal family of Kapilavatthu and attained maturity. He was known as Paripuṇṇaka due to his abundant prosperity. Due to his abundant prosperity, he always enjoyed food called 'satarasa'. Hearing that the Teacher partook of mixed food, he reflected: “Even the delicate-bodied Blessed One, desiring the bliss of Nibbāna, lives as he does. Why should we, greedy for food, be concerned with the purity of food? We should seek only the bliss of Nibbāna.” Feeling urgency towards the cycle of existence, he abandoned household life and went forth in the Teacher’s presence. The Blessed One assigned him the meditation on mindfulness of the body. Establishing himself there, making the attained jhāna his foundation, and performing the work of insight, he developed insight and reached arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nibbute lokanāthamhi, dhammadassīnarāsabhe;

Āropesiṃ dhajatthambhaṃ, buddhaseṭṭhassa cetiye.

“When the world’s protector, Dhammadassī, the foremost of men, had passed away, I erected a flagstaff at the stupa of the supreme Buddha.”

“Nisseṇiṃ māpayitvāna, thūpaseṭṭhaṃ samāruhiṃ;

Jātipupphaṃ gahetvāna, thūpamhi abhiropayiṃ.

“Having had a staircase made, I ascended the chief stupa; taking a jasmine flower, I offered it at the stupa.”

“Aho [M 1.0241] buddho aho dhammo, aho no satthu sampadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, thūpapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ah, the Buddha! Ah, the Dhamma! Ah, the perfection of our Teacher! I do not experience any woeful state; this is the fruit of worshiping the stupa.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, thūpasīkhasanāmakā;

Soḷasāsiṃsu rājāno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, sixteen kings named Thūpasīkhasa were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0207] pana patvā dhamme gāravabahumānena pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ [P 1.0201] udānaṃ udānento “na tathā mataṃ satarasa”nti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, with great respect and reverence for the Dhamma, he uttered an inspired utterance released with a surge of joy, and spoke the stanza beginning, “Not so esteemed is that of a hundred flavors.”

91. Tattha na tathā mataṃ satarasaṃ, sudhannaṃ yaṃ mayajja paribhuttanti tathāti tena pakārena. Matanti abhimataṃ. Satarasanti satarasabhojanaṃ “satarasabhojanaṃ nāma satapākasappiādīhi abhisaṅkhataṃ bhojana”nti vadanti. Atha vā anekattho satasaddo “sataso sahassaso”tiādīsu viya. Tasmā yaṃ bhojanaṃ anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ, taṃ anekarasatāya “satarasa”nti vuccati, nānārasabhojananti attho. Sudhā eva annaṃ sudhābhojanaṃ devānaṃ āhāro. Yaṃ mayajja paribhuttanti yaṃ mayā ajja anubhuttaṃ. “Yaṃ mayā paribhutta”nti ca idaṃ “satarasaṃ sudhanna”nti etthāpi yojetabbaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ mayā ajja etarahi nirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanavasena phalasamāpattisamāpajjanavasena ca accantameva santaṃ paṇītaṃ nibbānasukhaṃ paribhuñjiyamānaṃ, taṃ yathā mataṃ abhimataṃ sambhāvitaṃ tathā rājakāle mayā paribhuttaṃ satarasabhojanaṃ devattabhāve paribhuttaṃ sudhannañca na mataṃ nābhimataṃ. Kasmā? Idañhi ariyanisevitaṃ nirāmisaṃ kilesānaṃ avatthubhūtaṃ, taṃ pana puthujjanasevitaṃ sāmisaṃ kilesānaṃ vatthubhūtaṃ, taṃ imassa saṅkhampi kalampi kalabhāgampi na upetīti. Idāni “yaṃ mayajja paribhutta”nti vuttadhammaṃ desento aparimitadassinā gotamena, buddhena sudesito dhammo”ti āha. Tassattho – aparimitaṃ aparicchinnaṃ uppādavayābhāvato santaṃ asaṅkhatadhātuṃ sayambhūñāṇena passī, aparimitassa anantāparimeyyassa ñeyyassa dassāvīti tena aparimitadassinā gotamagottena sammāsambuddhena [M 1.0242] “khayaṃ virāgaṃ amataṃ paṇīta”nti (khu. pā. 6.4; su. ni. 227) ca “madanimmadano pipāsavinayo” (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti (a. ni. 5.140; 10.6) ca ādinā suṭṭhu desito dhammo, nibbānaṃ mayā ajja paribhuttanti yojanā.

91. Therein, ‘tathā’ means ‘in that way.’ ‘Mata’ means ‘approved’ or ‘desired.’ ‘Satarasa’ means ‘food of a hundred flavors.’ They say that ‘food of a hundred flavors’ is food prepared with ghee cooked a hundred times and so on. Alternatively, the word ‘sata’ (hundred) has multiple meanings, as in ‘by hundreds, by thousands’ and so on. Therefore, any food with many soups and many curries is called ‘satarasa’ due to its many tastes; the meaning is ‘food of diverse flavors.’ ‘Sudhanna’ (divine food) is indeed food, divine food, the sustenance of the devas. ‘Yaṃ mayajja paribhuttaṃ’ means ‘that which I have experienced today.’ And this ‘that which I have enjoyed’ should also be connected here with ‘satarasa’ and ‘sudhanna.’ This is what is said: The supremely peaceful and sublime bliss of Nibbāna, which I am enjoying today, now, by way of attaining the attainment of cessation and by way of attaining the attainment of fruition—that, as it is approved, desired, and esteemed, is not approved or desired in the same way as the food of a hundred flavors I enjoyed during my time as a king, or the divine food I enjoyed in my divine existence. Why? Because this [Nibbāna] is cultivated by the noble ones, free from sensual taints, and is not a basis for defilements. But that [worldly food] is cultivated by ordinary people, tainted by sensuality, and serves as a basis for defilements; it does not even approach a calculation, a fraction, or a part of a fraction of this [Nibbāna]. Now, explaining the teaching referred to by ‘that which I have enjoyed today,’ he says: ‘The Dhamma has been well taught by the Buddha Gotama, the one of infinite vision.’ The meaning is: He saw the unconditioned element, infinite and boundless, peaceful due to the absence of arising and passing away, with his self-awakened knowledge—thus, he is called ‘the one of infinite vision’ because he is a seer of the infinite, immeasurable object of knowledge. The Dhamma—Nibbāna—was well taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One of the Gotama clan with phrases such as ‘the destruction [of craving], dispassion, the deathless, the sublime’ (Khuddakapāṭha 6.4; Sutta Nipāta 227), ‘the subduer of intoxication, the removal of thirst’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34; Itivuttaka 90), and ‘the stilling of all formations’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.140; 10.6). The connection is: Nibbāna, which I have enjoyed today.

Paripuṇṇakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Paripuṇṇaka is concluded.

2. Vijayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vijaya

Yassāsavā [P 1.0202] parikkhīṇāti āyasmato vijayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro piyadassissa bhagavato kāle vibhavasampanne kule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute tassa thūpassa ratanakhacitaṃ vedikaṃ kāretvā tattha uḷāraṃ vedikāmahaṃ [V 1.0208] kāresi. So tena puññakammena anekasate attabhāve maṇiobhāsena vicari. Evaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, vijayotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gato tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane jhānalābhī hutvā viharanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā uppannappasādo satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.10-14) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Vijaya begins with ‘Yassāsavā parikkhīṇā’ (Whose taints are destroyed). What is his origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a prosperous family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī. Having reached maturity, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he had a jeweled railing constructed around his stupa and performed a grand festival of offerings there. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through hundreds of existences, shining like a gem. Thus, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī, and his name was Vijaya. When he came of age, he became proficient in brahminical knowledge and went forth into the ascetic life. Dwelling in a forest abode, he attained meditative absorption. Hearing of the Buddha’s arising, faith arose in him. He approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Hearing the Dhamma, he went forth, established insight, and before long attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.15.10–14):

“Nibbute lokanāthamhi, piyadassīnaruttame;

Pasannacitto sumano, muttāvedimakāsahaṃ.

“When the world’s protector, Piyadassī, the supreme among men, had attained Nibbāna, with a joyful and serene mind, I made a pearl railing.”

“Maṇīhi parivāretvā, akāsiṃ vedimuttamaṃ;

Vedikāya mahaṃ katvā, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Having surrounded it with gems, I made a supreme railing; having performed a festival for the railing, there I passed away.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Maṇī dhārenti ākāse, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In whatever womb I am born, be it divine or human, gems appear in the sky; this is the fruit of meritorious deeds.”

“Soḷasito kappasate, maṇippabhāsanāmakā;

Chattiṃsāsiṃsu rājāno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Sixteen hundred aeons ago, there were thirty-six kings named Maṇippabhāsa, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0243] pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto “yassāsavā parikkhīṇā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Having attained arahantship, while declaring his final knowledge, he uttered the verse: “Whose taints are destroyed.”

92. Tattha yassāsavā parikkhīṇāti yassa uttamapuggalassa kāmāsavādayo cattāro āsavā sabbaso khīṇā ariyamaggena khepitā. Āhāre ca anissitoti yo ca āhāre taṇhādiṭṭhinissayehi anissito agadhito anajjhāpanno, nidassanamattaṃ, āhārasīsenettha cattāropi paccayā gahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paccayapariyāyo vā idha āhāra-saddo veditabbo. “Suññato animitto cā”ti ettha appaṇihitavimokkhopi gahitoyeva, tīṇipi cetāni nibbānasseva nāmāni. Nibbānañhi rāgādīnaṃ abhāvena suññaṃ, tehi vimuttañcāti suññatavimokkho, tathā rāgādinimittābhāvena saṅkhāranimittābhāvena ca animittaṃ[P 1.0203], tehi vimuttañcāti animittavimokkho, rāgādipaṇidhīnaṃ abhāvena appaṇihitaṃ, tehi vimuttañcāti appaṇihito vimokkhoti vuccati. Phalasamāpattivasena taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā viharantassa ayampi tividho vimokkho yassa gocaro, ākāseva sakuntānaṃ, padaṃ tassa durannayanti yathā ākāse [V 1.0209] gacchantānaṃ sakuṇānaṃ “imasmiṃ ṭhāne pādehi akkamitvā gatā, idaṃ ṭhānaṃ urena paharitvā gatā, idaṃ sīsena, idaṃ pakkhehī”ti na sakkā ñātuṃ, evameva evarūpassa bhikkhuno “nirayapadādīsu iminā nāma padena gato”ti ñāpetuñca na sakkāti.

92. Herein, ‘whose taints are destroyed’ (yassāsavā parikkhīṇā) means that for that supreme person, the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, are completely destroyed, eradicated by the noble path. And ‘he is independent of nutriment’ (āhāre ca anissito) means that he is not dependent, not clinging, not obsessed with nutriment through craving, views, or attachment. This is merely an example; it should be understood that all four requisites are included here under the heading of nutriment. Or, the word ‘nutriment’ here should be understood as a synonym for requisites. ‘Empty and signless’ (suññato animitto ca) also includes the desireless liberation. These three are indeed names for Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is empty because of the absence of lust and so forth, and because it is liberated from them; thus it is called the liberation of emptiness. Similarly, because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, and because of the absence of the signs of formations, it is signless, and because it is liberated from them; thus it is called the signless liberation. Because of the absence of longing for lust and so forth, it is desireless, and because it is liberated from them; thus it is called the desireless liberation. For one who dwells making that (Nibbāna) the object through fruition attainment, this threefold liberation is his domain. ‘Like birds in the sky, his path is hard to trace’ (ākāseva sakuntānaṃ, padaṃ tassa durannayaṃ) means that just as it is impossible to know of birds flying in the sky, “They stepped here with their feet, they struck here with their chests, here with their heads, here with their wings,” so too it is impossible to point out of such a monk, “He went by such and such a path to the realms of hell or elsewhere.”

Vijayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vijaya is concluded.

3. Erakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Eraka

Dukkhā kāmā erakāti āyasmato erakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso satthu kiñci dātabbayuttakaṃ alabhanto “handāhaṃ kāyasāraṃ puññaṃ karissāmī”ti satthu gamanamaggaṃ sodhetvā samaṃ akāsi. Satthā tena tathākataṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji[M 1.0244]. So tattha bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha pasannacitto yāva dassanupacārasamatikkamā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ avijahanto aṭṭhāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ sambhāvanīyassa kuṭumbiyassa putto hutvā nibbatti, erakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko itikattabbatāsu paramena veyyattiyena samannāgato. Tassa mātāpitaro kulena rūpena ācārena vayena kosallena ca anucchavikaṃ dārikaṃ ānetvā vivāhakammaṃ akaṃsu[P 1.0204]. So tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsena gehe vasanto pacchimabhavikattā kenacideva saṃvegavatthunā saṃsāre saṃviggamānaso satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji, tassa satthā kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā katipayadivasātikkamena ukkaṇṭhābhibhūto vihāsi. Atha satthā tassa cittappavattiṃ ñatvā ovādavasena “dukkhā kāmā erakā”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi. So taṃ sutvā “ayuttaṃ mayā kataṃ, yohaṃ evarūpassa satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā taṃ vissajjento micchāvitakkabahulo vihāsi”nti saṃvegajāto vipassanāya yuttappayutto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.32-36) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Eraka begins with ‘Dukkhā kāmā erakā’ (Painful are sensual pleasures, Eraka). What is his origin? This elder too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a mind of faith, not finding anything suitable to offer the Teacher, thought, “Well then, I will make merit with the strength of my body,” and he cleared and leveled the path for the Teacher’s journey. The Teacher walked on that path thus prepared. Seeing the Blessed One there, with a mind of faith, he paid homage, raised his joined palms, and with a delighted heart, stood there without losing the joy focused on the Buddha until he was out of sight. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world. Continuously performing meritorious deeds, he wandered in happy destinies until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a respectable householder in Sāvatthī, and his name was Eraka—handsome, pleasing, and endowed with the highest skill in various arts. His parents, considering his family, appearance, conduct, age, and skill, brought a suitable maiden and performed the marriage ceremony. Living with her in the household, due to his being in his final existence, his mind was stirred with urgency regarding saṃsāra by some cause. Approaching the Teacher, he heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. The Teacher gave him a meditation subject. Taking up the meditation subject, after a few days, he dwelt, overcome by discontent. Then the Teacher, knowing the state of his mind, spoke this verse by way of advice: “Painful are sensual pleasures, Eraka.” Hearing this, he thought, “I have acted improperly, for having taken up a meditation subject in the presence of such a Teacher, I abandoned it and dwelt full of wrong thoughts.” Stirred by urgency, he applied himself to insight and soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.15.32–36):

“Uttaritvāna nadikaṃ, vanaṃ gacchati cakkhumā;

Tamaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, siddhatthaṃ varalakkhaṇaṃ.

“Having crossed a river, the One with Vision went to the forest; I saw the Fully Enlightened One, Siddhattha, endowed with excellent marks.

“Kudālapiṭakamādāya[V 1.0210], samaṃ katvāna taṃ pathaṃ;

Satthāraṃ abhivādetvā, sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādayiṃ.

“Taking a spade and a basket, having leveled that path; having paid homage to the Teacher, I gladdened my mind.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, maggadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, the deed I did then; I have not known a bad destination, this is the fruit of the gift of a path.

“Sattapaññāsakappamhi, eko āsiṃ janādhipo;

Nāmena suppabuddhoti, nāyako so narissaro.

“Fifty-seven aeons ago, I was a sole ruler of men, named Suppabuddha, a leader, a lord of men.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahā pana hutvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having become an arahant, he declared his final knowledge:

93.

93.

“Dukkhā [M 1.0245] kāmā eraka, na sukhā kāmā eraka;

Yo kāme kāmayati, dukkhaṃ so kāmayati eraka;

Yo kāme na kāmayati, dukkhaṃ so na kāmayati erakā”ti. –

“Painful are sensual pleasures, Eraka, not pleasant are sensual pleasures, Eraka. Whoever desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering, Eraka. Whoever does not desire sensual pleasures, does not desire suffering, Eraka.”

Tameva bhagavatā vuttagāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

He repeated that same verse spoken by the Blessed One.

Tattha dukkhā kāmāti ime vatthukāmakilesakāmā dukkhavatthutāya vipariṇāmadukkhasaṃsāradukkhasabhāvato ca, dukkhā dukkhamā dukkhanibbattikā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādi (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.234). Erakāti paṭhamaṃ tāva bhagavā taṃ ālapati, pacchā pana thero attānaṃ nāmena kathesi. Na sukhā kāmāti kāmā nāmete jānantassa sukhā na honti, ajānantassa pana sukhato upaṭṭhahanti. Yathāha – “yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 4.253; itivu. 53; theragā. 986). Yo kāme kāmayati, dukkhaṃ so kāmayatīti yo satto kilesakāmena vatthukāme kāmayati, tassa taṃ kāmanaṃ sampati sapariḷāhatāya[P 1.0205], āyatiṃ apāyadukkhahetutāya ca vaṭṭadukkhahetutāya ca dukkhaṃ. Vatthukāmā pana dukkhassa vatthubhūtā. Iti so dukkhasabhāvaṃ dukkhanimittaṃ dukkhavatthuñca kāmayatīti vutto. Itaraṃ paṭipakkhavasena tamevatthaṃ ñāpetuṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā tassattho vuttavipariyāyena veditabbo.

Herein, ‘painful are sensual pleasures’ refers to these sensual pleasures of objects and sensual pleasures of defilements, which are painful because they are the basis of suffering, because they are by nature suffering due to change, and because they are by nature the suffering of the round of existence; they are painful, they are suffering, they produce suffering. For it has been said: “Sensual pleasures have little enjoyment, much suffering, and great distress; the danger in them is even greater” (Pāc. 417; MN 1.234). ‘Eraka’—first, the Blessed One addresses him thus, and later the Elder refers to himself by name. ‘Not pleasant are sensual pleasures’ means that these sensual pleasures are not pleasant to one who knows them, but to one who does not know, they appear as pleasant. As it is said: “He who sees pleasure as suffering, and suffering as a dart” (SN 4.253; Iti. 53; Thag. 986). ‘Whoever desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering’ means that for that being who, driven by defiled desires, craves sensual objects, that craving is suffering because it is immediately burning and painful, and in the future, it becomes a cause of suffering in the states of misery and a cause of the suffering of the round of existence. Moreover, sensual objects themselves are the basis of suffering. Thus, it is said that one who desires them desires what is inherently suffering, a sign of suffering, and the basis of suffering. The other part is stated to convey the same meaning from the opposite perspective. Therefore, its meaning should be understood in contrast to what has been said.

Erakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Eraka is concluded.

4. Mettajittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mettaji

Namo [M 1.0246][V 1.0211] hi tassa bhagavatoti āyasmato mettajittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira anomadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto sāsane abhippasanno hutvā bodhirukkhassa iṭṭhakāhi vedikaṃ cinitvā sudhāparikammaṃ kāresi. Satthā tassa anumodanaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, mettajītissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññe viharanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā pubbahetunā codiyamāno satthu santikaṃ gantvā pavattinivattiyo ārabbha pañhaṃ pucchitvā satthārā pañhe vissajjite paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.26-31) –

“Homage to that Blessed One!” This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Mettaji. What is his origin? It is said that, in the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was born into a good family. Having attained maturity, he gained deep faith in the Dispensation and built a brick railing around the Bodhi tree, having it plastered with whitewash. The Teacher rejoiced in his meritorious deed. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world. After repeatedly performing meritorious deeds and wandering among divine and human realms, in this Buddha-era he was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin in the country of Magadha, and his name was Mettaji. When he came of age, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he went forth into the ascetic life and dwelt in the forest. Hearing of the Buddha’s appearance, urged on by past causes, he went to the Teacher. After asking questions concerning arising and cessation, and receiving answers from the Teacher, he gained faith, went forth, established insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.15.26-31):

“Anomadassīmunino, bodhivedimakāsahaṃ;

Sudhāya piṇḍaṃ datvāna, pāṇikammaṃ akāsahaṃ.

“For Anomadassī, the sage, I made a railing for the Bodhi tree. Having given a lump of plaster, I performed the work with my own hand.”

“Disvā taṃ sukataṃ kammaṃ, anomadassī naruttamo;

Bhikkhusaṅghe ṭhito satthā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Seeing that well-done deed, Anomadassī, the supreme man, the Teacher, standing in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses.”

“Iminā sudhakammena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Sampattiṃ anubhotvāna, dukkhassantaṃ karissati.

“By this deed of plastering, and by aspirations of intention, having experienced prosperity, he will make an end to suffering.”

“Pasannamukhavaṇṇomhi, ekaggo susamāhito;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsane.

“My countenance is bright and clear, I am one-pointed and well-composed; I bear this final body in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

“Ito kappasate āsiṃ, paripuṇṇe anūnake;

Rājā sabbaghano nāma, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“One hundred full aeons ago, not one less, I was King Sabbaghana, a wheel-turning monarch of great might.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthāraṃ thomento –

Having attained arahantship, while praising the Teacher, he spoke thus:

94.

94.

“Namo hi tassa bhagavato, sakyaputtassa sirīmato;

Tenāyaṃ aggappattena, aggadhammo sudesito”ti. – gāthaṃ [P 1.0206] abhāsi;

“Homage to that Blessed One, the glorious son of the Sakyans! By him, who has attained the supreme, the supreme Dhamma has been well taught.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha [M 1.0247] namoti namakkāro. Hīti nipātamattaṃ. Tassāti yo so bhagavā samattiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā [V 1.0212] sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, sakyarājassa puttoti sakyaputto. Anaññasādhāraṇāya puññasampattiyā ca sambhāvito uttamāya rūpakāyasiriyā dhammakāyasiriyā ca samannāgatattā sirīmā, tassa bhagavato sakyaputtassa sirīmato namo atthu, taṃ namāmīti attho. Tenāti tena bhagavatā. Ayanti tassa dhammassa attano paccakkhatāya vadati. Aggappattenāti aggaṃ sabbaññutaṃ, sabbehi vā guṇehi aggabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ pattena. Aggadhammoti aggo uttamo navavidhalokuttaro dhammo suṭṭhu aviparītaṃ desito paveditoti.

Here, 'namo' means homage. 'Hi' is merely a particle. 'Tassa' refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment—the son of the Sakyan king, thus 'Sakyaputta'. Esteemed for unparalleled merit and endowed with the supreme glory of the physical form and the glory of the Dhamma-body, he is 'sirīmā' (glorious). The meaning is: 'Homage be to that Blessed One, the glorious son of the Sakyans; I pay homage to him.' 'Tena' means by that Blessed One. 'Ayaṃ' refers to that Dhamma, spoken of as his own direct experience. 'Aggappattena' means having attained the highest, omniscience, or the supreme and excellent state in all virtues. 'Aggadhammo' means the supreme, the excellent, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, well taught and proclaimed without distortion.

Mettajittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mettaji is concluded.

5. Cakkhupālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cakkhupāla

Andhohaṃ hatanettosmīti āyasmato cakkhupālattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavati parinibbute thūpamahe kayiramāne umāpupphaṃ gahetvā thūpaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ mahāsuvaṇṇassa nāma kuṭumbikassa putto hutvā nibbatti, tassa pāloti nāmamakaṃsu. Mātā tassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle aññaṃ puttaṃ labhi. Tassa mātāpitaro cūḷapāloti nāmaṃ katvā itaraṃ mahāpāloti vohariṃsu. Atha te vayappatte gharabandhanena bandhiṃsu. Tasmiṃ samaye satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane. Tattha mahāpālo jetavanaṃ gacchantehi upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho kuṭumbabhāraṃ kaniṭṭhabhātikasseva bhāraṃ katvā sayaṃ pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike [P 1.0207] pañcavassāni vasitvā vuṭṭhavasso pavāretvā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā saṭṭhimatte [M 1.0248] sahāyabhikkhū labhitvā tehi saddhiṃ bhāvanānukūlaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesanto aññataraṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya gāmavāsikehi upāsakehi kāretvā dinnāya araññāyatane paṇṇasālāya vasanto samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Tassa akkhirogo uppanno. Vejjo bhesajjaṃ sampādetvā adāsi. So vejjena vuttavidhānaṃ na paṭipajji. Tenassa rogo vaḍḍhi. So “akkhirogavūpasamanato kilesarogavūpasamanameva mayhaṃ vara”nti akkhirogaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā vipassanāyayeva yuttappayutto ahosi. Tassa bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpentassa apubbaṃ acarimaṃ akkhīni ceva kilesā ca bhijjiṃsu. So sukkhavipassako arahā ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.21-25) –

'I am blind, my eyes are destroyed,' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Cakkhupāla. What is his origin? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, was born into a householder's family. Having reached the age of discernment, after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, when a great stupa festival was being held, he took an umā flower and offered it to the stupa. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds, wandering between the divine and human realms. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn as the son of a householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa in Sāvatthī, and they named him Pāla. His mother, while running about and attending to her affairs, conceived another son. His parents named him Cūḷapāla and called the other Mahāpāla. When they came of age, they bound them with the ties of household life. At that time, the Teacher was dwelling in Sāvatthī at Jetavana. There, Mahāpāla went to the monastery with lay devotees who were visiting Jetavana. After hearing the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence, he gained faith. He entrusted the burden of the household to his younger brother and himself went forth. Having received higher ordination, he stayed for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors. After completing his rains residence and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he received a meditation subject from the Teacher. He then found about sixty companion bhikkhus and, together with them, sought a dwelling place suitable for meditation. Relying on a border village, he stayed in a leaf hut in a forest hermitage, which was built and offered by the village lay devotees, and practiced the duties of a recluse. Then, an eye disease arose in him. A physician prepared medicine and gave it to him, but he did not follow the physician’s instructions. As a result, his illness worsened. Thinking, 'The pacification of the disease of defilements is better for me than the pacification of this eye disease,' he disregarded the eye ailment and devoted himself solely to insight meditation. As he ardently pursued his meditation, at one and the same time both his eyes and his defilements were destroyed. He became an arahant, a dry-insight meditator. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.15.21-25):

“Nibbute [V 1.0213] lokamahite, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahe;

Siddhatthamhi bhagavati, mahāthūpamaho ahu.

"When the world-honored one, the receiver of offerings, the Blessed One Siddhattha, had attained Parinibbāna, a great festival for the Great Stupa took place."

“Mahe pavattamānamhi, siddhatthassa mahesino;

Umāpupphaṃ gahetvāna, thūpamhi abhiropayiṃ.

"When the festival of the great sage Siddhattha was taking place, taking an umā flower, I offered it at the stupa."

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, thūpapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-four aeons ago, when I offered that flower, I do not recall any bad rebirth—this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa."

“Ito ca navame kappe, somadevasanāmakā;

Pañcāsītisu rājāno, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

"And in the ninth aeon from this one, there were eighty-five kings named Somadeva, wheel-turning monarchs of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Atha there akkhirogena vihāre ohīne gāmaṃ piṇḍāya gate bhikkhū disvā upāsakā “kasmā thero nāgato”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā sokābhibhūtā piṇḍapātaṃ upanetvā, “bhante, kiñci mā cintayittha, idāni mayameva piṇḍapātaṃ ānetvā upaṭṭhahissāmā”ti tathā karonti. Bhikkhū therassa ovāde ṭhatvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā vuṭṭhavassā pavāretvā, “satthāraṃ vandituṃ sāvatthiṃ gamissāma, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. Thero, “ahaṃ dubbalo acakkhuko, maggo ca saupaddavo, mayā saddhiṃ gacchantānaṃ tumhākaṃ parissayo bhavissati, tumhe paṭhamaṃ gacchatha, gantvā satthāraṃ mahāthere ca mama vandanāya vandatha, cūḷapālassa mama [M 1.0249] pavattiṃ kathetvā kañci purisaṃ peseyyāthā”ti āha. Te punapi yācitvā gamanaṃ alabhantā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā upāsake āpucchitvā anukkamena jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ mahāthere ca tassa vandanāya vanditvā dutiyadivase sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā [P 1.0208] cūḷapālassa taṃ pavattiṃ vatvā tena “ayaṃ, bhante, mayhaṃ bhāgineyyo pālito nāma, imaṃ pesissāmī”ti vutte, “maggo saparissayo, na sakkā ekena gahaṭṭhena gantuṃ, tasmā pabbājetabbo”ti taṃ pabbājetvā pesesuṃ. So anukkamena therassa santikaṃ gantvā attānaṃ tassa orocetvā taṃ gahetvā āgacchanto antarāmagge aññatarassa gāmassa sāmantā araññaṭṭhāne ekissā kaṭṭhahāriyā gāyantiyā saddaṃ sutvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ vissajjetvā “tiṭṭhatha, bhante, muhuttaṃ yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmī”ti vatvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā tattha sīlavipattiṃ pāpuṇi. Thero idānimeva itthiyā gītasaddo suto, sāmaṇero ca cirāyati, nūna sīlavipattiṃ patto bhavissatī”ti cintesi. Sopi āgantvā “gacchāma, bhante”ti āha. Thero “kiṃ pāpo jātosī”ti pucchi. Sāmaṇero tuṇhī hutvā puna pucchitopi na kathesi. Thero “tādisena pāpena mayhaṃ yaṭṭhigahaṇakiccaṃ natthi, gaccha tva”nti vatvā puna tena “bahuparissayo [V 1.0214] maggo, tumhe ca andhā, kathaṃ gamissathā”ti vutte “bāla idheva me nipajjitvā marantassāpi aparāparaṃ parivattentassāpi tādisena gamanaṃ nāma natthī”ti imamatthaṃ dassento –

Then, when the elder with the eye disease was left behind in the monastery while the other bhikkhus had gone to the village for alms, the lay followers saw them and asked, 'Why hasn't the elder come?' Hearing the reason, they were overcome with sorrow and brought almsfood, saying, 'Venerable sir, do not worry about anything. From now on, we ourselves will bring almsfood and attend to you.' And they did so. The bhikkhus, having abided by the elder’s instruction, before long attained arahantship. After completing the rains residence and performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they said, 'Venerable sir, we will go to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher.' The elder replied, 'I am weak and sightless, and the road is perilous. It will be a hardship for you to go with me. You go first. Having gone, pay homage to the Teacher and the great elders in my name. Tell Cūḷapāla about my situation and have him send someone.' They pleaded again but, unable to gain his consent for him to go, they agreed, saying, 'Very well.' They set their lodgings in order, took leave of the lay followers, and in due course went to Jetavana. There, they paid homage to the Teacher and the great elders in his name. The next day, after going for alms in Sāvatthī, they told Cūḷapāla about his situation. He said, 'Venerable sirs, this nephew of mine named Pālita—I will send him.' They replied, 'The road is perilous; it is not possible for a single householder to go, therefore he should be given the going forth.' So they gave him the going forth and sent him. He in due course went to the elder, announced himself, and, taking him, was coming back. On the way, near a certain village in a forest area, he heard the sound of a woman gathering firewood singing. His mind became captivated, and dropping the end of the staff, he said, 'Wait a moment, venerable sir, until I return.' He went to her and there he fell into a breach of moral discipline. The elder thought: 'Just now the sound of a woman's song was heard, and the novice is taking a long time. Surely he must have fallen into a breach of moral discipline.' When the novice returned, he said, 'Let us go, venerable sir.' The elder asked, 'Have you committed an evil deed?' The novice was silent. Even when asked again, he did not speak. The elder said, 'I have no need to have my staff held by such an evil person. Go away!' When the other replied, 'The road is very difficult, and you are blind. How will you go?' the elder, showing this meaning, said: 'Fool! Even if I have to lie down right here and die, rolling over and over, there is no going for me with such a one as you.'

95.

95.

“Andhohaṃ hatanettosmi, kantāraddhānapakkhando;

Sayamānopi gacchissaṃ, na sahāyena pāpenā”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsittha;

“I am blind, my eyes are destroyed, I have entered a long wilderness path; even while lying down I would go, but not with an evil companion.” Thus he spoke this verse.

Tattha andhoti cakkhuvikalo. Hatanettoti vinaṭṭhacakkhuko, tena “payogavipattivasenāhaṃ upahatanettatāya andho, na jaccandhabhāvenā”ti yathāvuttaṃ andhabhāvaṃ viseseti. Atha vā “andho”ti idaṃ “andhe [M 1.0250] jiṇṇe mātāpitaro posetī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.288) viya maṃsacakkhuvekalladīpanaṃ, “sabbepime paribbājakā andhā acakkhukā” (udā. 54) “andho ekacakkhu dvicakkhū”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.29) viya na paññācakkhuvekalladīpananti dassetuṃ “hatanettosmī”ti vuttaṃ, tena mukhyameva andhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Kantāraddhānapakkhandoti [P 1.0209] kantāre vivane dīghamaggaṃ anupaviṭṭho, na jātikantārādigahanaṃ saṃsāraddhānaṃ paṭipannoti adhippāyo. Tādisañhi kantāraddhānaṃ ayaṃ thero samatikkamitvā ṭhito, sayamānopīti sayantopi, pādesu avahantesu urena jaṇṇukāhi ca bhūmiyaṃ saṃsaranto parivattentopi gaccheyyaṃ. Na sahāyena pāpenāti tādisena pāpapuggalena sahāyabhūtena saddhiṃ na gacchissanti yojanā. Taṃ sutvā itaro saṃvegajāto “bhāriyaṃ vata mayā sāhasikakammaṃ kata”nti bāhā paggayha kandanto vanasaṇḍaṃ pakkhando ca ahosi. Atha therassa sīlatejena paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Tena sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā therassa santikaṃ gantvā sāvatthigāmipurisaṃ viya attānaṃ ñāpetvā yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ gaṇhanto maggaṃ saṅkhipitvā tadaheva sāyanhe sāvatthiyaṃ theraṃ netvā tattha jetavane cūḷapālitena kāritāya paṇṇasālāya phalake nisīdāpetvā tassa sahāyavaṇṇena therassa āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā pakkāmi; cūḷapālitopi taṃ yāvajīvaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhāsīti.

Herein, andho means blind, defective in sight. Hatanetto means one whose eyes are destroyed. Thereby he specifies the aforesaid state of blindness thus: 'I am blind because my eyes have been impaired due to a failure of treatment, not from being blind by birth.' Or, to show that the word andho here indicates the lack of the fleshly eye—as in such passages as 'he supports his blind, aged parents'—and not the lack of the wisdom eye—as in such passages as 'all these wanderers are blind, without vision' and 'blind, one-eyed, two-eyed'—the words hatanettosmi were spoken. Thus he indicates the primary state of blindness. Kantāraddhānapakkhando means: he has entered upon a long road in a wilderness, a forest. The meaning is that he has not entered upon the long road of saṃsāra, the wilderness of birth, etc. For this elder stands having transcended such a long wilderness road. Sayamānopi means: even while lying down; even while crawling on the ground with my chest and knees, my feet not carrying me, rolling over and over, I would go. Na sahāyena pāpenā: the construction is 'I will not go together with such an evil person who has become my companion.' Hearing that, the other, stirred by a sense of urgency, raising his arms and weeping, 'Alas, what a grave and reckless deed I have done!', plunged into the forest thicket. Then, through the power of the elder’s virtue, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed signs of heat. Thereupon Sakka, having understood the reason, went to the elder and, making himself known as a man from a village near Sāvatthī, took the end of the staff, shortened the path, and that very evening led the elder to Sāvatthī. There in Jetavana, he had the elder sit on a plank in a leaf-hut that had been built by Cūḷapālita, and, in the guise of his companion, informed Cūḷapālita of the elder’s arrival, and then departed. And Cūḷapālita attended on him respectfully for the rest of his life.

Cakkhupālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Cakkhupāla is finished.

6. Khaṇḍasumanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Khaṇḍasumana

Ekapupphaṃ [V 1.0215] cajitvānāti āyasmato khaṇḍasumanattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute tassa thūpassa samantato candanavedikāya parikkhipitvā mahantaṃ pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu uḷāraṃ sampattiṃ anubhavanto kassapassa bhagavato kāle kuṭumbikakule [M 1.0251] nibbatto satthari parinibbute kanakathūpaṃ uddissa raññā pupphapūjāya kayiramānāya pupphāni alabhanto ekaṃ khaṇḍasumanapupphaṃ disvā mahatā mūlena [P 1.0210] taṃ kiṇitvā gaṇhanto cetiye pūjaṃ karonto uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppādesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā asīti vassakoṭiyo saggasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde pāvāyaṃ mallarājakule nibbatti. Tassa jātakāle gehe khaṇḍasakkharā sumanapupphāni ca uppannāni ahesuṃ. Tenassa khaṇḍasumanoti nāmamakaṃsu. So viññutaṃ patto bhagavati pāvāyaṃ cundassa ambavane viharante upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.15-20) –

“Having given a single flower”: this is the verse of the Venerable Khaṇḍasumana. What is his origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a good family. Having reached maturity, when the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he surrounded his stupa with a sandalwood railing and performed a great offering. By that meritorious deed, he enjoyed great prosperity among gods and humans. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a householder’s family. When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, while a flower offering was being made by the king for the golden stupa, he was unable to obtain any flowers. Then he saw a single broken jasmine flower and, purchasing it for a great price, he made an offering at the shrine, arousing immense joy and delight. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and enjoyed heavenly bliss for eighty crores of years. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the royal family of the Mallas in Pāvā. At the time of his birth, lump sugar and jasmine flowers appeared in his house. For that reason, they gave him the name Khaṇḍasumana. Having reached maturity, when the Blessed One was dwelling in Cunda’s Mango Grove in Pāvā, he approached him, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. He went forth and, while undertaking the practice of insight meditation, before long he attained the six supernormal knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Jalitvā aggikkhandhova, sambuddho parinibbuto.

“The Conqueror named Padumuttara, chief of the world, bull among men, having blazed like a mass of fire, the Perfectly Enlightened One attained final Nibbāna.

“Nibbute ca mahāvīre, thūpo vitthāriko ahu;

Dūratova upaṭṭhenti, dhātugehavaruttame.

“When the Great Hero had attained Nibbāna, a vast stupa came to be. From afar they attend upon it, at that best and highest relic-shrine.

“Pasannacitto, sumano, akaṃ candanavedikaṃ;

Dissati thūpakhandho ca, thūpānucchaviko tadā.

“With a confident and glad mind, I made a sandalwood platform. And a section of the stupa, befitting it, was then visible.

“Bhave nibbattamānamhi, devatte atha mānuse;

Omattaṃ me na passāmi, pubbakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“While being reborn in existence, whether in a divine state or a human one, I see no inferiority in myself: this is the fruit of my past kamma.

“Pañcadasakappasate, ito aṭṭha janā ahuṃ;

Sabbe samattanāmā te cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Fifteen hundred kappas ago from now, there were eight persons, all named Samatta, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano purimajātiṃ anussaranto tattha attano sumanapupphapariccāgassa saggasampattinimittakaṃ nibbānūpanissayatañca disvā udānavasena tamatthaṃ pakāsento –

But having attained arahantship and recollecting his own past birth, seeing there that his offering of a jasmine flower was a cause for the attainment of heavenly fortune and a decisive support for Nibbāna, he proclaimed that meaning by way of an inspired utterance:

96.

96.

“Ekapupphaṃ [V 1.0216] cajitvāna, asīti vassakoṭiyo;

Saggesu paricāretvā, sesakenamhi nibbuto”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;
