He spoke this verse: “Having offered a single flower, for eighty crores of years I enjoyed myself in the heavens; with the remainder I am quenched.”

Tattha [M 1.0252] ekapupphanti ekaṃ kusumaṃ, taṃ pana idha sumanapupphaṃ adhippetaṃ. Cajitvānāti satthu thūpapūjākaraṇavasena pariccajitvā pariccāgahetu. Asīti vassakoṭiyoti manussagaṇanāya vassānaṃ asīti koṭiyo, accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, idañca chasu kāmasaggesu dutiye aparāparuppattivasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tasmā saggesūti tāvatiṃsasaṅkhāte saggaloke, punappunaṃ uppajjanavasena hettha bahuvacanaṃ. Paricāretvāti rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu indriyāni paricāretvā sukhaṃ anubhavitvā, devaccharāhi vā attānaṃ paricāretvā [P 1.0211] upaṭṭhāpetvā. Sesakenamhi nibbutoti pupphapūjāya vasena pavattakusalacetanāsu bhavasampatti dāyakakammato sesena yaṃ tattha vivaṭṭūpanissayabhūtaṃ, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Bahū hi tattha pubbāparavasena pavattā cetanā. Sesakenāti vā tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena aparikkhīṇeyeva tasmiṃ kammavipāke nibbuto amhi, kilesaparinibbānena parinibbutosmi. Etena yasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā attanā arahattaṃ sacchikataṃ, sopi carimattabhāvo tassa kammavipākoti dasseti. Yādisaṃ sandhāya aññatthāpi “tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenā”ti (pārā. 228; saṃ. ni. 1.131) vuttaṃ.

Herein, a single flower means one blossom; in this context a jasmine flower is intended. Having offered means having relinquished it by way of making an offering at the Teacher’s stupa, on account of that relinquishment. Eighty crores of years means eighty crores of years by human reckoning; this is a usage in the sense of continuous connection. This should be understood as stated with reference to successive rebirths in the second of the six sensual heavens. Therefore, in the heavens refers to the heavenly world called Tāvatiṃsa; the plural is used here because of being reborn there again and again. I enjoyed myself means: having experienced pleasure by letting the sense faculties roam among objects such as forms, or having had oneself attended upon and served by celestial nymphs. With the remainder I am quenched: he says this referring to what remained from the kamma that gave the fortune of existence—from among the wholesome volitions that arose by way of the flower offering—which was a decisive support for the rolling back of saṃsāra. For many volitions arose there in succession. Alternatively, with the remainder means: by the residual result of that very kamma, while that kamma-result was not yet exhausted, I was quenched; I have attained final Nibbāna with the final quenching of the defilements. By this he shows that the final existence in which he stood and realized arahantship was itself a result of that kamma. It is with reference to such a case that it is said elsewhere: “by the residual result of that very kamma”.

Khaṇḍasumanattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Khaṇḍasumana is finished.

7. Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Tissa

Hitvā satapalaṃ kaṃsanti āyasmato tissattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro vipassissa bhagavato kāle yānakārakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso candanakhaṇḍena phalakaṃ katvā bhagavato upanāmesi, tañca bhagavā paribhuñji. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde roruvanagare rājakule nibbatti. So vayappatto pitari kālaṅkate rajje patiṭṭhito bimbisārarañño adiṭṭhasahāyo hutvā tassa maṇimuttāvatthādīni paṇṇākārāni pesesi. Tassa rājā bimbisāro puññavantataṃ [M 1.0253] sutvā paṭipābhataṃ pesento cittapaṭe buddhacaritaṃ [V 1.0217] suvaṇṇapaṭṭe ca paṭiccasamuppādaṃ likhāpetvā pesesi. So taṃ disvā purimabuddhesu katādhikāratāya pacchimabhavikatāya ca cittapaṭe dassentaṃ buddhacaritaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭake likhitaṃ paṭiccasamuppādakkamañca oloketvā [P 1.0212] pavattinivattiyo sallakkhetvā sāsanakkamaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā sañjātasaṃvego “diṭṭho mayā bhagavato veso, sāsanakkamo ca ekapadesena ñāto, bahudukkhā kāmā bahupāyāsā, kiṃ dāni mayhaṃ gharāvāsenā”ti rajjaṃ pahāya kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādento bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitvā mattikāpattaṃ gahetvā rājā pukkusāti viya mahājanassa paridevantasseva nagarato nikkhamitvā anukkamena rājagahaṃ gantvā tattha sappasoṇḍikapabbhāre viharantaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammadesanaṃ sutvā vipassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā yuttappayutto viharanto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.37-42) –

“Having abandoned a bronze bowl of a hundred palas”: this is the verse of the Venerable Tissa. What is his origin? He too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in the family of a chariot-maker. Having reached discernment, one day he saw the Blessed One and, with a confident mind, he made a plank from a piece of sandalwood and presented it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One used it. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Having performed meritorious deeds again and again, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in the royal family in the city of Roruva. Having come of age, when his father died he was established in the kingdom. He became an unseen friend of King Bimbisāra and sent him gifts of gems, pearls, cloth, and so on. Having heard of his meritorious character, King Bimbisāra sent him a return gift: he had the life of the Buddha depicted on a painted cloth and the dependent origination inscribed on a golden plate. Seeing this, on account of his aspiration made under previous Buddhas and because he was in his final existence, he looked at the life of the Buddha shown on the painted cloth and the sequence of dependent origination inscribed on the golden plate. Having discerned the round of existence and its cessation, he established the sequence of the teaching in his heart. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him, and he thought: “I have seen the likeness of the Blessed One, and the sequence of the teaching is known to me in part. Sensual pleasures are very painful, very troublesome. What use is the household life to me now?” Abandoning his kingdom, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, he went forth with the Blessed One as his destination. Taking an earthenware bowl, just like King Pukkusāti, he departed from the city while the great populace was lamenting. He went in stages to Rājagaha and approached the Blessed One who was dwelling on the Sappasoṇḍika Slope. He paid homage to him and sat down to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma teaching, he took up a meditation subject for insight. Dwelling diligently, he intensified his insight and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.15.37–42):

“Yānakāro pure āsiṃ, dārukamme susikkhito;

Candanaṃ phalakaṃ katvā, adāsiṃ lokabandhuno.

“Formerly I was a vehicle-maker, well-trained in woodwork. Having made a sandalwood plank, I gave it to the Kinsman of the World.

“Pabhāsati idaṃ byamhaṃ, suvaṇṇassa sunimmitaṃ;

Hatthiyānaṃ assayānaṃ, dibbayānaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ.

“This celestial mansion shines, well-made of gold. Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles are at my service.

“Pāsādā sivikā ceva, nibbattanti yadicchakaṃ;

Akkhubbhaṃ ratanaṃ mayhaṃ, phalakassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Palaces and palanquins, too, arise as I wish. An imperturbable jewel is mine: this is the fruit of the plank.

“Ekanavutito kappe, phalakaṃ yamahaṃ dadiṃ;

Duggati nābhijānāmi, phalakassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first eon from now, when I gave that plank, I know of no bad destination because of it: this is the fruit of the plank.

“Sattapaññāsakappamhi, caturo nimmitāvhayā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“In the fifty-seventh eon from now, there were four named Nimmita, wheel-turning monarchs of great power endowed with the seven treasures.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā udānavasena attano paṭipattiṃ kathento –

But having attained arahantship, relating his own practice by way of an inspired utterance, he said:

97.

97.

“Hitvā [M 1.0254] satapalaṃ kaṃsaṃ, sovaṇṇaṃ satarājikaṃ;

Aggahiṃ mattikāpattaṃ, idaṃ dutiyābhisecana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

He spoke this verse: “Having abandoned a bronze bowl of a hundred palas, and a golden one of a hundred patterns, I have taken an earthenware bowl: this is my second consecration.”

Tattha hitvāti pariccajitvā. Satapalanti sataṃ palāni yassa, taṃ satapalaparimāṇaṃ. Kaṃsanti thālaṃ. Sovaṇṇanti suvaṇṇamayaṃ. Satarājikanti bhittivicittatāya ca anekarūparājicittatāya ca anekalekhāyuttaṃ. Aggahiṃ mattikāpattanti evarūpe mahārahe bhājane pubbe [V 1.0218] bhuñjitvā buddhānaṃ ovādaṃ karonto “idānāhaṃ taṃ chaḍḍetvā mattikāmayapattaṃ aggahesiṃ[P 1.0213], aho, sādhu, mayā kataṃ ariyavataṃ anuṭhita”nti bhājanakittanāpadesena rajjapariccāgaṃ pabbajjūpagamanañca anumodanto vadati. Tenāha “idaṃ dutiyābhisecana”nti. Paṭhamaṃ rajjābhisecanaṃ upādāya idaṃ pabbajjūpagamanaṃ mama dutiyaṃ abhisecanaṃ. Tañhi rāgādīhi saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ sāsaṅkaṃ saparisaṅkaṃ kammaṃ anatthasañhitaṃ dukkhapaṭibaddhaṃ nihīnaṃ, idaṃ pana taṃvipariyāyato uttamaṃ paṇītanti adhippāyo.

Herein, having abandoned means having relinquished. Of a hundred palas means that which has a measure of a hundred palas. A bronze bowl means a dish. A golden one means made of gold. Of a hundred patterns means endowed with many lines because its sides were variegated and because it was decorated with many kinds of patterns. Regarding I have taken an earthenware bowl: having formerly eaten from such a valuable vessel, he now speaks rejoicing in his renunciation of kingship and his going forth into homelessness under the pretext of praising the bowl, thinking: “Now I have discarded that and taken a bowl made of clay. Ah, it is good! The noble practice has been undertaken by me!” Therefore he said: this is my second consecration. In relation to the first consecration to kingship, this going forth is my second consecration. The meaning is that the former was defiled by lust and so on, perilous, fraught with danger, connected with what is unbeneficial, bound up with suffering, and inferior; but this, being the opposite, is supreme and sublime.

Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa is finished.

8. Abhayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya

Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhāti āyasmato abhayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sumedhaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto saḷalapupphehi pūjamakāsi. So tena puññakammena devesu nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā abhayoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto hetusampattiyā codiyamāno ekadivasaṃ vihāraṃ gato satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto viharati. Athassa ekadivasaṃ gāmaṃ [M 1.0255] piṇḍāya paviṭṭhassa alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mātugāmaṃ disvā ayonisomanasikāravasena tassa rūpaṃ ārabbha chandarāgo uppajji, so vihāraṃ pavisitvā “satiṃ vissajjitvā olokentassa rūpārammaṇe mayhaṃ kileso uppanno, ayuttaṃ mayā kata”nti attano cittaṃ niggaṇhanto tāvadeva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.43-47) –

“Having seen a form, mindfulness was lost”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Abhaya. What is its origin? He, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences that served as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he was born into a good family and, having reached the age of discernment, one day saw the Blessed One Sumedha. With a confident mind, he made an offering of saḷala flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the devas. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds, wandering only in happy destinies. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was given the name Abhaya. Having reached the age of discernment and being prompted by the maturity of his conditions, one day he went to the monastery. Hearing the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he gained faith, went forth, and having fulfilled his preliminary duties, he dwelled applying himself to the work of insight meditation. Then one day, as he entered a village for alms, he saw a woman who was adorned and beautifully dressed. Through unwise attention, sensual desire arose in him based on her form. Entering the monastery, he reflected: “Having let go of mindfulness while looking at a form-object, a defilement has arisen in me. What I have done is improper.” Restraining his own mind, he immediately developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.15.43–47):

“Sumedho [P 1.0214] nāma nāmena, sayambhū aparājito;

Vivekamanubrūhanto, ajjhogahi mahāvanaṃ.

“Sumedha by name, the Self-become, the Unconquered; cultivating seclusion, he plunged into the great forest.

“Saḷalaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, ganthitvāna vaṭaṃsakaṃ;

Buddhassa abhiropesiṃ, sammukhā lokanāyakaṃ.

“Seeing a saḷala tree in bloom, I wove a chaplet; I placed it upon the Buddha, the Leader of the World, in his very presence.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty thousand eons since I offered that flower, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping a Buddha.

“Ūnavīse [V 1.0219] kappasate, soḷasāsuṃ sunimmitā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Nineteen hundred eons ago, there were sixteen kings named Sunimmita; endowed with the seven treasures, they were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano kilesuppattinidassanena “kilese anuvattentassa vaṭṭadukkhato nattheva sīsukkhipanaṃ. Ahaṃ pana te nānuvatti”nti dassento –

But having attained arahantship, by pointing to the arising of a defilement in himself in order to show, “For one who follows the defilements, there is no lifting of the head from the suffering of the round of rebirth, but I did not follow them,” he uttered this verse:

98.

98.

“Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati;

“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost for one who gives attention to an attractive sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and one abides clinging to it.

Tassa vaḍḍhanti āsavā, bhavamūlopagāmino”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

For him the taints increase, those that lead to the root of existence.”

Tattha rūpanti rajjanīyaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, taṃ panettha itthirūpaṃ adhippetaṃ. Disvāti cakkhunā disvā, cakkhudvārānusārena nimittānubyañjanasallakkhaṇavasena taṃ gahetvā, tassa tathāgahaṇahetūti attho. Sati muṭṭhāti asubhasabhāve kāye “asubha”ntveva pavattanasati naṭṭhā. Yathā pana rūpaṃ disvā sati naṭṭhā, taṃ dassento āha “piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto”ti. Yathāupaṭṭhitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ “subhaṃ sukha”ntiādinā piyanimittaṃ katvā [M 1.0256] ayonisomanasikārena manasikaroto sati muṭṭhāti yojanā. Tathā bhūtova sārattacitto vedetīti suṭṭhu rattacitto hutvā taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ anubhavati abhinandati, abhinandanto pana tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati ajjhosāya taṃ ārammaṇaṃ gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā vattati ceva, evaṃbhūtassa ca tassa vaḍḍhanti āsavā bhavamūlopagāminoti bhavassa saṃsārassa mūlabhāvaṃ kāraṇabhāvaṃ upagamanasabhāvā kāmāsavādayo cattāropi āsavā tassa puggalassa uparūpari vaḍḍhantiyeva, na hāyanti. Mayhaṃ pana paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saccāni paṭivijjhantassa maggapaṭipāṭiyā te cattāropi āsavā anavasesato pahīnā parikkhīṇāti adhippāyo.

Herein, form means an enticing form-base; in this context, the form of a woman is intended. Having seen means having seen with the eye, that is, having grasped it through the eye-door by way of attending to its general mark and its details; the meaning is that this is the reason for grasping it in such a way. Mindfulness is lost means that the mindfulness that should be directed to the impure nature of the body as “impure” has been lost. To show how mindfulness is lost upon seeing a form, he said: for one who gives attention to an attractive sign. The connection is that mindfulness is lost for one who gives unwise attention to the object as it has presented itself, having made it an attractive sign by thinking, “It is beautiful, it is pleasant,” and so on. Being thus, with an impassioned mind one feels means that, having become thoroughly impassioned, one experiences and delights in that form-object. And while delighting, one abides clinging to it means that one clings to, swallows, and becomes fixated on that object. For such a person, the taints increase, those that lead to the root of existence means that for that person the four taints beginning with the taint of sensual desire—which by nature lead to the root of existence, that is, the cause of the round of saṃsāra—only increase, they do not diminish. The intended meaning is: ‘But for me, who stood firm in reflection, developed insight, and penetrated the truths in the sequence of the path, those four taints have been abandoned without remainder, they are utterly destroyed.’

Abhayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhaya is finished.

9. Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya

Saddaṃ [P 1.0215] sutvā sati muṭṭhāti āyasmato uttiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle [V 1.0220] kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto gonakādiatthataṃ sauttaracchadaṃ buddhārahaṃ pallaṅkaṃ gandhakuṭiyaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sakyarājakule nibbatti, tassa uttiyoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto satthu ñātisamāgame buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto ekadivasaṃ nāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho antarāmagge mātugāmassa gītasaddaṃ sutvā ayonisomanasikāravasena tattha chandarāge uppanne paṭisaṅkhānabalena taṃ vikkhambhetvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā sañjātasaṃvego divāṭṭhāne nisīditvā tāvadeva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.15.48-52) –

“Having heard a sound, mindfulness was lost”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Uttiya. What is its origin? This one, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences that served as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he was born into a good family and, having reached the age of discernment, one day he saw the Teacher. With a confident mind, he prepared in the fragrant chamber a couch worthy of a Buddha, spread with a long-fleeced coverlet and furnished with a canopy, and gave it as an offering. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn in the Sakyan royal family at Kapilavatthu. His name was Uttiya. Having come of age, he witnessed the Buddha’s spiritual power at the gathering of his kinsmen and, gaining faith, he went forth. While practicing the recluse’s duties, one day as he entered a village for alms, he heard on the road the sound of a woman singing. Through unwise attention, sensual desire arose in him. But by the power of reflection he suppressed it, entered the monastery, and sat down in his daytime quarters. Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he immediately developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.15.48–52):

“Sumedhassa [M 1.0257] bhagavato, lokajeṭṭhassa tādino;

Pallaṅko hi mayā dinno, sauttarasapacchado.

“To the Blessed One Sumedha, the world’s chief, the Such-like One, a couch was given by me, with a canopy and a cover.

“Sattaratanasampanno, pallaṅko āsi so tadā;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, nibbattati sadā mama.

“That couch was then endowed with the seven treasures; discerning my intention, it always appears for me.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, pallaṅkamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pallaṅkassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty thousand kappas ago I gave that couch; I have known no bad destination: this is the fruit of that couch.

“Vīsakappasahassamhi, suvaṇṇābhā tayo janā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Twenty thousand kappas ago, there were three men of golden complexion; endowed with the seven treasures, they were mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano kilesuppattinidassanena “kilese ajigucchantassa natthi vaṭṭadukkhato sīsukkhipanaṃ, ahaṃ pana te jigucchimevā”ti dassento –

But having attained arahantship, by pointing to the arising of a defilement in himself in order to show, “For one who does not abhor the defilements, there is no lifting of the head from the suffering of the round, but I do abhor them,” he uttered this verse:

99.

99.

“Saddaṃ sutvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasikaroto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati;

“Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost for one who gives attention to an attractive sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and one abides clinging to it.

Tassa vaḍḍhanti āsavā, saṃsāra upagāmino”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

For him the taints increase, those that lead towards saṃsāra.”

Tattha saddanti rajjanīyaṃ saddārammaṇaṃ, saṃsāraupagāminoti –

Herein, sound means an enticing sound-object. Those that lead towards saṃsāra means—

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti. –

“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and bases, proceeding uninterruptedly, is called saṃsāra.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0221][P 1.0216] vuttasaṃsāravaṭṭakāraṇaṃ hutvā upagamentīti saṃsāraupagāmino, “saṃsārūpagāmino”ti vā pāṭho. Sesaṃ anantaragāthāya vuttanayameva.

Because they become a cause for the round of saṃsāra thus described and lead towards it, they are called saṃsāraupagāmino. Or the reading may be saṃsārūpagāmino. The rest is to be understood in the same way as was explained for the preceding verse.

Uttiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttiya is finished.

10. (Dutiya) devasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Devasabha (Second)

Sammappadhānasampannoti [M 1.0258] āyasmato devasabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso bandhujīvakapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sakyarājakule nibbatti, tassa devasabhoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto cumbaṭakalahavūpasamanatthaṃ satthari āgate buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā pasannamānaso saraṇesu patiṭṭhito puna nigrodhārāme satthari viharante satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.1-6) –

The verse beginning “Accomplished in right effort” is by the Venerable Devasabha. What is his origin story? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma in various existences that serves as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One Sikhī and, with a confident mind, he made an offering of bandhujīvaka flowers. By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in the royal family of the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu; his name was Devasabha. When he came of age, the Teacher arrived to settle a quarrel among the Sakyans. Seeing the Buddha’s power, with a confident mind, he became established in the refuges. Later, while the Teacher was dwelling in the Nigrodha Park, he approached the Teacher, gained faith, and went forth. Having done the preliminary duties, he developed insight and before long attained arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhaṃ, vippasannamanāvilaṃ;

Nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ loke visattikaṃ.

“Like the moon, stainless and pure, clear and untroubled; he whose delight in existence is destroyed, has crossed over attachment in the world.

“Nibbāpayantaṃ janataṃ, tiṇṇaṃ tārayataṃ varaṃ;

Muniṃ vanamhi jhāyantaṃ, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.

“The one who brings quenching to the people, the excellent one, himself crossed over, who helps others to cross; the sage meditating in the forest, one-pointed and well-composed.

“Bandhujīvakapupphāni, lagetvā suttakenahaṃ;

Buddhassa abhiropayiṃ, sikhino lokabandhuno.

“Having strung bandhujīvaka flowers with a thread, I offered them to the Buddha Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, because of the deed I did then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of revering the Buddha.

“Ito sattamake kappe, manujindo mahāyaso;

Samantacakkhunāmāsi, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In the seventh eon from now, I was a lord of men of great fame, named Samantacakkhu, a wheel-turning monarch of great strength.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0222] pana patvā attanā adhigataṃ vimuttisukhaṃ nissāya uppannapītisomanasso udānavasena –

Then, having attained arahantship, based on the bliss of liberation that he had personally realized, with joy and gladness arisen, he uttered this inspired utterance:

100.

100.

“Sammappadhānasampanno[M 1.0259], satipaṭṭhānagocaro;

Vimuttikusumasañchanno, parinibbissatyanāsavo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Accomplished in the right strivings, with the establishments of mindfulness as his pasture, covered with the flowers of liberation, being taintless, he will attain final Nibbāna.” Thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha sammappadhānasampannoti sampannacatubbidhasammappadhāno, tehi kattabbakiccaṃ sampādetvā ṭhitoti attho. Satipaṭṭhānagocaroti kāyānupassanādayo satipaṭṭhānā gocaro [P 1.0217] pavattiṭṭhānaṃ etassāti satipaṭṭhānagocaro, catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhitacittoti attho. Guṇasobhena paramasugandhā vimuttiyeva kusumāni, tehi sabbaso sammadeva sañchanno vibhūsito alaṅkatoti vimuttikusumasañchanno. Parinibbissatyanāsavoti evaṃ sammā paṭipajjanto bhikkhu nacirasseva anāsavo hutvā parinibbissati saupādisesāya anupādisesāya ca nibbānadhātuyāti attho. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

Herein, accomplished in the right strivings means one who is accomplished in the fourfold right striving; the meaning is that one stands having fulfilled the duty to be done by them. With the establishments of mindfulness as his pasture means that the establishments of mindfulness, such as the contemplation of the body, are his pasture, his sphere of activity; the meaning is that his mind is established in the four establishments of mindfulness. Covered with the flowers of liberation means: liberation itself, supremely fragrant with the beauty of its qualities, are the flowers; by these he is altogether rightly covered, beautified, and adorned. Being taintless, he will attain final Nibbāna means that a bhikkhu practicing rightly in this way will, before long, become taintless and attain final Nibbāna by means of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. And this was the elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

(Dutiya) devasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Devasabha (Second) is finished.

Dasamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tenth Chapter is finished.

11. Ekādasamavaggo

11. The Eleventh Chapter

1. Belaṭṭhānikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhānika

Hitvā [V 1.0223] gihittaṃ anavositattotiādikā āyasmato belaṭṭhānikattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro ito ekatiṃse kappe vessabhussa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā isīhi parivuto vicaranto ekadivasaṃ vessabhuṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pītisomanassajāto satthu ñāṇasampattiṃ nissāya pasannamānaso ñāṇaṃ uddissa pupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā belaṭṭhānikoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ [M 1.0260] patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kosalaraṭṭhe araññe viharanto alaso kāyadaḷhibahulo pharusavāco ahosi, samaṇadhamme cittaṃ na uppādesi. Atha naṃ bhagavā ñāṇaparipākaṃ oloketvā –

The verse beginning “Having abandoned the household life, with task unfinished…” is by the Venerable Belaṭṭhānika. What is his origin story? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a brahmin family in the thirty-first eon from now, in the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū. Having come of age and achieved mastery in the brahminical sciences, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. While wandering surrounded by ascetics, one day he saw the Blessed One Vessabhū and, filled with joy and gladness, with a confident mind on account of the Teacher’s accomplishment in knowledge, he made an offering of flowers dedicated to that knowledge. By that meritorious act, wandering among gods and humans, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a brahmin family at Sāvatthī and was named Belaṭṭhānika. Having reached maturity and heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he gained faith and went forth. Taking a meditation subject, he dwelled in a forest in the Kosalan country, but he was lazy, very robust in body, and harsh in speech; he did not arouse his mind to the duties of a recluse. Then the Blessed One, perceiving the maturity of his knowledge, said:

101.

101.

“Hitvā gihittaṃ anavositatto, mukhanaṅgalī odariko kusīto;

Mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho, punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando”ti. –

“Having abandoned the household life, with task unfinished, ploughing with the mouth, devoted to his belly, lazy; like a great boar fattened on fodder, the fool enters the womb again and again.”

Imāya [P 1.0218] obhāsagāthāya saṃvejesi. So satthāraṃ purato nisinnaṃ viya disvā tañca gāthaṃ sutvā saṃvegajāto ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.14.41-46) –

The Blessed One stirred him with this verse of illumination. Seeing the Teacher as if seated before him and hearing that verse, he was overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency. As his knowledge had reached maturity, he established insight and before long attained arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva jotantaṃ, nisinnaṃ pabbatantare;

Obhāsentaṃ disā sabbā, osadhiṃ viya tārakaṃ.

“Shining like a kaṇikāra tree, seated in a mountain cleft, illuminating all directions, like the morning star.

“Tayo māṇavakā āsuṃ, sake sippe susikkhitā;

Khāribhāraṃ gahetvāna, anventi mama pacchato.

“There were three young men, well-trained in their own craft; taking up a carrying pole, they followed behind me.

“Puṭake satta pupphāni, nikkhittāni tapassinā;

Gahetvā tāni ñāṇamhi, vessabhussābhiropayiṃ.

“An ascetic had placed seven flowers in a leaf-container; taking them, I offered them to Vessabhū in honor of his knowledge.

“Ekatiṃse [V 1.0224] ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ñāṇapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, when I offered that flower, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of revering knowledge.

“Ekūnatiṃsakappamhi, vipulābhasanāmako;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“In the twenty-ninth eon from now, I was one named Vipulābhasa, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great strength.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthu ovādaṃ paṭipūjento byatirekamukhena ca aññaṃ byākaronto tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi.

Then, having attained arahantship, honoring the Teacher’s instruction and declaring his final knowledge by way of contrast, he recited that same verse in response.

Tattha [M 1.0261] hitvā gihittanti gahaṭṭhabhāvaṃ pariccajitvā pabbajitvāti attho. Anavositattoti anurūpaṃ avositatto, yadatthaṃ sāsane pabbajantassa anurūpapariññādīnaṃ atīritattā apariyositabhāvo akatakaraṇīyoti attho. Atha vā anavositattoti anuavositasabhāvo, visuddhīnaṃ maggānañca anupaṭipāṭiyā vasitabbavāsassa akatāvī, dasasu ariyavāsesu avusitavāti attho. Mukhasaṅkhātaṃ naṅgalaṃ imassa atthīti mukhanaṅgalī. Naṅgalena viya pathaviṃ paresu pharusavācappayogena attānaṃ khanantoti attho. Odarikoti udare pasuto udaraposanatapparo. Kusītoti alaso, bhāvanaṃ ananuyuñjanto. Evaṃbhūtassa nipphattiṃ dassento āha “mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho, punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando”ti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Ettha ca yathā pabbajitvā anavositādisabhāvatāya punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando, na evaṃ mādiso paṇḍito. Tabbiparītasabhāvatāya pana sammāpaṭipattiyā matthakaṃ pāpitattā parinibbāyatīti byatirekamukhena aññaṃ byākāsīti daṭṭhabbanti.

Herein, having abandoned the household life means having given up the state of a householder and gone forth. With task unfinished means his task is unfinished in the proper way; the meaning is that since the appropriate duties for one who has gone forth in the Dispensation, such as full understanding, have not been brought to fulfillment, his task is undone. Or alternatively, with task unfinished means his state is unfulfilled; he has not lived the life that should be lived in accordance with the sequence of the purifications and the paths; the meaning is he has not dwelt in the ten noble dwellings. Ploughing with the mouth means he has a plough that is the mouth. The meaning is that, like with a plough, he injures himself by using harsh speech towards others. Devoted to his belly means intent on his belly, devoted to nourishing his belly. Lazy means indolent, not applying himself to meditation. Showing the outcome for such a one, he said: like a great boar fattened on fodder, the fool enters the womb again and again. The meaning of this has been stated above. And here, it should be understood that he declared his final knowledge by way of contrast, thus: just as a fool who has gone forth but has an unfinished task and other such qualities enters the womb again and again, it is not so for a wise one like myself. Rather, because of having the opposite qualities, having brought the right practice to its culmination, he attains final Nibbāna.

Belaṭṭhānikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Belaṭṭhānika is finished.

2. Setucchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Setuccha

Mānena [P 1.0219] vañcitāseti āyasmato setucchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto tissassa sammāsambuddhassa kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ tissaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sumadhuraṃ panasaphalaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ nāḷikerasāḷavaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde aññatarassa maṇḍalikarañño [V 1.0225] putto hutvā nibbatti, setucchotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So pitari mate rajje patiṭṭhito ussāhasattīnaṃ abhāvena rājakiccāni virādhento rajjaṃ parahatthagataṃ katvā dukkhappattiyā saṃvegajāto janapadacārikaṃ carantaṃ bhagavantaṃ [M 1.0262] disvā upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā parikammaṃ karonto tadaheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.17.13-17) –

The verse beginning “Deceived by conceit” is that of the venerable elder Setuccha. What is its origin? This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in successive existences that serves as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Tissa. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One Tissa and, with a confident mind, he gave him a very sweet jackfruit prepared with tender coconut. By that meritorious deed he was reborn in a deva world. Wandering on from one existence to another among devas and humans, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn as the son of a certain provincial king. His name was Setuccha. When his father died, he was established in the kingdom. But due to a lack of energy and power, he failed in his royal duties and let the kingdom fall into the hands of another. Having fallen into suffering, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. Seeing the Blessed One wandering on tour through the country, he approached him, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. While undertaking the preliminary work, he attained arahantship on that very day. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Tissassa kho bhagavato, pubbe phalamadāsahaṃ;

Nāḷikerañca pādāsiṃ, khajjakaṃ abhisammataṃ.

“To the Blessed One Tissa, I formerly gave fruit; I also gave a coconut and a much-esteemed edible.

“Buddhassa tamahaṃ datvā, tissassa tu mahesino;

Modāmahaṃ kāmakāmī, upapajjiṃ yamicchakaṃ.

“Having given that to the Buddha, to Tissa, the great seer, I, a desirer of sensual pleasures, rejoiced; I was reborn wherever I wished.

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-second eon from now, when I gave that gift, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of giving fruit.

“Ito terasakappamhi, rājā indasamo ahu;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Thirteen eons ago from now, I was a king equal to Inda, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā kilese garahanto –

But having attained arahantship, reproaching the defilements, he uttered this verse:

102.

102.

“Mānena vañcitāse, saṅkhāresu saṃkilissamānāse;

Lābhālābhena mathitā, samādhiṃ nādhigacchantī”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Deceived by conceit, being defiled in the formations, agitated by gain and loss, they do not attain concentration.”

Tattha mānena vañcitāseti “seyyohamasmī”tiādinayappavattena mānena attukkaṃsanaparavambhanādivasena kusalabhaṇḍacchedanena vippaladdhā. Saṅkhāresu saṃkilissamānāseti ajjhattikabāhiresu cakkhādīsu ceva rūpādīsu ca saṅkhatadhammesu saṃkilissamānā, “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti taṃnimittaṃ taṇhāgāhādivasena saṃkilesaṃ āpajjamānā. Lābhālābhena mathitāti pattacīvarādīnañceva [P 1.0220] vatthādīnañca lābhena tesaṃyeva ca alābhena taṃnimittaṃ uppannehi anunayapaṭighehi mathitā madditā abhibhūtā. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ avasiṭṭhalokadhammānampettha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Samādhiṃ nādhigacchantīti te evarūpā puggalā samādhiṃ samathavipassanāvasena cittekaggataṃ kadācipi na vindanti na paṭilabhanti na pāpuṇanti samādhisaṃvattanikānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhāvato, itaresañca bhāvato. Idhāpi yathā mānādīhi abhibhūtā [V 1.0226] aviddasuno samādhiṃ [M 1.0263] nādhigacchanti, na evaṃ viddasuno. Te pana mādisā tehi anabhibhūtā samādhiṃ adhigacchantevāti byatirekamukhena aññābyākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, deceived by conceit means they are deluded by the conceit that proceeds in the manner of “I am superior,” etc., which cuts off their stock of wholesome things by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others. Being defiled in the formations means being defiled in regard to internal and external conditioned phenomena—that is, the eye, etc., and forms, etc.—and on that account, by way of craving, grasping, etc., they incur defilement, thinking: “This is mine, this I am, this is my self.” Agitated by gain and loss means they are agitated, crushed, and overwhelmed by the favor and disfavor that arise on account of the gain of such things as the bowl and robes, and on account of their loss. This is just an example; it should be seen that the remaining worldly conditions are included here. They do not attain concentration means that such persons never find, obtain, or attain concentration—the one-pointedness of mind by way of serenity and insight—because of the absence of things conducive to concentration and the presence of their opposites. Here, too, just as the unwise, being overwhelmed by conceit and so on, do not attain concentration, it is not so for the wise. But those like me, not being overwhelmed by these things, do indeed attain concentration. This should be understood as a declaration of final knowledge by way of contrast.

Setucchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Setuccha is finished.

3. Bandhurattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bandhura

Nāhaṃ etena atthikoti āyasmato bandhurattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle aññatarassa rañño antepure gopako hutvā ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ saparisaṃ rājaṅgaṇena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannacitto kaṇaverapupphāni gahetvā sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sīlavatīnagare seṭṭhiputto hutvā nibbatti, bandhurotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto kenacideva karaṇīyena sāvatthiyaṃ gato upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gato satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā ñāṇassa paripākattā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.17.7-12) –

The verse beginning “I have no need of this” is that of the venerable elder Bandhura. What is its origin? This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, was a guard in the inner quarters of a certain king in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. One day, seeing the Blessed One with his assembly passing through the royal courtyard, with a confident mind he took oleander flowers and honored the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha. By that meritorious deed he was reborn in a deva world. Wandering on only in happy destinations, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in the city of Sīlavatī. His name was Bandhura. Having reached maturity, he went to Sāvatthī on some business. He went to the monastery with some lay followers, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, gained faith, and went forth. As his knowledge was mature, he established insight and before long attained arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Siddhattho nāma bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Purakkhato sāvakehi, nagaraṃ paṭipajjatha.

“The Blessed One named Siddhattha, the world’s foremost, the bull among men, attended by his disciples, was entering the city.

“Rañño antepure āsiṃ, gopako abhisammato;

Pāsāde upaviṭṭhohaṃ, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“I was an esteemed guard in the king’s inner quarters. Seated on the upper floor of the palace, I saw the Leader of the World.

“Kaṇaveraṃ gahetvāna, bhikkhusaṅghe samokiriṃ;

Buddhassa visuṃ katvāna, tato bhiyyo samokiriṃ.

“Taking an oleander flower, I scattered it over the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Making a special offering for the Buddha, I scattered even more over him.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-fourth eon from now, when I worshipped with a flower, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Sattāsītimhito [M 1.0264] kappe, caturāsuṃ mahiddhikā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Eighty-seven eons ago from now, there were four of great psychic power, endowed with the seven treasures, wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā kataññubhāve ṭhatvā attano upakārassa rañño paccupakāraṃ kātuṃ sīlavatīnagaraṃ gantvā [P 1.0221] rañño dhammaṃ desento saccāni pakāsesi. Rājā saccapariyosāne sotāpanno [V 1.0227] hutvā attano nagare sudassanaṃ nāma mahantaṃ vihāraṃ kāretvā therassa niyyātesi. Mahālābhasakkāro ahosi. Thero vihāraṃ sabbañca lābhasakkāraṃ saṅghassa niyyātetvā sayaṃ purimaniyāmeneva piṇḍāya caritvā yāpento katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā sāvatthiṃ gantukāmo ahosi. Bhikkhū, “bhante, tumhe idheva vasatha, sace paccayehi vekallaṃ, mayaṃ taṃ paripūressāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Thero, “na mayhaṃ, āvuso, uḷārehi paccayehi attho atthi, itarītarehi paccayehi yāpemi, dhammarasenevamhi titto”ti dassento –

But having attained arahantship, abiding in gratitude, he went to the city of Sīlavatī to return the favor to the king who had been his benefactor. While teaching the Dhamma to the king, he proclaimed the truths. At the end of the discourse on the truths, the king became a stream-enterer. He had a great monastery named Sudassana built in his city and presented it to the elder. Great gain and honor arose for him. The elder presented the monastery and all the gain and honor to the Saṅgha, and he himself went for almsfood in the same way as before to maintain himself. Having lived there for some days, he wished to go to Sāvatthī. The bhikkhus said to him: “Venerable sir, please live right here. If there is any lack of requisites, we will provide it.” The elder, indicating, “Friends, I have no need for splendid requisites; I maintain myself with simple ones, for I am satisfied with the taste of the Dhamma”—

103.

103.

“Nāhaṃ etena atthiko, sukhito dhammarasena tappito;

Pitvā rasaggamuttamaṃ, na ca kāhāmi visena santhava”nti. –

“I have no need of this; I am happy, satisfied by the taste of the Dhamma. Having drunk the supreme, highest taste, I will not make an intimacy with poison.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha nāhaṃ etena atthikoti yena maṃ tumhe tappetukāmā “paripūressāmā”ti vadatha, etena āmisalābhena paccayāmisarasena nāhaṃ atthiko, mayhaṃ etena attho natthi, santuṭṭhi paramaṃ sukhanti itarītareheva paccayehi yāpemīti attho. Idāni tena anatthikabhāve padhānakāraṇaṃ dassento āha “sukhito dhammarasena tappito”ti. Sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammarasena ceva navavidhalokuttaradhammarasena ca tappito pīṇito sukhito uttamena sukhena suhitoti attho. Pitvā rasaggamuttamanti sabbarasesu aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ tatoyeva uttamaṃ yathāvuttaṃ dhammarasaṃ pivitvā ṭhito, tenāha – “sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jinātī”ti (dha. pa. 354). Na ca kāhāmi visena santhavanti evarūpaṃ rasuttamaṃ [M 1.0265] dhammarasaṃ pivitvā ṭhito visena visasadisena visarasena santhavaṃ saṃsaggaṃ na karissāmi, tathākaraṇassa kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho.

Herein, I have no need of this means: I have no need for this material gain, for the taste of material requisites, by which you, wishing to satisfy me, say, “We will provide.” The meaning is: I have no use for this; since “contentment is the highest happiness,” I maintain myself with whatever simple requisites I get. Now, showing the main reason for this lack of need, he says: happy, satisfied by the taste of the Dhamma. The meaning is: satisfied, gratified, happy, and well-content with the supreme happiness by the taste of the thirty-seven things pertaining to enlightenment and by the taste of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Having drunk the supreme, highest taste means: he abides having drunk the aforesaid taste of the Dhamma, which is the foremost, the best, and therefore the highest of all tastes. Thus it is said: “The taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes” (Dhp 354). I will not make an intimacy with poison means: abiding having drunk such a supreme taste, the taste of the Dhamma, I will not make an intimacy or an association with poison—that is, with the taste of poison, which is like poison—for there is no reason to do so. This is the meaning.

Bandhurattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Bandhura is finished.

4. Khitakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Khitaka

Lahuko [P 1.0222] vata me kāyoti āyasmato khitakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle yakkhasenāpati hutvā nibbatto ekadivasaṃ yakkhasamāgame nisinno satthāraṃ aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ pavedento apphoṭento uṭṭhahitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā [V 1.0228] padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, khitakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto mahāmoggallānattherassa mahiddhikabhāvaṃ sutvā “iddhimā bhavissāmī”ti pubbahetunā codiyamāno pabbajitvā bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā samathavipassanāsu kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.17.1-6) –

“Light indeed is my body”—this is the verse of the Venerable Khitaka. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn as a general of the yakkhas in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. One day, while seated in a gathering of yakkhas, he saw the Teacher seated at the foot of a certain tree. He approached the Teacher, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, expressing his lofty joy and gladness, he clapped his hands, rose, paid homage to the Teacher, circumambulated him respectfully, and departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans and in this Buddha-era was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; his name was Khitaka. When he came of age, he heard of the great psychic power of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and, impelled by a past cause, he thought, “I will become one with psychic power.” He went forth, and having received a meditation subject from the Blessed One, he worked at serenity and insight and before long became a possessor of the six direct knowledges. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Padumo nāma nāmena, dvipadindo narāsabho;

Pavanā abhinikkhamma, dhammaṃ deseti cakkhumā.

“The one named Paduma, leader of bipeds, bull among men, the One with Vision, has come forth from the forest and teaches the Dhamma.

“Yakkhānaṃ samayo āsi, avidūre mahesino;

Yena kiccena sampattā, ajjhāpekkhiṃsu tāvade.

“An assembly of yakkhas took place not far from the Great Sage. For whatever purpose they had arrived, they then looked on expectantly.

“Buddhassa giramaññāya, amatassa ca desanaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, apphoṭetvā upaṭṭhahiṃ.

“Discerning the Buddha’s utterance and his teaching of the Deathless, with confident and gladdened mind, I clapped my hands and attended on him.

“Suciṇṇassa phalaṃ passa, upaṭṭhānassa satthuno;

Tiṃsakappasahassesu, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“Behold the fruit of my good deed, of my attendance on the Teacher: for thirty thousand eons I was not reborn in a bad destination.

“Ūnatiṃse [M 1.0266] kappasate, samalaṅkatanāmako;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Twenty-nine hundred eons ago, I was a wheel-turning monarch of great power named Samalaṅkata, endowed with the seven treasures.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā savisesaṃ iddhīsu vasībhāvena anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhonto iddhipāṭihāriyena anusāsanīpāṭihāriyena ca sattānaṃ anuggahaṃ karonto viharati. So bhikkhūhi, “kathaṃ tvaṃ, āvuso, iddhi vaḷañjesī”ti puṭṭho tamatthaṃ ācikkhanto –

Having attained arahantship, he dwelled benefiting beings by means of the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of instruction, experiencing various kinds of psychic power through his special mastery over them. When he was asked by the bhikkhus, “Friend, how do you exercise psychic power?” he explained the matter thus:

104.

104.

“Lahuko vata me kāyo, phuṭṭho ca pītisukhena vipulena;

Tūlamiva eritaṃ mālutena, pilavatīva me kāyo”ti. –

“Light indeed is my body, and it is suffused with abundant rapture and happiness. Like a cotton tuft tossed by the wind, my body seems to float.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi. “Udānavasenā”tipi vadantiyeva.

He spoke this verse. It is also said that it was an inspired utterance.

Tattha lahuko vata me kāyoti nīvaraṇādivikkhambhanena cuddasavidhena cittaparidamanena caturiddhipādakabhāvanāya suṭṭhu ciṇṇavasībhāvena ca me rūpakāyo sallahuko vata, yena dandhaṃ mahābhūtapaccayampi nāma imaṃ karajakāyaṃ [P 1.0223] cittavasena pariṇāmemīti adhippāyo. Phuṭṭho ca pītisukhena [V 1.0229] vipulenāti sabbatthakameva pharantena mahatā uḷārena pītisahitena sukhena phuṭṭho ca me kāyoti yojanā. Idañca yathā kāyo lahuko ahosi, taṃ dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhasaññokkamanena hi saddhiṃyeva lahusaññokkamanaṃ hoti. Sukhassa pharaṇañcettha taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ kathaṃ pana catutthajjhānasamaṅgino pītisukhapharaṇaṃ, samatikkantapītisukhañhi tanti ce? Saccametaṃ, idaṃ pana na catutthajjhānalakkhaṇavasena vuttaṃ, atha kho pubbabhāgavasena. “Pītisukhenā”ti pana pītisahitasadisena sukhena, upekkhā hi idha santasabhāvatāya ñāṇavisesayogato ca sukhanti adhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.101). Pādakajjhānārammaṇena rūpakāyārammaṇena vā iddhicittena sahajātaṃ sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamati pavisati phusati sampāpuṇātīti [M 1.0267] ayampi tattha attho. Tathā cāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.3.12) – “sukhasaññā nāma upekkhāsampayuttā saññā. Upekkhā hi santaṃ sukhanti vuttaṃ sāyeva saññā nīvaraṇehi ceva vitakkādipaccanīkehi ca vimuttattā lahusaññātipi veditabbā. Taṃ okkantassa panassa karajakāyopi tūlapicu viya sallahuko hoti. So evaṃ vātakkhittatūlapicuno viya sallahukena dissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gacchatī”ti. Tenāha “tūlamiva eritaṃ mālutena, pilavatīva me kāyo”ti. Tassattho – yadāhaṃ brahmalokaṃ aññaṃ vā iddhiyā gantukāmo homi, tadā mālutena vāyunā eritaṃ cittaṃ tūlapicu viya ākāsaṃ laṅghantoyeva me kāyo hotīti.

Herein, ‘light indeed is my body’: the meaning is that through the suppression of the hindrances and so on, through the fourteenfold taming of the mind, and through the well-practiced cultivation of the four bases for psychic power and the mastery over them, my form-body has become very light. By this, even this foul body, which is conditioned by the great elements, I can transform by the power of the mind. ‘And it is suffused with abundant rapture and happiness’: the construction is that my body is suffused with great, lofty happiness accompanied by rapture, which pervades it entirely. This is said to show how the body became light, for the entering upon the perception of lightness occurs together with the entering upon the perception of happiness. Here, the suffusion with happiness should be seen in terms of the form produced from it. But how can there be a suffusion with rapture and happiness for one who is in the fourth jhāna, since rapture and happiness have been transcended? That is true. But this is not spoken of in terms of the characteristics of the fourth jhāna, but in terms of the preliminary stage. ‘With rapture and happiness’: this means with a happiness that is similar to that accompanied by rapture, for here equanimity is intended as happiness because of its peaceful nature and its connection with special knowledge. For thus it is said: “He enters upon the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness” (Paṭi I 101). Another meaning here is that he enters upon, touches, and attains the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness that are co-nascent with the mind of psychic power, which has either the base jhāna or the form-body as its object. Thus it is said in the commentary (Paṭi-a II 365): “The perception of happiness is the perception associated with equanimity. For equanimity is called ‘peaceful happiness.’ That same perception, because it is liberated from the hindrances and from opposing factors such as thought, should be known as the perception of lightness. For one who has entered upon it, even this foul body becomes as light as a cotton tuft. With a body that appears as light as a cotton tuft tossed by the wind, he goes to the Brahmā world.” Therefore he said: ‘Like a cotton tuft tossed by the wind, my body seems to float.’ The meaning is: When I wish to go to the Brahmā world or elsewhere by means of psychic power, then my body becomes one that leaps into the sky just like a cotton tuft tossed by the wind.

Khitakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Khitaka is finished.

5. Malitavambhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Malitavambha

Ukkaṇṭhitoti [P 1.0224] āyasmato malitavambhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle himavantato avidūre aññatarasmiṃ jātassare sakuṇo hutvā nibbatti, padumuttaro bhagavā taṃ anuggaṇhanto tattha gantvā jātassaratīre caṅkamati. Sakuṇo bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sare kumudāni gahetvā bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kurukacchanagare aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, malitavambhotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto pacchābhūmahātheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto viharati. Tassa ca ayaṃ sabhāvo, yattha bhojanasappāyo dullabho, itare sulabhā, tato na pakkamati. Yattha pana bhojanasappāyo sulabho, itare dullabhā, tattha na vasati pakkamateva. Evaṃ viharanto [V 1.0230] ca hetusampannatāya mahāpurisajātikatāya ca nacirasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.51-57) –

“Restless” is a verse of the Venerable Malitavambha. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a bird in a certain lake not far from the Himalayas. The Blessed One Padumuttara, wishing to favor him, went there and walked on the bank of the lake. Seeing the Blessed One, the bird, with a confident mind, took water lilies from the lake and honored the Blessed One. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era he was reborn as the son of a certain brahmin in the city of Kurukaccha. His name was Malitavambha. Having attained understanding, he approached the Great Elder Pacchābhū, listened to the Dhamma in his presence, and, having gained faith, went forth. He dwelt practicing insight meditation. And this was his nature: where suitable food was difficult to obtain but the other requisites were easy to obtain, he would not depart from there; but where suitable food was easy to obtain but the other requisites were difficult, he would not stay but would depart. Dwelling thus, because he was endowed with the right conditions and was of the lineage of a great man, before long he developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre[M 1.0268], mahājātassaro ahu;

Padumuppalasañchanno, puṇḍarīkasamotthaṭo.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there was a great lake, covered with lotuses and water lilies, and abounding with white lotuses.

“Kukuttho nāma nāmena, tatthāsiṃ sakuṇo tadā;

Sīlavā buddhisampanno, puññāpuññesu kovido.

“Kukuttha was my name; I was a bird there then, virtuous, endowed with wisdom, skilled in merit and demerit.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Jātassarassāvidūre, sañcarittha mahāmuni.

“Padumuttara, knower of worlds, recipient of offerings, the great sage, wandered not far from the lake.

“Jalajaṃ kumudaṃ chetvā, upanesiṃ mahesino;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, paṭiggahi mahāmuni.

“Having plucked a water-born water lily, I offered it to the great seer; understanding my intention, the great sage accepted it.

“Tañca dānaṃ daditvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“Having given that gift, urged on by a wholesome root, for a hundred thousand eons I was not reborn in a bad destination.

“Soḷaseto kappasate, āsuṃ varuṇanāmakā;

Aṭṭha ete janādhipā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Sixteen hundred eons ago, there were eight rulers of men named Varuṇa, mighty wheel-turning monarchs.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā udānento –

But having attained Arahantship, reflecting on his own practice, he uttered this inspired utterance:

105.

105.

“Ukkaṇṭhitopi na vase, ramamānopi pakkame;

Na tvevānatthasaṃhitaṃ, vase vāsaṃ vicakkhaṇo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Though dissatisfied, one should not stay; though delighting, one should depart. The discerning person should not take up a dwelling connected with what is unbeneficial.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha ukkaṇṭhitopi na vaseti yasmiṃ āvāse vasantassa me bhojanasappāyālābhena adhikusalesu dhammesu ukkaṇṭhā anabhirati uppajjati, tattha ukkaṇṭhitopi vasāmiyeva itarasappāyalābhena na pakkame na pakkamāmi. Na vaseti ettha na-kārenapi pakkametipadaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ. Ramamānopi pakkameti yasmiṃ [P 1.0225] pana āvāse vasantassa me paccayavekallābhāvena natthi ukkaṇṭhā, aññadatthu abhiramāmi, evaṃ abhiramamānopi avasesasappāyālābhena tato pakkame, na vaseyyaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipajjantovāhaṃ nacirasseva sakatthaṃ paccupādinti. Ayañcettha attapaṭipattipaccavekkhaṇāyaṃ yojanā. Parassa ovādadāne pana vaseyya na pakkameyyāti vidhānavasena [M 1.0269] yojetabbaṃ. Na tvevānatthasaṃhitaṃ, vase vāsaṃ vicakkhaṇoti yasmiṃ āvāse paccayā sulabhā[V 1.0231], samaṇadhammo na pāripūriṃ gacchati, yasmiñca āvāse paccayā dullabhā, samaṇadhammopi pāripūriṃ na gacchati, evarūpo āvāso idha anatthasaṃhito nāma avaḍḍhisahitoti katvā. Evarūpaṃ vāsaṃ vicakkhaṇo viññujātiko sakatthaṃ paripūretukāmo natveva vaseyya. Yattha pana pañcaṅgasamannāgato āvāso labbhati, sattapi sappāyā labbhanti, tattheva vaseyyāti attho.

Therein, Though dissatisfied, one should not stay: this refers to a dwelling where, while I was residing, dissatisfaction and non-delight arose in me regarding higher wholesome states due to not obtaining suitable food. [My wrong tendency was:] 'Though dissatisfied, I will stay, since I get other suitable things; I will not depart.' The negative in should not stay implies that one should depart. Though delighting, one should depart: this refers to a dwelling where, while I was residing, there was no dissatisfaction on account of not lacking requisites—on the contrary, I was delighting—but even while so delighting, if the other suitable conditions were not obtained, I should depart from there, I should not stay. It was by practicing thus that I quickly attained my own goal. This is the application here in reviewing one's own practice. But when giving advice to another, it should be applied in a prescriptive sense: 'One should stay, one should not depart' [where conditions are suitable]. The discerning person should not take up a dwelling connected with what is unbeneficial: this means a dwelling where requisites are easy to obtain but the ascetic’s duties are not fulfilled, or a dwelling where requisites are hard to obtain and the ascetic’s duties are also not fulfilled. Such a dwelling is here called 'connected with what is unbeneficial,' that is, 'connected with decline.' A discerning person, one who is wise, wishing to fulfill their own goal, should certainly not dwell in such a residence. But where a dwelling endowed with the five factors is found, and the seven kinds of suitability are also obtained, one should dwell right there—this is the meaning.

Malitavambhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Malitavambha is finished.

6. Suhemantattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Suhemanta

Sataliṅgassa atthassāti āyasmato suhemantattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito dvānavute kappe tissassa bhagavato kāle vanacaro hutvā vane vasati, taṃ anuggahituṃ bhagavā araññaṃ pavisitvā tassa āsanne ṭhāne aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. So bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto sugandhāni punnāgapupphāni ocinitvā bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde pāriyantadese vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, suhemantotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto saṅkassanagare migadāye viharantaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā tepiṭako hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño [P 1.0226] paṭisambhidāpatto ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.46-50) –

“Of the meaning with a hundred signs…” is a verse of the Venerable Suhemanta. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merit that serves as a basis for liberation, ninety-two eons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Tissa, was a forest-dweller living in the woods. To favor him, the Blessed One entered the forest and sat at the foot of a certain tree near him. Seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind he gathered fragrant punnāga flowers and honored the Blessed One. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in a deva world, and thereafter, having repeatedly performed meritorious deeds while wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in a border region. His name was Suhemanta. Having reached maturity, he approached the Blessed One dwelling in the Deer Park at Saṅkassa, listened to the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. He became a master of the Tipiṭaka, established insight, and before long attained the six direct knowledges and the analytical knowledges. Thus it was said in the Apadāna (apa. thera 1.16.46-50):

“Kānanaṃ vanamogayha, vasāmi luddako ahaṃ;

Punnāgaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, buddhaseṭṭhaṃ anussariṃ.

“Having entered the forest grove, I lived as a hunter; seeing a punnāga tree in bloom, I recollected the Supreme Buddha.”

“Taṃ [M 1.0270] pupphaṃ ocinitvāna, sugandhaṃ gandhitaṃ subhaṃ;

Thūpaṃ karitvā puline, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“Having plucked that flower—fragrant, scented, and beautiful—I made a stūpa on a sandbank and offered it to the Buddha.”

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-two eons ago, when I honored him with that flower, I have known no bad destination: this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.”

“Ekamhi navute kappe, eko āsiṃ tamonudo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Ninety-one eons ago, I was a dispeller of darkness, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up … the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0232] pana patvā evaṃ cintesi – “mayā kho yaṃ sāvakena pattabbaṃ, taṃ anuppattaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ idāni bhikkhūnaṃ anuggahaṃ kareyya”nti. Evaṃ cintetvā pabhinnapaṭisambhidatāya akilāsutāya ca attano santikaṃ upagate bhikkhū yathārahaṃ ovadanto anusāsanto kaṅkhaṃ chindanto dhammaṃ kathento kammaṭṭhānaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā ācikkhanto viharati. Athekadivasaṃ attano santikaṃ upagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ viññūnañca puggalānaṃ visesaṃ ācikkhanto –

But having attained arahantship, he reflected thus: “Whatever is to be attained by a disciple has been attained by me. Now, let me help the bhikkhus.” Having reflected thus, because of his attainment of the analytical knowledges and his tirelessness, he dwelt instructing and advising the bhikkhus who came to him as was fit, cutting off their doubts, teaching the Dhamma, and explaining the meditation subject, making it clear and disentangled. Then one day, while explaining the distinction to the wise persons and bhikkhus who had come to him,

106.

106.

“Sataliṅgassa atthassa, satalakkhaṇadhārino;

Ekaṅgadassī dummedho, satadassī ca paṇḍito”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Of a meaning that has a hundred signs, that bears a hundred characteristics, the fool sees only one aspect, but the wise person sees a hundred.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha sataliṅgassāti līnamatthaṃ gamentīti liṅgāni, atthesu saddassa pavattinimittāni, tāni pana sataṃ anekāni liṅgāni etassāti sataliṅgo. Anekattho hi idha satasaddo, “sataṃ sahassa”ntiādīsu viya na saṅkhyāvisesattho tassa sataliṅgassa. Atthassāti ñeyyassa, ñeyyañhi ñāṇena araṇīyato “attho”ti vuccati. So ca ekopi anekaliṅgo, yathā “sakko purindado maghavā”ti, “paññā vijjā medhā ñāṇa”nti ca. Yena liṅgena pavattinimittena tāvatiṃsādhipatimhi indasaddo pavatto, na tena tattha sakkādisaddā pavattā, atha kho aññena. Tathā yena sammādiṭṭhimhi paññāsaddo pavatto, na tena vijjādisaddā. Tena vuttaṃ “sataliṅgassa atthassā”ti.

Therein, of one with a hundred signs: 'signs' (liṅgāni) are so called because they make a hidden meaning understood; they are the grounds for the application of a word to its meanings. One for whom there are a hundred, that is, many, signs is 'one with a hundred signs' (sataliṅgo). For here the word 'hundred' (sata) means 'many,' as in such phrases as 'a hundred thousand'; it does not mean a specific number. Of the meaning: of the knowable. The knowable is called 'meaning' (attha) because it is to be approached by knowledge. And that meaning, though one, has many signs, as for example, 'Sakka, Purindada, Maghavā,' and 'wisdom (paññā), true knowledge (vijjā), intelligence (medhā), knowledge (ñāṇa).' The sign by which the word 'Inda' is applied to the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa devas is not the one by which the words 'Sakka,' etc., are applied to him; rather, they are applied by another. Similarly, the sign by which the word 'wisdom' is applied in the case of right view is not the one by which the words 'true knowledge,' etc., are applied. Therefore it was said, of the meaning with a hundred signs.

Satalakkhaṇadhārinoti [M 1.0271] anekalakkhaṇavato. Lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, paccayabhāvino atthassa attano phalaṃ paṭicca paccayabhāvo, tena hi so ayaṃ imassa kāraṇanti lakkhīyati. So ca ekasseva atthassa anekappabhedo upalabbhati[P 1.0227], tenāha “satalakkhaṇadhārino”ti. Atha vā lakkhīyantīti lakkhaṇāni, tassa tassa atthassa saṅkhatatādayo pakāravisesā te pana atthato avatthāvisesā veditabbā. Te ca pana tesaṃ aniccatādisāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ liṅgenti ñāpentīti “liṅgānī”ti ca vuccanti. Tassime ākārā, yasmā ekassāpi atthassa aneke upalabbhanti. Tena vuttaṃ “sataliṅgassa atthassa, satalakkhaṇadhārino”ti. Tenāha āyasmā dhammasenāpati – “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchantī”ti (mahāni. 156; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5).

'Satalakkhaṇadhārinoti' means 'possessing many characteristics.' 'Lakkhaṇa' (characteristic) is that by which something is marked—its being a cause in relation to its own effect. For by this, one discerns, 'This is the cause of that.' And this characteristic is found in many varieties for a single phenomenon, hence it is said, 'possessing a hundred characteristics.' Alternatively, 'lakkhaṇāni' (characteristics) are what is marked: the particular modes of each phenomenon, such as its being conditioned, etc., though these should be understood as particular states, not different in substance. And these, by indicating the universal characteristics such as impermanence, etc., are also called 'liṅgāni' (signs). These are its aspects, since many are found even for a single phenomenon. Therefore it was said, 'of a meaning with a hundred signs, possessing a hundred characteristics.' Therefore, the Venerable General of the Dhamma said: 'All phenomena, in all their aspects, come within the range of the Blessed Buddha’s knowledge' (Mahāni. 156; Cūḷani. Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5).

Ekaṅgadassī dummedhoti evaṃ anekaliṅge anekalakkhaṇe atthe yo tattha ekaṅgadassī aputhupaññatāya ekaliṅgamattaṃ ekalakkhaṇamattañca disvā attanā diṭṭhameva “idameva sacca”nti abhinivissa [V 1.0233] “moghamañña”nti itaraṃ paṭikkhipati, hatthidassanakaandho viya ekaṅgagāhī dummedho duppañño tattha vijjamānānaṃyeva pakāravisesānaṃ ajānanato micchā abhinivisanato ca. Satadassī ca paṇḍitoti paṇḍito pana tattha vijjamāne anekepi pakāre attano paññācakkhunā sabbaso passati. Yo vā tattha labbhamāne aneke paññācakkhunā attanāpi passati, aññesampi dasseti pakāseti, so paṇḍito vicakkhaṇo atthesu kusalo nāmāti. Evaṃ thero ukkaṃsagataṃ attano paṭisambhidāsampattiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vibhāvesi.

The one-sided seer is foolish—so in a matter with many signs and many characteristics, one who, due to limited wisdom, sees only a single sign and a single characteristic, clings to what he himself has seen, thinking, 'This alone is true,' and rejects the other as vain—like the blind men who saw the elephant, he is one-sided, foolish, unwise, due to not knowing the various modes present there and clinging wrongly. The hundred-sided seer is wise—but the wise one, with the eye of wisdom, sees all the various modes present there completely. Or one who, with the eye of wisdom, sees for himself the many aspects attainable there and also shows and makes them clear to others—he is called wise, discerning, skilled in matters. Thus, the elder revealed to the monks his own supreme attainment of the analytical knowledges.

Suhemantattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Suhemanta is concluded.

7. Dhammasavattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhammasava

Pabbajiṃ [M 1.0272] tulayitvānāti āyasmato dhammasavattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle suvaccho nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū gharāvāse dosaṃ [P 1.0228] disvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane pabbatantare assamaṃ kāretvā bahūhi tāpasehi saddhiṃ vasi. Athassa kusalabījaṃ ropetukāmo padumuttaro bhagavā assamasamīpe ākāse ṭhatvā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. So taṃ disvā pasannamānaso pūjetukāmo nāgapupphāni ocināpesi. Satthā, “alaṃ imassa tāpasassa ettakaṃ kusalabīja”nti pakkāmi. So pupphāni gahetvā satthu gamanamaggaṃ okiritvā cittaṃ pasādento añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā dhammasavoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto hetusampattiyā codiyamāno gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ pabbajjāya ānisaṃsañca disvā dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ viharantaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.39-45) –

The verse 'Having weighed, I went forth' is by the Venerable Dhammasava. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this one was a brahmin named Suvaccho, who was proficient in the three Vedas. Seeing the faults in household life, he took up the ascetic life and, having had a hermitage built in the mountain interior in the wilderness, lived together with many ascetics. Then, desiring to plant a seed of merit in him, the Blessed One Padumuttara stood in the sky near the hermitage and displayed a miracle of psychic power. Seeing this, with a joyful mind, he wished to honor him and had nāga flowers picked. The Teacher, thinking, 'This much seed of merit is enough for this ascetic,' departed. Taking the flowers, the ascetic scattered them along the path where the Teacher had walked, and making his mind serene, he stood with his hands raised in reverence. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Wandering from one happy existence to another, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the Magadha country during this Buddha’s Dispensation. Named Dhammasava, he attained maturity and, urged by favorable conditions, saw the drawbacks of household life and the benefits of going forth. Approaching the Blessed One dwelling in Dakkhiṇāgiri, he heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. Doing the work of insight meditation, he soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaccho nāma nāmena, brāhmaṇo mantapāragū;

Purakkhato sasissehi, vasate pabbatantare.

“Named Suvaccha, a brahmin proficient in mantras, honored by his disciples, he dwells in the mountain interior.”

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mamuddharitukāmo so, āgacchi mama santikaṃ.

“The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the recipient of offerings, wishing to uplift me, came into my presence.”

“Vehāsamhi caṅkamati, dhūpāyati jalate tathā;

Hāsaṃ mamaṃ viditvāna, pakkāmi pācināmukho.

“He walks in the sky, emits smoke and blazes forth; knowing my delight, he departed facing east.”

“Tañca [V 1.0234] acchariyaṃ disvā, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Nāgapupphaṃ gahetvāna, gatamaggamhi okiriṃ.

“Having seen that amazing, wonderful, and hair-raising sight, taking nāga flowers, I scattered them on the path he had gone.”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ pupphaṃ okiriṃ ahaṃ;

Tena cittappasādena, duggatiṃ nupapajjahaṃ.

“A hundred thousand aeons ago, I scattered those flowers; by that joyful confidence of mind, I was not reborn in a bad destination.”

“Ekatiṃse [M 1.0273] kappasate, rājā āsi mahāraho;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Thirty-one hundred aeons ago, I was a king of great worth, endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning monarch.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā somanassappatto udānavasena –

Having attained arahantship, reflecting on his own practice, filled with gladness, he uttered this inspired utterance:

107.

107.

“Pabbajiṃ tulayitvāna, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Having weighed it, I went forth from the home to the homeless life; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha pabbajiṃ tulayitvānāti “sambādho gharāvāso rajāpatho”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.191; ma. ni. 2.10; saṃ. ni. 2.154) gharāvāse, “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā”tiādinā (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.177) kāmesu ādīnavaṃ tappaṭipakkhato nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ tulabhūtāya paññāya vicāretvā vīmaṃsitvāti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Herein, 'having weighed, I went forth' means having considered and investigated with wisdom like a balance the household life as 'confined, a path of dust,' and so on, and the drawbacks in sensual pleasures as 'of little enjoyment, much suffering, much despair,' and so on, and, conversely, the benefits of renunciation—such is the meaning. The rest is as stated before. And this was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Dhammasavattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Dhammasava is concluded.

8. Dhammasavapituttheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhammasava’s Father

Sa vīsavassasatikoti [P 1.0229] āyasmato dhammasavapituttherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro buddhasuññe loke kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhūtagaṇe nāma pabbate viharantaṃ paccekasambuddhaṃ disvā pasannamānaso tiṇasūlapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi.
