So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto dārapariggahaṃ katvā dhammasavaṃ nāma puttaṃ labhitvā tasmiṃ pabbajite sayampi vīsavassasatiko hutvā, “mama putto tāva taruṇo pabbaji[M 1.0274], atha kasmā nāhaṃ [V 1.0235] pabbajissāmī”ti sañjātasaṃvego satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.35-38) –

The verse beginning 'Being one hundred and twenty years old' is by the Venerable Elder Dhammasava’s Father. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under past Buddhas, was reborn in a good family during a time when the world was empty of Buddhas. Having attained maturity, he saw a Paccekabuddha dwelling on a mountain named Bhūtagaṇa and, with a joyful mind, made an offering with grass-blade flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Wandering repeatedly in happy destinations, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the Magadha country during this Buddha’s Dispensation. Having attained maturity, he took a wife and fathered a son named Dhammasava. When his son went forth, he himself, being one hundred and twenty years old, thought, “My son has gone forth while still young—why should I not go forth?” Stirred by urgency, he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and went forth. Establishing insight, he soon realized arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre, bhūtagaṇo nāma pabbato;

Vasateko jino tattha, sayambhū lokanissaṭo.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Bhūtagaṇa; there dwells a single Victor, self-enlightened, detached from the world.”

“Tiṇasūlaṃ gahetvāna, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ;

Ekūnasatasahassaṃ, kappaṃ na vinipātiko.

“Taking a blade of grass, I offered it to the Buddha; for ninety-nine thousand aeons, I did not fall into a state of woe.”

“Ito ekādase kappe, ekosiṃ dharaṇīruho;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Eleven aeons ago, I was a single monarch, endowed with the seven treasures, a mighty wheel-turning king.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā sañjātasomanasso udānento –

Having attained arahantship, reflecting on his own practice, and with joy arisen, he uttered this inspired utterance:

108.

108.

“Sa vīsavassasatiko, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Being one hundred and twenty years old, I went forth into homelessness; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.” – thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha sa vīsavassasatikoti so vīsaṃvassasatiko, so ahaṃ jātiyā vīsādhikavassasatiko samāno. Pabbajinti pabbajjaṃ upagacchiṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Idameva ca imassa therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

Herein, 'sa vīsavassasatiko' means 'he, being one hundred and twenty years old'; that is, 'I, being one hundred and twenty years old by birth.' 'Pabbajiṃ' means 'I undertook the going forth.' The rest is as previously explained. And this was this Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Dhammasavapituttheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhammasava’s Father is concluded.

9. Saṅgharakkhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita

Na nūnāyaṃ paramahitānukampinoti āyasmato saṅgharakkhitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Sopi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito catunavute kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ pabbatapāde [P 1.0230] vasante satta paccekasambuddhe [M 1.0275] disvā pasannamānaso kadambapupphāni gahetvā pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ibbhakule nibbatti, tassa saṅgharakkhitoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0236] aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ sahāyaṃ katvā araññe viharati. Therassa vasanaṭṭhānato avidūre vanagumbe ekā migī vijāyitvā taruṇaṃ chāpaṃ rakkhantī chātajjhattāpi puttasinehena dūre gocarāya na gacchati, āsanne ca tiṇodakassa alābhena kilamati. Taṃ disvā thero, “aho vatāyaṃ loko taṇhābandhanabaddho mahādukkhaṃ anubhavati, na taṃ chindituṃ sakkotī”ti saṃvegajāto tameva aṅkusaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.30-34) –

“Surely, this one, secluded, does not ponder the teaching of the supremely compassionate.” This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Saṅgharakkhita. What is its origin? This Elder, too, having performed deeds of merit under past Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family ninety-four aeons ago and attained maturity. One day, while dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he saw seven Paccekabuddhas and, with a joyful mind, took kadamba flowers and offered them. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world and, again and again performing deeds of merit, wandered only in happy destinations until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. His name was Saṅgharakkhita. Having attained maturity and gained faith, he went forth, took a meditation subject, and lived in the forest with a monk as his companion. Not far from the Elder’s dwelling place, in a forest thicket, a doe gave birth and, protecting her young fawn, though afflicted by hunger, due to affection for her offspring, she did not go far to graze. And lacking grass and water nearby, she was afflicted. Seeing this, the Elder thought, “Alas, this world is bound by the bonds of craving, experiencing great suffering, and is unable to cut them.” Stirred by spiritual urgency, he made that very thing his goad, developed insight-meditation, and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.16.30–34):

“Himavantassāvidūre, kukkuṭo nāma pabbato;

Tamhi pabbatapādamhi, satta buddhā vasanti te.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Kukkuṭa. At the foot of that mountain, those seven Buddhas dwell.”

“Kadambaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, dīparājaṃva uggataṃ;

Ubho hatthehi paggayha, satta buddhe samokiriṃ.

“Seeing the kadamba tree in full bloom, like a king of lamps rising up, I raised both hands and scattered flowers over the seven Buddhas.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, I made that flower offering; I do not know of any bad destination—this is the fruit of worshipping a Buddha.”

“Dvenavute ito kappe, sattāsuṃ pupphanāmakā;

Sattaratanasampannā, cakkavattī mahabbalā.

“Ninety-two aeons ago, there were seven named Puppha; endowed with the seven treasures, they were wheel-turning monarchs of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano dutiyakaṃ bhikkhuṃ micchāvitakkabahulaṃ viharantaṃ ñatvā tameva migiṃ upamaṃ karitvā taṃ ovadanto –

Having attained arahantship, and knowing that his companion monk was dwelling with an abundance of wrong thoughts, he admonished him, using that very doe as a simile:

109.

109.

“Na nūnāyaṃ paramahitānukampino, rahogato anuvigaṇeti sāsanaṃ;

Tathāhayaṃ viharati pākatindriyo, migī yathā taruṇajātikā vane”ti. –

“Surely, this one, secluded, does not ponder the teaching of the supremely compassionate one. He dwells with senses unrestrained, just like a young doe in the forest.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [M 1.0276] na nūnāyanti na-iti paṭisedhe nipāto. Nūnāti parivitakke. Nūna ayanti padacchedo. Paramahitānukampinoti paramaṃ ativiya, paramena vā anuttarena hitena satte anukampanasīlassa bhagavato. Rahogatoti rahasi gato, suññāgāragato kāyavivekayuttoti attho. Anuvigaṇetīti ettha “na nūnā”ti padadvayaṃ ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ “nānuvigaṇeti nūnā”ti, na cintesi maññe, “nānuyuñjatī”ti takkemīti attho. Sāsananti paṭipattisāsanaṃ, catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvananti adhippāyo[P 1.0231]. Tathā hīti teneva kāraṇena, satthu sāsanassa ananuyuñjanato eva. Ayanti ayaṃ bhikkhu. Pākatindriyoti manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ yathāsakaṃ visayesu vissajjanato sabhāvabhūtaindriyo[V 1.0237], asaṃvutacakkhudvārādikoti attho. Yassa taṇhāsaṅgassa acchinnatāya so bhikkhu pākatindriyo viharati, tassa upamaṃ dassento “migī yathā taruṇajātikā vane”ti āha. Yathā ayaṃ taruṇasabhāvā migī puttasnehassa acchinnatāya vane dukkhaṃ anubhavati, na taṃ ativattati, evamayampi bhikkhu saṅgassa acchinnatāya pākatindriyo viharanto vaṭṭadukkhaṃ nātivattatīti adhippāyo. “Taruṇavijātikā”ti vā pāṭho. Abhinavappasutā bālavacchāti attho. Taṃ sutvā so bhikkhu sañjātasaṃvego vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Herein, 'na' is a particle of negation. 'Nūna' is for conjecture. The words should be split as 'nūna ayaṃ.' 'Paramahitānukampino' refers to the Blessed One, who by nature is compassionate towards beings with the highest, unsurpassed welfare. 'Rahogato' means gone to a secluded place, gone to an empty dwelling; the meaning is endowed with bodily solitude. Regarding 'anuvigaṇeti,' the two words 'na nūnā' should be brought forward and connected to it, meaning: 'he does not ponder, I suppose,' or 'he does not apply himself, I reckon.' 'Sāsana' refers to the teaching of practice, with the intention being the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Truths. 'Tathāhayaṃ' means for that very reason, due to not applying himself to the Teacher’s instruction. 'Ayaṃ' means this monk. 'Pākatindriyo' refers to one whose faculties—the six including the mind—are in their natural state, released toward their respective objects, meaning one with unrestrained sense-doors, such as the eye. To illustrate why that monk dwells with unrestrained faculties due to the uncut bond of craving, the simile is given: 'like a young doe in the forest.' The intention is: just as this doe of a young nature, because her affection for her offspring is uncut, experiences suffering in the forest and does not overcome it, so too this monk, because his attachment is uncut, dwells with unrestrained faculties and does not overcome the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. Alternatively, the reading may be 'taruṇavijātikā,' meaning one who has recently given birth to a young calf. Hearing this, that monk, stirred by spiritual urgency, developed insight-meditation, and before long attained arahantship.

Saṅgharakkhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita is concluded.

10. Usabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verse of Elder Usabha

Nagā nagaggesu susaṃvirūḷhāti āyasmato usabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppati? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni karonto ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle devaputto hutvā nibbatto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso dibbapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. Sā pupphapūjā sattāhaṃ pupphamaṇḍapākārena aṭṭhāsi. Devamanussānaṃ mahāsamāgamo ahosi. So [M 1.0277] tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe ibbhakule nibbatti, tassa usabhoti nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe satthari laddhappasādo pabbajitvā katapubbakicco araññe pabbatapāde viharati. Tena ca samayena pāvusakālameghe abhippavuṭṭhe pabbatasikharesu rukkhagacchalatāya ghanapaṇṇasaṇḍino honti[P 1.0232]. Athekadivasaṃ thero leṇato nikkhamitvā taṃ vanarāmaṇeyyakaṃ pabbatarāmaṇeyyakañca disvā yonisomanasikāravasena “imepi nāma rukkhādayo acetanā utusampattiyā vaḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇanti, atha kasmā nāhaṃ utusappāyaṃ labhitvā guṇehi vaḍḍhiṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti cintento –

“The trees have grown well on the mountain peaks”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Usabha. What is its origin? This Elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating in various existences merits that support liberation, was reborn as a deva thirty-one aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Sikhi. One day, seeing the Teacher, his mind was gladdened, and he made an offering with divine flowers. That flower offering remained for seven days in the form of a floral pavilion. There was a great gathering of devas and humans. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a wealthy family in the Kosala country. His name was Usabha. Having come of age, he gained faith in the Teacher at the dedication of Jetavana. Having gone forth and fulfilled his preliminary duties, he dwelt at the foot of a mountain in the forest. At that time, when the rainy-season clouds had poured down, the trees, shrubs, and creepers on the mountain peaks became dense with thick foliage. Then one day, the elder emerged from his cave and, seeing the beauty of the forest and the mountain, through wise attention he thought: “If even these trees and so on, though insentient, attain growth when the season is favorable, why then should I not, having obtained a suitable season, attain growth in virtues?”

110.

110.

“Nagā nagaggesu susaṃvirūḷhā, udaggameghena navena sittā;

Vivekakāmassa araññasaññino, janeti bhiyyo usabhassa kalyata”nti. –

“Trees well-grown on mountain peaks, watered by new rain from rising clouds, further increase the fitness of Usabha, who desires solitude and is percipient of the forest.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered the verse.

Tattha nagāti rukkhā, “nāgā”ti keci vadanti, nāgarukkhāti attho. Nagaggesūti pabbatasikharesu. Susaṃvirūḷhāti suṭṭhu samantato virūḷhamūlā hutvā parito upari ca sammadeva sañjātasākhaggapallavappasākhāti [V 1.0238] attho. Udaggameghena navena sittāti paṭhamuppannena uḷārena mahatā pāvusameghena abhippavuṭṭhā. Vivekakāmassāti kilesavivittaṃ cittavivekaṃ icchantassa, araññavāsena tāva kāyaviveko laddho, idāni upadhivivekādhigamassa nissayabhūto cittaviveko laddhabboti taṃ patthayamānassa, jāgariyaṃ anuyuñjantassāti attho, tenāha “araññasaññino”ti. Araññavāso nāma satthārā vaṇṇito thomito. So ca kho yāvadeva samathavipassanābhāvanāpāripūriyā, tasmā sā mayā hatthagatā kātabbāti evaṃ araññagatasaññino nekkhammasaṅkappabahulassāti attho. Janetīti uppādenti, puthutte [M 1.0278] hi idaṃ ekavacanaṃ. Keci pana “janentī”ti paṭhanti. Bhiyyoti uparūpari. Usabhassāti attānameva paraṃ viya vadati. Kalyatanti kalyabhāvaṃ cittassa kammaññataṃ bhāvanāyogyataṃ. Svāyamattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Evaṃ thero imaṃ gāthaṃ vadantoyeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.25-29) –

There, ‘nagā’ means trees; some call them ‘nāgā,’ meaning nāga trees. ‘Nagaggesu’ refers to mountain peaks. ‘Susaṃvirūḷhā’ means well-grown all around, with roots spreading evenly and branches, twigs, and sub-branches properly produced all around and above. ‘Udaggameghena navena sittā’ means drenched by the first-arisen, vast, great rainy-season cloud, pouring down heavily. ‘Vivekakāmassa’ refers to one who desires the seclusion of mind, free from defilements. First, bodily seclusion is attained through forest dwelling; now, mental seclusion, which is the basis for the attainment of seclusion from the substrates of existence, should be achieved. Thus, it means one who is devoted to wakefulness, as stated: “perceiving the forest.” Forest dwelling is praised and commended by the Teacher, but only to the extent of perfecting serenity and insight meditation. Therefore, one should think, “I must achieve it.” Thus, it means one who perceives the forest and is inclined toward renunciation. ‘Janeti’ means it produces. Here, the singular form is used for generality, though some read it as ‘janenti’ (plural). ‘Bhiyyo’ means more and more. ‘Usabhassa’ refers to oneself, speaking as if of another. ‘Kalyataṃ’ means the state of readiness, the mind’s fitness, its suitability for meditation. This meaning has been stated above. Thus, while reciting this verse, the elder, having diligently aroused insight, attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.16.25–29):

“Devaputto [P 1.0233] ahaṃ santo, pūjayiṃ sikhināyakaṃ;

Mandāravena pupphena, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“Being a deva, I honored Sikhi, the Leader; with a mandārava flower, I made an offering to the Buddha.”

“Sattāhaṃ chadanaṃ āsi, dibbaṃ mālaṃ tathāgate;

Sabbe janā samāgantvā, namassiṃsu tathāgataṃ.

“For seven days there was a canopy, a divine garland for the Tathāgata; all people gathered together and paid homage to the Tathāgata.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first aeon from now, when I offered that flower, I have not known a bad rebirth—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Ito ca dasame kappe, rājāhosiṃ jutindharo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“And in the tenth aeon from now, I was a king, a bearer of splendor; endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosīti.

This, indeed, was the Elder’s verse of declaration of final knowledge.

Usabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Usabha is concluded.

Ekādasamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Eleventh Chapter is concluded.

12. Dvādasamavaggo

12. The Twelfth Chapter

1. Jentattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jenta

Duppabbajjaṃ [V 1.0239] ve duradhivāsā gehāti āyasmato jentattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle devaputto hutvā nibbatti. So ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto kiṃkirātapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto [M 1.0279] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe jentagāme ekassa maṇḍalikarājassa putto hutvā nibbatti, jentotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto daharakāleyeva hetusampattiyā codiyamāno pabbajjāninnamānaso hutvā puna cintesi – “pabbajjā nāma dukkarā, gharāpi durāvāsā, dhammo ca gambhīro, bhogā ca duradhigamā, kiṃ nu kho kattabba”nti evaṃ pana cintābahulo hutvā vicaranto ekadivasaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇi. Sutakālato paṭṭhāya pabbajjābhirato hutvā satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sukhāya paṭipadāya khippābhiññāya arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.21-24) –

“Difficult is the going forth, hard to endure is the household life,” so spoke the verse of the venerable Elder Jenta. What is its origin? This one too, having made his aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulating wholesome actions as a basis for turning away from existence, was reborn as a deva during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. One day, seeing the Teacher, his mind filled with faith, he made an offering with kiṅkirāta flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a provincial king in the village of Jenta in the Magadha country, and his name was Jenta. Having attained understanding, even in his youth, urged by a favorable confluence of circumstances, his mind inclined toward renunciation. Yet he pondered: “Going forth is difficult, household life is hard to endure, the Dhamma is profound, and material possessions are hard to obtain—what should I do?” While wandering, preoccupied with these thoughts, one day he went to the Teacher and listened to the Dhamma. From the moment he heard it, he became devoted to renunciation, took ordination under the Teacher, took a meditation subject, developed insight, and attained arahantship through the path of ease and swift direct knowledge. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.16.21–24):

“Devaputto ahaṃ santo, pūjayiṃ sikhināyakaṃ;

Kakkārupupphaṃ paggayha, buddhassa abhiropayiṃ.

“Being a deva, I honored Sikhi, the Leader. Taking up a kakkāru flower, I offered it to the Buddha.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first aeon from now, when I offered that flower, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Ito ca navame kappe, rājā sattuttamo ahuṃ;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“And in the ninth aeon from now, I was King Sattuttama; endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhanto, “asakkhiṃ vatāhaṃ ādito mayhaṃ uppannavitakkaṃ chinditu”nti somanassajāto [P 1.0234] vitakkassa uppannākāraṃ tassa ca sammadeva chinnataṃ dassento –

Having attained arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, feeling joyful that “Indeed, I was able from the beginning to cut off the thought that arose in me,” and showing the manner in which the thought arose and its proper cutting off, he spoke this verse:

111.

111.

“Duppabbajjaṃ [V 1.0240] ve duradhivāsā gehā, dhammo gambhīro duradhigamā bhogā;

Kicchā vutti no itarītareneva, yuttaṃ cintetuṃ satatamaniccata”nti. –

“Difficult is the going forth, and hard to endure are households; the Dhamma is profound, and wealth is hard to acquire; difficult is our livelihood, not so that of others; it is right to constantly reflect on impermanence.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha duppabbajjanti appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhañceva ñātiparivaṭṭañca pahāya imasmiṃ sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajanassa dukkarattā dukkhaṃ pabbajanaṃ, dukkarā pabbajjāti duppabbajjaṃ. Veti nipātamattaṃ, daḷhattho vā “pabbajjā dukkhā”ti[M 1.0280]. Gehañce āvaseyyaṃ, duradhivāsā gehā, yasmā gehaṃ adhivasantena raññā rājakiccaṃ, issarena issarakiccaṃ, gahapatinā gahapatikiccaṃ kattabbaṃ hoti, parijano ceva samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca saṅgahetabbā, tasmiṃ tasmiñca kattabbe kariyamānepi gharāvāso chiddaghaṭo viya mahāsamuddo viya ca duppūro, tasmā gehā nāmete adhivasituṃ āvasituṃ dukkhā dukkarāti katvā duradhivāsā durāvāsāti. Pabbajjañce anutiṭṭheyyaṃ dhammo gambhīro, yadatthā pabbajjā, so pabbajitena adhigantabbo paṭivedhasaddhammo gambhīro, gambhīrañāṇagocarattā duddaso, duppaṭivijjho dhammassa gambhīrabhāvena duppaṭivijjhattā. Gehañce āvaseyyaṃ, duradhigamā bhogā yehi vinā na sakkā gehaṃ āvasituṃ, te bhogā dukkhena kasirena adhigantabbatāya duradhigamā. Evaṃ sante gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajjaṃyeva anutiṭṭheyyaṃ, evampi kicchā vutti no itarītarena idha imasmiṃ buddhasāsane itarītarena yathāladdhena paccayena amhākaṃ vutti jīvikā kicchā dukkhā, gharāvāsānaṃ duradhivāsatāya bhogānañca duradhigamatāya gehe itarītarena paccayena yāpetabbatāya kicchā kasirā vutti amhākaṃ, tattha kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti? Yuttaṃ cintetuṃ satatamaniccataṃ sakalaṃ divasaṃ pubbarattāpararattañca tebhūmakadhammajātaṃ aniccatanti, tato uppādavayavantato ādiantavantato [P 1.0235] tāvakālikato ca na niccanti “anicca”nti cintetuṃ vipassituṃ yuttaṃ. Aniccānupassanāya siddhāya itarānupassanā sukheneva sijjhantīti aniccānupassanāva ettha vuttā, aniccassa dukkhānattatānaṃ abyabhicaraṇato sāsanikassa sukhaggahaṇato ca. Tenāha – “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15), “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhammaṃ” (mahāva. 16; dī. ni. 2.371; saṃ. ni. 5.1081), “vayadhammā saṅkhārā”ti (dī. ni. 2.218) ca tadaminā evaṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭipakkhavasena aparāparaṃ uppanne vitakke niggahetvā aniccatāmukhena vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā idāni katakicco jātoti dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ “attano paṭipatti”ntiādi. Idameva therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

Here, 'duppabbajja' means the difficulty of going forth, because it is hard to abandon, whether small or great, a mass of wealth and a circle of relatives, and to undertake the going forth in this dispensation with determination; because of the difficulty of going forth, the going forth is painful, and a difficult going forth is 'duppabbajja.' The word 've' is merely a particle, or it has the emphatic meaning: 'Going forth is difficult.' If one were to dwell in a household, households are hard to endure, for one living in a household must perform royal duties for a king, lordly duties for a lord, and householder's duties for a householder. Family members, ascetics, and brahmins must be supported. Even while engaged in these various tasks, household life is like a pot with holes, like a vast ocean—hard to fill. Therefore, these households are difficult to live in, hard to endure. If one were to undertake the going forth, the Dhamma is profound. The Saddhamma of penetration, for the sake of which one goes forth and which is to be attained by one who has gone forth, is profound, hard to see due to its being within the range of profound knowledge, and hard to penetrate because of the profundity of the Dhamma. If one were to dwell in a household, wealth is hard to obtain, for without wealth, it is impossible to sustain household life. Such wealth is hard to gain because it requires great effort and hardship. This being so, one should abandon household life and undertake the going forth. Even so, our livelihood is difficult. Here in this Buddha’s dispensation, our livelihood, subsisting on whatever requisites are obtained by any means, is difficult and painful. Because households are hard to endure and wealth is hard to obtain, and because one must subsist in the home on whatever is at hand, our livelihood is difficult and arduous. What, then, should be done? It is fitting to constantly reflect on impermanence—throughout the entire day, the early and late parts of the night—on all phenomena of the three realms as impermanent. Then, from their nature of arising and passing away, having a beginning and an end, and being temporary, it is fitting to reflect and contemplate: 'This is impermanent.' When the contemplation of impermanence is accomplished, the other contemplations succeed easily. Therefore, only the contemplation of impermanence is mentioned here, because impermanence invariably implies suffering and non-self, and because it is easy for the practitioner to grasp. Hence it is said: 'What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self' (SN 3.15). 'Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease' (Mhv 16; DN 2.371; SN 5.1081). 'Conditioned things are subject to cessation' (DN 2.218). By this means, by suppressing the thoughts that arise one after another by way of mutual opposition, and by commencing insight through the door of impermanence, it is now shown that one has become one who has done what is to be done. Thus it is said: 'One’s own practice,' etc. This was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Jentattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jenta is concluded.

2. Vacchagottattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vacchagotta

Tevijjohaṃ [M 1.0281][V 1.0241] mahājhāyīti āyasmato vacchagottattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalabījaṃ ropento vipassissa bhagavato kāle bandhumatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ raññā nāgarehi ca saddhiṃ buddhapūjaṃ katvā tato paraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, tassa vacchagottatāya vacchagottotveva samaññā ahosi. So viññutaṃ patvā brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gato vimuttiṃ gavesanto tattha sāraṃ adisvā paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vicaranto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā tasmiṃ vissajjite pasannamānaso satthu santike pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.15-20) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Vacchagotta Thera: 'I am one who possesses the three knowledges, a great meditator.' What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, planting here and there in his existences the wholesome seed that is the supporting condition for rolling back the round of rebirths, was born in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, in the city of Bandhumatī, into a family of good standing. Having reached the age of discretion, one day he, together with the king and the citizens, made an offering to the Buddha. After that, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy brahmin. Due to his belonging to the Vacchagotta lineage, he was known as Vacchagotta. Having reached the age of discretion and becoming accomplished in the brahminical sciences, he sought liberation. Not finding the essence in them, he went forth into the life of a wandering ascetic. Traveling about, he approached the Teacher, asked a question, and upon its being answered, his mind became serene. He went forth in the Teacher's presence and, undertaking the practice of insight, soon became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.16.15-20):

“Udentaṃ [P 1.0236] sataraṃsiṃva, pītaraṃsiṃva bhāṇumaṃ;

Pannarase yathā candaṃ, niyyantaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

Like the rising sun with its hundred rays, the golden-rayed shining one; as the moon on the fifteenth day, so the world leader goes forth.

“Aṭṭhasaṭṭhisahassāni, sabbe khīṇāsavā ahuṃ;

Parivāriṃsu sambuddhaṃ, dvipadindaṃ narāsabhaṃ.

Sixty-eight thousand, all were ones whose taints were destroyed; they surrounded the Perfectly Awakened One, the lord of bipeds, the bull among men.

“Sammajjitvāna taṃ vīthiṃ, niyyante lokanāyake;

Ussāpesiṃ dhajaṃ tattha, vippasannena cetasā.

Having swept that road, as the world leader passed by; there I raised a banner, with a serene mind.

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ dhajaṃ abhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dhajadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-one aeons ago, when I raised that banner; I know no bad destination, this is the fruit of that banner-offering.

“Ito catutthake kappe, rājāhosiṃ mahabbalo;

Sabbākārena sampanno, sudhajo iti vissuto.

Four aeons ago from now, I was a king of great power, endowed in every way, renowned as Sudhaja.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā somanassajāto udānavasena –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, and reflecting on his own practice, with joy arisen, he uttered this inspired utterance:

112.

112.

“Tevijjohaṃ [M 1.0282] mahājhāyī, cetosamathakovido;

Sadattho me anuppatto, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

I am one possessing the three knowledges, a great meditator, skilled in the serenity of mind; my own goal has been attained, the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Tattha [V 1.0242] tevijjohanti yadipi maṃ pubbe tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ gatattā “brāhmaṇo tevijjo”ti sañjānanti, taṃ pana samaññāmattaṃ vedesu vijjākiccassa abhāvato. Idāni pana pubbenivāsañāṇādīnaṃ tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ adhigatattā paramatthato tevijjo ahaṃ, mahantassa anavasesassa samudayapakkhiyassa kilesagaṇassa jhāpanato, mahantena maggaphalajhānena mahantassa uḷārassa paṇītassa nibbānassa jhāyanato ca mahājhāyī. Cetosamathakovidoti cittasaṅkhobhakarānaṃ saṃkilesadhammānaṃ vūpasamanena cetaso samādahane kusalo. Etena tevijjabhāvassa kāraṇamāha. Samādhikosallasahitena hi āsavakkhayena tevijjatā, na kevalena. Sadatthoti sakattho ka-kārassāyaṃ da-kāro kato “anuppattasadattho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.9; a. ni. 3.38) viya. “Sadattho”ti ca arahattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tañhi attapaṭibandhaṭṭhena attānaṃ avijahanaṭṭhena attano paramatthaṭṭhena attano atthattā “sakattho”ti vuccati. Svāyaṃ sadattho me mayā anuppatto adhigato. Etena yathāvuttaṃ mahājhāyibhāvaṃ sikhāpattaṃ katvā dasseti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Here, regarding 'tevijjo' (possessing the three knowledges): although in the past people recognized me as 'a brahmin versed in the three Vedas' because I had mastered the three Vedas, that was merely a conventional designation, due to the absence of the function of true knowledge in the Vedas. But now, having attained the three knowledges—namely, the knowledge of past lives and so forth—I am truly a 'tevijjo' in the ultimate sense. I am a great meditator (mahājhāyī) because I have burnt up the great, entire mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination, and because I contemplate the great, sublime, and excellent Nibbāna with the great meditation of the path and fruition. 'Skilled in the serenity of mind' means being adept in calming the mind by pacifying the defiling states that disturb it. By this, he states the reason for being a 'tevijjo.' For the state of being a 'tevijjo' is achieved through the destruction of the taints accompanied by skill in concentration, not by that alone. 'Sadattho' means 'one's own goal' (sakattho); here, the 'ka' sound is changed to 'da,' as in phrases like 'anuppattasadattho' (MN 1.9; AN 3.38). 'Sadattho' should be understood as arahantship. For it is called 'sakattho' (one's own goal) because it is bound to oneself, because it does not abandon oneself, because it is one's own ultimate goal, and because it is one's own welfare. This 'sadattho' has been attained and realized by me. Through this, he shows that he has brought the state of being a great meditator, as previously described, to its peak. The rest is as has been explained.

Vacchagottattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vacchagotta is completed.

3. Vanavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vanavaccha

Acchodikā puthusilāti āyasmato vanavacchattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalabījaṃ ropento vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto parassa kammaṃ [P 1.0237] katvā jīvanto kassaci aparādhaṃ katvā maraṇabhayena tajjito palāyanto antarāmagge bodhirukkhaṃ [M 1.0283] disvā pasannamānaso tassa mūlaṃ sammajjitvā piṇḍibandhehi asokapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā vanditvā bodhiṃ abhimukho namassamāno pallaṅkena nisinno māretuṃ āgate paccatthike disvā tesu cittaṃ akopetvā bodhiṃ eva āvajjento sataporise papāte papati. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, “vaccho”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto bimbisārasamāgame paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.16.7-14) –

"Acchodikā puthusilā" is a verse of the Venerable Elder Vanavaccha. What is its origin? This elder too, having performed meritorious deeds in the time of previous Buddhas, planted seeds of merit here and there as a supporting condition for release from the cycle of existence. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a good family, and having reached maturity, he made a living by working for another. Having committed some offense, he was threatened by the fear of death and fled. On the way, he saw a Bodhi tree, and with a serene mind, he swept its base, made an offering with bunches of Asoka flowers, paid homage, and facing the Bodhi tree in reverence, he sat down in the cross-legged posture. Seeing his enemies who had come to kill him, he did not become angry at them but kept his mind fixed on the Bodhi tree. He fell into a precipice a hundred persons deep. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds, wandering between the deva and human realms. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha. His name was "Vaccha." Having come of age, he gained faith at a meeting with King Bimbisāra, went forth, and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.16.7-14):

“Parakammāyane [V 1.0243] yutto, aparādhaṃ akāsahaṃ;

Vanantaṃ abhidhāvissaṃ, bhayaverasamappito.

"Engaged in the service of another, I committed an offense; I rushed to the forest, oppressed by fear and hostility."

“Pupphitaṃ pādapaṃ disvā, piṇḍibandhaṃ sunimmitaṃ;

Tambapupphaṃ gahetvāna, bodhiyaṃ okiriṃ ahaṃ.

"Seeing the flowering tree, a well-formed cluster, I took copper-colored flowers and scattered them upon the Bodhi tree."

“Sammajjitvāna taṃ bodhiṃ, pāṭaliṃ pādaputtamaṃ;

Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāna, bodhimūle upāvisiṃ.

"Having swept that Bodhi tree, the excellent Pāṭali tree, I sat down cross-legged at the foot of the Bodhi tree."

“Gatamaggaṃ gavesantā, āgacchuṃ mama santikaṃ;

Te ca disvānahaṃ tattha, āvajjiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

"Seeking the path I had taken, they came into my presence; and seeing them there, I turned my mind to the supreme Bodhi tree."

“Vanditvāna ahaṃ bodhiṃ, vippasannena cetasā;

Anekatāle papatiṃ, giridugge bhayānake.

"Having paid homage to the Bodhi tree with a serene mind, I fell a distance of many palm-tree heights into a dreadful and impassable mountain place."

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bodhipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"In the ninety-first aeon from now, when I offered those flowers, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Bodhi tree."

“Ito ca tatiye kappe, rājā susaññato ahaṃ;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

"In the third aeon from now, I was King Susaññata, endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vivekābhiratiyā vaneyeva vasi, tena vanavacchoti samaññā udapādi. Atha kadāci thero ñātijanānuggahatthaṃ rājagahaṃ [M 1.0284] gato tattha ñātakehi upaṭṭhiyamāno katipāhaṃ vasitvā gamanākāraṃ sandasseti. Taṃ ñātakā, “bhante, amhākaṃ anuggahatthaṃ dhuravihāre vasatha, mayaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmā”ti yāciṃsu. Thero tesaṃ pabbatarāmaṇeyyakittanāpadesena vivekābhiratiṃ nivedento –

Having attained Arahantship, delighting in seclusion, he lived in the forest; therefore, the designation Vanavaccha arose. Then on one occasion, the elder, for the purpose of benefiting his relatives, went to Rājagaha. There, being attended to by his relatives, he stayed for some days and indicated his intention to depart. His relatives requested, "Venerable sir, for the purpose of benefiting us, dwell in a monastery near the village; we will attend to you." The elder, under the pretext of praising the delights of the mountain, revealed his delight in seclusion, saying:

113.

113.

“Acchodikā puthusilā, gonaṅgulamigāyutā;

Ambusevālasañchannā, te selā ramayanti ma”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

"With clear waters and broad rocks, frequented by monkeys and deer, covered with water-moss—those cliffs delight me." – he spoke this verse.

Tattha acchodikāti acchaṃ abahalaṃ sukhumaṃ udakaṃ etesūti “acchodakā”ti vattabbe liṅgavipallāsena acchodikā”ti vuttaṃ. Etena tesaṃ udakasampattiṃ dasseti. Puthusilāti puthulā vitthatā mudusukhasamphassā silā etesūti puthusilā. Etena nisajjanaṭṭhānasampattiṃ dasseti. Gunnaṃ viya naṅgulaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ etesanti gonaṅgulā, kāḷamakkaṭā, “pakatimakkaṭā”tipi vadantiyeva[P 1.0238]. Gonaṅgulehi ca pasadādikehi migehi ca tahaṃ tahaṃ vicarantehi āyutā missitāti gonaṅgulamigāyutā[V 1.0244]. Etena tesaṃ amanussūpacāritāya araññalakkhaṇūpetataṃ dasseti. Ambusevālasañchannāti pasavanato satataṃ paggharamānasalilatāya tahaṃ tahaṃ udakasevālasañchāditā. Te selā ramayanti manti yatthāhaṃ vasāmi; te edisā selā pabbatā vivekābhiratiyā maṃ ramayanti, tasmā tatthevāhaṃ gacchāmīti adhippāyo. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

Therein, 'acchodikā' means having clear, not thick, fine water. Although it should be 'acchodakā,' it is said as 'acchodikā' due to a change of gender. By this, he shows the excellence of their water. 'Puthusilā' means having broad, wide, soft, and pleasantly textured rocks. By this, he shows the excellence of their sitting places. 'Gonaṅgulā' are those with tails like cattle, meaning black monkeys; they are also called 'pakatimakkaṭā' (common monkeys). 'Gonaṅgulamigāyutā' means frequented by and mingled with these 'gonaṅgulā' and by deer and other wild animals wandering here and there. By this, he shows that the place is frequented by non-human beings and possesses the characteristics of a wilderness. 'Ambusevālasañchannā' means covered here and there with water-moss due to the water constantly trickling from the springs. 'Te selā ramayanti maṃ' means: those rocks and mountains where I dwell delight me with their seclusion; therefore, I will go there—this is the intention. This itself was the elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Vanavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vanavaccha is concluded.

4. Adhimuttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Adhimutta

Kāyaduṭṭhullagarunoti āyasmato adhimuttattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? So kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gato kāmesu ādīnavaṃ [M 1.0285] disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññe viharanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā manussūpacāraṃ upagantvā satthāraṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso attano vākacīraṃ satthu pādamūle patthari. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā tasmiṃ aṭṭhāsi. Tattha ṭhitaṃ bhagavantaṃ kāḷānusārena gandhena pūjetvā “samuddharasimaṃ loka”ntiādikāhi dasahi gāthāhi abhitthavi. Taṃ satthā “anāgate ito satasahassakappamatthake gotamassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā chaḷabhiñño bhavissatī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā tato yāvāyaṃ buddhuppādo, tāva devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā adhimuttoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gantvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto pacchimabhavikattā nissaraṇaṃ gavesanto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho satthu santike pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ [P 1.0239] paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.40.304-332) –

"The heaviness and coarseness of the body"—this is a verse of the Venerable Elder Adhimutta. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a brahmin family. Having attained maturity and mastered the brahminical sciences, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures, abandoned household life, and went forth as an ascetic. Dwelling in the forest, he heard of the appearance of a Buddha. Approaching human settlements, he saw the Teacher surrounded by the monastic community and, with a serene mind, spread his bark-fiber garment at the Teacher’s feet. The Teacher, knowing his inclination, stood upon it. While the Blessed One stood there, he honored him with the fragrance of black sandalwood and praised him with ten verses beginning with, "Lift up this world." The Teacher then declared, "In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from now, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, he will go forth and possess the six super-knowledges." Having made this prediction, the Teacher departed. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. From then until the appearance of this Buddha, he wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Adhimutta. Having attained maturity and mastered the brahminical sciences, he found no essence in them. Seeking liberation as one in his final existence, he witnessed the Buddha’s power during the dedication of Jetavana. Gaining faith, he went forth in the Teacher’s presence, established insight meditation, and before long attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.40.304-332)—

“Kaṇikāraṃva jalitaṃ, dīparukkhaṃva ujjalaṃ;

Osadhiṃva virocantaṃ, vijjutaṃ gagane yathā.

"Like a blazing Kaṇikāra tree, like a radiant lamp-tree; shining like a medicinal herb, like lightning in the sky."

“Asambhītaṃ anuttāsiṃ, migarājaṃva kesariṃ;

Ñāṇālokaṃ pakāsentaṃ, maddantaṃ titthiye gaṇe.

"Fearless, not trembling, like a lion, king of beasts; illuminating with the light of knowledge, crushing the crowds of sectarians."

“Uddharantaṃ imaṃ lokaṃ, chindantaṃ sabbasaṃsayaṃ;

Gajjantaṃ migarājaṃva, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

"Lifting up this world, cutting off all doubt, roaring like the king of beasts, I saw the leader of the world."

“Jaṭājinadharo [V 1.0245] āsiṃ, brahā uju patāpavā;

Vākacīraṃ gahetvāna, pādamūle apatthariṃ.

"I was a wearer of matted hair and an animal hide, a brahmin, upright and majestic. Taking a bark garment, I spread it at his feet."

“Kāḷānusāriyaṃ gayhaṃ, anulimpiṃ tathāgataṃ;

Sambuddhamanulimpetvā, santhaviṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

"Taking black sandalwood, I anointed the Tathāgata; having anointed the Perfectly Enlightened One, I extolled the Leader of the World."

“Samuddharasimaṃ lokaṃ, oghatiṇṇa mahāmuni;

Ñāṇālokena jotesi, nāvaṭaṃ ñāṇamuttamaṃ.

"O great sage who has crossed the flood, you lift up this world! You illuminate it with the light of knowledge, with supreme knowledge, which is like a boat."

“Dhammacakkaṃ [M 1.0286] pavattesi, maddase paratitthiye;

Usabho jitasaṅgāmo, sampakampesi medaniṃ.

"You set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma, you crush the other sectarians; O Bull, victorious in battle, you made the earth quake."

“Mahāsamudde ūmiyo, velantamhi pabhijjare;

Tatheva tava ñāṇamhi, sabbadiṭṭhī pabhijjare.

"As waves in the great ocean break upon the shore, even so all views are broken apart by your wisdom."

“Sukhumacchikajālena, saramhi sampatānite;

Antojālīkatā pāṇā, pīḷitā honti tāvade.

"When a fine-meshed net is cast upon a lake, the creatures caught within the net are instantly afflicted."

“Tatheva titthiyā loke, puthupāsaṇḍanissitā;

Antoñāṇavare tuyhaṃ, parivattanti mārisa.

Even so, the heretics in the world, relying on various sects, revolve within your supreme knowledge, O wise one.

“Patiṭṭhā vuyhataṃ oghe, tvañhi nātho abandhunaṃ;

Bhayaṭṭitānaṃ saraṇaṃ, muttitthīnaṃ parāyaṇaṃ.

You are a firm ground for those being swept away in the flood; you are indeed the protector of the friendless, the refuge of those struck by fear, the final resort of those who wish to be released.

“Ekavīro asadiso, mettākaruṇasañcayo;

Asamo susamo santo, vasī tādī jitañjayo.

A single hero, without equal, a store of loving-kindness and compassion; unequaled, well-composed, peaceful, controlled, such a one, a victorious conqueror.

“Dhīro vigatasammoho, anejo akathaṃkathī;

Tusito vantadososi, nimmalo saṃyato suci.

Wise, rid of confusion, unagitated, free from doubt; content, having cast out faults, immaculate, controlled, pure.

“Saṅgātigo hatamado, tevijjo tibhavantago;

Sīmātigo dhammagaru, gatattho hitavabbhuto.

Gone beyond attachment, with pride destroyed, possessor of the threefold knowledge, gone to the end of the three existences; gone beyond boundaries, revering the Dhamma, having attained the goal, a wondrous benefactor.

“Tārako tvaṃ yathā nāvā, nidhīvassāsakārako;

Asambhīto yathā sīho, gajarājāva dappito.

You are a deliverer like a boat, a source of assurance like a treasure; fearless as a lion, majestic as a king of elephants.

“Thometvā dasagāthāhi, padumuttaraṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Vanditvā satthuno pāde, tuṇhī aṭṭhāsahaṃ tadā.

Having praised the greatly renowned Padumuttara with ten verses, and having paid homage at the Teacher's feet, I then stood silent.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Bhikkhusaṅghe ṭhito satthā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

Padumuttara, the world-knower, receiver of offerings, the Teacher, standing amidst the Sangha of monks, spoke these verses.

“Yo me sīlañca ñāṇañca, saddhammañcāpi vaṇṇayi;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

Whoever has praised my virtue, knowledge, and also the true Dhamma, him I shall extol; listen to me as I speak.

“Saṭṭhi kappasahassāni, devaloke ramissati;

Aññe devebhibhavitvā, issaraṃ kārayissati.

For sixty thousand aeons he will delight in the heavenly world; having surpassed the other gods, he will exercise sovereignty.

“So [M 1.0287][V 1.0246] pacchā pabbajitvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Gotamassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajissati.

Later, impelled by the root of merit, he will go forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One, Gotama.

“Pabbajitvāna kāyena, pāpakammaṃ vivajjiya;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

Having gone forth, abandoning evil deeds with the body, and having fully understood all the taints, he, taintless, will attain final Nibbāna.

“Yathāpi megho thanayaṃ, tappeti medaniṃ imaṃ;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, dhammena tappayī mamaṃ.

Just as a thundering cloud satisfies this earth, so too, O great hero, you have satisfied me with the Dhamma.

“Sīlaṃ paññañca dhammañca, thavitvā lokanāyakaṃ;

Pattomhi paramaṃ santiṃ, nibbānaṃ padamaccutaṃ.

Having praised the world's leader, his virtue, wisdom, and the Dhamma, I have attained the supreme peace, Nibbāna, the imperishable state.

“Aho nūna sa bhagavā, ciraṃ tiṭṭheyya cakkhumā;

Aññātañca vijāneyyuṃ, phuseyyuṃ amataṃ padaṃ.

Oh, may that Blessed One, the Seeing One, long endure; may they come to fully know the unknown and realize the Deathless State.

“Ayaṃ me pacchimā jāti, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

This is my last birth; all states of becoming are eradicated. Having fully understood all the taints, I dwell taintless.

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhithomayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, kittanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

A hundred thousand aeons ago, when I extolled the Buddha, I have known no ill destiny since; this is the fruit of that praise.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attanā saha vasante kāyadaḷhibahule bhikkhū ovadanto –

Having attained Arahantship, while dwelling with monks who were much given to bodily robustness, he advised them:

114.

114.

“Kāyaduṭṭhullagaruno, hiyyamānamhi jīvite;

Sarīrasukhagiddhassa, kuto samaṇasādhutā”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

For one who esteems bodily coarseness, while life is dwindling away, for one greedy for bodily pleasures, whence the goodness of a recluse?

Tattha kāyaduṭṭhullagarunoti duṭṭhullaṃ asubhayogyatā, kāyassa duṭṭhullaṃ kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ, kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ garu sambhāvitaṃ yassa so kāyaduṭṭhullagaru, anissaraṇappañño hutvā kāyaposanappasuto kāyadaḷhibahuloti attho, tassa kāyaduṭṭhullagaruno. Hiyyamānamhi jīviteti kunnadīnaṃ udakaṃ viya jīvitasaṅkhāre lahuso khīyamāne. Sarīrasukhagiddhassāti paṇītāhārādīhi attano kāyassa sukhena gedhaṃ āpannassa[M 1.0288]. Kuto samaṇasādhutāti evarūpassa puggalassa samaṇabhāvena sādhutā susamaṇatā kuto kena kāraṇena siyā, ekaṃsato pana kāye jīvite ca nirapekkhassa itarītarasantosena santuṭṭhassa āraddhavīriyasseva samaṇasādhutāti adhippāyo.

Herein, 'kāyaduṭṭhullagaru' means: 'coarseness' (duṭṭhulla) is unsuitability for contemplating the unattractive; the body's coarseness is 'kāyaduṭṭhulla.' One for whom this bodily coarseness is esteemed is 'kāyaduṭṭhullagaru.' The meaning is that such a person, lacking the wisdom of escape and being devoted to nourishing the body, is one much given to bodily robustness; this is the meaning of 'kāyaduṭṭhullagaru.' 'When life is dwindling' means when the life-formations are quickly being exhausted, like the water in small rivers. 'Greedy for bodily pleasures' refers to one who has fallen into attachment to the pleasure of their own body through fine food and the like. 'Whence the goodness of a recluse?' means how, or for what reason, could such a person possess the goodness of a recluse, the excellence of a true recluse? The intended meaning, however, is that the goodness of a recluse belongs exclusively to one who is indifferent to the body and life, content with whatever is at hand, and energetically resolute.

Adhimuttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Adhimutta is concluded.

5. Mahānāmattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahānāma

Esāvahiyyase [V 1.0247] pabbatenāti āyasmato mahānāmattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gato gharāvāsaṃ pahāya aññatarāya nadiyā tīre assamaṃ kāretvā sambahule brāhmaṇe mante vācento viharati. Athekadivasaṃ bhagavā taṃ anuggaṇhituṃ tassa asamapadaṃ upagacchi. So bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto āsanaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi[P 1.0240]. Nisinne bhagavati sumadhuraṃ madhuṃ upanāmesi. Taṃ bhagavā paribhuñjitvā heṭṭhā adhimuttattheravatthumhi vuttanayena anāgataṃ byākaritvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā mahānāmoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto bhagavato santikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nesādake nāma pabbate viharanto kilesapariyuṭṭhānaṃ vikkhambhetuṃ asakkonto “kiṃ me iminā saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa jīvitenā”ti attabhāvaṃ nibbindanto uccaṃ pabbatasikharaṃ abhiruhitvā “ito pātetvā taṃ māressāmī”ti attānaṃ paraṃ viya niddisanto –

The verse of the Venerable Mahānāma Thera begins, "Esāvahiyyase pabbatenāti." What is its origin? This elder, too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits in various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having mastered the brahminical sciences, he abandoned the household life and had a hermitage built on the bank of a certain river, where he dwelt teaching mantras to many brahmins. Then one day, the Blessed One, wishing to favor him, approached his hermitage. Seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind, he prepared a seat and offered it. When the Blessed One was seated, he presented him with very sweet honey. The Blessed One partook of it and, in the manner described above in the story of the Elder Adhimutta, declared his future before departing. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Revolving only in happy destinies again and again, during this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthi. Having received the name Mahānāma and attained understanding, he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. After going forth, he took up a meditation subject and dwelt on a mountain called Nesādaka. Unable to suppress the arising of defilements, he became disgusted with his existence, thinking, "What use is this life to me with a defiled mind?" He climbed a high mountain peak, intending to throw himself down and kill himself, addressing himself as if he were another:

115.

115.

“Esāvahiyyase pabbatena, bahukuṭajasallakikena;

Nesādakena girinā, yasassinā paricchadenā”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

You are being undone by this mountain, abundant with kuṭaja and sallakī trees; by this renowned mountain named Nesādaka, with its surrounding thicket.

Tattha [M 1.0289] esāvahiyyaseti eso tvaṃ mahānāma avahiyyase parihāyasi. Pabbatenāti nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtena iminā pabbatena. Bahukuṭajasallakikenāti bahūhi kuṭajehi indasālarukkhehi sallakīhi indasālarukkhehi vā samannāgatena. Nesādakenāti evaṃnāmakena. Girināti selena. Selo hi sandhisaṅkhātehi pabbehi ṭhitattā “pabbato”ti, pasavanādivasena jalassa, sārabhūtānaṃ bhesajjādivatthūnañca giraṇato “girī”ti vuccati. Tadubhayatthasambhavato panettha “pabbatenā”ti vatvā “girinā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Yasassināti sabbaguṇehi vissutena pakāsena. Paricchadenāti nānāvidharukkhagacchalatāhi samantato channena, vasanaṭṭhānatāya vā tuyhaṃ paricchadabhūtena. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – mahānāma, yadi kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā vitakkabahulo hosi, evaṃ tvaṃ iminā chāyūdakasampannena sappāyena [P 1.0241] nivāsanaṭṭhānabhūtena nesādakagirinā parihāyasi, idānihaṃ taṃ ito pātetvā māressāmi, tasmā na labbhā vitakkavasikena bhavitunti. Evaṃ thero [V 1.0248] attānaṃ santajjentoyeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.40.333-352) –

Therein, 'esāvahiyyase' means: 'you, Mahānāma, are being undone, you are declining.' 'By the mountain' means by this mountain that is your dwelling place. 'Abundant with kuṭaja and sallakī trees' means endowed with many kuṭaja trees, that is, Indasāla trees, and sallakī trees, or Indasāla trees. 'By Nesādaka' means by the one so-named. 'By the mountain' (girinā) means by the rock (selena). A rock (selo), because it stands with what are called joints (pabba), is called a 'pabbata'; and because it emits water and absorbs essential things like medicinal substances, it is called a 'girī.' Since both meanings are possible here, 'pabbatena' was said first and then 'girinā.' 'Renowned' means famous and well-known for all its qualities. 'With its surrounding thicket' means covered all around by various kinds of trees, shrubs, and creepers, or because it serves as your dwelling place, it is your requisite. This is the intended meaning here: Mahānāma, if you abandon your meditation subject and become full of thoughts, you are thus declining by means of this Nesādaka mountain, which is endowed with shade and water and is a suitable dwelling place. Now I will throw you down from here and kill you; therefore, it is not permissible to be under the sway of thoughts. Thus, the elder, while admonishing himself, intensified his insight and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sindhuyā nadiyā tīre, sukato assamo mama;

Tattha vācemahaṃ sisse, itihāsaṃ salakkhaṇaṃ.

On the bank of the river Sindhu, my hermitage was well-made; there I taught my students the Itihāsa with its characteristics.

“Dhammakāmā vinītā te, sotukāmā susāsanaṃ;

Chaḷaṅge pāramippattā, sindhukūle vasanti te.

They were lovers of the Dhamma, disciplined, eager to hear the good teaching; they had attained mastery in the six auxiliary disciplines and dwelt on the bank of the Sindhu.

“Uppātagamane ceva, lakkhaṇesu ca kovidā;

Uttamatthaṃ gavesantā, vasanti vipine tadā.

Skilled in portents and their interpretation, and in bodily marks, seeking the highest goal, they dwelt in the forest then.

“Sumedho nāma sambuddho, loke uppajji tāvade;

Amhākaṃ anukampanto, upāgacchi vināyako.

The Buddha named Sumedha arose in the world at that time; the Guide, having compassion for us, approached.

“Upāgataṃ mahāvīraṃ, sumedhaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Tiṇasanthārakaṃ katvā, lokajeṭṭhassadāsahaṃ.

When the great hero, Sumedha, the world-leader, approached, having made a grass mat, I offered it to the foremost in the world.

“Vipināto madhuṃ gayha, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Sambuddho paribhuñjitvā, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

Having taken honey from the forest, I gave it to the Supreme Buddha. The Sambuddha, having partaken of it, spoke this word.

“Yo [M 1.0290] taṃ adāsi madhuṃ me, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

He who gave me that honey, pleased, with his own hands—him I shall praise; listen to me as I speak.

“Iminā madhudānena, tiṇasanthārakena ca;

Tiṃsa kappasahassāni, devaloke ramissati.

By this gift of honey and this grass mat, for thirty thousand aeons he will delight in the world of the devas.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

In the thirtieth thousand aeon, born in the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama will be in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

An heir to his Dhamma, a true son, created by the Dhamma; having fully understood all the taints, he will attain Nibbāna, taintless.

“Devalokā idhāgantvā, mātukucchiṃ upāgate;

Madhuvassaṃ pavassittha, chādayaṃ madhunā mahiṃ.

Having come here from the world of the devas, when he entered his mother's womb, a shower of honey rained down, covering the earth with honey.

“Mayi nikkhantamattamhi, kucchiyā ca suduttarā;

Tatrāpi madhuvassaṃ me, vassate niccakālikaṃ.

As soon as I came forth from the womb, so very difficult to escape, even then a rain of honey rained for me, constantly and perpetually.

“Agārā abhinikkhamma, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ;

Lābhī annassa pānassa, madhudānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

Having gone forth from the home, I went forth into homelessness; I am a recipient of food and drink—this is the fruit of the gift of honey.

“Sabbakāmasamiddhohaṃ, bhavitvā devamānuse;

Teneva madhudānena, pattomhi āsavakkhayaṃ.

Having been endowed with all sensual pleasures among gods and humans, by that very gift of honey, I have attained the destruction of the taints.

“Vuṭṭhamhi [V 1.0249] deve caturaṅgule tiṇe, sampupphite dharaṇīruhe sañchanne;

Suññe ghare maṇḍaparukkhamūlake, vasāmi niccaṃ sukhito anāsavo.

When the rain has fallen, on grass four fingers high, when the plants of the earth are in full bloom and covered; in an empty house, at the root of a maṇḍapa tree, I dwell always, happy and taintless.

“Majjhe mahante hīne ca, bhave sabbe atikkamiṃ;

Ajja me āsavā khīṇā, natthi dāni punabbhavo.

I have transcended all states of existence—middling, great, and inferior; today my taints are destroyed, there is no further becoming for me now.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, madhudānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

For thirty thousand aeons, since I gave that gift, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the gift of honey.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.

Ayameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthā ahosīti.

And this was the Elder's verse of declaration of final knowledge.

Mahānāmattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahānāma is concluded.

6. Pārāpariyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Pārāpariya

Chaphassāyatane [M 1.0291] hitvāti āyasmato pārāpariyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto piyadassissa bhagavato kāle nesādayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā tassa viññutaṃ pattassa vicaraṇaṭṭhāne aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe piyadassī bhagavā taṃ anuggaṇhituṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. So ca mige pariyesanto taṃ ṭhānaṃ gato satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso bhagavantaṃ anto katvā kataṃ sākhāmaṇḍapaṃ padumapupphehi kūṭāgārākārena sañchādetvā uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedento sattāhaṃ namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Divase divase ca milātamilātāni apanetvā abhinavehi chādesi. Satthā sattāhassa accayena nirodhato vuṭṭhahitvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anussari. Tāvadeva asītisahassamattā bhikkhū satthāraṃ parivāresuṃ. “Madhuradhammakathaṃ suṇissāmā”ti devatā sannipatiṃsu, mahā samāgamo ahosi. Satthā anumodanaṃ karonto tassa devamanussesu bhāviniṃ sampattiṃ imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvakabodhiñca byākaritvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā [P 1.0242] parāparagottatāya pārāpariyoti laddhasamañño bahū brāhmaṇe mante vācento satthu rājagahagamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.40.353-385) –

“Having abandoned the six sense bases” is a verse of the Venerable Elder Pārāpariya. What is its origin? This elder too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences, was reborn into a hunter family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī. Having come of age, while he was wandering in a certain forest grove, the Blessed One Piyadassī, in order to favor him, entered the attainment of cessation and sat there. That hunter, searching for deer, came to that place. Seeing the Teacher, his mind became joyful. Enclosing the Blessed One, he made a shelter of branches and covered it with lotus flowers in the shape of a peaked house. Experiencing sublime joy and happiness, he stood paying homage for seven days. Each day, he removed the withered flowers and replaced them with fresh ones. After seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and recollected the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Immediately, eighty thousand bhikkhus surrounded the Teacher. Thinking, “We will listen to the sweet Dhamma talk,” the deities gathered, and a great assembly took place. The Teacher, giving his blessing, declared the man's future prosperity among gods and humans and his attainment of a disciple’s enlightenment in this Buddha’s dispensation, then departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through saṃsāra among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Rājagaha. Having come of age and mastered the three Vedas, he became known as Pārāpariya due to his Parāpara lineage. While teaching mantras to many brahmins, he saw the Buddha’s majesty when the Teacher came to Rājagaha. Gaining faith, he went forth and, practicing insight meditation, soon attained Arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Piyadassī [V 1.0250] nāma bhagavā, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Vivekakāmo sambuddho, samādhikusalo muni.

The Blessed One named Piyadassī, the Self-existent, the Leader of the world; desiring seclusion, the Sambuddha, the sage skilled in concentration.

“Vanasaṇḍaṃ samoggayha, piyadassī mahāmuni;

Paṃsukūlaṃ pattharitvā, nisīdi purisuttamo.

Having entered the dense forest, the Great Sage Piyadassī, spread out his rag-robe and sat down, the supreme among men.

“Migaluddo pure āsiṃ, araññe kānane ahaṃ;

Pasadaṃ migamesanto, āhiṇḍāmi ahaṃ tadā.

Formerly I was a deer hunter, in the forest, in the wilderness; seeking spotted deer, I wandered then.

“Tatthaddasāsiṃ [M 1.0292] sambuddhaṃ, oghatiṇṇamanāsavaṃ;

Pupphitaṃ sālarājaṃva, sataraṃsiṃva uggataṃ.

There I saw the Sambuddha, who had crossed over the flood, the Taintless One; like a flowering royal sal tree, like the risen sun with its hundred rays.

“Disvānahaṃ devadevaṃ, piyadassiṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Jātassaraṃ samoggayha, padumaṃ āhariṃ tadā.

Having seen the God of gods, Piyadassī of great fame, I entered a natural lake and brought a lotus then.

“Āharitvāna padumaṃ, satapattaṃ manoramaṃ;

Kūṭāgāraṃ karitvāna, chādayiṃ padumenahaṃ.

Having brought a lotus, a hundred-petaled and delightful one, and having made a peaked house, I covered it with the lotus.

“Anukampako kāruṇiko, piyadassī mahāmuni;

Sattarattindivaṃ buddho, kūṭāgāre vasī jino.

Compassionate and merciful, the Great Sage Piyadassī, the Buddha, the Conqueror, dwelt in the peaked house for seven days and nights.

“Purāṇaṃ chaḍḍayitvāna, navena chādayiṃ ahaṃ;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, aṭṭhāsiṃ tāvade ahaṃ.

Having discarded the old one, I covered it with a new one; having raised my joined hands in homage, I stood right there.

“Vuṭṭhahitvā samādhimhā, piyadassī mahāmuni;

Disaṃ anuvilokento, nisīdi lokanāyako.

Having risen from concentration, the Great Sage Piyadassī, the Leader of the world, sat down, looking around in all directions.

“Tadā sudassano nāma, upaṭṭhāko mahiddhiko;

Cittamaññāya buddhassa, piyadassissa satthuno.

Then one named Sudassana, an attendant of great psychic power, knowing the thought of the Buddha, the Teacher Piyadassī,

“Asītiyā sahassehi, bhikkhūhi parivārito;

Vanante sukhamāsīnaṃ, upesi lokanāyakaṃ.

surrounded by eighty thousand bhikkhus, approached the Leader of the World as he sat comfortably at the edge of the forest.

“Yāvatā vanasaṇḍamhi, adhivatthā ca devatā;

Buddhassa cittamaññāya, sabbe sannipatuṃ tadā.

And whatever deities dwelt within that forest grove, knowing the Buddha's thought, they all assembled then.

“Samāgatesu yakkhesu, kumbhaṇḍe saharakkhase;

Bhikkhusaṅghe ca sampatte, gāthā pabyāharī jino.

When the yakkhas, kumbhaṇḍas, and rākṣasas had assembled, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had arrived, the Conqueror uttered these verses.

“Thomaṃ sattāhaṃ pūjesi, āvāsañca akāsi me;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

He honored me with praise for seven days, and made me a dwelling; I shall praise him, listen to me as I speak.

“Sududdasaṃ sunipuṇaṃ, gambhīraṃ suppakāsitaṃ;

Ñāṇena kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

That which is very hard to see, very subtle, deep, and well-proclaimed, I shall proclaim with wisdom; listen to me as I speak.

“Catuddasāni kappāni, devarajjaṃ karissati;

Kūṭāgāraṃ mahantassa, padmapupphehi chāditaṃ.

For fourteen aeons he will reign as king of the devas; a great peaked house of his will be covered with lotus flowers.

“Ākāse [M 1.0293][V 1.0251] dhārayissati, pupphakammassidaṃ phalaṃ;

Catubbīse kappasate, vokiṇṇaṃ saṃsarissati.

It will be held in the sky for him; this is the fruit of the flower-deed. For twenty-four hundred aeons, he will wander through saṃsāra interspersed.

“Tattha pupphamayaṃ byamhaṃ, ākāse dhārayissati;

Yathā padumapattamhi, toyaṃ na upalimpati.

There, a flowery canopy will be borne for him in the sky; just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf,

“Tathevīmassa ñāṇamhi, kilesā nopalimpare;

Manasā vinivaṭṭetvā, pañca nīvaraṇe ayaṃ.

even so, defilements do not cling to his knowledge; this one, having averted the five hindrances with his mind,

“Cittaṃ janetvā nekkhamme, agārā pabbajissati;

Tato pupphamaye byamhe, dhārente nikkhamissati.

having generated the thought of renunciation, will go forth from the household life; then, while a flowery canopy is borne for him, he will depart.

“Rukkhamūle vasantassa, nipakassa satīmato;

Tattha pupphamayaṃ byamhaṃ, matthake dhārayissati.

While he is dwelling at the foot of a tree, discerning and mindful, a flowery canopy will be borne there above his head.

“Cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca, paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ;

Datvāna bhikkhusaṅghassa, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“Having given robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodging to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the taintless one will attain Nibbāna.”

“Kūṭāgārena caratā, pabbajjaṃ abhinikkhamiṃ;

Rukkhamūle vasantampi, kūṭāgāraṃ dharīyati.

“Though wandering with a gabled house, I went forth into homelessness; even while dwelling at the foot of a tree, a gabled house was borne for me.”

“Cīvare piṇḍapāte ca, cetanā me na vijjati;

Puññakammena saṃyutto, labhāmi pariniṭṭhitaṃ.

“I have no intention regarding robes or almsfood; connected with meritorious deeds, I obtain that which is perfected.”

“Gaṇanāto asaṅkheyyā, kappakoṭī bahū mama;

Rittakā te atikkantā, pamuttā lokanāyakā.

“Beyond calculation, immeasurable, are my many crores of aeons; those have passed by empty, the leaders of the world were missed.”

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, piyadassī vināyako;

Tamahaṃ payirupāsitvā, imaṃ yoniṃ upāgato.

“Eighteen hundred aeons ago, there was Piyadassī, the Guide; having attended upon him, I came to this existence.”

“Idha passāmi sambuddhaṃ, anomaṃ nāma cakkhumaṃ;

Tamahaṃ upagantvāna, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ.

“Here I see the Fully Enlightened One, the One with Vision, named Anoma. Having approached him, I went forth into homelessness.”

“Dukkhassantakaro buddho, maggaṃ me desayī jino;

Tassa dhammaṃ suṇitvāna, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“The Buddha, the ender of suffering, the Conqueror, showed me the path. Having heard his Dhamma, I have attained the unshakable state.”

“Tosayitvāna sambuddhaṃ, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

“Having pleased the Fully Enlightened One, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans, and having fully understood all the taints, I dwell taintless.”

“Aṭṭhārase [M 1.0294] kappasate, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Since I revered the Buddha eighteen hundred aeons ago, I do not know a bad destination; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā sañjātasomanasso udānavasena –

But having attained arahantship and reflecting on his own practice, with joy arisen, he uttered this inspired utterance:

116.

116.

“Chaphassāyatane [V 1.0252] hitvā, guttadvāro susaṃvuto;

Aghamūlaṃ vamitvāna, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Having abandoned the six sense bases, with guarded doors, well-restrained, having vomited out the root of misery, I have attained the destruction of the taints.” Thus he spoke this verse.

Tattha chaphassāyatane hitvāti cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ channaṃ samphassānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānatāya “phassāyatanānī”ti laddhanāmāni cakkhādīni cha ajjhattikāyatanāni tappaṭibaddhasaṃkilesappahānavasena pahāya. Guttadvāro susaṃvutoti tato eva cakkhudvārādīnaṃ guttattā, tattha pavattanakānaṃ abhijjhādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pavesananivāraṇena satikavāṭena suṭṭu pihitattā guttadvāro susaṃvuto. Atha vā manacchaṭṭhānaṃ channaṃ dvārānaṃ vuttanayena rakkhitattā guttadvāro, kāyādīhi suṭṭhu saññatattā susaṃvutoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Aghamūlaṃ vamitvānāti aghassa vaṭṭadukkhassa mūlabhūtaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ dosaṃ, sabbaṃ vā kilesadosaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātavamanayogapānena uggiritvā santānato bahi katvā, bahikaraṇahetu vā. Patto me āsavakkhayoti kāmāsavādayo āsavā ettha khīyanti, tesaṃ vā khayena pattabboti āsavakkhayo, nibbānaṃ arahattañca. So āsavakkhayo patto adhigatoti udānavasena aññaṃ byākāsi.

Herein, “having abandoned the six sense bases” means having abandoned, by way of abandoning the defilements connected with them, the six internal bases—the eye and so on—which have received the name “sense bases” because they are the place of origin for the six kinds of contact, such as eye-contact. “With guarded doors, well-restrained” means that because the eye-door and so on are guarded, and because the entrance of unwholesome states like covetousness that arise there is prevented and well-closed by the bolt of mindfulness, he is “with guarded doors, well-restrained.” Alternatively, he is “with guarded doors” because the six doors, with the mind as the sixth, are protected in the manner stated, and he is “well-restrained” because he is thoroughly restrained in body and so on. This is how the meaning should be understood here. “Having vomited out the root of misery” means having expelled and cast out from the continuity of existence the fault that is the root of the misery of the cycle of rebirth—namely, the fault identified as ignorance and craving for existence, or all the faults of the defilements—by drinking the emetic medicine of the noble path, or because it is the cause of their expulsion. “I have attained the destruction of the taints” means that the destruction of the taints—Nibbāna and arahantship—is so called because the taints, such as the taint of sensual desire, are destroyed therein, or because it is to be attained by their destruction. Having attained that destruction of the taints, he declared his final knowledge by way of an inspired utterance.

Pārāpariyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Pārāpariya is concluded.

7. Yasattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Yasa

Suvilitto [M 1.0295][P 1.0243] suvasanoti āyasmato yasattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle mahānubhāvo nāgarājā hutvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ attano bhavanaṃ netvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Bhagavantaṃ mahagghena ticīvarena acchādesi, ekamekañca bhikkhuṃ mahaggheneva paccekadussayugena sabbena samaṇaparikkhārena acchādesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle seṭṭhiputto hutvā mahābodhimaṇḍaṃ sattahi ratanehi pūjesi. Kassapassa bhagavato kāle sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhino putto hutvā nibbatti, yaso nāma nāmena paramasukhumālo. “Tassa tayo pāsādā”ti sabbaṃ khandhake (mahāva. 25) āgatanayena veditabbaṃ.

“Well-anointed and well-clothed” is the verse of the venerable Elder Yasa. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and having accumulated merits in various existences that are a supporting condition for liberation, in the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, became a nāga king of great power. He brought the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, with the Buddha at its head, to his own abode and held a great almsgiving. He clothed the Blessed One with a magnificent triple robe, and he clothed each and every bhikkhu with a pair of magnificent individual cloths and with all the monastic requisites. By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born as the son of a wealthy merchant and honored the great Bodhi-terrace with the seven kinds of jewels. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he went forth in the dispensation and practiced the ascetic’s duties. Thus, wandering only in happy destinations, in the time of this our Blessed One, he was born in Bārāṇasī as the son of a merchant of great wealth. His name was Yasa, and he was extremely delicate. “He had three palaces”—all this should be understood according to the account given in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 25).

So [V 1.0253] pubbahetunā codiyamāno rattibhāge niddābhibhūtassa parijanassa vippakāraṃ disvā sañjātasaṃvego suvaṇṇapādukārūḷhova gehato niggato devatāvivaṭena nagaradvārena nikkhamitvā isipatanasamīpaṃ gato “upaddutaṃ vata, bho, upassaṭṭhaṃ vata, bho”ti āha. Tena samayena bhagavatā isipatane viharantena tasseva anuggaṇhanatthaṃ abbhokāse caṅkamantena “ehi, yasa, idaṃ anupaddutaṃ, idaṃ anupassaṭṭha”nti vutto, “anupaddutaṃ anupassaṭṭhaṃ kira atthī”ti somanassajāto suvaṇṇapādukā oruyha bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisinno satthārā anupubbikathaṃ kathetvā saccadesanāya katāya saccapariyosāne sotāpanno hutvā gavesanatthaṃ āgatassa pitu bhagavatā saccadesanāya kariyamānāya arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.40.456-483) –

Impelled by a past cause, in the middle of the night, he saw the disarray of his retinue, who were overcome by sleep. A sense of urgency arose in him, and, still mounted on his golden sandals, he went out of the house. Exiting through the city gate, which had been opened by a deity, he went near Isipatana and exclaimed, “Oh, what affliction! Oh, what oppression!” At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Isipatana. For the purpose of assisting him, the Blessed One was walking in the open air and said, “Come, Yasa. Here there is no affliction, here there is no oppression.” With joy arisen at the thought, “It seems there is a place without affliction and without oppression,” he descended from his golden sandals, approached the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. The Teacher gave him a progressive discourse, and when the teaching on the truths was given, at the conclusion of the truths, he became a stream-enterer. While the discourse on the truths was being given by the Blessed One to his father, who had come searching for him, he realized arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Mahāsamuddaṃ oggayha, bhavanaṃ me sunimmitaṃ;

Sunimmitā pokkharaṇī, cakkavākapakūjitā.

“Having entered the great ocean, my abode is well-built; well-built is the lotus pond, resounding with ruddy geese.”

“Mandālakehi [M 1.0296] sañchannā, padumuppalakehi ca;

Nadī ca sandate tattha, supatitthā manoramā.

“It is covered with mandārava flowers, and with lotuses and water lilies; and a delightful river with good fords flows there.”

“Macchakacchapasañchannā, nānādijasamotthatā;

Mayūrakoñcābhirudā, kokilādīhi vagguhi.

“Covered with fish and turtles, strewn with various kinds of birds, resounding with peacocks and curlews, and with melodious cuckoos and others.”

“Pārevatā ravihaṃsā ca, cakkavākā nadīcarā;

Dindibhā sāḷikā cettha, pammakā jīvajīvakā.

“Doves and royal swans, ruddy geese and river-dwellers; dindibha birds, mynas here, as well as pammakā birds and jīvajīvaka birds.”
