“Haṃsā koñcāpi naditā, kosiyā piṅgalā bahū;

Sattaratanasampannā, maṇimuttikavālukā.

“Swans and curlews also resound, along with many owls and tawny birds; endowed with the seven treasures, with sand of jewels and pearls.”

“Sabbasoṇṇamayā rukkhā, nānāgandhasameritā;

Ujjotenti divārattiṃ, bhavanaṃ sabbakālikaṃ.

“All the trees are made of gold, wafting various fragrances; they illuminate the abode day and night, at all times.”

“Saṭṭhitūriyasahassāni, sāyaṃ pāto pavajjare;

Soḷasitthisahassāni, parivārenti maṃ sadā.

“Sixty thousand musical instruments are played evening and morning; sixteen thousand women always attend upon me.”

“Abhinikkhamma bhavanā, sumedhaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, vandayiṃ taṃ mahāyasaṃ.

“Having gone forth from my abode to Sumedha, the leader of the world, with a serene and glad mind, I venerated that greatly renowned one.”

“Sambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā, sasaṅghaṃ taṃ nimantayiṃ;

Adhivāsesi so dhīro, sumedho lokanāyako.

“Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, I invited him together with the Saṅgha; that wise one, Sumedha, the leader of the world, accepted.”

“Mama dhammakathaṃ katvā, uyyojesi mahāmuni;

Sambuddhaṃ abhivādetvā, bhavanaṃ me upāgamiṃ.

“Having given me a Dhamma talk, the Great Sage dismissed me; having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, I went to my abode.”

“Āmantayiṃ parijanaṃ, sabbe sannipatātha vo;

Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ buddho, bhavanaṃ āgamissati.

“I addressed my retinue: ‘All of you, gather together! In the forenoon, the Buddha will come to the abode.’”

“Lābhā [V 1.0254] amhaṃ suladdhaṃ no, ye vasāma tavantike;

Mayampi buddhaseṭṭhassa, pūjaṃ kassāma satthuno.

“‘A gain for us, well gained by us, that we dwell near you; we too shall make an offering to the supreme Buddha, the Teacher.’”

“Annaṃ pānaṃ paṭṭhapetvā, kālaṃ ārocayiṃ ahaṃ;

Vasīsatasahassehi, upesi lokanāyako.

“Having prepared food and drink, I announced the time; the leader of the world approached with a hundred thousand sages.”

“Pañcaṅgikehi tūriyehi, paccuggamanamakāsahaṃ;

Sabbasoṇṇamaye pīṭhe, nisīdi purisuttamo.

“With five-membered musical instruments, I went forth to meet him; on an all-golden seat, the supreme man sat down.”

“Uparicchadanaṃ [M 1.0297] āsi, sabbasoṇṇamayaṃ tadā;

Bījaniyo pavāyanti, bhikkhusaṅghassa antare.

“There was a canopy overhead, entirely made of gold at that time; fans were being waved among the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”

“Pahūtenannapānena, bhikkhusaṅghamatappayiṃ;

Paccekadussayugaḷe, bhikkhusaṅghassadāsahaṃ.

“With abundant food and drink, I satisfied the community of monks; I gave a pair of cloths to each one in the community of monks.

“Yaṃ vadanti sumedhoti, lokāhutipaṭiggahaṃ;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“He whom they call Sumedha, receiver of offerings in the world, having sat in the community of monks, spoke these verses.

“Yo me annena pānena, sabbe ime ca tappayiṃ;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

“‘He who satisfied me and all of these with food and drink, I shall praise him; listen to me as I speak.

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, devaloke ramissati;

Sahassakkhattuṃ rājā ca, cakkavattī bhavissati.

“‘For eighteen hundred aeons, he will delight in the heavenly world; and a thousand times he will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch.

“Upapajjati yaṃ yoniṃ, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Sabbadā sabbasovaṇṇaṃ, chadanaṃ dhārayissati.

“‘Whatever birth he takes, whether divine or human, he will always wear an entirely golden covering.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“‘In thirty thousand aeons, born in the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will arise in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“‘An heir to his Dhamma, a true son, created by the Dhamma, having fully understood all the taints, he will attain Nibbāna, taintless.

“Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, sīhanādaṃ nadissati;

Citake chattaṃ dhārenti, heṭṭhā chattamhi ḍayhatha.

“‘Sitting in the community of monks, he will roar a lion’s roar. They hold a parasol over the pyre; beneath the parasol, you will be consumed by fire.

“Sāmaññaṃ me anuppattaṃ, kilesā jhāpitā mayā;

Maṇḍape rukkhamūle vā, santāpo me na vijjati.

“‘The state of a recluse has been attained by me, my defilements have been burnt up; whether in a pavilion or at the foot of a tree, no torment is found in me.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, sabbadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“‘In the thirty thousand aeons since I gave that gift, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that entire gift.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“‘My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.’”

Atha [V 1.0255][P 1.0244] bhagavā āyasmantaṃ yasaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ bāhuṃ pasāretvā “ehi bhikkhū”ti āha. Vacanasamanantarameva dvaṅgulamattakesamassu aṭṭhaparikkhāradharo vassasaṭṭhikatthero [M 1.0298] viya ahosi. So attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā udānento ehibhikkhubhāvappattito purimāvatthavasena –

Then the Blessed One, stretching out his right arm, said to the Venerable Yasa, “Come, monk.” Immediately upon that utterance, he had hair and beard two finger-breadths long, and appeared bearing the eight requisites, like an elder of sixty rains. Reflecting on his own practice, and considering his former state before attaining the ‘ehi-bhikkhu’ status, he uttered this inspired utterance:

117.

117.

“Suvilitto suvasano, sabbābharaṇabhūsito;

Tisso vijjā ajjhagamiṃ, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Well-anointed, well-clothed, adorned with all ornaments, I have attained the three knowledges; the Buddha’s teaching has been done.” Thus he spoke this verse.

Tattha suvilittoti sundarena kuṅkumacandanānulepanena vilittagatto. Suvasanoti suṭṭhu mahagghakāsikavatthavasano. Sabbābharaṇabhūsitoti sīsūpagādīhi sabbehi ābharaṇehi alaṅkato. Ajjhagaminti adhigacchiṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Herein, ‘well-anointed’ means having a body anointed with beautiful saffron and sandalwood paste. ‘Well-clothed’ means well-clothed in expensive Kāsī cloth. ‘Adorned with all ornaments’ means adorned with all ornaments, such as head ornaments and so on. ‘Ajjhagamiṃ’ means ‘I attained.’ The rest is as previously stated.

Yasattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Yasa is concluded.

8. Kimilattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Kimila

Abhisattova nipatatīti āyasmato kimilattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto kakusandhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto parinibbute satthari tassa dhātuyo uddissa saḷalamālāhi maṇḍapākārena pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena tāvatiṃse nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare sākiyarājakule nibbatti, kimilotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto bhogasampattiyā sampanno viharati. Tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ disvā saṃvegajananatthaṃ anupiyāyaṃ viharanto satthā paṭhamayobbane ṭhitaṃ dassanīyaṃ itthirūpaṃ abhinimminitvā purato dassetvā puna anukkamena yathā jarārogavipattīhi abhibhūtā dissati, tathā akāsi. Taṃ disvā kimilakumāro ativiya saṃvegaṃ pakāsento –

“As if cursed, it falls away”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kimila. What is its origin? He too, having made his resolve under past Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha. Having come to understanding, after the Teacher’s final Nibbāna, he honored the relics by making an offering in the form of a pavilion with garlands of salala flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering repeatedly among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was born in the city of Kapilavatthu into a Sakyan royal family, and his name was Kimila. Having reached maturity, he lived replete with wealth and possessions. Seeing that his knowledge was mature, the Teacher, dwelling in Anupiyā to generate a sense of spiritual urgency, manifested a beautiful woman in the prime of youth before him. Then, gradually, he made her appear as if afflicted by aging, sickness, and misfortune. Seeing this, Prince Kimila, expressing extreme spiritual urgency, exclaimed—

118.

118.

“Abhisattova [M 1.0299] nipatati vayo, rūpaṃ aññamiva tatheva santaṃ;

Tasseva [P 1.0245] sato avippavasato, aññasseva sarāmi attāna”nti. –

“Youth falls away as if cursed; the form, though existing just as it is, seems like another’s. Though I am that very same person, not gone away, I regard myself as if I were another.”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this verse.

Tattha abhisattovāti “tvaṃ sīghaṃ gaccha mā tiṭṭhā”ti devehi anusiṭṭho āṇatto viya. “Abhisaṭṭho [V 1.0256] vā”tipi pāṭho, “tvaṃ lahuṃ gacchā”ti kenaci abhilāsāpito viyāti attho. Nipatatīti atipatati abhidhāvati na tiṭṭhati, khaṇe khaṇe khayavayaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho. Vayoti bālyayobbanādiko sarīrassa avatthāviseso. Idha panassa yobbaññaṃ adhippetaṃ, taṃ hissa abhipatantaṃ khīyantaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhitaṃ. Rūpanti rūpasampadāti vadati. Rūpanti pana sarīraṃ “aṭṭhiñca paṭicca nhāruñca paṭicca maṃsañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito rūpaṃtveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.306) viya. Aññamiva tatheva santanti idaṃ rūpaṃ yādisaṃ, sayaṃ tatheva tenevākārena santaṃ vijjamānaṃ aññaṃ viya mayhaṃ upaṭṭhātīti adhippāyo. “Tadeva santa”nti ca keci paṭhanti. Tasseva satoti tasseva me anaññassa sato samānassa. Avippavasatoti na vippavasantassa, ciravippavāsena hi sato anaññampi aññaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti idampi idha natthīti adhippāyo. Aññasseva sarāmi attānanti imaṃ mama attabhāvaṃ aññassa sattassa viya sarāmi upadhāremi sañjānāmīti attho. Tassevaṃ aniccataṃ manasi karontassa daḷhataro saṃvego udapādi, so saṃvegajāto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.56.42-48) –

Therein, ‘as if cursed’ means as if instructed by the gods, “Go quickly, do not stay,” like one commanded. There is also the reading ‘abhisaṭṭho,’ meaning as if urged by someone with desire, “Go swiftly,” like one entreated. ‘It falls away’ means it rushes past, it runs on, it does not stay; it signifies reaching decay and passing away moment by moment. ‘Youth’ refers to the distinct stages of the body, such as childhood and youth. Here, youth is intended, for it is seen rushing forward and decaying as it appears. ‘Form’ refers to perfection of form, it is said. But ‘form’ also means the body, as in the passage: “Dependent on bones, sinews, and flesh, and space enclosed—this is called ‘form.’” ‘As if another, though existing just so’ means this form, existing in the same way, with the same appearance, appears to me as if it were another. And some read, ‘tadeva santaṃ.’ ‘Of that very same one existing’ means ‘of me, the very same, existing, not different.’ ‘Not having departed’ means not having gone far away; for when one has been long separated, even what is not another may appear as if it were another, but here, this is not the case. ‘I regard myself as if another’ means ‘I recall this self of mine as if it were another being,’ I consider, I perceive, I recognize. Reflecting thus on its impermanence, a stronger sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. Filled with this spiritual urgency, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, acquired faith, went forth, established insight, and soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Nibbute kakusandhamhi, brāhmaṇamhi vusīmati;

Gahetvā saḷalaṃ mālaṃ, maṇḍapaṃ kārayiṃ ahaṃ.

“When Kakusandha, the brahmin who had lived the holy life, had attained Nibbāna, I took up a salala garland and had a pavilion made.

“Tāvatiṃsaṃ gato santo, labhimha byamhamuttamaṃ;

Aññe devetirocāmi, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Having gone to Tāvatiṃsa, being there, I obtained a supreme mansion; I outshine the other gods; this is the fruit of that meritorious deed.

“Divā [M 1.0300] vā yadi vā rattiṃ, caṅkamanto ṭhito cahaṃ;

Channo saḷalapupphehi, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Whether by day or by night, whether walking or standing, I am covered by salala flowers; this is the fruit of that meritorious deed.

“Imasmiṃyeva kappamhi, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In this very eon, because I revered the Buddha, I have not known a bad destination: this is the fruit of revering the Buddha.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvāpi thero attano purimuppannaṃ aniccatāmanasikāraṃ vibhāvento tameva gāthaṃ paccudāhāsi. Tenetaṃ imassa therassa aññābyākaraṇampi ahosi.

But even after attaining Arahantship, the Elder, making manifest his previously arisen contemplation of impermanence, recited that very verse again. Thus, this also became the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Kimilattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Kimila is concluded.

9. Vajjiputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Verses of the Elder Vajjiputta

Rukkhamūlagahanaṃ [V 1.0257][P 1.0246] pasakkiyāti āyasmato vajjiputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe ekaṃ paccekasambuddhaṃ bhikkhāya gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kadaliphalāni adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ licchavirājaputto hutvā nibbatti, vajjirājaputtattā vajjiputtotveva cassa samaññā ahosi. So daharo hutvā hatthisikkhādisikkhanakālepi hetusampannatāya nissaraṇajjhāsayova hutvā vicaranto satthu dhammadesanākāle vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante nisinno dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho satthu santike pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.57-62) –

"Having penetrated the thicket at the root of a tree"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vajjiputta. What is its origin? He too, having made a resolution in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulating merit that serves as a foundation for liberation in various existences, ninety-four aeons ago from now, saw a Paccekabuddha going for alms. With a joyful mind, he gave banana fruits. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. After repeatedly performing good deeds, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a Licchavi king in Vesāli. Because he was a Vajji prince, his designation was Vajjiputta. As a youth, even during the time of learning elephant training and other skills, being endowed with the necessary conditions, he wandered about with an inclination only towards renunciation. He went to the monastery during the Teacher's Dhamma talk, and sitting at the edge of the assembly, he heard the Dhamma and gained faith. He went forth in the Teacher's presence and, applying himself to insight meditation, soon attained the six higher knowledges. As it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.51.57-62):

“Sahassaraṃsī bhagavā, sayambhū aparājito;

Vivekā vuṭṭhahitvāna, gocarāyābhinikkhami.

“The Blessed One, with a thousand rays, the self-existent, unconquered, having arisen from solitude, went forth for his alms-round.

“Phalahattho ahaṃ disvā, upagacchiṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, avaṭaṃ adadiṃ phalaṃ.

“With fruit in hand, I saw and approached the bull among men; with a serene and glad mind, I gave the fruit into his bowl.

“Catunnavutito [M 1.0301] kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad destination: this is the fruit of giving fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā aparabhāge aciraparinibbute satthari dhammaṃ saṅgāyituṃ saṅketaṃ katvā mahātheresu tattha tattha viharantesu ekadivasaṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sekhaṃyeva samānaṃ mahatiyā parisāya parivutaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā tassa uparimaggādhigamāya ussāhaṃ janento –

But having attained the six higher knowledges, later, after the Teacher had recently attained final Nibbāna, when the great elders had made an agreement to chant the Dhamma and were dwelling here and there, one day, seeing the Venerable Ānanda, who was still a learner, teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly, and wishing to inspire him to strive for the attainment of the higher path—

119.

119.

“Rukkhamūlagahanaṃ pasakkiya, nibbānaṃ hadayasmiṃ opiya;

Jhāya gotama mā ca pamādo, kiṃ te biḷibiḷikā karissatī”ti. –

“Having penetrated the thicket at the root of a tree, placing Nibbāna in your heart; meditate, Gotama, and do not be heedless. What will this prattling do for you?”

Gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered the verse.

Tattha rukkhamūlagahananti rukkhamūlabhūtaṃ gahanaṃ, gahanañhi atthi, na [P 1.0247] rukkhamūlaṃ, rukkhamūlañca [V 1.0258] atthi, na gahanaṃ, tesu rukkhamūlaggahaṇena ṭhānassa chāyāsampannatāya vātātapaparissayābhāvaṃ dasseti. Gahanaggahaṇena nivātabhāvena vātaparissayābhāvaṃ janasambādhābhāvañca dasseti, tadubhayena ca bhāvanāyogyataṃ. Pasakkiyāti upagantvā. Nibbānaṃ hadayasmiṃ opiyāti “evaṃ mayā paṭipajjitvā nibbānaṃ adhigantabba”nti nibbutiṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā citte karitvā. Jhāyāti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena jhāya, vipassanābhāvanāsahitaṃ maggabhāvanaṃ bhāvehi. Gotamāti dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ gottena ālapati. Mā ca pamādoti adhikusalesu dhammesu mā pamādaṃ āpajji. Idāni yādiso therassa pamādo, taṃ paṭikkhepavasena dassento “kiṃ te biḷibiḷikā karissatī”ti āha. Tattha biḷibiḷikāti viḷiviḷikiriyā, biḷibiḷīti saddapavatti yathā niratthakā, evaṃ biḷibiḷikāsadisā janapaññatti kiṃ te karissati kīdisaṃ atthaṃ tuyhaṃ sādheti, tasmā janapaññattiṃ pahāya sadatthapasuto hohīti ovādaṃ adāsi.

Therein, 'the thicket at the root of a tree' means a thicket that is at the base of a tree. For there can be a thicket without a tree base, and there can be a tree base without a thicket. By mentioning 'the root of a tree,' he shows the absence of danger from wind and sun due to the place being endowed with shade. By mentioning 'thicket,' he shows the absence of danger from wind due to it being a sheltered place, and the absence of crowds of people. And by both, he shows its suitability for meditation. 'Pasakkiya' means having gone near. 'Placing Nibbāna in your heart' means having established quenching in the heart, having fixed it in the mind, thinking, 'By practicing thus, I must attain Nibbāna.' 'Meditate' means meditate by closely contemplating the characteristics; develop the path-development accompanied by insight-development. 'Gotama' addresses the treasurer of the Dhamma by his clan-name. 'Do not be heedless' means do not fall into heedlessness regarding the higher skillful qualities. Now, showing by way of refutation what kind of heedlessness the Elder had, he said, 'What will this prattling do for you?' Herein, 'biḷibiḷikā' means the act of prattling; just as the sound 'biḷibiḷī' is meaningless, so too is popular designation similar to 'biḷibiḷikā'. 'What will it do for you?' means what kind of benefit will it accomplish for you? Therefore, abandoning popular designation, be intent on your own true goal—thus he gave his advice.

Taṃ [M 1.0302] sutvā aññehi vuttavisagandhavāyanavacanena saṃvegajāto bahudeva rattiṃ caṅkamena vītināmento vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā mañcake nipannamattova arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Hearing that, stirred to a sense of urgency by the words spoken by another that carried the scent of poison, he spent much of the night in walking meditation. Having diligently applied himself to insight, upon entering his dwelling and just as he was lying down on the bed, he attained arahantship.

Vajjiputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verse of the Elder Vajjiputta is concluded.

10. Isidattattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verse of the Elder Isidatta

Pañcakkhandhā [P 1.0248] pariññātāti āyasmato isidattattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ rathiyaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso madhuraṃ āmodaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde avantiraṭṭhe vaḍḍhagāme aññatarassa satthavāhassa putto hutvā nibbatti, isidattotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto macchikāsaṇḍe cittassa gahapatino adiṭṭhasahāyo hutvā tena buddhaguṇe likhitvā pesitasāsanaṃ paṭilabhitvā sāsane sañjātappasādo therassa mahākaccānassa santike pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.80-84) –

“The five aggregates are fully understood”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Isidatta. What is its origin? He too, having made a resolution under past Buddhas, accumulated merit here and there in various existences conducive to liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a good family and, having reached an age of understanding, one day saw the Blessed One walking along the road. With a joyful mind, he offered a sweet, fragrant fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Again and again performing meritorious deeds, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a caravan leader in Vaḍḍhagāma in the Avanti country. His name was Isidatta. When he came of age, he became a friend whom he had not seen of the householder Citta in Macchikāsaṇḍa. Having received a message sent by him in which the virtues of the Buddha were written, he developed faith in the Dispensation. He went forth under the Elder Mahākaccāna, began insight meditation, and soon became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.51.80-84)—

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, āmodamadadiṃ phalaṃ.

“The golden-hued Perfectly Enlightened One, recipient of offerings, was walking along the road; I gave him a fragrant fruit.”

“Ekanavutito [V 1.0259] kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of giving fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā “buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmī”ti theraṃ āpucchitvā anukkamena majjhimadesaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno[M 1.0303], “kacci, bhikkhu, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā satthārā katapaṭisanthāro paṭivacanamukhena, “bhagavā tumhākaṃ sāsanaṃ upagatakālato paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ sabbadukkhaṃ apagataṃ, sabbo parissayo vūpasanto”ti pavedanavasena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, he took leave of the elder, saying, “I will go to attend upon the Buddha.” Gradually, he journeyed to the Middle Country, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Having been greeted by the Teacher with kind words, such as, “I hope you are keeping well, monk? I hope you are comfortable?” he, in his reply, by way of announcement, declared his final knowledge, saying, “Since the time I came under your dispensation, Blessed One, all my suffering has departed, all distress has been allayed”—

120.

120.

“Pañcakkhandhā pariññātā, tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā;

Dukkhakkhayo anuppatto, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti. – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“The five aggregates are fully understood, they stand with their roots cut off; the end of suffering has been attained, the destruction of taints has been reached by me.” – thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha pañcakkhandhā pariññātāti pañcapi me upādānakkhandhā vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti sabbaso paricchijja ñātā, na tesu kiñcipi pariññātabbaṃ atthīti [P 1.0249] adhippāyo. Tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakāti sabbaso pariññātattā eva tesaṃ avijjātaṇhādikassa mūlassa samucchinnattā ariyamaggena pahīnattā yāvacarimacittanirodhā te tiṭṭhanti. Dukkhakkhayo anuppattoti chinnamūlakattāyeva ca nesaṃ vaṭṭadukkhassa khayo parikkhayo anuppatto, nibbānaṃ adhigataṃ. Patto me āsavakkhayoti kāmāsavādīnaṃ sabbesaṃ āsavānaṃ khayante abhigantabbatāya “āsavakkhayo”ti laddhanāmaṃ arahattaṃ pattaṃ paṭiladdhanti attho. Keci pana antimāyaṃ samussayo”ti paṭhanti. Nibbānassa adhigatattāyeva ayaṃ mama samussayo attabhāvo antimo sabbapacchimako, natthi dāni punabbhavoti attho. Yaṃ pana tattha tattha avuttaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānaṃyevāti.

Here, “the five aggregates are fully understood”—that is, my five clinging-aggregates have been thoroughly known by the wisdom of insight combined with the wisdom of the path, by discerning: “This is suffering, this much suffering; there is nothing beyond this.” The meaning is that there is nothing more to be fully understood about them. “They remain with roots cut off”—because they have been fully understood, and because their root, consisting of ignorance, craving, and so on, has been completely uprooted and abandoned by the noble path, they persist only until the cessation of the final consciousness. “The cessation of suffering has been attained”—because their roots have been cut off, the exhaustion and complete destruction of the suffering of the round of existence has been reached, and Nibbāna has been realized. “I have reached the destruction of the taints”—that is, all the taints, beginning with the taint of sensual desire, have been destroyed, and thus the state named “the destruction of the taints,” arahantship, has been attained and obtained. Some, however, read the phrase “this is my last aggregation”—meaning that because Nibbāna has been realized, this aggregation, this individual existence, is the final one, the very last. There is now no further becoming. As for what is not explicitly stated here and there, it is clear from what has been explained earlier.

Isidattattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Isidatta is concluded.

Dvādasamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Twelfth Chapter is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca paramatthadīpaniyaṃ theragāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ

Thus ends the commentary on the Theragāthā in the Paramatthadīpanī.

Vīsādhikasatattheragāthāpaṭimaṇḍitassa ekakanipātassa

The chapter of the single collection, adorned with the verses of one hundred and twenty elders.

Atthavaṇṇanā.

Commentary.

2. Dukanipāto

2. The Book of Twos

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Uttarattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara

Dukanipāte [M 1.0304][V 1.0260][P 2.0001] natthi koci bhavo niccotiādikā āyasmato uttarattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle vijjādharo hutvā ākāsena vicarati. Tena ca samayena satthā tassa anuggaṇhanatthaṃ vanantare aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi chabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo vissajjento. So antalikkhena gacchanto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto ākāsato oruyha suvisuddhehi vipulehi kaṇikārapupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjesi, pupphāni buddhānubhāvena satthu upari chattākārena aṭṭhaṃsu, so tena bhiyyosomattāya pasannacitto hutvā aparabhāge kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃse nibbattitvā uḷāraṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanto yāvatāyukaṃ tattha ṭhatvā tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇamahāsālaputto hutvā nibbatti, uttarotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gantvā jātiyā rūpena vijjāya vayena sīlācārena ca lokassa sambhāvanīyo jāto. Tassa taṃ sampattiṃ disvā vassakāro magadhamahāmatto attano dhītaraṃ dātukāmo hutvā attano adhippāyaṃ pavedesi. So nissaraṇajjhāsayatāya taṃ paṭikkhipitvā kālena kālaṃ dhammasenāpatiṃ payirupāsanto tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vattasampanno hutvā theraṃ upaṭṭhahati.

The verse of the Venerable Elder Uttara, beginning with “No existence is permanent,” is in the Dukanipāta. What is its origin? This elder, too, had performed deeds of merit under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit here and there in various existences conducive to the turning away from the round of existence. During the time of the Blessed Sumedha, he became a knowledge-holder and traveled through the sky. At that time, the Teacher, to favor him, sat at the foot of a certain tree in the forest, radiating the six-colored Buddha rays. As he was passing through the air, he saw the Blessed One and, with a joyful heart, descended from the sky. With very pure and abundant kaṇikāra flowers, he honored the Blessed One. By the power of the Buddha, the flowers remained in the form of a canopy above the Teacher. Filled with even greater joy, he passed away at a later time and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, enjoying abundant divine prosperity for his entire lifespan there. After passing away from there, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in Rājagaha, and his name was Uttara. Having reached maturity, he mastered brahminical knowledge and became esteemed in the world for his birth, beauty, knowledge, age, and virtuous conduct. Seeing his prosperity, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, wishing to give him his daughter, expressed his intention. However, due to his inclination toward renunciation, he declined. From time to time, he attended upon the General of the Dhamma, listened to the Dhamma in his presence, and acquired faith. Eventually, he went forth, became accomplished in the monastic observances, and attended upon the elder.

Tena ca samayena therassa aññataro ābādho uppanno, tassa bhesajjatthāya uttaro sāmaṇero pātova pattacīvaramādāya vihārato nikkhanto antarāmagge taḷākassa tīre pattaṃ ṭhapetvā udakasamīpaṃ gantvā mukhaṃ dhovati. Atha aññataro umaṅgacoro ārakkhapurisehi [M 1.0305] anubaddho aggadvāreneva nagarato nikkhamitvā palāyanto attanā gahitaṃ ratanabhaṇḍikaṃ sāmaṇerassa patte pakkhipitvā palāyi. Sāmaṇero pattasamīpaṃ [P 2.0002] upagato. Coraṃ anubandhantā rājapurisā [V 1.0261] sāmaṇerassa patte bhaṇḍikaṃ disvā, “ayaṃ coro, iminā coriyaṃ kata”nti sāmaṇeraṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā vassakārassa brāhmaṇassa dassesuṃ. Vassakāro ca tadā rañño vinicchaye niyutto hutvā chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsati. So “pubbe mama vacanaṃ nādiyi, suddhapāsaṇḍiyesu pabbajī”ti ca baddhāghātattā kammaṃ asodhetvāva jīvantameva taṃ sūle uttāsesi.

At that time, a certain illness arose in the elder. For his medicine, the novice Uttara took his bowl and robe early in the morning and left the monastery. On the way, he placed his bowl on the bank of a pond and went near the water to wash his face. Then, a certain tunnel-thief, pursued by guards, fled through the main gate of the city. As he ran, he placed a bundle of jewels he had taken into the novice’s bowl and escaped. The novice approached his bowl. The royal officers, chasing the thief, saw the bundle in the novice’s bowl and said, “This is the thief! He has committed this theft!” They bound the novice’s hands behind his back and brought him before Vassakāra the brahmin. Vassakāra, at that time, was appointed to the king’s judgment and decreed punishments of mutilation and breaking. Because he held a grudge, declaring, “He did not heed my words before—he went forth among pure sectarians!” and, without investigating the deed, had him impaled alive on a stake.

Athassa bhagavā ñāṇaparipākaṃ oloketvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā vipphurantahatthanakhamaṇimayūkhasambhinnasitābhatāya paggharantajātihiṅgulakasuvaṇṇarasadhāraṃ viya jālāguṇṭhitamudutalunadīghaṅgulihatthaṃ uttarassa sīse ṭhapetvā, “uttara, idaṃ te purimakammassa phalaṃ uppannaṃ, tattha tayā paccavekkhaṇabalena adhivāsanā kātabbā”ti vatvā ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Uttaro amatābhisekasadisena satthu hatthasamphassena sañjātappasādasomanassatāya uḷāraṃ pītipāmojjaṃ paṭilabhitvā yathāparicitaṃ vipassanāmaggaṃ samārūḷho ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā satthu ca desanāvilāsena tāvadeva maggapaṭipāṭiyā sabbakilese khepetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.56.55-92) –

Then the Blessed One, observing the maturity of his wisdom, went to that place. Placing his hand—with its white lustre mingled with the rays from his sparkling fingernail-gems, like a stream of flowing natural vermilion and liquid gold, his soft, tender, long-fingered hand covered with a web-like pattern—on Uttara’s head, he said, “Uttara, this fruit of your former kamma has arisen; you must endure it through the power of reflection.” Then he taught him the Dhamma in accordance with his inclination. Uttara, having gained great joy and gladness due to the serene joy and confidence that arose from the Teacher’s touch—like an anointment with the deathless—ascended the path of insight he had long practiced. As his wisdom had reached maturity and through the Teacher’s graceful delivery of the teaching, he immediately destroyed all defilements in due order along the path and became one with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.56.55-92):

“Sumedho nāma sambuddho, bāttiṃsavaralakkhaṇo;

Vivekakāmo bhagavā, himavantamupāgami.

“The Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha, possessing the thirty-two excellent marks, desiring seclusion, the Blessed One approached the Himalayas.

“Ajjhogāhetvā himavantaṃ, aggo kāruṇiko muni;

Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāna, nisīdi parisuttamo.

“Having plunged into the Himalayas, the foremost compassionate sage, folding his legs cross-wise, the best among the pure, sat down.

“Vijjādharo tadā āsiṃ, antalikkhacaro ahaṃ;

Tisūlaṃ sugataṃ gayha, gacchāmi ambare tadā.

“Then I was a knowledge-holder, a sky-walker was I; having taken the trident, I went happily through the sky at that time.

“Pabbatagge yathā aggi, puṇṇamāyeva candimā;

Vanaṃ obhāsate buddho, sālarājāva phullito.

“Just as a fire on a mountain peak, or the moon on the full-moon day, the Buddha illuminates the forest, like a blossoming king-sāl tree.

“Vanaggā [M 1.0306] nikkhamitvāna, buddharaṃsībhidhāvare;

Naḷaggivaṇṇasaṅkāsā, disvā cittaṃ pasādayiṃ.

“Having come forth from the treetops, the Buddha's rays were shining, resembling the color of a blazing reed-fire. Having seen them, I gladdened my heart.

“Vicinaṃ addasaṃ pupphaṃ, kaṇikāraṃ devagandhikaṃ;

Tīṇi pupphāni ādāya, buddhaseṭṭhamapūjayiṃ.

“While searching, I saw a Kaṇikāra flower, divinely scented; taking three flowers, I worshipped the supreme Buddha.

“Buddhassa ānubhāvena, tīṇi pupphāni me tadā;

Uddhaṃvaṇṭā adhopattā, chāyaṃ kubbanti satthuno.

“By the Buddha's power, my three flowers then, with stems upward and petals downward, cast a shade for the Teacher.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-performed deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.

“Tattha [V 1.0262] me sukataṃ byamhaṃ, kaṇikārīti ñāyati;

Saṭṭhiyojanamubbedhaṃ, tiṃsayojanavitthataṃ.

“There my well-made celestial palace is known as Kaṇikāra, sixty leagues in height and thirty leagues in breadth.

“Sahassakaṇḍaṃ satabheṇḍu, dhajālu haritāmayaṃ;

Satasahassaniyyūhā, byamhe pātubhaviṃsu me.

“A thousand sections, a hundred globes, banners of green and gold; a hundred thousand pinnacles appeared for me in the palace.

“Soṇṇamayā maṇimayā, lohitaṅkamayāpi ca;

Phalikāpi ca pallaṅkā, yenicchakā yadicchakā.

“Couches of gold, of gems, and also of coral, and crystal couches too, appearing as one desires, as one wishes.

“Mahārahañca sayanaṃ, tūlikā vikatīyutaṃ;

Uddhalomiñca ekantaṃ, bimbohanasamāyutaṃ.

“And a bed of great value, with a mattress of various designs, and an excellent coverlet with fleece on one side, furnished with pillows.

“Bhavanā nikkhamitvāna, caranto devacārikaṃ;

Yathā icchāmi gamanaṃ, devasaṅghapurakkhato.

“Having departed from my mansion, wandering on a divine journey, my going is as I wish, preceded by a host of deities.

“Pupphassa heṭṭhā tiṭṭhāmi, uparicchadanaṃ mama;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, kaṇikārehi chāditaṃ.

I stand beneath a flower, a canopy above me; for a hundred leagues around, it is covered with kaṇikāra blossoms.

“Saṭṭhitūriyasahassāni, sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhahuṃ;

Parivārenti maṃ niccaṃ, rattindivamatanditā.

Sixty thousand musical instruments attended upon me morning and evening. They constantly surrounded me, untiringly, day and night.

“Tattha naccehi gītehi, tāḷehi vāditehi ca;

Ramāmi khiḍḍā ratiyā, modāmi kāmakāmahaṃ.

There, with dances, songs, clapping, and instrumental music, I delight in sport and pleasure; I, a desirer of sensual pleasures, rejoice.

“Tattha bhutvā pivitvā ca, modāmi tidase tadā;

Nārīgaṇehi sahito, modāmi byamhamuttame.

Having eaten and drunk there, I then rejoice among the thirty gods; surrounded by groups of women, I rejoice in my supreme palace.

“Satānaṃ [M 1.0307] pañcakkhattuñca, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Satānaṃ tīṇikkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

Five hundred times I ruled as king of the gods; three hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch; and extensive regional kingship I held an incalculable number of times.

“Bhave bhave saṃsaranto, mahābhogaṃ labhāmahaṃ;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Wandering from existence to existence, I obtain great wealth; there is no lack of wealth for me. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Duve bhave saṃsarāmi, devatte atha mānuse;

Aññaṃ gatiṃ na jānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

I transmigrate in two existences: as a god or as a human. I know no other destination. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Duve kule pajāyāmi, khattiye cāpi brāhmaṇe;

Nīce kule na jānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

I am born into two families: either a noble family or a brahmin family. I do not know a low family. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Hatthiyānaṃ assayānaṃ, sivikaṃ sandamānikaṃ;

Labhāmi sabbamevetaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Elephant vehicles, horse vehicles, and swiftly moving palanquins—all these I obtain. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Dāsīgaṇaṃ dāsagaṇaṃ, nāriyo samalaṅkatā;

Labhāmi sabbamevetaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

A retinue of female slaves, a retinue of male slaves, and women adorned with ornaments—all these I obtain. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Koseyyakambaliyāni[V 1.0263], khomakappāsikāni ca;

Labhāmi sabbamevetaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Silken and woolen garments, and linen and cotton cloths—all these I obtain. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Navavatthaṃ navaphalaṃ, navaggarasabhojanaṃ;

Labhāmi sabbamevetaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

New clothes, new fruits, and food with new, excellent flavors—all these I obtain. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Imaṃ khāda imaṃ bhuñja, imamhi sayane saya;

Labhāmi sabbamevetaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Eat this, enjoy this, lie on this bed”—all this I obtain. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Sabbattha pūjito homi, yaso accuggato mama;

Mahāpakkho sadā homi, abhejjapariso sadā;

Everywhere I am honored, my fame is exceedingly high; I always have a large following, my assembly is always unbreakable.

Ñātīnaṃ uttamo homi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

I am the best among my relatives. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ na jānāmi, pariḷāho na vijjati;

Atho cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ, hadaye me na vijjati.

I know neither cold nor heat; no fever is found in me. Nor is there any mental pain, no suffering in my heart.

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hutvāna, saṃsarāmi bhavābhave;

Vevaṇṇiyaṃ na jānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Having a golden complexion, I transmigrate from existence to existence; I do not know discoloration. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Devalokā [M 1.0308] cavitvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Sāvatthiyaṃ pure jāto, mahāsāle suaḍḍhake.

Having passed away from the heavenly realm, impelled by a root of merit, I was born in the city of Sāvatthī, in a great, very wealthy family.

“Pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ;

Jātiyā sattavassohaṃ, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, I went forth into homelessness. At seven years of age, I attained arahantship.

“Upasampādayī buddho, guṇamaññāya cakkhumā;

Taruṇo pūjanīyohaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

The Buddha, the One with Vision, ordained me, recognizing my qualities. Though young, I am worthy of reverence. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Dibbacakkhu visuddhaṃ me, samādhikusalo ahaṃ;

Abhiññāpāramippatto, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

My divine eye is purified; I am skilled in concentration. I have attained the perfection of direct knowledge. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Paṭisambhidā anuppatto, iddhipādesu kovido;

Dhammesu pāramippatto, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

I have attained the analytical knowledges; I am skilled in the bases of psychic power. I have reached perfection in the Dhammas. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, I venerated the Buddha. I do not know a bad destination. This is the fruit of venerating the Buddha.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Chaḷabhiñño puna hutvā sūlato uṭṭhahitvā parānuddayāya ākāse ṭhatvā pāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Mahājano acchariyabbhutacittajāto ahosi. Tāvadevassa vaṇo saṃrūḷhi, so bhikkhūhi, “āvuso, tādisaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanto kathaṃ tvaṃ vipassanaṃ anuyuñjituṃ asakkhī”ti puṭṭho, “pageva me, āvuso, saṃsāre ādīnavo, saṅkhārānañca sabhāvo sudiṭṭho, evāhaṃ [V 1.0264] tādisaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantopi asakkhiṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā visesaṃ adhigantu”nti dassento –

Having again become one possessing the six direct knowledges, he rose from the stake and, out of compassion for others, stood in the air and displayed a miracle. The great multitude was filled with amazement and wonder. Immediately, his wound healed. When the monks asked him, “Friend, how were you able to apply yourself to insight meditation while experiencing such suffering?” he replied, explaining, “Friends, the danger in saṃsāra and the nature of conditioned things had already been clearly seen by me. Thus, even while experiencing such suffering, I was able to develop insight and attain a special distinction.”

121.

121.

“Natthi koci bhavo nicco, saṅkhārā vāpi sassatā;

Uppajjanti ca te khandhā, cavanti aparāparaṃ.

No existence is permanent, nor are conditioned things eternal. These aggregates arise and pass away again and again.

122.

122.

“Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, bhavenamhi anatthiko;

Nissaṭo sabbakāmehi, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti. –

Having known this danger, I am disinterested in existence. Freed from all sensual pleasures, I have attained the destruction of the taints.

Imaṃ gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha [M 1.0309][P 2.0003] natthi koci bhavo niccoti kammabhavo upapattibhavo kāmabhavo rūpabhavo arūpabhavo saññībhavo asaññībhavo nevasaññīnāsaññībhavo ekavokārabhavo catuvokārabhavo pañcavokārabhavoti evaṃbhedo, tatthāpi hīno majjhimo ukkaṭṭho dīghāyuko sukhabahulo vomissasukhadukkhoti evaṃvibhāgo yokoci nicco dhuvo thiro apalokiyadhammo natthi taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca samuppannattā. Yasmā ca etadevaṃ, tasmā saṅkhārā vāpi sassatā natthīti yojanā. Paccayehi saṅkhatattā “saṅkhārā”ti laddhanāme hi pañcakkhandhe upādāya bhavasamaññāya saṅkhārāva hutvā sambhūtā jarāmaraṇena ca vipariṇamantīti asassatā vipariṇāmadhammā. Tathā hi te “saṅkhārā”ti vuccanti. Tenāha uppajjanti ca te khandhā, cavanti aparāparanti. Te bhavapariyāyena saṅkhārapariyāyena ca vuttā pañcakkhandhā yathāpaccayaṃ aparāparaṃ uppajjanti, uppannā ca jarāya paripīḷitā hutvā cavanti paribhijjantīti attho. Etena “bhavo, saṅkhārā”ti ca laddhavohārā pañcakkhandhā udayabbayasabhāvāti dasseti. Yasmā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasantassa tayopi bhavā ādittaṃ viya saṅkhate ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ pageva vipassanāpaññāya jānitvā aniccalakkhaṇehi diṭṭhā saṅkhārā dukkhānattā vibhūtatarā upaṭṭhahanti, tenāha bhagavā – “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15).

Here, 'no existence is permanent' refers to the existence of kamma, the existence of rebirth, the existence of sensual desire, the existence of form, the formless existence, the percipient existence, the non-percipient existence, the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, the one-constituent existence, the four-constituent existence, and the five-constituent existence—thus differentiated. Even within these distinctions, whether inferior, middling, or superior, long-lived, abundant in pleasure, or mixed with pleasure and pain—none of these is permanent, stable, firm, or not subject to decay, because they arise dependent on their respective causes. Since this is so, the connection is that 'formations are also not eternal.' For the five aggregates, which are conditioned by causes and thus designated as 'formations,' having come into being as formations by way of the designation of existence, are subject to aging and death, and thus are impermanent and subject to change. That is why they are called 'formations.' Hence it is said: 'These aggregates arise and pass away again and again.' The meaning is that these five aggregates, spoken of in terms of existence and formations, arise successively according to conditions, and having arisen, they are oppressed by aging and then pass away, disintegrating. By this, it is shown that the five aggregates, conventionally termed 'existence' and 'formations,' have the nature of arising and ceasing. Because when one contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics, all three existences appear like a burning house, and one has already known the danger and fault in the conditioned by insight-wisdom. When formations are seen with the characteristic of impermanence, suffering and non-self become even more clearly manifest. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self' (SN 3.15).

Yasmā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasantassa tayopi bhavā ādittaṃ viya agāraṃ sappaṭibhayā upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā āha “bhavenamhi anatthiko”ti. Evaṃ pana sabbaso bhavehi vinivattiyamānassa kāmesu apekkhāya lesopi na sambhavatiyeva, tenāha “nissaṭo sabbakāmehī”ti, amhīti yojanā. Mānusehi viya dibbehipi kāmehi nivattitacittosmīti attho. Patto me āsavakkhayoti yasmā evaṃ suparimajjitasaṅkhāro bhavesu suparidiṭṭhādīnavo kāmesu [V 1.0265] ca anāsattamānaso tasmā sūlamatthake nisinnenāpi me mayā patto adhigato [M 1.0310] āsavakkhayo nibbānaṃ arahattañcāti. Aññehi ca sabrahmacārīhi appattamānasehi tadadhigamāya ussāho karaṇīyoti bhikkhūnaṃ ovādamadāsi.

Since for one who reflects on formations by applying the three characteristics, all three existences appear as fearful as a burning house, therefore he said: 'I am disinterested in existence.' Moreover, for one who is being completely turned away from all existences, not even the slightest trace of longing for sensual pleasures can arise. Hence it is said: 'I am freed from all sensual pleasures,' which is to be connected with 'amhi.' The meaning is: 'I have turned my mind away from sensual pleasures, whether human or divine.' 'Attained is the destruction of the taints' means that because he had thus thoroughly cleansed the formations, clearly seen the danger in existences, and had a mind unattached to sensual pleasures, therefore, even while sitting on the tip of a stake, the destruction of the taints—Nibbāna and arahantship—was attained by him. And since other fellow practitioners, with minds not yet attained, should make effort for its attainment, he thus gave advice to the monks.

Uttarattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara is completed.

2. Piṇḍolabhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja

Nayidaṃ [P 2.0004] anayenātiādikā āyasmato piṇḍolabhāradvājattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle sīhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā pabbataguhāyaṃ viharati. Bhagavā tassa anuggahaṃ kātuṃ gocarāya pakkantakāle sayanaguhaṃ pavisitvā nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Sīho gocaraṃ gahetvā nivatto guhādvāre bhagavantaṃ disvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho jalajathalajapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā cittaṃ pasādento bhagavato ārakkhatthāya araññe vāḷamige apanetuṃ tīsu velāsu sīhanādaṃ nadanto buddhagatāya satiyā aṭṭhāsi. Yathā paṭhamadivasaṃ, evaṃ sattāhaṃ pūjesi. Bhagavā sattāhaccayena nirodhā vuṭṭhahitvā “vattissati imassa ettako upanissayo”ti tassa passantasseva ākāsaṃ pakkhanditvā vihārameva gato. Sīho pālileyyakahatthī viya buddhaviyogadukkhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto kālaṃ katvā haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule nibbattitvā vayappatto nagaravāsīhi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle kosambiyaṃ rañño utenassa purohitaputto hutvā nibbatti bhāradvājo nāma nāmena. So vayappatto tayo vede uggahetvā pañca māṇavakasatāni mante vācento mahagghasabhāvena ananurūpācārattā tehi pariccajjanto rājagahaṃ gantvā bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca lābhasakkāraṃ disvā sāsane pabbajitvā bhojane amattaññū hutvā vicaranto satthārā upāyena [M 1.0311] mattaññutāya patiṭṭhāpito vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.104-109) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, beginning with “Nayidaṃ anayena.” What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born as a lion and dwelt in a mountain cave. The Blessed One, wishing to bestow his grace upon him, entered his sleeping cave while he was away foraging, attained cessation, and sat there. The lion, returning from foraging, saw the Blessed One at the cave entrance and, filled with joy and delight, worshipped him with water-born and land-born flowers. With a serene mind, he stood guard to protect the Blessed One from wild beasts in the forest, roaring a lion’s roar three times a day, with his mindfulness directed towards the Buddha. Just as on the first day, so he worshipped for seven days. After seven days, the Blessed One emerged from cessation and, thinking, “This will be sufficient basis for his future attainment,” rose into the sky right before the lion’s eyes and returned to the monastery. Unable to endure the sorrow of separation from the Buddha, like the elephant Pālileyyaka, the lion died and was reborn in a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When he came of age, he went to the monastery with the townspeople, listened to the Dhamma discourse, and held a great almsgiving for seven days. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and, wandering through successive existences among devas and humans, in the time of our Blessed One, he was born in Kosambī as Bhāradvāja, the son of King Udena’s chaplain. When he came of age, he mastered the three Vedas and taught mantras to five hundred young brahmins. Due to his expensive habits and inappropriate conduct, they abandoned him. He went to Rājagaha and, seeing the gains and honor received by the Blessed One and the monastic community, he went forth into the teaching. Being immoderate in food, he wandered about until the Teacher skillfully established him in moderation. He then developed insight and soon became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna: (Apadāna, Thera 2.50.104-109)

“Migaluddo pure āsiṃ, vipine vicaraṃ tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ.

“Once, I was a deer hunter, roaming in the wilds then. I saw the stainless Buddha, the one gone beyond all phenomena.”

“Piyālaphalamādāya, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Puññakkhettassa vīrassa, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

“Taking a piyāla fruit, I gave it to the supreme Buddha, the hero, the field of merit. With my own hands, with a serene mind.”

“Ekatiṃse [V 1.0266] ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from now, when I gave that fruit then; I have not known a bad destination, this is the fruit of that fruit-offering.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā “bhagavato sammukhā yaṃ sāvakehi pattabbaṃ, taṃ mayā patta”nti, bhikkhusaṅghe ca “yassa magge vā phale vā kaṅkhā atthi, so maṃ pucchatū”ti sīhanādaṃ nadi. Tena taṃ bhagavā, “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīhanādikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolabhāradvājo”ti (a. ni. 1.188, 195) etadagge ṭhapesi. So [P 2.0005] ekadivasaṃ attano santikaṃ upagataṃ gihikāle sahāyabhūtaṃ macchariṃ micchādiṭṭhibrāhmaṇaṃ anukampamāno tassa dānakathaṃ kathetvā tena ca “ayaṃ mama dhanaṃ vināsetukāmo”ti bhakuṭiṃ katvāpi “tuyhaṃ ekabhattaṃ demī”ti vutte, “taṃ saṅghassa dehi mā mayha”nti saṅghassa pariṇāmesi. Puna brāhmaṇena “ayaṃ maṃ bahūnaṃ dāpetukāmo”ti appaccaye pakāsite dutiyadivasaṃ dhammasenāpatinā saṅghagatāya dakkhiṇāya mahapphalabhāvappakāsanena taṃ pasādetvā, “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo ‘āhāragedhena maṃ dāne nīyojesī’ti maññati, āhārassa pana mayā sabbaso pariññātabhāvaṃ na jānāti, handa naṃ jānāpemī”ti –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, he declared, “Whatever can be attained by the disciples in the presence of the Blessed One, that I have attained.” And to the community of monks, he roared the lion’s roar: “Let anyone who has doubts about the path or the fruit question me.” Because of this, the Blessed One placed him foremost among his monk disciples who roar the lion’s roar, saying, “Monks, this Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja is the foremost among my monk disciples who roar the lion’s roar.” One day, out of compassion for a stingy brahmin with wrong views, who had been a friend in his householder life and had approached him, he spoke to him about giving. Though the brahmin frowned, thinking, “This man wants to destroy my wealth,” when he said, “I will give you one meal,” Piṇḍola replied, “Give it to the Sangha, not to me,” and thus redirected it to the Sangha. Again, when the brahmin showed displeasure, thinking, “This man wants me to give to many,” on the next day, the General of the Dhamma pleased him by explaining the great fruitfulness of a donation given to the Sangha. Piṇḍola reflected: “This brahmin thinks, ‘He induces me to give out of greed for food,’ but he does not know that I have fully understood the nature of food. Come, let me make him understand.”

123.

123.

“Nayidaṃ anayena jīvitaṃ, nāhāro hadayassa santiko;

Āhāraṭṭhitiko samussayo, iti disvāna carāmi esanaṃ.

“This life is not by wrong means, nor is food a solace to the heart; this aggregate is sustained by food—seeing this, I wander seeking alms.”

124.

124.

“Paṅkoti [M 1.0312] hi naṃ avedayuṃ, yāyaṃ vandanapūjanā kulesu;

Sukhumaṃ sallaṃ durubbahaṃ, sakkāro kāpurisena dujjaho”ti. –

“Indeed, they declared it to be a mire, this homage and veneration in families; a subtle dart, hard to extract, honor is hard for a base person to abandon.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tattha nayidaṃ anayena jīvitanti idaṃ mama jīvitaṃ anayena añāyena veḷudānapupphadānādianesanāya na hoti jīvitanikantiyā abhāvato. Nāhāro hadayassa santikoti āhāro ca āhariyamāno maggaphalañāṇaṃ viya hadayassa cittassa santikaro na hoti, kevalaṃ pana sajjukaṃ khudāpaṭighātamattaṃ karotīti adhippāyo. Atha vā nāhāro hadayassa santikoti āhāro rasataṇhāvatthu me hadayassa santiko āsatto na hoti rasataṇhāya eva abhāvato. “Santike”tipi paṭhanti. Yo hi āhāragiddho lābhasakkārappasuto vicarati, tassa āhāro hadayassa santike nāma abhiṇhaṃ manasikātabbato. Yo pana pariññātāhāro, so tattha pahīnacchandarāgo, na tassāhāro hadayassa [V 1.0267] santike nāma – “kathaṃ nu kho labheyya”ntiādimanasikaraṇasseva abhāvato. Yadi hi jīvitanikanti āhārarasataṇhā ca natthi, atha kasmā piṇḍāya carasīti anuyogaṃ manasi katvā āha “āhāraṭṭhitiko samussayo, iti disvāna carāmi esana”nti. Āhāro bhojanaṃ ṭhiti ṭhānaṃ paccayo etassāti āhāraṭṭhitiko. “Āhārapaṭibaddhavuttiko samussayo kāyo”iti disvāna evaṃ ñatvā imamatthaṃ buddhiyaṃ [P 2.0006] ṭhapetvā carāmi esanaṃ, bhikkhāpariyesanaṃ karomīti attho.

Here, “this life is not by wrong means” means that my life is not sustained by wrong means, by improper means, such as seeking offerings of bamboo, flowers, etc., because there is no clinging to life. “Nor is food a solace to the heart” means that food, even when consumed, does not bring solace to the heart, to the mind, like the knowledge of the path and fruition does. It merely serves to temporarily relieve hunger—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, “nor is food a solace to the heart” means that food, being the basis of craving for taste, is not attached to my heart because there is no craving for taste. Some also read “santike” (near). For one who is greedy for food and obsessed with gain and honor, food is indeed always near the heart, as it is constantly to be kept in mind. But for one who has fully understood food, and has abandoned desire and lust for it, food is not near the heart—because there is no such thought as, “How can I obtain it?” If there is no clinging to life or craving for the taste of food, then why do you go for alms? Reflecting on this question, he says: “This aggregate is sustained by food; seeing this, I wander seeking alms.” “This aggregate is sustained by food” means that food is the condition for its existence and sustenance. Having understood this truth—that “this body, this aggregate, is dependent on food for its sustenance”—and established it in my wisdom, I wander seeking alms.

Paccayanimittaṃ kulāni upasaṅkamanto tattha vandanapūjanāhi lābhasakkārehi ca bajjhatīti evaṃ mādisesu na cintetabbanti dassento “paṅko”tigāthaṃ abhāsi. Tassattho – yā ayaṃ paccayanimittaṃ upagatānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ kulesu gehavāsīsu pavattissati guṇasambhāvanā pūjanā ca, yasmā taṃ abhāvitattānaṃ osīdāpanaṭṭhena malīnabhāvakaraṇena ca paṅko kaddamoti buddhādayo avedayuṃ abbhaññāsuṃ pavedesuṃ vā, tasmā sā sappurisānaṃ [M 1.0313] bandhāya na hoti sakkārāsāya pageva pahīnattā. Asappurisassa pana sakkārāsā duviññeyyasabhāvatāya pīḷājananato anto tudanato uddharituṃ asakkuṇeyyato ca sukhumaṃ sallaṃ durubbahaṃ. Tato eva tena sakkāro kāpurisena dujjaho durubbaheyyo tassa pahānapaṭipattiyā appaṭipajjanato, sakkārāsāpahānena pahīno hotīti. Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo there abhippasanno ahosi.

Showing that the thought, ‘Approaching families for the sake of requisites, one becomes bound by their veneration, honor, and material gains,’ should not be entertained in regard to those like him, he recited the verse beginning “Paṅko.” Its meaning is this: The esteem and veneration that will arise among householders in families for those gone forth who approach them for the sake of requisites—since the Buddhas and others declared this to be a mire, a mud, because it causes the uncultivated to sink and creates a state of impurity, it is therefore not a bond for virtuous people, as the craving for honor has already been abandoned. But for an unvirtuous person, the craving for honor, due to its nature that is difficult to know, is a subtle dart, hard to bear, because it is a source of oppression, pricks within, and is difficult to pull out. Therefore, honor is hard to abandon and hard to bear for that inferior person, because he does not undertake the practice for its abandonment. It is abandoned by abandoning the craving for honor. Hearing this, the brahmin became deeply devoted to the elder.

Piṇḍolabhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja is completed.

3. Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Valliya

Makkaṭo pañcadvārāyantiādikā āyasmato valliyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena araññaṃ gato tattha nāradaṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ rukkhamūle vasantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso naḷehi sālaṃ katvā tiṇehi chādetvā adāsi. Caṅkamanaṭṭhānañcassa sodhetvā vālukā okiritvā adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā nibbatti, valliyotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto yobbanamanuppatto indriyavasiko hutvā vicaranto kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā [V 1.0268] vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.93-103) –

The verses beginning with 'The monkey at the five gates...' are those of the Venerable Valliya Thera. What is their origin? He too, having established a basis of merit in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family in the thirty-first aeon from now. There, having attained maturity, one day he went into the forest for some business. Seeing the Paccekabuddha named Nārada dwelling at the foot of a tree, his mind became joyful. He made a hall with reeds, covered it with grass, and offered it. He also cleaned his walking path, scattered sand, and gave it. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a great brahmin family in Sāvatthī, named Valliyotissa. Coming of age and reaching his youth, while living under the sway of his senses, through association with good friends, he approached the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma, acquired faith, and went forth. Establishing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.50.93-103)—

“Himavantassāvidūre, hārito nāma pabbato;

Sayambhū nārado nāma, rukkhamūle vasī tadā.

“Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Hārita; the Self-Awakened One, Nārada by name, dwelt at the foot of a tree at that time.”

“Naḷāgāraṃ karitvāna, tiṇena chādayiṃ ahaṃ;

Caṅkamaṃ sodhayitvāna, sayambhussa adāsahaṃ.

“Having built a hut of reeds, I covered it with grass; having cleaned the promenade, I gave it to the Self-Awakened One.”

“Tena [M 1.0314] kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.”

“Tattha me sukataṃ byamhaṃ, naḷakuṭikanimmitaṃ;

Saṭṭhiyojanamubbedhaṃ, tiṃsayojanavitthataṃ.

“There a well-made celestial mansion arose for me, created from the reed hut, sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in breadth.”

“Catuddasesu kappesu, devaloke ramiṃ ahaṃ;

Ekasattatikkhattuñca, devarajjamakārayiṃ.

“For fourteen aeons I rejoiced in the heavenly world; seventy-one times I ruled as a divine king.”

“Catuttiṃsatikkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

“Thirty-four times I was a wheel-turning monarch, and my regional kingships were vast and innumerable.”

“Dhammapāsādamāruyha, sabbākāravarūpamaṃ;

Yadicchakāhaṃ vihare, sakyaputtassa sāsane.

“Having ascended the palace of Dhamma, endowed with all excellent qualities, I dwell as I wish in the dispensation of the son of the Sakyans.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, naḷakuṭiyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago, when I performed that deed, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the reed hut.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [P 2.0007] pana patvā puthujjanakāle attano cittassa rūpādiārammaṇesu yathākāmappavattiyā, idāni ariyamaggena niggahitabhāvassa ca vibhāvanena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, however, he declared his final knowledge by way of explaining the tendency of his own mind to proceed as it pleased among objects such as forms when he was an ordinary person, and its state of being restrained now by the Noble Path:

125.

125.

“Makkaṭo pañcadvārāyaṃ, kuṭikāyaṃ pasakkiya;

Dvārena anupariyeti, ghaṭṭayanto muhuṃ muhuṃ.

“A monkey, attached to this five-gated hut, circles around from door to door, striking them again and again.”

126.

126.

“Tiṭṭha makkaṭa mā dhāvi, na hi te taṃ yathā pure;

Niggahītosi paññāya, neva dūraṃ gamissasī”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Stop, monkey, do not run! It is not for you as it was before. You are restrained by wisdom; you will not go far.” – He spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha [V 1.0269] ghaṭṭayantoti attano lolabhāvena rukkhassa aññaṃ sākhaṃ muñcitvā aññassa gahaṇena anekavāraṃ tattha rukkhaṃ cālento phalūpabhogamakkaṭo viya tena tena cakkhādidvārena rūpādiārammaṇesu aññaṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ gaṇhanto cittasantānassa samādānavasena niccalaṃ ṭhātuṃ [M 1.0315] appadānena abhikkhaṇaṃ ghaṭṭayanto cālento tasmiṃyeva rūpādiārammaṇe anuparivattati yathākāmaṃ vicarati. Vattamānasamīpatāya cettha vattamānavacanaṃ. Evaṃ anupariyanto ca tiṭṭha, makkaṭa, mā dhāvi tvaṃ, cittamakkaṭa, idāni tiṭṭha mā dhāvi, ito paṭṭhāya te dhāvituṃ na sakkā, tasmā na hi te taṃ yathā pūre yasmā taṃ attabhāvagehaṃ pubbe viya na te sevitaṃ pihitadvārabhāvato, kiñca niggahītosi paññāya sayañca idāni maggapaññāya kilesābhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātānaṃ pādānaṃ chedanena accantikaṃ niggahaṃ pattosi, tasmā neva dūraṃ gamissasi ito attabhāvato dūraṃ dutiyādiattabhāvaṃ neva gamissasi yāvacarimakacittaṃ eva te gamananti dasseti. “Neto dūra”ntipi pāṭho, so evattho.

Therein, 'striking' means: like a monkey enjoying fruit, which, due to its restlessness, releases one branch of a tree and grasps another, repeatedly shaking the tree; similarly, this mind, through the doors of the eye and so on, releases one sense-object such as form and grasps another. By not allowing the mental continuum to remain still through restraint, it constantly strikes and shakes it, revolving around that very sense-object, wandering as it pleases. The present tense is used here to indicate imminence. Thus, being admonished, it means: 'Stop, monkey, do not run! You, mind-monkey, stop now, do not run! From now on you cannot run. Therefore, it is not for you as it was before, because that house which is the self-state is not to be frequented by you as before, since its doors are closed. Moreover, you are restrained by wisdom. Now, through the wisdom of the path, by cutting off the feet called 'formations of defilements,' you have attained ultimate restraint. Therefore, you will not go far; from this self-state you will not go far to a second self-state and so on. Your journey is only up to the final consciousness.' This is what is shown. There is also the reading 'neto dūraṃ,' which has the same meaning.

Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Valliya is concluded.

4. Gaṅgātīriyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gaṅgātīriya

Tiṇṇaṃ me tālapattānantiādikā āyasmato gaṅgātīriyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto sāsane abhippasanno hutvā bhikkhusaṅghassa pānīyamadāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa gahapatissa putto hutvā nibbatti, “datto”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So [P 2.0008] vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto agamanīyaṭṭhānabhāvaṃ ajānitvā vītikkamaṃ katvā puna agamanīyaṭṭhānabhāvaṃ ñatvā saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā taṃ kammaṃ jigucchitvā lūkhapaṭipattiṃ anutiṭṭhanto paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ chavasittasadisaṃ mattikāpattañca gahetvā gaṅgātīre tīhi tālapattehi kuṭikaṃ katvā vihāsi, tenevassa gaṅgātīriyoti samaññā ahosi. So “arahattaṃ appatvā na kenaci sallapissāmī”ti cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāya paṭhamaṃ saṃvaccharaṃ tuṇhībhūto vacībhedaṃ akarontova vihāsi. Dutiye saṃvacchare gocaragāme aññatarāya itthiyā “mūgo nu kho no”ti vīmaṃsitukāmāya patte khīraṃ āsiñcantiyā [M 1.0316] hatthavihāre katepi okirite, “alaṃ, bhaginī”ti vācaṃ nicchari. Tatiye pana saṃvacchare antaravasseva ghaṭayanto vāyamanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.51-56) –

The verses beginning with 'Tiṇṇaṃ me tālapattānaṃ' are those of the Venerable Gaṅgātīriya. What is their origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in a good family, and having attained understanding, he became deeply devoted to the Dispensation and offered drinking water to the community of monks. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. After repeatedly performing meritorious deeds and wandering between the deva and human realms, in this Buddha-era he was born as the son of a certain householder in Sāvatthī. His name was Datta. Having come of age, while living the household life, he unknowingly transgressed by going to an improper place. Later, realizing it was an improper place, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. He went forth and, disgusted by that action, he undertook austere practices. Taking up a rag-robe like a shroud and a clay bowl, he built a hut with three palm leaves on the bank of the Ganges and dwelt there. For that reason, his designation became 'Gaṅgātīriya.' Resolving, 'I will not speak with anyone until I attain arahantship,' for the first year he remained silent, not breaking his speech. In the second year, in a village where he went for alms, a certain woman, wishing to test, 'Is he mute or not?', poured milk into his bowl. Even when it was spilled due to a movement of her hand, he uttered the words, 'Enough, sister.' Then, in the third year, striving and making an effort during the rains-retreat itself, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.50.51-56):

“Padumuttarabuddhassa[V 1.0270], bhikkhusaṅghe anuttare;

Pasannacitto sumano, pānīghaṭamapūrayiṃ.

“For the unsurpassed community of monks of the Buddha Padumuttara, with a confident and joyful mind, I filled a water pot.”

“Pabbatagge dumagge vā, ākāse vātha bhūmiyaṃ;

Yadā pānīyamicchāmi, khippaṃ nibbattate mama.

“Whether on a mountain peak, in the treetops, in the sky, or on the ground—whenever I desire drinking water, it swiftly arises for me.”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dakadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the hundred-thousandth aeon from now, when I gave that gift, I have known no bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the gift of water.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahā pana hutvā attano pubbabhāgapaṭipattiyā vibhāvanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having become an Arahant, however, he declared his final knowledge by way of explaining his own preliminary practice:

127.

127.

“Tiṇṇaṃ me tālapattānaṃ, gaṅgātīre kuṭī katā;

Chavasittova me patto, paṃsukūlañca cīvaraṃ.

“My hut on the bank of the Ganges was made of three palm leaves; my bowl was like a shroud, and my robe was a rag-robe.”

128.

128.

“Dvinnaṃ antaravassānaṃ, ekā vācā me bhāsitā;

Tatiye antaravassamhi, tamokhandho padālito”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“During two rains-retreats, only one utterance was spoken by me; in the third rains-retreat, the mass of darkness was rent asunder.” – He spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha tiṇṇaṃ me tālapattānaṃ, gaṅgātīre kuṭī katāti tālarukkhato pahitehi tīhi tālapaṇṇehi mayhaṃ vassanapariharaṇatthaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre kuṭikā katā. Tena attano senāsanasantosaṃ dasseti. Vuttañhi dhammasenāpatinā –

Therein, 'My hut on the bank of the Ganges was made of three palm leaves' means: a small hut was made for me on the bank of the river Ganges with three palm leaves taken from a palm tree, for the purpose of keeping off the rain. By this, he shows his contentment with his dwelling. For it was said by the General of the Dhamma:

“Pallaṅkena nisinnassa, jaṇṇuke nābhivassati;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 985; mi. pa. 6.1.1);

“For one seated cross-legged, the rain does not fall upon the knees; this is sufficient for a pleasant abiding for a monk with a resolute mind.”

“Tālapattīna”ntipi pāṭho, so evattho. Chavasittova me pattoti mayhaṃ patto chavasittasadiso, matānaṃ khīrasecanakuṇḍasadisoti attho[M 1.0317]. Paṃsukūlañca cīvaranti cīvarañca me antaramaggasusānādīsu chaḍḍitanantakehi kataṃ paṃsukūlaṃ. Padadvayena parikkhārasantosaṃ dasseti.

“Tālapattīna” is also a reading, with the same meaning. ‘My bowl is like a corpse-vessel’ means my bowl is similar to a corpse-vessel, that is, like a milk-pouring vessel for the dead—this is the meaning. ‘And my robe is a rag-robe’ means my robe is a rag-robe made from innumerable discarded cloths from places like roadsides and cemeteries. With these two phrases, he shows his contentment with the requisites.

Dvinnaṃ [P 2.0009] antaravassānanti dvīsu antaravassesu pabbajitato arahattamappattasaṃvaccharesu. Ekā vācā me bhāsitāti ekā, “alaṃ, bhaginī”ti khīrapaṭikkhepavācā eva mayā vuttā, añño tattha vacībhedo nāhosi. Tena ukkaṃsagataṃ kāyavacīsaṃyamaṃ dasseti. Tatiye antaravassamhīti [V 1.0271] tatiyassa saṃvaccharassa abbhantare, tasmiṃ aparipuṇṇeyeva. Tamokhandho padālitoti aggamaggena tamokhandho bhinno, avijjānusayo samucchinnoti attho. Tena tadekaṭṭhatāya sabbakilesānaṃ anavasesappahānaṃ vadati.

‘Between two rainy seasons’ means in the two intervening years after going forth, the years before attaining arahantship. ‘A single word was spoken by me’ means one word, “Enough, sister,” the word refusing milk, was spoken by me; there was no other kind of speech there. By this, he shows the exalted restraint of body and speech. ‘In the third intervening year’ means within the third year, while it was still incomplete. ‘The mass of darkness was split’ means the mass of darkness was broken by the highest path, meaning the underlying tendency of ignorance was eradicated. By this, due to its single meaning, he declares the abandonment of all defilements without remainder.

Gaṅgātīriyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gaṅgātīriya is concluded.

5. Ajinattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajina

Api ce hoti tevijjotiādikā āyasmato ajinattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto buddhasuññe loke kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kenacideva karaṇīyena araññaṃ gato tattha sucintitaṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ ābādhena pīḷitaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā bhesajjatthāya pasannamānaso ghatamaṇḍaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa daliddabrāhmaṇassa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ vijāyanakāle ajinacammena sampaṭicchiṃsu. Tenassa ajinotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So bhogasaṃvattaniyassa kammassa akatattā daliddakule nibbatto vayappattopi appannapānabhojano hutvā vicaranto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.43.78-87) –

The verses of the Venerable Elder Ajina begin with ‘Even if one is a master of the threefold knowledge’ (Api ce hoti tevijjo). What is their origin? This venerable one too, having made aspirations under past Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences. Born into a family home in a world empty of Buddhas, he attained maturity and went to the forest for some task. There, he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sucintita, afflicted by illness and sitting. Approaching, he paid homage and, with a devoted mind, gave him cream of ghee for medicine. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm. Again and again, he performed meritorious deeds, wandering only in happy destinies. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he took rebirth in the home of a poor brahmin in Sāvatthī. At his birth, they received him with a deer hide, so they named him Ajina. Due to not having done deeds leading to prosperity, he was born into a poor family. Even when grown, he wandered with little food and drink. Seeing the Buddha’s majesty at the acceptance of Jetavana, he gained faith and went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he soon became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.43.78-87):

“Sucintitaṃ [M 1.0318] bhagavantaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Upaviṭṭhaṃ mahāraññaṃ, vātābādhena pīḷitaṃ.

“The Blessed One Sucintita, the world’s foremost, the bull of men, sitting in the great forest, afflicted by a wind-related illness.

“Disvā cittaṃ pasādetvā, ghatamaṇḍamupānayiṃ;

Katattā ācitattā ca, gaṅgā bhāgīrathī ayaṃ.

“Having seen him, and with a gladdened mind, I offered cream of ghee. Through this deed having been done and accumulated, this Ganges, the Bhāgīrathī,

“Mahāsamuddā cattāro, ghataṃ sampajjare mama;

Ayañca pathavī ghorā, appamāṇā asaṅkhiyā.

“The four great oceans become ghee for me; and this fearsome earth, immeasurable, countless,

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, bhavate madhusakkarā;

Cātuddīpā ime rukkhā, pādapā dharaṇīruhā.

“Knowing my intention, becomes honey and sugar; these trees of the four continents, trees, those grown from the earth,

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, kapparukkhā bhavanti te;

Paññāsakkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ.

“Knowing my intention, they become wish-fulfilling trees. Fifty times as king of devas, I reigned in the deva realm.

“Ekapaññāsakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

“Fifty-one times I was a wheel-turning monarch; and regional kingship was extensive, countless in number.

“Catunnavutito [V 1.0272] kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, ghatamaṇḍassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, when I gave that gift, I do not recall any bad rebirth: this is the fruit of the cream of ghee.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvāpi purimakammanissandena appalābhī appaññātova ahosi. Uddesabhattasalākabhattānipi lāmakāneva pāpuṇanti. Kammaphaleneva ca naṃ puthujjanā bhikkhū sāmaṇerā ca “appaññāto”ti avamaññanti. Thero te bhikkhū saṃvejento –

Even after attaining Arahantship, however, due to the result of his past kamma, he remained of little gain and little renown. He received only the poorest designated meals and ticket-meals. And because of the fruit of his kamma, ordinary monks and novices despised him, saying, “He is unrenowned.” The Elder, wishing to stir those monks, said:

129.

129.

“Api ce hoti tevijjo, maccuhāyī anāsavo;

Appaññātoti naṃ bālā, avajānanti ajānatā.

“Even if one is endowed with the threefold knowledge, one who has abandoned death, taintless, fools, not knowing, despise him as ‘unrenowned’.

130.

130.

“Yo [M 1.0319][P 2.0010] ca kho annapānassa, lābhī hotīdha puggalo;

Pāpadhammopi ce hoti, so nesaṃ hoti sakkato”ti. –

“But whatever person here obtains food and drink, even if he is of evil nature, is respected by them.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tattha apīti sambhāvane nipāto. Ceti parikappane. Hotīti bhavati. Tisso vijjā etassāti tevijjo. Maccuṃ pajahatīti maccuhāyī. Kāmāsavādīnaṃ abhāvena anāsavo.
