Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇanti imāsaṃ tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ adhigatattā tevijjo tato eva sabbaso kāmāsavādīnaṃ parikkhīṇattā anāsavo āyatiṃ punabbhavassa aggahaṇato maraṇābhāvena maccuhāyī yadipi hoti, evaṃ santepi appaññātoti naṃ bālā avajānanti yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti, taṃ sadatthaṃ anupāpuṇitvā ṭhitampi naṃ uttamaṃ purisaṃ “dhutavādo bahussuto dhammakathiko”ti uppannalābhassa abhāvato “na paññāto na pākaṭo”ti bālā dummedhapuggalā avajānanti, kasmā? Ajānatā ajānanakāraṇā guṇānaṃ ajānanameva tattha kāraṇanti dasseti.

Herein, ‘api’ is a particle indicating possibility. ‘Ce’ signifies supposition. ‘Hoti’ means ‘becomes.’ ‘He has three knowledges’—thus, he is ‘one with the threefold knowledge.’ ‘He leaves death behind’—thus, he is ‘one who has abandoned death.’ Through the absence of the taints of sensual desire and so on, he is ‘taintless.’ This is what is meant: because he has attained these three knowledges—the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—he is ‘one with the threefold knowledge.’ For that very reason, because all the taints of sensual desire and so on are completely exhausted, he is ‘taintless.’ Because he does not grasp a future existence, through the absence of death, he is ‘one who has abandoned death.’ Even though he is such a person, fools despise him as ‘unrenowned.’ Although he is a supreme person who has attained and abides in that true goal for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, foolish, dull-witted individuals despise him. Because he has no material gain, which is associated with being a proponent of ascetic practices, a learned person, or a preacher of the Dhamma, they say, “He is not known, not famous.” Why? Due to not knowing. This shows that the reason is simply ignorance of his qualities.

Yathā ca guṇānaṃ ajānanato bālā lābhagarutāya sambhāvanīyampi avajānanti, evaṃ guṇānaṃ ajānanato lābhagarutāya evaṃ avajānitabbampi sambhāventīti dassento dutiyaṃ gāthaṃ āha. Tattha yoti aniyamavacanaṃ. Ca-saddo byatireke, tena yathāvuttapuggalato imassa puggalassa vuccamānaṃyeva visesaṃ janeti. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Annapānassāti nidassanamattaṃ. Lābhīti lābhavā. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Jarāmaraṇehi tassa tassa sattāvāsassa pūraṇato galanato [V 1.0273] ca puggalo. Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo. Ayañhettha attho – yo pana puggalo cīvarādipaccayamattasseva lābhī hoti, na jhānādīnaṃ, so pāpicchatāya dussīlabhāvena hīnadhammopi samāno idha imasmiṃ loke bālānaṃ lābhagarutāya sakkato garukato hotīti.

To show that just as fools, from not knowing qualities and from esteeming gain, despise one who should be respected, so too, from not knowing qualities and from esteeming gain, they respect one who should be despised, he spoke the second verse. Here, ‘yo’ is an indefinite word. The particle ‘ca’ indicates contrast; thereby it generates a specific distinction for this person being spoken of from the person mentioned before. ‘Kho’ is for emphasis. ‘Annapānassa’ is merely illustrative. ‘Lābhī’ means one with gain. ‘Idha’ means in this world. Because he fills up and falls away from this and that abode of beings through old age and death, he is a ‘puggalo’ (person). ‘Pāpadhammo’ means one of inferior nature. This is the meaning here: But that person who is an obtainer merely of requisites such as robes, and not of attainments such as jhāna, although being of inferior nature due to evil wishes and immorality, is honored and respected here in this world by fools due to their esteem for gain.

Ajinattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ajina is concluded.

6. Meḷajinattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Meḷajina

Yadāhaṃ [M 1.0320] dhammamassosintiādikā āyasmato meḷajinattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ [P 2.0011] patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso madhuraṃ āmodaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bārāṇasiyaṃ khattiyakule nibbattitvā meḷajinoti laddhanāmo vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato paṇḍito byatto disāsu pākaṭo ahosi. So bhagavati bārāṇasiyaṃ isipatane viharante vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā tadaheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.57-62) –

The verses of the Venerable Elder Meḷajina begin with, 'When I heard the Dhamma.' What is their origin? He too, having made aspirations in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulated merit here and there in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he was born into a respectable family and, having reached maturity, one day saw the Blessed One going for alms. With a joyful mind, he offered a sweet and fragrant fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among the deva and human realms. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a khattiya family in Bārāṇasī and was named Meḷajina. He became accomplished in arts and crafts, learned and articulate, and renowned in all directions. When the Blessed One was dwelling at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, he went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. He went forth, established insight meditation, and attained arahantship that very day. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 2.51.57-62):

“Sahassaraṃsī bhagavā, sayambhū aparājito;

Vivekā vuṭṭhahitvāna, gocarāyābhinikkhami.

“The Blessed One, with a thousand rays, the Self-existent, the Unconquered, having arisen from solitude, went forth for his alms round.”

“Phalahattho ahaṃ disvā, upagacchiṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, avaṭaṃ adadiṃ phalaṃ.

“With fruit in hand, I saw and approached the noblest of men; with a serene and glad mind, I offered the choice fruit.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving a fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aparabhāge bhikkhūhi, “āvuso, kiṃ tayā uttarimanussadhammo adhigato”ti puṭṭho sīhanādaṃ nadanto –

Having attained arahantship, later, when asked by the bhikkhus, “Friend, have you attained any superhuman state?” he roared a lion’s roar:

131.

131.

“Yadāhaṃ [V 1.0274] dhammamassosiṃ, bhāsamānassa satthuno;

Na kaṅkhamabhijānāmi, sabbaññū aparājite.

“When I heard the Dhamma as it was spoken by the Teacher, the All-Knowing, the Unconquered, I recognized no doubt.”

132.

132.

“Satthavāhe mahāvīre, sārathīnaṃ varuttame;

Magge paṭipadāyaṃ vā, kaṅkhā mayhaṃ na vijjatī”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Regarding the caravan leader, the great hero, the best of guides, or regarding the path and the practice, no doubt exists in me.” —he spoke these two verses.

Tattha [M 1.0321] yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati. Dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ. Assosinti suṇiṃ. Satthunoti diṭṭhadhammikādiatthehi veneyyānaṃ sāsanaṭṭhena satthuno. Kaṅkhanti saṃsayaṃ. Saṅkhatamasaṅkhatañca anavasesato jānanaṭṭhena sabbaññū. Kutocipi parājitā bhāvena aparājite. Veneyyasattānaṃ saṃsārakantārato nibbānaṃ paṭivāhanaṭṭhena satthavāhe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yato pabhuti ahaṃ satthuno dhammaṃ desentassa catusaccadhammaṃ assosiṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhāresiṃ upalabhiṃ, tato paṭṭhāya anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutidhammānaṃ sayambhūñāṇena jānanato sabbaññū anāvaraṇadassāvimhi, pañcannampi mārānaṃ abhibhavanato tehi aparājitattā sadevake loke appaṭihatadhammacakkattā ca aparājite, veneyyasattānaṃ lobhakantārādito vāhanaṭṭhena satthavāhe, mahāvikkantatāya mahāvīre, aññehi duddamānaṃ purisadammānaṃ saraṇato accantikena damathena damanato sārathīnaṃ pavarabhūte uttame sammāsambuddhe[P 2.0012], “buddho nu kho no nu kho”ti kaṅkhaṃ nābhijānāmi aparappaccayabhāvato. Tathārūpe desite ariyamagge tadupādāyabhūtāya ca sīlādipaṭipadāya “niyyāniko nu kho na nu kho”ti kaṅkhā vicikicchā na vijjati natthīti. Ettha ca ariyadhamme saṃsayābhāvakathanena ariyasaṅghepi saṃsayābhāvo kathitoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ tattha patiṭṭhitassa anaññathābhāvatoti.

Herein, ‘when’ (yadā) means at which time. ‘I’ (ahaṃ) indicates oneself. ‘Dhamma’ (dhammaṃ) means the four-truth Dhamma. ‘Heard’ (assosiṃ) means I listened. ‘Of the Teacher’ (satthuno) refers to the Teacher in the sense of instructing those to be trained for their welfare in this life and beyond. ‘Doubt’ (kaṅkhaṃ) means uncertainty. ‘All-Knowing’ (sabbaññū) is in the sense of knowing the conditioned and unconditioned in their entirety. ‘Unconquered’ (aparājite) is in the sense of being unconquered by anyone. ‘Caravan leader’ (satthavāhe) is in the sense of leading beings to be trained from the wilderness of saṃsāra to Nibbāna. This is what is said: From the time I heard the four-truth Dhamma as the Teacher was expounding it, and through the ear-door considered and understood it, from that moment onward, regarding the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—who is All-Knowing because he knows all conditioned, unconditioned, and conventional dhammas with his self-arisen knowledge; who is the one with unobstructed vision; who is Unconquered because he has overcome the five Māras and is thus undefeated by them, and because his Dhamma-wheel is unimpeded in the world with its devas; who is the caravan leader because he leads beings to be trained from the wilderness of greed and so on; who is the Great Hero because of his great courage; who is the supreme charioteer, the highest of guides, because he tames with the ultimate taming those men who are difficult for others to tame—I do not recognize any doubt such as, “Is he a Buddha or is he not?” because my knowledge is not dependent on another. Regarding the Noble Path thus taught, and the practice of virtue and so forth which is its basis, there is no doubt or uncertainty such as, “Is it liberating or is it not?”—it does not exist. Here, by stating the absence of doubt regarding the Noble Dhamma, it should be understood that the absence of doubt is also declared regarding the Noble Sangha, for one established therein does not become otherwise.

Meḷajinattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Meḷajina is concluded.

7. Rādhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Rādha

Yathā agāraṃ ducchannantiādikā āyasmato rādhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno satthārā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭibhāneyyakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapiyamānaṃ disvā sayaṃ taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā mahādānaṃ [M 1.0322] pavattesi. Satthu uḷārañca pūjaṃ akāsi. So evaṃ katapaṇidhāno tato cuto tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya gacchantaṃ [V 1.0275] disvā pasannamānaso madhurāni ambaphalānī adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā rādhoti laddhanāmo vayappatto hutvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto mahallakakāle puttadārehi apasādito, “kiṃ me gharāvāsena, pabbajissāmī”ti vihāraṃ gantvā there bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā tehi “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo jiṇṇo na sakkoti vattapaṭivattaṃ pūretu”nti paṭikkhitto satthu santikaṃ gantvā attano ajjhāsayaṃ pavedetvā satthārā upanissayasampattiṃ oloketvā āṇattena dhammasenāpatinā pabbājito vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.63-67) –

The verses of the Venerable Elder Rādha begin with, 'Just as a poorly thatched house…' What is their origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached maturity, he went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu as foremost among those with inspired speech, he himself aspired for that position and made a great offering. He also made a splendid offering to the Teacher. Having made this aspiration, after passing away from there, he accumulated merits in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a respectable family and, having reached maturity, one day saw the Teacher going for alms. With a mind full of faith, he offered sweet mangoes. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Continuing to perform merits in successive lives, he wandered among gods and humans until, in the time of our Blessed One, he was born into a brahmin family in Rājagaha and was named Rādha. Having grown to maturity, while living the household life, he was rejected by his wife and children in his old age. Thinking, “What use is household life to me? I shall go forth,” he went to the monastery, approached the elder bhikkhus, and requested ordination. They refused him, saying, “This brahmin is old; he cannot fulfill the duties and observances.” He then went to the Teacher and expressed his intention. The Teacher, seeing his supportive conditions for attainment, instructed the General of the Dhamma to ordain him. Having established insight meditation, he soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 2.51.63-67):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, pādaphalaṃ adāsahaṃ.

“To the golden-hued Sambuddha, the receiver of offerings, as he was walking along the road, I gave a fruit at his feet.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving a fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthu santikāvacaro hutvā vicaranto satthu dhammadesanāpaṭibhānassa paccayabhūtānaṃ paṭibhānajānanakānaṃ aggo jāto. Therassa hi diṭṭhisamudācārañca āgamma dasabalassa [P 2.0013] navanavā dhammadesanā paṭibhāti. Tenāha bhagavā – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭibhāneyyakānaṃ yadidaṃ rādho”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 233). So ekadivasaṃ “ime sattā abhāvanāya rāgena abhibhuyyanti, bhāvanāya sati taṃ natthī”ti bhāvanaṃ thomento “yathā agāra”ntiādinā gāthādvayamāha.

Having attained arahantship and, living as an attendant in the Teacher’s presence, he became the foremost of those who knew inspired speech, being a condition for the Teacher’s inspired Dhamma teachings. Indeed, on account of the Elder's views and conduct, new and fresh Dhamma teachings would become manifest to the Ten-Powered One. Therefore, the Blessed One declared: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are skilled in inspired speech, Rādha is the foremost” (AN 1.219, 233). One day, while extolling cultivation, saying, “These beings are overcome by lust through lack of cultivation, but when there is cultivation, that is not so,” he spoke the two verses beginning with, 'Just as a house…'

133-4. Tattha agāranti yaṃkiñci gehaṃ. Ducchannanti viraḷacchannaṃ chiddāvachiddaṃ. Samativijjhatīti vassavuṭṭhi vinivijjhati. Abhāvitanti taṃ agāraṃ vuṭṭhi viya bhāvanāya [M 1.0323] rahitattā abhāvitaṃ cittaṃ. Rāgo samativijjhatīti na kevalaṃ rāgova dosamohamānādayopi sabbakilesā tathārūpaṃ cittaṃ ativijjhantiyeva. Subhāvitanti samathavipassanābhāvanāhi suṭṭhu bhāvitaṃ, evarūpaṃ cittaṃ succhannaṃ gehaṃ vuṭṭhi viya rāgādayo kilesā ativijjhituṃ na sakkontīti.

133-4. Here, ‘agāra’ means any kind of house. ‘Ducchanna’ means poorly thatched, sparsely thatched with holes and gaps. ‘Samativijjhati’ means rain penetrates. ‘Abhāvita’ (undeveloped) refers to a mind that, like that house, is undeveloped because it lacks cultivation. ‘Rāgo samativijjhati’ (lust penetrates) means not only lust, but also hatred, delusion, conceit, and all other defilements penetrate such a mind. ‘Subhāvita’ (well-developed) means well-developed through the cultivation of serenity and insight meditation; such a mind, like a well-thatched house, cannot be penetrated by defilements such as lust and others.

Rādhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Rādha is concluded.

8. Surādhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Surādha

Khīṇā [V 1.0276] hi mayhaṃ jātītiādikā āyasmato surādhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso mātuluṅgaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde anantaraṃ vuttassa rādhattherassa kaniṭṭho hutvā nibbatti, surādhotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So jeṭṭhabhātari rādhe pabbajite sayampi pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.68-72) –

“Destroyed is birth for me,” and so forth, are the verses of the Venerable Elder Surādha. What is the origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born in a well-to-do family and, having come of age, one day saw the Teacher. With a joyful mind, he offered a citron fruit. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. Again and again, performing meritorious deeds, he wandered only in happy destinations. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was born as the younger brother of the aforementioned Elder Rādha, and was named Surādha. When his elder brother Rādha went forth, he himself also went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.51.68-72):

“Kaṇikāraṃva jalitaṃ, puṇṇamāyeva candimaṃ;

Jalantaṃ dīparukkhaṃva, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Like a blazing Kaṇikāra tree, like the full moon; I saw the Leader of the World, blazing like a burning lampstand.”

“Mātuluṅgaphalaṃ gayha, adāsiṃ satthuno ahaṃ;

Dakkhiṇeyyassa vīrassa, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

“Taking a citron fruit, I offered it to the Teacher, the Hero worthy of offerings, with a serene mind, with my own hands.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago from now, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad destination. This is the fruit of that fruit-offering.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ aññaṃ byākaronto “khīṇā hī mayha”ntiādinā gāthādvayamāha.

Having attained Arahantship, to show the liberating nature of the Dispensation, he made his declaration of final knowledge by speaking two verses beginning with, “Destroyed is birth for me.”

135-6. Tattha [M 1.0324] khīṇāti khayaṃ [P 2.0014] pariyosānaṃ gatā. Jātīti bhavo bhavanibbatti vā. Vusitaṃ jinasāsananti jinassa sammāsambuddhassa sāsanaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ vuṭṭhaṃ parivuṭṭhaṃ. Pahīno jālasaṅkhātoti sattasantānassa ottharaṇato nissarituṃ appadānato ca “jālasaṅkhāto”ti ca laddhanāmā diṭṭhi avijjā ca pahīnā maggena samucchinnā. Bhavanetti samūhatāti kāmabhavādikassa bhavassa nayanato pavattanato bhavanettisaññitā taṇhā samugghāṭitā. Yassatthāya pabbajitoti yassa atthāya yadatthaṃ ahaṃ agārasmā gehato anagāriyaṃ pabbajjaṃ pabbajito upagato. So sabbesaṃ orambhāgiyuddhambhāgiyappabhedānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ bandhanānaṃ khayabhūto attho nibbānasaṅkhāto paramattho arahattasaṅkhāto sadattho ca mayā anuppatto adhigatoti attho.

135-6. Here, ‘khīṇā’ means gone to destruction, to the end. ‘Jāti’ refers to existence or the production of existence. ‘Vusitaṃ jinasāsanaṃ’ means the teaching of the Victor, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the holy life of the path, has been lived, fully lived. ‘Pahīno jālasaṅkhāto’ refers to the view and ignorance, which are called ‘the net’ because they spread over the continuity of beings and do not allow one to escape, having been abandoned, utterly cut off by the path. ‘Bhavanetti samūhatā’ means craving, known as the conduit of existence because it leads and causes to arise various states of existence like sensual existence, has been uprooted. ‘Yassatthāya pabbajito’ means for whose sake, for what purpose, I went forth from home to homelessness. That purpose—the goal that is the destruction of all fetters and bonds, both lower and higher, the ultimate goal called Nibbāna, and the true goal called Arahantship—has been attained, achieved by me.

Surādhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Surādha is concluded.

9. Gotamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gotama

Sukhaṃ [V 1.0277] supantīti āyasmato gotamattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso āmodaphalamadāsi. Tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā gotamoti laddhanāmo sattavassikakāle upanayanaṃ katvā ratanabhikkhaṃ caritvā sahassaṃ labhitvā taṃ tādise ṭhāne ṭhapetvā vataṃ caranto soḷasasattarasavassuddesikakāle akalyāṇamittehi kāmesu parinīyamāno ekissā rūpūpajīviniyā taṃ sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ datvā brahmacariyavināsaṃ patvā tāya cassa brahmacārirūpaṃ disvā virattākāre dassite ekarattivāseneva nibbinnarūpo attano brahmacariyanivāsaṃ dhanajāniñca saritvā “ayuttaṃ mayā kata”nti vippaṭisārī ahosi. Satthā tassa hetusampattiṃ cittācārañca ñatvā [P 2.0015] tassa āsannaṭṭhāne [M 1.0325] attānaṃ dassesi. So satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso upasaṅkami, tassa bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajanto khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.80-84) –

“Happy in sleep”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Gotama. What is the origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds in the time of previous Buddhas, accumulating merit that was conducive to liberation in various existences, was born into a respectable family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Reaching the age of understanding, one day he saw the Blessed One and, with a joyful mind, offered a mango. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva world. Continuing to perform meritorious deeds and wandering only in happy destinations, he was born into a brahmin family in Rājagaha at the time of this Buddha’s appearance. Named Gotama, at the age of seven the thread ceremony was performed for him. He begged for jewels, and obtained a thousand [coins]. Setting that aside in a suitable place, he observed a certain vow. At sixteen or seventeen, influenced by bad friends, he was being led into sensual pleasures. Giving that thousand [coins] to a woman who earned her living through her beauty, he underwent the destruction of his celibacy. Seeing her show a disaffected attitude towards his celibate appearance, he became disenchanted in just one night. Remembering his dwelling in the holy life and the loss of his wealth, he thought, “I have acted improperly,” and felt remorse. The Teacher, knowing his potential and disposition, revealed himself in his vicinity. Seeing the Teacher, with a joyful mind, he approached. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. Hearing the Dhamma, he regained faith, went forth, and attained Arahantship even as his head was being shaved. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.51.80-84):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, āmodamadadiṃ phalaṃ.

“The golden-colored Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, acceptor of offerings, walking along the street, I gave him a delightful fruit.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad destination. This is the fruit of that fruit-offering.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā jhānasukhena phalasukhena vītināmentaṃ eko gihisahāyo upagantvā, “āvuso, tayā ratanabhikkhāya laddhaṃ pabbajanto kiṃ akāsī”ti pucchi. Taṃ sutvā thero “idaṃ nāma kata”nti anācikkhitvā mātugāme dosaṃ pakāsetvā attano vītarāgabhāvena aññaṃ byākaronto “sukhaṃ supantī”tiādinā gāthādvayamāha.

Having attained Arahantship and passing his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition, a lay friend approached him and asked, ‘Friend, what did you do with what you obtained by begging for jewels when you went forth?’ Hearing this, the Elder, without revealing what he had done, pointed out the fault in womankind and, indicating his own state of being free from lust, made his declaration of final knowledge by speaking two verses beginning with, ‘The sages sleep happily.’

137. Tattha sukhaṃ supanti munayo, ye itthīsu na bajjhareti ye itthīsu visayabhūtāsu nimittabhūtāsu vā rāgabandhanena na bajjhanti, te munayo tapassino saṃyatindriyā sukhaṃ supanti sukhaṃ viharanti, natthi tesaṃ dukkhanti adhippāyo. “Supantī”ti hi nidassanamattametaṃ. Sadā ve [V 1.0278] rakkhitabbāsūti ekaṃsena sabbakālaṃ rakkhitabbāsu. Itthiyo hi sattabhūmike nippurise pāsāde uparibhūmiyaṃ vasāpetvāpi, kucchiyaṃ pakkhipitvāpi na sakkā rakkhituṃ, tasmā tā kiṭṭhādigāviyo viya sabbakālaṃ rakkhaṇīyā honti. Bahucittatāya vā sāmikena vatthālaṅkārānuppadānādinā cittaññathattato sabbakālaṃ rakkhitabbā. Sarīrasabhāvaṃ vā mālāgandhādīhi paṭicchādanavasena rakkhitabbacittatāya rakkhitabbāti. Yāsu saccaṃ sudullabhanti yāsu saccavacanaṃ laddhuṃ na sakkā, itthiyo hi aggimpi pavisanti, visampi khādanti, satthampi āharanti, ubbandhitvāpi kālaṃ karonti, na pana sacce ṭhātuṃ sakkonti. Tasmā evarūpā itthiyo vajjetvā ṭhitā munayo sukhitā vatāti dasseti.

137. Here, ‘The sages sleep happily, those who are not bound to women’ means that those sages, ascetics with restrained senses, who are not entangled by the bondage of lust towards women who are objects of sensual pleasure or signs of it, sleep happily and dwell happily; for them, there is no suffering—this is the meaning. ‘They sleep’ is merely an illustration. Women should always be guarded—this is the absolute rule. For even if women are placed in a seven-story palace devoid of men, or even confined within the belly, they cannot be fully guarded. Therefore, like cows that eat crops, they must be watched at all times. Or, they should always be guarded on account of their fickleness, or because their minds change due to their husbands not giving them clothes, ornaments, and the like. Or, they must be guarded because their minds need to be protected by concealing the nature of their bodies with garlands, perfumes, and so on. ‘Among whom truth is exceedingly rare’ means among whom truthful speech is hard to find. For women will enter fire, consume poison, take up weapons, hang themselves, and even die, yet they cannot abide in truth. Therefore, it is shown that the sages, avoiding such women, remain happy.

138. Idāni [M 1.0326] yassa appahīnattā evarūpāsu itthīsupi bajjhanti, tassa kāmassa attano suppahīnataṃ accantaniṭṭhitatañca dassento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Vadhaṃ carimha te kāmāti ambho kāma, [P 2.0016] tava vadhaṃ accantasamucchedaṃ ariyamaggena carimha, “vadhaṃ carimhase”tipi pāṭho, vadhāya pahānāya maggabrahmacariyaṃ acarimhāti attho. Anaṇā dāni te mayanti idāni aggamaggapattito paṭṭhāya iṇabhāvakarāya pahīnattā kāma te anaṇā mayaṃ, na tuyhaṃ iṇaṃ dhārema. Avītarāgo hi rāgassa vase vattanato tassa iṇaṃ dhārento viya hoti, vītarāgo pana taṃ atikkamitvā paramena cittissariyena samannāgato. Anaṇattā eva gacchāma dāni nibbānaṃ, yattha gantvā na socati yasmiṃ nibbāne gamanahetu sabbaso sokahetūnaṃ abhāvato na socati, taṃ anupādisesanibbānameva idāni gacchāma anupāpuṇāmāti attho.

138. Now, to show his own complete abandoning and final cessation of that craving, due to the non-abandoning of which one is bound even to such women, he speaks the second verse. 'We have wrought your destruction, O craving!' means: O craving, we have brought about your destruction, your utter extermination, by the Noble Path. 'Vadhaṃ carimhase' is also a reading; the meaning is: we have practiced the holy life of the path for the purpose of destruction, for abandoning. 'Now we are free from debt to you' means: now, starting from the attainment of the highest path, because that which causes the state of debt has been abandoned, O craving, we are free from debt to you; we do not bear your debt. For one who is not free from lust, because he lives under the power of lust, is like one who bears its debt. But one who is free from lust has transcended it and is endowed with supreme mastery of mind. 'Because we are free from debt, we now go to Nibbāna, where, having gone, one does not sorrow' means: in that Nibbāna, because of the complete absence of all causes of sorrow, one does not sorrow upon going there. We now go to, we attain, that very Nibbāna without residue of aggregates.

Gotamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gotama is concluded.

10. Vasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vasabha

Pubbe hanati attānanti āyasmato vasabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto buddhasuññe loke brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā nekkhammajjhāsayatāya gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā cuddasasahassatāpasaparivāro himavantassa avidūre samagge nāma pabbate assamaṃ kāretvā vasanto jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā tāpasānaṃ ovādānusāsaniyo dento ekadivasaṃ evaṃ cintesi – “ahaṃ kho dāni imehi tāpasehi sakkato garukato pūjito viharāmi, mayā pana pūjetabbo na upalabbhati, dukkho kho panāyaṃ [V 1.0279] loke yadidaṃ agaruvāso”ti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā purimabuddhesu katādhikāratāya purimabuddhānaṃ cetiye attanā kataṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ anussaritvā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ purimabuddhe uddissa pulinacetiyaṃ katvā pūjaṃ kareyya”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho [M 1.0327] iddhiyā pulinathūpaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ māpetvā suvaṇṇamayādīhi tisahassamattehi pupphehi devasikaṃ pūjaṃ karonto yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatto. Tatthapi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto tāvatiṃse nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ licchavirājakule nibbattitvā vasabhoti laddhanāmo vayappatto bhagavato vesāligamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā [P 2.0017] nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.57-92) –

"First he harms himself" is the verse of the Elder Vasabha. What is its origin? He, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the time of former Buddhas, accumulating merit in various lives, was born into a Brahmin family in a world without a Buddha. Reaching adulthood, he became proficient in the Brahmin arts and sciences. Inclined towards renunciation, he abandoned household life and took up the ascetic life. With a retinue of fourteen thousand ascetics, he had a hermitage built on a mountain called Samagga, not far from the Himalayas. Living there, he developed jhānas and supernormal powers, giving advice and instructions to the ascetics. One day he thought to himself: "Now I dwell here, honored, respected, and revered by these ascetics, but there is no one I can revere. Truly, painful in this world is living without a superior." Thinking thus, because of the meritorious deeds he had performed in the time of former Buddhas, he remembered the honors and offerings he had made to the shrines of former Buddhas. "Why should I not build a sand shrine dedicated to the former Buddhas and make offerings?" Delighted, he used his psychic power to fashion a golden sand stūpa and made daily offerings with about three thousand golden flowers and the like. Having accumulated merit for as long as he lived, and without his jhānas declining, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma world. Having lived there for as long as his life-span lasted, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering on and on among devas and humans, in the dispensation of this Buddha, he was born into a Licchavi royal family in Vesāli and was given the name Vasabha. Reaching adulthood, when the Blessed One visited Vesāli, he saw the power of the Blessed One, gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and soon attained arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna (Thera 2.50.57-92):

“Himavantassāvidūre, samaggo nāma pabbato;

Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.

"Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Samagga. My hermitage was well-made, a leaf-hut beautifully constructed."

“Nārado nāma nāmena, jaṭilo uggatāpano;

Catuddasasahassāni, sissā paricaranti maṃ.

"Named Nārada, I was a matted-hair ascetic, one of fierce austerity; fourteen thousand disciples attended upon me."

“Paṭisallīnako santo, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

Sabbo jano maṃ pūjeti, nāhaṃ pūjemi kiñcanaṃ.

"Secluded and serene, I reflected thus at that time: 'All people honor me, but I honor no one.'"

“Na me ovādako atthi, vattā koci na vijjati;

Anācariyupajjhāyo, vane vāsaṃ upemahaṃ.

"There is no one to advise me, no one to teach me is found; without a teacher or preceptor, I dwell in the forest."

“Upāsamāno yamahaṃ, garucittaṃ upaṭṭhahe;

So me ācariyo natthi, vanavāso niratthako.

"Whom I might attend upon, establishing a respectful mind—that teacher I do not have; my forest-dwelling is pointless."

“Āyāgaṃ me gavesissaṃ, garuṃ bhāvaniyaṃ tathā;

Sāvassayo vasissāmi, na koci garahissati.

"I shall seek an object of veneration, and likewise a respected one worthy of cultivation; I shall live with a support, and no one will reproach me."

“Uttānakūlā nadikā, supatitthā manoramā;

Saṃsuddhapulinākiṇṇā, avidūre mamassamaṃ.

"Not far from my hermitage was a delightful river with gently sloping banks, good fords, and teeming with very pure sand."

“Nadiṃ amarikaṃ nāma, upagantvānahaṃ tadā;

Saṃvaḍḍhayitvā pulinaṃ, akaṃ pulinacetiyaṃ.

"Having then approached the river named Amarika, and having heaped up the sand, I made a sand shrine."

“Ye te ahesuṃ sambuddhā, bhavantakaraṇā munī;

Tesaṃ etādiso thūpo, taṃ nimittaṃ karomahaṃ.

"Those who were the Fully Awakened Ones, the sages who made an end to becoming—for them such is a stūpa; I make this as a symbol of them."

“Karitvā [M 1.0328] pulinaṃ thūpaṃ, sovaṇṇaṃ māpayiṃ ahaṃ;

Soṇṇakiṅkaṇipupphāni, sahasse tīṇi pūjayiṃ.

"Having made a stūpa of sand, I caused it to be golden; I offered three thousand golden kiṅkaṇi flowers."

“Sāyapātaṃ [V 1.0280] namassāmi, vedajāto katañjalī;

Sammukhā viya sambuddhaṃ, vandiṃ pulinacetiyaṃ.

"Evening and morning I pay homage, filled with joy, with hands joined in reverence; as if face to face with the Fully Awakened One, I venerated the sand shrine."

“Yadā kilesā jāyanti, vitakkā gehanissitā;

Sarāmi sukataṃ thūpaṃ, paccavekkhāmi tāvade.

"When defilements arise, thoughts connected with the household, I remember the well-made stūpa and reflect upon it immediately."

“Upanissāya viharaṃ, satthavāhaṃ vināyakaṃ;

Kilese saṃvaseyyāsi, na yuttaṃ tava mārisa.

"Dwelling in dependence on the Caravan Leader, the Guide—it is not fitting for you, good sir, to live together with defilements."

“Saha āvajjite thūpe, gāravaṃ hoti me tadā;

Kuvitakke vinodesiṃ, nāgo tuttaṭṭito yathā.

"As soon as the stūpa was brought to mind, reverence arose in me then; I dispelled wrong thoughts, like an elephant struck by the goad."

“Evaṃ viharamānaṃ maṃ, maccurājābhimaddatha;

Tattha kālaṅkato santo, brahmalokamagacchahaṃ.

"Thus dwelling, the King of Death struck me down. Having died there, serene, I went to the Brahma world."

“Yāvatāyuṃ vasitvāna, tidive upapajjahaṃ;

Asītikkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ.

"Having lived out my lifespan, I was reborn in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. Eighty times I ruled as Sakka, king of the devas."

“Satānaṃ tīṇikkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

"And three hundred times I was a wheel-turning monarch; countless and vast were the times I ruled a regional kingdom."

“Soṇṇakiṅkaṇipupphānaṃ, vipākaṃ anubhomahaṃ;

Dhātīsatasahassāni, parivārenti maṃ bhave.

"I experience the result of the golden kiṅkaṇi flowers; hundreds of thousands of nurses attend upon me in this existence."

“Thūpassa pariciṇṇattā, rajojallaṃ na limpati;

Gatte sedā na muccanti, suppabhāso bhavāmahaṃ.

"Because of having attended to the stūpa, dust and dirt do not cling to me; sweat is not released from my body; I am of excellent radiance."

“Aho me sukato thūpo, sudiṭṭhāmarikā nadī;

Thūpaṃ katvāna pulinaṃ, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

"Ah, well-made was my stūpa; well-seen was the river Amarika. Having made a stūpa of sand, I have attained the unshakable state."

“Kusalaṃ kattukāmena, jantunā sāragāhinā;

Natthi khettaṃ akhettaṃ vā, paṭipattīva sādhakā.

"For a being who desires to do what is skillful and who grasps the essence, there is no such thing as a 'field' or a 'non-field'; it is practice alone that is the accomplisher."

“Yathāpi balavā poso, aṇṇavaṃtaritussahe;

Parittaṃ kaṭṭhamādāya, pakkhandeyya mahāsaraṃ.

"Just as a strong man, able to cross the ocean, might take a small piece of wood and plunge into the great sea."

“Imāhaṃ [M 1.0329] kaṭṭhaṃ nissāya, tarissāmi mahodadhiṃ;

Ussāhena vīriyena, tareyya udadhiṃ naro.

"'Relying on this piece of wood, I shall cross the great ocean.' By striving and energy, a person could cross the ocean."

“Tatheva me kataṃ kammaṃ, parittaṃ thokakañca yaṃ;

Taṃ kammaṃ upanissāya, saṃsāraṃ samatikkamiṃ.

"Just so, the deed that I did was small and slight; relying on that deed, I have crossed beyond saṃsāra."

“Pacchime bhave sampatte, sukkamūlena codito;

Sāvatthiyaṃ pure jāto, mahāsāle suaḍḍhake.

"Having reached my final existence, impelled by the root of merit, I was born in the city of Sāvatthī, in a very wealthy and prominent family."

“Saddhā mātā pitā mayhaṃ, buddhassa saraṇaṃ gatā;

Ubho diṭṭhapadā ete, anuvattanti sāsanaṃ.

"My mother and father, full of faith, had gone for refuge to the Buddha; both had seen the path, they followed the teaching."

“Bodhipapaṭikaṃ [V 1.0281] gayha, soṇṇathūpamakārayuṃ;

Sāyapātaṃ namassanti, sakyaputtassa sammukhā.

"Taking a sacred object from the Bodhi tree, they had a golden stūpa made; they pay homage evening and morning in the presence of the Sakyan Son."

“Uposathamhi divase, soṇṇathūpaṃ vinīharuṃ;

Buddhassa vaṇṇaṃ kittentā, tiyāmaṃ vītināmayuṃ.

"On the Uposatha day, they would bring forth the golden stūpa; praising the Buddha’s qualities, they would pass the three watches of the night."

“Saha disvānahaṃ thūpaṃ, sariṃ pulinacetiyaṃ;

Ekāsane nisīditvā, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

"As soon as I saw the stūpa, I remembered the sand shrine; having sat down in a single session, I attained arahantship."

“Gavesamāno taṃ vīraṃ, dhammasenāpatiddasaṃ;

Agārā nikkhamitvāna, pabbajiṃ tassa santike.

"Seeking that hero, I saw the General of the Dhamma; having gone forth from home, I was ordained in his presence."

“Jātiyā sattavassena, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ;

Upasampādayī buddho, guṇamaññāya cakkhumā.

"At seven years of age, I attained arahantship; the Buddha, the One with Vision, knowing my virtue, gave me the higher ordination."

“Dārakeneva santena, kiriyaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ mayā;

Kataṃ me karaṇīyajja, sakyaputtassa sāsane.

"Though I was but a boy, the task was finished by me; what had to be done has been done by me today in the teaching of the Sakyan Son."

“Sabbaverabhayātīto, sabbasaṅgātigo isi;

Sāvako te mahāvīra, soṇṇathūpassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Gone beyond all enmity and fear, a sage who has surpassed all attachments; Your disciple, O great hero, this is the fruit of the golden stūpa.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā dāyakānuggahaṃ karonto tehi upanīte paccaye na paṭikkhipati, yathāladdheyeva paribhuñjati. Taṃ puthujjanā “ayaṃ kāyadaḷhibahulo arakkhitacitto”ti maññamānā avamaññanti. Thero taṃ [M 1.0330] agaṇentova viharati. Tassa pana avidūre aññataro kuhakabhikkhu pāpiccho samāno appiccho viya santuṭṭho viya attānaṃ dassento lokaṃ vañcento viharati. Mahājano taṃ arahantaṃ viya sambhāveti. Athassa sakko devānamindo taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, kiṃ nāma kuhako karotī”ti pucchi. Thero pāpicchaṃ garahanto –

But having attained arahantship, acting for the benefit of the donors, he does not refuse the requisites brought by them, but partakes of them just as he receives them. Ordinary people, thinking, “This one is strong in body and unguarded in mind,” look down upon him. The elder, however, dwells paying no heed to it. Not far from him, another deceitful bhikkhu, being of evil wishes, dwells deceiving the world, presenting himself as if he were of few wants and content. The great populace honors him as if he were an arahant. Then, Sakka, the king of the devas, having learned of this matter, approached the elder and asked, “Venerable sir, what is this hypocrite doing?” The elder, censuring the one of evil wishes, said—

139.

139.

“Pubbe hanati attānaṃ, pacchā hanati so pare;

Suhataṃ hanti attānaṃ, vītaṃseneva pakkhimā.

“First he harms himself, then afterwards he harms others; He harms himself thoroughly, like a fowler with a decoy bird.”

140.

140.

“Na brāhmaṇo bahivaṇṇo, antovaṇṇo hi brāhmaṇo;

Yasmiṃ pāpāni kammāni, sa ve kaṇho sujampatī”ti. – gāthādvayamāha;

“A brahmin is not so by outward quality, for a brahmin is of inward quality. He in whom there are evil deeds, he indeed is base, O Sujampati.” – He spoke these two verses.

Tattha pubbe hanati attānanti kuhakapuggalo attano kuhakavuttiyā lokaṃ vañcento pāpicchatādīhi pāpadhammehi paṭhamameva attānaṃ hanati, attano kusalakoṭṭhāsaṃ vināseti. Pacchā hanati so pareti so kuhako paṭhamaṃ tāva vuttanayena attānaṃ hantvā pacchā pare yehi “ayaṃ [V 1.0282] bhikkhu pesalo ariyo”ti vā sambhāventehi kārā katā, te hanati tesaṃ kārāni attani katāni amahapphalāni katvā paccayavināsanena vināseti. Satipi kuhakassa ubhayahanane attahanane pana ayaṃ visesoti dassento āha suhataṃ hanti attānanti. So kuhako attānaṃ hananto suhataṃ katvā hanti vināseti, yathā kiṃ? Vītaṃseneva pakkhimāti, vītaṃsoti dīpakasakuṇo, tena. Pakkhimāti sākuṇiko. Yathā tena vītaṃsasakuṇena aññe sakuṇe vañcetvā hananto attānaṃ idha lokepi hanati viññugarahasāvajjasabhāvādinā, samparāyaṃ pana duggatiparikkilesena hanatiyeva, na pana te sakuṇe pacchā hantuṃ sakkoti, evaṃ kuhakopi kohaññena lokaṃ vañcetvā idha lokepi [P 2.0018] attānaṃ hanati vippaṭisāraviññugarahādīhi, paralokepi duggatiparikkilesehi, na pana te paccayadāyake apāyadukkhaṃ pāpeti. Apica kuhako dakkhiṇāya amahapphalabhāvakaraṇeneva [M 1.0331] dāyakaṃ hanatīti vutto, na nipphalabhāvakaraṇena. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “dussīlassa manussabhūtassa dānaṃ datvā sahassaguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379). Tenāha “suhataṃ hanti attāna”nti.

Therein, ‘first he harms himself’ refers to a deceitful person who, through his deceitful conduct, deceives the world with evil wishes and other unwholesome qualities. First, he harms himself, ruining his own portion of merit. ‘Then he harms others’—that deceiver, having first harmed himself in the manner described, later harms those who, thinking, ‘This monk is amiable and noble,’ have made offerings to him. He harms them by rendering their offerings made to him of little fruit, destroying them by wasting the requisites. Although the deceiver harms both himself and others, to show this distinction in self-harm, the verse says, ‘he harms himself thoroughly.’ That deceiver, in harming himself, does so thoroughly. To what can this be compared? ‘Like a fowler with a decoy bird.’ Just as the fowler, by means of the decoy-bird, deceives and harms other birds, and thereby also harms himself in this world through censure and reproach from the discerning, and in the next world through the defilements of a miserable destination, yet cannot harm those other birds afterwards—so too, the deceiver, by deceiving the world with his hypocrisy, harms himself in this world through remorse and censure from the discerning, and in the next world through the defilements of a miserable destination, but does not lead those donors of requisites to the suffering of the lower realms. Moreover, it is said that the deceiver harms the donor only by making their offering of little fruit, not by rendering it fruitless. For it has been said by the Blessed One: “Having given a gift to an immoral human being, a thousandfold return from the offering is to be expected” (MN 3.379). Therefore, it is said, ‘he harms himself thoroughly.’”

Evaṃ bāhiraparimajjanamatte ṭhitā puggalā suddhā nāma na honti, abbhantarasuddhiyā eva pana suddhā hontīti dassento “na brāhmaṇo”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tassattho – iriyāpathasaṇṭhapanādibahisampattimattena brāhmaṇo na hoti. Sampattiattho hi idha vaṇṇa-saddo. Abbhantare pana sīlādisampattiyā brāhmaṇo hoti, “bāhitapāpo brāhmaṇo”ti katvā. Tasmā “yasmiṃ pāpāni lāmakāni kammāni saṃvijjanti, ekaṃsena so kaṇho nihīnapuggalo”ti sujampati, devānaminda, jānāhi. Taṃ sutvā sakko kuhakabhikkhuṃ tajjetvā “dhamme vattāhī”ti ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

To show that persons who rely merely on external polishing are not truly pure, but are pure only through inner purity, he spoke the second verse beginning, “A brahmin is not…”. Its meaning is this: one does not become a brahmin merely by external accomplishments such as proper deportment. For here the word vaṇṇa has the meaning of ‘accomplishment’. But one becomes a brahmin through inner accomplishments, such as virtue, because ‘a brahmin is one who has banished evil.’ Therefore, ‘Know this, O Sujampati, lord of the devas: he in whom evil and base actions are found is assuredly a dark, ignoble person.’ Having heard this, Sakka rebuked the deceitful monk, advised him, “Conduct yourself according to the Dhamma!”, and returned to his own dwelling.

Vasabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vasabha is concluded.

Dukanipāte paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first chapter of the Book of Twos is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Mahācundattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahācunda

Sussūsāti [V 1.0283] āyasmato mahācundattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kumbhakārakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kumbhakārakammena jīvanto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso ekaṃ mattikāpattaṃ svābhisaṅkhataṃ katvā bhagavato adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe nālakagāme rūpasāriyā brāhmaṇiyā putto sāriputtattherassa kaniṭṭhabhātā hutvā nibbatti, cundotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto dhammasenāpatiṃ anupabbajitvā taṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ [M 1.0332] paṭṭhapetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.39-50) –

The verses of the Venerable Mahācunda beginning Sussūsā. What is their origin? He too, having made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in a potter’s family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having attained understanding, he made his living by the potter’s craft. One day, seeing the Teacher, his mind was filled with faith, and he fashioned a clay bowl well with his own hands and offered it to the Blessed One. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered on among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country as the son of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī, the younger brother of the Elder Sāriputta. His name was Cunda. Coming of age, he went forth under the General of the Dhamma and, relying on him, established insight meditation. Striving and exerting himself, he soon attained the six direct knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera 2.51.39–50):

“Nagare haṃsavatiyā, kumbhakāro ahosahaṃ;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, oghatiṇṇamanāsavaṃ.

“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a potter. I saw the dust-free Buddha, who had crossed the flood, taintless.”

“Sukataṃ mattikāpattaṃ, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Pattaṃ datvā bhagavato, ujubhūtassa tādino.

“A well-made clay bowl I gave to the Buddha, the foremost. Having offered the bowl to the Blessed One, who was upright and Such.”

“Bhave nibbattamānohaṃ, soṇṇathāle labhāmahaṃ;

Rūpimaye ca sovaṇṇe, taṭṭike ca maṇīmaye.

“As I was reborn into existence, I obtained golden plates; and silver, golden, and jeweled plates.”

“Pātiyo paribhuñjāmi, puññakammassidaṃ phalaṃ;

Yasānañca dhanānañca, aggabhūto ca homahaṃ.

“I partake of food from fine bowls, the fruit of this meritorious deed. And I was foremost in glory and riches.”

“Yathāpi bhaddake khette, bījaṃ appampi ropitaṃ;

Sammādhāraṃ pavecchante, phalaṃ toseti kassakaṃ.

“Just as in a good field, even a small seed sown, when rain is properly supplied, its fruit satisfies the farmer.”

“Tathevidaṃ pattadānaṃ, buddhakhettamhi ropitaṃ;

Pītidhāre pavassante, phalaṃ maṃ tosayissati.

“Just so, this gift of a bowl, planted in the Buddha-field, when streams of joy pour forth, its fruit will satisfy me.”

“Yāvatā khettā vijjanti, saṅghāpi ca gaṇāpi ca;

Buddhakhettasamo natthi, sukhado sabbapāṇinaṃ.

“As far as fields exist, whether of Sanghas or of groups, none equals the Buddha-field, which brings happiness to all living beings.”

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Ekapattaṃ daditvāna, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man! Having given a single bowl, I have attained the unwavering state.”

“Ekanavutito [V 1.0284] kappe, yaṃ pattamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pattadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave that bowl, I have not known a miserable destination; this is the fruit of the gift of a bowl.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Chaḷabhiñño [P 2.0019] pana hutvā attanā paṭiladdhasampattiyā kāraṇabhūtaṃ garūpanissayaṃ vivekavāsañca kittento –

But having become one endowed with the six direct knowledges, he praised the reliance on a teacher and the dwelling in seclusion, which were the causes of the accomplishment he had attained:

141.

141.

“Sussūsā sutavaddhanī, sutaṃ paññāya vaddhanaṃ;

Paññāya atthaṃ jānāti, ñāto attho sukhāvaho.

“Eagerness to listen increases learning; learning is an increase of wisdom; by wisdom one understands the meaning; the understood meaning brings happiness.”

142.

142.

“Sevetha [M 1.0333] pantāni senāsanāni, careyya saṃyojanavippamokkhaṃ;

Sace ratiṃ nādhigaccheyya tattha, saṅghe vase rakkhitatto satīmā”ti. –

“One should frequent secluded lodgings, and practice for release from the fetters. If one finds no delight there, one should dwell in the Saṅgha, self-protected and mindful.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha sussūsāti sotabbayuttassa sabbasutassa sotumicchā, garusannivāsopi. Diṭṭhadhammikādibhedañhi atthaṃ sotumicchantena kalyāṇamitte upasaṅkamitvā vattakaraṇena payirupāsitvā yadā te payirupāsanāya ārādhitacittā kañci upanisīditukāmā honti, atha ne upanisīditvā adhigatāya sotumicchāya ohitasotena sotabbaṃ hotīti garusannivāsopi sussūsāhetutāya “sussūsā”ti vuccati. Sā panāyaṃ sussūsā saccapaṭiccasamuppādādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ sutaṃ taṃsamaṅgino puggalassa vaḍḍheti brūhetīti sutavaddhanī, bāhusaccakārīti attho. Sutaṃ paññāya vaddhananti yaṃ taṃ “sutadharo sutasannicayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.339; a. ni. 4.22) “idhekaccassa bahukaṃ sutaṃ hoti suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇa”nti (a. ni. 4.6) ca evamādinā nayena vuttaṃ bāhusaccaṃ, taṃ akusalappahānakusalādhigamanahetubhūtaṃ paññaṃ vaddhetīti sutaṃ paññāya vaddhanaṃ, vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Therein, 'eagerness to listen' means the wish to hear what is suitable to be heard, and also association with teachers. For one who wishes to hear the meaning, which is of various kinds such as pertaining to this life, should approach good friends, serve them by performing duties, and when their minds are pleased by such service and they wish for someone to sit near for instruction, then one should sit near them and listen with an attentive ear, with the acquired wish to hear what is suitable to be heard. Therefore, because association with teachers is a cause for 'eagerness to listen,' it is called 'eagerness to listen.' This eagerness to listen increases and nourishes the learning of a person who is endowed with it, learning connected with the truths, dependent origination, and so on. Thus, it is called 'growth in learning,' meaning it makes one accomplished in much learning. 'Learning is an increase of wisdom' means that which is called 'one who retains what is learned, accumulates what is learned' (MN 1.339; AN 4.22) and 'here someone has learned much: discourses, verses, explanations' (AN 4.6)—this much learning, being the cause for abandoning the unwholesome and attaining the wholesome, increases wisdom. For this has been said by the Blessed One—

“Sutāvudho kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 7.67).

“Monks, a noble disciple whose weapon is learning abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself pure.” (AN 7.67)

Paññāya atthaṃ jānātīti bahussuto sutamayañāṇe ṭhito taṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjanto sutānusārena atthūpaparikkhāya dhammanijjhānena bhāvanāya ca lokiyalokuttarabhedaṃ diṭṭhadhammādivibhāgaṃ [V 1.0285] dukkhādivibhāgañca atthaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti ca paṭivijjhati ca, tenāha bhagavā –

‘By wisdom one understands the meaning’; thus, the much-learned one, established in the knowledge born of learning, undertakes that practice. Following what has been learned, by examining the meaning, by contemplating the Dhamma, and by development, one truly knows and penetrates the meaning—differentiated as worldly and supramundane, with distinctions such as pertaining to this life, and with distinctions of suffering and so on. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

“Sutassa yathāpariyattassa atthamaññāya dhammamaññāya dhammānudhammappaṭipanno hotī”ti (a. ni. 4.6).

“Having understood the meaning of what has been learned, as it has been learned, and having understood the Dhamma, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma.” (AN 4.6)

“Dhatānaṃ [M 1.0334] dhammānaṃ atthaṃ upaparikkhati, atthaṃ upaparikkhato dhammā nijjhānaṃ khamanti, dhammanijjhānakkhantiyā sati chando jāyati, chandajāto ussahati, ussahitvā tuleti, tulayitvā padahati, pahitatto samāno [P 2.0020] kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca naṃ ativijjha passatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.432) ca.

“He examines the meaning of the teachings that have been retained. By examining the meaning, the teachings are approved of for contemplation. When there is acceptance of the teachings upon reflection, desire arises. With desire arisen, he strives. Having striven, he weighs. Having weighed, he exerts himself. Being resolute, he realizes the supreme truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.” (MN 2.432)

Ñāto attho sukhāvahoti yathāvutto diṭṭhadhammikādiattho ceva dukkhādiattho ca yāthāvato ñāto adhigato lokiyalokuttarabhedaṃ sukhaṃ āvahati nipphādetīti attho.

‘A known meaning is conducive to happiness’ means that when the aforesaid meaning—that is, the meaning pertaining to this life and so forth, and the meaning pertaining to suffering and so forth—is known and realized as it truly is, it brings about and produces happiness, differentiated as worldly and supramundane.

Ṭhitāya bhāvanāpaññāya sutamatteneva na sijjhatīti tassā paṭipajjanavidhiṃ dassento “sevetha…pe…vippamokkha”nti āha. Tattha sevetha pantāni senāsanānīti kāyavivekamāha. Tena saṃyojanappahānassa ca vakkhamānattā vivekārahasseva vivekavāsoti sīlasaṃvarādayo idha avuttasiddhā veditabbā. Careyya saṃyojanavippamokkhanti yathā saṃyojanehi cittaṃ vippamuccati, tathā vipassanābhāvanaṃ maggabhāvanañca careyya paṭipajjeyyāti attho. Sace ratiṃ nādhigaccheyya tatthāti tesu pantasenāsanesu yathāladdhesu adhikusaladhammesu ca ratiṃ pubbenāparaṃ visesassa alābhato abhiratiṃ na labheyya, saṅghe bhikkhusamūhe rakkhitatto kammaṭṭhānaparigaṇhanato rakkhitacitto chasu dvāresu satiārakkhāya upaṭṭhapanena satimā vaseyya vihareyya, evaṃ viharantassa ca api nāma saṃyojanavippamokkho bhaveyyāti adhippāyo.

For one established in the wisdom of development, success is not achieved by mere hearing; thus, to show the method of practice, it is said: 'One should frequent... up to liberation.' Herein, 'One should frequent secluded dwellings' refers to physical seclusion. Because the abandoning of the fetters will be described, and because dwelling in seclusion is for one who is worthy of seclusion, the restraint of virtue and so forth should be understood here as implied though not explicitly stated. 'One should practice for the liberation from fetters' means that one should practice insight meditation and path meditation so that the mind is liberated from the fetters—this is the meaning. 'If one does not find delight there' means that in those secluded dwellings and in the wholesome qualities one has attained, one does not gain delight due to not achieving further distinctions, that is, a lack of superior attainments. In the Sangha, the community of monks, one should dwell, self-guarded, with mind protected by taking up a meditation subject, and mindful by establishing mindfulness as protection at the six sense doors. For one dwelling thus, there may indeed be liberation from the fetters—this is the intention.

Mahācundattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahācunda is concluded.

2. Jotidāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jotidāsa

Ye kho teti āyasmato jotidāsattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā [V 1.0286] viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya gacchantaṃ disvā pasannacitto kāsumārikaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ [M 1.0335] buddhuppāde pādiyatthajanapade vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, jotidāsotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patvā gharamāvasanto ekadivasaṃ mahākassapattheraṃ attano gāme piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannacitto bhojetvā therassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā attano gāmasamīpe pabbate mahantaṃ vihāraṃ kāretvā theraṃ tattha vāsetvā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahanto therassa dhammadesanāya paṭiladdhasaṃvego pabbajitvā [P 2.0021] vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.51-56) –

The verses beginning 'Ye kho te' are those of the Venerable Jotidāsa Thera. What is their origin? This elder too, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having attained maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher going for alms, with a confident mind he offered a kāsumārika fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha-era, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin in the country of Pādiyattha. His name was Jotidāsa. Having attained maturity, while living as a householder, one day he saw the Elder Mahākassapa wandering for alms in his village. With a confident mind, he offered him food and, having heard the Dhamma from the Elder, he had a large monastery built on a mountain near his village. He had the Elder reside there and attended to him with the four requisites. Stirred by the Elder’s teachings, he went forth and, undertaking the practice of insight meditation, soon attained the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva jotantaṃ, nisinnaṃ pabbatantare;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ.

“Like a shining kaṇikāra flower, seated in a mountain cleft, I saw the stainless Buddha, the foremost in the world, the bull among men.”

“Pasannacitto sumano, sire katvāna añjaliṃ;

Kāsumārikamādāya, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ.

“With a confident and gladdened mind, placing my hands in reverence on my head, I took a kāsumārika fruit and gave it to the supreme Buddha.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-one aeons since I gave that fruit, I know of no bad destination; this is the fruit of that offering of fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā visesato vinayapiṭake sukusalabhāvaṃ patvā dasavassiko parisupaṭṭhāko ca hutvā bahūhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ vandituṃ sāvatthiṃ gacchanto antarāmagge addhānaparissamavinodanatthaṃ titthiyānaṃ ārāmaṃ pavisitvā ekamantaṃ nisinno ekaṃ pañcatapaṃ tapantaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā, “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, aññasmiṃ tapanīye aññaṃ tapatī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo kupito, “bho, muṇḍaka, kiṃ aññaṃ tapanīya”nti āha. Thero tassa –

Having attained the six higher knowledges, learned the three Piṭakas, and especially attained great skill in the Vinaya Piṭaka, and having been an attendant of the assembly for ten years, he set out for Sāvatthī with many bhikkhus to pay homage to the Blessed One. Along the way, to relieve the fatigue of the journey, he entered a hermitage belonging to sectarians. Sitting to one side, he saw a brahmin practicing the fivefold austerity and asked, “Brahmin, when there is another that ought to be tormented, why do you torment this other thing?” Hearing this, the brahmin became angry and said, “Hey, shaveling, what other thing ought to be tormented?” The Elder replied to him:

“Kopo ca issā paraheṭhanā ca, māno ca sārambhamado pamādo;

Taṇhā avijjā bhavasaṅgatī ca, te tappanīyā na hi rūpakhandho”ti. –

“Anger, envy, and harming others; pride, rivalry, arrogance, and negligence; craving, ignorance, and attachment to becoming—these are what ought to be tormented, not the form aggregate.”

Gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi. Taṃ sutvā so brāhmaṇo tasmiṃ titthiyārāme sabbe aññatitthiyā ca therassa santike pabbajiṃsu. Thero tehi [M 1.0336] saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā attano jātibhūmiṃyeva gato dassanatthaṃ upagatesu ñātakesu nānāladdhike yaññasuddhike ovadanto –

He taught the Dhamma with this verse. Hearing it, that brahmin and all the other sectarians in that sectarian hermitage went forth under the Elder. The Elder, together with them, went to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after staying there for a few days, returned to his own birthplace. When relatives who held various doctrines and believed in purification by sacrifice came to see him, he advised them, saying:

143.

143.

“Ye [V 1.0287] kho te veṭhamissena, nānattena ca kammunā;

Manusse uparundhanti, pharusūpakkamā janā;

Tepi tattheva kīranti, na hi kammaṃ panassati.

“Those people who, with deceit and various actions, oppress human beings, being harsh in their undertakings—they too are afflicted right there, for a deed is never lost.”

144.

144.

“Yaṃ karoti naro kammaṃ, kalyāṇaṃ yadi pāpakaṃ;

Tassa tasseva dāyādo, yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ pakubbatī”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Whatever deed a person does, whether good or evil, of that very deed he is the heir, whatever deed he performs.” Thus, the two verses were spoken.

Tattha yeti aniyamuddeso. Teti aniyamato eva paṭiniddeso. Padadvayassāpi “janā”ti iminā sambandho. Khoti nipātamattaṃ. Veṭhamissenāti varattakhaṇḍādinā sīsādīsu veṭhadānena. “Vedhamissenā”tipi pāḷi, so evattho. Nānattena ca kammunāti hananaghātanahatthapādādicchedanena khuddakaseḷadānādinā [P 2.0022] ca nānāvidhena parūpaghātakammena. Manusseti nidassanamattaṃ, tasmā ye keci satteti adhippāyo. Uparundhantīti vibādhenti. Pharusūpakkamāti dāruṇapayogā, kurūrakammantāti attho. Janāti sattā. Tepi tattheva kīrantīti te vuttappakārā puggalā yāhi kammakāraṇāhi aññe bādhiṃsu. Tattheva tāsuyeva kāraṇāsu sayampi kīranti pakkhipīyanti, tathārūpaṃyeva dukkhaṃ anubhavantīti attho. “Tatheva kīrantī”ti ca pāṭho, yathā sayaṃ aññesaṃ dukkhaṃ akaṃsu, tatheva aññehi karīyanti, dukkhaṃ pāpīyantīti attho, kasmā? Na hi kammaṃ panassati kammañhi ekantaṃ upacitaṃ vipākaṃ adatvā na vigacchati, avasesapaccayasamavāye vipaccatevāti adhippāyo.

Here, ‘ye’ is an indefinite reference. ‘Te’ is the corresponding definite reference. The connection between the two words is established by ‘janā’. ‘Kho’ is merely a particle. ‘Veṭhamissena’ means by binding the head and other parts with strips of leather or similar materials. The Pāli also reads ‘Vedhamissena,’ and the meaning is the same. ‘Nānattena ca kammunā’ refers to various cruel actions such as killing, slaying, cutting off hands and feet, giving minor blows, and other forms of harming others. ‘Manusse’ is merely illustrative; thus, the intention is ‘whatever beings.’ ‘Uparundhanti’ means they oppress. ‘Pharusūpakkamā’ means harsh applications—cruel deeds, in other words. ‘Janā’ means beings. ‘Te pi tattheva kīranti’ means those very individuals who, by those very actions by which they harmed others, are now tormented in that very place—they experience the same kind of suffering. Another reading is ‘tatheva kīranti,’ meaning just as they inflicted suffering on others, so too are they made to suffer by others, and thus they reach suffering. Why? Because no deed is lost—a deed, once accumulated, does not disappear without yielding its result; it inevitably ripens when the remaining conditions are met—this is the intended meaning.

Idāni “na hi kammaṃ panassatī”ti saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vibhajitvā sattānaṃ kammassakataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “yaṃ karotī”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tassattho yaṃ kammaṃ kalyāṇaṃ kusalaṃ, yadi vā pāpakaṃ akusalaṃ satto [M 1.0337] karoti, karonto ca tattha yaṃ kammaṃ yathā phaladānasamatthaṃ hoti, tathā pakubbati upacinoti. Tassa tasseva dāyādoti tassa tasseva kammaphalassa gaṇhanato tena tena kammena dātabbavipākassa bhāgī hotīti attho. Tenāha bhagavā – “kammassakā, māṇava, sattā kammadāyādā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.289). Imā gāthā sutvā therassa ñātakā kammassakatāyaṃ patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

Now, to explain in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief, “for a deed is not lost,” the verse “Whatever one does” was spoken to elucidate the ownership of deeds by beings. The meaning is this: whatever action, wholesome or unwholesome, a being does, and while doing it, accumulates that action in such a way that it is capable of yielding results, so he performs it. He is the heir to that very deed, meaning that by receiving the fruit of that very deed, he is the recipient of the ripening results to be given by that action. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Young man, beings are owners of their deeds, heirs to their deeds,” and so on (M. iii. 289). Having heard these verses, the Thera’s relatives were established in the ownership of deeds.

Jotidāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Jotidāsa is concluded.

3. Heraññakānittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Heraññakāni

Accayanti [V 1.0288] ahorattāti āyasmato heraññakānittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto paresaṃ bhatako hutvā jīvanto ekadivasaṃ sujātassa nāma satthusāvakassa paṃsukūlaṃ pariyesantassa upaḍḍhadussaṃ pariccaji. So tena puññakammena tāvatiṃsesu nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalarañño gāmabhojakassa coravosāsakassa putto hutvā [P 2.0023] nibbatti, heraññakānītissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto pitu accayena raññā tasmiṃyeva gāmabhojakaṭṭhāne ṭhapito jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho attano kaniṭṭhassa taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ dāpetvā rājānaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.31-40) –

“The nights and days pass by”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Heraññakāni. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having come of age, he lived as a hired servant for others. One day, when a disciple of the Teacher named Sujāta was searching for a rag-robe, he donated half of his cloth. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Wandering repeatedly among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era, he was born as the son of a village headman under the King of Kosala, who was a punisher of thieves. His name was Heraññakāni. When he came of age, upon his father’s passing, the king appointed him to that same position of village headman. At the acceptance of Jetavana, he saw the Buddha’s power and gained faith. He then arranged for his younger brother to be given that position, took leave of the king, and went forth. Establishing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.50.31-40):

“Padumuttarabhagavato, sujāto nāma sāvako;

Paṃsukūlaṃ gavesanto, saṅkāre carate tadā.

“Of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there was a disciple named Sujāta. Searching for a rag-robe, he was then wandering among the rubbish heaps.

“Nagare haṃsavatiyā, paresaṃ bhatako ahaṃ;

Upaḍḍhadussaṃ datvāna, sirasā abhivādayiṃ.

“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a servant for others. Having given half a cloth, I bowed with my head.”

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-performed deed, and by my volition and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.”

“Tettiṃsakkhattuṃ [M 1.0338] devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Sattasattatikkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

“Thirty-three times I was Sakka, king of devas; I ruled the deva kingdom. And seventy-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.”

“Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ;

Upaḍḍhadussadānena, modāmi akutobhayo.

“Vast regional kingdoms, countless in number—by the gift of half a cloth, I rejoice, fearless from any quarter.”

“Icchamāno cahaṃ ajja, sakānanaṃ sapabbataṃ;

Khomadussehi chādeyyaṃ, aḍḍhadussassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“If I wished today, I could cover the land with its forests and mountains with linen cloths. This is the fruit of half a cloth.”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ dānamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, aḍḍhadussassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“A hundred thousand aeons ago, when I gave that gift, I do not know of any bad destination. This is the fruit of half a cloth.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt away… the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano kaniṭṭhabhātaraṃ tato kammato nivattetukāmo tasmiṃyeva kamme abhirataṃ disvā taṃ codento –

But having attained arahantship, wishing to turn his younger brother away from that action, and seeing him still delighting in that very action, he admonished him thus:

145.

145.

“Accayanti [V 1.0289] ahorattā, jīvitaṃ uparujjhati;

Āyu khīyati maccānaṃ, kunnadīnaṃva odakaṃ.

“Days and nights pass away, life ceases; the lifespan of mortals dwindles, like water in small streams.”

146.

146.

“Atha pāpāni kammāni, karaṃ bālo na bujjhati;

Pacchāssa kaṭukaṃ hoti, vipāko hissa pāpako”ti. –

“Then the fool, doing evil deeds, does not understand; later it is bitter for him, for his result is indeed evil.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha accayantīti atikkamanti, lahuṃ lahuṃ apagacchantīti attho. Ahorattāti rattindivā. Jīvitaṃ uparujjhatīti jīvitindriyañca khaṇikanirodhavasena nirujjhati. Vuttañhi “khaṇe khaṇe, tvaṃ bhikkhu, jāyasi ca jiyyasi ca miyyasi ca cavasi ca upapajjasi cā”ti. Āyu khīyati maccānanti maritabbasabhāvattā maccāti laddhanāmānaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyu “yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti (dī. ni. 2.91; saṃ. ni. 2.143; a. ni. 7.74) evaṃ paricchinnakālaparamāyu khīyati khayañca sambhedañca gacchati, yathā kiṃ? Kunnadīnaṃva odakaṃ yathā nāma kunnadīnaṃ pabbateyyānaṃ khuddakanadīnaṃ udakaṃ ciraṃ na tiṭṭhati, lahutaraṃ khīyati, āgatamattaṃyeva vigacchati, evaṃ sattānaṃ āyu lahutaraṃ khīyati khayaṃ gacchati. Ettha ca udakameva “odaka”nti vuttaṃ, yathā manoyeva mānasanti.

Here, ‘accayanti’ means they pass by; the meaning is they go away very quickly. ‘Ahorattā’ refers to night and day. ‘Jīvitaṃ uparujjhati’ means the life faculty ceases by way of momentary cessation. For it has been said: “Moment by moment, O monk, you are born, you age, you die, you pass away, and you arise.” The life of mortals diminishes—‘maccānaṃ’ refers to the life of these beings who are called ‘mortals’ because they are of a nature to die. Their maximum lifespan, defined as “whoever lives long, lives a hundred years or a little more” (Dī. Ni. 2.91; Saṃ. Ni. 2.143; A. Ni. 7.74), thus having a limited duration, diminishes and comes to destruction and dissolution. Like what? Like the water of small streams: just as the water of small mountain streams does not remain for long, swiftly diminishes, and disappears as soon as it arrives, so too the lifespan of beings swiftly diminishes and comes to destruction. And here, ‘udaka’ itself is said as ‘odaka,’ just as ‘mano’ is ‘mānasa’.

Atha [M 1.0339] pāpāni kammāni, karaṃ bālo na bujjhatīti evaṃ saṃsāre aniccepi samāne bālo lobhavasena vā kodhavasena vā pāpāni kammāni karoti, karontopi na bujjhati, pāpaṃ karonto ca “pāpaṃ karomī”ti abujjhanako nāma natthi, “imassa kammassa evarūpo dukkho vipāko”ti pana ajānanato “na bujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Pacchāssa kaṭukaṃ hotīti yadipi pāpassa kammassa āyūhanakkhaṇe “imassa kammassa evarūpo vipāko”ti na bujjhati, tato pacchā pana nirayādīsu nibbattassa [P 2.0024] assa bālassa kaṭukaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ dukkhameva hoti. Vipāko hissa pāpako yasmā assa pāpakammassa nāma vipāko pāpako nihīno aniṭṭho evāti. Imaṃ pana ovādaṃ sutvā therassa kaniṭṭhabhātā rājānaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva sadatthaṃ nipphādesi.

“Then the fool, doing evil deeds, does not understand.” Thus, even though saṃsāra is impermanent, the fool, driven by greed or hatred, commits evil deeds, and even while doing so, he does not understand. For there is no one who commits evil and does not know, “I am committing evil.” But it is said, “He does not understand,” because he does not know, “This deed will have such a painful result.” Later, it becomes bitter for him. Even though at the moment of accumulating the evil deed, he does not understand, “This deed will have such a result,” later, when that fool is reborn in hell or other miserable states, it becomes bitter, unpleasant, and painful for him. For the result of his evil deed is indeed evil, inferior, and undesirable. However, having heard this advice, the elder’s younger brother, after taking leave of the king, went forth and soon accomplished his own welfare.

Heraññakānittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Heraññakāni is concluded.

4. Somamittattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Somamitta

Parittaṃ [V 1.0290] dārunti āyasmato somamittattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto buddhaguṇe sutvā pasannamānaso ekadivasaṃ kiṃsukarukkhaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā pupphāni gahetvā satthāraṃ uddissa ākāse khipitvā pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bārāṇasiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā somamittoti laddhanāmo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā vimalena nāma therena kataparicayattā abhiṇhaṃ tassa santikaṃ gacchanto dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane laddhappasādo pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado vattapaṭivattaṃ pūrento vicarati. Vimalatthero pana kusīto middhabahulo rattindivaṃ vītināmeti. Somamitto “kusītaṃ nāma nissāya ko guṇo”ti taṃ pahāya mahākassapattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa ovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.25-30) –

The verse ‘Parittaṃ dāru…’ is by the Venerable Elder Somamitta. What is its origin? This elder, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a family during the time of the Buddha Sikhī. Having attained maturity, he heard the virtues of the Buddha and, with a joyful mind, one day saw a kiṃsuka tree in bloom. He plucked its flowers and, dedicating them to the Master, scattered them in the air as an offering. By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī and was named Somamitta. Having mastered the three Vedas, he became acquainted with an elder named Vimala. Frequently going to him, he heard the Dhamma, gained faith in the Dispensation, went forth, and having received the higher ordination, wandered about fulfilling his duties. However, the Elder Vimala was lazy and very drowsy, and thus passed his days and nights. Somamitta thought, ‘What good is there in relying on a lazy person?’ Abandoning him, he approached the Elder Mahākassapa. Abiding by his advice, he established insight, and before long was established in Arahantship. As it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 2.50.25-30):

“Kiṃsukaṃ [M 1.0340] pupphitaṃ disvā, paggahetvāna añjaliṃ;

Buddhaseṭṭhaṃ saritvāna, ākāse abhipūjayiṃ.

“Having seen the kiṃsuka tree in bloom, I raised my hands in añjali; Remembering the Supreme Buddha, I worshipped him in the air.”

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-performed deed, and by my aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one eons ago, for the deed I performed then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

“My defilements are burnt away, all existences are uprooted; like a great elephant that has broken its bonds, I dwell taintless.”

“Svāgataṃ vata me āsi, mama buddhassa santike;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“Welcome indeed was my coming to the Buddha’s presence; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimalattheraṃ ovādena tajjento –

Having attained Arahantship, he then admonished the Elder Vimala with this advice:

147.

147.

“Parittaṃ dārumāruyha, yathā sīde mahaṇṇave;

Evaṃ kusītamāgamma, sādhujīvīpi sīdati;

Tasmā taṃ parivajjeyya, kusītaṃ hīnavīriyaṃ.

“Just as one who boards a small log sinks in the great ocean, so even one of good livelihood sinks by associating with the lazy. Therefore, one should avoid that lazy person of deficient energy.”

148.

148.

“Pavivittehi ariyehi, pahitattehi jhāyibhi;

Niccaṃ āraddhavīriyehi, paṇḍitehi sahāvase”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“One should dwell with the noble ones who are secluded, resolute, meditative, ever energetic, and wise.” Thus he spoke these two verses.
