Tattha [V 1.0291] parittaṃ dārumāruyha, yathā sīde mahaṇṇaveti pesalopi kulaputto kusītaṃ alasapuggalaṃ nissāya sīdati saṃsāre patati, na tassa pāraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati. Yasmā [P 2.0025] etadevaṃ, tasmā taṃ adhikusaladhammavasena sīsaṃ anukkhipitvā kucchitaṃ sīdanato kusītaṃ vīriyārambhābhāvato hīnavīriyaṃ puggalaṃ sabbathā vajjeyya, na tassa diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjeyyāti attho.

Herein, ‘Just as one who boards a small log sinks in the great ocean’ means that even an amiable son of good family, by relying on a lazy, indolent person, sinks, falls into saṃsāra, and does not reach the far shore, Nibbāna. Since this is so, therefore, one should in every way avoid that person who is ‘lazy’ (kusītaṃ) because he sinks wretchedly, not lifting his head with respect to higher wholesome states, and who is ‘of deficient energy’ (hīnavīriyaṃ) due to the absence of initiating effort. One should not follow his example—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya gāthāya kosajje ādīnavaṃ dassetvā idāni vīriyārambhe ānisaṃse dassetuṃ “pavivittehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassattho [M 1.0341] – ye pana kāyavivekasambhavena pavivittā, tato eva kilesehi ārakattā ariyā, nibbānaṃ patipesitattatāya pahitattā ārammaṇūpanijjhānavasena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānavasena ca jhāyino, sabbakālaṃ paggahitavīriyatāya āraddhavīriyā, lokiyalokuttarabhedāya paññāya samannāgatattā paṇḍitā, tehiyeva saha āvaseyya sadatthaṃ nipphādetukāmo saṃvaseyyāti. Taṃ sutvā vimalatthero saṃviggamānaso vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sadatthaṃ ārādhesi. Svāyamattho parato āgamissati.

Thus, having shown the dangers of laziness in the verse based on the individual, now, to show the benefits of initiating effort, the verse beginning ‘With the secluded’ was spoken. Its meaning is: those who are secluded by virtue of bodily seclusion, and thus are noble ones because they are far removed from defilements; because they have sent forth their minds towards Nibbāna, they are resolute; meditators by way of contemplating the object and contemplating the characteristics; being always of aroused energy, they are energetic; wise due to being endowed with wisdom that distinguishes between the mundane and the supramundane. One who wishes to accomplish his own goal should dwell, associating with them. Hearing this, the Elder Vimala, with a mind stirred to urgency, established insight and attained his own goal. This matter will come up again later.

Somamittattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Somamitta is concluded.

5. Sabbamittattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sabbamitta

Jano janamhi sambaddhoti āyasmato sabbamittattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito dvānavute kappe tissassa bhagavato kāle nesādakule nibbattitvā vanacāriko hutvā vane mige vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādanto jīvati. Athassa bhagavā anuggaṇhanatthaṃ vasanaṭṭhānasamīpe tīṇi padacetiyāni dassetvā pakkāmi. So atītakāle sammāsambuddhesu kataparicayattā cakkaṅkitāni disvā pasannamānaso koraṇḍapupphehi pūjaṃ katvā tena puññakammena tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, sabbamittotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharanto vassaṃ upagantvā vuṭṭhavasso bhagavantaṃ vandituṃ sāvatthiṃ gacchanto antarāmagge māgavikehi oḍḍite pāse migapotakaṃ baddhaṃ addasa. Mātā panassa migī pāsaṃ appaviṭṭhāpi puttasinehena dūraṃ na gacchati, maraṇabhayena pāsasamīpampi na upagacchati migapotako ca bhīto ito cito ca parivattento karuṇaṃ vilapati, taṃ disvā thero[V 1.0292], “aho sattānaṃ snehahetukaṃ dukkha”nti gacchanto tato paraṃ sambahule core ekaṃ [M 1.0342] purisaṃ jīvagāhaṃ gahetvā [P 2.0026] palālaveṇiyā sarīraṃ veṭhetvā jhāpente, tañca mahāviravaṃ viravantaṃ disvā tadubhayaṃ nissāya sañjātasaṃvego tesaṃ corānaṃ suṇantānaṃyeva –

The verse ‘Jano janamhi sambaddho…’ is by the Venerable Elder Sabbamitta. What is its origin? This elder, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of past Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a hunter’s family ninety-two eons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Living as a forest wanderer, he killed deer in the forest and lived by eating their flesh. Then, to favor him, the Blessed One displayed three footprint shrines near his dwelling place and departed. Due to his past familiarity with Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, upon seeing the wheel-marked footprints, his mind became joyful. He made an offering with koraṇḍa flowers. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Wandering through successive happy destinations, in this Buddha’s Dispensation he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthi, and his name was Sabbamitta. Having attained maturity, he saw the Buddha’s majesty at the dedication of Jetavana. Having gained faith, he went forth, took up a meditation subject, and dwelled in the forest. After completing the rains retreat, he set out for Sāvatthi to pay homage to the Blessed One. Along the way, he saw a young deer caught in a snare set by hunters. Its mother, the doe, though not caught in the snare, could not go far due to her love for her offspring, nor could she approach the snare due to fear of death. The fawn, terrified, kept turning this way and that, crying pitifully. Seeing this, the Elder thought, ‘Alas, how beings suffer because of affection!’ Proceeding further, he saw a group of bandits seizing a man alive, wrapping his body in a straw rope and setting him on fire, while he screamed loudly. Witnessing both scenes, the Elder was struck with urgency. Even as those bandits listened, he spoke:

149.

149.

“Jano janamhi sambaddho, janamevassito jano;

Jano janena heṭhīyati, heṭheti ca jano janaṃ.

“A person is bound to a person, a person relies on a person; a person is harmed by a person, and a person harms a person.”

150.

150.

“Ko hi tassa janenattho, janena janitena vā;

Janaṃ ohāya gacchaṃ taṃ, heṭhayitvā bahuṃ jana”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“What use are people to one, or being born of people? I am going forth, leaving people behind, having harmed many beings.” Thus he spoke these two verses.

Tattha janoti andhabālajano. Janamhīti aññe jane. Sambaddhoti taṇhābandhanena baddho. “Ayaṃ me putto, mātā”tiādinā paṭibaddho. Ayameva vā pāṭho, “ime maṃ posenti, ahaṃ ime nissāya jīvāmī”ti paṭibaddhacittoti attho. Janamevassito janoti “ayaṃ me putto, dhītā”tiādinā aññameva janaṃ añño jano assito taṇhāya allīno pariggayha ṭhito. Jano janena heṭhīyati, heṭheti ca jano jananti kammassakatāya yathābhūtāvabodhassa ca abhāvato ajjhupekkhanaṃ akatvā lobhavasena yathā jano janaṃ assito, evaṃ dosavasena jano janena heṭhīyati vibādhīyati. “Tayidaṃ mayhaṃva upari heṭhanaphalavasena paripatissatī”ti ajānanto heṭheti ca jano janaṃ.

Herein, ‘person’ (jano) means the blind, foolish person. ‘To a person’ (janamhi) means to other people. ‘Bound’ (sambaddho) means bound by the bond of craving, attached by thinking, ‘This is my son, my mother,’ and so on. Or this is the reading: ‘These support me, I live relying on them’—the meaning is having an attached mind. ‘A person relies on a person’ (janamevassito jano) means one person, thinking, ‘This is my son, my daughter,’ and so on, relies on another person, clinging through craving, grasping and remaining. ‘A person is harmed by a person, and a person harms a person’ (jano janena heṭhīyati, heṭheti ca jano janaṃ) means that due to the absence of understanding ownership of kamma and of seeing things as they truly are, by not practicing equanimity, just as a person relies on another through greed, so through aversion a person is harmed and oppressed by another. Not knowing, ‘This very thing will fall back upon me as the fruit of oppression,’ a person harms another person.

Ko hi tassa janenatthoti tassa aññajanassa aññena janena taṇhāvasena assitena dosavasena heṭhitena vā ko attho. Janena janitena vāti mātāpitā hutvā tena aññena janena janitena vā ko attho. Janaṃ ohāya gacchaṃ taṃ, heṭhayitvā bahuṃ jananti yasmā saṃsāre carato janassa ayamevānurūpā paṭipatti, tasmā taṃ janaṃ, tassa ca bādhikā yā sā taṇhā ca, yo ca so doso eva bahuṃ janaṃ bādhayitvā ṭhito, tañca ohāya sabbaso pahāya pariccajitvā [M 1.0343] gacchaṃ, tehi anupaddutaṃ ṭhānaṃ gaccheyyaṃ pāpuṇeyyanti attho. Evaṃ [P 2.0027] pana vatvā thero tāvadeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattamapāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.15-24) –

‘What use is there to him in people?’ (ko hi tassa janenattho) means what use is there to that other person in another person, relied upon due to craving, or harmed due to aversion? ‘Or in being born of people?’ (janena janitena vā) means what use is there in being born of another person, having been a mother or father? ‘Leaving those people behind, going forth, after harming many people’ (janaṃ ohāya gacchaṃ taṃ, heṭhayitvā bahuṃ janaṃ) means: since this is the appropriate practice for a person wandering in saṃsāra, therefore, abandoning those people, and also that craving which is their affliction, and that aversion which stands oppressing many people—having completely abandoned and relinquished these, going forth, the meaning is: ‘May I reach a place undisturbed by them.’ Having said this, the Elder immediately intensified his insight and attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 2.50.15-24):

“Vanakammiko pure āsiṃ, pitumātumatenahaṃ;

Pasumārena jīvāmi, kusalaṃ me na vijjati.

“Formerly I was a forest worker, by the will of my father and mother; I lived by slaughtering animals, no wholesome deed was found in me.”

“Mama [V 1.0293] āsayasāmantā, tisso lokagganāyako;

Padāni tīṇi dassesi, anukampāya cakkhumā.

“Near my abode, Tissa, the Leader of the world, the All-Seeing One, showed three footprints out of compassion.”

“Akkante ca pade disvā, tissanāmassa satthuno;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, pade cittaṃ pasādayiṃ.

“And seeing the footprints of the Master named Tissa, delighted, with a joyful mind, I made my mind serene at the footprints.”

“Koraṇḍaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, pādapaṃ dharaṇīruhaṃ;

Sakosakaṃ gahetvāna, padaseṭṭhamapūjayiṃ.

“Seeing the koraṇḍa tree in bloom, a tree rooted in the earth, taking it with its bud, I worshipped the supreme footprint.”

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-performed deed, and by my aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonupapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Koraṇḍakachavi homi, suppabhāso bhavāmahaṃ.

“In whatever womb I am reborn, whether divine or human, I have the complexion of a koraṇḍaka flower; I am exceedingly radiant.”

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, padapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-two aeons ago, when I performed that deed, I do not recall a bad rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the footprint.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Te pana corā therassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā saṃvegajātā pabbajitvā dhammānudhammaṃ paṭipajjiṃsūti.

But those thieves, having heard the Dhamma from the Elder, were stirred by a sense of urgency, went forth, and practiced in accordance with the Dhamma.

Sabbamittattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sabbamitta is concluded.

6. Mahākāḷattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākāḷa

Kāḷī [M 1.0344] itthīti āyasmato mahākāḷattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kenacideva karaṇīyena araññaṃ gato tattha aññatarassa rukkhassa sākhāya olambamānaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ disvā “ariyaddhajo olambatī”ti pasannacitto kiṅkaṇipupphāni gahetvā paṃsukūlaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde setabyanagare satthavāhakule nibbattitvā mahākāḷoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā vāṇijjavasena sāvatthiṃ gato ekamantaṃ sakaṭasatthaṃ nivesetvā addhānaparissamaṃ vinodetvā attano parisāya saddhiṃ nisinno sāyanhasamayaṃ gandhamālādihatthe upāsake jetavanaṃ gacchante disvā sayampi tehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā sosānikaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāya susāne vasati. Athekadivasaṃ kāḷī nāma ekā itthī chavaḍāhikā therassa kammaṭṭhānatthāya aciramatasarīraṃ ubho satthī [V 1.0294] bhinditvā ubho ca bāhū bhinditvā sīsañca dadhithālakaṃ viya bhinditvā sabbaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ sambandhameva katvā therassa oloketuṃ yogyaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Thero taṃ disvā attānaṃ ovadanto –

The verse of the Venerable Mahākāḷa begins with 'Kāḷī, the woman.' What is its origin? This Elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a respectable family ninety-one aeons ago. Having come of age, he went to the forest for some business. There, seeing a discarded-cloth robe hanging from the branch of a tree, he thought, 'The banner of the Noble Ones is hanging,' and with a faithful mind, he took kiṅkaṇi flowers and offered them to the robe. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in the city of Setabyā in the household of a caravan leader. He became known as Mahākāḷa and, having come of age, lived the household life. Taking goods with five hundred carts, he went to Sāvatthī for trade. Having parked the caravan to one side and relieved the fatigue of the journey, he sat with his retinue. In the evening, seeing lay devotees going to Jetavana with perfumes and garlands in hand, he too went to the monastery with them. Hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and went forth. He undertook the ascetic practice of dwelling in charnel grounds and lived in a cemetery. One day, a woman named Kāḷī, a charnel ground attendant, for the elder's meditation subject, took a recently deceased body, broke both thighs, broke both arms, and broke the head like a curd bowl, and having arranged all its major and minor limbs so they were still connected, placed it in a suitable spot for the elder to observe and sat to one side. Seeing it, the elder admonished himself:

151.

151.

“Kāḷī itthī brahatī dhaṅkarūpā, satthiñca bhetvā aparañca satthiṃ;

Bāhañca bhetvā aparañca bāhaṃ, sīsañca bhetvā dadhithālakaṃva;

Esā nisinnā abhisandahitvā.

“Kālī, the woman, huge and crow-like in form, having broken one thigh and then another, having broken one arm and then another, and having broken the head like a curd-bowl, she sits there, having reassembled them.”

152.

152.

“Yo [M 1.0345][P 2.0028] ve avidvā upadhiṃ karoti, punappunaṃ dukkhamupeti mando;

Tasmā pajānaṃ upadhiṃ na kayirā, māhaṃ puna bhinnasiro sayissa”nti. –

“The fool, unknowing, makes an acquisition; again and again he comes to suffering. Therefore, knowing, one should not make an acquisition, lest I lie down again with a broken head.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tattha kāḷīti tassā nāmaṃ, kāḷavaṇṇattā vā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Brahatīti mahāsarīrā ārohapariṇāhavatī. Dhaṅkarūpāti kāḷavaṇṇattā eva kākasadisarūpā. Satthiñca bhetvāti matasarīrassa satthiṃ jaṇṇubhedanena bhañjitvā. Aparañca satthinti itarañca satthiṃ bhañjitvā. Bāhañca bhetvāti bāhaṭṭhiñca aggabāhaṭṭhāneyeva bhañjitvā. Sīsañca bhetvā dadhithālakaṃvāti matasarīrassa sīsaṃ bhinditvā bhinnattā eva leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paggharantaṃ dadhithālakaṃ viya, paggharantaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ katvāti attho. Esā nisinnā abhisandahitvāti chinnabhinnāvayavaṃ matasarīraṃ te avayave yathāṭhāneyeva ṭhapanena sandahitvā sahitaṃ katvā maṃsāpaṇaṃ pasārentī viya esā nisinnā.

Therein, 'Kālī' is her name, or she is so called because of her dark complexion. 'Brahatī' means large-bodied, possessing height and girth. 'Dhaṅkarūpā' means having a crow-like appearance due to her dark color. 'Satthiñca bhetvā' means having broken the thigh of the dead body by breaking it at the knee. 'Aparañca satthiṃ' means having broken the other thigh as well. 'Bāhañca bhetvā' means having broken the arm bone, specifically at the upper arm. 'Sīsañca bhetvā dadhithālakaṃva' means having broken the head of the dead body so that, being broken, it is like a curd-bowl from which the contents ooze when struck by clods, sticks, and so on; the meaning is, having made the brain ooze out. 'Esā nisinnā abhisandahitvā' means having joined the cut and broken limbs of the dead body by placing those limbs back in their proper positions, thus putting it together, she sits there as if spreading out a butcher's stall.

Yo ve avidvā upadhiṃ karotīti yo imāya upaṭṭhāpitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ disvāpi avidvā akusalo kammaṭṭhānaṃ chaḍḍetvā ayonisomanasikārena kilesūpadhiṃ uppādeti, so mando mandapañño saṃsārassa anativattanato punappunaṃ aparāparaṃ nirayādīsu dukkhaṃ upeti. Tasmā pajānaṃ upadhiṃ na kayirāti tasmāti yasmā cetadevaṃ, tasmā. Pajānaṃ upadhinti “idha yaṃ dukkhaṃ sambhotī”ti pajānanto yoniso manasikaronto kilesūpadhiṃ na kayirā na uppādeyya. Kasmā? Māhaṃ puna bhinnasiro sayissanti yathayidaṃ matasarīraṃ bhinnasarīraṃ sayati, evaṃ kilesūpadhīhi saṃsāre punappunaṃ uppattiyā kaṭasivaḍḍhako hutvā bhinnasiro ahaṃ mā sayissanti. Evaṃ vadanto eva thero vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.50.8-14) –

The phrase 'One who, being ignorant, makes an acquisition' means: one who, being ignorant and unskillful, even after seeing this meditation subject presented by her, abandons the meditation subject and, through unwise attention, gives rise to the acquisitions of defilements—that fool, of weak wisdom, because of not transcending saṃsāra, repeatedly undergoes suffering again and again in hell and other realms. The phrase 'Therefore, knowing, one should not make an acquisition' means: since this is so, therefore, one who knows, understanding that suffering arises in this world and reflecting wisely, should not create or give rise to the acquisitions of defilements. Why? 'Lest I lie down again with a broken head' means: just as this dead body lies with a broken body, so too, due to the acquisitions of defilements, by being reborn again and again in saṃsāra, having become one who increases the charnel ground, may I not lie with a broken head. Speaking thus, the Elder intensified his insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.50.8-14):

“Himavantassāvidūre[M 1.0346][V 1.0295], udaṅgaṇo nāma pabbato;

Tatthaddasaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, dumaggamhi vilambitaṃ.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Udaṅgaṇa. There I saw a discarded-cloth robe hanging on a treetop.”

“Tīṇi kiṅkaṇipupphāni, ocinitvānahaṃ tadā;

Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, paṃsukūlamapūjayiṃ.

“Having picked three kiṅkaṇi flowers then, with a joyful and delighted mind, I worshipped the discarded-cloth robe.”

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my volitional aspirations, having left the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pūjitvā arahaddhajaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I performed that deed, I do not recall any bad rebirth, having worshipped the banner of the Arahant.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Mahākāḷattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākāḷa is concluded.

7. Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa

Bahū [P 2.0029] sapatte labhatīti āyasmato tissattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto piyadassissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto sippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane sālavane assamaṃ kāretvā vasati. Bhagavā tassa anuggaṇhanatthaṃ assamassa avidūre sālavane nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. So assamato nikkhamitvā phalāphalatthāya gacchanto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso cattāro daṇḍe ṭhapetvā bhagavato upari pupphitāhi sālasākhāhi sākhāmaṇḍapaṃ katvā sattāhaṃ navanavehi sālapupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjento aṭṭhāsi buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ avijahanto. Satthā sattāhassa accayena nirodhato vuṭṭhahitvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ cintesi. Tāvadeva satasahassamattā khīṇāsavā satthāraṃ parivāresuṃ. Bhagavā tassa bhāviniṃ sampattiṃ vibhāvento anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devaloke nibbattitvā aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde [M 1.0347] rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā tissoti laddhanāmo vayappatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū hutvā pañcamattāni māṇavakasatāni mante vācento lābhaggayasaggappatto hutvā satthu rājagahagamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.190-220) –

"One gains many enemies"—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Tissa. What is its origin? This one too, having made his aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences as a condition for release, was born into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī. Having attained understanding and perfected the various arts, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life. He went forth into the ascetic life, had a hermitage built in a sāla forest, and dwelt there. The Blessed One, wishing to favor him, entered the attainment of cessation in the sāla forest not far from his hermitage and sat there. Emerging from his hermitage to gather various fruits, he saw the Blessed One. With a serene mind, he set up four posts, made a pavilion of flowering sāla branches above the Blessed One, and for seven days he stood honoring the Blessed One with ever-fresh sāla flowers, never relinquishing the joy that has the Buddha as its object. After seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and brought to mind the community of monks. Immediately, a hundred thousand destroyers of the taints surrounded the Teacher. The Blessed One, making clear his future accomplishment, spoke words of appreciation and departed. Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the deva realm. Wandering only in happy destinies, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family in Rājagaha. Named Tissa, upon coming of age, he became a master of the three Vedas and taught the sacred texts to five hundred young brahmins. He attained the pinnacle of gain and fame. When the Teacher came to Rājagaha, he saw the Buddha’s power, gained faith, and went forth. Establishing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Ajjhogāhetvā [V 1.0296] sālavanaṃ, sukato assamo mama;

Sālapupphehi sañchanno, vasāmi vipine tadā.

"Having entered deep into the sāla forest, my hermitage was well-made; covered with sāla blossoms, I lived in the woods then.

“Piyadassī ca bhagavā, sayambhū aggapuggalo;

Vivekakāmo sambuddho, sālavanamupāgami.

"And the Blessed One Piyadassī, the Self-become, the supreme person, the Fully Enlightened One desiring seclusion, approached the sāla grove.

“Assamā abhinikkhamma, pavanaṃ agamāsahaṃ;

Mūlaphalaṃ gavesanto, āhiṇḍāmi vane tadā.

"Leaving the hermitage, I went into the forest; seeking roots and fruits, I wandered in the woods at that time.

“Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, piyadassiṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Sunisinnaṃ samāpannaṃ, virocantaṃ mahāvane.

"There I saw the Fully Enlightened One, Piyadassī of great fame, well-seated, absorbed in attainment, shining in the great forest.

“Catudaṇḍe ṭhapetvāna, buddhassa uparī ahaṃ;

Maṇḍapaṃ sukataṃ katvā, sālapupphehi chādayiṃ.

"Having placed four posts above the Buddha, I made a well-constructed pavilion and covered it with sāla flowers.

“Sattāhaṃ dhārayitvāna, maṇḍapaṃ sālachāditaṃ;

Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, buddhaseṭṭhamavandahaṃ.

"Having maintained the sāla-covered pavilion for seven days, there, with a serene mind, I paid homage to the best of Buddhas.

“Bhagavā tamhi samaye, vuṭṭhahitvā samādhito;

Yugamattaṃ pekkhamāno, nisīdi purisuttamo.

"The Blessed One at that time, rising from concentration, gazing a yoke's length before him, sat down, the supreme among men.

“Sāvako varuṇo nāma, piyadassissa satthuno;

Vasīsatasahassehi, upagacchi vināyakaṃ.

"A disciple named Varuṇa, of the Teacher Piyadassī, approached the Leader with a hundred thousand who had mastery.

“Piyadassī ca bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvāna, sitaṃ pātukarī jino.

"And the Blessed One Piyadassī, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, having sat amidst the community of monks, the Victor revealed a smile.

“Anuruddho upaṭṭhāko, piyadassissa satthuno;

Ekaṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā, apucchittha mahāmuniṃ.

"Anuruddha, the attendant of the Teacher Piyadassī, arranging his robe over one shoulder, asked the Great Sage:

“Ko nu kho bhagavā hetu, sitakammassa satthuno;

Kāraṇe vijjamānamhi, satthā pātukare sitaṃ.

"‘What, Blessed One, is the cause for the Teacher’s act of smiling? When a reason exists, the Teacher reveals a smile.’

“Sattāhaṃ [M 1.0348] sālacchadanaṃ, yo me dhāresi māṇavo;

Tassa kammaṃ saritvāna, sitaṃ pātukariṃ ahaṃ.

"‘The young man who maintained a sāla covering for me for seven days—remembering his deed, I revealed a smile.

“Anokāsaṃ na passāmi, yattha puññaṃ vipaccati;

Devaloke manusse vā, okāsova na sammati.

"‘I see no lack of opportunity for merit to ripen; whether in the deva world or among humans, the opportunity does not cease.

“Devaloke vasantassa, puññakammasamaṅgino;

Yāvatā parisā tassa, sālacchannā bhavissati.

"‘For one dwelling in the deva realm, endowed with meritorious deeds, his entire assembly will be covered by sāla flowers.

“Tattha dibbehi naccehi, gītehi vāditehi ca;

Ramissati sadā santo, puññakammasamāhito.

"‘There, with divine dances, songs, and music, the peaceful one, concentrated on his meritorious deeds, will always rejoice.

“Yāvatā parisā tassa, gandhagandhī bhavissati;

Sālassa pupphavasso ca, pavassissati tāvade.

"‘His entire assembly will be fragrant with scents, and a shower of sāla flowers will rain down at that time.

“Tato [V 1.0297] cutoyaṃ manujo, mānusaṃ āgamissati;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, sabbakālaṃ dharissati.

"‘Having passed away from there, this person will come to the human realm; here also, he will always have a sāla covering.

“Idha naccañca gītañca, sammatāḷasamāhitaṃ;

Parivāressanti maṃ niccaṃ, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"‘Here, dance and song, accompanied by proper rhythm, will constantly surround me. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Uggacchante ca sūriye, sālavassaṃ pavassati;

Puññakammena saṃyuttaṃ, vassate sabbakālikaṃ.

"‘As the sun rises, a rain of sāla flowers will fall; connected to his meritorious deed, it will rain perpetually.

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

"‘In eighteen hundred aeons, born in the Okkāka lineage, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will be in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

"‘He will be an heir to his Dhamma, a legitimate son, created by the Dhamma; having fully understood all the taints, he will, being taintless, attain Nibbāna.

“Dhammaṃ abhisamentassa, sālacchannaṃ bhavissati;

Citake jhāyamānassa, chadanaṃ tattha hessati.

"‘For him who is fully understanding the Dhamma, there will be a sāla covering; for him being cremated on the pyre, that will be his covering there.

“Vipākaṃ kittayitvāna, piyadassī mahāmuni;

Parisāya dhammaṃ desesi, tappento dhammavuṭṭhiyā.

"Having declared the fruition, the great sage Piyadassī taught the Dhamma to the assembly, delighting them with a rain of Dhamma.

“Tiṃsakappāni devesu, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Saṭṭhi ca sattakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

"‘For thirty aeons I reigned as king among the devas, and sixty-seven times I was a wheel-turning monarch.

“Devalokā [M 1.0349] idhāgantvā, labhāmi vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, maṇḍapassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

"‘Having come here from the deva world, I obtain abundant happiness; here too, the sāla covering is the fruit of that pavilion.

“Ayaṃ pacchimako mayhaṃ, carimo vattate bhavo;

Idhāpi sālacchadanaṃ, hessati sabbakālikaṃ.

"‘This is my last existence, my final becoming is proceeding; here too, a sāla covering will be mine for all time.

“Mahāmuniṃ tosayitvā, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Pattomhi acalaṃ ṭhānaṃ, hitvā jayaparājayaṃ.

"‘Having pleased the Great Sage, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans, I have attained the unshakable state, having abandoned victory and defeat.

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"‘Eighteen hundred aeons ago, I honored the Buddha; I know of no bad rebirth. This is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"‘My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.’"

So arahattaṃ pana patvā visesato lābhaggayasaggappatto ahosi. Tattha keci puthujjanabhikkhū therassa lābhasakkāraṃ disvā bālabhāvena asahanākāraṃ pavedesuṃ. Thero taṃ ñatvā lābhasakkāre ādīnavaṃ tattha attano alaggabhāvañca pakāsento –

Having attained arahantship, he became especially eminent, having reached the pinnacle of gain and fame. There, some ordinary monks, seeing the elder's gain and honor, displayed their immaturity by showing intolerance. Knowing this, the elder, proclaiming the danger in gain and honor and his own non-attachment to them, said:

153.

153.

“Bahū sapatte labhati, muṇḍo saṅghāṭipāruto;

Lābhī annassa pānassa, vatthassa sayanassa ca.

"The shaven-headed one, clad in the patchwork robe, obtains many enemies, being a recipient of food, drink, clothing, and lodging.

154.

154.

“Etamādīnavaṃ [V 1.0298] ñatvā, sakkāresu mahabbhayaṃ;

Appalābho anavassuto, sato bhikkhu paribbaje”ti. –

"‘Having known this danger, this great fear in honors, a monk of little gain, unattached, should wander mindfully.’"

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tassattho [P 2.0030] – sikhampi asesetvā muṇḍitakesatāya muṇḍo, chinditvā saṅghāṭitakāsāvadhāritāya saṅghāṭipāruto, evaṃ vevaṇṇiyaṃ ajjhupagato parāyattavuttiko pabbajito sace annapānādīnaṃ lābhī hoti, sopi bahū sapatte labhati, tassa usūyantā bahū sambhavanti. Tasmā etaṃ evarūpaṃ lābhasakkāresu mahabbhayaṃ vipulabhayaṃ ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ viditvā appicchataṃ santosañca hadaye ṭhapetvā anavajjuppādassāpi uppannassa lābhassa parivajjanena appalābho, tato eva tattha taṇhāvassutābhāvena anavassuto, saṃsāre bhayassa ikkhanato bhinnakilesatāya vā bhikkhu santuṭṭhiṭṭhānīyassa satisampajaññassa [M 1.0350] vasena sato hutvā paribbaje careyya vihareyyāti. Taṃ sutvā te bhikkhū tāvadeva theraṃ khamāpesuṃ.

Its meaning is this: A monk who, having shaved off all his hair, is bald-headed, and having cut and stitched his robe, wears the patched-up cloth, thus having adopted an inferior appearance and living dependent on others—if such a one becomes a recipient of food, drink, and so forth, he too gains many enemies; many become envious of him. Therefore, knowing this great danger, this abundant peril, this drawback, this fault in gains and honors, one should establish contentment and fewness of wishes in the heart. Having little gain (by avoiding even blameless gains that have arisen), and being unattached (due to the absence of craving's outflow), or seeing fear in saṃsāra, or due to the destruction of defilements, a monk, being mindful by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension, which is a basis for contentment, should wander, conduct himself, and dwell. Hearing this, those monks immediately asked forgiveness of the elder.

Tissattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tissa is concluded.

8. Kimilattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kimila

Pācīnavaṃsadāyamhītiādikā āyasmato kimilattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Tassa pubbayogo saṃveguppatti pabbajjā ca ekakanipāte “abhisatto”ti gāthāya saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttāyeva. Tāya ca gāthāya therena attano visesādhigamassa kāraṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Idha pana adhigatavisesassa attano āyasmatā ca anuruddhena āyasmatā ca nandiyena saha samaggavāso dassitoti veditabbaṃ. Samaggavāsaṃ pana vasantā te yathā ca vasiṃsu, taṃ dassento –

Beginning with 'In the eastern bamboo grove' are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kimila. What is their origin? His prior history, the arising of spiritual urgency, and his going forth have already been stated in the commentary to the verse 'Abhisatto' in the Ekakanipāta. By that verse, the Elder showed the reason for his attainment of a special distinction. Here, however, it should be understood that, having attained distinction, he demonstrated his harmonious dwelling with the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Nandiya. And showing how they dwelt, living in harmony, he spoke:

155.

155.

“Pācīnavaṃsadāyamhi, sakyaputtā sahāyakā;

Pahāyānappake bhoge, uñche pattāgate ratā.

“In the eastern bamboo grove, the Sakyan sons, companions, having abandoned considerable wealth, delight in gleanings and what has come into the bowl.

156.

156.

“Āraddhavīriyā pahitattā, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā;

Ramanti dhammaratiyā, hitvāna lokiyaṃ rati”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“With energy roused, their minds resolute, ever striving with firm effort, they delight in the joy of the Dhamma, having abandoned worldly pleasures.” – he spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha pācīnavaṃsadāyamhīti pācīnavaṃsanāmake rakkhitagopite sahaparicchede vane. Tañhi vanaṃ [V 1.0299] gāmassa pācīnadisāyaṃ ṭhitattā vaṃsagumbaparikkhittattā ca “pācīnavaṃsadāyo”ti vutto, vaṃsavanabhāvena vāti. Sakyaputtāti [P 2.0031] anuruddhattherādayo sakyarājakumārā. Sahāyakāti saṃveguppattipabbajjāsamaṇadhammakaraṇasaṃvāsehi saha ayanato pavattanato sahāyakā. Pahāyānappake bhogeti uḷārena puññānubhāvena adhigate kulaparamparāgate ca mahante bhogakkhandhe chaḍḍetvā. “Sahāyānappake”tipi pāḷi. Uñche pattāgate ratāti uñchācariyāya ābhatattā [M 1.0351] uñche patte āgatattā pattāgate pattapariyāpanne ratā abhiratā, saṅghabhattādiatirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā jaṅghabalaṃ nissāya bhikkhācariyāya laddhena missakabhatteneva santuṭṭhāti attho.

There, 'in the eastern bamboo grove' means in a guarded and protected forest named Pācīnavaṃsa, within its own boundary. For that forest, being situated to the east of the village and surrounded by clumps of bamboo, is called 'Pācīnavaṃsadāya,' or because it is a bamboo forest. 'Sakyaputtā' (Sons of the Sakyans) refers to the Elder Anuruddha and other Sakyan princes. 'Sahāyakā' (companions) means those who were companions by virtue of their common going forth, arising of spiritual urgency, practice of ascetic duties, and living together. 'Pahāyānappake bhoge' (having abandoned not-insignificant wealth) means having abandoned great heaps of wealth acquired through the power of immense merit and inherited through family lineage. The reading 'sahāyānappake' is also found. 'Uñche pattāgate ratā' (delighting in gleanings and what has come into the bowl) means they delighted and rejoiced in gleanings brought by the practice of gleaning and in the food that had come into and was contained in the bowl. The meaning is that they were content only with mixed almsfood obtained through the almsround, relying on the strength of their legs, having rejected extra gains such as meals offered to the Saṅgha.

Āraddhavīriyāti uttamatthassa adhigamāya āditova pageva sampāditavīriyā. Pahitattāti ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena kālena kālaṃ samāpajjanena ca nibbānaṃ patipesitacittā. Niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamāti vattapaṭipattīsu diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānuyogena sabbakālaṃ asithilaparakkamā. Ramanti dhammaratiyā, hitvāna lokiyaṃ ratinti loke viditatāya lokapariyāpannatāya ca lokiyaṃ rūpārammaṇādiratiṃ pahāya maggapaññāya pajahitvā lokuttaradhammaratiyā aggaphalanibbānābhiratiyā ca ramanti abhiramantīti.

'Āraddhavīriyā' (with energy roused) means they had generated effort right from the beginning, even from the outset, for the attainment of the highest goal. 'Pahitattā' (with minds resolute) means their minds were sent forth towards Nibbāna by way of inclination, leaning, and tending, and by entering attainments from time to time. 'Niccaṃ daḷhaparakkamā' (ever striving with firm effort) means they were unremitting in effort at all times through engagement in the practice of duties and the cultivation of dwelling in happiness visible in this very life. 'Ramanti dhammaratiyā, hitvāna lokiyaṃ rati' (they delight in the joy of the Dhamma, having abandoned worldly joy) means having abandoned worldly joy, which is known in the world and involved with the world, such as joy associated with visible forms, etc., having abandoned it by means of the wisdom of the path, they delight and rejoice in the joy of the supramundane Dhamma and the supreme fruition of Nibbāna.

Kimilattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kimila is concluded.

9. Nandattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nanda

Ayoniso manasikārāti āyasmato nandattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavato santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pūjāsakkārabahulaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā, “ahampi anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa evarūpo sāvako bhaveyya”nti paṇidhānaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya devamanussesu saṃsaranto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle vinatāya nāma nadiyā mahanto kacchapo hutvā nibbatto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ nadiyā pāraṃ gantuṃ tīre ṭhitaṃ disvā sayaṃ bhagavantaṃ tāretukāmo satthu pādamūle nipajji[P 2.0032]. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhi. So haṭṭhatuṭṭho vegena sotaṃ chindanto sīghataraṃ paratīrameva pāpesi. Bhagavā tassa anumodanaṃ vadanto bhāviniṃ sampattiṃ kathetvā pakkāmi.

“Ayoniso manasikārā” (from unwise attention) is a verse of the Venerable Elder Nanda. What is its origin? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this being was born into a family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having come of age, he listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One. Seeing the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who guarded the sense doors, he himself also aspired to attain that same rank. He then offered a great almsgiving with abundant honor and offerings to the Blessed One and the community of monks, making the aspiration: “May I too, in the future, become such a disciple of a Buddha like you.” From that time onward, he wandered among devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn as a large turtle in a river named Vinatā. One day, seeing the Teacher standing on the bank of the river, intending to cross to the other side, he himself wished to ferry the Blessed One across. He lay down at the Teacher’s feet. The Teacher, discerning his intention, stepped onto his back. Overjoyed and thrilled, he swiftly cut through the current and quickly brought him to the far shore. The Blessed One, expressing appreciation, spoke of his future attainment and then departed.

So [M 1.0352][V 1.0300] tena puññakammena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ suddhodanamahārājassa putto hutvā mahāpajāpatiyā gotamiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase ñātisaṅghaṃ nandento jātoti nandotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa vayappattakāle satthā pavattavaradhammacakko lokānuggahaṃ karonto kapilavatthuṃ gantvā ñātisamāgame pokkharavassaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā vessantarajātakaṃ (jā. 2.22.1655 ādayo) kathetvā dutiyadivase piṇḍāya paviṭṭho “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”ti (dha. pa. 168) gāthāya pitaraṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā nivesanaṃ gantvā “dhammaṃ care sucarita”nti (dha. pa. 169) gāthāya mahāpajāpatiṃ sotāpattiphale rājānaṃ sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā tatiye divase nandakumārassa abhisekanivesanappavesanavivāhamaṅgalesu vattamānesu piṇḍāya pavisitvā nandakumārassa hatthe pattaṃ datvā maṅgalaṃ vatvā tassa hatthato pattaṃ agahetvāva vihāraṃ gato taṃ pattahatthaṃ vihāraṃ āgataṃ anicchamānaṃyeva pabbājetvā tathā pabbajitattāyeva anabhiratiyā pīḷitaṃ ñatvā upāyena tassa taṃ anabhiratiṃ vinodesi. So yoniso paṭisaṅkhāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.148-163) –

By that meritorious deed, wandering only among happy destinies, he was reborn in this Buddha-era in Kapilavatthu as the son of King Suddhodana, in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. On the day of his naming ceremony, his relatives named him Nanda, because he was born gladdening the assembly of relatives. When he came of age, the Teacher, setting in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma for the benefit of the world, went to Kapilavatthu. At the gathering of his relatives, he made the occasion of the 'lotus rain' and taught the Vessantara Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.1655, etc.). The next day, while going for alms, he recited the verse, “Arise, do not be heedless” (Dhp. 168), establishing his father in the fruit of stream-entry. Upon returning to the palace, he recited the verse, “Practice the Dhamma with good conduct” (Dhp. 169), establishing Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning. On the third day, during the ceremonies of Prince Nanda’s consecration, house-entry, and marriage, he entered for alms. He placed his bowl in Prince Nanda’s hands, spoke a blessing, and without taking the bowl back from his hand, went to the monastery. He then ordained that Prince Nanda, who had come to the monastery with the bowl in his hand, even though he was unwilling. Knowing that Nanda was afflicted by discontent due to having been ordained in that way, the Buddha skillfully dispelled his discontent. Reflecting wisely, Nanda developed insight and soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.49.148-163):

“Atthadassī tu bhagavā, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Vinatānadiyā tīraṃ, upāgacchi tathāgato.

“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-Born, Leader of the World, the Tathāgata, approached the bank of the Vinatā River.

“Udakā abhinikkhamma, kacchapo vārigocaro;

Buddhaṃ tāretukāmohaṃ, upesiṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Having emerged from the water, I, a turtle whose resort is the water, desiring to ferry the Buddha across, approached the Leader of the World.

“Abhirūhatu maṃ buddho, atthadassī mahāmuni;

Ahaṃ taṃ tārayissāmi, dukkhassantakaro tuvaṃ.

“May the Buddha, Atthadassī, the Great Sage, ascend upon me; I will ferry you across, you are the Ender of Suffering.

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya, atthadassī mahāyaso;

Abhirūhitvā me piṭṭhiṃ, aṭṭhāsi lokanāyako.

“Knowing my intention, Atthadassī, of great renown, the Leader of the World, having ascended upon my back, stood.

“Yato sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ;

Sukhaṃ me tādisaṃ natthi, phuṭṭhe pādatale yathā.

“Since I remember myself, since I attained understanding, there is no such happiness for me as when the sole of his foot was touched.”

“Uttaritvāna sambuddho, atthadassī mahāyaso;

Naditīramhi ṭhatvāna, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Having crossed over, the Perfectly Awakened One, Atthadassī, of great renown, standing on the riverbank, spoke these verses.”

“Yāvatā [M 1.0353] vattate cittaṃ, gaṅgāsotaṃ tarāmahaṃ;

Ayañca kacchapo rājā, tāresi mama paññavā.

“As far as the mind extends, I have crossed the stream of the Ganges; and this wise turtle-king has ferried me across.”

“Iminā buddhataraṇena, mettacittavatāya ca;

Aṭṭhārase kappasate, devaloke ramissati.

“By this ferrying of the Buddha, and by possessing a mind of loving-kindness, for eighteen hundred aeons, he will delight in the heavenly world.”

“Devalokā [V 1.0301] idhāgantvā, sukkamūlena codito;

Ekāsane nisīditvā, kaṅkhāsotaṃ tarissati.

“Having come here from the heavenly world, urged on by the root of merit, sitting in a single seat, he will cross the stream of doubt.”

“Yathāpi bhaddake khette, bījaṃ appampi ropitaṃ;

Sammādhāraṃ pavecchante, phalaṃ toseti kassakaṃ.

“Just as in a good field, even a small seed sown, when proper rain is provided, the fruit satisfies the farmer.”

“Tathevidaṃ buddhakhettaṃ, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ;

Sammādhāraṃ pavecchante, phalaṃ maṃ tosayissati.

“Just so is this Buddha-field, taught by the Perfectly Awakened One; when proper support is bestowed, its fruit will satisfy me.”

“Padhānapahitattomhi, upasanto nirūpadhi;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

“I am resolute in striving, calm, free from substrates; having fully understood all the taints, I dwell without taints.”

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, taraṇāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Eighteen hundred aeons ago, for the deed I did then, I know no bad destination; this is the fruit of that ferrying.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimuttisukhaṃ anubhavanto “aho satthu upāyakosallaṃ, yenāhaṃ bhavapaṅkato uddharitvā nibbānathale patiṭṭhāpito”ti attano pahīnasaṃkilesaṃ paṭiladdhañca sukhaṃ paccavekkhitvā sañjātasomanasso udānavasena –

But having attained arahantship and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he surveyed his own abandoned defilements and the happiness he had gained. With joy arisen from reflecting, 'Ah, the Teacher’s skill in means, by which I was lifted from the swamp of existence and established on the ground of Nibbāna!' he uttered this inspired exclamation:

157.

157.

“Ayoniso manasikārā, maṇḍanaṃ anuyuñjisaṃ;

Uddhato capalo cāsiṃ, kāmarāgena aṭṭito.

“Through unwise attention, I pursued adornment; I was arrogant and fickle, afflicted by sensual lust.”

158.

158.

“Upāyakusalenāhaṃ, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Yoniso paṭipajjitvā, bhave cittaṃ udabbahi”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Through the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, who is skillful in means, having practiced wisely, I uprooted my mind from existence.” – he spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha [P 2.0033] ayoniso manasikārāti anupāyamanasikārato asubhaṃ kāyaṃ subhato manasi karitvā subhato manasikārahetu, asubhaṃ [M 1.0354] kāyaṃ subhasaññāyāti attho. Maṇḍananti hatthūpagādiābharaṇehi ceva mālāgandhādīhi ca attabhāvassa alaṅkaraṇaṃ. Anuyuñjisanti anuyuñjiṃ, sarīrassa vibhūsanappasuto ahosinti attho. Uddhatoti jātigottarūpayobbanamadādīhi uddhato avūpasantacitto. Capaloti vanamakkaṭo viya anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lolo, kāyamaṇḍanavatthamaṇḍanādicāpalye yuttatāya vā capalo ca. Āsinti ahosiṃ. Kāmarāgenāti vatthukāmesu chandarāgena aṭṭito pīḷito vibādhito āsinti yojanā.

Herein, 'through unwise attention' means that due to improper attention, one regards the impure body as pure; the meaning is to have a perception of purity towards the impure body. 'Adornment' refers to the decoration of one's person with ornaments such as those for the hands, as well as garlands and perfumes. 'I pursued' means 'I was engaged in,' that is, 'I was devoted to beautifying the body.' 'Arrogant' (`uddhato`) means one whose mind is agitated, not calmed, due to pride in birth, lineage, beauty, youth, and so forth. 'Fickle' (`capalo`) means unsteady, like a forest monkey, due to an unstable mind, or fickle from being engaged in the fickleness of adorning the body, clothes, and so on. 'I was' means 'I was.' 'By sensual lust' (`kāmarāgena`) is to be construed thus: 'I was afflicted, oppressed, and distressed by desire and passion with regard to sensual objects.'

Upāyakusalenāti [V 1.0302] vineyyānaṃ damanūpāyacchekena kovidena buddhena bhagavatā hetubhūtena. Hetuatthe hi etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Paluṭṭhamakkaṭīdevaccharādassanena hi upakkitavādacodanāya attano kāmarāgāpanayanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Bhagavā hi āyasmantaṃ nandattheraṃ paṭhamaṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ upādāya “yathāyaṃ makkaṭī, evaṃ kakuṭapādiniyo upādāya janapadakalyāṇī”ti mahatiyā āṇiyā khuddakaṃ āṇiṃ nīharanto chaḍḍako viya, sinehapānena sarīraṃ kiledetvā vamanavirecanehi dosaṃ nīharanto bhisakko viya ca kakuṭapādinidassanena janapadakalyāṇiyaṃ virattacittaṃ kāretvā puna upakkitavādena kakuṭapādinīsupi cittaṃ virājetvā sammadeva samathavipassanānuyogena ariyamagge patiṭṭhāpesi. Tena vuttaṃ “yoniso paṭipajjitvā, bhave cittaṃ udabbahi”nti. Upāyena ñāyena sammadeva samathavipassanāya visuddhipaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjitvā bhave saṃsārapaṅke nimuggañca me cittaṃ ariyamaggena hatthena uttāriṃ, nibbānathale patiṭṭhāpesinti attho.

'By one skillful in means' refers to the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is the cause, being clever and expert in the means of taming those to be trained. This instrumental case indeed indicates the cause. For he speaks with reference to the removal of his own sensual lust, which was achieved by showing him a singed female monkey and celestial nymphs, and by the accusation of being a hireling. For the Blessed One, in order to make the Venerable Nanda disenchanted with Janapadakalyāṇī, first made a comparison, saying, 'As this monkey is to Janapadakalyāṇī, so is Janapadakalyāṇī to the hen-footed nymphs.' He was like one who extracts a small peg with a large one, or like a physician who first moistens the body with a soothing drink and then removes the ailment with emetics and purgatives. By showing the hen-footed nymphs, he caused Nanda's mind to become dispassionate towards Janapadakalyāṇī. Then, with the accusation of being a hireling, he made his mind dispassionate even towards the hen-footed nymphs, and rightly established him on the noble path through the practice of serenity and insight. Hence it is said, 'Having practiced wisely, I uprooted my mind from existence.' The meaning is: by practicing the path of purification through serenity and insight with proper means and method, I lifted my mind, which was sunk in the swamp of existence, with the hand of the noble path and established it on the ground of Nibbāna.

Imaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā thero punadivase bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – “yaṃ me, bhante, bhagavā pāṭibhogo pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ paṭilābhāya kakuṭapādānaṃ, muñcāmahaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ etasmā paṭissavā”ti (udā. 22). Bhagavāpi, “yadeva kho te, nanda, anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuttaṃ, athāhaṃ mutto etasmā paṭissavā”ti (udā. 22) āha. Athassa [P 2.0034] bhagavā savisesaṃ [M 1.0355] indriyesu guttadvārataṃ ñatvā taṃ guṇaṃ vibhāvento, “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ yadidaṃ nando”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 230) indriyesu guttadvārabhāvena aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Thero hi “yamevāhaṃ indriyānaṃ asaṃvaraṃ nissāya imaṃ vippakāraṃ patto, tamevāhaṃ suṭṭhu niggahessāmī”ti ussāhajāto balavahirottappo tattha ca katādhikārattā indriyasaṃvare ukkaṃsapāramiṃ agamāsīti.

Having uttered this inspired utterance, the Elder approached the Blessed One the next day and said: 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One was my guarantor for my obtaining five hundred hen-footed celestial nymphs. I release the Blessed One, venerable sir, from this pledge.' The Blessed One replied: 'Nanda, when your mind, without clinging, is liberated from the taints, then I am released from this pledge.' Then the Blessed One, recognizing his special guardedness of the sense faculties, extolled this quality of his, saying: 'Monks, among my monastic disciples who are guarded in their sense faculties, Nanda is the foremost.' Thus, he placed him in the foremost position on account of his guardedness of the sense faculties. For the Elder, thinking, 'It was because of my lack of restraint over the senses that I experienced this trouble, therefore I will thoroughly restrain them,' with effort generated, strong in conscience and fear of blame, and having made a past aspiration for this, he reached the highest perfection in sense restraint.

Nandattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nanda is concluded.

10. Sirimattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirimat

Pare ca naṃ pasaṃsantīti āyasmato sirimattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato pāramiyo pūretvā tusitabhavane ṭhitakāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ [V 1.0303] pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ sakkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ padako veyyākaraṇo lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo nekkhammajjhāsayatāya kāme pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā caturāsītisahassaparimāṇena tāpasagaṇena parivuto himavantappadese devatābhinimmite assame jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā vasanto purimabuddhesu katādhikāratāya lakkhaṇamantesu āgataniyāmena ca buddhaguṇe anussaritvā atīte buddhe uddissa aññatarasmiṃ nadīnivattane pulinacetiyaṃ katvā pūjāsakkārābhirato ahosi. Taṃ disvā tāpasā, “kaṃ uddissa ayaṃ pūjāsakkāro karīyatī”ti pucchiṃsu. So tesaṃ lakkhaṇamante āharitvā tattha āgatāni mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni vibhajitvā tadanusārena attano bale ṭhatvā buddhaguṇe kittesi. Taṃ sutvā tepi tāpasā pasannamānasā tato paṭṭhāya sammāsambuddhaṃ uddissa thūpapūjaṃ karontā viharanti.

'Others also praise him'—this is the verse of the Venerable Sirimat. What is its origin? This elder too, having made aspirations in the presence of former Buddhas and having accumulated merits in various existences, fulfilled his perfections in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. At a time when he was dwelling in the Tusita heaven, he was reborn in a brahmin family. Having attained maturity, he mastered the three Vedas, along with the Nighaṇḍu, the Ketubha, the analysis of syllables, and the Itihasa as the fifth; he was a master of the Pada, a grammarian, flawless in Lokāyata and the marks of a great man. Due to his inclination toward renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and took up the ascetic life. Surrounded by a company of 84,000 ascetics, he dwelt in a hermitage created by deities in the Himalayan region, developing meditative attainments and psychic powers. Because of his past aspirations made to former Buddhas and in accordance with the method described in the mantras of the marks, he recollected the virtues of the Buddha. In honor of a past Buddha, he constructed a sand-shrine at a river bend and was devoted to offerings and veneration. Seeing this, the ascetics asked, 'For whom is this honor and veneration performed?' He then recited the mantras of the marks to them, explained the characteristics of a great man described therein, and, standing firm in his own strength, proclaimed the virtues of the Buddha. Hearing this, those ascetics too, with joyful minds, from that time onward lived honoring the stupa dedicated to the Fully Enlightened One.

Tena ca samayena padumuttarabodhisatto tusitakāyā cavitvā mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti. Carimabhave dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni pāturahesuṃ[M 1.0356], sabbe ca acchariyabbhūtadhammā. Tāpaso tāni antevāsikānaṃ dassetvā bhiyyosomattāya sammāsambuddhesu tesaṃ pasādaṃ vaḍḍhetvā kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbattitvā tehi attano sarīrassa pūjāya karīyamānāya dissamānarūpo āgantvā, “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ ācariyo brahmaloke nibbatto, tumhe appamattā pulinacetiyapūjamanuyuñjatha, bhāvanāya [P 2.0035] ca yuttappayuttā hothā”ti vatvā brahmalokameva gato.

At that time, the Bodhisatta Padumuttara, having passed away from the Tusita realm, had entered his mother’s womb. In his final existence, the thirty-two premonitory signs appeared, and all were marvelous and extraordinary phenomena. The ascetic, showing these to his disciples, further increased their faith in the Perfectly Enlightened Ones. After passing away, he was reborn in the Brahma world. While they were performing rites for his body, he appeared in visible form and said, 'I, your teacher, have been reborn in the Brahma world. You, being diligent, should devote yourselves to honoring the sand cetiya and be constantly engaged in meditation.' Having spoken thus, he returned to the Brahma world.

Evaṃ so devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ gahapatikule nibbatti, tassa jātadivasato paṭṭhāya tasmiṃ kule sirisampattiyā vaḍḍhamānattā sirimātveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle kaniṭṭhabhātā nibbatti, tassa “ayaṃ siriṃ vaḍḍhento jāto”ti sirivaḍḍhoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Te ubhopi jetavanappaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddhā pabbajiṃsu. Tesu sirivaḍḍho na tāva uttarimanussadhammassa lābhī ahosi, catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ lābhī, gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sakkato garukato, sirimatthero pana pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya tādisena kammacchiddena appalābhī ahosi bahujanāsambhāvito, samathavipassanāsu kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.111-147) –

Thus, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in a householder’s family in Sāvatthī during this Buddha’s dispensation. From the day of his birth, the family’s prosperity grew, and they named him Sirimat. When he began to walk, his younger brother was born, and they named him Sirivaḍḍha, thinking, 'This one was born increasing prosperity.' Both of them, upon seeing the Buddha’s power at the acceptance of Jetavana, acquired faith and went forth. Among them, Sirivaḍḍha had not yet attained superhuman states but was a recipient of the four requisites, respected and revered by both laypeople and monastics. The elder Sirimat, however, from the time of his ordination, received few offerings due to a certain defect in his kamma, and was unesteemed by many. Devoting himself to serenity and insight, he soon became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Pabbate himavantamhi, devalo nāma tāpaso;

Tattha me caṅkamo āsi, amanussehi māpito.

“On the Himavant mountain, there was an ascetic named Devala. There, my walking path was made by non-humans.”

“Jaṭābhārena [V 1.0304] bharito, kamaṇḍaludharo sadā;

Uttamatthaṃ gavesanto, vipinā nikkhamiṃ tadā.

“Burdened by a mass of matted hair, always carrying a water pot, seeking the highest good, I then went out from the forest.”

“Cullāsītisahassāni, sissā mayhaṃ upaṭṭhahuṃ;

Sakakammābhipasutā, vasanti vipine tadā.

“Eighty-four thousand disciples attended me; devoted to their own practices, they dwelt in the forest then.”

“Assamā abhinikkhamma, akaṃ pulinacetiyaṃ;

Nānāpupphaṃ samānetvā, taṃ cetiyamapūjayiṃ.

“Having left the hermitage, I made a sand cetiya; gathering various flowers, I worshipped that cetiya.”

“Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, assamaṃ pavisāmahaṃ;

Sabbe sissā samāgantvā, etamatthaṃ pucchiṃsu maṃ.

“Having made my mind serene there, I entered the hermitage; all the disciples gathered and asked me about this matter.”

“Pulinena [M 1.0357] kato thūpo, yaṃ tvaṃ deva namassasi;

Mayampi ñātumicchāma, puṭṭho ācikkha no tuvaṃ.

“‘The stupa made of sand, which you, O venerable one, venerate; we too wish to know, so being asked, please explain it to us.’”

“Niddiṭṭhā nu mantapade, cakkhumanto mahāyasā;

Te kho ahaṃ namassāmi, buddhaseṭṭhe mahāyase.

“‘Those with vision, of great glory, are indicated in the sacred texts; it is them I venerate, the supreme Buddhas, of great glory.’”

“Kīdisā te mahāvīrā, sabbaññū lokanāyakā;

Kathaṃvaṇṇā kathaṃsīlā, kīdisā te mahāyasā.

“What are those great heroes like, the all-knowing leaders of the world? Of what complexion, of what virtue, what are those of great glory like?”

“Bāttiṃsalakkhaṇā buddhā, cattālīsadijāpi ca;

Nettā gopakhumā tesaṃ, jiñjukā phalasannibhā.

“Buddhas have thirty-two marks, and also forty teeth; their eyes have eyelashes like a cow's and are like the jiñjuka fruit.”

“Gacchamānā ca te buddhā, yugamattañca pekkhare;

Na tesaṃ jāṇu nadati, sandhisaddo na suyyati.

“And when those Buddhas walk, they look a yoke's length ahead; their knees do not make a sound, nor is the sound of their joints heard.”

“Gacchamānā ca sugatā, uddharantāva gacchare;

Paṭhamaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ pādaṃ, buddhānaṃ esa dhammatā.

“And when the Fortunate Ones walk, they proceed as if lifting their feet; placing the right foot first—this is the nature of Buddhas.”

“Asambhītā ca te buddhā, migarājāva kesarī;

Nevukkaṃsenti attānaṃ, no ca vambhenti pāṇinaṃ.

“And fearless are those Buddhas, like the lion, the king of beasts; they neither exalt themselves, nor do they disparage other beings.”

“Mānāvamānato muttā, samā sabbesu pāṇisu;

Anattukkaṃsakā buddhā, buddhānaṃ esa dhammatā.

“Freed from honor and dishonor, impartial towards all beings, not exalting themselves are the Buddhas; this is the nature of Buddhas.”

“Uppajjantā ca sambuddhā, ālokaṃ dassayanti te;

Chappakāraṃ pakampenti, kevalaṃ vasudhaṃ imaṃ.

“And when the Fully Enlightened Ones arise, they reveal a light; they cause this entire earth to tremble in six ways.”

“Passanti nirayañcete, nibbāti nirayo tadā;

Pavassati mahāmegho, buddhānaṃ esa dhammatā.

“And they see hell, and then that hell is extinguished; a great cloud pours down—this is the nature of Buddhas.”

“Īdisā te mahānāgā, atulā ca mahāyasā;

Vaṇṇato anatikkantā, appameyyā tathāgatā.

“Such are those great beings, incomparable and of great glory; in beauty unsurpassed, immeasurable are the Tathāgatas.”

“Anumodiṃsu me vākyaṃ, sabbe sissā sagāravā;

Tathā ca paṭipajjiṃsu, yathāsatti yathābalaṃ.

“All the disciples respectfully rejoiced in my words, and they practiced accordingly, each according to their ability and strength.”

“Paṭipūjenti [V 1.0305] pulinaṃ, sakakammābhilāsino;

Saddahantā mama vākyaṃ, buddhasakkatamānasā.

“They honor the sand-heap, desiring their own kamma; trusting in my words, with minds revering the Buddha.”

“Tadā [M 1.0358] cavitvā tusitā, devaputto mahāyaso;

Uppajji mātukucchimhi, dasasahassi kampatha.

“Then, having passed away from Tusita, the devaputta of great glory arose in his mother’s womb, and the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.”

“Assamassāvidūramhi, caṅkamamhi ṭhito ahaṃ;

Sabbe sissā samāgantvā, āgacchuṃ mama santike.

“Not far from the hermitage, I stood on the walking path; all the disciples gathered and came into my presence.”

“Usabhova mahī nadati, migarājāva kūjati;

Susumārova saḷati, kiṃ vipāko bhavissati.

“‘The earth resounds like a bull, it roars like the king of beasts; it makes a sound like a crocodile—what will the result of this be?’”

“Yaṃ pakittemi sambuddhaṃ, sikatāthūpasantike;

So dāni bhagavā satthā, mātukucchimupāgami.

“‘The Fully Enlightened One whom I praised near the sand stupa, that Blessed One, the Teacher, has now entered his mother’s womb.’”

“Tesaṃ dhammakathaṃ vatvā, kittayitvā mahāmuniṃ;

Uyyojetvā sake sisse, pallaṅkamābhujiṃ ahaṃ.

“Having given them a talk on the Dhamma, having praised the Great Sage, having exhorted my own disciples, I sat cross-legged.”

“Balañca vata me khīṇaṃ, byādhinā paramena taṃ;

Buddhaseṭṭhaṃ saritvāna, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“Indeed, my strength was depleted by that severe illness; remembering the best of Buddhas, there I passed away.”

“Sabbe sissā samāgantvā, akaṃsu citakaṃ tadā;

Kaḷevarañca me gayha, citakaṃ abhiropayuṃ.

“All the disciples gathered together and then built a pyre; taking my body, they placed it upon the pyre.”

“Citakaṃ parivāretvā, sīse katvāna añjaliṃ;

Sokasallaparetā te, vikkandiṃsu samāgatā.

“Having surrounded the pyre, raising their joined hands to their heads, they, overcome by the dart of sorrow, wailed together.”

“Tesaṃ lālappamānānaṃ, agamaṃ citakaṃ tadā;

Ahaṃ ācariyo tumhaṃ, mā socittha sumedhasā.

“While they were lamenting, I then approached the pyre and said: ‘I am your teacher; do not grieve, O wise ones.’”

“Sadatthe vāyameyyātha, rattindivamatanditā;

Mā vo pamattā ahuttha, khaṇo vo paṭipādito.

“‘Strive for your own true good, day and night, unwearied. Do not be heedless; the opportune moment has been presented to you.’”

“Sake sissenusāsitvā, devalokaṃ punāgamiṃ;

Aṭṭhārasa ca kappāni, devaloke ramāmahaṃ.

“Having instructed my own disciples, I returned to the deva world; for eighteen aeons I rejoiced in the deva world.”

“Satānaṃ pañcakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ;

Anekasatakkhattuñca, devarajjamakārayiṃ.

“I was a wheel-turning monarch five hundred times, and I ruled as king of the devas many hundreds of times.”

“Avasesesu kappesu, vokiṇṇo saṃsariṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, uppādassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the remaining aeons, I wandered through various states; I do not recall any unhappy destination—this is the fruit of the Buddha’s arising.”

“Yathā [M 1.0359] komudike māse, bahū pupphanti pādapā;

Tathevāhampi samaye, pupphitomhi mahesinā.

“Just as in the Komudī month, many trees burst into bloom, so too at that time I blossomed through the Great Sage.”

“Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ, yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ;

Nāgova bandhanaṃ chetvā, viharāmi anāsavo.

“My energy is a beast of burden, carrying me to the security from bondage. Like a great elephant breaking its bonds, I dwell without defilements.”

“Satasahassito [V 1.0306] kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhikittayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, kittanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“A hundred thousand aeons ago, I praised the Buddha; I do not recall any unhappy destination—this is the fruit of that praise.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiññañhi samānaṃ āyasmantaṃ sirimattheraṃ “ariyo”ti ajānantā puthujjanā bhikkhū sāmaṇerā ca appalābhitāya lokassa anabhigatabhāvena asambhāventā yaṃkiñci kathetvā garahanti. Sirivaḍḍhattheraṃ pana paccayānaṃ lābhibhāvena lokassa sakkatagarukatabhāvato sambhāventā pasaṃsanti. Thero “avaṇṇārahassa nāma vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ, vaṇṇārahassa ca avaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ assa puthujjanabhāvassa doso”ti puthujjanabhāvañca garahanto –

Indeed, ordinary monks and novices, not knowing that the venerable elder Sirimat was a noble one endowed with the six higher knowledges, and not esteeming him due to his receiving few offerings and the world's lack of understanding, would criticize him for whatever reason. However, they praise the elder Sirivaḍḍha because he is a recipient of the requisites and is respected and revered by the world. The elder, rebuking this state of being an ordinary person, said: “To speak praise of one unworthy of praise and to speak dispraise of one worthy of praise—this is the fault of being an ordinary person.”

159.

159.

“Pare ca naṃ pasaṃsanti, attā ce asamāhito;

Moghaṃ pare pasaṃsanti, attā hi asamāhito.

“And others may praise him, but if he himself is uncomposed, vain is the praise of others, for he himself is uncomposed.”

160.

160.

“Pare ca naṃ garahanti, attā ce susamāhito;

Moghaṃ pare garahanti, attā hi susamāhito”ti.

“And others may blame him, but if he himself is well-composed, vain is the blame of others, for he himself is well-composed.”

– Gāthādvayamabhāsi.

He uttered two verses.

Tattha pareti attato aññe pare nāma, idha pana paṇḍitehi aññe bālā pareti adhippetā. Tesañhi ajānitvā apariyogāhetvā bhāsanato garahā viya pasaṃsāpi appamāṇabhūtā. Nanti naṃ puggalaṃ. Pasaṃsantīti aviddasubhāvena taṇhāvipannatāya vā, atha vā abhūtaṃyeva [P 2.0036] puggalaṃ “asuko bhikkhu jhānalābhī, ariyo”ti vā abhūtaguṇaropanena kittenti abhitthavanti. Yo panettha ca-saddo, so [M 1.0360] attūpanayattho. Tena pare naṃ puggalaṃ pasaṃsanti ca, tañca kho tesaṃ pasaṃsanamattaṃ, na pana tasmiṃ pasaṃsāya vatthu atthīti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Attā ce asamāhitoti yaṃ puggalaṃ pare pasaṃsanti, so ce sayaṃ asamāhito maggasamādhinā phalasamādhinā upacārappanāsamādhimatteneva vā na samāhito, samādhānassa paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ kilesānaṃ appahīnattā vikkhitto vibbhantacitto hoti ceti attho. “Asamāhito”ti ca etena samādhinimittānaṃ guṇānaṃ abhāvaṃ dasseti. Moghanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu viya. Pare pasaṃsantīti ye taṃ asamāhitaṃ puggalaṃ pasaṃsanti, te moghaṃ mudhā amūlakaṃ pasaṃsanti. Kasmā? Attā hi asamāhito yasmā tassa puggalassa cittaṃ asamāhitaṃ, tasmāti attho.

There, ‘pare’ means others apart from oneself; but here, it is intended that ‘pare’ are fools, who are other than the wise. For them, because of speaking without knowing or investigating, praise as well as blame becomes immeasurable. ‘Naṃ’ means that person. ‘Pasaṃsantīti’—they praise either due to their lack of insight or being corrupted by craving, or else they extol and laud a person with non-existent qualities, attributing false virtues by saying, “Such and such a monk is an attainer of jhāna, he is a noble one.” The word ‘ca’ here serves to connect to the subject. It shows this meaning: others praise that person, and yet that is merely their praise; there is no actual basis for such praise in him. ‘Attā ce asamāhito’—if the person whom others praise is himself uncomposed, not concentrated by the concentration of the path, the concentration of fruition, or even by access and absorption concentration, and his mind is scattered and bewildered because the defilements that are the opponents of concentration have not been abandoned, this is the meaning. And by ‘asamāhito,’ he shows the absence of the qualities that are the basis for concentration. ‘Moghaṃ’ is a neuter noun indicating a state, as in passages such as “the sun and moon revolve unevenly.” It means that those who praise that uncomposed person praise in vain, uselessly, and without foundation. Why? Because that person’s mind is uncomposed; this is the meaning.

Dutiyagāthāyaṃ garahantīti attano aviddasubhāvena dosantarāya vā ariyaṃ jhānalābhiñca samānaṃ [V 1.0307] “asuko bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ nānuyuñjati antamaso goduhanamattampi kālaṃ kevalaṃ kāyadaḷhibahulo niddārāmo bhassārāmo saṅgaṇikārāmo viharatī”tiādinā appaṭipajjamānatāvibhāvanena vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā garahanti nindanti, upakkosanti vāti attho. Sesaṃ paṭhamagāthāya vuttapariyāyena veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ therena imāhi gāthāhi attano nikkilesabhāve sirivaḍḍhassa ca sakilesabhāve pakāsite taṃ sutvā sirivaḍḍho saṃvegajāto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva sadatthaṃ paripūresi, garahakapuggalā ca theraṃ khamāpesuṃ.

In the second verse, ‘garahanti’ means that due to their own lack of insight or some other fault, they criticize a noble one who has attained jhāna, either by pointing out his lack of practice or by disparaging his virtues, saying, “Such and such a monk does not apply himself to wakefulness, not even for the time it takes to milk a cow; he just lives with a robust body, delighting in sleep, delighting in talk, delighting in company,” and so on. They blame, censure, or reproach—this is the meaning. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained in the first verse. Thus, when the elder had, through these verses, revealed his own state of being without defilements and Sirivaḍḍha’s state of being with defilements, Sirivaḍḍha heard it, became spiritually stirred, established insight, and before long fulfilled his own true goal. And the people who had criticized him asked the elder for forgiveness.

Sirimattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sirimā is completed.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second chapter is completed.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Uttarattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara

Khandhā [M 1.0361][V 1.0308] mayā pariññātāti āyasmato uttarattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito catunavute kappe siddhatthassa bhagavato [P 2.0037] kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto sāsane laddhappasādo hutvā upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi. So satthari parinibbute attano ñātake sannipātetvā bahuṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ sambharitvā dhātupūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sākete brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā uttaroti laddhanāmo vayappatto kenacideva karaṇīyena sāvatthiṃ gato kaṇḍambamūle kataṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā pasīditvā puna kāḷakārāmasuttadesanāya (a. ni. 4.24) abhivaḍḍhamānasaddho pabbajitvā satthārā saddhiṃ rājagahaṃ gantvā upasampajjitvā tattheva vasanto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.106-110) –

“The aggregates are fully understood by me”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Uttara. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome deeds that are a supportive condition for release in various existences, was reborn in a good family ninety-four aeons ago, in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having reached maturity and gained faith in the teaching, he declared himself a lay follower. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he gathered his relatives, prepared many offerings and honors, and performed a veneration of the relics. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, during this Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāketa and was given the name Uttara. When he came of age, he went to Sāvatthī on some business. Seeing the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, he was inspired. Later, his faith grew even stronger during the discourse on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta (AN 4.24). He went forth, accompanied the Teacher to Rājagaha, received full ordination, and stayed there. Establishing insight, he soon attained the six higher knowledges. As it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 2.49.106-110):

“Nibbute lokanāthamhi, siddhatthe lokanāyake;

Mama ñātī samānetvā, dhātupūjaṃ akāsahaṃ.

“When the World-Protector, Siddhattha the World-Leader, had attained final Nibbāna, I gathered my relatives and performed a veneration of the relics.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ dhātumabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dhātupūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, I venerated the relics. I know of no bad destination since then; this is the fruit of venerating the relics.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt away… the Buddha's instruction has been carried out.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā satthari sāvatthiyaṃ viharante buddhupaṭṭhānatthaṃ rājagahato sāvatthiṃ upagato bhikkhūhi “kiṃ, āvuso, pabbajjākiccaṃ tayā matthakaṃ pāpita”nti puṭṭho aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained the six higher knowledges, while the Teacher was dwelling in Sāvatthī, he went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī to attend upon the Buddha. When asked by the monks, “Friend, has the task of the homeless life been brought to its culmination by you?” he answered in another way, declaring:

161.

161.

“Khandhā mayā pariññātā, taṇhā me susamūhatā;

Bhāvitā mama bojjhaṅgā, patto me āsavakkhayo.

“The aggregates have been fully understood by me, my craving has been thoroughly uprooted; my factors of enlightenment have been developed, I have attained the destruction of the taints.”

162.

162.

“Sohaṃ [M 1.0362][V 1.0309] khandhe pariññāya, abbahitvāna jāliniṃ;

Bhāvayitvāna bojjhaṅge, nibbāyissaṃ anāsavo”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“I, having fully understood the aggregates, having pulled out the net of craving, having developed the factors of enlightenment, shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.” — He spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha khandhāti pañcupādānakkhandhā. Pariññātāti “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti paricchijja ñātā bhāvitā. Tena dukkhassa ariyasaccassa pariññābhisamayamāha. Taṇhāti tasati paritasatīti taṇhā. Susamūhatāti samugghāṭitā. Etena samudayasaccassa pahānābhisamayaṃ vadati. Bhāvitā mama bojjhaṅgāti bodhisaṅkhātāya satiādidhammasāmaggiyā, taṃsamaṅgino vā bodhisaṅkhātassa ariyapuggalassa aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātā maggapariyāpannā dhammā mayā bhāvitā uppāditā vaḍḍhitā. Bojjhaṅgaggahaṇeneva cettha taṃsahacaritatāya sabbe maggadhammā, sabbe ca bodhipakkhiyadhammā gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Eteneva maggasaccassa bhāvanābhisamayaṃ dasseti. Patto me āsavakkhayoti kāmāsavādayo āsavā khīyanti etthāti āsavakkhayoti laddhanāmo asaṅkhatadhammo mayā [P 2.0038] patto adhigato. Etena nirodhasaccassa sacchikiriyābhisamayaṃ katheti. Ettāvatā attano saupādisesanibbānasampattiṃ dasseti.

Therein, ‘aggregates’ means the five aggregates of clinging. ‘Fully understood’ means they are known and developed by defining them as, ‘This is suffering, there is nothing more than this.’ By this, he speaks of the penetration of the noble truth of suffering by way of full understanding. ‘Craving’ (taṇhā) is so called because it thirsts and trembles. ‘Thoroughly uprooted’ means eradicated. By this, he speaks of the penetration of the noble truth of the origin by way of abandoning. ‘My factors of enlightenment have been developed’—the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā) are the components of the noble person, who is designated as ‘enlightened’ because he is endowed with the collection of mental states, beginning with mindfulness, that are designated as ‘enlightenment.’ The states included in the path—namely, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—have been developed, produced, and cultivated by me. It should be seen that by the inclusion of the factors of enlightenment, all path-factors and all things pertaining to enlightenment are included here due to their association. By this, he shows the penetration of the noble truth of the path by way of development. ‘I have attained the destruction of the taints’—the unconditioned element, which is named ‘destruction of the taints’ because the taints such as the taint of sensual desire are destroyed in it, has been attained and realized by me. By this, he speaks of the penetration of the noble truth of cessation by way of realization. By this much, he shows his attainment of Nibbāna with a remainder of aggregates.

Idāni pana anupādisesanibbānasampattiṃ dassento “soha”ntiādinā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tassattho – sohaṃ evaṃ vuttanayena khandhe pariññāya parijānitvā, tathā parijānanto eva sakaattabhāvaparaattabhāvesu ajjhattikabāhirāyatanesu atītādibhedabhinnesu saṃsibbanākāraṃ punappunaṃ pavattisaṅkhātaṃ jālaṃ etassa atthīti jālinīti laddhanāmaṃ taṇhaṃ abbahitvāna mama cittasantānato uddharitvā, tathā naṃ uddharantoyeva vuttappabhede bojjhaṅge bhāvayitvāna te bhāvanāpāripūriṃ pāpetvā tato eva anāsavo hutvā ṭhito idāni carimakacittanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissaṃ parinibbāyissāmīti.

Now, however, to show the attainment of Nibbāna without a remainder of aggregates, he spoke the second verse beginning with ‘Sohaṃ.’ Its meaning is: I, having fully understood and comprehended the aggregates in the manner described, and while thus comprehending, having pulled out and removed from my mental continuum that craving which is called ‘Jālinī’ (the ensnaring one) because it has a net characterized by the recurring act of stitching together one's own and others' existences, the internal and external sense bases, and the divisions of past, present, and future. And while thus removing it, having developed the aforementioned kinds of enlightenment factors and brought them to the fulfillment of development, and having thereby become taintless, I now stand firm. With the cessation of the final consciousness, like a fire without fuel, I shall be extinguished, I shall attain final Nibbāna.

Uttarattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttara is completed.

2. Bhaddajittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhaddaji

Panādo [M 1.0363] nāma so rājāti āyasmato bhaddajittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu pāraṃ gantvā kāme pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane assamaṃ kāretvā vasanto ekadivasaṃ [V 1.0310] satthāraṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā ākāsato otari. Otiṇṇassa pana bhagavato madhuñca bhisamuḷālañca sappiñca khīrañca upanāmesi, tassa taṃ bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi.
