So tena puññakammena tusite nibbatto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto vipassissa bhagavato kāle mahaddhano seṭṭhi hutvā aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusahassaṃ bhojetvā ticīvarena acchādesi.

The verse beginning with "Panādo nāma so rājā" belongs to the Venerable Bhaddaji Thera. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, this one was born into a brahmin family. Having attained maturity and mastered the brahminical arts and sciences, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life, and lived in a hermitage in a forest retreat. One day, seeing the Teacher passing through the sky, his mind filled with faith, he stood with hands clasped in reverence. The Teacher, knowing his inclination, descended from the sky. He then offered honey, lotus roots and stalks, ghee, and milk to the Buddha who had descended. The Buddha accepted them out of compassion, gave a blessing, and departed. Through this meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven, where he lived out his lifespan. Afterward, wandering through favorable realms, in the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he became a wealthy merchant, feeding and clothing 68,000 monks with the three robes.

Evaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattitvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā manussesu uppanno buddhasuññe loke pañca paccekabuddhasatāni catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahitvā tato cuto rājakule nibbattitvā rajjaṃ anusāsanto puttaṃ paccekabodhiṃ adhigantvā ṭhitaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tassa parinibbutassa dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ katvā pūjesi. Evaṃ tattha tattha tāni puññāni katvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bhaddiyanagare asītikoṭivibhavassa bhaddiyaseṭṭhissa ekaputtako hutvā nibbatti, bhaddajītissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa kira issariyabhogaparivārādisampatti carimabhave [P 2.0039] bodhisattassa viya ahosi.

Having performed much merit and having been reborn in the deva realms, he dwelt there for as long as his lifespan lasted. Then, having passed away from there, he was born among humans in a world devoid of a Buddha. There, he attended to five hundred Paccekabuddhas with the four requisites. After passing away from there, he was reborn into a royal family and, while ruling the kingdom, supported his son who had attained Paccekabodhi. After his son's Parinibbāna, he took his relics, built a cetiya, and honored them. Having performed such meritorious deeds in various places, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in Bhaddiyanagara as the only son of the wealthy Bhaddiya-seṭṭhi, who possessed eighty crores of wealth; his name was Bhaddaji. It is said his prosperity, enjoyments, retinue, and other such attainments were like those of a Bodhisatta in his final existence.

Tadā satthā sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā bhaddajikumāraṃ saṅgaṇhituṃ mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ bhaddiyanagaraṃ gantvā jātiyāvane vasi tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno. Sopi upari pāsāde nisinno sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokento bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sotuṃ gacchantaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā “katthāyaṃ mahājano gacchatī”ti pucchitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā sayampi mahatā parivārena satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto [M 1.0364] sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitova sabbakilese khepetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.56.98-116) –

At that time, the Teacher, having spent the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, went to the city of Bhaddiya with a large company of monks to take Bhaddaji Kumāra under his care. He stayed in the Jātiyāvana grove, awaiting the ripening of his wisdom. Seated atop his palace, Bhaddaji opened the lion-window and looked out. Seeing a great crowd going to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he asked, "Where is this great crowd going?" Upon hearing the reason, he too, accompanied by a large retinue, went to the Teacher's presence. While listening to the Dhamma, adorned with all his ornaments, he eradicated all defilements and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Oggayha yaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ, nānākuñjarasevitaṃ;

Uddharāmi bhisaṃ tattha, ghāsahetu ahaṃ tadā.

"Having plunged into that lotus pond, frequented by various elephants, I then drew out a lotus stalk from there for the sake of food.

“Bhagavā tamhi samaye, padumuttarasavhayo;

Rattambaradharo buddho, gacchate anilañjase.

"At that time, the Blessed One, known as Padumuttara, the Buddha clad in a red robe, was traveling on the path of the wind.

“Dhunanto paṃsukūlāni, saddaṃ assosahaṃ tadā;

Uddhaṃ nijjhāyamānohaṃ, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

"As he shook his dust-heap robes, I then heard a sound; looking upwards, I saw the Leader of the World.

“Tattheva ṭhitako santo, āyāciṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Madhuṃ bhisehi sahitaṃ, khīraṃ sappiṃ muḷālikaṃ.

"Standing right there, serene, I requested the Leader of the World to accept honey with lotus roots, milk, ghee, and lotus stalks.

“Paṭiggaṇhātu [V 1.0311] me buddho, anukampāya cakkhumā;

Tato kāruṇiko satthā, orohitvā mahāyaso.

"'May the Buddha, the Possessor of Vision, accept this from me out of compassion.' Then the compassionate Teacher, the greatly renowned one, descended.

“Paṭiggaṇhi mamaṃ bhikkhaṃ, anukampāya cakkhumā;

Paṭiggahetvā sambuddho, akā me anumodanaṃ.

"The Possessor of Vision, out of compassion, accepted my alms; having accepted it, the Fully Awakened One gave me his blessing.

“Sukhī hotu mahāpuñña, gati tuyhaṃ samijjhatu;

Iminā bhisadānena, labhassu vipulaṃ sukhaṃ.

"'May you be happy, greatly meritorious one, may your destiny be fulfilled; by this gift of a lotus stalk, may you obtain abundant happiness.'

“Idaṃ vatvāna sambuddho, jalajuttamanāmako;

Bhikkhamādāya sambuddho, ākāsenāgamā jino.

"Having spoken these words, the Fully Awakened One, named Supreme Lotus, taking the alms, the Victor departed through the sky.

“Tato bhisaṃ gahetvāna, āgacchiṃ mama assamaṃ;

Bhisaṃ rukkhe laggetvāna, mama dānaṃ anussariṃ.

"Then, taking a lotus stalk, I came to my hermitage; having hung the lotus stalk on a tree, I recollected my gift.

“Mahāvāto uṭṭhahitvā, sañcālesi vanaṃ tadā;

Ākāso abhinādittha, asanī ca phalī tadā.

"A great wind arose, shaking the forest then; the sky resounded, and a thunderbolt then cracked.

“Tato me asanīpāto, matthake nipatī tadā;

Sohaṃ nisinnako santo, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

"Then a thunderbolt fell upon my head; as I was seated there, I died on that very spot.

“Puññakammena saññutto, tusitaṃ upapajjahaṃ;

Kaḷevaraṃ me patitaṃ, devaloke ramāmahaṃ.

"Connected with that meritorious deed, I arose in Tusita; my body fell away, and I rejoiced in the world of the devas.

“Chaḷasītisahassāni[M 1.0365], nāriyo samalaṅkatā;

Sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhanti, bhisadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Eighty-six thousand women, well-adorned, attend upon me evening and morning—this is the fruit of the gift of a lotus stalk.

“Manussayonimāgantvā, sukhito homahaṃ tadā;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, bhisadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Having come to a human birth, I was then happy; there is no lack in my possessions—this is the fruit of the gift of a lotus stalk.

“Anukampitako tena, devadevena tādinā;

Sabbāsavā parikkhīṇā, natthi dāni punabbhavo.

"I was shown compassion by him, by that god of gods, that Such One; all my taints are destroyed, there is now no future existence.

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ bhisaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bhisadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"One hundred thousand aeons ago, when I gave that lotus stalk, I do not recall any unhappy rebirth—this is the fruit of the gift of a lotus stalk.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Arahatte pana tena adhigate satthā bhaddiyaseṭṭhiṃ āmantesi – “tava putto alaṅkatapaṭiyatto dhammaṃ suṇanto arahatte patiṭṭhāsi, tenassa idāneva pabbajituṃ yuttaṃ, no ce pabbajati, parinibbāyissatī”ti. Seṭṭhi “na mayhaṃ puttassa daharasseva sato parinibbānena kiccaṃ atthi, pabbājetha na”nti āha. Taṃ satthā pabbājetvā upasampādetvā tattha sattāhaṃ vasitvā koṭigāmaṃ pāpuṇi, so ca gāmo gaṅgātīre. Koṭigāmavāsino buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ pavattesuṃ. Bhaddajitthero satthārā anumodanāya āraddhamattāya bahigāmaṃ gantvā [V 1.0312] “gaṅgātīre maggasamīpe satthu āgatakāle vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Mahātheresu āgacchantesupi avuṭṭhahitvā satthu āgatakāleyeva vuṭṭhahi. Puthujjanabhikkhū, “ayaṃ adhunā pabbajito mahātheresu āgacchantesu mānatthaddho hutvā na vuṭṭhāsī”ti ujjhāyiṃsu. Koṭigāmavāsino satthu bhikkhusaṅghassa ca bahū nāvāsaṅghāṭe bandhiṃsu, satthā “handassa ānubhāvaṃ pakāsemī”ti nāvāsaṅghāṭe ṭhatvā, “kahaṃ, bhaddajī”ti pucchi. Bhaddajitthero “esohaṃ, bhante”ti satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā añjaliṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi. Satthā, “ehi, bhaddaji, amhehi saddhiṃ ekanāvaṃ abhiruhā”ti. So uppatitvā satthu ṭhitanāvāyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Satthā gaṅgāmajjhaṃ gatakāle, “bhaddaji, tayā mahāpanādarājakāle ajjhāvuṭṭharatanapāsādo kaha”nti āha. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne nimuggo”ti. “Tena hi, bhaddaji, sabrahmacārīnaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindā”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero [M 1.0366] satthāraṃ vanditvā iddhibalena gantvā pāsādathūpikaṃ pādaṅgulantarena sannirumbhitvā pañcavīsatiyojanaṃ pāsādaṃ [P 2.0040] gahetvā ākāse uppati, uppatanto ca paññāsa yojanāni pāsādaṃ udakato ukkhipi. Athassa purimabhave ñātakā pāsādagatena lobhena macchakacchapamaṇḍūkā hutvā tasmiṃ pāsāde uṭṭhahante parivattitvā udake patiṃsu. Satthā te patante disvā “ñātakā te, bhaddaji, kilamantī”ti āha. Thero satthu vacanena pāsādaṃ vissajjesi. Pāsādo yathāṭhāne eva patiṭṭhahi. Satthā pāraṅgato bhikkhūhi “kadā, bhante, bhaddajittherena ayaṃ pāsādo ajjhāvuṭṭho”ti puṭṭho mahāpanādajātakaṃ (jā. 1.3.40-41) kathetvā mahājanaṃ dhammāmataṃ pāyesi. Thero pana attano ajjhāvuṭṭhapubbaṃ suvaṇṇapāsādaṃ dassetvā –

When he attained Arahantship, the Teacher addressed Bhaddiya the treasurer: "Your son, adorned and prepared, while listening to the Dhamma, has become established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is fitting for him to go forth now. If he does not go forth, he will attain final Nibbāna." The treasurer replied, "My son is still young; he has no need for final Nibbāna yet. Ordain him." The Teacher ordained him and gave him the higher ordination. After staying there for seven days, he reached the village of Koṭigāma, which was situated on the banks of the Ganges. The residents of Koṭigāma arranged a great almsgiving for the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. The Elder Bhaddaji, just as the Teacher began the blessing, went outside the village and sat down after entering a meditative attainment, thinking, "When the Teacher arrives near the path by the Ganges, I will rise." Even when the great elders arrived, he did not rise, but only rose when the Teacher arrived. The ordinary monks complained, "This newly ordained monk, being stiff with pride, did not rise when the great elders arrived." The residents of Koṭigāma prepared many rafts of boats tied together for the Teacher and the Sangha of monks. The Teacher, standing on the raft of boats, thought, "Come, I will display his power," and asked, "Where is Bhaddaji?" The Elder Bhaddaji replied, "Here I am, venerable sir," approached the Teacher, made the añjali gesture, and stood there. The Teacher said, "Come, Bhaddaji, board the same boat with us." He rose into the air and stood on the boat where the Teacher was. When the Teacher reached the middle of the Ganges, he asked, "Bhaddaji, where is the jeweled palace that you dwelt in during the time of King Mahāpanāda?" "It is submerged in this very place," he replied. "Then, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubts of your fellow practitioners of the holy life." At that moment, the Elder paid homage to the Teacher and, by his psychic power, went to the pinnacle of the palace, holding it with the tip of his toe. Lifting the twenty-five-yojana high palace, he rose into the sky, and as he did so, he raised the palace fifty yojanas out of the water. Then, his relatives from a past life, who had been reborn as fish, turtles, and frogs due to their greed for the palace, turned over and fell back into the water as the palace rose. Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, "Bhaddaji, your relatives are weary." Following the Teacher's words, the Elder released the palace, and it settled back in its original place. Having crossed to the other shore, the Teacher was asked by the monks, "Venerable sir, when did the Elder Bhaddaji dwell in this palace?" The Teacher then narrated the Mahāpanāda Jātaka (Jā. 1.3.40-41) and gave the great assembly the nectar of the Dhamma to drink. The Elder, for his part, displaying the golden palace he had previously dwelt in, said:

163.

163.

“Panādo nāma so rājā, yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayo;

Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho, ubbhamāhu sahassadhā.

"Panāda was the name of that king, whose sacrificial post was golden; sixteen ubbedhas in breadth, and a thousandfold high, they say.

164.

164.

“Sahassakaṇḍo satageṇḍu, dhajālu haritāmayo;

Anaccuṃ tattha gandhabbā, cha sahassāni sattadhā”ti. –

"A thousand-sectioned, hundred-knobbed, bannered, made of harita-gold; there the gandhabbas danced, six thousand in seven ways."

Dvīhi gāthāhi vaṇṇento aññaṃ byākāsi.

Describing this with two verses, he declared his final knowledge.

Tattha panādo nāma so rājāti atīte panādo nāma so rājā ahosīti attabhāvaantarahitatāya attānaṃ paraṃ viya niddisati. So eva hi rajje ṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya sadā ussāhasampattiādinā mahatā rājānubhāvena mahatā ca kittisaddena samannāgatattā “rājā mahāpanādo”ti paññāyittha. Yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayoti yassa rañño ayaṃ yūpo pāsādo suvaṇṇamayo. Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedhoti vitthārato soḷasakaṇḍapātappamāṇo. So pana aḍḍhayojanamatto [V 1.0313] hoti. Ubbhāmāhu sahassadhāti ubbhaṃ uccaṃ evamassa pāsādassa sahassadhā sahassakaṇḍappamāṇamāhu. So pana [M 1.0367] yojanato pañcavīsatiyojanappamāṇo hoti. Keci panettha gāthāsukhatthaṃ “āhū”ti dīghaṃ kataṃ. Āhu ahosīti atthaṃ vadanti.

Therein, Panādo nāma so rājā means: in the past, there was a king named Panāda. Due to the disappearance of his own state of existence, he indicates himself as if he were another. Indeed, from the time he was established in the kingdom, because he was always endowed with great royal power, such as the attainment of energy, and with a great sound of fame, he became known as 'King Mahāpanāda.' Yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayo means: of which king this sacrificial post, that is, the palace, was made of gold. Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho means: in breadth, it was the measure of sixteen arrow-shots. This is about half a yojana. Ubbhamāhu sahassadhā means: they say the height of this palace was a thousandfold, a measure of a thousand arrow-shots. This is a measure of twenty-five yojanas. Some say that here 'āhū' is made long for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. They say the meaning of 'āhu' is 'it was'.

Sahassakaṇḍoti sahassabhūmiko. Satageṇḍūti anekasataniyyūhako. Dhajālūti tattha tattha niyyūhasikharādīsu patiṭṭhāpitehi yaṭṭhidhajapaṭākadhajādidhajehi sampanno. Haritāmayoti cāmīkarasuvaṇṇamayo. Keci pana “haritajātimaṇisarikkhako”ti vadanti[P 2.0041]. Gandhabbāti naṭā. Cha sahassāni sattadhāti chamattāni gandhabbasahassāni sattadhā tassa pāsādassa sattasu ṭhānesu rañño abhiramāpanatthaṃ nacciṃsūti attho. Te evaṃ naccantāpi rājānaṃ hāsetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Atha sakko devarājā devanaṭe pesetvā samajjaṃ kāresi, tadā rājā hasīti.

Sahassakaṇḍo means having a thousand floors. Satageṇḍu means having many hundreds of pinnacles. Dhajālu means endowed with banners such as staff-banners, flag-banners, streamer-banners, and so on, established here and there on the tops of the pinnacles and elsewhere. Haritāmayo means made of cāmīkara gold. Some, however, say it means 'resembling a gem of the emerald type.' Gandhabbā means dancers. Cha sahassāni sattadhā means: six thousand gandhabbas danced in seven ways in seven places of that palace to delight the king. Even dancing thus, they were not able to make the king laugh. Then Sakka, king of the devas, sent divine dancers and had a festival performed; then the king laughed.

Bhaddajittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhaddaji is finished.

3. Sobhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sobhita

Satimā paññavāti āyasmato sobhitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ pubbenivāsañāṇalābhīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ uddissa patthanaṃ katvā puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā nekkhammādhimutto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantassa samīpe araññāyatane assamaṃ kāretvā vanamūlaphalāphalena yāpento buddhuppādaṃ sutvā sabbattha ekarattivāseneva bhaddavatīnagare satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pasannamānaso “tuvaṃ satthā ca ketu cā”tiādīhi chahi gāthāhi abhitthavi[M 1.0368], satthā cassa bhāviniṃ sampattiṃ pakāsesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Sobhitotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So aparena samayena satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Pubbenivāsañāṇe ciṇṇavasī ca ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.46-74) –

Satimā paññavā is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sobhita. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits in various existences, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among the monks who were obtainers of the knowledge of past lives. He himself, aspiring for that same position, made an aspiration and performed meritorious deeds. Wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having attained understanding, he became proficient in the knowledges and arts of the brahmins. With a mind intent on renunciation, he left the household life, went forth into the ascetic life, and had a hermitage built in a forest tract near the Himalayas, sustaining himself on roots and fruits of the forest. He heard of the Buddha’s appearance and, travelling by staying only one night in each place, approached the Teacher in the city of Bhaddavatī. With a devoted mind, he praised the Teacher with six verses beginning, 'You are the Teacher and the banner.' The Teacher then declared his future attainment. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They named him Sobhita. In time, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, gained faith, and went forth. Developing insight, he became one endowed with the six higher knowledges, and he was well-practiced in the knowledge of past lives. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.49.46-74):

“Dakkhiṇe [V 1.0314] himavantassa, sukato assamo mama;

Uttamatthaṃ gavesanto, vasāmi vipine tadā.

"To the south of the Himavant, well-made was my hermitage; seeking the highest goal, I dwelt in the forest then.

“Lābhālābhena santuṭṭho, mūlena ca phalena ca;

Anvesanto ācariyaṃ, vasāmi ekako ahaṃ.

"Content with gain and loss, with roots and fruits; seeking a teacher, I dwelt alone.

“Sumedho nāma sambuddho, loke uppajji tāvade;

Catusaccaṃ pakāseti, uddharanto mahājanaṃ.

"Sumedha by name, a Sambuddha, arose in the world at that time; he proclaimed the Four Truths, uplifting the great multitude.

“Nāhaṃ suṇomi sambuddhaṃ, napi me koci saṃsati;

Aṭṭhavasse atikkante, assosiṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

I did not hear of the Perfectly Enlightened One, nor did anyone inform me; after eight years had passed, I heard of the Leader of the World.

“Aggidāruṃ nīharitvā, sammajjitvāna assamaṃ;

Khāribhāraṃ gahetvāna, nikkhamiṃ vipinā ahaṃ.

Having brought out the firewood and swept the hermitage, taking up a carrying-pole load, I departed from the forest.

“Ekarattiṃ vasantohaṃ, gāmesu nigamesu ca;

Anupubbena candavatiṃ, tadāhaṃ upasaṅkamiṃ.

Dwelling for one night in villages and towns, I gradually approached Candavatī.

“Bhagavā tamhi samaye, sumedho lokanāyako;

Uddharanto bahū satte, deseti amataṃ padaṃ.

At that time, the Blessed One Sumedha, the Leader of the World, uplifting many beings, taught the Deathless State.

“Janakāyamatikkamma, vanditvā jinasāgaraṃ;

Ekaṃsaṃ ajinaṃ katvā, santhaviṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

Having passed through the populace, I paid homage to the Victor, the ocean of virtues. Arranging my antelope-skin garment over one shoulder, I praised the Leader of the World.

“Tuvaṃ satthā ca ketu ca, dhajo yūpo ca pāṇinaṃ;

Parāyano patiṭṭhā ca, dīpo ca dvipaduttamo.

You are the Teacher and the banner, the flag and the standard for beings; the ultimate resort and the support, the lamp and the best of bipeds.

“Nepuñño dassane vīro, tāresi janataṃ tuvaṃ;

Natthañño tārako loke, tavuttaritaro mune.

O hero, skilled in insight, you ferry the multitude across; there is no other ferryman in the world, none superior to you, O Sage.

“Sakkā [M 1.0369] theve kusaggena, pametuṃ sāgaruttame;

Na tveva tava sabbaññu, ñāṇaṃ sakkā pametave.

One might be able to measure the great ocean with the tip of a kusa grass blade, but one could never measure your knowledge, O All-Knowing One.

“Tuladaṇḍe ṭhapetvāna, mahiṃ sakkā dharetave;

Natveva tava paññāya, pamāṇamatthi cakkhuma.

It might be possible to weigh the earth, having placed it on a balance-beam; but for your wisdom, O Visionary One, there is no measure.

“Ākāso minituṃ sakkā, rajjuyā aṅgulena vā;

Natveva tava sabbaññu, sīlaṃ sakkā pametave.

One might be able to measure the sky with a rope or a finger-length, but one could never measure your virtue, O All-Knowing One.

“Mahāsamudde udakaṃ, ākāso ca vasundharā;

Parimeyyāni etāni, appameyyosi cakkhuma.

The water in the great ocean, the sky, and the earth—these can be measured, but you, O Visionary One, are immeasurable.

“Chahi gāthāhi sabbaññuṃ, kittayitvā mahāyasaṃ;

Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, tuṇhī aṭṭhāsahaṃ tadā.

Having praised the All-Knowing One, the greatly renowned one, with six verses, I raised my joined hands and then stood in silence.

“Yaṃ vadanti sumedhoti, bhūripaññaṃ sumedhasaṃ;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

He whom they call Sumedha, of extensive wisdom and truly wise, having sat down in the assembly of monks, spoke these verses:

“Yo [V 1.0315] me ñāṇaṃ pakittesi, vippasannena cetasā;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

“He who praised my knowledge with a serene mind, him I shall extol; listen to me as I speak.

“Sattasattati kappāni, devaloke ramissati;

Sahassakkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjaṃ karissati.

For seventy-seven aeons, he will delight in the deva world; a thousand times he will be the lord of devas, ruling the divine kingdom.

“Anekasatakkhattuñca, cakkavattī bhavissati;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

And for many hundreds of times, he will become a wheel-turning monarch; his regional kingship will be vast, beyond all reckoning.

“Devabhūto manusso vā, puññakammasamāhito;

Anūnamanasaṅkappo, tikkhapañño bhavissati.

Whether born as a deva or a human, devoted to meritorious deeds, he will have undiminished resolve and sharp wisdom.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

Thirty thousand aeons from now, born in the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama will arise in the world.

“Agārā abhinikkhamma, pabbajissatikiñcano;

Jātiyā sattavassena, arahattaṃ phusissati.

Having gone forth from the household life, possessing nothing, at seven years of age he will attain arahantship.

“Yato sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi sāsanaṃ;

Etthantare na jānāmi, cetanaṃ amanoramaṃ.

From the time I can remember myself, from when I attained the teaching, in all that time I know of no disagreeable intention.

“Saṃsaritvā [M 1.0370] bhave sabbe, sampattānubhaviṃ ahaṃ;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, phalaṃ ñāṇassa thomane.

Wandering through all states of existence, I have experienced all attainments; there is no lack of enjoyments for me—this is the fruit of praising knowledge.

“Tiyaggī nibbutā mayhaṃ, bhavā sabbe samūhatā;

Sabbāsavā parikkhīṇā, natthi dāni punabbhavo.

My three fires are extinguished, all states of existence are uprooted; all taints are destroyed, now there is no more rebirth.

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ ñāṇamathaviṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phalaṃ ñāṇassa thomane.

Since I praised that knowledge thirty thousand aeons ago, I do not recall any woeful state; such is the fruit of praising knowledge.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burned up... the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

So arahattaṃ pana patvā attano pubbenivāsaṃ anupaṭipāṭiyā anussaranto yāva asaññabhave acittakapaṭisandhi, tāva addasa. Tato pañca kappasatāni cittappavattiṃ adisvā avasāneva disvā “kimeta”nti [P 2.0042] āvajjento nayavasena “asaññabhavo bhavissatī”ti niṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, asaññasattā nāma dīghāyukā devā, tato cuto sobhito idhūpapanno, so etaṃ bhavaṃ jānāti, sobhito anussaratī”ti (pārā. 232 atthato samānaṃ). Evaṃ nayavasena anussarantassa anussaraṇakosallaṃ disvā satthā theraṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tato eva cāyaṃ āyasmā savisesaṃ attano pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ [V 1.0316] tassa ca paccayabhūtaṃ paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā somanassajāto tadatthadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānento –

Having attained arahantship, he recollected his past lives in sequence, recalling as far back as the rebirth in the realm of non-percipient beings, a rebirth devoid of consciousness. Then, not seeing the arising of consciousness for five hundred aeons, he saw it again at the end and, directing his mind with the thought, ‘What is this?’ he concluded through inference, ‘It must have been the realm of non-percipient beings.’ Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘Monks, there are long-lived devas called the non-percipient beings. Having passed away from there, Sobhita was reborn here. He knows this existence; Sobhita recollects it.’ (Parā. 232, similar in meaning). Seeing his skill in recollection through inference, the Teacher placed the elder foremost among those who recollect past lives. Then, this venerable one, reflecting on his own special knowledge of recollecting past lives and the practice that was its cause, filled with joy, uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning:

165.

165.

“Satimā paññavā bhikkhu, āraddhabalavīriyo;

Pañca kappasatānāhaṃ, ekarattiṃ anussariṃ.

“A mindful and wise bhikkhu, with aroused strength and energy, I recollected five hundred aeons as if in a single night.

166.

166.

“Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne, satta aṭṭha ca bhāvayaṃ;

Pañca kappasatānāhaṃ, ekarattiṃ anussari”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

Developing the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven, and the eight, I recollected five hundred aeons as if in a single night.” Thus he spoke this pair of verses.

Tattha satimāti sayaṃ samudāgamanasampannāya satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāpāripūriyā sativepullappattiyā ca satimā. Paññavāti chaḷabhiññāpāripūriyā paññāvepullappattiyā ca paññavā. Bhinnakilesatāya bhikkhu. Saddhādibalānañceva [M 1.0371] catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyassa ca saṃsiddhipāripūriyā āraddhabalavīriyo. Saddhādīnañhettha balaggahaṇena gahaṇaṃ satipi satiādīnaṃ balabhāve, yathā “gobalibaddhā puññañāṇasambhārā”ti. Pañca kappasatānāhaṃ, ekarattiṃ anussarinti ekarattiṃ viya anussariṃ. Viya-saddo hi idha luttaniddiṭṭho, etena pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇe attano ñāṇavasībhāvaṃ dīpeti.

Therein, ‘mindful’ means mindful through the perfection of the development of the foundations of mindfulness, which arises spontaneously, and through the attainment of an abundance of mindfulness. ‘Wise’ means wise through the perfection of the six direct knowledges and through the attainment of an abundance of wisdom. A ‘bhikkhu’ because his defilements are shattered. He has ‘aroused strength and energy’ through the perfection and accomplishment of the powers of faith and so forth, and of the fourfold right effort. Here, faith and so forth are included under the term ‘strength’, even though mindfulness and other qualities are also powers, just as it is said: ‘The provisions of merit and knowledge are bound as if by the strength of an ox.’ ‘I recollected five hundred aeons as one night’ means ‘I recollected as if it were one night.’ The word ‘as if’ is here elliptically expressed; by this, he demonstrates his mastery over the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

Idāni yāya paṭipattiyā attano satimantādibhāvo sātisayaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇañca siddhaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “cattāro”tiādinā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha cattāro satipaṭṭhāneti kāyānupassanādike attano visayabhedena catubbidhe lokiyalokuttaramissake satisaṅkhāte satipaṭṭhāne. Sattāti satta bojjhaṅge. Aṭṭhāti aṭṭha maggaṅgāni. Satipaṭṭhānesu hi suppatiṭṭhitacittassa satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gatā eva honti, tathā ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Tenāha dhammasenāpati – “catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā satta bojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā”tiādīhi (dī. ni. 3.143) sattakoṭṭhāsikesu sattatiṃsāya [P 2.0043] bodhipakkhiyadhammesu ekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchante itare agacchantā nāma natthīti. Bhāvayanti bhāvanāhetu. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Now, to show the practice by which his own state of being mindful and so forth, and the extraordinary knowledge of past lives, were accomplished, he spoke the second verse beginning with “four.” Herein, “four foundations of mindfulness” refers to the fourfold foundations of mindfulness, which are reckoned as mindfulness, consisting of both mundane and supramundane aspects, distinguished by their respective objects, such as the contemplation of the body. “Seven” refers to the seven factors of enlightenment. “Eight” refers to the eight factors of the path. For one whose mind is well-established in the foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment naturally reach full development in cultivation, as does the Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma said: “Having rightly developed the seven factors of enlightenment with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so on (Dī. Ni. 3.143). This means that among the thirty-seven qualities conducive to enlightenment, which are divided into seven sections, when one section reaches full development in cultivation, the others do not remain undeveloped. “Developing” is for the purpose of cultivation. The rest is as explained.

Sobhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sobhita is concluded.

4. Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Valliya

Yaṃ [V 1.0317] kiccaṃ daḷhavīriyenātiādikā āyasmato valliyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato asītikoṭivibhavaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pabbatapāde araññāyatane ekissā nadiyā tīre assamaṃ kāretvā viharanto attano anuggaṇhanatthaṃ upagataṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso ajinacammaṃ pattharitvā adāsi[M 1.0372]. Tattha nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ pupphehi ca candanena ca pūjetvā ambaphalāni datvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vandi. Tassa bhagavā nisinnāsanasampattiṃ pakāsento anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā “kaṇhamitto”ti laddhanāmo vayappatto satthu vesāligamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho mahākaccānattherassa santike pabbaji. So mandapañño dandhaparakkamo ca hutvā ciraṃ kālaṃ viññuṃ sabrahmacāriṃ nissāyeva vasati. Bhikkhū “yathā nāma valli rukkhādīsu kiñci anissāya vaḍḍhituṃ na sakkoti, evamayampi kañci paṇḍitaṃ anissāya vaḍḍhituṃ na sakkotī”ti valliyotveva samudācariṃsu. Aparabhāge pana veṇudattattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa ovāde ṭhatvā sato sampajāno hutvā viharanto ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā paṭipattikkamaṃ theraṃ pucchanto –

The verses of the Venerable Elder Valliya begin with “Whatever task requires firm vigor.” What is their origin? This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, was born in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having attained maturity and become accomplished in knowledge and crafts, he abandoned wealth amounting to eighty crores and took up the ascetic life. Dwelling at the foot of a mountain in a forest hermitage, he had a hermitage built on the bank of a river. Seeing the Teacher who had come to favor him, his mind became joyful. He spread out a deerskin and offered it. Seated there, he honored the Blessed One with flowers and sandalwood, gave him mango fruits, and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. The Blessed One, revealing the excellence of the offered seat, spoke words of appreciation and departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a brahmin family in Vesāli. Named “Kaṇhamitta,” he came of age. Seeing the Buddha’s majesty when the Teacher visited Vesāli, he gained faith and went forth under the Venerable Mahākaccāna Thera. Being of dull wisdom and slow effort, he spent a long time dwelling in dependence on a wise fellow bhikkhu. The bhikkhus said, “Just as a valli (creeper) cannot grow without depending on a tree or the like, so too this one cannot grow without depending on someone wise.” Thus, they called him “Valliya.” Later, however, he approached the Venerable Veṇudatta Thera and, following his advice, dwelt mindful and clearly aware. As his wisdom matured, he questioned the elder about the sequence of practice—

167.

167.

“Yaṃ kiccaṃ daḷhavīriyena, yaṃ kiccaṃ boddhumicchatā;

Karissaṃ nāvarajjhissaṃ, passa vīriyaṃ parakkamaṃ.

“Whatever task requires firm vigor, whatever task one desiring awakening undertakes, I shall accomplish it without fail. Behold my vigor and exertion.”

168.

168.

“Tvañca me maggamakkhāhi, añjasaṃ amatogadhaṃ;

Ahaṃ monena monissaṃ, gaṅgāsotova sāgara”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“And you, show me the path, direct, leading to the Deathless; I will know it through wisdom, like the Ganges’ current to the ocean.” – Thus he spoke the two verses.

Tattha [P 2.0044] yaṃ kiccaṃ daḷhavīriyenāti daḷhena vīriyena thirena parakkamena, daḷhavīriyena vā purisadhorayhena yaṃ kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiccaṃ boddhumicchatāti cattāri ariyasaccāni nibbānameva vā boddhuṃ bujjhituṃ icchantena paṭivijjhitukāmena yaṃ kiccaṃ karaṇīyaṃ. Karissaṃ nāvarajjhissanti tamahaṃ dāni karissaṃ na virādhessaṃ, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjissāmi. Passa vīriyaṃ parakkamanti yathā paṭipajjamāne dhamme vidhinā īraṇato “vīriyaṃ”, paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato “parakkamo”ti ca laddhanāmaṃ sammāvāyāmaṃ passa na saddhamevāti attano kattukāmataṃ dasseti.

Here, “whatever task requires firm vigor” means what should be done or practiced with firm energy, with steadfast exertion, or what should be done by one who is a leader among men, endowed with firm vigor. “Whatever task one desiring awakening undertakes” refers to the duty to be undertaken by one who desires to comprehend or penetrate the Four Noble Truths or Nibbāna itself. “I will accomplish it without fail” means “Now I will do it; I will not fail; I will practice as instructed.” “Behold my vigor and exertion” shows his determination, where “vigor” is so called because of pressing forward lawfully in the Dhamma, and “exertion” because of advancing to a further and further state—see my right effort, not merely my faith.

Tvañcāti [M 1.0373][V 1.0318] kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ ālapati. Meti mayhaṃ. Maggamakkhāhīti ariyamaggaṃ kathehi, lokuttaramaggasampāpakaṃ catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathehīti attho. Añjasanti ujukaṃ majjhimapaṭipadābhāvena antadvayassa anupagamanato. Amate nibbāne sampāpakabhāvena patiṭṭhitattā amatogadhaṃ. Monenāti ñāṇena maggapaññāya. Monissanti jānissaṃ nibbānaṃ paṭivijjhissaṃ pāpuṇissaṃ. Gaṅgāsotova sāgaranti yathā gaṅgāya soto sāgaraṃ samuddaṃ avirajjhanto ekaṃsato ogāhati, evaṃ “ahaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto maggañāṇena nibbānaṃ adhigamissāmi, tasmā taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ me ācikkhathā”ti theraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ yāci.

“And you” he addresses the good friend who gives the meditation subject. “Me” means “to me.” “Show me the path” means “Explain the Noble Path, that is, the meditation subject of the Four Truths, which leads to the supramundane path.” “Direct” means straight, by way of the Middle Way, as it avoids the two extremes. “Leading to the Deathless” means established as leading to the Deathless, Nibbāna. “Through wisdom” means with knowledge, with the wisdom of the path. “I will know” means “I will know, penetrate, attain Nibbāna.” “Like the Ganges’ current to the ocean” means, just as the Ganges’ stream flows unerringly into the sea, so too, “I, applying myself to the meditation subject, will attain Nibbāna through the knowledge of the path; therefore, teach me that meditation subject,” he requested the elder for the meditation subject.

Taṃ sutvā veṇudattatthero tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Sopi kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto nacirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.75-105) –

Hearing this, the Venerable Elder Veṇudatta gave him the meditation subject. Applying himself to that meditation subject, he soon intensified his practice of insight and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā, piyarūpe manorame;

Asīti koṭiyo hitvā, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ.

“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, so pleasing and delightful, and having abandoned eighty crores, I went forth into homelessness.

“Pabbajitvāna kāyena, pāpakammaṃ vivajjayiṃ;

Vacīduccaritaṃ hitvā, nadīkūle vasāmahaṃ.

“Having gone forth, I avoided evil bodily action; having abandoned verbal misconduct, I dwelt on the riverbank.

“Ekakaṃ maṃ viharantaṃ, buddhaseṭṭho upāgami;

Nāhaṃ jānāmi buddhoti, akāsiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ.

“While I was dwelling alone, the Supreme Buddha came to me; not knowing that it was the Buddha, I made him welcome.

“Karitvā paṭisanthāraṃ, nāmagottamapucchahaṃ;

Devatānusi gandhabbo, adu sakko purindado.

“After making him welcome, I asked for his name and clan: ‘Are you a deva, a gandhabba, or Sakka, giver of cities?

“Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, mahābrahmā idhāgato;

Virocesi disā sabbā, udayaṃ sūriyo yathā.

“‘Who are you? Whose son are you? Are you Mahābrahmā who has come here? You illuminate all directions like the rising sun.

“Sahassārāni cakkāni, pāde dissanti mārisa;

Ko vā tvaṃ kassa vā putto, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

“‘Thousand-spoked wheels, O noble sir, are visible on your feet. Who are you? Whose son are you? How can we know you?

“Nāmagottaṃ pavedehi, saṃsayaṃ apanehi me;

Namhi devā na gandhabbo, namhi sakko purindado.

“‘Declare your name and lineage, dispel my doubt.’ ‘I am not a deva, nor a gandhabba, nor Sakka, giver of cities.

“Brahmabhāvo ca me natthi, etesaṃ uttamo ahaṃ;

Atīto visayaṃ tesaṃ, dālayiṃ kāmabandhanaṃ.

“‘I have no becoming in Brahma’s realm, I am the highest of these; I have transcended their sphere, I have shattered the bonds of sensual pleasure.

“Sabbe [M 1.0374] kilese jhāpetvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ;

Tassa vācaṃ suṇitvāhaṃ, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

“‘Having burnt away all defilements, I have attained the supreme enlightenment.’ Hearing his words, I spoke this utterance:

“Yadi buddhosi sabbaññū, nisīda tvaṃ mahāmune;

Tamahaṃ pūjayissāmi, dukkhassantakaro tuvaṃ.

“‘If you are the Buddha, the All-Knowing One, sit down, O Great Sage; I will honor you, for you are the one who puts an end to suffering.’

“Pattharitvājinacammaṃ[V 1.0319], adāsi satthuno ahaṃ;

Nisīdi tattha bhagavā, sīhova girigabbhare.

“Spreading out a deerskin, I offered it to the Teacher; there the Blessed One sat, like a lion in a mountain cave.

“Khippaṃ pabbatamāruyha, ambassa phalamaggahiṃ;

Sālakalyāṇikaṃ pupphaṃ, candanañca mahārahaṃ.

“Quickly climbing the mountain, I picked mango fruits; and the finest Sāla flowers, and very valuable sandalwood.

“Khippaṃ paggayha taṃ sabbaṃ, upetvā lokanāyakaṃ;

Phalaṃ buddhassa datvāna, sālapupphamapūjayiṃ.

“Swiftly gathering all those, I approached the Leader of the World; after giving the fruit to the Buddha, I worshipped him with Sāla flowers.

“Candanaṃ anulimpitvā, avandiṃ satthuno ahaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, vipulāya ca pītiyā.

“Having anointed him with sandalwood, I paid homage to the Teacher; with a joyful and uplifted mind, and with abundant delight.

“Ajinamhi nisīditvā, sumedho lokanāyako;

Mama kammaṃ pakittesi, hāsayanto mamaṃ tadā.

“Seated on the deerskin, Sumedha, the World-Leader, proclaimed my deed, gladdening me at that time:

“Iminā phaladānena, gandhamālehi cūbhayaṃ;

Pañcavīse kappasate, devaloke ramissati.

“‘Through this gift of fruit and both fragrant garlands, for twenty-five hundred eons he will rejoice in the heavenly realm.

“Anūnamanasaṅkappo, vasavattī bhavissati;

Chabbīsatikappasate, manussattaṃ gamissati.

“‘With undiminished resolve, he will become a sovereign ruler; for twenty-six hundred eons, he will attain human existence.

“Bhavissati cakkavattī, cāturanto mahiddhiko;

Vebhāraṃ nāma nagaraṃ, vissakammena māpitaṃ.

“‘He will be a wheel-turning monarch, ruler of the four quarters, of great power; with a city named Vebhāra, created by Vissakamma.

“Hessati sabbasovaṇṇaṃ, nānāratanabhūsitaṃ;

Eteneva upāyena, saṃsarissati so bhave.

“‘It will be entirely golden, adorned with various jewels; in this very way, he will wander through existence.

“Sabbattha pūjito hutvā, devatte atha mānuse;

Pacchime bhave sampatte, brahmabandhu bhavissati.

“‘Having been honored everywhere, in the divine and human realms, when his final existence is reached, he will be a brahmin.

“Agārā abhinikkhamma, anagārī bhavissati;

Abhiññāpāragū hutvā, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“‘Having gone forth from home, he will become homeless; having gone to the far shore of direct knowledge, he will attain Nibbāna, taintless.’

“Idaṃ [M 1.0375] vatvāna sambuddho, sumedho lokanāyako;

Mama nijjhāyamānassa, pakkāmi anilañjase.

“Having spoken these words, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Sumedha, the Leader of the World, departed on the path of the wind while I was contemplating.

“Tena kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“By that well-done deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to Tāvatiṃsa.

“Tusitato cavitvāna, nibbattiṃ mātukucchiyaṃ;

Bhoge me ūnatā natthi, yamhi gabbhe vasāmahaṃ.

“Having passed away from the Tusita realm, I was reborn in my mother’s womb; there was no lack of wealth for me while I dwelt in that womb.”

“Mātukucchigate mayi, annapānañca bhojanaṃ;

Mātuyā mama chandena, nibbattati yadicchakaṃ.

“While I was in my mother’s womb, food, drink, and nourishment arose; according to my mother’s desire, whatever she wished for came to be.”

“Jātiyā pañcavassena, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ;

Oropitamhi kesamhi, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

“At the age of five, I went forth into homelessness; when my hair was brought down, I attained arahantship.”

“Pubbakammaṃ [V 1.0320] gavesanto, orena nāddasaṃ ahaṃ;

Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, mama kammamanussariṃ.

“Seeking my past deeds, I saw nothing in the near past; I recalled my kamma from thirty thousand aeons ago.”

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Tava sāsanamāgamma, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man; having come to your teaching, I have attained the unshakeable state.”

“Tiṃsakappasahassamhi, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty thousand aeons ago, I venerated the Buddha; I know of no bad destination since then; this is the fruit of venerating the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto thero imāyeva gāthā abhāsīti.

Having attained arahantship, the elder spoke these very verses, declaring his final knowledge.

Valliyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Valliya is concluded.

5. Vītasokattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vītasoka

Kese me olikhissantītiādikā āyasmato vītasokattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇānaṃ [P 2.0045] vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato kāme pahāya [M 1.0376] isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahatā isigaṇena parivuto araññe vasanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho “udumbarapupphasadisā dullabhadassanā buddhā bhagavanto, idāneva upagantabbā”ti mahatiyā parisāya saddhiṃ satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ gacchanto diyaḍḍhayojane sese byādhiko hutvā buddhagatāya saññāya kālaṅkato devesu uppajjitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde aṭṭhārasavassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ vassasatānaṃ matthake dhammāsokarañño kaniṭṭhabhātā hutvā nibbatti, tassa vītasokoti nāma ahosi. So vayappatto khattiyakumārehi sikkhitabbavijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato giridattattheraṃ nissāya gihibhūto suttantapiṭake abhidhammapiṭake ca visārado hutvā ekadivasaṃ massukammasamaye kappakassa hatthato ādāsaṃ gahetvā kāyaṃ olokento valitapalitādīni disvā sañjātasaṃvego vipassanāya cittaṃ otāretvā bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā tasmiṃyeva āsane sotāpanno hutvā giridattattherassa santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.9-26) –

The verses beginning, “The barber approached to shave my hair,” are those of the venerable Vītasoka. What is their origin? He, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having mastered the brahminical arts and sciences, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life. Surrounded by a great company of sages, he dwelt in the forest. Hearing of the Buddha’s appearance, he was delighted and overjoyed, thinking, “Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are as rare to see as an udumbara flower. I must go to him now!” Setting out with a large assembly to see the Teacher, he fell ill when only one and a half yojanas remained. With his mind fixed on the Buddha, he passed away and was reborn among the devas. Wandering between the deva and human realms, he was reborn at the time of this Buddha’s appearance, after two hundred and eighteen years had passed, as the youngest brother of King Dhammāsoka. His name was Vītasoka. When he came of age, he mastered the arts and sciences to be learned by khattiya princes. Relying on the Elder Giridatta, while still a layman he became skilled in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas. One day, at the time of having his beard trimmed, he took a mirror from the barber’s hand and, looking at his body, saw wrinkles, gray hairs, and so on. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him, and directing his mind to insight, he strove in his meditation. Right there, in that very seat, he became a stream-enterer. He then went forth in the presence of the Elder Giridatta and before long attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.49.9-26):

“Ajjhāyako [V 1.0321] mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Lakkhaṇe itihāse ca, sanighaṇḍusakeṭubhe.

“A reciter, a bearer of mantras, a master of the three Vedas; skilled in the marks of a great man, in legends, and in the Nighaṇḍu with the Keṭubha.”

“Nadīsotapaṭibhāgā, sissā āyanti me tadā;

Tesāhaṃ mante vācemi, rattindivamatandito.

“Like a river’s current, disciples came to me then; to them I recited the mantras, tirelessly day and night.”

“Siddhattho nāma sambuddho, loke uppajji tāvade;

Tamandhakāraṃ nāsetvā, ñāṇālokaṃ pavattayi.

“The Perfectly Enlightened One named Siddhattha arose in the world at that time; having destroyed that darkness, he set in motion the light of knowledge.”

“Mama aññataro sisso, sissānaṃ so kathesi me;

Sutvāna te etamatthaṃ, ārocesuṃ mamaṃ tadā.

“A certain disciple of mine told the other disciples; having heard this matter, they then reported it to me.”

“Buddho loke samuppanno, sabbaññū lokanāyako;

Tassānuvattati jano, lābho amhaṃ na vijjati.

“The Buddha has arisen in the world, the All-knowing One, the Leader of the World; people follow him, but for us there is no gain.”

“Adhiccuppattikā buddhā, cakkhumanto mahāyasā;

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ buddhaseṭṭhaṃ, passeyyaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Buddhas arise exceptionally, possessing vision and great glory; oh, that I might see the foremost Buddha, the Leader of the World!”

“Ajinaṃ [M 1.0377] me gahetvāna, vākacīraṃ kamaṇḍaluṃ;

Assamā abhinikkhamma, sisse āmantayiṃ ahaṃ.

“Taking my antelope hide, bark garment, and water pot, I went forth from the hermitage and addressed the disciples.”

“Odumbarikapupphaṃva, candamhi sasakaṃ yathā;

Vāyasānaṃ yathā khīraṃ, dullabho lokanāyako.

“Like the flower of the udumbara tree, like the hare in the moon, like milk from crows, rare is the Leader of the World.”

“Buddho lokamhi uppanno, manussattampi dullabhaṃ;

Ubhosu vijjamānesu, savanañca sudullabhaṃ.

“A Buddha has arisen in the world, and human existence is also rare; when both are present, hearing the teaching is exceedingly rare.”

“Buddho loke samuppanno, cakkhuṃ lacchāma no bhavaṃ;

Etha sabbe gamissāma, sammāsambuddhasantikaṃ.

“The Buddha has arisen in the world; sirs, we shall obtain the eye of wisdom. Come, let us all go to the presence of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

“Kamaṇḍaludharā sabbe, kharājinanivāsino;

Te jaṭābhārabharitā, nikkhamuṃ vipinā tadā.

“All carrying water pots, clad in rough antelope skins, laden with the burden of their matted hair, they then departed from the forest.”

“Yugamattaṃ pekkhamānā, uttamatthaṃ gavesino;

Āsattidosarahitā, asambhītāva kesarī.

“Looking a yoke’s length ahead, seeking the highest good, free from the fault of attachment, fearless as a lion.”

“Appakiccā aloluppā, nipakā santavuttino;

Uñchāya caramānā te, buddhaseṭṭhamupāgamuṃ.

“With few duties, ungreedy, prudent, living tranquilly, they, wandering for gleanings, approached the supreme Buddha.”

“Diyaḍḍhayojane sese, byādhi me upapajjatha;

Buddhaseṭṭhaṃ saritvāna, tattha kālaṅkato ahaṃ.

“When one and a half yojanas remained, an illness befell me; remembering the foremost Buddha, I passed away there.”

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhasaññāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gained that perception, I have not known a bad destination since; this is the fruit of perception of the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [V 1.0322] pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, declaring his final knowledge—

169.

169.

“Kese me olikhissanti, kappako upasaṅkami;

Tato ādāsamādāya, sarīraṃ paccavekkhisaṃ.

“The barber approached to shave my hair; then, taking a mirror, I inspected my body.”

170.

170.

“Tuccho kāyo adissittha, andhakāre tamo byagā;

Sabbe coḷā samucchinnā, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“The body was seen as empty, the darkness has departed; all defilements are cut off, now there is no further becoming.” – he spoke these two verses.

Tattha [M 1.0378] kese me olikhissanti, kappako upasaṅkamīti gihikāle massukammasamaye “mama kese olikhissaṃ kappemī”ti kesādīnaṃ chedanādivasena kappanato kappako nhāpito maṃ upagacchi. Tatoti kappakato. Sarīraṃ paccavekkhisanti sabbakāyike ādāse palitavalitamukhanimittādidassanamukhena “abhibhūto vata jarāya me kāyo”ti jarābhibhūtaṃ attano sarīraṃ paccavekkhiṃ. Evaṃ paccavekkhato ca tuccho kāyo adissittha niccadhuvasukhasabhāvādīhi ritto hutvā me kāyo adissatha paññāyi. Kasmā? Andhakāre tamo byagā yena ayonisomanasikārasaṅkhātena [P 2.0046] tamasā attano kāye andhagatā vijjamānampi asubhādisabhāvaṃ apassantā avijjamānaṃ subhādiākāraṃ gaṇhanti, tasmiṃ andhakāre andhakaraṇaṭṭhāne kāye yonisomanasikārasaṅkhātena ñāṇālokena avijjātamo vigato, tato eva sabbe coḷā samucchinnā corā viya kusalabhaṇḍacchedanato, sādhūhi alātabbato asaṅgahetabbato saṅkārakūṭādīsu chaḍḍitapilotikakhaṇḍaṃ viya issarajanena ariyajanena jigucchitabbatāya coḷā viyāti vā “coḷā”ti laddhanāmā kilesā samucchinnā. Aggamaggena samugghāṭitattā eva ca nesaṃ natthi dāni punabbhavo āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti natthīti.

Here, regarding “The barber approached to shave my hair”: in household life, at the time of having his beard trimmed, the barber (`nhāpito`), so-called because he cuts (`kappanato`), approached me to cut my hair and so on. “Then” means from the barber. Regarding “I inspected my body”: seeing in a mirror the signs of gray hairs, wrinkles, and so on, I reflected on my own body, “Indeed, my body is overcome by old age.” And upon so reflecting, “The body was seen as empty” means my body appeared, was known, as empty, devoid of the nature of permanence, stability, happiness, and so on. Why? Regarding “the darkness has departed”: by the darkness called unwise attention, those blinded in their own body, not seeing its existing foul nature, grasp at a non-existent appearance of beauty. In that darkness, that blinding place which is the body, the darkness of ignorance was dispelled by the light of knowledge called wise attention. Therefore, “all defilements are cut off”: the defilements, called ‘rags’ (`coḷā`), were cut off. They are so-called because they are like thieves (`corā`) who destroy wholesome things; or because they are not to be taken up by good people; or because they are like pieces of discarded rags on a rubbish heap, despised by noble ones. And because they were uprooted by the highest path, “now there is no further becoming” means there is no future arising of becoming.

Vītasokattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Vītasoka is concluded.

6. Puṇṇamāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa

Pañca nīvaraṇe hitvātiādikā āyasmato puṇṇamāsattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthari araññe viharante paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ dumasākhāya laggetvā gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe dhanuhattho gahanaṃ paviṭṭho satthu paṃsukūlaṃ disvā pasannamānaso [V 1.0323] dhanuṃ nikkhipitvā buddhaguṇe anussaritvā [M 1.0379] paṃsukūlaṃ vandi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kuṭumbiyakule nibbatti. Tassa kira jātadivase tasmiṃ gehe sabbabhājanāni suvaṇṇaratanamayehi māsehi paripuṇṇāneva ahesuṃ. Tenassa puṇṇamāsotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto dārapariggahaṃ katvā ekasmiṃ putte uppanne gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā gāmakāvāse vasanto ghaṭento vāyamanto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.49.1-8) –

The verses of the Venerable Puṇṇamāsa Thera, beginning with 'Having abandoned the five hindrances.' What is their origin? He too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa and reached maturity. One day, when the Teacher was dwelling in the forest, having hung his rag-robe on a tree branch and entered the fragrant hut, a man with a bow in hand entered the thicket. Seeing the Teacher’s rag-robe, his mind became serene. Putting down his bow, he recollected the virtues of the Buddha and paid homage to the rag-robe. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans, and in this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn into a householder's family in Sāvatthī. It is said that on the day of his birth, all the vessels in that house were completely filled with gold and jewel coins. Therefore, they named him Puṇṇamāsa. Having come of age, he took a wife and had a son. Then, abandoning the household life, he went forth. Dwelling in a village monastery, striving and exerting himself, he attained the six higher knowledges. As it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.49.1-8):

“Tisso nāmāsi bhagavā, sayambhū aggapuggalo;

Paṃsukūlaṃ ṭhapetvāna, vihāraṃ pāvisī jino.

“The Blessed One was named Tissa, the Self-Become One, the foremost person; having laid aside his rag-robe, the Conqueror entered his dwelling.”

“Vinataṃ dhanumādāya, bhakkhatthāya cariṃ ahaṃ;

Maṇḍalaggaṃ gahetvāna, kānanaṃ pāvisiṃ ahaṃ.

“Taking up a bent bow, I wandered for game; grasping a sword, I entered the forest.”

“Tatthaddasaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, dumagge laggitaṃ tadā;

Cāpaṃ tattheva nikkhippa, sire katvāna añjaliṃ.

“There I saw a rag-robe hanging on a treetop at that time. Laying down my bow right there, I placed my joined hands on my head in homage.”

“Pasannacitto sumano, vipulāya ca pītiyā;

Buddhaseṭṭhaṃ saritvāna, paṃsukūlaṃ avandahaṃ.

“With a serene and joyful mind, and with abundant delight, recollecting the Supreme Buddha, I paid homage to the rag-robe.”

“Dvenavute ito kappe, paṃsukūlamavandahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, vandanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-two aeons ago from now, I paid homage to that rag-robe. I know of no bad destination since then; this is the fruit of that veneration.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā sāvatthiṃ upagantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā susāne vasati, tassa ca acirāgatasseva sato putto kālamakāsi. Dārakamātā therassa āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā, “mā idaṃ aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājāno hareyyu”nti taṃ uppabbājetukāmā mahatā parivārena [P 2.0047] therassa santikaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā palobhetuṃ ārabhi. Thero attano vītarāgabhāvajānāpanatthaṃ ākāse ṭhatvā attano paṭipattikittanamukhena tassā dhammaṃ desento –

Having become one with the six higher knowledges, he went to Sāvatthī, paid homage to the Teacher, and dwelt in a charnel ground. Not long after his arrival, his son passed away. The boy’s mother, hearing of the elder’s arrival and desiring to make him disrobe, thinking, “Lest the kings seize this heirless property,” went to the elder with a large retinue, exchanged courteous greetings, and began to entice him. The elder, to make known his state of dispassion, stood in the air and, by way of extolling his own practice, taught her the Dhamma:

171.

171.

“Pañca nīvaraṇe hitvā, yogakkhemassa pattiyā;

Dhammādāsaṃ gahetvāna, ñāṇadassanamattano.

“Having abandoned the five hindrances for the attainment of security from the yokes, having taken the mirror of the Dhamma, one’s own knowledge and vision,

172.

172.

“Paccavekkhiṃ [M 1.0380] imaṃ kāyaṃ, sabbaṃ santarabāhiraṃ;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, tuccho kāyo adissathā”ti. –

“I contemplated this body, all of it, internal and external. Both internally and externally, the body appeared empty.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha [V 1.0324] pañca nīvaraṇe hitvāti kāmacchandādike pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya jhānādhigamena viddhaṃsetvā. Yogakkhemassa pattiyāti kāmayogādīhi catūhi yogehi khemassa anupaddutassa nibbānassa adhigamāya. Dhammādāsanti dhammabhūtaṃ ādāsaṃ. Yathā hi ādāso olokentassa rūpakāye guṇāguṇaṃ ādaṃseti, evaṃ vipassanāsaṅkhāto dhammānaṃ sāmaññavisesāvabodhanato ñāṇadassanabhūto dhammādāso vipassantassa vodānasaṃkilesadhammavibhāvanena tappahānasādhanena ca visesato nāmakāye guṇaṃ ādaṃseti. Tenāha –

Herein, 'Having abandoned the five hindrances' means having forsaken the five hindrances, such as sensual desire, and having destroyed them through the attainment of jhāna. 'For the attainment of security from the yokes' means for the attainment of Nibbāna, which is secure and untroubled by the four yokes, such as the yoke of sensuality. 'The mirror of the Dhamma' means the mirror that is the Dhamma. For just as a mirror shows the qualities and faults in the physical body of one who looks, so too the mirror of the Dhamma—which is called insight, and which is knowledge and vision due to its understanding of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena—especially shows the qualities in the mental body of one who practices insight, by means of clarifying pure and defiled states and by the means for their abandonment. Therefore, he said:

“Dhammādāsaṃ gahetvāna, ñāṇadassanamattano;

Paccavekkhiṃ imaṃ kāyaṃ, sabbaṃ santarabāhira”nti. –

“Having taken the mirror of the Dhamma, one’s own knowledge and vision, I contemplated this body, all of it, internal and external.”

Imaṃ kāyaṃ dhammasamūhaṃ mama attabhāvaṃ ajjhattikabāhirāyatanabhāvato santarabāhiraṃ sabbaṃ anavasesaṃ dhammādāsaṃ gahetvā “anicca”ntipi “dukkha”ntipi “anattā”tipi patiavekkhiṃ ñāṇacakkhunā passiṃ. Evaṃ passatā ca mayā ajjhattañca bahiddhā cāti attano santāne parasantāne ca tuccho kāyo adissatha niccasārādivirahito tuccho khandhapañcakasaṅkhāto attabhāvakāyo ñāṇacakkhunā yāthāvato apassittha. Sakalampi hi khandhapañcakaṃ “avijjānivutassa, bhikkhave, bālassa taṇhāsaṃyuttassa evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgato”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.19) “kāyo”ti vuccati. “Adissathā”ti ca iminā yadeva kāye daṭṭhabbaṃ, taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, na dānissa kiñci mayā passitabbaṃ atthīti katakiccataṃ dassento aññaṃ byākāsi. Evaṃ thero imāhi gāthāhi purāṇadutiyikāya dhammaṃ desetvā taṃ saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca sampatiṭṭhāpetvā uyyojesi.

Having taken the mirror of Dhamma, I contemplated this body—this aggregate of phenomena, my own personal existence, which is internal and external on account of being the internal and external sense bases, all of it without remainder—as ‘impermanent,’ ‘suffering,’ and ‘not-self’; I saw it with the eye of wisdom. And by me, seeing thus, both internally and externally—that is, in my own continuum and in the continua of others—the body appeared empty. That is, this personal existence, known as the five aggregates, empty and devoid of any permanent essence and so on, was truly seen as it is with the eye of wisdom. For indeed, the entire five aggregates are called ‘body’ in passages such as: ‘Bhikkhus, for the fool enveloped in ignorance, yoked to craving, this body has thus arisen’ (SN 2.19). And by this word ‘appeared,’ he declared his final knowledge, showing that his task was done: ‘Whatever was to be seen in the body has been seen; now there is nothing further for me to see in it.’ In this way, the elder, having taught the Dhamma through these verses to his former wife, established her in the refuges and precepts, and then sent her away.

Puṇṇamāsattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Puṇṇamāsa is finished.

7. Nandakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nandaka

Yathāpi [M 1.0381] bhaddo ājaññoti āyasmato nandakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto sikhissa bhagavato kāle paccantadese uppajjitvā viññutaṃ patto [P 2.0048] vanacāriko hutvā vicaranto ekadivasaṃ satthu caṅkamanaṭṭhānaṃ disvā pasannacitto vālukā okiri. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde campāyaṃ gahapatikule nibbatti, tassa nandakoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Jeṭṭhakabhātā panassa bharato nāma. Tassa pubbayogo anantaravatthusmiṃ āvibhavissati. Te ubhopi [V 1.0325] viññutaṃ patvā āyasmantaṃ soṇaṃ koḷivisaṃ pabbajitaṃ sutvā “soṇopi nāma tathāsukhumālo pabbaji, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya”nti pabbajiṃsu. Tesu bharato nacirasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Nandako pana kilesānaṃ balavabhāvena tāva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetuṃ nāsakkhi, vipassanāya kammaṃ karoti eva. Athassa bharatatthero āsayaṃ ñatvā avassayo bhavitukāmo taṃ pacchāsamaṇaṃ katvā vihārato nikkhamitvā maggasamīpe nisinno vipassanākathaṃ kathesi.

“Just as a fine thoroughbred,” is the verse of the Venerable Nandaka Thera. What is its origin? He, too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds in various existences, was born in a border region during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity, he became a forest-dweller. While wandering, one day he saw the Teacher’s walking path and, with a serene mind, scattered sand on it. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born into a householder’s family in Campā. They named him Nandaka. His elder brother was named Bharata. His past connection will be revealed in the following account. Both of them, having reached maturity, heard that the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa had gone forth and thought, “If even Soṇa, who is so delicate, has gone forth, what then of us?” and so they too went forth. Among them, Bharata soon developed insight and became one with the six higher knowledges. Nandaka, however, due to the strength of his defilements, was not yet able to arouse effort for insight; he was simply doing the practice of insight. Then, the Elder Bharata, knowing his inclination and wishing to be a support for him, made him his attendant. Leaving the monastery, he sat by the roadside and gave a talk on insight.

Tena ca samayena sakaṭasatthe gacchante eko sakaṭe yutto goṇo cikkhallaṭṭhāne sakaṭaṃ uddharituṃ asakkonto paripati. Tato naṃ satthavāho sakaṭā mocetvā tiṇañca pānīyañca datvā parissamaṃ apanetvā puna dhure yojesi. Tato goṇo vūpasantaparissamo laddhabalo taṃ sakaṭaṃ cikkhallaṭṭhānato uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhāpesi. Atha bharatatthero nandakassa “passasi no tvaṃ, āvuso nandaka, imassa kamma”nti taṃ nidassetvā tena “passāmī”ti vutte “imamatthaṃ suṭṭhu upadhārehī”ti āha. Itaro “yathāyaṃ goṇo vūpasantaparissamo paṅkaṭṭhānato bhāraṃ ubbahati, evaṃ mayāpi saṃsārapaṅkato attā uddharitabbo”ti tamevārammaṇaṃ katvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.90-95) –

At that time, as a cart caravan was traveling, an ox yoked to a cart, being unable to pull the cart out of a muddy place, collapsed. Then the caravan leader unyoked it from the cart, gave it grass and water, removed its weariness, and yoked it again to the yoke. Then the ox, its weariness calmed and strength regained, pulled that cart out of the muddy place and set it on dry ground. Then the elder Bharata, pointing this out to Nandaka, said, “Friend Nandaka, do you see this deed?” When he replied, “I see,” the elder said, “Attend well to this matter.” The other thought, “Just as this ox, its weariness calmed, lifts the burden from the muddy place, so too must I lift myself out of the mire of saṃsāra.” Making that very thing his object and practicing insight meditation, before long he attained arahantship. Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:

“Migaluddo [M 1.0382] pure āsiṃ, araññe kānane ahaṃ;

Vātamigaṃ gavesanto, caṅkamaṃ addasaṃ ahaṃ.

“Formerly I was a deer-hunter, in the forest, in the wilderness; seeking an antelope, I saw a walking path.

“Ucchaṅgena pulinaṃ gayha, caṅkame okiriṃ ahaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, sugatassa sirīmato.

“Taking sand in my lap, I scattered it on the walking path; with a clear and joyful mind, for the glorious Sugata.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, pulinaṃ okiriṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pulinassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one eons ago from now, I scattered that sand; I do not recall a bad rebirth. This is the fruit of that sand.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano jeṭṭhabhātikassa bharatattherassa santike aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge in the presence of his elder brother, the elder Bharata:

173.

173.

“Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño, khalitvā patitiṭṭhati;

Bhiyyo laddhāna saṃvegaṃ, adīno vahate dhuraṃ.

“Just as a fine thoroughbred, having stumbled, stands firm again; gaining even more urgency, undaunted, it bears the yoke.”

174.

174.

“Evaṃ dassanasampannaṃ, sammāsambuddhasāvakaṃ;

Ājānīyaṃ maṃ dhāretha, puttaṃ buddhassa orasa”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Thus, one endowed with vision, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One; regard me as a thoroughbred, a true-born son of the Buddha.” – He spoke these two verses.

Tattha [V 1.0326][P 2.0049] bhiyyo laddhāna saṃvegaṃ, adīno vahate dhuranti “mayhaṃ jātibalavīriyānaṃ ananucchavikametaṃ yadidaṃ āgatassa bhārassa avahana”nti saṃvegaṃ labhitvā adīno adīnamānaso alīnacitto. “Alīno”ti vā pāṭho, so eva attho. Bhiyyo punappunaṃ bhiyyosomattāya attano dhuraṃ bhāraṃ vahate ubbahati. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā ramaṇīyavihārittherassa gāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayameva.

Therein, ‘gaining even more urgency, undaunted, it bears the yoke’ means: having gained urgency by thinking, “This is unsuitable for my birth, strength, and energy—this not bearing of the burden that has come,” he is undaunted (adīno), with an undaunted mind (adīnamānaso), with an unshrinking mind (alīnacitto). Or the reading is ‘alīno,’ and the meaning is the same. Again and again, exceedingly, he bears and lifts his own yoke, his burden. The rest is in the same way as was explained below in the commentary on the verses of the Elder Ramaṇīyavihārin.

Nandakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nandaka is concluded.

8. Bharatattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bharata

Ehi[M 1.0383], nandaka, gacchāmāti āyasmato bharatattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira anomadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ manuññadassanaṃ mudusukhasamphassaṃ upāhanadvayaṃ gahetvā gacchanto satthāraṃ caṅkamantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso upāhanā upanāmetvā, “abhiruhatu bhagavā upāhanā, yaṃ mama assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti āha. Abhiruhi bhagavā tassa anuggaṇhanatthaṃ upāhanā. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde campānagare gahapatikule nibbatti, bharatotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto soṇattherassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā “sopi nāma pabbajī”ti sañjātasaṃvego pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.71-89) –

“Come, Nandaka, let us go” is a verse of the venerable elder Bharata. What is its origin? It is said that this elder was born in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī. Having reached maturity, one day he was going along carrying a pair of sandals that were pleasing to see and soft and pleasant to the touch. Seeing the Teacher on his walking path, with a clear mind he offered the sandals, saying, “May the Blessed One step on these sandals, so that it may be for my long-term welfare and happiness.” The Blessed One stepped on the sandals to show him favor. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, during this Buddha’s appearance, he was born into a householder’s family in the city of Campā, and his name was Bharata. Having reached maturity and hearing that the elder Soṇa had gone forth, he thought, “Even he has gone forth!” and with a sense of urgency arising, he went forth. Having completed his preliminary duties and practicing insight meditation, he soon attained the six higher knowledges. Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:

“Anomadassī bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Divāvihārā nikkhamma, pathamāruhi cakkhumā.

“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the world’s foremost, the bull of men; emerging from his day’s abiding, the one with the Eye set out upon the path.

“Pānadhiṃ sukataṃ gayha, addhānaṃ paṭipajjahaṃ;

Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, pattikaṃ cārudassanaṃ.

“Taking a well-made pair of sandals, I set out on a journey; there I saw the Sambuddha, of pleasing appearance, walking on foot.

“Sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā, nīharitvāna pānadhiṃ;

Pādamūle ṭhapetvāna, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

“Having cleared my mind, and taking out the sandals, I placed them at his feet and spoke these words:

“Abhirūha mahāvīra, sugatinda vināyaka;

Ito phalaṃ labhissāmi, so me attho samijjhatu.

“‘Step upon them, great hero, chief of Sugatas, leader; from this I shall obtain the fruit, may that purpose of mine succeed.’

“Anomadassī bhagavā, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho;

Pānadhiṃ abhirūhitvā, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“The Blessed One Anomadassī, the world’s foremost, the bull of men, having stepped on the sandals, spoke these words:

“Yo [V 1.0327] pānadhiṃ me adāsi, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

“‘He who gave me sandals, with a clear mind and his own hands; I will extol him, listen to me as I speak.

“Buddhassa giramaññāya, sabbe devā samāgatā;

Udaggacittā sumanā, vedajātā katañjalī.

“‘Having understood the Buddha’s words, all the gods assembled; with uplifted and glad minds, filled with joy, with hands joined in homage.

“Pānadhīnaṃ [M 1.0384] padānena, sukhitoyaṃ bhavissati;

Pañcapaññāsakkhattuñca, devarajjaṃ karissati.

“‘By this gift of sandals, this one will be happy; and fifty-five times he will rule as king of the gods.

“Sahassakkhattuṃ rājā ca, cakkavattī bhavissati;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

“‘A thousand times he will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch; his widespread regional kingship will be beyond counting.

“Aparimeyye ito kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“‘In an incalculable eon from now, born of the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama will be in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“‘He will be an heir to his Dhamma, a true-born son created by the Dhamma; having fully understood all the taints, he will attain Nibbāna without taints.

“Devaloke manusse vā, nibbattissati puññavā;

Devayānapaṭibhāgaṃ, yānaṃ paṭilabhissati.

“‘This meritorious one will be reborn in the world of gods or among humans; he will obtain a vehicle comparable to that of the gods.

“Pāsādā sivikā vayhaṃ, hatthino samalaṅkatā;

Rathā vājaññasaṃyuttā, sadā pātubhavanti me.

“‘Mansions, palanquins, and litters, well-adorned elephants, chariots yoked with thoroughbreds, always appear for me.

“Agārā nikkhamantopi, rathena nikkhamiṃ ahaṃ;

Kesesu chijjamānesu, arahattamapāpuṇiṃ.

“‘Even when going forth from home, I went forth in a chariot; while my hair was being cut, I attained arahantship.

“Lābhā mayhaṃ suladdhaṃ me, vāṇijjaṃ suppayojitaṃ;

Datvāna pānadhiṃ ekaṃ, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“‘A gain for me, well-gained by me, my commerce well-applied; having given a single pair of sandals, I have attained the unshakable state.

“Aparimeyye ito kappe, yaṃ pānadhimadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, pānadhissa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“‘In an incalculable eon ago, when I gave those sandals, I do not recall a bad rebirth. This is the fruit of those sandals.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“‘My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.’”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā attano kaniṭṭhabhātikena nandakattherena heṭṭhā vuttanayena aññābyākaraṇe kate “idāni nandakopi arahā jāto, handa mayaṃ ubhopi satthu santikaṃ gantvā vusitabrahmacariyataṃ nivedessāmāti uppannaṃ parivitakkaṃ nandakattherassa kathento –

Having become one with the six higher knowledges, when his younger brother, the elder Nandaka, made his declaration of final knowledge in the way described above, the following reflection arose in him: “Now Nandaka too has become an arahant. Come, let us both go to the Teacher’s presence and announce that we have lived the holy life.” Relating this reflection to the elder Nandaka, he said:

175.

175.

“Ehi nandaka gacchāma, upajjhāyassa santikaṃ;

Sīhanādaṃ nadissāma, buddhaseṭṭhassa sammukhā.

“Come, Nandaka, let us go to our preceptor’s presence; we shall roar the lion’s roar before the best of Buddhas.

176.

176.

“Yāya [M 1.0385] no anukampāya, amhe pabbājayī muni;

So no attho anuppatto, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“‘The purpose for which the sage, out of compassion for us, ordained us—that purpose has been attained by us: the destruction of all fetters.’” – He spoke these two verses.

Tattha [V 1.0328][P 2.0050] nandakāti ālapanaṃ. Ehīti tassa attano santikakaraṇaṃ. Gacchāmāti tena attanā ca ekajjhaṃ kātabbakiriyāvacanaṃ, upajjhāyassāti sammāsambuddhassa, sammāsambuddho hi samantacakkhunā buddhacakkhunā ca sattānaṃ āsayānusayacaritādīnaṃ yathābhūtavilokanena sadevakassa lokassa vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyatīti visesato upajjhāyoti vattabbataṃ arahati. Yadatthaṃ gamanaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “sīhanādaṃ nadissāma, buddhaseṭṭhassa sammukhā”ti āha. Yathābhuccaguṇābhibyāhāratāya abhītanādabhāvato sīhanādaṃ buddhassa sammāsambuddhassa tato eva sabbasattuttamatāya seṭṭhassa, buddhānaṃ vā sāvakabuddhādīnaṃ seṭṭhassa sammukhā purato nadissāmāti attho.

Here, 'Nandaka' is an address. 'Come' is drawing him into one's own presence. 'We shall go' is a statement of action to be done together by oneself and him. 'To the Preceptor' refers to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, with the all-seeing eye and the Buddha-eye, truly observes the inclinations, latent tendencies, and behaviors of beings as they really are, thus examining the faults and virtues of the world, including its gods. Therefore, He is especially worthy of being called the Preceptor. To indicate the purpose of going, he said, 'We shall roar the lion's roar in the presence of the Supreme Buddha.' Because it is a fearless roar due to the declaration of qualities as they truly are, it is called the lion’s roar. In the presence of the Supreme Buddha—supreme among all beings due to His very enlightenment—or in the presence of the foremost among Buddhas, such as Paccekabuddhas and disciple-Buddhas, we shall roar. This is the meaning.

Yathā pana sīhanādaṃ naditukāmo, taṃ dassento “yāyā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha yāyāti yadatthaṃ, yāya yadatthānuppattiyāti attho. Noti amhākaṃ. Anukampāyāti anuggaṇhanena amhe dvepi pabbājayi pabbājesi. Munīti bhagavā. So no attho anuppattoti so attho sabbesaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khayabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ no amhehi anuppatto, adhigatoti attho.

Now, demonstrating this, as one wishing to roar the lion's roar, he spoke the verse beginning 'Yāyā.' Here, 'Yāyā' means 'for what purpose,' or 'for the attainment of what purpose.' 'No' means 'for us.' 'Out of compassion' means that out of favor he made both of us go forth, he ordained us. 'The Sage' means the Blessed One. 'That goal has been attained by us' means that goal, the fruit of arahantship, which is the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by us, realized—this is the meaning.

Bharatattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bharata is concluded.

9. Bhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhāradvāja

Nadanti evaṃ sappaññāti āyasmato bhāradvājattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sumanaṃ nāma paccekabuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso [M 1.0386] paripakkaṃ vallikāraphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā gottanāmena bhāradvājotveva paññāyittha. So vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekaputtaṃ labhi. Tassa “kaṇhadinno”ti nāmaṃ akāsi. Tassa viññutaṃ pattakāle “tāta, asukassa nāma ācariyassa santike sippaṃ sikkhitvā ehī”ti taṃ takkasilaṃ pesesi. So gacchanto antarāmagge satthu sāvakaṃ aññataraṃ mahātheraṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ labhitvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā katapubbakicco vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.66-70) –

'Thus do the wise proclaim'—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bhāradvāja. What is its origin? This elder too had made his resolve in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences. In the thirty-first aeon from now, he was born into a good family.
