Having come of age, one day he saw the Paccekabuddha named Sumana wandering for alms. With a joyful mind, he offered him a fully ripened vallikāra fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, at the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Rājagaha. He became known by the clan name Bhāradvāja. When he came of age and while living the household life, he obtained a single son. He named him 'Kaṇhadinna.' When his son came of age, he said, 'Dear son, go and learn a craft from such-and-such a teacher, then return.' Thus, he sent him to Takkasilā. On the way, his son met a great elder, a disciple of the Teacher and a noble friend. Hearing the Dhamma from him, he gained faith, went forth, and fulfilled his preliminary duties. Applying himself to insight meditation, he soon attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.48.66-70):

“Sumano [V 1.0329] nāma sambuddho, takkarāyaṃ vasī tadā;

Vallikāraphalaṃ gayha, sayambhussa adāsahaṃ.

“The Sambuddha named Sumana dwelt in Takkara at that time; taking a vallikāra fruit, I gave it to the Self-Become One.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that fruit-offering.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Athassa [P 2.0051] pitā bhāradvājo veḷuvane viharantaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Atha putto satthāraṃ vandituṃ rājagahaṃ āgato satthu santike nisinnaṃ pitaraṃ disvā tuṭṭhacitto “pitāpi kho me pabbajito, kiṃ nu kho tena pabbajjākiccaṃ matthakaṃ pāpita”nti vīmaṃsanto khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ sīhanādaṃ nadāpetukāmo, “sādhu, kho tumhehi kataṃ pabbajantehi, pabbajjākiccaṃ pana matthakaṃ pāpita”nti pucchi. Bhāradvājo puttassa adhigamaṃ dīpento –

Then his father, Bhāradvāja, approached the Blessed One dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, heard the Dhamma, went forth, and soon actualized arahantship. Then his son came to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher. Seeing his father seated near the Teacher, he was delighted and thought, 'My father too has gone forth. Has he brought the purpose of going forth to completion?' Investigating thus, and knowing his father’s state of having destroyed the taints, he wished to make him roar the lion’s roar, and asked, 'It is good indeed that you have gone forth, but has the purpose of going forth been brought to its culmination?' Bhāradvāja, revealing his own attainment to his son, said:

177.

177.

“Nadanti evaṃ sappaññā, sīhāva girigabbhare;

Vīrā vijitasaṅgāmā, jetvā māraṃ savāhanaṃ.

“Thus roar the wise, like lions in mountain caves, heroes victorious in battle, having conquered Māra with his mount.

178.

178.

“Satthā ca pariciṇṇo me, dhammo saṅgho ca pūjito;

Ahañca vitto sumano, puttaṃ disvā anāsava”nti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“The Teacher has been attended to by me, the Dhamma and the Sangha have been honored; and I am delighted and glad, seeing my son taintless.” — He spoke these two verses.

Tattha [M 1.0387] nadantīti yathābhuccaguṇābhibyāhāravasena abhītanādaṃ nadanti gajjanti. Evanti idāni vattabbākāradassanaṃ. Sappaññāti aggamaggapaññādhigamena sabbapaññādhigamena sabbapaññāvepullappattā. Vīrāti catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyasampannatāya vīrā, tato eva anavasesasaṃkilesapakkhanimmathanena savāhanaṃ kilesamāraṃ abhisaṅkhāramāraṃ devaputtamārañca jetvā sabbaso vijitasaṅgāmā nadanti sappaññāti sambandho.

There, 'they roar' means they roar and thunder a fearless roar by way of proclaiming qualities as they truly are. 'Thus' indicates the manner of what is to be stated now. 'The wise' means those who have attained the full development of all wisdom by acquiring the wisdom of the highest path. 'Heroes' means they are heroes, endowed with the four kinds of right effort. Therefore, having utterly crushed the entire faction of defilements, having conquered the defilement-Māra with its mount, the Māra of formations, and the Māra of the devas, they are completely victorious in battle. Thus, 'the wise roar' is the connection.

Evaṃ vijetabbavijayena sīhanādaṃ dassetvā idāni ārādhetabbasamārādhanena icchitabbasiddhiyā ca taṃ dassetuṃ, “satthā ca pariciṇṇo me”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha satthā ca pariciṇṇo meti mama satthā sammāsambuddho yathānusiṭṭhaṃ ovādānusāsanīkaraṇena mayā pariciṇṇo upāsito, na dhammādhikaraṇaṃ visositoti adhippāyo. Dhammo saṅgho ca pūjitoti navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo, yathāpaṭipattiyāgatamaggānuppattiyā sīladiṭṭhisāmaññagamanena ariyasaṅgho ca mayā pūjito mānito. Ahañca vitto sumano, puttaṃ disvā anāsavanti mama puttaṃ [V 1.0330] anāsavaṃ sabbaso khīṇāsavaṃ disvā dassanahetu ahampi vitto nirāmisāya pītiyā tuṭṭho, tatoyeva nirāmisena somanassena sumano jātoti attho.

Having thus shown the lion's roar by means of the victory that should be won, he now spoke the second verse, 'The Teacher has been attended to by me,' in order to show it by means of the accomplishment that should be achieved and the success that should be desired. Here, 'The Teacher has been attended to by me' means that my Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, has been attended to and served by me by carrying out his advice and instruction, with the intention that the matter of the Dhamma should not be neglected. 'The Dhamma and the Sangha have been honored' means that the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, and the Noble Sangha—through arriving at commonality in virtue and views by attaining the path that comes from right practice—have been honored and revered by me. 'And I am delighted and glad, seeing my son taintless' means that because of seeing my son taintless, entirely free from taints, I too am delighted, pleased with non-sensual joy, and from that very non-sensual happiness, I have become glad.

Bhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Bhāradvāja is concluded.

10. Kaṇhadinnattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kaṇhadinna

Upāsitā [P 2.0052] sappurisāti āyasmato kaṇhadinnattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito catunavute kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sobhitaṃ nāma paccekabuddhaṃ disvā pasannacitto punnāgapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā kaṇhadinnoti laddhanāmo vayappatto upanissayasampattiyā codiyamāno dhammasenāpatiṃ upasaṅkamitvā [M 1.0388] dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.61-65) –

'Good people have been attended to'—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Kaṇhadinna. What is its origin? He too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family ninety-four aeons ago. Reaching maturity, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sobhita and, with a serene mind, made an offering with punnāga flowers. Through that meritorious act, wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Rājagaha at the arising of this Buddha, and was named Kaṇhadinna. Coming of age, urged by his supportive conditions, he approached the General of the Dhamma, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.48.61-65):

“Sobhito nāma sambuddho, cittakūṭe vasī tadā;

Gahetvā giripunnāgaṃ, sayambhuṃ abhipūjayiṃ.

“The Sambuddha named Sobhita dwelt on Cittakūṭa at that time; taking a mountain punnāga flower, I worshipped the Self-Become One.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I worshipped the Buddha, I do not recall any bad rebirth—this is the fruit of that Buddha-worship.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, he then declared his final knowledge:

179.

179.

“Upāsitā sappurisā, sutā dhammā abhiṇhaso;

Sutvāna paṭipajjissaṃ, añjasaṃ amatogadhaṃ.

“Good people have been attended to, the Dhamma has been frequently heard; having heard, I shall practice the straight path that leads to the deathless.

180.

180.

“Bhavarāgahatassa me sato, bhavarāgo puna me na vijjati;

Na cāhu na ca me bhavissati, na ca me etarahi vijjatī”ti. –

“For me, who was afflicted by craving for existence, that craving for existence is no longer found; it was not, nor will it be, nor is it present in me now.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha upāsitāti paricaritā paṭipattipayirupāsanāya payirupāsitā. Sappurisāti santehi [V 1.0331] sīlādiguṇehi samannāgatā purisā, ariyapuggalā sāriputtattherādayo. Etena purimacakkadvayasampattimattano dasseti. Na hi patirūpadesavāsena vinā sappurisūpanissayo sambhavati. Sutā dhammāti saccapaṭiccasamuppādādipaṭisaṃyuttadhammā sotadvārānusārena upadhāritā. Etena attano bāhusaccaṃ dassento pacchimacakkadvayasampattiṃ dasseti. Abhiṇhasoti bahuso na kālena kālaṃ. Idañca padaṃ “upāsitā sappurisā”ti etthāpi yojetabbaṃ. Sutvāna paṭipajjissaṃ, añjasaṃ amatogadhanti te dhamme sutvā tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme salakkhaṇādito pariggahetvā anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā amatogadhaṃ nibbānapatiṭṭhaṃ taṃsampāpakaṃ añjasaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃ pāpuṇiṃ.

Here, upāsitā means served, attended upon, closely associated with through practice. Sappurisā refers to virtuous men endowed with qualities such as morality, noble individuals like the Elder Sāriputta and others. By this, he indicates his own possession of the first two wheels of progress. For without residing in a suitable place, association with the virtuous is not possible. Sutā dhammā refers to the teachings connected with the truths, dependent origination, and so on, grasped through the ear-door. By this, in showing his extensive learning, he indicates his possession of the latter two wheels of progress. Abhiṇhaso means repeatedly, not just from time to time. This phrase should also be connected with upāsitā sappurisā. Sutvāna paṭipajjissaṃ, añjasaṃ amatogadhan means: having heard those teachings, having comprehended the phenomena of form and formlessness described therein according to their characteristics, and having developed insight step by step, I practiced and attained the direct Noble Eightfold Path which leads to the deathless, the foundation of Nibbāna.

Bhavarāgahatassa [M 1.0389] me satoti bhavarāgena bhavataṇhāya anādimati [P 2.0053] saṃsāre hatassa upaddutassa mama sato samānassa, aggamaggena vā hatabhavarāgassa. Bhavarāgo puna me na vijjatīti tato eva puna idāni bhavarāgo me natthi. Na cāhu na me bhavissati, na ca me etarahi vijjatīti yadipi pubbe puthujjanakāle sekkhakāle ca me bhavarāgo ahosi, aggamaggappattito pana paṭṭhāya na cāhu na ca ahosi, āyatimpi na me bhavissati, etarahi adhunāpi na ca me vijjati na ca upalabbhati, pahīnoti attho. Bhavarāgavacaneneva cettha tadekaṭṭhatāya mānādīnampi abhāvo vuttoti sabbaso parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanataṃ dasseti.

Bhavarāgahatassa me sato means: of me, who was afflicted and harassed by craving for existence—by craving for becoming—in beginningless saṃsāra; or of me, whose craving for existence has been destroyed by the supreme path. Bhavarāgo puna me na vijjatī means: for that very reason, craving for becoming is no longer present in me now. Na cāhu na ca me bhavissati, na ca me etarahi vijjatī means: although in the past, during my time as a worldling and as a learner, craving for existence was present in me, from the attainment of the supreme path onwards it was not, nor will it be for me in the future, nor is it found or present in me now—the meaning is, it has been abandoned. By the mention of ‘craving for existence,’ the absence of conceit and other defilements is also stated here, due to their having one and the same basis, thus showing the complete destruction of the fetters of existence.

Kaṇhadinnattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kaṇhadinna is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third chapter is concluded.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter

1. Migasirattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Migasira

Yato [V 1.0332] ahaṃ pabbajitoti āyasmato migasirattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto kassapassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto kusaṭṭhakaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā migasiranakkhattena jātattā migasiroti laddhanāmo vayappatto brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato chavasīsamantaṃ nāma sikkhi, yaṃ parijappetvā tivassamatthake matānampi sīsaṃ nakhena ākoṭetvā “ayaṃ satto asukaṭṭhāne nibbatto”ti jānāti.

“Since I went forth…”: these are the verses of the Venerable Migasira. What is their origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was born into a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Having attained understanding, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a confident mind, offered a handful of kusa grass. By that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, during this Buddha-era he took rebirth in a brahmin family in the Kosala country. As he was born under the Migasira constellation, he was given the name Migasira. Having reached maturity, he became accomplished in the knowledge and arts of the brahmins and learned a spell called the Chavasīsamanta. By reciting it, he could strike the head of a dead person with his fingernail, even one dead for three years, and know, “This being was reborn in such-and-such a place.”

So gharāvāsaṃ anicchanto paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā taṃ vijjaṃ nissāya lokena sakkato garukato lābhī hutvā vicaranto sāvatthiṃ upagato [M 1.0390] satthu santikaṃ gantvā attano ānubhāvaṃ pakāsento – “ahaṃ, bho gotama, matānaṃ nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānāmī”ti vatvā, “kathaṃ pana tvaṃ jānāsī”ti vutte, “chavasīsāni āharāpetvā mantaṃ parijappetvā nakhena sīsaṃ ākoṭento nirayādikaṃ tehi tehi nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānāmī”ti kathesi. Athassa bhagavā parinibbutassa bhikkhuno sīsakapālaṃ āharāpetvā, “kathehi tāva tassa gatiṃ, yassidaṃ sīsakapāla”nti āha. So taṃ kapālaṃ mantaṃ parijappetvā nakhena ākoṭetvā neva antaṃ na koṭiṃ passati. Atha satthārā, “na sakkosi paribbājakā”ti vutte[P 2.0054], “upaparikkhissāmi tāvā”ti vatvā punappunaṃ parivattentopi na passateva. Bāhirakamantena hi khīṇāsavassa gatiṃ kathaṃ jānissati, athassa matthakato kacchehi ca sedo mucci. So lajjitvā tuṇhībhūto aṭṭhāsi. Satthā “kilamasi paribbājakā”ti āha. So “āma, kilamāmi, na imassa gatiṃ jānāmi, tumhe pana jānāthā”ti. “Ahaṃ etaṃ jānāmi, ito uttaritarampi jānāmī”ti vatvā “nibbānaṃ gato so”ti āha. Paribbājako “imaṃ vijjaṃ mayhaṃ dethā”ti āha. “Tena hi pabbajā”ti vatvā taṃ pabbājetvā paṭhamaṃ samathakammaṭṭhāne niyojetvā [V 1.0333] jhānābhiññāsu patiṭṭhitassa vipassanāya kammaṃ upadisi. So vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.56-60) –

Not desiring the household life, he went forth into the homeless life of a wanderer. Relying on that knowledge, he was honored, respected, and esteemed by the world, and he became a recipient of gains. While wandering, he came to Sāvatthī and approached the Teacher. Displaying his own power, he said, “Venerable Gotama, I know the places of rebirth of the dead.” When asked, “But how do you know?” he explained, “Having skulls brought, reciting a spell, and tapping the skull with my fingernail, I know their various places of rebirth, such as in hell.” Then the Blessed One had the skull of a bhikkhu who had attained final Nibbāna brought and said, “Then tell me the destination of the one to whom this skull belongs.” The wanderer recited his spell over that skull and tapped it with his fingernail, but he could perceive neither its beginning nor its end. When the Teacher said, “You cannot, wanderer,” he replied, “I will examine it further,” but even after turning it over again and again, he still saw nothing. For how could he know the destination of one whose taints were destroyed by means of an external spell? Then sweat poured from his head and from his armpits. Ashamed, he stood in silence. The Teacher asked, “Are you weary, wanderer?” He replied, “Yes, I am weary. I do not know this one’s destination, but do you know?” The Teacher said, “I know this, and I know even beyond this,” and he declared, “He has gone to Nibbāna.” The wanderer said, “Give this knowledge to me.” The Teacher replied, “In that case, go forth.” Having ordained him, he first engaged him in a meditation subject for serenity. Once he was established in the jhānas and the higher knowledges, the Teacher instructed him in the practice of insight. Practicing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kassapassa bhagavato, brāhmaṇassa vusīmato;

Pasannacitto sumano, kusaṭṭhakamadāsahaṃ.

“To the Blessed One Kassapa, the brahmin who has lived the holy life; with a confident and joyful mind, I gave a handful of kusa grass.

“Imasmiṃyeva kappasmiṃ, kusaṭṭhakamadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, kusaṭṭhakassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In this very eon, I gave a handful of kusa grass; I know of no bad destination since. This is the fruit of that handful of kusa grass.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Then, having attained arahantship, he declared his final knowledge:

181.

181.

“Yato ahaṃ pabbajito, sammāsambuddhasāsane;

Vimuccamāno uggacchiṃ, kāmadhātuṃ upaccagaṃ.

“Since I went forth in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, becoming liberated, I ascended; I transcended the sense-sphere realm.

182.

182.

“Brahmuno [M 1.0391] pekkhamānassa, tato cittaṃ vimucci me;

Akuppā me vimuttīti, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayā”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“While the supreme Brahmā was looking on, my mind was then liberated. My liberation is unshakeable, through the destruction of all fetters.” — He spoke these two verses.

Tattha yato ahaṃ pabbajito, sammāsambuddhasāsaneti yato pabhuti ahaṃ pabbajito buddhassa bhagavato sāsane, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya. Vimuccamāno uggacchinti saṃkilesapakkhato paṭhamaṃ tāva samathavipassanāhi vimuccamāno vodānadhammasavanena uṭṭhahiṃ. Evaṃ uggacchanto kāmadhātuṃ upaccagaṃ anāgāmimaggena accantameva kāmadhātuṃ atikkamiṃ.

Here, Yato ahaṃ pabbajito, sammāsambuddhasāsane means: from the time I went forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One, the Buddha; that is, from the time of my going forth. Vimuccamāno uggacchiṃ means: being liberated, I ascended—first, being liberated from the side of the defilements by serenity and insight, I was uplifted by hearing the purifying Dhamma. Thus ascending, kāmadhātuṃ upaccagaṃ means: I completely transcended the sense-sphere realm by means of the path of the non-returner.

Brahmuno pekkhamānassa, tato cittaṃ vimucci meti sadevakassa lokassa aggabhūtattā seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmuno buddhassa bhagavato mahākaruṇāyogena “ayaṃ kulaputto mama sāsane pabbajitvā kathaṃ nu kho paṭipajjatī”ti pekkhantassa tato anāgāmimaggādhigamato pacchā aggamaggādhigamena mama cittaṃ sabbasaṃkilesato accantameva mucci. Akuppā [P 2.0055] me vimuttīti, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayāti tathāvimuttacittattā eva sabbesaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ khayā parikkhayā iti evaṃ akuppā me vimuttīti aññaṃ byākāsi.

Brahmuno pekkhamānassa, tato cittaṃ vimucci me means: while Brahmā—that is, the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is Brahmā in the sense of being the best, as he is foremost in the world with its gods—was looking on, and who, out of great compassion, was watching and thinking, “This clansman has gone forth in my dispensation; how will he practice?”—then, after attaining the path of the non-returner, my mind was completely liberated from all defilements through the attainment of the highest path. Akuppā me vimuttīti, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayā means: ‘My liberation is unshakeable, through the destruction of all fetters.’ Because his mind was thus liberated, with the destruction and complete exhaustion of all fetters, he thus declared his final knowledge: “My liberation is unshakeable.”

Migasirattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Migasira is concluded.

2. Sivakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sivaka

Aniccāni [V 1.0334] gahakānīti āyasmato sivakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ passitvā pasannamānaso pattaṃ ādāya kummāsassa pūretvā adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, sivakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ [M 1.0392] gato nekkhammajjhāsayatāya kāme pahāya paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vicaranto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.56.117-121) –

‘Impermanent are houses’ is the verse of the Venerable Elder Sivaka. What is his origin? He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in a family home during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One walking for alms and, with a confident mind, took his bowl, filled it with sour gruel, and gave it. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Rājagaha, and his name was Sivaka. Having come of age and attained proficiency in the arts and sciences, with an inclination for renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth as a wandering ascetic. While wandering, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. After going forth and practicing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.56.117–121)—

“Esanāya carantassa, vipassissa mahesino;

Rittakaṃ pattaṃ disvāna, kummāsaṃ pūrayiṃ ahaṃ.

“While the great sage Vipassī was wandering in search of alms, I saw his empty bowl and filled it with sour gruel.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ bhikkhamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, kummāsassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first aeon from now, for the alms I gave then, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of the sour gruel.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, he then made this declaration—

183.

183.

“Aniccāni gahakāni, tattha tattha punappunaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

“Impermanent are houses, here and there again and again; seeking the house-builder, painful is birth again and again.”

184.

184.

“Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, thūṇikā ca vidālitā;

Vimariyādikataṃ cittaṃ, idheva vidhamissatī”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“House-builder, you are seen; you will not build a house again. All your rafters are broken, your pillar is shattered. My mind has been made boundless; it will be utterly extinguished right here.” Thus he uttered these two verses.

Tattha aniccāni gahakāni, tattha tattha punappunanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave punappunaṃ nibbattamānāni gahakāni attabhāvagehāni na nibbāni anavaṭṭhitāni ittarāni parittakālāni. Gahakāraṃ gavesantoti imassa attabhāvagehassa kārakaṃ taṇhāvaḍḍhakiṃ pariyesanto ettakaṃ kālaṃ anuvicarinti adhippāyo. Dukkhā jāti punappunanti idaṃ gahakārakagavesanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ[P 2.0056]. Yasmā [V 1.0335] jarābyādhimaraṇamissatāya jāti nāmesā punappunaṃ upagantuṃ dukkhā, na ca sā tasmiṃ adiṭṭhe nivattati, tasmā taṃ gavesanto vicarinti attho.

Therein, “impermanent are houses, here and there again and again” means that the houses—the dwellings of individual existence—that are repeatedly produced in this and that state of being, are not permanent, are unstable, transient, and short-lived. “Seeking the house-builder” means: “I have been wandering for so long searching for the maker of this dwelling of individual existence, the craving-carpenter”—this is the intention. “Painful is birth again and again” is a statement of the reason for seeking the house-builder. The meaning is: because birth, being mixed with aging, sickness, and death, is painful to undergo again and again, and it does not cease as long as that house-builder is unseen, therefore I wander seeking him.

Gahakāraka [M 1.0393] diṭṭhosīti idāni pana yena so sakkā daṭṭhuṃ, tena ariyamaggañāṇacakkhunā gahakāraka diṭṭho asi. Puna gehanti puna imasmiṃ saṃsāravaṭṭe attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ mama gehaṃ na kāhasi na karissasi. Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggāti tava sabbā anavasesakilesaphāsukā mayā bhaggā. Thūṇikā ca vidālitāti idāni tayā kātabbassa attabhāvagehassa avijjāsaṅkhātā kaṇṇikā ca bhinnā. Vimariyādikataṃ cittanti mama cittaṃ vigatantaṃ kataṃ, āyatiṃ anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditaṃ. Tato eva idheva vidhamissati imasmiṃyeva bhave viddhaṃsissati, carimakacittanirodhena nirujjhissatīti attho.

“House-builder, you are seen!” means: now, by that with which it is possible to see, by the eye of the knowledge of the noble path, you, house-builder, are seen. “You will not build a house again” means: you will not again make for me a house, that is, an individual existence, in this round of saṃsāra. “All your rafters are broken” means: all your defilement-rafters have been broken by me, without remainder. “And the pillar is shattered” means: now the peak of the roof, that is, ignorance, for the house of individual existence that was to be built by you, has been shattered. “My mind has been made boundless” means: my mind has been made without limit; it has been brought to a state of non-arising in the future. For that very reason, “it will be utterly extinguished right here” means: it will be extinguished in this very existence; it will cease with the cessation of the final consciousness—this is the meaning.

Sivakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Sivaka is concluded.

3. Upavāṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upavāṇa

Arahaṃ sugatoti āyasmato upavāṇattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle daliddakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavati parinibbute tassa dhātuṃ gahetvā manussadevanāgagaruḷakumbhaṇḍayakkhagandhabbehi sattaratanamaye sattayojanike thūpe kate tattha sudhotaṃ attano uttarāsaṅgaṃ veḷagge ābandhitvā dhajaṃ katvā pūjaṃ akāsi. Taṃ gahetvā abhisammatako nāma yakkhasenāpati devehi cetiyapūjārakkhaṇatthaṃ ṭhapito adissamānakāyo ākāse dhārento cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. So taṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso ahosi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā upavāṇoti laddhanāmo vayappatto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto arahattaṃ patvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.56.122-178) –

‘The Arahant, the Well-gone’ is the verse of the Venerable Elder Upavāṇa. What is his origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a poor family. Having attained understanding, after the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna, he took a relic. When a stūpa seven yojanas high and made of the seven kinds of jewels was built by humans, gods, nāgas, garuḍas, kumbhaṇḍas, yakkhas, and gandhabbas, he washed his upper robe, tied it to the tip of a bamboo pole to make a flag, and made an offering. A yakkha general named Abhisammataka, appointed by the gods to guard the shrine, took that flag and, becoming invisible, held it in the sky and circumambulated the shrine three times. Seeing this, his mind became even more confident and joyful. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. Named Upavāṇa, he came of age and, witnessing the Buddha’s power at the dedication of Jetavana, gained faith. He went forth, practiced insight, attained arahantship, and became endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 2.56.122–178)—

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Jalitvā aggikkhandhova, sambuddho parinibbuto.

“The Conqueror named Padumuttara, who had gone to the far shore of all things, having blazed like a mass of fire, the Fully Awakened One passed into final Nibbāna.”

“Mahājanā [M 1.0394] samāgamma, pūjayitvā tathāgataṃ;

Cittaṃ katvāna sugataṃ, sarīraṃ abhiropayuṃ.

“A great crowd of people gathered and, having honored the Tathāgata, they built a pyre for the Sugata and placed his body upon it.”

“Sarīrakiccaṃ katvāna, dhātuṃ tattha samānayuṃ;

Sadevamanussā sabbe, buddhathūpaṃ akaṃsu te.

“Having performed the funeral rites, they gathered the relics there; all of them, gods and humans together, built a stūpa for the Buddha.”

“Paṭhamā [V 1.0336] kañcanamayā, dutiyā ca maṇimayā;

Tatiyā rūpiyamayā, catutthī phalikāmayā.

“The first was made of gold, the second of jewels, the third of silver, and the fourth of crystal.”

“Tattha pañcamikā ceva, lohitaṅkamayā ahu;

Chaṭṭhā masāragallassa, sabbaṃ ratanamayūpari.

“There, the fifth was made of ruby, and the sixth of masāragalla; the entire upper part was made of jewels.”

“Jaṅghā maṇimayā āsi, vedikā ratanāmayā;

Sabbasoṇṇamayo thūpo, uddhaṃ yojanamuggato.

“The drum was made of jewels, the railing of precious gems; the entire stūpa was made of gold, rising a yojana in height.”

“Devā tattha samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Mayampi thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino.

“The gods gathered there and then consulted together: ‘We too shall build a stūpa for the World-Protector, the steadfast one.’”

“Dhātu āveṇikā natthi, sarīraṃ ekapiṇḍitaṃ;

Imamhi buddhathūpamhi, kassāma kañcukaṃ mayaṃ.

“‘There are no separate relics, as the body is a single mass; on this very stūpa of the Buddha, we shall make a casing.’”

“Devā sattahi ratnehi, aññaṃ vaḍḍhesuṃ yojanaṃ;

Thūpo dviyojanubbedho, timiraṃ byapahanti so.

“The gods extended it by another yojana with seven jewels; the stūpa, two yojanas in height, dispels the darkness.”

“Nāgā tattha samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Manussā ceva devā ca, buddhathūpaṃ akaṃsu te.

“Nāgas gathered there and then consulted together: ‘Humans and gods have built a stūpa for the Buddha.’”

“Mā no pamattā assumha, appamattā sadevakā;

Mayampi thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino.

“‘Let us not be heedless; let us be diligent as the gods were. We too shall build a stūpa for the World-Protector, the steadfast one.’”

“Indanīlaṃ mahānīlaṃ, atho jotirasaṃ maṇiṃ;

Ekato sannipātetvā, buddhathūpaṃ achādayuṃ.

“Gathering together indanīla, mahānīla, and also the jotirasa jewel, they covered the Buddha’s stūpa.”

“Sabbaṃ maṇimayaṃ āsi, yāvatā buddhacetiyaṃ;

Tiyojanasamubbedhaṃ, ālokakaraṇaṃ tadā.

“The entire Buddha-shrine was made of jewels; three yojanas in height, it was a source of light at that time.”

“Garuḷā ca samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Manussā devanāgā ca, buddhapūjaṃ akaṃsu te.

“Garuḷas too gathered and consulted together then: ‘Humans, devas, and nāgas have made offerings to the Buddha.’”

“Mā [M 1.0395] no pamattā assumha, appamattā sadevakā;

Mayampi thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino.

“‘Let us not be heedless; let us be diligent as the gods were. We too shall build a stūpa for the World-Protector, the steadfast one.’”

“Sabbaṃ maṇimayaṃ thūpaṃ, akaruṃ te ca kañcukaṃ;

Yojanaṃ tepi vaḍḍhesuṃ, āyataṃ buddhacetiyaṃ.

“They too made a casing for the stūpa, entirely of jewels; they extended the long Buddha-shrine by another yojana.”

“Catuyojanamubbedho, buddhathūpo virocati;

Obhāseti disā sabbā, sataraṃsīva uggato.

“Four yojanas in height, the Buddha’s stūpa gleams; it illuminates all directions, like the rising sun with its rays.”

“Kumbhaṇḍā ca samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Manussā ceva devā ca, nāgā ca garuḷā tathā.

“Kumbhaṇḍas too gathered and consulted together then: ‘Humans and gods, and nāgas and garuḷas likewise…’”

“Paccekaṃ buddhaseṭṭhassa, akaṃsu thūpamuttamaṃ;

Mā no pamattā assumha, appamattā sadevakā.

“‘…they have each built an excellent stūpa for the supreme Buddha. Let us not be heedless; let us be diligent as the gods were.’”

“Mayampi [V 1.0337] thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino;

Ratanehi chādessāma, āyataṃ buddhacetiyaṃ.

“We too shall build a stupa for the World-protector, the steadfast one; We shall cover the extended Buddha-shrine with jewels.”

“Yojanaṃ tepi vaḍḍhesuṃ, āyataṃ buddhacetiyaṃ;

Pañcayojanamubbedho, thūpo obhāsate tadā.

“They increased that Buddha-shrine by a yojana; The stupa then shone, five yojanas in height.”

“Yakkhā tattha samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Manussā devanāgā ca, garuḷā ca kumbhaṇḍakā.

“Yakkhas too gathered and consulted together then: Humans, gods, nāgas, garuḷas, and kumbhaṇḍas (had built stupas).”

“Paccekaṃ buddhaseṭṭhassa, akaṃsu thūpamuttamaṃ;

Mā no pamattā assumha, appamattā sadevakā.

“For each individual Supreme Buddha, they had built an excellent stupa. Let us not be heedless; let us be diligent, together with the devas.”

“Mayampi thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino;

Phalikā chādayissāma, āyataṃ buddhacetiyaṃ.

“We too shall build a stupa for the World-protector, the steadfast one; We shall cover the extended Buddha-shrine with crystal.”

“Yojanaṃ tepi vaḍḍhesuṃ, āyataṃ buddhacetiyaṃ;

Chayojanikamubbedho, thūpo obhāsate tadā.

“They increased that Buddha-shrine by a yojana; Then the stupa, six yojanas in height, shone forth.”

“Gandhabbā ca samāgantvā, ekato mantayuṃ tadā;

Manujā devatā nāgā, kumbhaṇḍā garuḷā tathā.

“Gandhabbas too gathered and consulted together then: Humans, deities, nāgas, kumbhaṇḍas, and garuḷas too (had built stupas).”

“Sabbe akaṃsu buddhathūpaṃ, mayamettha akārakā;

Mayampi thūpaṃ kassāma, lokanāthassa tādino.

“All built a Buddha-stupa; we were non-doers here. We too shall build a stupa for the World-protector, the steadfast one.”

“Vediyo [M 1.0396] satta katvāna, dhajaṃ chattaṃ akaṃsu te;

Sabbasoṇṇamayaṃ thūpaṃ, gandhabbā kārayuṃ tadā.

“Having made seven railings, they made a banner and a parasol; Then the gandhabbas had a stupa made entirely of gold.”

“Sattayojanamubbedho, thūpo obhāsate tadā;

Rattindivā na ñāyanti, āloko hoti sabbadā.

“Seven yojanas in height, the stupa shone forth at that time; Day and night were not discernible, light was everywhere.”

“Abhibhonti na tassābhā, candasūrā satārakā;

Samantā yojanasate, padīpopi na pajjali.

“The radiance of the moon, sun, and stars could not overcome its splendor; For a hundred yojanas around, not even a lamp could burn.”

“Tena kālena ye keci, thūpaṃ pūjenti mānusā;

Na te thūpaṃ āruhanti, ambare ukkhipanti te.

“At that time, whatever people worshipped the stupa, they did not climb the stupa; they tossed them up into the sky.”

“Devehi ṭhapito yakkho, abhisammatanāmako;

Dhajaṃ vā pupphadāmaṃ vā, abhiropeti uttariṃ.

A yakkha named Abhisammata, stationed by the devas, would raise banners or flower garlands even higher.

“Na te passanti taṃ yakkhaṃ, dāmaṃ passanti gacchato;

Evaṃ passitvā gacchantā, sabbe gacchanti suggatiṃ.

They did not see that yakkha, but they saw the garland moving. Seeing it thus as they went, all went to a good destination.

“Viruddhā ye pāvacane, pasannā ye ca sāsane;

Pāṭihīraṃ daṭṭhukāmā, thūpaṃ pūjenti mānusā.

Those who were hostile to the Dispensation and those who were devoted to the Teaching, desiring to see a miracle, people worshipped the stupa.

“Nagare haṃsavatiyā, ahosiṃ bhatako tadā;

Āmoditaṃ janaṃ disvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā.

In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was then a servant. Seeing the delighted populace, I thought thus at that time:

“Uḷāro [V 1.0338] bhagavā neso, yassa dhātughare disaṃ;

Imā ca janatā tuṭṭhā, kāraṃ kubbaṃ na tappare.

“This Blessed One is sublime, in whatever direction his reliquary may be. And this populace is delighted, making offerings without tiring.”

“Ahampi kāraṃ kassāmi, lokanāthassa tādino;

Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, bhavissāmi anāgate.

“I too shall perform service for the World-Lord, the Such One. I shall become an heir to his Dhamma in the future.”

“Sudhotaṃ rajakenāhaṃ, uttareyyaṃ paṭaṃ mama;

Veḷagge ālaggetvāna, dhajaṃ ukkhipimambare.

I had my upper garment well-washed by a washerman. Having fastened it to the top of a bamboo pole, I raised a banner into the sky.

“Abhisammatako gayha, ambare hāsi me dhajaṃ;

Vāteritaṃ dhajaṃ disvā, bhiyyo hāsaṃ janesahaṃ.

Abhisammata took my banner and raised it in the sky. Seeing the banner stirred by the wind, I aroused even more delight.

“Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā, samaṇaṃ upasaṅkamiṃ;

Taṃ bhikkhuṃ abhivādetvā, vipākaṃ pucchahaṃ dhaje.

Having gladdened my mind there, I approached a recluse. Having paid homage to that bhikkhu, I asked him about the result of the banner.

“So [M 1.0397] me kathesi ānandī, pītisañjananaṃ mama;

Tassa dhajassa vipākaṃ, anubhossasi sabbadā.

He spoke to me joyfully, generating joy in me: “You will always experience the result of that banner.”

“Hatthiassarathāpattī, senā ca caturaṅginī;

Parivāressanti taṃ niccaṃ, dhajadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Elephants, horses, chariots, and foot soldiers, a fourfold army will always surround you—this is the fruit of the banner-offering.

“Saṭṭhitūriyasahassāni, bheriyo samalaṅkatā;

Parivāressanti taṃ niccaṃ, dhajadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Sixty thousand musical instruments and adorned drums will always surround you—this is the fruit of the banner-offering.

“Chaḷasīti sahassāni, nāriyo samalaṅkatā;

Vicittavatthābharaṇā, āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā.

“Eighty-six thousand women, well-adorned, with variegated garments and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings.

“Aḷārapamhā hasulā, susaññā tanumajjhimā;

Parivāressanti taṃ niccaṃ, dhajadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“With charming eyelashes, smiling, of fine figure, slender-waisted, they will always surround you—this is the fruit of the banner-offering.

“Tiṃsakappasahassāni, devaloke ramissasi;

Asītikkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjaṃ karissasi.

“For thirty thousand aeons you will rejoice in the world of devas. Eighty times you will reign as Sakka, king of devas.

“Sahassakkhattuṃ rājā ca, cakkavattī bhavissati;

Padesarajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

“A thousand times you will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch. Vast regional kingship, countless in number.

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“In a hundred thousand aeons, born of the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will arise in the world.

“Devalokā cavitvāna, sukkamūlena codito;

Puññakammena saññutto, brahmabandhu bhavissasi.

“Having fallen away from the world of devas, impelled by wholesome roots, endowed with meritorious kamma, you will be a kinsman of Brahmā.

“Asītikoṭiṃ chaḍḍetvā, dāse kammakare bahū;

Gotamassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajissasi.

“Having abandoned eighty crores, many slaves and hired workers, you will go forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama.

“Ārādhayitvā sambuddhaṃ, gotamaṃ sakyapuṅgavaṃ;

Upavāṇoti nāmena, hessasi satthu sāvako.

“Having propitiated the Sambuddha, Gotama, the Sakyan bull, by the name Upavāṇa, you will be the Teacher's disciple.

“Satasahasse [V 1.0339] kataṃ kammaṃ, phalaṃ dassesi me idha;

Sumutto saravegova, kilese jhāpayiṃ mama.

“The kamma done a hundred thousand aeons ago showed its fruit to me here. Well-released, like the speed of an arrow, I have burned up my defilements.

“Cakkavattissa santassa, cātuddīpissarassa me;

Tīṇi yojanāni sāmantā, ussīyanti dhajā sadā.

“For me, the peaceful wheel-turning monarch, lord of the four continents, banners always rose up for three leagues around.

“Satasahassito [M 1.0398] kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dhajadānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“The kamma I did then, a hundred thousand aeons ago, I do not know of any bad destination—this is the fruit of the banner-offering.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up...the Buddha's Dispensation has been done.”

Athāyasmā [P 2.0057] upavāṇo bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Tena ca samayena bhagavato vātābādho uppajji. Therassa ca gihisahāyo devahito nāma brāhmaṇo sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasati. So theraṃ catūhi paccayehi pavedesi. Athāyasmā upavāṇo nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya tassa brāhmaṇassa nivesanaṃ upagacchi. Brāhmaṇo “kenaci aññena payojanena thero āgato”ti ñatvā, “vadeyyātha, bhante, kenattho”ti āha. Thero tassa brāhmaṇassa payojanaṃ ācikkhanto –

Then the Venerable Upavāṇa was the Blessed One's attendant. And at that time, a wind ailment arose in the Blessed One. The elder’s lay friend, a brahmin named Devahita, was residing in Sāvatthī. He supported the elder with the four requisites. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went to that brahmin’s dwelling. The brahmin, knowing that the elder had come for some other purpose, said, 'Please say, venerable sir, what is the need?' The elder, explaining his purpose to that brahmin, spoke thus:

185.

185.

“Arahaṃ sugato loke, vātehābādhiko muni;

Sace uṇhodakaṃ atthi, munino dehi brāhmaṇa.

“The Arahant, the Sugata in the world, the sage is afflicted by winds. If there is warm water, brahmin, give it to the sage.”

186.

186.

“Pūjito pūjaneyyānaṃ, sakkareyyāna sakkato;

Apacitopaceyyānaṃ, tassa icchāmi hātave”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Honored by those worthy of honor, revered by those worthy of reverence, esteemed by those worthy of esteem—for him I wish to bring it.”

Tassattho – yo imasmiṃ loke pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjetabbehi sakkādīhi devehi mahābrahmādīhi ca brahmehi pūjito, sakkareyyānaṃ sakkātabbehi bimbisārakosalarājādīhi sakkato, apaceyyānaṃ apacāyitabbehi mahesīhi khīṇāsavehi apacito, kilesehi ārakattādinā arahaṃ, sobhanagamanādinā sugato sabbaññū muni mayhaṃ satthā devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā, so dāni vātehi vātahetu vātakkhobhanimittaṃ ābādhiko jāto. Sace, brāhmaṇa, uṇhodakaṃ atthi, tassa vātābādhavūpasamanatthaṃ taṃ hātave upanetuṃ icchāmīti. Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo uṇhodakaṃ tadanurūpaṃ vātārahañca [M 1.0399] bhesajjaṃ bhagavato upanāmesi. Tena ca satthu rogo vūpasami. Tassa bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsīti.

The meaning is this: He who in this world is honored by those worthy of honor—such as Sakka and other devas, and Mahābrahmā and other brahmās—who is respected by those worthy of respect—such as King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and others—who is revered by those worthy of esteem—such as chief queens and arahants—he is the Arahant due to being far from defilements and so forth, the Sugata due to his excellent going and so forth, the All-Knowing Muni, my Teacher, the God of Gods, surpassing even Sakka, surpassing even Brahmā—he has now become afflicted by winds, due to wind, or as a result of a wind disturbance. If, brahmin, there is hot water, I wish to bring it to him for the alleviation of his wind ailment. Hearing this, the brahmin brought hot water and medicine suitable for the wind ailment to the Blessed One. And thereby, the Teacher’s illness subsided. The Blessed One then expressed his appreciation.

Upavāṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Elder Upavāṇa’s verses is concluded.

4. Isidinnattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Elder Isidinna's Verses

Diṭṭhā [V 1.0340] mayāti āyasmato isidinnattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bījaniṃ gahetvā bodhiyā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sunāparantajanapade seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā isidinnoti laddhanāmo vayappatto satthu candanamāḷapaṭiggahaṇe pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā pasannamānaso satthāraṃ [P 2.0058] upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā sotāpanno hutvā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. Tassa hitānukampinī devatā taṃ codentī –

“Seen by me”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Isidinna. What is their origin? This elder too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. Having attained maturity, he took a fan and paid homage to the Bodhi tree. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered on in saṃsāra among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in a wealthy family in the Sunāparanta country. Having received the name Isidinna, he came of age. He witnessed the miracle of the Teacher’s acceptance of the sandalwood pavilion. With a mind inspired by faith, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, became a stream-enterer, and dwelt in the household life. A deity, out of compassion for his welfare, urging him on, said:

187.

187.

“Diṭṭhā mayā dhammadharā upāsakā, kāmā aniccā iti bhāsamānā;

Sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu, puttesu dāresu ca te apekkhā.

“I have seen lay followers, upholders of the Dhamma, declaring that sensual pleasures are impermanent; yet they are deeply infatuated and attached to jeweled earrings, and have longing for their children and spouses.”

188.

188.

“Addhā na jānanti yatodha dhammaṃ, kāmā aniccā iti cāpi āhu;

Rāgañca tesaṃ na balatthi chettuṃ, tasmā sitā puttadāraṃ dhanañcā”ti. –

“Surely they do not truly understand the Dhamma here, even though they say that sensual pleasures are impermanent; and they do not have the strength to cut off their lust, therefore they cling to sons, wives, and wealth.”

Gāthādvayamabhāsi.

She spoke two verses.

Tattha diṭṭhā mayā dhammadharā upāsakā, kāmā aniccā iti bhāsamānāti idhekacce pariyattidhammadharā upāsakā mayā diṭṭhā, pariyattidhammadharattā [M 1.0400] eva “kāmā nāmete aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā”ti kāmesu ādīnavapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammaṃ bhāsamānā, sayaṃ pana sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu, puttesu dāresu ca te apekkhāti sārattā hutvā bahalarāgarattā maṇīsu kuṇḍalesu ca, maṇicitesu vā kuṇḍalesu, puttesu puttadhītāsu dāresu ca adhigatasnehā, aññaṃ bhaṇantā aññaṃ karontā diṭṭhā mayāti attho.

There, “I have seen lay followers, upholders of the Dhamma, declaring, ‘Sensual pleasures are impermanent.’” Here, some lay followers who are upholders of the Dhamma by way of study were seen by me. Because they are upholders of the Dhamma by way of study, they speak the Dhamma connected with the danger in sensual pleasures, saying, “Indeed, these sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.” Yet they themselves, “being deeply infatuated and attached to jeweled earrings, and having longing for sons and wives”—that is, being deeply infatuated, strongly attached with lust for jewels and earrings (or for earrings studded with jewels), and having developed affection for their sons, daughters, and wives—they were seen by me saying one thing and doing another. This is the meaning.

Yatoti yasmā te upāsakā sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu puttesu dāresu ca apekkhavanto, tasmā idha imasmiṃ buddhasāsane dhammaṃ yāthāvato addhā ekaṃsena na jānanti. Evaṃ bhūtā ca “kāmā aniccā”iti cāpi āhu ahosi, sattapakati vicittasabhāvāti adhippāyo. Rāgañca tesaṃ na balatthi chettunti tesaṃ upāsakānaṃ yasmā rāgaṃ chettuṃ samucchindituṃ tādisaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ natthi, tasmā tena kāraṇena sitā taṇhāvasena nissitā puttadāraṃ dhanañca allīnā na vissajjentīti sabbametaṃ devatā taṃyeva upāsakaṃ uddissa aññāpadesena kathesi. Taṃ sutvā upāsako saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.46-50) –

“Because”—since those lay followers are deeply infatuated and attached to jeweled earrings, and have longing for sons and wives, therefore, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, they do not truly and unequivocally understand the Dhamma as it is. Even though they are such, they also say “sensual pleasures are impermanent”—the meaning is that the nature of beings is varied. “And they do not have the strength to cut off lust”—since those lay followers do not have such power of knowledge to cut off or eradicate lust, therefore, for that reason, clinging by way of craving, they are dependent on sons, wives, and wealth, clinging to them and not relinquishing them. All this the deity spoke by way of an indirect reference, intending it for that very lay follower. Having heard this, the lay follower, filled with a sense of urgency, went forth and, not long after, attained Arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Vipassino [V 1.0341] bhagavato, bodhiyā pādaputtame;

Sumano bījaniṃ gayha, abījiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

“At the supreme foot of the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Vipassī, with a gladdened mind, taking a fan, I fanned the supreme Bodhi.

“Ekanavutito kappe, abījiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bījanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, I fanned the supreme Bodhi tree; I have not known a bad destination—this is the fruit of that fanning.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā aññaṃ byākaronto imā eva gāthā abhāsīti.

Having attained Arahantship, and then declaring his attainment, he spoke these very verses.

Isidinnattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Isidinna is concluded.

5. Sambulakaccānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sambulakaccāna

Devo [M 1.0401][P 2.0059] cāti āyasmato sambulakaccānattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto ito catunavutikappamatthake kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ sataraṃsiṃ nāma paccekabuddhaṃ nirodhā vuṭṭhahitvā piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso tālaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe gahapatikule nibbattitvā “sambulo”ti laddhanāmo kaccānagottatāya sambulakaccānoti paññāyittha.

“And the cloud...”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sambulakaccāna. What is their origin? This elder too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and performing meritorious deeds in various existences, ninety-four aeons ago from now, was reborn in a good family. Having attained maturity, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Sataraṃsi, who had emerged from cessation and was walking for alms. With a mind inspired by faith, he offered a palm fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered on in saṃsāra among devas and humans. In this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in a householder’s family in the Magadha country, and, having received the name “Sambulo,” he became known as Sambulakaccāna due to his Kaccāna clan.

So vayappatto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā himavantasamīpe bheravāya nāma pabbataguhāyaṃ vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto viharati. Athekadivasaṃ mahā akālamegho satapaṭalasahassapaṭalo thanento gajjanto vijjullatā nicchārento gaḷagaḷāyanto uṭṭhahitvā vassituṃ ārabhi, asaniyo phaliṃsu. Taṃ saddaṃ sutvā acchataracchuvanamahiṃsahatthiādayo bhītatasitā bhītaravaṃ viraviṃsu. Thero pana āraddhavipassanattā kāye jīvite ca nirapekkho vigatalomahaṃso taṃ acintento vipassanāyameva kammaṃ karonto ghammāpagamena utusappāyalābhena samāhitacitto tāvadeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā saha abhiññāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.85-90) –

Having reached maturity, he heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, gained faith, and went forth. Dwelling near the Himalayas in a fearsome mountain cave named Bheravā, he lived, applying himself to the work of insight. Then one day, a great unseasonal cloud, with hundreds and thousands of layers, arose, thundering, roaring, emitting flashes of lightning, and rumbling, and it began to rain; thunderbolts struck. Hearing that sound, bears, hyenas, wild buffaloes, elephants, and others, terrified and trembling, uttered cries of fear. But the elder, having undertaken the practice of insight, indifferent to body and life, with no bristling of hair, not minding it, but applying himself only to insight, with the passing of the heat and the attainment of suitable weather, his mind composed, at that very moment, having intensified insight, together with the higher knowledges, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Sataraṃsī nāma bhagavā, sayambhū aparājito;

Vivekā vuṭṭhahitvāna, gocarāyābhinikkhami.

“The Blessed One named Sataraṃsī, the Self-Existent, the Unconquered, having risen from seclusion, went out for his alms-round.

“Phalahattho [V 1.0342] ahaṃ disvā, upagacchiṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, tālaphalaṃ adāsahaṃ.

“I, with fruit in hand, seeing that bull among men, approached him. With a mind inspired by faith and glad, I offered him a palm fruit.

“Catunnavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-four aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that gift of fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0402] pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā somanassajāto udānavasena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained Arahantship, reflecting on his own practice, and filled with joy, he declared his attainment by way of an utterance of exultation:

189.

189.

“Devo ca vassati, devo ca gaḷagaḷāyati,

Ekako cāhaṃ bherave bile viharāmi;

Tassa mayhaṃ ekakassa bherave bile viharato,

Natthi bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā.

“The cloud rains, and the cloud rumbles. And I dwell alone in a fearsome cave. For me, dwelling alone in that fearsome cave, there is no fear, no terror, no bristling of hair.

190.

190.

“Dhammatā mamesā yassa me, ekakassa bherave bile;

Viharato natthi bhayaṃ vā, chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā”ti. –

“This is my nature—that for me, dwelling alone in a fearsome cave, there is no fear, no terror, no bristling of hair.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tattha [P 2.0060] devo ca vassati, devo ca gaḷagaḷāyatīti devo megho vassati ca, “gaḷagaḷā”ti ca karonto gajjatīti attho. Gajjantassa hi anukaraṇametaṃ. Ekako cāhaṃ bherave bile viharāmīti ahañca ekako asahāyo sappaṭibhayāyaṃ pabbataguhāyaṃ vasāmi, tassa mayhaṃ evaṃbhūtassa me sato natthi bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vāti cittutrāsasaññitaṃ bhayaṃ vā taṃnimittakaṃ sarīrassa chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃsanamattaṃ vā natthi.

There, “the cloud rains, and the cloud rumbles”—this means the cloud rains and, making the sound “gaḷagaḷā,” it thunders. For this is an imitation of the sound of thunder. And “I dwell alone in a fearsome cave”—this means I, alone, without a companion, live in a terrifying mountain cave. “For me, being such, there is no fear, no terror, no bristling of hair”—this means there is no fear characterized by mental agitation, nor bodily trembling caused by that, nor even mere bristling of hair.

Kasmāti tattha kāraṇamāha “dhammatā mamesā”ti. Apariññātavatthukassa hi tattha appahīnacchandarāgatāya bhayādinā bhavitabbaṃ, mayā pana sabbaso tattha pariññātaṃ, tattha ca chandarāgo samucchinno, tasmā bhayādīnaṃ abhāvo dhammatā mamesā mama dhammasabhāvo esoti aññaṃ byākāsi.

Why? The reason for that is stated as “This is my nature.” For one who has not fully comprehended the object, there would indeed be fear and so on due to unabandoned desire and lust for it. But by me, it has been fully comprehended in every respect, and desire and lust for it have been utterly eradicated. Therefore, the absence of fear and so on is my nature—this is my inherent nature—thus he declared his attainment.

Sambulakaccānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sambulakaccāna is concluded.

6. Nitakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nitaka

Kassa [M 1.0403][V 1.0343] selūpamaṃ cittanti āyasmato nitakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto vipassissa bhagavato kāle bandhumatīnagare ārāmagopako hutvā jīvanto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso nāḷikeraphalaṃ dātukāmo ahosi. Satthā taṃ anuggaṇhanto ākāseyeva ṭhatvā paṭiggaṇhi. So taṃ datvā uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā nitakoti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharanto ghaṭento arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.91-99) –

“Whose mind is like a rock?”—this is the verse of the Venerable Elder Nitaka. What is its origin? This elder too had made aspirations under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was living as a park-keeper in the city of Bandhumatī. One day, seeing the Blessed One traveling through the sky, his mind filled with confidence, he wished to offer a coconut fruit. The Teacher, showing him favor, stood in the sky and accepted it. Having given it, he experienced immense joy and mental gladness. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the Kosala country and received the name Nitaka. Having attained understanding, hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher and gaining faith, he went forth. Taking up a meditation subject, he dwelt in the forest, striving until he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Theragāthā 2.51.91-99)—

“Nagare bandhumatiyā, ārāmiko ahaṃ tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, gacchantaṃ anilañjase.

“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was then a park-keeper; I saw the stainless Buddha traveling on the path of the wind.”

“Nāḷikeraphalaṃ gayha, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Ākāse ṭhitako santo, paṭiggaṇhi mahāyaso.

“Taking a coconut fruit, I gave it to the supreme Buddha. Standing in the sky, the greatly renowned one accepted it.”

“Vittisañjanano mayhaṃ, diṭṭhadhammasukhāvaho;

Phalaṃ buddhassa datvāna, vippasannena cetasā.

“This act produced joy for me, bringing happiness in this very life. Having given the fruit to the Buddha with a clearly confident mind,”

“Adhigacchiṃ tadā pītiṃ, vipulañca sukhuttamaṃ;

Uppajjateva ratanaṃ, nibbattassa tahiṃ tahiṃ.

“Then I attained joy and abundant, supreme bliss. Indeed, treasure arose for me wherever I was reborn.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad destination; this is the fruit of the gift of a fruit.”

“Dibbacakkhu visuddhaṃ me, samādhikusalo ahaṃ;

Abhiññāpāramippatto, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“My divine eye is purified; I am skilled in concentration. I have attained the perfection of direct knowledge; this is the fruit of the gift of a fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā there phalasukhena nibbānasukhena viharante padhānapariggāhako thero taṃ āraññāyatanaṃ gantvā tattha vasantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pariggaṇhanatthaṃ “kassa selūpama”ntiādinā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha.

Now, having attained arahantship, while the elder was dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, an elder who was an encourager of striving went to that forest dwelling. There, for the purpose of examining the monks dwelling there, he first spoke the verse beginning, “Whose mind is like a rock?”

191. Tattha [M 1.0404][V 1.0344][P 2.0061] kassa selūpamaṃ cittaṃ, ṭhitaṃ nānupakampatīti imasmiṃ araññāyatane vasantesu kassa bhikkhuno cittaṃ aggaphalādhigamena ekaghanasilāmayapabbatūpamaṃ sabbesaṃ iñjanānaṃ abhāvato vasībhāvappattiyā ca ṭhitaṃ sabbehipi lokadhammehi nānukampati na vedhati. Idānissa akampanākāraṃ saddhiṃ kāraṇena dassetuṃ “viratta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha virattaṃ rajanīyesūti virāgasaṅkhātena ariyamaggena rajanīyesu rāguppattihetubhūtesu tebhūmakadhammesu virattaṃ, tattha sabbaso samucchinnarāganti attho. Kuppanīyeti paṭighaṭṭhānīye, sabbasmimpi āghātavatthusmiṃ. Na kuppatīti na dussati na vikāraṃ āpajjati. Yassevaṃ bhāvitaṃ cittanti yassa ariyapuggalassa cittaṃ mano evaṃ vuttanayena tādibhāvena bhāvitaṃ, kuto taṃ dukkhamessatīti taṃ puggalaṃ kuto sattato saṅkhārato vā dukkhaṃ upagamissati, na tādisassa dukkhaṃ atthīti attho.

191. Herein, “Whose mind is like a rock, steady, and does not tremble?” means: among those dwelling in this forest retreat, which bhikkhu’s mind, through the attainment of the highest fruit, is like a mountain made of a single solid mass of rock; is steady due to the absence of all agitation and the attainment of mastery; and does not tremble or shake on account of all worldly conditions? Now, to show its unshakeable nature along with its cause, what begins with “detached” is said. Therein, “detached from what is enticing” means detached from the phenomena of the three realms, which are the cause for the arising of lust, by means of the noble path known as dispassion; the meaning is that lust for them is utterly eradicated. “In what is provocative” means in grounds for aversion, in any object of malice. “Does not get upset” means one is not corrupted, does not undergo alteration. “Whose mind is thus developed” means: for which noble person the mind is developed in this way, with such a nature; “from where will suffering come to them?” means from what source, whether from a being or from formations, will suffering approach that person? The meaning is that for such a one, there is no suffering.

192. Evaṃ aniyamavasena pucchitamatthaṃ nitakatthero attūpanāyikaṃ katvā vissajjento “mama selūpamaṃ citta”ntiādinā dutiyagāthāya aññaṃ byākāsi. Taṃ vuttatthameva.

192. Thus, the Elder Nitaka, answering the matter that was asked in a general way by applying it to himself, declared with the second verse beginning, “My mind is like a rock.” Its meaning is as has been stated.

Nitakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Nitaka is concluded.

7. Soṇapoṭiriyaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Soṇapoṭiriyaputta

Na tāva supituṃ hotīti āyasmato soṇassa poṭiriyaputtassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro sikhissa bhagavato kāle vanacaro hutvā jīvanto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto kurañjiyaphalaṃ [P 2.0062] satthuno adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ poṭiriyassa nāma gāmabhojakassa putto hutvā nibbatti, soṇotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto bhaddiyassa sākiyarañño senāpati ahosi. Atha bhaddiyarāje heṭṭhā vuttanayena pabbajite, senāpati [M 1.0405] “rājāpi nāma pabbaji, kiṃ mayhaṃ gharāvāsenā”ti pabbaji? Pabbajitvā pana niddārāmo viharati, na bhāvanamanuyuñjati. Taṃ bhagavā anupiyāyaṃ ambavane viharanto attano obhāsaṃ pharāpetvā tenassa satiṃ janetvā imāya gāthāya taṃ ovadanto –

“Not yet is it time to sleep”—this is the verse of the Venerable Soṇa, son of Poṭiriyā. What is its origin? This one too, having made aspirations under previous Buddhas, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, lived as a forest dweller. One day, seeing the Teacher, with a confident mind, he offered a kurañjiya fruit to the Teacher. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in Kapilavatthu as the son of a village headman named Poṭiriyā, and his name was Soṇa. When he came of age, he became the general of Bhaddiya, the Sakyan king. Then, when King Bhaddiya had gone forth in the manner previously described, the general thought, “Even the king has gone forth; what use is the household life for me?” and he went forth. But after going forth, he lived delighting in sleep and did not apply himself to mental development. The Blessed One, dwelling in the mango grove at Anupiyā, suffused him with his radiance, thereby arousing mindfulness in him, and admonished him with this verse:

193.

193.

“Na tāva supituṃ hoti, ratti nakkhattamālinī;

Paṭijaggitumevesā, ratti hoti vijānatā.

“Not yet is it time to sleep, this night garlanded with stars; for one who is discerning, this night is indeed for being vigilant.”

194.

194.

“Hatthikkhandhāvapatitaṃ[V 1.0345], kuñjaro ce anukkame;

Saṅgāme me mataṃ seyyo, yañce jīve parājito”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“Should an elephant pursue one fallen from its back, better for me to die in battle than that I should live on, defeated.” — thus he spoke the two verses.

Tattha na tāva supituṃ hoti, ratti nakkhattamālinīti aṭṭhahi akkhaṇehi vajjitaṃ navamaṃ khaṇaṃ labhitvā ṭhitassa viññujātikassa yāva na arahattaṃ hatthagataṃ hoti, tāva ayaṃ nakkhattamālinī ratti supituṃ niddāyituṃ na hoti, supanassa kālo na hoti. Apica kho paṭijaggitumevesā, ratti hoti vijānatāti esā ratti nāma manussānaṃ migapakkhīnañca niddūpagamanena visesato nissaddavelābhūtā paṭipattiṃ attani sañjaggituṃ jāgariyānuyogamanuyuñjitumeva vijānatā viññunā icchitā hotīti.

Herein, “Not yet is it time to sleep, this night garlanded with stars” means: for a person of wise nature who stands having obtained the ninth opportune moment, which is free from the eight inopportune moments, for as long as arahantship has not come to hand, this night garlanded with stars is not for sleeping, not for slumbering; it is not the time for sleep. Furthermore, “this night is indeed for being vigilant, for one who is discerning” means: this night, being a time of special quietude because humans, beasts, and birds have gone to sleep, is desired by a discerning wise person for the very purpose of cultivating the practice in oneself and applying oneself to the practice of wakefulness.

Taṃ sutvā soṇo saṃviggataramānaso hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto “hatthikkhandhova patita”nti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha avapatitanti avamukhaṃ patitaṃ uddhaṃpādaṃ adhomukhaṃ patitaṃ. Kuñjaro ce anukkameti kuñjaro anukkameyya ce. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadāhaṃ hatthimāruhitvā saṅgāmaṃ paviṭṭho hatthikkhandhato patito, tadāhaṃ saṅgāme tena hatthinā maddito mato ahosiṃ ce, taṃ me maraṇaṃ seyyo, yañce idāni kilesehi parājito jīveyyaṃ, taṃ na seyyoti. Imaṃ gāthaṃ vadantoyeva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.1-6) –

Hearing that, Soṇa, with his mind deeply stirred, established moral shame and moral dread, undertook the ascetic practice of living in the open, and while doing the work of insight meditation, he spoke the second verse: “Fallen from an elephant’s back.” Therein, “fallen” means fallen headfirst, fallen with feet up and head down. “Should an elephant pursue” means: if the elephant were to pursue. This is what is said: “If, when I had mounted an elephant and entered a battle, I had fallen from the elephant’s back and then been crushed and killed by that elephant in the battle, that death would be better for me than that I should now live on, defeated by the defilements—that would not be better.” Even while speaking this verse, he intensified his insight meditation and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Theragāthā 2.52.1-6):

“Migaluddo [M 1.0406][P 2.0063] pure āsiṃ, vipine vicaraṃ ahaṃ;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ.

“Formerly, I was a deer hunter, wandering in the forest; I saw the stainless Buddha, the one gone beyond all dhammas.”

“Kurañjiyaphalaṃ gayha, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Puññakkhettassa tādino, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

“Taking a kurañjiya fruit, I gave it to the supreme Buddha, to the field of merit, the Such One, confident, with my own hands.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad destination; this is the fruit of the gift of a fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā “satthārā vuttaṃ, attanā vutta”nti ubhayañhi gāthaṃ “hatthikkhandhāvapatita”ntiādinā paccudāhāsi. Tena idameva aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Having attained arahantship, he recited both verses, “spoken by the Teacher, spoken by myself,” beginning with “fallen from an elephant’s shoulder.” Therefore, this very thing was his declaration of final knowledge.

Soṇapoṭiriyaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Soṇapoṭiriyaputta is finished.

8. Nisabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nisabha

Pañca [V 1.0346] kāmaguṇe hitvāti āyasmato nisabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannacitto kapitthaphalamadāsi. So tena puññakammena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde koliyajanapade kulagehe nibbattitvā nisabhoti laddhanāmo vayappatto sākiyakoliyānaṃ saṅgāme buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā tadaheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.7-11) –

“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure”—this is the verse of the Elder Nisabha. What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached an age of discernment, one day, seeing the Teacher walking for alms, with a mind of faith he offered a wood-apple. Through that meritorious deed, wandering only in happy states of existence, in this Buddha era he was reborn in a good family in the Koliyan country. Having received the name Nisabha, upon reaching maturity, he witnessed the Buddha's power during the battle between the Sākyans and Koliyans. Having gained faith, he went forth and on that very day attained arahantship. Thus it was said in the Apadāna:

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, kapitthaṃ adadiṃ phalaṃ.

“To the golden-hued Fully Enlightened One, the recipient of offerings, as he was walking along the road, I gave a wood-apple fruit.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving that fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

So [M 1.0407] arahattaṃ pana patvā attano sahāyabhikkhū pamādavihārena kālaṃ vītināmente disvā te ovadanto –

Having attained arahantship, seeing his companion monks spending their time living in heedlessness, he admonished them:

195.

195.

“Pañca kāmaguṇe hitvā, piyarūpe manorame;

Saddhāya gharā nikkhamma, dukkhassantakaro bhave”ti. –

“Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are dear and delightful, going forth from home in faith, one should make an end of suffering.”

Paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke the first verse.

Tassattho – bālaputhujjanassa piyāyitabbasabhāvatāya piyarūpe manuññasabhāvatāya manorame rūpādike pañca kāmaguṇe kāmakoṭṭhāse hitvā pahāya pariccajitvā kammaphalasaddhāya ratanattayasaddhāya ca vasena gharā gharabandhanato nikkhamma nikkhamitvā pabbajjaṃ upagato viññujātiko pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya ghaṭento vāyamanto vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaro bhave bhaveyyāti. Evaṃ te bhikkhū ovaditvā “ayaṃ pare eva saññāpento viharati, “sayaṃ [P 2.0064] pana akārako’ti mā cintayitthā”ti tesaṃ attano paṭipannabhāvaṃ pakāsento –

Its meaning is this: Having abandoned, given up, and relinquished the five strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms—which are constituents of sensual pleasure, dear because it is their nature to be cherished by foolish worldlings, and delightful due to their pleasing nature—and having gone forth from the bonds of household life through faith in kamma and its results and faith in the Triple Gem, a discerning person, striving and endeavoring from the time of ordination, should become an end-maker of the suffering of the cycle of existence. Having thus advised those monks, and in order to reveal his own state of practice to them lest they think, “This one dwells instructing only others, but is himself inactive,” he spoke the following:

196.

196.

“Nābhinandāmi [V 1.0347] maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, sampajāno patissato”ti. –

“I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; I await the time, clearly comprehending and mindful.”

Dutiyagāthāya aññaṃ byākāsi. Tattha nābhinandāmi maraṇanti maraṇaṃ na abhikaṅkhāmi. Nābhinandāmi jīvitanti idaṃ pana tassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ, tasmā nābhinandāmi maraṇanti. Yo hi āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇāya kilesābhisaṅkhāre ācinoti upacinoti, so punabbhavābhinibbattiṃ abhinandanto nāntariyakatāya attano maraṇampi abhinandati nāma kāraṇassa appahīnattā, khīṇāsavo pana sabbaso ācayagāmidhamme pahāya apacayagāmidhamme patiṭṭhito pariññātavatthuko sabbaso jīvitaṃ anabhinandanto maraṇampi anabhinandati nāma kāraṇassa eva suppahīnattā. Tenāha – “nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvita”nti. Yadi evaṃ khīṇāsavassa parinibbānābhikaṅkhā, yāva parinibbānā avaṭṭhānañca kathanti āha “kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, sampajāno patissato”ti, kilesaparinibbāne siddhe satipaññāvepullappattiyā sato sampajāno kevalaṃ [M 1.0408] khandhaparinibbānakālaṃ paṭikaṅkhāmi, taṃ udikkhamāno āgamayamāno viharāmi, na pana me maraṇe jīvite vā abhinandanā atthi arahattamaggeneva tassa samugghāṭitattāti.

With the second verse, he declared his final knowledge. Therein, “I do not delight in death” means I do not long for death. “I do not delight in life”—this is a statement of the reason: because I do not delight in life, therefore I do not delight in death. For one who accumulates and increases defilements and volitional formations for the sake of future birth, aging, and death, delighting in new becoming, by necessity also delights in their own death, because the cause has not been abandoned. But one whose taints are destroyed, having entirely abandoned things that lead to accumulation and being established in things that lead to non-accumulation, with the basis fully understood, does not delight in life at all and thus does not delight in death either, because the cause has been thoroughly abandoned. Therefore, he said: “I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life.” If this is so, and one whose taints are destroyed longs for final Nibbāna, how do they remain until that final Nibbāna? He explains: “I await the time, clearly comprehending and mindful.” This means: when the Nibbāna of the defilements has been achieved, due to the attainment of abundant mindfulness and wisdom, being mindful and clearly comprehending, I simply await the time of the final Nibbāna of the aggregates, watching for it, expecting it, while living thus. But there is no delight in death or life for me, because it has been uprooted by the path of arahantship itself.

Nisabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nisabha is concluded.

9. Usabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Usabha

Ambapallavasaṅkāsanti āyasmato usabhattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kosambaphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthusmiṃ sākiyarājakule nibbattitvā usabhoti laddhanāmo vayappatto satthu ñātisamāgame buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbaji. So pabbajitakālato [P 2.0065] paṭṭhāya samaṇadhammaṃ akatvā divā saṅgaṇikārāmo sakalarattiṃ niddāyamāno vītināmeti. So ekadivasaṃ muṭṭhassati asampajāno niddaṃ okkanto supine kesamassuṃ ohāretvā ambapallavavaṇṇaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā hatthigīvāyaṃ nisīditvā nagaraṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ tattheva manusse sampatte disvā lajjāya hatthikkhandhato oruyha attānaṃ disvā paṭibuddho, “īdisaṃ nāma supinaṃ muṭṭhassatinā asampajānena [V 1.0348] niddāyamānena mayā diṭṭha”nti uppannasaṃvego vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.12-16) –

“Like a mango sprout”—this is the verse of the Elder Usabha. What is its origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and performing merits in various existences, was born in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached an age of discernment, one day he saw the Teacher walking for alms and, with a mind of faith, offered a kosamba fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in the Sakyan royal family of Kapilavatthu and was named Usabha. When he came of age, he saw the Buddha’s power at the gathering of relatives and, having gained faith, he went forth. From the time of his ordination, not practicing the ascetic’s duties, he was fond of company by day and spent the whole night sleeping. One day, with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension, he fell asleep and dreamed that he shaved off his hair and beard, donned a robe the color of mango sprouts, sat on an elephant’s neck, and entered the city for alms. Upon seeing the people who had gathered there, he was overcome with shame, descended from the elephant’s back, and saw himself. Awakening, he thought, “Such a dream was seen by me while sleeping with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension.” A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him, and establishing insight, he before long attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Kakudhaṃ vilasantaṃva, devadevaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, kosambaṃ adadiṃ tadā.

“Like a shining kakudha tree, the deva of devas, a bull among men; as he was walking along the road, I then gave a kosamba fruit.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-one aeons since I gave that fruit, I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of giving that fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Atha [M 1.0409] thero yathādiṭṭhaṃ supinaṃ aṅkusaṃ katvā arahattassa adhigatattā tasseva supinassa kittanavasena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Then the elder, having made the dream he had seen into a goad, and having attained arahantship, declared his final knowledge by way of recounting that very dream:

197.

197.

“Ambapallavasaṅkāsaṃ, aṃse katvāna cīvaraṃ;

Nisinno hatthigīvāyaṃ, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ.

“Having placed a robe like a mango sprout on my shoulder, seated on an elephant’s neck, I entered the village for alms.”

198.

198.

“Hatthikkhandhato oruyha, saṃvegaṃ alabhiṃ tadā;

Sohaṃ ditto tadā santo, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti. – gāthādvayamāha;

“Having descended from the elephant's shoulder, I then gained a sense of spiritual urgency; I, who was then proud, became serene, and for me the destruction of the taints was attained.” Thus, he spoke these two verses.

Tattha ambapallavasaṅkāsaṃ, aṃse katvāna cīvaranti ambapallavākāraṃ pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ cīvaraṃ khandhe karitvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā.
