Gāmanti attano rājadhāniṃ hatthikkhandhe nisinno piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ, paviṭṭhamattova mahājanena olokiyamāno hatthikkhandhato oruyha ṭhito paṭibujjhiṃ, pabuddhova saṃvegaṃ alabhiṃ tadā “muṭṭhassati asampajāno hutvā niddāyokkamanena etaṃ jāta”nti. Apare pana “rājāva hutvā rattibhāge evarūpaṃ supinaṃ disvā vibhātāya rattiyā hatthikkhandhaṃ āruyha nagaravīthiyaṃ caranto taṃ supinaṃ saritvā hatthikkhandhato oruyha saṃvegaṃ labhitvā satthu santike pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patvā udānaṃ udānento imā gāthā abhāsī”ti vadanti. Dittoti tasmiṃ rājakāle jātimadabhogamadādiparidappito samāno saṃvegamalabhinti yojanā.

Therein, 'ambapallavasaṅkāsaṃ, aṃse katvāna cīvaraṃ' means: having placed on the shoulder a coral-colored robe shaped like a mango sprout, having made it an upper robe. 'Gāmaṃ' means my own royal capital. Seated on an elephant's back, I entered for alms. Just as I entered, being watched by the great crowd, I descended from the elephant's back, stood still, and awakened. Upon awakening, I then felt spiritual urgency, thinking, 'This happened because I was of lapsed mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, and had succumbed to sleep.' Others, however, say: 'Having been a king, he saw such a dream during the night. When the night grew light, he mounted an elephant's back and, while proceeding along a city street, remembered that dream. Descending from the elephant's back, he felt spiritual urgency, went forth in the Teacher's presence, attained arahantship, and, uttering an inspired utterance, spoke these verses.' 'Ditto' (puffed up): the connection is that during that time as a king, being intoxicated with the pride of birth, the pride of wealth, and so on, I felt spiritual urgency.

Usabhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Usabha is finished.

10. Kappaṭakurattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kappaṭakura

Ayamiti [V 1.0349][P 2.0066] kappaṭoti āyasmato kappaṭakurattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ vinatāya nāma nadiyā tīre aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ketakapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde [M 1.0410] sāvatthiyaṃ duggatakule nibbattitvā yāva vayappatti, tāva aññaṃ upāyaṃ ajānanto kappaṭakhaṇḍanivāsano sarāvahattho tattha tattha kuraṃ pariyesanto vicari, tena kappaṭakurotveva paññāyittha. So vayappatto tiṇaṃ vikkiṇitvā jīvikaṃ kappento ekadivasaṃ tiṇalāvanatthaṃ araññaṃ gato tattha aññataraṃ khīṇāsavattheraṃ disvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā nisīdi. Tassa thero dhammaṃ kathesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho “kiṃ me imāya kicchajīvikāyā”ti pabbajitvā attano nivatthakappaṭacoḷaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nikkhipi. Yadā cassa anabhirati uppajjati, tadā taṃ kappaṭaṃ olokentassa anabhirati vigacchati, saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi. Evaṃ karonto sattakkhattuṃ uppabbaji. Tassa taṃ kāraṇaṃ bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ kappaṭakuro bhikkhu dhammasabhāyaṃ parisapariyante nisinno niddāyati, taṃ bhagavā codento –

'This is the rag' is the verse of the Venerable Kappaṭakura. What is its origin? This elder, too, having made a resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences, was reborn in a family of good standing during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One seated at the foot of a certain tree on the bank of the river Vinatā. With a confident mind, he made an offering of ketaka flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, during this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a poor family in Sāvatthī. Until he reached maturity, knowing no other means of livelihood, he wandered about wearing a piece of worn cloth and carrying a bowl in hand, searching for rice-gruel here and there. For that reason, he became known as Kappaṭakura. Having reached maturity, he made a living by selling grass. One day, having gone to the forest to cut grass, he saw a certain elder who was an arahant. Approaching him, he paid homage and sat down. The elder taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith and thought, 'What is this difficult livelihood to me?' and went forth. He put aside the worn-out rag he had been wearing in a certain place. Whenever discontent arose in him, upon looking at that rag, his discontent would vanish, and he would regain a sense of spiritual urgency. In this way, he left the order seven times. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then one day, the monk Kappaṭakura was sitting at the edge of the assembly in the Dhamma hall, dozing. The Blessed One, admonishing him, said:

199.

199.

“Ayamiti kappaṭo kappaṭakuro, acchāya atibharitāya;

Amataghaṭikāyaṃ dhammakaṭamatto, katapadaṃ jhānāni ocetuṃ.

“This is the rag, O Kappaṭakura! In this very clear and full vessel of the deathless, you are discontented with the Dhamma. Make a foundation for plunging into the jhānas.”

200.

200.

“Mā kho tvaṃ kappaṭa pacālesi, mā tvaṃ upakaṇṇamhi tāḷessaṃ;

Na hi tvaṃ kappaṭa mattamaññāsi, saṅghamajjhamhi pacalāyamāno”ti. –

“Do not, Kappaṭa, doze off! Lest I strike you near the ear. For you, Kappaṭa, do not know the measure, dozing in the midst of the Saṅgha.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke two verses.

Tattha ayamiti kappaṭo kappaṭakuroti kappaṭakuro bhikkhu “ayaṃ mama kappaṭo, imaṃ paridahitvā yathā tathā jīvāmī”ti evaṃ uppannamicchāvitakko acchāya atibharitāya amataghaṭikāyaṃ mama amataghaṭe tahaṃ tahaṃ vassante “amatamadhigataṃ ahamanusāsāmi, ahaṃ [P 2.0067] dhammaṃ desemi” (mahāva. 12; ma. ni. 1.286; 2.342). “Andhībhūtasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, āhañchaṃ amatadundubhi”ntiādinā (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341) ghosetvā [M 1.0411] mayā dhammāmate pavassiyamāne katapadaṃ jhānāni ocetuṃ lokiyalokuttarajjhānāni upacetuṃ bhāvetuṃ katapadaṃ kaṭamaggavihitabhāvanāmaggaṃ idaṃ mama sāsanaṃ, tathāpi dhammakaṭamatto mama sāsanadhammato [V 1.0350] ukkaṇṭhacitto apagatamānaso kappaṭakuroti taṃ codetvā punapissa sahoḍḍhaṃ coraṃ gaṇhanto viya pamādavihāraṃ dassento “mā kho tvaṃ, kappaṭa, pacālesī”ti gāthamāha.

Therein, 'This is the rag, Kappaṭakura' means: the monk Kappaṭakura had the wrongly arisen thought, 'This is my rag; wearing this, I will live somehow.' In my clear and very full vessel of the deathless, while the deathless rains down here and there, and while I, having proclaimed, 'I teach the deathless I have attained, I teach the Dhamma' and 'In a world gone blind, I have beaten the drum of the deathless,' and so on, cause the deathless nectar of the Dhamma to rain down—this teaching of mine is the path of practice established, the way of development laid out, for accumulating and developing worldly and supramundane jhānas, for plunging into the jhānas. Nevertheless, Kappaṭakura is discontented with the Dhamma, his mind is dissatisfied with and has turned away from the Dhamma of my teaching. Thus, having admonished him, and again, pointing out his heedless way of living as if catching a thief red-handed with the stolen goods, he spoke the verse beginning, 'Do not, Kappaṭa, doze off!'

Tattha mā kho tvaṃ, kappaṭa, pacālesīti tvaṃ, kappaṭakura, “mama dhammaṃ suṇissāmī”ti nisīditvā mā kho pacālesi mā pacalāhi mā niddaṃ upagacchi. Mā tvaṃ upakaṇṇamhi tāḷessanti taṃ niddāyamānaṃ upakaṇṇamhi kaṇṇasamīpe desanāhatthena ahaṃ mā patāḷessaṃ. Yathā ito paraṃ kilesappahānāya ahaṃ taṃ na ovadeyyaṃ, tathā paṭipajjāhīti attho. Na hi tvaṃ, kappaṭa, mattamaññāsīti tvaṃ, kappaṭa, saṅghamajjhamhi pacalāyamāno mattaṃ pamāṇaṃ na vā maññasi, “ayamatidullabho khaṇo paṭiladdho, so mā upajjhagā”ti ettakampi na jānāsi, passa yāva ca te aparaddhanti codesi.

Therein, 'Do not, Kappaṭa, doze off' means: You, Kappaṭakura, having sat down thinking, 'I will listen to his Dhamma,' should not doze off, should not nod, should not fall asleep. 'Lest I strike you near the ear' means: lest I strike you, who are dozing, near the ear with the hand of my teaching. The meaning is: practice in such a way that hereafter I will not have to advise you for the sake of abandoning the defilements. 'For you, Kappaṭa, do not know the measure' means: You, Kappaṭa, dozing in the midst of the Saṅgha, do not know the measure or limit; you do not even know this much: 'This extremely rare opportunity has been obtained; may it not be wasted!' See how greatly you have erred!—thus he admonished him.

Evaṃ bhagavatā dvīhi gāthāhi gāḷhaṃ taṃ niggayha codanāya katāya aṭṭhivedhaviddho viya caṇḍagajo maggaṃ otaranto viya ca sañjātasaṃvego vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.52.17-22) –

Thus, having been firmly rebuked and admonished by the Blessed One with these two verses, he became filled with spiritual urgency, like a fierce elephant pierced to the very bone or like one descending into the path. Establishing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vinatānadiyā tīre, vihāsi purisuttamo;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.

“On the bank of the river Vinatā, the Supreme Person dwelt; I saw the Stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-composed.”

“Madhugandhassa pupphena, ketakassa ahaṃ tadā;

Pasannacitto sumano, buddhaseṭṭhamapūjayiṃ.

“With a sweet-smelling ketaka flower, at that time, with a confident and joyful mind, I worshipped the Supreme Buddha.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I worshipped with that flower, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0412] pana patvā satthārā vuttagāthādvayameva attano arahattādhigamanassa aṅkusabhūtanti paccudāhāsi. Tenassa tadeva aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Having attained arahantship, however, he recited the very two verses spoken by the Teacher, stating that they had been the goad for his attainment of arahantship. Thus, that itself became his declaration of final knowledge.

Kappaṭakurattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Kappaṭakura is finished.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth chapter is finished.

5. Pañcamavaggo

5. The Fifth Chapter

1. Kumārakassapattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Kumārakassapa

Aho [V 1.0351][P 2.0068] buddhā aho dhammāti āyasmato kumārakassapattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ pāpuṇi. “Kulagehe”ti pana aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.217) vuttaṃ. So satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ cittakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhanto paṇidhānaṃ katvā tadanurūpāni puññāni karonto kassapassa bhagavato kāle samaṇadhammaṃ katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe seṭṭhidhītāya kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā kira kumārikākāleyeva pabbajitukāmā hutvā mātāpitaro yācitvā pabbajjaṃ alabhamānā kulagharaṃ gatāpi gabbhasaṇṭhitampi ajānantī sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā tena anuññātā bhikkhunīsu pabbajitā. Tassā gabbhinibhāvaṃ disvā bhikkhuniyo devadattaṃ pucchiṃsu. So “assamaṇī”ti āha. Puna dasabalaṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthā upālittheraṃ paṭicchāpesi. Thero sāvatthinagaravāsīni kulāni visākhañca upāsikaṃ pakkosāpetvā sarājikāya parisāya vinicchinanto “pure laddho gabbho, pabbajjā arogā”ti āha. Satthā “suvinicchitaṃ adhikaraṇa”nti therassa sādhukāraṃ adāsi.

"Ah, the Buddhas! Ah, the Dhamma!"—these are the verses of the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa Thera. What is the origin of this story? This elder too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a brahmin family and attained understanding. However, in the Aṅguttara Commentary, it is said he was born in a noble family. He went to the Teacher’s presence and, while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk as the foremost among those skilled in giving elaborate discourses. Aspiring for that position himself, he made a resolution and performed meritorious deeds accordingly. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he practiced the ascetic life and wandered through happy destinies. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was conceived in the womb of a chief householder's daughter in Rājagaha. It is said that even in her youth, this maiden wished to go forth. She asked her parents for permission but, being unable to obtain it, entered the household life. Without even knowing that she was pregnant, she pleased her husband and, with his consent, was ordained among the bhikkhunīs. When the bhikkhunīs saw that she was pregnant, they asked Devadatta, who declared, "She is not a true renunciant." They then asked the Ten-Powered One. The Teacher instructed the Elder Upāli to investigate. The elder summoned the families living in Sāvatthi and the laywoman Visākhā, and in an assembly that included the king, he investigated the case. He concluded, "The conception occurred before her ordination, and her going forth was valid." The Teacher gave his approval to the elder, saying, "The legal issue has been well-decided."

Sā bhikkhunī suvaṇṇabimbasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ rājā pasenadikosalo posesi. “Kassapo”ti cassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Aparabhāge [M 1.0413] alaṅkaritvā satthu santikaṃ netvā pabbājesi. Kumārakāle pabbajitattā bhagavatā “kassapaṃ pakkosatha, idaṃ phalaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā kassapassa dethā”ti vutte “katarakassapassā”ti. “Kumārakassapassā”ti. Evaṃ gahitanāmattā rañño posāvanikaputtattā ca vuḍḍhakālepi kumārakassapotveva paññāyittha.

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son resembling a golden statue. King Pasenadi of Kosala raised him. They named him "Kassapa." Later, having adorned him, they brought him to the Teacher and ordained him. Having gone forth in his youth, when the Blessed One would say, "Summon Kassapa, give this fruit or snack to Kassapa," if asked, "Which Kassapa?" he would reply, "Kumāra Kassapa." Thus, being known by this name and being the king's foster son, even in his old age he was still known as Kumāra Kassapa.

So pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya vipassanāya ceva kammaṃ karoti, buddhavacanañca uggaṇhāti. Atha tena saddhiṃ pabbatamatthake samaṇadhammaṃ katvā anāgāmī hutvā suddhāvāse nibbatto [V 1.0352] mahābrahmā “vipassanāya mukhaṃ dassetvā maggaphalappattiyā upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti pañcadasa pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā andhavane vasantassa [P 2.0069] therassa “ime pañhe satthāraṃ puccheyyāsī”ti ācikkhitvā gato. So te pañhe bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Bhagavāpissa byākāsi. Thero satthārā kathitaniyāmeneva te uggaṇhitvā vipassanaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.54.150-177) –

From the time of his going forth, he practiced insight meditation and learned the Buddha’s teachings. Then, a certain Mahābrahmā, who had practiced the ascetic life with him on a mountain peak and become a non-returner, was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm. He thought, "I will show the way to insight and help him attain the path and fruition." Having formulated fifteen questions, he went to the elder who was dwelling in the Andhavana forest, instructing him, "Ask the Teacher these questions." The elder then asked the Blessed One these questions. The Blessed One explained them to him, and the elder, learning them according to the Teacher’s explanation, established insight and attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Ito satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji nāyako;

Sabbalokahito vīro, padumuttaranāmako.

“One hundred thousand eons ago, the Leader arose; the hero named Padumuttara, who worked for the welfare of all the world.

“Tadāhaṃ brāhmaṇo hutvā, vissuto vedapāragū;

Divāvihāraṃ vicaraṃ, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Then, as a brahmin, renowned and a master of the Vedas, roaming in search of a daytime dwelling, I saw the Leader of the World.

“Catusaccaṃ pakāsentaṃ, bodhayantaṃ sadevakaṃ;

Vicittakathikānaggaṃ, vaṇṇayantaṃ mahājane.

“Revealing the four truths, awakening the world with its gods; extolling before the great assembly the one foremost among speakers of varied discourses.

“Tadā muditacittohaṃ, nimantetvā tathāgataṃ;

Nānārattehi vatthehi, alaṅkaritvāna maṇḍapaṃ.

“Then, with a joyful mind, I invited the Tathāgata, and having adorned a pavilion with various colorful garments,

“Nānāratanapajjotaṃ, sasaṅghaṃ bhojayiṃ tahiṃ;

Bhojayitvāna sattāhaṃ, nānaggarasabhojanaṃ.

“Shining with various jewels, I fed him with the Saṅgha there; having fed them for seven days with food of diverse, excellent flavors.

“Nānācittehi pupphehi, pūjayitvā sasāvakaṃ;

Nipacca pādamūlamhi, taṃ ṭhāna patthayiṃ ahaṃ.

“With flowers of various colors, I honored him and his disciples; bowing at his feet, I aspired to that position.

“Tadā munivaro āha, karuṇekarasāsayo;

Passathetaṃ dijavaraṃ, padumānanalocanaṃ.

“Then the noble sage, whose heart is a mine of compassion, said: ‘Look at this excellent twice-born one, with lotus-like eyes.

“Pītipāmojjabahulaṃ[M 1.0414], samuggatatanūruhaṃ;

Hāsamhitavisālakkhaṃ, mama sāsanalālasaṃ.

“‘Abundant in joy and gladness, with the hairs of his body standing erect; with a smiling, wide-eyed gaze, longing for my teaching.

“Patitaṃ pādamūle me, ekāvatthasumānasaṃ;

Esa pattheti taṃ ṭhānaṃ, vicittakathikattanaṃ.

“‘Fallen at my feet, with a joyful and single-minded intent, this one aspires to that position: the state of being a speaker of varied discourses.

“Satasahassito kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“‘A hundred thousand eons hence, born of the Okkāka lineage, Gotama by clan name, he will be the Teacher in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Kumārakassapo nāma, hessati satthu sāvako.

“‘He will be an heir in his Dhamma, a true son, created by the Dhamma; Kumārakassapa by name, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.

“Vicittapupphadussānaṃ, ratanānañca vāhasā;

Vicittakathikānaṃ so, aggataṃ pāpuṇissati.

“‘By means of varied floral cloths and jewels, he will reach the foremost place among those who speak in diverse ways.

“Tena [V 1.0353] kammena sukatena, cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Jahitvā mānusaṃ dehaṃ, tāvatiṃsamagacchahaṃ.

“‘By that well-done deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, having left the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

“Paribbhamaṃ bhavābhave, raṅgamajjhe yathā naṭo;

Sākhamigatrajo hutvā, migiyā kucchimokkamiṃ.

“Wandering from existence to existence, like an actor on a stage, having become the son of the deer Sākha, I entered a doe's womb.

“Tadā mayi kucchigate, vajjhavāro upaṭṭhito;

Sākhena cattā me mātā, nigrodhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā.

“Then, while I was in the womb, the turn for slaughter arrived. My mother, abandoned by Sākha, went to Nigrodha for refuge.

“Tena sā migarājena, maraṇā parimocitā;

Pariccajitvā sapāṇaṃ, mamevaṃ ovadī tadā.

“By that deer king she was freed from death, as he gave up his own life. Then my mother advised me thus:

“Nigrodhameva seveyya, na sākhamupasaṃvase;

Nigrodhasmiṃ mataṃ seyyo, yañce sākhamhi jīvitaṃ.

“‘One should associate only with Nigrodha; one should not live with Sākha. Better to die with Nigrodha than to live with Sākha.’

“Tenānusiṭṭhā migayūthapena, ahañca mātā ca tathetare ca;

Āgamma rammaṃ tusitādhivāsaṃ, gatā pavāsaṃ sagharaṃ yatheva.

“Instructed by that leader of the deer herd, my mother and I, and the others, went to the delightful abode of Tusita, just as one returns home from abroad.

“Puno kassapavīrassa, atthamentamhi sāsane;

Āruyha selasikharaṃ, yuñjitvā jinasāsanaṃ.

“Again, when the dispensation of the heroic Kassapa was declining, having climbed a rocky peak, I applied myself to the Victor’s teaching.

“Idānāhaṃ [M 1.0415] rājagahe, jāto seṭṭhikule ahuṃ;

Āpannasattā me mātā, pabbaji anagāriyaṃ.

“Now, in Rājagaha, I was born in a chief householder's family; my mother, being pregnant, went forth into the homeless life.

“Sagabbhaṃ taṃ viditvāna, devadattamupānayuṃ;

So avoca vināsetha, pāpikaṃ bhikkhuniṃ imaṃ.

“Knowing that she was pregnant, they brought the case to Devadatta. He said, ‘Destroy this wicked nun!’

“Idānipi munindena, jinena anukampitā;

Sukhinī ajanī mayhaṃ, mātā bhikkhunupassaye.

“But now, shown compassion by the Lord of Sages, the Victor, my mother happily gave birth in the nuns’ quarters.

“Taṃ viditvā mahīpālo, kosalo maṃ aposayi;

Kumāraparihānena, nāmenāhañca kassapo.

“Knowing this, the king of Kosala raised me; I was Kassapa by name, and known as Kumāra on account of my princely upbringing.

“Mahākassapamāgamma, ahaṃ kumārakassapo;

Vammikasadisaṃ kāyaṃ, sutvā buddhena desitaṃ.

“I, Kumārakassapa, having approached Mahākassapa, heard the teaching delivered by the Buddha that the body is like an anthill.

“Tato cittaṃ vimucci me, anupādāya sabbaso;

Pāyāsiṃ damayitvāhaṃ, etadaggamapāpuṇiṃ.

“Then my mind was completely liberated, without any clinging. Having subdued Pāyāsi, I attained this foremost position.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“‘My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.’”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā cittakathikabhāvena satthārā etadagge ṭhapito attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā ratanattayaguṇavibhāvanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained Arahantship and been placed by the Teacher at the forefront of those who give inspiring talks, he reflected on his own practice and, by way of expounding the qualities of the Triple Gem, declared his final knowledge:

201.

201.

“Aho [V 1.0354] buddhā aho dhammā, aho no satthu sampadā;

Yattha etādisaṃ dhammaṃ, sāvako sacchikāhiti.

“Wonderful are the Buddhas! Wonderful is the Dhamma! Wonderful is the accomplishment of our Teacher, in whose teaching a disciple can realize such a Dhamma.

202.

202.

“Asaṅkheyyesu kappesu, sakkāyādhigatā ahū;

Tesamayaṃ pacchimako, carimoyaṃ samussayo;

Jātimaraṇasaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi;

“‘For incalculable eons, I was overcome by identity. This is my last existence, this is my final body. The wandering through birth and death is ended; now there is no renewed existence.’” Thus, he spoke these two verses.

Tattha ahoti acchariyatthe nipāto. Buddhāti sabbaññubuddhā, gāravavasena bahuvacanaṃ, aho acchariyā sambuddhāti attho. Dhammāti pariyattidhammena saddhiṃ nava lokuttaradhammā. Aho no satthu sampadāti amhākaṃ satthu dasabalassa aho sampattiyo. Yatthāti yasmiṃ satthari [M 1.0416] brahmacariyavāsena. Etādisaṃ dhammaṃ, sāvako sacchikāhitīti etādisaṃ evarūpaṃ suvisuddhajjhānābhiññāparivāraṃ anavasesakilesakkhayāvahaṃ santaṃ paṇītaṃ anuttaraṃ dhammaṃ sāvakopi nāma sacchikarissati, tasmā evaṃvidhaguṇavisesādhigamahetubhūtā aho acchariyā buddhā bhagavanto, acchariyā dhammaguṇā, acchariyā amhākaṃ satthu sampattiyoti ratanattayassa guṇādhimuttiṃ pavedesīti. Dhammasampattikittaneneva hi saṅghasuppaṭipatti kittitā hotīti.

Here, 'aho' is a particle in the sense of wonder. 'Buddhā' refers to the All-Knowing Buddhas, the plural being used out of reverence, meaning, 'Oh, how wonderful are the Fully Awakened Ones!' 'Dhammā' refers to the nine supramundane Dhammas together with the scriptural teachings. 'Aho no satthu sampadā' means, 'Oh, the accomplishments of our Teacher!'—that is, 'Oh, the accomplishments of our Teacher, the Possessor of the Ten Powers!' 'Yattha' means 'in which Teacher,' by living the holy life. 'Such a Dhamma a disciple will realize' means: a Dhamma of this kind—exceedingly pure, attended by jhāna and direct knowledge, leading to the destruction of defilements without remainder, peaceful, sublime, and unsurpassed—even a disciple will realize. Therefore, because they are the cause for attaining such extraordinary qualities, 'Oh, how wonderful are the Blessed Buddhas, how wonderful are the virtues of the Dhamma, how wonderful are the accomplishments of our Teacher!' Thus, he declared his conviction in the virtues of the Triple Gem. Indeed, by extolling the accomplishment of the Dhamma, the Saṅgha’s good practice is also extolled.

Evaṃ sādhāraṇavasena dassitaṃ dhammassa sacchikiriyaṃ idāni attupanāyikaṃ katvā dassento “asaṅkheyyesū”ti gāthamāha. Tattha asaṅkheyyesūti gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattesu mahākappesu. Sakkāyāti pañcupādānakkhandhā. Te hi paramatthato vijjamānadhammasamūhatāya “sakkāyā”ti vuccanti. Ahūti nivattanūpāyassa anadhigatattā anapagatā ahesuṃ. Tesamayaṃ pacchimako carimoyaṃ samussayoti [P 2.0070] yasmā ayaṃ sabbapacchimako, tato eva carimo, tasmā jātimaraṇasahito khandhādipaṭipāṭisaññito saṃsāro idāni āyatiṃ punabbhavābhāvato punabbhavo natthi, ayamantimā jātīti attho.

Having thus shown the realization of the Dhamma in a general way, he now speaks the verse beginning 'In countless aeons,' illustrating it by applying it to himself. Here, 'in countless aeons' means in great aeons that have gone beyond the scope of reckoning. 'Personal existence' (sakkāya) means the five aggregates subject to clinging. For these are called 'personal existence' because, in the ultimate sense, they are a collection of existing phenomena. 'There were' (ahū) means they had not been abandoned, because the means of turning back had not been attained. 'This is the last, the final embodied state' (ayaṃ pacchimako carimo samussayo)—because this is the very last, it is therefore the final one. Therefore, the cycle of existence, characterized by birth and death and known as the succession of aggregates, now, in the future, due to the absence of further becoming, there is no further becoming; the meaning is, 'This is the final birth.'

Kumārakassapattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kumārakassapa is concluded.

2. Dhammapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammapāla

Yo have daharo bhikkhūti āyasmato dhammapālattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kenacideva karaṇīyena vanantaṃ upagato satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso [V 1.0355] pilakkhaphalamadāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde satthari parinibbute avantiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā dhammapāloti laddhanāmo vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggahetvā paṭinivattento antarāmagge ekasmiṃ vihāre aññataraṃ theraṃ disvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā [M 1.0417] vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.21-25) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Dhammapāla, beginning 'Truly, that young bhikkhu.' What is its origin? He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, was born into a respectable family and attained maturity. On some business, he went into the forest, saw the Teacher, and with a joyful mind, offered a pilakkha fruit. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era, after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he was born into a brahmin family in the Avanti region. He was named Dhammapāla and, coming of age, went to Takkasilā to learn a craft. On his return journey, he saw an elder in a monastery along the way. Hearing the Dhamma from him, he gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 1.39.21-25):

“Vanantare buddhaṃ disvā, atthadassiṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, pilakkhassādadiṃ phalaṃ.

'Seeing the Buddha in the forest, Atthadassī, the greatly renowned; With a joyful and serene mind, I offered the pilakkha fruit.'

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, yaṃ phalamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

'Eighteen hundred aeons ago, when I gave that fruit; I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that fruit-offering.'

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

'My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.'

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā samāpattisukhena vītināmento ekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ vihāre dve sāmaṇere rukkhagge pupphāni ocinante ārūḷhasākhāya bhaggāya patante disvā thero iddhānubhāvena hatthena gahetvā arogeyeva bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā tesaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ dhammaṃ desento –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, while spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainments, one day in that monastery, seeing two novice monks picking flowers at the treetop, as the branch they climbed on broke, falling down, the elder, through his psychic power, caught them with his hand and placed them safely on the ground. Then, teaching those novice monks the Dhamma, he said:

203.

203.

“Yo have daharo bhikkhu, yuñjati buddhasāsane;

Jāgaro sa hi suttesu, amoghaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ.

'Truly, that young bhikkhu who devotes himself to the Buddha's teaching, being awake among those who sleep—his life is not in vain.'

204.

204.

“Tasmā saddhañca sīlañca, pasādaṃ dhammadassanaṃ;

Anuyuñjetha medhāvī, saraṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti. – imā dve gāthā abhāsi;

'Therefore, faith, virtue, confidence, and vision of the Dhamma—the wise one should cultivate, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.' These two verses he spoke.

Tattha yoti aniyamavacanaṃ. Haveti daḷhatthe nipāto. Daharoti taruṇo. Bhikkhatīti bhikkhu. Yuñjatīti ghaṭati vāyamati. Jāgaroti [P 2.0071] jāgaraṇadhammasamannāgato. Suttesūti supantesu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti yo bhikkhu daharova samāno taruṇo “tathāhaṃ pacchā vuḍḍhakāle jānissāmī”ti acintetvā buddhānaṃ sāsane appamādapaṭipattiyaṃ yuñjati samathavipassanābhāvanāya yogaṃ karoti, so suttesu avijjāniddāya suttesu pamattesu saddhādijāgaradhammasamannāgamena jāgaro, tato eva attahitaparahitapāripūriyā amoghaṃ avañjhaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ, yasmā ca etadevaṃ, tasmā saddhañca “atthi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko”tiādinayappavattaṃ kammaphalasaddhañca, saddhūpanibandhattā sīlassa tadupanissayaṃ catupārisuddhisīlañca[M 1.0418], “sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti evaṃ pavattaratanattayappasādañca[V 1.0356], vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya pariññādivasena catusaccadhammadassanañca medhāvī dhammojapaññāya samannāgato bhikkhu buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādaṃ anusiṭṭhiṃ anussaranto ādittampi attano sīsaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā anuyuñjetha, tattha anuyogaṃ ātappaṃ kareyyāti attho.

Here, 'yo' is an indefinite term. 'Have' is a particle indicating emphasis. 'Daharo' means young. A bhikkhu is one who begs (bhikkhati). 'Yuñjati' means strives or exerts. 'Jāgaro' means endowed with the quality of wakefulness. 'Suttesu' means among those who are asleep. This is what is said: A bhikkhu who, though young, does not think, 'I will understand this in old age later,' but instead applies himself diligently to the Buddha's teaching, engaging in the practice of serenity and insight meditation—he is awake among those asleep in the slumber of ignorance, among the heedless, endowed with the quality of wakefulness through faith and so on. Because of this, his life is not in vain or fruitless, fulfilling both his own welfare and the welfare of others. And since it is so, therefore, a wise bhikkhu endowed with the wisdom that is the essence of the Dhamma, recollecting the Buddha's teaching, advice, and instruction, should diligently cultivate faith—that is, the faith in the result of kamma, such as the conviction 'there is action, there is the result of action'—and the virtue dependent on faith, the fourfold purified virtue, and confidence in the Triple Gem—'The Blessed One is the fully enlightened one, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is practicing rightly'—as well as the vision of the Dhamma, which is the seeing of the four truths by means of path-wisdom together with insight-wisdom through full understanding and so on, disregarding even his own head if it were ablaze. The meaning is that he should make an ardent effort in that practice.

Dhammapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammapāla is concluded.

3. Brahmālittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Brahmāli

Kassindriyāni samathaṅgatānīti āyasmato brahmālittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā pādaphalaṃ adāsi. Satthā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brahmālīti laddhanāmo viññutaṃ patto hetusampattiyā codiyamāno saṃsāre sañjātasaṃvego tādisena kalyāṇamittasannissayena buddhasāsane pabbajitvā patirūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe viharanto ñāṇassa paripākagatattā nacirasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.51.63-67) –

“Whose faculties are calmed”—this verse was spoken by the Venerable Elder Brahmāli. What is its origin? This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome deeds here and there as a basis for liberation from existence, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher walking for alms, with a mind filled with faith, he paid homage and offered a fruit for the bowl. The Teacher gave his appreciation and departed. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the Kosala country and was named Brahmāli. Having reached maturity, being urged by the maturity of causes, he developed a sense of urgency about saṃsāra. Through reliance on such good friends, he went forth in the Buddha’s Dispensation, took up a suitable meditation subject, and dwelling in the forest, due to the maturation of his knowledge, he soon developed insight and became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 2.51.63–67):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, pādaphalaṃ adāsahaṃ.

“The golden-hued Perfectly Enlightened One, the receiver of offerings, as he was proceeding along the road, I gave him a fruit for the bowl.”

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one eons ago, when I gave that fruit, I do not know of any bad destination—this is the fruit of that fruit-offering.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño [M 1.0419][P 2.0072] pana hutvā maggasukhena phalasukhena vītināmento ekadivasaṃ padhānapariggāhakena therena tasmiṃ araññāyatane bhikkhū uddissa vuttaṃ padhānānuyogaṃ pariggaṇhanto –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, and passing his time in the bliss of the path and the bliss of fruition, one day, while accepting the exhortation to striving spoken by the elder who supervised practice in that forest dwelling for the sake of the monks—

205.

205.

“Kassindriyāni [V 1.0357] samathaṅgatāni, assā yathā sārathinā sudantā;

Pahīnamānassa anāsavassa, devāpi kassa pihayanti tādino.

“Whose faculties are calmed, / like horses well-trained by a charioteer? / To whom, having abandoned conceit, taintless, / do even the devas long for such a one?”

206.

206.

“Mayhindriyāni samathaṅgatāni, assā yathā sārathinā sudantā;

Pahīnamānassa anāsavassa, devāpi mayhaṃ pihayanti tādino”ti. –

“My faculties are calmed, / like horses well-trained by a charioteer. / Having abandoned conceit, taintless, / even the devas long for me, such a one.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tassattho – imasmiṃ araññāyatane vasantesu bhikkhūsu kassa bhikkhuno therassa vā navassa vā majjhimassa vā chekena sārathinā sudantā assā viya manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni samathaṃ dantabhāvaṃ nibbisevanabhāvaṃ gatāni. Kassa navavidhampi mānaṃ pahāya ṭhitattā pahīnamānassa catunnampi āsavānaṃ abhāvena anāsavassa iṭṭhādīsu tādilakkhaṇappattiyā tādino devāpi pihayanti manussāpi sammāpaṭipattidassanādinā ca ādarena patthentīti.

Its meaning is this: Among the monks dwelling in this forest abode, whose faculties—the six, with the mind as the sixth—are calmed, tamed, and free from indulgence, like horses well-trained by a skilled charioteer? And to whom, having abandoned the ninefold conceit, and being without the four taints, and having attained the characteristic of impartiality towards the desirable and undesirable, do even the devas long for, and humans, by seeing his proper practice and so forth, desire him with reverence?

Tattha ca gāthāyaṃ purimaḍḍhena anāgāmimaggādhigamo puṭṭho, anāgāminopi hi indriyāni pahīnakāmarāgabyāpādatāya samathaṃ nibbisevanataṃ gatāni honti. Itarena arahattamaggapaṭilābho, arahā hi “pahīnamāno anāsavo tādī”ti ca vuccati.

In that verse, by the first half, the attainment of the non-returner path is questioned, for the faculties of non-returners too are calmed and have reached a state of non-indulgence through the abandoning of sensual desire and ill-will. By the other half, the attainment of the Arahant path is indicated, for an Arahant is indeed called “one who has abandoned conceit, taintless, such a one.”

Athāyasmā brahmāli padhānapariggāhakena vuttaṃ “kassindriyānī”ti gāthaṃ paccanubhāsi. Tadatthaṃ attūpanāyikavasena vissajjento “mayhindriyānī”tiādikāya dutiyagāthāya aññaṃ byākāsi, tattha mayhindriyānīti mama cakkhādīni indriyāni. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Then the Venerable Brahmāli recited in response the verse “Whose faculties?” spoken by the one who encouraged striving. Answering its meaning by applying it to himself, he declared his final knowledge with the second verse beginning, “My faculties.” Here, “My faculties” means my faculties such as the eye, etc. The rest is as previously explained.

Brahmālittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Brahmāli is concluded.

4. Mogharājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mogharāja

Chavipāpaka [M 1.0420] cittabhaddakāti āyasmato mogharājattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthu [P 2.0073] santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhanto paṇidhānaṃ katvā tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato brāhmaṇamāṇave vijjāsippāni sikkhāpento ekadivasaṃ atthadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ gacchantaṃ [V 1.0358] disvā pasannamānaso pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā sirasi añjaliṃ katvā “yāvatā rūpino sattā”tiādinā chahi gāthāhi abhitthavitvā bhājanaṃ pūretvā madhuṃ upanāmesi. Satthā madhuṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ akāsi.

“Chavipāpaka cittabhaddakā”—this verse was spoken by the Venerable Elder Mogharāja. What is its origin? This venerable one, too, having made an aspiration under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher establishing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who wore coarse robes. Desiring that rank for himself, he made a resolution and performed meritorious deeds in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn in a brahmin family, attained expertise in the arts and sciences of brahmins, and taught those arts and sciences to brahmin youths. One day, seeing the Blessed One Atthadassī walking surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, with a joyful mind, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, raised his joined hands to his head, and with six verses beginning “Yāvatā rūpino sattā,” he praised him and, having filled a vessel, offered honey. The Teacher accepted the honey and gave his appreciation.

So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle kaṭṭhavāhanassa nāma rañño amacco hutvā tena satthu ānayanatthaṃ purisasahassena pesito satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ katvā tato cuto ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā mogharājāti laddhanāmo bāvarībrāhmaṇassa santike uggahitasippo saṃvegajāto tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tāpasasahassaparivāro ajitādīhi saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ pesito tesaṃ pannarasamo hutvā pañhe pucchitvā pañhavissajjanapariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.4.64-83) –

Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he became a minister of the king named Kaṭṭhavāhana. Sent by the king with a thousand men to bring the Teacher, he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. Having practiced the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years, after passing away from there, he was reborn only in happy destinations for one Buddha-interval. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a brahmin family and received the name Mogharāja. Having mastered the arts in the presence of the brahmin Bāvarī, he felt spiritual urgency and went forth into the ascetic life. With a retinue of a thousand ascetics, he was sent to the Teacher along with Ajita and the others. Being the fifteenth among them, he asked his questions, and at the conclusion of the explanation of the questions, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera Apadāna 1.4.64–83):

“Atthadassī tu bhagavā, sayambhū aparājito;

Bhikkhusaṅghaparibyūḷho, rathiyaṃ paṭipajjatha.

“The Blessed One Atthadassī, the Self-become, the Unconquered, / surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, proceeded along the road.”

“Sissehi samparivuto, gharamhā abhinikkhamiṃ;

Nikkhamitvānahaṃ tattha, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Surrounded by disciples, I departed from my house; / having departed, there I saw the Leader of the World.”

“Abhivādiya sambuddhaṃ, sire katvāna añjaliṃ;

Sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā, santhaviṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Having paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, placing my joined hands on my head, / having gladdened my mind, I praised the Leader of the World.”

“Yāvatā [M 1.0421] rūpino sattā, arūpī vā asaññino;

Sabbe te tava ñāṇamhi, anto honti samogadhā.

“Whatever beings there are with form, or formless, or without perception— / all of them are encompassed within your knowledge, fully included.”

“Sukhumacchikajālena, udakaṃ yo parikkhipe;

Ye keci udake pāṇā, antojāle bhavanti te.

“Like one who might surround the water with a fine-meshed net— / whatever creatures are in the water, they are within the net.”

“Yesañca cetanā atthi, rūpino ca arūpino;

Sabbe te tava ñāṇamhi, anto honti samogadhā.

“And those who have volition, both with form and without form— / all of them are encompassed within your knowledge, fully included.”

“Samuddharasimaṃ lokaṃ, andhakārasamākulaṃ;

Tava dhammaṃ suṇitvāna, kaṅkhāsotaṃ taranti te.

“You rescue this world, which is filled with darkness; / having heard your Dhamma, they cross the stream of doubt.”

“Avijjānivute loke, andhakārena otthaṭe;

Tava ñāṇamhi jotante, andhakārā padhaṃsitā.

“In a world shrouded by ignorance, covered with darkness, / when your knowledge shines, the darkness is dispelled.”

“Tuvaṃ cakkhūsi sabbesaṃ, mahātamapanūdano;

Tava dhammaṃ suṇitvāna, nibbāyati bahujjano.

“You are the eye for all, the dispeller of great darkness; / having heard your Dhamma, many people attain Nibbāna.”

“Puṭakaṃ [V 1.0359] pūrayitvāna, madhukhuddamaneḷakaṃ;

Ubho hatthehi paggayha, upanesiṃ mahesino.

“Having filled a basket with pure honey and honeycomb, / raising it with both hands, I offered it to the Great Sage.”

“Paṭiggaṇhi mahāvīro, sahatthena mahā isi;

Bhuñjitvā tañca sabbaññū, vehāsaṃ nabhamuggami.

“The Great Hero, the Great Seer, accepted it with his own hand; / having eaten it, the All-Knowing One ascended into the sky.”

“Antalikkhe ṭhito satthā, atthadassī narāsabho;

Mama cittaṃ pasādento, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“Standing in the sky, the Teacher, Atthadassī, the Bull of Men, / gladdening my mind, spoke these verses:”

“Yenidaṃ thavitaṃ ñāṇaṃ, buddhaseṭṭho ca thomito;

Tena cittappasādena, duggatiṃ so na gacchati.

“Because he has praised this knowledge and extolled the Supreme Buddha, / through that confidence of mind, he will not go to a bad destination.”

“Catuddasañca khattuṃ so, devarajjaṃ karissati;

Pathabyā rajjaṃ aṭṭhasataṃ, vasudhaṃ āvasissati.

“Fourteen times he will exercise the sovereignty of the devas; / eight hundred times he will rule the kingdom of the earth, he will hold sway over the wealth-bearer.”

“Pañceva satakkhattuñca, cakkavattī bhavissati;

Padesarajjaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ, mahiyā kārayissati.

“And five hundred times he will be a wheel-turning monarch; / countless times, he will exercise regional sovereignty over the earth.”

“Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Gotamassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajissati.

“A reciter, a master of mantras, one who has gone to the far shore of the three Vedas, / he will go forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama.”

“Gambhīraṃ [M 1.0422] nipuṇaṃ atthaṃ, ñāṇena vicinissati;

Mogharājāti nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

“With knowledge, he will investigate the deep and subtle meaning; / by the name of Mogharāja, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.”

“Tīhi vijjāhi sampannaṃ, katakiccamanāsavaṃ;

Gotamo satthavāhaggo, etadagge ṭhapessati.

“Endowed with the three knowledges, having done what was to be done, taintless, / Gotama, the foremost leader of the caravan, will place him in the foremost position.”

“Hitvā mānusakaṃ yogaṃ, chetvāna bhavabandhanaṃ;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, viharāmi anāsavo.

“Having abandoned the human yoke, having cut the fetter of existence, / fully understanding all taints, I dwell taintless.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthalūkhaṃ suttalūkhaṃ rajanalūkhanti visesena tividhenapi lūkhena samannāgataṃ paṃsukūlaṃ dhāresi. Tena naṃ satthā lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Aparabhāge purimakammappaccayā parihārassa akaraṇato therassa sarīre daddupīḷakādīni uppajjitvā vaḍḍhiṃsu. So “senāsanaṃ dussatī”ti hemantepi magadhakkhettesu palālasanthārāni attharitvā seti. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ satthā paṭisanthāravasena “chavipāpakā”tiādinā [P 2.0074] paṭhamagāthāya pucchi.

Having attained Arahantship, he wore cast-off robes that were especially rough in three ways: rough from the loom, rough from the thread, and rough from dye. Because of this, the Teacher placed him foremost among those who wear rough robes. Later, due to past kamma and a failure to take precautions, boils and sores arose and spread on the elder’s body. Thinking, "The bedding will be soiled," he spread straw mats in the Magadha fields even in winter and lay there. One day, after approaching the Teacher for attendance, paying homage, and sitting to one side, the Teacher questioned him with the first verse, beginning with "Chavipāpakā," by way of a friendly greeting.

207. Tattha chavipāpakāti daddukacchupīḷakāhi bhinnacchavibhāvato hīnacchavika duṭṭhacchavika[V 1.0360]. Cittabhaddakāti anavasesakilesappahānena brahmavihārasevanāya ca bhaddacitta sundaracitta. Mogharājāti tassa ālapanaṃ. Satataṃ samāhitoti aggaphalasamādhinā niccakālaṃ abhiṇhaṃ samāhitamānaso. Hemantikasītakālarattiyoti hemantasamaye sītakālarattiyo. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. “Hemantikā sītakālarattiyo”tipi pāḷi. Tattha hemantikāti hemantogadhā hemantapariyāpannāti attho. Bhikkhu tvaṃ sīti bhikkhu ko tvaṃ asi, evaṃbhūto paresu tava senāsanaṃ katvā adentesu saṅghikañca senāsanaṃ apavisanto. Kathaṃ karissasīti yathāvutte sītakāle kathaṃ attabhāvaṃ pavattesīti satthā pucchi. Evaṃ pana puṭṭho thero satthu tamatthaṃ kathento –

207. There, 'of bad skin' means having broken skin due to ringworm, scabies, or boils—thus, one with inferior skin, of afflicted skin. 'Of good mind' means having a beautiful and excellent mind through the complete abandonment of defilements and the cultivation of the divine abidings. 'Mogharāja' is his name, used as a form of address. 'Ever concentrated' means constantly and repeatedly having a mind absorbed in the highest fruition attainment. 'In the cold winter nights' refers to the cold nights of the winter season. This is a locative case denoting continuous duration. There is also the Pāli reading: 'Hemantikā sītakālarattiyo.' Herein, 'winter' means immersed in winter, pertaining to winter. The question 'Monk, how will you manage?' implies: 'Being such a monk, when others do not provide you with a dwelling and you do not enter the communal dwelling, how will you manage?' Thus, the Teacher asked how he would sustain himself in the cold season as described. When questioned thus, the elder, explaining the matter to the Teacher, said—

208.

208.

“Sampannasassā [M 1.0423] magadhā, kevalā iti me sutaṃ;

Palālacchannako seyyaṃ, yathaññe sukhajīvino”ti. – gāthamāha;

"Magadha is entirely rich in crops, so I have heard; I lie on a bed covered with straw, like others who live a life of ease." – thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha sampannasassāti nipphannasassā. Magadhāti magadharaṭṭhaṃ vadati. Magadhā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīvasena “magadhā”tveva bahuvacanena vuccati. Kevalāti anavasesā. Iti me sutanti evaṃ mayā sutaṃ. Tattha yo adiṭṭho padeso, tassa vasena sutanti vuttaṃ. Tena edise kāle magadhesu yattha katthaci mayā vasituṃ sakkāti dasseti. Palālacchannako seyyaṃ, yathaññe sukhajīvinoti yathā aññe sukhajīvino bhikkhū senāsanasappāyaṃ laddhā sundarehi attharaṇapāvuraṇehi sukhena sayanti, evaṃ ahampi palālasanthārameva heṭṭhā santharitvā upari tiriyañca palālacchadaneneva chāditasarīratāya palālacchannako seyyaṃ sayiṃ, seyyaṃ kappesinti attano yathālābhasantosaṃ vibhāveti.

There, 'sampannasassā' means crops that are fully grown. 'Magadhā' refers to the Magadha country. The princes of the countryside are called 'Magadhā,' and by customary usage, even a single region where they dwell is referred to in the plural as 'Magadhā.' 'Kevalā' means without exception. 'Iti me sutaṃ' means 'thus have I heard.' There, regarding a place that was unseen, it is said to have been 'heard.' This shows that at such a time he was able to dwell anywhere in Magadha. The phrase 'I lie on a bed covered with straw, like others who live a life of ease' means: just as other monks who live comfortably, having obtained suitable lodgings, sleep happily with beautiful coverings and spreads, so too I, having spread a straw mat beneath and having my body covered above and crosswise with just a straw covering, lay down. Thus, being 'covered with straw,' I make my bed. In this way, he expresses his contentment with whatever he obtains.

Mogharājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Mogharāja is completed.

5. Visākhapañcālaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Visākha Pañcālaputta

Na [P 2.0075] ukkhipe no ca parikkhipe pareti āyasmato visākhassa pañcālaputtassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito cuddase kappe paccantagāme daliddakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ phalapariyesanaṃ carantehi tasmiṃ gāme manussehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ gato tattha ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā pasannamānaso valliphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ [V 1.0361] buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe maṇḍalikarājakule nibbattitvā visākhoti laddhanāmo pañcālarājadhītuyā puttabhāvato pacchā pañcālaputtoti paññāyittha. So pitari mate rajjaṃ kārento satthari attano gāmasamīpagate satthu santikaṃ gantvā [M 1.0424] dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā satthārā saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ gato vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.31-36) –

"One should not exalt oneself nor disparage others," this is the verse of the Venerable Visākha Pañcālaputta. What is its origin? He too, having made aspirations under past Buddhas, accumulated merit here and there in his existences, merit that supports liberation. Fourteen aeons ago from this one, he was born in a poor family in a border village. Having reached maturity, one day while searching for fruits with the people of that village, he went to the forest and saw a Paccekabuddha. With a serene mind, he offered a fruit from a creeper. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was born into a ruling family in the Magadha country and was given the name Visākha. Because he was the son of the daughter of the king of Pañcāla, he later became known as Pañcālaputta. When his father died, he ruled the kingdom. When the Teacher came near his village, he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. Having gone forth, he accompanied the Teacher to Sāvatthī, established insight, and soon attained the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.39.31-36):

“Sabbe janā samāgamma, agamiṃsu vanaṃ tadā;

Phalamanvesamānā te, alabhiṃsu phalaṃ tadā.

"All the people gathered together and went to the forest then; seeking fruit, they obtained fruit at that time.

“Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, sayambhuṃ aparājitaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, valliphalamadāsahaṃ.

"There I saw the Sambuddha, the Self-Awakened, the Unconquered One; with a serene and joyful mind, I gave a fruit from a creeper.

“Catuddase ito kappe, yaṃ phalamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Fourteen aeons ago from this one, when I gave that fruit; I know of no bad destination since then—this is the fruit of giving that fruit.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burned up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā thero ñātīnaṃ anukampāya jātibhūmiṃ agamāsi. Tattha manussā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā kālena kālaṃ dhammaṃ suṇantā ekadivasaṃ “katihi nu kho, bhante, aṅgehi samannāgato dhammakathiko hotī”ti dhammakathikalakkhaṇaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero tesaṃ dhammakathikalakkhaṇaṃ kathento –

The elder, having attained the six higher knowledges, went to his birthplace out of compassion for his relatives. There, people approached the elder and, listening to the Dhamma from time to time, one day asked, "Venerable sir, with how many qualities is a Dhamma preacher endowed?" The elder, explaining to them the characteristics of a Dhamma preacher, said:

209.

209.

“Na ukkhipe no ca parikkhipe pare, na okkhipe pāragataṃ na eraye;

Na cattavaṇṇaṃ parisāsu byāhare, anuddhato sammitabhāṇi subbato.

"One should not exalt oneself nor disparage others; one should not belittle nor provoke one who has gone beyond. One should not speak of one's own praise in assemblies; be unagitated, speak moderately, and be of good conduct.

210.

210.

“Susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā, matikusalena nivātavuttinā;

Saṃsevitabuddhasīlinā, nibbānaṃ na hi tena dullabha”nti. –

"By one who sees very subtle and refined meanings, who is skilled in intellect and of humble conduct, by one accustomed to associating with the wise—for such a one, Nibbāna is not hard to attain."

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

Tattha na ukkhipeti attānaṃ na ukkhipeyya, jātiādīhi bāhusaccādīhi ca attukkaṃsanaṃ na kareyya. No ca parikkhipe pareti pare parapuggale teheva jātiādīhi no parikkhipe paricchinditvā na [P 2.0076] khipeyya guṇaparidhaṃsanavasena [M 1.0425] vā na khipeyya. Na okkhipe pare iccevaṃ sambandho. Pare ojjhāpanavasena na okkhipe heṭṭhato katvā pare na olokāpeyya, na ojjhāpeyyāti attho. “Na ukkhipe”ti keci paṭhanti, so evattho. Pāragatanti [V 1.0362] saṃsārapāraṃ viya vijjāya pāraṃ gataṃ khīṇāsavaṃ tevijjaṃ chaḷabhiññaṃ vā na eraye na ghaṭṭaye na āsādeyya. Na cattavaṇṇaṃ parisāsu byāhareti attano vaṇṇaṃ guṇaṃ lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamāno khattiyaparisādīsu na bhāseyya. Anuddhatoti uddhaccarahito. Uddhatassa hi vacanaṃ nādiyanti. Sammitabhāṇīti sammadeva mitabhāṇī, kālena sāpadesaṃ pariyantavatiṃ atthasañhitameva vācaṃ bhāsanasīloti attho. Ito aññathā vadantassa vacanaṃ agahaṇīyaṃ hoti. Subbatoti sundaravato sīlasampanno. “Siyā”ti kiriyāpadaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ.

There, 'one should not exalt' means one should not exalt oneself; one should not boast about one's birth, extensive learning, and so forth. 'Nor should one disparage others' means one should not disparage other individuals based on those same factors like birth; one should not reject them by discriminating against them, nor disparage them by diminishing their virtues. The connection is thus: 'one should not belittle others.' This means one should not belittle others by way of reproaching them; one should not look down upon them or cause them to be looked down upon. Some read 'na ukkhipe' here; the meaning is the same. 'One who has gone beyond' means one who has gone to the far shore of knowledge, as if to the far shore of saṃsāra—an Arahant endowed with the threefold knowledge or the six higher knowledges. One should not provoke, agitate, or treat such a person with disrespect. 'One should not speak of one's own praise in assemblies' means one should not speak of one's own praise, virtue, gains, honor, or fame in assemblies of nobles and others, out of desire for them. 'Unagitated' means free from restlessness. For the words of a restless person are not heeded. 'A measured speaker' means one whose nature is to speak in a measured way, that is, to speak at the right time, with reason, with limits, and only what is connected to the goal. The words of one who speaks otherwise are not to be accepted. 'Of good conduct' means one of beautiful vows, endowed with virtue. The verb 'siyā' ('one should be') should be supplied to complete the sense.

Evaṃ thero saṅkhepeneva dhammakathikalakkhaṇaṃ vatvā tesaṃ guṇānaṃ attani labbhamānataṃ adhimuccitvā bhiyyosomattāya abhippasannaṃ mahājanaṃ ñatvā “evaṃvidhassa dhammakathikassa vimuttāyatanasannissitassa na nibbānaṃ dullabhaṃ, atha kho sulabhamevā”ti dassento “susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā”ti dutiyagāthamāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

Thus the elder, having briefly explained the characteristics of a Dhamma speaker, and having become convinced that these qualities were found within himself, and having known that the great assembly was even more devoted, spoke the second verse, 'Susukhumanipuṇatthadassinā,' showing that for such a Dhamma speaker who is dependent on a basis for liberation, Nibbāna is not difficult to attain, but is indeed easily attainable. The meaning of this has already been stated below.

Visākhapañcālaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Visākha Pañcālaputta is completed.

6. Cūḷakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Cūḷaka

Nadanti morā susikhā supekhuṇāti āyasmato cūḷakattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso chattapaṇṇiphalaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā cūḷakoti laddhanāmo vayappatto dhanapāladamane satthari [M 1.0426] laddhappasādo pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto indasālaguhāyaṃ vasati, so ekadivasaṃ guhādvāre nisinno magadhakkhettaṃ olokesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pāvusakālamegho gambhīramadhuranigghoso satapaṭalasahassapaṭalo añjana [P 2.0077] sikharasannikāso nabhaṃ pūretvā pavassati, mayūrasaṅghā ca meghagajjitaṃ sutvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā kekāsaddaṃ muñcitvā tattha tattha padese naccantā vicaranti. Therassapi āvāsagabbhe meghavātaphassehi apagatadhammattā passaddhakarajakāye kallataṃ patte utusappāyalābhena cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi, kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ otari, so taṃ ñatvā kālasampadādikittanamukhena attānaṃ bhāvanāya ussāhento –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Cūḷaka begins: 'The peacocks cry, with beautiful crests and lovely plumage...' What is its origin? This one, too, had performed meritorious deeds in the time of previous Buddhas. Relying on the support of liberation wherever he was reborn, accumulating wholesome deeds conducive to unbinding, he was born in a household in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, thirty-one eons ago. Having attained maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a joyful mind, offered him a chattapaṇṇi fruit. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a brahmin family in Rājagaha. Named Cūḷaka, he came of age and, gaining faith in the Teacher at the subduing of Dhanapāla, he went forth. Practicing the ascetic life, he dwelled in the Indasāla Cave. One day, seated at the cave’s entrance, he surveyed the Magadha countryside. At that moment, a monsoon cloud, with a deep and sweet sound, with hundreds and thousands of layers, resembling a peak of collyrium, filled the sky and rained down. Hearing the thunder, flocks of peacocks, delighted and thrilled, released their 'kekā' cries and danced here and there. In the Elder’s dwelling, too, due to the heat having departed by the touch of the cloud-wind, his body, with its defilements calmed, became fit. His mind became one-pointed and entered the course of the meditation subject. Knowing this, he encouraged himself in development by praising the perfection of time and other conditions:

211.

211.

“Nadanti [V 1.0363] morā susikhā supekhuṇā, sunīlagīvā sumukhā sugajjino;

Susaddalā cāpi mahāmahī ayaṃ, subyāpitambu suvalāhakaṃ nabhaṃ.

“The peacocks cry out, with fine crests and beautiful plumage, with lovely blue necks, fair faces, and fine voices; and this great earth is very grassy, well-spread with water, and the sky has fine clouds.”

212.

212.

“Sukallarūpo sumanassa jhāyataṃ, sunikkamo sādhu subuddhasāsane;

Susukkasukkaṃ nipuṇaṃ sududdasaṃ, phusāhi taṃ uttamamaccutaṃ pada”nti. –

“Being well-disposed in body, meditating with a joyful mind, strive well in the good teaching of the Buddha; attain that supreme, deathless state, which is exceedingly pure, subtle, and very difficult to see.”

Dve gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke two verses.

Tattha nadanti morā susikhā supekhuṇā, sunīlagīvā sumukhā sugajjinoti ete matthake uṭṭhitāhi sundarāhi sikhāhi samannāgatattā susikhā, nānāvaṇṇehi anekehi sobhanehi bhaddakapiñchehi samannāgatattā supekhuṇā, rājīvavaṇṇasaṅkāsāya sundarāya nīlavaṇṇāya gīvāya samannāgatattā sunīlagīvā, sundaramukhatāya sumukhā, manuññavāditāya sugajjino, morā sikhaṇḍino chajjasaṃvādī kekāsaddaṃ muñcantā [M 1.0427] nadanti ravanti. Susaddalā cāpi mahāmahī ayanti ayañca mahāpathavī susaddalā sundaraharitatiṇā. Subyāpitambūti abhinavavuṭṭhiyā tahaṃ tahaṃ vissandamānasalilatāya suṭṭhu byāpitajalā vitatajalā. “Susukkatambū”tipi pāṭho, suvisuddhajalāti attho. Suvalāhakaṃ nabhanti idañca nabhaṃ ākāsaṃ nīluppaladalasannibhehi samantato pūretvā ṭhitehi sundarehi valāhakehi meghehi suvalāhakaṃ.

Therein, 'the peacocks cry, with beautiful crests, lovely plumage, splendid blue necks, charming faces, and delightful calls': 'beautiful-crested' (susikhā) because they are endowed with beautiful crests that have risen on their heads; 'lovely-plumaged' (supekhuṇā) because they are adorned with many splendid and colorful feathers; 'splendid blue-necked' (sunīlagīvā) because they possess beautiful blue necks resembling the color of a blue lotus; 'charming-faced' (sumukhā) because of their charming faces; and 'delightful-calling' (sugajjino) because of their pleasant calls. The peacocks (morā), the crested ones (sikhaṇḍino), singing in the sixth note of the scale, release their 'kekā' sound and cry out. 'And this great earth is very grassy': this great earth (mahāpathavī) is 'very grassy' (susaddalā), meaning it has beautiful green grass. 'Well-spread with water' (subyāpitambu) means that due to the recent rain, it is thoroughly pervaded with water, with water spread about, as it flows here and there. There is also the reading 'susukkatambū,' which means 'with very pure water.' 'The sky has fine clouds' (suvalāhakaṃ nabhaṃ) means this sky, this expanse, has fine clouds (suvalāhakaṃ) because it is filled all around with beautiful clouds (valāhakehi) resembling blue lotus petals.

Sukallarūpo [P 2.0078] sumanassa jhāyatanti idāni utusappāyalābhena suṭṭhu kallarūpo kammaniyasabhāvo tvaṃ, nīvaraṇehi anajjhārūḷhacittatāya sundaramanassa yogāvacarassa yaṃ ārammaṇūpanijjhānavasena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānavasena ca jhāyataṃ. Sunikkamo…pe… accutaṃ padanti evaṃ jhāyanto ca sādhu subuddhassa sammāsambuddhassa sāsane sundaranikkamo hutvā suparisuddhasīlatāya susukkaṃ, visuddhasabhāvatāya sabbassapi saṃkilesassa gocarabhāvānupagamanato sukkaṃ, nipuṇañāṇagocaratāya nipuṇaṃ, paramagambhīratāya sududdasaṃ, paṇītabhāvena seṭṭhabhāvena ca uttamaṃ, niccasabhāvatāya accutaṃ padaṃ taṃ nibbānaṃ phusāhi attapaccakkhakaraṇena sammāpaṭipattiyā sacchikarohīti.

'Well-disposed in body, meditating with a joyful mind': now, because you have obtained a favorable season, you are truly well-disposed, in a workable state. You are a meditator with a beautiful mind, due to your mind not being overcome by the hindrances, who meditates by way of sustained reflection on the object and by way of sustained reflection on the characteristics. 'Strive well... the deathless state': thus meditating, having striven well in the good teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, 'attain that Nibbāna.' It is 'exceedingly pure' (susukkaṃ) due to perfectly pure virtue; it is 'pure' (sukkaṃ) due to its pure nature, as it does not fall within the range of any defilement. It is 'subtle' because it is the domain of subtle knowledge; it is 'very difficult to see' due to its extreme profundity. It is 'supreme' because it is sublime and excellent. It is the 'deathless' (accutaṃ) 'state' (padaṃ) due to its eternal nature. 'Attain' it, meaning, realize it for yourself through right practice.

Evaṃ thero attānaṃ ovadantova utusappāyalābhena samāhitacitto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.37-42) –

Thus the elder, while admonishing himself in this way, having obtained a conducive season, with a concentrated mind, made an effort in insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it was said in the Apadāna:

“Kaṇikāraṃva jalitaṃ, puṇṇamāyeva candimaṃ;

Jalantaṃ dīparukkhaṃva, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“Like a blazing Kaṇikāra tree, like the moon on a full-moon night, like a shining lampstand, I saw the Leader of the World.”

“Kadaliphalaṃ [V 1.0364] paggayha, adāsiṃ satthuno ahaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, vanditvāna apakkamiṃ.

“Holding up a banana fruit, I gave it to the Teacher; with a confident and joyful mind, having paid homage, I departed.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ phalamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the thirty-first eon from now, when I gave that fruit, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of the gift of fruit.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ [M 1.0428] pana patvā thero attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā pītisomanassajāto “nadanti morā”tiādinā tāyeva gāthā paccudāhāsi. Tenassa idameva aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

Having attained arahantship, the elder reflected on his own practice, and with joy and gladness arisen, he recited those very same verses beginning with 'The peacocks cry.' Thus, this itself was his declaration of final knowledge.

Cūḷakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Cūḷaka is completed.

7. Anūpamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Anūpama

Nandamānāgataṃ cittāti āyasmato anūpamattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ padumaṃ nāma paccekabuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ rathiyaṃ disvā pasannamānaso aṅkolapupphehi pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe ibbhakule nibbattitvā rūpasampattiyā anūpamoti laddhanāmo vayappatto upanissayasampannatāya kāme pahāya pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto araññe viharati. Tassa cittaṃ bahiddhā rūpādiārammaṇesu vidhāvati. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ parivaṭṭati. Thero vidhāvantaṃ cittaṃ niggaṇhanto –

'The mind, delighting, has come': these are the verses of the Venerable Anūpama. What is their origin? This one, too, had performed meritorious deeds in the time of previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation. Thirty-one eons ago, he was born into a family, and having attained maturity, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Paduma walking for alms in the street. With a joyful mind, he honored him with Aṅkola flowers. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was born into a wealthy family in the Kosala country. Due to his perfection of form, he was named Anūpama. Coming of age, endowed with supporting conditions, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth, and, while practicing insight meditation, dwelled in the forest. His mind would run about towards external objects such as forms. His meditation subject became unsettled. The elder, restraining his wandering mind:

213.

213.

“Nandamānāgataṃ [P 2.0079] cittaṃ, sūlamāropamānakaṃ;

Tena teneva vajasi, yena sūlaṃ kaliṅgaraṃ.

“O mind, you have come delighting, placing one upon a stake. You go to that very place where the stake, the worthless log, is.”

214.

214.

“Tāhaṃ cittakaliṃ brūmi, taṃ brūmi cittadubbhakaṃ;

Satthā te dullabho laddho, mānatthe maṃ niyojayī”ti. –

“That I call a stain on the mind; that I call a betrayer of the mind. A Teacher, so hard to find, has been found by you. Do not engage me in what is harmful!”

Imāhi dvīhi gāthāhi ovadi.

He admonished it with these two verses.

Tattha nandamānāgataṃ cittāti nandamāna abhinandamāna citta abhinandamānaṃ āgataṃ uppannaṃ[V 1.0365]. Sūlamāropamānakanti dukkhuppattiṭṭhānatāya sūlasadisattā sūlaṃ taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ kammakilesehi ettakaṃ kālaṃ āropiyamānaṃ. Tena teneva vajasi, yena sūlaṃ kaliṅgaranti yattha yattha sūlasaṅkhātā [M 1.0429] bhavā kaliṅgarasaṅkhātā adhikuṭṭanakā kāmaguṇā ca tena teneva, pāpacitta, vajasi, taṃ tadeva ṭhānaṃ upagacchasi, attano anatthaṃ na sallakkhesi.

Herein, 'the mind, delighting, has come' means the mind that delights, that greatly delights, that has come, that has arisen, delighting. 'As if being impaled on a stake' means that which is like a stake because it is the place of origin of suffering, namely, that existence, being impaled for so long by kamma and defilements. 'By that very path you go, wherever the stake, the kaliṅgara, is' means, O evil mind, you go by that very path, you approach that very place, wherever existences are called the stake, and sense pleasures are called the kaliṅgara, the crushing things; you do not discern your own harm.

Tāhaṃ cittakaliṃ brūmīti taṃ tasmā pamattabhāvato cittakaliṃ cittakālakaṇṇiṃ ahaṃ kathayāmi. Punapi taṃ brūmi kathemi cittadubbhakaṃ cittasaṅkhātassa attano bahūpakārassa santānassa anatthāvahanato cittadubbhiṃ. “Cittadubbhagā”tipi paṭhanti. Cittasaṅkhātaalakkhikaappapuññāti attho. Kinti brūhīti ce? Āha “satthā te dullabho laddho, mānatthe maṃ niyojayī”ti. Kappānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyampi nāma buddhasuñño loko hoti, satthari uppannepi manussattasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo dullabhā eva, laddhesu ca tesu satthāpi dullabhoyeva hoti. Evaṃ dullabho satthā idāni tayā laddho, tasmiṃ laddhe sampatipi anatthe ahite āyatiñca anatthāvahe dukkhāvahe akusale maṃ mā niyojesīti. Evaṃ thero attano cittaṃ ovadanto eva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.37.16-19) –

'That, I say, is a blemish on the mind' means, because of its heedless nature, I declare that to be a blemish on the mind, a black mark on the mind. Again, I declare it a betrayer of the mind, because it brings harm to one's own continuity, which is called the mind and is of great benefit. Some also recite 'cittadubbhagā' (unfortunate mind). The meaning is: unlucky and of little merit, associated with the mind. If it is asked, 'What do you declare?' he said: 'A Teacher is hard to find—you have found one, yet you urge me to conceit.' For countless aeons, the world is indeed devoid of Buddhas. Even when a Teacher has arisen, human birth, the acquisition of faith, and so on, are indeed rare; and when these have been obtained, a Teacher is still hard to find. Such a rare Teacher has now been found by you. Now that he has been found, do not urge me to what is unprofitable, unwholesome, bringing harm and suffering in the future, to what is unskillful. Thus admonishing his own mind, the Elder developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.37.16–19):

“Padumo [P 2.0080] nāma sambuddho, cittakūṭe vasī tadā;

Disvāna taṃ ahaṃ buddhaṃ, sayambhuṃ aparājitaṃ.

"The Buddha named Paduma was dwelling on Cittakūṭa then; having seen that Buddha, the Self-Enlightened One, the Unconquered One,"

“Aṅkolaṃ pupphitaṃ disvā, ocinitvānahaṃ tadā;

Upagantvāna sambuddhaṃ, pūjayiṃ padumaṃ jinaṃ.

"Seeing the Aṅkola tree in bloom, I gathered its flowers then; approaching the Buddha, the Conqueror Paduma, I worshipped him."

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Thirty-one aeons ago, when I offered that flower, I have not known a bad rebirth—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been done."

Anūpamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Anūpama is concluded.

8. Vajjitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vajjita

Saṃsaraṃ [M 1.0430] dīghamaddhānanti āyasmato vajjitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito pañcasaṭṭhime kappe ekasmiṃ paccantagāme nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto vanacarako hutvā vicaranto ekadivasaṃ upasantaṃ [V 1.0366] nāma paccekabuddhaṃ pabbataguhāyaṃ viharantaṃ addasa. So tassa upasamaṃ disvā pasannamānaso campakapupphena pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe ibbhakule nibbatto jātadivasato paṭṭhāya mātugāmahatthaṃ gato rodati. Brahmalokato kira cavitvā idhāgato yasmā mātugāmasamphassaṃ na sahati, tasmā mātugāmasamphassavajjanato vajjitotveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. So vayappatto satthu yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā tadaheva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.37.27-30) –

"Long is the round of transmigration"—this is the verse of the Elder Vajjita. What is its origin? This elder, too, had made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various existences. Sixty-five aeons ago, he was born in a border village. Having attained maturity, he became a forest-dweller. While wandering, one day he saw a Paccekabuddha named Upasanta dwelling peacefully in a mountain cave. Seeing his serenity, his mind became joyful, and he offered worship with campaka flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn into a wealthy family in the Kosala country. From the day of his birth, whenever he was touched by a woman, he would cry. It is said that he had passed away from the Brahma world and come here. Because he could not bear the touch of women, he was named Vajjita (the Averted One) due to his aversion to female contact. When he came of age, he witnessed the Teacher's Twin Miracle. Gaining faith, he went forth. Developing insight, he attained the six higher knowledges on that very day. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Th. 1.37.27–30):

“Upasanto ca sambuddho, vasatī pabbatantare;

Ekacampakamādāya, upagacchiṃ naruttamaṃ.

"The Paccekabuddha Upasanta was dwelling in a mountain cave; taking a single campaka flower, I approached that supreme man."

“Pasannacitto sumano, paccekamunimuttamaṃ;

Ubho hatthehi paggayha, pūjayiṃ aparājitaṃ.

"With a serene and joyful mind, raising both hands, I worshipped the unsurpassed Paccekabuddha, the Unconquered One."

“Pañcasaṭṭhimhito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Sixty-five aeons ago, when I worshipped with a flower, I have not known a bad rebirth: this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been done."

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā attano pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā dhammasaṃvegena –

Having attained the six higher knowledges, recollecting his own past existences, he was stirred by a sense of urgency concerning the Dhamma—

215.

215.

“Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, gatīsu parivattisaṃ;

Apassaṃ ariyasaccāni, andhabhūto puthujjano.

"Wandering this long journey, I revolved through the destinations; a blind worldling, I did not see the Noble Truths.

216.

216.

“Tassa me appamattassa, saṃsārā vinaḷīkatā;

Sabbā gatī samucchinnā, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. – dve gāthā abhāsi;

"For me, heedful, the round of transmigration has been uprooted; all destinations are cut off; now there is no more renewed existence." Thus he spoke two verses.

Tattha [M 1.0431] saṃsaranti saṃsaranto, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave ādānanikkhepavasena aparāparaṃ sandhāvanto. Dīghamaddhānanti cirakālaṃ anādimati saṃsāre aparimāṇakālaṃ. Gatīsūti sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ [P 2.0081] vasena sugatiduggatīsu. Parivattisanti ghaṭīyantaṃ viya paribbhamanto cavanupapajjanavasena aparāparaṃ parivattiṃ. Tassa pana parivattanassa kāraṇamāha “apassaṃ ariyasaccāni, andhabhūto puthujjano”ti. Dukkhādīni cattāri ariyasaccāni ñāṇacakkhunā apassanto appaṭivijjhanto, tato eva avijjandhatāya andhabhūto puthūnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjano honto gatīsu parivattisanti yojanā, tenevāha bhagavā –

Herein, 'wandering' means wandering, running back and forth in each existence by way of taking up and laying down. 'For a long time' means for a long period, for an immeasurable period in beginningless transmigration. 'Through destinations' means in happy and miserable destinations by way of well-done and ill-done kamma. 'I revolved' means I revolved again and again by way of passing away and reappearing, wandering like a potter's wheel. He states the reason for that revolving: 'Not seeing the Noble Truths, the ordinary person, being blind.' Not seeing, not penetrating with the eye of wisdom the four Noble Truths beginning with suffering, hence being blinded by the blindness of ignorance, becoming an ordinary person for reasons such as being born in many ways, he revolves through destinations—this is the connection. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Catunnaṃ[V 1.0367], bhikkhave, ariyasaccānaṃ ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamidaṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ mamañceva tumhākañcā”ti (mahāva. 287; dī. ni. 2.155; saṃ. ni. 5.1091; netti. 114).

"Monks, it is through not comprehending, not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that this long journey has been traversed and wandered through, both by me and by you." (Mv. 287; DN 2.155; SN 5.1091; Nett. 114)

Tassa mayhaṃ vuttanayena pubbe puthujjanasseva sato idāni satthārā dinnanayena appamattassa appamādapaṭipattiyā samathavipassanābhāvanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā ṭhitassa.
