Saṃsārā vinaḷīkatāti saṃsaranti sattā etehīti “saṃsārā”ti laddhanāmā kammakilesā aggamaggena samucchinnattā vigatanaḷā nimmūlā katā. Sabbā gatī samucchinnāti evaṃ kammakilesavaṭṭānaṃ vinaḷīkatattā nirayādikā sabbāpi gatiyo sammadeva ucchinnā viddhaṃsitā, tato eva natthi dāni āyatiṃ punabbhavoti idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosīti.

For me, who was previously an ordinary person in the manner described, now, by the method given by the Teacher, being heedful, having brought the development of serenity and insight to its culmination through the practice of heedfulness, I stand established. 'The round of transmigration has been uprooted' means that kamma and defilements, which are called 'transmigration' because beings transmigrate by means of them, have been utterly cut off by the noble path, and thus have been made devoid of sprouts, uprooted. 'All destinations are cut off' means that since the round of kamma and defilements has thus been uprooted, all destinations, beginning with the hells, have been utterly cut off, destroyed. Therefore, there is now no renewed existence in the future—and this was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge.

Vajjitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vajjita is concluded.

9. Sandhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sandhita

Assatthe haritobhāseti āyasmato sandhitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle eko gopālako ahosi. So satthari parinibbute aññataraṃ theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā [M 1.0432] tassa santike buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso “kuhiṃ bhagavā”ti pucchitvā parinibbutabhāvaṃ sutvā “evaṃ mahānubhāvā buddhāpi nāma aniccatāvasaṃ gacchanti, aho saṅkhārā addhuvā”ti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Taṃ thero bodhipūjāya ussāhesi. So kālena kālaṃ bodhirukkhasamīpaṃ gantvā [P 2.0082] vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā buddhaguṇe anussaranto bodhiṃ vandati. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe ibbhakule nibbattitvā sandhitoti laddhanāmo vayappatto aniccatāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā saṃvegajāto pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. So attano pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranto sikhissa bhagavato kāle bodhivandanaṃ buddhānussatiṃ aniccasaññāpaṭilābhañca anussaritvā tadupanissayena attano visesādhigamaṃ pakāsento –

“The Assattha tree shines green,” a verse by the Venerable Elder Sandhita. What is its origin? This elder too had performed meritorious deeds in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences. In the thirty-first aeon from now, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was a cowherd. When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he approached a certain elder and, hearing Dhamma connected with the virtues of the Buddha, his mind became serene. He asked, “Where is the Blessed One?” and upon hearing of his final Nibbāna, he reflected, “Even Buddhas, so mighty, succumb to impermanence! Alas, all conditioned things are impermanent!” Thus, he gained the perception of impermanence. That elder encouraged him to pay homage to the Bodhi tree. From time to time, he would go to the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, establish insight meditation, recollect the virtues of the Buddha, and pay homage to the Bodhi tree. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s Dispensation, he was reborn in the Kosala country in a wealthy household. Named Sandhita, when he came of age, upon hearing a Dhamma talk on impermanence, he was stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency. He went forth into homelessness, established insight meditation, and as his knowledge matured, he soon attained the six higher knowledges. Recollecting his past lives, he remembered how, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he had paid homage to the Bodhi tree, practiced recollection of the Buddha's virtues, and gained the perception of impermanence. Recalling these as the supporting conditions for his own special attainment, he declared:

217.

217.

“Assatthe haritobhāse, saṃvirūḷhamhi pādape;

Ekaṃ buddhagataṃ saññaṃ, alabhitthaṃ patissato.

“Beneath the Assattha tree, shining green, a well-grown tree, I gained a single perception directed to the Buddha, being mindful.

218.

218.

“Ekatiṃse [V 1.0368] ito kappe, yaṃ saññamalabhiṃ tadā;

Tassā saññāya vāhasā, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti. –

Thirty-one aeons from now, the perception I gained then—by the force of that perception, the destruction of the taints has been attained by me.”

Dve gāthā abhāsi.

He uttered two verses.

Tattha assattheti assatthaṭṭhānīye, yvāyaṃ etarahi amhākaṃ bhagavato bodhirukkho assattho, etassa ṭhāne tadā sikhissa bhagavato bodhirukkho puṇḍarīko ṭhitoti so assatthaṭṭhānīyatāya “assatthe”ti vuttaṃ. Sattānaṃ assāsajananato vā. Apare pana “assattharukkhamūle nisīditvā tadā buddhānussatiyā bhāvitattā thero ‘assatthe’ti avocā”ti vadanti. Haritobhāseti haritehi sāramaṇivaṇṇehi obhāsamāne. Saṃvirūḷhamhīti suṭṭhu virūḷhe suppatiṭṭhite, sughananicitapattapalāsapallavehi virūḷhasañchanneti ca vadanti. Pādapeti rukkhe. Ekaṃ buddhagataṃ saññaṃ, alabhitthaṃ patissatoti buddhārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0433] ārammaṇassa ekajātiyattā ekaṃ “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinayappavattaṃ buddhānussatisahagataṃ saññaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ patipatisaraṇato patissato hutvā alabhiṃ.

Herein, ‘assatthe’ means the place of the assattha tree; that is, where now stands the Bodhi tree of our Blessed One, the Assattha tree. In that very spot at that time stood the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Sikhī, the Puṇḍarīka tree. Thus, because it was in the place of an assattha tree, it is called ‘assatthe.’ Or, because it generates comfort for beings. Others, however, say: “Because the elder sat at the foot of an assattha tree at that time and developed recollection of the Buddha, he said ‘assatthe.’” ‘Haritobhāse’ means shining with green hues, with the color of emeralds. ‘Saṃvirūḷhamhi’ means well-grown, firmly established; and some say, ‘well-covered with dense, closely-packed leaves and fresh shoots.’ ‘Pādape’ means ‘tree.’ ‘Ekaṃ buddhagataṃ saññaṃ, alabhitthaṃ patissato’ means: because the object was solely the Buddha, I gained a single perception accompanied by recollection of the Buddha, arising in the manner of “Indeed, the Blessed One is...” and so forth, being mindful due to repeatedly recollecting the virtues of the Buddha.

Kadā pana sā saññā laddhā, kīvatāya siddhāti āha “ekatiṃse ito kappe”tiādi. Ito bhaddakappato uddhaṃ ārohanavasena ekatiṃse kappe. Yaṃ saññanti yaṃ buddhānussatisahagataṃ saññaṃ, yaṃ vā buddhānaṃ aniccataṃ disvā tadanusārena sabbāsaṅkhāresu tadā aniccasaññaṃ alabhiṃ. Tassā saññāya vāhasāti tassā yathāvuttāya saññāya kāraṇabhāvena taṃ upanissayaṃ katvā. Patto me āsavakkhayoti idāni [P 2.0083] mayā āsavānaṃ khayo nirodho adhigatoti imāyeva ca imassa therassa apadānagāthāpi. Yathāha (apa. thera 1.22.27-30) –

When was that perception gained, and how was it accomplished? He said, “In the thirty-first aeon from now,” and so forth. Counting upwards from this auspicious aeon, it was the thirty-first aeon. What is ‘that perception’? It refers to the perception accompanied by recollection of the Buddha, or the perception of impermanence in all conditioned things that he gained at that time by seeing the impermanence of the Buddhas and following that. ‘By the force of that perception’ means making that perception as described the cause and strong supporting condition. ‘The destruction of the taints has been attained by me’ means that now the destruction and cessation of the taints has been attained by me. These are also the Apadāna verses of this elder. As it is said:

“Assatthe haritobhāse…pe… patto me āsavakkhayo.

“Ito terasakappamhi, dhaniṭṭho nāma khattiyo;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

“Beneath the Assattha tree, shining green… the destruction of the taints has been attained by me. Thirteen aeons from now, there was a khattiya named Dhaniṭṭha, endowed with the seven treasures, a powerful Wheel-turning Monarch.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt away… the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished.”

Sandhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sandhita is concluded.

Pañcamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fifth Chapter is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca dukanipātavaṇṇanā.

And the Commentary on the Book of Twos is concluded.

3. Tikanipāto

3. The Book of Threes

1. Aṅgaṇikabhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja

Tikanipāte [M 1.0434][V 1.0369] ayoni suddhimanvesanti āyasmato aṅgaṇikabhāradvājattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito ekatiṃse kappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā añjaliṃ paggaṇhi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde himavantasamīpe ukkaṭṭhe nāma nagare vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa gehe nibbattitvā aṅgaṇikabhāradvājoti laddhanāmo vayappatto vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato nekkhammajjhāsayatāya paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā amaraṃ tapaṃ caranto tattha tattha vicaranto sammāsambuddhaṃ janapadacārikaṃ carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā taṃ micchātapaṃ pahāya sāsane pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.23.48-51) –

In the Book of Threes, “Seeking purity by improper means,” are the verses of the Venerable Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja. What is its origin? This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulating merit that served as a supporting condition for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a noble household during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, thirty-one aeons from now. Having attained discernment, one day he saw the Teacher going on alms round and, with a serene mind, paid homage with a five-point prostration and raised his joined hands. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha's Dispensation, he was reborn in the city named Ukkaṭṭha, near the Himalayas, in the household of a wealthy brahmin, and was named Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja. When he came of age, he became accomplished in the sciences and arts but, due to his inclination for renunciation, he went forth into the wandering ascetic's life. Practicing austerities for immortality, wandering here and there, he saw the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One traveling through the countryside. With a serene mind, he listened to the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, abandoned that misguided austerity, and went forth into the Dispensation. Applying himself to insight meditation, he soon attained the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Usabhaṃ pavaraṃ vīraṃ, vessabhuṃ vijitāvinaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, buddhaseṭṭhamavandahaṃ.

“With a serene and joyful mind, I paid homage to Vessabhū, the supreme bull, the hero, the victorious one, the foremost of Buddhas.

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, vandanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

Thirty-one aeons from now, for the deed I performed then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of paying homage.

“Catuvīsatikappamhi, vikatānandanāmako;

Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo.

Twenty-four aeons from now, there was one named Vikatānanda, endowed with the seven treasures, a powerful Wheel-turning Monarch.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt away… the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā vimuttisukhena viharanto ñātīnaṃ anukampāya attano jātibhūmiṃ gantvā bahū ñātake saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpetvā tato nivattitvā kururaṭṭhe kuṇḍiyassa [V 1.0370] nāma nigamassa avidūre [M 1.0435] araññe vasanto kenacideva karaṇīyena uggārāmaṃ gato uttarāpathato āgatehi sandiṭṭhehi brāhmaṇehi [P 2.0084] samāgato tehi, “bho bhāradvāja, kiṃ disvā brāhmaṇānaṃ samayaṃ pahāya imaṃ samayaṃ gaṇhī”ti pucchito tesaṃ ito buddhasāsanato bahiddhā suddhi natthīti dassento –

Having attained the six higher knowledges and dwelling in the bliss of deliverance, out of compassion for his kinsmen, he went to his native land. There he established many kinsmen in the refuges and precepts, then returned and dwelt in a forest not far from the town named Kuṇḍiya in the Kuru realm. On some business, he went to Uggārāma, where he met some brahmins who had come from the northern region and were known to him. They asked him, “Friend Bhāradvāja, what have you seen that you have abandoned the ways of the brahmins and taken up this way?” To show them that outside the Buddha's Dispensation there is no purity, he said:

219.

219.

“Ayoni suddhimanvesaṃ, aggiṃ paricariṃ vane;

Suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto, akāsiṃ amaraṃ tapa”nti. – paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha;

“Seeking purity by improper means, I tended the fire in the forest; not knowing the path to purity, I practiced austerities for immortality.”

Tattha ayonīti ayoniso anupāyena. Suddhinti saṃsārasuddhiṃ bhavanissaraṇaṃ. Anvesanti gavesanto. Aggiṃ paricariṃ vaneti “ayaṃ suddhimaggo”ti adhippāyena araññāyatane aggihutasālāyaṃ agyāgāraṃ katvā āhutiṃ paggaṇhanto aggidevaṃ paricariṃ vede vuttavidhinā pūjesiṃ. Suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto, akāsiṃ amaraṃ tapanti suddhiyā nibbānassa maggaṃ ajānanto aggiparicaraṇaṃ viya pañcatapatappanādiattakilamathānuyogaṃ “suddhimaggo”ti maññāya akāsiṃ acariṃ paṭipajjiṃ.

Herein, 'ayonī' means 'improperly,' 'by improper means.' 'Suddhi' means 'purification from saṃsāra,' 'escape from becoming.' 'Anvesaṃ' means 'seeking.' 'Aggiṃ paricariṃ vane' means: thinking, 'This is the path to purity,' I worshipped the fire god according to the method described in the Vedas, having made a fire-house in a fire-offering hall in a forest retreat and offering oblations. 'Suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto, akāsiṃ amaraṃ tapa' means: not knowing the path to purity, to Nibbāna, I practiced, undertook, and acted, thinking that self-mortification such as fire worship and the practice of the five austerities was the path to purity.

Evaṃ thero assamato assamaṃ gacchanto viya vede vuttavidhinā aggiparicaraṇādinā anuṭṭhāya suddhiyā appattabhāvena bahiddhā suddhiyā abhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni imasmiṃyeva sāsane suddhi ca mayā adhigatāti dassento –

Thus the elder, as if wandering from hermitage to hermitage, having shown the absence of external purity due to not having attained purity by performing the prescribed Vedic rituals such as tending the fire, now, demonstrating that purity has been attained by me in this very Dispensation—

220.

220.

“Taṃ sukhena sukhaṃ laddhaṃ, passa dhammasudhammataṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. – dutiyagāthamāha;

“That bliss was gained with ease—see the true excellence of the Dhamma! The three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished.” – he uttered the second verse;

Tattha tanti yassatthāya suddhiṃ anvesanto tassa maggaṃ ajānanto aggiṃ paricariṃ amaraṃ tapaṃ acariṃ, taṃ nibbānasukhaṃ sukhena samathavipassanāya sukhāya paṭipadāya attakilamathānuyogaṃ anupagamma mayā laddhaṃ pattaṃ adhigataṃ. Passa dhammasudhammatanti satthu sāsanadhammassa sudhammataṃ aviparītaniyyānikadhammasabhāvaṃ [M 1.0436] passa jānāhīti dhammālapanavasena vadati, attānaṃ vā ālapati. Tassa laddhabhāvaṃ pana dassento –

Herein, 'that' refers to: for the sake of which I sought purity, not knowing its path, I tended the fire, I practiced immortal austerity; that bliss of Nibbāna has been gained, reached, attained by me with ease, by the pleasant practice of serenity and insight, without resorting to self-mortification. 'Passa dhammasudhammataṃ' means: he speaks by way of addressing the Dhamma, or he addresses himself, saying 'see, understand the excellence of the Teacher's Dispensation-Dhamma, its nature as the unperverted Dhamma that leads to deliverance.' And showing his attainment—

“Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. –

“The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished.”

Āha[V 1.0371], taṃ vuttatthameva. Evaṃ suddhiyā adhigatattā “ito paṭṭhāyāhaṃ paramatthato brāhmaṇo”ti dassento –

The meaning of this has been stated. Thus, having attained purity, to show, “From this point on, I am a brahmin in the ultimate sense”—

221.

221.

“Brahmabandhu [P 2.0085] pure āsiṃ, idāni khomhi brāhmaṇo;

Tevijjo nhātakocamhi, sottiyo camhi vedagū”ti. – tatiyaṃ gāthamāha;

“Formerly, I was a kinsman of Brahmā; now I am truly a brahmin. I am one possessing the three knowledges, a bath-graduate am I; a pure one and a knower of the Veda.” —Thus he spoke the third verse.

Tassattho – ito pubbe jātimattena brāhmaṇabhāvato brāhmaṇānaṃ samaññāya brahmabandhu nāma āsiṃ. Bāhitapāpattā pana idāni kho arahattādhigamena paramatthato brāhmaṇo ca amhi. Ito pubbe bhavasañcayakarānaṃ tissannaṃ vedasaṅkhātānaṃ vijjānaṃ ajjhayanena samaññāmattena tevijjo nāma hutvā idāni bhavakkhayakarāya vijjāya vasena tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ adhigatattā paramatthato tevijjo ca amhi. Tathā ito pubbe bhavassādagadhitāya nhātakavatanipphattiyā samaññāmattena nhātako nāma hutvā idāni aṭṭhaṅgikamaggajalena suvikkhālitakilesamalatāya paramatthato nhātako camhi. Ito pubbe avimuttabhavassādamantajjhānena vohāramattato sottiyo nāma hutvā idāni suvimuttabhavassādadhammajjhānena paramatthato sottiyo camhi. Ito pubbe appaṭinissaṭṭhapāpadhammānaṃ vedānaṃ gatamattena vedagū nāma hutvā idāni vedasaṅkhātena maggañāṇena saṃsāramahoghassa vedassa catusaccassa ca pāraṃ gatattā adhigatattā ñātattā paramatthato vedagū jātoti. Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇā sāsane uḷāraṃ pasādaṃ pavedesuṃ.

The meaning of this is: In the past, by mere birth into the brahmin caste, I was called a kinsman of Brahmā by conventional designation. But now, having abandoned evil and attained arahantship, I am truly a brahmin in the highest sense. In the past, by studying the three knowledges designated as Vedas, which accumulate existence, I was conventionally known as 'one possessing the three knowledges.' But now, having attained the three knowledges by means of the knowledge that destroys existence, I am truly 'one possessing the three knowledges' in the highest sense. Similarly, in the past, being greedy for the pleasures of existence, I was conventionally called a 'bath-graduate' due to the completion of the bath-graduate's vows. But now, having thoroughly washed away the stains of defilements with the water of the Noble Eightfold Path, I am truly a 'bath-graduate' in the highest sense. In the past, through recitation of mantras while not yet freed from the pleasures of existence, I was merely called a 'sotthiya' by conventional usage. But now, being fully liberated through meditation on the Dhamma free from the pleasures of existence, I am truly a 'sotthiya' in the highest sense. In the past, having merely gone to the Vedas without abandoning evil qualities, I was called a 'knower of the Vedas.' But now, by means of the path-knowledge designated as Veda, having crossed beyond, attained, and known the great flood of saṃsāra, the Veda, and the four truths, I have become a 'knower of the Veda' in the ultimate sense. Hearing this, the brahmins developed supreme confidence in the Teaching.

Aṅgaṇikabhāradvājattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Aṅgaṇikabhāradvāja is concluded.

2. Paccayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Paccaya

Pañcāhāhaṃ [M 1.0437] pabbajitoti āyasmato paccayattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto ito ekanavute kappe vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ vinatāya nāma nadiyā tīre gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso manuññadassanāni mahantāni udumbaraphalāni ocinitvā upanāmesi. So tena puññakammena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ bhaddakappe kassape bhagavati loke uppajjitvā pavattavaradhammacakke veneyyajanānuggahaṃ karonte tassa sāsane pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā bhāvanamanuyuñjanto ekadivasaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ cintetvā

“Five days since I went forth”—these are the verses of the Venerable Elder Paccaya. What is the origin? He too, having made a resolution in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, ninety-one aeons ago from now, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, was reborn in a good family and attained maturity. One day, seeing the Teacher walking on the bank of the river named Vinatā, his mind became joyful. Gathering large, delightful-looking udumbara fruits, he offered them. Through that meritorious deed, wandering only in happy realms, in this auspicious aeon, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, when the supreme Wheel of Dhamma was turning and assisting receptive beings, he went forth under his dispensation. Establishing insight and striving in meditation, one day, reflecting on the suffering of saṃsāra,

Ativiya [V 1.0372] sañjātasaṃvego vihāre nisinno “arahattaṃ appatvā ito na nikkhamissāmī”ti [P 2.0086] cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāya vāyamanto ñāṇassa aparipakkattā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. So kālaṅkatvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rohitanagare khattiyakule nibbattitvā paccayoti laddhanāmo vayappatto pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhito ekadivasaṃ mahārājabaliṃ kātuṃ ārabhi. Tattha mahājano sannipati. Tasmiṃ samāgame tassa pasādañjananatthaṃ satthā mahājanassa pekkhantasseva ākāse vessavaṇena nimmite ratanamayakūṭāgāre ratanamayasīhāsane nisīditvā dhammaṃ desesi. Mahato janakāyassa dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Taṃ dhammaṃ sutvā paccayarājāpi rajjaṃ pahāya purimahetusañcodito pabbaji. So yathā kassapassa bhagavato kāle paṭiññaṃ akāsi, evaṃ paṭiññaṃ katvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā tāvadeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.15-20) –

he became deeply agitated. Sitting in his dwelling, he resolved, “Without attaining arahantship, I will not leave this place,” and exerted himself. But due to the immaturity of his knowledge, he could not bring insight to a climax. Passing away, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s time, he was reborn in a Khattiya clan in the city of Rohita. Named Paccaya, he came of age and, after his father’s passing, was established on the throne. One day, he began to perform a great royal sacrifice. A large crowd gathered there. To inspire faith in him, the Teacher, while the people were watching, appeared in the sky in a jeweled pavilion created by Vessavaṇa, seated on a jeweled lion throne, and taught the Dhamma. A great multitude attained understanding of the Dhamma. Hearing that Dhamma, King Paccaya, prompted by his past cause, renounced his kingdom and went forth. Just as he had made a vow during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he made that vow again, entered the monastery, developed insight, and, when his knowledge matured, immediately attained arahantship. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vinatānadiyā tīre, vihāsi purisuttamo;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.

“On the bank of the Vinatā River, the Supreme Person dwelt; I saw the Stainless Buddha, one-pointed and well-composed.

“Tasmiṃ pasannamānaso, kilesamaladhovane;

Udumbaraphalaṃ gayha, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ.

“With a mind full of faith in him, the washer-away of defilement's stain, taking an udumbara fruit, I gave it to the Supreme Buddha.

“Ekanavutito [M 1.0438] kappe, yaṃ phalamadadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Ninety-one aeons ago, when I gave that fruit, I have known no bad rebirth. This is the fruit of that fruit-offering.

“Imamhi bhaddake kappe, saṃviggamānamānaso;

Kassapassa bhagavato, sāsane pabbajiṃ ahaṃ.

“In this auspicious aeon, with a mind stirred to urgency, I went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.

“Tathā pabbajito santo, bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjisaṃ;

Na vihārā nikkhamissaṃ, iti katvāna mānasaṃ.

“Thus gone forth, I devoted myself to meditation, resolving in my mind: ‘I shall not leave the monastery.’

“Uttamatthaṃ asampatto, na ca pattomhi tāvade;

Idāni pana ñāṇassa, paripākena nibbuto;

“Not having attained the highest goal, I did not attain it at that time; but now, through the maturation of knowledge, I am extinguished.

Pattomhi acalaṃ ṭhānaṃ, phusitvā accutaṃ padaṃ.

“I have reached the unshakable state, having touched the deathless state.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattikittanamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained arahantship, declaring his final knowledge by way of proclaiming his own practice—

222.

222.

“Pañcāhāhaṃ [V 1.0373] pabbajito, sekho appattamānaso;

Vihāraṃ me paviṭṭhassa, cetaso paṇidhī ahu.

“Five days since I went forth, a trainee, my goal not yet reached; as I entered my dwelling, a resolution arose in my mind.

223.

223.

“Nāsissaṃ na pivissāmi, vihārato na nikkhame;

Napi passaṃ nipātessaṃ, taṇhāsalle anūhate.

“‘I will not eat, I will not drink, nor from my dwelling shall I leave; nor will I lay my side to rest, till craving’s dart is not retrieved.’

224.

224.

“Tassa mevaṃ viharato, passa vīriyaparakkamaṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti. –

“For me dwelling thus, behold my energy and striving! The three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha's teaching has been done.”

Imā tisso gāthā abhāsi.

These three verses were uttered.

Tattha pañcāhāhaṃ pabbajitoti pañcāho ahaṃ, pabbajito hutvā pañcāho, pabbajitadivasato pañcamo aho niṭṭhitoti attho. Sekho appattamānasoti adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ sikkhanato sekho. Anavasesato mānaṃ siyati samucchindatīti mānaso, aggamaggo, taṃnibbattito mānasato āgataṃ mānasaṃ, arahattaṃ, taṃ, so vā appatto [M 1.0439] etenāti appattamānaso. Vihāraṃ me paviṭṭhassa, cetaso paṇidhī ahūti evaṃ sekhassa me vasanakavihāraṃ ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassa sato evarūpo idāni vuccamānākāro cetopaṇidhi ahosi, evaṃ mayā cittaṃ paṇihitanti attho.

Here, 'Pañcāhāhaṃ pabbajito' means 'I am five days gone forth,' or 'five days have passed since I went forth,' or 'the fifth day from the day of going forth was completed.' 'Sekho appattamānaso' means 'a trainee' because he is training in higher virtue and so on. One who completely cuts off conceit (mānaṃ) is called 'mānaso,' which refers to the supreme path (aggamaggo). 'Mānasaṃ' is that which arises from that mānaso, namely arahantship. He has not attained that arahantship, therefore he is 'appattamānaso.' 'Vihāraṃ me paviṭṭhassa, cetaso paṇidhī ahu' means that when I, a trainee, entered my dwelling place, my lodging, such a determination of mind, of the kind about to be described, arose; that is, 'Thus I resolved my mind.'

Nāsissantiādinā [P 2.0087] cittapaṇidhiṃ dasseti. Tattha nāsissanti yaṃkiñci bhojanaṃ na bhuñjissaṃ na bhuñjissāmi taṇhāsalle mama hadayagate anūhate anuddhateti evaṃ sabbapadesu yojetabbaṃ. Na pivissāmīti yaṃkiñci pātabbaṃ na pivissāmi. Vihārato na nikkhameti imasmā idāni mayā nisinnagabbhato na nikkhameyyaṃ. Napi passaṃ nipātessanti mama sarīrassa dvīsu passesu ekampi passaṃ kāyakilamathavinodanatthaṃ na nipātessaṃ, ekapassenapi na nipajjissāmīti attho.

'Nāsissaṃ' and so on, shows the determination of the mind. Here, 'Nāsissaṃ' means: 'I will not eat any food whatsoever, I will not consume it, while the dart of craving remains unextracted and unremoved in my heart.' This should be applied in all cases. 'Na pivissāmi' means: 'I will not drink any drink whatsoever.' 'Vihārato na nikkhame' means: 'From this chamber where I am now sitting, I will not go out.' 'Napi passaṃ nipātessaṃ' means: 'I will not lay down even one of my two sides to relieve bodily fatigue; that is, I will not lie down on even one side.' This is the meaning.

Tassa mevaṃ viharatoti tassa me evaṃ cittaṃ paṇidhāya daḷhavīriyādhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanānuyogavasena viharato. Passa vīriyaparakkamanti vidhinā īrayitabbato “vīriyaṃ” paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato “parakkamo”ti ca laddhanāmaṃ ussoḷhībhūtaṃ vāyāmaṃ passa jānāhi. Yassa panānubhāvena mayā tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsananti vuttatthameva.

'Tassa mevaṃ viharato' means: 'For me, dwelling thus, having made such a determination of mind and a firm resolve of energy, devoted to the practice of insight.' 'Passa vīriyaparakkamaṃ' means: 'Behold this exertion, which is called "energy" because it is to be urged on in the proper way, and "striving" because it advances to the supreme state.' And by its power the three knowledges have been attained by me, and the Buddha's teaching has been done—this is the meaning as stated.

Paccayattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Paccaya is concluded.

3. Bākulattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bākula

Yo [V 1.0374] pubbe karaṇīyānīti āyasmato bākulattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi kira atīte ito kappasatasahassādhikassa asaṅkhyeyyassa matthake anomadassissa bhagavato uppattito puretarameva brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tayo vede uggahetvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto “samparāyikatthaṃ gavesissāmī”ti isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pabbatapāde viharanto pañcābhiññāaṭṭhasamāpattilābhī hutvā viharanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu [M 1.0440] patiṭṭhito satthu udarābādhe uppanne araññato bhesajjāni āharitvā taṃ vūpasametvā tattha puññaṃ ārogyatthāya pariṇāmetvā tato cuto brahmaloke nibbattitvā ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto padumuttarabuddhakāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ appābādhānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayaṃ taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhanto paṇidhānaṃ katvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto vipassissa bhagavato nibbattito puretarameva bandhumatīnagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatto purimanayeneva isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññālābhī hutvā pabbatapāde vasanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu [P 2.0088] patiṭṭhito bhikkhūnaṃ tiṇapupphakaroge uppanne taṃ vūpasametvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto brahmaloke nibbattitvā ekanavutikappe devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekaṃ jiṇṇaṃ vinassamānaṃ mahāvihāraṃ disvā tattha uposathāgārādikaṃ sabbaṃ āvasathaṃ kāretvā tattha bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbaṃ bhesajjaṃ paṭiyādetvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato uppattito puretarameva kosambiyaṃ seṭṭhigehe nibbatti. So arogabhāvāya mahāyamunāya nhāpiyamāno dhātiyā hatthato macchena gilito macche kevaṭṭahatthagate bārāṇasiseṭṭhibhariyāya vikkiṇitvā gahite phāliyamānepi puññabalena arogoyeva hutvā tāya puttoti gahetvā posiyamāno taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā janakehi mātāpitūhi “ayaṃ amhākaṃ putto, detha no putta”nti anuyoge kate raññā “ubhayesampi sādhāraṇo hotū”ti dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ dāyādabhāvena vinicchayaṃ katvā ṭhapitattā bākuloti laddhanāmo vayappatto hutvā mahatiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavanto āsītiko hutvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā sattāhameva puthujjano ahosi, aṭṭhame aruṇe saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.40.386-411) –

This is the verse of the Venerable Elder Bākula, beginning with "Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni." What is its origin? In the past, more than a hundred thousand aeons and an incalculable period ago, even before the arising of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was born in a brahmin family. Having reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas but, finding no essence in them, thought, "I will seek the goal for the next life," and took up the ascetic life of a seer. Dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he attained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. Hearing of the Buddha's appearance, he went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and was established in the refuges. When an abdominal ailment arose in the Teacher, he brought medicines from the forest and cured him, dedicating the merit for the sake of health. After passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma world. For one incalculable aeon, he wandered among devas and humans. During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born in a household in the city of Haṃsavatī. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those with few ailments, he himself aspired to that state, made a resolve, and accumulated wholesome karma for his entire life. Wandering only in happy states of existence, before the arising of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī. Following the same course as before, he took up the ascetic life of a seer, attained the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and dwelt at the foot of a mountain. Hearing of the Buddha's appearance, he went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and was established in the refuges. When an illness caused by grass and flowers arose among the monks, he cured it. Having remained there for the duration of his life, after passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma world. For ninety-one aeons, he wandered among devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was born in a household in Bārāṇasī. While living the household life, he saw a great monastery that was old and decaying, and had all its residences, including the Uposatha hall, rebuilt. He provided all necessary medicines for the Saṅgha of monks there and performed wholesome deeds for his entire life. For one Buddha-interval, he wandered among devas and humans. Before the arising of our Blessed One, he was born into a merchant's family in Kosambī. While being bathed in the great Yamunā river for his health, he slipped from his nurse's hands and was swallowed by a fish. The fish was caught by fishermen and sold to the wife of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī. When it was cut open, by the power of his merit, he was unharmed. She took him as her son and raised him. When this story became known, his birth parents made a claim, saying, "This is our son, give us our son!" The king ruled, "Let him be common to both," and established him as the heir to both families. For this reason, he received the name Bākula. Having reached maturity, he enjoyed great prosperity. At the age of eighty, he heard the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, gained faith, and went forth. For only seven days he remained an ordinary person; at dawn on the eighth day, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Himavantassāvidūre[M 1.0441][V 1.0375], sobhito nāma pabbato;

Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, sakasissehi māpito.

"Not far from the Himālaya, there is a mountain named Sobhita; my well-made hermitage was built there by my own disciples.

“Maṇḍapā ca bahū tattha, pupphitā sindhuvārakā;

Kapitthā ca bahū tattha, pupphitā jīvajīvakā.

"Many pavilions were there, and sindhuvāra trees were in bloom; many kapittha trees were there, and jīvajīvaka plants were in bloom.

“Nigguṇḍiyo bahū tattha, badarāmalakāni ca;

Phārusakā alābū ca, puṇḍarīkā ca pupphitā.

"Many nigguṇḍi shrubs were there, and jujube and myrobalan trees; phārusaka and gourd vines, and white lotuses were in bloom.

“Āḷakā beluvā tattha, kadalī mātuluṅgakā;

Mahānāmā bahū tattha, ajjunā ca piyaṅgukā.

"Āḷaka and beluva trees were there, plantains and citrons; many mahānāma trees were there, and ajjuna and piyaṅgu plants.

“Kosambā saḷalā nimbā, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Ediso assamo mayhaṃ, sasissohaṃ tahiṃ vasiṃ.

"Kosamba, saḷala, and nimba trees, banyans and kapitthanas; such was my hermitage, and there I lived with my disciples.

“Anomadassī bhagavā, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Gavesaṃ paṭisallānaṃ, mamassamamupāgami.

"The Blessed One Anomadassī, the Self-become, the Leader of the World, seeking solitude, approached my hermitage.

“Upetamhi mahāvīre, anomadassimahāyase;

Khaṇena lokanāthassa, vātābādho samuṭṭhahi.

"When the Great Hero, the glorious Anomadassī, was approached, in an instant a wind-ailment arose for the Protector of the World.

“Vicaranto araññamhi, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Upagantvāna sambuddhaṃ, cakkhumantaṃ mahāyasaṃ.

"Wandering in the forest, I saw the Leader of the World; I approached the Sambuddha, the one with vision, of great glory.

“Iriyañcāpi disvāna, upalakkhesahaṃ tadā;

Asaṃsayañhi buddhassa, byādhi no udapajjatha.

"Having observed even his deportment, I then took note; for surely, no illness had arisen in the Buddha.

“Khippaṃ assamamāgañchiṃ, mama sissāna santike;

Bhesajjaṃ kattukāmohaṃ, sisse āmantayiṃ tadā.

"Quickly I went to the hermitage, to my disciples; wishing to prepare medicine, I then addressed my disciples.

“Paṭissuṇitvāna me vākyaṃ, sissā sabbe sagāravā;

Ekajjhaṃ sannipatiṃsu, satthugāravatā mama.

"Having respectfully assented to my words, all the disciples, out of reverence for me, their teacher, gathered together in one place.

“Khippaṃ pabbatamāruyha, sabbosadhamahāsahaṃ;

Pānīyayogaṃ katvāna, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ.

"Quickly ascending the mountain, a great repository of all herbs, I prepared a medicinal drink and gave it to the Supreme Buddha.

“Paribhutte mahāvīre, sabbaññulokanāyake;

Khippaṃ vāto vūpasami, sugatassa mahesino.

"When the Great Hero, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, had consumed it, the wind ailment of the Sugata, the Great Sage, swiftly subsided.

“Passaddhaṃ [M 1.0442] darathaṃ disvā, anomadassī mahāyaso;

Sakāsane nisīditvā, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

"Seeing the affliction calmed, the glorious Anomadassī, seated upon his own seat, spoke these verses:

“Yo me pādāsi bhesajjaṃ, byādhiñca samayī mama;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

“He who gave me medicine and relieved my sickness—I shall proclaim his praise—listen as I speak.”

“Kappasatasahassāni, devaloke ramissati;

Vādite tūriye tattha, modissati sadā ayaṃ.

“For a hundred thousand eons, he will rejoice in the heavenly realm; there, while musical instruments are played, this one will always delight.”

“Manussalokamāgantvā[V 1.0376], sukkamūlena codito;

Sahassakkhattuṃ rājā ca, cakkavattī bhavissati.

“Having come to the human world, impelled by a wholesome root, he will become a wheel-turning monarch a thousand times.”

“Pañcapaññāsakappamhi, anomo nāma khattiyo;

Cāturanto vijitāvī, jambumaṇḍassa issaro.

“In the fifty-fifth eon from now, there will be a noble named Anoma, a conqueror of the four quarters, lord over Jambumaṇḍala.”

“Sattaratanasampanno, cakkavattī mahabbalo;

Tāvatiṃsepi khobhetvā, issaraṃ kārayissati.

“Endowed with the seven treasures, a wheel-turning monarch of great power, he will even agitate Tāvatiṃsa and exercise his dominion.”

“Devabhūto manusso vā, appābādho bhavissati;

Pariggahaṃ vivajjetvā, byādhiṃ loke tarissati.

“Whether he becomes a god or a human being, he will have few illnesses; abandoning attachments, he will overcome sickness in the world.”

“Aparimeyye ito kappe, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“In an incalculable eon from now, born of the Okkāka lineage, Gotama by clan name, a Teacher will arise in the world.”

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Sabbāsave pariññāya, nibbāyissatināsavo.

“An heir to his Dhamma, a true son, created by the Dhamma; having fully understood all the taints, he will attain Nibbāna without taints.”

“Kilese jhāpayitvāna, taṇhāsotaṃ tarissati;

Bākulo nāma nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

“Having burned away the defilements, he will cross the stream of craving; Bākula by name, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.”

“Idaṃ sabbaṃ abhiññāya, gotamo sakyapuṅgavo;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, etadagge ṭhapessati.

“Having fully known all this, Gotama, chief of the Sakyans, seated in the assembly of bhikkhus, will place him in the foremost position.”

“Anomadassī bhagavā, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Vivekānuvilokento, mamassamamupāgami.

“The Blessed One, Anomadassī, the Self-become, the Leader of the World, contemplating seclusion, approached my hermitage.”

“Upāgataṃ mahāvīraṃ, sabbaññuṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Sabbosadhena tappesiṃ, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

“When the Great Hero, the All-Knowing Leader of the World, arrived, I satisfied him with all medicines, pleased, with my own hands.”

“Tassa [M 1.0443] me sukataṃ kammaṃ, sukhette bījasampadā;

Khepetuṃ neva sakkomi, tadā hi sukataṃ mama.

“That well-done deed of mine, like a good seed in a fertile field, I am unable to exhaust—for it was well done by me then.”

“Lābhā mama suladdhaṃ me, yohaṃ addakkhi nāyakaṃ;

Tena kammāvasesena, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“A gain it was for me, well-gained by me, that I saw the Leader; by the remainder of that kamma, I have attained the unshakable state.”

“Sabbametaṃ abhiññāya, gotamo sakyapuṅgavo;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.

“Having fully understood all this, Gotama, chief of the Sakyans, seated in the assembly of bhikkhus, placed me in the foremost position.”

“Aparimeyye ito kappe, yaṃ kammamakariṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, bhesajjassa idaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the incalculable eons since I performed that deed, I have not known a woeful destination; this is the fruit of the medicine.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā ekadivasaṃ satthārā attano sāvake paṭipāṭiyā ṭhānantare ṭhapentena appābādhānaṃ [V 1.0377] aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapito so parinibbānasamaye saṅghamajjhe bhikkhūnaṃ ovādamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained Arahantship, one day, when the Teacher was placing his disciples in their respective positions in due order, he was placed in the foremost position among those with few illnesses. At the time of his final Nibbāna, in the midst of the Saṅgha, while giving advice to the bhikkhus, he made another declaration:

225.

225.

“Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni, pacchā so kātumicchati;

Sukhā so dhaṃsate ṭhānā, pacchā ca manutappati.

“He who wishes to do later what should be done before, falls away from the state of happiness, and afterwards he laments.”

226.

226.

“Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

“What one would do, that one should say; what one would not do, that one should not say. The wise discern one who speaks but does not act.”

227.

227.

“Susukhaṃ vata nibbānaṃ, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ;

Asokaṃ virajaṃ khemaṃ, yattha dukkhaṃ nirujjhatī”ti. – gāthāttayamabhāsi;

“Oh, how truly blissful is Nibbāna, taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; sorrowless, stainless, secure, where suffering ceases.” – He spoke these three verses.

Tattha [P 2.0089] yo pubbe karaṇīyāni, pacchā so kātumicchatīti yo puggalo pubbe puretaraṃ jarārogādīhi anabhibhūtakāleyeva kātabbāni attano hitasukhāvahāni kammāni pamādavasena akatvā pacchā so kātabbakālaṃ atikkamitvā kātuṃ icchati. Soti ca nipātamattaṃ. Tadā pana jarārogādīhi abhibhūtattā kātuṃ na sakkoti, asakkonto ca sukhā so dhaṃsate ṭhānā, pacchā ca manutappatīti so puggalo sukhā [M 1.0444] ṭhānā saggato nibbānato ca tadupāyassa anuppāditattā parihāyanto “akataṃ me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.248; netti. 120) pacchā ca anutappati vippaṭisāraṃ āpajjati. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro. Ahaṃ pana karaṇīyaṃ katvā eva tumhe evaṃ vadāmīti dassento “yañhi kayirā”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha.

Herein, ‘He who wishes to do later what should be done before’ means: a person who, through heedlessness, does not do in former times—while not yet overcome by old age, sickness, and so on—those deeds which are conducive to his own welfare and happiness, and later, after the time for doing them has passed, wishes to do them. ‘So’ is merely a particle. But then, being overcome by old age, sickness, and so on, he is unable to act, and being unable, ‘he falls away from the state of happiness, and afterwards he laments.’ This means that person, because he has not produced the means for it, declines from the state of happiness—from heaven and Nibbāna—and afterwards laments and falls into remorse, thinking, ‘I have done no good,’ and so forth (MN III 248; Nett. 120). The letter ‘ma’ is for euphonic connection. To show, ‘But I, having done what should be done, speak to you thus,’ he spoke the second verse, ‘What one would do…’

Tattha parijānantīti “ettako aya”nti paricchijja jānanti na bahuṃ maññantīti attho. Sammāpaṭipattivasena hi yathāvādī tathākārī eva sobhati, na tato aññathā. Karaṇīyapariyāyena sādhāraṇato vuttamatthaṃ idāni sarūpato dassetuṃ “susukhaṃ vatā”tiādinā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tassattho – sammā sāmaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhena bhagavatā desitaṃ sabbaso sokahetūnaṃ abhāvato asokaṃ vigatarāgādirajattā virajaṃ catūhi yogehi anupaddutattā khemaṃ nibbānaṃ suṭṭhu sukhaṃ vata, kasmā? Yattha yasmiṃ nibbāne sakalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ nirujjhati accantameva vūpasamatīti.

Herein, ‘they discern’ means they know by delimiting, ‘This one is only so much,’ and do not hold him in high esteem. For by way of right practice, one who acts as he speaks truly shines, not otherwise. Now, to show in its specific nature the meaning that was stated generally by way of ‘what should be done,’ he spoke the third verse, beginning ‘Oh, how truly blissful!’ Its meaning is: Nibbāna, taught by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—so-called because he has rightly and by himself awakened to all things—is truly very blissful. Why? Because in that Nibbāna all the suffering of the round of existence ceases, is utterly stilled; it is sorrowless due to the complete absence of the causes of sorrow, stainless due to the absence of the dust of lust and so on, and secure due to being unassailed by the four yokes.

Bākulattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bākula is concluded.

4. Dhaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhaniya

Sukhañce [V 1.0378] jīvituṃ iccheti āyasmato dhaniyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso naḷamālāya pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe kumbhakārakule nibbattitvā dhaniyoti laddhanāmo vayappatto kumbhakārakammena jīvati. Tena ca samayena satthā dhaniyassa kumbhakārassa sālāyaṃ nisīditvā pukkusātissa kulaputtassa chadhātuvibhaṅgasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo) desesi. So taṃ sutvā katakicco ahosi. Dhaniyo tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ sutvā “niyyānikaṃ vata buddhasāsanaṃ, yattha ekarattiparicayenāpi vaṭṭadukkhato muñcituṃ sakkā”ti paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā [P 2.0090] kuṭimaṇḍanānuyutto [M 1.0445] viharanto kuṭikaraṇaṃ paṭicca bhagavatā garahito saṅghike senāsane vasanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.1-7) –

‘If one wishes to live happily’ is a verse of the Venerable Elder Dhaniya. What is its origin? This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a confident mind, made an offering of a reed garland. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a potter's family in Rājagaha. He received the name Dhaniya, and having come of age, he made his living by the potter's craft. At that time, the Teacher, seated in the hall of Dhaniya the potter, taught the Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Elements (MN III 237 ff.) to the clansman Pukkusāti. Hearing it, he accomplished his task. Dhaniya, hearing of his attainment of final Nibbāna, gained faith, thinking, ‘Truly, the Buddha's Dispensation is emancipating, where one can be freed from the suffering of the round of existence even by a single night's association!’ and went forth. While dwelling devoted to decorating his hut, he was rebuked by the Blessed One concerning hut-making. Thereafter, dwelling in a lodging belonging to the Saṅgha, he developed insight and attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.48.1–7):

“Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Vipinaggena gacchantaṃ, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ.

“I saw the Leader of the World, the Self-Enlightened One of golden hue, the recipient of offerings, walking through the forest.”

“Naḷamālaṃ gahetvāna, nikkhamanto ca tāvade;

Tatthaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ, oghatiṇṇamanāsavaṃ.

“Taking a reed garland, as I was going out at that very moment, there I saw the Self-Enlightened One, who had crossed the flood, free from taints.”

“Pasannacitto sumano, naḷamālamapūjayiṃ;

Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ mahāvīraṃ, sabbalokānukampakaṃ.

“With a confident and glad mind, I offered a reed garland to the Great Hero, worthy of offerings, compassionate to the whole world.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ mālamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, buddhapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one eons ago, when I offered that garland, I do not recall any woeful destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burned up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā ye bhikkhū dhutaṅgasamādhānena attānaṃ ukkaṃsetvā saṅghabhattādiṃ sādiyante aññe bhikkhū avajānanti, tesaṃ ovādadānamukhena aññaṃ byākaronto –

Having attained Arahantship, by way of giving advice to those bhikkhus who exalt themselves by undertaking ascetic practices and, while partaking of communal meals and so on, disparage other bhikkhus, he made another declaration:

228.

228.

“Sukhañce jīvituṃ icche, sāmaññasmiṃ apekkhavā;

Saṅghikaṃ nātimaññeyya, cīvaraṃ pānabhojanaṃ.

“If one wishes to live happily, having regard for the ascetic life, one should not despise the Saṅgha’s robes, drink, and food.”

229.

229.

Sukhañce [V 1.0379] jīvituṃ icche, sāmaññasmiṃ apekkhavā;

Ahi mūsikasobbhaṃva, sevetha sayanāsanaṃ.

“If one wishes to live happily, having regard for the ascetic life, one should frequent a lodging like a snake a mouse-hole.”

230.

230.

Sukhañce jīvituṃ icche, sāmaññasmiṃ apekkhavā;

Itarītarena tusseyya, ekadhammañca bhāvaye”ti. – tisso gāthā abhāsi;

If one wishes to live happily, with regard for the ascetic life, one should be content with this and that, and cultivate the one quality.” Thus he spoke three verses.

Tattha sukhañce jīvituṃ icche, sāmaññasmiṃ apekkhavāti sāmaññasmiṃ samaṇabhāve apekkhavā sikkhāya tibbagāravo hutvā sukhaṃ jīvituṃ iccheyya ce, anesanaṃ pahāya sāmaññasukhena sace jīvitukāmoti attho[M 1.0446]. Saṅghikaṃ nātimaññeyya, cīvaraṃ pānabhojananti saṅghato ābhataṃ cīvaraṃ āhāraṃ na avamaññeyya, saṅghassa uppajjanakalābho nāma parisuddhuppādo hotīti taṃ paribhuñjantassa ājīvapārisuddhisambhavena sāmaññasukhaṃ hatthagatamevāti adhippāyo. Ahi mūsikasobbhaṃvāti ahi viya mūsikāya khatabilaṃ sevetha seveyya senāsanaṃ. Yathā nāma sappo sayamattano āsayaṃ akatvā mūsikāya aññena vā kate āsaye vasitvā yena kāmaṃ pakkamati, evamevaṃ bhikkhu sayaṃ senāsanakaraṇā saṃkilesaṃ anāpajjitvā yattha katthaci vasitvā pakkameyyāti attho.

Herein, “If one wishes to live happily, with regard for the ascetic life” means: if one wishes to live happily, being desirous of the ascetic state, being deeply respectful of the training, having abandoned wrong livelihood—that is, if one wishes to live by the happiness of the ascetic life. “One should not despise the Sangha’s robes, drinks, and food” means one should not despise the robes and food brought from the Sangha. The meaning is that the gain that arises for the Sangha is a pure arising, and by partaking of it, the purity of livelihood is achieved, and the happiness of the ascetic life is directly within one’s grasp. “Like a snake a mouse-hole” means one should frequent a resting place and lodging like a snake a hole dug by a mouse. Just as a snake, without making its own dwelling, dwells in a dwelling made by a mouse or another and departs as it wishes, so too a monk, without incurring defilement by making his own dwelling, should dwell wherever and depart as he wishes. This is the meaning.

Idāni vutte avutte ca paccaye yathālābhasantoseneva sāmaññasukhaṃ hoti, na aññathāti dassento āha “itarītarena tusseyyā”ti, yena kenaci hīnena vā paṇītena vā yathāladdhena paccayena santosaṃ āpajjeyyāti attho. Ekadhammanti appamādabhāvaṃ, tañhi anuyuñjantassa anavajjaṃ sabbaṃ lokiyasukhaṃ lokuttarasukhañca hatthagatameva hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “appamatto hi jhāyanto, pappoti vipulaṃ sukha”nti (ma. ni. 2.352; dha. pa. 27).

Now, showing that the happiness of the ascetic life comes only through contentment with whatever is obtained, whether the requisites are mentioned or not, and not otherwise, he said: “One should be content with this and that.” This means one should attain contentment with any requisite, whether inferior or superior, as it has been obtained. “The one quality” means the state of heedfulness. For one who applies himself to that, all blameless worldly happiness and supramundane happiness are as if held in the hand. Therefore the Blessed One said: “For the heedful one, meditating, attains abundant happiness” (MN II 352; Dhp 27).

Dhaniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Dhaniya is concluded.

5. Mātaṅgaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mātaṅgaputta

Atisītanti [P 2.0091] āyasmato mātaṅgaputtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle himavantasamīpe mahato jātassarassa heṭṭhā mahati nāgabhavane mahānubhāvo nāgarājā hutvā nibbatto ekadivasaṃ nāgabhavanato nikkhamitvā vicaranto satthāraṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso attano sīsamaṇinā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe mātaṅgassa nāma kuṭumbikassa putto [V 1.0380] hutvā nibbatto [M 1.0447] mātaṅgaputtotveva paññāyittha. So viññutaṃ patto alasajātiko hutvā kiñci kammaṃ akaronto ñātakehi aññehi ca garahito “sukhajīvino ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā”ti sukhajīvitaṃ ākaṅkhanto bhikkhūhi kataparicayo hutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā aññe bhikkhū iddhimante disvā iddhibalaṃ patthetvā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.48.8-29) –

“Too cold” is the verse of the Venerable Elder Mātaṅgaputta. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this one was reborn as a powerful nāga king in a great nāga palace beneath a vast natural lake near the Himalayas. One day, having gone forth from his nāga palace and while wandering around, he saw the Teacher passing through the sky. With a joyful mind, he paid homage with the jewel on his head. Through that meritorious deed, while transmigrating among devas and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as the son of a householder named Mātaṅga in the Kosala country. He was known as “Mātaṅgaputta.” Having attained maturity but being naturally lazy, he did no work and was criticized by relatives and others. Desiring a comfortable life, thinking, “These ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, live comfortably,” he became acquainted with the monks, approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. After going forth, he saw other monks possessing psychic powers and aspired for such abilities. Receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he devoted himself to meditation and attained the six higher knowledges. As stated in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.48.8-29):

“Padumuttaro nāma jino, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Vivekakāmo sambuddho, gacchate anilañjase.

“The Conqueror named Padumuttara, gone beyond all phenomena, desiring seclusion, the Perfectly Enlightened One, goes on the path of the wind.”

“Avidūre himavantassa, mahājātassaro ahu;

Tattha me bhavanaṃ āsi, puññakammena saṃyutaṃ.

“Not far from the Himalayas, there was a great natural lake. There my dwelling was, associated with meritorious deeds.”

“Bhavanā abhinikkhamma, addasaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Indīvaraṃva jalitaṃ, ādittaṃva hutāsanaṃ.

“Having gone forth from my dwelling, I saw the leader of the world, blazing like a blue lotus, like a burning fire.”

“Vicinaṃ naddasaṃ pupphaṃ, pūjayissanti nāyakaṃ;

Sakaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā, avandiṃ satthuno ahaṃ.

“Searching, I did not see a flower with which to honor the leader; having gladdened my own mind, I paid homage to the Teacher.”

“Mama sīse maṇiṃ gayha, pūjayiṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Imāya maṇipūjāya, vipāko hotu bhaddako.

“Having taken the jewel from my head, I honored the leader of the world; by this offering of a jewel, may the result be auspicious.”

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Antalikkhe ṭhito satthā, imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsatha.

“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings; the Teacher, standing in the sky, uttered this verse:”

“So te ijjhatu saṅkappo, labhassu vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Imāya maṇipūjāya, anubhohi mahāyasaṃ.

“May that intention of yours succeed, may you obtain abundant happiness; through this offering of a jewel, may you experience great glory.”

“Idaṃ vatvāna bhagavā, jalajuttamanāmako;

Agamāsi buddhaseṭṭho, yattha cittaṃ paṇīhitaṃ.

“Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, named Foremost of the Water-Born, the supreme Buddha, went to the place where his mind was inclined.”

“Saṭṭhikappāni devindo, devarajjamakārayiṃ;

Anekasatakkhattuñca, cakkavattī ahosahaṃ.

“For sixty eons I was the lord of devas, ruling the divine realm; and many hundreds of times I was a wheel-turning monarch.”

“Pubbakammaṃ sarantassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Maṇi nibbattate mayhaṃ, ālokakaraṇo mamaṃ.

“For me, mindful, having become a deva and recalling my past deeds, a jewel manifests, bringing me light.”

“Chaḷasītisahassāni[M 1.0448], nāriyo me pariggahā;

Vicittavatthābharaṇā, āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā.

“Eighty-six thousand women were my attendants, adorned with various garments and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings.”

“Aḷārapamhā hasulā, susaññā tanumajjhimā;

Parivārenti maṃ niccaṃ, maṇipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“With curved eyelashes, smiling, well-proportioned, slender-waisted, they constantly surround me; this is the fruit of the jewel offering.”

“Soṇṇamayā [V 1.0381] maṇimayā, lohitaṅkamayā tathā;

Bhaṇḍā me sukatā honti, yadicchasi piḷandhanā.

“Golden, made of gems, and also made of ruby; my ornaments are well-crafted, whatever adornments I desire.”

“Kūṭāgārā gahā rammā, sayanañca mahārahaṃ;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, nibbattanti yadicchakaṃ.

“Pinnacled buildings, delightful houses, and beds of great value; knowing my intention, they arise as I desire.”

“Lābhā tesaṃ suladdhañca, ye labhanti upassutiṃ;

Puññakkhettaṃ manussānaṃ, osadhaṃ sabbapāṇinaṃ.

“A gain, a well-gained one, is theirs who obtain an opportunity to hear of the field of merit for humans, the medicine for all living beings.”

“Mayhampi sukataṃ kammaṃ, yohaṃ adakkhi nāyakaṃ;

Vinipātā pamuttomhi, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“For me, too, the deed is well done, that I beheld the Leader; freed from downfall, I have attained the unshakable state.”

“Yaṃ yaṃ yonūpapajjāmi, devattaṃ atha mānusaṃ;

Divasañceva rattiñca, āloko hoti me sadā.

“In whatever womb I am reborn, whether divine or human, day and night, there is always light for me.”

“Tāyeva maṇipūjāya, anubhotvāna sampadā;

Ñāṇāloko mayā diṭṭho, pattomhi acalaṃ padaṃ.

“By that very offering of the jewel, having experienced prosperity, the light of wisdom was seen by me, and I attained the unshakeable state.”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ maṇiṃ abhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, maṇipūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“A hundred thousand eons ago, I honored that jewel; I know of no bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the jewel offering.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā puggalādhiṭṭhānavasena kosajjaṃ garahanto attano ca vīriyārambhaṃ kittento –

But having attained the six higher knowledges, criticizing idleness by way of reference to individuals, and praising his own undertaking of energy—

231.

231.

“Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu;

Iti vissaṭṭhakammante, khaṇā accenti māṇave.

“‘Too cold, too hot, it’s too late in the evening’—thus, for people who neglect their work, the opportunities pass by.”

232.

232.

“Yo ca sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, so sukhā na vihāyati.

“But one who regards cold and heat as no more than grass, performing the duties of a man, does not fall away from happiness.”

233.

233.

“Dabbaṃ [M 1.0449] kusaṃ poṭakilaṃ, usīraṃ muñjapabbajaṃ;

Urasā panudissāmi, vivekamanubrūhaya”nti. – gāthāttayamāha;

“Dabba grass, kusa grass, rushes, usīra roots, and muñja reeds, I will push aside with my chest, cultivating seclusion!”—he spoke these three verses.

Tattha atisītanti himapātavaddalādinā ativiya sītaṃ, idaṃ ahūti ānetvā sambandho. Atiuṇhanti dhammaparitāpādinā ativiya uṇhaṃ, ubhayenapi utuvasena kosajjavatthumāha. Atisāyanti divasassa pariṇatiyā atisāyaṃ, sāyaggahaṇeneva cettha pātopi saṅgayhati[P 2.0092], tadubhayena kālavasena kosajjavatthumāha. Itīti iminā pakārena. Etena “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kattabbaṃ hotī”tiādinā (a. ni. 8.80; dī. ni. 3.334) vuttaṃ kosajjavatthuṃ [V 1.0382] saṅgaṇhāti. Vissaṭṭhakammanteti pariccattayogakammante. Khaṇāti buddhuppādādayo brahmacariyavāsassa okāsā. Accentīti atikkamanti. Māṇaveti satte. Tiṇā bhiyyo na maññatīti tiṇato upari na maññati, tiṇaṃ viya maññati, sītuṇhāni abhibhavitvā attanā kattabbaṃ karoti. Karanti karonto. Purisakiccānīti vīrapurisena kattabbāni attahitaparahitāni. Sukhāti sukhato, nibbānasukhatoti adhippāyo. Tatiyagāthāya attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

Here, “too cold” refers to extreme cold from snowfall and frost, etc., and “this was” connects to it. “Too hot” refers to extreme heat from scorching winds, etc. Both illustrate grounds for laziness due to weather. “Too late” refers to the extreme lateness of the day, and by mentioning evening, morning is also included. Both illustrate grounds for laziness due to time. “Thus” refers to this manner. This encompasses the grounds for laziness mentioned in, “Here, monks, a monk has work to do…” (AN 8.80; DN 3.334). “Neglecting their duties” means abandoning the work of effort. “Opportunities” refers to the rare chances like the arising of a Buddha, opportunities for living the holy life. “Waste” means letting them pass by. “Young men” refers to beings. “No more than grass” means not regarding them as more than grass, regarding them as grass, overcoming cold and heat and doing what must be done. “Performing” means doing. “The tasks of a man” refers to duties for one’s own and others’ welfare, to be done by a heroic person. “From happiness” means happiness, the happiness of Nibbāna—this is the intention. The meaning of the third verse is as stated below.

Mātaṅgaputtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mātaṅgaputta is concluded.

6. Khujjasobhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khujjasobhita

Ye cittakathī bahussutāti āyasmato khujjasobhitattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso dasahi gāthāhi abhitthavi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde pāṭaliputtanagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, “sobhito”tissa nāmaṃ [M 1.0450] ahosi. Thokaṃ khujjadhātukatāya pana khujjasobhitotveva paññāyittha. So vayappatto satthari parinibbute ānandattherassa santike pabbajitvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.49-58) –

“Ye cittakathī bahussutāti” is the verse of the Venerable Khujjasobhita Thera. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in a respectable family and, having come of age, one day saw the Blessed One traveling with a great assembly of monks. With a joyful mind, he praised Him with ten verses. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a brahmin family in the city of Pāṭaliputta. His name was “Sobhita,” but due to a slight hunchback, he became known as “Khujjasobhita.” When he came of age, after the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, he went forth under the Venerable Ānanda Thera and became one endowed with the six superknowledges. Thus, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.47.49–58):

“Kakudhaṃ vilasantaṃva, devadevaṃ narāsabhaṃ;

Rathiyaṃ paṭipajjantaṃ, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“Like a splendid Kakudha flower, the god of gods, the bull among men, going along the road; who, having seen him, would not be pleased?”

“Tamandhakāraṃ nāsetvā, santāretvā bahuṃ janaṃ;

Ñāṇālokena jotantaṃ, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“Having dispelled that darkness, having led many people across, shining with the light of wisdom, who, seeing him, would not be pleased?”

“Vasīsatasahassehi, nīyantaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Uddharantaṃ bahū satte, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“Who, seeing the Leader of the World, escorted by a hundred thousand masters, delivering many beings, would not be pleased?”

“Āhanantaṃ dhammabheriṃ, maddantaṃ titthiye gaṇe;

Sīhanādaṃ vinadantaṃ, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“Beating the Dhamma drum, subduing the groups of sectarians, roaring the lion’s roar—who, on seeing him, would not be pleased?”

“Yāvatā brahmalokato, āgantvāna sabrahmakā;

Pucchanti nipuṇe pañhe, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“Having come from as far as the Brahmā realm, together with Brahmās, they ask subtle questions. Who, on seeing him who answers them, would not be pleased?”

“Yassañjaliṃ karitvāna, āyācanti sadevakā;

Tena puññaṃ anubhonti, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“To whom, having made the añjali gesture, the world with its devas entreats; through that they experience merit—who, on seeing him, would not be pleased?”

“Sabbe [V 1.0383] janā samāgantvā, sampavārenti cakkhumaṃ;

Na vikampati ajjhiṭṭho, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“All people gather together and invite the One with Vision; unshaken when entreated—who, having seen him, would not be pleased?”

“Nagaraṃ pavisato yassa, ravanti bheriyo bahū;

Vinadanti gajā mattā, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“When he enters the city, many drums sound; the intoxicated elephants roar—who, seeing him, would not be pleased?”

“Vīthiyā gacchato yassa, sabbābhā jotate sadā;

Abbhunnatā samā honti, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“When he walks along the path, his radiance always shines in every direction; the uneven becomes even—who, seeing him, would not be pleased?”

“Byāharantassa buddhassa, cakkavāḷampi suyyati;

Sabbe satte viññāpeti, ko disvā na pasīdati.

“When the Buddha speaks, his voice is heard even throughout the universe; he makes all beings understand—who, having seen him, would not be pleased?”

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ buddhamabhikittayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, kittanāya idaṃ phalaṃ.

“A hundred thousand eons ago, I praised the Buddha; I have not known a bad destination—this is the fruit of that praise.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño [M 1.0451] pana hutvā paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle rājagahe sattapaṇṇiguhāyaṃ sannipatitena saṅghena “āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantehī”ti āṇatto pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā therassa purato uṭṭhahitvā saṅghassa sāsanaṃ ārocetvā sayaṃ puretaraṃ ākāsena gantvā sattapaṇṇiguhādvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Tena ca samayena mārassa mārakāyikānañca paṭisedhanatthaṃ devasaṅghena pesitā aññatarā devatā sattapaṇṇiguhādvāre ṭhitā hoti, tassā khujjasobhito thero attano āgamanaṃ kathento –

Having become one with the six superknowledges, during the time of the First Great Council in Rājagaha, in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, when the Saṅgha had gathered and ordered, “Invite Venerable Ānanda,” he submerged into the earth and rose up in front of the elder. After informing him of the Saṅgha’s instruction, he himself went ahead through the sky and arrived at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. At that time, to prevent Māra and his hosts, a certain deity sent by the assembly of gods was standing at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. The Elder Khujjasobhita, announcing his arrival, said—

234.

234.

“Ye [P 2.0093] cittakathī bahussutā, samaṇā pāṭaliputtavāsino;

Tesaññataroyamāyuvā, dvāre tiṭṭhati khujjasobhito”ti. – paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha;

“Those ascetics who are skilled in discourse, learned, dwelling in Pāṭaliputta—among them is this venerable one, Khujjasobhita, standing at the door.” – thus he spoke the first verse.

Tattha cittakathīti vicittadhammakathikā, saṅkhipanaṃ, vitthāraṇaṃ gambhīrakaraṇaṃ uttānīkaraṇaṃ kaṅkhāvinodanaṃ dhammapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādīhi nānānayehi paresaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammassa kathanasīlāti attho. Bahussutāti pariyattipaṭivedhabāhusaccapāripūriyā bahussutā. Sabbaso samitapāpatāya samaṇā. Pāṭaliputtavāsino, tesaññataroti pāṭaliputtanagaravāsitāya pāṭaliputtavāsino, tesaṃ aññataro, ayaṃ āyuvā dīghāyu āyasmā. Dvāre tiṭṭhatīti sattapaṇṇiguhāya dvāre tiṭṭhati, saṅghassa anumatiyā pavisitunti attho. Taṃ sutvā sā devatā therassa āgamanaṃ saṅghassa nivedentī –

There, “cittakathī” means one skilled in teaching the Dhamma in various ways—summarizing, elaborating, making the profound deep, making the abstruse clear, dispelling doubts, and establishing the Dhamma—thus having the nature of speaking the Dhamma in accordance with others’ inclinations. “Bahussuta” means very learned with the fullness of scriptural learning and penetration. “Samaṇā” are those who have completely calmed evil. “Pāṭaliputtavāsino, tesaññataro” means a resident of Pāṭaliputta city, one of them, this venerable, long-lived one. “Dvāre tiṭṭhati” means he stands at the door of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, intending to enter with the Saṅgha’s permission. Hearing this, that deity, informing the Saṅgha of the Elder’s arrival—

235.

235.

“Ye [V 1.0384] cittakathī…pe… dvāre tiṭṭhati māluterito”ti. – dutiyaṃ gāthamāha;

“Those who are skilled in speech… impelled by the wind, he stands at the door.” – thus she spoke the second verse.

Tattha māluteritoti iddhicittajanitena vāyunā erito, iddhibalena āgatoti attho.

There, “māluterito” means impelled by wind generated through a mind of psychic power; the meaning is that he arrived by the power of psychic ability.

Evaṃ [M 1.0452] tāya devatāya niveditena saṅghena katokāso thero saṅghassa santikaṃ gacchanto –

Thus informed by that deity, the Elder, having been granted an opportunity by the Saṅgha, approached the Saṅgha—

236.

236.

“Suyuddhena suyiṭṭhena, saṅgāmavijayena ca;

Brahmacariyānuciṇṇena, evāyaṃ sukhamedhatī”ti. –

“Through good fighting, good offering, and victory in battle, through the practice of the holy life, thus does this one increase in happiness.”

Imāya tatiyagāthāya aññaṃ byākāsi.

With this third verse, he declared his final knowledge.

Tattha suyuddhenāti pubbabhāge tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānavasena kilesehi suṭṭhu yujjhanena. Suyiṭṭhenāti antarantarā kalyāṇamittehi dinnasappāyadhammadānena. Saṅgāmavijayena cāti samucchedappahānavasena sabbaso kilesābhisaṅkhāranimmathanena laddhasaṅgāmavijayena ca. Brahmacariyānuciṇṇenāti anuciṇṇena aggamaggabrahmacariyena. Evāyaṃ sukhamedhatīti evaṃ vuttappakārena ayaṃ khujjasobhito nibbānasukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhañca edhati, anubhavatīti attho.

Here, “suyuddhena” means by thoroughly battling the defilements in the initial stages by means of abandonment through substitution and through suppression. “Suyiṭṭhena” means by the gift of suitable Dhamma given from time to time by good friends. “And victory in battle” means by the victory in battle gained through the complete destruction of all defilements and formations by means of eradication. “By practicing the holy life” means by the practiced holy life of the supreme path. “Thus does this one increase in happiness” means that in this way, this Khujjasobhita increases in—that is, experiences—the happiness of Nibbāna and the happiness of fruition attainment; this is the meaning.

Khujjasobhitattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khujjasobhita is concluded.

7. Vāraṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vāraṇa

Yodha koci manussesūti āyasmato vāraṇattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto ito dvānavute kappe tissassa bhagavato uppattito puretarameva [P 2.0094] brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu pāragū hutvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā catupaṇṇāsasahassānaṃ antevāsikānaṃ mante vācento vasati. Tena ca samayena tissassa bhagavato bodhisattabhūtassa tusitā kāyā cavitvā carimabhave mātukucchiṃ okkamanena mahāpathavikampo ahosi. Taṃ disvā mahājano bhīto saṃviggo naṃ isiṃ upasaṅkamitvā pathavikampanakāraṇaṃ pucchi. So “mahābodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkami, tenāyaṃ pathavikampo, tasmā mā bhāyathā”ti buddhuppādassa pubbanimittabhāvaṃ kathetvā samassāsesi, buddhārammaṇañca pītiṃ paṭivedesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu [M 1.0453] saṃsaranto imasmiṃ [V 1.0385] buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vāraṇoti laddhanāmo vayappatto aññatarassa āraññakassa therassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā laddhappasādo pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. So ekadivasaṃ buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge ahinakule aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ katvā kālaṅkate disvā “ime sattā aññamaññavirodhena jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā”ti saṃviggamānaso hutvā bhagavato santikaṃ gato, tassa bhagavā cittācāraṃ ñatvā tadanurūpameva ovādaṃ dento –

The verse beginning 'Whoever here among men...' is a verse of the Venerable Elder Vāraṇa. What is its origin? This one, too, having made a foundation of merit in the presence of former Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was born ninety-two eons ago, even before the arising of the Blessed One Tissa, in a brahmin family. Becoming an expert in the brahminical arts and sciences, he went forth into the ascetic life and lived teaching mantras to fifty-four thousand disciples. At that time, when the Bodhisatta who was to become the Blessed One Tissa passed away from the Tusita realm and descended into his mother’s womb for his final existence, a great earthquake occurred. Seeing this, the great populace, terrified and agitated, approached that sage and asked the reason for the earthquake. He reassured them, explaining it as a precursor to the Buddha’s arising, saying, 'The Great Bodhisatta has entered his mother’s womb—that is why there is this earthquake. Therefore, do not be afraid,' and he experienced joy with the Buddha as its object. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha-era, he was born in a brahmin family in the Kosala country. Having received the name Vāraṇa, he reached maturity and, hearing the Dhamma from a certain forest-dwelling elder, gained faith and went forth, practicing the duties of a recluse. One day, while going to attend upon the Buddha, he saw on the way a family of mongooses who had died after quarreling with one another. His mind agitated, he thought: 'These beings have met their end through mutual hostility.' He then went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing the state of his mind, gave him advice suited to it, saying:

237.

237.

“Yodha koci manussesu, parapāṇāni hiṃsati;

Asmā lokā paramhā ca, ubhayā dhaṃsate naro.

Whoever here among human beings harms other living beings, from this world and from the next, that person falls away from both.

238.

238.

“Yo ca mettena cittena, sabbapāṇānukampati;

Bahuñhi so pasavati, puññaṃ tādisako naro.

But one who, with a mind of loving-kindness, has compassion for all beings; such a person generates much merit.

239.

239.

“Subhāsitassa sikkhetha, samaṇūpāsanassa ca;

Ekāsanassa ca raho, cittavūpasamassā cā”ti. – tisso gāthā abhāsi;

One should train in what is well-spoken, and in associating with recluses; in sitting alone in seclusion, and in the calming of the mind.' Thus he spoke three verses.

Tattha yodha koci manussesūti idha manussesu yo koci khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā. Manussaggahaṇañcettha ukkaṭṭhasattanidassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Parapāṇāni hiṃsatīti parasatte māreti vibādhati ca. Asmā lokāti idha lokato. Paramhāti paralokato. Ubhayā dhaṃsateti ubhayato dhaṃsati, ubhayalokapariyāpannahitasukhato parihāyatīti attho. Naroti satto.

Herein, 'whoever here among humans' means any noble, brahmin, merchant, laborer, householder, or renunciant among human beings. The mention of 'human beings' here should be understood as an indication of superior beings. 'Harms other living beings' means he kills and oppresses other beings. 'From this world' means from this world here. 'From the other' means from the other world. 'Falls away from both' means he falls away from both; that is, he is deprived of the welfare and happiness pertaining to both worlds. 'Person' means a being.

Evaṃ parapīḷālakkhaṇaṃ pāpadhammaṃ dassetvā idāni parapīḷānivattilakkhaṇaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ dassento “yo ca mettenā”tiādinā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha mettena cittenāti mettāsampayuttena cittena appanāpattena itarītarena vā. Sabbapāṇānukampatīti sabbe pāṇe attano orasaputte viya mettāyati. Bahuñhi so pasavati, puññaṃ tādisako naroti [P 2.0095] so tathārūpo mettāvihārī puggalo bahuṃ mahantaṃ anappakaṃ kusalaṃ pasavati paṭilabhati adhigacchati.

Having thus shown the unwholesome quality characterized by harming others, he now speaks the second verse, beginning 'But one who, with a mind of loving-kindness,' showing the wholesome quality characterized by desisting from harming others. Here, 'with a mind of loving-kindness' means with a mind endowed with loving-kindness, whether it has attained absorption or is of a lesser degree. 'Has compassion for all beings' means he extends loving-kindness to all beings as if they were his own legitimate children. 'Such a person generates much merit' means that such a person, dwelling in loving-kindness, generates, obtains, and attains abundant, great, and substantial wholesome kamma.

Idāni [M 1.0454] taṃ sasambhāre samathavipassanādhamme niyojento “subhāsitassā”tiādinā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha subhāsitassa sikkhethāti appicchakathādibhedaṃ subhāsitaṃ pariyattidhammaṃ savanadhāraṇaparipucchādivasena sikkheyya. Samaṇūpāsanassa cāti samitapāpānaṃ samaṇānaṃ kalyāṇamittānaṃ upāsakānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsanañceva paṭipattiyā tesaṃ samīpacariyañca [V 1.0386] sikkheyya. Ekāsanassa ca raho cittavūpasamassa cāti ekassa asahāyassa kāyavivekaṃ anubrūhantassa raho kammaṭṭhānānuyogavasena āsanaṃ nisajjaṃ sikkheyya. Evaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhāvanañca matthakaṃ pāpento samucchedavasena kilesānaṃ cittassa vūpasamañca sikkheyya. Yāhi adhisīlasikkhādīhi kilesā accantameva vūpasantā pahīnā honti, tā maggaphalasikkhā sikkhantassa accantameva cittaṃ vūpasantaṃ nāma hotīti. Gāthāpariyosāne vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.59-72) –

Now, directing him to the practice of serenity and insight with their requisites, he spoke the third verse, beginning 'One should train in what is well-spoken.' Herein, 'one should train in what is well-spoken' means one should train in the Dhamma of the scriptures, which is well-spoken and includes such aspects as talk on contentment, by way of listening, memorizing, questioning, and so forth. 'And in associating with recluses' means one should train in approaching and attending upon, from time to time, the recluses who have calmed evil, who are good friends, and in following their conduct closely through practice. 'And in solitary sitting in seclusion and in the calming of the mind' means one who cultivates physical seclusion without a companion should train in sitting alone in a secluded place by way of applying oneself to a meditation subject.
