Thus, applying oneself to meditation and bringing development to its peak, one should train in the calming of the mind by way of cutting off defilements. The defilements are utterly calmed and abandoned by means of the higher training in morality and so forth; for one who trains in the training of the path and fruition, the mind is said to be utterly calmed. At the end of the verses, having developed insight, he attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna-Thera 2.47.59-72):

“Ajjhogāhetvā himavaṃ, mante vācemahaṃ tadā;

Catupaññāsasahassāni, sissā mayhaṃ upaṭṭhahuṃ.

Having entered the Himalayas, I then taught mantras; fifty-four thousand disciples attended me.

“Adhitā vedagū sabbe, chaḷaṅge pāramiṃ gatā;

Sakavijjāhupatthaddhā, himavante vasanti te.

All were learned, masters of the Vedas, having gone to perfection in the six branches; proud of their own knowledge, they dwelt in the Himalayas.

“Cavitvā tusitā kāyā, devaputto mahāyaso;

Uppajji mātukucchismiṃ, sampajāno patissato.

Having passed away from the Tusita realm, the greatly glorious deva-son arose in his mother's womb, mindful and clearly comprehending.

“Sambuddhe upapajjante, dasasahassi kampatha;

Andhā cakkhuṃ alabhiṃsu, uppajjantamhi nāyake.

When a Perfectly Enlightened One arises, the ten-thousandfold world system trembles; the blind regained their sight when the Leader arose.

“Sabbākāraṃ pakampittha, kevalā vasudhā ayaṃ;

Nigghosasaddaṃ sutvāna, ubbijjiṃsu mahājanā.

This entire earth shook in every way; having heard the resounding noise, the great multitude was terrified.

“Sabbe janā samāgamma, āgacchuṃ mama santikaṃ;

Vasudhāyaṃ pakampittha, kiṃ vipāko bhavissati.

All the people, having gathered together, came into my presence, saying: 'The earth has trembled; what will be the outcome?'

“Avacāsiṃ [M 1.0455] tadā tesaṃ, mā bhetha natthi vo bhayaṃ;

Visaṭṭhā hotha sabbepi, uppādoyaṃ suvatthiko.

Then I said to them: 'Do not be afraid, there is no danger for you. All of you, be at ease; this arising is very auspicious.'

“Aṭṭhahetūhi samphussa, vasudhāyaṃ pakampati;

Tathā nimittā dissanti, obhāso vipulo mahā.

The earth trembles, touched by eight causes; such signs are seen: a vast and mighty radiance.

“Asaṃsayaṃ buddhaseṭṭho, uppajjissati cakkhumā;

Saññāpetvāna janataṃ, pañcasīle kathesahaṃ.

Without a doubt, the supreme Buddha, the One with Vision, will arise. Having informed the people, I taught the five precepts.

“Sutvāna pañcasīlāni, buddhuppādañca dullabhaṃ;

Ubbegajātā sumanā, tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā ahaṃsu te.

Having heard of the five precepts and the rare arising of a Buddha, they became agitated yet glad, pleased and delighted.

“Dvenavute ito kappe, yaṃ nimittaṃ viyākariṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, byākaraṇassidaṃ phalaṃ.

Ninety-two eons ago, I declared that sign; I do not know of any bad destination—this is the fruit of that declaration.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been done.

Vāraṇattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vāraṇa is concluded.

8. Vassikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vassika

Ekopi [V 1.0387] saddho medhāvīti āyasmato vassikattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannacitto pilakkhaphalāni adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kosalaraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vassikoti laddhanāmo vayappatto satthu yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto ābādhiko ahosi. Atha naṃ ñātakā vejjaparidiṭṭhena bhesajjavidhinā upaṭṭhahitvā arogamakaṃsu. So tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhito saṃvegajāto bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.40-44) –

"One who is faithful and wise"—this is the verse of Elder Vassika. What is its origin? This one, having made an aspiration under former Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds in various existences, was born into a family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassi. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher, and with a confident mind, he offered pilakkha fruits. Through that meritorious act, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born into a brahmin family in the Kosala country. Named Vassika, having come of age and witnessed the Teacher's Twin Miracle, he gained faith. He then went forth and, while practicing the duties of a recluse, became ill. Then his relatives attended to him with medical treatment prescribed by a physician and made him well. Having recovered from that illness, he was stirred by a sense of urgency, roused himself to meditation, and became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera 2.47.40-44):

“Vanantare [M 1.0456] buddhaṃ disvā, atthadassiṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Pasannacitto sumano, pilakkhassa phalaṃ adā.

"Having seen the Buddha Atthadassi, of great renown, in the forest, with a confident and gladdened mind, I offered a pilakkha fruit."

“Aṭṭhārase kappasate, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"For eighteen hundred aeons since I gave that fruit, I have not known an unhappy destination; this is the fruit of that offering of fruit."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burned up… the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled."

Chaḷabhiñño [P 2.0096] pana hutvā ākāsena ñātakānaṃ santike gantvā ākāse ṭhito dhammaṃ desetvā te saraṇesu sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpesi. Tesu keci kālaṅkatā saraṇesu sīlesu ca patiṭṭhitattā sagge nibbattiṃsu. Atha naṃ satthā buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ upagataṃ “kiṃ te, vassika, ñātīnaṃ ārogya”nti pucchi. So ñātīnaṃ attanā kataṃ upakāraṃ satthu kathento –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, he went through the air to his relatives and, standing in the sky, taught them the Dhamma, establishing them in the refuges and precepts. Some of them, having passed away, were reborn in a heavenly world because they had been established in the refuges and precepts. Then, when he came to attend upon the Buddha, the Teacher asked him, "Vassika, are your relatives well?" He then related to the Teacher the help he had given to his relatives, saying:

240.

240.

“Ekopi saddho medhāvī, assaddhānīdha ñātinaṃ;

Dhammaṭṭho sīlasampanno, hoti atthāya bandhunaṃ.

"Even one who is faithful and wise, for his faithless relatives here, established in Dhamma, accomplished in virtue, becomes for the welfare of his kinsmen."

241.

241.

“Niggayha anukampāya, coditā ñātayo mayā;

Ñātibandhavapemena, kāraṃ katvāna bhikkhusu.

"Urged on by me out of compassion, having been admonished, my relatives, through affection for their kinsman, rendered service to the bhikkhus."

242.

242.

“Te abbhatītā kālaṅkatā, pattā te tidivaṃ sukhaṃ;

Bhātaro mayhaṃ mātā ca, modanti kāmakāmino”ti. –

"They have passed on, having died, and have reached heavenly happiness; my brothers and my mother now rejoice, enjoying all they desire."

Tisso gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke these three verses.

Tatthāyaṃ [V 1.0388] paṭhamagāthāya attho – yo kammaphalasaddhāya ca ratanattayasaddhāya ca vasena saddho, tato eva kammassakatañāṇādiyogato medhāvī, satthu ovādadhamme navalokuttaradhamme ca ṭhitattā dhammaṭṭho, ācārasīlassa maggasīlassa phalasīlassa ca vasena sīlasampanno, so ekopi yathāvuttāya saddhāya abhāvena assaddhānaṃ idha imasmiṃ loke “amhākaṃ ime”ti ñātabbaṭṭhena ñātīnaṃ, tathā pemabandhanena bandhanaṭṭhena “bandhū”ti ca laddhanāmānaṃ bandhavānaṃ atthāya hitāya hotīti.

Here is the meaning of the first verse: One who is faithful through faith in kamma and its results and in the Triple Gem, and who is wise through connection with the knowledge of ownership of kamma and so forth; one who is established in Dhamma because of being grounded in the Teacher’s instructional Dhamma and the nine supramundane Dhammas; one who is accomplished in virtue by way of the virtue of conduct, the virtue of the path, and the virtue of fruition—even one such person is for the welfare and benefit of his faithless relatives here in this world, who are known as ‘ñāti’ in the sense of being recognized as ‘ours,’ and for his kinsmen, who are called ‘bandhu’ in the sense of being bound by the bond of affection.

Evaṃ [M 1.0457] sādhāraṇato vuttamatthaṃ attūpanāyikaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “niggayhā”tiādinā itaragāthā vuttā. Tattha niggayha anukampāya, coditā ñātayo mayāti idānipi duggatā kusalaṃ akatvā āyatiṃ parikkilesaṃ puna mānubhavitthāti niggahetvā ñātayo mayā ovaditā. Ñātibandhavapemena “amhākaṃ ayaṃ bandhavo”ti evaṃ pavattena pemena mama ovādaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkontā kāraṃ katvāna bhikkhūsu pasannacittā hutvā cīvarādipaccayadānena ceva upaṭṭhānena ca bhikkhūsu sakkārasammānaṃ katvā te abbhatītā kālaṅkatā hutvā imaṃ lokaṃ atikkantā. Puna teti nipātamattaṃ. Tidivaṃ sukhanti devalokapariyāpannasukhaṃ, sukhaṃ vā iṭṭhaṃ tidivaṃ adhigatā. “Ke pana te”ti āha. “Bhātaro mayhaṃ mātā ca, modanti kāmakāmino”ti. Attanā yathākāmitavatthukāmasamaṅgino hutvā abhiramantīti attho.

To show the general meaning that was stated by applying it to himself, the other verses beginning with "Niggayhā" were spoken. Therein, 'Urged on by me out of compassion, having been admonished, my relatives' means: 'My relatives were advised by me, having been admonished with the thought: “Even now you are in a wretched state; having not done what is wholesome, do not experience future defilements again!”' 'Through affection for their kinsman,' unable to disregard my advice because of the affection that arose from thinking, 'This is our kinsman,' 'rendered service to the bhikkhus,' that is, with confident minds, they showed respect and honor to the bhikkhus by giving requisites such as robes and by attending upon them. 'They have passed on, having died,' means they have departed from this world. The word 'te' is merely a particle. 'Heavenly happiness' means happiness pertaining to the deva world, or they attained the desired heaven, which is happiness. To the question, 'But who are they?' he said: 'My brothers and my mother now rejoice, enjoying all they desire.' The meaning is that they delight in being endowed with the objects of sensual pleasure that they themselves desired.

Vassikattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of Elder Vassika is finished.

9. Yasojattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Yasoja

Kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāsoti [P 2.0097] āyasmato yasojattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ārāmagopakakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso labujaphalaṃ adāsi.

The verse of the Venerable Yasoja begins with 'Kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāso.' What is its origin? This one, having made an aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences, was born into the family of a park-keeper during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One Vipassī traveling through the air. With a confident mind, he offered a labuja fruit.

So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagaradvāre kevaṭṭagāme pañcakulasatajeṭṭhakassa kevaṭṭassa putto hutvā nibbatti, yasojotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto attano sahāyehi kevaṭṭaputtehi saddhiṃ macchagahaṇatthaṃ aciravatiyaṃ nadiyaṃ jālaṃ khipi. Tattheko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo mahāmaccho antojālaṃ pāvisi. Taṃ te rañño pasenadissa dassesuṃ[V 1.0389]. Rājā “imassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa macchassa vaṇṇakāraṇaṃ bhagavā jānātī”ti macchaṃ gāhāpetvā bhagavato [M 1.0458] dassesi. Bhagavā “ayaṃ kassapassa sammāsambuddhassa sāsane osakkamāne pabbajitvā micchā paṭipajjanto sāsanaṃ osakkāpetvā niraye nibbatto ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā tato cuto aciravatiyaṃ maccho hutvā nibbatto”ti vatvā tassa bhaginīnañca niraye nibbattabhāvaṃ, tassa bhātikattherassa parinibbutabhāvañca teneva kathāpetvā imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā kapilasuttaṃ desesi.

By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a fishermen's village near the city of Sāvatthī as the son of the chief fisherman of five hundred families. They named him Yasoja. When he came of age, he cast a net into the Aciravatī River with his fellow fishermen's sons to catch fish. There, a great golden-colored fish entered the net. They showed it to King Pasenadi. The king, thinking, “The Blessed One knows the reason for the golden color of this fish,” had the fish brought and presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “This one went forth in the dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa when it was declining. Practicing wrongly, he caused the dispensation to decline. He was reborn in hell and, after suffering there for one Buddha-interval, he passed away from there and was reborn as this fish in the Aciravatī.” Then, having made that very one relate that his sisters had been reborn in hell and that his elder brother, the Thera, had attained final Nibbāna, he taught the Kapila Sutta in connection with this origin story.

Satthu desanaṃ sutvā yasojo saṃvegajāto saddhiṃ attano sahāyehi bhagavato santike pabbajitvā patirūpe ṭhāne vasanto ekadivasaṃ sapariso bhagavantaṃ vandituṃ jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tassa āgamane senāsanapaññāpanādinā vihāre uccāsaddamahāsaddo ahosi. Taṃ sutvā “bhagavā saparisaṃ yasojaṃ paṇāmesī”ti (udā. 23) sabbaṃ udāne āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Paṇāmito pana āyasmā yasojo kasābhihato bhaddo assājānīyo viya saṃviggamānaso saddhiṃ parisāya vaggumudāya nadiyā tīre vasanto ghaṭento vāyamanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā antovasseyeva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.32-39) –

Having heard the Teacher’s discourse, Yasoja was stirred with a sense of urgency. Together with his companions, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Dwelling in a suitable place, one day he went with his retinue to Jetavana to pay homage to the Blessed One. Upon his arrival, a great loud noise arose in the monastery due to the arrangement of lodgings and so forth. Hearing this, 'The Blessed One dismissed Yasoja with his retinue'—all of which should be understood in accordance with the account in the Udāna (Ud. 23). After being dismissed, the Venerable Yasoja, like a fine thoroughbred horse struck by a whip, with a mind stirred by urgency, dwelt with his retinue on the banks of the Vaggumudā River. Striving and exerting himself, he developed insight and within that same rains-retreat became one endowed with the six higher knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera 2.47.32-39):

“Nagare bandhumatiyā, ārāmiko ahaṃ tadā;

Addasaṃ virajaṃ buddhaṃ, gacchantaṃ anilañjase.

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a park-keeper then; I saw the stainless Buddha traveling through the sky."

“Labujaṃ phalamādāya, buddhaseṭṭhassadāsahaṃ;

Ākāseva ṭhito santo, paṭiggaṇhi mahāyaso.

"Taking a labuja fruit, I offered it to the foremost of Buddhas. Standing in the sky, serene, the glorious one accepted it."

“Vittisañjānano mayhaṃ, diṭṭhadhammasukhāvaho;

Phalaṃ buddhassa datvāna, vippasannena cetasā.

"Having given the fruit to the Buddha with an utterly serene mind, it produced joy for me and brought happiness in this very life."

“Adhigañchiṃ tadā pītiṃ, vipulaṃ sukhamuttamaṃ;

Uppajjateva ratanaṃ, nibbattassa tahiṃ tahiṃ.

"I then attained rapture, vast and supreme happiness; indeed, a treasure arises for one reborn here and there."

“Ekanavutito kappe, yaṃ phalaṃ adadiṃ tadā;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, phaladānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"In the ninety-first eon, when I gave that fruit, I do not recall any unhappy destination; this is the fruit of that fruit-offering."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are consumed... the Buddha's Dispensation has been accomplished."

Chaḷabhiññaṃ [M 1.0459] pana samānaṃ saparisaṃ āyasmantaṃ yasojaṃ satthā pakkositvā āneñjasamāpattinā paṭisanthāramakāsi. So sabbepi [P 2.0098] dhutaṅgadhamme samādāya vattati. Tenassa sarīraṃ kisaṃ ahosi lūkhaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ, taṃ bhagavā paramappicchatāya pasaṃsanto –

The Teacher, having summoned the Venerable Yasoja, who was one endowed with the six higher knowledges, together with his following, greeted him with the attainment of the imperturbable. He lived undertaking all the ascetic practices. Because of this, his body became thin, rough, and unsightly. Praising him for his supreme fewness of wishes, the Blessed One said—

243.

243.

“Kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāso[V 1.0390], kiso dhamanisanthato;

Mattaññū annapānamhi, adīnamānaso naro”ti. – paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha;

"Resembling the joint of a dark creeper, lean, with veins spread out; knowing moderation in food and drink, a man with an undaunted mind."—this is the first verse spoken;

Tattha kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāsoti maṃsūpacayavigamena kisadusaṇṭhitasarīrāvayavatāya dantilatāpabbasadisaṅgo, tenāha “kiso dhamanisanthato”ti. Kisoti moneyyapaṭipadāpūraṇena kisasarīro. Dhamanisanthatoti dhamanīhi santhatagatto appamaṃsalohitatāya pākaṭīhi kaṇḍarasirāhi vitatasarīro. Mattaññūti pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogavissajjanesu pamāṇaññū. Adīnamānasoti kosajjādīhi anabhibhūtattā alīnacitto akusītavutti. Naroti puriso, porisassa dhurassa vahanato porisalakkhaṇasampanno purisadhorayhoti adhippāyo.

There, 'Kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāso' means having limbs resembling the joint of a danti creeper due to the loss of accumulated flesh, which made his body parts thin and ill-formed. Therefore he said, 'thin, with veins spread out.' 'Kiso' means having a thin body due to fulfilling the practice of sagely conduct. 'Dhamanisanthato' means having a body spread with veins, a body stretched out with visible tendons and veins due to the lack of flesh and blood. 'Mattaññū' means knowing the measure in seeking, receiving, consuming, and relinquishing. 'Adīnamānaso' means having an unfeeble mind, not being overcome by laziness and so forth, having an unyielding mind, and diligent conduct. 'Naro' means a man; the intention is that he is a leader among men, endowed with the characteristics of a man, due to bearing the burden of manhood.

Evaṃ thero satthārā pasaṭṭho pasaṭṭhabhāvānurūpaṃ attano adhivāsanakhantivīriyārambhavivekābhiratikittanamukhena bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ kathento –

Thus, the elder, praised by the Teacher, taught the Dhamma to the monks by way of proclaiming his own endurance, patience, energetic striving, and delight in solitude, in accordance with that praise—

244.

244.

“Phuṭṭho ḍaṃsehi makasehi, araññasmiṃ brahāvane;

Nāgo saṅgāmasīseva, sato tatrādhivāsaye.

"Assailed by gadflies and mosquitoes in the wilderness, in the great forest, one should mindfully endure there, like a great elephant at the forefront of battle."

245.

245.

“Yathā brahmā tathā eko, yathā devo tathā duve;

Yathā gāmo tathā tayo, kolāhalaṃ tatuttari”nti. –

"As Brahmā, so one; as a god, so two; as a village, so three; beyond that, uproar."

Imā dve gāthā abhāsi.

He uttered these two verses.

Tattha nāgo saṅgāmasīsevāti yathā nāma ājāneyyo hatthināgo yuddhamaṇḍale asisattitomarādippahāre adhivāsetvā parasenaṃ viddhaṃseti, evaṃ bhikkhu araññasmiṃ brahāvane araññāniyaṃ ḍaṃsādiparissaye sato [M 1.0460] sampajāno adhivāseyya, adhivāsetvā ca bhāvanābalena mārabalaṃ vidhameyya.

There, 'like a great elephant at the forefront of battle' (nāgo saṅgāmasīseva) means: Just as a noble elephant, a nāga, in the battlefield endures the strikes of swords, spears, and javelins, and then crushes the enemy army, so too should a monk in the wilderness, in the great forest, in a wild forest dwelling, remain mindful and clearly aware while enduring the troubles of gadflies and other pests. Having endured them, he should then crush the power of Māra through the strength of meditation.

Yathā brahmāti yathā brahmā ekako cittappakoparahito jhānasukhena niccameva sukhito viharati tathā ekoti bhikkhupi eko adutiyo vivekasukhamanubrūhento sukhaṃ viharati. Ekassa sāmaññasukhaṃ paṇītanti hi vuttaṃ. Etena ekavihārī bhikkhu “brahmasamo”ti ovādaṃ deti. Yathā devo tathā duveti yathā devānaṃ antarantarā [P 2.0099] cittappakopopi siyā, tathā dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sahavāse ghaṭṭanāpi bhaveyyāti sadutiyavāsena bhikkhu “devasamo”ti vutto. Yathā gāmo tathā tayoti asmimeva pāṭhe tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sahavāso gāmavāsasadiso vivekavāso na hotīti adhippāyo[V 1.0391]. Kolāhalaṃ tatuttarinti tato tayato upari ca bahūnaṃ saṃvāso kolāhalaṃ uccāsaddamahāsaddamahājanasannipātasadiso, tasmā ekavihārinā bhavitabbanti adhippāyoti.

As Brahmā: Just as Brahmā, alone, free from mental agitation, dwells constantly happy with the bliss of jhāna, so too a monk, alone, without a second, cultivating the bliss of seclusion, dwells happily. For it is said, 'The bliss of the ascetic life for a solitary one is sublime.' By this, he gives the advice that a solitary monk is 'like Brahmā.' As a god, so two: Just as among gods there may occasionally be mental agitation, so too when two monks live together, there may be friction. Therefore, a monk who lives with a companion is said to be 'like a god.' As a village, so three: In this very passage, the meaning is that the dwelling of three monks together is like village life; it is not a life of seclusion. Commotion beyond that: Beyond three, the dwelling of many is commotion—like loud noise, great noise, a gathering of a great crowd. Therefore, one should be a solitary dweller—this is the meaning.

Yasojattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Verses of the Elder Yasoja is completed.

10. Sāṭimattiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sāṭimattiya

Ahu tuyhaṃ pure saddhāti āyasmato sāṭimattiyattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso tālavaṇṭaṃ adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā sāṭimattiyoti laddhanāmo vayappatto hetusampannatāya āraññakabhikkhūnaṃ santike pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.38.43-47) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Sāṭimattiya begins: 'Once you had faith.' What is its origin? He too, having made aspirations under past Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences, was born in a respectable family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and with a joyful mind offered a palm-leaf fan. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born in a brahmin family in the Magadha country. Named Sāṭimattiya, when he came of age, due to his potential, he went forth in the presence of the forest-dwelling monks. Practicing insight, he became one with the six supernormal knowledges. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Siddhatthassa [M 1.0461] bhagavato, tālavaṇṭamadāsahaṃ;

Sumanehi paṭicchannaṃ, dhārayāmi mahārahaṃ.

"To the Blessed One Siddhattha, I gave a palm-leaf fan, covered with sumana flowers, a thing of great worth."

“Catunnavutito kappe, tālavaṇṭamadāsahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, tālavaṇṭassidaṃ phalaṃ.

"Ninety-four eons ago, I gave a palm-leaf fan. I do not recall any bad rebirth; this is the fruit of the palm-leaf fan."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā bhikkhū ovadati anusāsati bahū ca satte dhammaṃ kathetvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpesi. Aññatarañca kulaṃ assaddhaṃ appasannaṃ saddhaṃ pasannaṃ akāsi. Tena tasmiṃ kule manussā there abhippasannā ahesuṃ. Tatthekā dārikā abhirūpā dassanīyā theraṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ sakkaccaṃ bhojanena parivisati. Athekadivasaṃ māro “evaṃ imassa ayaso vaḍḍhissati, appatiṭṭho bhavissatī”ti cintetvā therassa rūpena gantvā taṃ dārikaṃ hatthe aggahesi. Dārikā “nāyaṃ manussasamphasso”ti ca aññāsi, hatthañca muñcāpesi. Taṃ disvā gharajano there appasādaṃ janesi. Punadivase thero taṃ kāraṇaṃ anāvajjento taṃ gharaṃ agamāsi. Tattha manussā anādaraṃ akaṃsu. Thero taṃ kāraṇaṃ āvajjento mārassa kiriyaṃ disvā “tassa gīvāyaṃ kukkurakuṇapaṃ paṭimuñcatū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā [V 1.0392] tassa mocanatthaṃ upagatena mārena atītadivase katakiriyaṃ [P 2.0100] kathāpetvā taṃ tajjetvā vissajjesi. Taṃ disvā gharasāmiko “khamatha, bhante, accaya”nti khamāpetvā “ajjatagge ahameva, bhante, tumhe upaṭṭhahāmī”ti āha. Thero tassa dhammaṃ kathento –

Having become one endowed with the six higher knowledges, the Elder advised and instructed the monks. He also taught the Dhamma to many beings and established them in the refuges and the precepts. He transformed a certain family from being faithless and lacking confidence to being faithful and confident. The people in that family became deeply devoted to the elder. There was a young girl in that family, beautiful and lovely, who respectfully served the elder with food when he entered for alms. One day, Māra thought, "In this way, his fame will grow, and he will become unshakeable." So, taking the form of the elder, he went and grabbed the girl's hand. The girl realized, "This is not the touch of a human," and freed her hand. Seeing this, the household generated displeasure toward the elder. The next day, the elder, not adverting to the incident, went to that house. There, the people treated him with disrespect. Reflecting on the matter, the elder saw Māra's deed. He resolved, "Let a rotting dog carcass be fastened around his neck." When Māra came to be freed from it, the elder made him confess the deed he had done the previous day. After rebuking him, he released him. Seeing this, the master of the house begged forgiveness, saying, "Forgive me, venerable sir, for my transgression." Having sought pardon, he declared, "From today onward, I myself will attend to you, venerable sir." The elder then taught him the Dhamma, saying:

246.

246.

“Ahu tuyhaṃ pure saddhā, sā te ajja na vijjati;

Yaṃ tuyhaṃ tuyhamevetaṃ, natthi duccaritaṃ mama.

"You once had faith, but that is not found in you today; what is yours is yours alone, there is no wrongdoing on my part."

247.

247.

“Aniccā hi calā saddhā, evaṃ diṭṭhā hi sā mayā;

Rajjantipi virajjanti, tattha kiṃ jiyyate muni.

"Faith is impermanent and unsteady; thus have I seen it. People are attracted and then become disaffected; how is the sage diminished by that?"

248.

248.

“Paccati munino bhattaṃ, thokaṃ thokaṃ kule kule;

Piṇḍikāya carissāmi, atthi jaṅghabalaṃ mamā”ti. –

"The sage's food is cooked, a little in this family, a little in that. I shall wander for alms, for I have strength in my legs."

Tisso gāthā abhāsi.

He uttered these three verses.

Tattha [M 1.0462] ahu tuyhaṃ pure saddhā, sā te ajja na vijjatīti, upāsaka, ito pubbe tava mayi “ayyo dhammacārī samacārī”tiādinā saddhā ahosi, sā saddhā te tava ajja idāni na upalabbhati. Tasmā yaṃ tuyhaṃ tuyhamevetanti catupaccayadānaṃ, tuyhameva etaṃ hotu, na tena mayhaṃ attho, sammā pasannacittena hi dānaṃ nāma dātabbanti adhippāyo. Atha vā yaṃ tuyhaṃ tuyhamevetanti yaṃ tava mayi ajja agāravaṃ pavattaṃ, taṃ tuyhameva, tassa phalaṃ tayā eva paccanubhavitabbaṃ, na mayāti attho. Natthi duccaritaṃ mamāti mama pana duccaritaṃ nāma natthi maggeneva duccaritahetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā.

Therein, 'Previously, you had faith, but today it is not found' means: O lay follower, before this you had faith in me, thinking, 'This venerable one practices the Dhamma, lives rightly,' and so on. That faith of yours is now no longer found. Therefore, 'what is yours, let it be yours' means: this gift of the four requisites, let it be yours alone; I have no need of it. For a gift should be given with a rightly serene mind—this is the intended meaning. Or else, 'what is yours, let it be yours' means that whatever disrespect toward me has now occurred on your part, that is yours alone. You yourself must experience its fruit, not I—this is the meaning. 'There is no misconduct on my part,' for on my part there is no misconduct whatsoever, because the defilements, the causes of misconduct, have been utterly cut off by the path itself.

Aniccā hi calā saddhāti yasmā pothujjanikā saddhā aniccā ekantikā na hoti, tato eva calā assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍaṃ viya, thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇukaṃ viya ca anavaṭṭhitā. Evaṃ diṭṭhā hi sā mayāti evaṃ bhūtā ca sā saddhā mayā tayi diṭṭhā paccakkhato viditā. Rajjantipi virajjantīti evaṃ tassā anavaṭṭhitattā eva ime sattā kadāci katthaci mittasanthavavasena rajjanti sinehampi karonti, kadāci virajjanti virattacittā honti. Tattha kiṃ jiyyate munīti tasmiṃ puthujjanānaṃ rajjane virajjane ca muni pabbajito kiṃ jiyyati, kā tassa hānīti attho.

'For faith is impermanent and unsteady' means that because the faith of ordinary people is impermanent and not absolute, it is therefore unsteady and unstable, like a pot placed on a horse's back or a stake driven into a heap of chaff. 'Thus have I seen it' means that such faith has been seen and directly known by me in you. 'They are attracted and also repelled' means that because of its instability, these beings are sometimes attracted and form affection somewhere on account of friendship, and at other times they are repelled, their minds becoming averse. 'Therein, what does the sage lose?' means: in the attraction and repulsion of ordinary people, what does the sage, the renunciant, lose? What is his loss? That is the meaning.

“Sace mama paccaye na gaṇhatha, kathaṃ tumhe yāpethā”ti evaṃ mā cintayīti dassento “paccatī”ti gāthamāha. Tassattho munino pabbajitassa bhattaṃ nāma kule kule anugharaṃ divase divase [V 1.0393] thokaṃ thokaṃ paccate, na ca tuyhaṃ eva gehe. Piṇḍikāya carissāmi, atthi jaṅghabalaṃ mamāti atthi me jaṅghabalaṃ, nāhaṃ obhaggajaṅgho na khañjo na ca pādarogī, tasmā [P 2.0101] piṇḍikāya missakabhikkhāya carissāmi, “yathāpi bhamaro puppha”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 49; netti. 123) satthārā vuttanayena piṇḍāya caritvā yāpessāmīti dasseti.

To show that one should not think, 'If you do not accept my requisites, how will you maintain yourself?', he spoke the verse beginning 'Paccati'. Its meaning is: For the renunciant sage, food is cooked little by little, day by day, in family after family, from house to house, and not only in your house. 'I will wander for alms-food; I have strength in my shins' means: I have strength in my shins. I am not one with broken shins, nor lame, nor afflicted with a disease of the feet. Therefore, I will wander for alms-food, for mixed alms. He shows: 'In the manner spoken by the Teacher, beginning with "Just as a bee from a flower...", having wandered for alms, I will maintain myself.'

Sāṭimattiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Sāṭimattiya is completed.

11. Upālittheragāthāvaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Upāli

Saddhāya [M 1.0463] abhinikkhammāti āyasmato upālittherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulaghare nibbatto ekadivasaṃ satthu dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ vinayadharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā adhikārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi. So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kappakagehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, upālītissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto anuruddhādīnaṃ channaṃ khattiyānaṃ pasādako hutvā tathāgate anupiyambavane viharante pabbajanatthāya nikkhamantehi chahi khattiyehi saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā pabbaji. Tassa pabbajjāvidhānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva (cūḷava. 330).

'Having gone forth in faith...' are the verses of the Venerable Elder Upāli. What is their origin? During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this one was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, he saw the Teacher placing a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among the masters of the Vinaya. Having performed a foundational act of merit, he aspired to that very rank. Having done good for his entire life and wandered among devas and humans, during this Buddha-era he took rebirth-linking in a barber's house. They gave him the name Upāli. When he came of age, he became the attendant barber to the six Khattiyas, including Anuruddha. When the Tathāgata was dwelling in the Anupiya mango grove, he went forth together with the six Khattiyas who were departing for the purpose of renunciation, and he too was ordained. The details of his ordination are found in the Pāli Canon itself (Cūḷavagga 330).

So pabbajitvā upasampanno satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, araññavāsaṃ anujānāthā”ti āha. Bhikkhu tava araññe vasantassa ekameva dhuraṃ vaḍḍhissati, amhākaṃ pana santike vasantassa ganthadhurañca vipassanādhurañca paripūressatīti. Thero satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.1.441-595) –

Having gone forth and received the higher ordination, he took a meditation subject from the Teacher and said, 'Venerable sir, please permit me to dwell in the forest.' The Teacher replied, 'Bhikkhu, if you dwell in the forest, only one yoke will develop for you; but if you dwell near us, you will fulfill both the yoke of the scriptures and the yoke of insight.' The Elder, accepting the Teacher's words and undertaking the practice of insight, before long attained Arahantship. Therefore it was said in the Apadāna:

“Nagare haṃsavatiyā, sujāto nāma brāhmaṇo;

Asītikoṭinicayo, pahūtadhanadhaññavā.

"In the city of Haṃsavatī, there was a brahmin named Sujāta, who had amassed eighty crores and was possessed of abundant wealth and grain."

“Ajjhāyako mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Lakkhaṇe itihāse ca, sadhamme pāramiṃ gato.

"A reciter and master of mantras, one who had gone to the further shore of the three Vedas; in the sciences of signs and legends, and in his own doctrine, he had reached perfection."

“Paribbājā ekasikhā, gotamā buddhasāvakā;

Carakā tāpasā ceva, caranti mahiyā tadā.

"Wandering mendicants with single topknots, sages of the Gotama clan, awakened disciples, Caraka ascetics, and hermits too, roamed the earth at that time."

“Tepi [V 1.0394] maṃ parivārenti, brāhmaṇo vissuto iti;

Bahujjano maṃ pūjeti, nāhaṃ pūjemi kiñcanaṃ.

"They too surrounded me, saying, 'He is a renowned brahmin.' Many people honored me, but I honored no one at all."

“Pūjārahaṃ na passāmi, mānatthaddho ahaṃ tadā;

Buddhoti vacanaṃ natthi, tāva nuppajjate jino.

"I saw no one worthy of honor; I was stiff with conceit at that time. The very word 'Buddha' was not to be heard, for the Conqueror had not yet arisen."

“Accayena ahorattaṃ, padumuttaranāmako;

Sabbaṃ tamaṃ vinodetvā, loke uppajji cakkhumā.

"With the passing of days and nights, the one named Padumuttara, having dispelled all darkness, the One with Vision, arose in the world."

“Vitthārike [M 1.0464] bāhujaññe, puthubhūte ca sāsane;

Upāgami tadā buddho, nagaraṃ haṃsasavhayaṃ.

"When the Dispensation had become widespread, known to many, and extensive, the Buddha then approached the city named Haṃsa."

“Pitu atthāya so buddho, dhammaṃ desesi cakkhumā;

Tena kālena parisā, samantā yojanaṃ tadā.

"For the benefit of his father, that Buddha, the One with Vision, taught the Dhamma. At that time, the assembly extended for a yojana all around."

“Sammato manujānaṃ so, sunando nāma tāpaso;

Yāvatā buddhaparisā, pupphehacchādayī tadā.

"Esteemed among humans was he, the ascetic named Sunanda; as far as the Buddha's assembly extended, he then covered it with flowers."

“Catusaccaṃ pakāsente, seṭṭhe ca pupphamaṇḍape;

Koṭisatasahassānaṃ, dhammābhisamayo ahu.

"While he was proclaiming the Four Truths in the excellent flower pavilion, for a hundred thousand koṭis of beings there was a breakthrough to the Dhamma."

“Sattarattindivaṃ buddho, vassetvā dhammavuṭṭhiyo;

Aṭṭhame divase patte, sunandaṃ kittayī jino.

"For seven nights and days, the Buddha, having rained down the rain of Dhamma, when the eighth day arrived, the Conqueror extolled Sunanda."

“Devaloke manusse vā, saṃsaranto ayaṃ bhave;

Sabbesaṃ pavaro hutvā, bhavesu saṃsarissati.

"Wandering in existence, whether in the world of devas or of humans, this one, having become the foremost of all, will continue to wander through states of being."

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

"After a hundred thousand aeons, one born of the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama by lineage, will arise in the world."

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Mantāṇiputto puṇṇoti, hessati satthu sāvako.

"An heir to his Dhamma, a true-born son created by the Dhamma, Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī, will be a disciple of that Teacher."

“Evaṃ kittayi sambuddho, sunandaṃ tāpasaṃ tadā;

Hāsayanto janaṃ sabbaṃ, dassayanto sakaṃ balaṃ.

"Thus did the Fully Enlightened One extol the ascetic Sunanda at that time, causing all the people to rejoice while displaying his own power."

“Katañjalī namassanti, sunandaṃ tāpasaṃ janā;

Buddhe kāraṃ karitvāna, sodhesi gatimattano.

"With palms joined in reverence, the people paid homage to the ascetic Sunanda. Having performed an act of reverence for the Buddha, he purified his own future destination."

“Tattha me ahu saṅkappo, sutvāna munino vacaṃ;

Ahampi kāraṃ kassāmi, yathā passāmi gotamaṃ.

"There, having heard the Sage's words, a resolve arose in me: 'I too shall perform such an act, so that I may see Gotama.'"

“Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, kiriyaṃ cintayiṃ mama;

Kyāhaṃ kammaṃ ācarāmi, puññakkhette anuttare.

"Having reflected thus, I considered what action I should take: 'What deed should I perform in this unsurpassed field of merit?'"

“Ayañca pāṭhiko bhikkhu, sabbapāṭhissa sāsane;

Vinaye agganikkhitto, taṃ ṭhānaṃ patthaye ahaṃ.

"This bhikkhu, a master of the texts, foremost in all texts of the Dispensation, preeminent in the Vinaya—that is the position I aspire to."

“Idaṃ [M 1.0465][V 1.0395] me amitaṃ bhogaṃ, akkhobhaṃ sāgarūpamaṃ;

Tena bhogena buddhassa, ārāmaṃ māpaye ahaṃ.

"This wealth of mine is immeasurable, unshakable, like the ocean; with this wealth, I shall have a monastery built for the Buddha."

“Sobhanaṃ nāma ārāmaṃ, nagarassa puratthato;

Kiṇitvā satasahassena, saṅghārāmaṃ amāpayiṃ.

"A monastery named Sobhana, to the east of the city, I purchased for a hundred thousand and had it built as a monastery for the Sangha."

“Kūṭāgāre ca pāsāde, maṇḍape hammiye guhā;

Caṅkame sukate katvā, saṅghārāmaṃ amāpayiṃ.

"Having had pinnacled halls, terraced buildings, pavilions, mansions, caves, and well-made walkways constructed, I had the monastery for the Sangha built."

“Jantāgharaṃ aggisālaṃ, atho udakamāḷakaṃ;

Nhānagharaṃ māpayitvā, bhikkhusaṅghassadāsahaṃ.

"A steam-bath house, a fire hall, and also a water chamber and a bathing house—having had these built, I gave them to the Sangha of bhikkhus."

“Āsandiyo pīṭhake ca, paribhoge ca bhājane;

Ārāmikañca bhesajjaṃ, sabbametaṃ adāsahaṃ.

"Long chairs and stools, vessels for use, monastery attendants, and medicine—all this I gave."

“Ārakkhaṃ paṭṭhapetvāna, pākāraṃ kārayiṃ daḷhaṃ;

Mā naṃ koci viheṭhesi, santacittāna tādinaṃ.

"Having established protection, I had a strong wall built, so that no one might harass them—the steadfast ones of peaceful mind."

“Satasahassenāvāsaṃ, saṅghārāme amāpayiṃ;

Vepullaṃ taṃ māpayitvā, sambuddhaṃ upanāmayiṃ.

“A dwelling worth a hundred thousand, I had built in the monastery. Having had that vast structure built, I presented it to the Sambuddha.

“Niṭṭhāpito mayārāmo, sampaṭiccha tuvaṃ muni;

Niyyādessāmi taṃ vīra, adhivāsehi cakkhuma.

“My monastery is now complete, accept it, O Sage; I will dedicate it to you, O Hero, consent, O One with the Eye.

“Padumuttaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama saṅkappamaññāya, adhivāsesi nāyako.

“Padumuttara, the Knower of the World, the Recipient of offerings, understanding my intention, the Leader consented.

“Adhivāsanamaññāya, sabbaññussa mahesino;

Bhojanaṃ paṭiyādetvā, kālamārocayiṃ ahaṃ.

“Understanding the consent of the All-Knowing One, the Great Sage, I prepared the meal and announced the time.

“Ārocitamhi kālamhi, padumuttaranāyako;

Khīṇāsavasahassehi, ārāmaṃ me upāgami.

“When the time was announced, Padumuttara, the Leader, with thousands of arahants, came to my monastery.

“Nisinnaṃ kālamaññāya, annapānena tappayiṃ;

Bhuttāviṃ kālamaññāya, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

“Knowing the time they were seated, I satisfied them with food and drink; knowing the time when he had eaten, I spoke this utterance:

“Kīto satasahassena, tattakeneva kārito;

Sobhano nāma ārāmo, sampaṭiccha tuvaṃ muni.

“‘Purchased for a hundred thousand, and built for that same amount, is the monastery named Sobhana; accept it, O Sage.’

“Iminārāmadānena[M 1.0466], cetanāpaṇidhīhi ca;

Bhave nibbattamānohaṃ, labhāmi mama patthitaṃ.

“Through this gift of a monastery, and through my intentions and aspirations, may I, being reborn in future existences, attain my desired aim.

“Paṭiggahetvā sambuddho, saṅghārāmaṃ sumāpitaṃ;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“Having accepted the well-built monastery, the Sambuddha, seated in the midst of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, spoke this utterance:

“Yo so buddhassa pādāsi, saṅghārāmaṃ sumāpitaṃ;

Tamahaṃ kittayissāmi, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

“‘He who gave to the Buddha a well-built monastery, I shall praise him; listen to me as I speak.

“Hatthī [V 1.0396] assā rathā pattī, senā ca caturaṅginī;

Parivāressantimaṃ niccaṃ, saṅghārāmassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“‘Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, a fourfold army, will always surround him—this is the fruit of a monastery.

“Saṭṭhi tūrasahassāni, bheriyo samalaṅkatā;

Parivāressantimaṃ niccaṃ, saṅghārāmassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“‘Sixty thousand musical instruments and well-adorned drums will always surround him—this is the fruit of a monastery.

“Chaḷasītisahassāni, nāriyo samalaṅkatā;

Vicittavatthābharaṇā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā.

“‘Eighty-six thousand women, well-adorned, with varied clothes and ornaments, wearing jeweled earrings,

“Aḷārapamhā hasulā, susaññā tanumajjhimā;

Parivāressantimaṃ niccaṃ, saṅghārāmassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“‘with curved eyelashes, smiling, well-proportioned, and slender-waisted, will always surround him—this is the fruit of a monastery.

“Tiṃsakappasahassāni, devaloke ramissati;

Sahassakkhattuṃ devindo, devarajjaṃ karissati.

“‘For thirty thousand aeons, he will rejoice in the deva world; a thousand times he will be the king of devas, and he will exercise kingship over the devas.

“Devarājena pattabbaṃ, sabbaṃ paṭilabhissati;

Anūnabhogo hutvāna, devarajjaṃ karissati.

“‘All that is to be attained by a king of devas, he will obtain; having become one of undiminished enjoyments, he will exercise kingship over the devas.

“Sahassakkhattuṃ cakkavattī, rājā raṭṭhe bhavissati.

Pathabyā rajjaṃ vipulaṃ, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyaṃ.

“‘A thousand times he will be a wheel-turning king in the land. His vast kingdom on earth will be beyond calculation.

“Kappasatasahassamhi, okkākakulasambhavo;

Gotamo nāma gottena, satthā loke bhavissati.

“‘In a hundred thousand aeons from now, born of the Okkāka clan, a Teacher named Gotama by clan will be in the world.

“Tassa dhammesu dāyādo, oraso dhammanimmito;

Upāli nāma nāmena, hessati satthu sāvako.

“He will be the heir in the Dhamma, a true son, Dhamma-created; by the name Upāli, he will be a disciple of the Teacher.

“Vinaye pāramiṃ patvā, ṭhānāṭhāne ca kovido;

Jinasāsanaṃ dhārento, viharissatināsavo.

“Having attained perfection in the Vinaya, skilled in what is proper and improper, he will dwell free from taints, maintaining the Victor’s teaching.

“Sabbametaṃ [M 1.0467] abhiññāya, gotamo sakyapuṅgavo;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, etadagge ṭhapessati.

“Having fully known all this, Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans, seated in the Sangha of monks, will establish him in the foremost position.

“Aparimeyyupādāya, patthemi tava sāsanaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo.

“On account of the immeasurable, I aspire to your dispensation; that goal has been attained by me—the destruction of all fetters.

“Yathā sūlāvuto poso, rājadaṇḍena tajjito;

Sūle sātaṃ avindanto, parimuttiṃva icchati.

“Just as a man impaled on a stake, terrified by the king’s punishment, finds no pleasure on the stake and longs for release,

“Tathevāhaṃ mahāvīra, bhavadaṇḍena tajjito;

Kammasūlāvuto santo, pipāsāvedanaṭṭito.

“So too, O great hero, terrified by the rod of becoming, I am impaled on the stake of kamma, afflicted by the pain of thirst.

“Bhave sātaṃ na vindāmi, ḍayhanto tīhi aggibhi;

Parimuttiṃ gavesāmi, yathāpi rājadaṇḍito.

“I find no satisfaction in existence, burning with the three fires; I seek release, like one punished by the king.

“Yathā visādo puriso, visena paripīḷito;

Agadaṃ so gaveseyya, visaghātāyupālanaṃ.

“Just as a man suffering from poison, afflicted by the venom, would seek an antidote for destroying the poison and for his protection.

“Gavesamāno [V 1.0397] passeyya, agadaṃ visaghātakaṃ;

Taṃ pivitvā sukhī assa, visamhā parimuttiyā.

“Searching, he might find an antidote that destroys poison; having drunk it, he would be happy, through release from the venom.

“Tathevāhaṃ mahāvīra, yathā visahato naro;

Sampīḷito avijjāya, saddhammāgadamesahaṃ.

“So too, Great Hero, like a man afflicted by poison, I was oppressed by ignorance and sought the antidote of the true Dhamma.

“Dhammāgadaṃ gavesanto, addakkhiṃ sakyasāsanaṃ;

Aggaṃ sabbosadhānaṃ taṃ, sabbasallavinodanaṃ.

“Searching for the Dhamma-antidote, I saw the Sakyan’s teaching—the foremost of all medicines, which removes all darts.

“Dhammosadhaṃ pivitvāna, visaṃ sabbaṃ samūhaniṃ;

Ajarāmaraṃ sītibhāvaṃ, nibbānaṃ phassayiṃ ahaṃ.

“Having drunk the Dhamma-medicine, I have uprooted all poison; I have experienced Nibbāna, the ageless, deathless, cool state.

“Yathā bhūtaṭṭito poso, bhūtaggāhena pīḷito;

Bhūtavejjaṃ gaveseyya, bhūtasmā parimuttiyā.

“Just as a man afflicted by a spirit, oppressed by spirit-possession, would seek a spirit-doctor for release from that spirit,

“Gavesamāno passeyya, bhūtavijjāsu kovidaṃ;

Tassa so vihane bhūtaṃ, samūlañca vināsaye.

“Searching, he might find one skilled in spirit-lore; that one would expel the spirit from him and destroy it root and all.

“Tathevāhaṃ mahāvīra, tamaggāhena pīḷito;

Ñāṇālokaṃ gavesāmi, tamato parimuttiyā.

“So too, O great hero, oppressed by the grip of darkness, I seek the light of knowledge for release from that darkness.

“Athaddasaṃ [M 1.0468] sakyamuniṃ, kilesatamasodhanaṃ;

So me tamaṃ vinodesi, bhūtavejjova bhūtakaṃ.

Then I saw the Sakyan Sage, the purifier of the darkness of defilements; he dispelled my darkness, like a spirit-doctor dispels a spirit.

“Saṃsārasotaṃ sañchindiṃ, taṇhāsotaṃ nivārayiṃ;

Bhavaṃ ugghāṭayiṃ sabbaṃ, bhūtavejjova mūlato.

I have cut the stream of saṃsāra, I have checked the stream of craving; I have uprooted all becoming, like a spirit-doctor from the root.

“Garuḷo yathā opatati, pannagaṃ bhakkhamattano;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, vikkhobheti mahāsaraṃ.

Just as a Garuḷa swoops down upon a serpent, its own prey, and stirs up the great lake for a hundred yojanas all around,

“Pannagaṃ so gahetvāna, adhosīsaṃ viheṭhayaṃ;

Ādāya so pakkamati, yenakāmaṃ vihaṅgamo.

seizing the serpent, tormenting it head-downwards, the bird carries it off, going wherever it wishes.

“Tathevāhaṃ mahāvīra, yathāpi garuḷo balī;

Asaṅkhataṃ gavesanto, dose vikkhālayiṃ ahaṃ.

Just so, O great hero, like the mighty Garuḷa, seeking the Unconditioned, I washed away my stains.

“Diṭṭho ahaṃ dhammavaraṃ, santipadamanuttaraṃ;

Ādāya viharāmetaṃ, garuḷo pannagaṃ yathā.

I have seen the excellent Dhamma, the unsurpassed state of peace; taking it up, I abide, as a Garuḷa does a serpent.

“Āsāvatī nāma latā, jātā cittalatāvane;

Tassā vassasahassena, ekaṃ nibbattate phalaṃ.

A creeper named Āsāvatī grows in the Cittalatā grove; after a thousand years, a single fruit is produced from it.

“Taṃ devā payirupāsanti, tāvadūraphale sati;

Devānaṃ sā piyā evaṃ, āsāvatī latuttamā.

The gods attend upon it, even while its fruit is still far off; thus is that supreme creeper, Āsāvatī, dear to the gods.

“Satasahassupādāya, tāhaṃ paricare muni;

Sāyaṃ pātaṃ namassāmi, devā āsāvatiṃ yathā.

For one hundred thousand aeons, I attended upon that Sage; evening and morning I pay homage, as the gods do to Āsāvatī.

“Avañjhā [V 1.0398] pāricariyā, amoghā ca namassanā;

Dūrāgatampi maṃ santaṃ, khaṇoyaṃ na virādhayi.

My service was not in vain, and my homage was not fruitless; though I had come from afar, this moment was not missed by me.

“Paṭisandhiṃ na passāmi, vicinanto bhave ahaṃ;

Nirūpadhi vippamutto, upasanto carāmahaṃ.

Searching through states of becoming, I see no further rebirth; without substrate, completely liberated, being at peace, I live.

“Yathāpi padumaṃ nāma, sūriyaraṃsena pupphati;

Tathevāhaṃ mahāvīra, buddharaṃsena pupphito.

Just as a lotus blooms by the rays of the sun, so too, O Great Hero, have I been brought to bloom by the rays of the Buddha.

“Yathā balākayonimhi, na vijjati pumo sadā;

Meghesu gajjamānesu, gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti tā sadā.

Just as among the species of herons a male is not always present, yet when the clouds rumble, they always conceive.

“Cirampi [M 1.0469] gabbhaṃ dhārenti, yāva megho na gajjati;

Bhārato parimuccanti, yadā megho pavassati.

For a long time they carry the embryo, as long as the cloud does not thunder; they are released from their burden when the cloud pours down rain.

“Padumuttarabuddhassa, dhammameghena gajjato;

Saddena dhammameghassa, dhammagabbhaṃ agaṇhahaṃ.

From the Buddha Padumuttara thundering with the cloud of Dhamma, by the sound of that Dhamma-cloud, I conceived the Dhamma-embryo.

“Satasahassupādāya, puññagabbhaṃ dharemahaṃ;

Nappamuccāmi bhārato, dhammamegho na gajjati.

For one hundred thousand aeons I carried the embryo of merit; I was not released from the burden, as the Dhamma-cloud did not thunder.

“Yadā tuvaṃ sakyamuni, ramme kapilavatthave;

Gajjasi dhammameghena, bhārato parimuccahaṃ.

But when you, O Sage of the Sakyans, thundered with the cloud of Dhamma in delightful Kapilavatthu, I was released from my burden.

“Suññataṃ animittañca, tathāppaṇihitampi ca;

Caturo ca phale sabbe, dhammevaṃ vijanayiṃ ahaṃ.

Emptiness, the signless, and the desireless as well; thus in the Dhamma I brought forth all four fruits.

“Aparimeyyupādāya, patthemi tava sāsanaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, santipadamanuttaraṃ.

For an immeasurable time I have aspired to your dispensation; that aim has been attained by me: the unsurpassed state of peace.

“Vinaye pāramiṃ patto, yathāpi pāṭhiko isi;

Na me samasamo atthi, dhāremi sāsanaṃ ahaṃ.

I have reached perfection in the Vinaya, like a sage who is a reciter; there is no one equal to me, and I uphold the dispensation.

“Vinaye khandhake cāpi, tikacchede ca pañcake;

Ettha me vimati natthi, akkhare byañjanepi vā.

In the Vinaya and also in the Khandhakas, in the sections of three and in the section of five, in these I have no doubt, whether in a letter or a consonant.

“Niggahe paṭikamme ca, ṭhānāṭhāne ca kovido;

Osāraṇe vuṭṭhāpane, sabbattha pāramiṃ gato.

I am skilled in censure and in rehabilitation, in what is a proper case and what is not; in reinstatement and in rehabilitation from an offense, in all these I have reached perfection.

“Vinaye khandhake vāpi, nikkhipitvā padaṃ ahaṃ;

Ubhato viniveṭhetvā, rasato osareyyahaṃ.

Whether in the Vinaya or the Khandhakas, having set down a topic, I can unravel it from both sides and penetrate to its essence.

“Niruttiyā sukusalo, atthānatthe ca kovido;

Anaññātaṃ mayā natthi, ekaggo satthu sāsane.

Highly skilled in language, expert in what is and is not the meaning, there is nothing unknown to me; I am single-minded in the Teacher’s dispensation.

“Rūpadakkho ahaṃ ajja, sakyaputtassa sāsane;

Kaṅkhaṃ sabbaṃ vinodemi, chindāmi sabbasaṃsayaṃ.

Today, in the dispensation of the Sakyan son, I am skilled in discerning the case; I dispel all doubt, I cut off all uncertainty.

“Padaṃ [V 1.0399] anupadañcāpi, akkharañcāpi byañjanaṃ;

Nidāne pariyosāne, sabbattha kovido ahaṃ.

In the word and what follows the word, in the letter and the consonant, in the introduction and the conclusion—in all these, I am skilled.

“Yathāpi [M 1.0470] rājā balavā, niggaṇhitvā parantape;

Vijinitvāna saṅgāmaṃ, nagaraṃ tattha māpaye.

Just as a powerful king, a scorcher of foes, having subdued them and conquered in battle, might have a city built there—

“Pākāraṃ parikhañcāpi, esikaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ;

Aṭṭālake ca vividhe, kāraye nagare bahū.

He would have walls and a moat built, gate pillars and gatehouses, and in the city, many and various watchtowers.

“Siṅghāṭakaṃ caccarañca, suvibhattantarāpaṇaṃ;

Kārayeyya sabhaṃ tattha, atthānatthavinicchayaṃ.

He would have crossroads and squares constructed, and well-laid-out market streets; and there, a council hall for judging what is beneficial and what is not.

“Nigghātatthaṃ amittānaṃ, chiddāchiddañca jānituṃ;

Balakāyassa rakkhāya, senāpaccaṃ ṭhapeti so.

For the destruction of enemies, to know its strengths and weaknesses, and for the protection of the army, he appoints a general.

“Ārakkhatthāya bhaṇḍassa, nidhānakusalaṃ naraṃ;

Mā me bhaṇḍaṃ vinassīti, bhaṇḍarakkhaṃ ṭhapeti so.

For the protection of the treasury, thinking, ‘May my goods not be lost,’ he appoints a man skilled in storing them as treasurer.

“Mamatto hoti yo rañño, vuddhiṃ yassa ca icchati;

Tassādhikaraṇaṃ deti, mittassa paṭipajjituṃ.

To one who is devoted to the king and desires his prosperity, he gives authority, to attend to matters as a friend.

“Uppātesu nimittesu, lakkhaṇesu ca kovidaṃ;

Ajjhāyakaṃ mantadharaṃ, porohicce ṭhapeti so.

He appoints as chaplain one who is skilled in portents, omens, and signs, a scholar and a bearer of sacred verses.

“Etehaṅgehi sampanno, khattiyoti pavuccati;

Sadā rakkhanti rājānaṃ, cakkavākova dukkhitaṃ.

Endowed with these components, he is called a Khattiya; they always protect the king, just as a ruddy goose protects its distressed mate.

“Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, hatāmittova khattiyo;

Sadevakassa lokassa, dhammarājāti vuccati.

In the same way, O Great Hero, like a warrior who has slain his foes, you are called the King of Dhamma for the world with its gods.

“Titthiye nihanitvāna, mārañcāpi sasenakaṃ;

Tamandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā, dhammanagaraṃ amāpayi.

Having struck down the sectarians, and Māra with his army, and having dispelled that darkness, you have created the City of Dhamma.

“Sīlaṃ pākārakaṃ tattha, ñāṇaṃ te dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ;

Saddhā te esikā vīra, dvārapālo ca saṃvaro.

Therein, your virtue is the city wall, your knowledge the gatehouse; your faith is the gate pillar, O Hero, and your restraint is the gatekeeper.

“Satipaṭṭhānamaṭṭālaṃ, paññā te caccaraṃ mune;

Iddhipādañca siṅghāṭaṃ, dhammavīthi sumāpitā.

The foundations of mindfulness are the watchtower, your wisdom is the city square, O Sage; the bases of psychic power are the crossroads, and the Dhamma-street is well-laid-out.

“Suttantaṃ abhidhammañca, vinayañcāpi kevalaṃ;

Navaṅgaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, esā dhammasabhā tava.

The Suttanta, the Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya in its entirety—the nine-limbed word of the Buddha—this is your Dhamma council hall.

“Suññataṃ [M 1.0471] animittañca, vihārañcappaṇīhitaṃ;

Āneñjañca nirodho ca, esā dhammakuṭī tava.

The dwelling in emptiness, the dwelling in the signless, and the dwelling in the desireless, the imperturbable, and cessation: this is your Dhamma-abode.

“Paññāya aggo nikkhitto, paṭibhāne ca kovido;

Sāriputtoti nāmena, dhammasenāpatī tava.

Appointed as foremost in wisdom, skilled in ready speech, the one known by the name Sāriputta is your General of the Dhamma.

“Cutūpapātakusalo[V 1.0400], iddhiyā pāramiṃ gato;

Kolito nāma nāmena, porohicco tavaṃ mune.

Skilled in the passing away and rebirth of beings, having reached the perfection of psychic power, the one known by the name Kolita is your chaplain, O Sage.

“Porāṇakavaṃsadharo, uggatejo durāsado;

Dhutavādīguṇenaggo, akkhadasso tavaṃ mune.

Bearer of the ancient lineage, of fierce energy and hard to approach, foremost in the quality of ascetic practice—he is your judge, O Sage.

“Bahussuto dhammadharo, sabbapāṭhī ca sāsane;

Ānando nāma nāmena, dhammārakkho tavaṃ mune.

Greatly learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a reciter of all the texts in the dispensation, the one named Ānanda is your guardian of the Dhamma, O Sage.

“Ete sabbe atikkamma, pamesi bhagavā mamaṃ;

Vinicchayaṃ me pādāsi, vinaye viññudesitaṃ.

Surpassing all of these, the Blessed One appointed me; you gave to me the judgment in the Vinaya taught by the wise.

“Yo koci vinaye pañhaṃ, pucchati buddhasāvako;

Tattha me cintanā natthi, taññevatthaṃ kathemahaṃ.

Whatever disciple of the Buddha asks a question concerning the Vinaya, for me there is no deliberation; I speak on that very matter.

“Yāvatā buddhakhettamhi, ṭhapetvā taṃ mahāmuni;

Vinaye mādiso natthi, kuto bhiyyo bhavissati.

Throughout the entire Buddha-field, setting you aside, O Great Sage, there is no one like me in the Vinaya; whence could there be one who is superior?

“Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, evaṃ gajjati gotamo;

Upālissa samo natthi, vinaye khandhakesu ca.

Having sat down in the Saṅgha of monks, thus Gotama roars: 'There is none equal to Upāli in the Vinaya, nor in the Khandhakas.'

“Yāvatā buddhabhaṇitaṃ, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ;

Vinayogadhaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ, vinayamūlapassino.

Whatever has been spoken by the Buddha, the nine-fold teaching of the Teacher, all of it is included in the Vinaya for one who sees the Vinaya as the root.

“Mama kammaṃ saritvāna, gotamo sakyapuṅgavo;

Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvā, etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.

Recalling my deeds, Gotama, the chief of the Sakyans, seated in the Saṅgha of monks, established me in the foremost position.

“Satasahassupādāya, imaṃ ṭhānaṃ apatthayiṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, vinaye pāramiṃ gato.

For a hundred thousand aeons, I have aspired to this position. That goal of mine has been attained; I have reached perfection in the Vinaya.

“Sakyānaṃ nandijanano, kappako āsahaṃ pure;

Vijahitvāna taṃ jātiṃ, putto jāto mahesino.

I, who brought joy to the Sakyans, was formerly a barber. Having abandoned that birth, I have become a son of the Great Sage.

“Ito [M 1.0472] dutiyake kappe, añjaso nāma khattiyo;

Anantatejo amitayaso, bhūmipālo mahaddhano.

In the second aeon from this one, there was a khattiya named Añjasa, of infinite power and immeasurable fame, a ruler of the earth, of great wealth.

“Tassa rañño ahaṃ putto, candano nāma khattiyo;

Jātimadenupatthaddho, yasabhogamadena ca.

I was the son of that king, a khattiya named Candana, arrogant with the pride of birth, and with the pride of fame and possessions.

“Nāgasatasahassāni, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā;

Tidhāpabhinnā mātaṅgā, parivārenti maṃ sadā.

A hundred thousand elephants, adorned with all ornaments, great elephants with ichor flowing from three places, always surround me.

“Sabalehi paretohaṃ, uyyānaṃ gantukāmako;

Āruyha sirikaṃ nāgaṃ, nagarā nikkhamiṃ tadā.

Surrounded by my forces, desiring to go to the park, I mounted the elephant Sirika and then departed from the city.

“Caraṇena ca sampanno, guttadvāro susaṃvuto;

Devalo nāma sambuddho, āgacchi purato mama.

Endowed with good conduct, with guarded sense-doors, well-restrained, the Perfectly Awakened One named Devala came before me.

“Pesetvā [V 1.0401] sirikaṃ nāgaṃ, buddhaṃ āsādayiṃ tadā;

Tato sañjātakopo so, nāgo nuddharate padaṃ.

Having sent forth the elephant Sirika, I then assailed the Buddha. Then, with anger arisen, that elephant would not lift its foot.

“Nāgaṃ ruṇṇamanaṃ disvā, buddhe kodhaṃ akāsahaṃ;

Vihesayitvā sambuddhaṃ, uyyānaṃ agamāsahaṃ.

Seeing the elephant with a distressed mind, I became angry at the Buddha; having harassed the Perfectly Awakened One, I went to the park.

“Sātaṃ tattha na vindāmi, siro pajjalito yathā;

Pariḷāhena ḍayhāmi, macchova baḷisādako.

I found no pleasure there, as if my head were ablaze; I am consumed by torment, like a fish that has taken the hook.

“Sasāgarantā pathavī, ādittā viya hoti me;

Pitu santikupāgamma, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

The earth, with its ocean boundaries, seems to me as if ablaze; having approached my father, I spoke this word:

“Āsīvisaṃva kupitaṃ, aggikkhandhaṃva āgataṃ;

Mattaṃva kuñjaraṃ dantiṃ, yaṃ sayambhumasādayiṃ.

It was like assailing an angered viper, like an advancing mass of fire, like a rutting, tusked elephant—that Self-Awakened One whom I assailed.

“Āsādito mayā buddho, ghoro uggatapo jino;

Purā sabbe vinassāma, khamāpessāma taṃ muniṃ.

The Buddha has been assailed by me, the fierce one of intense asceticism, the Victor. Before we all perish, let us ask forgiveness of that sage.

“No ce taṃ nijjhāpessāma, attadantaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Orena sattadivasā, raṭṭhaṃ me vidhamissati.

If we do not appease him, the self-controlled and composed one, within seven days my kingdom will be destroyed.

“Sumekhalo kosiyo ca, siggavo cāpi sattako;

Āsādayitvā isayo, duggatā te saraṭṭhakā.

Sumekhala, Kosiya, Siggava, and also Sattaka—having offended the sages, they came to a bad end along with their kingdoms.

“Yadā [M 1.0473] kuppanti isayo, saññatā brahmacārino;

Sadevakaṃ vināsenti, sasāgaraṃ sapabbataṃ.

When the sages, the restrained holy-life practitioners, become angry, they destroy the world with its gods, its oceans, and its mountains.

“Tiyojanasahassamhi, purise sannipātayiṃ;

I gathered men within a distance of three thousand yojanas.

Accayaṃ desanatthāya, sayambhuṃ upasaṅkamiṃ.

To confess my transgression, I approached the Self-Awakened One.

“Allavatthā allasirā, sabbeva pañjalīkatā;

Buddhassa pāde nipatitvā, idaṃ vacanamabravuṃ.

With wet clothes and wet hair, all with hands folded in reverence, having fallen at the Buddha’s feet, they spoke this word:

“Khamassu tvaṃ mahāvīra, abhiyācati taṃ jano;

Pariḷāhaṃ vinodehi, mā no raṭṭhaṃ vināsaya.

Forgive, O Great Hero, the people entreat you; dispel the torment, do not let our kingdom be destroyed.

“Sadevamānusā sabbe, sadānavā sarakkhasā;

Ayomayena kūṭena, siraṃ bhindeyyu me sadā.

May all gods and humans, with the dānavas and rakkhasas, forever smash my head with an iron hammer.

“Dake aggi na saṇṭhāti, bījaṃ sele na rūhati;

Agade kimi na saṇṭhāti, kopo buddhe na jāyati.

Fire does not persist in water, a seed does not grow on a rock; a worm does not exist in an antidote, anger does not arise in a Buddha.

“Yathā ca bhūmi acalā, appameyyo ca sāgaro;

Anantako ca ākāso, evaṃ buddhā akhobhiyā.

Just as the earth is unmoving, and the ocean is immeasurable, and the sky is endless, so are the Buddhas unshakeable.

“Sadā khantā mahāvīrā, khamitā ca tapassino;

Khantānaṃ khamitānañca, gamanaṃ taṃ na vijjati.

Always patient are the great heroes, and forgiving are the ascetics; for the patient and the forgiving, that course of action is not found.

“Idaṃ [V 1.0402] vatvāna sambuddho, pariḷāhaṃ vinodayaṃ;

Mahājanassa purato, nabhaṃ abbhuggamī tadā.

Having spoken thus, the Perfectly Awakened One, dispelling the torment, then rose into the sky before the great assembly.

“Tena kammenahaṃ vīra, hīnattaṃ ajjhupāgato;

Samatikkamma taṃ jātiṃ, pāvisiṃ abhayaṃ puraṃ.

Through that kamma, O hero, I came to a low state; having transcended that birth, I entered the fearless city.

“Tadāpi maṃ mahāvīra, ḍayhamānaṃ susaṇṭhitaṃ;

Pariḷāhaṃ vinodesi, sayambhuñca khamāpayiṃ.

Even then, O Great Hero, as I was burning and established in suffering, he dispelled my torment, and I appeased the Self-Awakened One.

“Ajjāpi maṃ mahāvīra, ḍayhamānaṃ tihaggibhi;

Nibbāpesi tayo aggī, sītibhāvañca pāpayiṃ.

Even today, O Great Hero, as I was burning with the three fires, he extinguished those three fires, and I have attained the state of coolness.

“Yesaṃ sotāvadhānatthi, suṇātha mama bhāsato;

Atthaṃ tuyhaṃ pavakkhāmi, yathā diṭṭhaṃ padaṃ mama.

Those of you who have attentive ears, listen to me as I speak; I will declare the meaning to you, just as I have seen the state.

“Sayambhuṃ [M 1.0474] taṃ vimānetvā, santacittaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Tena kammenahaṃ ajja, jātomhi nīcayoniyaṃ.

Having disrespected that Self-Awakened One, of serene and composed mind, through that kamma, I am today born in a low station.

“Mā vo khaṇaṃ virādhetha, khaṇātītā hi socare;

Sadatthe vāyameyyātha, khaṇo vo paṭipādito.

Do not let the opportune moment pass you by, for those who miss the moment grieve; strive for your own welfare, the moment has been afforded to you.

“Ekaccānañca vamanaṃ, ekaccānaṃ virecanaṃ;

Visaṃ halāhalaṃ eke, ekaccānañca osadhaṃ.

For some, an emetic; for others, a purgative; for some, halāhala poison; and for others, medicine.

“Vamanaṃ paṭipannānaṃ, phalaṭṭhānaṃ virecanaṃ;

Osadhaṃ phalalābhīnaṃ, puññakkhettaṃ gavesinaṃ.

An emetic for those who are practicing, a purgative for those established in the fruit; medicine for those who have obtained the fruit, a field of merit for those who are seeking.

“Sāsanena viruddhānaṃ, visaṃ halāhalaṃ yathā;

Āsīviso diṭṭhaviso, evaṃ jhāpeti taṃ naraṃ.

For those opposed to the Teaching, it is like halāhala poison; like a viper that kills by its glance, so it burns that person.

“Sakiṃ pītaṃ halāhalaṃ, uparundhati jīvitaṃ;

Sāsanena virujjhitvā, kappakoṭimhi ḍayhati.

Halāhala, drunk once, destroys life; having opposed the Teaching, one burns for ten million aeons.

“Khantiyā avihiṃsāya, mettacittavatāya ca;

Sadevakaṃ so tāreti, tasmā te avirādhiyā.

Through patience, non-harming, and a mind of loving-kindness, he saves the world with its gods; therefore, they are not to be opposed.

“Lābhālābhe na sajjanti, sammānanavimānane;

Pathavīsadisā buddhā, tasmā te na virādhiyā.

They do not cling to gain and loss, to honor and dishonor; the Buddhas are like the earth, therefore, they are not to be opposed.

“Devadatte ca vadhake, core aṅgulimālake;

Rāhule dhanapāle ca, sabbesaṃ samako muni.

Towards Devadatta the murderer, and the thief Aṅgulimāla; towards Rāhula, and Dhanapāla, the sage is equal to all.

“Etesaṃ paṭigho natthi, rāgomesaṃ na vijjati;

Sabbesaṃ samako buddho, vadhakassorasassa ca.

For them, there is no aversion; for them, no lust is found. The Buddha is equal to all, to the murderer and to his own son.

“Panthe disvāna kāsāvaṃ, chaḍḍitaṃ mīḷhamakkhitaṃ;

Sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ katvā, vanditabbaṃ isiddhajaṃ.

Having seen on the path a saffron robe, discarded and smeared with excrement, placing the joined palms upon one's head, one should venerate that banner of the sages.

“Abbhatītā [V 1.0403] ca ye buddhā, vattamānā anāgatā;

Dhajenānena sujjhanti, tasmā ete namassiyā.

Whatever Buddhas are past, present, and yet to come—by this banner are they purified; therefore, they are worthy of veneration.

“Satthukappaṃ suvinayaṃ, dhāremi hadayenahaṃ;

Namassamāno vinayaṃ, viharissāmi sabbadā.

The excellent discipline, which is like the Teacher, I bear in my heart; venerating the discipline, I will always dwell.

“Vinayo [M 1.0475] āsayo mayhaṃ, vinayo ṭhānacaṅkamaṃ;

Kappemi vinaye vāsaṃ, vinayo mama gocaro.

The Discipline is my refuge, the Discipline is my place for standing and walking; I make my dwelling in the Discipline, the Discipline is my pasture.

“Vinaye pāramippatto, samathe cāpi kovido;

Upāli taṃ mahāvīra, pāde vandati satthuno.

Having reached perfection in the Discipline, and being skilled also in serenity, O Great Hero, Upāli venerates the feet of the Teacher.

“So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ.

So I shall wander from village to village, from city to city, venerating the Perfectly Enlightened One and the excellent nature of the Dhamma.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

Tattha hi naṃ satthā sayameva sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. So aparabhāge bhārukacchakavatthuṃ (pārā. 78) ajjukavatthuṃ (pārā. 158) kumārakassapavatthunti imāni tīṇi vatthūni vinicchayi. Satthā ekekasmiṃ vinicchite sādhukāraṃ datvā tayopi vinicchaye aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā theraṃ vinayadharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So aparabhāge ekasmiṃ uposathadivase pātimokkhuddesasamaye bhikkhū ovadanto –

For there, the Teacher himself had him learn the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. Later, he adjudicated these three cases: the Bhārukacchaka case, the Ajjuka case, and the Kumārakassapa case. The Teacher, having given his approval for each adjudication and having established the origin story for all three decisions, placed the elder in the foremost position among the experts in the Vinaya. Later, on an Uposatha day, at the time of the Pātimokkha recitation, while advising the monks:

249.

249.

“Saddhāya [P 2.0102] abhinikkhamma, navapabbajito navo;

Mitte bhajeyya kalyāṇe, suddhājīve atandite.

Having gone forth out of faith, a new one, newly ordained, should associate with good friends who are of pure livelihood and diligent.

250.

250.

“Saddhāya abhinikkhamma, navapabbajito navo;

Saṅghasmiṃ viharaṃ bhikkhu, sikkhetha vinayaṃ budho.

Having gone forth out of faith, a new one, newly ordained, a wise bhikkhu dwelling in the Saṅgha, should train in the Discipline.

251.

251.

“Saddhāya abhinikkhamma, navapabbajito navo;

Kappākappesu kusalo, careyya apurakkhato”ti. – tisso gāthā abhāsi;

“Having gone forth out of faith, a new one, newly ordained, skilled in what is allowable and unallowable, should live without being put forward.” He spoke these three verses.

Tattha saddhāyāti saddhānimittaṃ, na jīvikatthanti attho. Saddhāyāti vā kammaphalāni ratanattayaguṇañca saddahitvā. Abhinikkhammāti gharāvāsato nikkhamitvā. Navapabbajitoti navo hutvā pabbajito, paṭhamavaye eva pabbajito. Navoti sāsane sikkhāya abhinavo daharo. Mitte bhajeyya kalyāṇe suddhājīve atanditeti “piyo garu bhāvanīyo”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.37) vuttalakkhaṇe kalyāṇamitte, micchājīvavivajjanena suddhājīve[M 1.0476], āraddhavīriyatāya atandite [V 1.0404] bhajeyya upasaṅkameyya, tesaṃ ovādānusāsanīpaṭiggahaṇavasena seveyya. Saṅghasmiṃ viharanti saṅghe bhikkhusamūhe vattapaṭivattapūraṇavasena viharanto. Sikkhetha vinayaṃ budhoti bodhañāṇatāsukusalo hutvā vinayapariyattiṃ sikkheyya. Vinayo hi sāsanassa āyu, tasmiṃ ṭhite sāsanaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti. “Buddho”ti ca paṭhanti, so evattho. Kappākappesūti kappiyākappiyesu kusalo suttavasena suttānulomavasena ca nipuṇo cheko. Apurakkhatoti na purakkhato taṇhādīhi kutoci purekkhāraṃ apaccāsīsanto hutvā vihareyya.

Herein, 'out of faith' means with faith as the cause, not for the sake of livelihood; or, having faith in the fruits of kamma and the qualities of the Triple Gem. 'Having gone forth' means having gone forth from the household life. 'Newly ordained' means having become ordained while new, ordained in the first stage of life. 'New' means new to the training in the Dispensation, a junior. 'He should associate with good friends who are of pure livelihood and diligent' means he should associate with, approach, and serve—by way of accepting their advice and instruction—good friends who possess the characteristics described as 'dear, respected, to be developed' (AN 7.37), who are of pure livelihood by avoiding wrong livelihood, and who are diligent through aroused effort. 'Dwelling in the Saṅgha' means dwelling in the Saṅgha, the community of bhikkhus, by way of fulfilling the various duties. 'A wise one should train in the Discipline' means, being skilled in the knowledge of awakening, he should train in the study of the Discipline. For the Discipline is the life of the Dispensation; when it stands, the Dispensation stands. Some also read 'Buddho' (awakened), and the meaning is the same. 'Skilled in what is allowable and unallowable' means skilled, clever, and expert in what is proper and improper according to the suttas and what is in conformity with the suttas. 'Without being put forward' means he should live not being put forward by craving and so on, not expecting honor from anyone.

Upālittheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the verses of the Elder Upāli is concluded.

12. Uttarapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

12. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttarapāla

Paṇḍitaṃ vata maṃ santanti āyasmato uttarapālattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato gamanamagge setuṃ kārāpesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā uttarapāloti laddhanāmo vayappatto yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Tassa ekadivasaṃ ayonisomanasikāravasena [P 2.0103] anubhūtārammaṇaṃ anussarantassa kāmarāgo uppajji. So tāvadeva sahoḍḍhaṃ coraṃ gaṇhanto viya attano cittaṃ niggahetvā saṃvegajāto paṭipakkhamanasikārena kilese vikkhambhetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto bhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.16-20) –

The verses of the Venerable Elder Uttarapāla begin, 'Though I was wise…' What is their origin? He, too, having made aspirations in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits in various existences, had a bridge built on the walking path of the Blessed One Vipassī. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was given the name Uttarapāla. Having come of age and witnessed the Twin Miracle, he gained faith and went forth to practice the ascetic’s duties. One day, through unwise attention, while recollecting a previously experienced sense-object, sensual lust arose in him. Instantly, like one seizing a thief with the stolen goods, he restrained his own mind. With a sense of urgency arisen, he suppressed the defilements by means of counter-attention, applied himself to insight, and, striving in the development of meditation, he attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

“Vipassino bhagavato, caṅkamantassa sammukhā;

Pasannacitto sumano, setuṃ kārāpayiṃ ahaṃ.

“In the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, as he was engaged in walking meditation, with a confident and joyful mind, I had a bridge built.”

“Ekanavutito [M 1.0477] kappe, yaṃ setuṃ kārayiṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, setudānassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“In the ninety-first aeon from now, when I had that bridge made, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of the gift of a bridge.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā sīhanādaṃ nadanto –

Then, having attained Arahantship and reviewing his own practice, roaring a lion’s roar, he said:

252.

252.

“Paṇḍitaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, alamatthavicintakaṃ;

Pañca kāmaguṇā loke, sammohā pātayiṃsu maṃ.

“Though I was indeed wise, capable of discerning the goal, the five strands of sensual pleasure in the world, through delusion, cast me down.”

253.

253.

“Pakkhando [V 1.0405] māravisaye, daḷhasallasamappito;

Asakkhiṃ maccurājassa, ahaṃ pāsā pamuccituṃ.

“Having plunged into Māra's domain, pierced by a firm dart, I was able to become free from the snare of the King of Death.”

254.

254.

“Sabbe kāmā pahīnā me, bhavā sabbe padālitā;

Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti. –

“All sensual pleasures have been abandoned by me, all states of existence have been shattered; the round of births is destroyed, now there is no more renewed existence.”

Tisso gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke these three verses.

Tattha paṇḍitaṃ vata maṃ santanti sutacintāmayāya paññāya vasena paññāsampannampi nāma maṃ samānaṃ. Alamatthavicintakanti attano ca paresañca atthaṃ hitaṃ vicintetuṃ samatthaṃ, alaṃ vā pariyattaṃ atthassa vicintakaṃ, kilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ atthadassinaṃ vā, sabbametaṃ attano antimabhavikatāya thero vadati. Pañca kāmaguṇāti rūpādayo pañca kāmakoṭṭhāsā. Loketi tesaṃ pavattiṭṭhānadassanaṃ. Sammohāti sammohanimittaṃ ayonisomanasikārahetu. Sammohāti vā sammohanā sammohakarā. Pātayiṃsūti dhīrabhāvato pātesuṃ, lokato vā uttaritukāmaṃ maṃ loke pātayiṃsūti attho.

Herein, 'Though I was indeed wise' means: though I was endowed with wisdom by way of the wisdom born of learning and reflection. 'Capable of discerning the goal' means: capable of considering the welfare and benefit of oneself and others; or, sufficient in discerning the goal; or, capable of destroying the defilements; or, one who sees the goal. The elder says all this because he is in his final existence. 'The five strands of sensual pleasure' are the five portions of sensuality, namely, forms and so on. 'In the world' indicates the place of their occurrence. 'Through delusion' is the cause of delusion, the reason being unwise attention. Or, 'sammohā' means deluding, causing delusion. 'They cast me down' means they cast me down from a state of steadfastness; or, the meaning is, 'they cast me, who wished to transcend the world, down into the world'.

Pakkhandoti anupaviṭṭho. Māravisayeti kilesavisaye kilesamārassa pavattiṭṭhāne, tassa vasaṃ gatoti adhippāyo. Devaputtamārassa vā issariyaṭṭhāne taṃ anupavisitvā ṭhito. Daḷhasallasamappitoti daḷhaṃ thiraṃ, daḷhena vā sallena samappito, rāgasallena hadayaṃ āhacca viddho. Asakkhiṃ maccurājassa, ahaṃ pāsā pamuccitunti aggamaggasaṇḍāsena rāgādisallaṃ anavasesato uddharantoyeva rāgabandhanasaṅkhātā [M 1.0478] maccurājassa pāsā ahaṃ parimuccituṃ asakkhiṃ, tato attānaṃ pamocesiṃ.

'Having plunged' means having entered. 'In Māra's domain' means in the sphere of defilements, the place where the Māra of defilements operates; the intention is that he had come under his power. Or, having entered and stood in the domain of the Māra who is a son of a deva. 'Pierced by a firm dart' means firm, stable; or, pierced by a firm dart, meaning struck and pierced in the heart by the dart of lust. 'I was able to become free from the snare of the King of Death' means: by extracting the dart of lust and so on without remainder with the pincers of the highest path, I was able to be completely freed from the snare of the King of Death, which is designated as the bond of lust; thus I freed myself.

Tato eva ca sabbe kāmā pahīnā me, bhavā sabbe padālitāti vatthārammaṇādibhedena anekabhedabhinnā [P 2.0104] sabbe kilesakāmā ariyamaggena samucchedavasena mayā pahīnā. Kilesakāmesu hi pahīnesu vatthukāmāpi pahīnā eva honti. Tathā kāmabhavakammabhavādayo bhavā sabbe maggañāṇāsinā padālitā viddhaṃsitā. Kammabhavesu hi padālitesu upapattibhavā padālitā eva honti. Evaṃ kammabhavānaṃ padālitattā eva vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavoti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Idameva ca therassa aññābyākaraṇaṃ ahosi.

‘All sensual desires are abandoned by me, all existences are shattered’ (sabbe kāmā pahīnā me, bhavā sabbe padālitā) means that all defilements of sensual desire, of various kinds divided by objects and so on, have been abandoned by me by way of complete eradication through the Noble Path. For when the defilements of sensual desire are abandoned, the objects of sensual desire are also abandoned. Similarly, all existences—such as sensual existence, kamma-generated existence, and others—have been shattered and destroyed by the sword of path-knowledge. For when kamma-generated existences are shattered, rebirth existences are likewise shattered. Thus, because these kamma-generated existences have been shattered, 'the cycle of birth is exhausted—there is now no further becoming' (vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, natthi dāni punabbhavo). The meaning of this has already been stated below. This, indeed, was the Elder’s declaration of final knowledge.

Uttarapālattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Uttarapāla is completed.

13. Abhibhūtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

13. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhibhūta
