Suṇātha [V 1.0406] ñātayo sabbeti āyasmato abhibhūtattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni upacinanto vessabhussa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tādisena kalyāṇamittasannissayena sāsane abhippasanno ahosi. So satthari parinibbute tassa dhātuṃ gahetuṃ mahājane ussāhaṃ karonte sayaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ gandhodakena citakaṃ nibbāpesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde veṭhapuranagare rājakule nibbattitvā abhibhūtoti laddhanāmo pitu accayena rajjaṃ kāreti. Tasmiñca samaye bhagavā janapadacārikaṃ caranto anupubbena taṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tato so rājā “bhagavā kira mama nagaraṃ anuppatto”ti sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā dutiyadivase mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Bhagavā bhuttāvī tassa rañño ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ anumodanaṃ karontoyeva vitthārato dhammaṃ desesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā laddhappasādo rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.11-15) –

“Listen, relatives, all of you,” are the verses of the Venerable Elder Abhibhūta. What is his origin? He too, having made a resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences, was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū. Having reached maturity, he became deeply devoted to the Dispensation through association with good friends. After the Teacher's Parinibbāna, when the great multitude was striving to obtain his relics, he himself was the very first to extinguish the funeral pyre with scented water. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans until, in this Buddha's era, he was reborn in a royal family in Veṭhapura city. Having received the name Abhibhūta, he ruled the kingdom after his father's passing away. At that time, the Blessed One, wandering through the countryside, gradually arrived at that city. Hearing that the Blessed One had arrived at his city, the king went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and on the following day arranged a great almsgiving. The Blessed One, having eaten, gave a Dhamma talk in detail in accordance with the king's inclination while giving his blessing. Hearing the Dhamma, he gained faith, renounced the kingdom, went forth, and realized arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Thera 2.47.11-15):

“Dayhamāne [M 1.0479] sarīramhi, vessabhussa mahesino;

Gandhodakaṃ gahetvāna, citaṃ nibbāpayiṃ ahaṃ.

“When the body of the Great Seer Vessabhū was burning, I, taking fragrant water, extinguished the pyre.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, citaṃ nibbāpayiṃ ahaṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, gandhodakassidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago I extinguished a funeral pyre; I do not recall any unhappy destination. This is the fruit of the scented water.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up…the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Arahattaṃ pana patvā vimuttisukhena viharante tasmiṃ tassa ñātakā amaccā pārisajjā nāgarā jānapadāti sabbe samāgantvā, “bhante, kasmā tvaṃ amhe anāthe katvā pabbajito”ti parideviṃsu. Thero te ñātipamukhe manusse paridevante disvā tesaṃ attano pabbajjakāraṇavibhāvanamukhena dhammaṃ kathento –

Having attained arahantship, while he was dwelling in the bliss of liberation, his relatives, ministers, courtiers, townspeople, and country folk all gathered and lamented, saying, “Venerable sir, why have you made us helpless and gone forth?” The Elder, seeing those people headed by his relatives lamenting, taught them the Dhamma by way of explaining the reason for his going forth:

255.

255.

“Suṇātha [P 2.0105] ñātayo sabbe, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Dhammaṃ vo desayissāmi, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

“Listen, all you relatives, as many as are gathered here. I will teach you the Dhamma: repeated birth is suffering.”

256.

256.

“Ārambhatha nikkamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane;

Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro.

“Strive, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha's Dispensation! Shake off Death's army, as an elephant a reed hut.”

257.

257.

“Yo [V 1.0407] imasmiṃ dhammavinaye, appamatto vihassati;

Pahāya jātisaṃsāraṃ, dukkhassantaṃ karissatī”ti. – tisso gāthā abhāsi;

“Whoever in this Dhamma and Discipline dwells heedfully, having abandoned the round of rebirth, will make an end to suffering.” He uttered these three verses.

Tattha suṇāthāti nisāmetha, idāni mayā vuccamānaṃ ohitasotā sotadvārānusārena upadhārethāti attho. Ñātayoti ñātī pamukhe katvā tesaṃ sabbesaṃ ālapanaṃ, tenāha “sabbe yāvantettha samāgatā”ti, yāvanto yattakā ettha samāgame, etissaṃ vā mama pabbajjāya samāgatāti attho.

Herein, 'Listen' (suṇātha) means 'pay attention'; that is, 'with attentive ears, comprehend through the ear-door what is now being said by me.' 'Relatives' (ñātayo) is an address to all of them, making kin foremost. Therefore he said, 'all, as many as are gathered here' (sabbe yāvantettha samāgatā), meaning 'as many as are gathered here in this assembly, or have gathered on account of my going forth'—this is the meaning.

Idāni yaṃ sandhāya “suṇāthā”ti savanāṇattikavacanaṃ kataṃ, taṃ “dhammaṃ vo desayissāmī”ti paṭijānitvā “dukkhā jāti punappuna”ntiādinā desetuṃ ārabhi. Tattha dukkhā jāti punappunanti jāti nāmesā gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedassa jarādibhedassa ca anekavihitassa dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato dukkhā. Sā punappunaṃ pavattamānā ativiya dukkhā.

Now, having promised 'I will teach you the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ vo desayissāmi) with reference to which the instruction to hear, 'Listen' (suṇātha), was given, he began to teach with 'repeated birth is suffering' (dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ) and so on. Herein, 'repeated birth is suffering': this thing called birth is suffering because it is the basis for various kinds of suffering, such as those rooted in entering the womb and those differentiated as aging and so on. Occurring again and again, it is exceedingly painful.

Tassā [M 1.0480] pana jātiyā samatikkamanatthaṃ ussāho karaṇīyoti dassento āha “ārambhathā”tiādi. Tattha ārambhathāti ārambhadhātusaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ karotha. Nikkamathāti kosajjapakkhato nikkhantattā nikkamadhātusaṅkhātaṃ taduttariṃ vīriyaṃ karotha. Yuñjatha buddhasāsaneti yasmā sīlasaṃvaro indriyesu guttadvāratā bhojane mattaññutā satisampajaññanti imesu dhammesu patiṭṭhitānaṃ jāgariyānuyogavasena ārambhanikkamadhātuyo sampajjanti, tasmā tathābhūtā samathavipassanāsaṅkhāte adhisīlasikkhādisaṅkhāte vā bhagavato sāsane yuttappayuttā hotha. Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaroti evaṃ paṭipajjantā ca tedhātuissarassa maccurājassa vasaṃ satte netīti tassa senāsaṅkhātaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ yathā nāma thāmabalūpapanno kuñjaro naḷehi kataṃ agāraṃ khaṇeneva viddhaṃseti, evameva kilesagaṇaṃ dhunātha vidhamatha viddhaṃsethāti attho.

To show that effort must be made to overcome that birth, he said, “Strive!” and so on. Herein, “Strive!” means: exert the energy called the element of initiative. “Go forth!” means: having departed from the side of laziness, exert the further energy called the element of exertion. “Apply yourselves to the Buddha's Dispensation!”—because for those established in such qualities as restraint in virtue, guarding the sense-doors, moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension, the elements of initiative and exertion are accomplished by way of applying oneself to wakefulness; therefore, be thus engaged and applied in the Blessed One's Dispensation, which consists of serenity and insight or the higher trainings in virtue and so forth. “Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant does a hut of reeds.”—By practicing thus, just as a mighty elephant endowed with strength instantly demolishes a hut made of reeds, even so shake off, scatter, and destroy the weak and feeble mass of defilements, which is known as the army of the King of Death, the lord of the three realms, because it leads beings under his sway—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ pana buddhasāsane ussāhaṃ karontassa ekaṃsiko jātidukkhassa samatikkamoti dassento “yo imasmi”ntiādinā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

To show that for one striving in the Buddha's Dispensation, the overcoming of the suffering of birth is certain, he spoke the third verse beginning with “Whoever in this.” It is indeed easy to understand.

Abhibhūtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Abhibhūta is finished.

14. Gotamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

14. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gotama

Saṃsaranti [V 1.0408][P 2.0106] āyasmato gotamattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayaṃ kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto sikhimhi bhagavati parinibbute tassa citakaṃ devamanussesu pūjentesu aṭṭhahi campakapupphehi citakaṃ pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sakyarājakule nibbattitvā gotamoti gottavaseneva abhilakkhitanāmo vayappatto satthu ñātisamāgame paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.47.6-10) –

“Wandering on” and so on are the verses of the Venerable Elder Gotama. What is his origin? It is said that he, having made a resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas and performed meritorious deeds in various existences, was reborn at the time of this Buddha’s arising. When the Blessed One Sikhī attained Parinibbāna, while gods and humans were venerating his pyre, he venerated the pyre with eight campaka flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among gods and humans and was reborn in the Sakyan royal family. Known by the clan name Gotama, he reached maturity and, gaining faith at the assembly of the Teacher’s relatives, he went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he attained the six supernormal knowledges. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.47.6-10):

“Jhāyamānassa [M 1.0481] bhagavato, sikhino lokabandhuno;

Aṭṭha campakapupphāni, citakaṃ abhiropayiṃ.

“When the Blessed One, the Kinsman of the World, Sikhī, was being cremated, I offered eight champaka flowers to the pyre.”

“Ekatiṃse ito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhiropayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, citapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

“Thirty-one aeons ago, I offered that flower; I do not recall any bad rebirth. This is the fruit of venerating the pyre.”

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

“My defilements are burnt up...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā vimuttisukhena viharanto ekadivasaṃ ñātakehi “kasmā, bhante, amhe pahāya pabbajito”ti puṭṭho saṃsāre attanā anubhūtadukkhañceva idāni adhigataṃ nibbānasukhañca pakāsento –

Having become one with the six supernormal knowledges and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one day, when asked by his relatives, “Venerable sir, why did you go forth, abandoning us?” he, declaring both the suffering he himself had experienced in saṃsāra and the bliss of Nibbāna now attained, said:

258.

258.

“Saṃsarañhi nirayaṃ agacchissaṃ, petalokamagamaṃ punappunaṃ;

Dukkhamamhipi tiracchānayoniyaṃ, nekadhā hi vusitaṃ ciraṃ mayā.

Indeed, wandering in saṃsāra, I went to hell; I went to the realm of ghosts again and again. In the painful animal realm, too, I have dwelt long in many ways.

259.

259.

“Mānusopi ca bhavobhirādhito, saggakāyamagamaṃ sakiṃ sakiṃ;

Rūpadhātusu arūpadhātusu, nevasaññisu asaññisuṭṭhitaṃ.

Even human existence was achieved; I reached the heavenly realms from time to time. In the realms of form and the formless, I arose in the realms of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the non-percipient.

260.

260.

“Sambhavā suviditā asārakā, saṅkhatā pacalitā saderitā;

Taṃ viditvā mahamahattasambhavaṃ, santimeva satimā samajjhaga”nti. –

Existences are well understood as coreless, conditioned, wavering, and ever agitated; having understood this nature that has arisen in myself, I, being mindful, have attained peace itself.

Tīhi gāthāhi tesaṃ dhammaṃ desesi.

He taught them the Dhamma with three verses.

Tattha saṃsaranti anādimati saṃsāre saṃsaranto kammakilesehi pañcasu gatīsu cavanupapātavasena aparāparaṃ saṃsarantoti attho. Hīti nipātamattaṃ. Nirayaṃ agacchissanti sañjīvādikaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ mahānirayaṃ, kukkuḷādikaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ ussadanirayañca paṭisandhivasena upagacchiṃ[V 1.0409]. “Punappuna”nti idaṃ idhāpi ānetabbaṃ[P 2.0107]. Petalokanti pettivisayaṃ, khuppipāsādibhedaṃ petattabhāvanti [M 1.0482] attho. Agamanti paṭisandhivasena upagacchiṃ upapajjiṃ. Punappunanti aparāparaṃ. Dukkhamamhipīti aññamaññaṃ tikhiṇakasāpatodābhighātādidukkhehi dussahāyapi. Liṅgavipallāsena hetaṃ vuttaṃ “dukkhamamhipī”ti. Tiracchānayoniyanti migapakkhiādibhedāya tiracchānayoniyaṃ. Nekadhā hīti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhādivasena ceva kākabalākakulalādivasena ca anekappakāraṃ anekavārañca ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ mayā vusitaṃ niccaṃ utrastamānasatādivasena dukkhaṃ anubhūtaṃ. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattasatto mahāmūḷhatāya cirataraṃ tattheva aparāparaṃ parivattatīti dassanatthaṃ idha “cira”nti vuttaṃ.

Therein, 'saṃsaranti' means wandering again and again in the beginningless cycle of existence, transmigrating through the five realms due to kamma and its defilements, passing away and being reborn repeatedly. 'Hī' is merely a particle. 'Nirayaṃ agacchissanti' means I went to the eight great hells like Sañjīva and so on, as well as the sixteen secondary hells like Kukkuḷa, taking rebirth there. 'Punappunaṃ' should also be brought in here. 'Petaloka' refers to the realm of the departed, the state of being a hungry ghost characterized by hunger and thirst. 'Agamanti' means I went there, I was reborn. 'Punappunaṃ' means again and again. 'Dukkhamamhipī' means even in the unbearable, with pains from mutual attacks with sharp whips, goads, and so on. This is said with a change of gender: 'dukkhamamhipī'. 'Tiracchānayoniyaṃ' refers to the animal realm, including various kinds of beasts and birds. 'Nekadhā hī' means in many ways, such as a camel, an ox, or a donkey, or as a crow, a heron, or a kite, experiencing suffering for a long time with a mind constantly terrified and agitated. The word 'cira' here is used to show that a being born in the animal realm, due to great delusion, keeps revolving there for a very long time.

Mānusopi ca bhavobhirādhitoti manussattabhāvopi mayā tādisena kusalakammunā samavāyena abhirādhito sādhito adhigato. Kāṇakacchapopamasuttamettha (ma. ni. 3.252; saṃ. ni. 5.1117) udāharitabbaṃ. Saggakāyamagamaṃ sakiṃ sakinti saggagatisaṅkhātaṃ kāmāvacaradevakāyaṃ sakiṃ sakiṃ kadāci kadāci upapajjanavasena agacchiṃ. Rūpadhātusūti puthujjanabhavaggapariyosānesu rūpabhavesu arūpadhātusūti arūpabhavesu. Nevasaññisu asaññisuṭṭhitanti rūpārūpadhātūsu ca na kevalaṃ saññīsu eva, atha kho nevasaññīnāsaññīsu asaññīsu ca upapajja ṭhitaṃ mayāti ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Nevasaññiggahaṇena hettha nevasaññīnāsaññībhavo gahito. Yadipime dve bhavā rūpārūpadhātuggahaṇeneva gayhanti, ye pana ito bāhirakā tattha niccasaññino bhavavimokkhasaññino ca, tesaṃ tassā saññāya micchābhāvadassanatthaṃ visuṃ gahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding 'Mānusopi ca bhavo abhirādhito': human existence too was achieved, accomplished, and attained by me through such wholesome kamma, due to such wholesome actions coming together. Here, the Kāṇakacchapa Sutta (MN 129; SN 56.47) should be cited. Regarding 'Saggakāyamagamaṃ sakiṃ sakiṃ': the divine realm of the sense-sphere, known as the heavenly destination, was reached by me occasionally, being reborn there from time to time. 'Rūpadhātusū' means in the form existences up to the highest existence for worldlings. 'Arūpadhātusū' means in the formless existences. Regarding 'Nevasaññisu asaññisuṭṭhitaṃ': in the realms of form and formlessness, not only among the percipient, but also 'I have stood, having been reborn in the realms of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the non-percipient'—this should be connected accordingly. Here, by the term 'nevasaññi', the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is included. Although these two existences are included by the mention of the form and formless realms, those outside these—such as beings with a perception of permanence or a perception of liberation from existence—are mentioned separately to show the wrongness of their perception. This should be understood.

Evaṃ dvīhi gāthāhi bhavamūlassa anupacchinnattā anādimati saṃsāre attano vaṭṭadukkhānubhavaṃ dassetvā idāni tadupacchedena vivaṭṭasukhānubhavaṃ dassento “sambhavā”tiādinā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha sambhavāti bhavā. Kāmabhavādayo eva hi hetupaccayasamavāyena bhavantīti idha sambhavāti vuttā. Suviditāti vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya suṭṭhu viditā. Asārakātiādi tesaṃ viditākāradassanaṃ. Tattha asārakāti niccasārādisārarahitā. Saṅkhatāti samecca sambhuyya paccayehi [M 1.0483] katā. Pacalitāti saṅkhatattā eva uppādajarādīhi pakārato calitā anavaṭṭhitā. Saderitāti sadā sabbakālaṃ bhaṅgena eritā, ittarā bhaṅgagāmino pabhaṅgunoti attho. Taṃ viditvā [P 2.0108] mahamattasambhavanti taṃ yathāvuttaṃ saṅkhatasabhāvaṃ attasambhavaṃ attani sambhūtaṃ attāyattaṃ issarādivasena aparāyattaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena ahaṃ viditvā tappaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ santimeva nibbānameva maggapaññāsatiyā satimā [V 1.0410] hutvā samajjhagaṃ adhigacchiṃ ariyamaggabhāvanāya anuppattoti. Evaṃ thero ñātakānaṃ dhammadesanāmukhena aññaṃ byākāsi.

Thus, with two verses, having shown his own experience of the suffering of the cycle in beginningless saṃsāra due to the unsevered root of existence, now, showing the experience of the happiness of that which is beyond the cycle by severing that root, he spoke the third verse beginning with 'sambhavā.' Herein, 'sambhavā' means existences. For the sensual existences and so on come to be through an assemblage of causes and conditions; hence they are here called 'sambhavā.' 'Suviditā' means well understood by the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight-wisdom. The words beginning with 'asārakā' show the manner in which they are understood. Herein, 'asārakā' means devoid of the essence of permanence and so forth. 'Saṅkhatā' means made by conditions coming together and assembling. 'Pacalitā' means that because they are conditioned, they are wavering and unstable in various ways due to arising, decay, and so on. 'Saderitā' means always, at all times, agitated by breaking up; the meaning is they are transient, heading for destruction, fragile. Regarding 'Taṃ viditvā... attasambhavaṃ': having understood that aforesaid conditioned nature which has arisen in myself—dependent on myself, not dependent on another such as a creator—through full understanding and realization, I, being mindful with the wisdom and mindfulness of the path, attained peace itself, Nibbāna itself, which is the opposite of that; I reached it through the development of the noble path. Thus, the elder, by way of a Dhamma discourse to his relatives, declared his final knowledge.

Gotamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Gotama is finished.

15. Hāritattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

15. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hārita

Yo pubbe karaṇīyānīti āyasmato hāritattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute tassa citakapūjāya kayiramānāya gandhena pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā hāritoti laddhanāmo vayappatto jātimānaṃ nissāya aññe vasalavādena samudācarati. So bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitopi ciraparicitattā vasalasamudācāraṃ na vissajji. Athekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā sañjātasaṃvego vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā attano cittappavattiṃ upaparikkhanto mānuddhaccaviggahitataṃ disvā taṃ pahāya vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.46.63-67) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Hārita begins with 'Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni'. What is its origin? He too, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, was reborn in a good family and attained understanding. When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, as the pyre-offering was being made for him, he made an offering with fragrance. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Hārita. Having reached maturity, relying on pride in his birth, he addressed others with the term 'outcast'. He went to the monks, listened to the Dhamma, and having gained faith, even after going forth, due to long familiarity, he did not relinquish addressing others as outcasts. Then one day, after hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he was stirred with a sense of urgency. Establishing insight, examining the activity of his own mind, he saw it was seized by conceit and restlessness. Abandoning that, he made an effort in insight and attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.46.63-67):

“Citāsu kurumānāsu, nānāgandhe samāhaṭe;

Pasannacitto sumano, gandhamuṭṭhimapūjayiṃ.

When the pyres were being made, with various fragrances gathered, with a serene and joyful mind, I offered a handful of fragrance.

“Satasahassito kappe, citakaṃ yamapūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, citapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

A hundred thousand aeons ago, when I worshipped the pyre, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of that pyre-worship.

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Arahā [M 1.0484] pana hutvā vimuttisukhaṃ anubhavanto “yo pubbe karaṇīyānī”tiādinā tīhi gāthāhi bhikkhūnaṃ ovādadānamukhena aññaṃ byākāsi. Tāsaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

Having become an Arahant and experiencing the bliss of liberation, he declared his final knowledge to the monks by way of giving advice, through three verses beginning with 'Yo pubbe karaṇīyāni'. Their meaning has already been stated below.

Hāritattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Hārita is finished.

16. Vimalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

16. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vimala

Pāpamitteti [V 1.0411][P 2.0109] āyasmato vimalattherassa gāthā. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthari parinibbute sādhukīḷanadivasesu vītivattesu satthu sarīraṃ gahetvā upāsakesu jhāpanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantesu satthu guṇe āvajjitvā pasannamānaso sumanapupphehi pūjamakāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bārāṇasiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vimaloti laddhanāmo vayappatto somamittattheraṃ nissāya sāsane pabbajitvā teneva ussāhito vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 2.46.58-62) –

The verse of the Venerable Elder Vimala begins with 'Pāpamitta'. What is its origin? He too, having made a resolve under previous Buddhas, accumulated merit in various existences that was a proximate condition for liberation. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a good family and attained maturity. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, when the days of festive celebration had passed, as the lay followers were taking the Teacher's body to the cremation ground, he reflected on the Teacher's virtues and, with a serene and joyful mind, made an offering with sumana flowers. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī and was named Vimala. Coming of age, he went forth into homelessness depending on the Elder Somamitta and, encouraged by him, established insight meditation. Before long, he attained arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna (Apadāna, Thera 2.46.58-62):

“Nīharante sarīramhi, vajjamānāsu bherisu;

Pasannacitto sumano, paṭṭipupphamapūjayiṃ.

"When the body was being carried out, and the drums were sounding, with a serene and joyful mind, I offered a sumana flower."

“Satasahassito kappe, yaṃ pupphamabhipūjayiṃ;

Duggatiṃ nābhijānāmi, dehapūjāyidaṃ phalaṃ.

"A hundred thousand aeons ago, when I offered that flower in worship, I have known no bad destination; this is the fruit of that offering to the body."

“Kilesā jhāpitā mayhaṃ…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

"My defilements are burnt up… the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Arahattaṃ pana patvā attano sahāyassa bhikkhussa ovādaṃ dento –

Having attained Arahantship, giving advice to his companion monk:

264.

264.

“Pāpamitte vivajjetvā, bhajeyyuttamapuggalaṃ;

Ovāde cassa tiṭṭheyya, patthento acalaṃ sukhaṃ.

"Having avoided evil friends, one should associate with the best of people; and one should stand firm in their advice, desiring unshakable happiness."

265.

265.

“Parittaṃ [M 1.0485] dārumāruyha, yathā sīde mahaṇṇave;

Evaṃ kusītamāgamma, sādhujīvīpi sīdati;

"Just as one who boards a small piece of wood would sink in the great ocean, so too, by relying on the lazy, even one of good livelihood sinks."

Tasmā taṃ parivajjeyya, kusītaṃ hīnavīriyaṃ.

Therefore, one should avoid him, the lazy one of low energy.

266.

266.

“Pavivittehi ariyehi, pahitattehi jhāyibhi;

Niccaṃ āraddhavīriyehi, paṇḍitehi sahāvase”ti. –

"One should live together with the secluded, noble, resolute, and meditative ones; with the wise who are constantly energetic."

Tisso gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke three verses.

Tattha pāpamitteti akalyāṇamitte asappurise hīnavīriye. Vivajjetvāti taṃ abhajanavasena dūrato vajjetvā. Bhajeyyuttamapuggalanti sappurisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ ovādānusāsanīgahaṇavasena [V 1.0412] seveyya. Ovāde cassa tiṭṭheyyāti assa kalyāṇamittassa ovāde anusiṭṭhiyaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjanavasena tiṭṭheyya. Patthentoti ākaṅkhanto. Acalaṃ sukhanti nibbānasukhaṃ phalasukhañca. Tampi hi akuppabhāvato “acala”nti vuccati. Sesaṃ vuttatthameva.

Herein, 'evil friends' means unwholesome friends, ignoble persons, those of diminished energy. 'Having avoided' means having avoided them from afar by not associating with them. 'One should associate with the best of people' means one should attend upon a noble person, a wise person, a good friend, by way of accepting their advice and instruction. 'And one should stand firm in their advice' means one should stand in the advice and instruction of that good friend by way of practicing as instructed. 'Desiring' means wishing for. 'Unshakable happiness' means the happiness of Nibbāna and the happiness of the fruit. For that too is called 'unshakable' because of its immutable nature. The rest has the meaning already stated.

Vimalattheragāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vimala is concluded.

Tikanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Threes is concluded.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is concluded.
